trips.title: The Donauradweg — Passau to Vienna Through the Wachau
trips.subRegion: Danube Valley, Upper and Lower Austria

bestPeriod.note: July and August fill the riverside hotels and the ferries; late September gives you the Wachau grape harvest and empty cycle path.

trips.gatewayAirport: Vienna (VIE)
trips.summary: Seven days downstream from Passau to Vienna on Europe's most-ridden river path, with hand-pulled ferries and the Wachau terraces at the centre.
trips.hook: The Danube does the work. You lose about 130 metres of altitude between Passau and Vienna and almost none of it feels like effort, which is why this route carries more cyclists than any other in Europe. The trick is to ride it in a way that is not a conveyor belt: cross by ferry whenever you can, sleep on the quiet bank, and give the Wachau two days instead of one.

snapshot.Base(s): Point-to-point: Passau → Schlögen → Linz → Grein → Melk → Krems → Vienna
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: 330–370 km, roughly 1,100 m cumulative gain; ~95% asphalt, short crushed-limestone sections in the Strudengau and on the Wachau south bank
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Vienna (VIE), CAT or S7 to Wien Mitte, then ÖBB westbound to Passau Hbf (approx 3h30, one change at Linz). Return from Krems or Tulln on the Franz-Josefs-Bahn
snapshot.Who It Suits: First-time tourers, families with teenagers, anyone who wants distance without climbing

itinerary.title: Out of Passau on the Schlögen bend
itinerary.morning: Collect bikes in Passau. Donau Touristik of Linz and Eurobike Aktiv-Reisen both deliver hire bikes and e-bikes to Passau hotels and take them back in Vienna — a one-way rental here should never involve a return journey. Check rack bolts at the Dreiflüsseeck, where the Inn, Ilz and Danube meet.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the German bank to Obernzell, cross into Austria near Jochenstein and pick up the Austrian Donauradweg signage. This upper stretch is quiet, wooded and slightly damp underfoot in the shaded cuttings. At Engelhartszell, the Trappist abbey of Stift Engelszell brews Gregorius and Nivard on site; the shop closes mid-afternoon.
itinerary.evening: The Schlögener Schlinge is the Danube's 180-degree hairpin, best seen from the water rather than above it. The Rollfähre at Au–Schlögen is a cable ferry that swings across on the current; approx €3.50 with a bike. Eat trout at the riverside and watch the barges take the bend.
itinerary.dayStats: 52 km, +160 m, asphalt throughout, one cable ferry.

itinerary.title: Locks, orchards and the Linz waterfront
itinerary.morning: North bank to Aschach, then the wide farmed flats below Eferding. The Aschach power station is the first of the run-of-river dams you cross; cyclists use the marked service deck.
itinerary.afternoon: Take the Ottensheim ferry to the south bank for the last 12 km into Linz — quieter, and it drops you at the Ars Electronica Center rather than in industrial Urfahr. The Lentos art museum and the Höhenrausch roof walks are both a five-minute push from the cycle path.
itinerary.evening: Linz eats late and well. The Altstadt around Hofgasse and Hauptplatz has the Linzer Torte in every window; the version at Konditorei Jindrak is the one locals argue about.
itinerary.dayStats: 63 km, +180 m, asphalt, two dam crossings and one ferry.

itinerary.title: The Strudengau narrows
itinerary.morning: Leave Linz on the south bank through Enns, the oldest chartered town in Austria, then Mauthausen. The memorial at the former concentration camp is 3 km uphill from the river; free, two hours, and it changes the tone of the day.
itinerary.afternoon: From Ardagger the valley tightens into the Strudengau. This is the only stretch where the path leaves asphalt for compacted limestone for a few kilometres, and where a modest headwind actually bites because the hills funnel it.
itinerary.evening: Grein is a small yellow-and-white river town with the oldest surviving theatre in Austria, the Greiner Stadttheater of 1791, still in its converted granary.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km, +210 m, asphalt with ~4 km crushed limestone.

itinerary.title: Nibelungengau to the gates of the Wachau
itinerary.morning: Persenbeug, Ybbs and the twin bridge at Ybbs-Persenbeug. The Nibelungengau is orchard country; roadside honesty stalls sell Most, the dry pressed cider, by the litre.
itinerary.afternoon: The pilgrimage church of Maria Taferl sits 120 m above the north bank on a spur — a genuine climb by this route's standards, and the terrace view down the valley is the reason to do it. Descend to Marbach and cross to Melk.
itinerary.evening: Stift Melk's baroque library and marble hall are worth the approx €15 entry; the last admission is around 16:30 outside high summer, so if you arrive late, do it first thing on Day 5.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km, +290 m including the Maria Taferl spur, asphalt.

itinerary.title: Wachau, both banks
itinerary.morning: The Wachau is 36 km of terraced Grüner Veltliner and Riesling between Melk and Krems, and it is UNESCO-listed for the terraces, not the castles. Ride the south bank first through Aggsbach and Rossatz — less traffic, better light before noon.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross at Spitz–Arnsdorf or Weißenkirchen–St. Lorenz (approx €3 with bike, roughly every 30 minutes in season) and climb the Ruine Aggstein spur or the path up to Burgruine Dürnstein, where Richard the Lionheart was held. The ruin is a 25-minute walk from the village; leave the bike locked in the church square rack.
itinerary.evening: Dürnstein at dusk, once the coach parties have gone, is a different town. Wachauer Marille — the protected apricot — turns up as schnapps, dumplings and jam in every second window.
itinerary.dayStats: 44 km, +330 m with the ruin walk, asphalt plus short cobbled village lanes.

itinerary.title: Krems, Göttweig and the Kremstal edge
itinerary.morning: A loop day with no luggage. From Krems-Stein, take the Mautern ferry and climb to Stift Göttweig, the Benedictine abbey on its hill above the Danube confluence — 240 m of gain in 6 km on a quiet asphalt road.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop north into the Kremstal and follow the vineyard lanes back through Rohrendorf and Gedersdorf. Loess terraces, cellar rows, almost no cars.
itinerary.evening: Krems has the Kunsthalle and a genuine student population, so kitchens run past 21:00. The Heuriger courtyards in Stein pour their own wine by the Viertel.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 km, +420 m, asphalt with a 2 km gravel vineyard track.

itinerary.title: Tullnerfeld and the run into Vienna
itinerary.morning: Krems to Tulln on the north bank, 40 km of dead-flat levee path through the Tullnerfeld. The never-used Zwentendorf nuclear plant still stands beside the path.
itinerary.afternoon: Two honest options. Ride on: Tulln to Vienna is another 42 km, entering via Klosterneuburg and the Donauinsel to the Reichsbrücke. Or stop at Tulln Stadt and take the REX on the Franz-Josefs-Bahn into Wien Franz-Josefs-Bahnhof in 35 minutes.
itinerary.evening: Drop the bike at the Vienna return point, then Schwedenplatz and a Schnitzel that overhangs the plate.
itinerary.dayStats: 40 km (or 82 km riding through), +120 m, asphalt.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Donauschlinge
accommodationStrategy.description: It sits directly on the hairpin at the Day 1 finish, with a locked bike room, an outdoor wash point and a drying room that matters more than you think in May. The restaurant terrace looks straight down the bend, and the ferry landing is 100 metres away, so you start Day 2 without a road transfer.
accommodationStrategy.booking: eight weeks ahead for June–September.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €95–150 per night for two, half board available

accommodationStrategy.name: Gasthof Sänger Blondel
accommodationStrategy.description: A long-running house behind the blue abbey tower, with a walled courtyard where bikes go under lock and the owner's own cellar list on the table. Staying inside Dürnstein rather than at a Krems chain is the difference between seeing the village at 07:00 and seeing it at 11:00 with 300 river-cruise passengers.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead; there are barely twenty rooms.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €120–170 per night for two with breakfast

accommodationStrategy.name: Steigenberger Hotel & Spa Krems
accommodationStrategy.description: The pragmatic Day 6 choice: underground garage with bike cages, a proper spa for a rest-day evening, and a five-minute roll to the Krems train station for a bail-out. Ask for a room on the vineyard side, not the road side.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks ahead, longer during the September harvest weekends.

logistics.emergency: 112 across Europe; in Austria, 144 for ambulance and 133 for police. Water rescue on the Danube is coordinated through 112.
logistics.money: Small Heurigen, ferry operators and honesty stalls are cash-only; carry €40–60 in small notes. Cards work everywhere else.

other.label: Bikes on ÖBB
other.text: Regional trains (REX, S-Bahn, Cityjet) take bikes without reservation — buy a bike day ticket, approx €5–7 for all of Austria. Long-distance Railjet and Intercity services require a compulsory bike reservation, approx €3 on top of the bike ticket, and the slots for the Linz–Vienna corridor sell out on summer Sundays. Book them in the ÖBB app the moment your dates are fixed.

other.label: The Wachaubahn
other.text: between Krems and Emmersdorf runs seasonally with open bike wagons and is the standard fallback if the weather turns on Day 5.

other.label: Ferries
other.text: The Wachau and Schlögen crossings are private operations, cash-friendly, roughly €2.50–4.00 per person with a bike, and they stop when the Danube runs high. Check water levels on the Austrian hydrographic service before you rely on a specific crossing.

other.label: Luggage transfer
other.text: Donau Touristik, Eurobike Aktiv-Reisen and Austria Radreisen all move bags hotel-to-hotel on this corridor for roughly €12–18 per bag per day. Book it as a package with the bike hire, not separately.

other.label: Data
other.text: Austrian coverage along the river is uniformly good. EU roaming applies; the German first day is on the same terms.

other.label: Opening traps
other.text: Village bakeries shut by 12:00 on Saturday and stay shut Sunday. Abbey ticket offices close admissions 45–60 minutes early; Monday closes many small museums.

other.label: Legal
other.text: Helmets are compulsory in Austria only for under-12s. Cycling with a blood alcohol level above 0.8‰ is an offence and is enforced in the Wachau. Bike lights are legally required from dusk.

proTips: Ride the Wachau west-to-east, which is what this itinerary does — the prevailing wind runs downstream and the terraces face you rather than glare at you.
Book the ÖBB bike reservation for the Passau approach on a Friday train, not a Saturday one; the Saturday morning westbound Railjets are the ones that fill with cyclists heading upstream.
Cross to the south bank at Ottensheim rather than riding into Linz on the north. It cuts the industrial approach and lands you at the Ars Electronica Center.
In Dürnstein, walk to the ruin at 07:30. The gate is unstaffed, the path is empty and the light down the valley is the reason people photograph the Wachau.
On the Göttweig climb, go up the Furth side and come down the Palt side. The descent is smoother and the abbey terrace faces the morning sun.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: 330–370 km, roughly 1,100 m cumulative gain; ~95% asphalt, short crushed-limestone sections in the Strudengau and on the Wachau south bank
raw.Who It Suits: First-time tourers, families with teenagers, anyone who wants distance without climbing

typeSpecific.surface: 330–370 km, roughly 1,100 m cumulative gain; ~95% asphalt, short crushed-limestone sections in the Strudengau and on the Wachau south bank
typeSpecific.audience: First-time tourers, families with teenagers, anyone who wants distance without climbing

packingNotes: Two pairs of padded shorts. Seven consecutive days on a saddle punishes a single pair.
A rain jacket that actually breathes — Danube valley showers are short, warm and heavy in June.
A cable lock long enough to pass through both wheels and a fixed rack; village churches and ruins have public racks but no supervision.
Two bottles minimum. Public drinking fountains are common in Upper Austria and scarce in the Tullnerfeld.
Spare tube, tyre levers, a multi-tool and a compact pump, even on a hire bike. The nearest shop can be 30 km away.
Cash in small denominations for ferries and Heurigen.
whatCouldGoWrong: **High water closes the ferries.** After heavy Alpine rain the Wachau crossings suspend service and stretches of the path near Grein flood. Fallback: the Wachaubahn or the north-bank road, and the ÖBB regional trains between Melk and Krems.

**The bike reservation you need is sold out.** Long-distance ÖBB bike slots are capped and non-flexible. Fallback: chain two regional trains — Passau–Linz–Amstetten runs frequently and takes bikes without reservation.
**A summer Föhn headwind.** The valley can blow hard upstream for a day. Fallback: the itinerary has slack on Day 5 and Day 6; shorten the Göttweig loop rather than compressing the Wachau.

**Accommodation gap in the Wachau.** Between Melk and Krems there are fewer than a dozen villages with rooms, and river-cruise season books them out. Fallback: sleep in Mautern or Rossatz on the south bank, which are quieter and rarely full.

trips.title: Kasseien and Bergs — A Week in the Flemish Ardennes

bestPeriod.note: Ride in April for Ronde van Vlaanderen atmosphere, September for dry cobbles and empty lanes; winter turns the kasseien into ice.

trips.gatewayAirport: Brussels (BRU)
trips.summary: Six days of short brutal cobbled climbs from a single Oudenaarde base, linked by Flanders' knooppunten network and the Ronde van Vlaanderen route.
trips.hook: Nothing here is more than 150 metres above sea level, and that is the joke. The Flemish Ardennes hide their difficulty in 400-metre ramps of granite setts pitched at 20 per cent, strung together by lanes so narrow two cars cannot pass. You will ride 400 km in a week and climb more than you expect, and you will do it all from one hotel in Oudenaarde.

snapshot.Base(s): Oudenaarde (single base, all seven nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: 380–430 km, approx 5,500 m cumulative gain; asphalt lanes with roughly 35 km of cobbled sectors (kasseien) split between climbs and flat sections
snapshot.Getting There: Brussels (BRU) → train to Brussel-Zuid/Bruxelles-Midi, then IC to Oudenaarde (approx 1h from Brussels, hourly)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Road cyclists who want short savage climbs rather than long ones, and anyone who has watched the Ronde on television for a decade

itinerary.title: Arrival, Koppenberg reconnaissance
itinerary.morning: Train in to Oudenaarde. The station has a Fietspunt — Flanders' network of station bike points, staffed by social-economy operators — where you can leave a bike box, and a Blue-bike rack for a cheap city hack bike. Build up, check the tyre pressure and drop it: 5.5–6 bar on 28 mm tyres is the local orthodoxy on cobbles, not the 7 bar you ride at home.
itinerary.afternoon: A short shakedown loop east to Melden and the Koppenberg. It is 600 metres long, averages 11.6 per cent and hits 22 per cent at the bend — the single hardest ramp in Flanders, and unrideable if you are boxed in behind someone who stalls. Ride it once, badly, then again.
itinerary.evening: The Centrum Ronde van Vlaanderen on the Markt has the race's archive, a cobble-simulator and a café that pours Kwaremont blond. Entry approx €10.
itinerary.dayStats: 38 km, +480 m, asphalt with 1.1 km of cobbles (Koppenberg, Mariaborrestraat).

itinerary.title: The Ronde finale, in order
itinerary.morning: Ride the closing sequence of the modern Tour of Flanders as the race does it. South to Kluisbergen, then the Oude Kwaremont: 2,200 m long, 1,500 m of it cobbled, averaging 4 per cent with an 11.6 per cent opening ramp through the hamlet.
itinerary.afternoon: Straight on to the Paterberg — 360 m, averaging 12.9 per cent, maxing at 20.3 — then loop and repeat both, which is what the race does. Finish over the Koppenberg and Steenbeekdries, and take the Mariaborrestraat descent slowly; it is cobbled and off-camber.
itinerary.evening: Back to Oudenaarde along the Schelde towpath, which is smooth asphalt and a relief. Eat at one of the Markt brasseries; the local beer is Adriaen Brouwer, brewed in the town by Roman.
itinerary.dayStats: 78 km, +1,050 m, approx 6 km cobbles.

itinerary.title: Geraardsbergen and the Muur
itinerary.morning: East across the Zwalm valley on knooppunten — the numbered node network that covers all of Flanders. Ride node to node rather than by GPS trace; the signs are green-on-white and never more than 2 km apart.
itinerary.afternoon: The Muur van Geraardsbergen: 1,075 m of cobbles through the town and up through the beech woods to the Kapelmuur, averaging 9.3 per cent with a 19.8 per cent section at the Chapel bend. Follow it with the Bosberg, 980 m at 5.8 per cent, which is the polite one.
itinerary.evening: Geraardsbergen makes mattentaart, a curdled-milk tart with EU protected status. Buy two at a bakery on the Markt and eat one immediately.
itinerary.dayStats: 92 km, +1,150 m, approx 4 km cobbles.

itinerary.title: The flat cobbles: Paddestraat and Haaghoek
itinerary.morning: A deliberately different day. Ride north-east through Zottegem to the Paddestraat at Velzeke — 2,300 metres of dead-flat protected historic cobbles, and a completely different skill from climbing them. Big gear, high cadence, hands light on the tops.
itinerary.afternoon: Link to the Haaghoek at Brakel, another 2,000 m of flat setts, then take the Leberg and Berendries (940 m at 7 per cent) on the way home. This is the day your wrists learn something.
itinerary.evening: Rest the hands. The Ename abbey ruins and archaeological park sit 3 km from Oudenaarde on the Schelde and are free to walk.
itinerary.dayStats: 85 km, +780 m, approx 7 km cobbles, almost all flat.

itinerary.title: Recovery on the Schelde and the Kluisbos
itinerary.morning: A genuine easy day. Follow the Schelde towpath south on smooth asphalt toward Kerkhove and Avelgem, then cross into Hainaut for coffee.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb the Kluisberg on its asphalt side to Mont-de-l'Enclus, the wooded ridge that marks the language border, and descend the Knokteberg. Total climbing under 500 m.
itinerary.evening: Oudenaarde's Adriaan Brouwer brewery tap and the Tacambaroplein terraces. Early night.
itinerary.dayStats: 62 km, +460 m, asphalt with 600 m of cobbles (Kluisberg lower section).

itinerary.title: The northern bergs and the Hotond ridge
itinerary.morning: North-west over the Eikenberg (1,200 m of cobbles at 5.2 per cent) and the Taaienberg, 530 m at 6.6 per cent with a 15.8 per cent kick — Tom Boonen's hill, and the one with the best surface.
itinerary.afternoon: Up onto the Hotondberg, at 150 m the high point of East Flanders, then the Kanarieberg (1,000 m at 7.7 per cent) and the Kruisberg into Ronse. On a clear day you can see the cooling towers at Doel from the Hotond ridge.
itinerary.evening: Ronse has a Flemish-French bilingual edge and a good Saturday market. Ride the last 12 km home in the low light along the Molenbeek.
itinerary.dayStats: 88 km, +1,180 m, approx 5 km cobbles.

itinerary.title: The Ronde sportive loop, short version
itinerary.morning: Whatever hurt most, ride it again. The standard local farewell loop is Oude Kwaremont–Paterberg–Koppenberg–Steenbeekdries–Taaienberg, roughly 55 km from Oudenaarde.
itinerary.afternoon: Wash the bike at the hotel bay, pack it, and take a late train. Bikes on NMBS require a bike supplement, roughly €4–8 depending on the ticket, and are barred from some Brussels-bound peak services on weekday mornings and evenings.
itinerary.evening: If your flight is next morning, sleep near Brussel-Zuid rather than at the airport; the bike carriage there is simpler.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 km, +720 m, approx 4 km cobbles.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Leopold
accommodationStrategy.description: Directly on the Markt, opposite the Ronde centre, with a locked bike room off the courtyard and staff who have handled cyclists for decades. Every one of the seven rides starts from the front door, which removes the daily car shuffle that ruins most cobble trips.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four months ahead, and immediately if your week touches the Ronde van Vlaanderen weekend in early April.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €110–150 per night for two with breakfast

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel De Rantere
accommodationStrategy.description: Quieter, on the Schelde a few hundred metres from the centre, with private parking and a ground-floor storage room. Its restaurant serves at a proper hour for people who come back at 19:00 covered in Flemish clay, which the Markt brasseries do not always do.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Steenhuyse
accommodationStrategy.style: Boutique rooms in a listed townhouse
accommodationStrategy.description: The upgrade: five suites in an eighteenth-century mansion on the square, with a secure interior courtyard for bikes. Worth it if you are two couples and want space to spread wet kit; not worth it if you need a workshop, which it does not have.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 for everything in Belgium. Ambulances reach the berg lanes slowly; give a knooppunt number, not a road name, when you call.
logistics.weather: Flanders is maritime and unstable. A 15 °C day with 30 km/h of westerly and rain is normal in April and will feel far colder on a 60 km/h descent.
logistics.money: Cards are universal. Village cafés close on Monday and Tuesday almost without exception; the Markt in Oudenaarde is the reliable fallback.

other.label: Knooppunten
other.text: The node network is the practical navigation layer. Buy the Vlaamse Ardennen fietsnetwerkkaart at the Oudenaarde tourist office, approx €8, and write the node sequence on bar tape. It is faster than a phone in rain.

other.label: Bikes on trains
other.text: NMBS charges a bike supplement of roughly €4 for a single journey and around €8 for a day, with no reservation and no guaranteed space. Bikes are restricted on weekday peak services into and out of Brussels, roughly 06:30–09:00 and 16:00–18:30. Folding bikes travel free.

other.label: Blue-bike and Fietspunt
other.text: Blue-bike rents from Oudenaarde station for a few euros a day for members; the Fietspunt does basic repairs and will store a bike box for the week. Neither rents road bikes — bring your own or hire from the Centrum Ronde van Vlaanderen, which keeps a fleet of road and e-road bikes at roughly €35–60 per day.

other.label: Luggage transfer
other.text: Deliberately not needed: one base for seven nights means nothing moves but you. The only transfer worth arranging is the bike box between Brussels Airport and Oudenaarde, which a local taxi will do for approx €120–150 each way, or which the train handles free if the box is on a folding trolley.

other.label: Cobble law
other.text: The historic sectors — Paddestraat, Haaghoek, the Muur — are protected monuments. Riding the smooth gutter is legal but locally frowned on and often full of gravel and glass.

proTips: Drop your tyre pressure by a full bar before the cobbled days and run 28–30 mm rubber. The single biggest cause of ruined trips here is a pinch flat on the Haaghoek.
Ride the Oude Kwaremont on the left-hand crown, not the centre. The crown is worn flatter and the gutter is where the punctures live.
Approach the Koppenberg with 200 m of clear road behind you and commit; there is no restarting once you stall on the 22 per cent bend.
On the Muur, the cobbles are worst in the town section and best above the treeline. Save something for the last 200 m to the Chapel.
Go to the Centrum Ronde van Vlaanderen on your first evening, not your last. Its route maps and the staff's advice on which sectors are currently resurfaced will change your week's planning.
Book Oudenaarde accommodation for the Ronde weekend a full year out, or ride the sportive on the Saturday and leave town before the professionals arrive.

typeSpecific.surface: 380–430 km, approx 5,500 m cumulative gain; asphalt lanes with roughly 35 km of cobbled sectors (kasseien) split between climbs and flat sections
typeSpecific.audience: Road cyclists who want short savage climbs rather than long ones, and anyone who has watched the Ronde on television for a decade

packingNotes: Tyres of 28 mm minimum, tubeless if possible, plus two spare tubes and a tyre boot.
Double-wrapped bar tape or gel inserts under the tape. Wrists take more punishment here than legs.
Full mudguards or clip-ons — Flemish farm lanes stay wet for days after rain, and the mud is fine clay.
A packable rain jacket and a spare base layer in a jersey pocket; the temperature swing between a sheltered climb and an exposed ridge is real.
Overshoes and long-finger gloves even in May.
A paper knooppunten map in a waterproof sleeve.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Rain turns the cobbles greasy.** Wet setts on a 20 per cent gradient are close to unrideable on a road bike. Fallback: Day 4's flat-cobble plan and Day 5's asphalt loop can swap into any slot; the Schelde towpath always works.
**Peak-hour bike ban strands you at Brussel-Zuid.** Fallback: take an IC to Ghent Sint-Pieters instead and change there for Oudenaarde outside the restricted window, or ride the 30 km from Ghent.

**A broken derailleur hanger 40 km from base.** There is no bike shop in most of these villages. Fallback: carry a spare hanger and a quick link; failing that, the Fietspunt at Oudenaarde station does same-day basic work and De Lijn buses take bikes only on limited routes, so budget for a taxi.

**You overcook Day 2 and lose the week.** Five thousand metres of climbing in short violent efforts wrecks people who train on long climbs. Fallback: Day 5 is a real recovery day — use it, and cut Day 6's Kanarieberg if the legs are gone.

trips.title: The Vennbahn — Aachen to Troisvierges on a Borrowed Railway
trips.subRegion: Ostbelgien and the High Fens, Liège Province

bestPeriod.note: The High Fens hold snow and freezing fog into April and the plateau is genuinely cold; September gives the driest surfaces and the heather.

trips.gatewayAirport: Brussels (BRU)
trips.summary: A converted railway from Aachen to Luxembourg at railway gradients, crossing the High Fens, five German exclaves and three countries in 125 km.
trips.hook: The Vennbahn is a Belgian strip of land running through Germany, which is why the map looks broken: five German villages sit as exclaves beside a cycle path that never leaves Belgian sovereignty. It also happens to be the gentlest way to cross the Ardennes, because trains do not climb more than two per cent. Seven days turns a 125 km trail into a proper week by adding the High Fens, two lakes and the Our valley.

snapshot.Base(s): Aachen → Monschau (2 nights) → Bütgenbach (2 nights) → Sankt Vith → Troisvierges
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx 290 km, roughly 2,100 m cumulative gain; 80% asphalt rail-trail, 20% compacted crushed stone and gravel, gradients almost never above 2%
snapshot.Getting There: Brussels (BRU) → ICE or IC to Aachen Hbf (approx 2h). Return from Troisvierges or Clervaux on CFL line 10 to Luxembourg City, then onward
snapshot.Who It Suits: Riders who want distance without gradient, families with children over ten, and anyone with a taste for absurd borders

itinerary.title: Aachen to Monschau through the exclaves
itinerary.morning: Pick up bikes in Aachen. Velocity Aachen on the Reichsweg hires trekking bikes and e-bikes and knows the Vennbahn well. Start at the Aachen Hauptbahnhof end of the trail and roll south through Kornelimünster, whose abbey and cobbled Benediktusplatz are worth ten minutes.
itinerary.afternoon: From Roetgen the trail turns strange. The trackbed is Belgian territory, so the German land east of it — Münsterbildchen, Roetgener Wald, Rückschlag, Mützenich, Ruitzhof — is cut off as five exclaves. Signposts change country every few kilometres. Asphalt, with crushed stone near Lammersdorf.
itinerary.evening: Drop off the plateau into Monschau, a half-timbered town wedged in the Rur gorge. The descent into town is steep and cobbled — walk it if the panniers are loaded.
itinerary.dayStats: 47 km, +390 m, asphalt with approx 4 km compacted crushed stone.

itinerary.title: The High Fens loop from Monschau
itinerary.morning: A luggage-free day onto the Hohes Venn. Ride via Kalterherberg and Sourbrodt to the Botrange Nature Centre and the Signal de Botrange, at 694 m the highest point in Belgium. The plateau boardwalks are for walkers only; bikes stay on the marked cycle routes and forest roads.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue past Baraque Michel and the Fagne de la Poleur, then descend the Hoëgne valley toward Sart before turning back east. This is the only day with real climbing, and the wind on the plateau does most of the damage.
itinerary.evening: Monschau's Senfmühle mustard mill and the glassblowers on the Marktplatz. Eat Rhenish — Sauerbraten, Reibekuchen — at one of the Rur-bank restaurants.
itinerary.dayStats: 58 km, +620 m, mixed asphalt and gravel forest track.

itinerary.title: Down the Warche to Bütgenbach
itinerary.morning: Rejoin the Vennbahn southbound past Kalterherberg's oversized church and Küchelscheid, crossing into Belgium proper. The trail runs on embankments and through cuttings with the old station buildings still standing at Sourbrodt and Weywertz.
itinerary.afternoon: Detour west to the Robertville dam and Reinhardstein castle, then east along the Warche to the Bütgenbach lake. The dam-top road gives the classic view down the reservoir.
itinerary.evening: Worriken sits on the lake shore. Swim if it is August, otherwise walk the 8 km shoreline path at dusk.
itinerary.dayStats: 42 km, +320 m, asphalt with approx 3 km gravel around the reservoirs.

itinerary.title: Elsenborn, Butgenbacher Heck and the Ourthe headwaters
itinerary.morning: A loop day. North-east across the Elsenborn ridge — open moorland, military training area boundaries clearly marked and to be respected — and down to Rocherath and Krinkelt.
itinerary.afternoon: Return via Bullingen and the Butgenbacher Heck woods on forestry gravel. This is the day to test a gravel bike or an e-MTB if you hired one; the surface is loose and the descents are fun rather than technical.
itinerary.evening: Ostbelgien's German-speaking Community has its own parliament in Eupen and its own beer culture. The Bütgenbach brewpubs pour local Ourdaller and Eifel beers.
itinerary.dayStats: 48 km, +540 m, roughly half compacted gravel.

itinerary.title: Bütgenbach to Sankt Vith
itinerary.morning: Straight down the Vennbahn through Weywertz and Born. This is textbook rail-trail: 1.5 per cent, cuttings, viaducts, and the occasional preserved goods shed. Surface is asphalt with a long crushed-limestone stretch approaching Sankt Vith.
itinerary.afternoon: Sankt Vith lost its railway and most of its old town in the Ardennes offensive of December 1944, and its history museum is direct about it. Short afternoon by design.
itinerary.evening: Sankt Vith eats better than a town of 9,000 has any right to. The dining room at Zur Post is the serious one in the German-speaking Community; book it before you leave home.
itinerary.dayStats: 36 km, +180 m, asphalt with approx 6 km crushed limestone.

itinerary.title: The Our valley and the three-country stone
itinerary.morning: South from Sankt Vith on the trail through Lommersweiler and Steinebrück into the Our valley, one of the prettiest and least visited river corridors in the Ardennes. Burg-Reuland's ruined keep sits directly above the path.
itinerary.afternoon: At Ouren the Our, the German border and the Luxembourg border meet. The Europadenkmal — three stones for the founding states — stands at the confluence. Cross the bridge, ride 300 metres, and you have been in three countries in five minutes. Then climb gently to Troisvierges over the Luxembourg border.
itinerary.evening: Troisvierges, Ëlwen in Luxembourgish, is the end of the Vennbahn and the northern terminus of CFL line 10. Modest, quiet, and the point where all your public transport becomes free.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 km, +420 m, asphalt with approx 5 km gravel in the Our valley.

itinerary.title: Clervaux and the train home
itinerary.morning: Follow Luxembourg's national cycle network south from Troisvierges toward Clervaux, a short and steadily descending run through the Öslek forests.
itinerary.afternoon: Clervaux's castle holds The Family of Man, Edward Steichen's photographic exhibition and a UNESCO Memory of the World listing; entry approx €6. The Benedictine abbey above the town sings Vespers.
itinerary.evening: Board CFL at Clervaux for Luxembourg City, about an hour. Public transport in Luxembourg is free, bikes included where there is space, and no reservation exists to buy.
itinerary.dayStats: 26 km, −180 m net, asphalt.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Horchem
accommodationStrategy.description: On the river in the old town, with a locked bike garage and a small wellness area that earns its keep after the High Fens day. Two nights here means you ride Day 2 unloaded, which is the difference between a pleasant plateau loop and a slog.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead; longer for the Christmas market weeks, which are not your season anyway.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €110–150 per night for two with breakfast

accommodationStrategy.name: Sport- und Freizeitzentrum Worriken
accommodationStrategy.description: Purpose-built for active groups on the Bütgenbach reservoir: bike storage, a hose-down point, its own rental fleet including e-MTBs, and rooms that are functional rather than charming. The location on the water at the trail's midpoint makes the Day 4 loop possible without moving bags.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks ahead, earlier for Belgian school holidays.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Zur Post
accommodationStrategy.style: Small hotel with a serious kitchen
accommodationStrategy.description: A handful of quiet rooms above one of the region's best-known dining rooms, with enclosed parking for bikes. Staying here on Day 5 rather than pushing on to Burg-Reuland lets you eat properly at the one place in Ostbelgien worth planning around.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead for the restaurant, which fills before the rooms do.

logistics.emergency: 112 works in all three countries. Mobile coverage on the High Fens plateau and in the Our valley cuttings is patchy — do not assume a signal between Baraque Michel and Sourbrodt.
logistics.money: Cards everywhere except some Fens refuges and farm cafés. Ostbelgien shops close Sunday and often Monday; German Sunday closure is near-total.

other.label: Bikes on German trains
other.text: Regional RE and RB services in North Rhine-Westphalia need a bike day ticket, approx €4.50–6.00, no reservation. ICE services require a compulsory bike reservation, approx €9, booked in advance and frequently sold out; the Deutschlandticket does not cover bikes at all.

other.label: Bikes on Belgian trains
other.text: NMBS charges a bike supplement of roughly €4 per journey. Note that Sankt Vith has no station — the line is the path you are riding. The nearest railheads are Gouvy and Trois-Ponts.

other.label: Bikes on Luxembourg trains
other.text: All CFL travel is free, including bikes, subject to space in the marked carriages. There is no reservation system, so a busy Sunday afternoon can leave you waiting an hour.

other.label: Luggage transfer
other.text: Radweg-Reisen and Rückenwind Reisen both run supported Vennbahn itineraries with hotel-to-hotel bag transport, roughly €12–20 per bag per stage, and will sell the transfer without the accommodation if you ask.

other.label: Rental and shuttles
other.text: Velocity Aachen at the northern end, Worriken at Bütgenbach in the middle. One-way rentals need a shuttle back: the Vennbahn office in Sankt Vith keeps the current list of operators running Troisvierges–Aachen bike transfers, typically €45–70 per person with bike.

other.label: Borders
other.text: Schengen means no checks, but three phone networks will hand you back and forth all day. EU roaming applies throughout; German, Belgian and Luxembourgish networks all appear.

other.label: Protected area rules
other.text: The Hautes Fagnes nature reserve has zoned access. Boardwalks and marked footpaths are walkers only, some sectors close entirely during fire risk or bird nesting, and the closure signs are legally enforceable. Cyclists stay on the numbered routes.

proTips: Ride north to south. The Vennbahn climbs steadily from Aachen to the Fens watershed and then falls all the way to Luxembourg; doing it in reverse gives you 60 km of imperceptible uphill into the prevailing wind.

Check the Hautes Fagnes access status on the Wallonia nature portal the night before Day 2. Sector closures during drought or nesting season can force a 15 km reroute and there is no signage until you reach the barrier.
Start Day 2 by 08:30. The plateau builds cloud and wind through the afternoon, and the Botrange view is a morning thing.
Fill bottles in Kalterherberg or Sourbrodt. There is no reliable water between the Fens edge and Weywertz.
At Ouren, cross the Our on the small road bridge rather than following the marked path straight on — it puts you at the Europadenkmal without a backtrack.
Once past Troisvierges, stop buying tickets. Luxembourg's free public transport means you can bail out of any stage onto a bus or train at no cost.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx 290 km, roughly 2,100 m cumulative gain; 80% asphalt rail-trail, 20% compacted crushed stone and gravel, gradients almost never above 2%
raw.Who It Suits: Riders who want distance without gradient, families with children over ten, and anyone with a taste for absurd borders

typeSpecific.surface: approx 290 km, roughly 2,100 m cumulative gain; 80% asphalt rail-trail, 20% compacted crushed stone and gravel, gradients almost never above 2%
typeSpecific.audience: Riders who want distance without gradient, families with children over ten, and anyone with a taste for absurd borders

packingNotes: Tyres of 35–40 mm. Half this route is compacted stone and forest gravel; 28 mm road rubber will punish you in the Our valley.
A genuine windproof shell. The Fens plateau at 690 m is exposed, treeless and reliably 6–8 °C colder than Monschau in the gorge.
Front and rear lights: several Vennbahn cuttings and two short tunnels are unlit.
Two litres of water capacity for Day 2, where refills are scarce.
A spare tube plus tubeless plugs; blackthorn hedge cuttings on the Ardennes forestry tracks are the local puncture source.
A paper RAVeL and Vennbahn map — GPS handovers between three national networks drop out in the valleys.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Fens weather arrives without warning.** Freezing fog and horizontal rain occur on the plateau in every month. Fallback: Day 2 is a loop, so turn back to Monschau at Kalterherberg and ride the Rur valley instead; the trail below the plateau is sheltered.

**A Hautes Fagnes sector closes.** Fire-risk closures shut whole zones at short notice. Fallback: the Vennbahn main line itself never closes, and the Sourbrodt–Weywertz section carries you through regardless.

**The one-way shuttle does not exist on your date.** Small operators run Vennbahn transfers seasonally and by demand. Fallback: return by train — Clervaux to Luxembourg City free, then CFL/SNCB to Liège and Aachen with a bike supplement, roughly four hours total.

trips.title: Into the Easterly: EuroVelo 6 Along the Bulgarian Danube, Vidin to Cherven
trips.subRegion: The Bulgarian Danube bank, the Danubian Plain and Rusenski Lom

bestPeriod.window: the second half of May, and the first three weeks of September
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (35–40 °C on unshaded II-11 asphalt, and no tree cover between the river towns)

accommodation.note: €140–€260 (€20–€37/night — Danube-town guesthouses are genuinely cheap)

transport.note: €150–€290 (bike rental/delivery €90–€190 + BDŽ trains, bridge shuttle, transfers)

activities.note: €35–€60 (Baba Vida, Kaleto, Ivanovo, Cherven, Persina, Radetzky)

profile.difficultyNote: Moderate

trips.gatewayAirport: Sofia (SOF) is the practical gateway. BDŽ runs Sofia–Vidin daily, roughly 5–5 h 30. Finish in Ruse: BDŽ Ruse–Sofia is ~6 h 30, or fly out of Bucharest Otopeni (OTP), 75 km north across the river.
trips.currency: Euro (EUR) — sole legal tender since 1 February 2026; mandatory dual BGN display ended 8 August 2026
trips.summary: Seven days on the least-ridden stretch of EuroVelo 6, where the river is a kilometre wide and the traffic is a tractor every twenty minutes. You climb a thousand metres inland to the sandstone towers of Belogradchik,…
trips.hook: Seven days on the least-ridden stretch of EuroVelo 6, where the river is a kilometre wide and the traffic is a tractor every twenty minutes. You climb a thousand metres inland to the sandstone towers of Belogradchik, drop back to a road crossing six tributary valleys, sleep in fishing towns nobody photographs, and finish at a UNESCO cave-church above a gorge. For self-sufficient riders who want distance without crowds and do not mind a headwind.

snapshot.Start / End: Vidin → Ruse (point-to-point, ~505 km, ~4,300 m ascent)
snapshot.Getting there: Sofia (SOF) is the practical gateway. BDŽ runs Sofia–Vidin daily, roughly 5–5 h 30. Finish in Ruse: BDŽ Ruse–Sofia is ~6 h 30, or fly out of Bucharest Otopeni (OTP), 75 km north across the river.

itinerary.title: Vidin, the fortress and the bridge
itinerary.morning: Arrive on the Sofia train, build or collect the bike, and ride the riverside promenade to **Baba Vida**, the only fully preserved medieval fortress in Bulgaria, its feet literally in the Danube [VERIFY: current Baba Vida entry fee and hours].
itinerary.afternoon: Spin north to the **New Europe Bridge** ramps and ride the cycle lane out over the water towards Calafat — 1,971 m of deck and the best view of Vidin there is. Return past the Ottoman **Stambol Kapiya** gate and the synagogue.
itinerary.evening: Eat on the promenade, drink Novo Selo wine, and repack. Tomorrow is the only real climbing day.

itinerary.title: The rocks above the plain
itinerary.morning: South-west out of Vidin on the Dimovo road: 25 km of gently rising farmland, then the ascent proper after **Dimovo**, where the road tips into the western Balkan foothills and stays up for 20 km.
itinerary.afternoon: Roll into **Belogradchik** at about 520 m, close to a thousand metres above the river. Take the last steep pitch to **Kaleto**, the fortress built into the sandstone towers themselves — Roman foundations, Ottoman walls, rock doing the work of ramparts [VERIFY: current Kaleto and Belogradchik Rocks entry fee].
itinerary.evening: Walk to the **Zbegovete** viewpoint for sunset, when the rock turns properly red. It is cold after dark up here even in a summer week.

itinerary.title: Back down to the river
itinerary.morning: A 12 km spur to the **Magura Cave** at Rabisha — bat colony, and prehistoric wall paintings drawn in bat guano — before the long descent [VERIFY: current Magura Cave hours].
itinerary.afternoon: Drop north-east through Dimovo to **Archar** — Roman **Ratiaria**, capital of Dacia Ripensis, now a ploughed field with a fence and a sign. Join **II-11** and turn east.
itinerary.evening: Into **Lom**, Bulgaria's second Danube port, for river fish on the quay. The wind will have been in your face for 40 km; this is the day you learn the week's rhythm.

itinerary.title: Two valleys and a nuclear town
itinerary.morning: East out of Lom across the **Tsibritsa** and the **Ogosta** — the first two rungs of the washboard, each a 70 m drop and climb with nothing to break the wind on the rim.
itinerary.afternoon: **Kozloduy**: the nuclear plant's stacks own the skyline, but stop for the **Radetzky**, a full-size replica of the Austrian paddle steamer Hristo Botev's rebels seized in 1876, moored where they landed [VERIFY: current Radetzky museum-ship hours].
itinerary.evening: On to **Oryahovo**, a hill town rising steeply off its own ferry terminal (the crossing runs to Bechet, Romania). Guesthouses sit on the upper terrace; the dusk view down the river pays for the last climb.

itinerary.title: Along the Iskar mouth to Nikopol
itinerary.morning: The best surface of the week: a resurfaced run east from Oryahovo across open grain country, the river appearing and disappearing on the left.
itinerary.afternoon: At **Gigen**, detour 2 km to **Ulpia Oescus**, the Roman colony at the mouth of the Iskar — a large, quiet, half-excavated field of foundations and column drums with almost no visitors.
itinerary.evening: Into **Nikopol**, the steepest town on the route, its ruined Byzantine and Ottoman fortress on the bluff above the Turnu Măgurele ferry. Fish soup, then bed — tomorrow is short and the hours belong on the island.

itinerary.title: The island and the marshes
itinerary.morning: An easy 12 km to **Belene**. Report to the **Persina Nature Park** visitor centre in town before riding the dykes — the park covers the whole Bulgarian Danube island complex and **Persin** is the largest island in the Bulgarian Danube [VERIFY: current Persina visitor centre opening hours and whether an island permit is required].
itinerary.afternoon: Persin's restored marshes are reintroduction ground for Dalmatian pelican, pygmy cormorant and ferruginous duck — ride the compacted dyke slowly, with binoculars. The island also held Bulgaria's principal labour camp; there is a memorial.
itinerary.evening: On to **Svishtov**, the northernmost point of Bulgaria: Kolyu Ficheto's **Sveta Troitsa** church, and the Roman legionary fortress of **Novae** on the eastern edge of town.

itinerary.title: The gorge, the cave church and little Vienna
itinerary.morning: Skip the truck-heavy 35 km of II-52: take the early bus or BDŽ connection with the bike to **Byala**, then ride south-east through Polsko Kosovo to **Dve Mogili** [VERIFY: current Svishtov–Byala bus and bike-carriage arrangement].
itinerary.afternoon: Drop into **Rusenski Lom Nature Park** and the Cherni Lom gorge to **Cherven**, a 12th–14th-century fortress town on a meander spur, reached by footbridge and a stiff walk. Then the gorge road north to the **Ivanovo Rock-Hewn Churches**, UNESCO-listed since 1979 — the Church of the Holy Virgin is a cave gallery in the cliff with 14th-century frescoes, up a steel stair [VERIFY: current Ivanovo entry fee and closing day].
itinerary.evening: Twenty easy kilometres north into **Ruse**. Finish on **ploshtad Svoboda** beneath the **Dohodno Zdanie**, among the neo-baroque façades that earned the "little Vienna" tag, and eat somewhere with a tablecloth.

accommodationStrategy.name: Upper-town guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: the rocks are floodlit and the town empties when the day coaches leave, so an overnight buys the site alone at dusk and again at 08:00. Courtyards take bikes; most houses cook dinner if you ask at booking.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–3 weeks ahead for May and September weekends, by phone or Booking.com; midweek walk-ins are fine [VERIFY: current Belogradchik guesthouse rates].

accommodationStrategy.name: Riverfront guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: both sit on the bank above the ferry terminal — secure yard, a 06:30 start straight onto II-11, dinner within 200 m, and the week's lowest rates at €20–€30.
accommodationStrategy.booking: a week ahead or on the day by phone. Outside August nobody is competing for beds.

accommodationStrategy.name: Central hotels around ploshtad Svoboda
accommodationStrategy.description: end-of-trip logistics — inside the neo-baroque core, 10 minutes from the BDŽ station for the bike train to Sofia, close to the bridge plaza for a Bucharest flight, with lockable luggage rooms.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead. Ruse fills with business travellers, so Tuesday and Wednesday are tightest.

logistics.connectivity: A1, Yettel and Vivacom cover the river road and every town on it; coverage drops in the Cherni Lom gorge and on parts of the Persin dykes. Download the route offline — EuroVelo 6 signage here is sporadic and cannot be navigated by.
logistics.emergency: **112**, with English-speaking operators. Quote the II-11 kilometre marker if you can see one; it is the fastest way to be located between towns.
logistics.weather: Continental and extreme. May can hold a 12 °C day of rain and a 32 °C day in the same week; July hits 38 °C with no shade between tributary valleys. Storms build on the plain late afternoon and cross fast. Carry 2.5 litres — gaps between village taps run to 25 km.
logistics.bookingWindows: Nothing needs months of notice except the Sofia bike delivery (4–6 weeks) and a Ruse hotel midweek (3–4 weeks).
logistics.money: Bulgaria uses the **euro**, lev fixed at 1 EUR = 1.95583 BGN, dual pricing still displayed. Cards work in Vidin, Lom, Svishtov and Ruse. **Carry €80–€120 in small notes** — village shops, the Cherven ticket hut, ferry kiosks and guesthouses between Lom and Nikopol are cash-first.
logistics.transportRules: The **Ruse–Giurgiu bridge cannot be ridden**; the **Vidin–Calafat bridge can**. Oryahovo–Bechet and Nikopol–Turnu Măgurele ferries take bikes.
logistics.permits: No permit for the EuroVelo 6 line. **Persina** restricts parts of the island complex in the breeding season and asks visitors to register at Belene; **Rusenski Lom** is marked paths only. No wild camping in either. Lights and reflective gear outside built-up areas are legally required — II-11 is unlit and busy with farm traffic at dusk.

proTips: **Ride the long eastbound days before 11:00.** The easterly is a morning breeze and an afternoon wall. On Days 4 and 5, leaving at 06:30 and finishing by 14:00 is the whole difference.
**Sleep in Belogradchik, don't day-trip it.** Sofia operators arrive at midday and leave by five; an overnight gives you the towers at dusk and dawn with nobody in them.

**Book the bike delivery before the flights.** Sofia fleets are finite in May and September, and a Vidin drop plus a Ruse collection is a 600 km round trip for the operator — it is the one piece that can fail.
**Learn three words:** *"чешма"* (public drinking fountain — ask in every village), *"баничарница"* (the pastry shop that opens at 06:00) and *"колело"* (bicycle).
**Keep the Oryahovo ferry as a fallback.** If wind or a mechanical wrecks Day 5, the Romanian bank is flatter, faster and better connected back to Bucharest.
**Eat river fish.** Danube carp (*шаран*) and catfish in Lom, Nikopol and Svishtov cost a third of the Black Sea equivalent. Order it grilled, not fried.

raw.Daily legs: D1 Vidin loop 24 km / +140 m. D2 Vidin → Belogradchik 55 km / +980 m. D3 Belogradchik → Archar → Lom 80 km / +320 / −850 m. D4 Lom → Kozloduy → Oryahovo 92 km / +560 m. D5 Oryahovo → Gigen → Nikopol 76 km / +520 m. D6 Nikopol → Belene → Svishtov 58 km / +330 m. D7 Byala → Cherven → Ivanovo → Ruse 77 km / +690 m.
raw.Surface split: Roughly **82% asphalt, 11% gravel or compacted dyke track, 7% badly patched or broken asphalt**. The spine is **republican road II-11**, which shadows the river from Vidin to Svishtov: two lanes, no shoulder, low traffic, and surface quality that changes at every municipal boundary. Gravel is concentrated on the **Persina** dykes and the **Rusenski Lom** tracks. Ride **35–40 mm tyres minimum**; a gravel bike or rigid tourer is right, a 25 mm road bike is not.
raw.The terrain is not flat: The river is flat; the road is not. The **Danubian Plain is a washboard** — the Lom, Tsibritsa, Ogosta, Iskar, Vit, Osam and Yantra each cut a 60–120 m valley across your line of travel, and II-11 drops into and climbs out of every one. Expect **500–700 m of ascent on a "flat" river day**, and nearly **1,000 m on the Belogradchik climb**, from about 35 m at the Danube to 520 m in town and 600 m at the Kaleto gate.
raw.The wind: A **persistent easterly to north-easterly** runs the corridor, strongest in spring and often 20–30 km/h through the afternoon. Riding west to east you ride **into it** most of the week — deliberate, since it front-loads the wind onto the short sheltered western days. Want it behind you? Run the route in reverse from Ruse.
raw.Bike rental and delivery: No walk-in rental counter exists in Vidin. Bikes come from Sofia: **Odysseia-In**, **Penguin Travel** and **Cycling Bulgaria** rent touring and gravel bikes and will deliver to Vidin and collect in Ruse, typically €90–€190 for the week including transfer [VERIFY: current rental and delivery rates]. Ruse has bike shops around ulitsa Aleksandrovska [VERIFY: current Ruse bike-shop names and hours]. Carry two tubes, a folding tyre and a chain link — between Lom and Nikopol there is nothing.
raw.Bike-friendly accommodation: Danube-town guesthouses have a courtyard, shed or garage; ask for *"стая за колело"* and the bike comes inside. Nowhere here has a formal bike room, and nowhere needs one.
raw.Trains with bikes (BDŽ): Bikes travel in the **baggage compartment of trains marked with a bicycle symbol**; buy a separate bike ticket at the counter, around €2 (4 BGN) [VERIFY: current BDŽ bicycle-ticket price]. Sofia–Vidin and Ruse–Gorna Oryahovitsa–Sofia services generally take them; some expresses do not, and on a crowded train the guard decides. Buy it at the station — conductors will not.
raw.Bridges to Romania: The **New Europe Bridge, Vidin–Calafat** (2013) has a **separate pedestrian and cycle lane** and can be ridden [VERIFY: current cyclist access and whether a fee applies]. The **Danube Bridge, Ruse–Giurgiu** (1954) is **closed to cyclists and pedestrians**; reach Giurgiu by bridge shuttle minibus or a lift arranged at the customs plaza, roughly €10–€15 [VERIFY: current Ruse bridge shuttle operation and fare].

typeSpecific.surface: Roughly **82% asphalt, 11% gravel or compacted dyke track, 7% badly patched or broken asphalt**. The spine is **republican road II-11**, which shadows the river from Vidin to Svishtov: two lanes, no shoulder, low traffic, and surface quality that changes at every municipal boundary. Gravel is concentrated on the **Persina** dykes and the **Rusenski Lom** tracks. Ride **35–40 mm tyres minimum**; a gravel bike or rigid tourer is right, a 25 mm road bike is not.
typeSpecific.windConditions: A **persistent easterly to north-easterly** runs the corridor, strongest in spring and often 20–30 km/h through the afternoon. Riding west to east you ride **into it** most of the week — deliberate, since it front-loads the wind onto the short sheltered western days. Want it behind you? Run the route in reverse from Ruse.
