provenance.sourceFormat: md with '## Metadata' bullet block (one file per trip)

trips.title: The Waterline Ride from Amsterdam to Kinderdijk

bestPeriod.note: Late April gives bulb fields and long light; the forts of the waterline mostly open from April to October only.

trips.gatewayAirport: Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS)
trips.summary: Amsterdam to Kinderdijk by knooppunten and the Waterlinieroute, following the UNESCO-listed Dutch Water Defence Lines through forts, dikes and river ferries.
trips.hook: This is a week spent inside a piece of military engineering. The Stelling van Amsterdam and the Nieuwe Hollandse Waterlinie were designed to drown an invading army in 40 cm of water, and since 2021 they have carried a joint UNESCO listing. Riding them means forts, sluices, inundation fields and dike tops, with the Vecht, the Lek and the Alblasserwaard windmills threaded in. There is no climbing. There is a great deal of wind.

snapshot.Base(s): Naarden (1 night), Utrecht (3), Gorinchem (1), Kinderdijk area (1), Rotterdam (1)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 300 km, +600 m cumulative. Asphalt and brick fietspaden, shell paths on the fort perimeters
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Schiphol, train to Amsterdam Centraal in 17 minutes; bikes need a day ticket and are banned in weekday rush hours
snapshot.Who It Suits: Anyone who can turn a pedal. The difficulty here is headwind and city traffic, not terrain

itinerary.title: Out of Amsterdam along the Stelling
itinerary.morning: Collect bikes. MacBike has rented in Amsterdam since 1984 and has a branch at Centraal Station; Black Bikes is the other reliable multi-branch option. For a trekking bike with racks, Frederic Rentabike on the Brouwersgracht is the long-standing choice. OV-fiets, the station hire system, is cheaper at around €4.75 for 24 hours but needs a Dutch NS-Flex account, so most visitors cannot use it.
itinerary.afternoon: East along the IJ and the Diemerzeedijk to Muiden, where Muiderslot has guarded the Vecht mouth since about 1285. Then Weesp and the earth ramparts of Naarden-Vesting, a twelve-pointed star fortress that is still fully moated.
itinerary.evening: Naarden. Walk the ramparts at sunset; the whole circuit is 3 km.
itinerary.dayStats: 40 km · +60 m · asphalt and brick cycle path, short shell sections on the ramparts.

itinerary.title: The Vecht to Utrecht
itinerary.morning: South along the Vecht, following the knooppunten rather than a route number: this stretch links 68, 70, 34 and 33 through Nigtevecht and Vreeland. The riverbanks carry the country houses that 17th-century Amsterdam merchants built to escape the city.
itinerary.afternoon: Loenen, Breukelen and Maarssen, then into Utrecht along the Vecht towpath. Fort bij Nigtevecht and Fort Uitermeer are passed en route and both are open in summer.
itinerary.evening: Utrecht. The wharf cellars along the Oudegracht are the medieval unloading level of the canal and now hold most of the city's restaurants.
itinerary.dayStats: 46 km · +50 m · asphalt, 6 km of compacted gravel towpath.

itinerary.title: Forts of the Nieuwe Hollandse Waterlinie
itinerary.morning: East out of Utrecht through the Amelisweerd estate woods to Fort Rijnauwen, the largest fort of the line, accessible on guided visits only because it is a bat and owl reserve.
itinerary.afternoon: Fort bij Vechten holds the Waterliniemuseum, built underground in 2015, with a working scale model of the inundation system that explains the entire week in twenty minutes. Loop back via Bunnik, Houten and the Kromme Rijn.
itinerary.evening: Utrecht again. The Rietveld Schröder House of 1924 is on the eastern edge and takes timed tickets released well ahead.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 km · +60 m · asphalt with shell paths inside the fort grounds.

itinerary.title: Down the Lek to Gorinchem
itinerary.morning: South from Utrecht through Nieuwegein and Vreeswijk, where the old lock complex meets the Lek. Cross the river on the Wijk bij Duurstede ferry or the Culemborg road bridge.
itinerary.afternoon: Follow the Lek dike west through Culemborg, past Werk aan het Spoel, then Everdingen, where Fort Everdingen houses a working brewery in its bomb-proof barracks. Continue on the dike to Gorinchem, entering through the 17th-century Dalempoort.
itinerary.evening: Gorinchem. The bastion walk over the Merwede is the best view of the week.
itinerary.dayStats: 58 km · +80 m · asphalt dike road, occasional cobbled village sections.

itinerary.title: Loevestein and the Alblasserwaard
itinerary.morning: Take the Riveer foot and bike ferry from Gorinchem to Woudrichem and on to Slot Loevestein, the moated castle at the meeting of the Waal and the Maas where Hugo de Groot escaped in a book chest in 1621.
itinerary.afternoon: Return by ferry and ride west into the Alblasserwaard, the deepest polder in the country, through Hoornaar and Bleskensgraaf. The land here sits below sea level and the ditches are the field boundaries.
itinerary.evening: Kinderdijk. Nineteen windmills of 1738–1740, UNESCO-listed since 1997, and almost empty after 18:00 when the visitor centre closes.
itinerary.dayStats: 52 km · +70 m · asphalt, two ferry crossings.

itinerary.title: Kinderdijk to Rotterdam
itinerary.morning: A slow first hour along the Kinderdijk mill canal before the coaches arrive, then the Lek dike west to the Krimpen ferry.
itinerary.afternoon: Into Rotterdam along the Nieuwe Maas. Cross the Erasmusbrug of 1996, ride Katendrecht and the Kop van Zuid, then the Van Nelle Factory of 1931, a UNESCO monument of Dutch functionalism. The Maastunnel has a dedicated cyclist escalator and tube under the river.
itinerary.evening: Rotterdam. The Markthal and the Fenix warehouses on Katendrecht are the two places to eat that are worth the detour.
itinerary.dayStats: 38 km · +90 m · asphalt, city traffic and one river tunnel.

itinerary.title: The Green Heart back to Gouda
itinerary.morning: North-east out of Rotterdam through the Rottemeren and Zevenhuizen into the Groene Hart proper, the open dairy landscape that Dutch planning law has protected from the Randstad cities since the 1950s.
itinerary.afternoon: Gouda for the Sint-Janskerk stained glass and, on Thursday mornings from April to August, the reconstructed cheese market on the Markt. Then the Reeuwijkse Plassen, a lake district created by peat digging, and on to Woerden or Gouda station.
itinerary.evening: Train back to Amsterdam, roughly 50 minutes with a bike day ticket. Return bikes at Centraal.
itinerary.dayStats: 50 km · +60 m · asphalt with brick village streets.

accommodationStrategy.name: Mother Goose Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: On the Ganzenmarkt, a few metres off the Oudegracht and 10 minutes from Utrecht Centraal, with an internal bike store. Three nights here removes two hotel changes and puts you in reach of the entire waterline by day ride, which is the structural point of the week.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead, three in April.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Gorinchem
accommodationStrategy.description: Just outside the old ramparts with parking and a lockable bike area, which matters because Gorinchem is the pivot between the Lek dike and the Loevestein ferries. The town's own hotel stock is tiny, so this is the reliable bed rather than the charming one.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel New York
accommodationStrategy.description: The former Holland America Line headquarters of 1901, on the water at the Wilhelminapier, with bike parking and the water taxi at the door. It is the right end point because you can ride in over the Erasmusbrug and never touch a car park.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead.

logistics.emergency: Emergency number is 112. Traffic police response is fast and cycle-lane rules are enforced, including lights after dark.

other.text: Emergency number is 112. Traffic police response is fast and cycle-lane rules are enforced, including lights after dark.

Bikes on trains need a Dagkaart Fiets, approximately €7.50, valid all day on NS and accepted by the regional operators. Bikes are banned on weekdays from 06:30 to 09:00 and 16:00 to 18:30. Folding bikes in a bag travel free at any time.

Navigate by fietsknooppunten, the numbered junction network. Write the sequence on a bar-mounted card. The LF Waterlinieroute is still signed along this stretch, but do not expect to see LF2 Stedenroute markers too — that numbering was retired and its signs came down in 2021, part of the national move away from numbered LF-routes toward the node network.

Ferries are part of the network. Riveer runs Gorinchem to Woudrichem and Loevestein; the Waterbus links Rotterdam, Kinderdijk and Dordrecht and takes bikes for a small supplement; the Lek pontjes at Wijk bij Duurstede and Krimpen run daily in season and cost €2–€4.
Look for the Fietsers Welkom certification on accommodation. It means covered locked storage, a repair kit and a place to dry kit.
Luggage transfer is a private arrangement. Dutch Bike Tours and Boat Bike Tours both run supported Waterline itineraries with bags moved daily.
Contactless card and phone payment work everywhere, but a few Dutch businesses accept only Maestro or local debit. Carry a modest amount of cash.
Fort interiors and museums typically open Tuesday to Sunday, April to October. Fort Rijnauwen is guided-visit only and books out weeks ahead.

proTips: Plan the week west to east if a strong south-westerly is forecast for the whole period, and reverse the itinerary. Wind is the only gradient here and 6 Bft on an open polder is harder than an Alpine col.
Ride the Kinderdijk mill canal before 09:00 or after 18:00. The path is public and free; only the visitor centre and the museum mills charge.
Book the Rietveld Schröder House the moment your dates are fixed. Slots are small-group, timed and released months ahead, and it is the one thing in Utrecht that sells out.
The Waterliniemuseum at Fort Vechten is best done on Day 3, not later. It explains the inundation sluices you will then ride past for four days.
Use the water taxi in Rotterdam to skip the Maastunnel with a loaded bike; it takes bikes and crosses in five minutes.
The Utrecht bike parking under the station holds 12,500 bikes and the first 24 hours are free. Use it rather than the street if you are exploring on foot.
Buy a €7.50 bike day ticket even for a short hop. There is no cheaper single fare and it lets you bail out of any headwind day at the next station.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 300 km, +600 m cumulative. Asphalt and brick fietspaden, shell paths on the fort perimeters
raw.Who It Suits: Anyone who can turn a pedal. The difficulty here is headwind and city traffic, not terrain

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 300 km, +600 m cumulative. Asphalt and brick fietspaden, shell paths on the fort perimeters
typeSpecific.audience: Anyone who can turn a pedal. The difficulty here is headwind and city traffic, not terrain

packingNotes: A genuinely windproof jacket. Rain gear alone does not cope with a polder crosswind.
35–40 mm tyres. Brick fietspaden and shell fort paths punish anything narrower.
Two locks, one of them a heavy chain. Bike theft in Amsterdam, Utrecht and Rotterdam is industrial.
Lights front and rear, legally required and checked. Dutch police fine tourists.
A bar-mounted phone holder or a knooppunten card holder; you will be reading junction numbers every few kilometres.
Sunscreen. There is no shade for hours at a time on the dikes.
A dry bag for the ferry crossings, which are open-decked.
Cash for the small pontjes, which sometimes take coins only.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Rush-hour bike ban.** If a day collapses at 16:30 you cannot take a train until 18:30. Plan bail-outs for late morning or wait it out in a station café.
**A cancelled pontje.** High water or wind stops the small Lek ferries. The alternatives are the Culemborg and Vianen road bridges, adding 10–15 km.
**Headwind from the south-west.** On a bad day the Alblasserwaard leg can take twice the expected time. Shorten by taking the Waterbus from Kinderdijk to Rotterdam.
**A fort that is shut.** Many open only at weekends outside July and August. Check openingstijden the night before rather than arriving hopeful.
**Amsterdam bike theft.** Never leave a hired touring bike on the street overnight. Use the hotel store or a guarded stalling.

trips.title: Frisian Dikes and the Wadden Coast

bestPeriod.note: May and September carry the wader migrations across the Wadden mudflats; July has the longest evenings and the fullest ferries.

trips.gatewayAirport: Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS)
trips.summary: A week along the Waddenzee sea dikes of Friesland and Groningen on EuroVelo 12, with two days on Ameland and the terp villages inland.
trips.hook: The northern coast of the Netherlands is a raised green line with the sea on one side and land that is lower than the sea on the other. There is nothing between you and the Wadden except a dike, and nothing between the dike and Denmark except sandbanks. This week rides that line eastward, takes a ferry to Ameland for two days, and returns through the terp villages that were the only dry ground before the dikes existed.

snapshot.Base(s): Leeuwarden (1 night), Harlingen (1), Dokkum (1), Ameland (2), Lauwersoog (1), Groningen (1)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 305 km, +500 m cumulative. Asphalt dike roads, brick village streets, shell and sand paths on Ameland
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Schiphol, then direct trains to Leeuwarden in about 2 h 15; bikes need a day ticket and are banned in weekday rush hours
snapshot.Who It Suits: Riders who want emptiness, big skies and tidal landscape, and who accept that the wind decides the day

itinerary.title: Leeuwarden, Franeker, Harlingen
itinerary.morning: Collect bikes in Leeuwarden. OV-fiets is available at the station but needs a Dutch NS-Flex account; visitors should book a trekking bike or e-bike from a Bike Totaal or Profile dealer in town, or have Dutch Bike Tours deliver a supported set-up with daily luggage transfer.
itinerary.afternoon: West on the Elfstedenroute alignment through Deinum and Dronrijp to Franeker. The Eise Eisinga Planetarium there, built into a canalside living room between 1774 and 1781, is the oldest working planetarium in the world and gained UNESCO listing in 2023. Continue to Harlingen on the Van Harinxmakanaal path.
itinerary.evening: Harlingen. The Noorderhaven is lined with 17th-century warehouses and the town still runs working ferries to Terschelling and Vlieland.
itinerary.dayStats: 38 km · +50 m · asphalt canal path and brick town streets.

itinerary.title: The sea dike to Dokkum
itinerary.morning: North out of Harlingen to the Waddenzeedijk at Koehool. From here you ride the dike crown east on EuroVelo 12, the North Sea Cycle Route, with the mudflats exposed at low tide and the salt marsh green at high.
itinerary.afternoon: Zwarte Haan, where a single row of houses faces the sea, then inland briefly through Sint-Jacobiparochie and the Bildt polders reclaimed in 1505. Rejoin the dike and continue to Holwerd, then cut south to Dokkum.
itinerary.evening: Dokkum, one of the eleven cities, ringed by bastions with two windmills on them. Boniface was killed near here in 754.
itinerary.dayStats: 62 km · +80 m · asphalt dike road, fully exposed.

itinerary.title: Wierum, Moddergat and the crossing to Ameland
itinerary.morning: North-east to Wierum, where the church sits directly against the dike, then Paesens-Moddergat and the memorial to the 1883 fishing disaster that drowned 83 men from two villages.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride back west to Holwerd for the Wagenborg ferry to Ameland, 45 minutes to Nes. A return passenger ticket runs about €18 and a bicycle about €10 return. Sailings are roughly every two hours and the last one leaves in the early evening.
itinerary.evening: Nes. Ride the 6 km out to Buren for the evening light on the dunes.
itinerary.dayStats: 34 km on the mainland plus 12 km on the island · +40 m · asphalt and shell paths.

itinerary.title: Ameland end to end
itinerary.morning: West to Ballum and Hollum. The Bornrif lighthouse at Hollum, built in 1880 and 55 m tall, can be climbed. The old Hollum lifeboat is still launched by draught horses in summer demonstrations.
itinerary.afternoon: The island is 25 km long. Cross to the north side and ride the dune paths east through the Nieuwlandsreid to the Oerd, the wild eastern end, where the path becomes sand and the terns nest above the tide line. Return along the Wadden side dike through Buren.
itinerary.evening: Nes. The island has no light pollution to speak of; on a clear night the Milky Way is visible from the Oerd track.
itinerary.dayStats: 48 km · +90 m · asphalt, shell paths and 4 km of soft sand.

itinerary.title: Back to the mainland and east to Lauwersoog
itinerary.morning: Early ferry to Holwerd. The crossing follows a dredged channel and can be delayed at the lowest tides.
itinerary.afternoon: East along the dike through Ternaard, Wierum and Anjum to the Lauwersmeer, a sea inlet closed by a dam in 1969 and now a national park. The Lauwersmeer is a certified dark-sky park and one of the few in the country.
itinerary.evening: Lauwersoog. The fish auction and the Wadden centre sit beside the harbour, and the mussel and shrimp boats unload late.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 km · +60 m · asphalt dike road with short gravel through the reserve.

itinerary.title: Groningen's north coast
itinerary.morning: East from Lauwersoog through Zoutkamp, the old Zuiderzee-style fishing village stranded inland when the dam went in, then north to Pieterburen. The seal rehabilitation centre here has treated Wadden seals since 1971.
itinerary.afternoon: The dike again through Westernieland and Usquert to Uithuizen, where Menkemaborg is a moated 14th-century manor with its formal gardens intact. This coast is emptier than the Frisian side and the villages are further apart.
itinerary.evening: Uithuizen or back to Lauwersoog. Wadlopen, guided mudflat walking, launches from Pieterburen and Wierum with licensed guides only. Book weeks ahead and expect hours of knee-deep mud.
itinerary.dayStats: 50 km · +70 m · asphalt.

itinerary.title: Terp villages to Groningen
itinerary.morning: Turn inland. Warffum, Baflo and Winsum sit on terpen, the artificial mounds raised from about 500 BC as the only dry ground in a tidal marsh. Niehove and Ezinge are the clearest surviving examples, laid out as concentric rings around a church.
itinerary.afternoon: Follow the Reitdiep south into Groningen, a canal that was the city's sea link until 1876. Finish at the Grote Markt under the Martinitoren.
itinerary.evening: Train back to Leeuwarden or south to Schiphol, roughly 2 h 20, with a bike day ticket.
itinerary.dayStats: 48 km · +60 m · asphalt with brick village streets.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Anna Casparii
accommodationStrategy.description: On the Noorderhaven quay, family-run, with bike storage in the rear and a kitchen that serves North Sea sole and Wadden shrimp. Harlingen is the correct first coastal night because the dike starts 4 km north of the door and the ferries give you a bad-weather escape to Terschelling.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead, three for July.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Nobel
accommodationStrategy.description: Run by the same family since 1889, in the smallest of the island villages, with a locked bike shed and a jenever distillery attached. Ballum sits mid-island, which halves the distance to both Hollum and the Oerd on the full island day.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four months ahead for July and August; the island has a hard bed ceiling.

accommodationStrategy.name: Vrienden op de Fiets network
accommodationStrategy.description: Not a hotel but a national scheme of private homes that host cyclists for a fixed rate of roughly €27.50 per person including breakfast, with membership around €12 a year. Dozens of addresses along this coast, all with somewhere dry to put a bike, and the cheapest way to ride the route.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct by phone, a week or two ahead.

logistics.emergency: Emergency number is 112. The KNRM lifeboat service and the Kustwacht handle incidents on the Wadden; never walk onto the mudflats without a licensed guide.

other.text: Emergency number is 112. The KNRM lifeboat service and the Kustwacht handle incidents on the Wadden; never walk onto the mudflats without a licensed guide.

Bikes on trains need a Dagkaart Fiets at approximately €7.50, valid on NS and the regional operator Arriva, which runs the Leeuwarden, Harlingen and Groningen lines. Bikes are barred on weekdays 06:30–09:00 and 16:00–18:30.

The Holwerd to Ameland ferry is run by Wagenborg Passagiersdiensten. Bikes are carried for a supplement of roughly €10 return and do not need booking, but the ferry itself can be delayed or rerouted at extreme low water. Lauwersoog to Schiermonnikoog is the same operator; Harlingen to Terschelling and Vlieland is Rederij Doeksen.
Navigate by fietsknooppunten. The LF Waddenzeeroute and EuroVelo 12 share the dike alignment; the LF Elfstedenroute covers the inland Frisian legs.

Tides govern everything visual on this coast. Check the getijden tables; at low water the flats extend for kilometres and the birds are distant, at high water the birds are pushed onto the salt marsh right beside the dike.
The Waddenzee has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2009. Salt marsh and mudflat access is restricted in the bird breeding season from mid-April to mid-July, and dogs must be leashed.
Village shops close at 18:00 and many shut on Sunday. Dokkum, Harlingen and Uithuizen have supermarkets; the dike between them has nothing.
Frisian is a separate official language, not a dialect, and signs carry both spellings. Leeuwarden is also Ljouwert.

proTips: Ride west to east. The prevailing wind here is south-westerly and this coast has no shelter at all, so an eastbound week converts a fight into a push.
Cross to Ameland on a mid-morning sailing rather than the first one. The first ferry carries the island's supply traffic and the bike deck fills.
On Ameland, ride the north-side dune paths in the morning and the Wadden-side dike in the afternoon. The sun is behind you both times and the wind is usually cross rather than head.
Book wadlopen at Pieterburen or Wierum for a rest half-day, not a riding day. It is exhausting and you will finish covered to the waist in mud.
When the wind is brutal, drop off the seaward dike crown onto the landward service road; it is two metres lower and noticeably calmer.
Join Vrienden op de Fiets before you travel. The membership pays for itself on the second night and it solves the bed shortage in villages with no hotel at all.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 305 km, +500 m cumulative. Asphalt dike roads, brick village streets, shell and sand paths on Ameland
raw.Who It Suits: Riders who want emptiness, big skies and tidal landscape, and who accept that the wind decides the day

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 305 km, +500 m cumulative. Asphalt dike roads, brick village streets, shell and sand paths on Ameland
typeSpecific.audience: Riders who want emptiness, big skies and tidal landscape, and who accept that the wind decides the day

packingNotes: A genuinely windproof shell and a spare warm layer. Wind chill off the Wadden in May is severe even in sunshine.
37–42 mm tyres. Ameland's shell and sand tracks bog down anything narrower.
Compact binoculars. This is a major wader coast in spring and autumn.
Sunscreen. Cloud does not stop the glare off wet mudflats.
Offline tidal tables and the ferry timetable.
Cash in small notes for the island bike sheds, the ferry kiosks and the village bakeries.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A storm-force westerly.** Riding an exposed dike in 7 Bft is unsafe. Fall back to the Arriva line between Harlingen, Leeuwarden and Groningen and ride the sheltered inland canal paths instead.
**A missed or delayed ferry.** Extreme low water can delay the Holwerd crossing by an hour or more. Build slack into Day 3 and Day 5 and do not plan a train connection tight to the arrival.
**No bed on Ameland.** The island sells out in July and during the Ameland Adventure and beach events. Book both island nights first, then build the rest of the week around them.
**Breeding-season closures.** Salt marsh paths shut from mid-April to mid-July without much warning. The dike crown always stays open; take it and skip the marsh detours.

**Mechanical trouble on the coast.** There is no bike shop between Harlingen and Zoutkamp. Carry tubes, a spare tyre boot and a chain link, and note that Dokkum and Uithuizen have the only workshops on the eastern half.

trips.title: Green Velo Through Podlasie: Marsh, Forest and the Eastern Trail
trips.subRegion: Podlaskie — Puszcza Knyszyńska, Narew & Biebrza valleys, Puszcza Białowieska

bestPeriod.window: the second half of May, when the Biebrza marshes are at their loudest and the aquatic warblers and great snipe are displaying
bestPeriod.avoid: April snowmelt (Carska Droga floods and the meadows are impassable) and the July mosquito peak on the Biebrza

accommodation.note: €230–€420 (€33–€60/night, agroturystyka and small hotels)

transport.note: €150–€230 (bike rental €80–€130 + PKP tickets, bike reservations, one shuttle transfer)

activities.note: €60–€110 (national park entry, licensed Białowieża guide, museums, boat trip)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy–Moderate

trips.gatewayAirport: Warsaw Chopin (WAW) or Modlin (WMI), then PKP Intercity Warszawa Centralna → Białystok, roughly 2 h 20 on the fastest services. Białystok also has a small airport at Krywlany with negligible traffic. Return from Białowieża via Hajnówka, the nearest passenger railhead, 20 km away.
trips.summary: Podlasie is the flattest, emptiest and least-visited corner of Poland, and the Green Velo runs straight through the middle of it. Seven days of near-zero gradient, wooden Orthodox churches, storks on every second…
trips.hook: Podlasie is the flattest, emptiest and least-visited corner of Poland, and the Green Velo runs straight through the middle of it. Seven days of near-zero gradient, wooden Orthodox churches, storks on every second telegraph pole, and two of Europe's great wetlands. You will ride 30 km of gravel causeway across a bog on the Tsar's Road and finish among the last lowland primeval forest on the continent. Bring binoculars and a headnet.

snapshot.Best period: Second half of May, June, or September
snapshot.Start / End: Białystok → Białowieża (linear, ~330 km ridden)
snapshot.Getting there: Warsaw Chopin (WAW) or Modlin (WMI), then PKP Intercity Warszawa Centralna → Białystok, roughly 2 h 20 on the fastest services. Białystok also has a small airport at Krywlany with negligible traffic. Return from Białowieża via Hajnówka, the nearest passenger railhead, 20 km away.

itinerary.title: Białystok: Branicki's palace and a shakedown spin
itinerary.morning: Arrive by Intercity, collect the bike, and ride the flat city loop. **Pałac Branickich**, the 18th-century "Versailles of Podlasie", now the medical university, with formal gardens open to walk through free of charge.
itinerary.afternoon: **Rynek Kościuszki** and the neo-Gothic *ratusz*, then the Jewish heritage trail — the Great Synagogue memorial on Suraska, and the birthplace plaque of Ludwik Zamenhof, who invented Esperanto in a city where five languages met on one street.
itinerary.evening: Eat Podlasie properly: **kartacze** (potato dumplings stuffed with meat), **babka** and **kiszka ziemniaczana**, and *sękacz*, the spit-baked layer cake. Finish with a *rurka z kremem* at a **Cukiernia Sowa**, the patisserie chain that started here [VERIFY: current Białystok restaurant recommendations and hours].

itinerary.title: Into the Knyszyn forest to Supraśl
itinerary.morning: Pick up the Green Velo waymarks north-east out of the city and into the **Park Krajobrazowy Puszczy Knyszyńskiej** — pine and spruce on sandy moraine, with the trail alternating asphalt and forest gravel. Detour to the **Arboretum w Kopnej Górze** and the adjacent **Silvarium** open-air forestry exhibition.
itinerary.afternoon: Roll into **Supraśl**, a spa-status town on the river of the same name. The **Monaster Zwiastowania NMP** — the Orthodox Monastery of the Annunciation, founded 1498, blown up in 1944 and painstakingly rebuilt — houses the **Muzeum Ikon**, the best icon collection in Poland and worth an unhurried hour [VERIFY: Muzeum Ikon current hours and ticket price].
itinerary.evening: Supraśl is small, walkable, and full of restored wooden villas. Stay here rather than doubling back to Białystok; the MPR guesthouses are cheap and the evening light on the monastery walls is the reason to be in Podlasie.

itinerary.title: West to the Narew and Poland's Amazon
itinerary.morning: Back through the forest edge and around Białystok's northern side to **Choroszcz**, where the Branicki summer palace sits in its rococo garden. Then west onto quiet county asphalt.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Narwiański Park Narodowy** — not one river but dozens of braided channels through 20 km of reed and sedge, which is why it is nicknamed the Polish Amazon. Park HQ is at **Kurowo**, in a restored manor, and the **kładka w Kurowie** carries you a kilometre out on a boardwalk over the marsh. Watch for marsh harriers, bitterns and, in May, a wall of noise from sedge warblers.
itinerary.evening: Sleep at Kurowo, in **Waniewo** — where a chain of hand-hauled pontoon footbridges crosses the whole valley — or in **Łapy** if you want a shop and a station. Dinner is whatever the agroturystyka is cooking, and it will be good.

itinerary.title: Tykocin: the synagogue, the castle, the bison at Kiermusy
itinerary.morning: North along the Narew's left bank on flat asphalt with the marsh on your right. Stop at **Góra Strękowa**, the low bluff above the river where Captain Władysław Raginis held the Wizna position in September 1939 — the bunker and memorial are on the trail.
itinerary.afternoon: **Tykocin**, the finest small town on this route. The **Wielka Synagoga** of 1642 is one of the oldest surviving synagogues in Poland, its bimah and painted Hebrew inscriptions intact, and now the **Muzeum w Tykocinie** [VERIFY: current hours and combined-ticket price]. Add the baroque **Alumnat**, the Czarniecki monument on the market square, and the reconstructed **Zamek w Tykocinie** across the river.
itinerary.evening: Three kilometres out at **Kiermusy Dworzysko nad Łąkami**, a cluster of relocated timber cottages with a **żubrowisko** — an enclosure holding European bison — and a kitchen doing old Podlasie recipes. Or eat at **Tejsza** in Tykocin, in the former Talmudic house beside the synagogue [VERIFY: current opening days].

itinerary.title: The Biebrza: Osowiec-Twierdza and the Carska Droga
itinerary.morning: North-west to **Osowiec-Twierdza**, the Russian fortress of 1882–1892 that sits on the only firm ground for miles and is the headquarters of the **Biebrzański Park Narodowy**, Poland's largest national park at roughly 592 km². Buy the day entry ticket here — 10 PLN (~€2.30) adult, 5 PLN reduced, with a weekend ticket at 20 PLN and a seven-day at 50 PLN, set by the park director's order of April 2025 and sold online at biebrza.eparki.pl as well as at the HQ — and take the guided fortress tour if the timing works.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Carska Droga**, the Tsar's Road: about 30 km of gravel causeway laid across the **Bagno Ławki** marsh between Osowiec and Laskowiec, dead straight, dead flat, with sedge and open water on both sides and elk crossing in the early evening. Climb the **wieża widokowa nad Bagnem Ławki** and the tower at **Barwik**, and walk the **Długa Luka** boardwalk out into the fen.
itinerary.evening: **Goniądz**, on its bluff above the Biebrza — the best sunset in Podlasie, over a floodplain that stretches to the horizon. Beds at **Dworek Bartlowizna** or a village agroturystyka [VERIFY: current rates]. Eat elk sausage and drink Biebrza-brewed beer.

itinerary.title: South to the great forest
itinerary.morning: The gap between the Biebrza and Białowieża is 130 km of not-very-much, and the honest move is to shortcut it: a pre-booked minibus with a bike trailer from Goniądz or Mońki to **Hajnówka** (roughly 2 h 15), or POLREGIO Mońki → Białystok → Hajnówka with a change and a bike ticket. Riding it is possible and adds a day.
itinerary.afternoon: From Hajnówka — visit the concrete-tented **Cerkiew św. Trójcy**, one of Poland's boldest modern Orthodox churches — ride the dedicated 20 km bike path north-east to **Białowieża**, arrow-straight through the forest beside the old road. Detour to the **Szlak Dębów Królewskich**, where each of ten giant oaks carries the name of a Lithuanian or Polish monarch.
itinerary.evening: Arrive in **Białowieża** village. Dinner at **Restauracja Carska**, in the restored tsarist railway station on the branch line the Romanovs built for their hunting trips — Russian-Polish cooking, samovar tea [VERIFY: current opening days and reservation policy].
itinerary.dayStats: transfer + 42 km / +240 m

itinerary.title: The strict reserve, the bison, and out
itinerary.morning: The **Obręb Ochrony Ścisłej** — the strict reserve of Białowieski Park Narodowy, the last fragment of primeval lowland forest in Europe and a UNESCO site — can **only be entered with a licensed guide**, on the fixed route to the Dąb Jagiełły — about 7 km there and back, roughly three hours — from the gate at the Palace Park. The cap is a hard **ten people per guide**; entry is by ticket bought alongside the guide, and you must book in advance. The park entry ticket is 10 PLN (~€2.30) adult and 5 PLN reduced; Białowieża agencies running scheduled reserve walks charge about 80 PLN (~€19) per head on top, usually with a seven-person minimum, so a small private party pays more per person. Book through an agency on the park's licensed-guide list at least a week ahead, longer in May.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the **Park Pałacowy**, the Museum of Nature and Forest, and the **Rezerwat Pokazowy Żubrów** 4 km west on the Hajnówka road — the show reserve where żubr, tarpan-type horses, elk and wolves are kept, and the reliable way to actually see a bison if the wild ones stay hidden.
itinerary.evening: Ride or shuttle back to Hajnówka for the POLREGIO to Białystok and the Intercity onward, or stay a last night in Białowieża and take the early train. Hand the bike to the rental operator's drop-off point before you go.
itinerary.dayStats: 35 km / +160 m + a 4 km guided walk

accommodationStrategy.name: An MPR-certified guesthouse in Supraśl
accommodationStrategy.description: MPR certification guarantees the locked bike parking, tools and water you actually need, and Supraśl puts the monastery, the icon museum and the Knyszyn forest trailheads within walking distance of the door.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–4 weeks ahead; Supraśl fills for the August theatre festival and for Orthodox feast days.

accommodationStrategy.name: Dworek Bartlowizna
accommodationStrategy.description: it is the established base for Biebrza birders, which means early breakfasts, drying space, secure storage and staff who know which section of the marsh is flooded this week. Fifteen minutes from the Carska Droga's northern end.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–8 weeks ahead for the May migration and display season — this is the one genuinely competitive booking of the trip [VERIFY: current rates].

accommodationStrategy.name: Restauracja Carska / a Białowieża village pensjonat
accommodationStrategy.description: staying in the village rather than in Hajnówka means you can make an 07:00 guided entry into the strict reserve, which is when the forest is worth the trip, and you are a short ride from the show reserve and the Royal Oaks.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–6 weeks ahead; Białowieża has limited beds and school groups take blocks of them in May and June.

logistics.connectivity: Play, Orange, T-Mobile and Plus all cover the towns. Signal is thin on the Carska Droga and patchy in the Białowieża forest interior, and near the eastern frontier your phone may latch onto a Belarusian network — turn off roaming to avoid non-EU charges. Download offline maps.
logistics.emergency: 112. Also useful: 985 for mountain and water rescue nationally, though here the real hazards are dehydration, ticks and getting benighted on a causeway. There are hospitals in Białystok, Mońki and Hajnówka.
logistics.weather: Podlasie has Poland's most continental climate. May can deliver 28 °C and a night frost in the same week; Biebrza fog sits until 09:00. Spring floods can close sections of the Carska Droga outright — check the Biebrzański PN website before you commit to Day 5.
logistics.bookingWindows: Białowieża strict-reserve guide, 1–3 weeks. Accommodation 2–4 weeks, 4–8 for Goniądz in May. PKP Intercity bike reservations as early as the timetable opens.
logistics.money: Polish złoty, roughly 4.2–4.4 PLN to €1. Cards and BLIK work almost everywhere including village shops, but carry 150–250 PLN for national park kiosks, guide fees and the smaller agroturystyka.
logistics.transportRules: Lights front and rear plus a rear reflector are compulsory after dark. Helmets are not legally required. The cyclist blood-alcohol limit is 0.2‰ and enforced. On shared county roads ride single file — Podlasie's agricultural traffic is fast and wide.
logistics.permits: Biebrzański PN charges a day entry fee and restricts cycling to marked routes; the Carska Droga is a public road and always open. Białowieski PN's strict reserve is **guided entry only, no exceptions, no cycling inside**. Critically, the frontier with Belarus runs through the forest and the **buffer zone (*strefa buforowa*) with a ban on presence is still in force** — first imposed in June 2024 and extended again from **1 September 2026 for a further 90 days**. It covers 78.29 km of the border across five Border Guard posts including **Białowieża and Narewka**: a 200 m strip along most of it, widening to about 2 km through the nature reserves and to about 4 km on one 3.79 km section. Villages and marked tourist trails are as a rule left outside it, so a normal Białowieża itinerary is unaffected — but the boundary is redrawn every renewal, entry inside it needs written permission from the local Border Guard post commander, and you should re-check the *strefa* with Straż Graniczna or the park before planning any route close to the border. Carry your passport at all times east of Hajnówka.

proTips: **Ride the Carska Droga in the last two hours of daylight.** Elk come out to the causeway edges, the marsh light goes copper, and the day-trip cars are gone. Carry lights and a headnet — this is also when the mosquitoes arrive.
**Book the Białowieża guide before you book anything else.** The strict reserve is the point of the week and the licensed guide slots, not the beds, are the limiting factor.
**Use MPR plaques as your planning grid.** They mark guaranteed water, tools and a toilet with no purchase required — space your Podlasie days between them rather than between towns.
**Go in the second half of May.** Aquatic warblers and great snipe are displaying on the Biebrza, the meadows are dry enough, and the mosquito peak is still three weeks away.

**The wind is the hill.** Podlasie's prevailing westerly means the west-to-east days (3, 6, 7) are easier. If a strong easterly is forecast, reverse Day 3 and take the train leg on the windy day instead.
**Say it right:** *"Czy jest przechowalnia na rower?"* (is there bike storage?) and *"Poproszę bilet na rower"* (a bike ticket, please) will handle 90% of the logistics.
**Eat at Kiermusy once, and order the game.** It is the one meal on this route worth planning a day around, and the bison enclosure is fifty metres from the table.

raw.The route: The **Wschodni Szlak Rowerowy Green Velo** is a single waymarked route of roughly 2,071 km across five eastern voivodeships; the podlaskie section is the longest and, most cyclists agree, the best. This week rides a ~330 km selection of it, not the whole voivodeship.
raw.Surface split: Across the podlaskie section expect roughly **70% asphalt** (much of it purpose-built or resurfaced low-traffic county road), **25% compacted gravel and crushed stone**, and **5% concrete slab, sand or grass track** — the sandy fraction concentrated in the Knyszyn forest and on the far side of the Narew. The **Carska Droga** through the Biebrza is a graded gravel causeway for its full ~30 km. A gravel bike or a trekking bike on 38–42 mm tyres is the right tool; a road bike is not. [VERIFY: current Green Velo podlaskie surface percentages — the operator resurfaces sections most years.]
raw.Elevation, honestly: Podlasie is a moraine plain. Białystok sits around 140 m, Goniądz at 120 m, the Biebrza floodplain at 105–110 m, Białowieża at 165 m. Daily gain runs **+120 to +350 m over 45–70 km** — the biggest single climb of the week is the moraine ramp out of the Narew valley at Góra Strękowa, all of 60 m. Wind, not gradient, is what makes a hard day here.
raw.Miejsca Przyjazne Rowerzystom (MPR): Green Velo's certified **cyclist-friendly places** scheme — several hundred cafés, guesthouses, museums, shops and campsites along the trail carrying the green MPR plaque. Certification obliges them to provide **free bike parking, a basic tool kit and pump, drinking water and a toilet, with no obligation to buy**. Many also offer bike washing and secure overnight storage. The trail is additionally punctuated by **MOR** (*Miejsce Obsługi Rowerzystów*) rest stops — timber shelters with racks, tables and information boards, roughly every 15–25 km.
raw.Bike rental and rates: Rental in Białystok runs about **€10–€15/day (45–65 PLN)** for a trekking bike and **€20–€28/day (90–120 PLN)** for a gravel or e-bike, with weekly rates around 30% lower; several Białystok and Supraśl operators will collect the bike in Białowieża for a fee of €25–€45 (110–200 PLN), which is what makes this linear route practical. [VERIFY: 2026 Białystok rental operators, rates and one-way drop-off fees.]
raw.Trains with a bike (PKP): On **PKP Intercity** a bike needs its own **bike reservation** in addition to your ticket, bought at the same time — capacity is a handful of spaces per train, and Warsaw–Białystok services sell those out on Friday and Sunday. Reserve online at intercity.pl or at a *kasa* well ahead; the bike ticket is a flat 11.90 PLN (~€2.75) regardless of distance, raised by about 31% in the July 2026 tariff. On **POLREGIO** regional trains (Białystok–Hajnówka, Białystok–Mońki) bikes go without reservation on a cheap bike ticket, subject to space. Note that **Białowieża has no passenger rail service** — Hajnówka is the railhead, then 20 km by bike or the local bus.
raw.Bike-friendly accommodation features: Ask for a *zamykana przechowalnia rowerów* (locked bike store), a drying room — Podlasie rain is horizontal — and breakfast before 08:00. MPR-certified stays advertise all three.

typeSpecific.surface: Across the podlaskie section expect roughly **70% asphalt** (much of it purpose-built or resurfaced low-traffic county road), **25% compacted gravel and crushed stone**, and **5% concrete slab, sand or grass track** — the sandy fraction concentrated in the Knyszyn forest and on the far side of the Narew. The **Carska Droga** through the Biebrza is a graded gravel causeway for its full ~30 km. A gravel bike or a trekking bike on 38–42 mm tyres is the right tool; a road bike is not. trips.title: Alentejo & Costa Vicentina Gravel

bestPeriod.window: Mid-March–May & late September–early November
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August — inland Alentejo regularly exceeds 40°C with no shade on the montado, and coastal accommodation triples in price
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-March–May & late September–early November

accommodation.note: Évora and Monsaraz €80–€140 pppn; coastal guesthouses €70–€120

food.note: Tasca mains €10–€16; a Milfontes seafood dinner €30–€45

transport.note: Airport transfers, one Odemira-line train leg, luggage shuttle

activities.note: Gravel hire €180–€260/week (usually delivered), Alqueva stargazing session €25

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5 — moderate gradients but long, exposed, low-traffic days with heavy gravel resistance and real water-carrying discipline

trips.gatewayAirport: LIS Lisbon Humberto Delgado, 1 h 30 min to Évora; FAO Faro, 1 h 45 min to Mértola and 2 h to Vila Nova de Milfontes
trips.summary: The Alentejo is Europe's emptiest agricultural landscape and its gravel is correspondingly generous — hundreds of kilometres of hard clay and schist farm track winding through montado, the cork-oak savannah that has been managed the same way for eight centuries. This week runs from Évora's Roman and Manueline core east to the walled hilltop of Monsaraz above the Alqueva reservoir, south through Mértola's Islamic castle to the Guadiana, then west to the Atlantic, where the Costa Vicentina delivers cliffs, storks nesting on sea stacks, and a headwind that defines the last two days. It is a route about space, silence and heat management rather than climbing, and it needs a rider comfortable being 30 km from the nearest café.

itinerary.title: Évora, and the first montado tracks
itinerary.morning: Arrive in Évora, take delivery of the gravel bike, and walk the walled centre: the Roman Templo de Diana, the Sé cathedral roof terrace, and the Capela dos Ossos with its wall of monastic bones.
itinerary.afternoon: A short shakedown east through the Herdade da Mitra estate tracks and the Valverde area, past the Cromeleque dos Almendres — a 95-stone Neolithic circle older than Stonehenge, reached on 3 km of rough gravel.
itinerary.evening: Botequim da Mouraria on Rua da Mouraria — nine counter seats, no reservations, exceptional Alentejo cooking. If it is full, Fialho on Travessa das Mascarenhas is the classic alternative.
itinerary.dayStats: 42 km / 460 m ascent / 55% clay track, 45% paved / Almendres access 3 km unsurfaced

itinerary.title: Évora to Monsaraz across the plain
itinerary.morning: East out of Évora on the empty N254 toward Reguengos de Monsaraz, dropping onto estate tracks at São Manços. This is textbook montado: cork oaks stripped to red trunks, black pigs, no shade at head height.
itinerary.afternoon: Reach the Alqueva shore and climb the 2.1 km ramp to Monsaraz's Porta da Vila, finishing on cobbles at 14%. The walled village is a single street and a castle keep, with the reservoir filling the whole eastern horizon.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Sabores de Monsaraz inside the walls, then an Alqueva Dark Sky session — this was the world's first Starlight Tourism Destination and the observatory at Cumeada runs guided sessions.
itinerary.dayStats: 68 km / 690 m ascent / 50% clay track, 40% paved, 10% cobbles / Monsaraz 232 m, max 14%
itinerary.sleep: São Lourenço do Barrocal, near Monsaraz

itinerary.title: The Alqueva montado circuit
itinerary.morning: The signature gravel day: a loop through São Marcos do Campo, Motrinos and Telheiro on estate tracks, with the Alqueva reservoir appearing and disappearing between oaks. Water at Motrinos; there is nothing else for 25 km.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend to the reservoir at Telheiro for a swim, then the last climb back to Monsaraz. Total ascent is modest but the clay resistance makes the effort feel 30% higher than the numbers.
itinerary.evening: Eat at São Lourenço do Barrocal's own restaurant — the estate's produce, its own wines, and a terrace looking at the same hill you rode all day.
itinerary.dayStats: 74 km / 780 m ascent / 70% clay estate track, 25% paved, 5% cobbles / longest waterless stretch 25 km
itinerary.sleep: São Lourenço do Barrocal, near Monsaraz

itinerary.title: South to Mértola and the Guadiana
itinerary.morning: Transfer south past Serpa, or ride the long option through Vidigueira and Vila de Frades — the region of talha wine, still fermented in clay amphorae, which you can taste at Herdade do Rocim.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride into Mértola on the Guadiana schist ramps. The town is a stack of white houses under a Moorish castle, and its mosque-turned-church retains the mihrab — one of very few in Portugal.
itinerary.evening: Tamuje, on the riverbank below the castle, for Guadiana fish and Alentejo black pork.
itinerary.dayStats: 58 km ridden / 820 m ascent / 45% schist track, 55% paved / repeated 1.5–3 km ramps at 6–8%
itinerary.sleep: Casa Amarela or the Hotel Museu, Mértola

itinerary.title: Guadiana valley to the Atlantic
itinerary.morning: North-west through the Vale do Guadiana Natural Park on schist tracks toward Castro Verde, an ochre landscape of open steppe that is one of Europe's most important great bustard habitats.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue toward Odemira. This is the transition day and the N120 corridor is the obvious line — treat it with caution: it is narrow, has no hard shoulder, carries heavy timber and eucalyptus trucks, and is genuinely unpleasant to ride. Use the parallel municipal roads and the Rota Vicentina signed gravel wherever they exist, even at the cost of 15 km.
itinerary.evening: Arrive Vila Nova de Milfontes. Tasca do Celso on Rua dos Aviadores is the town's institution — book, or eat at 19:00.
itinerary.dayStats: 96 km / 1,010 m ascent / 40% schist and clay track, 60% paved / N120 exposure minimised to under 8 km
itinerary.sleep: HS Milfontes Beach Hotel, Vila Nova de Milfontes

itinerary.title: Costa Vicentina: Almograve, Cabo Sardão, Zambujeira
itinerary.morning: South from Milfontes on the coastal lanes and signed Rota Vicentina cycling routes to Almograve, then Cavaleiro and the Cabo Sardão lighthouse, where white storks nest on the sea stacks — the only place in the world they nest on ocean cliffs.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue on hardpack and sand to Zambujeira do Mar. Remember the cliff-edge Fishermen's Trail here is walking-only; the parallel gravel and municipal lanes are the legal cycling line.
itinerary.evening: O Sacas at Entrada da Barca below Zambujeira — a shack above the fishing cove serving whatever came in that morning.
itinerary.dayStats: 46 km / 620 m ascent / 45% hardpack, 35% paved, 20% loose sand / Fishermen's Trail closed to bikes
itinerary.sleep: Herdade do Touril, Zambujeira do Mar

itinerary.title: Cork country and the ride out
itinerary.morning: Inland loop east from Zambujeira through São Teotónio and the cork estates toward Odemira, on the best clay tracks of the week. Watch for freshly stripped cork oaks numbered with the year of harvest — they are cut once every nine years.
itinerary.afternoon: Return the bike to the delivery operator at Odemira or Zambujeira, then transfer to Faro or Lisbon.
itinerary.evening: If you have time in Lisbon, eat in Cais do Sodré before the flight; otherwise a final grilled fish at Milfontes harbour.
itinerary.dayStats: 54 km / 560 m ascent / 65% clay track, 35% paved / transfer to FAO 1 h 45 min
itinerary.sleep: Herdade do Touril, or an airport hotel

accommodationStrategy.name: São Lourenço do Barrocal
accommodationStrategy.description: A 200-year-old monte turned hotel on 780 hectares, with secure bike storage, its own fleet for guests, a wine cellar producing on site, and direct access to estate gravel tracks from the door. Expensive at roughly €280–€420 double, but it is the only property that lets you ride the Alqueva circuit without touching a public road for the first 8 km.

accommodationStrategy.name: Convento do Espinheiro
accommodationStrategy.description: A fifteenth-century convent 3 km from Évora's walls, with a lockable cloister storeroom for bikes and a pool that matters after a 40°C day. Positioned on the eastern side, so you leave toward Monsaraz without crossing the city. Around €150–€230 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Herdade do Touril
accommodationStrategy.description: A working farm on the cliff edge with a bike outbuilding, an outdoor hose, and a private path down to the beach. Breakfast is served early enough for a pre-wind coastal start, which is the single most valuable feature on the Costa Vicentina. €120–€190 double.

logistics.connectivity: 4G is reasonable in towns and along the coast, but there are real dead zones in the Guadiana valley and on interior estates. Portugal is in the EU so roaming applies. Download offline maps: many estate tracks are gated and unmapped, and gates in the montado are often locked without notice.
logistics.emergency: 112. Portugal honours EHIC/GHIC. The nearest full hospitals are in Évora, Beja and Faro; the Costa Vicentina's nearest is at Odemira health centre with transfers to Beja. Response times in the interior can exceed an hour — carry a satellite messenger if riding solo on estate tracks.
logistics.weather: The nortada, a persistent north-westerly Atlantic wind, blows almost every afternoon on the coast from April to September, frequently at 30–45 km/h. Ride south, and ride early. Inland the risk is heat, not wind — a 40°C day on unshaded clay is genuinely dangerous. Coastal fog (nevoeiro) can cut visibility on the cliff lanes at dawn.
logistics.bookingWindows: São Lourenço do Barrocal books three to six months for spring. Coastal guesthouses fill entirely in August. Delivered rental bikes need four weeks. Botequim da Mouraria does not take bookings and seats nine — arrive at opening. Alqueva stargazing sessions need a few days.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards are accepted in towns; rural tascas and village cafés in the Guadiana valley are frequently cash-only, and ATMs are scarce between Mértola and Odemira. Tipping is 5–10% at a restaurant, rounding elsewhere.
logistics.transportRules: Portuguese motorway tolls on the A22 and parts of the A2 are electronic-only — a rental car needs a transponder or a registered plate. CP Regional and InterRegional trains carry bikes free in designated spaces; Alfa Pendular and Intercidades require bagging with limited bookable spaces. Rede Expressos coaches take boxed bikes at driver's discretion.
logistics.permits: The Parque Natural do Sudoeste Alentejano e Costa Vicentina restricts off-track riding, and the Fishermen's Trail is closed to bicycles. Cork oaks are legally protected trees — do not lean bikes on freshly stripped trunks, which are open wounds. Estate tracks cross private land under customary access; close every gate you open. Drones need ANAC registration and are restricted over the natural park.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable across the region but often heavily mineralised inland. Carry a minimum of three litres on montado days. Ticks are present in cork-oak scrub. Portuguese man o' war occasionally wash onto Costa Vicentina beaches on westerly swells. Sun exposure, not traffic, is the main medical risk on this route.

proTips: Ride the coast north to south. The nortada is a tailwind going south and a wall going north; the same 46 km leg can take two hours or four.
Do not plan any bike section on the Fishermen's Trail, however tempting the GPX looks. It is a walking route on erodible dune and cliff, and riding it is both prohibited and locally resented.
Start montado days at first light. The clay tracks are firm and cool before 10:00 and turn to dust-and-glare afterwards, and there is no shade to wait in.
Ask São Lourenço do Barrocal or your Évora hotel which estate gates are currently open. Locked farm gates are the most common route failure in the Alentejo and no map shows them.
Taste talha wine at Vila de Frades or Herdade do Rocim rather than in Évora. Clay-amphora Alentejo wine barely leaves its villages and the November talha season is when the pots are opened.
Carry two spare tubes and a tyre boot. Alentejo schist cuts sidewalls, and there is no bike shop between Évora and Odemira.
Book the Alqueva Dark Sky observatory session for a moonless night — the reservoir has among the lowest light pollution in Europe and the difference between new and full moon is total.
Use the Linha do Sul railheads at Funcheira or Ourique to skip the worst of the N120 if the transition day looks hot. CP Regional takes bikes free.
Cork harvest runs roughly May to August. Estate tracks in harvest see slow trucks and stacked bark — pass wide and expect diversions.

raw.Signature gravel day — the Alqueva monta: 74 km, 780 m ascent, on hard clay estate tracks between cork oaks with three short 12% pitches on the Monsaraz approach.
raw.Monsaraz wall ramp: 2.1 km at 6.4% from the Alqueva shore, maximum 14% on the final cobbled approach to Porta da Vila, summit 232 m. Short but it is the only meaningful gradient for 40 km in any direction.
raw.Serra de Serpa/Mértola schist climbs: the Guadiana valley delivers repeated 1.5–3 km ramps at 6–8% on broken schist, with the day's high point around 220 m — low numbers that mislead badly, because the surface is loose plate and the sun is unrelenting.
raw.Coastal leg — Vila Nova de Milfontes to: 46 km, 620 m ascent, on sand-over-hardpack and paved lanes via Almograve and Cavaleiro, with the Cabo Sardão lighthouse detour.
raw.Week surface split: approximately 45% hard clay and schist farm track, 30% paved (narrow, empty municipal roads), 15% loose sand on the coastal sections, 10% cobbled village setts. Run 45–50 mm tyres; anything narrower will bog in the Costa Vicentina sand.
raw.Rota Vicentina rules — read this before: the Fishermen's Trail (Trilho dos Pescadores) is a walking route along cliff edge and dune and is not a cycling route; do not plan bike days on it. The Historical Way is the one long-distance Rota Vicentina route that has historically been open to cyclists, and the network now also publishes over 1,000 km of dedicated MTB and gravel trails across 38 signed routes in four difficulty grades, a 145 km long-distance MTB trail through the Odemira area with train-station connections, and a roughly 500 km touring route between Lisbon and Faro suited to gravel, hybrid and touring bikes. Use those, and treat cliff-edge singletrack as off-limits.
raw.Bike hire: local rental in the Alentejo interior is genuinely scarce — the practical model is a Lisbon operator such as Bike Iberia delivering gravel or touring bikes to Évora and collecting from the coast, at roughly €30–€40/day for a gravel bike and €160–€260/week including delivery, or booking through a Rota Vicentina bike-friendly partner in Odemira or São Teotónio. E-bike hire is easier to find on the coast than inland. One-way drop-off across the region is normal with delivery operators but should be priced at booking; bike-box storage is usually held by the operator in Lisbon, not locally.
raw.Bike-friendly accommodation logistics: São Lourenço do Barrocal near Monsaraz has a secure bike store and its own bikes; Herdade do Touril at Zambujeira do Mar keeps bikes in a farm outbuilding with a hose; Convento do Espinheiro outside Évora will lock bikes in a cloister storeroom. Ask about a hose specifically — Alentejo clay dust in the drivetrain is the mechanical risk of the week.
raw.Bike on public transport: Comboios de Portugal carries bikes free on Regional and InterRegional services in designated spaces, subject to capacity; Alfa Pendular and Intercidades require the bike bagged or dismantled, with limited spaces bookable in advance. The Linha do Sul stops at Funcheira and Ourique are the useful railheads for the Odemira area. Rede Expressos coaches take boxed bikes in the hold for a fee at driver's discretion.

typeSpecific.surface: approximately 45% hard clay and schist farm track, 30% paved (narrow, empty municipal roads), 15% loose sand on the coastal sections, 10% cobbled village setts. Run 45–50 mm tyres; anything narrower will bog in the Costa Vicentina sand.

sources.verified: Rota Vicentina's own cycling page confirming that the Historical Way was the original route open to cyclists, that the network now publishes a dedicated bike offer of more than 1,000 km across 38 routes in four difficulty levels, a 145 km long-distance MTB trail in the Odemira area with train-station connections, and roughly 500 km of touring route between Lisbon and Faro for hybrid, gravel and touring bikes, plus a bike-friendly partner accommodation scheme. The Fishermen's Trail is presented as a walking route and is not offered as a cycling route.
sources.confidenceNotes: Rental logistics are the weakest point in this file — inland Alentejo hire is thin, and the named delivery model plus its indicative pricing must be confirmed with the operator before publishing. Whether cycling is formally prohibited or merely not offered on the Fishermen's Trail should be checked against current park regulations, as enforcement and signage have changed. Hotel rates for São Lourenço do Barrocal, Convento do Espinheiro and Herdade do Touril are prior-season estimates. Mértola accommodation names should be re-verified as trading. CP bike-carriage rules by service class and Rede Expressos coach policy need confirmation. The Alqueva Dark Sky observatory session format and price change seasonally. trips.hook: A carved stone every kilometre, an orange T on a fence post, and 300 km of Transylvania that no road atlas makes look interesting. This is riding through hay meadows and oak forest between Saxon villages with fortified churches and forty remaining German speakers, on a surface that swings from smooth commune asphalt to clay ruts that would stop a tractor. The hills are short and relentless, the guesthouse dinners are enormous, and the shepherd dogs are the real terrain.

snapshot.Start / End: Sighișoara → Sibiu (point-to-point, ~305 km, ~5,200 m ascent)
snapshot.Getting there: Fly into Sibiu (SBZ), Târgu Mureș (TGM) or Cluj (CLJ). CFR trains reach Sighișoara from Brașov (2 h 15), Cluj (3 h 30) and Bucharest (4 h 30–5 h). Finish on a train or flight out of Sibiu.

itinerary.title: Sighișoara and a shakedown
itinerary.morning: Arrive in **Sighișoara**, collect or build the bike, and walk the citadel — the Clock Tower, the Covered Stairway up to the Church on the Hill, and the last inhabited medieval citadel in Europe still functioning as a town.
itinerary.afternoon: A short loop east on the Via Transilvanica towards **Hetiur** and back, purely to find the orange T, meet your first milestone, and check that the gearing and tyre pressure suit 10% pasture ramps.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in the lower town. Set the bike up properly tonight: mud clearance, spare hanger, two tubes, and a chain that will survive clay.

itinerary.title: A taste of Terra Siculorum
itinerary.morning: Transfer or train north-east to **Odorheiu Secuiesc**, the Székely town at the heart of Terra Siculorum — Hungarian-speaking, with its own architecture and a completely different village pattern from the Saxon lands.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the Via Transilvanica back south-west out of Odorheiu through the Székely hill villages: long grassy doubletrack, oak woodland, and milestones set into hedgerows. This is the quietest riding of the week.
itinerary.evening: Finish at a guesthouse on the section end and eat *kürtőskalács* fresh off the spit. Székely cooking runs to *gulyás* and stuffed cabbage — order both.

itinerary.title: Saschiz, Criț and the clay
itinerary.morning: Back to Sighișoara and out west on the route to **Saschiz**, whose fortified church and hilltop citadel are UNESCO-listed as part of the Villages with Fortified Churches in Transylvania.
itinerary.afternoon: The section on to **Criț** is the first serious clay. Ridable and enjoyable dry; a shoulder-carry wet. Criț's church has a Saxon graveyard with almost no living German community left to fill it.
itinerary.evening: Down to **Viscri**. Guesthouse dinner — this village's houses were restored under the Mihai Eminescu Trust and the whole street is lime-washed in blues and greens.

itinerary.title: Viscri, Bunești and Rupea
itinerary.morning: The **Viscri fortified church**, UNESCO-listed, white-walled and unheated, plus the village blacksmith and the woollen-sock cooperative. Do this before riding; the coaches arrive at 11:00.
itinerary.afternoon: Out via **Bunești** — the junction village on the DN13 — and the pasture climb to **Rupea**, where a huge basalt-hilltop citadel stands over the road, restored and open. The Rupea approach is the best descent of the week.
itinerary.evening: Guesthouse in Rupea or Homorod. *Ciorbă*, *sarmale*, *palincă*; ask the host to fill your bottles from the well rather than the tap.

itinerary.title: Homorod, Cața, Ungra
itinerary.morning: **Homorod**'s Romanesque-cored fortified church, then a long forest-track section south — genuinely remote riding, with more roe deer than people.
itinerary.afternoon: **Cața** and **Ungra**, the two quietest Saxon villages on the route, on rolling clay and pasture. Ungra sits above the Olt; from the ridge the **Făgăraș** wall appears to the south, 2,500 m and usually with snow on it.
itinerary.evening: Guesthouse in the Făgăraș foothills. This is the day to check the forecast properly — everything from here west depends on whether the clay stays hard.

itinerary.title: North-west to Biertan and Richiș
itinerary.morning: Transfer or ride north-west to **Biertan**, whose fortified church — a triple ring of walls, the famous multi-locked sacristy door — was the seat of the Saxon Lutheran bishops and is the best-preserved of the lot.
itinerary.afternoon: The short, beautiful ride over the hill to **Richiș**, a village with a strikingly Gothic-Cistercian church and a slow trickle of returning Saxon descendants, then on towards **Mediaș**.
itinerary.evening: **Mediaș**: the leaning Trumpeters' Tower, a real town centre, and a proper restaurant meal after five days of guesthouse cooking.

itinerary.title: Into Sibiu
itinerary.morning: West out of Mediaș on the Terra Vinum ground — vineyards on the south-facing slopes, gravel between them, easier gradients than anything so far.
itinerary.afternoon: The long approach into **Sibiu** through Șura Mare, finishing in the Piața Mare. Wash the bike before you box it; Transylvanian clay sets like cement.
itinerary.evening: Sibiu. Eat on the Piața Mică under the Bridge of Lies, drink something local, and count how many andesite milestones you photographed.

accommodationStrategy.name: A restored Saxon house at Viscri
accommodationStrategy.description: Viscri's guesthouses are restored 18th-century Saxon houses with barns — meaning a lockable stone outbuilding for the bikes, an outdoor tap and hose for the clay, and a host who cooks dinner because there is nowhere else to eat.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–5 weeks ahead, direct by phone; Viscri fills at weekends [VERIFY: current nightly rates].

accommodationStrategy.name: A guesthouse in Rupea or Homorod
accommodationStrategy.description: the midpoint of the Saxon crossing, on the DN13 so a support car or a bail-out taxi can reach you, with the Rupea citadel and a railway station both within reach if the weather turns and you need to skip a section.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–3 weeks ahead; half-board is standard and worth taking.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel or pension in the Sighișoara lower town
accommodationStrategy.description: bookending the trip in the lower town rather than the citadel means level access, parking, a bike-build space and a five-minute walk to the station — the citadel's cobbles and stairs are a nightmare with a bike bag.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead; confirm secure indoor bike storage explicitly before you pay.

logistics.connectivity: Romanian mobile data is fast and cheap, and 4G reaches most Saxon villages. Forest sections between Homorod and Cața have gaps. Download the whole route offline — the blaze is not a substitute for a GPX in fog.
logistics.emergency: **112**. In the hills, **Salvamont 0725 826 668**. Dog bites need medical attention and a rabies risk assessment the same day — Romania is not rabies-free and rural dogs are frequently unvaccinated.
logistics.weather: Transylvanian summer storms build fast in the afternoon; the danger to a cyclist is not lightning but the clay, which goes from rideable to impossible in twenty minutes of rain and takes 24–48 hours of sun to recover. Build a rest day into a seven-day plan.
logistics.bookingWindows: Guesthouses 2–5 weeks; Viscri and Biertan longer at weekends. Bike hire and luggage transfer 4–8 weeks — the operators are small and their fleets are smaller.
logistics.money: Village guesthouses, church keyholders and roadside honey sellers are cash. Carry 700–1,000 RON (€135–€190). ATMs exist in Sighișoara, Rupea, Mediaș and Sibiu and nowhere between them.
logistics.transportRules: CFR needs a **bicycle supplement** and a service with bike space; *Regio* trains are the dependable ones. If you drive a support car, the **rovinietă** applies on national roads — category A, 1 day €3.50 (~18 RON), 10 days €6 (~31 RON), 30 days €9.50 (~50 RON); there is no 7-day product.
logistics.permits: No permit for the Via Transilvanica; it is free to walk and ride. Fortified churches charge small entry fees and several are opened on request by a keyholder living nearby [VERIFY: current fortified-church entry fees at Viscri, Biertan and Saschiz]. Wild camping is tolerated off the route in unfenced forest but not on pasture in use.

proTips: Check rainfall for the previous **three days**, not the forecast. The clay's state is a function of what already fell, and a sunny morning after a wet night is the worst trap on this route.
Fit a **40–45 mm tyre with real mud clearance** and carry a stick or a length of dowel — for scraping the clay off the frame, and not incidentally for the dogs.
Photograph the milestone number at every junction you doubt. If you lose the blaze, the last number you saw is what Tășuleasa Social or a local will use to find you.
Arrive at Viscri and Biertan **before 10:00 or after 16:00**. Both are on the coach circuit from Brașov and both are empty either side of the middle of the day.
Learn *"Ciobane, cheamă câinii!"* — shepherd, call the dogs. Said loudly and early, it resolves 90% of encounters before they start.
Book **half-board everywhere**. Saxon villages have no restaurants; the guesthouse kitchen is the only food, it costs €8–€12, and it is better than the towns.
Ride the section **into** Sibiu rather than out of it. The Terra Vinum gradients favour the westbound direction and finishing in the Piața Mare beats starting there.

raw.The route: The **Via Transilvanica** is a **waymarked long-distance route of roughly 1,400 km** running diagonally across Romania from **Putna** in Bucovina to **Drobeta-Turnu Severin** on the Danube, built from 2018 onwards by the **Asociația Tășuleasa Social** with volunteer labour. It is divided into named *terras* — Bucovinei, Dacica, Siculorum, **Saxonica**, Vinum, Ardealului, Banatica. This week rides the **Terra Saxonica** heart, with a taste of **Terra Siculorum** and a Terra Vinum finish into Sibiu.
raw.Waymarking: Two systems, both used. The **orange "T" blaze** is painted on posts, trees, walls and rocks, and it is the one you follow minute to minute. The **carved andesite milestones** — one roughly every kilometre, each numbered, quarried and cut by hand — are the route's signature and the best confirmation you are still on it. Milestone numbers run from the Putna end, so they count **down** as you ride south-west. Download the official GPX before you leave; the blaze is good but not infallible on pasture.
raw.Is it legally rideable?: The Via Transilvanica is **designed and promoted for walking, cycling and horseback**, and the great majority of it is legally open to bikes. It is not, however, uniformly *practically* rideable: sections cross narrow single-track through forest, steep eroded gullies and, in the mountain *terras*, terrain where you will push. Within Terra Saxonica the ridable proportion is high — call it 85–90% — but expect short carries. Some segments cross private pasture on customary access; ride through, do not stop, and close gates. [VERIFY: current official cycling guidance and any walkers-only segments in Terra Saxonica]
raw.Surface split: Roughly: **35% forest track and gravel doubletrack**, **25% sheep-pasture doubletrack** (grass over hard-packed earth, fine when dry, greasy when not), **25% commune asphalt** linking villages, and **15% clay**. That last figure is the one that decides your week. **The clay sections between Saschiz, Criț and Bunești, and again around Cața and Ungra, are genuinely unrideable after rain** — the soil balls up in the frame and drivetrain within fifty metres and the bike becomes a wheelbarrow. This is a **40–45 mm gravel-tyre trip** with generous mud clearance; anything narrower is wrong and anything wider is unnecessary.
raw.Per-day distance and elevation: Day 1 shakedown 22 km / +350 m. Day 2 (Terra Siculorum) 48 km / +820 m. Day 3 52 km / +900 m. Day 4 46 km / +780 m. Day 5 58 km / +950 m. Day 6 47 km / +810 m. Day 7 62 km / +680 m. Total ~305 km / ~5,200 m. **The Transylvanian hills roll harder than the map suggests** — these are 60–120 m rises repeated a dozen times a day at 8–12%, and the accumulated climbing is closer to an Alpine col day than the profile implies.
raw.Shepherd dogs — the single biggest hazar: Not bears, not traffic. Transylvanian flocks are guarded by **Ciobănesc Românesc Carpatin, Mioritic and de Bucovina** dogs, 40–60 kg, bred to drive off wolves, and a cyclist moving fast past a flock triggers exactly the behaviour they exist for. **The technique:** slow down and **stop pedalling well before you reach them**; **dismount and put the bike between you and the dogs**; walk steadily on, without running, without shouting, without eye contact; keep the bike as a barrier and keep moving away from the flock, which is what they want. Shout for the shepherd — ***"Ciobane!"*** — and he will normally call them off. Never sprint: they are faster than you uphill and they will chase. Carrying a stick or riding with a group helps. **The legal position:** Romania's hunting law (Legea 407/2006) caps sheepfold dogs in hunting grounds at **three in mountain areas, two in hills and one in the plains**, each required to wear a *jujeu* — a wooden restraint on the collar to stop them chasing game. **In practice this is very widely ignored**; flocks of eight or ten unrestrained dogs are common. Know the rule, but plan for the reality.
raw.Bikes: hire and logistics: Dedicated gravel-bike hire in **Sighișoara** is thin to non-existent; the practical options are a Brașov- or Bucharest-based operator delivering a bike to your first guesthouse, or bringing your own in a bag. Several Romanian cycling tour operators run supported Via Transilvanica trips and will hire out bikes with luggage transfer between guesthouses, which is the sensible way to do this route without a support car [VERIFY: current gravel-bike hire rates and delivery to Sighișoara].
raw.CFR trains with a bike: Romanian Railways carries bicycles only on services with designated bike space, and you need a **bicycle supplement in addition to your own ticket**; on Interregio and long-distance trains this is not guaranteed and staff can refuse a bike if the space is taken. Regional (*Regio*) trains on the Sighișoara–Mediaș–Sibiu and Brașov–Rupea lines are the reliable ones. Bag the bike if you can — a boxed or bagged bike travels as luggage without argument [VERIFY: current CFR bicycle supplement price and which services accept bikes].
