trips.title: Kattegattleden: Gothenburg to Helsingborg

bestPeriod.window: May to late September; warmest swimming July–August; best light and empty roads late August–mid September
bestPeriod.raw: May to late September; warmest swimming July–August; best light and empty roads late August–mid September

accommodation.note: €95–170 per night, double; STF hostels €40–60 pp; two seaside spa nights push the top end

food.note: €50–75 per day (bakery breakfast, harbour lunch, one proper dinner)

transport.note: €150–220: bike hire €120–160 for the week, plus one-way rail return Helsingborg–Gothenburg

activities.note: €50–90: Tjolöholm Castle, Varberg fortress and cold bathhouse, museum entries

profile.difficultyNote: Easy. Sweden's flattest long-distance route; 45–70 km per day, rarely more than 250 m gain, one real climb over Hallandsåsen

trips.summary: A seven-day cycling trip itinerary in Halland & northwest Skåne coast, Sweden.

itinerary.title: Gothenburg to Kungsbacka
itinerary.morning: Collect touring bikes in central Gothenburg — reserve panniers and a rear rack explicitly, most shops rent them separately. Coffee at Da Matteo in Magasinsgatan before you roll.
itinerary.afternoon: Out through Askim and Billdal on segregated cycleway, then the coastal stretch past Särö Västerskog nature reserve, a rare wind-sculpted oak forest on the shore. Swim stop at Vallda Sandö if the wind is off the land.
itinerary.evening: Kungsbacka's old town on Storgatan for dinner. Short day by design: the first afternoon on a loaded bike is where blisters get decided.
itinerary.dayStats: 43 km, asphalt

itinerary.title: Kungsbacka to Varberg
itinerary.morning: Tjolöholm Castle, an Arts-and-Crafts manor on its own peninsula, opens at 11:00 in season — the stables café does a good early lunch.
itinerary.afternoon: Through Åsa and Frillesås on quiet lanes, then the long open coast toward Varberg. The last 10 km run past Apelviken, Sweden's most consistent surf and windsurf beach — expect to be overtaken by kite buggies.
itinerary.evening: Varberg. Swim from the Varberg Kallbadhus, a Moorish-style 1903 cold bathhouse on the pier with separate sex-segregated open-air pools and a wood sauna. Dinner in the Societetsparken pavilion.
itinerary.dayStats: 62 km, 240 m gain

itinerary.title: Varberg to Falkenberg (32 km) plus Ätran valley loop
itinerary.morning: Varberg Fortress, where the Bocksten Man — a fully clothed 14th-century bog body — is displayed. One hour, genuinely unsettling.
itinerary.afternoon: Short flat coastal ride via Träslövsläge and Ugglarps to Falkenberg. Check in early, then ride the Ätran river loop inland: the Ätran is one of Europe's original catch-and-release salmon rivers and the old town of wooden houses around Tullbron bridge is the prettiest hour on the whole route.
itinerary.evening: Falkenberg has a serious brewing scene; the town's brewery taproom plus a river-side dinner.
itinerary.dayStats: 20 km

itinerary.title: Falkenberg to Halmstad
itinerary.morning: Coastal cycleway via Skrea Strand and Glommen, a working fishing harbour where the smoked prawn stands open around 10:00.
itinerary.afternoon: Steninge and the Möllegård cliffs, then into Halmstad along the Nissan river. Detour to Tylösand, a 7 km white-sand beach that is essentially Sweden's summer capital.
itinerary.evening: Halmstad Castle waterfront, dinner in the Stora Torg quarter, evening swim at Tylösand where the sun sets straight into the Kattegat.
itinerary.dayStats: 42 km

itinerary.title: Halmstad to Båstad over Hallandsåsen
itinerary.morning: South via Trönninge and Eldsberga, gently rolling farmland. Fuel properly in Laholm — the ascent is next.
itinerary.afternoon: Hallandsåsen ridge: a steady 5–6 km climb to about 200 m with a fast, technical descent into Båstad on the Bjäre peninsula. Not steep, but it is where the day is won.
itinerary.evening: Båstad. Tennis town, old harbour, Norrviken Gardens on the headland. Dinner overlooking Laholm Bay.
itinerary.dayStats: 48 km, the route's only real climb

itinerary.title: Bjäre peninsula and on to Ängelholm
itinerary.morning: The Bjäre loop is the best riding on the route: Kattvik, Hovs Hallar's red cliffs (where Bergman filmed *The Seventh Seal*), and the potato fields the Bjärehalvön is famous for. Rolling, hedged, lanes barely wider than a car.
itinerary.afternoon: Down the west side via Torekov and Båstad's back roads, then south through Skälderviken to Ängelholm.
itinerary.evening: Ängelholm Havsbaden beach and a quiet last-but-one night.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 km, 300 m gain

itinerary.title: Ängelholm to Helsingborg and out
itinerary.morning: The finest final stretch on Kattegattleden: Rönnen nature reserve, then the cliff-edge cycleway past Domsten and Viken with Denmark two miles across the Sound.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive Helsingborg. Climb Kärnan tower for the view over to Helsingør. Return bikes, then train north to Gothenburg (about 2 h 15) or the 20-minute ferry to Denmark for a Copenhagen flight.
itinerary.dayStats: 38 km

accommodationStrategy.name: Varbergs Kusthotell
accommodationStrategy.description: Directly on the promenade beside the Kallbadhus, with a spa you will want on Day 2 evening. Secure bike room and a drying cabinet for wet kit. Book a sea-side room, the rail-side ones face the tracks.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Skansen / Båstad harbour properties
accommodationStrategy.description: Base for the Bjäre loop day. Choose a property in the harbour rather than upper Båstad: after the Hallandsåsen descent you will not want the extra 60 m of climbing home each evening.

accommodationStrategy.name: STF Hostels along the route
accommodationStrategy.description: Sweden's touring club network — clean, cheap, always with a kitchen and a lockable cycle shed, and the standard fallback if you decide to reshape the stages mid-week. Bring or hire bed linen; it is charged extra by default.

logistics.emergency: 112. Hospitals in Varberg, Halmstad and Helsingborg. Sweden's *Trafikverket* road-condition service and the SMHI weather app are both usable in English.
logistics.weather: Southwesterly prevailing wind. A frontal day in Halland means 10–14 m/s straight off the sea with no shelter for 20 km at a stretch. Build one flex day into a 7-day plan or accept a train hop.
logistics.bookingWindows: July is Swedish industrial holiday season — coastal hotels sell out 3–4 months out and prices roughly double. Late August and September are half the price with better riding.

other.label: Signage
other.text: Kattegattleden is Sweden's first national tourist cycle route and is fully signposted with distinctive blue-and-white markers in both directions. Signage is reliable enough that a GPX file is a backup, not a necessity.

other.label: Bikes on trains
other.text: Rules differ by operator and change often: Skåne's Pågatåg and Öresundståg carry bikes with restrictions in rush hour; long-distance SJ services generally require a boxed bike or a booked bike space on selected trains. Plan the return leg before you book — this is the single most common trip-ruining detail on this route. `verify: true`

other.label: Luggage transfer
other.text: Several Halland-based operators run pannier transfer between the standard overnight towns, roughly €20–30 per bag per stage. Worth it if you are riding on a light road bike rather than a tourer.

other.label: Right to roam
other.text: *Allemansrätten* allows wild camping for one night on unenclosed land away from dwellings — but not on the Bjäre peninsula's fenced farmland, and not on the beach reserves, which are explicitly excluded.

proTips: Ride **north to south**. Finishing at Helsingborg gives you a fast train home, a Danish ferry option, and a downhill last day.
The **Kallbadhus at Varberg** is open early. Go at 07:00 on Day 3 before you ride — sauna, cold Kattegat, empty pier.
Swedish *fika* is a logistics tool, not a cliché: bakeries in Falkenberg and Torekov open at 07:00 and close at 15:00. Plan the long afternoon stages with a packed lunch, not a hopeful one.
Hovs Hallar is packed 11:00–15:00 with car tourists. Ride it at **08:30** and you will have the cliffs to yourself.
If a headwind day arrives, take the regional train **Halmstad–Ängelholm** and use the saved hours on the Bjäre loop instead. The Bjäre is the good part; the flat farmland is not what you came for.
Book Tjolöholm Castle's guided tour slot online the night before — the walk-up queue on a July Saturday is over an hour.

trips.title: Soča Valley & Goriška Brda Gravel Week

bestPeriod.window: Mid-May–late June & early September–mid-October
bestPeriod.avoid: November–March — Kolovrat ridge roads ice or snow-block and most Kobarid guesthouses close
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-May–late June & early September–mid-October

accommodation.note: Kobarid guesthouses €70–€110 pppn; Brda wine estates €110–€145

food.note: Gostilna mains €12–€18; one Hiša Franko blowout adds €150–€300

transport.note: Airport transfer, Bohinj railway leg, luggage shuttle Kobarid→Brda

activities.note: Gravel hire €210–€260/week, Kobarid Museum €8, two winery tastings €40

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5 — six riding days of 900–1,800 m ascent with sustained 9–12% gravel ramps on the Kolovrat side roads

trips.gatewayAirport: TRS Trieste–Ronchi dei Legionari, 75 min drive to Kobarid; LJU Ljubljana 1 h 50 min; VCE Venice 2 h 15 min
trips.summary: Two textures in one week. The first half climbs repeatedly out of Kobarid onto the Kolovrat ridge, a militarised limestone spine where Isonzo Front trenches still cut the grass and tarmac gives way to white dolomite without warning. The second half drops 900 m into Goriška Brda, where gradients shorten but never stop, hills are terraced in ribolla gialla, and the Italian border is a line you cross four times a day. It suits riders who like climbing in 6–14 km doses on 40–45 mm tyres. Distances stay at 55–80 km because the ascent-per-kilometre ratio is punishing.

itinerary.title: Landing in Kobarid, legs open on the Napoleon bridge loop
itinerary.morning: Transfer from Trieste to Kobarid and collect the gravel bike from Positive Sport on Mučeniška ulica, insisting on a 40 mm minimum tyre. Walk ten minutes to the Kobarid Museum for the Isonzo Front context that makes every ridge this week legible.
itinerary.afternoon: Shakedown loop: Kobarid, the Napoleon bridge, the Drežnica turn, Trnovo ob Soči and back on the right bank, dipping to the Great Soča Gorge.
itinerary.evening: Hiša Polonka on Gregorčičeva, Ana Roš's casual room. Order the frika with Tolminc cheese and a glass of Movia.
itinerary.dayStats: 34 km / 480 m ascent / 90% paved, 10% gravel access track / max gradient 9%

itinerary.title: Kolovrat ridge, the week's hardest hour
itinerary.morning: Roll south to Volarje and start the Kolovrat ascent via Selišče. The first 5 km are steepest; settle into a gear you can hold for 75 minutes. Tarmac ends above Ježa.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the crest gravel west to the Kolovrat Outdoor Museum at 1,114 m — restored Italian third-line trenches, tunnels and observation posts, Julian Alps one side, Friulian plain the other. Continue to the Solarji saddle, then descend the paved Livek road to Kobarid.
itinerary.evening: Topli Val at Hotel Hvala for Soča trout and the Brda white list.
itinerary.dayStats: 61 km / 1,780 m ascent / 65% paved, 35% dolomite gravel / summit 1,114 m / 12.8 km at 7.9%

itinerary.title: Vršno hairpins and the Tolminka gorge
itinerary.morning: Warm up on the left-bank road to Kamno, then take the Vršno switchbacks — eleven turns, 340 m, the poet Simon Gregorčič's birthplace at the top. Descend the same way.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride to Tolmin and walk the Tolminska korita gorge circuit, roughly 90 minutes past the Devil's Bridge and the wedged Bear's Head boulder. Then a gravel loop up Zatolmin toward Čadrg.
itinerary.evening: Gostilna Zatolmin outside Tolmin for štruklji and grilled meat at half Kobarid prices.
itinerary.dayStats: 58 km / 1,250 m ascent / 70% paved, 30% gravel / Vršno 3.9 km at 8.7%, max 14%

itinerary.title: Most na Soči, the Bača valley, transfer south to Brda
itinerary.morning: Take the quiet right-bank road via Idrsko and Kred to Most na Soči, where the dammed Soča turns mint green, then the Bača valley spur toward Grahovo.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the Kanalski Lom ridge to Dobrovo, or shorten it with one stop on the Bohinj railway. Cross into Brda by the Neblo road; the landscape becomes terraced vine inside a kilometre.
itinerary.evening: Klinec in Medana for macerated ribolla and slow-cooked lamb. Book three days ahead — one sitting only.
itinerary.dayStats: 72 km / 1,120 m ascent / 80% paved, 20% hardpack / bike-on-train €3, paid on board

itinerary.title: Brda hill circuit: Šmartno, Medana, Ceglo, Vipolže
itinerary.morning: The ridge road from Šmartno to the Gonjače lookout tower, then drop and climb repeatedly through Kozana, Medana and Plešivo. Nothing is long; everything is 8–12%.
itinerary.afternoon: Two tastings, no more — Marjan Simčič at Ceglo for the Opoka single-vineyard whites, then Ščurek at Plešivo for Stara Brajda and the sculpture park. Recover on the flat cypress avenue at Vipolže.
itinerary.evening: Gredič at Ceglo for the tasting menu, or the cheaper terrace at Hiša Marica.
itinerary.dayStats: 64 km / 1,340 m ascent / 75% paved, 25% vineyard hardpack / no climb over 3 km but 22 ramps above 8%

itinerary.title: Cross-border day: Collio, Cormòns and Nova Gorica
itinerary.morning: Drop west into Italian Collio via Vipolže — identical geology, different signage. Ride the Plessiva ridge above Cormòns, then the vine lanes through Ruttars and Lonzano.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop east to Nova Gorica and roll across Trg Evrope / Piazza Transalpina, the square split by the border where the twin cities ran their joint European Capital of Culture year in 2025.
itinerary.evening: Belica in Medana, a farm restaurant with a terrace over the vines; order the cherry dishes in late May and June.
itinerary.dayStats: 78 km / 1,180 m ascent / 88% paved, 12% gravel / two Schengen border crossings, no checks

itinerary.title: Sabotin, Solkan and out
itinerary.morning: Final climb: Sabotin from Solkan, 6.7 km at 7.2% to 609 m, a WWI battleground with summit tunnels and the best single view of the Soča leaving the mountains.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend to Solkan for the stone arch railway bridge — at 85 m, the longest stone arch span ever built for a railway. Return the bike via the pre-arranged shuttle to Positive Sport.
itinerary.evening: Hiša Franko in Kobarid, which retained three Michelin stars in the 2026 guide. Book three to six months ahead.
itinerary.dayStats: 46 km / 780 m ascent / 95% paved / Sabotin 6.7 km at 7.2%, summit 609 m
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Hvala, Kobarid, or an airport hotel at Ronchi

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Hvala
accommodationStrategy.description: Combines a secure ground-floor bike room, breakfast from 07:00 for early Kolovrat starts, and Topli Val downstairs. Around €95–€130 double B&B, two minutes from Positive Sport for a mid-week mechanical.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hiša Marica
accommodationStrategy.description: Inside Šmartno's walled medieval core, so you ride out of a village gate straight into vineyards. The cellar locks around six bikes, there is an outdoor tap for washing, and the terrace kitchen saves you descending to Dobrovo after a hard day. Roughly €110–€145 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Nebesa Chalets
accommodationStrategy.description: The luxury option at 700 m directly above the Livek climb: your morning is an 8 km descent, your evening an 8 km penalty. Glass-fronted cabins, shared sauna, dinner included, roughly €280–€340 per cabin.

logistics.connectivity: 4G is solid on the valley floor and in Brda, patchy on the Kolovrat crest, absent in the Bača side valleys. EU roaming applies. Load offline tiles: the gravel forks at Solarji are badly signed.
logistics.emergency: 112 covers GRZS mountain rescue on Kolovrat. Slovenia honours EHIC/GHIC but recovery costs may not be — carry sports insurance naming off-road cycling. Nearest hospital: Šempeter pri Gorici, 45 min from Kobarid.
logistics.weather: One of Europe's wettest basins; storms build over the Krn massif from 14:00 in June and September. In autumn the burja accelerates through the Vipava and Brda gaps at 80–120 km/h and stops you dead on exposed ridges. Check meteo.si daily.
logistics.bookingWindows: Hiša Franko three to six months. Klinec and Belica three to five days. Positive Sport gravel bikes six weeks for June weekends. Hiša Marica two months for September.
logistics.money: Slovenia is in the eurozone. Cards work almost everywhere, but mountain gostilnas above Livek and the Kolovrat hut are cash-only. Tipping means rounding up, or 10% for a full meal.
logistics.transportRules: A Slovenian e-vinjeta (€16 weekly) is required if your car uses the A1/H4 — buy online before crossing. Bikes on trains cost €3 per journey, no advance reservation. Cross-border rental into Italy is generally free; into Croatia it usually is not. Carry ID for Schengen crossings.
logistics.permits: Triglav National Park lies north of the route, so its rules do not bite, but the Kolovrat trenches are protected heritage: no metal detecting, no removing objects, and unexploded WWI ordnance still surfaces. Drones need Slovenian CAA registration and are banned over the Kobarid Museum and military cemeteries.
logistics.health: Tap water is drinkable throughout, fountains included. Ticks on Kolovrat grassland April–October are the real hazard: Slovenia has one of Europe's highest tick-borne encephalitis rates, so consider vaccination and check nightly. The Soča runs 8–12°C in August — cold shock, not depth, is the swimming risk.

proTips: Climb Kolovrat on a weekday before 08:00 — the ridge gravel stays shaded until mid-morning and the motorcyclists who own the Livek–Solarji road do not appear before eleven.
The Solarji crossing drops you into Italy on an unsigned dirt road toward Clabuzzaro on far worse tarmac. Ride out and back on the Slovenian side unless you are on 45 mm+ tyres.
Tell Positive Sport your frame model when booking and ask them to fit a spare rear mech hanger. Nothing between Tolmin and Nova Gorica will stock one.
Brda tastings are farm visits, not tasting rooms. Phone or email a day ahead; arriving unannounced at Simčič or Ščurek on a Tuesday gets you a locked gate.
Buy the €3 bike ticket the second the conductor appears at Most na Soči — the Bohinj railway carriages cap bikes at a handful, first come first served.
The Brda cherry harvest peaks in the first fortnight of June with open-cellar weekends. Best riding of the year, and also when Šmartno beds vanish first.
Refill at the public fountain on Šmartno's square; the Brda ridge has almost no shade and 64 km there drinks like 100 km elsewhere.
Carry €40 cash for the Kolovrat and Livek huts. They serve outstanding jota and none of them takes cards.

raw.Signature climb — Kolovrat from Tolmin v: 12.8 km, 1,010 m ascent, 7.9% average, 15% maximum on the Selišče hairpins, cresting at 1,114 m at the Kolovrat Outdoor Museum. Tarmac to Ježa, then 4 km of graded white gravel along the ridge.
raw.Livek pass from Kobarid: 8.4 km, 470 m, 5.6% average, summit 679 m, fully paved — the warm-up and the gateway to the Solarji border ridge at 1,000 m via 6 km of packed forest gravel.
raw.Vršno hairpins: 3.9 km, 340 m, 8.7% average with two 14% ramps out of Kamno; eleven switchbacks, all paved, dropping straight to the river.
raw.Week surface split: approximately 62% paved (narrow, chip-sealed, near-empty), 28% white dolomite and forest hardpack, 8% vineyard farm track, 2% short singletrack link at Most na Soči. A 40–45 mm gravel tyre is the correct tool; 32 mm road rubber costs you the two best days.
raw.Bike hire: Positive Sport, Mučeniška ulica 8B, Kobarid (+386 40 821 810) is the valley's main rental and workshop — gravel, MTB and e-MTB, roughly €35–€45/day gravel and €50–€60 e-bike, weekly €210–€260, free bike-box storage for hirers. Marko Munih's shop at Cankarjeva ulica 3, Tolmin (+386 5 3811 464) covers spares and wheel-truing; Outdoor Galaxy (Ledina 1, Bovec) and Soča Experience (Čezsoča 129) serve the upper valley. One-way drop-off in Brda is not standard — budget a €40–€60 recovery fee.
raw.Bike-friendly accommodation: Hotel Hvala and Nebesa Chalets both give locked ground-floor bike storage; Hiša Marica in Šmartno stores bikes in the stone cellar with an outdoor tap for washing. No property here has a full workshop stand — carry a multitool and a spare mech hanger.
raw.Bike on public transport: Slovenske železnice charges €3 per bicycle per journey, paid to the conductor on board; no reservation is possible and space is genuinely limited, so avoid 06:00–08:00 and 14:00–16:00 weekday peaks. The Bohinj railway from Most na Soči is the useful line. Bikes are barred from ICS Pendolino services. Italian regional trains out of Gorizia charge €3.50 for a 24-hour bike ticket.

typeSpecific.surface: approximately 62% paved (narrow, chip-sealed, near-empty), 28% white dolomite and forest hardpack, 8% vineyard farm track, 2% short singletrack link at Most na Soči. A 40–45 mm gravel tyre is the correct tool; 32 mm road rubber costs you the two best days.

trips.title: Two Rivers: The Váh Cycle Trunk and the Danube Dyke from Žilina to Štúrovo
trips.subRegion: Považie (the Váh valley) and the Slovak Danube

bestPeriod.window: the first three weeks of September — warm, dry, the Danube dyke empty of Austrian weekend traffic
bestPeriod.avoid: late July–August (35 °C on the shadeless dyke) and March–April, when the Danube floodplain paths can be under water

accommodation.note: €245–€420 (€35–€60/night, cyklopríjemné penzióny)

transport.note: €120–€210 (bike rental €70–€120, ZSSK trains + bike tickets, one-way fee)

activities.note: €50–€90 (Trenčín castle, Komárno fortress, Piešťany spa island)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy–Moderate

trips.gatewayAirport: Fly Bratislava (BTS) or Vienna (VIE); ZSSK train Bratislava → Žilina, 2 h 20, bikes carried. Return from Štúrovo by train to Bratislava (~2 h 15) or cross the Mária Valéria bridge for Esztergom and Budapest.

trips.hook: Slovakia has one finished long-distance cycle route and one that is half-built, and this week rides both honestly. The Danube dyke below Bratislava is flat, smooth asphalt across Europe's largest river island, with a basilica in another country as the finish line. The Váh is the opposite: castle rock after castle rock, a spa town with a colonnade bridge, and stretches where the cycleway simply stops and you take the road. Come for the rivers, not for perfect infrastructure.

snapshot.Start / End: Žilina → Štúrovo (point-to-point, ~430 km ridden)
snapshot.Getting there: Fly Bratislava (BTS) or Vienna (VIE); ZSSK train Bratislava → Žilina, 2 h 20, bikes carried. Return from Štúrovo by train to Bratislava (~2 h 15) or cross the Mária Valéria bridge for Esztergom and Budapest.

itinerary.title: Through the Strečno gorge
itinerary.morning: From Žilina's Mariánske námestie, pick up the Váh downstream. The **Strečno** gorge comes at 12 km: the castle on its limestone crag above the river, and the route's worst infrastructure — short shared stretches on road I/18. Ride it early, before the truck traffic.
itinerary.afternoon: Past Vrútky, a spur into **Martin** for the Slovak National Museum's open-air Museum of the Slovak Village at Jahodnícke háje, then back onto the valley route through Považská Bystrica.
itinerary.evening: Reach **Trenčín** under its castle rock. Eat on Mierové námestie and look up: the castle is floodlit and vertical.

itinerary.title: The Roman inscription
itinerary.morning: Climb into **Trenčín Castle** first. Behind the Hotel Elizabeth, cut into the rock, is the **Roman inscription of 179 AD** recording the victory of Legio II Adiutrix at Laugaricio — **the only Roman inscription north of the Danube limes**, and viewable through a window in the hotel [VERIFY: current viewing arrangement and hours].
itinerary.afternoon: An easy 48 km on the finished cycleway south to **Piešťany**. This is the best-surfaced stretch of the whole Váh strand.
itinerary.evening: Cross the **Kolonádový most**, the 1933 covered colonnade bridge, to the spa island. Eat on the Winterova pedestrian street.

itinerary.title: Spa island to the Váh dams
itinerary.morning: A thermal soak or a walk round the spa island — the mud here has treated rheumatism since the 18th century [VERIFY: current spa day-pass price].
itinerary.afternoon: South to **Hlohovec** on levee and quiet road, past the Empire château above the town. The **Hlohovec–Sereď** section is the second unfinished gap: signed, partly unsurfaced, and with two short stretches on a busy road.
itinerary.evening: **Sereď** is unremarkable and that is fine — it is a bed, a supper and 62 km done. The Holocaust museum in the former labour camp is worth an hour if it is open.

itinerary.title: Onto the Danube
itinerary.morning: West through the Trnava lowlands on quiet farm roads to Senec, then down into **Bratislava**. If the wind is against you, take the regional train from Sereď — it is a legitimate shortcut and costs a few euros.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the Bratislava riverfront under the Nový most and out to Devín, where the Morava joins the Danube under the castle ruin. Then back into the Old Town.
itinerary.evening: Change bikes if you are switching rental, and sleep in Bratislava. Tomorrow is the flat river.

itinerary.title: Žitný ostrov and the barrage
itinerary.morning: Leave on **EuroVelo 6** along the left-bank dyke into the **Žitný ostrov (Csallóköz)** — at roughly 1,600 km², **Europe's largest river island**, formed between the Danube and the Little Danube, flat, agricultural and Hungarian-speaking.
itinerary.afternoon: Smooth asphalt all the way to **Šamorín** and on to the **Gabčíkovo** barrage — the vast, contested hydroelectric works on the Danube, whose locks you can ride across and watch from above.
itinerary.evening: Stay in Gabčíkovo or Vojka nad Dunajom. Fish soup, and an early night.

itinerary.title: The dyke to the fortress town
itinerary.morning: Pure dyke riding: asphalt, no traffic, no gradient, the Danube on your right and the Hungarian bank beyond it. The **Vojka–Kyselica ferry** and the **Šamorín-area crossings** operate seasonally if you want the right bank [VERIFY: current Danube ferry timetables and fares].
itinerary.afternoon: Into **Komárno**, where the Váh finally meets the Danube. The **Komárno fortress system** is one of the largest surviving 19th-century bastion complexes in central Europe — the Old and New Fortress plus the Monostor works across the river [VERIFY: current Monostor and Nová pevnosť opening hours].
itinerary.evening: Komárno is a bilingual Slovak-Hungarian town; eat *halászlé* or *kapustnica* depending on which side of the menu you read.

itinerary.title: To the basilica
itinerary.morning: Continue east on EuroVelo 6, still on the dyke, through Iža — where the Roman fort of **Kelemantia**, a bridgehead of the Danube limes, sits in a field — and Radvaň nad Dunajom.
itinerary.afternoon: Roll into **Štúrovo**, with **Esztergom's basilica** — the largest church in Hungary — filling the far bank. Cross the **Mária Valéria bridge**, destroyed in 1944 and not rebuilt until 2001; it is open to cyclists and pedestrians, there is no border check inside Schengen, and the crossing takes four minutes.
itinerary.evening: Climb to the basilica dome for the view back over Slovakia, then take the train from Štúrovo to Bratislava — or from Esztergom to Budapest, which is the better ending.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Elizabeth
accommodationStrategy.description: the Roman inscription of 179 AD is literally in the building's basement rock face, the castle is a ten-minute climb, and there is enclosed parking for bikes. Worth the one splurge night of the week.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct, 3–4 weeks ahead [VERIFY: current nightly rate].

accommodationStrategy.name: Penzión Sandra
accommodationStrategy.description: a locked bike room, a hose and a drying line, five minutes from the Kolonádový most, so you can wash the bike, wash yourself in the thermal water and be back for dinner. Central, cheap, and used to touring riders.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct or Booking.com, 2–3 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Penzión Panoráma
accommodationStrategy.description: on the flat right in the fortress quarter, secure storage, and walkable to the Nová pevnosť and the Danube confluence — plus a station five minutes away if the last day's weather turns and you want the train to Štúrovo.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct, 2 weeks ahead; earlier around the Komárno Days festival in late April.

logistics.connectivity: Continuous 4G/5G on both strands. The Žitný ostrov dyke is open farmland with excellent signal and no shade — the risk here is sun, not isolation.
logistics.emergency: 112. The Danube strand is never more than 8 km from a village. On the Váh, the Strečno gorge is the one place with poor shoulder and fast traffic — ride it defensively, with lights on, and use a mirror.
logistics.weather: The Danube plain gets 33–36 °C in July with no tree cover on the dyke; carry 2 L and start at 07:00. Spring high water can close short floodplain sections between Gabčíkovo and Komárno. The Váh valley funnels afternoon thunderstorms off the Strážovské vrchy.
logistics.bookingWindows: Guesthouses 2–4 weeks. The exception is the **IC bike reservation** — book it the moment you fix your dates, because the bike spaces on the Bratislava–Žilina IC sell out well before the seats.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards work in towns; carry €60–€100 cash for village *potraviny*, ferries and small guesthouses, which sometimes prefer it. ATMs in every town on the route.
logistics.transportRules: ZSSK carries bikes only on services with the bike pictogram, needs a separate bicycle ticket, and **requires a compulsory bike-space reservation on IC trains**. Slovak law requires a **helmet outside built-up areas** for all cyclists (and everywhere for under-15s), **lights and a rear reflector after dark**, and a **reflective element outside built-up areas at night**. Cyclist blood-alcohol tolerance is effectively **0.0‰**, same as drivers.
logistics.permits: No permits. The Mária Valéria bridge and the Danube ferries are inside Schengen — no checks, but carry ID. Cycling on the Gabčíkovo barrage structures is permitted only on the marked route.

proTips: Ride the Danube **west to east**. The prevailing north-westerly gives you 180 km of tailwind to Štúrovo, and reversing the direction turns an easy week into a hard one.

Do the Váh first and the Danube second, as here. The Váh's rough sections are best done on fresh legs, and finishing on flat asphalt under Esztergom's dome is a far better last day than grinding through the Strečno gorge.

If the Žilina–Strečno shared section worries you, take the local train Žilina–Vrútky (15 minutes, bikes carried without reservation) and start riding there. You lose the castle view and gain the least stressful morning of the trip.
Book the **IC bike space** before anything else. It is the hardest reservation of the week and the fallback — a regional stopping train from Bratislava to Žilina — costs you three and a half hours.
Ask specifically for *"cyklopríjemné ubytovanie"* when you phone a guesthouse. The phrase gets you the locked bike room; asking whether you can "keep a bike somewhere" gets you a corridor.
Carry 32–35 mm tyres. The Danube dyke would take anything, but the Hlohovec–Sereď levee and the Považská gravel connectors will punish 25 mm.
Finish in Esztergom, not Štúrovo. The direct trains to Budapest are frequent, the basilica is the natural full stop, and the border crossing on a bike bridge is a good last kilometre.

raw.Daily distances and elevation: Day 1 Žilina–Trenčín 78 km / +380 m. Day 2 Trenčín–Piešťany 48 km / +180 m. Day 3 Piešťany–Sereď via Hlohovec 62 km / +190 m. Day 4 Sereď–Bratislava 58 km / +120 m (or train the last section). Day 5 Bratislava–Gabčíkovo 62 km / +40 m. Day 6 Gabčíkovo–Komárno 58 km / +30 m. Day 7 Komárno–Štúrovo 62 km / +90 m. Total ~428 km, ~1,030 m of climbing — almost all of it in the first three days.
raw.Surface split, and this is the honest pa: The **EuroVelo 6 / Danube** strand from Bratislava to Štúrovo is roughly **85% smooth asphalt on the flood dyke, 10% quiet paved lane, 5% short gravel or village cobble** — genuinely flat, genuinely finished, rideable on 28 mm tyres. The **Vážska cyklomagistrála** down the Váh is roughly **50% dedicated asphalt cycleway, 35% quiet secondary road, and 15% unfinished gaps where you share a main road with traffic**. The gaps that matter: **Žilina–Strečno** (short shared sections through the gorge on road I/18, narrow, with trucks — this is the least pleasant hour of the week); **Púchov–Trenčín**, where the completed cycleway is discontinuous and drops you onto road II/507 in places; and **Hlohovec–Sereď**, where the route is signed but partly unsurfaced levee. The Piešťany–Nové Mesto nad Váhom middle section, by contrast, is finished, wide and excellent [VERIFY: current completion status of the Považská cyklotrasa gap sections — new segments open most years].
raw.Elevation per day: is negligible on the Danube (+30 to +120 m) and modest but real on the Váh, where the route repeatedly climbs off the floodplain to skirt Strečno, Považská Bystrica and Trenčín.
raw.Prevailing wind: The Danube corridor blows predominantly from the **north-west**, which means riding Bratislava → Komárno → Štúrovo is a tailwind week and the reverse is a grind. This is the single reason to ride the Danube strand west to east.
raw.Bike rental by name: In Bratislava, **Bratislava Bike Point** and **Cyklopožičovňa Trnka** rent trekking and gravel bikes from roughly €18–€28 a day with panniers and helmet, with one-way drop-off negotiable to Komárno or Štúrovo for a fee [VERIFY: current rental rates and one-way drop fees]. In Žilina, **CykloCentrum Žilina** rents trekking bikes; one-way returns down the Váh are harder to arrange, so many riders rent in Bratislava and take the bike north on the train.
raw.Bike-friendly accommodation: Look for the **cyklopríjemné ubytovanie** mark — it means a locked room or cage for bikes, a wash point, basic tools and a drying line, and it is the thing to ask about before price. Standard along the Váh in Trenčín and Piešťany, and on the Danube dyke at Šamorín, Gabčíkovo and Komárno.
raw.Trains with bikes (ZSSK): ZSSK carries bicycles on services marked with a bike pictogram in the timetable; you buy a separate **cestovný lístok pre bicykel** at a fraction of the passenger fare [VERIFY: current ZSSK bicycle ticket price]. On **IC services a bike-space reservation is compulsory and capacity is small — book it when you book the seat**, not at the station. Regional trains on the Bratislava–Komárno and Bratislava–Štúrovo lines take bikes without reservation but fill on summer weekends.

trips.title: Nordkette Skyline — A Running Week Above Innsbruck

bestPeriod.note: Old snow lingers in the north-facing gullies of the Karwendel until late June; September gives the cleanest rock and the shortest lift queues.

trips.gatewayAirport: Innsbruck (INN)
trips.summary: Seven days of lift-assisted vertical above Innsbruck, from the Nordkette crest to the Zirbenweg, with the recovery days built in.
trips.hook: Innsbruck is the rare city where you can drink a coffee on Maria-Theresien-Straße and be standing on a 2,300 m limestone ridge forty minutes later, without a car. That funicular-and-cable-car chain is the point of the week: it lets you spend your legs on descending and ridge running instead of grinding up the same forest road twice. Karwendel rock and exposure to the north, rolling larch trail to the south.

snapshot.Base(s): Innsbruck (single base, all week)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 95–115 km, 5,500–6,500 m vert; limestone ridge (T3), larch singletrack (T1–T2), river gravel
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Innsbruck (INN), 20 min by bus F into town; or rail via Munich / Zürich to Innsbruck Hbf
snapshot.Who It Suits: Runners comfortable with exposure and 1,000 m descents; not a first mountain-running week

itinerary.title: Legs open on the Höttinger terraces
itinerary.morning: Land, drop bags, do nothing hard. Walk the Innpromenade to the Hungerburgbahn valley station at Congress.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the Hungerburgbahn to 860 m and run the Höttinger Alm loop: west on the Höhenweg past the Höttinger Bild chapel, up forest track to Höttinger Alm (1,487 m), then down the Höttinger Graben to Hötting. Shaded almost throughout, which matters in July.
itinerary.evening: Eat early in Wilten and go to bed. Innsbruck's tap water comes from the Mühlau springs — fill from any Altstadt fountain rather than buying bottles.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 550 m vert, 550 m descent. Grade T1–T2, forest road and firm singletrack, no exposure. Water: Höttinger Alm (staffed in summer), Altstadt fountains. Bail-out: the Hungerburgbahn or a walk of 30 min down to Hötting.

itinerary.title: The Goetheweg into the Karwendel
itinerary.morning: First cabin on the Nordkettenbahnen. Hungerburg to Seegrube (1,905 m), change, Seegrube to Hafelekar (2,269 m). From the top station take the Goetheweg east — a narrow, cable-secured traverse under the Hafelekarspitze and Gleirschspitze that stays high on scree and slabs before dropping through the Mandlscharte to Pfeishütte (1,922 m).
itinerary.afternoon: Soup and a litre of water at Pfeishütte, then return on the same line or, if legs are good, descend the Arzler Scharte to Arzler Alm (1,067 m) and finish on forest trail into Hungerburg.
itinerary.evening: Rehydrate hard. There is no water at all between Hafelekar and Pfeishütte.
itinerary.dayStats: 18–21 km, 700 m vert (lift-assisted), 1,300–1,600 m descent. Grade T3 with short secured sections; loose scree, exposure to the north on the Goetheweg traverse. Water: Seegrube restaurant, Pfeishütte, Arzler Alm. Bail-out: back to Hafelekar and ride down, or the Arzler Scharte valley path.

itinerary.title: Recovery on the Zirbenweg
itinerary.morning: Bus to Igls, then the Patscherkofelbahn to 1,952 m. The Zirbenweg contours east through one of the largest stone-pine stands in the Alps, almost flat, with the whole Nordkette opposite.
itinerary.afternoon: Run gently to Boscheben and Tulfeinalm, then take the Glungezerbahn down to Tulfes and the bus back. Conversational pace only.
itinerary.evening: Swim at the Baggersee on the western edge of town.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km, 250 m vert, 200 m descent. Grade T1, wide compacted path, no exposure. Water: Patscherkofel top station, Boscheben, Tulfeinalm. Bail-out: the path is never more than 40 min from a lift or a road.

itinerary.title: Vertical session, then nothing
itinerary.morning: The quality day. Warm up along the Inn, then run the Hungerburg-to-Seegrube line as one sustained climb: roughly 1,050 m on switchbacked forest and open grass. Threshold effort, not a race. Ride the cable car down — descending 1,000 m on tired quads after a vertical effort is how weeks end early.
itinerary.afternoon: Twenty easy minutes on the Innpromenade gravel, then stop.
itinerary.evening: Bergisel and the Zaha Hadid ski jump tower, on foot, slowly.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km running, 1,050 m vert, 100 m descent. Grade T2, steep switchback trail, no exposure. Water: Seegrube. Bail-out: the Hungerburgbahn intersects the route at 860 m.

itinerary.title: Rest day with a rope-free ridge walk
itinerary.morning: No running. The Hofkirche, the Domplatz, a long breakfast.
itinerary.afternoon: If you cannot sit still, ride to Hungerburg and walk — walk — the Umbrüggler Alm circuit, 300 m of gain, 90 minutes round trip.
itinerary.evening: Check the forecast. Tomorrow only works with a clear morning window.
itinerary.dayStats: 6 km walked, 300 m vert. Grade T1. Water: Umbrüggler Alm. Bail-out: not applicable.

itinerary.title: Long day: Hochzirl, Solsteinhaus and the Erlsattel
itinerary.morning: Early S-Bahn west to Hochzirl (10 minutes from Innsbruck Hbf). Climb the Solsteinhaus trail through beech and then pine to Solsteinhaus (1,806 m) — steady, runnable in the lower half, hiking pace above.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue east over the Erlsattel, traverse the flank of the Großer Solstein toward Höttinger Alm, then descend the long forest line into Hötting and run home along the Inn. Hours of limestone with nobody on it.
itinerary.evening: Kaspressknödelsuppe and a Gröstl will do more for you than a protein bar.
itinerary.dayStats: 26–29 km, 1,600 m vert, 1,900 m descent. Grade T2–T3, rooty forest below, scree and rock steps above the hut; moderate exposure on the Erlsattel traverse. Water: Solsteinhaus (staffed June–October), Höttinger Alm; nothing in between, so carry 1.5 L. Bail-out: return to Hochzirl station, or drop south to Zirl and take the train.

itinerary.title: Sunrise on the Hafelekarspitze
itinerary.morning: First lift again, this time only to stand on it. From Hafelekar station the scramble to Hafelekarspitze (2,334 m) takes 20 minutes and gives the whole Inn valley in low light.
itinerary.afternoon: Run down from Seegrube on the Seegrubensteig for a last 1,000 m descent, or ride down if the week has taken enough. Shower, eat, airport bus.
itinerary.evening: Out.
itinerary.dayStats: 6–10 km, 150 m vert, 150–1,150 m descent. Grade T3 on the summit scramble, T2 on the descent. Water: Seegrube. Bail-out: the cable car runs all day.

accommodationStrategy.name: Nepomuks
accommodationStrategy.description: Small, long-running, and 90 seconds from the Altstadt fountains and the bus stops that feed Igls and Hungerburg. Rooms are simple but there is space to hang wet kit. Best if you are solo and want walking distance to every trailhead bus.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead for July–August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Innsbruck
accommodationStrategy.description: Directly on the Inn, so the recovery jog starts at the door, and a 10-minute walk to the Hungerburgbahn valley station. The pool and sauna are the single most useful hotel feature on a vert-heavy week.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–10 weeks ahead; it fills during Innsbruck congress weeks.

accommodationStrategy.name: Apartments in Hötting or Mühlau
accommodationStrategy.description: The north bank is the correct side of the river for the Nordkette trails, and a kitchen matters when you are eating 3,500 kcal a day. Look for anything within 10 minutes of the Hungerburgbahn line.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Austrian alpine rescue is **140**, which reaches the Bergrettung dispatcher directly. Save both before you leave the valley.
logistics.weather: The Karwendel is a north-facing limestone wall that generates its own cloud, and convective storms build from about 13:00 in July and August. Check the GeoSphere Austria forecast the night before and plan to be off the crest by early afternoon.
logistics.money: Cards work across the city, but several alms are cash-only or have unreliable terminals — carry €40–€60 in small notes. Huts close one day a week, usually Monday or Tuesday, and shut for the season in early October. Supermarkets close at 18:00–19:00 and all day Sunday.

other.label: Guest card
other.text: Most Innsbruck-region accommodations issue a Welcome Card at check-in covering regional buses and trains, with lift discounts that vary by property and season. Confirm the exact terms at check-in.

other.label: Lift hours
other.text: The Nordkettenbahnen run roughly 08:00 to 17:30 in summer, the Hafelekar section closing first. Missing the last cabin from Seegrube means a 1,000 m descent on tired legs in fading light.

other.label: Water is scarce, not absent
other.text: Limestone drains instantly. Above 1,900 m there is effectively no surface water and the huts are the supply. Plan 1.5–2 L for any Goetheweg or Solsteinhaus day.

other.label: Camping and drones
other.text: Camping in the Tyrolean alpine zone is prohibited outside designated sites, and the Karwendel Nature Park adds its own restrictions. Drones are restricted over the park and inside Innsbruck airport's control zone, which covers most of the valley floor.

proTips: Buy the Nordkettenbahnen return even if you intend to run down. The price gap is small and it removes the temptation to descend 1,300 m on shredded quads.
Take the first cabin of the day, not the second. The Goetheweg is single-file with passing places; twenty minutes earlier means an empty path and cooler rock.
Run the Zirbenweg west to east in the afternoon. The light is behind you, the Nordkette opposite is lit, and you finish at a lift instead of starting at one.
Use the S-Bahn as a trail shuttle. Hochzirl, Zirl and Hall in Tirol are 10–20 minutes from Innsbruck Hbf and open point-to-point routes that a car would ruin.
Fill both flasks at Pfeishütte even if you feel fine. The return over the Mandlscharte is dry and slower than it looks.
If Day 6 is stormed off, the Rumer Alm and Arzler Alm circuit from Hungerburg stays below the treeline and runs in weather that closes the ridge.
Innsbruck's public fountains are drinking water unless marked *Kein Trinkwasser* — the cheapest hydration strategy in the Alps.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 95–115 km, 5,500–6,500 m vert; limestone ridge (T3), larch singletrack (T1–T2), river gravel
raw.Who It Suits: Runners comfortable with exposure and 1,000 m descents; not a first mountain-running week

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 95–115 km, 5,500–6,500 m vert; limestone ridge (T3), larch singletrack (T1–T2), river gravel
typeSpecific.audience: Runners comfortable with exposure and 1,000 m descents; not a first mountain-running week

packingNotes: Shoes with a real rock plate and moderate lugs; sharp limestone scree shreds soft trail shoes and offers nothing on slabs.
1.5 L carrying capacity: two soft flasks plus a collapsible half-litre for hut taps.
A wind shell that actually blocks wind. Hafelekar runs 15°C colder than the Altstadt.
Light gloves and a beanie even in August, for the Day 7 sunrise.
Foldable poles — they pay for themselves on the Solsteinhaus climb and the Arzler Scharte descent.
Sunscreen and a cap: the ridge is unshaded above 2,200 m.
Cash in small notes for hut soup.
A headtorch, even on days you plan to finish at 16:00. Lift closures change plans.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Afternoon storm on the Goetheweg.** A cable-secured traverse is the worst possible place in lightning. Fallback: turn at the Mandlscharte and descend to Pfeishütte, a staffed hut with beds, rather than continuing on the crest.
**Hafelekar closed for wind.** It happens several times a summer. Fallback: Seegrube still runs — use it for the Day 4 vertical session and shift the Karwendel day later in the week.

**Old snow in the Mandlscharte in early season.** The north-facing gully holds hard névé into late June. Fallback: ask the Nordkettenbahnen staff at Hafelekar before committing, and substitute the Zirbenweg or the Solsteinhaus day.
**Quad failure by Day 5.** Common on a lift-assisted week, where ascents are cheap and descents are long. Fallback: the Day 5 rest day is structural, not padding, and ride the lift down on Day 7.
**Hut closed on the day you counted on its tap.** Fallback: carry the full day's water on any Karwendel route and treat hut taps as a bonus, not a plan.

trips.title: Boardwalks and Bog — Running the Hautes Fagnes
trips.subRegion: Hautes Fagnes & Amblève Valley, Liège Province

bestPeriod.note: The plateau closes to walkers during high fire risk in dry spring spells; late September gives dry boardwalks, russet moor grass and no ticks.

trips.gatewayAirport: Brussels (BRU)
trips.summary: A high-volume running week on Belgium's peat plateau, with two genuinely technical valley days in the Amblève gorges to break up the flat.
trips.hook: The Hautes Fagnes is not mountainous and pretending otherwise wastes the week. It is a 700 m peat plateau of cotton grass, black water and duckboard, cold and open, and it lets you run long. Treat it as a volume block: five flat-to-rolling days on the moor, two hard technical days in the Amblève and Warche gorges.

snapshot.Base(s): Malmedy (5 nights), one night option at Robertville / Ovifat
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 115–135 km, 2,400–3,000 m vert; peat, boardwalk, forest track, rock-and-root river trail
snapshot.Getting There: Brussels (BRU) or Liège; train to Verviers-Central or Trois-Ponts, then hire car or TEC bus
snapshot.Who It Suits: Runners chasing weekly volume and comfort in bad weather, not vertical gain

itinerary.title: Signal de Botrange and the Poleur boardwalk
itinerary.morning: Collect the car at Liège or Verviers and drive to the Centre Nature de Botrange. Sort access here: the reserve is zoned and the staff will tell you which zones are open today.
itinerary.afternoon: An easy opener. From Botrange, run the boardwalk loop across the Fagne de la Poleur, touch the Signal de Botrange (694 m, the highest point in Belgium, with a stone staircase built to push it past 700 m), and return on the plateau tracks. Duckboard running is a skill — short quick steps, land flat, never push off a wet plank.
itinerary.evening: Settle in Malmedy and eat around Place de Rome.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 180 m vert. Grade T1, boardwalk and peat track, fully exposed to wind. Water: Centre Nature de Botrange (café and taps). Bail-out: the N676 plateau road is never far.

itinerary.title: The GR56 to Baraque Michel and the Fagne Wallonne
itinerary.morning: The signature moor day. Pick up the GR56 near Botrange and run north-west across the Fagne Wallonne to Baraque Michel, the old inn and the Chapelle Fischbach at the crossroads on the plateau. The peat here is dark and deep and the sightlines are enormous.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to the Mont Rigi research station, then loop south past the Noir Flohay — the stand of dead bleached spruce that is now the plateau's landmark — and back to Botrange on duckboard and sand track.
itinerary.evening: Wash your shoes. Peat stains everything.
itinerary.dayStats: 24 km, 320 m vert. Grade T1–T2, boardwalk, wet peat, occasional ankle-deep bog. High exposure to wind and rain, no shelter. Water: Baraque Michel (inn, seasonal hours), Mont Rigi, Botrange. Bail-out: the N68 and N676 cross the plateau; both carry traffic and TEC buses.

itinerary.title: Vertical day above Robertville: Reinhardstein and Bayehon
itinerary.morning: Drive 20 minutes to Robertville, where the Fagnes finally has gradient. Descend into the Warche gorge below the Barrage de Robertville, run up under the walls of the Château de Reinhardstein, and climb out the far side.
itinerary.afternoon: Link east to the Cascade du Bayehon, Belgium's highest waterfall at about nine metres, on a rooty trail along the stream. Repeat the gorge climb: 180 m of gain in under a kilometre, three times, is a proper hill session.
itinerary.evening: Back to Malmedy. Legs up.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km, 750 m vert. Grade T2, wet rock, roots, steep switchbacks; short exposed sections above the Warche. Water: Robertville village, Ovifat. Bail-out: the Robertville–Ovifat road sits above both valleys.

itinerary.title: Recovery on the Vennbahn and the Warche
itinerary.morning: Nothing hard. Run out of Malmedy on the Vennbahn RAVeL — the old railway rebuilt as a crushed-stone greenway — north toward Sourbrodt. Flat, wide and forgiving, which is the point after Day 3.
itinerary.afternoon: Turn back at will; 60–75 minutes total. Then the cathedral and the Malmundarium in the old abbey buildings.
itinerary.evening: Early night.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 150 m vert. Grade T1, crushed limestone greenway, no exposure. Water: Malmedy public fountains, Sourbrodt. Bail-out: the greenway parallels the road throughout.

itinerary.title: Ninglinspo and the Fonds de Quarreux
itinerary.morning: Drive or train to Aywaille and start at Nonceveux. The Ninglinspo is the closest thing Belgium has to an alpine stream trail: a narrow path crossing and re-crossing a clear brook over rock slabs, past the Bain de Diane pools, climbing through beech to Sedoz.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop back down the Chefna valley, then run the Amblève bank through the Fonds de Quarreux, the field of huge quartzite boulders in the river. Technical, slow, the best running of the week.
itinerary.evening: Check the plateau's fire-risk status before planning Day 6.
itinerary.dayStats: 21 km, 700 m vert. Grade T2–T3, wet rock slabs, roots, stream crossings; slippery rather than exposed. Water: Nonceveux and Aywaille village taps; do not drink the Amblève. Bail-out: the valley road at Nonceveux, and Aywaille station for the train back to Verviers.

itinerary.title: Long traverse: Ternell to Hockai across the plateau
itinerary.morning: The big one. Start at Haus Ternell, the nature centre in the beech forest east of Eupen, and run south past the Getzbach and the Eupen dam catchment onto the open moor. Join the GR56 near Botrange.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross the plateau west via Baraque Michel and the Fagne de la Poleur, then descend through the Hockai woods to Hockai. Arrange a pickup, or add 8 km down to Francorchamps. Four to five hours of continuous moor running is a real endurance day even without gradient.
itinerary.evening: Eat everything. Trout is on most local menus.
itinerary.dayStats: 30–34 km, 550 m vert. Grade T1–T2, forest track, peat, boardwalk; sustained wind exposure with no shelter for long stretches. Water: Haus Ternell, Botrange, Baraque Michel. Bail-out: Botrange and Mont Rigi both sit on roads with bus stops at roughly the halfway mark.

itinerary.title: Dawn on the moor, then out
itinerary.morning: Drive up before sunrise. The Fagnes in low light with mist in the hollows is the reason to come; 45 easy minutes on the Poleur boardwalk is enough.
itinerary.afternoon: Coffee at Botrange, drop the car at Verviers or Liège, train onward.
itinerary.evening: Travel.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km, 90 m vert. Grade T1, boardwalk. Water: Botrange. Bail-out: none needed.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel-restaurant options on Place de Rome and Rue Devant les Religieuses, Malmedy
accommodationStrategy.description: The only town of size within 20 minutes of both the plateau and the Amblève gorges, with supermarkets, a pharmacy and kitchens serving after 21:00. Ask for a room away from the N68 traffic and confirm parking, which is tight.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead, longer over Belgian school holidays and the Spa-Francorchamps race weekends.

accommodationStrategy.name: Gîtes and holiday cottages around Ovifat and Robertville
accommodationStrategy.description: A gîte at Ovifat is five minutes from the Warche gorge and fifteen from Botrange, with a kitchen for the volume of food this week needs and space to dry sodden kit. You will drive to eat out. Good for a group splitting the cost.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead for autumn weekends.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €110–€180 per night for the whole cottage

accommodationStrategy.name: Guesthouses in Eupen
accommodationStrategy.description: Worth one night for the Ternell forest and the Vesdre catchment without a long drive. Eupen has a station with direct trains to Verviers and Liège — the practical choice if you are doing the week car-free.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead.

logistics.connectivity: Mobile coverage is patchy mid-moor and in the Ninglinspo gorge. Download offline maps; the white-red GR waymarks are reliable but sparse in fog.
logistics.emergency: 112. There is no mountain rescue service here; the plateau is served by ordinary ambulance and fire brigade, and the limiting factor is that they cannot drive to you. Know which road you are nearest to.
logistics.weather: The plateau makes its own weather and holds fog for days. It can be 8°C with horizontal rain in June while Malmedy is dry 300 m below. Carry a shell every day.
logistics.money: Cards work everywhere in Belgium, including small cafés. Kitchens in the East Cantons stop serving around 21:00 and many restaurants close Monday and Tuesday.

other.label: Reserve zoning is a legal rule
other.text: The Hautes Fagnes reserve is divided into zones; some are freely accessible on marked paths, some (notably zones C and D) may only be entered with an accredited guide, and leaving the marked path elsewhere is prohibited. The Centre Nature de Botrange posts the current status.

other.label: Fire-risk closures
other.text: In dry spells the plateau closes outright — the ban is publicised in stages and enforced with fines, most often in March–May. Always check before driving up.

other.label: Boardwalks are slippery
other.text: Wet duckboard with algae is the single most common injury cause here; some sections have chicken wire, some do not. Shorten your stride and never corner hard on a plank.

other.label: Language
other.text: Malmedy is French-speaking; Robertville, Bütgenbach, Eupen and Ovifat are in the German-speaking Community, and signage flips accordingly. *Fagne* and *Venn* mean the same bog.

other.label: Camping, fires and ticks
other.text: Wild camping and fires are prohibited in the reserve without exception. Ticks are numerous all season and Lyme is endemic in the Ardennes — check after every run.

proTips: Start plateau runs from the Mont Rigi car park rather than Botrange at weekends. Botrange takes the coach traffic and its boardwalks become a queue by 11:00.
Run the Fagne Wallonne early and the wooded Amblève valleys in the afternoon. The moor is at its best in low morning light and its worst under a flat midday sky.
Use the Vennbahn as your recovery surface. Crushed limestone at zero gradient is kinder than any forest track here and it runs straight out of Malmedy.
Do the Ninglinspo upstream, not down. The path crosses the brook repeatedly and reading the line uphill is far easier; downstream you will end up wading.
Peat-black water is not drinkable and no filter fixes the tannin. Plan every run around the four reliable named water points — Botrange, Mont Rigi, Baraque Michel, Haus Ternell — and carry the rest.
If a fire-risk closure kills the plateau, move the whole week south to the Amblève and Salm valleys around Trois-Ponts, Coo and Stavelot, all on the Liège–Luxembourg rail line.
Buy food at the Saturday market on Place Albert I in Malmedy. Sunday supply in the East Cantons is thin.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 115–135 km, 2,400–3,000 m vert; peat, boardwalk, forest track, rock-and-root river trail
raw.Who It Suits: Runners chasing weekly volume and comfort in bad weather, not vertical gain

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 115–135 km, 2,400–3,000 m vert; peat, boardwalk, forest track, rock-and-root river trail
typeSpecific.audience: Runners chasing weekly volume and comfort in bad weather, not vertical gain

packingNotes: Shoes with soft, widely spaced lugs. Deep aggressive lugs clog in peat and slide on wet planks; moderate sticky rubber is better here than a mud spike.
A second pair kept dry, and newspaper to stuff them. You will soak one pair a day.
A genuinely waterproof hooded jacket, not a wind shell. The plateau delivers sustained cold rain.
Low gaiters — peat, sand and grit get into everything on the moor tracks.
Full-length tights or long shorts for the Ninglinspo; the beech scrub scratches.
Tick removal tool and antiseptic, used nightly.
Offline map plus a paper 1:25,000 of the Fagnes. Fog on the plateau is total and featureless.
Two 500 ml flasks and a 1 L reserve for the Day 6 traverse.
Headtorch and something reflective for early Vennbahn runs; it passes through cuttings and short tunnels.
About €30 cash for the Baraque Michel inn, which is not always card-friendly.
whatCouldGoWrong: **The plateau is closed for fire risk on your long-traverse day.** Fallback: run the Amblève valley network from Trois-Ponts to Coo and Stavelot — similar distance, more shade, more gradient, no closure risk.

**Fog reduces visibility to 30 m mid-moor.** Fallback: navigate to the nearest of the two crossing roads, the N68 or the N676, rather than trying to hold a line to the next waypoint, and walk out on tarmac. That is the standard local advice and it is correct.

**You roll an ankle in the Ninglinspo.** It is narrow, wet and 45 minutes from a road at the top end, with unreliable signal on the gorge floor. Fallback: descend to Nonceveux rather than continuing over the plateau, and climb toward the ridge to make the call.

**Bus timings strand you at Hockai.** Rural TEC services run a handful of times a day and thin out after 18:00. Fallback: pre-book a taxi from Malmedy for the Day 6 finish, or leave a second car at Hockai.
**Cold-wet hypothermia on an easy day.** The risk here is not altitude, it is 6°C, 40 km/h wind and rain in a t-shirt. Fallback: never leave the car park without a shell and gloves, even in July.

trips.title: Musala to Vihren: A Rila and Pirin Running Week Above 2,500 m

bestPeriod.window: mid-August to the end of September — snowfields gone from the Musala couloirs, storm frequency falling, lifts still turning
bestPeriod.avoid: before late June (cornices and wet slab on the north sides) and the first half of July, when the klek is soaking and afternoon cells fire daily

accommodation.note: €180–€300 (€25–€45/night, guesthouses and mountain huts)

transport.note: €90–€160 (Sofia transfers, Yastrebets and Panichishte gondolas, Bansko gondola, taxis to trailheads)

activities.note: €0–€200 (no trail fees; a local guide day is optional)

profile.difficultyNote: Hard

trips.gatewayAirport: Sofia (SOF) is 75 km from Govedartsi and Borovets — one hour by transfer, or bus to Samokov then a local minibus. Bansko is 2 h 45 from Sofia by direct bus, or 2 h from Borovets over the Yundola road.
trips.currency: Euro (EUR) — sole legal tender since 1 February 2026; mandatory dual BGN display ended 8 August 2026
trips.summary: Two ranges, six days of running, and the two highest summits in the Balkans in the same week. Rila gives you granite slab, a hundred cirque lakes and dwarf-pine tunnels that will remove the skin from your shins.…
trips.hook: Two ranges, six days of running, and the two highest summits in the Balkans in the same week. Rila gives you granite slab, a hundred cirque lakes and dwarf-pine tunnels that will remove the skin from your shins. Pirin gives you white marble that eats outsoles and drops away on both sides. The trails are waymarked and almost entirely unmaintained. Bring a headtorch, a jacket, and the discipline to be off the ridge by one o'clock.

snapshot.Best period: July–September, best mid-August to end of September
snapshot.Start / End: Govedartsi → Bansko (two bases, ~150 km and ~8,000 m of running)
snapshot.Getting there: Sofia (SOF) is 75 km from Govedartsi and Borovets — one hour by transfer, or bus to Samokov then a local minibus. Bansko is 2 h 45 from Sofia by direct bus, or 2 h from Borovets over the Yundola road.

itinerary.title: Arrival and a legs-opener
itinerary.morning: Fly into Sofia, transfer to **Govedartsi** (1,200 m) in the Cherni Iskar valley — quieter, cheaper and better for sleeping than Borovets.
itinerary.afternoon: Shake out on the forest road up the **Malyovishka river** towards Hizha Malyovitsa. Runnable, shaded, and useful for gauging how the altitude sits on you.
itinerary.evening: Eat at a village *mehana* — grilled trout, *shopska salata*, no *rakia* the night before Musala. Lay out kit and check the Yastrebets gondola's first cabin time.

itinerary.title: Musala, 2,925 m, the highest point in the Balkans
itinerary.morning: Drive to **Borovets** and take the **Yastrebets gondola** to 2,369 m [VERIFY: current Yastrebets gondola summer fare]. Run the traverse to **Musala hut (2,389 m)**, fill at the spring, then follow the **Musalenski lakes** chain — Everest, Ledeno, Alekovo — up the cirque.
itinerary.afternoon: The final 300 m is stepped rock and often has old snow in the gully. Touch the summit block and the weather station, then reverse. Two and a half hours up, ninety minutes down.
itinerary.evening: Back down the gondola before the last cabin. Recovery food in Borovets, then back to Govedartsi.

itinerary.title: Malyovitsa and the Fish Lakes
itinerary.morning: From **Hizha Malyovitsa (1,750 m)** climb the granite steps past the Malyovishki waterfall to the **Malyovitsa (2,729 m)** summit block — a genuine hands-on scramble at the top, T4 for ten metres.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop to the **Ribni Ezera** (Fish Lakes) basin and the hut on the shore, then run back over the **Kobilino Branishte** saddle. Big day; carry food and refill at the lake outflow.
itinerary.evening: Legs up in Govedartsi. This is the day that decides whether the Pirin loop later in the week is realistic.

itinerary.title: The Seven Rila Lakes and Haramiyata
itinerary.morning: Transfer to **Panichishte** and take the **Pionerska gondola** to the **Rilski Ezera hut (2,150 m)**. Run the full circuit of the seven: **Dolnoto** (the Lower), **Ribnoto** (the Fish), **Trilistnika** (the Trefoil), **Bliznaka** (the Twin), **Babreka** (the Kidney), **Okoto** (the Eye) — at 37.5 m the deepest cirque lake in Bulgaria — and **Salzata** (the Tear).
itinerary.afternoon: Climb the ridge to the **Haramiyata** viewpoint (2,465 m) for the classic overhead of all seven, then descend the klek-tunnel path towards Skakavitsa.
itinerary.evening: Return by gondola [VERIFY: current Pionerska gondola fare]. Overnight at the hut if you want the lakes to yourselves at dawn.

itinerary.title: Rila Monastery, then transfer to Pirin
itinerary.morning: Drive over to the **Rila Monastery (1,147 m)** — the Hrelyo Tower and the striped arcades of the Church of the Nativity — and run the river track up the Rilska valley to **Kirilova Polyana (1,400 m)** and back. Fast, forested, restorative.
itinerary.afternoon: Transfer south to **Bansko** via Blagoevgrad, two to two and a half hours [VERIFY: current Rila–Bansko transfer options and cost].
itinerary.evening: Bansko *mehana* dinner: *kavarma*, *banitsa*, a Melnik red. Reconnoitre the gondola base for tomorrow's early cabin.

itinerary.title: The Vihren–Todorka loop
itinerary.morning: Up the **Bunderitsa** road or the Bansko gondola to **Hizha Vihren (1,950 m)**. Climb the **Kazana** cirque to **Vihren (2,914 m)**, Bulgaria's second summit, on white marble that is unrunnable in the wet.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend to the **Banderishka porta**, traverse the ridge to **Todorka (2,746 m)**, then drop past the **Banderishki lakes** to the hut. Two litres minimum — the marble section holds no water at all.
itinerary.evening: Down to Bansko, mineral bath, and an honest assessment of quads before Day 7.

itinerary.title: Banderishki lakes cruise and out
itinerary.morning: A gentle last lap from Hizha Vihren around the upper and lower **Banderishki lakes** on granite slab, with a detour to **Baikushev's Pine**, a Bosnian pine over 1,300 years old.
itinerary.afternoon: Gondola or jeep down to Bansko [VERIFY: current summer Bansko gondola fare]. Late lunch on the old square.
itinerary.evening: Bus to Sofia, or stay the night and take the narrow-gauge train from Dobrinishte for the view.

accommodationStrategy.name: Guesthouse in Govedartsi
accommodationStrategy.description: 1,200 m of free altitude while you sleep, twenty minutes from the Malyovitsa trailhead and forty from Borovets, at half Borovets prices. Family kitchens will do an early breakfast if you ask the night before.
accommodationStrategy.booking: Booking.com or direct by phone, two to four weeks ahead [VERIFY: current Govedartsi guesthouse rates].

accommodationStrategy.name: Rilski Ezera hut
accommodationStrategy.description: puts you inside the cirque for a dawn circuit before the gondola delivers the day crowds at 10:00. Dormitory beds, hot soup, cash only.
accommodationStrategy.booking: phone the hut direct, a week ahead midweek, longer for weekends [VERIFY: current Rilski Ezera hut bed rate].

accommodationStrategy.name: Hizha Vihren
accommodationStrategy.description: removes 1,000 m of road climbing from the Vihren–Todorka loop and lets you start on the marble at 06:00 rather than 09:00. Spring water at the door.
accommodationStrategy.booking: phone direct, two weeks ahead; cash only.

logistics.connectivity: A1 and Yettel cover Borovets, Bansko and most ridgelines; the Fish Lakes basin and the Bunderitsa cirque are patchy. Download offline maps for both ranges before leaving town.
logistics.emergency: **PSS 1470** or **112**. Report your position by hut, lake or saddle name and waymark colour. Carry a foil blanket — a twisted ankle at 2,700 m becomes a hypothermia problem within an hour.
logistics.weather: Afternoon thunderstorms from mid-June to mid-August, typically firing at 13:00. Rila also produces fast hill fog that erases the marker poles. Hail is common above 2,500 m.
logistics.bookingWindows: Guesthouses two to four weeks; huts one to two weeks by phone, more for the September holiday weekends.
logistics.money: Bulgaria has adopted the **euro**, with prices still dual-displayed in **BGN** at the fixed 1.95583 rate. Huts and jeep taxis are **cash only**; gondolas take cards.
logistics.transportRules: The Bunderitsa road above Hizha Banderitsa is unsurfaced — gondola or jeep taxi. Gondolas stop for lightning and wind without warning; always know the walking descent.
logistics.permits: No fees or permits in either Rila or Pirin National Park, but both ban **wild camping outside marked bivouac zones**, **open fires**, **dogs** and drones. Marked trails only, and no shortcutting the Seven Lakes switchbacks.

proTips: Wear long socks or calf sleeves for every Rila run. The klek will otherwise take your shins apart in a single descent, and the cuts get infected fast at altitude.
Take the first gondola cabin at Borovets and at Panichishte. You will have Musala's summit and the Seven Lakes ridge to yourself for two hours before the day-trip buses land.
Sleep at the Rilski Ezera hut and run the circuit at 06:00. The lakes are mirror-flat, the light is sideways, and Haramiyata is empty.
Carry two litres for the Pirin marble day and fill at the Hizha Vihren spring. The karst drains everything; there is no stream between the Kazana and the Banderishki lakes.
Learn *"Kade e pateka za…?"* — where is the path to…? Waymarks vanish in cloud, and shepherds and hut wardens give reliable directions by hut name.
Use Govedartsi, not Borovets, as the Rila base. Cheaper, quieter, closer to Malyovitsa, and you sleep at 1,200 m instead of in a ski resort.
Keep Day 7 flexible. If a front comes through, swap the Banderishki lakes for the low, forested Rila Monastery run — it works in any weather.

raw.The runs, with numbers: **Musala (2,925 m)** from the Yastrebets gondola top: 13 km, +680/−680 m, **T3**, granite blocks and one steep summit staircase. **Seven Rila Lakes circuit with Haramiyata**: 14 km, +780 m, **T2–T3**. **Malyovitsa (2,729 m) and Ribni Ezera**: 26 km, +1,450 m, **T3** with a T4 scramble on the summit block. **Rila Monastery to Kirilova Polyana and back**: 16 km, +420 m, **T1–T2**, runnable river track. **Vihren–Todorka loop, Pirin**: 18 km, +1,500 m, **T3–T4**. **Banderishki lakes loop**: 12 km, +600 m, **T2**.
raw.Terrain, honestly: Rila is **granite** — slab that grips when dry and skates when wet, plus long boulder fields where you hop rather than run. Pirin's north is **marble karst**: sharp, fissured, and hard on soft-lugged shoes. Both ranges have **scree**, some of it live.
raw.The klek is the real hazard: *Klek* is dwarf mountain pine (*Pinus mugo*), and above about 1,900 m in Rila it forms dense, waist-to-chest-high thickets that trails tunnel through. The branches are woody, springy and hidden under the canopy; they shred shins, hook laces, and conceal the trail surface completely, so you cannot see the rock you are about to land on. Klek sections are why Rila runners wear **calf sleeves or long socks in August**. Never leave a marked line to shortcut through klek — you will not get through, and you will not be visible from the air.
raw.Water points by name: The **Musala hut spring** at 2,389 m (the last reliable water before the summit). The **outflow streams of the Rila lakes** — the Fish Lake and Lower Lake outflows below Rilski Ezera hut, and the Okoto outflow. The **Malyovishka river** below Malyovitsa hut. In Pirin: the **Banderitsa** stream and the spring at Hizha Vihren. Between Kutelo and Todorka on the marble there is **nothing** — carry two litres.
raw.Waymarks and maintenance: The **BTS/KKS** white–colour–white blaze plus tall marker poles above the treeline. **Red** is the ridge line and the **E4**. Be clear-eyed: Bulgarian ridge trails are **marked but not maintained**. Paint fades, poles fall, drainage does not exist, and a "path" on the map may be a braided scar across scree. Carry a phone with an offline map and do not rely on continuous waymarking in cloud.
raw.Bail-outs: **Yastrebets gondola** to Borovets from the Musala side; the **Panichishte–Pionerska gondola** from the Seven Lakes; the **Bansko gondola** from Banderishka polyana; the **Bezbog chairlift** on the far side of Pirin. All are weather-dependent and stop early [VERIFY: current gondola operating hours and last-down times].
raw.Rescue: **PSS (Planinska Spasitelna Sluzhba) on 1470**, or **112**. Rila and Pirin teams are ground-based out of Borovets, Samokov and Bansko; helicopter is not something to plan around. Insure for mountain running above 2,500 m.
raw.Storm timing: From roughly 20 June to 20 August, convective cells fire over both ranges from about **13:00**, often earlier over Rila. On Musala and the Pirin ridge you are the highest object for kilometres. Start at first light and treat 13:00 as a hard turnaround.

typeSpecific.surface: Rila is **granite** — slab that grips when dry and skates when wet, plus long boulder fields where you hop rather than run. Pirin's north is **marble karst**: sharp, fissured, and hard on soft-lugged shoes. Both ranges have **scree**, some of it live.
