trips.title: Thin Air — The Engadin Ridge Week

bestPeriod.note: Piz Languard's summit ridge holds snow into early July, and the high huts shut in early October.

trips.gatewayAirport: Zürich (ZRH)
trips.summary: Seven days of altitude running above Pontresina, from a 1,800 m valley floor to the 3,262 m summit of Piz Languard, with lifts and rail as the safety net.
trips.hook: The Oberengadin's valley floor sits at 1,800 metres, which means you sleep higher than most Alpine summits and everything you run starts with an advantage. It is a training environment before it is a holiday: long, graded, panoramic paths, three cable cars that sell you vertical metres, and a railway that will always take you home.

snapshot.Base(s): Pontresina, with runs from Muottas Muragl, Surlej, Sils, Morteratsch and St. Moritz
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 105–115 km and 5,200–5,800 m of ascent; larch forest track, alp meadow, granite blockfield and scree, T1–T3
snapshot.Getting There: Fly Zürich (ZRH), train via Chur and the Albula line to Pontresina (approx. 4 h)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Runners who want altitude adaptation and long climbs, not exposure and cables

itinerary.title: Val Roseg, Flat and High
itinerary.morning: Arrive in Pontresina and do nothing energetic. At 1,805 m, the first day is about drinking water and letting the resting heart rate settle.
itinerary.afternoon: Easy out-and-back up the Val Roseg on the gravel carriage road from the edge of the village to Hotel Roseg Gletscher — about 7 km each way, almost level, with the Roseg glacier tongue and Piz Bernina closing the head of the valley. T1, fully runnable, and a perfect first-day aerobic dose at 1,800–2,000 m.
itinerary.evening: Pontresina. Eat early and sleep long; altitude disrupts the first two nights.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km, 300 m ascent, T1. Water: Hotel Roseg Gletscher (open through the summer season) and the village fountains in Pontresina, which are drinking water unless signed otherwise. **Bail-out:** horse-drawn carriages run the valley road all summer and will take a passenger.

itinerary.title: Muottas Muragl to Alp Languard
itinerary.morning: Funicular from Punt Muragl to Muottas Muragl at 2,456 m — the view down the chain of Engadin lakes to Maloja is the region's signature. Start running from the top station on the Panoramaweg that traverses east under Piz Muragl.
itinerary.afternoon: The path climbs gently to the Segantinihütte (Chamanna Segantini, 2,731 m), where the painter Giovanni Segantini died in 1899, then contours down to Alp Languard at 2,326 m. Broad, stony, T2 and largely runnable. Take the Alp Languard chairlift down or run the forest path to Pontresina.
itinerary.evening: Legs will feel heavier than the numbers justify. That is altitude, not fitness.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 480 m ascent, T2. Water: Chamanna Segantini (staffed roughly late June to mid-October, drinks bought), Restaurant Alp Languard at the chairlift top station. **Bail-out:** funicular or chairlift at either end; there is no committing ground.

itinerary.title: Fuorcla Surlej and the Long Descent
itinerary.morning: Bus to Surlej, cable car to Corvatsch's Murtèl middle station at 2,702 m, then the short traverse to Fuorcla Surlej (2,755 m). The Berghaus there looks straight across at the Bernina group's north faces — Piz Roseg, Piz Scerscen, Piz Bernina in one frame.
itinerary.afternoon: Run north over the shoulder and down past the Hahnensee to St. Moritz Bad, then along the lake path to St. Moritz station. It is 1,400 m of descent on stone, alp track and finally forest — eccentric loading, and the point of the day.
itinerary.evening: Train back to Pontresina, ten minutes. Ice the quads.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km, 420 m ascent, 1,430 m descent, T2. Water: Berghaus Fuorcla Surlej (staffed in summer), Restaurant Hahnensee at 2,153 m. **Bail-out:** ride the Corvatsch cable car back down instead of descending.

itinerary.title: Sils, the Lakes and Val Fex
itinerary.morning: Postbus down the valley to Sils Maria. Run the shoreline path along the Silsersee and out onto the Chastè peninsula, where the Nietzsche stone sits among the larches — flat, soft, T1.
itinerary.afternoon: Turn up the Val Fex on the near-level valley road to Fex Crasta and its 15th-century church, then back. A genuine recovery day at 1,800–2,000 m, which is the whole reason to sit in the Engadin rather than train at sea level.
itinerary.evening: Sils Maria for cake, then the bus home. Nothing after 20:00.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km, 260 m ascent, T1, entirely runnable. Water: village fountains in Sils Maria and Fex Crasta. **Bail-out:** postbus stops at Sils, Silvaplana and along the Val Fex road.

itinerary.title: Peak Day: Piz Languard, 3,262 m
itinerary.morning: Leave Pontresina at first light on the direct path towards Alp Languard, then up the long, graded zigzags past Chamanna Paradis at 2,540 m. This is 1,460 m of continuous climbing, T2 on the lower half and T3 on the granite blockfield above the hut, with a marked but hands-on final ridge to the summit.
itinerary.afternoon: From the top the whole Bernina massif, the Morteratsch and Pers glaciers and — on a clear day — a line of peaks into Italy. Descend to Alp Languard, then take the Panoramaweg west past the Segantinihütte to Muottas Muragl and down the Schafberg path to Punt Muragl.
itinerary.evening: Pontresina. Eat everything. This is the hardest single day of the week by a wide margin.
itinerary.dayStats: 22 km, 1,600 m ascent, T3 above 2,800 m. Water: Chamanna Paradis (small and not always staffed — treat as unreliable), Chamanna Segantini on the return. Carry 2 l. **Bail-out:** turn at Chamanna Paradis; descend to Alp Languard and ride the chairlift, or take the funicular down from Muottas Muragl.

itinerary.title: Chamanna Boval and the Glacier Front
itinerary.morning: Train two stops to Morteratsch. Run the Gletscherweg up the moraine, past the year-markers showing where the glacier stood in 1900, 1950 and 2000, then climb the lateral moraine path to Chamanna Boval at 2,495 m — an SAC hut hung directly above the ice.
itinerary.afternoon: Return by the same route or the higher variant, then run the flat valley path back to Pontresina through the larch woods rather than taking the train. Roughly 800 m of climbing on tired legs.
itinerary.evening: Last dinner in Pontresina.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km, 820 m ascent, T3 on the moraine, T2 below. Water: Chamanna Boval (staffed roughly late June to mid-October; water is bought). **Bail-out:** the Morteratsch station and the Diavolezza cable car are both within reach of the valley floor.

itinerary.title: Stazerwald and Home
itinerary.morning: Easy loop from Pontresina through the Stazerwald larch forest to the Lej da Staz and on to St. Moritz — soft, level, T1, 40 minutes of genuine shakeout at 1,800 m.
itinerary.afternoon: Train from St. Moritz over the Albula line to Chur and Zürich. Sit on the right leaving St. Moritz for the Landwasser viaduct.
itinerary.evening: Zürich.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km, 180 m ascent, T1. Water: fountains in Pontresina and St. Moritz Dorf.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Saratz
accommodationStrategy.description: A 19th-century house with a modern wing, a large park, indoor and outdoor pools and a sauna — the recovery infrastructure that a 5,500 m week actually needs. It sits directly on the Val Roseg and Alp Languard trailheads, so three days start on foot from the door.
accommodationStrategy.booking: February for July and August.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: CHF 250–420 (approx. €260–€440) per night for two, half board available

accommodationStrategy.name: Romantik Hotel Muottas Muragl
accommodationStrategy.description: Reached only by funicular and sitting 650 m above the valley floor, which turns two or three nights here into real altitude exposure rather than daytime visits. Sunrise runs on the Panoramaweg start outside the front door.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead; there are very few rooms.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: CHF 300–450 (approx. €310–€470) per night for two, half board

accommodationStrategy.name: Jugendherberge Pontresina
accommodationStrategy.description: A large, well-run hostel with private rooms, half board included, a drying room and gear storage, five minutes from the station. The cheapest way to spend a week in one of the most expensive valleys in the Alps.
accommodationStrategy.booking: April.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: CHF 90–130 (approx. €95–€135) per person per night with half board

logistics.emergency: works; the number that matters in the Swiss mountains is **1414** for Rega helicopter rescue. A Rega patronage costs about CHF 40 a year and removes the argument about who pays.

other.text: works; the number that matters in the Swiss mountains is **1414** for Rega helicopter rescue. A Rega patronage costs about CHF 40 a year and removes the argument about who pays.

Most Engadin hotels include the summer mountain railways and regional buses in the room rate through the regional guest card — Muottas Muragl, Corvatsch, Diavolezza and Alp Languard among them. Confirm it at booking; it is worth well over CHF 200 across a week.
The Rhaetian Railway runs Pontresina–Morteratsch–St. Moritz frequently, and PostAuto covers the lakes. Both are punctual to the minute; the timetable is a contract, not a suggestion.
Weather flips fast at 3,000 m. MeteoSwiss and the SAC's hut pages are the two sources to check the night before and the morning of; afternoon convective storms build from late July.
SAC huts including Chamanna Boval take reservations online and by phone. Even for a day visit, water and food are bought, not free, and cash is still welcome.
Village fountains in Graubünden are drinking water by default; anything not potable is signed *kein Trinkwasser*. Glacier meltwater is heavy with rock flour — do not drink it.

Nothing in this itinerary enters the Swiss National Park, but if you add it, be aware its rules are the strictest in the Alps: no leaving the path, no running off-trail, no dogs, no bivouac. Wild camping is also restricted across much of Graubünden above the treeline.
Mobile coverage is good on the lift-served ridges and unreliable in the Val Roseg and the upper Morteratsch valley.

proTips: Spend the first 48 hours below 2,500 m. The Val Roseg and Sils days exist to let haemoglobin adapt before Piz Languard, and skipping them is why people bonk at 3,000 m on day three.
Take the first Muottas Muragl funicular and run the Panoramaweg eastwards in the morning. It faces south-west, so the afternoon light is better but the heat and the crowds are worse.
Ride the lifts up and run down on Day 3, then reverse the pattern on Day 5. Alternating loading direction across the week is what keeps quads intact through a seven-day block.
Buy the Corvatsch and Diavolezza rides as part of the guest card rather than at the counter — walk-up single fares in the Engadin run CHF 30–50 each.
The Val Roseg carriage road is the region's best tempo surface: 14 km of near-flat, well-drained gravel at 1,900 m, with no traffic and no navigation.
If Piz Languard is snowbound or stormy, substitute Piz Nair from Corviglia — lift-assisted, 3,057 m, and a fraction of the commitment.
Book the Segantinihütte or Chamanna Boval for lunch by phone in high season; both are small and both fill with walkers from 12:00.

typeSpecific.audience: Runners who want altitude adaptation and long climbs, not exposure and cables

packingNotes: Shoes with a real rock plate for the Piz Languard blockfield and the Boval moraine — Engadin granite is angular and unforgiving.
Two-litre carrying capacity for Day 5; 750 ml is plenty on the lift-served days.
A warm layer and a proper wind shell. It can be 25°C in Pontresina and near freezing on the Languard ridge in the same hour.
Sun protection at strength. UV at 3,000 m is brutal, and the Engadin averages more sunshine than almost anywhere in Switzerland.
Light gloves and a beanie for the summit ridge, even in August.
Swiss francs in small notes for hut drinks; card acceptance at 2,700 m is inconsistent.
Poles for the Languard climb and the 1,400 m Fuorcla Surlej descent.
A head torch for the pre-dawn start on Day 5.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Altitude hits harder than expected.** Headache, poor sleep and a raised resting heart rate are normal for 48 hours. If they persist, drop Day 5 to the Muottas Muragl traverse and try Piz Languard on Day 6 instead.
**Afternoon thunderstorm on the Languard ridge.** The summit block is exposed granite. Be off the top by noon; the escape is straight down to Chamanna Paradis and Alp Languard.
**Early snow.** A September cold front can put 20 cm on everything above 2,800 m overnight. The lake paths at Sils and the Val Roseg stay runnable in any conditions.
**Lift closures.** Corvatsch, Diavolezza and Alp Languard each have a short summer season and maintenance days. Check operating dates before planning a day around a descent you have not earned.
**Sticker shock.** Switzerland at altitude is expensive. Half-board rates and the hostel option are what make a seven-day block affordable; buying lunch at 2,700 m every day is not.

trips.title: The Main Ridge — Running the Krkonoše Border Path

bestPeriod.note: Several ridge and glacial-cirque paths are legally closed 1 November to 31 May for grouse and vegetation; June is open, empty and still cold up top.

trips.gatewayAirport: Prague (PRG)
trips.summary: Seven days on the Czech-Polish crest of the Krkonoše, from the Elbe source to Sněžka, using the boudy as water stops and the chairlifts as escape routes.
trips.hook: The Krkonoše look modest on paper — nothing tops 1,603 m — and then you get on the crest and find arctic-alpine tundra, dwarf pine, and a wind that has come off the North European Plain with nothing in its way. This is a subtle, weather-driven range with a superb hut network and a marking system so good you can navigate it by colour alone. Run it as a ridge week: the boudy are your aid stations, the valleys are your recovery, and Sněžka waits until Friday.

snapshot.Base(s): Špindlerův Mlýn (4 nights), Pec pod Sněžkou (3 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 120–140 km, 5,000–5,800 m vert; granite paving, tundra path, forest track, boardwalk
snapshot.Getting There: Prague (PRG) → direct coach to Špindlerův Mlýn (approx. 2h45), or train to Vrchlabí and bus
snapshot.Who It Suits: Runners who like long exposed days, cold wind and cheap hut soup

itinerary.title: Arrival and the Svatý Petr valley
itinerary.morning: Coach from Prague's Černý Most or Florenc terminal to Špindlerův Mlýn. Buy a bus ticket in advance online; the seats sell out on summer Fridays.
itinerary.afternoon: Shake the coach out of your legs. Run up the Svatý Petr valley on the green-marked path toward Pláň, turn at the top of the piste, and come back down the Labe riverside path through town. Nothing above threshold.
itinerary.evening: Learn the Czech marking system before you need it: 10 cm painted stripes, a coloured band between two white ones, red for the main ridge, then blue, green and yellow for connectors. Junction posts carry timings in hours, not kilometres.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km, 400 m vert. Grade T1, forest track and gravel road, no exposure. Water: Špindlerův Mlýn taps and shops; the Labe here is not drinking water. Bail-out: you are never more than 20 min from town.

itinerary.title: Western crest: Zlaté návrší, the Elbe source and the Sněžné jámy
itinerary.morning: Take the Medvědín chairlift out of Špindlerův Mlýn to 1,235 m — this is the cheap 600 m of the week, use it. Run west along the red-marked ridge over Zlaté návrší to Labská bouda (1,340 m), perched above the Labský důl cirque.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue north on the border path past Pramen Labe, the ceremonial source of the Elbe, then up over Vysoké Kolo (1,509 m) and along the rim of the Sněžné jámy — two deep glacial cirques falling away on the Polish side, and the most dramatic drop in the range. Return via Vosecká bouda and Martinova bouda, then descend the blue trail to Špindlerův Mlýn.
itinerary.evening: Eat at one of the town's pubs. Kulajda, svíčková, dumplings, a large mineral water.
itinerary.dayStats: 26 km, 950 m vert (lift-assisted), 1,450 m descent. Grade T2, granite slab paving and tundra path; serious wind exposure on the crest, vertical drops on the cirque rims — stay behind the barriers. Water: Labská bouda, Vosecká bouda, Martinova bouda. Bail-out: Horní Mísečky road at Zlaté návrší; the Medvědín chairlift.

itinerary.title: Recovery in the Labský důl
itinerary.morning: Easy and low. Run the valley path from Špindlerův Mlýn up the Labe to the Labský vodopád viewpoint below Labská bouda, on shaded forest road with a gentle constant gradient.
itinerary.afternoon: Turn around before the steep zig-zags. Total 70 minutes at conversational pace. Spend the afternoon flat — the town has a heated outdoor pool and several hotel saunas that sell day access.
itinerary.evening: Check the forecast for the week's two big days. The Krkonoše ridge is the windiest place in Czechia and gusts routinely make running the crest pointless.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 350 m vert. Grade T1, forest road. Water: Špindlerův Mlýn. Bail-out: the valley road runs the whole way.

itinerary.title: Climb session to Luční bouda by the Bílé Labe
itinerary.morning: The quality day. From Špindlerův Mlýn follow the Bílé Labe (White Elbe) valley east on the Weberova cesta — a rocky, rooty, cascade-lined path that is one of the prettiest lines in the park — then take the steep climb up to Luční bouda (1,410 m), the enormous inter-war hut on the Bílá louka plateau.
itinerary.afternoon: Soup and refill at Luční bouda, then descend to Špindlerova bouda on the ridge and drop the blue trail home. Treat the climb as one sustained tempo effort and the rest of the day as easy.
itinerary.evening: Pack. You move base tomorrow.
itinerary.dayStats: 22 km, 900 m vert. Grade T2 with short T3 rock steps in the Bílé Labe gorge; wet granite, roots, no fall exposure. Water: Bouda u Bílého Labe (seasonal), Luční bouda, Špindlerova bouda. Bail-out: the Bílé Labe path exits back to town at any point; the Špindlerova bouda road has a bus stop.

itinerary.title: Transfer to Pec pod Sněžkou, easy legs in the Obří důl
itinerary.morning: Bus over the ridge road via Vrchlabí or the direct seasonal connection to Pec pod Sněžkou. Drop bags.
itinerary.afternoon: A short, easy reconnaissance of tomorrow's start: run the blue path up the Obří důl — the great glacial trench under the south face of Sněžka — as far as the Kaplička and the old mine adits, then turn back. Look up. That headwall is the last climb of Day 6.
itinerary.evening: Early food in Pec. Buy tomorrow's supplies; the shops here shut by 19:00.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km, 400 m vert. Grade T1–T2, gravel service road and stony path. Water: Pec pod Sněžkou taps; Obří důl streams are clean but untreated. Bail-out: single valley, one road, trivial.

itinerary.title: Sněžka and the Path of Czech-Polish Friendship
itinerary.morning: Out at first light. Climb the Obří důl to the Obří sedlo, then the final rocky steps to Sněžka (1,603 m) — the highest point in Czechia, with the baroque Chapel of St Lawrence, the Czech post office building and, forty metres below on the Polish side, the Dom Śląski refuge.
itinerary.afternoon: Head west on the Cesta česko-polského přátelství, the Path of Czech-Polish Friendship, which runs the border crest with markers on both sides. Over Svorová hora, past Slezský dům, across the Bílá louka to Luční bouda, then Studniční hora's flank and down to Výrovka (1,370 m). Descend the Zelený důl to Pec.
itinerary.evening: This is the day of the week. Eat, drink, do not set an alarm.
itinerary.dayStats: 29 km, 1,500 m vert, 1,500 m descent. Grade T2–T3; the Obří důl headwall is steep rock steps with chains in places, the crest is paved granite and tundra with total wind exposure and no shelter for 8 km. Water: Dom Śląski and the Sněžka summit buildings, Luční bouda, Výrovka. Bail-out: the Sněžka cable car from the summit down via Růžová hora to Pec; from the crest, the Luční bouda–Pec valley path.

itinerary.title: Růžová hora at dawn, then out
itinerary.morning: Ride the first cable-car section from Pec to Růžová hora (1,390 m), watch the light come onto Sněžka's cone, and run the ridge path down through the dwarf pine to Pec — 500 m of gentle, forgiving descent.
itinerary.afternoon: Coffee, shower, coach back to Prague from Pec pod Sněžkou.
itinerary.evening: Prague.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km, 100 m vert, 550 m descent. Grade T2, stone path and boardwalk. Water: Růžová hora buffet, Pec. Bail-out: the cable car runs both directions.

accommodationStrategy.name: Pensions on the Labe in Špindlerův Mlýn
accommodationStrategy.description: Špindlerův Mlýn is a purpose-built mountain town, which means abundant, cheap, unglamorous pensions with drying rooms and half-board — exactly what a running week needs. Take one within walking distance of the Medvědín chairlift base so you are not adding a bus leg to every morning. Half-board is worth taking: the kitchen opens for breakfast before the lifts.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead for July–August; longer for weekends.

accommodationStrategy.name: Luční bouda
accommodationStrategy.description: The largest and oldest of the ridge boudy, sitting where the two big traverses cross. Worth one night mid-week if you want to start Day 6 already on the plateau and watch the sunrise on the Bílá louka rather than climbing to it. It has proper beds, a restaurant, and it is the single most useful water point in the range.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–10 weeks ahead in summer; it fills fast.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €35–€60 per person in a shared room

accommodationStrategy.name: Pensions in Pec pod Sněžkou
accommodationStrategy.description: Pec is smaller and quieter than Špindlerův Mlýn and sits directly under the Obří důl and the Sněžka cable car, which puts the two escape options and the biggest day's trailhead on your doorstep. Ask about parking if you drive — the village restricts vehicle access to the upper valley.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European. Czech mountain rescue is Horská služba, reachable on **1210** — save it; they run stations at Špindlerův Mlýn, Pec pod Sněžkou and Luční bouda.
logistics.weather: You will cross into Poland repeatedly on the crest path, which is normal and requires nothing. Carry ID anyway. Polish huts price in złoty; most take cards.
logistics.money: Czechia uses the koruna. Cards are near-universal, including in most boudy, but carry 500–1,000 CZK for the smaller huts and the Polish side. Refuse dynamic currency conversion at card terminals.
logistics.transportRules: Direct coaches run Prague–Špindlerův Mlýn and Prague–Pec pod Sněžkou daily; book online in advance for a reserved seat. Within the park, seasonal shuttle buses connect the valleys and the ridge road.

other.label: You must stay on marked trails
other.text: Krkonoše is a national park with strict zoning; leaving the marked path in the first zone is an offence and is enforced by rangers on the ridge. This is not a place for improvised lines.

other.label: Seasonal closures are legal, not advisory
other.text: A number of ridge and cirque trails close from 1 November to 31 May. Some paths also close temporarily for grouse breeding. Signs are in Czech, Polish, German and English.

other.label: Wind is the primary hazard
other.text: Sněžka records some of the strongest sustained winds in Central Europe. If the summit forecast shows gusts above 70 km/h, the crest is not runnable — swap to a valley day.

other.label: Opening hours
other.text: Village shops close around 18:00–19:00 and many close Sunday afternoon. Huts serve food all day but stop hot dishes earlier than you expect at altitude.

other.label: Camping, fires and drones
other.text: All prohibited within the national park. Bivouacking is not tolerated.

proTips: Ride the Medvědín chairlift up and run the crest west-to-east. You buy 600 m of altitude for the price of a coffee, and the prevailing wind then pushes you along the ridge instead of into your face.

Climb Sněžka from the Obří důl on the Czech side and descend the Path of Czech-Polish Friendship. The Polish approach from Karpacz carries most of the summit traffic; the Obří důl is steeper, wilder and quieter before 09:00.
Time the summit for before 09:00 or after 16:00. Between those hours Sněžka is one of the busiest mountaintops in Europe and the summit path becomes a single-file queue.

Use the junction post timings as a pacing tool. Czech signs give walking hours; a fit trail runner covers them at roughly 0.4–0.5 of the posted time on the flat crest and far closer to 1.0 on the rocky descents.
Luční bouda is open all year and is the only reliable water on the Bílá louka. Fill both flasks there even if you feel fine — the plateau has no springs and the tundra streams are peaty.
Buy the Sněžka cable-car ticket as a single up, not a return, and only on the day. Weather stops it regularly and the queue at Pec is worst between 10:00 and 12:00.
Špindlerův Mlýn's outdoor pool and the hotel saunas sell day passes cheaply. On a five-figure-descent week, that is the highest-value €10 you will spend.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 120–140 km, 5,000–5,800 m vert; granite paving, tundra path, forest track, boardwalk
raw.Who It Suits: Runners who like long exposed days, cold wind and cheap hut soup

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 120–140 km, 5,000–5,800 m vert; granite paving, tundra path, forest track, boardwalk
typeSpecific.audience: Runners who like long exposed days, cold wind and cheap hut soup

packingNotes: Shoes with firm, moderately lugged outsoles. The crest is paved with granite slabs and quartzite blocks; soft mud shoes are wasted and the rock chews soft foam.
A proper windproof jacket, not a rain shell. Wind, not rain, is what stops days here.
Gloves and a beanie, June through September, without exception.
Long tights or leg covers for the Bílé Labe gorge and the dwarf-pine sections, which scratch.
1 L carrying capacity is enough given the hut density, plus a collapsible cup for spring taps.
A small amount of Czech cash and a card that does not charge for foreign transactions.
Offline maps plus the KČT colour logic: red = main ridge, and every junction post names the next two destinations with times.
Sunglasses and sunscreen — the plateau is treeless tundra and reflects hard even under cloud.
Trekking poles for the Obří důl headwall and the Zelený důl descent.
A dry bag for the Day 6 kit change; the crest and the valley can be 15°C apart.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Ridge-strength wind cancels Day 6.** Fallback: run the Bílé Labe and Modrý důl valleys from Pec, both sheltered and both offering 800 m of gain, and push Sněžka to Day 7 with the cable car as insurance.

**A trail you planned on is under seasonal closure.** Fallback: check the KRNAP closure map before the trip and again at your pension. The Path of Czech-Polish Friendship and the main valley routes are open in summer; the cirque descents are the ones that close.

**Fog on the Bílá louka.** The plateau is flat, featureless tundra and disorienting in cloud. Fallback: the crest is lined with tall wooden marker poles specifically for this — follow them, do not cut corners, and aim for Luční bouda, which is heated and open year-round.
**The Prague coach is sold out on your return day.** Fallback: local bus to Trutnov or Vrchlabí and a train onward; slower but frequent.

**Storms on the crest.** Convective storms build in July and August afternoons and there is no shelter for kilometres on the border path. Fallback: the boudy are spaced roughly an hour apart along the ridge — plan every crest day so you are never more than 30 minutes from one.

trips.title: Watzmann Weeks — Running the Berchtesgaden Ridges

bestPeriod.note: North-facing gullies below the Watzmann and Hochkalter hold old snow into late June.

trips.gatewayAirport: Salzburg (SZG)
trips.summary: A coached week of ridge running in Berchtesgaden National Park, built around one big Watzmann day and supported by huts, boats and buses.
trips.hook: Berchtesgaden gives you more vertical per kilometre than almost anywhere in Germany, and it gives you an escape route from nearly all of it — a boat, a gondola, a valley track. That combination is what makes it a training week rather than a survival week. You build for three days, you spend everything on one, and you let the Königssee put you back together.

snapshot.Base(s): Schönau am Königssee, with runs from Ramsau, Hintersee and Wimbachbrücke
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 105–115 km and 6,000–6,500 m of ascent; limestone, root, scree and cabled rock, T1–T3
snapshot.Getting There: Fly Salzburg (SZG), bus 840 to Berchtesgaden Hbf (approx. 50 min), then RVO bus 841/842 to Schönau
snapshot.Who It Suits: Runners comfortable with sustained 1,000 m+ climbs, hands-on-rock scrambling and loose descents

itinerary.title: Salt, Water, Legs
itinerary.morning: Land, take the bus down and drop bags in Schönau. Ask for the Berchtesgadener Land Gästekarte at check-in — it covers the RVO valley buses and pays for itself before Thursday.
itinerary.afternoon: Shakeout on the Soleleitungsweg, the 19th-century brine-pipeline path between Berchtesgaden and Ramsau. It is a graded, largely traversing forest track — T1, fully runnable, soft underfoot, with a handful of short tunnels and constant views to the Watzmann's east face. Run it out to Ramsau and back to the bus at the Pfarrkirche St. Sebastian.
itinerary.evening: Walk the Königssee shore to Malerwinkel, eat early, sleep long. At 600 m there is nothing to acclimatise to — this week's adaptation is muscular, not respiratory.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 320 m ascent, T1. Water: fountain beside St. Sebastian in Ramsau, reliable all summer.

itinerary.title: Grünstein, the Honest Warm-Up
itinerary.morning: From the Königssee car park take the Grünstein trail via the Kühroint junction. It is 700 m of steady, rooty climbing to the Grünsteinhütte at 1,220 m, then a short scramble to the 1,304 m cross. Grade T2, with one exposed step near the top; the via ferrata variants alongside are for climbers, not runners — stay on the walkers' path.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend the Rabensteinsteig side towards Schönau — steeper, looser, good practice for controlling cadence on limestone gravel.
itinerary.evening: Cold-water legs in the Königssee at the Seelände, then dinner in Schönau. This is a nervous-system day, not a fitness day.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 780 m ascent, T2. Water: Grünsteinhütte, staffed roughly May to October, closed in poor weather. **Bail-out:** the ascent path is the descent path — no committing terrain.

itinerary.title: Jenner to Schneibstein, Lift-Assisted Vert
itinerary.morning: Jennerbahn gondola from Königssee to the top station, then run the ridge to the Jenner summit (1,874 m) before dropping to the Königsbergalm saddle. Continue south to Torrener Joch and the Carl-von-Stahl-Haus (1,733 m), which sits exactly on the German–Austrian border.
itinerary.afternoon: From the Stahlhaus climb Schneibstein (2,276 m) — an open, stony ridge at T2, runnable in long sections, with the Hoher Göll filling the eastern sky. Return over the Joch and descend the Königsbachalm track to Hinterbrand, then the forest road to Königssee.
itinerary.evening: Refuel properly. Tomorrow is deliberately easy so that Friday can be hard.
itinerary.dayStats: 19 km, 950 m ascent (plus 700 m bought with the gondola), 1,600 m descent, T2. Water: Carl-von-Stahl-Haus (staffed nearly year-round, most dependable water on the ridge) and Königsbachalm (Almsommer only, roughly mid-June to mid-September). **Bail-out:** ride the Jennerbahn back down instead of descending on foot.

itinerary.title: Hintersee and the Zauberwald, Recovery Pace
itinerary.morning: Bus to Hintersee. Loop the lake, then run the Zauberwald — a boulder-strewn moss forest on the Ramsauer Ache — up to the Klausbachtal entrance. Flat, cushioned, T1.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue up the Klausbachtal valley road as far as the hanging bridge, then turn. If your legs feel good, the temptation is the Blaueis climb; resist it, that is Saturday's job.
itinerary.evening: Ramsau for the postcard view of the church against the Reiter Alpe, then early bed.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km, 300 m ascent, T1, all runnable. Water: taps at the Hintersee car park area and the Klausbachtal information point; the lakeside guesthouses serve non-guests. **Bail-out:** the Klausbachtal shuttle and RVO bus 846 both return to Ramsau.

itinerary.title: Peak Day: Wimbach to the Watzmannhaus and Hocheck
itinerary.morning: Leave at first light from Wimbachbrücke. Through the Wimbachklamm gorge, then break right onto the Watzmann path. The climb to the Watzmannhaus (1,930 m) via the Stubenalm and Mitterkaseralm is 1,300 m of relentless, well-graded T2 — forest, then meadow, then limestone terrace.
itinerary.afternoon: From the hut, the summit of Hocheck (2,651 m) is a further 720 m on marked rock, T3, with cables on the final rib and real exposure to the east. It is a hike-fast section, not a running section. Return the same way to the Watzmannhaus, then traverse the balcony path to Kührointhütte and descend the Rinnkendlsteig or the Kühroint forest road to the Königssee.
itinerary.evening: Food and salt in Schönau. Plan nothing after 20:00.
itinerary.dayStats: 26 km, 2,150 m ascent, T3 at the top, T2 below. Water: Watzmannhaus (bought, not free — carry cash), Kührointhütte (staffed roughly late May to October), Wimbachschloss on the alternative valley return. **Bail-out:** turn at the Watzmannhaus, or descend Kühroint and take the last Königssee boat; RVO buses run from Wimbachbrücke and Königssee until evening.

itinerary.title: Blaueis, the Northernmost Glacier
itinerary.morning: Bus to Hintersee. Climb the Blaueishütte path (1,680 m) under the Hochkalter's north face — 1,050 m of steep, stepped, partly cabled T3 through the Schärtenalm. The glacier cirque above the hut still holds ice; it is the northernmost in the Alps and it is visibly shrinking.
itinerary.afternoon: Optional out-and-back towards the Blaueisscharte for another 250 m, then a controlled descent — fast below, not above.
itinerary.evening: Ramsau. Eat, stretch, pack down.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km, 1,150 m ascent, T3. Water: Schärtenalm (Almsommer only) and Blaueishütte (staffed roughly late May to mid-October, water sold). **Bail-out:** single valley, single path back to Hintersee and bus 846.

itinerary.title: Kehlstein and a Flat Finish
itinerary.morning: Obersalzberg bus, then the Kehlstein road walk-run to the Kehlsteinhaus at 1,834 m — closed to private cars, served by its own bus, and a clean 800 m of graded tarmac if you want one last climb. The Hoher Göll fills the view south.
itinerary.afternoon: Bus down, then a shakeout: there is no shore path to St. Bartholomä, so take the boat and jog the peninsula loop past the pilgrimage church.
itinerary.evening: Bus 840 to Salzburg. Arrive at the airport with wrecked quads and a much better descent technique than you had on Monday.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km, 850 m ascent (mostly road), T1. Water: Kehlsteinhaus terrace, open daily in season.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Zechmeisterlehen
accommodationStrategy.description: Ten minutes on foot from the Königssee bus terminus, which is the trailhead for Grünstein, Jenner and Kühroint, so three of the week's seven days start without transport. It has a pool and sauna, which matter more than they sound after Day 5, and a drying room for the inevitable afternoon storm.
accommodationStrategy.booking: February for July and August dates.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €130–€190 per night for two, half board available

accommodationStrategy.name: Alpenhotel Denninglehen
accommodationStrategy.description: Perched at 900 m on the Obersalzberg side, with a wellness area and a genuinely quiet setting. It suits runners who want the Kehlstein and Rossfeld side of the valley on the doorstep and do not mind a bus down to the Königssee trailheads.
accommodationStrategy.booking: March.

logistics.emergency: Emergency is **112** across Germany. Bergwacht Bayern is dispatched through 112 — give the trail name, the nearest hut, and your grid position from the map app before your battery dies.

other.text: Emergency is **112** across Germany. Bergwacht Bayern is dispatched through 112 — give the trail name, the nearest hut, and your grid position from the map app before your battery dies.
Mobile coverage is good on the Jenner and Kehlstein ridges, patchy in the Wimbachgries, absent in the lower Klausbachtal gorge.
Berchtesgaden National Park rules are enforced: stay on marked paths, no wild camping, no bivouacs, no drones anywhere in the park, dogs on a lead. Rangers do check.

Afternoon thunderstorms are the defining hazard from mid-July. Build every day around being off the ridges by 14:00; the DWD WarnWetter app and the Bergwetter forecast from the Alpenverein are the two to trust.
Huts want cash. The Watzmannhaus, Blaueishütte and Kührointhütte have limited or no card acceptance and no free drinking water — budget €4–€6 per litre bought at altitude.

The Königssee boats are electric, timetabled and stop early — last departures from St. Bartholomä are usually mid- to late afternoon in shoulder season. Do not plan a day that depends on a boat you have not checked that morning.
The Gästekarte from your accommodation gives free RVO valley bus travel — just show it to the driver.

proTips: Take the first Jennerbahn cabin of the day. It buys 700 m of climb, puts you on the Schneibstein ridge before the cloud builds, and halves the crowding on the summit path.
Run the Königssee's east shore in the morning and the Wimbach side in the afternoon — the valley is deep and narrow, and the light and shade flip hard around midday.

The Rinnkendlsteig off Kühroint is closed after heavy rain and after rockfall; check the notice at the Königssee trailhead before committing to it as your Day 5 descent, and default to the Kühroint forest road if in doubt.
If Friday's forecast is bad, swap Day 5 and Day 6 — Blaueis is a single-valley objective with a hut halfway, far safer in unsettled weather than the Watzmann's east ridge.
The Wimbachgries riverbed is 6 km of near-flat gravel at 1,200 m — an ideal tempo session on a light day.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 105–115 km and 6,000–6,500 m of ascent; limestone, root, scree and cabled rock, T1–T3
raw.Who It Suits: Runners comfortable with sustained 1,000 m+ climbs, hands-on-rock scrambling and loose descents

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 105–115 km and 6,000–6,500 m of ascent; limestone, root, scree and cabled rock, T1–T3
typeSpecific.audience: Runners comfortable with sustained 1,000 m+ climbs, hands-on-rock scrambling and loose descents

packingNotes: Shoes with a real lug pattern and a stiff-ish rock plate. Berchtesgaden limestone is sharp, wet in the morning and polished on the popular sections.
Lightweight gloves for the cabled sections on Hocheck and above the Blaueishütte — the steel is cold and greasy.
A 1.5 l carrying capacity minimum. Between the Watzmannhaus and the valley there is no reliable water on Day 5.
Cash in small notes for hut drinks and the Königssee boat if you buy on the day.
Wind shell and a warm layer, always. The Schneibstein ridge at 2,276 m can be fifteen degrees colder than Schönau.
Head torch even for day runs: the Wimbachklamm tunnels are dark, and any Day 5 overrun finishes in forest.
Poles, foldable. The 1,300 m Watzmann climb and the Blaueis descent both justify them.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Thunderstorm on the Watzmann ridge.** The Hocheck section is cabled and exposed. The fallback is to stop at the Watzmannhaus, sit it out on the terrace, and descend to Kühroint once the cell passes; the hut will take you for the night if it does not.
**Old snow in the north-facing gullies.** Below the Blaueisscharte and on the Schneibstein's north side snow can survive into early July. Without microspikes, turn around — the runout is rock.
**Hut closed or full.** Alm kitchens close in bad weather and outside the Almsommer. Carry the full day's water on any route where your plan relies on a single hut.
**Missing the last Königssee boat.** The shore is not walkable from St. Bartholomä. Check the final departure time in the morning and set a phone alarm for one hour before it.

**Bus timetable thinning in September.** RVO frequencies drop after the Bavarian school holidays. On late-season days finishing at Hintersee or Wimbachbrücke, confirm the last service before you start running.

trips.title: Sierra Nevada & Las Alpujarras
trips.subRegion: Andalucía — Sierra Nevada National Park & the Alpujarra Granadina

bestPeriod.window: Late May–late June & mid-September–late October
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (38 °C+ in the villages, acequias switched to irrigation, no shade below 2,000 m); December–April (high summits snowbound, Hoya del Portillo road closed)
bestPeriod.raw: Late May–late June & mid-September–late October

accommodation.note: Alpujarra guesthouses €55–€95 dbl/night; Refugio Poqueira dorm ~€20, half-board ~€38–€48

food.note: Menú del día €12–€16; tapas free with drinks in Granada province

transport.note: Rental car 7 days €190–€300, fuel, plus the national park high-mountain shuttle

activities.note: Park shuttle bus, refuge night, Alhambra ticket if you add Granada

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5 — the running is rarely technical but you climb 2,000 m in a day to 3,479 m, in dry heat, on exposed ground

trips.gatewayAirport: GRX — Granada Federico García Lorca (1 h 15 to Capileira); AGP — Málaga is 2 h 15 and usually has better fares
trips.summary: This week runs the biggest vertical relief in Western Europe outside the Alps: from white Berber-plan villages at 1,050 m to Mulhacén at 3,479 m, the highest ground on the Iberian mainland, in a single climb. The Alpujarra south slope gives you terraced chestnut and almond terrain threaded by *acequias* — Moorish snowmelt channels that double as the region's only reliable water — while the Granada north side gives the Vereda de la Estrella, a long, cool, glacial-valley approach to the north faces. The arc is deliberate: two acclimatisation days on the GR-7 and the acequia paths, a refuge night at 2,500 m, the Mulhacén day, a genuine recovery day in the gorge at Monachil, then a high traverse to finish. It suits a runner who is more worried about heat and altitude than about scrambling.

itinerary.title: Arrive, and the Poqueira village triangle
itinerary.morning: Fly into Granada (GRX) or Málaga, collect the car, and drive up the Lecrín valley and the Órgiva road to **Capileira** (1,436 m). Buy food — the villages have small shops that close 14:00–17:30.
itinerary.afternoon: Easy orientation loop on the GR-7 down through **Bubión** to **Pampaneira** and back up the Poqueira barranco path — 300 m of descent and the same back up, on cobbles and terrace paths, with the acequia channels running beside you.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **El Corral del Castaño** in Capileira — plato alpujarreño, migas, and a Contraviesa red.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km / 480 m D+ / ~60% cobbled village path / 1 h 20–1 h 50; transfer 1 h 15 from GRX.

itinerary.title: GR-7 to Trevélez
itinerary.morning: Run the **GR-7 east** from Capileira through **Pitres, Pórtugos** (stop at the iron-red **Fuente Agria**) and **Busquístar**, dropping into and out of the Trevélez river gorge on old mule paths through chestnut terraces.
itinerary.afternoon: Finish in **Trevélez** (1,476 m), one of the highest permanently inhabited villages in Spain. Taxi or pre-positioned second car back, or run the high acequia return for a 34 km day.
itinerary.evening: Eat at **Mesón La Fragua** in Trevélez — jamón de Trevélez cured at altitude, and choto al ajillo.
itinerary.dayStats: 21 km / 1,050 m D+ / 950 m D- / ITRA 2 / 2 h 45–3 h 45 / 5 village fountains en route.

itinerary.title: Climb to Refugio Poqueira and sleep at 2,500 m
itinerary.morning: Leave Capileira at 08:00 on the **Cebadillas path** up the Poqueira barranco — pine plantation, then open high pasture, following the río to the **Refugio Poqueira (2,500 m)**, 84 places and staffed year-round.
itinerary.afternoon: Deliberately easy: a 5 km reconnaissance jog toward the **Río Mulhacén** and back for altitude exposure, then rest, hydrate and eat early. Do not chase the summit today.
itinerary.evening: Refuge half-board — lentil stew and a communal table full of Spanish mountaineers who will tell you exactly what the snow line is doing.
itinerary.dayStats: 11.5 km / 1,100 m D+ / 2 h–2 h 45 plus a 5 km shakeout; sleeping at 2,500 m.

itinerary.title: Mulhacén, 3,479 m
itinerary.morning: Out of the refuge by 06:30. Climb to the **Laguna de la Caldera** (3,050 m), then the west flank onto the **Mulhacén summit at 3,479 m** — the highest point on the Iberian mainland, with the Alcazaba and the 700 m north face falling away on the other side.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend the broad south ridge to **Alto del Chorrillo** and pick up the track to **Hoya del Portillo**, then the forest descent to Capileira. Long, hot and relentless — save water for the last hour.
itinerary.evening: Recovery beers and tapas in Capileira; in Granada province the tapa comes free with the drink.
itinerary.dayStats: 24 km / 1,050 m up / 2,050 m down / high point 3,479 m / 4 h 30–6 h / zero water after the Caldera.

itinerary.title: Recovery day at Los Cahorros de Monachil
itinerary.morning: Drive north over the Puerto de la Ragua or round via Granada to **Monachil**. Run the **Los Cahorros** gorge loop — 8 km of hanging bridges, a cabled rock traverse and a tunnel beside the Río Monachil, cool and shaded the whole way.
itinerary.afternoon: Nothing strenuous. Granada: the Albaicín, a long lunch, and free tapas on Calle Navas. Optional cold-water soak in the river.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Granada; return to the Alpujarra or overnight in the city.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km / 350 m D+ / ITRA 3 (bridges and cables) / 1 h–1 h 20 / total drive ~1 h 45 each way.

itinerary.title: Vereda de la Estrella, the north side
itinerary.morning: Drive to **Güéjar Sierra** and the Barranco de San Juan trailhead. Run the **Vereda de la Estrella** — the old mining track along the Genil, under chestnut and holm oak, with the **Mulhacén and Alcazaba north walls** opening ahead — to Cueva Secreta and back.
itinerary.afternoon: Extend to the **Cortijo de la Estrella** ruins if legs allow, then drive back over the Sierra to Capileira for the last night; stop at the **Hoya de la Mora** (2,500 m) viewpoint for the Veleta.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Mesón Poqueira in Capileira — soup, grilled meat, and an early night.
itinerary.dayStats: 18 km out-and-back / 700 m D+ / 2 h 15–3 h / two stream fords / no signal in the valley.

itinerary.title: Veleta and out
itinerary.morning: Early drive to **Hoya de la Mora** (2,500 m) above the ski station and run the old road and ridge to **Veleta (3,396 m)** — the fastest 3,000 m summit in Spain, with the Alpujarra, the Mediterranean and, on the clearest mornings, the Rif of Morocco visible together.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend, drive to Granada or Málaga, and eat properly before the flight.
itinerary.evening: Departure from GRX or AGP.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km / 950 m D+ / high point 3,396 m / 2 h 15–3 h; 45 min drive to Granada.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Real de Poqueira
accommodationStrategy.description: Right in the middle of Capileira at 1,436 m, so both the GR-7 and the Poqueira barranco start from the door and you never move the car on running days. Small pool, parking, and breakfast from 08:00 (ask for a bag earlier). €65–€95 double outside August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Refugio Poqueira
accommodationStrategy.description: The only shelter on the south high mountain and the key to doing Mulhacén sanely: sleeping at 2,500 m turns a brutal 1,750 m ascent into a manageable 1,050 m one and gives you real acclimatisation. 84 places, open all year, half-board available; book directly by phone or its own site.

accommodationStrategy.name: Finca Los Llanos
accommodationStrategy.style: garden hotel on the edge of Capileira
accommodationStrategy.description: Quieter, with a pool, terrace and parking, and better for the recovery half of the week. Five minutes from the village centre, with space to spread wet kit. Similar price band, worth the swap after the refuge night.

logistics.connectivity: Spain is EU; roaming at domestic rates. Movistar has the best mountain coverage. **No signal in the Poqueira barranco floor, in the Vereda de la Estrella valley or in Los Cahorros.** Download offline maps and the park's shuttle timetable before leaving Capileira.
logistics.emergency: **112**; the Guardia Civil's GREIM mountain unit covers Sierra Nevada and is based at Pinos Genil. Rescue in Andalucía is not routinely billed to the casualty, but insurance covering activity above 3,000 m is still sensible. Give your route to the refuge guardian before summit days.
logistics.weather: The defining phenomena are the **terral** (a hot, dry down-slope wind that can push village temperatures past 40 °C) and sudden high-mountain cloud that drops visibility on the Mulhacén–Veleta crest with almost no warning. Afternoon thunderstorms build over the summits from June. Snow and névé can persist in the Caldera and on the Veleta north side into early July.
logistics.bookingWindows: **Refugio Poqueira** and the **national park high-mountain shuttle** (Servicio de Interpretación de Altas Cumbres, Capileira to Mirador de Trevélez) both need advance booking and both fill on summer weekends — reserve 2–4 weeks out. The Alhambra needs weeks. Ultra Sierra Nevada entries open months before its early-summer date.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards work in hotels and most restaurants; carry €100 cash for village bars, the refuge and the shuttle. Tipping is minimal — round up or leave 5%.
logistics.transportRules: A car is effectively required; Alsa buses reach Capileira and Trevélez but only once or twice a day. The A-44 and A-92 are toll-free. The **Hoya del Portillo forest road above Capileira is gated seasonally** and the last section to the high mountain is closed to private vehicles — the park shuttle is the legal way up. Ski-station road to Hoya de la Mora is open and free in summer.
logistics.permits: Sierra Nevada National Park has **no entry fee and no running permit**, but the high zone above roughly 2,700 m has restricted vehicle access and camping rules: bivouacking is permitted above 2,500 m from sunset to sunrise only, with tents pitched no earlier than an hour before dusk. Drones need park authorisation. Fires are banned outright.
logistics.health: Village tap water is potable. **Acequia water is irrigation water** — treat it, or drink only from named fountains. Real risks here are heat exhaustion, sunburn at altitude and dehydration, not falls. Snakes (Montpellier, ladder snake) are harmless to humans. There is no avalanche concern in the recommended season, but check the park's snow report before any pre-June summit attempt.

proTips: **Use the park shuttle as an uphill lift, not a tour.** Book the Capileira bus to the Mirador de Trevélez (about 2,700 m), run Mulhacén from there and descend on foot to the village — you get the summit at a third of the climbing cost, and it is the only motorised access allowed.
**Book the refuge night before you book flights.** Refugio Poqueira is the difference between a good Mulhacén day and an altitude-headache slog, and its 84 places go on summer weekends.

**Time the week to the acequia charge.** The channels above Capileira run hardest in the six weeks after the main snowmelt, roughly mid-May to late June — that's when the mountain is greenest and water is everywhere.
**Take the second car to Trevélez.** The GR-7 point-to-point is far better run one-way; a €40 taxi or a shuttled second car buys you the whole traverse instead of an out-and-back.
**Run Veleta on your last morning, not your first.** It's the easiest 3,000 m in Spain but only if you have already slept high — done cold on day one it will cost you the rest of the week.
**Eat the tapas system.** In Granada province and much of the Alpujarra, each drink comes with a substantial free tapa. Three beers is dinner, for about €9.

**Cool down in Los Cahorros deliberately.** The Monachil gorge is 15 °C cooler than the south-facing Alpujarra slopes and the river pools are a legitimate recovery tool between the Mulhacén and Veleta days.
**Watch for the Ultra Sierra Nevada weekend.** Race week fills every bed in Güéjar Sierra and Capileira — either enter it, or avoid it.

raw.Signature routes: (1) **Mulhacén from Capileira** via Hoya del Portillo (2,150 m), Alto del Chorrillo and the Mirador de Trevélez: 26 km, 1,750 m D+ to **3,479 m**, mid-pack 4 h 30–6 h; shortened to 14 km / 900 m by taking the park shuttle to the Mirador. (2) **Refugio Poqueira (2,500 m) from Capileira** by the Cebadillas/Río Naute path: 11.5 km, 1,100 m D+, 2 h–2 h 45. (3) **Veleta (3,396 m) from the Hoya de la Mora** (2,500 m): 17 km, 950 m D+, 2 h 15–3 h. (4) **Vereda de la Estrella** from the Barranco de San Juan to Cueva Secreta, under the Mulhacén–Alcazaba north walls: 18 km out-and-back, 700 m D+, 2 h 15–3 h. (5) **Los Cahorros de Monachil gorge loop**: 8 km, 350 m D+, 1 h–1 h 20. (6) **GR-7 village link, Pampaneira–Bubión–Capileira–Pitres–Pórtugos–Busquístar–Trevélez**: 21 km, 1,050 m D+, 2 h 45–3 h 45.
raw.Technicality (ITRA-style 1–5; 1 = fire r: GR-7 and acequia paths **2**. Mulhacén by the normal south route **2**, mostly a rideable gravel track and broad ridge — the altitude, not the terrain, is the difficulty. Veleta ridge **3** on loose micaschist blocks. Vereda de la Estrella **2–3** with two stream crossings. Los Cahorros **3** — hanging bridges, a cable traverse and a low tunnel. Nothing here needs hands except by choice.
raw.Terrain split, week average: ~30% stony mule track and cobbled village path, ~25% high-mountain gravel road (the old Veleta road and the Hoya del Portillo track), ~20% micaschist scree and blocky ridge above 2,800 m, ~15% terraced almond/chestnut singletrack, ~10% forest fire road in the Poqueira pine plantation. Dry, abrasive, dusty — sand gaiters earn their place.
raw.Waymarking: **GR-7 (part of E4)** in red-and-white; **PR-A** local routes in yellow-and-white; national park boards at Hoya del Portillo, Alto del Chorrillo and the Poqueira refuge junction. High above 2,800 m the marking thins to cairns and painted dots — the Mulhacén–Veleta crest is navigated by feature, not by paint.
raw.Water refill points and month reliabilit: *Acequias* are the system: the **Acequia Alta and Acequia Baja above Capileira** and the **Acequia de Mecina** flow strongly **April–June** on snowmelt, are switched to field irrigation in July–August (channels can run dry or foul), and refill with autumn rain from late September. Named fixed points: **village fountains at Capileira, Bubión, Pampaneira, Trevélez, Pórtugos (the ferruginous Fuente Agria) and Busquístar** — potable year-round. **Refugio Poqueira** — water and drinks all year, hut open year-round. **Río Mulhacén and Laguna de la Caldera** — snowmelt, filter or treat, reliable to about mid-July then thin. **Nothing at all on the Hoya del Portillo–Alto del Chorrillo track**: carry 2 L for the Mulhacén day.
raw.Navigation: Editorial Penibética 1:40,000 "Sierra Nevada" and 1:25,000 "Alta Montaña" sheets; GPX from Wikiloc (dense Spanish coverage), the Ultra Sierra Nevada course files, and the park's Ventana del Visitante portal. Coverage: good in villages and on summits, **dead in the Poqueira barranco bottom, in the Vereda de la Estrella valley and in Los Cahorros**. Bail-outs: the Poqueira refuge is staffed all year and is the only shelter on the south side; from the Veleta ridge, the old road drops to Hoya de la Mora; from the Vereda, the only exit is back down the valley.
raw.Recovery, altitude and heat: Day 5 is a true low day. This is the only trip in the region where **altitude genuinely matters**: 3,479 m after sleeping at 1,436 m is a real dose, hence the refuge night at 2,500 m first. Start every summit day by 06:30 — the south slope has zero shade after 09:00 — and carry 500 ml/hour above 2,500 m in June. Expect 3–4 °C at dawn at the refuge even when the village is 25 °C.

typeSpecific.surface: ~30% stony mule track and cobbled village path, ~25% high-mountain gravel road (the old Veleta road and the Hoya del Portillo track), ~20% micaschist scree and blocky ridge above 2,800 m, ~15% terraced almond/chestnut singletrack, ~10% forest fire road in the Poqueira pine plantation. Dry, abrasive, dusty — sand gaiters earn their place.
typeSpecific.technicalRating: GR-7 and acequia paths **2**. Mulhacén by the normal south route **2**, mostly a rideable gravel track and broad ridge — the altitude, not the terrain, is the difficulty. Veleta ridge **3** on loose micaschist blocks. Vereda de la Estrella **2–3** with two stream crossings. Los Cahorros **3** — hanging bridges, a cable traverse and a low tunnel. Nothing here needs hands except by choice.

sources.verified: Refugio Poqueira sits at 2,500 m, has 84 places and is open year round with half-board available; Mulhacén 3,479 m and Veleta 3,396 m as the two highest Iberian mainland summits; Sierra Nevada is a UTMB-index race venue (Ultra Sierra Nevada, ~100 km with roughly 6,200 m of ascent, plus shorter distances); GRX and AGP transfer times.
sources.confidenceNotes: Re-verify (a) **Refugio Poqueira current nightly and half-board prices** — the figures circulating online date from 2022 and Federación Andaluza rates change annually; (b) **the national park high-mountain shuttle's operating dates, route ends and fare**, which shift year to year and are sometimes suspended; (c) **exact Ultra Sierra Nevada 2026/2027 dates and the distance ladder**; (d) **acequia flow status in the travel month** — irrigation scheduling is set locally and cannot be assumed; (e) **Hoya del Portillo gate status and the snow line on Mulhacén** before any pre-June trip; (f) current guesthouse price bands in Capileira and Trevélez.

trips.title: Faroese Ridgelines: Streymoy & Vágar

bestPeriod.window: Late May to early September. June and July give near-endless daylight; September brings the clearest air but the first autumn gales
bestPeriod.raw: Late May to early September. June and July give near-endless daylight; September brings the clearest air but the first autumn gales

accommodation.note: €120–200 per night, double; guesthouses €80–130

food.note: €55–85 per day; a heimablídni home-dinner runs €70–110 per person

transport.note: €250–380: flights to Vágar, car hire €70–95 per day (essentially mandatory), tunnel tolls

activities.note: €80–200: landowner hiking fees, one guided ridge day, Mykines boat or helicopter

profile.difficultyNote: Hard, and hard in an unusual way — the terrain is not technically difficult but it is steep, wet, trackless in places, and navigationally serious in fog

trips.summary: A seven-day trail running itinerary in Streymoy, Vágar and Eysturoy, Faroe Islands.

itinerary.title: Arrive Vágar, Trøllkonufingur and Sandavágur
itinerary.morning: Land at Vágar Airport, collect the hire car, buy food in Miðvágur — supplies outside Tórshavn are thin.
itinerary.afternoon: The short cliff run out to the Trøllkonufingur viewpoint above Sandavágur — the "witch's finger" sea stack, 313 m of basalt. Grass path, steep, wildly exposed at the end.
itinerary.evening: Check in near Sørvágur. **Water:** the stream behind Sandavágur village; fill before you climb.

itinerary.title: Trælanípa and Sørvágsvatn
itinerary.morning: The optical-illusion route: the lake Sørvágsvatn appears to hang hundreds of metres above the sea when seen from the Trælanípa cliff. Pay the landowner fee at the trailhead — it is collected in person and by card.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue past Bøsdalafossur, where the lake pours directly into the Atlantic, and run the ridge line above Miðvágur back. Add the Gásadalur road and the Múlafossur waterfall village at the western tip for the classic Faroese photograph.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Sørvágur. **Water:** lake outflows are drinkable after filtering; there is nothing on the Trælanípa cliff itself.

itinerary.title: Slættaratindur, the highest point
itinerary.morning: Drive to Eysturoy via the subsea tunnel and up to the Eiðisskarð pass. Slættaratindur is 880 m, the highest mountain in the Faroes, and from the pass it is a direct 600 m climb on grass, scree and rock.
itinerary.afternoon: The summit view on a clear day reaches most of the archipelago. In fog it is a compass-and-cairn exercise and should be abandoned rather than improvised — the north face falls away sharply.
itinerary.evening: Drive on to Gjógv, a village built around a natural sea gorge, and stay there. **Water:** streams on the lower third of the ascent only.
itinerary.dayStats: 5 km, 600 m — short, steep, serious

itinerary.title: Saksun to Tjørnuvík, the old postal route
itinerary.morning: Start at Saksun — a turf-roofed church, a tidal lagoon, and about ten inhabitants. The old walking route climbs over the pass to Tjørnuvík on the north coast, marked by traditional cairns (*varðar*) that predate any signage.
itinerary.afternoon: Tjørnuvík's black-sand beach faces the Risin og Kellingin sea stacks. It is also the Faroes' surf beach; the water is 9–11 °C.
itinerary.evening: Arrange a shuttle or leave a second car — there is no bus link between the two ends that works in a single day. `verify: true` **Water:** the pass streams; the Saksun valley is heavily grazed, so filter.
itinerary.dayStats: 7–8 km point-to-point, 500 m

itinerary.title: Tórshavn ridge day: Húsareyn and the Kirkjubøur old road
itinerary.morning: From the capital, run up Húsareyn (347 m) directly from the northern edge of town — the local training hill, runnable throughout.
itinerary.afternoon: The Kirkjubøhálsur old road, a stone-marked historic route over the ridge from Tórshavn to Kirkjubøur, where the ruined 14th-century Magnus Cathedral and the Kirkjubøargarður farmhouse — reportedly one of the oldest inhabited wooden houses in the world — sit on the shore.
itinerary.evening: Tórshavn. Book a **heimablídni** — a home-hosted dinner in a private house, a Faroese institution that predates the current food scene. **Water:** carry it; the Kirkjubøur ridge is dry.

itinerary.title: Skælingsfjall or the Nordradalsskarð traverse
itinerary.morning: The Nordradalsskarð pass road south of Tórshavn gives high starts. Skælingsfjall (767 m) is a long grassy ridge with almost no trail and no other people, looking across Hestfjørður to the islands of Koltur and Hestur.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend to Kvívík and run the coastal lane. This is the day to have GPX loaded and a compass bearing rehearsed — the plateau is featureless in cloud.
itinerary.evening: Last night in Tórshavn; if the reservation gods have been kind, this is the night for a tasting menu at the fermentation-focused end of the Faroese food scene. `verify: true` **Water:** stream at the col below the summit ridge.

itinerary.title: Sea day and departure
itinerary.morning: If wind allows, take the Mykines boat from Sørvágur for the puffin colony and the lighthouse ridge — but treat it as a bonus, since it cancels often.
itinerary.afternoon: Fly out from Vágar. Allow slack: Faroese departures are the most weather-delayed in this dataset.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Føroyar
accommodationStrategy.description: Turf-roofed, built into the hillside above the capital, with a view over the whole harbour. Practically: it is at the top of the Húsareyn trailhead, so two of the week's runs start from the car park, and the drying facilities cope with genuinely wet kit.

accommodationStrategy.name: Gjáargarður Guesthouse
accommodationStrategy.description: A guesthouse in the most beautiful village in the archipelago, positioned for the Slættaratindur and Saksun–Tjørnuvík days. Home-cooked evening meals available if booked at check-in, which matters because Gjógv has no restaurant.

accommodationStrategy.name: Sørvágur / Bøur guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: Ten minutes from the airport and from the Sørvágsvatn trailhead. Best first and last nights, and the correct base if you are attempting Mykines, since the boat leaves from Sørvágur harbour and decisions are made at 07:00.

logistics.connectivity: Surprisingly good 4G on populated coasts, absent on plateaux. Download offline maps for every route. Faroese numbers are cheap on a local SIM; EU roaming does not apply. `verify: true`
logistics.emergency: 112. Search and rescue is competent but the terrain is unforgiving: the standard accident is a slip on wet grass above a cliff. Wear shoes with aggressive lugs, and treat 35° wet grass as you would treat ice.
logistics.weather: Four seasons in an hour is the local joke and it is literal. Sea fog can drop visibility to 20 m on a ridge in minutes. Faroese forecasts are given per-village because the weather differs across a single fjord. Build two flexible days into a seven-day plan and expect to use one.
logistics.bookingWindows: Cars: 2–3 months ahead for summer, the island fleet is small and genuinely sells out. Mykines boat: as soon as the season opens. Tórshavn's serious restaurants: 2–4 months. Guesthouses in Gjógv: 3 months.

other.label: Hiking fees and guides
other.text: Since 2019, landowners charge for access to several of the most-photographed routes and some require a guide. Fees are typically 200–500 DKK per person. Trespassing is taken seriously and has led to prosecutions. Check each route's status before you drive to it. `verify: true`

other.label: Driving and tunnels
other.text: Subsea tunnels connect Vágar, Streymoy and Eysturoy; the Vágar and Eysturoy tunnels are tolled automatically via the hire car's registration and billed by the rental company. The Eysturoy tunnel contains the world's only undersea roundabout. Single-lane mountain roads use passing bays — the vehicle nearest a bay reverses.

proTips: Run the popular routes at **06:00 or after 19:00** in June. The Sørvágsvatn path holds hundreds of people between 10:00 and 16:00 and almost nobody before or after — and the light at both ends is better.
Book a **heimablídni** early in the trip, not late. Your hosts will reshape the rest of your week with local knowledge no guidebook has.
Faroese sheep have made every hillside a network of contour paths. On trackless ground, follow the sheep line that maintains altitude — it is almost always the safest and the driest.

Take the **helicopter**. The government-subsidised Atlantic Airways helicopter serves remote villages at a fixed, absurdly low fare for a scheduled sector. Seats are released on a fixed schedule and go instantly, and tourists may be restricted to one-way legs. `verify: true`
Wind assessment is more useful than rain assessment. Above 12 m/s, cancel the exposed ridges — not because of comfort but because gusts on a cliff edge are the actual danger.
Carry **two pairs of shoes**. Nothing dries overnight in Faroese humidity, and a wet shoe on Day 3 is a wet shoe on Day 7.

raw.technical_rating: T3 with severe exposure on cliff-edge sections; grass-on-rock at 35–40° is the real hazard, not scrambling
raw.water_strategy: Streams everywhere, but every catchment is grazed by sheep — carry a filter or purification tablets and drink from fast water high in the catchment only
raw.access_note: Many routes cross private land and charge a per-person fee or require a licensed guide. This has been enforced since 2019 and is not optional.

typeSpecific.technicalRating: T3 with severe exposure on cliff-edge sections; grass-on-rock at 35–40° is the real hazard, not scrambling
