trips.title: The Balcons — A Chamonix Running Week Facing Mont Blanc

bestPeriod.note: Lac Blanc and the Aiguillette des Posettes hold hard snow into early July; most refuges shut between mid and late September.

trips.gatewayAirport: Geneva (GVA)
trips.summary: Seven days on the two great balcony trails of the Chamonix valley, with the lifts doing the climbing and the recovery days built into the plan.
trips.hook: Chamonix runs on two horizontal lines. The Grand Balcon Nord traverses the Aiguilles Rouges side of nothing — it clings to the Mont Blanc massif itself, under the granite spires, on moraine and slab. The Grand Balcon Sud sits opposite on the Aiguilles Rouges, in the sun, looking straight across at the whole range. Between them and the lifts that reach them, you can build a week of genuine alpine running without ever carrying a rope or sleeping above 2,000 m.

snapshot.Base(s): Chamonix-Mont-Blanc (all week; Argentière is the quieter alternative)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 105–125 km, 6,500–7,500 m vert; moraine, granite slab, alpine singletrack, forest balcon
snapshot.Getting There: Geneva (GVA) → shared shuttle or coach to Chamonix, approx. 1h15; or rail via Saint-Gervais and the Mont-Blanc Express
snapshot.Who It Suits: Experienced mountain runners comfortable with exposure, ladders and 1,500 m descents

itinerary.title: Petit Balcon Sud and the Chalet de la Floria
itinerary.morning: Arrive, get your Carte d'Hôte from the accommodation — it covers the valley buses and the Mont-Blanc Express train between Servoz and Vallorcine, and you will use it every day.
itinerary.afternoon: Open the legs low. The Petit Balcon Sud is a forest traverse at around 1,200 m running the whole length of the valley. Pick it up above Chamonix, run north-east to the Chalet de la Floria — a flower-covered buvette with the best cheap terrace view in the valley — then descend to Les Praz and jog the Arve riverside path home.
itinerary.evening: Eat early. Altitude in Chamonix is only 1,035 m, but you will feel the first days regardless.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 500 m vert. Grade T1–T2, forest singletrack and root, no exposure. Water: Chamonix town fountains, Chalet de la Floria, Les Praz. Bail-out: the balcon is 20–30 min above the valley floor at any point.

itinerary.title: Grand Balcon Nord: Plan de l'Aiguille to Montenvers
itinerary.morning: First cable car on the Aiguille du Midi, but only to the mid-station at Plan de l'Aiguille (2,317 m). From the Refuge du Plan de l'Aiguille the Grand Balcon Nord traverses east under the Aiguille du Midi, the Blaitière and the Grands Charmoz on moraine, slab and scree, with the Mer de Glace opening below.
itinerary.afternoon: Reach Montenvers (1,913 m) and its hotel and railway station. Refill, then descend either by the rack railway or on foot down the Grand Balcon Nord's lower path and the Signal Forbes trail to Chamonix. Choose the train if the quads are new to this.
itinerary.evening: Stretch. Tomorrow is deliberately empty.
itinerary.dayStats: 14–18 km, 400 m vert (lift-assisted), 700–1,300 m descent. Grade T3 in sections — cable-secured slabs, moraine crossings, real exposure above the glacier. Water: Refuge du Plan de l'Aiguille, Montenvers. Bail-out: the Montenvers rack railway; the Aiguille du Midi cable car back down from Plan de l'Aiguille.

itinerary.title: Recovery: Les Bois, the Arve and Vallorcine
itinerary.morning: Genuinely easy. Run the flat Arve path from Chamonix through Les Praz to Les Bois and the hamlet of Le Lavancher, on gravel and packed earth, then loop back. Forty-five to sixty minutes, nose-breathing.
itinerary.afternoon: Take the Mont-Blanc Express to Vallorcine (free with the Carte d'Hôte) and walk — do not run — the valley floor to the Cascade de Bérard. Coffee, then train home.
itinerary.evening: Look hard at the forecast. Days 4 and 6 both need clear mornings.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km run, 150 m vert. Grade T1, riverside gravel. Water: fountains in Chamonix, Les Praz, Argentière and Vallorcine — all drinkable. Bail-out: trivial, the train parallels the whole route.

itinerary.title: Aiguillette des Posettes and the Col de Balme
itinerary.morning: The quality day. Train to Le Tour and climb the ridge of the Aiguillette des Posettes (2,201 m) as one sustained effort — roughly 850 m of gain on a clean, runnable spur with the whole Mont Blanc range at your back. This ridge appears in the closing stages of the big Chamonix ultra courses and it is worth understanding why: it is steep enough to hurt and smooth enough to keep running.
itinerary.afternoon: From the summit, drop north-west to the Col des Montets and Tré-le-Champ, or extend north-east over the Col de Balme (2,191 m) on the Swiss frontier and descend to Charamillon for the gondola down to Le Tour. Train back.
itinerary.evening: Refuel properly. Savoyard food is heavy and appropriate.
itinerary.dayStats: 18–22 km, 1,050 m vert, 1,050–1,300 m descent. Grade T2, with a T3 rocky section on the Posettes crest and moderate ridge exposure. Water: Le Tour village fountain, the Charamillon mid-station buvette, Tré-le-Champ. Bail-out: the Charamillon/Balme gondola from Le Tour; the Col des Montets road with valley buses.

itinerary.title: Rest day
itinerary.morning: No running at all. Chamonix rewards a slow morning — the Maison de la Montagne, the guides' office noticeboard with the day's conditions, the market on Place du Mont-Blanc on Saturdays.
itinerary.afternoon: If you must move, ride the Montenvers train and walk the gallery to look at the Mer de Glace, which is retreating fast enough that the staircase down to it is extended most years. Otherwise: the Chamonix outdoor pool at the Centre Sportif, and a long nap.
itinerary.evening: Pack for Day 6 tonight. It starts early.
itinerary.dayStats: Rest. 0 km. Water: everywhere. Bail-out: not applicable.

itinerary.title: Grand Balcon Sud: Bellachat, Brévent, Flégère, Lac Blanc
itinerary.morning: The week's big day, and it starts on foot. Bus to Les Houches and climb the Bellachat trail — a long, steady 1,400 m through forest then open alpage past the Refuge de Bellachat to Le Brévent (2,525 m). Sunrise on the way up puts Mont Blanc directly in front of you the whole climb.
itinerary.afternoon: From Brévent, run the Grand Balcon Sud north-east across Planpraz and the Aiguillette des Houches side of the ridge to La Flégère (1,877 m), then climb to Lac Blanc (2,352 m) and its refuge. Return along the balcon and descend to Argentière, or take the Flégère cable car down to Les Praz if the day has taken enough. Bus or train home.
itinerary.evening: Eat, drink, sleep. Nothing else.
itinerary.dayStats: 28–32 km, 2,100 m vert, 1,700–2,200 m descent. Grade T2–T3; the Lac Blanc approach and the Tête aux Vents area include bolted metal ladders and cable on granite slabs, with genuine exposure. Water: Refuge de Bellachat, Brévent and Planpraz stations, La Flégère restaurant, Refuge du Lac Blanc. Bail-out: three separate lifts intersect this route — Brévent/Planpraz, Flégère, and the valley buses at either end.

itinerary.title: Loriaz or the Bois du Bouchet, then out
itinerary.morning: Short and beautiful. Train to Vallorcine and run the climb to the Refuge de Loriaz (2,020 m), a quiet alpage terrace looking straight down the valley at the Aiguille Verte, then descend the same way. If the legs are finished, jog the flat Bois du Bouchet loops in Chamonix instead.
itinerary.afternoon: Shower, one last fondue or one last salad, and the shuttle to Geneva.
itinerary.evening: Travel.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 700 m vert. Grade T2, alpage path and forest. Water: Vallorcine fountain, Refuge de Loriaz (staffed in season). Bail-out: single valley path back to Vallorcine station.

accommodationStrategy.name: Auberge de Jeunesse de Chamonix
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits on the valley bus line at the Les Houches end, which is exactly where Day 6 begins, and has drying space, self-catering, a bag store and a genuinely international climbing and running crowd. The cheapest way to spend a week in one of the most expensive valleys in the Alps.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3 months ahead for July–August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotels and apartments around Argentière
accommodationStrategy.description: Argentière is quieter than Chamonix, 200 m higher, and closer to the Posettes, Balme and Lac Blanc trailheads — three of this week's six sessions start nearer here. It has a train station on the Mont-Blanc Express, a supermarket and enough restaurants. Choose it if you value sleep over nightlife.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 months ahead, and avoid the UTMB week entirely unless you are running it.

accommodationStrategy.name: Self-catering apartments in Chamonix Sud
accommodationStrategy.description: An apartment with a washing machine and a kitchen changes a running week. Chamonix Sud is walking distance to the Aiguille du Midi and Brévent lift stations and to the bus hub, which removes a transfer from every morning. Look for a ground-floor unit with a ski locker — it becomes the wet kit room.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4 months ahead for August.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €150–€260 per night for two to four

logistics.emergency: 112. Mountain rescue in the Chamonix valley is run by the PGHM; calling 112 routes you to them. Give your position as a named trail plus altitude, not GPS coordinates read aloud.
logistics.weather: Afternoon convective build-up is routine from mid-July. Météo-France publishes a specific Mont-Blanc massif bulletin; the guides' office in Chamonix posts it daily. Be off the Balcon Sud ladders before storms arrive.
logistics.bookingWindows: Chamonix accommodation for August should be booked in spring. The UTMB week in late August fills the entire valley and doubles prices — either plan around it or embrace it.
logistics.money: The Chamonix Mont-Blanc Multipass covers the valley's lifts and the Montenvers train; a single day runs to roughly €70–€90 per adult, with 2–6 day passes bringing the daily rate down substantially. Buy the number of days you will actually use, not more.

other.label: The Carte d'Hôte is free and essential
other.text: Every registered accommodation issues one at check-in. It covers the valley bus network and the Mont-Blanc Express train between Servoz and Vallorcine. It does not cover the lifts.

other.label: Glacial water is not drinkable and no filter helps
other.text: The Arve and every torrent draining a glacier carries suspended rock flour. Use the village fountains — Chamonix, Les Praz, Argentière, Le Tour, Vallorcine all have them — and the refuges.

other.label: Refuge water in late summer
other.text: High refuges like Lac Blanc rely on stored or piped supply and can be short in a dry August; some charge for water or ask you to buy a drink. Never plan a day whose only water is a single high refuge.

other.label: Money
other.text: Cards everywhere, including refuges, though signal can fail. Carry €30–€40.

other.label: Drones
other.text: Prohibited over much of the massif and inside the Réserve Naturelle des Aiguilles Rouges, which covers the whole Balcon Sud. Assume no.

other.label: The Aiguilles Rouges reserve
other.text: Dogs banned, camping banned, staying on marked paths required, no picking anything. Rangers patrol Lac Blanc.

proTips: Take the first Aiguille du Midi cabin at around 07:00 and get off at Plan de l'Aiguille. The Grand Balcon Nord is a narrow traverse; an hour earlier means an empty path and firmer overnight-frozen moraine.

Run the Grand Balcon Sud south-west to north-east in the afternoon and the Grand Balcon Nord in the morning. The Aiguilles Rouges side catches evening light on Mont Blanc; the Mont Blanc side is in shadow and cold by 16:00.
Buy lift passes as a multi-day Multipass only if you will use three or more days. Otherwise the free valley train plus one single lift ticket beats it easily.
Climb Bellachat from Les Houches on foot rather than riding Brévent up. It is the finest sustained climb in the valley, it faces Mont Blanc the whole way, and it is almost empty before 09:00.
The Chalet de la Floria and the Refuge de Bellachat are both cheap places to refill and both are staffed daily in season — worth more to your planning than any high refuge.
Check the guides' office conditions board in Chamonix each evening. It reports snow on the Lac Blanc and Posettes approaches, which is the specific information that decides your next day.
If the Balcon Sud is stormed off, the Petit Balcon Nord runs the shaded valley side at 1,200 m from Argentière to Les Tines and stays runnable in almost any weather.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 105–125 km, 6,500–7,500 m vert; moraine, granite slab, alpine singletrack, forest balcon
raw.Who It Suits: Experienced mountain runners comfortable with exposure, ladders and 1,500 m descents

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 105–125 km, 6,500–7,500 m vert; moraine, granite slab, alpine singletrack, forest balcon
typeSpecific.audience: Experienced mountain runners comfortable with exposure, ladders and 1,500 m descents

packingNotes: Shoes with sticky rubber and a rock plate. The Balcon Nord is polished granite slab and moraine block; lugs matter less than grip on rock.
A light pack that carries 1.5 L, a shell and a spare layer without bouncing. Half of these days are three to six hours from a road.
Wind shell plus a waterproof — different garments, both needed on Day 6.
Gloves. The ladders near Tête aux Vents are cold metal and often wet.
Sunglasses with real UV rating and high-factor sunscreen: you are at 2,300 m on reflective granite and snow patches.
Poles for the Bellachat climb and the Montenvers descent.
A headtorch for the pre-dawn start on Day 6.
A buff or light beanie — the Balcon Nord holds cold air off the Mer de Glace all morning.
Cash of €30–€40 for refuges with intermittent card signal.
A dry bag for the phone: afternoon storms here arrive faster than you can descend.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Storm on the Grand Balcon Sud.** The ladders and slabs above Tête aux Vents are the last place to be in lightning. Fallback: descend immediately to La Flégère and take the cable car down; it is 25–40 minutes from most of the balcon.

**The Aiguille du Midi is closed for wind and Day 2 has no start.** Fallback: run the Grand Balcon Nord in reverse from Montenvers, reached by the rack railway which operates in weather that grounds the cable car.

**Old snow on the Lac Blanc approach in early July.** North-facing slabs hold hard névé and people fall on them every season. Fallback: check the guides' office board, and substitute the Aiguillette des Posettes, which clears earlier.

**Quads destroyed by Day 5.** Two 1,500 m descents in a week is a lot of eccentric load. Fallback: take the lifts down. The Day 5 rest day is structural, not filler — skipping it is how this week ends in a strained calf.

**Everything is full and twice the price.** If your dates land on the UTMB week in late August, the valley is at capacity. Fallback: base in Vallorcine or Les Houches, both on the free valley transport, or move the trip to the first half of September when the refuges are still open and the crowds have gone.

trips.title: High Cols and Engraved Rock — Mercantour by Vésubie and Merveilles

bestPeriod.note: The cols above 2,400 m hold snow into early July and the CAF refuges close between mid and late September, after which there is no staffed water above the valleys.

trips.gatewayAirport: Nice Côte d'Azur (NCE)
trips.summary: A two-base week in the southern Alps, running the Vésubie cirques and the Vallée des Merveilles with no lifts and no shortcuts.
trips.hook: The Mercantour is an hour and a half from the Mediterranean and behaves nothing like it. Above Saint-Martin-Vésubie the valleys close into granite cirques with cold lakes, and over the watershed the Vallée des Merveilles holds thousands of Bronze Age engravings under Mont Bégo. There are no cable cars here. Every metre is earned, every bail-out is a valley path, and that is exactly why the trails are empty in August.

snapshot.Base(s): Saint-Martin-Vésubie (4 nights), Castérino / Tende (3 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 110–130 km, 6,000–7,000 m vert; granite slab, larch forest, scree, high lake basins
snapshot.Getting There: Nice (NCE) → Zou! regional bus to Saint-Martin-Vésubie, or the Nice–Tende railway to Saint-Dalmas-de-Tende for the Merveilles side
snapshot.Who It Suits: Self-sufficient mountain runners who want remoteness rather than infrastructure

itinerary.title: Le Boréon, gently
itinerary.morning: Arrive from Nice. If you are driving, take the Vésubie road up through Lantosque and Roquebillière and notice how much of it is new — the valley was rebuilt after the October 2020 floods and reconstruction is still visible.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive or ride 8 km up to Le Boréon (1,500 m) and run an easy loop: the lake, the Cascade du Boréon, and the forest track up the Vallon de Salèse under Norway spruce. Altitude adjustment, nothing more.
itinerary.evening: Back down to Saint-Martin-Vésubie. Walk the Rue du Docteur Cagnoli, the old street with a channel of spring water running down its middle, and fill your bottles from the fountains on the square.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 450 m vert. Grade T1–T2, forest track and lakeside path, no exposure. Water: Le Boréon (Vacherie du Boréon, fountains), Saint-Martin-Vésubie fountains — all reliable year-round. Bail-out: the Boréon road runs to the trailhead.

itinerary.title: Les Lacs de Prals from La Madone de Fenestre
itinerary.morning: Drive the 12 km up the Vallon de la Madone to the sanctuary and the Refuge de la Madone de Fenestre (1,903 m), a stone chapel and CAF hut in a bare granite bowl. Climb the marked path east to the Cinq Lacs de Prals (2,270 m), five small tarns on a grassy shelf.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to the Cime de la Valette de Prals for the view over the whole Vésubie, then descend the loop back to the Madone. Watch for flocks: this is patou country, and the descent path runs through summer grazing.
itinerary.evening: Eat in Saint-Martin. Trout, gnocchi, tourte de blettes — the Niçois mountain kitchen is heavier than the coast's.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km, 900 m vert. Grade T2, grass, scree and slab; moderate exposure on the Valette ridge. Water: Refuge de la Madone de Fenestre, streams below the lakes (running until roughly late August, unreliable in September). Bail-out: the Madone road, with a hut at the trailhead.

itinerary.title: Recovery in the Boréon forest
itinerary.morning: Easy only. Run the forest tracks and the Vallon du Boréon path on soft larch duff, 60 minutes at conversational pace, no climbing above 1,800 m.
itinerary.afternoon: Visit Alpha, the wolf park at Le Boréon — wolves returned to the Mercantour in the 1990s and shape everything about how livestock is managed here, which in turn shapes the dogs you will meet on the trail.
itinerary.evening: Legs up. Tomorrow is the biggest day on the Vésubie side.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km, 350 m vert. Grade T1, forest track. Water: Le Boréon. Bail-out: trivial.

itinerary.title: Cougourde, the Pas des Ladres and the Col de Fenestre
itinerary.morning: From Le Boréon climb the Vallon de la Cougourde to the Refuge de la Cougourde (2,090 m), under the granite tooth of the Cime de la Cougourde. Continue up to Lac de Trecolpas and over the Pas des Ladres (2,448 m).
itinerary.afternoon: Descend the far side to the Refuge de la Madone de Fenestre, refill, then climb north to the Col de Fenestre (2,474 m) on the Italian frontier — an old salt-trade pass with military ruins on the crest — and turn around. Return to Le Boréon over the Pas des Ladres, or arrange a pickup at the Madone road head to save 500 m of re-ascent.
itinerary.evening: Big meal, early night, and pack: you change valleys tomorrow.
itinerary.dayStats: 24–27 km, 1,600 m vert. Grade T2–T3; rocky, cairned sections near both cols, loose scree on the north side of the Ladres, moderate exposure. Water: Refuge de la Cougourde, Refuge de la Madone de Fenestre, Lac de Trecolpas outflow (reliable), and nothing at all on the Fenestre climb. Bail-out: descend to the Madone road head and the hut, which is staffed and has a phone.

itinerary.title: Over to the Roya, and easy legs at Castérino
itinerary.morning: The transfer. Drive east over the Col de Turini and down through Sospel and the Roya to Tende, then up the side road to Castérino (roughly 2h to 2h30 — this is a mountain road, do not underestimate it). Without a car, the alternative is the Nice–Tende railway and a taxi or seasonal shuttle up from Saint-Dalmas-de-Tende.
itinerary.afternoon: Shake the drive out on the Castérino valley track toward the Refuge de Valmasque, turning back at the first lake basin. Easy pace, 45–60 minutes.
itinerary.evening: Sort tomorrow's water and food in Castérino, which is a hamlet, not a town. Tende, 15 km below, has the shops.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km, 300 m vert. Grade T1, jeep track and forest path. Water: Castérino hamlet, Refuge de Valmasque approach streams. Bail-out: single valley track.

itinerary.title: The Merveilles circuit under Mont Bégo
itinerary.morning: The big one, and the reason you came east. From Castérino climb the Vallon de la Valmasque past the Lac Vert and the Lac Noir to the Refuge de Valmasque (2,221 m), then up to the Baisse de Valmasque (2,549 m) on bare granite.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop south-west into the Vallée des Merveilles, past the Lac Long Supérieur and the Refuge des Merveilles (2,111 m). This is the archaeological core: thousands of Bronze Age petroglyphs on the ice-polished schist under Mont Bégo. Stay on the marked path — leaving it inside the engravings zone is prohibited without an accredited guide. Return to Castérino over the Pas de l'Arpette on the GR52.
itinerary.evening: Nothing but food and sleep.
itinerary.dayStats: 27–30 km, 1,500 m vert, 1,500 m descent. Grade T3 on the Baisse de Valmasque and the Arpette — cairned slab, scree, some hands-on rock; sustained exposure to weather above 2,200 m for four hours. Water: Refuge de Valmasque, Refuge des Merveilles, the lake outflows (reliable all season). Bail-out: both refuges are staffed in season; the Merveilles valley descends to the Lac des Mesches road head.

itinerary.title: Lac Vert at dawn, then the Train des Merveilles
itinerary.morning: Short and slow. Run the Valmasque track back up to the Lac Vert for the reflection at first light and come straight back down. Ninety minutes total.
itinerary.afternoon: Down to Tende. Walk the old town's stacked lanes, then take the Nice–Tende railway back to the coast — one of the great mountain railways in France, spiralling down the Roya in tunnels and viaducts.
itinerary.evening: Nice.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km, 400 m vert. Grade T1–T2, jeep track and stony path. Water: Castérino, Tende fountains. Bail-out: not needed.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotels and gîtes in Saint-Martin-Vésubie
accommodationStrategy.description: The only place in the valley with a pharmacy, a bakery, restaurants and a bus link to Nice, and it sits equidistant from the Boréon and Madone de Fenestre road heads — the two trailheads that carry four of this week's sessions. Ask for parking and a place to dry kit; and confirm the property's status, as some village stock was affected by the 2020 floods and rebuilding has been staged.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead for August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Refuge de la Madone de Fenestre
accommodationStrategy.description: Worth one night if you want the Pas des Ladres and Col de Fenestre day to start at altitude instead of 900 m below it. Half-board, dormitories, cold running water and a guardian who knows the snow conditions on both cols better than any website. Book through the Club Alpin Français reservation system.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead; weekends in August go early.

accommodationStrategy.name: Gîtes and small hotels at Castérino
accommodationStrategy.description: Castérino is a scattering of buildings at the road head, which is precisely its value: the Merveilles circuit starts from the doorstep and you skip an hour of driving each way. Expect half-board, limited menu choice and no shop. Bring your own trail food from Tende.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead for July–August.

logistics.emergency: 112. Mountain rescue in the Alpes-Maritimes is handled by the PGHM, based at Saint-Sauveur-sur-Tinée, and reached through 112. Coverage in the Valmasque and Fenestre cirques is patchy — expect to move to a col or ridge to get signal.
logistics.weather: Southern-Alps convection is violent and early. Storms can build by midday in August. Both big days should have you off the high ground by mid-afternoon.
logistics.money: Cards work in the villages; refuges vary and several are cash-preferred. Village shops close for a long lunch, roughly 12:30–15:00, and are shut on Sunday afternoons.

other.label: National park core-zone rules
other.text: Dogs are banned outright, even on a lead. Camping is banned; bivouac is tolerated only between 19:00 and 09:00 and at more than an hour's walk from the park boundary or a road. No fires, no drones, no picking anything, no leaving marked paths in the archaeological zone.

other.label: The Merveilles engravings zone
other.text: Off-path access requires an accredited guide. Rangers patrol in summer and the rule is enforced. The marked GR52 through the valley passes plenty of visible engravings — you do not need to leave it.

other.label: Patous
other.text: Livestock guardian dogs work these alpages unsupervised because wolves are present. If one comes at you: stop running, walk, keep your arms down, do not shout, do not swing poles, detour wide around the flock, and let the dog escort you out. Running through a flock is the one reliable way to get bitten.

other.label: Storm damage and trail status
other.text: Storm Alex in October 2020 destroyed roads, bridges and trails throughout the Vésubie and Roya. Much is rebuilt, some routes are still rerouted. Check the Parc national du Mercantour's trail-status page and the Saint-Martin-Vésubie tourist office before committing to a plan.

other.label: Water in late summer
other.text: The lakes and their outflows run all season; the grass-slope streams do not, and by September many are dry. The refuges are the reliable points, and they close from mid-September.

other.label: Roads
other.text: The Col de Turini and the Castérino side road are narrow, hairpinned and shared with cyclists and motorbikes at weekends. Budget more time than the map suggests.

proTips: Start the Day 4 and Day 6 loops before 07:00. The cols are the exposed part, the storms come in the afternoon, and this is a range where a single lift-served escape does not exist.

Run the Merveilles circuit anticlockwise — Valmasque first, Merveilles second. The Baisse de Valmasque is a steep granite climb best done fresh and in shade, and you then arrive at the engravings in the good afternoon light.

Ask the guardian at the Refuge de la Madone de Fenestre about the Pas des Ladres and Col de Fenestre before you go up. In early July they will tell you exactly which north-facing gully still holds hard snow.
Use the Nice–Tende railway as a one-way tool. It gets you to Saint-Dalmas-de-Tende and Tende without the Turini drive, and it means you can plan a point-to-point rather than a loop on your last day.
Refill at every refuge you pass, not at every second one. Between the Cougourde and the Madone there is nothing, and between the Baisse de Valmasque and the Merveilles refuge there is nothing.
Saint-Martin-Vésubie's street channel and square fountains are the cheapest and best water in the valley. Fill the night before rather than queuing at a refuge tap in the morning.
If the high cols are out, the Vallon de Salèse and the Col de Salèse give 700 m of gain on forest and alpage entirely below 2,050 m, and stay runnable in weather that shuts the cirques.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 110–130 km, 6,000–7,000 m vert; granite slab, larch forest, scree, high lake basins
raw.Who It Suits: Self-sufficient mountain runners who want remoteness rather than infrastructure

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 110–130 km, 6,000–7,000 m vert; granite slab, larch forest, scree, high lake basins
typeSpecific.audience: Self-sufficient mountain runners who want remoteness rather than infrastructure

packingNotes: Shoes with a stiff midsole and real rock grip. Mercantour granite is abrasive and the scree above the cols is coarse and mobile.
2 L carrying capacity for the two big days. This is the single most important item on the list here.
A wind shell and a genuine waterproof — southern-Alps storms are short, violent and cold.
Light gloves and a warm layer: the Col de Fenestre and the Baisse de Valmasque sit near 2,500 m and hold wind.
Poles. Two 1,500 m days with no lift assistance, on scree, make them worth their weight.
High-factor sunscreen, a cap and proper sunglasses. This is 44° north at 2,400 m with granite and lake reflection.
Offline mapping plus a paper 1:25,000 of the Vallée des Merveilles. Cairned slab sections are easy to lose in cloud.
A survival blanket and a whistle — the standard alpine minimum, and here the rescue response is genuinely distant.
Cash for refuges, €40–€60, plus a card.
Insect repellent for the Boréon forest evenings and a tick tool; the lower larch woods have both.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A trail or road you planned on is still closed from flood damage.** Fallback: check the park's trail-status page the week before, and keep the Boréon–Salèse and Prals loops as substitutes since both are on the intact upper roads.

**Thunderstorm on the Baisse de Valmasque.** There is no shelter and no lift. Fallback: the Refuge de Valmasque and the Refuge des Merveilles bracket the col; commit to whichever is closer and wait it out rather than pushing over.
**A patou confronts you at speed on the Prals descent.** Fallback: stop, walk, and go wide. Plan the descent so you are not running blind into an alpage at 18:00 when the flock is being moved.

**Snow in the Pas des Ladres in early July.** North-facing and steep. Fallback: ask the Madone guardian, and if in doubt run the Cougourde and Trecolpas out-and-back instead, which stays below the col.

**You arrive after the refuges have closed for the season.** From roughly late September the huts shut, taking the water and the emergency shelter with them. Fallback: shift the trip earlier, or plan strictly valley-based days with full water carried from Saint-Martin-Vésubie.

trips.title: Zagori & the Vikos Gorge

bestPeriod.window: Mid-May–late June & mid-September–late October
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (35 °C+ on the gorge floor, springs dry, vipers active); November–April (Tymfi under snow, Astraka refuge shut)
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-May–late June & mid-September–late October

accommodation.note: Guesthouses €70–€110 dbl/night; Astraka refuge dorm ~€18–€22

food.note: Taverna meal with wine €14–€22; refuge half-board ~€30

transport.note: Rental car 7 days €200–€300 plus fuel; a car is effectively mandatory

activities.note: Refuge night, Voidomatis raft, Anavasi maps

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5 — comfortable with 1,000 m climbs on rough limestone and back-to-back 20 km days; no alpinism required

trips.gatewayAirport: IOA — Ioannina "King Pyrrhus" (45 min to Monodendri, 1 h 15 to Papingo); fallback PVK — Preveza/Aktion, 2 h 15
trips.summary: Zagori offers two entirely different running surfaces twenty minutes apart: the shaded limestone floor of the Vikos Gorge — 900 m deep from the Oxya rim to the Voidomatis bed — and the bare karst amphitheatre of Mt Tymfi above Papingo, where a 1,000 m climb lands you at a refuge on a 1,950 m col. Linking them are forty-six stone villages joined by 18th-century mule paths and single-arch packhorse bridges. The week's arc is deliberate: two orientation days, a two-day Tymfi block with a night at altitude, a genuine recovery day on the river, then a fast village-path day and a rim finish. It suits an experienced runner who wants technical volume without glacier travel.

itinerary.title: Land at Ioannina, shake out on the Vradeto Steps
itinerary.morning: Fly into IOA, collect the car, stock up in Ioannina — Zagori shops are tiny. Drive 45 minutes to Kapesovo.
itinerary.afternoon: Shake-out down the **Skala Vradetou**, roughly 1,100 restored zigzag steps into the Mezaria ravine, up to Vradeto (1,340 m) and out to the **Beloi viewpoint** facing the gorge's north wall. Take the descent slow — first contact with polished Zagori limestone.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **Sterna** in Kapesovo; order the hortopita and a Zitsa white.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km / 520 m D+ / ~70% kalderimi flagstone / 1 h 30–2 h; 45 min transfer.

itinerary.title: The full Vikos Gorge traverse
itinerary.morning: Leave Monodendri by 07:00. Drop from the **Agia Paraskevi monastery** trailhead — 450 m down in 2.5 km on the loosest ground of the week — then north-west along the dry bed on cobble, slab and beech shade.
itinerary.afternoon: Refill at the **Voidomatis springs** at Klima where the river resurfaces, then climb 250 m in 40 minutes to **Vikos village**. Pickup, or add the kalderimi link down to Aristi.
itinerary.evening: **Kanela kai Garyfallo** in Vitsa — book ahead; order the daily wild-greens dish.
itinerary.dayStats: 12.8 km / 320 m up, 690 m down / 2 h 15–3 h / no signal for 9 km / one reliable water point.

itinerary.title: Up to Astraka, the thousand-metre climb
itinerary.morning: Drive to **Mikro Papingo** (960 m) and start the O3 climb at 07:00: box scrub to the **Antalki spring**, then open karst and the traverse to the **Astraka col, 1,950 m**, where the refuge sits between Astraka and Lapatos. 1 h 45–2 h 20 with power-hiking.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop the pack, then the 45-minute out-and-back across the plateau to **Drakolimni** (2,050 m) with its alpine newts, on the lip above the Aoos gorge.
itinerary.evening: Refuge fixed menu — soup, bean stew, feta — and sunset from the terrace over the Papingo towers.
itinerary.dayStats: 9.5 km / 1,050 m D+ to the refuge, plus 5.5 km / 220 m D+ for the lake; refuge 1,950 m, 51 beds.

itinerary.title: Astraka summit ridge, then the long descent
itinerary.morning: Away by 06:45. **Astraka (2,436 m)** by the south-east flank from the col, 55–75 minutes with a short easy scramble on good rock. Strong runners add the plateau traverse to **Gamila I (2,497 m)**, +2 h.
itinerary.afternoon: Reverse the Papingo descent, 1,000 m of karst and cobble that punishes quads harder than the climb did lungs. Finish in the **Rogovo rock pools** above Megalo Papingo as an ice bath.
itinerary.evening: Grilled meats and tsipouro at Kalliopi's in Megalo Papingo, then a very early night.
itinerary.dayStats: 19 km / 1,600 m D+ / 4 h 30–6 h / technicality 4 on the summit block / high point 2,436 m.

itinerary.title: Recovery day on the Voidomatis
itinerary.morning: Deliberate low day: 6 km flat on the **Voidomatis riverside path, Klidonia bridge to Aristi bridge** — packed gravel, plane-tree shade, 40 m total elevation change, conversational pace only.
itinerary.afternoon: A half-day Class II raft on the Voidomatis, or nothing at all. Drive out to the **Kokkorou** and **Plakidas (Kalogeriko)** packhorse bridges near Kipoi.
itinerary.evening: Aristi Mountain Resort restaurant — Epirot cheeses, trahana, Glinavos wine.
itinerary.dayStats: 6 km / 40 m D+ / 100% flat gravel / ~35 minutes running.

itinerary.title: The village kalderimi link
itinerary.morning: Point-to-point **Kipoi → Koukouli → Dilofo → Vitsa** on restored mule paths across three single-arch bridges. Constant short climbs, deep forest, no exposure — the fast, flowing day of the week.
itinerary.afternoon: Extend on the **Kapesovo–Tsepelovo** link if the legs are good, or drive to Tsepelovo for the short Mezaria ravine loop and coffee under the plane tree.
itinerary.evening: Tsepelovo taverna — order gida vrasti (boiled goat) if it is on the board.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km / 600 m D+ / ~50% forest singletrack, 35% kalderimi, 15% asphalt / 1 h 45–2 h 30.

itinerary.title: Rim run at Oxya, then out
itinerary.morning: Drive to the **Oxya viewpoint** above Monodendri and run the rim path north — 8 km out-and-back on pine-needle singletrack directly above the 900 m drop, seeing Day 2's route from above.
itinerary.afternoon: Pita and coffee in Monodendri, then the 45-minute drive to Ioannina; an hour in the Ottoman castle quarter if the flight allows.
itinerary.evening: Late departure from IOA, or a night on the Ioannina lakefront.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km / 260 m D+ / 1 h–1 h 20; 45 min drive to IOA.

accommodationStrategy.name: Archontiko Zarkada
accommodationStrategy.description: Two minutes' jog from the Agia Paraskevi gorge trailhead, so the Vikos traverse starts on foot at 07:00 without moving the car. Early breakfast on request if you ask the night before. Roughly €70–€95 double in shoulder season, with secure indoor storage for shoes and packs.

accommodationStrategy.name: Papaevangelou Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: The Tymfi base: ten minutes from the Mikro Papingo trailhead, balcony view of the Astraka towers, and owners who know real-time refuge and snow conditions — worth more than any website. Ask for a 06:00 coffee flask before the summit day.

accommodationStrategy.name: Aristi Mountain Resort
accommodationStrategy.description: The recovery base. Indoor pool, sauna and massage make it the right place to sit between the Astraka block and the kalderimi day, five minutes from the Voidomatis path. €130–€200 a night — you are paying for the recovery.

logistics.connectivity: Greece is EU, so roaming is at domestic rates; Cosmote has the best Zagori coverage. Assume **no signal on the gorge floor** and patchy service on the north Tymfi plateau. Download offline maps in the village.
logistics.emergency: **112** for everything; the Hellenic Rescue Team's Epirus section covers Tymfi. Forest fire **199**. Buy insurance that explicitly covers mountain running above 2,000 m — standard policies often exclude it.
logistics.weather: Pindus afternoon convection is the defining hazard — clear mornings turn to lightning on the treeless Tymfi karst from about 14:00 in June and September. Autumn cold fronts off the Ionian can flood the gorge bed within a day.
logistics.bookingWindows: **Astraka refuge** books by phone/email and fills on summer weekends and Greek holidays — 2–4 weeks ahead, more for August. It opens around **22 May** and closes in October; outside that only the unstaffed winter room, with no water. Aristi Mountain Resort goes 2–3 months ahead for late September.
logistics.money: Euro. Hotels and larger tavernas take cards; **the refuge, kafeneia and small tavernas are frequently cash-only**. Carry €150–€200 from Ioannina — Zagori ATMs are limited to Tsepelovo and Papingo and run dry at weekends. Round up or leave 5–10%.
logistics.transportRules: A rental car is non-negotiable; buses run once or twice daily at best. Egnatia Odos from Ioannina is tolled (a few euros per gate). Inter-village roads are narrow, unlit and full of sheep — do not plan fast night driving.
logistics.permits: Vikos–Aoos National Park has **no entry fee** and needs no permit to run. Wild camping in the core zone is prohibited. Drones need park permission. Open fires are banned May–October.
logistics.health: Village taps and named springs are potable; treat lake and standing water. **Ticks** in beech leaf litter May–July — check nightly. Nose-horned vipers live on sunny limestone; make noise on rock ledges. Sheepdogs guarding flocks on the plateau are serious — stop, don't run, wait for the shepherd.

proTips: **Run the gorge north-to-south.** Almost everyone starts at Monodendri; start at Vikos village and you meet the crowd head-on for twenty minutes then have empty trail, and the brutal 450 m Monodendri climb becomes a known quantity at the end rather than a surprise descent on tired ankles.
**Sleep at the refuge mid-week.** Astraka fills with Greek groups Friday and Saturday; a Tuesday night can mean fifteen people in a 51-bed hut.
**Pre-position water for the Tymfi descent.** Stash a litre at the Antalki junction on the way up in July–September; the last 700 m of descent in afternoon sun is where people cook.
**Use the refuge as a weather oracle.** Call the hut the day before your ridge day — the guardian's read on plateau cloudbase beats any app.
**Do the Vradeto Steps at 18:30.** The Mezaria ravine faces west, the light on the stone is extraordinary, and the Beloi coach parties are long gone.
**Carry the Anavasi paper sheet anyway.** Above the Astraka col the karst is featureless and a phone inside a rain shell is a liability.
**Book the Voidomatis raft for a rest-day morning.** The river is shaded until midday at 8–10 °C — accidental cold-water recovery after the Astraka block.

raw.Signature routes: (1) **Vikos Gorge traverse, Monodendri→Vikos village**: 12.8 km, 320 m up / 690 m down, mid-pack 2 h 15–3 h. (2) **Astraka refuge & Drakolimni from Mikro Papingo**: 15.5 km, 1,290 m D+, 3 h 15–4 h 15. (3) **Astraka summit (2,436 m) via the col and Lapatos**: 19 km, 1,600 m D+, 4 h 30–6 h. (4) **Vradeto Steps + Beloi rim loop from Kapesovo**: 11 km, 520 m D+, 1 h 30–2 h. (5) **Kalderimi link Kipoi–Koukouli–Dilofo–Vitsa**: 14 km, 600 m D+, 1 h 45–2 h 30.
raw.Technicality (ITRA-style 1–5; 1 = fire r: Gorge floor **3–4** (loose cobble, wet slab, two boulder-hop crossings); Tymfi ascent **3**; Astraka summit ridge **4**, with 20–30 m of easy exposed scrambling below the summit block; village kalderimia **2**, though polished flagstone is genuinely slick when damp. SAC equivalents: gorge T2–T3, Astraka T3.
raw.Terrain split, week average: ~45% limestone cobble and rock step, ~20% karst pavement and scree above 1,800 m, ~20% beech and black-pine singletrack with deep leaf litter, ~10% engineered kalderimi flagstone, ~5% asphalt connectors. Bring 4 mm+ lugs and a rock plate — Tymfi karst destroys soft midsoles.
raw.Waymarking: Gorge and Tymfi approaches carry **O3** (Greek national long-distance path) in red/white paint plus wooden Zagori NP posts timed in hours. Village links use yellow diamonds. Above the treeline, cairns matter more than paint.
raw.Water refill points and month reliabilit: *Voidomatis springs* at Klima below Vikos village — permanent, 8 °C, the most reliable source in Epirus. *Astraka refuge* — piped spring, reliable while staffed (from ~22 May), dry when the hut is shut. *Drakolimni* — lake water, filter or treat. *Mikro/Megalo Papingo, Kipoi, Koukouli, Vradeto, Kapesovo, Tsepelovo* village fountains — year-round. *Antalki/Trafos spring* on the Papingo ascent — reliable May–June, often dry August–September. Assume **nothing between Mikro Papingo and the refuge after mid-July**.
raw.Navigation: Anavasi 1:25,000 sheets 6.1 (Zagori–Vikos–Aoos) and 6.11 (Tymfi); GPX from the Anavasi topo app and Wikiloc ("O3 Vikos"). **Zero signal on the gorge floor for ~9 km** between Monodendri and the springs, patchy on the north Tymfi plateau. Bail-outs: from the gorge, side paths to Vikos village and the Klidonia road bridge; from Tymfi, only the refuge and the Papingo descent — the Tsepelovo side is a 4 h+ commitment.
raw.Recovery and heat management: Day 5 is a true low day (under 8 km, flat). Gorge days start by 07:00 — the east rim shades the floor to about 10:00, then it becomes an oven. Tymfi days start 06:30 to clear the treeless plateau before the 14:00–16:00 Pindus convective build-up. High point 2,497 m (Gamila); no acclimatisation needed, but the refuge night is a useful sleep-high dose.

typeSpecific.surface: ~45% limestone cobble and rock step, ~20% karst pavement and scree above 1,800 m, ~20% beech and black-pine singletrack with deep leaf litter, ~10% engineered kalderimi flagstone, ~5% asphalt connectors. Bring 4 mm+ lugs and a rock plate — Tymfi karst destroys soft midsoles.
typeSpecific.technicalRating: Gorge floor **3–4** (loose cobble, wet slab, two boulder-hop crossings); Tymfi ascent **3**; Astraka summit ridge **4**, with 20–30 m of easy exposed scrambling below the summit block; village kalderimia **2**, though polished flagstone is genuinely slick when damp. SAC equivalents: gorge T2–T3, Astraka T3.

sources.verified: Astraka refuge's official site confirms 1,950 m, 51 beds and a stated 2026 opening of 22 May; Vikos–Aoos National Park charges no entry fee; IOA as base airport; Greece EU roaming.
sources.confidenceNotes: Re-verify (a) **Astraka refuge exact opening/closing dates and current nightly and half-board prices**, set year to year by the guardian; (b) **spring reliability at Antalki/Trafos**, which tracks the winter snowpack — confirm with the refuge in the booking month; (c) **taverna trading status and shoulder-season opening days** for Sterna, Kanela kai Garyfallo and Kalliopi; (d) **accommodation price bands**, especially Aristi Mountain Resort; (e) **O3 paint condition and flood damage on the gorge floor** — the Voidomatis bed reshapes in flood years and crossings move.

trips.title: Velebit Dry-Stone: Running the Premužić Trail

bestPeriod.window: Mid-June–early July & September–mid-October
bestPeriod.avoid: November–April — the Oltari–Zavižan forest road is snow-gated, Alan is unstaffed, and bura closes the coastal approach; late July–August is brutally dry with every cistern at its lowest.
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-June–early July & September–mid-October

accommodation.note: Krasno/Starigrad rooms €45–€75 pppn; Zavižan and Alan hut bunks €15–€25

food.note: Lika konoba mains €10–€16; hut meals €8–€12; carried food for three days

transport.note: Hire car for the week (essential), fuel, the Oltari–Zavižan gravel road

activities.note: Northern Velebit NP and Paklenica NP entries, Botanical Garden, one guided day

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5 — five running days of 12–22 km with up to 1,450 m of vertical on limestone, plus genuine self-sufficiency on water

trips.gatewayAirport: ZAD Zadar — 55 min to Starigrad-Paklenica, 2 h 15 min to Krasno; RJK Rijeka 1 h 45 min to Senj; ZAG Zagreb 2 h 30 min to Krasno
trips.summary: Velebit is a 145 km limestone wall standing between the Adriatic and the Lika plateau, and almost none of it holds water. That single fact shapes everything: the running is fast, pale, waterless and strangely engineered, because in 1930–33 the forestry engineer **Ante Premužić** cut a graded dry-stone path across the wildest section of the range — 57 km from Zavižan south to Baške Oštarije, laid so gently that a laden horse could walk it, threading between the Rožanski and Hajdučki kukovi towers without ever needing a hand. This week runs the northern half of that path properly, adds the botanical high ground around Zavižan, drops to Paklenica for the canyon and the Vaganski vrh ridge, and builds in one genuine rest day on the coast. It suits self-sufficient runners who are comfortable carrying two litres and reading a limestone landscape with no streams in it.

itinerary.title: Zadar in, up the Lika side to Krasno
itinerary.morning: Land at ZAD, collect a car, and drive north — the coastal Adriatic road to Senj, then inland over to **Krasno**, Croatia's highest village and the Northern Velebit NP headquarters. Buy park tickets and the 1:30,000 map at **Kuća Velebita**.
itinerary.afternoon: Easy legs-opener on the forest tracks around Krasno at 700 m — nothing technical, just an hour of soft ground to shake off the flight and check the shoes against the first limestone.
itinerary.evening: Lika cooking in Krasno: lamb, cheese from the plateau, and *škripavac*. Buy three days of trail food here; the shop options above 1,000 m are none.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km / 180 m D+ / T1 / 50 min–1 h; drive 2 h 15; NP entry ≈€10

itinerary.title: Up the gravel to Zavižan, the botanical high ground
itinerary.morning: Drive the **Oltari–Zavižan forest road** — roughly 15 km of gravel with a barrier, slow and rough but manageable in a normal hire car when dry. Arrive at **Planinarski dom Zavižan (1,594 m)**, beside the highest permanently staffed meteorological station in Croatia.
itinerary.afternoon: Run the acclimatiser loop over **Veliki Zavižan** and **Vučjak** through the **Velebit Botanical Garden**, a 1967 reserve set in a limestone sinkhole holding the endemic Velebit degenia. Short, sharp and 1,600 m high.
itinerary.evening: Dinner and a bunk in the hut. Twenty-eight beds, a wood stove, and the whole Kvarner archipelago below you at sunset.
itinerary.dayStats: 7.2 km / 310 m D+ / T2 / 50 min–1 h 15; hut 1,594 m; carry 1.5 L

itinerary.title: Premužićeva staza to Rossijeva koliba and back
itinerary.morning: Onto the dry-stone path itself. Within two kilometres the trail enters the **Rožanski kukovi**, a strict reserve of limestone towers where leaving the marked path is forbidden — and the path threads it at a runnable grade the whole way.
itinerary.afternoon: Turn at **Rossijeva koliba**, an emergency shelter about two hours' walk from Zavižan and roughly the halfway feel of the northern section. Return the same way; the surface rewards a faster second half.
itinerary.evening: Back at Zavižan. Log the next day's route in the hut book — it is the only meaningful safety net up here.
itinerary.dayStats: 12.4 km / 380 m D+ / T1–T2 / 1 h 20–1 h 50 / ≈70% dry-stone path; no water on route

itinerary.title: The full northern Premužić section to Alan
itinerary.morning: Run the whole northern section south to **Planinarski dom Alan (≈1,340 m)** — 16.5 km of continuous engineered path, past the Hajdučki kukovi and above the Lubenovac basin, dropping steadily toward the Alan saddle.
itinerary.afternoon: Add the **Lubenovac circuit** from Alan if legs are fresh: sinkhole pasture, roofless shepherd huts and a silence that is genuinely total. Otherwise recover; the hut is basic, self-catering, and has no electric lighting.
itinerary.evening: Cook at Alan or eat what the warden is serving. Confirm your descent transport — this is a point-to-point day and the car is still at Zavižan.
itinerary.dayStats: 16.5 km / 560 m D+ / 810 m D− / T2 / 2 h–2 h 50 (+11 km, 420 m if adding Lubenovac); carry 2 L
itinerary.sleep: Planinarski dom Alan, or drive down to Starigrad-Paklenica

itinerary.title: Recovery on the coast: Zrmanja and sea
itinerary.morning: Down to **Starigrad-Paklenica**. Swim. The Adriatic here is clear and cold enough to work as an ice bath on tired quads.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive to the **Zrmanja canyon** rim near Obrovac and walk or jog the easy rim path — 6 km, no vertical worth naming, and the green river 200 m below in a limestone slot.
itinerary.evening: Fish and *šparoge* in Starigrad, on a terrace, with the Velebit wall going pink behind you. Rehydrate deliberately: you have been running on cistern rations for three days.
itinerary.dayStats: 6 km / 120 m D+ / T1 / 35–50 min; drive Alan→Starigrad ≈1 h 20

itinerary.title: Velika Paklenica: Anića kuk and Manita peć
itinerary.morning: Enter **Paklenica NP** at the Velika Paklenica gate and run up the canyon floor beneath **Anića kuk**, the 350 m limestone face that is the Balkans' most important big wall. Look up: on any dry morning there are climbers on it.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb the cabled rock steps to **Manita peć**, the show cave open on a restricted schedule, then loop via **Lugarnica** forest hut and the **Planinarski dom Paklenica** at 480 m before descending.
itinerary.evening: Konoba dinner in Starigrad. Sleep early — tomorrow starts before light.
itinerary.dayStats: 13.2 km / 720 m D+ / T2–T3 / 1 h 45–2 h 30; Paklenica NP entry ≈€10; Manita peć limited opening days

itinerary.title: Struge and Vaganski vrh, 1,757 m
itinerary.morning: From the Paklenica dom, take the long climb through beech to the **Struge** shelter at ≈1,400 m — the last water on the mountain, and it may not be there. Fill at Struge if the cistern holds; if not, turn the day around.
itinerary.afternoon: The ridge to **Vaganski vrh (1,757 m)**, Velebit's summit, with the Adriatic on one side and the Lika plateau on the other. Loose karst, real exposure to the seaward wind, T3 running. Descend by the ascent route — do not improvise a new line down this face.
itinerary.evening: Down, wash, and drive to Zadar. Last dinner in the old town inside the Roman forum walls.
itinerary.dayStats: 22 km / 1,450 m D+ / T3 on the ridge / 3 h 30–4 h 45; carry 2.5–3 L; summit 1,757 m
itinerary.sleep: Zadar, or out on a late flight

accommodationStrategy.name: Planinarski dom Zavižan
accommodationStrategy.description: Twenty-eight beds across small rooms and a dormitory, open **year-round**, with electricity and a telephone — genuinely unusual at this altitude in Croatia. It is the only sane base for the Premužić days, saving 90 minutes of gravel driving each way. The cistern is small: bring your own water for running and buy drinks from the warden rather than draining the supply. Bunk roughly €15–€25.

accommodationStrategy.name: Planinarski dom Alan
accommodationStrategy.description: Forty beds, a wooden cabin with a kitchen, **no electric lighting**, staffed daily from the end of May to the end of October and typically only on Sundays outside that. It is the natural end of the northern Premužić section and the gateway to Lubenovac. Bring a headtorch, food and a sleeping bag liner. The nearby Shepherds' Huts Alan sleep 24 from 1 May to 31 October with wood stoves and solar power, but their rainwater cistern is **not potable**.

accommodationStrategy.name: Seafront room in Starigrad-Paklenica
accommodationStrategy.location: coastal base for the southern half
accommodationStrategy.description: Two minutes from the Paklenica NP gate, so the Vaganski day starts without a drive, and directly on the water for post-run recovery. Rooms €45–€75 per night; most have a terrace, secure shoe-drying space and parking. Choose one on the north side of town to shorten the park approach.

logistics.connectivity: Croatia is inside EU roaming, so no surcharge. Signal is usable on seaward ridges and in Starigrad, **absent in Lubenovac, Šugarska duliba, the Rožanski towers and much of the Velika Paklenica floor**, and intermittent on the Oltari–Zavižan road. Offline maps are mandatory, not advisable.
logistics.emergency: **112** reaches **HGSS** (Hrvatska gorska služba spašavanja), the Croatian Mountain Rescue Service, whose Karlobag, Gospić and Zadar stations cover Velebit. Response to the Rožanski kukovi or the Vaganski ridge is measured in hours, not minutes. Croatia is in the EU and Schengen, so **EHIC/GHIC covers state treatment**, but helicopter extraction and repatriation are not covered — carry sports insurance that names mountain running.
logistics.weather: The **bura** is the headline: a cold, gusting, katabatic north-easterly that accelerates over the Velebit crest and hits the coast in violent bursts, closing the Maslenica bridge and the coastal road to high-sided vehicles. It can arrive in clear blue conditions. Summer afternoon thunderstorms build over the ridge from about 14:00. Temperature swing between Starigrad and Zavižan is routinely 12–15 °C.
logistics.bookingWindows: Zavižan and Alan bunks should be reserved through the huts or HPS **2–4 weeks ahead for June and September weekends**; midweek is usually walk-in-able but never assume. Manita peć runs on a **restricted opening schedule** — check the Paklenica NP site before building Day 6 around it. Starigrad rooms: 4–6 weeks in shoulder season, months in July–August.
logistics.money: Croatia uses the **euro** (since 2023). Cards work in Krasno, Starigrad and Zadar. **The mountain huts are cash** — carry €80–€120 in small notes for bunks, meals and water.
logistics.transportRules: A hire car is effectively mandatory; public transport does not reach Zavižan or Alan. Croatian motorway tolls are paid at barriers or by ENC transponder; the coastal Adriatic road is toll-free. The **Oltari–Zavižan forest road is a barriered gravel road**, snow-closed roughly November–May and unpleasant in a low car after heavy rain — check the gate status with the NP before committing. Cross-border hire into Bosnia (relevant if you detour to the Una) needs written permission and a green card.
logistics.permits: **Northern Velebit NP** and **Paklenica NP** charge separate daily entries of roughly €10 in season, sold at the gates and online. The **Rožanski and Hajdučki kukovi are a strict reserve**: staying on the marked Premužić trail is a legal requirement, not a suggestion, and off-trail movement there is prohibited. Wild camping is banned in both parks; bivouacking is tolerated only at designated points. Drones need permission. Do not take limestone, plants or the endemic Degenia velebitica.
logistics.health: Tap water in Krasno and Starigrad is potable; **cistern water is not, unless the warden says so** — carry a filter or purification tablets. **Ticks** are abundant in the beech and pasture zones April–October and Croatia has tick-borne encephalitis in the Lika region; check nightly and consider vaccination. **Poskok** (nose-horned viper, *Vipera ammodytes*) is genuinely present and genuinely venomous on the sunny southern slopes and in Paklenica — do not put hands into unseen rock. Brown bear, wolf and lynx live in Northern Velebit; encounters are rare and avoidance is simply noise.

proTips: **Treat water as the route-planning variable, not distance.** Plan every Velebit day backwards from where you can fill. If Struge's cistern is dry — and in September it often is — the Vaganski route becomes a 3 L carry or it does not happen.
**Phone Zavižan or Alan the day before and ask two questions:** is the cistern holding, and what is the wind doing on the ridge. The wardens give a better forecast than any app.

**Run the Premužić trail northbound if you can arrange the shuttle.** Alan → Zavižan gives you the Kvarner islands ahead of you in the light for the whole second half, and the net ascent lands earlier when you are fresh.

**Book a Zavižan bunk to skip the gravel road twice a day.** The Oltari approach eats 45 minutes each way and punishes hire-car suspension. Sleeping up there converts two commutes into two extra runs.

**Time Manita peć to its published opening days.** It runs on a short seasonal schedule with fixed hours, and a wasted 400 m climb to a locked cave gate is a genuinely dispiriting way to spend a morning.
**On a bura day, go into the Velika Paklenica canyon.** The walls shelter the floor almost completely while the ridge above is unrunnable, and the canyon is a full day on its own.
**Buy the paper 1:30,000 Velebit sheet at Kuća Velebita in Krasno.** Phone batteries die at 5 °C on the ridge, and the junction signage assumes you know which basin you are in.
**Wear shoes with a rock plate and full-cover uppers.** The *škrape* fissures here are the sharpest limestone in the Dinarides and will open both a mesh upper and a shin inside one week.
**Do the Zrmanja rest day properly.** Six easy kilometres and a cold swim between the Alan and Vaganski efforts is the difference between finishing the week and limping it.

raw.Zavižan – Premužićeva staza – Rossijeva: 12.4 km, 380 m D+, **1 h 20–1 h 50**. The purest stretch of the dry-stone path, running past the flanks of the Rožanski kukovi.
raw.Zavižan → Alan, full northern Premužić s: 16.5 km, 560 m D+ / 810 m D−, **2 h–2 h 50**. Point-to-point; needs a car shuttle or a hut night at Alan.
raw.Alan – Lubenovac – Alan circuit: 11 km, 420 m D+, **1 h 15–1 h 45**. Sinkhole pasture and abandoned shepherd settlements.
raw.Planinarski dom Paklenica → Struge → Vag: 22 km, 1,450 m D+, **3 h 30–4 h 45**. The week's big day and Velebit's highest point.
raw.Starigrad seafront + Zrmanja canyon rim: 6 km, 120 m D+, **35–50 min**. Recovery pace only.
raw.Technicality, stated on the SAC hiking s: The Premužić trail itself is a remarkable **T1–T2** for its altitude: graded, dry-stone-walled, never exposed, runnable at pace even where the surrounding terrain is vertical. Zavižan's summit spurs and the Lubenovac circuit are **T2**. Manita peć and the Anića kuk approach are **T2–T3** on polished, cabled rock steps. The Struge–Vaganski vrh ridge is **T3**: loose karst, a section of rock steps and real exposure on the seaward side in wind. Nothing on this itinerary requires a rope; nothing above T3 is included.
raw.Terrain composition, week average: ≈35% engineered dry-stone path and rock steps (the Premužić signature — hand-laid, wide enough for two, superb running surface), ≈25% bare fluted karst and rubble, ≈20% beech and black-pine forest singletrack, ≈12% gravel forest road, ≈8% grass sinkhole pasture. Croatian karst here is *škrape* — knife-edged fissured limestone that destroys soft uppers and lacerates hands in a fall. Rock plate, reinforced toe box, light gloves.
raw.Exposure and waymarking: Balkan standard **red circle with a white centre dot**, plus wooden signposts with hiking times (halve them for running). The Premužić trail is signed at both ends and at every junction; the **Velebitski planinarski put (VPP)** long-distance route shares much of it. Exposure on the Premužić section is negligible even where the drop beside it is not — the dry-stone parapets are the point. Exposure on the Vaganski ridge is real.
raw.Water refill points and month-by-month r: Velebit is porous karst with essentially **no surface water above 500 m**. Everything is cisterns and snowmelt.
raw.Zavižan hut (1,594 m): staffed year-round, but on a **limited-capacity cistern**. Water is available to guests and is sold; do not plan on filling four bottles for free. Reliable all season with courtesy.
raw.Rossijeva koliba: an unstaffed emergency shelter only. **No water, ever.**
raw.Alan hut (≈1,340 m): cistern water; staffed daily **end of May to end of October**, off-season usually only Sundays. Outside that window assume nothing.
raw.Shepherds' huts, Alan (1 May–31 Oct): rainwater cistern explicitly **not potable** — treat or boil.
raw.Lubenovac: the old shepherd cisterns are unreliable and often fouled. Do not count on them in any month.
raw.Struge (≈1,400 m, Paklenica): cistern fed by snowmelt and rain. Usually good **May–June**, dropping through July, and **frequently low or empty in late August and September**. This is the failure point on the Vaganski day.
raw.Velika Paklenica stream: flows well **March–May**, reduces to pools by July, often **dry August–September**. **Lugarnica** forest refreshment hut operates broadly April–October in daylight.
raw.Reliable taps: Krasno village, Starigrad-Paklenica, the Paklenica NP entrance. Fill there, every day, without exception. **Carry 2 L minimum on any Velebit ridge day and 2.5–3 L on the Vaganski route.**
raw.GPX sources and phone blackspots: GPX from the Croatian Mountaineering Association (HPS) Velebit Hiking Trail pages, the Northern Velebit NP site, Wikiloc and Komoot; the printed 1:30,000 Velebit sheets sold at the **Kuća Velebita** visitor centre in Krasno remain the reference. **Coverage:** decent on seaward-facing ridges with line of sight to the coast and around Starigrad; **dead in the Lubenovac and Šugarska duliba bowls, in the Rožanski kukovi, and for long stretches of the Velika Paklenica canyon floor.** The Oltari–Zavižan forest road has intermittent signal at best. Carry a fully offline map and tell the hut your plan.
raw.Bura management: The Senj–Velebit channel produces Europe's most notorious katabatic wind. Gusts of 150–200 km/h are recorded at the Maslenica bridge, which closes to high-sided vehicles and sometimes entirely. **A bura day is not a ridge day.** Signs: crystalline visibility, a lenticular cap on the ridge, a hard-edged cloud roll spilling seaward. Move the day to the sheltered Paklenica canyon floor or the Lika-side forest. Check DHMZ (meteo.hr) and the Zavižan station reading, which is the best real-time proxy for the ridge.
raw.Recovery: Day 5 is a true rest day: sea, the Zrmanja, and nothing above 120 m of ascent.

trips.title: Blue Blazes and Dry Karst: A Trail-Running Week in the Bükk and the Mátra
trips.subRegion: Északi-középhegység — the Bükk and Mátra ranges

bestPeriod.window: late April to mid-May, and the last two weeks of September into mid-October
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (35 °C in the Eger basin, no water on the Bükk plateau) and February–March (mud, ice on the north-facing rim)

accommodation.note: €145–€265 (€21–€38/night in panzió and turistaház beds)

food.note: €90–€140 (€13–€20/day — village konyha lunches, hut goulash)

transport.note: €45–€80 (trains, the Szalajka and Mátra forest railways, buses, one transfer taxi)

activities.note: €25–€65 (cave tours, lookout towers, a stamping book)

profile.difficultyNote: Moderate–Hard

trips.gatewayAirport: Budapest (BUD). Train Budapest-Keleti → Eger via Füzesabony, ~2 h; bus Eger → Szilvásvárad, ~45 min. Home: Gyöngyös → Vámosgyörk → Budapest, ~1 h 45.
trips.summary: Hungary's mountains top out at 1,014 m, which is why runners underrate them and then get quietly taken apart. Seven days of beech singletrack, limestone rim path and the oldest waymarked long-distance trail in…
trips.hook: Hungary's mountains top out at 1,014 m, which is why runners underrate them and then get quietly taken apart. Seven days of beech singletrack, limestone rim path and the oldest waymarked long-distance trail in Europe. The Bükk plateau is the hook: a karst tableland with almost no surface water, sinkholes underfoot, and a rock rim that drops 400 m in one step. Runnable, beautiful, and unforgiving about hydration.

snapshot.Start / End: Szilvásvárad → Mátrafüred (two bases, ~115 km running, ~4,300 m ascent)
snapshot.Getting there: Budapest (BUD). Train Budapest-Keleti → Eger via Füzesabony, ~2 h; bus Eger → Szilvásvárad, ~45 min. Home: Gyöngyös → Vámosgyörk → Budapest, ~1 h 45.

itinerary.title: Arrival and the Szalajka shakeout
itinerary.morning: Train from Budapest-Keleti to Eger, change at Füzesabony, then the bus north to **Szilvásvárad**. Drop bags and buy a *bélyegzőfüzet* before the shops shut.
itinerary.afternoon: Run the **Szalajka-völgy** floor: trout ponds, the open-air forestry museum, then the **Fátyol-vízesés**, a travertine cascade spreading like a veil over stepped limestone. Continue to the **Szalajka-forrás** at the valley head and turn back — 9 km of near-flat gravel and boardwalk.
itinerary.evening: Eat trout at one of the Szalajka út kitchens, then walk to the Lipizzaner stud paddocks. Check the plateau forecast: on the Bükk, fog matters more than rain.

itinerary.title: Istállós-kő, the roof of the Bükk
itinerary.morning: Away by 07:30 on the yellow trail up the valley's north side. Relentless but entirely runnable — beech, then hornbeam, then the sudden thin light of the summit meadow at **Istállós-kő (959 m)**. Stamp box at the top.
itinerary.afternoon: Follow the ridge west, turn south on the red trail toward **Bánya-hegy**, and drop back to Szilvásvárad on forest road and singletrack. Refill only at the Szalajka source — there is nothing on the ridge.
itinerary.evening: Arrange tomorrow's lift to Bánkút; there is no useful bus onto the plateau and a village taxi runs about €18–€25 (7,000–10,000 HUF) [VERIFY: current Szilvásvárad–Bánkút transfer fare].

itinerary.title: The rim: Bálvány, Tar-kő, Három-kő
itinerary.morning: Start at **Bánkút** (~890 m), the ski clearing on the plateau's western shoulder. Run east on the blue and red lines to **Bálvány (956 m)**, then out along the rim — the best running in Hungary: open grassy karst, dolina after dolina on your right, the Sajó basin below on your left.
itinerary.afternoon: **Tar-kő (950 m)** and **Három-kő (932 m)** are limestone prows standing clear of the forest above a 300–400 m drop, the only airy metres of the week. Then the interior: Nagy-mező's frost-hollow meadows, and **Jávorkút** for the day's only reliable water, before the forestry track back.
itinerary.evening: Sleep at **Bánkút** or drop to Szilvásvárad. Either way eat twice — the dry plateau air dehydrates you without your noticing [VERIFY: current Bánkút turistaház bed rates].

itinerary.title: Lillafüred, caves and the Garadna
itinerary.morning: Move east to **Lillafüred** (~320 m), where the Palotaszálló hangs over the Hámori lake. Run the green trail past the **Szinva-vízesés** — about 20 m, the highest waterfall in Hungary — then climb the Garadna on forestry track.
itinerary.afternoon: Up to Fehérkő-lápa and back down the ridge: shaded, spring-fed, gentle, exactly what tired quads need after the rim. Finish at the **Anna-barlang**, a rare limestone-tufa cave formed inside the waterfall's own deposits, and the dripstone **Szent István-barlang** next door; both guided, both short [VERIFY: current cave tour times and ticket prices].
itinerary.evening: LÁEV narrow-gauge into Miskolc for dinner, or stay and eat trout at Lillafüred. Reposition to the Mátra tonight or at dawn.

itinerary.title: Into the Mátra: Muzsla and Sástó
itinerary.morning: Eger to Gyöngyös by bus, then the **Mátravasút** narrow-gauge or the local bus up to **Mátrafüred** (~340 m). A different mountain entirely: andesite, softer contours, running water everywhere.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb the blue-triangle spur to **Muzsla-tető (805 m)** and its lookout, traverse north to **Sástó**, and descend on the red trail. Sástó's tower — a converted oil rig on the lakeshore — gives the cleanest view of the Kékes massif short of climbing it.
itinerary.evening: Mátrafüred is a small spa village with cheap kitchens; eat *bableves* and lay out tomorrow's kit. The Kékestető day is long.

itinerary.title: Kékestető and Galyatető on the Blue Trail
itinerary.morning: Out of Mátrafüred on the OKT's blue blaze, climbing through Sástó to **Mátraháza (~715 m)**, then the last pull to **Kékestető (1,014 m)** — the highest ground in Hungary, marked by a television tower with a public viewing deck [VERIFY: current Kékestető tower lookout hours and entry price]. Stamp the book.
itinerary.afternoon: West on the Kéktúra along the Mátrabérc ridge to **Galyatető (964 m)**, the country's second summit, with its stone tower above the beeches. Refill at Mátraháza and Galyatető — this is where the Mátra's springs earn their keep.
itinerary.evening: Bus down road 24 to Mátrafüred. Dinner, legs up, four stamp boxes in the book.

itinerary.title: Sirok, and out
itinerary.morning: An unhurried last run on the OKT's eastern Mátra section toward **Parádsasvár** and the volcanic ruin of **Sirok castle** on its tuff spike — the trail's hinge between the Mátra and the Bükk.
itinerary.afternoon: Bus to Gyöngyös, an hour in the baroque centre and the Mátra Museum, then the branch train to Vámosgyörk.
itinerary.evening: Train to Budapest-Keleti, 1 h 45. Eat *lecsó* and drink Egri Bikavér somewhere with a tablecloth.

accommodationStrategy.name: Szilvásvárad village panzió cluster
accommodationStrategy.description: Szilvásvárad sits at the mouth of the Szalajka valley, so Days 1 and 2 start from the door. The Egri út and Szalajka út guesthouses have drying space, laundry sinks, and hosts who will drive you up to Bánkút for the rim day.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead direct by phone or email; 2–3 months for May and October weekends.

accommodationStrategy.name: Bánkút turistaház
accommodationStrategy.description: the only bed actually on the Bükk plateau. It turns the 24 km rim traverse into a run starting at 900 m instead of 300 m, and puts you on the karst at dawn while the dolinas still hold mist. Bunk rooms, cash-friendly, no reliable signal.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct, 4–6 weeks ahead; confirm the kitchen is running before counting on dinner.

accommodationStrategy.name: Mátrafüred guesthouses off Parádi út
accommodationStrategy.description: the best vertical-to-doorstep ratio in the Mátra — Muzsla starts 200 m from the street and the OKT to Kékestető runs through the village. On the Mátravasút line and the road-24 bus route, so every run has a bail-out.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–3 weeks ahead; avoid the mid-August holiday fortnight when the village is full.

logistics.connectivity: Telekom, Yettel and Vodafone cover the Mátra ridge and Kékestető comprehensively. The Bükk plateau interior — Nagy-mező, the Tar-kő rim, the upper Garadna — is patchy to dead. Download offline maps; the OSM hiking layer renders the blaze colours accurately.
logistics.emergency: **112**, unified dispatch, English-speaking operators. There is no dedicated mountain-rescue corps; county disaster management and the volunteer *Magyar Barlangi Mentőszolgálat* handle cave incidents. Give your position by trail colour and nearest named feature — dispatchers know Tar-kő and Jávorkút.
logistics.weather: Continental and abrupt. Storms build over the Mátra from mid-May afternoons; the Kékes summit runs 8–10 °C colder than Gyöngyös. On the plateau the real hazard is autumn fog, which erases the rim and makes the dolina field genuinely disorienting. Frost hollows sit well below surrounding forest temperature at dawn.
logistics.bookingWindows: Nothing sells out except May and October weekends and mid-August. Lillafüred cave tours run to fixed departures and fill on summer Saturdays — take the first.
logistics.money: Forint, roughly **395 HUF to the euro** [VERIFY: current exchange rate]. Cards work in Eger, Gyöngyös and Miskolc, but the Bánkút hut, the Szalajka railway kiosk and village kitchens prefer cash — carry €50–€70 in small notes. Never change money at an airport kiosk or a street *pénzváltó* advertising "no commission".
logistics.transportRules: MÁV trains are cheap and reliable; buy in the MÁVPlusz app. With a bike, the **kerékpárjegy is 500 HUF**, valid 24 hours and one journey, plus a *kerékpárhelyjegy* of 100–990 HUF on InterCity and express services. Both forest railways are seasonal.
logistics.permits: This is **Bükki Nemzeti Park** and protected landscape. No permit or fee for running marked trails, but stay on them — leaving the blaze in a strictly protected zone (*fokozottan védett terület*) is an offence, and several plateau dolinas and cave mouths sit inside them. No wild camping, no open fire, no drones without written permission, dogs on leads.

proTips: **Treat the Bükk plateau as a desert crossing.** Two litres, salt, and a plan that touches **Jávorkút**. Runners get into trouble here not from terrain but from assuming a green Central European mountain must have streams. The water is 400 m below you, inside the rock.

**Buy the stamping book on day one.** Pressing a rubber stamp at Istállós-kő, Bánkút, Kékestető and Galyatető turns four separate runs into one coherent thing, and Hungarians will talk to you about it on the trail.
**Run the rim traverse west to east.** Bálvány first puts the morning sun behind you on Tar-kő and Három-kő, and lands Jávorkút's water at the two-thirds point rather than the start.
**Use the forest railways as one-way lifts.** The Szalajka line up the valley and the Mátravasút to Lajosháza let you run down instead of up. Locals do it routinely.

**September beats May by a nose** — same temperatures, drier limestone, fewer ticks, and the beech turn in the second week of October is the best week of the Bükk year. May's one advantage is wild garlic in the Garadna.

**Vaccinate against tick-borne encephalitis.** Hungary is endemic, these forests are prime habitat, and the schedule needs starting months ahead. Carry a tick remover: Nagy-mező's grass is thick with them from April.

raw.Named routes, distance and vertical: (1) **Szalajka–Istállós-kő loop**: Szilvásvárad (~300 m) up the *Szalajka-völgy* past the **Fátyol-vízesés** and the Szalajka source to **Istállós-kő (959 m)**, the Bükk's highest summit, back over Bánya-hegy — **18 km / +720 m**. (2) **The rim traverse**: Bánkút (~890 m) → **Bálvány (956 m)** → **Tar-kő (950 m)** → **Három-kő (932 m)** → Nagy-mező → **Jávorkút** → Bánkút, **24 km / +650 m**. (3) **Lillafüred–Jávorkút loop** up the Garadna and back over Fehérkő-lápa, **17 km / +610 m**. (4) **Muzsla circuit** from Mátrafüred (~340 m) over **Muzsla-tető (805 m)** and **Sástó**, **15 km / +620 m**. (5) **The Kéktúra spine**, Mátrafüred → Mátraháza → **Kékestető (1,014 m)** → **Galyatető (964 m)**, **26 km / +1,050 m** point-to-point.
raw.Waymarking: The **Országos Kéktúra (OKT)** — the National Blue Trail, laid out from 1938, the oldest long-distance marked path in Europe, roughly 1,170 km from Írott-kő to Hollóháza. Its blaze is a **horizontal blue bar on a white square**. All Hungarian trails share the grammar: horizontal bar for main lines; triangle for a summit spur, circle for a spring (*forrás*), L for a lookout.
raw.Technical grade: T1 to a soft T2, with short T2+ steps on the **Tar-kő** and **Három-kő** rim scrambles — no exposure needing hands for more than three moves. The difficulty is elsewhere: wet beech litter over polished limestone in October, ankle-swallowing *dolina* rims, and unmarked forestry junctions that look identical under closed canopy.
raw.Terrain split: Roughly 55% forest singletrack, 25% packed forestry road, 15% bare karst — plates, runnels, grikes — 5% asphalt. The Mátra is andesite: rounder, grassier, with real streams. The Bükk is Triassic limestone: faster when dry, treacherous when not.
raw.Water — the critical section: **The Bükk plateau has essentially no surface water.** Rain drains straight into the karst and re-emerges in valley springs hundreds of metres below the rim. Plan every plateau run around named sources: **Jávorkút** (piped, the plateau's one dependable tap), **Bolhás-forrás** near the Bálvány meadows, **Vörös-kő-forrás** below the northern rim — a genuine descent-and-reclimb, not a detour — and the **Szalajka-forrás** at the valley head. Carry **2 litres minimum** on the rim traverse and treat Jávorkút as the only guaranteed refill [VERIFY: current flow reliability of Bolhás-forrás and Vörös-kő-forrás in a dry autumn]. The Mátra is the opposite: Mátraháza, Kékestető, Sástó and Galyatető all have taps, and the Csörgő and Nagy streams run year-round.
raw.Bail-outs: Bánkút is driveable from Nagyvisnyó and Mályinka; Nagy-mező and Jávorkút sit on forestry roads. Lillafüred and Garadna are on the **LÁEV narrow-gauge** from Miskolc [VERIFY: current LÁEV timetable and fares]. In the Mátra, road 24 runs Gyöngyös–Mátrafüred–Sástó–Mátraháza–Kékestető with regular buses, so no route is more than 4 km from a stop. The **Szalajka forest railway** cuts 5 km off the valley when your legs are done [VERIFY: current fare and running season].
raw.The stamping book: The Kéktúra's *bélyegzőfüzet* is a passport carried by tens of thousands of Hungarians: stamp boxes (*bélyegzőhely*) hang at huts, lookouts and summit posts, and you press the rubber stamp into the book to prove passage. Buy one through the **Magyar Természetjáró Szövetség** or a tourist shop in Eger or Gyöngyös [VERIFY: current price of the bélyegzőfüzet]. On this route you can collect **Istállós-kő, Bánkút, Kékestető and Galyatető**. A phone app with GPS check-in exists; the physical stamps are the point.
raw.Race calendar: **Ultrabalaton** in mid-May — 221 km round Lake Balaton, solo or relay — is the gravitational centre of the Hungarian endurance year and empties every other May start list for a fortnight; enter it or avoid its weekend. In the mountains, the **Kékes uphill race** to the 1,014 m summit and the Bükk trail events based on Miskolc and Lillafüred are the fixtures [VERIFY: 2027 race dates, distances and entry fees].
