bestPeriod.raw: May to early October. May–June for long light and drier bog; September for firm ground and heather; avoid February–March when the peat is saturated

trips.summary: A seven-day trail running itinerary in County Wicklow / Dublin Mountains, Ireland.

itinerary.title: Arrive Dublin, Bray Head to Greystones
itinerary.morning: Fly into Dublin, DART train south to Bray — 45 minutes, right along the coast.
itinerary.afternoon: The Bray Head cliff path to Greystones: sea on one side, gorse on the other, a runnable 7 km with an optional climb to the cross on Bray Head (241 m). DART back from Greystones.
itinerary.evening: Fish and chips in Bray, then transfer inland to your Wicklow base. **Water:** town taps at both ends; carry a flask.

itinerary.title: Great Sugar Loaf and Djouce
itinerary.morning: Great Sugar Loaf (501 m) is a 45-minute quartzite cone from the Red Lane car park — steep, scree-topped, and the finest small hill in Ireland for effort-to-view ratio.
itinerary.afternoon: Move to the Wicklow Way at Crone Wood: the loop past Powerscourt Waterfall — Ireland's highest at 121 m — then up to Maulin and along the boardwalk over White Hill to Djouce (725 m), with Lough Tay, the "Guinness Lake", black below.
itinerary.evening: Roundwood, Ireland's highest village, and a pub dinner. **Water:** the Dargle stream below Powerscourt Waterfall; the Djouce boardwalk section is dry.

itinerary.title: Glendalough Spinc and Camaderry loop
itinerary.morning: From the Upper Lake car park, the railway-sleeper boardwalk climbs to the Spinc ridge above the Glendalough valley — the classic view down onto the monastic city and both lakes.
itinerary.afternoon: Extend north over Camaderry (700 m) on open bog, then descend the miners' road past the abandoned lead workings at Glendasan. Finish through the 6th-century monastic settlement with its round tower.
itinerary.evening: Glendalough. Early dinner; tomorrow is the long one. **Water:** the Glenealo river above the miners' village is excellent; the boardwalk ridge has none.

itinerary.title: Lugnaquilla, the county top
itinerary.morning: Lugnaquilla is 925 m and the highest mountain in Ireland outside Kerry. **Critical rule: the western approach through the Glen of Imaal crosses a live Defence Forces artillery range.** Check the published firing notices before you go, and if in doubt use the eastern approach from Glenmalure instead. `verify: true`
itinerary.afternoon: From Baravore in Glenmalure, climb through Fraughan Rock Glen — a hanging valley with waterfalls — onto the plateau. The summit is a broad flat dome called the Percy's Table with cliffs (the North and South Prisons) on either side; in cloud, navigate on a bearing and do not shortcut.
itinerary.evening: Glenmalure Lodge for food and a fire. This is the deepest glacial valley in Ireland and there is no phone signal at the head of it. **Water:** the Avonbeg river and the Fraughan Rock Glen streams — abundant and clean.

itinerary.title: Tonelagee, Lough Ouler and the Wicklow Gap
itinerary.morning: From the Wicklow Gap road, up Tonelagee (817 m). Lough Ouler sits in its northeast corrie in the shape of a heart — Wicklow's most photographed corrie lake, and it is a run, not a climb.
itinerary.afternoon: Traverse toward Turlough Hill and the pumped-storage reservoir on top, then down the Glenmacnass valley past the waterfall. The bog between Tonelagee and Turlough Hill is the deepest on this itinerary; keep to the peat ridges.
itinerary.evening: Laragh village. **Water:** Glenmacnass river; Lough Ouler's outflow.

itinerary.title: Mullaghcleevaun and the high bog crossing
itinerary.morning: Mullaghcleevaun (849 m), Wicklow's second summit, from the Oasis car park on the military road. Long featureless plateau running; this is the day you find out whether you can navigate.
itinerary.afternoon: Return via Duff Hill and Gravale on a rough line, or drop to the Sally Gap and run the military road — built by the British after 1798 to open the mountains, and now the loneliest tarmac in Leinster.
itinerary.evening: Return to Dublin, or a last night in Enniskerry. If it is a summer weekday evening, enter an **IMRA** race — the Irish Mountain Running Association runs a weekly midweek series across these hills, entry is a few euro on the night, and it is the fastest way into the local scene. `verify: true` **Water:** the Cleevaun Lough outflow; the plateau is otherwise a bog with no running water.

itinerary.title: Dublin shakeout and out
itinerary.morning: Easy 8 km around Phoenix Park — 707 hectares, twice the size of Central Park, with a resident fallow deer herd — or the Howth cliff loop if you prefer sea air.
itinerary.afternoon: Dublin Airport, 30 minutes from the city.

accommodationStrategy.name: Glenmalure Lodge
accommodationStrategy.description: An old coaching inn at the head of Ireland's deepest glacial valley, right at the Lugnaquilla and Fraughan Rock Glen trailheads. Rooms are simple; the location is unbeatable and the kitchen serves late enough for a slow day on the hill. No mobile coverage — tell someone your plan before you drive in.

accommodationStrategy.name: Wicklow Way Lodge / Roundwood-area B&Bs
accommodationStrategy.description: Purpose-built for walkers and runners, with drying space, early breakfasts and lifts to trailheads by arrangement. Central for Days 2, 3 and 5, and 30 minutes from the Sally Gap.

accommodationStrategy.name: Glendalough International Hostel (An Óige)
accommodationStrategy.description: Inside the national park beside the monastic site, with a kitchen and secure storage. Cheapest way to run the Spinc at dawn before the coach parties arrive at 10:00, which is the single best hour of the week.

logistics.connectivity: Good in the valleys and towns, absent on the plateaux and in Glenmalure. Download OSI 1:50,000 or OS Maps offline layers before you leave Dublin.
logistics.emergency: 112 or 999, ask for **Mountain Rescue**. Dublin and Wicklow Mountain Rescue covers these hills. Register your route with someone; there is no signal in Glenmalure, at the head of Glenmacnass, or on much of the Mullaghcleevaun plateau.
logistics.weather: Wicklow is only 900 m high but Atlantic cloud sits on the plateaux for days. The classic accident is a competent runner navigating off a featureless summit in 30 m visibility. Carry map, compass and the ability to use them — a phone with a dead battery in horizontal rain is not a navigation system.
logistics.bookingWindows: Glendalough and Glenmalure accommodation: 6–8 weeks for summer weekends. Car hire in Ireland: book early and read the insurance excess terms closely, Irish CDW rules differ from mainland Europe. `verify: true`

other.label: Live firing
other.text: The Glen of Imaal artillery range is active and marked with red flags and warning signs. Firing schedules are published in advance. Never cross a marked range boundary, never pick up metal objects, and use the Glenmalure or Camara Hill approaches when firing is scheduled. `verify: true`

other.label: Bog craft
other.text: After heavy rain, the peat between Tonelagee and Turlough Hill and around Duff Hill will take you to mid-thigh. Follow the drier heather ridges, not the direct line, and expect 30–50% slower splits than the distance suggests.

other.label: Access
other.text: Ireland has no general right to roam; upland access is by long-standing tolerance, not law. Close gates, never cross a field with livestock, and park only in designated car parks — the Wicklow parking situation at Glendalough and Sally Gap is a live local grievance.

proTips: Run the **Spinc at 07:00**. The Glendalough Upper Lake car park fills by 10:00 in summer and the boardwalk becomes a queue; at dawn the valley is yours and the light comes down the lake.
Enter a midweek **IMRA** race. It costs less than a pint, the courses are the local secret lines you would never find on a map, and the pub afterwards will tell you exactly which bog to avoid.
The **Military Road** over Sally Gap is the best warm-down drive in Ireland and the worst place to break down. Fuel up in Laragh or Enniskerry.
Two-car logistics unlock the good linear routes. Leave a car at Glenmalure and run Wicklow Way sections point-to-point instead of doing out-and-backs.
**Guinness Lake (Lough Tay) is private land** — the viewpoint from the R759 is the legal one, and the drone-shot angle everyone chases is not.

Pack for water, not for cold. Wicklow rarely goes below 5 °C in season but it will soak you completely; a waterproof with a stiff hood brim and spare dry socks in a bag beats an extra insulating layer.

raw.technical_rating: T2–T3; peat hags, deep heather, granite slabs, boardwalk sections
raw.water_strategy: Wicklow's upland streams run off granite and blanket bog — clear, peat-brown and generally safe above grazing, but filter anything below a sheep line

typeSpecific.technicalRating: T2–T3; peat hags, deep heather, granite slabs, boardwalk sections

trips.title: Cortina d'Ampezzo Ridgelines

bestPeriod.window: Late June–mid-July & early September–early October
bestPeriod.avoid: Late July–third week of August (peak Italian holidays, refuge queues, Tre Cime gridlock); November–May (snow on all high traverses, refuges closed)
bestPeriod.raw: Late June–mid-July & early September–early October

accommodation.note: Cortina 3★ €110–€190 dbl/night; rifugio half-board €65–€85

food.note: Refuge lunch €18–€26; Cortina dinner €35–€60

transport.note: Cortina Express both ways ~€52, local Dolomitibus, Tre Cime toll road, taxis

activities.note: Tre Cime road toll ~€30/car, Lagazuoi cable car ~€22 single, Faloria ~€20, tunnel headtorch

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5 — repeated 1,200–1,600 m days on high, exposed limestone; you need descending legs and a head for drops

trips.gatewayAirport: VCE — Venice Marco Polo (2 h 15 by Cortina Express coach, ~€26 one way, or 2 h drive); TSF — Treviso is a similar transfer
trips.summary: Cortina sits at 1,224 m in a bowl ringed by Tofane, Cristallo, Sorapis, Croda da Lago and Nuvolau, and almost every classic run here is a lift-assisted or road-assisted ascent onto a limestone balcony followed by a very long, very technical descent. The week builds from the postcard laps — Tre Cime, Cinque Torri, Lago Federa — into two genuine ridge days on the Nuvolau–Averau crest and the Lagazuoi WWI tunnel system, with one full recovery day on the valley Dolomiti bike path. Trails are CAI-numbered, superbly signed and busy: the whole game is being on them at 07:00 rather than 11:00. It suits a confident mountain runner who can descend 1,200 m of scree and rock step without wrecking their quads on day two.

itinerary.title: Arrive, and an easy Cinque Torri orientation lap
itinerary.morning: Cortina Express from Venice Marco Polo (2 h 15). Drop bags, collect a Tabacco 03 map from the newsagent on Corso Italia, and get lunch.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive or bus to the Bai de Dones lift and run the easy loop up to **Rifugio Scoiattoli** (2,255 m) and around the **Cinque Torri** WWI open-air museum trenches on CAI 439 — short, low-commitment, and the fastest way to learn what dolomite gravel feels like underfoot.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **Baita Fraina** above town — casunziei (beetroot ravioli) and a Lagrein.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km / 450 m D+ / T2 / 1 h 15–1 h 45; transfer 2 h 15.

itinerary.title: Tre Cime circuit at dawn
itinerary.morning: Leave Cortina at 06:00 for Misurina and the **Tre Cime toll road** to Rifugio Auronzo (2,320 m; car toll around €30, and access is periodically shuttle-only in high season — check the day before). Run the circuit anticlockwise on CAI 101 past Rifugio Lavaredo and **Forcella Lavaredo** for the classic north-face reveal at **Rifugio Locatelli**.
itinerary.afternoon: Complete the loop via Malga Langalm and CAI 105, then add the short spur to **Forcella Col di Mezzo** if legs are fresh. Coffee at Auronzo, down before the coach traffic peaks.
itinerary.evening: Aperitivo on Corso Italia, then dinner at **Al Camin** — smoked ricotta, deer, and grappa.
itinerary.dayStats: 10.2 km circuit / 380 m D+ / 1 h 10–1 h 40 / high point 2,454 m / toll ~€30 per car.

itinerary.title: Lago Federa and the Croda da Lago loop
itinerary.morning: Start at **Ponte de Ru Curto** on the Passo Giau road. Climb CAI 434 through larch forest to **Rifugio Palmieri al Lago Federa** (2,046 m), where the Croda da Lago wall drops straight into the lake — the best 20 minutes of forest running in the Ampezzo.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue on CAI 437 under the Croda's east face to Forcella Ambrizzola, then close the loop down to Ru Curto. Strong runners extend over Forcella Giau to Passo Giau and bus back.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **SanBrite** on the Alverà road — a working malga kitchen, everything from the family's own herd.
itinerary.dayStats: 14.5 km / 900 m D+ / T2–T3 / 2 h 30–3 h 20 / water at Palmieri only.

itinerary.title: Recovery day on the Lunga Via delle Dolomiti
itinerary.morning: True rest day. Jog or ride the **Lunga Via delle Dolomiti**, the old Calalzo–Dobbiaco railway bed, from Cortina north to **Ospitale** — packed gravel, 2% average gradient, viaducts and tunnels, zero technical demand.
itinerary.afternoon: Legs up. Cortina's outdoor pool, a massage, or the Museo della Grande Guerra. Restock food for the ridge days.
itinerary.evening: Pizza and a beer at a Corso Italia trattoria; nothing ambitious.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km out-and-back / 180 m D+ / 100% gravel rail-trail / 1 h 10 easy.

itinerary.title: Nuvolau ridge and a night at 2,413 m
itinerary.morning: Bus to **Passo Falzarego** (2,105 m). Climb CAI 441/440 to **Forcella Nuvolau**, then the cabled final steps to **Rifugio Nuvolau (2,575 m)** — a 360° platform over the Averau, Tofane and Marmolada.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop to **Rifugio Averau (2,413 m)**, run the Cinque Torri traverse on CAI 439/443 and the Averau circumnavigation, then return to Averau for the night. Sunset from the Nuvolau terrace is worth a second climb.
itinerary.evening: Half-board at Rifugio Averau — its kitchen is the best of any refuge in the Ampezzo; book weeks ahead.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km / 1,150 m D+ / T3 with cables / 3 h–4 h / sleeping at 2,413 m.

itinerary.title: Lagazuoi tunnels and the Sentiero Astaldi
itinerary.morning: Descend to Falzarego, take the **Lagazuoi cable car** to 2,778 m, and explore the **Galleria del Lagazuoi** WWI tunnel entrances with a headtorch — the running exit is the CAI 402 path down the Falzarego side, not the ferrata.
itinerary.afternoon: Transfer to **Rifugio Angelo Dibona** (2,083 m) and run the **Sentiero Astaldi** balcony under the Tofana di Rozes south face on CAI 404/412 to Pomedes, then descend to Cortina. Narrow, cabled in two places, and utterly exposed to the wall above.
itinerary.evening: Recovery dinner in town; order the local Ampezzo cheese board and go to bed early.
itinerary.dayStats: 18 km combined / 900 m up / 1,700 m down / T3 / cable car ~€22 / headtorch mandatory.

itinerary.title: Faloria descent and out
itinerary.morning: First Faloria cable car (2,123 m), then the long, fast descent via **Son Forca** and the CAI 215/212 forest trails toward **Passo Tre Croci** — the classic Cortina Trail (now branded Lavaredo 50K) descent section, and a chance to run one of the race's best fifteen kilometres.
itinerary.afternoon: Shower, a last plate of casunziei, and the Cortina Express back to Venice.
itinerary.evening: Departure from VCE.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km / 400 m up, 1,200 m down / 1 h 40–2 h 20; coach 2 h 15 to VCE.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Montana
accommodationStrategy.description: The pragmatic base: central enough to walk to the Dolomitibus stops and the Faloria lift, cheap by Cortina standards (€110–€160 double in shoulder season), and used to runners leaving before breakfast — ask for a packed bag the night before. Ski/boot room doubles as gear-drying space.

accommodationStrategy.name: Rifugio Averau
accommodationStrategy.description: The one night you should sleep high. Half-board, bunk rooms, and a kitchen with a reputation that fills the place on weekends — book six to eight weeks out for late June or September. It removes the Falzarego shuttle from both ends of the biggest ridge day.

accommodationStrategy.name: Camina Suite & Spa
accommodationStrategy.description: Last-night comfort with a proper wellness area for the post-Astaldi legs, ten minutes' walk from the centre and with parking, which in Cortina is the real luxury. €160–€240 a night, worth it once.

logistics.connectivity: Italy is EU; roaming at domestic rates. TIM and Vodafone both cover the valley and ridges well. **No signal in the Lagazuoi tunnels, in Val Travenanzes or in the Federa forest** — carry offline maps.
logistics.emergency: **112** for everything; the Soccorso Alpino Veneto operates helicopters out of Pieve di Cadore. Italian mountain rescue can bill non-residents for helicopter recovery — carry insurance with explicit heli-evacuation cover, and note that many policies exclude "via ferrata" ground, which the Astaldi and Lagazuoi sections may be read as.
logistics.weather: Afternoon convective storms are near-daily from mid-July to late August, typically firing between 14:00 and 17:00; the Dolomites also get sudden Adriatic-driven fog banks that erase visibility on the Nuvolau ridge in minutes. Check the ARPAV Veneto Dolomiti bulletin each morning. Early-season névé lingers in north-facing gullies into early July.
logistics.bookingWindows: Refuges take direct bookings by phone/email or through their own sites; **Averau, Nuvolau, Scoiattoli and Locatelli are the ones that sell out** — book 6–8 weeks ahead, more for August weekends. Cortina hotels for the first two weeks of August need 4–6 months. The Lavaredo/Cortina Trail races fill by lottery months ahead of the late-June event weekend.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards work almost everywhere including most refuges, but carry €80–€100 in cash — some high refuges and the Tre Cime toll booth prefer or require it. Tipping is not expected; round up.
logistics.transportRules: The **Tre Cime toll road** to Rifugio Auronzo charges roughly €30 per car and is subject to seasonal shuttle-only restrictions and daily quotas — verify the current rule before driving. Dolomitibus serves Falzarego, Giau and Tre Croci but with sparse timetables; check the last return. Italian motorways to Venice are tolled. Rental cars into Austria are usually permitted but need a vignette.
logistics.permits: No permit or fee to run the trails. Wild camping is prohibited across the Dolomiti d'Ampezzo natural park; bivouacking above 2,500 m from dusk to dawn is tolerated in practice but not guaranteed. Drones are banned over the park. The WWI tunnels are open free but you enter at your own risk.
logistics.health: Tap water throughout Cortina and the refuges is potable and excellent. Ticks are present in the larch forest below 1,800 m. Rockfall is the real hazard on the Astaldi and under the Tofana — a helmet is not absurd on that section. No altitude sickness risk below 2,800 m, but UV at 2,500 m is severe.

proTips: **Do Tre Cime before 07:30 or after 17:00.** The toll road and Auronzo car park saturate by 09:00 in summer; the same 10 km loop is a different, almost empty experience at dawn, with the north faces in shadow and the Cadini spires lit.

**Sleep at Averau to own the Nuvolau sunrise.** Guests can be on the 2,575 m summit terrace at first light with nobody else on the ridge — the single best photograph of the week and a 25-minute climb from your bunk.

**Halve the CAI signpost times.** Every wooden junction post gives walking hours. A mid-pack runner reliably does 50–55% of them on ascent and 40% on descent — use that to plan turnarounds rather than trusting a GPS estimate.
**Buy a Cortina Skyline / Dolomiti Supersummer lift pass only if you'll use three lifts.** Single rides on Faloria and Lagazuoi are €20–€22 and often cheaper than a multi-day pass for this itinerary.
**Carry a real headtorch, not a phone light, for Lagazuoi.** The tunnels are pitch dark, wet and uneven, and phone torches die fast in the cold.

**Run the Cortina Trail descent sections in reverse of race direction.** Faloria down to Tre Croci and the Ospitale rail-trail let you preview the course's decisive kilometres without the 48 km / ~2,650 m of the full race.
**Use the Lunga Via delle Dolomiti as your weather bail-out.** When the ridges are electric, the old railway gives you a shaded, safe, tunnel-covered 20 km at 2% gradient.
**Eat lunch at a refuge, not in Cortina.** A €20 plate of canederli at Palmieri or Averau at 2,000 m is both cheaper and better than the valley equivalent, and it solves your water resupply.

raw.Signature routes: (1) **Tre Cime di Lavaredo circuit** from Rifugio Auronzo (2,320 m) via CAI 101 → Forcella Lavaredo → **Rifugio Locatelli/Dreizinnenhütte** (2,405 m) → Malga Langalm → CAI 105: 10.2 km, 380 m D+, mid-pack 1 h 10–1 h 40. (2) **Croda da Lago loop to Rifugio Palmieri al Lago Federa** (2,046 m) from Ponte de Ru Curto on CAI 434/437: 14.5 km, 900 m D+, 2 h 30–3 h 20. (3) **Cinque Torri–Averau–Nuvolau ridge** from Passo Falzarego via CAI 441/439/440 to **Rifugio Nuvolau** (2,575 m, the oldest refuge in the Dolomites, 1883) and **Rifugio Averau** (2,413 m): 16 km, 1,150 m D+, 3 h–4 h. (4) **Sentiero Astaldi balcony**, Rifugio Angelo Dibona (2,083 m) → Pomedes under the Tofana di Rozes south face on CAI 404/412: 11 km, 700 m D+, 1 h 45–2 h 30. (5) **Faloria–Son Forca–Passo Tre Croci descent** off the Faloria cable car (2,123 m): 13 km, 400 m up / 1,200 m down, 1 h 40–2 h 20.
raw.Technicality (SAC hiking scale T1–T5, st: Tre Cime circuit **T2**, entirely runnable. Croda da Lago loop **T2–T3**. Nuvolau final ridge **T3** with cabled steps and genuine exposure on the summit approach. Sentiero Astaldi **T3**, a narrow balcony with fixed cable on two short sections — a slip is consequential. Lagazuoi tunnel exit **T3** and requires a headtorch; the full Galleria descent is via ferrata territory and beyond scope for running.
raw.Terrain split, week average: ~35% dolomite scree and gravel, ~25% hard rock step and slab, ~20% larch and pine forest singletrack on needle duff, ~15% white-gravel refuge access track, ~5% asphalt. Scree above Forcella Nuvolau is small, ball-bearing dolomite — light shoes with sticky rubber beat maximal cushioning.
raw.Waymarking: CAI red-white-red flashes with **numbered trail signs on wooden posts at every junction, with walking times in hours** — halve them for a mid-pack run. Alta Via 1 (marked "1" in a triangle) crosses the Falzarego–Nuvolau ground; Alta Via 3 runs the Cristallo side. Numbers used this week: 101, 104, 105, 401, 402, 404, 412, 434, 437, 439, 440, 441.
raw.Water refill points and month reliabilit: Refuges are the water system here: **Auronzo, Lavaredo, Locatelli, Palmieri, Scoiattoli, Averau, Dibona, Faloria, Lagazuoi** all sell or dispense water while open (roughly **20 June–20 September**, some to early October). **Rifugio Nuvolau has no spring** — water is hauled up, so buy, don't expect to refill free. Cortina town fountains and the Fanes/Ru Curto stream crossings are reliable all summer. Natural sources on the high karst plateaux are effectively **nil from mid-July** — this is porous limestone and it does not hold water. Plan 1.5 L minimum per high day.
raw.Navigation: Tabacco 1:25,000 sheet **03 "Cortina d'Ampezzo e Dolomiti Ampezzane"** is the standard; GPX from Dolomiti Trekking/Cortina Skyline portals, Komoot and the Lavaredo race site. Phone coverage is good on ridges and around refuges but **dead in the Lagazuoi tunnels, in the Val Travenanzes trench and on the Federa north side**. Bail-outs: Passo Falzarego, Passo Giau and Passo Tre Croci all have bus stops; the Faloria and Lagazuoi cable cars will take you down if the weather turns.
raw.Recovery, altitude and heat: Day 4 is a genuine low day on the valley floor. Working altitude is 2,000–2,800 m; sleeping at 1,224 m in Cortina means no acclimatisation problem, but expect 10–15% slower climbing pace on day one at altitude. Dolomite thunderstorms are near-daily from mid-July: be off the Nuvolau and Lagazuoi ridges by 14:00, and treat a rising anvil cloud over the Tofane as a hard turnaround signal.

typeSpecific.surface: ~35% dolomite scree and gravel, ~25% hard rock step and slab, ~20% larch and pine forest singletrack on needle duff, ~15% white-gravel refuge access track, ~5% asphalt. Scree above Forcella Nuvolau is small, ball-bearing dolomite — light shoes with sticky rubber beat maximal cushioning.
typeSpecific.technicalRating: Tre Cime circuit **T2**, entirely runnable. Croda da Lago loop **T2–T3**. Nuvolau final ridge **T3** with cabled steps and genuine exposure on the summit approach. Sentiero Astaldi **T3**, a narrow balcony with fixed cable on two short sections — a slip is consequential. Lagazuoi tunnel exit **T3** and requires a headtorch; the full Galleria descent is via ferrata territory and beyond scope for running.

sources.verified: The Lavaredo Ultra Trail by UTMB event is held in the last week of June out of Cortina and the historic Cortina Trail 50K is now presented within the UTMB-branded distance ladder (Lavaredo 120K/80K/50K/20K/10K); Rifugio Locatelli/Dreizinnenhütte at 2,405 m and Rifugio Auronzo at 2,320 m; Rifugio Nuvolau at 2,575 m as the oldest Dolomites refuge; VCE as base airport with a ~2 h 15 coach transfer.
sources.confidenceNotes: Re-verify (a) the **Tre Cime toll road price and whether private-car access is restricted to shuttle-only or a daily quota** in the travel month — this rule has changed repeatedly; (b) **exact 2026 race names, dates and course distances/elevation for the Cortina Trail / Lavaredo 50K**, which UTMB has re-branded; (c) **refuge opening and closing dates and half-board prices** for Averau, Nuvolau, Scoiattoli, Palmieri and Locatelli; (d) **Lagazuoi and Faloria cable-car fares and operating dates**; (e) **Sentiero Astaldi condition** — it is closed for rockfall repair in some seasons; (f) Cortina Express fares and timetable.

provenance.sourceFormat: md with '## Metadata' bullet block (one file per trip)

trips.title: The Principality Ridge — Fürstensteig and the Drei Schwestern

bestPeriod.note: The Fürstensteig ledges stay iced or snow-patched until mid-June and again from late October.

trips.gatewayAirport: Zürich (ZRH)
trips.summary: Liechtenstein's whole running country is one 25 km ridge — so you learn it, rehearse it, then run it end to end in a single day.
trips.hook: Liechtenstein is 160 square kilometres, and almost all of its good running sits on a single limestone crest above the Rhine. That is not a limitation once you accept it. You get to run the same ground twice, in different directions and different light, and you get to know a mountain range properly instead of collecting it.

snapshot.Base(s): Vaduz (nights 1–3), Malbun (nights 4–7)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 95–105 km and 5,500–6,000 m of ascent; Rhine gravel, alp track, limestone ledge and cabled rock, T1–T4
snapshot.Getting There: Fly Zürich (ZRH), train to Sargans or Buchs SG, LIEmobil bus 11 to Vaduz (approx. 25–30 min)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Runners with a head for exposure who would rather learn one range deeply than tick five

itinerary.title: The Rhine, Flat and Fast
itinerary.morning: Arrive in Vaduz, drop bags, fill bottles at the fountain in the Städtle. The country's only genuinely flat running is the Rhine dyke, and it is worth using properly.
itinerary.afternoon: Run the dyke path north from Vaduz through Schaan to Bendern and back — hard-packed gravel, T1, dead level at 450 m, the Drei Schwestern wall on your right throughout. Forty-odd minutes each way at easy pace.
itinerary.evening: Walk up to Schloss Vaduz's gate for the light on the crest, then eat in the Städtle.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 90 m ascent, T1, fully runnable. Water: Städtle fountain in Vaduz and the village fountain in Bendern.

itinerary.title: Eschnerberg, Aerobic Volume
itinerary.morning: Bus to Bendern and pick up the Historischer Höhenweg Eschnerberg, the 15 km way-marked route over the low limestone island of the Eschnerberg to Schellenberg. Forest, orchard edge and gravel farm track at 500–700 m, T1 with brief T2 root sections, and almost entirely runnable.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop back past the ruins of Obere Burg Schellenberg. If the legs allow, add the Schaan–Planken climb as a single 400 m tempo effort — a preview of Friday's approach.
itinerary.evening: Back in Vaduz. Eat early; tomorrow you learn the technical ground.
itinerary.dayStats: 20 km, 520 m ascent, T1–T2. Water: village fountains in Bendern, Schellenberg and Planken. **Bail-out:** LIEmobil buses run the valley floor constantly; nothing here is more than 3 km from a stop.

itinerary.title: Fürstensteig, the Rehearsal
itinerary.morning: Bus to Triesenberg and up to Gaflei (check the LIEmobil timetable — the Gaflei service is seasonal and thin; the alternative is a 500 m climb on foot from Triesenberg). From Gaflei the Fürstensteig starts almost at once: a ledge blasted into the west face in 1898, one metre wide in places, cable-secured, with several hundred metres of air below.
itinerary.afternoon: Follow the path to the Alpspitz saddle and on to the Kuegrat (2,123 m), the crest's high point, then return the same way. T4 where it is exposed — walking pace with hands — and T3 between. Reversing it while tired is the point: the ledges must be familiar before Friday.
itinerary.evening: Triesenberg for the terrace view down the Rhine valley, then Vaduz.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 900 m ascent, T4 on the ledges. Water: none on the ridge — carry 1.5 l; fill at the Triesenberg village fountain. **Bail-out:** the Fürstensteig is an out-and-back with no mid-route escape; the decision point is the Gaflei end.

itinerary.title: Relocation and the Fürstin-Gina-Weg
itinerary.morning: Move up to Malbun (1,600 m) on bus 21 via Triesenberg and Steg. Check in, then take the Sareisbahn chairlift to Sareis at 2,000 m.
itinerary.afternoon: Run the Fürstin-Gina-Weg south along the Sareiserjoch flank to the Bettlerjoch and the Pfälzerhütte (2,108 m) — a broad, grassy, panoramic traverse at T2, genuinely runnable for long stretches, with the Rätikon opening up into Austria and Switzerland. Descend from the hut into the Valünatal and out to Steg, or run back over the Joch to Malbun.
itinerary.evening: Malbun. Eat well and sleep; tomorrow is the whole point of the week.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km, 620 m ascent (plus 400 m bought on the chairlift), T2. Water: Bergrestaurant Sareis at the top station (open when the lift runs), Pfälzerhütte (staffed roughly mid-June to mid-October). **Bail-out:** ride the Sareisbahn back down; from Steg, bus 21 to Malbun.

itinerary.title: Peak Day: The Whole Crest, Planken to Gaflei
itinerary.morning: Early bus down to Schaan and on to Planken (800 m). Climb the forest path to the Gafadurahütte (1,428 m), then up onto the border crest for the Drei Schwestern (2,052 m) — the ridge that separates Liechtenstein from Vorarlberg, with the Austrian approach from Frastanz joining from the north-east. The Drei-Schwestern-Steig is cabled, ladder-assisted in two places, and unambiguously T4.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue south over the Garsellikopf (2,105 m) and along the crest to the Kuegrat, then reverse Tuesday's Fürstensteig down to Gaflei and the descent to Triesenberg. It is the length of the country's alpine skyline in one push, and the technical rehearsal on Day 3 is what makes the second half safe when you are tired.
itinerary.evening: Bus back to Malbun. Do nothing else.
itinerary.dayStats: 24 km, 1,750 m ascent, T4 in three distinct sections, T2–T3 between. Water: Gafadurahütte (staffed weekends and summer high season — treat it as a bonus, not a plan) and nothing else until Triesenberg. Carry 2 l. **Bail-out:** descend west from the Gafadurahütte to Planken, or bail from Gaflei; there is no exit from the crest between them.

itinerary.title: Naafkopf and the Three Countries
itinerary.morning: Sareisbahn again, then the ridge to the Augstenberg (2,359 m) — a straightforward, stony T3 line with big drops on the Austrian side but no cables — and down to the Pfälzerhütte.
itinerary.afternoon: From the hut, climb the Naafkopf (2,570 m), where Liechtenstein, Austria and Switzerland meet on one summit. T3, loose in the upper section, and a proper 460 m of climbing on tired legs. Return to the hut, then descend the Valünatal track to Steg — a fast, non-technical 6 km on alp road that lets you actually run.
itinerary.evening: Steg or Malbun for dinner.
itinerary.dayStats: 18 km, 1,150 m ascent, T3. Water: Pfälzerhütte (twice on this route — the single most useful refill in the country), Berggasthaus Sücka above Steg. **Bail-out:** the Valünatal track from the Pfälzerhütte is drivable by rescue vehicles and joins bus 21 at Steg.

itinerary.title: Valüna, Gänglesee, Home
itinerary.morning: Easy loop from Steg around the Gänglesee and up the Valünatal on the flat alp road as far as Alp Valüna, then back. Gravel, gentle gradient, T1 — 45 minutes of genuine recovery running at 1,300–1,500 m.
itinerary.afternoon: Bus 21 to Vaduz, then bus 11 to Sargans or Buchs for the train.
itinerary.evening: Zürich.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km, 220 m ascent, T1. Water: Alp Valüna in summer; the Steg fountain year-round.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Turna Malbun
accommodationStrategy.description: Fifty metres from the Sareisbahn base station, which is the start of three of this week's days, with a sauna, a drying room and a kitchen that will feed you after a long day out. Being at 1,600 m also means the last hour of every evening is spent recovering at altitude rather than in the valley.
accommodationStrategy.booking: March for July and August.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: CHF 160–230 (approx. €165–€240) per night for two, half board available

accommodationStrategy.name: Gasthof Löwen Vaduz
accommodationStrategy.description: A 14th-century building in the Städtle, five minutes from the bus interchange that reaches every trailhead in the country and directly on the flat Rhine running. The right base for the low, high-volume first half of the week.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead; Vaduz has very few beds.

logistics.emergency: works throughout Liechtenstein. Locally: 117 police, 118 fire, 144 ambulance. Helicopter rescue is flown by Swiss **Rega — 1414** — and a Rega patronage membership is worth more here than travel insurance small print.

other.text: works throughout Liechtenstein. Locally: 117 police, 118 fire, 144 ambulance. Helicopter rescue is flown by Swiss **Rega — 1414** — and a Rega patronage membership is worth more here than travel insurance small print.
Liechtenstein uses the Swiss franc. Cards work everywhere including huts, but the Pfälzerhütte and Gafadurahütte appreciate cash and can lose connectivity.
Liechtenstein is in Schengen and the Swiss customs union but outside the EU, so no EU roaming deal applies — buy a Swiss eSIM. Coverage is good on the crest, patchy in the Valünatal.

LIEmobil bus 21 (Vaduz–Triesenberg–Steg–Malbun) is the spine of the week and runs roughly hourly, more often in high season. Buy a day ticket from the driver or use the LIEmobil app; the Gaflei branch is seasonal and sparse.

Wild camping and bivouacking are prohibited in the Liechtenstein alpine zone, and much of the ridge is a protected area. Drones require authorisation and are effectively off-limits near the border crest.

The Fürstensteig closes after rockfall and stays closed until the route is cleared. The Liechtenstein Marketing hiking pages and notices at the Gaflei and Malbun trailheads carry the status — check the morning you plan to run it.
The Pfälzerhütte is run by the Liechtensteiner Alpenverein and takes bookings by phone and online; even for a day visit, a call the evening before tells you whether the kitchen is open.

proTips: Run the Fürstensteig southbound in the morning and northbound in the afternoon. The face is west-facing, so morning gives you shade and dry rock, and afternoon gives you light down the Rhine.
The Sareisbahn's first ride of the day is usually mid-morning, not dawn. If you want an early start on Day 6, climb to Sareis on foot in 55 minutes and save the lift for the descent.
The Liechtenstein Trail's 75 km of way-marked route links all eleven municipalities and is signposted throughout — use its markers as a backup navigation layer when cloud drops onto the crest.
Stay in Malbun and ask about the guest card: several hotels include LIEmobil bus travel, which covers your entire transport budget for the second half of the week.
Weekdays on the Drei Schwestern are close to solitary; on Sundays Vorarlberg day walkers arrive from the Austrian side and the cabled sections become single-file queues.
Book one night at the Pfälzerhütte (2,108 m) to turn Day 6 into a two-day traverse and drop the Sareisbahn dependency.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 95–105 km and 5,500–6,000 m of ascent; Rhine gravel, alp track, limestone ledge and cabled rock, T1–T4
raw.Who It Suits: Runners with a head for exposure who would rather learn one range deeply than tick five

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 95–105 km and 5,500–6,000 m of ascent; Rhine gravel, alp track, limestone ledge and cabled rock, T1–T4
typeSpecific.audience: Runners with a head for exposure who would rather learn one range deeply than tick five

packingNotes: Shoes with a firm edge and reliable grip on smooth limestone. Soft, cushioned trainers slide on the polished Fürstensteig ledges.
Light gloves. There is more cable-handling on the Drei-Schwestern-Steig than most runners expect.
Two-litre carrying capacity for Day 3 and Day 5 — the crest has no water at all.
Swiss francs in small notes for hut drinks and bus tickets.
A wind shell that survives a Rätikon föhn, plus a warm layer for the Naafkopf summit.
Sun protection: the ridge is entirely shadeless from the Alpspitz southwards.
A paper 1:25,000 map of the Liechtenstein Alps or an offline map layer — cloud on the crest removes every visual reference at once.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Wet rock on the Fürstensteig.** The ledges are slick and unforgiving in rain. Swap to the Eschnerberg or the Valünatal on any wet morning; the ridge is not worth it.
**Fürstensteig closed for rockfall.** The fallback peak day is Malbun–Sareis–Augstenberg–Pfälzerhütte–Naafkopf–Steg, which delivers similar distance and vert without exposure.
**Thin bus service.** Miss the last bus 21 from Malbun and you are looking at a 15 km road descent to Triesenberg. Photograph the timetable at the stop on your first day.

**Underestimating a small country.** Ninety-five kilometres with 6,000 m of ascent in a week is a serious load regardless of the map's scale. If Day 5 goes badly, cut Day 6 to the Sareis–Pfälzerhütte traverse and keep the recovery day intact.

trips.title: Little Switzerland Underfoot — The Mullerthal Trail

bestPeriod.note: Sandstone slabs, roots and wooden steps turn treacherous once leaf-fall and winter damp set in.

trips.gatewayAirport: Luxembourg (LUX)
trips.summary: Three linked Mullerthal Trail routes through sandstone crevices and beech plateau, run from Echternach on Luxembourg's free public transport.
trips.hook: Nothing here goes above 420 metres, and that fools people. The Mullerthal's vertical arrives in fifty-metre instalments — down a rock crevice, up a wooden staircase, along a root ladder — a hundred times a day. It is the most technical low-altitude running in the Benelux, and the whole week is reachable on buses that cost nothing.

snapshot.Base(s): Echternach, with runs from Berdorf, Consdorf, Mullerthal, Beaufort and Larochette
snapshot.Best Period: April to June and September to October
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 125–135 km and 3,200–3,600 m of ascent; sandstone slab, root, beech leaf-litter, wooden steps and iron rungs, T1–T2 with short T3 passages
snapshot.Getting There: Fly Luxembourg (LUX), RGTR bus 111 to Echternach (approx. 50 min) — free, like all Luxembourg public transport
snapshot.Who It Suits: Runners who want technical footwork and daily volume rather than altitude

itinerary.title: Echternach, the Lake and the Zickzack
itinerary.morning: Arrive, drop bags, and walk the abbey quarter — the Basilica of St Willibrord and the arcaded Denzelt on the Place du Marché are the town's two fixed points, and the market square fountain is your most reliable refill of the week.
itinerary.afternoon: Easy shakeout on the Lac d'Echternach circuit, roughly 3.5 km of flat gravel, then take the Zickzack switchbacks up to the Troosknäppchen viewpoint above town for a first taste of what Luxembourg calls a climb. Sandstone underfoot, beech overhead, T1.
itinerary.evening: Eat on the Place du Marché. Check the Mullerthal Trail signage system before tomorrow: white on black, with route numbers 1, 2 and 3 and lettered Extra Tours.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km, 220 m ascent, T1, fully runnable. Water: Place du Marché fountain, Echternach; taps at the lake recreation area in season.

itinerary.title: Route 1 into the Crevices
itinerary.morning: Start from Echternach on Mullerthal Trail Route 1 heading west. The trail climbs onto the plateau and then drops you straight into the sandstone: the Wolfsschlucht (Gorge du Loup), a metre-wide fissure with fixed steps, and the Hohllay, a Roman-era quarried cave where millstones were cut.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue past the Perekop rock stack and the Kohlscheuer to Berdorf. The plateau between the rock groups runs beautifully — firm, level, shaded — while the crevices are strictly walking. Pace swings between 5 and 15 minutes per kilometre inside the same hour.
itinerary.evening: Bus back to Echternach, ten minutes. Berdorf sits directly above the town and the service is frequent.
itinerary.dayStats: 19 km, 520 m ascent, T2 with short T3 steps and ladders. Water: Berdorf village centre and the campsite tap on the Berdorf–Echternach road; nothing drinkable in the gorges. **Bail-out:** the plateau road from Berdorf to Echternach shadows the trail the whole way.

itinerary.title: Route 2 and the Schiessentümpel
itinerary.morning: Bus to Berdorf, then Route 2 south through the Kasselt and the Aesbach valley. This is the wettest, mossiest ground of the week: black sandstone walls, ferns, and long stretches of duckboard and step. Grade T2, with a real premium on foot placement.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop to Mullerthal village and the Schiessentümpel, the triple-stepped waterfall under a stone footbridge that ends up on every postcard of the region. Pick up the trail again past the Heringer Millen mill complex and climb to Consdorf, then take the bus back.
itinerary.evening: Echternach. Legs will be sore in unfamiliar places — the ankles and the hip stabilisers, not the quads.
itinerary.dayStats: 23 km, 680 m ascent, T2. Water: Heringer Millen at Mullerthal has a restaurant and visitor centre (closed one or two days a week outside high season — check before relying on it), and Consdorf village has a fountain. **Bail-out:** buses serve Mullerthal and Consdorf; the Mullerthal valley road runs alongside the trail for most of its length.

itinerary.title: The Sûre, Flat and Wide
itinerary.morning: Deliberate down day. Run the Sûre valley path east from Echternach along the German border towards Rosport and Steinheim — level, open, gravel and grass, with the river on one side and vineyard-facing slopes on the other.
itinerary.afternoon: Turn at Rosport, where the Henri Tudor museum occupies the battery inventor's family home, and run back. No rock, no steps, no technical work at all. That is the point.
itinerary.evening: An early night. Tomorrow is 33 kilometres.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km, 160 m ascent, T1, entirely runnable. Water: Rosport village fountain; the Echternach lake taps at the finish. **Bail-out:** hourly buses shadow the Sûre road on both the Luxembourg and German banks.

itinerary.title: Peak Day: Larochette to Echternach
itinerary.morning: First bus to Larochette, under its ruined 11th-century castle. Pick up Mullerthal Trail Route 3 heading north-east through the Nommerlayen rock group's beech woods and on across the plateau towards Beaufort.
itinerary.afternoon: At Beaufort, the medieval castle and its Renaissance neighbour sit side by side above the Hallerbach; it is the natural food-and-water halfway point at roughly 15 km. From there run east on Route 2 through the Schnellert, then join Route 1 at Berdorf for the last long descent past the Werschrumschlëff crevice into Echternach.
itinerary.evening: Do not attempt anything except food. This is the day the week is built around, and 33 km of Mullerthal footwork costs more than 33 km of anything flatter.
itinerary.dayStats: 33 km, 1,050 m ascent, T2 throughout with several T3 crevice passages. Water: Beaufort village and castle area at 15 km, Berdorf at 25 km. Carry 1.5 l between them. **Bail-out:** Beaufort, Berdorf and Consdorf all have bus stops on the route; the trail is never more than 3 km from a village.

itinerary.title: Berdorf's Rock Gymnasium
itinerary.morning: Bus to Berdorf for the shortest, most technical day. Work the Extra Tour loops around the village: the Werschrumschlëff, the Predigtstuhl, the Siwenschlëff's seven pinnacles, the Huel Lee, and the Kuelscheier passage, where the trail squeezes between walls barely wider than your shoulders.
itinerary.afternoon: Finish at the Amphitheatre Breechkaul, a former quarry with tiered stone seating still used for summer performances. Then run the plateau back down to Echternach on Route 1 in reverse.
itinerary.evening: Echternach for the last proper dinner.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km, 480 m ascent, T2–T3 in the crevices. Water: Berdorf village centre. **Bail-out:** every loop returns to Berdorf within 4 km, and the bus runs from the village square.

itinerary.title: Weilerbach and Out
itinerary.morning: Easy 8 km along the Sûre to Weilerbach and back, or a second lap of the Echternach lake. Twenty-five minutes out, twenty-five minutes back, nothing hard.
itinerary.afternoon: Coffee on the Place du Marché, then bus 111 out. With three spare hours, break the journey in the capital and walk the Chemin de la Corniche above the Grund.
itinerary.evening: Fly out.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km, 100 m ascent, T1. Water: Echternach market square fountain.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Bel Air Sport & Wellness
accommodationStrategy.description: Set in its own park on the edge of town with a pool, sauna and gardens to stretch in, and a five-minute jog from the Route 1 trailhead and the lake. The wellness side matters on a week whose damage is tendon-and-ankle rather than lung.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead; May and the Whitsun dancing-procession weekend sell out.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel-Restaurant Bisdorff
accommodationStrategy.description: Long-established in the middle of Berdorf, which puts you inside the rock groups rather than below them: the Werschrumschlëff, Predigtstuhl and Hohllay are all within twenty minutes on foot. It has a pool, a serious kitchen and the local knowledge to tell you which passages are closed.
accommodationStrategy.booking: March for spring dates.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €120–€180 per night for two, half board available

logistics.emergency: Emergency is **112** for rescue and ambulance, **113** for police. In the gorges, give the nearest named rock formation — the trail signage names them and rescuers know them.

other.text: Emergency is **112** for rescue and ambulance, **113** for police. In the gorges, give the nearest named rock formation — the trail signage names them and rescuers know them.
All public transport in Luxembourg — bus, train and tram, second class — has been free since 2020. There is no ticket, no validation and no zone. Use the Mobiliteit.lu app for live timetables.
Mobile coverage is strong on the plateau and unreliable at the bottom of the Wolfsschlucht, Kuelscheier and Aesbach. Download offline maps before you start.
Sandstone is the whole story. Wet rock, wet roots and wet wooden steps are all slippery; after rain, expect the technical sections to take fifty per cent longer.
Rock climbing in the Berdorf sector is regulated and zoned, and some passages close seasonally for nesting birds or after rockfall. Signage at the trailhead is authoritative.
Wild camping and open fires are prohibited across the Mullerthal, and dogs must be leashed in the nature reserve zones.
Luxembourg keeps banking hours: village shops shut for a long lunch and most close on Sunday. Buy running food in Echternach on Saturday.

proTips: Run the crevices early. The Wolfsschlucht and Kuelscheier are single-file passages that fill with family walking groups from about 10:30 in season; before nine you will have them entirely.

Order the Mullerthal Trail map from the regional tourist office in Echternach rather than relying on GPX alone — the numbered junction posts on the ground match the printed sheet and make improvised shortcuts trivial.
The plateau above Berdorf is where you do actual running training: long, flat, firm forest track. Save your interval sessions for it and treat the gorges as strength work.
Use the free buses to run everything one-way. There is no reason to do out-and-backs here, and linear days let you follow the trail's logic instead of fighting it.
Beaufort's two castles are the only substantial refreshment point on Day 5's middle third. Check their opening season before you plan your water around them.
If it has rained hard, swap the Aesbach and Kasselt sections for the Sûre valley path — the gorge duckboards become genuinely dangerous, and the river route runs the same distance flat.
Echternach's Hopping Procession falls on Whit Tuesday and fills every bed for miles. Come for it deliberately or avoid that week.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 125–135 km and 3,200–3,600 m of ascent; sandstone slab, root, beech leaf-litter, wooden steps and iron rungs, T1–T2 with short T3 passages
raw.Who It Suits: Runners who want technical footwork and daily volume rather than altitude

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 125–135 km and 3,200–3,600 m of ascent; sandstone slab, root, beech leaf-litter, wooden steps and iron rungs, T1–T2 with short T3 passages
typeSpecific.audience: Runners who want technical footwork and daily volume rather than altitude

packingNotes: Aggressive lugs and a soft, grippy outsole. This is mud-and-wet-rock terrain, not alpine scree, and stiff mountain shoes are the wrong tool.
Long socks or light gaiters — the crevice passages are abrasive and the plateau has nettles through summer.
1.5 l carrying capacity for Day 5; 750 ml is enough for every other day.
A light waterproof. The Mullerthal is wooded and sheltered, so wind shells matter less than staying dry.
Offline maps plus the printed Mullerthal Trail sheet — the beech canopy degrades GPS accuracy in the valleys.
A head torch if you run in October: the gorges are dark by 17:30 well before the plateau is.
Tick protection from April onwards. Luxembourg's beech woods have a real tick population and TBE is present in the wider region.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Rain turns the technical sections lethal.** Wooden steps and mossy slabs shed grip almost completely. Fall back to the Sûre valley and the Echternach lake circuit; both give volume with no consequence.
**A closed passage.** Rockfall and nesting closures happen and are enforced. Every rock group has a marked bypass on the plateau — take it rather than improvising through private forest.

**Underestimating cumulative load.** Three thousand-plus metres of stair-stepping in a week wrecks calves and Achilles tendons. If Day 3 leaves you limping, cut Day 5 to the Beaufort–Echternach half and keep the week intact.

**Missing the last rural bus.** Village services thin out sharply after 19:00 and on Sundays. Check the return before you start any linear day, and note that Echternach has no railway station — the nearest is Wasserbillig.

trips.title: Sea Level to Summit — Running Monaco's Hinterland

bestPeriod.note: July and August bring heat above 30°C and prefectural fire closures on the limestone massifs.

basecamps: Monaco (or Beausoleil, 200 m across the border)
trips.gatewayAirport: Nice Côte d'Azur (NCE)
trips.summary: A Riviera running week from a two-square-kilometre basecamp, climbing straight from the Mediterranean to the 900 m limestone ridges above Monaco.
trips.hook: Monaco is two square kilometres and you can run across it in eleven minutes. That is precisely why it works: the border is invisible, the mountains start at the last apartment block, and within twenty minutes of leaving the port you are on a limestone path with nothing but sea below you. Everything in this week except the first and last kilometre happens in France.

snapshot.Country: Monaco (routes run into the Alpes-Maritimes, France)
snapshot.Base(s): Monaco or Beausoleil, with runs from Cap d'Ail, La Turbie, Èze, Roquebrune and Menton
snapshot.Best Period: March to May and October to November
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 115–125 km and 5,800–6,400 m of ascent; limestone, pine needle, scree, stone stairway and coastal path, T1–T3
snapshot.Getting There: Fly Nice (NCE), then the airport express bus or tram plus TER to Monaco-Monte-Carlo (approx. 45–60 min)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Runners who like relentless gradient, sea views and a base where dinner costs more than the flight

itinerary.title: The Sentier du Littoral, Sea Level
itinerary.morning: Arrive, drop bags, and start with Monaco's own peculiar terrain: the public lifts and escalators linking the tiers of the city, and the stone ramps to the Rocher. The Rampe Major from port to Palace is the classic — a genuine strength session if you take it four times.
itinerary.afternoon: Train or run west to Cap d'Ail and pick up the Sentier du Littoral below the Cap, from Plage Marquet round to Plage Mala. Rock-cut steps, sea spray, pine tunnels and a few exposed sections above the water — T2 because of the steps, not the difficulty.
itinerary.evening: Eat in the Condamine market hall, which is the only sensible-value food in the Principality.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 400 m ascent, T1–T2. Water: public taps at Plage Marquet and Plage Mala (seasonal, spring to autumn), fountains throughout Monaco's parks. **Bail-out:** Cap-d'Ail station sits directly above the path.

itinerary.title: Mont des Mules and the Trophée
itinerary.morning: Climb out of Beausoleil on the Sentier du Mont des Mules, the botanical path up the 520 m limestone knuckle behind Monaco. Short, sharp, well-marked T2, with an Iron Age oppidum on top.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue north towards La Turbie and the Trophée des Alpes, Augustus's 6 BC victory monument on the Grande Corniche at 480 m, then drop back down the old mule path to Beausoleil.
itinerary.evening: Stretch. The gradient is unforgiving in both directions and the descents are what hurt.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km, 750 m ascent, T2. Water: the village fountain in La Turbie's old centre, reliable year-round; nothing on the Mont des Mules loop. **Bail-out:** the Monaco–La Turbie bus runs from the village square down to Monaco.

itinerary.title: Tête de Chien and the Grande Corniche
itinerary.morning: Train one stop to Cap-d'Ail, then climb to the Tête de Chien — the 550 m headland hanging directly over Monaco, capped by a 19th-century fort that is military property and closed. The path to the belvedere edge is public, and the view down onto the Rocher is the defining image of the region.
itinerary.afternoon: Traverse north to La Turbie on the Grande Corniche paths, then descend the long ridge line back towards Monaco. Roughly 800 m of climbing with a fast, stony descent — T2, with short T3 steps where the path crosses slab.
itinerary.evening: Larvotto for a swim — around 16–18°C in April, 20–22°C in October.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km, 830 m ascent, T2–T3. Water: La Turbie village fountain; the Golf de Monte-Carlo clubhouse at La Turbie serves non-members. **Bail-out:** drop west to Èze-sur-Mer or east to Cap-d'Ail, both on the Nice–Ventimiglia line.

itinerary.title: Cap Martin, Deliberately Flat
itinerary.morning: Recovery day. Train to Roquebrune-Cap-Martin and run the Promenade Le Corbusier round the headland to Menton — a paved and rock-cut sea-level path past the Cabanon Le Corbusier built for himself in 1952 and the villa Eileen Gray designed above it.
itinerary.afternoon: Menton: the Marché des Halles, the old-town stairways to the cemetery terrace, then the train home.
itinerary.evening: Early bed. Tomorrow is the big one.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 250 m ascent, T1. Water: fountains along the Carnolès promenade and in Menton's old town. **Bail-out:** three stations within 5 km of any point on this route.

itinerary.title: Peak Day: Sainte-Agnès, Col de la Madone, Mont Agel
itinerary.morning: First train to Menton, then climb the old path towards Sainte-Agnès, at 800 m the highest coastal village in Europe and a fortified balcony above the sea. It is a sustained 800 m of hot, stony, exposed T2 climbing — start at first light.
itinerary.afternoon: Contour west to the Col de la Madone at 925 m, the pass professional cyclists use for testing, then work along the flank of Mont Agel. Be clear about Agel: its 1,148 m summit is a French Air Force radar station, permanently closed. The runnable ground is the shoulder below it, past the Golf de Monte-Carlo course at around 900 m, then the long descent through La Turbie to Monaco.
itinerary.evening: Salt, carbohydrate, sleep.
itinerary.dayStats: 30 km, 1,750 m ascent, T2 with T3 sections above Sainte-Agnès. Water: Sainte-Agnès village fountain at 8 km, Gorbio village fountain on the alternative line, La Turbie at 24 km. Carry 2 l — the Madone traverse is dry and shadeless. **Bail-out:** descend from Sainte-Agnès or Gorbio to Menton, both served by local buses; from La Turbie, the bus to Monaco.

itinerary.title: Parc de la Grande Corniche and the Sentier Nietzsche
itinerary.morning: Bus or train west to Èze and into the Parc naturel départemental de la Grande Corniche. Run the plateau paths past the Fort de la Revère at 740 m — a Second Empire fort now a viewpoint and picnic area — over the Plateau de la Justice and the Mont Bataille top on the ridge above La Turbie.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop to Mont Bastide, the Ligurian hill settlement above Èze village, then descend the Sentier Nietzsche — the stepped path the philosopher walked while composing part of *Zarathustra* — 400 m to Èze-sur-Mer. Steep, stony, T2, hard on tired quads.
itinerary.evening: Train back along the coast at sunset.
itinerary.dayStats: 19 km, 900 m ascent, T2. Water: the picnic area at the Fort de la Revère has a tap that runs seasonally — do not plan on it; the fountains in Èze village are dependable. **Bail-out:** the Moyenne Corniche bus between Nice and Beausoleil stops at Èze village; Èze-sur-Mer station is at the bottom of the Sentier Nietzsche.

itinerary.title: Stairs, Gardens, Departure
itinerary.morning: Shakeout inside the Principality: the Jardin Exotique cliff terraces, the Parc Princesse Antoinette, then down through the public lifts to the port and a lap of Larvotto.
itinerary.afternoon: Coffee on the Place d'Armes, then the train or express bus to Nice airport.
itinerary.evening: Out.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km, 300 m ascent, mostly stairs and paved terrace, T1.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Olympia
accommodationStrategy.description: Two hundred metres over the French border and roughly a third of Monaco's room rate, which is the single biggest saving available on this trip. It also sits at the foot of the Mont des Mules path, so Day 2 starts at the door and every La Turbie run begins uphill from reception.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead; avoid Grand Prix weekend entirely.

accommodationStrategy.name: Novotel Monte-Carlo
accommodationStrategy.description: Built into the slope above the station on Boulevard Princesse Charlotte, with a pool, a garden terrace and direct lift access down to the port. Being on top of Monaco-Monte-Carlo station matters when four of the week's days start with a train.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four months ahead in spring and autumn.

logistics.emergency: works in both Monaco and France; inside the Principality 17 is police and 18 fire and medical. In the French hinterland rescue comes through 112 — name the commune and the nearest marked path.

other.text: works in both Monaco and France; inside the Principality 17 is police and 18 fire and medical. In the French hinterland rescue comes through 112 — name the commune and the nearest marked path.
There are no border controls and the currency is the euro, but EU roaming does not apply on Monaco's own network — lock your phone onto a French operator.

The TER Nice–Ventimiglia line is the backbone: every 20–30 minutes, stopping at Cap-d'Ail, Monaco-Monte-Carlo, Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, Carnolès and Menton. Buy on SNCF Connect; validate any paper ticket before boarding.
Zou! bus line 100 runs the Basse Corniche between Nice and Menton for a couple of euros; the Moyenne Corniche line serves Èze village, and Monaco's CAM buses cover the Principality and La Turbie.

From roughly 1 July to 30 September the Alpes-Maritimes prefecture publishes a daily fire-risk map, and access to the wooded massifs — including the Grande Corniche park — can be closed outright. Check the prefecture site the night before.
Monaco's public lifts and escalators are free and run from early morning to around midnight — the fastest link between port, station and Jardin Exotique.
Heat, not gradient, is the hazard. From May the south-facing limestone reflects hard and there is no shade above 400 m; start before 07:00.
The Grand Prix, usually the last weekend in May, closes streets and triples room rates. Plan around it.

proTips: Run every climb in the morning and every coastal path in the afternoon. The ridges face south and east; by 11:00 in spring they are ovens, while the Sentier du Littoral stays half-shaded.
Use the train as a chairlift. Descending 800 m to a station and riding one stop home is far kinder on quads than reversing your climb, and a single ticket costs less than a coffee.
The Col de la Madone is a road pass, so it always has a legal, gradient-consistent escape route. Make it your turning point when weather or legs go wrong on Day 5.
Fill up at La Turbie every time you pass — its fountain sits on four of the week's seven routes.
Buy running food at the Condamine market, not at a Monte-Carlo café — the price differential is roughly fourfold.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 115–125 km and 5,800–6,400 m of ascent; limestone, pine needle, scree, stone stairway and coastal path, T1–T3
raw.Who It Suits: Runners who like relentless gradient, sea views and a base where dinner costs more than the flight

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 115–125 km and 5,800–6,400 m of ascent; limestone, pine needle, scree, stone stairway and coastal path, T1–T3
typeSpecific.audience: Runners who like relentless gradient, sea views and a base where dinner costs more than the flight

packingNotes: Shoes with firm lugs for dry, dusty limestone. Grip here is a dust-on-rock problem, not a mud problem.
Two-litre carrying capacity for Day 5 and a 500 ml flask for everything else.
Electrolyte tablets — sweat rates on a south-facing Riviera ridge run high.
A cap, sunglasses and high-factor sunscreen — 90 per cent of this week is shadeless.
Lightweight windproof for the ridge above the Madone, where the mistral's tail end can cut ten degrees off the temperature.
Swim shorts: Larvotto and Plage Mala are legitimate recovery tools.
Offline maps: the GR51 and the local yellow waymarks overlap confusingly around the Grande Corniche.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Fire closure in summer.** If the massifs shut, everything above 300 m is off. Fall back on the coastal paths — Cap d'Ail, Cap Martin and the Menton stairways give 15 km and 500 m without entering the woods.

**Heat exhaustion on Day 5.** Thirty kilometres with 1,750 m of ascent in Riviera sun is a genuine risk. Break it at Sainte-Agnès, descend to Menton and take the train — you lose the traverse, not the week.
**Expecting Mont Agel's summit.** It is a closed military installation and the fences are real. Plan the ridge and the golf-course shoulder instead, and do not push past signage.
**Grand Prix or a race weekend.** Roads close, trains fill and prices spike. Check the Monaco events calendar before booking flights.
**Assuming Monaco is the running.** It is the bed, the food and the station. The routes are French, and every day from Day 2 crosses an unmarked border repeatedly.

trips.title: Durmitor Ridges
trips.subRegion: Durmitor National Park & Žabljak, northern Montenegro

bestPeriod.window: Mid-June–mid-July & early September–early October
bestPeriod.avoid: November–May (Sedlo pass road snow-blocked, high ridges unrunnable, Žabljak is a ski town); late July–August has the crowds and afternoon storms
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-June–mid-July & early September–early October

accommodation.note: Žabljak guesthouses €35–€70 dbl/night; Škrka mountain hut ~€15–€20

food.note: Main course €7–€12; a full dinner with rakija under €20

transport.note: Rental car 7 days €180–€280, fuel, Sozina/Tara tolls

activities.note: NP daily entry ~€5, or the all-parks card ~€13.50; Tara rafting half-day €40–€55

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5 — 1,000–1,400 m days on sharp karst with short exposed scrambles; no glacier, but very little forgiving ground

trips.gatewayAirport: TGD — Podgorica (2 h–2 h 30 drive to Žabljak via Nikšić or the Tara bridge); TIV — Tivat is 2 h 45
trips.summary: Durmitor is a compact, savage limestone massif with 48 peaks over 2,000 m packed into an area you can drive across in forty minutes, and Žabljak at 1,456 m is the highest town in the Balkans — which means you sleep at altitude and start every run from a car park rather than a valley. The rock is pale, fluted karst with almost no soil, so the running is fast on the grass shelves and genuinely sharp on the ridges. The week arcs from a lake-circuit warm-up through the two showpiece summits, Bobotov Kuk and Prutaš, into a two-day Škrčka lakes excursion with a hut night, then a recovery day on the Tara canyon rim and a fast finish on Savin Kuk. It suits runners who like empty mountains, do not need refuge comfort, and can carry their own water.

itinerary.title: Drive up from Podgorica, warm up at Crno jezero
itinerary.morning: Land at TGD, collect the car, drive north through the Moraća canyon and over to **Žabljak (1,456 m)** — 2 h to 2 h 30 depending on route. Buy the national park ticket at the Crno jezero booth or the visitor centre.
itinerary.afternoon: Shake out on the **Crno jezero (Black Lake) circuit**, 3.6 km around both basins on flat forest track, then add the gentle climb to the **Zminje jezero** for another 4 km. Enough to feel the altitude, not enough to cost anything.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Žabljak — cicvara, kajmak and lamb ispod sača at one of the town's konobas; wash it down with a local Vranac.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km / 220 m D+ / T1 / 55 min–1 h 15; drive 2 h–2 h 30; NP entry ~€5.

itinerary.title: Prutaš, the slab mountain
itinerary.morning: Drive the **P14 road to Sedlo pass (1,907 m)**, 25 minutes from Žabljak, and park at the col. Run the ridge south-west to **Prutaš (2,393 m)** — grass shelves, then the famous banded limestone strata tilted like the pages of a book.
itinerary.afternoon: Return over Sedlo and add the short spur north toward **Velika Previja** for the first sight of the Škrka cirque and Bobotov's south face. Back to Žabljak by mid-afternoon.
itinerary.evening: Beer on the Žabljak main street; early dinner and a properly early night before tomorrow.
itinerary.dayStats: 8.2 km / 560 m D+ / T2–T3 / 1 h 30–2 h / high point 2,393 m / no water above Žabljak.

itinerary.title: Bobotov Kuk, 2,523 m
itinerary.morning: Leave Žabljak at 06:15 for Sedlo. Climb the scree gully and the traverse to **Velika Previja**, then the cabled, exposed final ridge onto **Bobotov Kuk (2,523 m)**, the classic Durmitor summit, with the whole Tara canyon system on one side and Bosnian ranges on the other.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend by the same route to Sedlo — or, if fit, take the long variant down to **Lokvice katun** and out via Ivan Do to Žabljak, refilling at the katun spring and buying cheese from the shepherds.
itinerary.evening: Recovery meal in Žabljak; a soak in the hotel wellness if it has one.
itinerary.dayStats: 9.9 km / 940 m D+ (or 19 km / 1,450 m by Lokvice) / T3 with cables / 2 h 15–3 h / 2 L water minimum.

itinerary.title: Down into the Škrka cirque, hut night
itinerary.morning: Sedlo again, but this time run north-west over **Velika Previja** and drop into the **Škrka cirque**, a 500 m descent on loose karst steps into the most isolated bowl in the park, holding **Veliko and Malo Škrčko jezero** at about 1,686 m.
itinerary.afternoon: Easy exploration of the two lakes and the surrounding pastures, then check into the **Škrka mountain hut** — basic, bunk-bed, hot food, and the only building for hours in any direction.
itinerary.evening: Hut dinner and one of the darkest night skies in Europe; the cirque walls block every light source.

itinerary.title: Climb out, then a genuine recovery afternoon on the Tara rim
itinerary.morning: Reverse the climb out of the cirque to Sedlo — 550 m up, taken slowly as the only hard effort of the day — and drive back to Žabljak.
itinerary.afternoon: True low day. An easy 7 km jog out to the **Ćurevac viewpoint (1,625 m)** on soft forest track for the head-on view 1,300 m down into the **Tara canyon**, the deepest in Europe. Then coffee and nothing else.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Žabljak; plan the last two days around the forecast.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km out / 550 m D+, then 7 km / 300 m D+ / total ~1 h 50 running / Tara canyon depth ~1,300 m.

itinerary.title: Savin Kuk and the Tara river
itinerary.morning: From Crno jezero, climb **Savin Kuk (2,313 m)** on the ski-area flank and the summit ridge — a shorter, less committing summit than Bobotov with an equally complete panorama over the Žabljak plateau and the Piva side.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive to the **Đurđevića Tara bridge** and take a half-day raft on the Tara — cold, fast, green water at the bottom of the canyon you looked into yesterday. The best possible active recovery.
itinerary.evening: Grilled trout and rakija at a riverside restaurant near the bridge.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km / 900 m D+ / T2–T3 / 2 h–2 h 45; rafting €40–€55 half-day; 35 min drive to the bridge.

itinerary.title: Katun loop and the drive out
itinerary.morning: Last run: the **Ivan Do–Lokvice katun** loop from Crno jezero, up through black pine to the shepherds' summer settlement at about 1,800 m and back on the Zminje side — the most characteristic Durmitor ground, all pasture, karst pavement and sheep bells.
itinerary.afternoon: Buy cheese and honey in Žabljak, then the drive south to Podgorica, ideally via the **Tara bridge and the Piva canyon** if the flight allows.
itinerary.evening: Departure from TGD.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km / 700 m D+ / 2 h–2 h 30; drive to TGD 2 h–2 h 30.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Soa
accommodationStrategy.description: The pragmatic town base: five minutes' drive from the Crno jezero park entrance and the P14 Sedlo road, parking, a proper breakfast, and staff who will do an early one if you ask the night before. Good value at €55–€90 double in shoulder season, and it has drying space, which matters when Durmitor weather turns.

accommodationStrategy.name: Planinarski dom Škrka
accommodationStrategy.description: The only accommodation inside the high massif and the reason Day 4 works. Bunks, a stove, simple hot food and no electricity to speak of — bring cash, a sleeping bag liner and a headtorch. Confirm it is staffed before you commit to descending into the cirque; outside high summer it may be locked.

accommodationStrategy.name: Guesthouse or apartman in Ivan Do
accommodationStrategy.description: The runner's alternative: apartments a kilometre from the Crno jezero trailhead, €35–€55 a night, with a kitchen for early breakfasts and late dinners. Ideal if you want to start on foot rather than driving to the lake each morning.

logistics.connectivity: Montenegro is **not** in the EU, but it participates in the Western Balkans roaming arrangement and most EU operators now apply reduced or roam-like-at-home terms — check your tariff, and consider a local Telekom/One prepaid SIM. **No signal in the Škrka cirque, the Tara canyon floor, or the deep forest bowls.**
logistics.emergency: **112**; mountain rescue in Montenegro is run by the Gorska služba spašavanja (GSS) and is volunteer-based, so response is slower than in the Alps. Helicopter availability is limited. Carry insurance with mountain cover and repatriation, and leave your route with your accommodation.
logistics.weather: Durmitor makes its own weather. Violent afternoon thunderstorms from mid-June through August, often building from 13:00; sudden temperature drops of 15 °C; and snow possible on the ridges in any month. The massif also catches Adriatic fronts, which arrive fast from the south-west. Check the Montenegrin hydrometeorological service each morning.
logistics.bookingWindows: Žabljak beds are plentiful except in the first three weeks of August — 2–4 weeks ahead is enough otherwise. The **Škrka hut** should be confirmed by phone through the Žabljak visitor centre a few days ahead. Tara rafting books same-day outside August. Rental cars for August need months.
logistics.money: **Montenegro uses the euro** although it is not in the eurozone. Cards work in hotels and larger restaurants in Žabljak; **the national park booth, the hut, katuns and small konobas are cash-only** — bring €200 in small notes. Tipping: round up, 10% for a good meal.
logistics.transportRules: A rental car is essentially required — buses reach Žabljak but nothing inside the park. Montenegro has no vignette; the **Sozina tunnel** on the coast route is tolled (a few euros). Check that your rental agreement permits the unpaved sections; the P14 to Sedlo is paved but narrow and gated by snow into June. Green Card insurance is needed to cross into Bosnia for the Piva loop.
logistics.permits: **Durmitor National Park charges a daily entry fee of roughly €5 per person**, collected at Crno jezero and other entry points; an all-parks annual card is around €13.50 and pays for itself in three days. No running permit needed. Wild camping is restricted to designated areas; drones need park permission. Do not disturb katun livestock or leave gates open.
logistics.health: Žabljak tap water is potable; treat all lake and stream water. **Nose-horned viper (poskok)** is present on sunny karst below 1,800 m — Europe's most venomous snake, though bites are rare; wear proper shoes and don't put hands blind onto ledges. Ticks in the pine and beech forest. Karst edges are sharp and undercut: a slip on Bobotov's summit block is a serious injury, not a graze.

proTips: **Buy the all-parks card, not day tickets.** At roughly €13.50 against ~€5 a day, it pays back on day three and also covers Biogradska Gora and Lovćen if you drive out via the coast.

**Do Bobotov Kuk from Sedlo, not from Crno jezero, on your first attempt.** The Sedlo start saves 500 m of climbing and puts you on the summit two hours earlier — which on a storm day is the whole safety margin.

**Refill at Lokvice katun and buy the cheese.** The shepherds' summer settlement is the only reliable water between Žabljak and the high ridges, and the sheep's cheese and kajmak sold there is better than anything in town.
**Check the Sedlo road before you plan the week.** The P14 over Sedlo is the key to three of the seven days and it can stay snow-blocked into mid-June and close early after an autumn storm.
**Descend into Škrka in the morning, never the afternoon.** The climb out is 500 m on loose karst with no water and no phone signal; doing it in evening light or a storm is the classic Durmitor epic.
**Run Prutaš in low side-light.** The banded strata that make the mountain famous only read properly early or late — mid-morning flattens them completely.
**Use the Tara raft as your recovery session.** Half a day of cold water and no impact after a Bobotov day does more for your legs than a rest morning in the hotel.
**Watch the sheepdogs at the katuns.** Šarplaninac guard dogs work loose around the summer settlements. Stop running, walk, and wait for a shepherd — never try to outrun one.

raw.Signature routes: (1) **Bobotov Kuk (2,523 m) from Sedlo pass (1,907 m)**: 9.9 km out-and-back, 940 m D+, mid-pack run 2 h 15–3 h (hiking guides quote 5 h 30). (2) **Bobotov Kuk the long way from Crno jezero** via Ivan Do, Lokvice katun and Velika Previja: 19 km, 1,450 m D+, 4 h–5 h 30. (3) **Prutaš (2,393 m) from Sedlo**: 8.2 km out-and-back, 560 m D+, 1 h 30–2 h — the most photogenic striated slabs in the Balkans. (4) **Škrčka jezera (1,686 m) circuit from Sedlo** down the Škrka cirque and back over Velika Previja: 17 km, 1,100 m D+, 3 h–4 h. (5) **Savin Kuk (2,313 m) from Crno jezero**: 12 km, 900 m D+, 2 h–2 h 45. (6) **Crno jezero circuit**: 3.6 km, 60 m D+, 22–30 min. (7) **Ćurevac (1,625 m) Tara rim** from Tepca road: 7 km, 300 m D+, 50 min–1 h 10.
raw.Technicality (SAC hiking scale T1–T5, st: Crno jezero circuit **T1**. Prutaš and Savin Kuk **T2–T3**. Bobotov Kuk **T3**, with a cabled section and about 80 m of easy but genuinely exposed scrambling on the summit block, plus a steep scree gully on the Sedlo side. Škrka descent **T3** on loose karst steps. Nothing needs a rope, but Bobotov Kuk in the wet is a different mountain — the polished limestone becomes lethal.
raw.Terrain split, week average: ~40% bare fluted karst and limestone slab, ~20% scree and gully, ~15% high grass shelf and katun pasture (the only genuinely fast ground), ~15% black-pine and beech forest singletrack around the lakes, ~10% gravel park track. The karst is razor-edged: it shreds soft uppers and destroys hands in a fall, so long shoes with a rock plate and light gloves are sensible.
raw.Waymarking: Balkan standard **red circle with a white dot**, plus numbered wooden posts installed by the national park and the Via Dinarica **White Trail** (a "VD" white blaze) crossing the massif. Marking is good on the main peaks and thin in the Škrka cirque, where cairns take over. Timings on posts are hiking times — halve them.
raw.Water refill points and month reliabilit: Durmitor is porous karst and **water is the planning constraint**. Reliable: **Žabljak town taps and the Crno jezero café**, all season; **Lokvice katun spring** (shepherds' summer settlement below Bobotov Kuk), reliable while the katun is occupied, roughly **mid-June to mid-September**, dry outside it; **Škrčka jezera** lake water and the hut at Škrka, treat or ask the hut; **Crno jezero** itself, treat. **Nothing at all at Sedlo pass, on Prutaš, on the Bobotov ridge or on the Ćurevac rim.** Snow patches in the north gullies give melt into early July and nothing after. Carry 2 L on any Sedlo day.
raw.Navigation: The Durmitor 1:25,000 hiking map sold at the NP visitor centre in Žabljak is the standard; GPX from the Via Dinarica portal, Wikiloc and Komoot.
