Coverage: reasonable in Žabljak and on ridges, **dead in the Škrka cirque, in the Tara canyon below the rim and in the Zminje/Crno forest bowls**. Bail-outs: from Bobotov Kuk, back to Sedlo (fastest) or down to Lokvice and Ivan Do; from Škrka, the Škrka hut is the only shelter and the exit is a 500 m climb — do not descend into that cirque late in the day.
raw.Recovery, altitude and heat: Day 5 is a real low day on the Tara rim. Working altitude 1,900–2,520 m from a 1,456 m base, so no acclimatisation problem but noticeably thinner air on the Bobotov scramble. Convective storms build over the massif from about 13:00 in July and are severe — the ridges are the highest ground for a long way and lightning strikes here are not theoretical. Be off Bobotov Kuk by early afternoon, every time.

typeSpecific.surface: ~40% bare fluted karst and limestone slab, ~20% scree and gully, ~15% high grass shelf and katun pasture (the only genuinely fast ground), ~15% black-pine and beech forest singletrack around the lakes, ~10% gravel park track. The karst is razor-edged: it shreds soft uppers and destroys hands in a fall, so long shoes with a rock plate and light gloves are sensible.
typeSpecific.technicalRating: Crno jezero circuit **T1**. Prutaš and Savin Kuk **T2–T3**. Bobotov Kuk **T3**, with a cabled section and about 80 m of easy but genuinely exposed scrambling on the summit block, plus a steep scree gully on the Sedlo side. Škrka descent **T3** on loose karst steps. Nothing needs a rope, but Bobotov Kuk in the wet is a different mountain — the polished limestone becomes lethal.

sources.verified: Durmitor National Park entry is charged per person per day at approximately €5, with a Montenegro all-national-parks card around €13.50; the Bobotov Kuk out-and-back from Sedlo is about 9.9 km with roughly 939 m of ascent and the Sedlo trailhead is around a 25-minute drive from Žabljak on the P14; Montenegro uses the euro without being in the eurozone.
sources.confidenceNotes: Re-verify (a) **the current Durmitor entry fee and card price**, which the park revises; (b) **Škrka mountain hut staffing, opening dates, price and booking channel** — it is the single most volatile item in this itinerary and should be confirmed by phone before Day 4 is committed; (c) **P14 Sedlo pass road opening date** for the travel month, which depends entirely on snow clearance; (d) **Ćurevac viewpoint access** — the approach road has been closed or restricted in some seasons for erosion; (e) **Montenegro roaming terms** for the traveller's specific EU operator; (f) named Žabljak restaurants and hotel price bands, which turn over frequently.

provenance.sourceFormat: md with '## Metadata' bullet block (one file per trip)

trips.title: Romsdal Ridges: Åndalsnes Skyrunning Week

bestPeriod.window: Late June to late September. Snow lingers on north-facing ridge sections into early July; September gives firm ground, no mosquitoes and cold clear air
bestPeriod.raw: Late June to late September. Snow lingers on north-facing ridge sections into early July; September gives firm ground, no mosquitoes and cold clear air

accommodation.note: €130–220 per night, double; DNT cabins €35–55 pp for members

food.note: €60–90 per day — Norway is the most expensive country in this dataset; self-cater breakfasts and trail food

transport.note: €180–300: Oslo–Åndalsnes rail via Dombås (the Rauma Line), local buses, one gondola ticket, optional car hire €65/day

activities.note: €90–160: Romsdalen Gondola, one guided ridge day, via ferrata option

profile.difficultyNote: Hard. Exposed ridgelines with scrambling sections, 1,000–1,400 m vertical on the big days, sustained steep descents

trips.summary: A seven-day trail running itinerary in Møre og Romsdal, Western Norway, Norway.

itinerary.title: Arrival and the Nesaksla shakeout
itinerary.morning: Rauma Line train from Dombås to Åndalsnes — 100 minutes through the Romsdalen gorge past the Trollveggen wall, Europe's tallest vertical rock face at around 1,100 m. Sit on the right.
itinerary.afternoon: Straight up the Rampestreken trail from town to the steel viewing platform cantilevered over the fjord, then continue to Nesaksla summit (715 m). Steep, stepped, stone-pitched — a perfect legs-opening effort at about 45–60 minutes climbing.
itinerary.evening: Ride the Romsdalen Gondola down (or run it), eat at the Eggen restaurant at the top station if you go up late instead. **Water:** the stream crossing at roughly 400 m on the Rampestreken path; nothing above it.

itinerary.title: Litlefjellet and Mjølva reconnaissance
itinerary.morning: Drive or bus 15 minutes to Venjesdalen. Litlefjellet is the short one — 45 minutes up to a knife of rock with the entire Romsdalen valley and Romsdalshorn opposite. Run it early with a headtorch for sunrise.
itinerary.afternoon: Mjølva above Åndalsnes: a runnable grassy ridge, 950 m of climb on trail the whole way, the best pure aerobic day of the week and a good test of whether tomorrow's big ridge is on.
itinerary.evening: Sauna and fjord swim. Trail food shopping at the Åndalsnes Coop for the ridge day. **Water:** Mjølvabekken crosses the trail at about 550 m — reliable all summer.

itinerary.title: Romsdalseggen, the main event
itinerary.morning: Take the early shuttle bus from Åndalsnes to Vengedalen — the standard start since the route was reversed and rebuilt. From the car park you climb steadily to the ridge proper.
itinerary.afternoon: The ridge: rock steps, chains at two short sections, sustained exposure with the Isterdalen valley 900 m below on one side and Romsdalen on the other. Highest point around 1,216 m at Blånebba if you take the optional extension. Finish over Nesaksla and descend Rampestreken into town — or take the gondola down to spare your quads.
itinerary.evening: Rest properly. **Water:** two streams in the first 300 m of climbing out of Vengedalen; after that the ridge is dry for 8 km. Carry 1.5 litres minimum.
itinerary.dayStats: 10–12 km, 970 m, 5–7 h hiking pace / 2.5–4 h running

itinerary.title: Recovery: Isterdalen valley and the Trollstigen approach
itinerary.morning: Easy running on the valley floor track through Isterdalen beneath the Trollstigen hairpins, with the peaks Bispen, Kongen and Dronningen (the Bishop, the King and the Queen) overhead.
itinerary.afternoon: The Trollstigen mountain road and its viewing platform have been subject to rockfall closures in recent seasons — check status before planning to run the hairpins. `verify: true` Substitute the Kløvstien old packhorse path if the road is shut.
itinerary.evening: Isfjorden village; the Norsk Tindesenter climbing centre in Åndalsnes has an indoor wall and the national mountaineering museum for a wet afternoon. **Water:** Istra river tributaries throughout; abundant.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km flat-ish, 350 m

itinerary.title: Kyrkjetaket or Skarven long day
itinerary.morning: From Isterdalen up to Kyrkjetaket (1,439 m) — a long, mostly runnable ascent on a marked path with a rocky final 200 m. Fewer people than Romsdalseggen by a factor of twenty, bigger views of the Trolltindane.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend the same line or traverse toward Alnesvatnet. Snowfields on the north side can persist to mid-July; micro-spikes are worth the 200 g in June and early July.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Hotel Aak — Norway's oldest tourist hotel, founded 1880 for the English salmon-fishing gentry. **Water:** the outflow of Alnesvatnet, and streams to about 1,100 m.

itinerary.title: Fjord ridge: Innfjorden and Middagstinden
itinerary.morning: Drive 20 minutes south to Innfjorden. The Middagstinden and Skorgedalen ridgelines look straight down the fjord, with sheep tracks that run better than the marked path.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend to the fjord and swim. On a clear day the Måsvassbu direction offers an add-on ridgeline traverse with no infrastructure at all.
itinerary.evening: Last dinner in Åndalsnes; pack for an early train. **Water:** Skorgedalselva at the valley floor; treat nothing above the last farm.

itinerary.title: Rauma Line and out
itinerary.morning: Optional 5 km shakeout along the Rauma river's salmon pools and the Kylling Bridge viewpoint if you have a car.
itinerary.afternoon: Train Åndalsnes–Dombås–Oslo, or the bus to Molde/Ålesund airports (1.5 h and 2 h respectively).

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Aak
accommodationStrategy.description: Two kilometres out of town at the foot of the valley, built for climbers and still run for them. Drying room, packed breakfasts on request from 06:00, and staff who know current ridge conditions better than any website. Trailheads for Mjølva and Isterdalen start effectively from the door.

accommodationStrategy.name: Grand Hotel Bellevue
accommodationStrategy.description: On the fjord, three minutes from the station and the gondola base. The practical choice if you are travelling car-free: the Vengedalen shuttle for Romsdalseggen leaves from town, and you can be on the ridge without ever hiring a vehicle.

accommodationStrategy.name: Trollstigen Camping / Åndalsnes cabins
accommodationStrategy.description: Simple hytter with kitchenettes, €70–110 for two, positioned for Days 4 and 5. Self-catering matters in Norway: three restaurant dinners will cost more than two nights of accommodation.

logistics.connectivity: 4G is good in the valleys, intermittent above 1,000 m. Norwegian eSIMs are cheap; EU roaming does **not** cover Norway on all plans since it is outside the EU — check your bundle. `verify: true`
logistics.emergency: 113 for medical, 112 for police and mountain rescue. Download the **Hjelp 113** app before you arrive — it transmits your GPS position to the emergency operator, and it is the standard tool used by Norwegian rescue services. Mobile coverage on the Romsdalseggen ridge is patchy but usually present at high points.
logistics.weather: Romsdal is a fjord-head microclimate: the town can be sunny at 18 °C while the ridge sits in cloud at 4 °C with 15 m/s wind and zero visibility. Yr.no gives point forecasts by altitude — use the 1,000 m layer, not the town figure. Turn around at the first sign of the ridge clouding in; the chained sections are unpleasant in wet fog.
logistics.bookingWindows: Hotel Aak and Bellevue: 3–4 months for July and August, the cruise-ship days fill the town. The Vengedalen shuttle: book the day before online in high season. Guided ridge days with Romsdal guides: 2–4 weeks.

other.label: Gear floor for the ridge days
other.text: Trail shoes with real lugs, waterproof shell and trousers, hat and gloves even in July, headtorch, 1.5–2 l capacity, whistle, a foil bivvy, and a charged phone. Poles help enormously on the descent and are a nuisance on the chained steps — collapsible only.

other.label: Allemannsretten
other.text: Norway's right to roam allows wild camping on uncultivated land, at least 150 m from any inhabited house, for up to two nights in the same place. Fires are banned in or near forest 15 April–15 September.

proTips: Run Romsdalseggen on the **first bus of the day**. The ridge takes 5–7 hours at hiking pace, which means the crowd is strung out between 10:00 and 16:00; leaving at 07:30 puts you ahead of all of it and lets you use the chained sections without queuing.
Buy a **single gondola down-ticket** rather than a return. The climb is the point; the 900 m descent on tired quads on day three is not.
The **Rauma Line** is one of Europe's great rail journeys and it is a normal scheduled service, not a tourist train — the tourist version costs several times as much for the same track.
Norwegian supermarkets close early (Coop and Rema 1000 around 21:00–23:00, and Sunday closures are near-total). Buy your Sunday food on Saturday, always.
The best free viewpoint nobody runs: **Litlefjellet at 05:30** in late June, when the sun hits Romsdalshorn and there is nobody within two kilometres.
If a storm cancels a ridge day, the fallback is not the hotel gym — it is the fjord-level Rauma river path plus the Norsk Tindesenter's 21 m indoor wall.

raw.technical_rating: T3–T4 alpine (UIAA I scrambling on Romsdalseggen); not suitable for runners without exposure tolerance
raw.water_strategy: Named refill points listed per day; running mountain streams above the treeline and above grazing are drinkable — filter anything below a farm

trips.title: Sandstone and Saucer: A Trail-Running Week in the Karkonosze and Góry Stołowe
trips.subRegion: The Sudetes — Karkonosze, Góry Stołowe and the Śnieżnik Massif

bestPeriod.window: the first three weeks of September — dry sandstone, stable air, empty ridge
bestPeriod.avoid: late July–August (Karpacz and Karłów at full crowd), and November–April when the paved ridge trails ice over

accommodation.note: €230–€400 (€33–€57/night, guesthouses and mountain schroniska)

food.note: €140–€210 (€20–€30/day — schronisko kitchens are cheap)

transport.note: €90–€160 (Wrocław transfer, one rental-car day, buses, Kopa chairlift)

activities.note: €35–€60 (two national park tickets, Szczeliniec, Błędne Skały, Jaskinia Niedźwiedzia)

profile.difficultyNote: Moderate–Hard

trips.gatewayAirport: Wrocław (WRO), 2 h by bus/car to Karpacz; Prague (PRG) 2 h 30 to Kudowa via Náchod. Rail to Jelenia Góra, then bus 100/200 to Karpacz (~40 min).
trips.summary: Two ranges, ninety kilometres apart, that run nothing alike. The Karkonosze give you a bald granite ridge on the Czech border, peat bog on duckboards, glacial cirques dropping away on your left, and stone-paved paths…
trips.hook: Two ranges, ninety kilometres apart, that run nothing alike. The Karkonosze give you a bald granite ridge on the Czech border, peat bog on duckboards, glacial cirques dropping away on your left, and stone-paved paths that turn into a skating rink the moment it rains. The Góry Stołowe give you a sandstone tabletop split into labyrinths you run through sideways. Come for the contrast, and bring shoes with a hard edge.

snapshot.Start / End: Karpacz → Kudowa-Zdrój (two bases, one relocation on Day 4)
snapshot.Getting there: Wrocław (WRO), 2 h by bus/car to Karpacz; Prague (PRG) 2 h 30 to Kudowa via Náchod. Rail to Jelenia Góra, then bus 100/200 to Karpacz (~40 min).

itinerary.title: Arrival and the Łomniczka warm-up
itinerary.morning: Fly into Wrocław, bus or drive to **Karpacz**. Buy the Karkonoski Park Narodowy ticket online at kpnmab.pl or at the gate — around 15 PLN (€3.50) a day, reduced roughly half [VERIFY: 2026 KPN daily entry tariff].
itinerary.afternoon: Ease in on the green trail up **Kocioł Łomniczki** from Karpacz Górny, following the Łomniczka stream past the waterfall to the cirque headwall. Turn at the Dom Śląski junction and descend the same way. It is steep, rooted and rocky — a calibration run for what the rest of the week costs your ankles.
itinerary.evening: Eat at Karczma Głodny Turysta on Konstytucji 3 Maja and walk the town's odd Norwegian stave church, **Świątynia Wang**, moved here from Vang in 1842 [VERIFY: current Wang opening hours].

itinerary.title: Śnieżka the honest way
itinerary.morning: Leave Karpacz Biały Jar by 07:00 on the blue trail through the Kocioł Łomniczki, then the zigzags to **Dom Śląski** at 1,400 m. Fill bottles here. The final cone to **Śnieżka (1,603 m)** is 25 minutes of stone stair.
itinerary.afternoon: On the summit: the three fibreglass discs of the **Wysokogórskie Obserwatorium Meteorologiczne** (1974, and it does look like a stack of flying saucers), the baroque **Kaplica św. Wawrzyńca** of 1681, and the Czech **Poštovna** hut serving soup. The border runs over the top; you cross it by walking.
itinerary.evening: Descend the red ridge west then the trail past **Strzecha Akademicka** and **Samotnia** at Mały Staw — the most photographed hut in Poland, on a tarn under a 200 m cirque wall — and down to Karpacz. Beer at Samotnia is worth the ten-minute stop.

itinerary.title: The full Droga Przyjaźni
itinerary.morning: First bus to **Szklarska Poręba**, chairlift or the black trail up to **Szrenica (1,362 m)**, then east on the red-blazed **Droga Przyjaźni Polsko-Czeskiej**. Łabski Szczyt, then the rim of the **Śnieżne Kotły** — two glacial cirques with 250 m walls and the mock-castle transmitter building on the lip.
itinerary.afternoon: Wielki Szyszak, Przełęcz Karkonoska (water at **Odrodzenie**), then the long boardwalk across **Równia pod Śnieżką**, a high peat bog at 1,400 m. This is the fastest running of the week and the coldest place to be caught in weather.
itinerary.evening: Second summit of Śnieżka if the sky allows, then the Kopa chairlift or the blue trail down to Karpacz. Pierogi ruskie and żurek at Bączek in Karpacz.

itinerary.title: Wielki Staw, then relocate
itinerary.morning: A short, beautiful loop: the trail from Karpacz to **Wielki Staw**, the larger of the two Karkonosze tarns, sitting in a cirque directly beneath the ridge, and back over Kopa. Run it before 09:00 and you will have the water to yourself.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive or take the bus via Jelenia Góra and Kłodzko to **Kudowa-Zdrój** (2 h 15 by car, longer by public transport). Book a car for Days 4–7 if you can — the Stołowe trailheads are poorly linked.
itinerary.evening: Walk the spa park in Kudowa, drink the mineral water from the pijalnia, and eat at Restauracja Sowia Dolina [VERIFY: current opening hours].

itinerary.title: The sandstone labyrinth
itinerary.morning: Drive to **Karłów** and take the 665 stone steps up **Szczeliniec Wielki (919 m)**, the flat-topped sandstone block that is the signature of the range. Entry is ticketed separately from the park [VERIFY: 2026 Szczeliniec entry price]. Inside: **Piekiełko** ("Little Hell"), the slot corridors, the ladders, and the Fotel Pradziada viewpoint over the whole Kłodzko basin.
itinerary.afternoon: It is a one-way circuit with fixed direction and you cannot run it — accept that. Descend to Karłów and run the yellow trail to **Schronisko Pasterka** and the Skały Puchacza viewpoint instead, which is properly runnable sandstone singletrack.
itinerary.evening: Back to Kudowa. If you want a genuinely odd hour, the Kaplica Czaszek at Czermna is a chapel lined with several thousand human skulls [VERIFY: current chapel opening hours].

itinerary.title: Błędne Skały and the Skalne Grzyby
itinerary.morning: Drive the toll road up to **Błędne Skały** (853 m) at opening. It is a maze of sandstone blocks with passages — Tunel, Kuchnia, the Ucho Igielne — narrow enough that a broad-shouldered runner with a vest on genuinely wedges. Take the pack off first. One-way, timed entry in summer.
itinerary.afternoon: Run the red then blue trails east across the plateau to the **Skalne Grzyby**, the "rock mushrooms" — free-standing sandstone toadstools scattered through the forest between Batorów and Karłów. This is the best running in the Stołowe: rolling, sandy, quiet, no ticket gate.
itinerary.evening: Return via Karłów. Eat at Bar Karłów by the car park; simple and open when everything else is not.

itinerary.title: Śnieżnik and a bear cave
itinerary.morning: Drive to **Kletno** (1 h 20 from Kudowa) and book the first slot at **Jaskinia Niedźwiedzia**, the Bear Cave — timed entry, limited daily numbers, and it fills [VERIFY: 2026 Jaskinia Niedźwiedzia ticket price and booking window].
itinerary.afternoon: Run the trail from Kletno up to **Schronisko na Śnieżniku** and on to the summit of **Śnieżnik (1,425 m)**, a bald grass dome on the Polish–Czech border with the new Czech observation tower on the far side. Open, fast, exposed — this is a run, not a scramble.
itinerary.evening: Descend the same way and drive out to Wrocław (2 h 30) or back to Kudowa for a last night.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Vivaldi
accommodationStrategy.description: on Olimpijska, ten minutes' jog from the Biały Jar trailhead and the Kopa chairlift base, with a pool and sauna that do real work on trashed calves after the ridge day.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–8 weeks ahead direct or via Booking; avoid Polish long weekends, when Karpacz doubles in price.

accommodationStrategy.name: Schronisko PTTK Samotnia
accommodationStrategy.description: one night sleeping on the ridge shortens the Droga Przyjaźni day at both ends and lets you be on Śnieżka at sunrise. Bunk rooms, shared bathrooms, a warden's kitchen.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct with the hut by phone or its own form, 2–3 months ahead for summer weekends [VERIFY: current Samotnia bed rate].

accommodationStrategy.name: Willa Sanssouci
accommodationStrategy.description: parking on site (non-negotiable for the Stołowe days), a drying room, breakfast from 07:00, and fifteen minutes' drive to both Karłów and Błędne Skały.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead, direct by phone for the early breakfast.

logistics.connectivity: Play, Orange and T-Mobile all cover Karpacz, Kudowa and the ridge itself; the cirque floors and Kocioł Łomniczki are dead. On the crest your phone will hop onto Czech networks — Poland and Czechia are both EU, so roaming is free, but turn off data if you are near your fair-use cap.
logistics.emergency: **GOPR — 985 or 601 100 300**, or 112. Install the *Ratunek* app, which sends GPS coordinates automatically. Give your position by trail colour and the nearest schronisko.
logistics.weather: Śnieżka is one of the windiest inhabited places in Europe. Mean annual temperature at the observatory is about **0.4 °C**, mean wind speed roughly **12–13 m/s**, and it records gusts above 100 km/h on well over a hundred days a year, with recorded extremes near **290 km/h** [VERIFY: exact record gust and mean wind figures from IMGW]. Cloud sits on the summit around 300 days a year. There is no shelter on Równia pod Śnieżką. Carry a windshell always, even in July.
logistics.bookingWindows: Ridge huts (Samotnia, Strzecha Akademicka, Odrodzenie) 2–3 months for weekends. Szczeliniec and Błędne Skały use timed entry in high season — buy the day before. Jaskinia Niedźwiedzia needs a week or more in July–August.
logistics.money: Poland uses the złoty; roughly 4.3 PLN to the euro. Cards work almost everywhere including most schroniska, but carry 150–200 PLN in cash for hut kitchens, the Błędne Skały toll road and small bufety.
logistics.transportRules: The **ridge is an international border**. Both countries are in Schengen so crossing is trivial and unmarked, but **carry photo ID** — Czech and Polish police do occasionally check on the crest and at Pec pod Sněžkou. Marked trails only: leaving the trail in either national park is an offence, and the Karkonosze bogs are the reason.
logistics.permits: **Karkonoski PN** and **Park Narodowy Gór Stołowych** both charge daily entry, payable at gates, online or by QR code at trailheads [VERIFY: 2026 Góry Stołowe PN daily entry tariff]. Both ban wild camping, drones and dogs off-lead. Szczeliniec and Błędne Skały have fixed one-way circulation and their own additional tickets on top of park entry.

proTips: **Run the paved ridge sections in the dry, and never at speed in the wet.** Those granite setts are the single biggest injury cause in the Karkonosze; GOPR's ankle callouts cluster on them. If it rains, swap the Droga Przyjaśni day for the Skalne Grzyby.

**Shoes matter more than usual.** Take one pair with a stiff rock plate and hard lugs for the granite, and one softer, grippier pair for the sandstone. A single soft-lugged shoe will feel wrong on both ranges.
**Do Szczeliniec at 08:30 or at 17:00.** Between 10:00 and 15:00 in summer the slots become a stationary queue and the one-way system means you cannot escape forwards.
**The Czech side is the cheap lunch.** Soup and a beer at Pec pod Sněžkou or on the Czech ridge huts undercuts Karpacz noticeably, and it is a legitimate 30-minute detour from Równia pod Śnieżką.
**Buy the 7-day park ticket if you are running four or more days.** It costs a fraction of daily entries and the QR is checked by roving rangers on the ridge, not only at the gates.
**Ask for *"schronisko"*, not "hut".** And *"Czy tędy do Śnieżki?"* — "is this the way to Śnieżka?" — gets you an answer from anyone.
**Start the Droga Przyjaźni from Szrenica, not from Karpacz.** Running west-to-east puts the prevailing wind behind you and the Kopa chairlift at the finish rather than the start.

raw.Named routes, distance and vertical: (1) **Droga Przyjaźni Polsko-Czeskiej**, the red-blazed main ridge trail: Szrenica → Śnieżne Kotły → Wielki Szyszak → Równia pod Śnieżką → **Śnieżka (1,603 m)** → Przełęcz Okraj, roughly 28–30 km with about 900 m of cumulative climb once you are on the crest. (2) **Śnieżka loop from Karpacz** via Kocioł Łomniczki: 17 km, +1,050 m. (3) **Mały Staw / Wielki Staw tarn circuit**: 21 km, +900 m. (4) **Szczeliniec Wielki (919 m)** from Karłów: 6 km, +230 m, but slow. (5) **Błędne Skały + Skalne Grzyby link**: 22 km, +550 m. (6) **Śnieżnik (1,425 m)** from Kletno: 16 km, +900 m.
raw.Technical grade: The ridge is T1–T2 walking terrain that runs like T3 because of the surface. Kocioł Łomniczki and the Czarny Kocioł zigzags are T3. Szczeliniec's Piekiełko slots and Błędne Skały's passages are T2 by grade and unrunnable by geometry — you turn sideways and shuffle.
raw.Terrain: Four distinct surfaces: **stone-paved ridge trail** (irregular granite setts, laid to stop erosion, brutal underfoot and genuinely dangerous wet); **peat-bog boardwalk** across Równia pod Śnieżką (wet timber, zero grip, run it flat-footed); **granite tor and blockfield** in the cirque rims; and **sandstone slab and step** throughout the Stołowe, which is grippy dry and soapy wet.
raw.Water points by name: Karkonosze: **Schronisko Na Hali Szrenickiej**, **Schronisko Pod Łabskim Szczytem**, **Schronisko Odrodzenie** (Przełęcz Karkonoska), **Samotnia** and **Strzecha Akademicka** at Mały Staw, **Dom Śląski** at Równia pod Śnieżką (the last water before the summit cone), and the Poštovna post office hut on Śnieżka itself. Stołowe: **Schronisko PTTK na Szczelińcu Wielkim**, the bufet at Karłów, **Schronisko Pasterka**. There is nothing drinkable between Szrenica and Odrodzenie — carry 1.5 L.
raw.Bail-outs: From the ridge above Karpacz: the **Kolej linowa Kopa** chairlift (top station 1,375 m, a 25-minute descent from Śnieżka's saddle) runs you down to Karpacz in about 15 minutes [VERIFY: 2026 Kopa chairlift fare and operating hours]. From the western ridge: drop north to Szklarska Poręba on the blue or yellow trails, 40–60 minutes. From Równia pod Śnieżką you can also drop **south into Czechia** to Pec pod Sněžkou. In the Stołowe, every ridge point is within 5 km of the road 387 between Radków, Karłów and Kudowa.

trips.title: Madeira: Pico Ruivo & the Levadas
trips.subRegion: Madeira — Central Massif, Laurissilva & the north coast

bestPeriod.window: March–May & late September–November
bestPeriod.avoid: Late July–August (heat on the exposed east, peak crowds, trail quotas fill); December–February is runnable but the massif is frequently closed by wind and fog
bestPeriod.raw: March–May & late September–November

accommodation.note: North-coast quintas €80–€140 dbl/night; Funchal 3★ from €70

food.note: Prato do dia €10–€14; a full dinner with wine €25–€40

transport.note: Rental car 7 days €180–€300 plus fuel; taxi shuttles for point-to-point runs €25–€45 each

activities.note: Official trail fees (from €4.50, PR1 at €10.50), booking charges, headtorch, one guided day

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5 — endless volcanic stair-climbing and 1,000 m descents; the cardiovascular load is high and the eccentric load is brutal

trips.gatewayAirport: FNC — Madeira Cristiano Ronaldo, Santa Cruz (20 min to Funchal, 40 min to Santana, 55 min to Porto Moniz)
trips.summary: Madeira is a 1,862 m volcanic wall dropped into the Atlantic, and running it means alternating between two utterly different systems: the *veredas*, stone staircases cut along the ridges of the central massif with 500 m of air on both sides, and the *levadas*, 18th-century irrigation channels contouring for kilometres at a steady gradient through dripping laurel forest and pitch-dark tunnels. The week alternates hard massif days with flat levada days, which is both the smartest recovery structure available here and the way MIUT racers actually train. You will climb more stairs in seven days than in a year at home. It suits a runner with strong quads, no fear of exposure or of the dark, and the patience to deal with an official booking system for almost every trail.

itinerary.title: Land, and an evening lap on Ponta de São Lourenço
itinerary.morning: Fly into FNC, collect the car, and drive fifteen minutes east to **Baía d'Abra**. Book the PR8 slot in advance on the SIMplifica portal — do it before you fly.
itinerary.afternoon: Run **PR8 Vereda da Ponta de São Lourenço** out to the Casa do Sardinha and the eastern viewpoint: red and ochre volcanic cliffs, no trees, the Atlantic on both sides, and a serious crosswind. Jetlag-proof, short, and the best introduction to Madeiran rock.
itinerary.evening: Drive to Funchal; dinner in the old town and a first poncha.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km / 400 m D+ / ITRA 2–3 / 1 h–1 h 20 / zero shade, zero water / fee from €4.50.

itinerary.title: PR1: the Areeiro–Ruivo traverse
itinerary.morning: At the **Pico do Areeiro** car park (1,818 m) for sunrise — it fills by 06:30 in season. Run **PR1** across **Pico das Torres (1,851 m)** to **Pico Ruivo (1,862 m)**, through the rock tunnels and along the cut staircases with the whole massif dropping away.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend **PR1.3 to Achada do Teixeira**, taxi or shuttle back to your car at Areeiro. Coffee and bolo do caco at the Pico Ruivo shelter on the way through.
itinerary.evening: Drive north to Santana. Dinner at **Quinta do Furão** — Madeiran beef espetada on a laurel skewer, and a Verdelho.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km PR1 + 2.8 km PR1.3 / ~700 m up, 850 m down / ITRA 3–4 / 1 h 45–2 h 30 / **PR1 fee €10.50** / headtorch for tunnels.

itinerary.title: PR9 Levada do Caldeirão Verde and the Inferno extension
itinerary.morning: From **Casa das Queimadas**, run the **PR9 Levada do Caldeirão Verde** — 6.5 km of contouring channel path through dense laurissilva, four unlit tunnels and a series of hanging ravines, ending at the Caldeirão Verde waterfall in its green amphitheatre.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue on **PR9.1 to the Caldeirão do Inferno** if the water level allows, then reverse. Flat, fast, cold and dark — a deliberate contrast to yesterday's stair-climbing.
itinerary.evening: Santana: the triangular palheiro houses, then a quiet dinner and legs up.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km (18 km with PR9.1) / 300 m D+ / ITRA 2 / 1 h 30–2 h 30 / 4+ tunnels, headtorch essential / fee from €4.50.

itinerary.title: Recovery day: Fanal and the north coast
itinerary.morning: Deliberate low day. Drive across the **Paul da Serra** plateau (1,400–1,500 m of treeless moor, often in cloud) to **Fanal** and run the short, flat loop among the thousand-year-old **til laurel trees** — 6 km of soft grass and mist, no climbing, no exposure.
itinerary.afternoon: Down to **Porto Moniz** for the natural volcanic swimming pools, then the coast road to São Vicente. No further running.
itinerary.evening: Fresh limpets, black scabbardfish with banana, and a Madeira at a Porto Moniz seafront restaurant.
itinerary.dayStats: 6 km / 120 m D+ / 100% flat grass and forest track / 45 min easy; Paul da Serra crossing ~40 min.
itinerary.sleep: Estalagem or quinta, São Vicente / Ponta Delgada

itinerary.title: PR1.2 Vereda da Encumeada, the big one
itinerary.morning: Start at **Encumeada (1,007 m)** at first light. Climb **PR1.2** onto the western ridge of the massif — the longest, most exposed and least crowded route to Pico Ruivo, with ladders, narrow arêtes and views into both the north and south valleys at once.
itinerary.afternoon: Summit **Pico Ruivo (1,862 m)**, drop to the shelter for food, then descend **PR1.3** to Achada do Teixeira for a pre-arranged pickup. This is the day that most resembles racing MIUT.
itinerary.evening: Recovery dinner in Santana or São Vicente; get horizontal early.
itinerary.dayStats: 11.5 km + 2.8 km / ~1,200 m up, 700 m down / ITRA 4 / 3 h 15–4 h 30 / one water point at the Ruivo shelter.

itinerary.title: Ribeiro Frio levadas and the Curral rim
itinerary.morning: From **Ribeiro Frio**, run the classic pair: the **Levada do Furado (PR10) toward Portela** through mossy laurel forest, or the short **Balcões** viewpoint spur for the head-on view of the massif you have just run across.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive to **Eira do Serrado** above **Curral das Freiras** and run the rim path down into and back out of the "Nuns' Valley" — 500 m of descent into a volcanic caldera surrounded by 1,500 m walls, then the climb back out.
itinerary.evening: Chestnut soup and cherry liqueur in Curral das Freiras, then back toward Funchal.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km levada + 9 km Curral / ~900 m D+ combined / ITRA 2–3 / 2 h 30–3 h 20.

itinerary.title: Funchal coastal shakeout and out
itinerary.morning: Easy 8 km along the **Funchal seafront promenade to Câmara de Lobos** — flat, paved, sea-level — then a poncha at the fishing harbour where the boats are painted.
itinerary.afternoon: Mercado dos Lavradores for passionfruit and bolo de mel, a Madeira tasting at Blandy's, then the twenty-minute drive to FNC.
itinerary.evening: Departure.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km / 80 m D+ / 100% paved promenade / 45 min–1 h; 20 min to the airport.

accommodationStrategy.name: Quinta do Furão
accommodationStrategy.description: The north-coast base and the right side of the island for the massif: 40 minutes from Achada do Teixeira, 20 from the PR9 trailhead at Queimadas, with an early breakfast, secure parking, drying space and one of the best restaurants on Madeira on site. €110–€170 double depending on season.

accommodationStrategy.name: Funchal Zona Velha aparthotel
accommodationStrategy.description: Cheap, central, and useful for the arrival and departure nights: walking distance to the seafront promenade, the market and the taxi ranks that get you to trailheads, from about €70. A kitchen matters when you are eating at 05:30 before an Areeiro sunrise start.

accommodationStrategy.name: A small quinta in São Vicente or Ponta Delgada
accommodationStrategy.description: For the middle of the week: it halves the driving to Encumeada and Fanal, sits on the wet, green side of the island where the recovery day belongs, and costs €80–€120. Check it has covered parking — north-coast rain is not a rumour.

logistics.connectivity: Portugal is EU — roaming at domestic rates, and coverage is good island-wide. **No signal in any levada tunnel**, in the Caldeirão ravine or in the upper Curral basin. Download offline maps; save your SIMplifica booking QR codes offline too, because rangers check them at trailheads.
logistics.emergency: **112**; Madeira's Serviço Regional de Proteção Civil coordinates mountain and coastal rescue, with helicopter support based near Funchal. Rescues from the massif ridges are technical and slow. Insurance covering hiking/trail running with exposure is essential; note that some policies exclude "unmarked trails", which is a reason to stay on PR routes.
logistics.weather: Madeira's defining phenomenon is the **north–south split**: it can be 24 °C and sunny in Funchal while the north coast is in horizontal rain and the massif is closed. The *capacete* cloud cap forms on Pico Ruivo most days from mid-morning. Winter and early spring bring Atlantic storms with 100 km/h+ gusts on the ridges, and the authorities close trails outright — check the IFCN trail-status page every morning, not just once.
logistics.bookingWindows: **Official trails require a paid online reservation through the SIMplifica portal** for a dated slot; book PR1 as far ahead as you can, because it is capped and it sells out. Fees in 2026 start at a **€4.50 minimum**, with a reduced €3.00 rate retained for operators under protocol, and **PR1 Vereda do Areeiro priced at €10.50**. MIUT (late April) fills the whole island's accommodation — book six months out or avoid that week.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards are accepted almost everywhere including small cafés; carry €50–€80 cash for rural bars and parking. Tipping 5–10% for good service.
logistics.transportRules: A rental car is the practical choice, but Madeira's roads are extreme — 20% gradients, hairpins, and old ER roads with rockfall. Take full insurance and never leave anything visible at a trailhead car park; Areeiro and Queimadas have had break-ins. For point-to-point runs, pre-book a taxi shuttle (€25–€45); Funchal-based drivers will do a fixed-price Areeiro-to-Achada transfer. Buses (Rodoeste, SAM, Horários do Funchal) reach most villages but not most trailheads.
logistics.permits: The paid reservation described above is a legal requirement on classified PR routes and is enforced by rangers with fines. Trails close for weather, fire damage and landslides frequently and without much notice. Camping is restricted to designated sites. Drone use over the natural park needs authorisation. Do not swim in levada channels.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable island-wide; **levada water is not**. The real hazards are falls from unfenced levada edges, rockfall on the north-coast veredas, and hypothermia on the ridge in wind-driven rain — carry a windproof shell even on a 25 °C day at sea level. No ticks or venomous snakes. The 2024 wildfires damaged the central massif and left loose ground and dead standing timber in places; stay on the path.

proTips: **Book PR1 the day the slot opens, and take the first one.** It is the island's flagship route, it is capped, and at sunrise you get the ridge to yourself before the tour groups start at 08:00 — after which the tunnels become a queue.
**Run the massif traverses one-way with a taxi shuttle.** Areeiro to Achada do Teixeira, or Encumeada to Achada, costs €25–€45 and doubles the quality of the running compared with any out-and-back.
**Carry two headtorches, not one.** The PR9 tunnels are long, wet, low and completely unlit; a failed torch a kilometre into a tunnel is an actual emergency and phones die in that humidity.

**Use the north–south split as a weather strategy.** When the massif is closed, the south-coast levadas and the Funchal promenade are usually dry; when Funchal bakes, the Fanal and Ribeiro Frio forests are 10 °C cooler.
**Check the IFCN trail-status page every single morning.** Madeira closes and reopens individual PR routes constantly for landslip and storm damage; a booking is not a guarantee the trail is open.
**Alternate stairs and contours.** Madeira's eccentric loading is exceptional — a levada day after every ridge day is what makes six running days in seven survivable.
**Do Fanal in the mist, not in the sun.** The ancient til trees only look the way people photograph them when the Paul da Serra fog is in, which is most mornings and almost no afternoons.

**Time a spring trip against MIUT, deliberately.** Late April brings the Madeira Island Ultra Trail; go the week before to run a marked course with course support around, or steer well clear if you want empty trails and available beds.

raw.Signature routes: (1) **PR1 Vereda do Areeiro, Pico do Areeiro (1,818 m) → Pico das Torres (1,851 m) → Pico Ruivo (1,862 m)**: 7 km one way, roughly 700 m up / 550 m down, mid-pack 1 h 15–1 h 50 (signed 3 h 30 walking); the reopened tunnel variant after the 2024 fire damage. (2) **PR1.2 Vereda da Encumeada**, Encumeada (1,007 m) → Pico Ruivo: 11.5 km, ~1,100 m D+, 2 h 30–3 h 30. (3) **PR1.3 Vereda da Ilha / Achada do Teixeira → Pico Ruivo**: 5.6 km out-and-back, 300 m D+, 45 min–1 h. (4) **PR9 Levada do Caldeirão Verde**, Queimadas → Caldeirão Verde: 13 km out-and-back, 300 m D+, 1 h 30–2 h, four unlit tunnels. (5) **PR8 Vereda da Ponta de São Lourenço**: 8 km out-and-back, 400 m D+, 1 h–1 h 20, fully exposed. (6) **PR13 Vereda do Fanal** across the Paul da Serra plateau to the Fanal laurel wood: 10.8 km, 300 m D+, 1 h 15–1 h 45.
raw.Technicality (ITRA-style 1–5; 1 = fire r: Levada paths **2**, but with a permanent unprotected drop on the outside edge — the danger is falling off, not falling over. PR1 massif ridge **3–4**: cut steps, cabled sections, three tunnels, severe exposure. PR1.2 Encumeada **4** — the most sustained exposure on the island, with narrow arêtes and ladders. PR8 São Lourenço **2–3**, with wind as the actual hazard. Add one grade to everything in wet conditions: basalt polished by two hundred years of feet is genuinely slippery.
raw.Terrain split, week average: ~30% cut basalt steps and rock staircase, ~25% levada-side dirt and cobble path, ~15% tunnel (unlit, wet, ankle-deep in places), ~15% laurissilva forest singletrack on root and leaf mould, ~10% volcanic gravel and ash on the high ridges, ~5% asphalt. Grip beats cushioning: sticky rubber and aggressive lugs, plus a spare dry pair, because nothing dries on the north coast.
raw.Waymarking: Official routes carry **PR numbers on yellow-topped wooden posts** with distance and walking time, plus green-and-yellow "Percursos Pedestres Recomendados" boards at each trailhead. Unofficial levada branches are unmarked and frequently unsafe. The **MIUT** course is signed only during race week; outside it, follow PR numbers.
raw.Water refill points and month reliabilit: *Levada water is irrigation water and not potable* — do not drink it untreated regardless of how clean it looks. Reliable fixed points: **Casa de Abrigo do Pico Ruivo** (shelter/café below the summit, drinks and water, generally open daily in season); **Casa das Queimadas** at the PR9 trailhead; **Ribeiro Frio** village fountain and cafés; **Achada do Teixeira** car park; **Encumeada** café; **Pico do Areeiro** café at the observatory; **Baía d'Abra** has nothing at all, so carry everything for PR8. Springs on the north slopes run year-round given Madeira's rainfall, but the **exposed east (São Lourenço) and the Paul da Serra plateau have no water at any time of year**.
raw.Navigation: Official route sheets and the **SIMplifica** booking portal from the regional forestry authority (IFCN); GPX from the visitmadeira trail pages, Komoot and the MIUT race site. Phone coverage is surprisingly good on the ridges and in the villages but **absent in every tunnel, in the Caldeirão Verde ravine, in Curral das Freiras' upper basin and in parts of the Fanal wood**. Bail-outs: the Pico Ruivo shelter and Achada do Teixeira road head are the massif's escape route; the Encumeada and Areeiro roads are the two other exits; on the levadas you simply reverse — there are rarely side exits.
raw.Recovery, exposure and weather managemen: Day 4 is the true low day. The structural rule for the week is **alternate ridge days with levada days**: the levadas are near-flat, shaded and cool, which lets you run six days out of seven. Start massif days at first light — the *capacete*, the cloud cap that forms on Pico Ruivo, typically builds from late morning and turns the ridge into a whiteout. Sea-level to 1,862 m in an hour's drive means no altitude issue, but the temperature difference between Funchal and the summit is routinely 12–15 °C and the wind on the ridge can be 60 km/h when the coast is still.

Grip beats cushioning: sticky rubber and aggressive lugs, plus a spare dry pair, because nothing dries on the north coast.

PR1 massif ridge **3–4**: cut steps, cabled sections, three tunnels, severe exposure. PR1.2 Encumeada **4** — the most sustained exposure on the island, with narrow arêtes and ladders. PR8 São Lourenço **2–3**, with wind as the actual hazard. Add one grade to everything in wet conditions: basalt polished by two hundred years of feet is genuinely slippery.

sources.verified: Madeira's classified walking routes require a paid dated reservation through the regional SIMplifica system, with a **€4.50 minimum fee for 2026** and a retained **€3.00 protocol rate**; **PR1 Vereda do Areeiro reopened in April 2026** after roughly two years closed following 2024 wildfire damage, and carries a **€10.50 fee**; PR1 links Pico do Areeiro (1,818 m), Pico das Torres (1,851 m) and Pico Ruivo (1,862 m) over about 7 km, signed at roughly 3 h 30 walking; **MIUT is scheduled for 25–26 April 2026**.
sources.confidenceNotes: Re-verify (a) **per-trail fee amounts and which routes are chargeable** — the IFCN fee schedule differs by trail and has changed more than once; (b) **live trail status for PR1, PR1.2, PR9/PR9.1 and PR8**, which close for storm and landslide damage at short notice; (c) whether the **PR1 tunnel variant or the original crest route** is the open alignment post-reopening; (d) **MIUT 2026/2027 distance ladder and elevation figures** (the 110–115 km flagship has been rebranded); (e) **Pico Ruivo shelter opening hours and whether it is currently serving food and water**; (f) taxi shuttle prices and rental car rates.

trips.title: The Knife and the Plateau: Running Piatra Craiului and the Bucegi
trips.subRegion: Piatra Craiului & Bucegi Mountains, Southern Carpathians

bestPeriod.window: mid-July to mid-September, once the ridge snow patches have gone and before the first autumn storms
bestPeriod.avoid: May–June (verglas and wet limestone on the chained sections) and any period of afternoon thunderstorm warnings — the Piatra Craiului ridge is a 25 km lightning rod with no escape

accommodation.note: €250–€430 (€35–€62/night, pensiuni and cabanas; cabana bunks far cheaper)

transport.note: €120–€200 (car hire or transfers Brașov–Zărnești–Bușteni, plus the Bușteni cable car)

activities.note: €60–€130 (park fees, one guided ridge day, cable car, Libearty sanctuary)

profile.difficultyNote: Hard

trips.gatewayAirport: Bucharest Otopeni (OTP) then CFR to Brașov (2 h 30–3 h) or Bușteni (2 h); Brașov → Zărnești by local train (~50 min) or road (~28 km, 40 min). Bușteni is on the DN1/Prahova valley main line, so the week's ending point is the easiest place in Romania to leave from.
trips.summary: Piatra Craiului is a 25 km limestone blade standing on end, and it is one of the few places in Europe where a runner meets fixed chains before breakfast. Then the Bucegi does the opposite: a vast tilted plateau at…
trips.hook: Piatra Craiului is a 25 km limestone blade standing on end, and it is one of the few places in Europe where a runner meets fixed chains before breakfast. Then the Bucegi does the opposite: a vast tilted plateau at 2,200 m where you can hold a pace for an hour. This week is fast grass, sharp karst, a 1,600 m descent that will ruin your quads, and a genuine obligation to think about bears. It suits confident mountain runners, not first-timers.

snapshot.Start / End: Zărnești → Bușteni (linear, ~135 km run, ~7,500 m of vertical)
snapshot.Getting there: Bucharest Otopeni (OTP) then CFR to Brașov (2 h 30–3 h) or Bușteni (2 h); Brașov → Zărnești by local train (~50 min) or road (~28 km, 40 min). Bușteni is on the DN1/Prahova valley main line, so the week's ending point is the easiest place in Romania to leave from.

itinerary.title: Zărnești, the gorge, and legs that remember the altitude
itinerary.morning: Train or transfer from Brașov to **Zărnești**. Register the week's plan with your accommodation and check the **Parcul Național Piatra Craiului** visitor centre for trail and bear notices [VERIFY: current park entry fee and visitor-centre hours].
itinerary.afternoon: Run the **Prăpăstiile Zărneștiului** from **Fântâna lui Botorog** past **Cabana Diana** — the gorge narrows to a slot, the temperature drops, and the trail turns to polished limestone — up to **Cabana Curmătura** at 1,470 m for the first view of the ridge you will be on in two days.
itinerary.evening: Back down the same way. Ciorbă de burtă and a beer in Zărnești, kit laid out, and a serious look at tomorrow's forecast — Piatra Craiului makes its own weather and the ridge day depends on it.

itinerary.title: Măgura and Peștera: the good-legs day
itinerary.morning: Shuttle or run the road up to **Măgura**, the scattered village on the shelf above Zărnești. Meadow trails between hay barns and limestone dolines, past **Peștera** and its cave, toward **Șirnea**.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop back with the entire east face of Piatra Craiului on your right — a 1,000 m wall of grey limestone running 20 km without a break. This is the run people remember, and it is easy enough to hold a conversation.
itinerary.evening: Down to **Bran** for the castle if you must, or better, the **Libearty Bear Sanctuary** at Zărnești, home to over a hundred rescued brown bears and the most useful hour you will spend on bear behaviour before the ridge [VERIFY: current hours and ticket price].

itinerary.title: Creasta Nordică: Curmătura to La Om
itinerary.morning: Out of Zărnești before first light, up the Prăpăstii, and at **Cabana Curmătura** by 07:30. Fill everything you carry. Onto the red stripe for **Vârful Turnu (1,923 m)** and the start of the ridge proper.
itinerary.afternoon: The crest: Padinile Frumoase, Vârful Ascuțit, the **lanțuri**, and the long airy walk to **La Om (Vârful Baciului), 2,238 m**. Drop east to **Izvorul lui Ivan** if you need water. Turn around at a hard time, not a hard place — 14:00 is the sensible cut-off with afternoon storms building.
itinerary.evening: Return over the ridge or descend via **Șaua Grindului** and **Refugiul Grind** to Plaiul Foii if you have arranged a pick-up. Eat everything. Sleep hard.

itinerary.title: Padina lui Călineț, or a rest day earned
itinerary.morning: Road transfer 12 km up the valley to **Cabana Plaiul Foii (849 m)**, the western trailhead. Into **Padina lui Călineț** — a raw, silent limestone valley where the trail crosses scree fans under 500 m walls.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb to **Șaua Călineț** on the ridge, touch the crest from the other side, and descend the same line. If the ridge day has taken more out of you than expected, swap this for an easy 8 km in the Zărnești forest and the thermal recovery of doing nothing.
itinerary.evening: Transfer to **Bușteni** over the Bran and Predeal saddles, about 70 km and 1 h 30. Check into a Prahova valley pension and shift your head from limestone to plateau.

itinerary.title: Babele, the Sfinx and Vârful Omu
itinerary.morning: First cabin on the **Bușteni–Babele cable car** — from 885 m to about 2,200 m in one lift, which is the honest way to get onto the Bucegi plateau with fresh legs [VERIFY: 2026 Telecabina Bușteni tariff, hours and any maintenance closure]. Run out to **Babele (2,206 m)** and the **Sfinxul (2,216 m)** before the coach crowd arrives at ten.
itinerary.afternoon: North across the plateau, high open gravel and grass, past Curmătura Văii Cerbului to **Cabana Omu** and **Vârful Omu, 2,505 m** — the roof of the Bucegi, with the Făgăraș on the horizon. Hot tea at the cabana, which is the highest staffed hut in Romania.
itinerary.evening: Back to Babele and down on the cable car, or run the whole plateau return if the weather is holding. Dinner in Bușteni on Bulevardul Libertății.

itinerary.title: Omu to Bușteni down Valea Cerbului
itinerary.morning: Cable car up, plateau traverse back to **Cabana Omu**, then commit: the **Valea Cerbului** descent drops 1,600 m into Bușteni in one uninterrupted line. Steep grass at the top, then a boulder-choked valley floor, then Poiana Coștilei and forest track.
itinerary.afternoon: This is a quad-destroying descent and the reason to have trained eccentric loading. Take it in stages, keep your feet quiet, and stop at the Poiana Coștilei meadow to look back up at the Coștila and Morarul walls — the alpine climbing heart of Romania.
itinerary.evening: Ice-cold feet in the Prahova, then papanași. Do not plan anything for tomorrow morning that requires stairs.

itinerary.title: Jepii Mici, Poiana Izvoarelor, and out
itinerary.morning: A choice. The hard version: the blue-stripe **Jepii Mici** rib straight out of Bușteni toward Cabana Piatra Arsă, 1,100 m of climbing on a rocky spur with the Caraiman cross above you. The kind version: the forest circuit to **Cabana Gura Diham** and **Cabana Poiana Izvoarelor (1,455 m)**, soft underfoot and shaded.
itinerary.afternoon: Down to Bușteni, a last look at the **Crucea Eroilor** on Caraiman — the 1928 monument standing 28 m tall at 2,291 m — and the Cantacuzino Castle gardens if there is time.
itinerary.evening: CFR from Bușteni: 2 h to Bucharest Nord, or 45 minutes back to Brașov. Kit smells of limestone dust and spruce. That is correct.

accommodationStrategy.name: A Zărnești pensiune near Strada Mitropolit Ioan Mețianu
accommodationStrategy.description: the Prăpăstii trailhead and **Fântâna lui Botorog** are a 3 km jog from town, transfers to Plaiul Foii and Măgura are easy to arrange from here, and the national park office is in town for trail and bear updates.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–4 weeks ahead for July–August; Zărnești has far more beds than it used to.

accommodationStrategy.name: Vila Hermani
accommodationStrategy.description: it sits at 900 m in the meadow village with the east wall of Piatra Craiului out of the window, which turns Day 2 into a run from the door. Long-established with walkers and runners, so early breakfasts and packed lunches are normal.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead in summer, direct by email [VERIFY: current rates].

accommodationStrategy.name: Cabana Curmătura
accommodationStrategy.description: sleeping at 1,470 m puts you on the ridge at dawn with 650 m of climbing already banked, which is the difference between finishing the Creasta Nordică before the storms and turning back. Bunks, blankets, no shower worth the name, cash only.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct by phone; bunks are first-come in practice, so arrive early or call the day before [VERIFY: current rate and whether reservations are taken].

logistics.connectivity: Orange, Vodafone and Digi cover the valleys and, surprisingly, much of the Piatra Craiului crest and the Bucegi plateau — the ridges are line-of-sight to Brașov and the Prahova valley. Expect nothing in Padina lui Călineț or the lower Valea Cerbului.
logistics.emergency: **112** for everything. **Salvamont** is the mountain rescue service; the national Salvamont dispatch number is **0725 826 668**, and **Salvamont Brașov** covers Piatra Craiului, Bran and Râșnov, with the Prahova county team covering the Bucegi from Bușteni. Carry a charged phone, a foil bivvy and a whistle. Tell your guesthouse your route and expected return time every single day.
logistics.weather: Convective storms build over both ranges from roughly 13:00 in July and August. On the Piatra Craiului ridge there is no shelter and no fast way down. Start at dawn, be off the crest by early afternoon, and treat a forecast of afternoon storms as a rest day rather than a gamble. Snow patches survive in north-facing gullies into early July.
logistics.bookingWindows: Guesthouses 2–6 weeks. A guide for the Creasta Nordică 2–3 weeks. Cabana Omu bunks are not really bookable — arrive or don't.
logistics.money: Romanian leu (RON), roughly 5 RON to €1. Cards work in Zărnești, Bran and Bușteni. **Every cabana above the treeline is cash only** — carry 300–500 RON in small notes for the week.
logistics.transportRules: No car is needed if you use transfers, but one makes Plaiul Foii and Măgura far easier. Local minibuses (*maxi-taxi*) run Brașov–Zărnești and Brașov–Bran frequently. The Bușteni cable car queues badly after 09:30 in August.
logistics.permits: No permit is needed to run in either national park, but **Parcul Național Piatra Craiului** and **Parcul Natural Bucegi** both restrict you to marked trails, ban wild camping outside designated areas, and ban fires. Bivouacking is tolerated only at named spots. **Bears:** Romania holds the largest brown bear population in the EU and the Zărnești–Bran corridor is among the most active areas in the country. Never run at dawn or dusk in the beech zone alone; make noise on blind corners; carry food sealed and never leave it outside a hut; if you meet a bear, **stop, do not run, back away slowly while facing it and talking**; a bear standing up is assessing you, not charging. Report any close encounter to Salvamont or 112 so it is logged. **Bear spray** is legal in Romania for personal defence — no permit, over-18s only — and sells for roughly **100–350 RON (€20–€70)** in outdoor and hunting shops in Brașov and online (TW1000 Bear Defender, Umarex, Sabre Frontiersman, Bear Stopper are the names on the shelf). The catch is that you cannot fly with it, in cabin *or* hold, so buy it on arrival and leave it behind; carry it on a hip belt where you can reach it in seconds, not buried in a running vest.

proTips: **Sleep at Cabana Curmătura the night before the ridge.** It removes 650 m of climbing and two hours from the front of the Creasta Nordică day, and it is the only way to be on the crest at sunrise.
**Set a turn-around time, not a turn-around summit.** 14:00 on the ridge, regardless of where you are. The chains in wet limestone are the single highest-consequence thing on this itinerary.

**Hire a local guide for the Creasta Nordică once.** One day with a Zărnești or Salvamont-affiliated guide teaches you the escape lines and the chain sequence, and makes every subsequent day safer. Roughly €90–€150 for a small group [VERIFY: current guide day rates].
**Take the cable car up and run down.** In the Bucegi the plateau is the good running and the ascent from Bușteni is a grind. Buying the lift buys you the best 14 km of the week.

**Carry more water than the profile suggests.** Both ranges are limestone: rain vanishes underground. Izvorul lui Ivan is a genuine spring but a detour, and the Bucegi plateau has nothing at all between the cabanas.
**Shoes with a rock plate, and take a second pair.** Piatra Craiului karst will cut a soft midsole in three days and the Valea Cerbului descent will find any weakness in your lacing.

**Learn three words:** *"Ajutor"* (help), *"potecă"* (trail) and *"urs"* (bear). Shepherds and their dogs are everywhere above the treeline — walk, don't run, past a flock, keep the shepherd between you and the dogs, and greet him loudly.

raw.Run 1 — Prăpăstiile Zărneștiului to Caba: 13 km round trip, +650 m / −650 m. From the **Fântâna lui Botorog** spring at the gorge mouth, the blue-triangle trail threads the **Prăpăstii** — a limestone slot barely three metres wide in places — then climbs scree and beech to **Cabana Curmătura** (1,470 m). Technical grade **T2–T3**: runnable up, genuinely runnable down, loose gravel on the exit ramp.
raw.Run 2 — Creasta Nordică, Curmătura to La: 18–20 km out-and-back from Curmătura, +1,150 m. The main ridge, red stripe: **Vârful Turnu (1,923 m)**, Padinile Frumoase, Vârful Ascuțit, Șaua Grindului, then the long summit ridge to **La Om, 2,238 m**, the range's high point. Grade **T4 with sections of secured scrambling**. This is not a running route end to end — expect 40% moving on hands, 30% careful walking, 30% actual running.
raw.Run 3 — Padina lui Călineț from Plaiul F: 16 km, +1,250 m. The western approach: a wild limestone valley of scree fans and pine, climbing to **Șaua Călineț** and the ridge. Grade **T4**, with a long unrunnable grohotiș (scree) middle section — a strong hiker's route done at running pace, and the quietest day of the week.
raw.Run 4 — Măgura and Peștera meadow circui: 17 km, +700 m. Hay meadows, haystacks and karst dolines between **Măgura**, **Peștera** and **Șirnea** villages, with Piatra Craiului's whole east wall as backdrop. Grade **T1–T2** and the most purely enjoyable running of the trip.
raw.Run 5 — Bucegi plateau: Babele to Vârful: 14 km round trip from the Babele cable-car top station, +550 m. **Babele (2,206 m)** and the **Sfinxul (2,216 m)** wind-carved rock, then the yellow-stripe plateau traverse north over Curmătura Văii Cerbului to **Cabana Omu** and **Vârful Omu, 2,505 m**. Grade **T2** on the plateau, **T3** on the final rocky pull.
raw.Run 6 — Omu down Valea Cerbului to Buște: 12 km, −1,600 m in one continuous drop from 2,505 m to Bușteni at ~880 m. Steep alpine grass, then boulder-strewn stream bed, then forest track. Grade **T3–T4** at the top, **T2** below the treeline. [VERIFY: current waymark colour on the Valea Cerbului trail — repainted in recent seasons.]
raw.Run 7 — Jepii Mici and Poiana Izvoarelor: 15 km, +900 m / −900 m. Blue-stripe from Bușteni up the **Jepii Mici** rib toward Cabana Piatra Arsă, or the gentler forest circuit via **Cabana Gura Diham** and **Cabana Poiana Izvoarelor (1,455 m)**. Grade **T2–T3**.
raw.Terrain: Piatra Craiului is **karst**: fluted limestone, sharp edges that shred a soft-lugged shoe, and mobile scree. Wear a stiffer shoe with a rock plate and expect to replace it. The Bucegi plateau is **alpine grass and gravel** — fast, high, exposed. Below the treeline both ranges are **root and mud** beech-and-spruce.
raw.The chains (lanțuri): The Creasta Nordică carries fixed chains and cables on several short exposed steps between Vârful Ascuțit and the summit ridge. They are old, sometimes loose, and lethal when wet or iced. Treat any of the following as a turn-around: rain on the limestone, cloud on the ridge, wind above ~50 km/h, or a thunderstorm within an hour. There is **no bail-out from the middle of the ridge** — the escape points are Curmătura at the north end and Șaua Funduri / the Grind descent, and both are long.
raw.Water points by name: **Fântâna lui Botorog** at the mouth of the Prăpăstii (reliable, the last certain water before the ridge). **Izvorul lui Ivan**, on the eastern flank below the main ridge, is the classic ridge-runner's refill and a signposted detour off the crest — allow 20–30 minutes there and back and do not count on it in a dry August. **Cabana Curmătura** and **Cabana Plaiul Foii** sell water and refill bottles. In the Bucegi, **Cabana Omu** and **Cabana Piatra Arsă** are the only reliable sources on the plateau; the plateau itself is dry karst and you must carry 2–2.5 L for the Babele–Omu day.
raw.Bail-outs and refuges: **Refugiul Grind (~1,620 m)** on the west side is an unstaffed emergency shelter, not accommodation. **Cabana Curmătura**, **Cabana Plaiul Foii (849 m)**, **Cabana Diana** at the Zărnești gorge entrance, **Cabana Omu (2,505 m)**, **Cabana Babele**, **Cabana Piatra Arsă**, **Cabana Gura Diham** and **Cabana Poiana Izvoarelor** are all staffed in season and all take walk-ins for soup and a bunk if you get caught out [VERIFY: current cabana bed rates and season dates].

trips.title: Julian Alps: Bohinj & Pokljuka
trips.subRegion: Gorenjska — Bohinj, Pokljuka & the Triglav Lakes Valley

bestPeriod.window: Mid-June–mid-July & September (huts staffed, snow gone, lakes running)
bestPeriod.avoid: Late July–mid-August (hut beds gone, Vogel and Savica car parks full by 08:00); late October–May (snow above 1,500 m, huts closed, Pokljuka is a cross-country ski plateau)
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-June–mid-July & September (huts staffed, snow gone, lakes running)

accommodation.note: Bohinj pensions €70–€120 dbl/night; mountain hut bed €25–€35, half-board €45–€60

food.note: Gostilna main €12–€18; hut dinner €12–€16; planina sour milk and cheese €5

transport.note: Rental car 7 days €190–€290, Slovenian motorway vignette, Vogel cable car

activities.note: Vogel return ~€28, Savica waterfall ~€4–€6, Blato/Savica parking, PZS membership if bought

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5 — sustained 1,200–1,600 m days on Julian limestone with one hut night at 1,685 m; no glacier, but plenty of loose rock and cable

trips.gatewayAirport: LJU — Ljubljana Jože Pučnik (1 h 15 drive to Bohinj; bus via Bled ~2 h); KLU Klagenfurt and TRS Trieste are both ~2 h
trips.summary: Bohinj is the quiet end of the Julian Alps — a 525 m glacial lake with a 1,400 m wall of the Lower Bohinj range on one side and the Triglav massif on the other — and it gives a runner two contrasting playgrounds within twenty minutes. South and west: the Vogel–Rodica ridge and the Komna plateau, high, dry limestone with enormous views to Triglav. North and east: the Pokljuka plateau, a 1,200–1,400 m spruce-and-karst tableland whose *planine* (summer dairy pastures) link into some of the most runnable singletrack in the Alps. The week builds through a lake orientation day and a Vogel ridge day into an overnight in the Triglav Lakes Valley, then swings to Pokljuka for the Debela peč rim and the planina circuit, with a deliberate recovery day on the Bohinj lake path. It suits a runner who wants alpine scale, a functioning hut network and Slovenian prices.

itinerary.title: Arrive at Bohinj, circle the lake
itinerary.morning: Land at LJU, collect the car, buy a Slovenian **motorway vignette** at the airport or first petrol station, and drive 1 h 15 via Bled to **Ribčev Laz** on Lake Bohinj (525 m).
itinerary.afternoon: Loosen off on the **Bohinj lake circuit** — 12 km around, gravel and lakeside root path, the north shore the quieter half, finishing at the stone bridge and St John the Baptist church. Swim if it is warm; the lake is around 18–20 °C in July.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **Gostilna Mihovc** in Stara Fužina — Bohinj cheese, ričet, and a Union beer.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km / 120 m D+ / SAC T1 / 55 min–1 h 15; transfer 1 h 15 from LJU.
itinerary.sleep: Pension in Stara Fužina or Ribčev Laz

itinerary.title: Vogel ridge to Rodica
itinerary.morning: First **Vogel cable car** from Ukanc (up to 1,535 m, return around €28). Run the ridge west over **Šija (1,880 m)** to **Rodica (1,966 m)** — grass, then limestone, with Triglav filling the northern horizon and the Soča side falling away south.
itinerary.afternoon: Return along the ridge and either ride down or run the steep old descent to Ukanc. Then the short walk to **Slap Savica**, the waterfall at the head of the valley (small entry fee).
itinerary.evening: Pizza and a beer in Bohinjska Bistrica at **Foksner**; get to bed early — tomorrow is a hut day.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km / 900 m D+ / SAC T2 with one T3 step / 2 h 15–3 h / high point 1,966 m / cable car ~€28.
itinerary.sleep: Pension in Stara Fužina or Ribčev Laz

itinerary.title: Into the Seven Lakes Valley
itinerary.morning: Drive to **Planina Blato (1,147 m)** and pay the parking. Climb through **Planina pri Jezeru (1,453 m)** — dairy hut, water, sour milk — then over the shoulder into the **Dolina Triglavskih jezer**, past **Črno jezero (1,294 m)**, the lowest of the seven.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue up the valley to **Koča pri Triglavskih jezerih (1,685 m)**, drop your pack, and run the easy upper-valley out-and-back past Dvojno jezero toward Zeleno jezero for the full sequence of lakes and the dolomite amphitheatre above.
itinerary.evening: Hut half-board — jota, štruklji, and a very early night in a 135-bed hut where the water is limited and the showers are cold.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km in / 900 m D+, plus 6 km / 300 m upper valley / SAC T2–T3 / 2 h 15–3 h / hut at 1,685 m, 135 beds.

itinerary.title: Over to Komna and down
itinerary.morning: From the hut, run south-west across the plateau to **Dom na Komni (1,520 m)**, a big old hut on the Komna shelf with the WWI Isonzo-front history and a view down the Bohinj trough.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend the **Komna zigzags to the Savica** trailhead at Ukanc — a 900 m drop on stepped, cobbled path that is a proper eccentric-strength test. Retrieve the car from Blato by taxi or a pre-arranged shuttle.
itinerary.evening: Recovery dinner at **Gostilna Rupa** in Srednja vas — Bohinj mutton, buckwheat žganci.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km / 400 m up, 1,150 m down / SAC T2 / 2 h 30–3 h 30 / water at Komna only.
itinerary.sleep: Pension in Stara Fužina or Srednja vas

itinerary.title: Recovery day in the Voje valley
itinerary.morning: True low day. An easy 9 km from **Stara Fužina up the Mostnica gorge** to the **Voje valley** and the Mostnica waterfall — flat, shaded, riverside, with the gorge's carved potholes and the famous "elephant" rock.
itinerary.afternoon: Nothing. Coffee at the Voje hut, the Bohinj cheese dairy museum in Stara Fužina, and legs up by the lake.
itinerary.evening: Grilled trout and a Rebula on the lakefront at Ribčev Laz.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km / 250 m D+ / SAC T1 / 55 min–1 h 10 easy / entirely shaded.
itinerary.sleep: Pension in Stara Fužina or Srednja vas

itinerary.title: Pokljuka: Lipanci and Debela peč
itinerary.morning: Drive up to **Rudno polje (1,347 m)**, the Pokljuka biathlon centre, and climb the Slovenska planinska pot line to **Blejska koča na Lipanci (1,630 m)**, then the rim over **Lipanski vrh** to **Debela peč (2,014 m)** — a narrow, cabled summit ridge looking straight across the Krma valley at Triglav's north side.
itinerary.afternoon: Return over **Brda and Mrežce** and descend through the spruce to Rudno polje. Add the **Planina Konjščica** loop if the legs allow.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Srednja vas or Bohinjska Bistrica; toast the last big day.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km / 800 m D+ / SAC T3 on the summit ridge / 2 h–2 h 45 / high point 2,014 m.
itinerary.sleep: Pension in Stara Fužina or Srednja vas

itinerary.title: Planina circuit and out
itinerary.morning: The best-value run of the week: the **Pokljuka planina circuit** — Rudno polje to **Zajamniki** (the photogenic row of hay barns on the ridge), across to **Uskovnica (1,154 m)** and down to Srednja vas. Fast, soft, forested, and dotted with dairy huts where you can buy sour milk mid-run.
itinerary.afternoon: Shower, buy Bohinj cheese and honey in Stara Fužina, and drive to Ljubljana — with an hour in the old town if the flight allows.
itinerary.evening: Departure from LJU.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km / 550 m D+ / SAC T1–T2 / 1 h 50–2 h 30; drive to LJU 1 h 15.

accommodationStrategy.name: A family pension in Stara Fužina
accommodationStrategy.description: The right base: on the Mostnica/Voje trailhead, five minutes from Ribčev Laz, twenty from the Blato and Rudno polje roads, and cheaper than the lakefront hotels at €70–€110 double. Slovenian pensions habitually do early breakfast or a packed one if you ask, and all of them have somewhere to hang wet kit.

accommodationStrategy.name: Koča pri Triglavskih jezerih
accommodationStrategy.description: The one high night, and the only way to see the Seven Lakes Valley without a punishing there-and-back. 135 places across rooms and dormitories, spring water outside the door, no hot showers, and a **compulsory advance reservation** — its 2026 season ran roughly 6 June to 30 September. Bring a sleeping-bag liner and cash for extras.

accommodationStrategy.name: A pension in Srednja vas or Bohinjska Bistrica
accommodationStrategy.description: For the Pokljuka half of the week: fifteen minutes closer to the Rudno polje road and noticeably quieter than the lake, with parking and easy access to Gostilna Rupa. Similar price band, and a better bet than the lake in the first three weeks of August.

logistics.connectivity: Slovenia is EU; roam at domestic rates. Coverage is good in the Bohinj basin and on ridges but **absent in the Mostnica gorge, patchy in the Lakes Valley and in the Krma-side gullies**. Download offline maps and the hut phone numbers.
logistics.emergency: **112**; Slovenia's mountain rescue (GRZS) is professional, fast and helicopter-equipped. Membership of the Alpine Association of Slovenia (PZS) includes rescue and repatriation cover and gives roughly 30–50% off hut beds — for a week with two or more hut nights it can pay for itself. Otherwise carry insurance with alpine rescue cover.
logistics.weather: Julian Alps summer convection is the main hazard — clear mornings, towering cumulus by 13:00, and violent lightning on exposed limestone ridges by mid-afternoon. The region also gets sudden **jugo**-driven Adriatic fronts from the south-west that dump remarkable rainfall on Bohinj (one of the wettest places in Slovenia). ARSO's mountain forecast is the source to use.
logistics.bookingWindows: **Mountain huts require reservation** and Koča pri Triglavskih jezerih fills for July and August weekends months ahead — book as soon as the season's calendar opens, and note it takes card payment for the reservation. Bohinj accommodation for August wants 3–4 months. Vogel cable car does not need booking.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards are widely accepted including at most huts, but carry €100 in cash for planina dairy huts, parking machines and small gostilne. Tipping: round up or 10%.
logistics.transportRules: Slovenia requires a **motorway vignette** (weekly e-vignette, around €16 for a car) — buy it before you touch the A2. Parking at **Savica, Planina Blato and Rudno polje is paid and limited**, and Blato in particular fills by 08:00 in summer. Bohinj runs a summer shuttle bus network, and the **Bohinj Card / Julian Alps guest card** given by many accommodations includes free buses — check before you rent. Bikes and dogs have their own rules on Pokljuka forest roads.
logistics.permits: **Triglav National Park charges no entry fee** and needs no running permit, but parking, the Savica waterfall and the Vogel lift are all paid. Wild camping and bivouacking are prohibited in the park. Drones need permission. Hut etiquette matters: reserve, arrive before dinner service, remove shoes at the door, and pay cash for anything the card machine won't take.
logistics.health: Tap and hut spring water is potable and excellent; treat surface water. **Tick-borne encephalitis is endemic in Slovenian forests** — the vaccine is genuinely worth considering for a week spent in Pokljuka spruce, and do daily tick checks. Vipers exist on sunny limestone but are rarely seen. Snow patches can linger in north-facing gullies above 1,800 m into early July.

proTips: **Buy a PZS (Alpine Association of Slovenia) membership before you travel.** It cuts hut bed prices substantially and includes mountain rescue and repatriation insurance — for a trip with a Lakes Valley night it is usually cheaper than the alternatives.
**Park at Planina Blato before 07:30 or take the shuttle.** It is the gateway to the Seven Lakes Valley, the car park is tiny, and by mid-morning in summer you will be turned around at the barrier.
**Use Pokljuka as the bad-weather plan.** When the Julians are electric, Rudno polje's forest tracks and planina circuits are safe, shaded, low-relief and genuinely enjoyable in rain.

**Buy lunch from the planina dairies.** Sour milk (kislo mleko), fresh cheese and štruklji sold from the huts at Uskovnica, Zajamniki and Blato cost a few euros, are excellent, and solve both food and water on the Pokljuka days.
**Ride Vogel up and run down.** The cable car buys you 1,000 m of ascent and turns a hard out-and-back into a ridge traverse with a long descent — the best value €28 on the trip.

**Do the lake circuit anticlockwise, starting on the north shore.** The south shore is where the day-trip crowds are; going the other way you get the quiet half of the loop first and the swimming spots to yourself.

**Confirm the hut season dates before booking flights.** Koča pri Triglavskih jezerih's summer window is roughly early June to end September, and a trip in late May or October has no high accommodation at all.
**Get the TBE vaccine if you can plan far enough ahead.** Slovenia has one of Europe's highest tick-borne encephalitis rates and this itinerary spends three days in exactly the habitat.

raw.Signature routes: (1) **Vogel–Šija–Rodica ridge** from the Vogel cable-car top station (1,535 m): 14 km, 900 m D+, mid-pack 2 h 15–3 h, with **Rodica at 1,966 m** and a continuous balcony over Bohinj. (2) **Komna plateau loop** from Ukanc via the Savica path to **Dom na Komni (1,520 m)** and back over Črna prst side paths: 17 km, 1,150 m D+, 3 h–4 h. (3) **Seven Lakes Valley (Dolina Triglavskih jezer)** from Planina Blato via Planina pri Jezeru and **Črno jezero (1,294 m)** to **Koča pri Triglavskih jezerih (1,685 m)**: 12 km, 900 m D+, 2 h 15–3 h. (4) **Debela peč (2,014 m) rim from Rudno polje (1,347 m)** via **Blejska koča na Lipanci (1,630 m)** and Lipanski vrh: 15 km, 800 m D+, 2 h–2 h 45. (5) **Pokljuka planina circuit**, Rudno polje–Zajamniki–Uskovnica–Konjščica: 21 km, 750 m D+, 2 h 30–3 h 30, the fastest ground of the week. (6) **Bohinj lake circuit** from Ribčev Laz: 12 km, 120 m D+, 55 min–1 h 15.
raw.Technicality (SAC hiking scale T1–T5, st: Bohinj lake path and Pokljuka planina tracks **T1–T2**. Vogel–Rodica ridge **T2**, with one short **T3** step near Šija. Seven Lakes approach **T2–T3**, with cabled sections above Planina pri Jezeru. Debela peč summit ridge **T3**, narrow, with a short cabled traverse and real exposure north into the Krma valley. Komna **T2**. Nothing on this itinerary needs a via ferrata set, but the Debela peč and Šija steps will feel serious to anyone who has only run forest trails.
raw.Terrain split, week average: ~30% Julian limestone slab, scree and rubble above 1,600 m, ~25% spruce forest singletrack on needle duff (Pokljuka, and it is glorious), ~20% grass pasture and cart track through the planine, ~15% cobbled and stepped hut approach path, ~5% gravel forest road, ~5% asphalt. Pokljuka's needle duff is the softest running of any trip in this collection; the Komna and Lakes limestone is the sharpest.
raw.Waymarking: The **Knafelc mark** — a red circle with a white centre — is used across Slovenia, backed by wooden signposts giving hut names and walking times. The **Slovenska planinska pot** (Slovenian Mountain Trail, the first European long-distance path, established 1953, 600+ km Maribor–Ankaran) crosses this whole area: its Pokljuka–Bohinj–Komna sections are the spine of Days 3, 4 and 6. Marking density is excellent; the weak spots are the open karst above Komna and the plateau between Lipanci and Debela peč in fog.
raw.Water refill points and month reliabilit: The **planina dairy huts are the water system**: **Planina Blato (1,147 m), Planina pri Jezeru (1,453 m), Planina Uskovnica (1,154 m), Planina Zajamniki, Planina Konjščica, Planina Viševnik** all have troughs or taps and most sell sour milk, cheese and štruklji — staffed roughly **mid-June to mid-September**, dry and shut outside that. Fixed points: **Koča pri Triglavskih jezerih** (spring tap outside the hut, drinkable, but consumption is limited and there are no hot showers), **Dom na Komni**, **Blejska koča na Lipanci**, **Koča na Uskovnici**, **Vogel top station**, and every village in the Bohinj basin. **The high limestone between Komna and the Lakes Valley, and the Debela peč rim, hold no surface water at all** — this is porous karst. Carry 1.5–2 L for any high day after mid-July.
raw.Navigation: PZS 1:25,000 "Bohinj" and "Triglav" sheets, or the Kartografija "Julijske Alpe – Vzhodni del"; GPX from the Hiking Bohinj and PZS portals, Komoot and the Slovenian Mountain Trail route files. Coverage: decent on ridges and in the Bohinj basin, **patchy to absent in the Voje valley, the Lakes Valley floor, and the Krma-side gullies below Debela peč**. Bail-outs: the **Vogel cable car** will take you down from the ridge in bad weather; from the Lakes Valley, the descent to Planina Blato is the only quick exit; from Pokljuka, forest roads run everywhere and you are never more than an hour from tarmac.
raw.Recovery, altitude and weather managemen: Day 5 is the low day. Altitude tops at 2,014 m from a 525 m base, so no acclimatisation issue, but the one night at 1,685 m is a useful stimulus. Julian Alps convective storms are frequent and violent from mid-June onward, typically firing between 13:00 and 17:00 — be off Rodica and Debela peč well before that. Pokljuka is the all-weather option: forest cover, low relief and a plateau that stays runnable in rain.
