trips.gatewayAirport: Bratislava (BTS) or Vienna (VIE) then rail to **Žilina** (2 h 30 from Bratislava); Žilina → Terchová by SAD bus, ~50 min. Krakow (KRK) is 3 h by road. Between the ranges: Terchová → Liptovský Mikuláš, ~100 km / 1 h 20 via Žilina and the D1.
trips.summary: The Krivánska Malá Fatra is Slovakia's most concentrated ridge — grass, limestone and chains packed into 20 km — and Veľký Rozsutec at the end of it is a rock horn you climb with your hands. Then you drive ninety…
trips.hook: The Krivánska Malá Fatra is Slovakia's most concentrated ridge — grass, limestone and chains packed into 20 km — and Veľký Rozsutec at the end of it is a rock horn you climb with your hands. Then you drive ninety minutes east and the Nízke Tatry give you the opposite: a long, rolling, above-treeline crest where Chopok to Ďumbier can be run. Two ranges, two temperaments, one week, and a legal closure you cannot argue with.

snapshot.Getting there: Bratislava (BTS) or Vienna (VIE) then rail to **Žilina** (2 h 30 from Bratislava); Žilina → Terchová by SAD bus, ~50 min. Krakow (KRK) is 3 h by road. Between the ranges: Terchová → Liptovský Mikuláš, ~100 km / 1 h 20 via Žilina and the D1.

itinerary.title: Terchová, and a gorge to loosen the legs
itinerary.morning: Bus or drive from Žilina to **Terchová**, birthplace of Juraj Jánošík, the outlaw whose 8 m tin statue stands above the village, and home of the Terchovská muzika string tradition on the UNESCO intangible heritage list.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Jánošíkove diery** from Podžiar: Dolné diery's ladders and catwalks, then the loop through Nové diery and back via Štefanová. Check the weather first — wet rock here is genuinely dangerous, and the one-way system means you cannot simply reverse out.
itinerary.evening: Move up the valley to **Štefanová**, a preserved hamlet of log houses with no through traffic. Bryndzové halušky and a Kofola, then sleep with the Rozsutec silhouette over the roofs.

itinerary.title: The Krivánska ridge, west half
itinerary.morning: Cable car from Vrátna to **Snilovské sedlo (1,524 m)** for a fast start [VERIFY: 2026 Vrátna cable car tariff, operating hours and any maintenance closure], then the short out-and-back to **Veľký Kriváň (1,709 m)** for the whole-range view before turning east.
itinerary.afternoon: The red waymark over **Chleb (1,646 m)**, **Hromové (1,636 m)** and the **Steny** section, where the trail runs along the top of a limestone wall with the Vrátna valley 800 m below on the right. Drop to **Chata pod Chlebom** for water, then run the grass to **Poludňový Grúň**.
itinerary.evening: Descend to **Chata na Grúni** for the terrace and a plate of halušky, then down to Štefanová. Total valley-floor version of this day is close to 2,000 m of vertical if you skip the lift — a legitimate and much better session.
itinerary.dayStats: 18 km / +1,050 m from the saddle

itinerary.title: Stoh, Medziholie and the chains of Veľký Rozsutec
itinerary.morning: Up from Štefanová to **Stoh (1,607 m)**, a steep grass cone with a summit the size of a table. Then the loose descent to **Medziholie (1,185 m)**, the saddle between the two halves of the range.
itinerary.afternoon: **Veľký Rozsutec (1,610 m)** — steel chains and staples on the upper rock, one-way ascent enforced by signs, and a genuinely airy top. Come down north over **Medzirozsutec** and **Malý Rozsutec (1,344 m)** into the Horné diery, which returns you to Štefanová through waterfalls.
itinerary.evening: Pizza and beer at one of the Štefanová chalets, and honest self-assessment: this is the hardest technical day of the week and it tells you whether the Nízke Tatry crest should be run or walked.

itinerary.title: Transfer east, valley legs, and the caves
itinerary.morning: Drive or bus Terchová → Žilina → **Liptovský Mikuláš**, roughly 100 km and 1 h 20 on the D1. Base yourself in **Demänovská Dolina** or in Liptovský Mikuláš itself for supermarkets and physio.
itinerary.afternoon: An easy shakeout in **Demänovská dolina** past **Vyvieranie**, the resurgence where the underground river reappears, then the **Demänovská jaskyňa slobody** or the **Demänovská ľadová jaskyňa** — guided tours only, fixed departure times, and they sell out in August [VERIFY: 2026 Demänovská cave tour times and ticket prices].
itinerary.evening: Liptovský Mikuláš for dinner and the **Múzeum Janka Kráľa** on the main square, then early to bed. Tomorrow is the range's high point.

itinerary.title: Chopok to Ďumbier on the main crest
itinerary.morning: Start at **Trangoška (1,130 m)** on the south side and climb the red waymark to **Chata M. R. Štefánika (1,728 m)**, the classic hut under Ďumbier — coffee, water, and the only shelter on the ridge.
itinerary.afternoon: Up to **Ďumbier (2,043 m)**, the highest point in the Nízke Tatry, with the whole High Tatras chain on the northern horizon. West along the crest over Krúpova hoľa to **Chopok (2,024 m)** — blocky and slow at first, then fast gravel. Descend the south side via Kosodrevina to Trangoška, or take the Jasná lifts down the north side into Demänovská.
itinerary.evening: Recovery in Liptovský Mikuláš — the **Tatralandia** thermal complex is unashamedly a waterpark but the 38 °C outdoor pools do the job [VERIFY: current hours and entry price].

itinerary.title: Bystrá dolina and the long runnable valleys
itinerary.morning: **Bystrá dolina** from Trangoška: forest track and single trail up a quiet valley on the Ďumbier massif's south flank, gaining height gently enough that you can actually run all of it.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross toward **Chopok Juh / Srdiečko** and drop back, or, if legs are good, take the yellow link over to the head of Demänovská and finish down the valley. The alternative base for this day is **Donovaly**, 40 km west, whose forest and meadow network is gentler and better in bad weather.
itinerary.evening: Last big dinner: bryndzové pirohy, kapustnica, and a Demänovka herbal bitter that tastes exactly like the valley it is named after.

itinerary.title: Chopok at dawn, then out
itinerary.morning: First lift up the Jasná side, out to **Chopok (2,024 m)** for sunrise over the Liptov basin, then a fast run down the north-side red-and-blue trails into Demänovská before the cable cars fill.
itinerary.afternoon: Clean kit, return the car, and walk the **Liptovský Mikuláš** old town. If there is time, the open-air museum at **Pribylina** or the Havránok Celtic hillfort above the Liptovská Mara reservoir.
itinerary.evening: Train west to Žilina and Bratislava, or east to Poprad for the High Tatras if you are not finished.

accommodationStrategy.name: A Štefanová chalet
accommodationStrategy.description: Štefanová is inside the national park at the foot of Rozsutec, closed to through traffic, and every route on Days 1–3 starts from the doorstep. No transfers, no parking fees, and you can decide on the weather at 06:00 instead of the night before.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–8 weeks ahead for July–August; Štefanová has very few beds [VERIFY: current rates].

accommodationStrategy.name: Chata pod Chlebom
accommodationStrategy.description: sleeping on the ridge means running the Krivánska crest at dawn with no lift queue and no 800 m of morning climbing. Basic bunks, a spring, and a warden who knows the conditions on Rozsutec better than any forecast.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct with the hut by phone or its own booking form — Slovak huts are not on a central system [VERIFY: current bed rate and season].

accommodationStrategy.name: Chata M. R. Štefánika
accommodationStrategy.description: the only accommodation on the Nízke Tatry main crest, which turns Day 5 from a 1,450 m day into two comfortable halves and puts you on Ďumbier for sunrise. Half-board, shared rooms, no card machine in practice.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct with the hut, 3–6 weeks ahead for summer weekends [VERIFY: current bed rate and half-board price].

logistics.connectivity: O2, Orange, Telekom and 4ka cover both crests well — the Malá Fatra ridge sees Žilina and the Nízke Tatry crest sees the Liptov basin. Signal drops in the Jánošíkove diery, in Bystrá dolina and in the lower Vrátna forest.
logistics.emergency: **112**, or **18 300** direct to the **Horská záchranná služba (HZS)**, Slovakia's mountain rescue service. Install the HZS app, which transmits your position with the call. **HZS intervention is charged to the person rescued** — travel insurance that explicitly covers mountain rescue and helicopter evacuation in Slovakia is effectively mandatory, and a European Health Insurance Card does **not** cover rescue costs.
logistics.weather: Both crests are fully exposed. Storms build from early afternoon in July and August, and the Malá Fatra ridge in particular funnels wind — 70–90 km/h gusts on Steny are not unusual outside summer. Fog on the Nízke Tatry crest between Chopok and Ďumbier hides the waymarks; carry a compass bearing and a headtorch even on a day run.
logistics.bookingWindows: Huts 3–8 weeks for summer weekends; Štefanová beds 4–8 weeks. Demänovská cave tours 1–2 weeks in August. Insurance before you leave home.
logistics.money: Slovakia uses the **euro**, so no conversion. Cards work in Terchová, Liptovský Mikuláš and the lift stations; **mountain huts are cash-only in practice** — carry €150–€250 in small notes.
logistics.transportRules: A motorway **diaľničná známka** e-vignette is required for the D1 between Žilina and Liptovský Mikuláš — buy online at eznamka.sk, it is plate-linked with no sticker [VERIFY: 2026 e-vignette 10-day and monthly prices]. Vrátna dolina charges for parking in season. SAD buses serve Terchová from Žilina and Demänovská from Liptovský Mikuláš roughly hourly, thinning at weekends.
logistics.permits: No permit, but hard rules. **Trails in the high zones of NAPANT (Národný park Nízke Tatry) and TANAP are closed each year from 1 November to 15 June**, and **Národný park Malá Fatra applies the same seasonal closure to its high routes** — the closure is legally enforced, fines are issued, and HZS will point out that a rescue from a closed trail is both charged and awkward. Beyond that: stay on marked trails (leaving them is an offence in a Slovak national park), no wild camping, no fires, no bivouacking, and no drones. Dogs must be leashed. [VERIFY: 2026 exact closure dates and any route-specific extensions published by NAPANT and NP Malá Fatra.]

other.label: Bears
other.text: Slovakia has a substantial brown bear population and the Nízke Tatry are among the most active areas. Make noise on forest sections, run with a partner at dawn and dusk, never leave food outside a hut, and if you meet one, stop, do not run, and back away while talking.

proTips: **Check the date before anything else.** Nothing on the crests is legal before 16 June. A trip planned for early June is a valley trip, and there is no negotiating this with a warden.

**Sleep at Chata pod Chlebom.** It converts the Krivánska ridge from a lift-dependent day trip into a dawn traverse with the whole crest to yourself, and the sunrise off Rozsutec is the image people come back for.
**Do Rozsutec in the morning, and only in the dry.** The chains face south-east and dry first; by midday the one-way ascent queues behind hikers, and in rain the limestone is unusable.

**Read the rázcestník times as your pacing tool.** Slovak signpost times are conservative hiking times. Once you know your own ratio to them — most fit runners land at 55–65% — you can plan a whole crest day off the signposts without a watch.
**Buy the rescue insurance, and print the policy number.** HZS charges for intervention. A helicopter off Ďumbier is a four-figure bill, and every Slovak hut warden will ask whether you are covered.
**Run the Nízke Tatry from Trangoška, not from the Chopok lift.** The lift version is 9 km of ridge tourism; from the valley it is a real 1,450 m mountain day with the hut in the middle of it.

**Learn the vocabulary that matters:** *chodník* (trail), *sedlo* (saddle), *rázcestník* (signpost junction), *chata* (hut), *uzavretý* (closed) and *pramen'/studnička* (spring). A closure sign in Slovak is the one word you must not misread.

raw.Run 1 — Jánošíkove diery circuit: 11 km, +650 m. From Biely Potok/Podžiar through **Dolné diery**, **Nové diery** and **Horné diery** — a gorge system of ladders, catwalks and chains through waterfalls, on a one-way system. Grade **T3, but not a running route in the true sense**: the ladders are enforced one-way, the rock is wet limestone, and **it should not be attempted in rain or after heavy rain**. Treat it as an active recovery morning, not a session.
raw.Run 2 — The Krivánska ridge: Chleb–Hromo: 18 km, +1,050 m from **Snilovské sedlo** (1,524 m) if you take the cable car, or **+2,000 m** if you start on the Vrátna valley floor at ~750 m and run the whole thing. Red waymark along the crest: **Chleb (1,646 m)**, **Hromové (1,636 m)**, **Steny (1,571 m)**, **Poludňový Grúň (1,460 m)**, with **Veľký Kriváň (1,709 m)**, the range's high point, an easy out-and-back from Snilovské sedlo. Grade **T2–T3**: grass, dwarf pine and rock steps, mostly runnable, exposed in wind.
raw.Run 3 — Stoh, Medziholie and Veľký Rozsu: 15 km, +1,300 m. The ridge's dramatic east end: **Stoh (1,607 m)**, down to **Medziholie (1,185 m)**, then the chained ascent of **Veľký Rozsutec (1,610 m)** — steel chains and staples on steep rock, one-way in the ascent direction. Grade **T4 / secured scrambling**. Descend north over **Medzirozsutec** to Štefanová. **Do not do the Rozsutec chains in the wet.**
raw.Run 4 — The Nízke Tatry crest: Chopok to: 9 km round trip from the Chopok top station, +450 m; 20 km / +1,450 m if run from **Trangoška** (1,130 m). Red waymark: **Chopok (2,024 m)**, Krúpova hoľa, **Ďumbier (2,043 m)**, the range's high point, with **Chata M. R. Štefánika (1,728 m)** tucked below the summit on the south side. Grade **T3** — blocky granite on the summit ridge, fast gravel and grass between.
raw.Run 5 — Bystrá dolina and Demänovská dol: 16–18 km, +700 m. Long forested valley trails with runnable gradients, linking Trangoška, Bystrá and the head of Demänovská. Grade **T1–T2** and the best pure-running surface of the week.
raw.Terrain: Malá Fatra is **grass over Mesozoic limestone and dolomite** — fast in the dry, greasy in the wet, with sharp karst edges through Rozsutec and the diery. The Nízke Tatry crest is **granite and gneiss with gravel and alpine grass**, plus long belts of **kosodrevina** (dwarf mountain pine) that will scratch bare legs to ribbons. Below the treeline both are spruce root and mud.
raw.The Slovak waymarking system (KST): Trails are marked by the **Klub slovenských turistov** with a horizontal colour band between two white bands, painted on rocks and trees at eye level, with a matching directional signpost (*rázcestník*) at every junction carrying times in hours and minutes, not kilometres. **Red = main ridge and long-distance routes** (the Malá Fatra and Nízke Tatry crests are both red). **Blue and green = connecting routes**, **yellow = short links and shortcuts**. Slovak signposted times are hiking times and honest; a fit runner does roughly 55–65% of them.
raw.Water points: In Malá Fatra: the spring at **Chata pod Chlebom (1,423 m)**, water at **Chata na Grúni (~1,100 m)** and **Chata Vrátna**, and the Vrátna valley streams below the ridge. **The Krivánska crest itself is dry** — carry 1.5–2 L. In the Nízke Tatry: **Chata M. R. Štefánika** below Ďumbier is the only reliable high source, plus **Trangoška** and the springs in Bystrá and Demänovská; the Chopok–Ďumbier crest has none. **Vyvieranie**, the karst resurgence in Demänovská dolina, is a sight rather than a refill.
raw.Bail-outs: Malá Fatra: the **Vrátna–Snilovské sedlo cable car** (up or down), **Chata pod Chlebom**, the descent from Poludňový Grúň to **Chata na Grúni** and Vrátna, and Medziholie down to Štefanová. Nízke Tatry: the **Chopok cable cars** on both the Jasná (north) and Srdiečko/Kosodrevina (south) sides, **Chata M. R. Štefánika**, and the walk-off to **Trangoška**. In both ranges the crest is exposed with almost no shelter — the huts are the plan, not the weather.

trips.title: Vienna — The Ring and Everything Behind It

bestPeriod.note: May and late September give warm terraces without the August closures; the Heuriger season peaks with Sturm in late September.

trips.gatewayAirport: Vienna (VIE)
trips.summary: Seven days of Vienna organised one district at a time, from Ringstrasse historicism to Ottakring's market streets and the Steinhof hill.
trips.hook: Vienna rewards people who stop moving. The city is small enough to walk, dense enough that one district will fill a day, and structured in rings — so the honest way to see it is to take one block at a time and finish each with a market, a Beisl or a Heuriger. Four of these seven days never touch the Innere Stadt at all, and they are the days you will remember.

snapshot.Base(s): Vienna, single base (Neubau/7th or Landstrasse/3rd)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 70–85 km on foot; flat except the Steinhof and Kahlenberg slopes; 9 of 23 districts covered
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to VIE; City Airport Train or S7 to Wien Mitte in 16–25 min. By rail, Wien Hauptbahnhof from Munich, Prague, Budapest and Zürich
snapshot.Who It Suits: Slow walkers, architecture readers, market shoppers; anyone allergic to a coach-tour itinerary

itinerary.title: The Ring, read as one building
itinerary.morning: Start at the Staatsoper (August Sicard von Sicardsburg and Eduard van der Nüll, 1869) and walk the Ring anticlockwise as a single block: Burggarten, Heldenplatz, then the Parlament (Theophil Hansen, 1883, reopened after restoration in 2023), the Rathaus (Friedrich von Schmidt, 1883), the Burgtheater (Gottfried Semper and Karl von Hasenauer, 1888) and the Universität (Heinrich von Ferstel, 1884). Each borrowed a style to match its function — Greek for parliament, Flemish Gothic for the town hall.
itinerary.afternoon: The Kunsthistorisches Museum (Semper and Hasenauer, 1891) for the Bruegel room and the Kunstkammer. Book the timed slot online the night before.
itinerary.evening: Coffee at Café Landtmann (opened 1873) on the Ring, then Stehplätze at the Staatsoper — standing tickets go on sale at the Operngasse standing-room entrance about 80 minutes before curtain for roughly €13–€18.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walked. Districts: 1. Ticket spend approx. €35–€50 (museum plus standing opera).

itinerary.title: Wienzeile: Wagner, the Secession and the Naschmarkt
itinerary.morning: One block, all morning: Linke Wienzeile. Otto Wagner's Majolikahaus at No. 40 and the gold-medallioned house at No. 38 (both 1899) face the market. Walk down to the Karlsplatz Stadtbahn Pavilions (Wagner, 1899) and the Secession (Joseph Maria Olbrich, 1898) for Klimt's Beethoven Frieze in the basement.
itinerary.afternoon: The Naschmarkt itself — the permanent stalls run Monday to Saturday, roughly 06:00 to 19:30, with Saturday the fullest day. Then Karlskirche (Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach, begun 1716) and the Wien Museum, whose permanent collection is free.
itinerary.evening: Café Sperl (1880) on Gumpendorfer Strasse, unrenovated on purpose, then dinner in Neubau around Siebensterngasse.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walked. Districts: 4, 6, 1. Ticket spend approx. €22–€30.

itinerary.title: Belvedere and the Landstrasse
itinerary.morning: The Oberes Belvedere (Johann Lucas von Hildebrandt, 1723) holds Klimt's *Der Kuss*. Book a timed slot online at least a week ahead in high season and take the first entry of the day, around 09:00 — the Klimt room is a single small gallery and by 11:00 it is three deep. The Unteres Belvedere and the garden are quieter all day.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk north into Landstrasse. The Rochusmarkt on Landstrasser Hauptstrasse (Monday to Friday, plus Saturday morning) is a working neighbourhood market, not a tourist one. Then the Hundertwasserhaus (Friedensreich Hundertwasser with Josef Krawina, 1985) at Kegelgasse — five minutes of looking, no ticket needed.
itinerary.evening: Gmoakeller on Am Heumarkt, a Beisl running since 1858, for Backhendl or Tafelspitz.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km walked. Districts: 3. Ticket spend approx. €19–€26.

itinerary.title: Ottakring: Brunnenmarkt and the Gemeindebau
itinerary.morning: Off the spine entirely. Take U6 to Josefstädter Strasse and walk into the Brunnenmarkt on Brunnengasse — the longest street market in Europe, Monday to Saturday, Turkish and Balkan produce, and prices a third below the Naschmarkt. Saturday adds a farmers' market on Yppenplatz.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk to the Sandleitenhof (1928, by Emil Hoppe, Otto Schönthal, Franz Matuschek and others), Red Vienna's largest scheme: 1,500 flats built as a small town with courtyards, a library and shops. Then the Ottakringer Brauerei (1837) on Ottakringer Strasse for a tour and a Zwickl.
itinerary.evening: Back to Yppenplatz. Kent on Brunnengasse has been grilling lahmacun and Adana for decades and the terrace runs late.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walked. Districts: 16, 17. Ticket spend approx. €12–€18.

itinerary.title: Penzing: Wagner's hill at Steinhof
itinerary.morning: The single most beautiful building in Vienna is a hospital chapel. Kirche am Steinhof (Otto Wagner, 1907) sits at the top of the former Otto-Wagner-Spital grounds in the 14th district — white marble panels bolted to brick, a copper dome, Kolo Moser glass. Access is by limited opening hours and guided tours, typically Saturday afternoon and Sunday midday; confirm the schedule, which shifts with the season and with works on the site. Get there by bus 48A from Ottakring U3.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk down through the pavilion grounds and take the tram to Hütteldorf for Wagner's own Villa I (1888) on Hüttelbergstrasse, now the Ernst Fuchs Museum. If the church is closed, substitute the Lainzer Tiergarten and the Hermesvilla (Karl von Hasenauer, 1886).
itinerary.evening: Eat in Hietzing or ride back to Neubau. A long, quiet, un-touristed day; take an early night.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km walked, including 120 m of climbing to Steinhof. Districts: 14, 13. Ticket spend approx. €14–€20.

itinerary.title: Döbling: Karl-Marx-Hof to the Heuriger
itinerary.morning: U4 to Heiligenstadt and out of the station straight into the Karl-Marx-Hof (Karl Ehn, 1930) — 1.1 km of ochre and red social housing with those four archway towers, still lived in. The Waschsalon museum in laundry courtyard 2 tells the Red Vienna story; it opens only a couple of afternoons a week.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk north to the Nussdorf Wehr- und Schleusenanlage (Otto Wagner, 1898), the sluice gate with the bronze lions where the Donaukanal begins. Then uphill through the vineyards on the Nussberg, with the whole city below you and the Danube flats beyond.
itinerary.evening: A proper Heuriger. Schübel-Auer on Kahlenberger Strasse and Mayer am Pfarrplatz in Heiligenstadt both serve their own wine by the Viertel with cold buffet food sold by weight. A pine branch over the door means open — *ausg'steckt*.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walked, 180 m of climbing on the Nussberg. Districts: 19. Ticket spend approx. €8–€12 plus wine.

itinerary.title: Leopoldstadt: Karmelitermarkt and the Augarten
itinerary.morning: Cross the Donaukanal into the 2nd. The Karmelitermarkt is small, and best on Saturday morning when the farmers set up. Eat breakfast at one of the stall counters.
itinerary.afternoon: The Augarten: a Baroque park laid out in the 1650s, the porcelain manufactory established in 1718, and two vast concrete Flaktürme from 1944 that cannot be demolished and so simply stand there among the chestnuts. Then walk the Prater Hauptallee, 4.5 km of horse-chestnut avenue, to the Riesenrad (1897).
itinerary.evening: Schweizerhaus in the Prater, open roughly March to October, for Stelze and Budvar from wooden barrels, in a beer garden running since the 1920s.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km walked. Districts: 2. Ticket spend approx. €14–€20 with the Riesenrad.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Altstadt Vienna
accommodationStrategy.description: A converted 19th-century apartment building in the 7th, each room done differently, with a salon where breakfast runs long. The location is the argument: five minutes from the Volkstheater U2/U3 interchange, walking distance to the Ring, the MuseumsQuartier and the Naschmarkt, and the Spittelberg lanes for dinner.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead; longer for the Christmas market weeks.

accommodationStrategy.name: An apartment in Landstrasse or Leopoldstadt
accommodationStrategy.description: For a week, a flat near Rochusmarkt or Karmelitermarkt beats a hotel: you shop the market instead of eating out twice a day, and both districts sit one or two U-Bahn stops from the centre at far lower rates. Check the building has a lift — Viennese *Altbau* stairwells are handsome and four flights high.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–10 weeks ahead.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming applies; free WLAN covers most U-Bahn stations and the city centre. Vienna's continental weather swings hard — 30°C afternoons and 12°C evenings in May — and thunderstorms build fast in July. Carry a layer every day.
logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European. Austrian specifics: ambulance 144, police 133, fire 122. Pharmacies post the rotating night service on the door.
logistics.bookingWindows: Belvedere, Albertina and Kunsthistorisches release timed slots online weeks ahead; take the first hour of the day. Spanish Riding School morning exercise sells out weeks out. Staatsoper standing room cannot be pre-booked — same day, at the Operngasse door.
logistics.money: Cards are near-universal, but small Beisln, market stalls and Heurigen prefer cash — carry €40–€60. Tip by rounding up plus 5–10 percent, handed to the waiter with payment, not left on the table.

other.label: The pass decision, honestly
other.text: The Wien Karte costs roughly €25–€35 for 24/48/72 hours and bundles travel with discounts usually worth €1–€3 per attraction — it rarely repays itself. For seven days the **Wochenkarte** at approx. €20 is far cheaper, but it is a calendar-week ticket, valid Monday 00:00 to the following Monday 09:00 whenever you buy it, so it is useless on a Thursday arrival. The clean answer for a mid-week arrival is the **8-Tage-Klimakarte**, approx. €45–€50: eight day-strips, not necessarily consecutive, transferable between travellers.

other.label: Validation
other.text: Wiener Linien runs on trust with heavy spot checks. Time and strip tickets must be stamped in the blue box at the platform entrance or on the tram before boarding. Unstamped is untkicketed: €105 on the spot.

other.label: Airport trap
other.text: The city zone ends at Wien Mitte, so every city pass needs an add-on for the airport. Use the S7 with an outer-zone ticket for about €4.60 instead of the €14–€16 CAT.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Most museums close Monday (Belvedere and Albertina excepted). Supermarkets shut at 19:00 or 20:00 and all day Sunday; the Hauptbahnhof and Westbahnhof shops are the exception. Heurigen close for weeks at a time.

proTips: Ride trams **1 and 2** around the Ring instead of paying for a sightseeing tram. Same track, same buildings, any valid ticket.
The Klimt room at the Oberes Belvedere is emptiest in the last hour before closing as well as the first. If 09:00 is gone, take the latest slot.
Buy Naschmarkt food from the stalls at the Kettenbrückengasse end, where locals shop. On Saturdays the Flohmarkt beyond it starts around 06:30 and the dealers have picked it over by 09:00.
Ride the U6 between Josefstädter Strasse and Nussdorfer Strasse for Otto Wagner's Stadtbahn viaducts and stations, still in daily use — the cheapest architecture tour in the city.
Vienna's street fountains are drinking water unless marked *Kein Trinkwasser*. The supply comes by aqueduct from the Rax; do not buy bottles.
For Steinhof, phone or email ahead. The church's opening pattern shifts with restoration work, and a wasted trip costs a whole morning.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 70–85 km on foot; flat except the Steinhof and Kahlenberg slopes; 9 of 23 districts covered
raw.Who It Suits: Slow walkers, architecture readers, market shoppers; anyone allergic to a coach-tour itinerary

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 70–85 km on foot; flat except the Steinhof and Kahlenberg slopes; 9 of 23 districts covered
typeSpecific.audience: Slow walkers, architecture readers, market shoppers; anyone allergic to a coach-tour itinerary

packingNotes: Shoes with real grip for granite setts and tram grooves, both slippery in rain.
A layer for museums: the Kunsthistorisches and Belvedere run cool even in July.
A folding shopping bag for the Brunnenmarkt and Karmelitermarkt; stalls charge for plastic.
One smart outfit — standing room at the Staatsoper is informal but not shorts.
A refillable bottle, for the fountains.
Cash in small notes for Heurigen, market stalls and older Beisln.
whatCouldGoWrong: **You buy the Wochenkarte on a Friday.** It expires Monday morning. Fallback: at any Wiener Linien machine switch to the 8-Tage-Klimakarte and validate one strip a day; nothing is wasted.

**Kirche am Steinhof is shut on the day you climb the hill.** Fallback: the Otto-Wagner-Spital grounds and pavilions are freely walkable, and the Wagner Villa in Hütteldorf plus the Hermesvilla make a full day.
**Everything is closed on Monday.** Fallback: build Monday around the Belvedere or Albertina, both of which open, plus the Ottakring markets and Gemeindebau walk, which need no ticket.
**The Klimt slot sells out.** Fallback: the Secession's Beethoven Frieze and the Leopold Museum's Schiele rooms cover the same ground with far shorter queues.

trips.title: Antwerp, With a Day in Ghent

bestPeriod.note: May and September give long evenings on the Scheldt quays; Flanders in July is warm but the Zuid empties for holidays.

trips.gatewayAirport: Brussels (BRU)
trips.summary: A week in Antwerp taken district by district — Rubens, the diamond and fashion quarters, the docks, Zurenborg — with one full day in Ghent.
trips.hook: Antwerp is a port city that behaves like a capital and a village at once: a Baroque cathedral, a fashion school that reset the industry in the 1980s, and a Sunday bird market where people still buy chickens. It is compact enough that each district is a morning's walk, and the tram network exists mainly to get you home. Ghent, fifty minutes away by train, is the counterweight — smaller, denser, and built entirely around one river fork.

snapshot.Base(s): Antwerp, single base; one day trip to Ghent
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 65–80 km on foot; entirely flat, cobbled in the centre; 6 Antwerp districts plus central Ghent
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Brussels (BRU), then direct train to Antwerpen-Centraal in about 45 min; Eurostar and ICE arrive at Brussels-Midi, 40 min further
snapshot.Who It Suits: People who like paintings, buildings and beer in roughly equal measure; a good first Belgian city week

itinerary.title: Grote Markt, Vlaeykensgang and the cathedral block
itinerary.morning: Arrive into Antwerpen-Centraal (Louis Delacenserie, 1905), which is worth twenty minutes before you leave it — the stone hall, the dome, and the four track levels stacked below. Then tram 3 or 5 to Groenplaats and start with the Onze-Lieve-Vrouwekathedraal (begun 1352, tower finished 1521), holding four Rubens altarpieces including *The Descent from the Cross*.
itinerary.afternoon: The block behind it: the Stadhuis (Cornelis Floris de Vriendt, 1565), the guild houses on Grote Markt, the Vleeshuis (Herman de Waghemakere, 1504) in its striped brick, and Het Steen on the quay. Slip into the Vlaeykensgang off Oude Koornmarkt — a 16th-century alley of cobbles and courtyards, free and almost always empty.
itinerary.evening: A Belgian beer café with a serious list, then dinner around Hoogstraat. Try Bolleke, the amber De Koninck brewed in Antwerp since 1833, served in its own round glass.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km walked. Districts: Historic Centre. Ticket spend approx. €14–€20.

itinerary.title: Sint-Andries: the fashion district and Kloosterstraat
itinerary.morning: The whole day fits inside a triangle of Nationalestraat, Kammenstraat and Kloosterstraat. Start at MoMu, the ModeMuseum on Nationalestraat, reopened in 2021 after a full rebuild — the rotating exhibitions cover the Antwerp Six and the school that produced them. Book online; capacity is small and Saturday sells out.
itinerary.afternoon: Nationalestraat for the flagship shops, including Dries Van Noten's Het Modepaleis at No. 16 in its 1881 corner building. Then Kloosterstraat, four blocks of antiques, lighting and mid-century dealers, and Sint-Andrieskerk with the memorial to Mary Stuart's ladies-in-waiting.
itinerary.evening: Eat in the Zuid end of Sint-Andries and walk the Scheldt quays at dusk — the whole west-facing waterfront gets the light.
itinerary.dayStats: 6 km walked. Districts: Sint-Andries. Ticket spend approx. €12–€18.

itinerary.title: Het Zuid: KMSKA and Leopold de Waelplaats
itinerary.morning: The Koninklijk Museum voor Schone Kunsten (Jacob Winders and Frans Van Dijk, 1890, with the white inserted galleries by KAAN Architecten, reopened 2022) is the reason for the day. Book a timed slot — they release online and the first hour, from opening, is by far the calmest. Van Eyck, Memling, Rubens, Ensor and Rik Wouters, hung with room to breathe.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Zuid grid: Leopold de Waelplaats, Volkstraat, Marnixplaats with its fountain, Vlaamsekaai and Waalsekaai. FOMU, the photography museum on Waalsekaai, is a good second stop and rarely crowded.
itinerary.evening: The Zuid is where Antwerp eats. Marnixplaats and Volkstraat have the terraces; the fish restaurants near Vlaamsekaai are the local default for a splurge.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km walked. Districts: Zuid. Ticket spend approx. €25–€35.

itinerary.title: Het Eilandje and the docks
itinerary.morning: North to the old dock island. The MAS (Neutelings Riedijk Architecten, 2011) stacks red Indian sandstone boxes ten storeys high; the spiral escalator route through the building to the rooftop is free and open late, and gives the best view of the port, the city and the Scheldt bend. Pay only for the collection floors if you want them.
itinerary.afternoon: The Red Star Line Museum in the old embarkation sheds on Montevideostraat — two million people left Europe from this quay for New York. Then walk the Bonapartedok and Willemdok, the Sint-Felixpakhuis warehouse, and out to Zaha Hadid's Havenhuis (2016), the glass hull landed on the old fire station at Mexicostraat.
itinerary.evening: Droogdokkenpark at sunset, then back for mussels or a shrimp croquette in the Eilandje cafés.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walked. Districts: Eilandje. Ticket spend approx. €16–€24.

itinerary.title: Ghent: Patershol, Graslei and the Van Eyck
itinerary.morning: Take an IC train from Antwerpen-Centraal to Gent-Sint-Pieters, roughly 50–60 minutes, about €11–€13 one way, four an hour. Tram 1 into the centre. Start at Sint-Baafskathedraal for the Van Eyck brothers' *Adoration of the Mystic Lamb* (1432), now shown in its own climate-controlled chapel. This is a strict timed entry: slots release online, they run every 15 minutes, and summer weekends sell out several days ahead. Take a morning slot.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Graslei and Korenlei guild fronts, then the Gravensteen (rebuilt 1180) if the queue is short, and the Patershol — the medieval lanes north of Kraanlei, now Ghent's restaurant quarter. Buy mustard scooped from the barrel at Tierenteyn-Verlent on Groentenmarkt, trading since 1790, and cuberdons from the stalls at Groentenmarkt.
itinerary.evening: A jenever bar near the Vrijdagmarkt, then the last train back — services run late, but check the final IC to Antwerp before you settle in.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km walked, plus 2 hours on trains. Districts: central Ghent. Ticket spend approx. €35–€45 including rail.

itinerary.title: Zurenborg and Berchem
itinerary.morning: Tram 11 or a 25-minute walk to Cogels-Osylei, the most concentrated street of late-19th-century domestic architecture in Belgium: eclectic, neo-Gothic and Art Nouveau villas built 1894–1906. Look for De Vier Seizoenen, the four-house cycle of the seasons at the Waterloostraat corner, and Jules Hofman's Zonnebloem (1900). It is all private housing — you walk and look, nothing is ticketed.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Draakplaats for the tram shelter and the Art Nouveau corners, then Dageraadplaats, the square Antwerp actually lives on: plane trees, playground, and a full ring of terraces. Zeezicht on the square has been the neighbourhood café for decades.
itinerary.evening: Stay put. Dageraadplaats at 20:00 on a warm evening is the point of the day.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walked. Districts: Zurenborg, Berchem. Ticket spend approx. €4–€8 (trams only).

itinerary.title: The Rubens circuit and the Sunday markets
itinerary.morning: If it is Sunday, start at the Vogelenmarkt on Theaterplein — birds, plants, food and clothing since the 18th century, roughly 08:00 to 13:00, with the Exotische Markt alongside. Then the Rubens itinerary that does not depend on one museum: Sint-Pauluskerk on Veemarkt for the Mysteries of the Rosary series, Sint-Jacobskerk on Lange Nieuwstraat where Rubens is buried behind the altar, and the Snijders&Rockoxhuis on Keizerstraat, the restored home of Rubens' patron Nicolaas Rockox.
itinerary.afternoon: The Plantin-Moretus Museum on Vrijdagmarkt — a UNESCO-listed printing house with the two oldest surviving printing presses in the world, still in the family rooms. Timed tickets online; it is small and caps numbers. Note that the Rubenshuis on Wapper has been closed for a multi-year renovation, so check its status before building a morning around it.
itinerary.evening: Last walk on the Scheldt quays, then a final Bolleke.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km walked. Districts: Historic Centre, Sint-Jacob. Ticket spend approx. €24–€34.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Julien
accommodationStrategy.description: Two merchant houses knocked together behind a plain door, with a roof terrace that looks straight at the cathedral tower. The location is the argument: three minutes to Grote Markt, ten to the Zuid trams, and you can walk home from anywhere in this itinerary except Zurenborg. Quiet rooms at the back for a centre-of-town address.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 10 weeks ahead, longer for weekends.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Banks
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits inside the fashion district triangle, one street from Nationalestraat, which makes Day 2 a stroll and Day 3's KMSKA a ten-minute walk. Bike rental at reception and secure storage — useful, because Antwerp is genuinely better by bicycle than by tram.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: An apartment in Zuid or Zurenborg
accommodationStrategy.description: A week is long enough that a kitchen pays. Zuid puts you among the restaurants and the museums; Zurenborg is quieter, cheaper and served by trams 11 and 24. Either way ask about the stairs — Antwerp townhouses are narrow and steep, and lifts are rare.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 across Belgium for all services. Non-urgent medical after hours: 1733. Pharmacies post the rotating night duty on the door.
logistics.bookingWindows: The Mystic Lamb in Ghent and the Plantin-Moretus are the two genuine sell-outs; book both a week or more ahead in summer. KMSKA and MoMu release timed slots online and are usually fine two or three days out, except Saturdays. Nothing else on this week requires advance purchase.
logistics.money: Cards, including contactless, work everywhere; Belgium is close to cashless. Keep €20 for market stalls and church donation boxes. Service is included — round up rather than tipping a percentage.

other.label: The transit maths
other.text: Antwerp's trams and buses are run by De Lijn. A single m-ticket bought in the app costs roughly €2.50; a day pass is around €7.50–€8, and a 10-journey card is cheaper per ride. There is no Antwerp weekly tourist ticket worth the name, and on this itinerary you will walk most days — buy singles or a couple of day passes rather than anything bundled.

other.label: The city pass trap
other.text: The Antwerp City Pass (roughly €45–€70 for 24 to 72 hours) includes museums plus De Lijn travel, and its clock runs continuously from first use, not by calendar day. It only wins if you compress KMSKA, MAS collection floors, Plantin-Moretus, MoMu and Red Star Line into two consecutive days — which is the opposite of how this week is built.

other.label: Rail to Ghent
other.text: Buy point-to-point online or at the machine. If you are two people travelling at a weekend, the SNCB/NMBS weekend return is significantly discounted; a 10-journey Rail Pass is the better buy if you add Bruges or Mechelen. Trains from Antwerpen-Centraal leave from the lower levels — allow ten minutes to descend.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Most Flemish museums close Monday, and several also close Tuesday. Churches keep their own hours: Sint-Pauluskerk and Sint-Jacobskerk typically open afternoons only, and close entirely in winter months. Shops shut around 18:00 and most are closed Sunday except in the centre.

other.label: Cycling law
other.text: If you rent a Velo Antwerpen bike, ride on the marked cycle paths where they exist, use lights after dark (enforced), and never leave a bike unlocked. Trams have absolute priority and their rails will take a wheel.

proTips: The MAS rooftop is free and stays open well beyond the museum floors, typically until 22:00 in summer. Go up at dusk when the port lights come on — it costs nothing and beats any paid viewpoint in the city.
Book the first Mystic Lamb slot of the day in Ghent and you will have the Van Eyck chapel almost to yourself for the first ten minutes; by 11:00 the room is at capacity for the rest of the day.
Antwerp's cathedral is free to enter for worship and charges for the art. Sunday morning services are the exception — respect them, and come back paying on a weekday.
Take tram 11 through Zurenborg rather than walking out. It runs down Cogels-Osylei's cross streets and gives you a moving preview of the façades.

The Ghent day works better in reverse if you are a late riser: take a mid-afternoon Lamb slot, eat in the Patershol, and walk the illuminated Graslei at night — Ghent's lighting plan is one of the best in Europe.
Buy chocolate and mustard in Ghent, not Antwerp. Tierenteyn-Verlent on Groentenmarkt fills a stoneware pot from the barrel, and it survives the flight home.
Skip the diamond district as a sight — it is offices and security doors — but the DIVA museum on Suikerrui gives the trade's actual history in an hour.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 65–80 km on foot; entirely flat, cobbled in the centre; 6 Antwerp districts plus central Ghent
raw.Who It Suits: People who like paintings, buildings and beer in roughly equal measure; a good first Belgian city week

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 65–80 km on foot; entirely flat, cobbled in the centre; 6 Antwerp districts plus central Ghent
typeSpecific.audience: People who like paintings, buildings and beer in roughly equal measure; a good first Belgian city week

packingNotes: A properly waterproof jacket with a hood, not an umbrella. Flanders rain arrives sideways off the North Sea in every month.
Shoes for cobbles and tram rails; Antwerp's setts are large, uneven and slick when wet.
One smarter layer — Antwerp dresses well and the Zuid restaurants notice.
A small daypack: several museums, including KMSKA, require larger bags in the cloakroom.
A refillable bottle; Belgian tap water is safe and restaurants will fill it.
A phone holder or paper map for the Zurenborg walk — the streets loop and the house numbers are the whole point.
Layers for museum interiors, which run cold, and for the Scheldt quays, which are windier than the streets behind them.
A folding bag for Ghent's market buys.
whatCouldGoWrong: **The Mystic Lamb is sold out on your Ghent day.** Fallback: move the Ghent day within the week — any day works — or see the cathedral without the chapel and spend the time on the Patershol, the Gravensteen and the Design Museum instead.

**Rain settles in for 48 hours.** Entirely plausible in April or October. Fallback: this itinerary has four indoor-heavy days (KMSKA, MoMu, Plantin-Moretus, MAS and Red Star Line). Reorder to put them against the weather and save Zurenborg and the quays for the clear day.

**Monday closures wipe out your museum plan.** Fallback: Monday is the day for Zurenborg, the docks walk, the Vlaeykensgang and the churches — none of which need a ticket. Keep it flexible rather than fixed.

**You count on the Rubenshuis.** It has been shut for a long renovation and its reopening has moved more than once. Fallback: the Day 7 circuit — Sint-Pauluskerk, Sint-Jacobskerk, the Rockoxhuis and the cathedral altarpieces — delivers more Rubens than the house ever did.

**You miss the last train from Ghent.** Fallback: services to Antwerp run until late evening, but if you do miss it, an IC via Brussels or a Gent–Sint-Niklaas connection usually still works; check the SNCB/NMBS app before ordering the last round.

trips.title: Sofia and Plovdiv: A Split Week Between Serdica and Philippopolis
trips.subRegion: Sofia Valley & the Upper Thracian Plain

bestPeriod.window: mid-May to mid-June, and the whole of September
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (35 °C+ on the Thracian plain, Plovdiv's Old Town cobbles unbearable by noon) and February fog in the Sofia basin

accommodation.note: €270–€480 (€39–€69/night, 4 nights Sofia + 3 nights Plovdiv)

transport.note: €35–€60 (metro/day cards, Sofia–Plovdiv train, Boyana and Vitosha buses)

activities.note: €70–€120 (Boyana, Nevsky crypt, Roman Theatre, Roman Stadium, museums)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy

trips.gatewayAirport: Sofia Airport (SOF) Terminal 2 sits on metro line **M4**; Serdika in the centre in ~20 min for a single-ride fare. Plovdiv Airport (PDV) has thin seasonal traffic — plan on Sofia both ways and take the train back on Day 7 morning.
trips.currency: Euro (EUR) — sole legal tender since 1 February 2026; mandatory dual BGN display ended 8 August 2026
trips.summary: Two cities, one week, one train. Sofia is a capital built on top of its own Roman street grid, where you change metro lines through 4th-century foundations and the mineral water still runs free from a public tap.…
trips.hook: Two cities, one week, one train. Sofia is a capital built on top of its own Roman street grid, where you change metro lines through 4th-century foundations and the mineral water still runs free from a public tap. Plovdiv is older and slower, a Thracian hill town wearing an Ottoman and National Revival coat, with a Roman stadium buried under the shopping street. Cheap, flat, unhurried and — for once in Europe — genuinely uncrowded.

snapshot.Start / End: Sofia (4 nights) → Plovdiv (3 nights) → fly out of Sofia or Plovdiv
snapshot.Getting there: Sofia Airport (SOF) Terminal 2 sits on metro line **M4**; Serdika in the centre in ~20 min for a single-ride fare. Plovdiv Airport (PDV) has thin seasonal traffic — plan on Sofia both ways and take the train back on Day 7 morning.

itinerary.title: Landing on the Roman Grid
itinerary.morning: M4 from Terminal 2 to Serdika. Drop bags, then descend into the **Serdica archaeological complex** under the Largo — a Roman street, drains and house walls, roofed and free to walk.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Rotunda of St George** through the Presidency courtyard (watch the hourly guard change), then Sveta Nedelya and the Banya Bashi mosque, then the **Central Mineral Baths** and its free taps — bring a bottle.
itinerary.evening: **Manastirska Magernitsa**, ul. Han Asparuh 67 — monastery recipes, rabbit in wine, wild-herb salads, an encyclopaedic menu. Reserve for after 20:00 [VERIFY: current hours].
itinerary.dayStats: Sofia, 5 km on foot

itinerary.title: Nevsky, Oborishte and the Doctor's Garden
itinerary.morning: **Alexander Nevsky Cathedral** at opening, when the light is on the eastern apse and the choir sometimes rehearses; then the crypt icon museum, the strongest single collection in the Balkans.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk north into **Oborishte** — the National Gallery in the former royal palace, then the **Doctor's Garden** and the streets of Art Nouveau villas around it. Coffee somewhere on ul. Oborishte.
itinerary.evening: **Cosmos**, ul. Lavele 19 — modern Bulgarian, small plates, a serious list of Melnik and Thracian Valley wines. Book two or three days ahead [VERIFY: current hours].
itinerary.dayStats: Sofia, 6 km

itinerary.title: Boyana and Vitosha
itinerary.morning: Bus 64 or 107 from Hladilnika to **Boyana Church**. Fifteen minutes, eight people, 1259 frescoes — the Christ Evergetes and the donor portraits of Sebastocrator Kaloyan and Desislava. It is the single best thing in Bulgaria.
itinerary.afternoon: Up to **Vitosha**: the Simeonovo gondola or Dragalevtsi chairlift to Aleko hut, then 1h30 on a broad path to **Cherni Vrah**, 2,290 m, with the Sofia basin below. Lifts often run weekends only outside high season [VERIFY: current Simeonovo/Dragalevtsi operating days].
itinerary.evening: Back down to the centre for something simple — shopska salad and a rakia.
itinerary.dayStats: Sofia, 20 km round trip + 4 km walking

itinerary.title: Zhenski Pazar, Vazov and NDK
itinerary.morning: **Zhenski Pazar** by 09:00 for the produce lines, cheese counters and a hot banitsa, then Sveti Sedmochislenitsi, an Ottoman mosque turned Orthodox church.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Ivan Vazov National Theatre** and City Garden, then Vitosha boulevard south to **NDK**; the National Archaeological Museum in the old Büyük mosque if it is hot.
itinerary.evening: Last Sofia dinner. Pack for an early train.
itinerary.dayStats: Sofia, 6 km

itinerary.title: The Train to Plovdiv, and Kapana
itinerary.morning: Train from Sofia Central to Plovdiv. Fifteen minutes' walk to your Kapana or Old Town base.
itinerary.afternoon: Get the ground under you: **Dzhumaya Square** and the exposed **Roman Stadium** sphendone, then the length of ul. Knyaz Alexander I — you are walking directly above the track.
itinerary.evening: **Pavaj**, ul. Zlatarska 7 — mismatched furniture, Bulgarian home cooking done properly, no reservations, go at 19:00 [VERIFY: current hours]. Then Kapana's bars.

itinerary.title: The Old Town, House by House
itinerary.morning: Climb into **Stariya Grad** early. **Balabanov House** (reconstructed National Revival merchant's house, symmetric plan, painted ceilings) and **Hindliyan House** (1835–40, the alabaster bathroom, the Venice and Constantinople murals on the walls). Both take an hour.
itinerary.afternoon: **Nebet Tepe** — Thracian walls of the 12th century BC on the top hill, and the best view over the Maritsa and the Rhodope foothills. Down the far side to the **Roman Theatre of Philippopolis**, which you should see empty in daylight and, if a performance is on, again at night.
itinerary.evening: **Shtastliveca**, ul. Knyaz Alexander I 31 — big terrace, generous portions, the reliable main-street table. Book for the terrace [VERIFY: current hours].
itinerary.dayStats: Plovdiv, 5 km

itinerary.title: Tsar Simeon Garden, Sahat Tepe, and Out
itinerary.morning: **Tsar Simeon Garden** — the 1892 layout by the Swiss gardener Lucien Chevalas, the lake, and the Singing Fountains, which perform in the evening but look better empty in the morning.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb **Sahat Tepe** to the clock tower and take a last long lunch at **Rahat Tepe**, the terrace restaurant on the hill.
itinerary.evening: Train or bus back to Sofia for the flight, or fly from Plovdiv if the schedule serves.
itinerary.dayStats: Plovdiv, 4 km

accommodationStrategy.name: Sense Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: opposite Alexander Nevsky, a rooftop bar level with the domes, 10 minutes from the Largo and the Doctor's Garden.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–5 weeks ahead direct.

accommodationStrategy.name: R34 Boutique Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: cheaper and quieter, a block from the National Theatre and inside the Serdika/NDK walking triangle.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–4 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Residence City Garden
accommodationStrategy.description: between Kapana and Tsar Simeon Garden — five minutes from Pavaj, eight from the Roman Theatre steps, and not above a Kapana bar.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–4 weeks ahead; longer during the September Plovdiv fair week.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming. Free wifi in metro stations and most cafés; patchy on Vitosha above Aleko.
logistics.emergency: 112, English usually answered; Vitosha mountain rescue is reached the same way.
logistics.weather: Sofia sits at 550 m, 5–8 °C cooler than Plovdiv; Cherni Vrah can be 15 °C colder again, with wind. Carry a shell even in June.
logistics.bookingWindows: Boyana same-day-to-24-hours; Cosmos 2–3 days; Shtastliveca terrace 2 days; trains no booking needed except on public holidays.
logistics.money: Bulgaria has moved to the **euro**, converted at the fixed rate of **1 EUR = 1.95583 BGN**. Mandatory dual EUR/BGN price display ran from 8 August 2025 and **ended on 8 August 2026** — from 9 August merchants price in euro only, and any lev figure you still see is voluntary reference. Lev notes and coins stopped being legal tender on 31 January 2026; banks exchange them until 31 December 2026 (some charge a fee after 30 June) and the **BNB exchanges them free of charge with no deadline**. Expect some ATMs and older tills to still think in leva. Cards are accepted almost everywhere; keep €20–€30 in small notes for Zhenski Pazar and village buses.
logistics.transportRules: validate a paper ticket on trams and buses; contactless taps at metro turnstiles are per-journey. Sofia's transport inspectors are frequent and unamused. Left luggage exists at Sofia Central station.
logistics.permits: no photography inside Boyana Church at all — this is enforced. Flash is banned in the Nevsky crypt. Drone use over the Old Town of Plovdiv and over Sofia's government quarter requires permission you will not get.

proTips: Do Boyana at the **first slot of the day**. Eight people at a time means the difference between arriving at 09:00 and 14:00 is an hour of standing in a car park.
Fill your bottle at the **Central Mineral Baths** taps rather than buying water. It is 37 °C, slightly sulphurous, free, and Sofians queue there with five-litre jerricans for a reason.
Take the **train** Sofia–Plovdiv and sit on the right-hand side heading east — you get Vitosha behind you and the Sredna Gora ridge for most of the run.

Plovdiv's Old Town houses are individually ticketed, but a **combined municipal-museums ticket** covers Balabanov, Hindliyan and several others for less than three singles [VERIFY: current combined ticket price and coverage].
Eat *banitsa* and drink *boza* at Zhenski Pazar for under €2. Then never drink boza again.
In Bulgaria a **head shake means yes and a nod means no**. It is real, it is inconsistent among younger people, and it will cost you a meal at least once. Say *da* and *ne* out loud.
Vitosha's lifts are the weak link. If Simeonovo is closed, bus 66 from Hladilnika reaches Aleko by road and the Cherni Vrah walk is unaffected.

raw.Walkable neighbourhood blocks (Sofia): the **Largo** — the socialist-classicist ensemble of the former Party House, Council of Ministers and TZUM, with the excavated **Serdica** decumanus and shops running beneath it and up into the Serdika metro concourse. **Oborishte and the Doctor's Garden (Doktorska gradina)** — embassy streets, plane trees and the 1884 memorial to the medical corps of the Russo-Turkish War; the quietest good-café district in the city. **Ivan Vazov** — the National Theatre, the City Garden chess tables and the axis down to NDK. **Zhenski Pazar** (the Women's Market) on ul. Stefan Stambolov — three blocks of produce, banitsa, lyutenitsa and Roma trade, best before 10:00. The **Central Mineral Baths** block behind the Banya Bashi mosque, where the 1913 Vienna-Secession bathhouse now holds the Sofia History Museum and the free 37 °C taps run on the north side.
raw.Walkable neighbourhood blocks (Plovdiv): **Kapana** ("the trap") — a dozen pedestrianised lanes of studios, third-wave coffee and craft beer between ul. Rayko Daskalov and Dzhumaya Square. **Stariya Grad (Old Town)** — the cobbled climb past Balabanov House and Hindliyan House to **Nebet Tepe**, the Thracian acropolis on the northernmost of the syenite hills. **Tsar Simeon Garden** and the Singing Fountains, south of the main street. **Sahat Tepe (Danov Hill)** for the clock tower and the sunset terrace.
raw.Transit passes and prices: Sofia runs four metro lines — **M1/M2** (the older cross), **M3** (Hadzhi Dimitar–Gorna Banya, the deep new line) and **M4**, which shares track with M1/M2 and serves the airport. A single ride is **€0.80 (1.56 BGN)**; a one-day all-modes card **€2.00 (3.91 BGN)**, or **€3.00 (5.87 BGN)** with the night lines included; a 72-hour card **€7.60 (14.86 BGN)** (2026 tariff, published in euro since 1 January 2026). Buy contactless at the turnstile or from the machine. Plovdiv has no metro and needs none — everything in this itinerary is inside a 25-minute walk.
raw.Sofia–Plovdiv, train vs. bus: the **train** from Sofia Central (Tsentralna Gara) takes **2h40–3h05** on the fast (BV/ICF) services, costs **€5.62 (11.00 BGN)** second class on the BDŽ distance tariff — **€7.62 (14.90 BGN)** on the services carrying compulsory seat reservation (2026 tariff) — and drops you at Plovdiv station a 15-minute walk south of Kapana. The **bus** from Serdika Bus Station or Sofia Central Bus Station is faster — about 1h50 — runs at least hourly and costs roughly **€8–€10 (16–20 BGN)**. Take the train: it is more comfortable, and the Trakiya motorway coach gains you forty minutes you will not use.
raw.Cultural booking timelines: **Boyana Church** is the one hard reservation. UNESCO-listed, with 1259 frescoes that predate Giotto by a generation, it admits a **maximum of eight visitors at a time for a strictly enforced 15 minutes** — the microclimate rule, not a queue-management one. Turn up at opening or reserve by phone the day before; on summer weekends the last slots go by early afternoon. Admission around €5 (10 BGN) [VERIFY: current Boyana admission and reservation procedure]. Nothing else in either city genuinely sells out, but the **Alexander Nevsky crypt** icon museum keeps shorter hours than the cathedral above it, and the **Roman Stadium** underpass has restricted afternoon access on some weekdays [VERIFY: current hours].
raw.Architectural focal points: **Alexander Nevsky Cathedral** (Alexander Pomerantsev, 1882–1912) — Neo-Byzantine, gold-leaf domes, a 45 m central cupola and the country's best icon collection in its crypt. The **Rotunda of St George**, early 4th century, the oldest building in Sofia, standing in the courtyard of the Presidency with three layers of medieval fresco under later Ottoman plaster. The **Largo** (1950s, Petso Zlatev and others) — Bulgaria's most complete Stalinist ensemble. **NDK**, the National Palace of Culture (Alexander Barov, 1981), a hexagonal concrete slab built for the 1,300th anniversary of the Bulgarian state. In Plovdiv: the **Roman Theatre of Philippopolis** (early 2nd century, under Trajan, ~5,000–7,000 seats, still used for opera) and the **Roman Stadium** (2nd century, ~240 m long, capacity around 30,000), of which the marble sphendone is exposed beneath Dzhumaya Square and the rest runs under the length of ul. trips.title: Brno — Functionalism, Cellars and Café Tables

bestPeriod.note: September brings the Moravian harvest and burčák into the wine bars; Villa Tugendhat closes for maintenance in parts of winter.

trips.gatewayAirport: Vienna (VIE)
trips.summary: A slow week in Czechia's second city built around interwar villas, a daily cabbage market, an underground labyrinth and Moravian wine.
trips.hook: Brno is not a smaller Prague. It is a manufacturing and university city that got rich in the 1920s and spent the money on white flat-roofed buildings, and it has never learned to perform for visitors. Nothing here has a queue except Villa Tugendhat. You sit down a lot, you drink Moravian white rather than lager, and you spend the week walking up and down a set of hills between villas.

snapshot.Base(s): Brno, single base; one day in the Moravian Karst
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 55–70 km on foot; the core is flat, the villa districts sit on wooded ridges with 80–150 m climbs; 6 city districts plus the Karst
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Vienna (VIE), then the direct RegioJet or ÖBB coach/train to Brno hlavní nádraží in about 2 hours; or train from Prague, 2h30
snapshot.Who It Suits: Architecture people, café sitters, anyone who found Prague too loud

itinerary.title: Zelný trh and the old town block
itinerary.morning: Begin on Zelný trh, the Cabbage Market — a working vegetable and flower market on the same sloping square since the 13th century, stalls out Monday to Saturday from early morning, with the Parnas Fountain (Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach, 1695) in the middle of it. Buy fruit, then walk up to the Cathedral of St Peter and St Paul on Petrov hill, its twin neo-Gothic spires added by August Kirstein in 1909 to a much older church.
itinerary.afternoon: The Old Town Hall on Radnická for the crooked pinnacle, the stuffed "dragon" and the tower view; then the Capuchin Crypt on Kapucínské náměstí, where 18th-century monks and local notables lie air-dried in the ventilated vaults. Finish at the Moravian Gallery's Pražák Palace on Husova for Czech modern art.
itinerary.evening: Coffee in the Alfa Passage on Poštovská, a 1930s arcade, then a standing beer at Výčep Na stojáka on Běhounská, where there are no chairs and no small talk.
itinerary.dayStats: 6 km walked, 60 m of climbing to Petrov. Districts: Brno-střed. Ticket spend approx. CZK 400–550 (€16–€23).

itinerary.title: Villa Tugendhat and Černá Pole
itinerary.morning: **Book this before you book anything else.** Villa Tugendhat (Ludwig Mies van der Rohe with Lilly Reich, completed 1930, UNESCO-listed) is guided tour only, with strict group sizes. Tickets are released online in batches — typically a new month opens roughly three months ahead, at the start of the calendar month, and the English-language slots and the longer 90-minute tour including the technical basement and the garden go within days. Nothing is held back for walk-ups in season. Tram 5 or 9 to Dětská, then a short climb up Černopolní.
itinerary.afternoon: Stay on the hill. The Löw-Beer Villa next door on Drobného (Alexander Neumann, 1904) belonged to Grete Tugendhat's father and is now a museum of the Brno bourgeoisie, with a path linking the two gardens. Then Lužánky, the oldest public park in the Czech lands, laid out in 1786.
itinerary.evening: Eat in Veveří or around Konečného náměstí, where the university crowd is.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walked, 90 m of climbing. Districts: Černá Pole, Veveří. Ticket spend approx. CZK 700–900 (€29–€37).

itinerary.title: The functionalist city centre walk
itinerary.morning: One block, the length of Česká and Jakubské náměstí. Hotel Avion at Česká 20 (Bohuslav Fuchs, 1928) is 8 metres wide and eight storeys tall, a split-level puzzle in a gap site. Along the same axis: the Morava Palace on Malinovského náměstí (Ernst Wiesner, 1929), the Vesna school buildings, and the former Baťa department store on Kobližná (1931), the chain's glass-fronted retail template.
itinerary.afternoon: Tram 1 to Výstaviště, the Brno Exhibition Centre built for the 1928 Exhibition of Contemporary Culture. Pavilion A (Josef Kalous and Jaroslav Valenta, 1928) is a reinforced-concrete parabolic hall that still hosts trade fairs; the grounds are freely walkable outside fair weeks. Walk up to the Anthropos Pavilion in Pisárky for the mammoth and the Moravian palaeolithic.
itinerary.evening: Zemanova kavárna, Fuchs's 1926 café pavilion by Koliště park, reconstructed on a new site — a glass box with a terrace and a long coffee list.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walked. Districts: Brno-střed, Pisárky. Ticket spend approx. CZK 300–450 (€12–€19).

itinerary.title: Špilberk, Mendel and Staré Brno
itinerary.morning: Špilberk castle on its hill, a 13th-century fortress turned Habsburg prison, with casemates you can walk and a city museum in the upper rooms. The ramparts give the only complete view of Brno's basin.
itinerary.afternoon: Down the west side into Staré Brno: the Augustinian Abbey on Mendlovo náměstí, where Gregor Mendel grew his pea plants between 1856 and 1863 — the Mendel Museum sits in the abbey and the reconstructed garden is behind it. Next door, the Basilica of the Assumption holds the Black Madonna of Brno. The Starobrno brewery has been on the same square since 1872.
itinerary.evening: A wine bar on Jánská or Kapucínské náměstí. Ask for Veltlínské zelené, Ryzlink rýnský or Pálava from the Mikulov and Velké Pavlovice subregions — Moravia grows almost all Czech wine and Brno drinks it by the deci.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walked, 120 m of climbing to Špilberk. Districts: Brno-střed, Staré Brno. Ticket spend approx. CZK 400–600 (€16–€25).

itinerary.title: The villa districts: Masarykova čtvrť, Stiassni and Jurkovič
itinerary.morning: The Masaryk quarter on the wooded slope above Pisárky is where Brno's interwar money built. Walk Barvičova, Vinařská and Preslova and read the villas from the pavement. The Stiassni Villa on Hroznová (Ernst Wiesner, 1929), the "Brno White House" that later hosted state guests, is open by guided tour with its original interiors and a large garden — book online, English tours are limited.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross to Žabovřesky for the Jurkovič House on Jana Nečase (Dušan Jurkovič, 1906), the architect's own home, a folk-inflected Arts and Crafts villa restored by the Moravian Gallery; entry is by timed slot and the house is small. Walk back through Wilson Forest, the ridge park that connects the whole district.
itinerary.evening: Back in the centre, Bar, který neexistuje on Dvořákova for cocktails, or a beer garden on Kraví hora.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km walked, 150 m of climbing. Districts: Masarykova čtvrť, Pisárky, Žabovřesky. Ticket spend approx. CZK 500–700 (€21–€29).

itinerary.title: The Moravian Karst
itinerary.morning: A day out of the city. Train from Brno hlavní nádraží to Blansko, roughly 25 minutes, then the seasonal shuttle bus into the Punkva valley. The Punkevní jeskyně cave tour walks a river gallery, drops to the floor of the Macocha abyss — 138 metres deep, open to the sky — and returns by boat on the underground Punkva. **Tickets are timed and sold online; summer and weekend slots routinely sell out days ahead, and the ticket office often has nothing left by late morning.** Book the moment your dates are set.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the cable car up to the Macocha upper bridge and walk the rim path, or take the Kateřinská or Balcarka cave instead if Punkevní is full. The whole area is limestone forest with marked Czech trails — green, blue, yellow and red bands on trees.
itinerary.evening: Back to Brno for dinner. If you would rather have wine than caves, swap this day for Mikulov: 50 minutes by train, a chateau, the Holy Hill, and the Pálava limestone ridge over the vineyards.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km walked, 130 m of climbing on the Macocha rim; 1h30 of travel. Districts: Moravian Karst. Ticket spend approx. CZK 700–900 (€29–€37) including rail.

itinerary.title: Underground Brno and the last glass
itinerary.morning: The Labyrinth under Zelný trh — three storeys of medieval cellars, storerooms and an alchemist's workshop under the market square, on a timed route with an audioguide. Then the Ossuary at the Church of St James, discovered in 2001 and holding the remains of more than 50,000 people, the second largest in Europe after the Paris catacombs. Both are ticketed, both are five minutes apart, and both are cool on a hot day.
itinerary.afternoon: The Church of St James itself, a late-Gothic hall church completed 1592, with a rude stone figure high on the south tower. Then Denisovy sady, the terraced gardens below Petrov, for the last view.
itinerary.evening: A long dinner and a bottle of Moravian white. Brno's kitchens run later than Prague's and its bar scene runs later still.
itinerary.dayStats: 5 km walked. Districts: Brno-střed. Ticket spend approx. CZK 400–550 (€16–€23).

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Continental
accommodationStrategy.description: A 1964 modernist block with a rooftop restaurant, sitting on the tram line between the centre and Černá Pole. It is exactly the right register for this week — unfussy, well positioned for the Tugendhat and villa days, and a fifteen-minute walk downhill to Zelný trh. Ask for a higher floor away from Kounicova.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4 weeks ahead; longer during the big Výstaviště trade fairs, which fill every bed in the city.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Barceló Brno Palace
accommodationStrategy.description: A restored 19th-century palace at the foot of Špilberk, two minutes from Zelný trh and the Labyrinth, with a courtyard atrium. Worth it if you want a comfortable base for a week and do not want to walk uphill at midnight. Quiet, because the old town has almost no nightlife noise.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: An apartment in Veveří or Černá Pole
accommodationStrategy.description: For seven days a flat with a kitchen and the Zelný trh market makes the food budget trivial. Veveří puts you on the 5 and 9 tram lines for Villa Tugendhat and near the university cafés; Černá Pole is quieter and greener. Check for a lift and note that Brno's tram network stops around midnight, with night buses converging on Malinovského náměstí.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead, avoiding fair dates.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European. Czech specifics: ambulance 155, police 158, fire 150. In the Karst, mountain-rescue style call-outs also go through 112.
logistics.bookingWindows: Villa Tugendhat first, three months out. Punkevní jeskyně second, as soon as the date is fixed. Then the Stiassni Villa and the Jurkovič House, both small-group and both easier, a week or two out. The Labyrinth and Ossuary can be bought on the day except on summer weekends.
logistics.money: Koruna, not euro. Card acceptance is high, including on trams via contactless in most vehicles, but market stalls, the smaller wine bars and cave ticket offices prefer cash. Withdraw from a bank ATM and decline dynamic currency conversion.

other.label: The ticket
other.text: Brno runs on IDS JMK, zones 100 and 101 covering the whole city. A 15-minute single is approx. CZK 20, a 60-minute single approx. CZK 25, a 24-hour ticket approx. CZK 99 and a **seven-day ticket for zones 100+101 approx. CZK 250–300 (about €10–€12)** — on a week-long stay that is the obvious buy. Purchase in the PID Lítačka or Poseidon app, at a DPMB kiosk, or from the yellow machines at major stops.

other.label: The trap
other.text: The SMS ticket (approx. CZK 35, 60 minutes) needs a Czech SIM and does not work on a foreign number. Paper tickets must be stamped in the orange machine on board at the start of the journey, not before. App tickets activate on purchase and cannot be pre-bought for later. Inspectors work in plain clothes and the fine is around CZK 1,500.

other.label: Getting to the Karst
other.text: Zone tickets do not cover Blansko — buy a separate České dráhy return, approx. CZK 60–80 each way. The Punkva shuttle bus and the cave tickets are separate again.

other.label: Trade fairs
other.text: Výstaviště hosts large international fairs several times a year, most notably the engineering fair in autumn. During those weeks hotel prices in Brno double or worse and Pavilion A is closed to casual visitors. Check the fair calendar before booking dates.

other.label: Café and wine habits
other.text: Brno's café culture is a genuine institution and nobody will move you along. Wine is sold by the deciliter — order "dvě deci" for a normal glass. In autumn, burčák is the part-fermented young wine sold for a few weeks only; it is stronger than it tastes.

proTips: Take the 90-minute extended Villa Tugendhat tour rather than the standard one. It adds the basement machine room with the motorised window mechanism and the air plant, which is where you actually understand the building, and it costs only a little more.
The Löw-Beer Villa and Villa Tugendhat share a garden path. Buy the Löw-Beer ticket for the same day and walk between them rather than doubling back up the hill.
Zelný trh's stalls are cheapest in the last hour before they pack up, roughly 16:00–17:00 on weekdays.

Ride tram 1 end to end — Bystrc to Řečkovice — for about CZK 25 with an ordinary ticket. It crosses the whole city, passes Výstaviště and the Pisárky villas, and ends at the Brno reservoir if you want a swim.

If Villa Tugendhat is sold out, the Moravian Gallery's Brno Architecture Manual (a free, well-made online and printed guide) maps every significant interwar building in the city with walking routes. Half the collection is on the street and free.
Order Moravian wine by producer rather than by grape in the Jánská bars — Sonberk, Stapleton & Springer and Nové Vinařství are widely poured and consistently good.
Book Punkevní jeskyně for the first tour of the morning. The boat section is slower and colder later in the day when the queue backs up at the abyss floor.
