typeSpecific.surface: approx. 55–70 km on foot; the core is flat, the villa districts sit on wooded ridges with 80–150 m climbs; 6 city districts plus the Karst
typeSpecific.audience: Architecture people, café sitters, anyone who found Prague too loud

packingNotes: A warm layer and closed shoes for the caves: Punkevní jeskyně sits at 7–8°C year-round and the boat leg is damp.
Shoes that handle a wooded hill climb — the Masaryk quarter and Wilson Forest are proper slopes with gravel paths.
Slip-on shoes are handy at Villa Tugendhat, where visitors wear protective overshoes on the travertine floors.
A layer for the Špilberk casemates and the Capuchin Crypt, which are cold in every season.
Cash in CZK for the market, the wine bars and the cave shuttle.
A refillable bottle; tap water is soft and drinkable everywhere in the city.
A camera with a wide lens if you care — Tugendhat's onyx wall and the Löw-Beer interiors reward it, and photography rules differ between the two, so ask at the desk.
An umbrella; South Moravia gets short, heavy summer storms.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Villa Tugendhat is sold out for your entire week.** The single most common Brno failure. Fallback: the garden and exterior can be seen from the Löw-Beer Villa's grounds on a cheap ticket, and the Stiassni Villa, the Jurkovič House and the Baťa-era centre give you a real functionalist week without it. Watch the booking page for released cancellations, which appear a day or two ahead.

**A trade fair is on and every hotel is triple price.** Fallback: check the Výstaviště calendar before setting dates; if you are locked in, stay in Vienna or Olomouc and day-trip, or take an apartment in Žabovřesky or Královo Pole, which fill last.

**Punkevní jeskyně is fully booked.** Fallback: Kateřinská and Balcarka caves in the same valley usually have same-day tickets, and the Macocha rim walk with the cable car needs no reservation. Or swap the whole day for Mikulov and the Pálava vineyards.

**You arrive on a Monday.** Most Brno museums, the Moravian Gallery houses and Villa Tugendhat close. Fallback: Monday is the day for the Špilberk ramparts, Zelný trh, the functionalist street walk and the Masaryk quarter — all of it exterior and free.

**The tram network stops before you do.** Fallback: night buses run from around midnight and all of them meet at Malinovského náměstí on a timed interchange, so you can always get home with one change if you know the hour of departure.

trips.title: Prague in Layers — Gothic, Baroque, Cubist, Functionalist

bestPeriod.note: May and late September avoid both the August coach season and the short, grey January days; the Vinohrady beer gardens open around April.

trips.gatewayAirport: Prague (PRG)
trips.summary: Prague read as four architectural centuries, one district a day, with Vinohrady and Karlín given as much weight as the Castle.
trips.hook: Prague was never bombed and never comprehensively rebuilt, so its centuries sit on top of one another on the same streets: a Gothic vault under a Baroque plaster ceiling, a Cubist façade three doors from a Renaissance one. Take one layer at a time and the city stops being a crowd problem and becomes legible. The Castle gets one morning. Vinohrady and Karlín get a day each, which is roughly the right proportion.

snapshot.Base(s): Prague, single base (Vinohrady or Karlín)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 65–80 km on foot; flat on the right bank, steep climbs to Hradčany, Vyšehrad and Vítkov; 8 districts
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to PRG, then bus 119 to Nádraží Veleslavín and metro A, about 35 min; or rail from Vienna, Dresden and Berlin to Praha hlavní nádraží
snapshot.Who It Suits: Repeat visitors and first-timers who want more than the Charles Bridge; anyone who reads buildings

itinerary.title: Staré Město: the Gothic core and the Cubist corner
itinerary.morning: Start early, genuinely early. Staroměstské náměstí at 07:30 is empty; at 10:00 it is not. The Týn Church (begun 1365), the astronomical clock on the Old Town Hall (mechanism 1410), and the Karolinum's oriel window on Ovocný trh belong to the same century. The Old Town Hall tower has timed entry and the first slots are the only calm ones.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk Celetná to the Dům U Černé Matky Boží — the House at the Black Madonna (Josef Gočár, 1912), the first Cubist building anywhere, with a Cubist café, Grand Café Orient, on the first floor. Coffee there, then the Convent of St Agnes (founded 1231) on the river side of Josefov, which holds the National Gallery's medieval Bohemian panels in a Gothic cloister almost nobody visits.
itinerary.evening: Havelské tržiště, the market on Havelská, runs daily until early evening; buy fruit, not souvenirs. Dinner in the Old Town away from the main axes — anywhere off Dlouhá.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walked. Districts: Staré Město, Josefov. Ticket spend approx. CZK 600–800 (€25–€33).

itinerary.title: Hradčany: the Castle at opening, then Nový Svět
itinerary.morning: Be at the Castle gates when they open. Buy the Circuit B ticket, which covers St Vitus Cathedral (begun 1344 by Matthias of Arras, continued by Peter Parler, completed 1929), the Old Royal Palace, St George's Basilica and Golden Lane. Cathedral entry is free only in the small entrance area; the nave is inside the ticket. Security screening at the gates adds 10–20 minutes from mid-morning.
itinerary.afternoon: Leave by the western gate into Hradčanské náměstí and walk down into Nový Svět, a lane of tiny 17th-century cottages behind the Castle where the crowd simply does not go. Then Loreta (Baroque complex, bell carillon on the hour) and the Strahov Monastery library (Theological Hall 1679, Philosophical Hall 1794) — you view the halls from the doorway unless you book the paid extended access.
itinerary.evening: Walk down the Petřín slope through the orchards for the classic dusk view, or ride the funicular, which is covered by any valid transit ticket.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walked, 130 m of climbing. Districts: Hradčany, Malá Strana. Ticket spend approx. CZK 700–950 (€29–€39).

itinerary.title: Malá Strana Baroque and Kampa
itinerary.morning: One block: the streets between Malostranské náměstí and Kampa. St Nicholas Church (Kryštof Dientzenhofer, continued by his son Kilián Ignác and completed 1755) is the finest Baroque interior in Central Europe and the one building worth the entry fee twice. Then the Wallenstein Palace garden (1630), free, with its dripstone wall and resident peacocks.
itinerary.afternoon: The Vrtba Garden off Karmelitská, a terraced Baroque garden climbing the hill, ticketed and almost always quiet. Then Kampa island, the Čertovka mill wheel, and the Kampa Museum for Czech modernism, including František Kupka.
itinerary.evening: Café Savoy on Vítězná, a restored 1893 café with a neo-Renaissance ceiling, does a proper dinner. Cross the Charles Bridge after 22:00 when it is briefly walkable again.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km walked. Districts: Malá Strana. Ticket spend approx. CZK 500–700 (€21–€29).

itinerary.title: Vyšehrad and the Cubist embankment
itinerary.morning: Metro C to Vyšehrad and walk into the fortress: the Basilica of St Peter and St Paul, the ramparts above the Vltava bend, and the Slavín cemetery where Dvořák, Smetana, Mucha and Čapek are buried. The casemates and the Gorlice hall underneath hold six original Charles Bridge statues.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend the north-west stairs to Podolí and the best Cubist architecture in the world, all within four streets: the Kovařovic Villa on Libušina, the triple house at Rašínovo nábřeží 6–10, and the apartment building at Neklanova 30 — all by Josef Chochol, all 1913. Walk the embankment north.
itinerary.evening: The Náplavka riverside quay below Výtoň. On Saturday mornings it holds Prague's biggest farmers' market; on weekday evenings the vaulted cellars in the wall are bars.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walked, 60 m of climbing. Districts: Vyšehrad, Podolí, Nové Město. Ticket spend approx. CZK 300–450 (€12–€19).

itinerary.title: Vinohrady: Plečnik, the vineyard and Jiřího z Poděbrad
itinerary.morning: Metro A to Jiřího z Poděbrad and out into the square. The Church of the Most Sacred Heart of Our Lord (Jože Plečnik, 1932) is unlike anything else — a dark brick liturgical ark with a glazed clock 7.5 metres across set into a slab tower. The interior is open around services and on scheduled afternoons. The farmers' market on the square runs Wednesday to Saturday, roughly 08:00 to 18:00, and Saturday is the full version.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk Vinohradská and the residential grid — Slovenská, Šumavská, Mánesova — for the National Revival and Art Nouveau apartment blocks. Then Havlíčkovy sady, known as Grébovka, a 19th-century landscape park with a working vineyard and a neo-Renaissance villa; the Viniční altán pavilion pours the estate's own wine.
itinerary.evening: Riegrovy sady beer garden for the sunset view over the city to the Castle. It is a local institution, cash-friendly, and gets busy from 18:00.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walked, 70 m of climbing. Districts: Vinohrady. Ticket spend approx. CZK 200–350 (€8–€15).

itinerary.title: Karlín and Žižkov
itinerary.morning: Karlín is the flat grid laid out in 1817 as Prague's first planned suburb, flooded catastrophically in 2002 and rebuilt since. Start at Karlínské náměstí with the Church of Sts Cyril and Methodius (Karl Roesner and Ignác Ullmann, 1863), a basilica in Romanesque revival on a scale the district no longer justifies. The square holds a farmers' market on Saturdays.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb Vítkov hill to the National Memorial (Jan Zázvorka, 1932), a granite functionalist mausoleum with the enormous equestrian Jan Žižka (Bohumil Kafka, cast 1950) outside and a rooftop terrace over the whole city. Descend into Žižkov for the Television Tower (1992) with David Černý's crawling babies bolted to it, and the Olšany cemeteries.
itinerary.evening: Eska on Pernerova, in a converted Karlín factory, does modern Czech baking and fermentation properly. Or drink in Žižkov, which has more pubs per capita than any district in the country.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km walked, 110 m of climbing to Vítkov. Districts: Karlín, Žižkov. Ticket spend approx. CZK 350–500 (€15–€21).

itinerary.title: Functionalism: Villa Müller, Baba and the Veletržní palác
itinerary.morning: Adolf Loos's Villa Müller (1930) in Střešovice is the Raumplan made real — a plain white cube outside, a spiralling sequence of differently proportioned rooms in travertine, mahogany and green marble inside. **It is guided tour only, small groups, and the tours book out weeks ahead in season.** Reserve online or by email as soon as your dates are fixed; tours typically run several times a day, closed Mondays, with a reduced winter schedule. Tram 1 or 18 to Ořechovka.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross to the Baba estate in Dejvice, 33 functionalist family villas built for the 1932 Werkbund exhibition by Gočár, Pavel Janák, Ladislav Žák and others, still lived in and walkable from the street. Then the Veletržní palác (Oldřich Tyl and Josef Fuchs, 1928), the first great functionalist building in Europe, now the National Gallery's modern collection.
itinerary.evening: Holešovice: the Pražská tržnice market halls, the Vnitroblock complex, and a last Czech lager somewhere with a proper tank.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walked. Districts: Střešovice, Dejvice, Holešovice. Ticket spend approx. CZK 600–800 (€25–€33).

accommodationStrategy.name: An apartment in Vinohrady
accommodationStrategy.description: Vinohrady is the right base for this itinerary: metro A runs through it to both the Castle side and the airport bus, the restaurants are for residents rather than tourists, and the Jiřího z Poděbrad market is your breakfast. Look for a flat with a lift and street-facing windows on a side street rather than on Vinohradská, which carries trams all night.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Pentahotel Prague
accommodationStrategy.description: Straightforward, reliable and priced well below the Old Town, with trams to Náměstí Míru and the Karlín and Vršovice restaurant streets on foot. Useful if you want a hotel desk and daily housekeeping without paying centre rates, and the location makes Days 5 and 6 start at the door.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 5 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Boutique rooms in Karlín
accommodationStrategy.description: Karlín gives you flat streets, the metro B line, the Vítkov climb, and a district that empties of visitors at 18:00. Bakeries and the Saturday market are on Karlínské náměstí; Forum Karlín handles the concerts. Ask for a courtyard room — Křižíkova is a tram street.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European. Czech specifics: ambulance 155, police 158, city police 156, fire 150. Pharmacies with 24-hour service are listed at the door of every lékárna.
logistics.bookingWindows: Villa Müller is the one true bottleneck — book it first and build the week around it. Prague Castle needs no advance ticket but the security queue does; arrive at opening. The Clementinum Baroque library and the Astronomical Clock tower run timed slots that sell out midday in summer. Restaurant reservations at Eska and the Ambiente group's places should be a week ahead for dinner.
logistics.money: Czechia uses the koruna, not the euro. Never change money at a street exchange booth in the centre — the advertised rate is for a different transaction. Use a bank ATM (ČSOB, Komerční banka, Česká spořitelna) and always decline dynamic currency conversion. Cards work almost everywhere; keep CZK 500 in cash for markets and small pubs.

other.label: The transit ticket that actually fits
other.text: Prague PID sells 30-minute (approx. CZK 30) and 90-minute (approx. CZK 40) singles, a 24-hour ticket at approx. CZK 120 and a **72-hour jízdenka at approx. CZK 330 (about €13.50)**. There is no 7-day tourist ticket. For a week, buy one 72-hour ticket for your heaviest three days and singles for the rest, or, if you are here longer, a monthly pass at approx. CZK 550 — but that requires a registered Lítačka card and a photo, which is rarely worth the errand.

other.label: Validation is a one-time act
other.text: Paper tickets are stamped once, in the yellow box at the metro entrance or on board a tram, at the *start* of validity — not at every change. Stamping twice voids it. Inspectors are plain-clothed and constant; the on-the-spot fine is around CZK 1,500.

other.label: Luggage
other.text: A bag over 25 × 45 × 70 cm needs its own half-price ticket, approx. CZK 20. Inspectors do check this on the airport bus.

other.label: Beer etiquette
other.text: In a traditional pub the beer arrives when you sit and keeps arriving until you put a beer mat on your glass. Tally marks on the slip are the bill. Tip by rounding up to the next CZK 10 or 20.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: National Gallery buildings and most state museums close Monday. Churches with paid entry close for services. Many kitchens stop at 21:30 even where the bar runs later.

proTips: The Charles Bridge is a different structure before 07:00 and after 22:30. Both windows are genuinely empty and free; every hour in between is a queue with a view.
Buy the Prague Castle ticket at the far Golden Lane end box office rather than the main courtyard one. The circuit is the same, the queue is a fraction.
The Petřín funicular, the Vltava ferries (přívoz lines P1–P7) and tram 42's historic cars all run on ordinary PID tickets. Ferry P5 across to Císařská louka is the cheapest boat ride in the city.
Tram 22 from Národní třída up to Pohořelec is the standing tourist route; ride it up in the morning and walk down instead of queueing for it in the afternoon crush.
Book the Villa Müller and, if you want the pair, Loos's Winternitz Villa in Střešovice on the same day — they are 15 minutes apart and share the same Raumplan logic.
Náplavka's Saturday farmers' market opens at 08:00 and the good bread is gone by 10:00. Go early, then walk the Cubist embankment while it is still cool.

Riegrovy sady in Vinohrady and Letná beer garden face each other across the river. Riegrovy gets the sunset over the Castle; Letná gets the bridges. Do one on Day 5 and the other after the Veletržní palác on Day 7.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 65–80 km on foot; flat on the right bank, steep climbs to Hradčany, Vyšehrad and Vítkov; 8 districts
raw.Who It Suits: Repeat visitors and first-timers who want more than the Charles Bridge; anyone who reads buildings

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 65–80 km on foot; flat on the right bank, steep climbs to Hradčany, Vyšehrad and Vítkov; 8 districts
typeSpecific.audience: Repeat visitors and first-timers who want more than the Charles Bridge; anyone who reads buildings

packingNotes: Shoes with grip for wet cobbles — Prague's setts polish smooth and the Malá Strana lanes are steep.
A layer for church interiors, which stay cold from October to May regardless of the street temperature.
A small cash reserve in CZK for markets, pub tabs and cloakroom attendants, who expect CZK 20.
A compact daypack; the National Gallery buildings and Villa Müller require bags and coats in the cloakroom.
A phone with offline maps — the Old Town's street numbering uses two systems and neither helps.
Sunglasses and a hat for the Vyšehrad ramparts and Vítkov, both fully exposed.
A refillable bottle; Prague tap water is soft, safe and free, and restaurants will fill it if asked.
Something smart enough for a concert at the Rudolfinum or Forum Karlín, if you plan one.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Villa Müller is fully booked for your whole week.** Fallback: book the Winternitz Villa instead, also Loos, also guided, and considerably easier to get into; add the Rothmayer House in Střešovice for a third interwar interior.

**You get stung by a currency exchange booth or a DCC prompt.** Fallback: withdraw from a bank-branded ATM, refuse the machine's own conversion, and if you have already changed money, Czech exchange offices are legally required to allow a cancellation within three hours for amounts under a threshold — go straight back with the receipt.

**The Old Town is unwalkable by mid-morning.** Fallback: this itinerary only spends one day there, and it front-loads it to 07:30. If you lose that window, swap Day 1 with Day 5 and do Vinohrady instead.

**Rain shuts the outdoor half of the week.** Fallback: the Veletržní palác, the Convent of St Agnes, the Kampa Museum and the Strahov libraries are four large interiors that between them absorb two full wet days.

**A pub bill is larger than expected.** Fallback: check the slip's tally marks against what you drank before paying, and be wary of unrequested bread, nuts or aperitifs in centre restaurants, which are charged. Politely send them back.

trips.title: Berlin, One Kiez at a Time

bestPeriod.note: July and August are hot and the city half-empties; January and February are dark by 16:00.

trips.gatewayAirport: Berlin Brandenburg (BER)
trips.summary: Seven days of Berlin taken district by district, from Museumsinsel to Neukölln, on one weekly BVG ticket and a lot of walking.
trips.hook: Berlin is not a centre with suburbs. It is a loose federation of Kieze, each with its own market hall, its own square and its own century. Treat it that way and the city stops feeling exhausting: one district a day, on foot, with the U-Bahn only to get in and out.

snapshot.Base(s): Kreuzberg (Bergmannkiez) or Mitte, single base all week
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: 65–80 km on foot over seven days, flat, cobbles in the old core
snapshot.Getting There: BER airport, FEX or S9/S45 to the centre in 30–50 min; ICE to Hauptbahnhof
snapshot.Who It Suits: Walkers, museum-goers, anyone who wants a city in cross-section rather than a highlight reel

itinerary.title: Museumsinsel and the Spandauer Vorstadt
itinerary.morning: Start on the island itself. The Neues Museum (August Stüler, 1855; rebuilt by David Chipperfield, 2009) holds Nefertiti, and Chipperfield's decision to leave the war damage legible is the real exhibit. Book a timed slot online; 09:00 and 10:00 release first and go last. The Alte Nationalgalerie (Stüler, 1876) is fifty metres away. Note honestly that the Pergamonmuseum's main building is closed for structural works and is not expected back in full before the late 2020s — the Pergamonmuseum. Das Panorama on Am Kupfergraben covers the gap.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk north into the Spandauer Vorstadt. The Hackesche Höfe (August Endell, 1906) is eight linked courtyards; the first, with its glazed polychrome tile, is the one Endell designed. Continue to Sophienstraße, then the Neue Synagoge on Oranienburger Straße (Eduard Knoblauch and Stüler, 1866), whose gilded dome is visible from three districts.
itinerary.evening: Eat at Zur letzten Instanz on Waisenstraße, a tavern trading since 1621, then walk the Nikolaiviertel after the coach groups have gone.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walking · districts: Mitte, Spandauer Vorstadt · tickets approx €26 (Neues Museum + Alte Nationalgalerie).

itinerary.title: Kreuzberg SO36 and the Landwehrkanal
itinerary.morning: Markthalle Neun on Eisenbahnstraße is the anchor: a small weekday market, a full Saturday one, and Street Food Thursday from 17:00 to 22:00. Come early for coffee and Sironi bread, then walk Wrangelkiez.
itinerary.afternoon: Oranienstraße end to end, then Oranienplatz and the Landwehrkanal towpath west to Kottbusser Brücke. If it is a Tuesday or Friday, the Türkischer Markt on Maybachufer runs 11:00–18:00 and is the best value produce in the city.
itinerary.evening: Cross the Oberbaumbrücke (Otto Stahn, 1896) at dusk for the classic Spree view, then back for a beer on Paul-Lincke-Ufer.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km walking · districts: Kreuzberg SO36, Wrangelkiez · tickets approx €0 (markets and streets only).

itinerary.title: Prenzlauer Berg and the Wall at Bernauer Straße
itinerary.morning: The Gedenkstätte Berliner Mauer on Bernauer Straße is free, open-air and the only place where the full depth of the border strip — outer wall, death strip, signal fence — is reconstructed. Allow ninety minutes and climb the viewing tower at the documentation centre.
itinerary.afternoon: Kollwitzplatz. The market runs Thursday 12:00–19:00 and Saturday 09:00–16:00. Loop Husemannstraße, Rykestraße and Zionskirchplatz, then the Kulturbrauerei, a Schultheiss brewery complex of 1891 now full of small halls.
itinerary.evening: Konnopke's Imbiss under the U2 viaduct at Eberswalder Straße has been selling Currywurst since 1930. Follow it with a table at the Prater Garten on Kastanienallee, a beer garden since 1837.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km walking · districts: Prenzlauer Berg, Gesundbrunnen edge · tickets approx €0 (memorial free).

itinerary.title: Neukölln and Tempelhofer Feld
itinerary.morning: Enter Tempelhofer Feld at the Columbiadamm gate. The runways are public park now; Ernst Sagebiel's terminal (1936–41) is 1.2 km of limestone curve and still one of Europe's largest buildings. Guided tours run several times daily and must be booked ahead.
itinerary.afternoon: Schillerkiez, then Richardplatz — the surviving core of Bohemian Rixdorf, a village settled by Czech Protestants in 1737. Körnerpark, a sunken neo-baroque garden in a former gravel pit, is three streets south.
itinerary.evening: Sunset from Klunkerkranich, the rooftop bar on the Neukölln Arcaden car park, entered by lift from the top parking deck. Small entry fee, queue after 19:00 in summer.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km walking · districts: Neukölln, Rixdorf, Tempelhof · tickets approx €19 (Tempelhof tour).

itinerary.title: Tiergarten, the Kulturforum and Potsdamer Platz
itinerary.morning: Mies van der Rohe's Neue Nationalgalerie (1968, refurbished by Chipperfield in 2021) opens at 10:00; the steel-and-glass upper hall is worth as much time as the collection below. Timed tickets online.
itinerary.afternoon: The Gemäldegalerie next door holds Germany's deepest old-master collection and is almost never full. Then Hans Scharoun's Philharmonie (1963); free lunchtime chamber concerts run Tuesdays in season, doors around 12:00.
itinerary.evening: Walk the Tiergarten paths to the Neuer See, eat at the Café am Neuen See beer garden, and finish at the Siegessäule if the light holds.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walking · districts: Tiergarten, Kulturforum, Potsdamer Platz · tickets approx €24 (two state museums, or free with the Museum Pass).

itinerary.title: Friedrichshain and Karl-Marx-Allee
itinerary.morning: Walk Karl-Marx-Allee from Frankfurter Tor to Strausberger Platz. Hermann Henselmann's towers (1952–60) and the tiled Stalinist blocks are the most complete piece of socialist urbanism west of Moscow, and the Café Sibylle at number 72 keeps a small display on the street's history.
itinerary.afternoon: Boxhagener Platz and the RAW-Gelände, a former railway repair yard. The Boxhagener Platz market runs Saturday (food) and Sunday (flea, from 10:00).
itinerary.evening: The East Side Gallery is best walked after 20:00 when the crowds thin. Dinner on Simon-Dach-Straße or at the Volkspark Friedrichshain beer garden.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km walking · districts: Friedrichshain, Stralauer Kiez · tickets approx €0.

itinerary.title: Charlottenburg and City West
itinerary.morning: Schloss Charlottenburg (Johann Arnold Nering, 1699; extended by Eosander and Knobelsdorff) with the Neuer Flügel and the baroque garden. The combined palace ticket is roughly €19.
itinerary.afternoon: Kantstraße for lunch, then the Kaiser-Wilhelm-Gedächtniskirche — Egon Eiermann's 1963 blue-glass hall beside the bombed 1895 tower. Rogacki on Wilmersdorfer Straße, a fish counter since 1928, is the food anchor here.
itinerary.evening: The sixth-floor food hall at KaDeWe, then a last U-Bahn ride east.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walking · districts: Charlottenburg, City West · tickets approx €19.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Oderberger
accommodationStrategy.style: Design hotel in a restored 1902 bathhouse
accommodationStrategy.description: The swimming hall is original and open to guests, which matters after four days of pavement. Oderberger Straße puts Mauerpark, Kastanienallee and the U2 within five minutes, and breakfast runs late enough for a slow start.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead, 4 months for a September weekend.

accommodationStrategy.name: Orania.Berlin
accommodationStrategy.description: A 1913 corner building on Oranienplatz with a ground-floor salon and live music most nights. You are inside the Kreuzberg walking radius, which removes a transit leg from three of these days.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–10 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Michelberger Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: Opposite Warschauer Straße station, so the S-Bahn ring, the U1 and the M10 tram are all at the door. Rooms are small and cheap at the lower tiers; the courtyard kitchen serves late.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–8 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 for fire and ambulance, 110 for police. Pharmacy after hours: the rota is posted in every Apotheke window under Notdienst.
logistics.money: Card acceptance has improved but is not universal: Spätis, Imbiss stands, market halls and some bars are cash-only. Carry €40 in notes.

other.label: Zones
other.text: Berlin runs on AB, BC and ABC. AB covers everything in this itinerary. ABC is only needed for BER airport and Potsdam. If you hold an AB ticket, buy a single Anschlussfahrausweis (extension ticket, approx €2.20) rather than a whole ABC fare.

other.label: The weekly ticket
other.text: The 7-Tage-Karte AB runs approx €43; the ABC version approx €53. A single AB is approx €3.80, a day ticket approx €10.50. The weekly pays for itself on about day four.

other.label: The traps
other.text: There are no barriers. A paper ticket is invalid until stamped in the yellow or red box on the platform or inside the bus or tram — inspectors work in plain clothes and the fine is €60 in cash or on the spot. App tickets (BVG Fahrinfo / Jelbi) validate at purchase, so buy them before you step onto the vehicle, not after. The Kurzstrecke (approx €2.40) is three stops on U- or S-Bahn with no changes, or six stops by bus or tram — it is not a short-distance-in-general ticket.

other.label: Museum Pass Berlin
other.text: is approx €34 for three consecutive days across roughly 30 museums, including everything on Museumsinsel and at the Kulturforum. It does not remove the need for a timed slot: reserve the free entry slot online with the pass number.

other.label: Reichstag dome
other.text: Free but registered. Apply at bundestag.de at least three days ahead — in practice two to three weeks in summer — and bring the passport whose number you registered.

other.label: Sunday closing
other.text: Supermarkets shut; bakeries, Spätis and station shops do not. Museums open Sundays and mostly close Mondays.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 for fire and ambulance, 110 for police. Pharmacy after hours: the rota is posted in every Apotheke window under Notdienst.

proTips: Book the Neues Museum's first slot and go straight to Nefertiti's room; by 11:00 there is a queue at that single gallery door.
The Berliner Philharmoniker release returned and standing seats at the box office 90 minutes before curtain; the acoustic in Scharoun's hall is worth the wait.
Tempelhofer Feld gates close at sunset, times posted at each gate; use Oderstraße in the evening, the last to lock.
Street Food Thursday at Markthalle Neun is heaving by 18:30. Arrive at 17:00 and leave before the door queue forms.
Take the S-Bahn Ring (S41 clockwise) once, all the way round, for 60 minutes and one fare. It is the cheapest architectural survey of the city.
For the Sunday flea markets, Mauerpark is the famous one and Boxhagener Platz is the one where locals actually buy things.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: 65–80 km on foot over seven days, flat, cobbles in the old core
raw.Who It Suits: Walkers, museum-goers, anyone who wants a city in cross-section rather than a highlight reel

typeSpecific.surface: 65–80 km on foot over seven days, flat, cobbles in the old core
typeSpecific.audience: Walkers, museum-goers, anyone who wants a city in cross-section rather than a highlight reel

packingNotes: Shoes with a real sole: Berlin's Mitte and Prenzlauer Berg pavements are granite setts and small cobbles.
A rain shell, not an umbrella — the wind across Tempelhofer Feld and the Spree bridges destroys umbrellas.
€40 in small notes and coins for Imbiss stands, Spätis and market halls.
A passport for the Reichstag registration and for ID checks at some club doors.
A refillable bottle; Berliner Wasserbetriebe runs public drinking fountains May to October.
Ear plugs if you take a room facing Oranienstraße, Simon-Dach-Straße or Kastanienallee.
A tote bag for the Türkischer Markt — the stalls do not give out plastic.
whatCouldGoWrong: **You arrive without an ABC ticket at BER.** The airport is in zone C. Buy an ABC single (approx €4.70) at the machine before the platform; the FEX and RE7 to Hauptbahnhof take 30 minutes and run twice hourly.

**A Museumsinsel museum is closed for works.** Beyond the Pergamonmuseum, rotating closures are routine. Check smb.museum the week before and swap in the Gemäldegalerie, the Bode-Museum or the Hamburger Bahnhof.
**A strike or U-Bahn works.** BVG runs replacement buses (SEV) on the same ticket, and the M-series trams cover most U-Bahn corridors. Allow 20 extra minutes at weekends, when closures cluster.
**Rain from noon.** Move the indoor anchor forward: the Kulturforum, the Museum für Naturkunde and the Jüdisches Museum (Daniel Libeskind, 2001) each absorb three hours.
**Refused at a club door.** Normal, not personal. Fall back on a late concert at the Kulturbrauerei or the bars on Weserstraße in Neukölln, which run past 03:00 without a door policy.

trips.title: Hamburg on the Water

bestPeriod.note: The Elbe wind is cold until late April; June and September give long light without August prices.

trips.gatewayAirport: Hamburg (HAM)
trips.summary: A week of Hamburg read through its water: Speicherstadt, HafenCity, the Alster, the Elbe ferries and a Sunday dawn at the Fischmarkt.
trips.hook: Hamburg makes sense only from the water. The city was built to move cargo, and every district still faces a canal, a basin or a lake. Ride the public ferries rather than the tourist barges, walk the warehouse quarters at low light, and let the harbour set the rhythm of the week.

snapshot.Base(s): Neustadt or St. Pauli, single base all week
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: 60–75 km on foot, flat, plus roughly 3 hours on public ferries
snapshot.Getting There: S1 from Hamburg Airport to Hauptbahnhof in 25 min; ICE from Berlin in 1h50
snapshot.Who It Suits: Architecture readers, harbour watchers, families who like boats more than queues

itinerary.title: Speicherstadt and the Kontorhausviertel
itinerary.morning: Start at Kornhausbrücke and walk the Speicherstadt north to south. Built from 1883 on oak piles, it is the largest continuous warehouse district in the world and, with the Kontorhausviertel, a UNESCO site since 2015. Cross Poggenmühlenbrücke for the Wasserschloss view; go before 10:00 and you will have it.
itinerary.afternoon: Over Meßberg into the Kontorhausviertel. Fritz Höger's Chilehaus (1924) is the definitive brick expressionist building — walk to the eastern point on Pumpen for the ship's-prow corner. The Sprinkenhof (Höger with the Gerson brothers, 1927–43) opposite is bigger and less visited.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at the Oberhafen-Kantine, a listed 1925 dock canteen that has been leaning at an angle since the 1962 flood, then a walk along the Zollkanal.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walking · districts: Speicherstadt, Altstadt, Kontorhausviertel · tickets approx €0.

itinerary.title: HafenCity and the Elbphilharmonie
itinerary.morning: Book the Elbphilharmonie Plaza slot. Herzog & de Meuron's glass wave (2017) sits on Werner Kallmorgen's 1963 Kaispeicher A; the Plaza at 37 m is a public terrace with an entry ticket of approx €5, timed online, with the long curved escalator ride included. Same-day slots exist but sell out by mid-morning in summer.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk east through HafenCity: Sandtorhafen and the Magellan-Terrassen, the Marco-Polo-Terrassen, Behnisch Architekten's Unilever-Haus (2009) at Strandkai, and the Lohsepark memorial on the site of the Hannoverscher Bahnhof deportation platform.
itinerary.evening: Miniatur Wunderland in the Speicherstadt runs late most nights and is the one attraction in Hamburg you must book weeks ahead; a timed ticket is approx €22 and evening slots are the quietest.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km walking · districts: HafenCity, Speicherstadt · tickets approx €27.

itinerary.title: Altstadt, Neustadt and the Binnenalster
itinerary.morning: The Rathaus (1897, Martin Haller and others) sits on 4,000 piles; guided tours run hourly and cost a few euros. Then the Alsterarkaden and the Binnenalster.
itinerary.afternoon: St. Michaelis — "der Michel" — by Johann Leonhard Prey and Ernst Georg Sonnin, consecrated 1762, with a 132 m tower and a lift to the viewing gallery for about €8. Behind it, the Krameramtsstuben on Krayenkamp (1676) are the last courtyard almshouses of their kind in the city.
itinerary.evening: Großneumarkt has the neighbourhood's restaurant tables; Café Paris on Rathausstraße, in a 1882 tiled butchers' hall, does a long dinner service.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walking · districts: Altstadt, Neustadt · tickets approx €14.

itinerary.title: St. Pauli, the Landungsbrücken and the harbour
itinerary.morning: From the Landungsbrücken (1907) take HADAG ferry line 62 to Finkenwerder. It is an ordinary scheduled service, included in any HVV ticket, and it runs the same water as the commercial harbour tours for a fraction of the price. Get off at Neumühlen/Övelgönne on the way back.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Alter Elbtunnel (1911), 426 m under the river with tiled reliefs of eels and rats; the pedestrian crossing is free and the old car lifts still run on a restricted timetable.
itinerary.evening: Up the Reeperbahn, through the Große Freiheit, then a Fischbrötchen at Brücke 10 before the bars fill.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km walking, 1h on ferries · districts: St. Pauli, Steinwerder · tickets approx €9 (HVV day ticket covers the ferries).

itinerary.title: Eppendorf, Winterhude and the Außenalster
itinerary.morning: The Isemarkt runs under the U3 viaduct on Isestraße every Tuesday and Friday, 08:30–14:00, and is the longest open-air market in Germany. This is the food anchor of the week.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Alsterrundweg — 7.4 km around the Außenalster, past the Krugkoppelbrücke and the boathouses. Cut into Winterhude for the Goldbekufer and the Stadtpark, laid out by Fritz Schumacher from 1910.
itinerary.evening: Hire a rowing or pedal boat at one of the Alster jetties for the last hour of light, then eat on Mühlenkamp.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km walking · districts: Eppendorf, Harvestehude, Winterhude · tickets approx €10 (market spend, boat hire).

itinerary.title: Sternschanze and the Karolinenviertel
itinerary.morning: Schanzenstraße, Susannenstraße and the Rote Flora, a squatted 1888 theatre. The Schanzenpark water tower (1910) is now a hotel and marks the high point of the quarter.
itinerary.afternoon: The Karolinenviertel behind the Messe: Marktstraße's small shops, then the Kunsthalle if the weather breaks — Georg Theodor Schirrmacher's 1869 building plus O. M. Ungers' cube-perfect Galerie der Gegenwart (1997), about €16.
itinerary.evening: The Saturday market on Neuer Pferdemarkt, or dinner on Bartelsstraße, then a gig at the Fabrik in Altona.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walking · districts: Sternschanze, Karolinenviertel, St. Georg edge · tickets approx €16.

itinerary.title: Altona, Ottensen and Blankenese
itinerary.morning: The Fischmarkt at Große Elbstraße runs Sunday from 05:00 in summer and 07:00 in winter, and ends at 09:30 sharp. The 1896 Fischauktionshalle beside it has a brass band and beer at breakfast, which is the point.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Elbe path from Neumühlen past the Museumshafen Övelgönne to the Elbstrand, then take the S1 from Klein Flottbek or Othmarschen to Blankenese and climb the Treppenviertel — 5,000 steps of car-free hillside village.
itinerary.evening: Back east for a last drink on the Altonaer Balkon over the container terminal.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km walking, 60 m of stair climbing · districts: Altona, Ottensen, Blankenese · tickets approx €9.

accommodationStrategy.name: 25hours Hotel HafenCity
accommodationStrategy.description: Puts you inside HafenCity, so the Elbphilharmonie, Speicherstadt and Miniatur Wunderland are all walkable and you never need a night transfer. The ground-floor bar keeps a late kitchen, which matters after an evening Plaza slot.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead; 4 months for a cruise-turnaround weekend.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Hafen Hamburg
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits on the bluff directly above the Landungsbrücken, so the ferries, the Alter Elbtunnel and the Reeperbahn are five minutes downhill. Ask for a harbour-facing room in the Turmzimmer wing; the container cranes work all night and the view is the reason to be here.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–10 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Superbude St. Pauli
accommodationStrategy.description: Family rooms with bunks, a laundry and bike hire, on the Schanze side rather than the Reeperbahn side, so it is quieter than the postcode suggests. U3 Feldstraße is four minutes away.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–8 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 for fire and ambulance, 110 for police. On the water, the DGzRS sea rescue service monitors VHF 16.
logistics.weather: Schmuddelwetter is the local word for it: horizontal drizzle off the Elbe most months. Keep an indoor fallback for every afternoon.
logistics.bookingWindows: Miniatur Wunderland: 3–6 weeks ahead in summer, longer for school holidays. Elbphilharmonie Plaza: online from about two weeks out, or same-day from 09:00. Elbphilharmonie concerts: the season goes on sale in a single spring release and the Grand Hall sells out within days.
logistics.money: Markets, Imbiss stands and Fischmarkt traders are cash. Restaurants take cards. Tip by rounding up and saying the total as you pay.

other.label: HVV zones
other.text: Ring A covers everything here except the airport, which sits in Ring B. A single Hamburg AB ticket is approx €3.90; the 9-Uhr-Tageskarte (valid from 09:00) approx €8.60; the all-day version approx €9.30. Buy in the hvv app or at machines.

other.label: The ferries are transit, not tours
other.text: HADAG lines 61, 62, 64, 72, 73 and 75 are part of HVV and included in every ticket. Line 62 to Finkenwerder is the long one; line 72 links Landungsbrücken to the Elbphilharmonie in six minutes.

other.label: Deutschlandticket
other.text: Approx €63 a month in 2026, valid on all regional and local transport nationwide including the whole HVV. It is a rolling subscription you must cancel, and it only beats a week of day tickets if you also travel to another German city. Buy it before the 1st of the month or it starts late.

other.label: Hamburg CARD
other.text: Approx €12.90 for one adult-day, roughly €33 for three days, with HVV travel plus 20–50% off many museums. It pays only if you use two paid attractions a day.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 for fire and ambulance, 110 for police. On the water, the DGzRS sea rescue service monitors VHF 16.

proTips: Ferry 62 westbound in the early evening puts the setting sun behind Steinwerder and the cranes; the same trip in the morning gives you flat grey light and no photographs.
St. Michaelis sells a combined ticket for the tower and the crypt; take the stairs down and the lift up, not the reverse, and go at opening for the clear eastward view before haze builds.
At the Fischmarkt, the traders start throwing in extras at 09:00 as they clear stock — the last thirty minutes is when the boxes of fruit get absurd.
Book the Elbphilharmonie Plaza for a slot after 19:00 in June and July; the Plaza stays open late and the harbour lights come on while you are up there.
Buy the day ticket rather than singles on any day involving a ferry: two ferry legs and one U-Bahn ride already beat the €9.30.
Blankenese's Treppenviertel has no through roads. Come down by the Süllbergsterrasse steps and out at the ferry pontoon rather than climbing back to the S-Bahn.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: 60–75 km on foot, flat, plus roughly 3 hours on public ferries
raw.Who It Suits: Architecture readers, harbour watchers, families who like boats more than queues

typeSpecific.surface: 60–75 km on foot, flat, plus roughly 3 hours on public ferries
typeSpecific.audience: Architecture readers, harbour watchers, families who like boats more than queues

packingNotes: A properly windproof shell with a hood; the Elbe funnel makes 20 km/h feel like 40.
Grippy soles for the Treppenviertel steps and wet warehouse cobbles in the Speicherstadt.
A warm layer for the ferries even in July — the open aft deck is where you want to stand and it is cold.
€30 in coins and small notes for the Fischmarkt and the Isemarkt.
A rain cover for a camera; harbour spray is real on line 62.
Smart shoes and a jacket if you plan an Elbphilharmonie concert — there is no formal code but the Grand Hall dresses up.
A tote for the Isemarkt; the stalls sell by weight and hand you paper.
whatCouldGoWrong: **The Plaza is sold out on your chosen day.** Same-day tickets go on sale at 09:00 at the visitor centre on Platz der Deutschen Einheit, and the queue clears by mid-morning outside school holidays.

**A storm surge (Sturmflut).** Autumn and winter westerlies push the Elbe over the Fischmarkt and the lower Speicherstadt streets several times a season. Warnings are broadcast by the Sturmflutwarndienst; the ferries stop and the U4 keeps running.
**A ferry line is suspended for fog or works.** The 62 and 72 are the first to go. The S1/S3 to Altona and the U3 ring cover the same corridors on the same ticket.

**Miniatur Wunderland has nothing left.** Its cancellation returns appear online through the day, and the last hour before closing usually has stock. Otherwise the Internationales Maritimes Museum in Kaispeicher B absorbs the afternoon.
**Sunday shutdown.** Almost all shops close and the Fischmarkt ends at 09:30. Museums and the ferries run normally; plan Sunday around water and food, not shopping.

trips.summary: A seven-day city trip itinerary in Zealand / Øresund, Denmark.

itinerary.title: Indre By: the medieval core and the Golden Age block
itinerary.morning: Arrive by Metro M2 from the airport, 14 minutes to Kongens Nytorv. Start at Nyhavn early — by 10:00 it is a cruise-passenger crush — then walk the Strøget spine as far as Gammeltorv.
itinerary.afternoon: Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek: Rodin, Gauguin and Etruscan bronzes around a glass-domed winter garden, all funded by beer. Then the Round Tower (Rundetårn) for its 1642 spiral ramp — Christian IV built it so a horse could carry instruments to the observatory.
itinerary.evening: Aperitivo at Ved Stranden 10, a canal-side natural-wine bar in a merchant's house, then dinner in the Gammel Strand block. Walk back along the canal at dusk.

itinerary.title: Vesterbro and Frederiksberg: meatpacking to marble
itinerary.morning: Coffee and cardamom pastry at a Vesterbro bakery, then the Carlsberg City District — the old brewery quarter, with the Elephant Gate and the new residential architecture around it.
itinerary.afternoon: Cisternerne: a former underground reservoir beneath Søndermarken, now a dripping, stalactite-hung art space that stays at 8 °C in August. Walk the Frederiksberg Gardens and the Chinese pavilion.
itinerary.evening: Kødbyen, the Meatpacking District: white-tiled 1930s halls now full of restaurants and bars. Eat at one of the seafood or Basque-leaning places, then bar-hop within three blocks — this is the densest nightlife square in the city.

itinerary.title: Christianshavn, Refshaleøen and the harbour block
itinerary.morning: Bike over to Christianshavn — Christian IV's 17th-century Dutch-planned canal district. Climb the external spiral of Vor Frelsers Kirke's spire, 400 steps with the last hundred outdoors.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross to Refshaleøen, the old shipyard island: Copenhagen Contemporary in a welding hall, the Reffen street-food yard, and the harbour bath at La Banchina. Then CopenHill (Amager Bakke) — Bjarke Ingels' waste-to-energy plant with a dry ski slope, hiking path and the world's tallest climbing wall on its flanks.
itinerary.evening: Dinner on Refshaleøen. Note that the Copenhagen fine-dining landscape has shifted significantly since 2023 — confirm what is open and taking bookings before you build an evening around it. `verify: true`

itinerary.title: Nørrebro and Østerbro: the lived-in city
itinerary.morning: Jægersborggade, one street of eleven shopfronts that contains a ceramicist, a natural-wine shop, a chocolatier and two of the best bakeries in Scandinavia. Then Assistens Cemetery — Kierkegaard and H.C. Andersen are buried in what is functionally the neighbourhood park.
itinerary.afternoon: Superkilen, the BIG/Superflex/Topotek urban park built from objects donated by residents of 60 nationalities — a red square, a black market and a green park in a line. Cycle east to Østerbro and the lakes.
itinerary.evening: Fælledparken and dinner in Østerbro's quieter restaurants, or return to Nørrebro for the wood-fired pizza and natural wine axis around Guldbergsgade.

itinerary.title: Architecture day: Grundtvig, Bagsværd, Ørestad
itinerary.morning: Grundtvig's Church in Bispebjerg — expressionist brick Gothic, six million yellow bricks, an organ facade of a west front, and usually empty. Bus 6A gets you there.
itinerary.afternoon: Utzon's Bagsværd Church (S-train + walk): plain outside, and inside a white concrete cloud ceiling that is one of the finest interior spaces in Europe. Opening hours are limited to specific afternoons. `verify: true` Then Metro M1 to Ørestad for BIG's 8 House and the VM Houses.
itinerary.evening: Back to town via the Royal Library's Black Diamond and a harbour-front walk.

itinerary.title: Louisiana and the coast
itinerary.morning: Train from Copenhagen Central to Humlebæk (36 minutes), then a 10-minute walk to the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art — a low glass-and-brick sequence of pavilions running through a sculpture park to the Øresund, with Sweden visible across the water. Half a day minimum.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue north to Helsingør for Kronborg Castle, the Hamlet castle, and the M/S Maritime Museum built into a dry dock beside it.
itinerary.evening: Return to Copenhagen. Last dinner in Indre By or the Torvehallerne market halls for a low-key final meal.

itinerary.title: Islands Brygge, Amalienborg and departure
itinerary.morning: Swim at the Islands Brygge harbour bath if it is summer — the harbour water is clean enough to swim in the middle of the city, which is the single fact that best explains Copenhagen. Then the changing of the guard at Amalienborg at noon.
itinerary.afternoon: Designmuseum Danmark for the Danish chair collection if you have time, then Metro to the airport.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Sanders
accommodationStrategy.description: Behind the Royal Theatre, a small hotel with a residential feel and a rooftop bar. The point is the block: Nyhavn, Kongens Nytorv and the canals are all within 400 m, which lets you use Day 1 and Day 7 fully without transit.

accommodationStrategy.name: Coco Hotel / Vesterbro boutique properties
accommodationStrategy.description: Mid-price, five minutes from Central Station and ten from Kødbyen. Best base if the food scene is your priority; you can walk home from dinner in the Meatpacking District, which no other neighbourhood allows.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Ottilia / Carlsberg district
accommodationStrategy.description: Built into the old Carlsberg brewhouse, with a rooftop terrace over the district. Quieter than the centre, on the S-train and metro network, and the right choice for a longer stay where you want space rather than a postcard address.

logistics.emergency: 112. Pharmacies: at least one 24-hour pharmacy operates near Central Station. EHIC/GHIC cards are accepted for EU/UK visitors.
logistics.weather: Grey and windy is the default from October to April; the wind chill off the harbour is worse than the temperature suggests. Summer evenings cool quickly — a layer, always.
logistics.bookingWindows: Top-tier tasting menus release seats on a fixed schedule 2–4 months out and sell in minutes. Louisiana and museums do not need advance booking except on rainy summer weekends. Tivoli: buy the entry online, skip the queue. Bagsværd Church: check the published visiting afternoons. `verify: true`
logistics.money: DKK, not euro. Denmark is functionally cashless; some places no longer accept cash at all.

other.label: Transit
other.text: The Metro's M1–M4 run 24 hours and are fully driverless. The City Pass covers metro, bus, S-train and the harbour buses (routes 991/992), which are effectively a public boat service along the harbour for the price of a bus ticket — the best-value sightseeing in the city. Rejsekort is being phased toward app-based ticketing; buy in the DOT Tickets app. `verify: true`

other.label: Cycling rules that are actually enforced
other.text: Hand signals are expected (arm out to turn, hand up to stop). Never stop in a cycle lane. Lights front and rear are mandatory after dark and police issue on-the-spot fines. Ride right, overtake left, and do not cross a bike lane on foot without looking — the traffic is fast and constant.

other.label: Christiania
other.text: The Freetown is in a period of significant change following the 2024 dismantling of its open cannabis trade. Photography restrictions have historically applied in parts of it; respect posted signs and residents' privacy. `verify: true`

proTips: **Rent a bike for the whole week, not the day.** Copenhagen's geography is designed around 20 km/h, and every block in this itinerary is 8–12 minutes from the next one by bike. Donkey Republic and hotel rentals both work; take a bike with a proper lock and use the wheel lock plus a chain.
Nyhavn before 09:00 and after 21:00 is a different place from Nyhavn at 13:00.
Torvehallerne market opens at 10:00 — go at 10:15 for a smørrebrød lunch built from three stalls, at half the price of a sit-down version.
The **harbour bus (line 991/992)** at sunset costs the price of a metro ticket and covers the same water as the €20 canal tours.

Museum trick: many Copenhagen museums have a free or reduced evening once a week, and SMK (the National Gallery) has free permanent-collection access. Check the day before you plan a paid ticket. `verify: true`
Book **one** ambitious dinner and let the rest of the week be bakeries, smørrebrød and wine bars. The city's best value is at the €20 end, not the €400 end.

trips.summary: A seven-day city trip itinerary in Harju County, Gulf of Finland, Estonia.

itinerary.title: Lower Old Town: the Hanseatic block
itinerary.morning: Tram 4 from the airport, 15 minutes. Start at Town Hall Square (Raekoja plats) with the only surviving Gothic town hall in Northern Europe, and the pharmacy on its corner — trading since 1422 and claiming to be Europe's oldest continuously operating one.
itinerary.afternoon: The merchant streets: Pikk with its guild halls, the Great Guild, the House of the Blackheads, and the Three Sisters merchant houses. Climb St Olaf's Church tower — briefly the tallest building in the world in the 16th century — for the best rooftop view in the Baltics.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in the Old Town but off Viru — Rataskaevu 16 and its neighbours are where Estonians actually eat inside the walls. Book ahead; it is small.

itinerary.title: Toompea and the bastion tunnels
itinerary.morning: Up the Lühike jalg passage to Toompea, the upper town of nobility and power: Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, the Riigikogu parliament in its pink Baroque castle, and the Kohtuotsa and Patkuli viewing platforms.
itinerary.afternoon: Kiek in de Kök and the **Bastion Passages** — 17th-century Swedish tunnels under the earthworks, later used as Soviet bomb shelters and, in the 1980s, by the city's punks. Guided entry only, and genuinely cold; take a jacket.
itinerary.evening: Walk the surviving town wall towers, then down to the Rotermann Quarter for dinner in the converted mill and factory buildings between the Old Town and the port.

itinerary.title: Kalamaja and Telliskivi
itinerary.morning: Kalamaja, the wooden district: pastel 1920s–30s "Lender houses" with limestone bases, once fishermen's and factory workers' homes and now the most desirable address in the city. Balti Jaam Market for breakfast — three floors of produce, street food and secondhand.
itinerary.afternoon: Telliskivi Creative City, a former railway repair complex: Fotografiska Tallinn, independent design shops, and a rotating wall of street art. Then walk the Kultuurikilomeeter seafront path.
itinerary.evening: Noblessner, the old submarine shipyard turned waterfront quarter — a brewery taproom, a seafront promenade, and the city's most ambitious restaurants. This is where to spend your one big dinner.

itinerary.title: Kadriorg and KUMU
itinerary.morning: Tram 1 or 3 to Kadriorg: Peter the Great's Baroque palace and gardens, built after the Great Northern War, with the Kadriorg Art Museum inside.
itinerary.afternoon: KUMU, the Estonian national art museum — a copper-and-limestone building cut into the escarpment. Its 20th-century floors, covering the occupation years and Soviet-era nonconformist art, are the most affecting museum experience in the Baltics.
itinerary.evening: Walk to Pirita along the sea, past the Song Festival Grounds where 300,000 people sang during the 1988 Singing Revolution. Eat at the Pirita marina.

itinerary.title: Seaplane Harbour and the Soviet edge
itinerary.morning: Lennusadam (Seaplane Harbour), a 1917 seaplane hangar of pioneering thin-shell concrete, now a maritime museum with the submarine *Lembit* sitting inside it. Excellent for all ages.
itinerary.afternoon: Patarei — a Tsarist sea fortress that became a Soviet prison, now partly open as a memorial to the victims of communism and Nazism. Sobering and essential; check the current opening status. `verify: true` Then Linnahall, the crumbling 1980 Olympic concrete monument on the shore, best seen from outside.
itinerary.evening: Kalamaja neighbourhood dinner, then a sauna — Estonian sauna culture is as serious here as in Finland and several public saunas operate in the city.

itinerary.title: Helsinki day trip or Lahemaa
itinerary.morning: Option A: the fast ferry to Helsinki, roughly 2 hours each way, giving five hours in the Finnish capital — enough for the Design District and a market lunch. Option B: drive or take a tour to Lahemaa National Park for manor houses, bog boardwalks and the Baltic coast.
itinerary.afternoon: Whichever you chose, be back for the evening; the last ferries fill in summer.
itinerary.evening: Old Town cellar bars, or a folk-music evening if one is on.

itinerary.title: Markets and departure
itinerary.morning: Balti Jaam Market or the Sunday flea section for last purchases; coffee in Kalamaja.
itinerary.afternoon: Tram 4 to the airport, or the ferry terminal for the Helsinki connection. Tallinn Airport is 4 km from the centre — the shortest airport transfer in this dataset.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Telegraaf
accommodationStrategy.description: The former telegraph exchange on Vene street, with a spa and a courtyard. Inside the walls but on a quiet lane, so you get the Old Town at 07:00 without the Viru street noise at 23:00.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Palace / Rotermann-area design hotels
accommodationStrategy.description: Between the Old Town and the port, on the modern side of the divide. Best if you are arriving or leaving by ferry, and the walk to Telliskivi is 15 minutes.

accommodationStrategy.name: Kalamaja apartments and small guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: The neighbourhood choice: wooden buildings, bakeries, and the district's own rhythm. Cheaper by a third than the Old Town, and it puts Days 3 and 5 on your doorstep. Look for buildings with renovated heating — the old wooden stock varies wildly in winter.

logistics.connectivity: Some of the fastest and cheapest mobile data in Europe; free public Wi-Fi is close to universal.
logistics.emergency: 112. The Estonian emergency system is well resourced and English-speaking. The North Estonia Medical Centre is the main hospital.
logistics.weather: Continental with a maritime edge: −10 °C and dry in February, 25 °C and humid in July. White nights in June mean it never gets properly dark; blackout curtains are worth checking for.
logistics.bookingWindows: Noblessner's top restaurants: 3–6 weeks. Bastion Passages tours: a few days, longer in summer. Helsinki ferries: book the specific sailing 1–2 weeks out in summer, walk-on the rest of the year. Hotels: 4–6 weeks except during the Song Festival years and December weekends.

other.label: Digital by default
other.text: Estonia is the most digitised state in Europe: transport tickets, parking, restaurant bookings and museum entry are all app-based and all work in English. Contactless bank-card tapping works on trams and buses.

other.label: Old Town surfaces
other.text: The limestone cobbles are savage in the wet and lethal in ice. Flat rubber soles, and in winter, spikes for shoes — sold in every Estonian pharmacy for a few euros, and locals genuinely use them.

other.label: Cruise-ship rhythm
other.text: From May to September, several thousand cruise passengers walk the same Old Town loop between 09:30 and 15:00. Their route is fixed: Viru Gate → Town Hall Square → Toompea. Invert it.

proTips: Do Toompea at **08:00**. The Kohtuotsa platform is empty, the light is on the Old Town roofs, and by 10:30 there are three tour groups on it.

The Old Town has two economies. Restaurants with medieval costumes and a menu in six languages are for cruise passengers; the ones on Vene, Rataskaevu and Sauna streets are for Estonians. The price difference is 40% and the quality difference is larger.
**KUMU on a Thursday evening** — the museum stays open late one evening a week and the top floors are silent. `verify: true`
Take the **Helsinki ferry as a foot passenger** and use the return leg as your restaurant: the ships' buffets are absurdly good value and the crossing gives you two hours of Gulf of Finland.
Estonian sauna is not a spa product, it is a social institution. Book a public sauna slot rather than the hotel's.
Winter visit? The Old Town in a snowstorm with Christmas-market glögi is the single most atmospheric week in this entire dataset, and hotel prices in January are less than half of July's.

trips.title: Seville Slow: Mudéjar Courtyards and Triana Nights

bestPeriod.window: Mid-March–early May & mid-October–end November
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (42°C is routine and the city genuinely shuts 14:00–20:00); Semana Santa and Feria de Abril triple hotel rates and close monuments.
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-March–early May & mid-October–end November

accommodation.note: Casa-palacio guesthouse double, per-person share, Santa Cruz or Alfalfa

food.note: Tapas €3.50–5 each, menú del día €14–18, one €45 dinner

transport.note: Tussam card, AVE/Media Distancia day trip, airport bus both ways

activities.note: Alcázar, Cathedral, Casa de Pilatos, Setas, flamenco, Córdoba Mezquita

profile.difficultyNote: 2 — flat city, 7–10 km a day, but heat is the limiting factor, not gradient.

trips.gatewayAirport: SVQ — Seville Airport; EA airport bus to Plaza de Armas 35 min (€4 single), taxi flat fare ~€25–33
trips.summary: Seville is a city of interiors: the whole point is what happens behind the door, in the courtyard, under the vine. This week is built around that — the Real Alcázar's Mudéjar rooms at opening hour, Casa de Pilatos's Renaissance-Roman patio in the empty midday, the Hospital de los Venerables's sunken courtyard fountain, and Triana's tiled bar fronts across the river at night. Days follow the Andalusian clock: monuments before 12:00, a long lunch, siesta, then the city reopens at 20:00 and stays up. Distances are small and flat; the discipline is timing, not stamina. A Córdoba or Cádiz day by fast train supplies the contrast.

itinerary.title: Arrival, Alfalfa and the first tapas crawl
itinerary.morning: EA bus in from SVQ, drop bags, orient on **Plaza de la Alfalfa**. Coffee and *tostada con manteca colorá* at **Bar El Comercio**, Calle Lineros 9, a 1904 tiled churro bar.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the **Setas de Sevilla** (Metropol Parasol) walkway (€16 including the Antiquarium's Roman house mosaics beneath) and Plaza de la Encarnación. Then the **Iglesia del Salvador** (€5, or included on the Cathedral combined ticket), a Baroque hall on a mosque footprint.
itinerary.evening: Crawl three bars: **Bodeguita Romero** (Calle Harinas 10, *pringá* roll), **Bar Las Teresas** (Calle Santa Teresa 2, jamón), **Casa Morales** (Calle García de Vinuesa 11, vermouth from the vats).
itinerary.dayStats: 5.8 km walked, flat; EA bus €4; Setas 09:30–00:30; tapas €3.50–5 each, three bars ~€30pp.
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Casa 1800, Calle Rodrigo Caro 6, Santa Cruz.

itinerary.title: Real Alcázar at opening, then Santa Cruz
itinerary.morning: **Real Alcázar** on the 09:30 opening slot (€15.50, +€5.50 for the Cuarto Real Alto; 09:30–19:00 April–September, to 17:00 in winter). Head straight to the Patio de las Doncellas before the groups, then the Salón de Embajadores dome and out into the Jardines with the Galería de Grutesco.
itinerary.afternoon: **Hospital de los Venerables** (Plaza de los Venerables 8, €12) for the sunken patio and Velázquez's *Santa Rufina*, then wander Callejón del Agua and Plaza de Doña Elvira in the emptier siesta hours.
itinerary.evening: Flamenco at **Casa de la Memoria**, Calle Cuna 6 — 90 minutes, no amplification, ~€22, book ahead. Late dinner at **Casa Ricardo**, Calle Hernán Cortés 2.
itinerary.dayStats: 6.4 km; Alcázar €15.50 + €5.50; Venerables €12; flamenco 19:30 & 21:00 sittings.

itinerary.title: Cathedral, Giralda and the riverside
itinerary.morning: **Catedral de Sevilla + Giralda** on a 10:00 slot (€14, €13 online) — the Almohad minaret's ramps were built for a horseman, not stairs; the Capilla Mayor retablo is the largest altarpiece in Christendom. Then the free **Archivo General de Indias** across the square.
itinerary.afternoon: **Torre del Oro** (€3) and the Guadalquivir bank, then **Plaza de España** and the Parque de María Luisa in late light — go at 18:30 when the ceramic province benches face west.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **Cañabota**, Calle Orfila 3 — Atlantic fish over coals, counter seating, book 2–3 weeks, €55–75pp. Alternative: **Casa Robles** for the classic version.
itinerary.dayStats: 8.1 km; Cathedral 10:45–18:00 Mon–Sat, Sun from 14:30; Archivo free, closed Mondays.

itinerary.title: Córdoba day trip by AVE
itinerary.morning: Santa Justa 08:00–08:30 AVE/Avant to Córdoba, 45–50 min. Walk 20 min to the **Mezquita-Catedral** for the 08:30–09:30 free early entry (Mon–Sat, no ticket, no groups) or the 10:00 paid slot (€13). The 856 double-arched columns of Abd al-Rahman's hall are the reason to make the trip.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Judería** lanes, **Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos** (€5), and Calleja de las Flores. Lunch of *salmorejo* and *flamenquín* at **Bodegas Campos**, Calle de Lineros 32.
itinerary.evening: Back on the 19:00–20:00 train. Late tapas at **Eslava**, Calle Eslava 3 in San Lorenzo (the *costilla* and the cigar-shaped *huevo sobre bizcocho*), no reservations for the bar.
itinerary.dayStats: 6.9 km walked in Córdoba; AVE 45–50 min, €25–38 return; Mezquita free 08:30–09:30 Mon–Sat.

itinerary.title: Casa de Pilatos, Macarena and the convents
itinerary.morning: **Casa de Pilatos** (Plaza de Pilatos 1, €12 full house, €10 ground floor only; free for EU citizens Mondays 15:00–18:00). The main patio's Roman busts, Genoese marble and Mudéjar *azulejo* dado in one square is the city's argument in miniature.
itinerary.afternoon: North up Calle San Luis through **Macarena**: the Baroque **Iglesia de San Luis de los Franceses** (€6), the **Basílica de la Macarena** and her Virgin (€5 museum), and the surviving Almohad **Muralla** stretch. Buy convent sweets through the *torno* at **Convento de Santa Paula**.
itinerary.evening: **Alameda de Hércules** — vermouth at **Bar Bulebar**, then dinner at **Sobretablas**, Calle Colombia 7 (book 1–2 weeks, €45–60pp) or the closer **Casa Ruperto** for quail.
itinerary.dayStats: 7.6 km; Pilatos €12, 09:00–18:00; San Luis closed Mondays; convent sweets €6–9 a box, cash.

itinerary.title: Triana across the river
itinerary.morning: Cross the **Puente de Isabel II** (1852, Gustavo Steinacher and Ferdinand Bernadet, modelled on the Pont du Carrousel) to the **Centro Cerámica Triana** (€2.10) built over the old Santa Ana kiln floors — the tile industry that surfaced half the city's façades.
itinerary.afternoon: **Mercado de Triana** for lunch at the counters, then Calle Betis for the classic river-facing view of the Torre del Oro, and the **Capilla de los Marineros**. Browse the surviving tile workshops on Calle Antillano Campos.
itinerary.evening: Triana flamenco with less theatre: **Casa Anselma**, Calle Pagés del Corro 49, opens around midnight, no sign, no entry fee, drinks-only, and no photographs. Eat first at **Blanca Paloma**, Calle San Jacinto 49.
itinerary.dayStats: 7.2 km; Centro Cerámica €2.10, 11:00–18:00; Anselma from ~00:00, closed Sundays.

itinerary.title: Fine art and departure
itinerary.morning: **Museo de Bellas Artes** in the Convento de la Merced (free for EU citizens, €1.50 otherwise) — the Zurbarán and Murillo rooms in the former church nave are the best-hung pictures in Andalucía.
itinerary.afternoon: Last vermouth and a *serranito* at **Bodega Santa Cruz "Las Columnas"**, Calle Rodrigo Caro 1, then bags and the EA bus to SVQ from Prado de San Sebastián.
itinerary.evening: Flight out.
itinerary.dayStats: 3.9 km; Bellas Artes 09:00–21:00 Tue–Sat, closed Mondays; EA bus 35 min, €4; allow 2 h at SVQ.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Casa 1800
accommodationStrategy.description: Thirty-odd rooms in a 19th-century house one lane from the Alcázar wall, with a roof terrace looking straight at the Giralda and free afternoon tea. You can be first through the Alcázar gate five minutes after breakfast. €180–260 double; ask for an interior patio room to escape the Mateos Gago noise.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Palacio de Villapanés
accommodationStrategy.description: An 18th-century palace with a proper Baroque staircase, a courtyard pool and enough distance from Santa Cruz to feel residential while staying a 10-minute walk from the Cathedral. €200–290.

accommodationStrategy.name: Corral del Rey
accommodationStrategy.description: Thirteen rooms in a 17th-century *casa señorial* with Roman columns in the courtyard, dropped into the best tapas grid in the city. €190–280; the roof plunge pool is the July argument.

logistics.connectivity: Full EU roaming; 5G throughout the centre and on the AVE corridor. Renfe requires the app or a printed ticket for barrier entry at Santa Justa.
logistics.emergency: 112. Municipal police 092. Pharmacies rotate a *farmacia de guardia* — the roster is posted on every pharmacy door. EU/EHIC applies; Spain's public system is straightforward for EU visitors.
logistics.weather: The *terral*, a dry inland wind, pushes July–August highs past 42°C; Seville regularly records Spain's national maximum. Even in May, 15:00–18:00 is for interiors. November brings short, heavy Atlantic rain.
logistics.bookingWindows: Real Alcázar 1–2 weeks (official infoticketing site only — resellers add 40%); Cathedral 3–5 days; Casa de la Memoria 4–7 days; Cañabota and Sobretablas 1–3 weeks; AVE to Córdoba 2–3 weeks for the cheap fare buckets.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards work almost everywhere, but old-guard bars (Casa Morales, Casa Anselma, convent *tornos*) are cash. Tipping is minimal — round up, or leave €1–2 per person after tapas.
logistics.transportRules: Validate the Tussam card on boarding; the EA bus takes cards. Renfe security-scans bags at Santa Justa — arrive 20 minutes before an AVE departure.
logistics.permits: Andalucía charges no municipal tourist tax as of 2026. The Alcázar and Cathedral both refuse large backpacks — no cloakroom at the Alcázar. Flamenco venues like Casa Anselma prohibit photography outright and will ask you to leave.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable. Heat is the hazard: carry 2 litres, walk the *sombra* side, treat 14:00–17:00 in summer as unwalkable. Petty theft concentrates on Calle Sierpes and the Cathedral perimeter.

proTips: The Alcázar's free slot is **Mondays 18:00–18:30, October–March**, released online only and gone within hours — set a reminder for the release, and note it is far too short for the gardens.
Córdoba's **Mezquita is free 08:30–09:30, Monday to Saturday**, with no ticket required and no tour groups. Take the 08:00 AVE and you are inside the arcades in near-silence.
Casa de Pilatos is **free to EU citizens on non-holiday Mondays, 15:00–18:00** — exactly the hours when everything else is shut for siesta.
Order tapas *de pie* at the bar, not at a table: the same plate costs 20–30% more seated on a terrace, and every price list posts both tariffs.
Book the **Giralda climb for the last hour before closing** — the ramp empties, and the bells at the hour from inside the belfry are worth the timing.
**Casa Anselma** has no sign and no fee; look for the plain door at Pagés del Corro 49 after midnight and buy a drink. It is the antidote to ticketed *tablao* flamenco.
Buy convent sweets through the revolving *torno* at Santa Paula — you never see the nun, you leave exact change, and the *dulce de membrillo* travels.
In heat, use the **Setas walkway at 09:30 or after 21:00**; the deck is unshaded and the midday version is punishing for the same €16.

raw.Walkable blocks: Santa Cruz (Calle Mateos Gago → Plaza de Doña Elvira → Callejón del Agua, 1.1 km of shaded lanes); Alfalfa/Encarnación (Plaza de la Alfalfa → Calle Pérez Galdós → Setas, 900 m); Alameda de Hércules (the 800 m boulevard itself, plus Calle Feria); Macarena (Basílica → Calle San Luis → Convento de Santa Paula, 1.3 km); Triana (Puente de Isabel II → Calle Betis → Calle San Jacinto → Mercado de Triana, 1.6 km).
raw.Transit pass: Tussam's **Tarjeta Multiviaje** — €1.50 refundable deposit, top-ups from €7, fares around €0.76 per ride versus €1.40 cash on board; the single Metro Line 1 and the T1 tram to San Bernardo take the same card. Most of this week needs zero transit.
raw.Airport transfer: **EA (Especial Aeropuerto)** bus, airport → Prado de San Sebastián → Plaza de Armas, every 20–30 min, ~35 min, €4 single / €6 return. Taxis run a fixed municipal tariff, roughly €25 weekday daytime, €33 nights and holidays.
raw.Booking timeline: **Real Alcázar** — timed entry, book 1–2 weeks ahead on alcazardesevilla.infoticketing.com (the only official channel); the free Monday evening slot (18:00–18:30, October–March) releases online and vanishes within hours. **Cathedral + Giralda** — 3–5 days ahead, €14 at the door or €13 online. **Flamenco at Casa de la Memoria** — 4–7 days, only 100 seats. **Córdoba AVE** — book 2–3 weeks for the €25–35 fare band.
raw.Architectural focal points: Almohad brickwork in the Giralda's sebka panelling (1184–98, Ahmad ibn Baso); Pedro I's 1360s Mudéjar palace inside the Alcázar, built by Toledan and Granadan craftsmen for a Christian king; Casa de Pilatos's 1520s fusion of Gothic, Mudéjar and Italian Renaissance; Leonardo de Figueroa's Baroque at the Hospital de los Venerables (1687); Aníbal González's 1929 regionalist Plaza de España; Jürgen Mayer's 2011 timber Metropol Parasol.
raw.Eating structure: stand-up tapas bars in Alfalfa and Santa Cruz, sit-down *guisos* in Triana, market lunch at Feria or Triana. Only the destination kitchens (Cañabota, Sobretablas) require booking; classic bars are elbows-only.
raw.Day trip: **Córdoba** by Renfe AVE/Avant, Santa Justa → Córdoba in 45–50 min, €25–38 return depending how early you book; Media Distancia takes 1h20 for less.

typeSpecific.transitPass: Santa Cruz (Calle Mateos Gago → Plaza de Doña Elvira → Callejón del Agua, 1.1 km of shaded lanes); Alfalfa/Encarnación (Plaza de la Alfalfa → Calle Pérez Galdós → Setas, 900 m); Alameda de Hércules (the 800 m boulevard itself, plus Calle Feria); Macarena (Basílica → Calle San Luis → Convento de Santa Paula, 1.3 km); Triana (Puente de Isabel II → Calle Betis → Calle San Jacinto → Mercado de Triana, 1.6 km).

sources.verified: Real Alcázar admission (€15.50), Cuarto Real Alto supplement (€5.50) and seasonal hours (09:30–19:00 Apr–Sep, to 17:00 Oct–Mar) confirmed on alcazarsevilla.org, which names alcazardesevilla.infoticketing.com as the sole official channel. Cathedral/Giralda (€14, €13 online), Casa de Pilatos (€12) and Setas (€16) checked against a June 2026 Seville monument price list. No municipal tourist tax in Andalucía.
sources.confidenceNotes: Tussam Multiviaje fare and deposit, the €4 EA bus fare and the fixed taxi tariff all drift annually. AVE Seville–Córdoba pricing is dynamic; €25–38 assumes 2–3 weeks' notice. The Mezquita free hour and the Alcázar/Casa de Pilatos free slots are the most volatile items and are periodically suspended. Restaurant lead times and Casa Anselma's opening nights need re-confirmation.
