trips.title: Rome in Seven Layers: Centro Storico to EUR

bestPeriod.window: Late March–mid-May & late September–mid-November
bestPeriod.avoid: August — 36 °C on unshaded travertine, half the good trattorie closed for *ferie*; and the Christmas–Epiphany fortnight, when the centre is impassable and museum slots vanish.
bestPeriod.raw: Late March–mid-May & late September–mid-November

accommodation.note: Monti or Trastevere double, per-person share, €160–€280 per room per night

food.note: Trattoria dinner €30–€45, pizza al taglio lunch €6–€10, coffee standing €1.20

transport.note: Leonardo Express return, ATAC weekly CIS, Ostia Antica return

activities.note: Vatican, Colosseum, Borghese, Palazzo Massimo, Case Romane, Ostia Antica

profile.difficultyNote: 2/5 — 7–11 km of walking a day on cobbles and stairs, with the Gianicolo and Celio climbs the only real vertical

trips.gatewayAirport: FCO Leonardo da Vinci–Fiumicino — Leonardo Express to Termini 32 min; CIA Ciampino for low-cost carriers, 40 min by bus
trips.summary: Rome is not a city you see, it is a city you cross-section. This week takes seven cuts through it: the Baroque theatre of the Centro Storico, the imperial spine of Colosseum–Forum–Palatine, the Vatican, the Republican and Imperial sculpture at Palazzo Massimo, the working-class kitchen of Testaccio, the industrial archaeology of Ostiense, and Mussolini's white marble suburb at EUR — closing with a day at Ostia Antica, the port city that is Pompeii without the crowds. The single hardest skill is ticketing: four of the week's set pieces require timed slots bought on specific official platforms at specific moments, and the difference between doing that and not is roughly three hours of queuing per day. Walking is the transport of choice; the metro is only three lines and mostly goes where you are not.

itinerary.title: Arrival, Centro Storico, and the Pantheon at dusk
itinerary.morning: Leonardo Express in to Termini, drop bags in Monti, and take the first coffee standing at a bar counter — sitting doubles the price by law and everyone knows it.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Centro Storico spine: **Piazza Navona**, **Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza**'s courtyard, the **Pantheon**, then **San Luigi dei Francesi** for the three Caravaggios of the **Contarelli Chapel** — bring €1 coins for the light box, and go at a quiet hour.
itinerary.evening: **Ai Tre Scalini** on Via Panisperna in Monti, standing at the bar with a glass of Cesanese and a plate of *polpette*.
itinerary.dayStats: 7.2 km walking / 60 m ascent; Leonardo Express €14, 32 min; CIS weekly card €29; Pantheon timed entry required

itinerary.title: The imperial spine: Colosseum, Forum, Palatine, Celio
itinerary.morning: Pre-booked **Colosseum** slot as early as the ticket allows. The 24-hour ticket covers the Forum and Palatine as one continuous visit — enter the Colosseum first, then walk out to the Forum through the Arch of Titus side.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Palatine** for the Farnese gardens and the Domus Augustana, then down to the **Roman Forum**. Late afternoon, cross to the **Celio** for the **Case Romane del Celio** beneath Santi Giovanni e Paolo — a frescoed Roman apartment block under a church, closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays — and finish at **San Clemente**, three buildings stacked: a 12th-century basilica over a 4th-century church over a Mithraeum.
itinerary.evening: **La Carbonara** on Via Panisperna. Order the carbonara; it is the correct place to be obvious.
itinerary.dayStats: 9.4 km / 120 m ascent; Colosseum €18 + €2 booking, 24 h validity; Case Romane ≈€8; San Clemente lower levels ticketed

itinerary.title: Vatican Museums early, Prati afternoon
itinerary.morning: Earliest possible **Vatican Museums** entry — €20 plus the €5 booking fee. Go directly through the Pinacoteca or the Egyptian rooms to reach the **Sistine Chapel** before the group tours converge; then double back for the Raphael Rooms and the Gallery of Maps at leisure.
itinerary.afternoon: **St Peter's Basilica** (free, security queue) and the dome climb, 551 steps, or the lift plus 320. Then west into **Prati** and lunch standing at **Bonci Pizzarium** by Cipro.
itinerary.evening: **Il Sorpasso**, Via Properzio — Roman-Iberian, cured meats and *maritozzi*. Walk back across Ponte Sant'Angelo.
itinerary.dayStats: 8.6 km / 90 m ascent; Vatican €25 all-in; dome 551 steps; Prati grid 2.6 km

itinerary.title: Galleria Borghese and Palazzo Massimo
itinerary.morning: Your **Galleria Borghese** two-hour shift — booked, non-negotiable, and genuinely enough. Look at Bernini's *Apollo and Daphne* and *Ratto di Proserpina* (the fingers in the marble thigh), then the six Caravaggios.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the **Villa Borghese** gardens down to the **Pincio** terrace and Piazza del Popolo, calling at **Santa Maria del Popolo** for the Cerasi Chapel Caravaggios. Then to **Palazzo Massimo alle Terme** by Termini for the Villa of Livia garden frescoes and the Boxer at Rest — the least-crowded great museum in Rome.
itinerary.evening: **Roscioli**, Via dei Giubbonari 21 — booked. Burrata, anchovies, and a serious wine list.
itinerary.dayStats: 8.8 km / 70 m ascent; Borghese €13 + €2, two-hour slot, closed Mondays; Palazzo Massimo on the Museo Nazionale Romano combined ticket

itinerary.title: Testaccio, Ostiense and Roman industry
itinerary.morning: **Mercato Testaccio** before 11:00 — the stalls, then a *trapizzino* or a *panino con allesso*. Walk to the **Piramide Cestia** (12 BC) and the **Cimitero Acattolico** for Keats and Shelley.
itinerary.afternoon: Down Via Ostiense to the **Centrale Montemartini** — classical marbles installed among the turbines and diesel engines of Rome's first public power station, and the best-staged museum in the city. Continue to the **Gazometro** and the Ostiense street art.
itinerary.evening: **Flavio al Velavevodetto**, Via di Monte Testaccio 97, in rooms cut into Monte dei Cocci — a 35 m hill made entirely of smashed Roman amphorae. Book.
itinerary.dayStats: 9.1 km / 50 m ascent; Mercato Testaccio Mon–Sat mornings; Montemartini open Tue–Sun; Metro B Piramide

itinerary.title: Ostia Antica day trip
itinerary.morning: Metro B to **Piramide**, cross to **Porta San Paolo**, and take the **Metromare** line to **Ostia Antica** — 25–35 minutes on a €1.50 BIT. Be at the gate for opening; the site is 150 hectares and there is almost no shade.
itinerary.afternoon: Work the Decumanus Maximus: the **Baths of Neptune** mosaics, the **theatre**, the **Piazzale delle Corporazioni** with its guild mosaics of ships and grain, the **Thermopolium** bar counter on Via di Diana, and the **Casa di Diana** insula. Four hours minimum. Bring water — refill points are limited.
itinerary.evening: Back into the city; dinner at **Da Enzo al 29** in Trastevere if you can face the queue, otherwise **Nannarella** on Piazza San Calisto.
itinerary.dayStats: 10.5 km walked at the site / return transit ≈70 min total / BIT €1.50 covers the whole journey / Ostia Antica entry ticket, sold by CoopCulture

itinerary.title: EUR, Trastevere and the Gianicolo
itinerary.morning: Metro B to **EUR Magliana/EUR Palasport** for the **Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana**, the **Palazzo dei Congressi** and the laghetto. An hour of white travertine, straight lines and total silence — the deliberate opposite of everything else this week.
itinerary.afternoon: Back to **Trastevere**: **Santa Maria in Trastevere** for the 12th-century apse mosaics and Cavallini's cycle, **Santa Cecilia** for the Cavallini Last Judgement, then up to **Bramante's Tempietto** at San Pietro in Montorio and the **Gianicolo** terrace.
itinerary.evening: **Antico Arco** on the Gianicolo for a proper last dinner, or a €3 negroni at **Bar San Calisto** and pizza at **Ai Marmi**.
itinerary.dayStats: 9.8 km / 130 m ascent (Gianicolo climb 2 km at 70 m); EUR by Metro B, 20 min from Termini
itinerary.sleep: Small hotel in Monti, or airport-side for an early flight

accommodationStrategy.name: Small hotel in Monti
accommodationStrategy.description: The best all-round base: ten minutes' walk to the Colosseum, twelve to Termini for the Leonardo Express, and a neighbourhood with its own bars and market rather than a museum queue. Streets are steep and cobbled, so a wheeled case is a genuine consideration. €160–€260 per room per night in shoulder season.

accommodationStrategy.name: A Trastevere guesthouse
accommodationStrategy.description: Right for a second visit or a trip weighted to the Vatican and the Gianicolo, and served directly by the FL1 regional train from Fiumicino at €8. The trade-off is noise: the Piazza Trilussa–San Calisto axis is loud until 02:00 at weekends, so ask for a courtyard room. €150–€240 per room.

accommodationStrategy.name: A Prati apartment
accommodationStrategy.description: Quiet, residential, on a grid, with the Mercato Trionfale and Via Cola di Rienzo for self-catering, and Cipro/Ottaviano metro for everything else. It is the sensible choice for a family or anyone who wants a kitchen and a lift. €140–€220 per apartment.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming applies with no surcharge. 4G/5G is excellent everywhere including underground on Metro A and B. Free municipal WiFi (*DigitRoma WiFi*) exists in many piazzas and is slow. Download an offline map anyway: the Centro Storico's alleys defeat GPS.
logistics.emergency: 112 for everything (Italy's single European emergency number). Pharmacies rotate a *farmacia di turno* overnight, posted on every pharmacy door. Italy is in the EU, so **EHIC/GHIC covers state care**; the main central hospitals are Ospedale Fatebenefratelli on Tiber Island and Policlinico Umberto I near Termini.
logistics.weather: Rome's real hazard is heat, not storms — July and August routinely hit 35–38 °C with the *ponentino* evening breeze the only relief, and Ostia Antica and the Forum are entirely unshaded. Autumn brings short, violent *acquazzoni* that flood cobbled streets in twenty minutes and stop taxi availability dead. Winter is mild and wet; January averages 12 °C.
logistics.bookingWindows: Vatican Museums 4–8 weeks. Colosseum on the 30-day rolling release at 09:00 CET — this is the single most time-critical booking of the week. Galleria Borghese 3–5 weeks. Armando al Pantheon and Da Felice several weeks. Roscioli, La Carbonara, Flavio 3–7 days. Case Romane and Palazzo Massimo, days or same-day.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards are accepted almost universally and merchants are legally required to accept them, but small trattorie and market stalls still prefer cash — carry €50–€100. **Tipping is not expected**; a *coperto* of €1.50–€3 per person appears on the bill instead, and *servizio* is occasionally added — check before adding anything.
logistics.transportRules: Validate paper tickets before boarding; contactless card taps at metro gates charge the BIT rate automatically. The historic centre is a **ZTL (Zona a Traffico Limitato)** with camera enforcement and automatic fines — **do not hire a car for this itinerary**. Taxis must use the metered fare within the city and the fixed €55/€40 airport fares to and from the walls; ranks are safer than hailing. Metro A closes early (around 21:00) on some nights for works, replaced by the MA bus.
logistics.permits: Rome's **city tourist tax** is charged per person per night by hotel category, roughly €4–€10, usually payable in cash at check-out. Sitting on the Spanish Steps, eating on church steps, and wading in fountains are all finable under municipal decorum rules and are actively policed. Drones are banned over the historic centre. Large backpacks are refused at the Vatican Museums and the Colosseum; cloakrooms are free but slow.
logistics.health: Tap water is excellent and free — the **nasoni**, the cast-iron street fountains, run continuously and are potable; block the spout hole with a finger and it arcs upward to drink from. Rome is a low-violence, high-pickpocket city: Termini, the 64 bus to the Vatican, Metro A and the Colosseum forecourt are the specific hotspots. Wear real shoes; the *sampietrini* cobbles are ankle-hostile and lethal in rain.

proTips: **Set an alarm for the Colosseum's 30-day release at 09:00 CET.** CoopCulture is the only official seller; everything else is a reseller charging a markup for the same slot. Buy the moment your date opens, and take the earliest entry offered.
**Buy the CIS weekly card at €29 on day one.** It beats seven Roma 24H passes, covers the Metromare line to Ostia Antica, and removes every decision about whether a bus is worth €1.50.
**The Colosseum ticket is valid 24 hours.** Do the Colosseum in the evening and the Forum and Palatine the next morning on the same ticket, and you avoid the worst of both crowds.

**At the Vatican, walk away from the Sistine first.** Everyone funnels straight down the Candelabra–Tapestries–Maps corridor. Go via the Pinacoteca or the Egyptian collection, hit the chapel from the far side, then walk the corridors backwards when they have emptied.
**Use the nasoni.** Around 2,500 of them run across the city with free, cold, potable water. In August this saves you €20 a day and a great deal of misery.
**Eat lunch standing.** Pizza al taglio is sold by weight — point, say *basta* when the slice is the right size, pay €6–€10, and put the ninety minutes into the Palatine instead.

**Go to Ostia Antica, not Pompeii.** It is 35 minutes each way on a €1.50 city ticket rather than a day on a train, it is bigger than most people expect, and on a Tuesday in October you will have whole streets to yourself.
**Book Galleria Borghese for the 09:00 shift.** Two hours is a hard limit and the rooms are small; the first shift gives you Bernini's *Daphne* without a phone in front of it.

**Check the Case Romane del Celio calendar before you plan Day 2.** It closes Tuesdays and Wednesdays, and it is the best small ancient site in Rome — a frescoed Roman house, complete, under a working basilica.
**Take one hour in EUR.** Nowhere else shows you what the twentieth century wanted to do to Rome, and the Metro B ride out is twenty minutes.

raw.Centro Storico: Piazza Navona → Corso del Rinascimento → Pantheon → Via del Corso → Piazza di Spagna, a 2.4 km spine with every Baroque set piece hung off it; add the Campo de' Fiori–Via Giulia loop for another 1.8 km.
raw.Monti: Via Nazionale → Via Panisperna → Via dei Serpenti → Piazza della Madonna dei Monti → Via Leonina, ≈1.3 km of the oldest surviving street grid in the city, all of it uphill from the Forum.
raw.Trastevere: Piazza Trilussa → Via del Moro → Piazza Santa Maria in Trastevere → Via della Lungaretta → Piazza San Cosimato, 1.5 km flat, plus the Gianicolo climb (2 km, 70 m ascent) for the terrace view.
raw.Testaccio: Piramide → Via Marmorata → Mercato Testaccio → Via di Monte Testaccio → the Mattatoio, 1.7 km, flat and entirely without tourists before noon.
raw.Ostiense: Piramide → Via Ostiense → Centrale Montemartini → Gazometro, 2.2 km of street art and gas holders.
raw.Prati: Piazza Cavour → Via Cola di Rienzo → Mercato Trionfale → Via della Meloria, 2.6 km on a Haussmann-style grid, the antidote to the medieval tangle.
raw.EUR: Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana → Viale della Civiltà del Lavoro → Palazzo dei Congressi → the laghetto, 1.9 km of monumental rationalism on empty boulevards.
raw.Transit products and exact fares: ATAC's integrated Metrebus tickets: **BIT €1.50** (100 minutes, one metro entry, unlimited surface changes), **Roma 24H €8.50**, **Roma 48H €15.00**, **Roma 72H €22.00**, and the **CIS weekly card €29.00**, valid to midnight of the seventh day including the day of validation. All are valid on metro lines A/B/B1/C, buses, trams, the Metromare (ex Roma–Lido) line and regional trains inside the city boundary. Contactless bank cards work directly at metro gates and on many buses at BIT rates. For a full week, the **CIS at €29 beats seven day passes outright**.
raw.Airport transfer options and cost: **Leonardo Express**, FCO → Roma Termini non-stop, **32 minutes, €14**, roughly every 15 minutes 06:23–23:23 — the reliable default. **FL1 regional train**, FCO → Trastevere / Ostiense / Tuscolana / Tiburtina, **€8**, better if you are sleeping in Trastevere or Testaccio. **Taxi from FCO** to any address inside the Aurelian Walls is a **fixed municipal fare of €55**, luggage included — insist on the flat fare, do not accept the meter. **Ciampino (CIA)**: Terravision/SIT coach to Termini, roughly **€6–€7, 40 minutes**; taxi flat fare inside the walls **€40**.
raw.Vatican Museums & Sistine Chapel: — museivaticani.va only. Standard admission **€20 plus a €5 online booking fee (€25 total)**. Closed Sundays except the last Sunday of the month (free, and unbearable). Book **4–8 weeks ahead** for spring; the early-entry and "Breakfast in the Museums" products release on the same site and go first.
raw.Colosseum, Roman Forum & Palatine: — coopculture.it, the only official seller. The **24-hour ticket is €18 plus a €2 booking fee**; the Full Experience with Arena and Underground costs more and is separately capped. Tickets release on a **rolling 30-day window at 09:00 CET** and high-season dates are gone in minutes. Set an alarm.
raw.Galleria Borghese: — galleriaborghese.beniculturali.it. **€13 plus a €2 mandatory booking fee**, Tuesday–Sunday 09:00–19:00, entry in hourly shifts with a **strict two-hour visit** (the 17:45 last shift is shorter and reduced to €8). Booking is compulsory even for free-entry categories. Book **3–5 weeks ahead**.
raw.Case Romane del Celio: — caseromane.it, around €8, **closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays**, small and rarely full; 2–3 days is enough.
raw.Palazzo Massimo alle Terme: — part of the Museo Nazionale Romano combined ticket covering Palazzo Altemps, the Terme di Diocleziano and Crypta Balbi over several days. Same-day entry is normally fine.
raw.Named architectural focal points, and wh: The **Pantheon** (Hadrian, 118–128 AD) — stand under the 43.3 m coffered concrete dome and find the drainage holes in the floor beneath the oculus. **Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza** (Borromini, 1642–60) — the spiral lantern, best seen from the courtyard. **San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane** (Borromini, 1638–41) — an oval dome on a site the size of a Vatican pier. **Sant'Andrea al Quirinale** (Bernini, 1658–70) — the reply, in pink marble. **Piazza Navona** (Bernini's Four Rivers, 1651) sits on the footprint of Domitian's stadium; the piazza *is* the arena. **Il Tempietto** at San Pietro in Montorio (Bramante, 1502) — the moment the Renaissance stops quoting antiquity and starts equalling it. **Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana** at EUR (Guerrini, La Padula and Romano, 1938–43) — the "Square Colosseum", six arches by nine, now Fendi's headquarters. **Ara Pacis Museum** (Richard Meier, 2006) — the first new building in the historic centre since the war, and still argued about. **MAXXI** (Zaha Hadid, 2010) in Flaminio, and **Auditorium Parco della Musica** (Renzo Piano, 2002) next door.
notes: *Centro Storico:* **Armando al Pantheon**, Salita dei Crescenzi 31 — €40–€55, book **weeks** ahead, tiny. **Roscioli Salumeria con Cucina**, Via dei Giubbonari 21 — €45–€60, booking essential. **Antico Forno Roscioli** next door for pizza bianca, €4–€8, no booking. **Sant'Eustachio Il Caffè** for the *gran caffè*, €1.50 standing.

*Monti:* **La Carbonara**, Via Panisperna 214 — €30–€40, book. **Ai Tre Scalini**, Via Panisperna 251 — wine bar, €20–€30, no booking, arrive before 20:00. **Mercato Monti Urban Market**, Via Leonina 46 — weekends only.

*Trastevere:* **Da Enzo al 29**, Via dei Vascellari 29 — €25–€35, minimal reservations and a permanent queue; go at 19:00 sharp. **Antico Arco** on the Gianicolo — €50–€70, book. **Bar San Calisto** for a €3 negroni among Romans.

*Testaccio:* **Da Felice a Testaccio**, Via Mastro Giorgio 29 — €35–€45, **book well ahead**, cacio e pepe tossed at the table. **Flavio al Velavevodetto**, Via di Monte Testaccio 97 — €30–€40, dining rooms cut into a hill of Roman amphora shards, book. **Trapizzino**, Via Giovanni Branca 88 — €4–€6 a pocket. **Mercato Testaccio**, Via Beniamino Franklin, Mon–Sat mornings. **Volpetti**, Via Marmorata 47, for cheese.

*Prati:* **Bonci Pizzarium**, Via della Meloria 43 by Cipro metro — €8–€15, standing, no booking. **Il Sorpasso**, Via Properzio 31–33 — €25–€35. **Mercato Trionfale**, Via Andrea Doria, Mon–Sat, the largest covered market in the city.
*Ostiense:* **Porto Fluviale**, Via del Porto Fluviale 22 — €25–€35, book at weekends.
raw.Day trip with exact line, time and fare: **Ostia Antica** — Metro B to **Piramide**, cross to the adjacent **Roma Porta San Paolo** station, take the **Metromare (ex Roma–Lido) line** toward Cristoforo Colombo, alight at **Ostia Antica**, roughly **25–35 minutes**. The whole journey is **inside the urban fare zone and covered by a €1.50 BIT** or any Roma pass — no separate ticket. The excavations are a 5-minute signed walk over the footbridge.

sources.verified: ATAC's official ticket page — **BIT €1.50 / 100 min, Roma 24H €8.50, Roma 48H €15.00, Roma 72H €22.00, CIS weekly €29.00**, valid on metro, bus, tram, Metromare and urban regional rail. Galleria Borghese's official ticket office — **€13 full, €2 mandatory booking fee, €8 for the last shift, open Tuesday–Sunday 09:00–19:00, hourly shifts with a two-hour visit, last entry 17:45, booking compulsory for all visitors including free categories**. Colosseum/Forum/Palatine **24-hour ticket at €18** on CoopCulture, the official seller. Vatican Museums standard admission **€20 plus a €5 online booking fee**.
sources.confidenceNotes: Re-verify before publishing — (1) the **Colosseum €2 booking fee and the exact 30-day release mechanism**, which CoopCulture has changed more than once and which differs between the standard and Full Experience products; (2) **Ostia Antica's current admission price**, which has moved substantially in recent seasons and varies between high and low season — treat any figure as provisional; (3) the **Museo Nazionale Romano combined ticket price and validity period** covering Palazzo Massimo, Palazzo Altemps, Terme di Diocleziano and Crypta Balbi; (4) **Case Romane del Celio** admission and its Tuesday/Wednesday closure, which has varied; (5) **Pantheon** timed-entry pricing and any exemptions, introduced recently and still being adjusted; (6) **Roma Pass** 48h/72h pricing, deliberately omitted from the budget above because it rarely beats the CIS plus individual tickets on this itinerary — confirm before recommending it; (7) **Leonardo Express €14 and the €55/€40 fixed taxi fares**, both set by decree and periodically revised; (8) restaurant reservation policies, particularly **Da Enzo al 29**, which changes its walk-in rules seasonally; (9) Rome's **city tourist tax bands**, revised in recent budgets.

trips.title: Luxembourg City, Fortress and Valley

bestPeriod.note: The Bock casemates and the palace tours are seasonal; both are shut for much of the winter.

trips.gatewayAirport: Luxembourg Findel (LUX)
trips.summary: A week in the only capital where every bus, tram and train is free, spent climbing between a fortress plateau and the valleys 70 metres below.
trips.hook: Luxembourg is a city with two floors. The plateau holds the banks, the palace and the ramparts; the Alzette and Pétrusse valleys, seventy metres down, hold the old mills, the abbey and the quiet. Nothing costs anything to reach, because since 2020 the whole country's public transport has been free.

snapshot.Base(s): Luxembourg City, single base all week
snapshot.Best Period: April to June, September and October
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: 55–70 km on foot with roughly 2,000 m of cumulative stair climbing
snapshot.Getting There: Findel airport, bus 16 to the centre in 25 min, free; TGV from Paris in 2h15
snapshot.Who It Suits: Fortification readers, architecture watchers, anyone who wants a capital they can finish

itinerary.title: Ville Haute and the UNESCO ramparts
itinerary.morning: Start on Place Guillaume II — the Knuedler — where the market runs Wednesday and Saturday mornings, roughly 08:00 to 14:00. Then the Grand Ducal Palace, a Spanish Renaissance town hall of 1573 whose state rooms open to guided tours only from mid-July to early September; tickets go on sale through the Luxembourg City Tourist Office at the end of June and are gone in days.
itinerary.afternoon: Notre-Dame Cathedral, a Jesuit church of 1613–21 with a 1930s neo-Gothic extension, then the Chemin de la Corniche along the old rampart wall. Batty Weber called it the most beautiful balcony in Europe and, looking down onto Grund, it is hard to argue.
itinerary.evening: Dinner on Rue de la Boucherie or Place d'Armes; the Chocolate House opposite the palace fills any gap beforehand.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km walking, 180 m of stairs · districts: Ville Haute · tickets approx €14 (palace tour in season).

itinerary.title: The Bock, the Rham plateau and Grund
itinerary.morning: The Bock Casemates, cut by the Spaniards in 1644 and vastly extended under Vauban from 1684, run 17 km through the rock. Entry is approx €8; they open roughly from February to early November and the first hour is the only quiet one. The Pétrusse Casemates are separate, guided-only, about €15, and must be booked through the tourist office.
itinerary.afternoon: Follow the Wenzel Circular Walk, a signposted 2.5 km loop that drops from the Bock to the Alzette, crosses under the Rham plateau's barracks and comes back up through Grund. It is the clearest single explanation of how the fortress worked.
itinerary.evening: Neimënster in Grund — the 1606 abbey, later a prison, now a cultural centre with a courtyard bar and a concert programme. Ride the free Grund lift back up to Ville Haute from Plateau du Saint-Esprit.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walking, 300 m of stairs and ramps · districts: Bock, Rham, Grund · tickets approx €8.

itinerary.title: Pfaffenthal, Clausen and the Kirchberg plateau
itinerary.morning: Take the Pfaffenthal panoramic lift (2016), a free 71 m glass shaft from the Pescatore park down into the valley, then walk Pfaffenthal's Vauban towers and the Trois Glands. The free funicular from Pfaffenthal–Kirchberg station lifts you to the plateau.
itinerary.afternoon: Kirchberg is the country's architectural showroom. Mudam, I. M. Pei's 2006 museum built on the ruined Fort Thüngen, is approx €8; the Musée Dräi Eechelen inside the 1732 fort below it is free. Add Christian de Portzamparc's Philharmonie (2005) and Dominique Perrault's gold-clad Court of Justice towers (2008).
itinerary.evening: Down to Clausen and the Rives de Clausen, the converted Mousel brewery, for dinner and a beer under the rock.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walking, 250 m of stairs · districts: Pfaffenthal, Kirchberg, Clausen · tickets approx €8.

itinerary.title: Gare quarter, Bonnevoie and the Pétrusse
itinerary.morning: Cross the Pont Adolphe (Paul Séjourné, 1903), for a while the largest stone arch bridge in the world, with its 2017 cycle-and-foot deck slung underneath. Then down into the Pétrusse valley park, reopened after several years of works, and along the stream bed under the viaducts.
itinerary.afternoon: The Gare quarter is the city's most mixed: Avenue de la Liberté's 1920s bank architecture, then Rue de Strasbourg and Bonnevoie's Portuguese and Cape Verdean grocers. Lunch here costs half what it does on the plateau.
itinerary.evening: Back up to Villa Vauban (1873), the city art museum built on a fort remnant, open late on Fridays.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km walking, 200 m of stairs · districts: Gare, Bonnevoie, Pétrusse · tickets approx €5.

itinerary.title: Belval and Esch-sur-Alzette
itinerary.morning: Train to Belval-Université, about 25 minutes and free. Two blast furnaces of the old ARBED steelworks stand preserved in the middle of a new university quarter; Furnace A can be climbed on a guided visit booked through the Fonds Belval.
itinerary.afternoon: Esch-sur-Alzette, one stop on, is the second city and the heart of the Minett iron basin, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 2020. Walk Rue de l'Alzette for the Art Nouveau and Art Deco facades.
itinerary.evening: Back to the capital in half an hour; eat in the Gare quarter, where the trains land you.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walking · districts: Belval, Esch centre · tickets approx €0 (transport free, furnace tour approx €10).

itinerary.title: Vianden and the Our valley
itinerary.morning: Train to Ettelbruck (35 min), then bus 570 to Vianden (25 min). All free. Vianden Castle, an eleventh-to-fourteenth-century Ottonian and Gothic seat rebuilt from ruin between 1977 and the 1990s, is approx €10 and opens at 10:00.
itinerary.afternoon: The chairlift climbs to a ridge café with the classic castle view; walk back down through the woods in 40 minutes. The Victor Hugo house by the bridge, where he stayed in 1871, is small and good.
itinerary.evening: Return by the same route; eat late in Grund or Clausen where the kitchens run past 22:00.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km walking, 220 m ascent · districts: Vianden · tickets approx €10.

itinerary.title: Limpertsberg, the Glacis and a last Corniche circuit
itinerary.morning: Limpertsberg's villa streets and the Glacis field, where the Glacismaart takes over the third Sunday of each month from March to November: food, plants and flea stalls together.
itinerary.afternoon: The Lëtzebuerg City Museum, in a set of medieval houses on Rue du Saint-Esprit, approx €5, with a glass lift running down through four floors of rock.
itinerary.evening: Walk the Corniche once more at dusk and take the Grund lift down for a last dinner by the Alzette.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walking, 150 m of stairs · districts: Limpertsberg, Glacis, Ville Haute · tickets approx €5.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Le Place d'Armes
accommodationStrategy.description: Seven joined historic houses on the main square, inside the pedestrian core, so every plateau day starts at the door and the Corniche is four minutes away. Its courtyard restaurant keeps a later kitchen than most of the Ville Haute.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–12 weeks ahead; avoid EU summit weeks entirely.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Parc Beaux-Arts
accommodationStrategy.description: Eleven suites in three eighteenth-century houses between the palace and the Bock. Quiet, and it puts the casemates and the Wenzel Walk literally below your window, which saves a lift ride each morning.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Vauban or the Gare-quarter chains
accommodationStrategy.location: Place Guillaume II and Avenue de la Liberté
accommodationStrategy.description: For a lower rate, stay near the station: trams and trains at the door, cheaper dinners in Bonnevoie, and a ten-minute walk or one free tram stop up to the plateau.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 for ambulance and fire, 113 for police. Pharmacies post the night rota (garde) in the window.
logistics.money: Cards work everywhere. Shops close at 18:00 or 19:00, and on Sunday almost everything but restaurants and the Grund bars is shut.
logistics.transportRules: Since 29 February 2020 all public transport in Luxembourg — bus, tram, train, the funicular and the Pfaffenthal lift — is free in second class, for everyone, with no ticket and no validation. First class on trains still requires a ticket (approx €3 for a day supplement).

other.label: Where free stops
other.text: At the border. Trains to Trier, Arlon, Thionville or Metz are free only to the last Luxembourgish station; buy the cross-border leg from CFL machines. The Pétrusse Express road train and guided tours are not public transport and are chargeable.

other.label: The tram
other.text: Line T1 runs Luxexpo–Kirchberg–Pont Rouge–Gare Centrale–Cloche d'Or. It is the fastest way between Kirchberg and the station and it is free.

other.label: The Luxembourg Card
other.text: costs roughly €13 for one day, €28 for three, and covers 90-plus sites nationwide. Because transport is already free, it only pays if you visit two or more ticketed sites in a day — on this itinerary, days 2, 3 and 6.

other.label: Opening traps
other.text: Most museums close Mondays; the Bock closes for winter; the palace opens for about seven weeks in summer. On National Day, 23 June, everything shuts and the city fills the night before.

other.label: Stairs
other.text: This is a vertical city. Lifts at Pfaffenthal, Grund and the Plateau du Saint-Esprit are free and run roughly 05:45 to 01:00; use them rather than the staircases when you are tired.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 for ambulance and fire, 113 for police. Pharmacies post the night rota (garde) in the window.

proTips: Do the Wenzel Walk anticlockwise: descend the Bock side in the morning, climb back through Grund in afternoon shade. The reverse means climbing into full sun.
Palace tour tickets go live at the tourist office on Place Guillaume II in late June for the whole season. Book the day they release or plan without them.
The Pfaffenthal lift is open around the clock and free, and at night the valley below it is lit — it is the best five-minute view in the city and nobody is there after 22:00.
Go to Belval on a weekday: the university quarter is alive and the furnace tours run. At weekends it is a ghost town.
Eat lunch in Bonnevoie or the Gare quarter: the same plate is €12 rather than €26.
If your dates cover a third Sunday, build them around the Glacismaart — it is the one day the capital feels crowded in a good way.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: 55–70 km on foot with roughly 2,000 m of cumulative stair climbing
raw.Who It Suits: Fortification readers, architecture watchers, anyone who wants a capital they can finish

typeSpecific.audience: Fortification readers, architecture watchers, anyone who wants a capital they can finish

packingNotes: Shoes with grip and ankle tolerance: the Wenzel Walk and the casemates involve wet stone stairs.
A phone light for the deeper Bock galleries, which are lit but dim.
A light waterproof; the Alzette valley holds mist long after the plateau clears.
Warm mid-layer even in June — the casemates hold about 10°C year-round.
Smart-casual for dinner; the Ville Haute and Clausen dining rooms dress up more than the city's size suggests.
A small daypack only. Large bags are refused at Mudam and the casemates.
whatCouldGoWrong: **The casemates are closed for the season.** From roughly November to February the Bock is shut. Substitute the Musée Dräi Eechelen and the Lëtzebuerg City Museum, both indoor and both open year-round.
**You visit on a Monday.** Mudam, Villa Vauban, the City Museum and the national museum all close. Make Monday your Vianden or Belval day instead.
**The palace tour is sold out.** Usually it is. The guard change on Place du Palais and the free Dräi Eechelen museum cover the same history for nothing.
**Rail works north.** CFL replaces the Ettelbruck trains with buses some weekends, adding 20–30 minutes each way. Check cfl.lu the night before and leave an hour earlier.
**Sunday shutdown.** Shops close. Plan Sunday around Grund, the Corniche, Neimënster and the Glacismaart, and buy food on Saturday.

trips.title: Riga: Art Nouveau, Market Halls & the Daugava

bestPeriod.window: May to September; June for the Jāņi midsummer festival; December for the Christmas market on Doma laukums; February is cheap, dark and atmospheric

accommodation.note: €65–140 per night, double; design hotels €170+; hostels €20–35 pp

food.note: €35–65 per day; a top tasting menu €80–140

trips.summary: A seven-day city trip itinerary in Riga & the Gulf of Riga, Latvia.

itinerary.title: Vecrīga: the Old Town block
itinerary.morning: Airport bus 22 into town, 30 minutes. Begin at Doma laukums with Riga Cathedral, the largest medieval church in the Baltics, and its 6,700-pipe organ.
itinerary.afternoon: The House of the Blackheads — a reconstructed Hanseatic guild house with an outrageous Dutch Renaissance facade — then St Peter's Church for the lift to the 72 m spire viewing platform, the definitive Riga panorama.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in the Old Town, then a beer in Folkklubs Ala Pagrabs, a cellar with Latvian folk music, local ciders and a crowd that is genuinely local despite the location.

itinerary.title: The Quiet Centre: Art Nouveau block
itinerary.morning: Alberta iela is the reason this city is on UNESCO's list: a single street of Mikhail Eisenstein facades with screaming masks, peacocks, sphinxes and blue-tiled reliefs. Walk it slowly, then Elizabetes iela and Strēlnieku iela.
itinerary.afternoon: The Riga Art Nouveau Museum in a restored 1903 apartment — the only place you see how these buildings were actually lived in, down to the kitchen and the servant's stair. Then the Latvian National Museum of Art in its neo-Baroque palace on the edge of the Esplanade.
itinerary.evening: Miera iela — "the street of peace" — for the city's independent coffee roastery, a chocolate factory, small bars and a distinctly unpolished bohemian energy.

itinerary.title: Central Market and the Moscow Suburb
itinerary.morning: Riga Central Market: five converted Zeppelin hangars from the First World War, one of the largest markets in Europe. Dairy hall, fish hall, meat hall, and the produce rows outside. Eat breakfast here — grey peas with bacon, smoked fish, rye bread, curd cheese.
itinerary.afternoon: Behind the market, the Latvian Academy of Sciences, a Stalinist skyscraper known locally as "Stalin's birthday cake", with a 17th-floor open observation terrace that costs a few euros and beats every other viewpoint in the city. Continue into the Maskavas forštate, the old wooden Moscow Suburb, sobering and half-abandoned.
itinerary.evening: The Spīķeri warehouse quarter beside the market for dinner and a riverside walk.

itinerary.title: Left bank: Āgenskalns, Kalnciema and wooden Riga
itinerary.morning: Cross the Daugava. Āgenskalns Market and the wooden residential streets around it are what Riga looked like before the boulevards.
itinerary.afternoon: The Kalnciema Quarter, a restored block of 19th-century wooden buildings that hosts a Saturday farmers' and craft market — time this day for a Saturday if you can. Then the Latvian National Library, Gunnar Birkerts' "Castle of Light", whose reading terraces give the classic skyline view back across the river.
itinerary.evening: Return over the bridge at dusk; the Old Town spires from the left bank at sunset are the postcard.

itinerary.title: Jūrmala and the pine coast
itinerary.morning: Commuter train from Riga Central to Majori, about 35 minutes. Jūrmala is a 25 km strip of white sand and pine forest with 4,000 wooden dachas, an aristocratic spa town first, a Soviet resort second, and now something in between.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk Jomas iela, then the beach itself as far as Dubulti and its modernist 1977 railway station. Dzintari forest park has a viewing tower over the canopy.
itinerary.evening: Spa treatment at one of the Jūrmala sanatorium-hotels, or a seafood dinner and the train back.

itinerary.title: Sigulda and the Gauja valley
itinerary.morning: Train to Sigulda, about 1 h 15. Turaida Castle's red-brick tower over the Gauja valley, the Dainu Hill sculpture park of Latvian folk songs, and Gūtmaņa cave with its centuries of carved graffiti.
itinerary.afternoon: The cable car across the valley, and Krimulda. In autumn this valley is the best foliage in the Baltics; in winter it has a bobsleigh track you can ride.
itinerary.evening: Back to Riga. Last dinner at one of the city's ambitious modern-Latvian kitchens — Latvia's restaurant scene has gained significant international recognition in recent years. `verify: true`

itinerary.title: Mežaparks or the Occupation Museum, then out
itinerary.morning: Choose: Mežaparks, Europe's first garden city (planned 1901), with wooden villas under pines and the vast Song Festival stage; or the Museum of the Occupation of Latvia in the centre, which explains the 20th century that made this city.
itinerary.afternoon: Bus 22 to the airport, 30 minutes.

accommodationStrategy.name: Grand Poet / Neiburgs
accommodationStrategy.location: Old Town and Quiet Centre edge
accommodationStrategy.description: Neiburgs occupies a 1903 Art Nouveau building in the Old Town — you sleep inside the architecture you came to look at, with apartment-style rooms. Grand Poet sits on the Esplanade side, closest to Alberta iela and the museums.

accommodationStrategy.name: Quiet Centre boutique apartments
accommodationStrategy.description: The residential blocks north of Elizabetes iela are quiet, elegant, and full of well-restored apartments at €70–110 a night. Best value in the city and a five-minute walk to both the Art Nouveau district and the Old Town.

accommodationStrategy.name: Āgenskalns / left-bank guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: Cheaper still, wooden-house neighbourhood, tram straight over the bridge. Choose this if you want the version of Riga that residents actually live in, and if the Kalnciema Saturday market is a fixed point in your week.

logistics.emergency: 112. Riga's East Clinical University Hospital is the main facility. Pharmacies (*aptieka*) are plentiful; some in the centre run 24 hours.
logistics.weather: Cold continental winters (−5 to −15 °C, dark by 16:00 in December), warm humid summers up to 28 °C. Spring arrives late — April is still bare.
logistics.bookingWindows: Hotels: 4–6 weeks; much longer for the Song and Dance Festival, held every five years, when the city fills completely. `verify: true` Top restaurants: 2–4 weeks. Jūrmala spa treatments: a week.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards are accepted almost everywhere, but the Central Market's produce rows are cash-friendlier and haggling is normal for volume.

other.label: Transit
other.text: One integrated tram, trolleybus and bus network. Buy an e-talons at a kiosk or tap a contactless card. Trams are the useful mode — routes 2, 5 and 10 cover most of this itinerary.

other.label: Language
other.text: Latvian is the state language; Russian is widely spoken and this is a live political subject. English is standard in hospitality and near-universal under 40.

other.label: Stag-party zones
other.text: Parts of the Old Town around Kaļķu iela have an aggressive nightlife economy with a long history of tourist overcharging. Check prices before ordering, avoid street touts for clubs entirely, and drink where locals do — Miera iela, Spīķeri, Kalnciema.

proTips: The **Academy of Sciences terrace** costs a fraction of St Peter's tower, has no queue, and gives you the view *including* the Old Town rather than from inside it. Go 90 minutes before sunset.
Central Market at **08:00** is a working market; at 12:00 it is a tourist attraction. The dairy hall before nine is one of the best food experiences in this dataset.
Time your week so Day 4 lands on a **Saturday** for the Kalnciema Quarter market.
Riga Black Balsam is the local herbal bitter and is punishing neat. The blackcurrant version, or a spoonful in coffee, is how Latvians actually drink it.
The Art Nouveau facades are all above eye level. Walk Alberta iela **twice** — once looking up, once looking at doorways and stairwell glass, which is where the real detail is.
Combine Days 5 and 6 differently if the weather turns: Jūrmala is a fair-weather day, Sigulda works in rain, and the museums absorb a whole wet afternoon.

raw.walkability: High. Old Town, the Quiet Centre and the Central Market are one continuous 3 km walk; Āgenskalns and Kalnciema need a tram or a short taxi
raw.transit_pass: Rīgas Satiksme e-talons card, or contactless; trams, trolleybuses and buses on one system
raw.architectural_focus: The largest concentration of Art Nouveau architecture in the world — roughly a third of central Riga's buildings — plus wooden suburbs and Stalinist monumentalism

trips.title: A Riviera Week from a Monaco Base

bestPeriod.note: Avoid the last week of May entirely; the Grand Prix closes half the streets and triples every room rate.

trips.gatewayAirport: Nice Côte d'Azur (NCE)
trips.summary: Monaco is 2 km² and takes a day and a half. Base there and let the Ventimiglia–Cannes railway deliver a different Riviera town every morning.
trips.hook: Monaco is two square kilometres. You can walk it end to end in forty-five minutes, and after two days you will have seen it properly. The reason to stay is the railway: a two-track line hugging the coast from Ventimiglia to Cannes, with Monaco-Monte-Carlo in the middle, putting six other towns within half an hour.

snapshot.Country: Monaco (with days in France and Italy)
snapshot.Base(s): Monaco, single base all week
snapshot.Best Period: April to June, September and October
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: 55–70 km on foot, steep and stepped; roughly 6 hours on TER trains
snapshot.Getting There: Nice airport, then tram T2 to Nice-Ville and TER to Monaco, about 55 min total
snapshot.Who It Suits: Belle Époque and modernist architecture readers, coastal-path walkers, people who dislike hire cars

itinerary.title: Le Rocher and Fontvieille
itinerary.morning: The Rocher is the old town on its 60 m limestone headland, one walkable block: Rue Basse, Place de la Visitation, and the Cathédrale de Monaco (Charles Lenormand, 1875) with Rainier III and Grace Kelly's tombs. The guard changes on Place du Palais at 11:55 daily.
itinerary.afternoon: The Musée Océanographique, opened 1910 to Paul Delefortrie's design and run by Jacques Cousteau from 1957 to 1988, is the serious institution here: approx €21, timed slots online. Walk down through the Jardins Saint-Martin afterwards to see its sheer sea facade.
itinerary.evening: Down the ramp to Fontvieille for the Princess Grace Rose Garden and the port. Marché de la Condamine on Place d'Armes, a covered hall trading since 1880, does barbagiuan and socca at its counters until mid-afternoon, and the restaurants around it run late.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walking, 200 m of climbing and public lifts · districts: Rocher, Fontvieille, Condamine · tickets approx €21.

itinerary.title: Monte-Carlo and Larvotto
itinerary.morning: The Casino de Monte-Carlo (Charles Garnier, 1878–79) opens for self-guided daytime visits from 10:00 to about 13:00, approx €18, and that is the only way to see the Salle Garnier opera house and the Salle Blanche without gambling. Bring a passport: ID is checked at the door, and 18 is the minimum age even for the tour.
itinerary.afternoon: The Jardins du Casino, the Hôtel de Paris (1864) and the Café de Paris (1868), then east to the Nouveau Musée National de Monaco's Villa Sauber on Avenue Princesse Grace, approx €6.
itinerary.evening: Larvotto beach, rebuilt in 2020, and the Japanese Garden. Dinner on the Port Hercule quays.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walking · districts: Monte-Carlo, Larvotto · tickets approx €24.

itinerary.title: Nice: Vieux-Nice, Cimiez and the Promenade
itinerary.morning: TER to Nice-Ville, 22 minutes, roughly €5.20. Walk down to Cours Saleya: flower and produce market Tuesday to Sunday, about 06:00 to 13:30, antiques on Mondays. Eat socca standing up.
itinerary.afternoon: Take the free lift at the east end of Quai des États-Unis to the Colline du Château, then bus 5 to Cimiez for the Musée Matisse in its seventeenth-century villa and the Musée Marc Chagall (André Hermant, 1973), built around the Biblical Message cycle.
itinerary.evening: The Promenade des Anglais past the Hôtel Negresco (Édouard-Jean Niermans, 1913) at sunset, then the last TER back — services run until roughly 23:30.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km walking · districts: Vieux-Nice, Cimiez, Promenade · tickets approx €22 (train, Lignes d'Azur bus, two museums).

itinerary.title: Menton and Ventimiglia
itinerary.morning: TER east to Menton, 11 minutes, about €3. The old town climbs in ramps to the Basilique Saint-Michel-Archange (1675) and the cemetery terrace above. The Halles municipales on Quai de Monléon, an 1898 market building, is the food anchor: Menton lemons, tourte de blettes, pissaladière.
itinerary.afternoon: The Jardin Botanique Val Rahmeh, approx €7, or the Serre de la Madone above town. Both are the reason Menton has a microclimate reputation.
itinerary.evening: On a Friday, take the TER 12 minutes further into Italy to Ventimiglia, whose market spreads along Via Roma and the seafront until about 13:00 — so go in the morning and reverse this day. Otherwise stay in Menton for an aperitif on Place aux Herbes.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km walking, 120 m ascent · districts: Menton old town, Garavan; Ventimiglia · tickets approx €12.

itinerary.title: Èze, the Chemin de Nietzsche and La Turbie
itinerary.morning: TER west to Èze-sur-Mer, 9 minutes. The Chemin de Nietzsche climbs from the seafront to Èze-Village: 1.6 km, about 430 m of ascent, 60–75 minutes, rough and stepped, no water. Nietzsche said he composed part of Zarathustra on it.
itinerary.afternoon: Èze-Village at 427 m is one vertical block of lanes ending in the Jardin Exotique d'Èze, approx €8, cactus terraces over Cap Ferrat. The Fragonard perfumery below runs free factory visits.
itinerary.evening: A Zou! bus or short taxi up to La Turbie for the Trophée d'Auguste, raised in 6 BC to mark Augustus's subjugation of the Alpine tribes, then down to Monaco in about 25 minutes.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walking, 520 m ascent · districts: Èze-sur-Mer, Èze-Village, La Turbie · tickets approx €14.

itinerary.title: Villefranche, Beaulieu and Cap Ferrat
itinerary.morning: TER to Villefranche-sur-Mer, 13 minutes. Jean Cocteau decorated the Chapelle Saint-Pierre on the quay in 1957; the covered thirteenth-century Rue Obscure runs under the old town; the Citadelle Saint-Elme dates from 1557.
itinerary.afternoon: One stop to Beaulieu-sur-Mer for Villa Kérylos, Emmanuel Pontremoli's 1902–08 reconstruction of a Delian Greek house, approx €13. Then bus 15 to Villa Ephrussi de Rothschild on Cap Ferrat (Aaron Messiah, 1912), approx €18: nine gardens and fountains that perform every twenty minutes. Book online in July and August.
itinerary.evening: Walk the Sentier du Littoral round Cap Ferrat toward Saint-Jean, then the train home.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km walking · districts: Villefranche old town, Beaulieu, Cap Ferrat · tickets approx €36.

itinerary.title: Roquebrune-Cap-Martin and the modernist cape
itinerary.morning: TER to Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, 6 minutes. Cap Moderne is the guided-only site holding Eileen Gray's Villa E-1027 (1929) and Le Corbusier's Cabanon (1952). Small groups, booked through the Centre des monuments nationaux, approx €18, sold out weeks ahead — book the moment your dates are fixed.
itinerary.afternoon: The Promenade Le Corbusier runs around the cape toward Monaco; then climb to Roquebrune village and its tenth-century keep, the oldest in France.
itinerary.evening: Back into Monaco to walk the Grand Prix circuit on foot: Sainte-Dévote, the hill to Casino Square, the tunnel, the harbour chicane. Forty minutes, no charge.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km walking, 250 m ascent · districts: Cap Martin, Roquebrune village · tickets approx €22.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Ambassador Monaco
accommodationStrategy.description: Two minutes from the Condamine market and the port, five from a station exit, and far below Carré d'Or rates. The practical base: you can walk home from anywhere in the principality.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 10–12 weeks ahead; never for Grand Prix week.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Métropole Monte-Carlo
accommodationStrategy.description: An 1889 building beside the Casino gardens, with a rooftop pool. Worth it only if the Belle Époque evening is the point of the trip; otherwise the money buys three days elsewhere.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 months ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Beausoleil across the border
accommodationStrategy.description: Beausoleil is Monaco's uphill French twin, one street away. Rates run 40–50% lower, the public lifts drop you into Monte-Carlo in ten minutes, and you pay French rather than Monégasque restaurant prices.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 across all three countries. In Monaco, 17 for police and 18 for fire and ambulance. Sea rescue on VHF 16.

other.label: The railway is the trip
other.text: TER Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur runs the Marseille–Ventimiglia line at two to four trains an hour in daytime. From Monaco-Monte-Carlo: Cap-d'Ail 4 min, Èze-sur-Mer 9, Roquebrune-Cap-Martin 6, Menton 11, Villefranche 13, Nice-Ville 22, Ventimiglia 23, Cannes about 1h05.

other.label: The station is inside the rock
other.text: Two long exits sit several hundred metres apart: Sainte-Dévote for the port, La Condamine and the Rocher; the Ostende end for Monte-Carlo. Pick the wrong one and you climb an extra 60 m.

other.label: Tickets
other.text: TER singles come from machines or SNCF Connect: Monaco–Nice approx €5.20, Monaco–Menton approx €3. The Pass Isabelle, roughly €12–15 a day, covers unlimited TER plus Zou! and Lignes d'Azur buses across the Alpes-Maritimes and pays for itself on the Nice and Cap Ferrat days. Not valid into Italy — buy the Ventimiglia leg separately.

other.label: Buses
other.text: Compagnie des Autobus de Monaco runs six lines inside the principality: single approx €2, day pass approx €5.50, contactless accepted. Zou! line 100 shadows the coast from Nice to Menton at approx €2–3, slower than the train but scenic on the Basse Corniche.

other.label: The lifts are free
other.text: Monaco has around thirty-five public lifts and escalators linking its levels, most running 06:00 to midnight, some around the clock. They are on the free CAM map and they save enormous amounts of climbing.

other.label: Timed entry
other.text: Oceanographic Museum and the Casino daytime visit: a day or two ahead in summer. Villa Ephrussi: same week. Cap Moderne: weeks, sometimes a month.

other.label: Law and habits
other.text: Monaco enforces public decorum: no swimwear or bare chests away from the beach, and it is policed. Cards work everywhere; keep €20 in cash for market stalls and Italian bars.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 across all three countries. In Monaco, 17 for police and 18 for fire and ambulance. Sea rescue on VHF 16.

proTips: Climb the Chemin de Nietzsche from Èze-sur-Mer in the morning shade rather than descending it in the afternoon; it is loose underfoot, and the bus down from the village is easy.
The Oceanographic Museum's roof terrace and café are included in the ticket and almost nobody goes up. It is the best free-with-entry view on the Rocher.
Ventimiglia's market is Friday only and winds down by 13:00. Build the week around it if Italian produce matters.
Buy the Pass Isabelle at an SNCF machine on the Nice day and use it for the Cimiez buses too; those museums are far enough uphill to matter.
Monaco's public lift from Larvotto to Boulevard d'Italie and the one at Sainte-Dévote turn a 30-minute uphill slog into a 90-second ride. Learn those two.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: 55–70 km on foot, steep and stepped; roughly 6 hours on TER trains
raw.Who It Suits: Belle Époque and modernist architecture readers, coastal-path walkers, people who dislike hire cars

typeSpecific.surface: 55–70 km on foot, steep and stepped; roughly 6 hours on TER trains
typeSpecific.audience: Belle Époque and modernist architecture readers, coastal-path walkers, people who dislike hire cars

packingNotes: Trail-capable shoes for the Chemin de Nietzsche and the Cap Ferrat littoral path: rock and loose stone, not promenade.
A collared shirt or equivalent for the Casino and the Métropole bar; trainers and shorts are refused after 20:00.
A passport, not just an ID card: the Casino checks it, and spot checks happen on the Ventimiglia train.
Two litres of water for the Èze and Cap Martin days; no fountains on either climb.
Sun protection in April as much as August; the reflection off the sea on these south-facing slopes is fierce.
Swimwear and a quick-dry towel; Larvotto, Plage Mala at Cap-d'Ail and Menton's Sablettes are each a short walk from a station.
whatCouldGoWrong: **You booked during Grand Prix week.** The circuit build starts about six weeks before the late-May race and stands stay up for two after. Streets close, grandstands block the harbour and rates triple. Check the ACM calendar before booking anything.
**A TER strike.** French rail strikes are common and announced days ahead. Zou! line 100 keeps running along the coast, slower but reliable.
**Cap Moderne is full.** Usually it is. Walk the free Promenade Le Corbusier instead; it passes directly below E-1027.
**Swell shuts the coastal paths.** The Sentier du Littoral at Cap-d'Ail and Cap Martin closes in heavy weather, posted at the trailheads. The Moyenne Corniche buses give the same coast from above.
**Monaco costs more than you planned.** Move two dinners to Beausoleil or Menton and one lunch to the Condamine market, and the week comes back into range.

trips.title: Three Capitals in One Country: Chișinău, Tiraspol and Comrat
trips.subRegion: Chișinău, Transnistria (de facto), and the Gagauz autonomy

bestPeriod.window: early September — warm, the wine harvest starting, and Chișinău's National Wine Day in the first weekend of October just beyond it
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (35 °C in a city of concrete), and January–February (grey, −10 °C, nothing outdoors works)

accommodation.note: €180–€350 (€26–€50/night, central Chișinău doubles)

food.note: €110–€180 (€16–€26/day — Moldova is genuinely cheap)

transport.note: €35–€70 (city trolleybuses, three intercity rutieră returns, airport transfers)

activities.note: €80–€140 (museums, opera, Kvint, winery tastings)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy

trips.gatewayAirport: Chișinău International (KIV), 13 km and 20–30 minutes from the centre. **No published airport taxi tariff and meters are unreliable** — order a **Bolt** or **Yandex Go** and take the fixed quote (roughly 160 MDL / ~€8). **Trolleybus 30** runs into town for **7 MDL** (~€0.35).
trips.currency: Moldovan leu (MDL); Transnistria uses the unrecognised Transnistrian rouble (PRB)
trips.summary: Chișinău is a low green city of chestnut trees and heavy Soviet concrete where the wine bars are better than the buildings and dinner for two costs €20. From it you can reach two other capitals in under two hours:…
trips.hook: Chișinău is a low green city of chestnut trees and heavy Soviet concrete where the wine bars are better than the buildings and dinner for two costs €20. From it you can reach two other capitals in under two hours: Tiraspol, seat of an internationally unrecognised de facto entity with its own money, and Comrat, capital of a Turkic-speaking Orthodox autonomy inside Moldova. One week, three self-images of the same small country.

snapshot.Start / End: Chișinău → Chișinău (single base, three day trips)
snapshot.Getting there: Chișinău International (KIV), 13 km and 20–30 minutes from the centre. **No published airport taxi tariff and meters are unreliable** — order a **Bolt** or **Yandex Go** and take the fixed quote (roughly 160 MDL / ~€8). **Trolleybus 30** runs into town for **7 MDL** (~€0.35).

itinerary.title: The boulevard
itinerary.morning: Land at KIV, drop bags, and start at **Grădina Publică Ștefan cel Mare și Sfânt** — the 1818 park with the **Aleea Clasicilor**, a double row of busts of Romanian and Moldovan writers under lime trees.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk **Bulevardul Ștefan cel Mare** east: the **Nativity Cathedral** and its detached bell tower, the **Triumphal Arch**, the Government building, and the Presidency. It is one straight kilometre and it contains most of what the city puts on postcards.
itinerary.evening: **Carpe Diem** on Strada Bulgară for the first orientation in Moldovan wine — Fetească Neagră, Rara Neagră, Fetească Albă — with a knowledgeable list and by-the-glass flights.

itinerary.title: Museums and the concrete city
itinerary.morning: The **National Museum of Ethnography and Natural History** on Strada Mihail Kogălniceanu, for the **Deinotherium** skeleton — a near-complete giant prehistoric proboscidean excavated in southern Moldova, the museum's and the country's single most famous object [VERIFY: current ethnography museum entry fee].
itinerary.afternoon: The **Pushkin Museum** in the small house where the exiled poet lodged in 1820–23, then north to Râșcani for the **State Circus** and the **Romanița tower** — the two buildings that explain late-Soviet Chișinău better than any museum.
itinerary.evening: **Valea Morilor** lake and park at sunset, then back to **Invino** on Strada Vlaicu Pârcălab, the city's most serious wine list.

itinerary.title: Tiraspol and Transnistria
itinerary.morning: Rutieră from **Gara Centrală**. Transnistria — officially the Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic — is an **internationally unrecognised de facto entity**: no state recognises it, Moldova claims it, and it has functioned with its own administration since 1992. At the crossing you fill in a **free migration slip** giving your name, passport number and where you are going; keep it, you surrender it on the way out. Slips are commonly issued for **up to 24 hours**; a longer stay must be registered at the migration office. **Do not photograph the checkpoint, the peacekeeping posts or any military site.**
itinerary.afternoon: In **Tiraspol**: the **House of Soviets** with its Lenin bust on 25 October Street, the war memorial and tank, and the **Kvint** distillery — brandy since 1897, the entity's best-known export, with tours and a shop. The **Sheriff Sports Complex** on the edge of town — stadium, academy and hypermarket — is the other half of the local economy [VERIFY: current Kvint tour times and price].
itinerary.evening: Twenty minutes back west, **Bendery (Tighina) fortress** on the Dniester, an Ottoman rebuild of the 1530s, is the best actual monument on this side of the river [VERIFY: current Bendery fortress hours and entry fee]. Return to Chișinău the same evening — the last rutiere run into the early evening, so check the return time before you settle in for lunch.

itinerary.title: Comrat and Gagauzia
itinerary.morning: Rutieră from **Gara de Sud** south across open steppe to **Comrat**, capital of **Găgăuzia**, an autonomous territorial unit within Moldova whose people are **Turkic-speaking Orthodox Christians** — a combination that exists almost nowhere else.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Gagauz National History and Ethnography Museum**, the **Cathedral of St John the Baptist**, the Assembly building and Comrat State University, where Gagauz is taught alongside Russian and Romanian.
itinerary.evening: Eat before you leave: **gözleme**, **kıvırma** (a coiled layered pie), **sarma**, lamb *kaurma*, and the heavy red house wine that every Gagauz household makes. Back in Chișinău by nine.

itinerary.title: Market day and the underground cellars
itinerary.morning: **Piața Centrală**, the central market: whole aisles of tomatoes, brânză sheep's cheese, dried fruit, sunflower seeds, walnuts, and a flower market that runs all year. Go before 10:00 and bring small notes.
itinerary.afternoon: **Cricova**, 15 km north — 120 km of limestone galleries entered **by vehicle**, driven through streets named after wines. Reservation is mandatory; the entry-level **Matinal** tour is 250 MDL and the tasting tours run from 400 MDL to 3,100 MDL per person.
itinerary.evening: **Vinăria Nouă** back in town for small-producer Moldovan bottles you will not find outside the country.

itinerary.title: The green city
itinerary.morning: The **Ciuflea Monastery** (Sfântul Teodor Tiron), the city's main working monastery, then the **Mazarache church** in the old lower town — the oldest surviving church in Chișinău, on the hill above the Bâc.
itinerary.afternoon: The **National Museum of History of Moldova** on Strada 31 August 1989, with the she-wolf statue outside, then the **National Art Museum** in the Herța house.
itinerary.evening: Dinner on **Strada 31 August 1989** — *zeamă* chicken broth, *plăcinte* pastries with cheese or pumpkin, *mămăligă* with brânză and sour cream, *sarmale*.

itinerary.title: Mileștii Mici, or the parks
itinerary.morning: **Mileștii Mici**, 20 minutes south: the largest wine cellar collection in the world by bottle count, again toured **by vehicle**, again reservation-only. The Excursie tour is 350 MDL on a weekday, more at evenings and weekends.
itinerary.afternoon: Or, if you have had enough underground: **Valea Trandafirilor** park, the Botanical Garden, and the Ethnographic Museum's outdoor section.
itinerary.evening: Last dinner, then Bolt to KIV — allow 40 minutes for the 13 km, more at rush hour.

accommodationStrategy.name: Central boulevard hotels
accommodationStrategy.description: everything in this itinerary except the day trips is within a 20-minute walk, and both bus stations are a short trolleybus ride. Ask for a rear-facing room — the boulevard is loud until midnight.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead, longer for the first weekend of October (National Wine Day).

accommodationStrategy.name: Apartment rentals
accommodationStrategy.description: Moldova's best-value beds. A central one-bedroom runs well under a hotel double, with a kitchen for market produce and a washing machine. Confirm the floor and whether the lift works — many blocks are 1970s.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 1–2 weeks ahead; supply is good outside festival dates.

accommodationStrategy.name: Guesthouses in Butuceni / Trebujeni
accommodationStrategy.description: if you want one night out of the city, this is the one — limestone cliffs, a cave monastery, and home cooking, an hour north. Reserve entry is 20 MDL adult, 10 MDL reduced.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–4 weeks ahead; the village has only a few dozen beds.

logistics.connectivity: Moldova is **not** in EU roaming — buy a local SIM (Orange or Moldcell) at the airport, or check your operator's Moldova rate first. City wifi is widespread and fast. **Transnistrian mobile networks are separate**; your Moldovan SIM may roam expensively or not at all across the river.
logistics.emergency: **112** works throughout Moldova. In Transnistria the local services answer their own numbers; **your consulate has no consular access there** — most foreign ministries state plainly that they cannot provide assistance in the de facto entity. Note this before you cross, not after.
logistics.weather: Continental extremes. Summer highs above 35 °C with no sea to moderate them; winters to −15 °C with ice on the pavements. Spring and autumn are short, mild and the reason to come then.
logistics.bookingWindows: Cellar tours several days to a week (they are genuinely reservation-only). Opera and Organ Hall, 2–3 days midweek. Nothing else needs advance booking.
logistics.money: The **Moldovan leu (MDL)**; roughly 19–20 MDL to the euro. Cards work well in Chișinău. **In Transnistria the currency is the unrecognised Transnistrian rouble, foreign cards do not work, and there is no international ATM** — the economy there is cash-only for a visitor. Change a modest amount of MDL into roubles at a Tiraspol exchange booth, spend it, and change back before you leave: the rouble is worthless outside the territory. Euro and dollar notes are also exchangeable there.
logistics.transportRules: Rutiere are hailed at marked stops, paid in cash, and do not run to a printed timetable so much as to a fill rate. Confirm the last return departure from Tiraspol and Comrat before you commit to the day.
logistics.permits: Entering Transnistria requires the **free migration slip** issued at the crossing; overstaying it, or losing it, causes trouble on exit. **No photography of checkpoints, peacekeepers or military installations.** Moldova asks you to enter and leave the country through territory it controls — do not plan to exit from Transnistria into Ukraine on this itinerary.

proTips: **Go to Tiraspol early and come back the same day.** A day slip is simple, an overnight adds a registration step, and a same-day return removes every complication that makes people nervous about the trip.
**Carry small Moldovan notes.** Rutiere, market stalls and trolleybus conductors do not break a 500 MDL note, and the ATM will hand you nothing else.

**Language reality: Romanian is the state language, Russian is the second working language of daily life.** Older people and almost everyone in Tiraspol and Comrat answer more comfortably in Russian; younger Chișinău answers in Romanian and often English. *Bună ziua* and *mulțumesc* go a long way; *здравствуйте* and *спасибо* go equally far in the other two cities.
**Book the cellars, don't turn up.** Cricova and Mileștii Mici both take you through the tunnels **in a vehicle**, both require advance reservation, and walk-ins are routinely turned away.

**On safety, be accurate rather than dramatic.** Chișinău's ordinary crime risk is low and comparable with other European capitals; the real annoyances are unmetered taxis, poor street lighting and broken pavements. Transnistria is calm for visitors, and the issue is legal and consular ambiguity, not danger.

**Do Comrat on a weekday.** The museum and university are open, the market is running, and the rutiere are frequent; on Sunday the town is closed and you will have made a two-hour trip for a cathedral.

**Time your visit to the first weekend of October** if you can. National Wine Day fills Piața Marii Adunări Naționale with every producer in the country pouring at market prices — but book a bed a month out.

raw.Walkable blocks by name: **Bulevardul Ștefan cel Mare și Sfânt** is the spine — Ștefan cel Mare park to the Government building, 1.5 km, everything on it. **Strada 31 August 1989** runs parallel one block north with the Organ Hall and the quieter cafés. **Strada Bulgară** and **Strada Vlaicu Pârcălab** hold the wine bars. **Strada Alexandru cel Bun** and the streets down to **Piața Centrală** are the market quarter. **Valea Morilor** park is a 20-minute walk south-west from the boulevard and swallows an afternoon.
raw.Transit fares: There is **no tourist travel card** and no need for one. **Trolleybus 7 MDL** (~€0.35), **municipal bus 6 MDL**, paid to a conductor or at the validator; a contactless bank card works on most trolleybuses. City **rutiere** (privately run minibuses) cost a little more and are hailed and paid in cash to the driver [VERIFY: current Chișinău city rutieră fare and e-ticket rollout].
raw.Intercity rutieră: **Chișinău → Tiraspol**: from **Gara Centrală** (the central bus station beside Piața Centrală), roughly hourly, 70 km, **1 h 30 – 2 h** including the crossing, around 50 MDL. **Chișinău → Comrat**: from **Gara de Sud**, every 30–60 minutes, 100 km, **1 h 45 – 2 h**, around 80 MDL. Both are cash, both are minibuses, neither takes reservations [VERIFY: current Tiraspol and Comrat rutieră fares].
raw.Cultural booking timelines: The **National Opera and Ballet Theatre "Maria Bieșu"** and the **Organ Hall (Sala cu Orgă)** sell online and at the box office; a mid-week seat is usually available two or three days ahead, a Friday or Saturday premiere wants two weeks. **Cricova** and **Mileștii Mici** cellar tours are **reservation-only** and are not reliable as walk-ins — book several days out. Museums need no advance ticket [VERIFY: current Opera and Organ Hall ticket bands].
raw.Architectural focal points: The **Nativity Cathedral** (Catedrala Nașterea Domnului, 1830s, Russian neoclassical, architect **Avraam Melnikov**) with its **detached bell tower** — the original was demolished in 1962 and rebuilt in 1997. The **Triumphal Arch** (1840, architect **Luca Zaușkevici**), facing it across the square. The **Organ Hall** (1911, the former City Bank, architect **Mihail Cekerul-Cuș**), Beaux-Arts. The **State Circus** (1981), the city's great **Soviet-modernist** set piece — a ribbed concrete crown on a hill in Râșcani, long derelict and under intermittent restoration; the exterior is the point [VERIFY: current circus restoration status and whether the site can be approached].
raw.Romanița tower: The 1986 **Turnul Romanița** on Strada Mihail Sadoveanu, a 22-storey cylindrical residential high-rise by **Oleg Vronski**, is late-Soviet Chișinău's signature object: a concrete stem with cantilevered flats, half brutalist, half chamomile flower. Residential, so admire from the street.
