trips.title: Amsterdam by Canal, Oost and Noord

bestPeriod.note: Tulip season runs April into early May; June and September give long light with fewer crowds than midsummer.

trips.gatewayAirport: Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS)
trips.summary: A week of Amsterdam in rings: the UNESCO canal belt, the newer architecture of Oost and Noord, and the free ferries that cross the IJ.
trips.hook: Amsterdam rewards a week the way a weekend never can: the canal belt stops feeling like a postcard once you have walked it three times, and the free ferries across the IJ turn Noord from an afterthought into half the trip. Book the timed-entry museums before you land, then let the neighbourhoods set the pace.

snapshot.Base(s): Jordaan or De Pijp, single base all week
snapshot.Best Period: April to June, September to October
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: 55–70 km on foot, flat, plus several short IJ ferry crossings
snapshot.Getting There: Direct train from Schiphol to Amsterdam Centraal in 15–20 min
snapshot.Who It Suits: First-time and repeat visitors who want depth over a checklist, families comfortable near bike lanes

itinerary.title: Brouwersgracht to the Golden Bend
itinerary.morning: Start at Brouwersgracht, the prettiest working canal in the belt, and walk south along Prinsengracht to the Westerkerk, Hendrick de Keyser's church of 1620–1631 with the 85 m Westertoren added in 1638. Climb the tower for the belt's clearest overview.
itinerary.afternoon: Book a timed slot at the Anne Frank House on Prinsengracht 263, inside the 1635 canal house where the Secret Annex is hidden behind the bookcase. Slots for six weeks out release online every Tuesday at 10:00 CET; a smaller batch opens two days ahead at 09:00.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in the Jordaan at Moeders on Rozengracht, a long-running Amsterdam kitchen with a wall of mismatched family photographs and honest stamppot.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walking · districts: Grachtengordel-West, Jordaan · tickets approx €16.

itinerary.title: Jordaan and the Negen Straatjes
itinerary.morning: The Noordermarkt runs a farmers' and organic market every Saturday 09:00–16:00, and a flea and textile market every Monday 09:00–13:00; either anchors the morning. Circle the Noorderkerk (1623) before the stalls close in.
itinerary.afternoon: The Negen Straatjes — nine cross-streets between Prinsengracht and Singel — hold Amsterdam's independent shops: vintage on Berenstraat, design on Hartenstraat, specialist food on Runstraat.
itinerary.evening: A canal-side beer at Café 't Smalle on Egelantiersgracht, a former genever distillery tasting house from 1786, then dinner nearby.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walking · districts: Jordaan, Grachtengordel-West · tickets approx €0 (market spend aside).

itinerary.title: Museumplein and the Golden Age masters
itinerary.morning: The Rijksmuseum, Pierre Cuypers' 1885 cathedral of a building, needs a booked timed slot; go straight for the Gallery of Honour and Rembrandt's Night Watch before the tour groups arrive at 10:30.
itinerary.afternoon: The Van Gogh Museum next door — Gerrit Rietveld's 1973 building plus Kisho Kurokawa's 1999 exhibition wing — releases tickets ten weeks ahead on Mondays at 10:00 and sells out for weekends within days.
itinerary.evening: Walk into Vondelpark for the open-air light, then dinner in Oud-Zuid on Cornelis Schuytstraat.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km walking · districts: Museumkwartier, Oud-Zuid · tickets approx €47.

itinerary.title: Oost
itinerary.morning: The Dappermarkt runs Monday to Saturday, 09:00–17:00, one of the city's most genuinely local street markets — Surinamese, Turkish and Dutch stalls side by side. This is the week's food anchor.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Muiderpoort, the 1770 city gate Napoleon rode through in 1811, then into the Amstelkwartier, where recent housing blocks by young Dutch practices face the Amstel across the water. The Tropenmuseum (Cuypers en Hulswit, 1926) covers a wet-weather hour well.
itinerary.evening: Dinner on Javastraat, Oost's food street, or Balistraat nearby.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km walking · districts: Oost, Dapperbuurt, Amstelkwartier · tickets approx €17.

itinerary.title: Noord across the IJ
itinerary.morning: Take the free GVB ferry from behind Centraal Station to Buiksloterweg — it runs every few minutes, day and night, and carries pedestrians, cyclists and prams at no charge. EYE Filmmuseum, Delugan Meissl's angular white building from 2012, sits right at the landing.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk or cycle along the NDSM-weg to NDSM-werf, a former shipyard now covered in murals, with the STRAAT street-art museum inside an old warehouse and the Kunststad studio complex.
itinerary.evening: Ride up A'DAM Lookout for the sunset view back over the Centraal Station roofline, then the free ferry home.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walking, 25 min on ferries · districts: Noord (Buiksloterham, NDSM) · tickets approx €15.

itinerary.title: De Pijp and Amsterdam School Zuid
itinerary.morning: The Albert Cuypmarkt, Monday to Saturday 09:00–17:00, runs the length of Albert Cuypstraat and is the country's largest daily street market — herring, stroopwafels, fabric and flowers in one 500 m stretch.
itinerary.afternoon: Sarphatipark for a break, then south into the Rivierenbuurt for De Dageraad, the 1918–1923 housing block by Michel de Klerk and Piet Kramer near Burgemeester Tellegenstraat — Amsterdam School brick expressionism at its most sculptural.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in De Pijp, still Amsterdam's densest restaurant neighbourhood per block.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km walking · districts: De Pijp, Rivierenbuurt · tickets approx €5.

itinerary.title: Nieuwmarkt, Plantage and Waterlooplein
itinerary.morning: Nieuwmarkt square and the Waag, a 1488 city-gate turned weigh house, then north up Zeedijk through the old sailors' quarter into Chinatown.
itinerary.afternoon: The Plantage: Hortus Botanicus (one of the world's oldest botanical gardens, founded 1638), and the Portuguese Synagogue (Elias Bouman, 1675), centrepiece of the Jewish Cultural Quarter.
itinerary.evening: Browse the Waterlooplein flea market before it closes at 18:00, then a last canal-side dinner near the Amstel — book a self-drive electric sloop from one of the canal-belt rental docks for a final hour on the water if the weather holds.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km walking · districts: Nieuwmarkt, Plantage, Waterlooplein · tickets approx €12.

accommodationStrategy.name: The Toren
accommodationStrategy.description: A pair of connected 17th-century canal houses on the Keizersgracht, close enough to the Jordaan and the Anne Frank House to make Days 1 and 2 entirely on foot. Rooms are small, as every canal house is — ask for one facing the water, not the courtyard.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–10 weeks ahead for spring and September.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Not Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: A converted school on Piri Reisplein with rooms built as a houseboat, a caravan and a tram carriage among conventional ones. It sits between the Jordaan and Museumplein, a genuine ten-minute walk to either, and works well for families who want a talking point as much as a bed.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Sir Adam
accommodationStrategy.location: base of the A'DAM Tower, Noord
accommodationStrategy.description: Puts Day 5 on your doorstep and turns the ferry commute into the fun part of the evening rather than the end of it. The rooftop bar looks straight down the IJ to Centraal Station.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 for police, fire and ambulance; canal water rescue is handled by the same number.

other.label: GVB fares
other.text: Contactless bank cards and phones tap in and out on buses, trams, the metro and the HADAG-style IJ ferries via OVpay, charged per journey capped daily. Multi-day GVB passes (24 through 168 hours) are better value if you are moving constantly; buy them in the GVB app or at Centraal Station.

other.label: The IJ ferries to Noord are free
other.text: for pedestrians and cyclists on the Buiksloterweg, IJplein and NDSM routes — no ticket, no tap, just walk on.

other.label: Timed-entry windows
other.text: Anne Frank House: six weeks out, Tuesdays 10:00 CET, plus a same-week release two days ahead at 09:00. Van Gogh Museum: ten weeks out, Mondays 10:00. Rijksmuseum: slots open roughly three months ahead and rarely sell out except peak weekends.

other.label: Bike lanes are traffic
other.text: The red-asphalt paths beside every canal carry real cyclist speed; look both ways before stepping onto one, always.

other.label: Cash is nearly extinct
other.text: Contactless card or phone covers almost everything, including most markets now; carry some coins only for the rare stall that does not.

other.label: Tourist tax
other.text: Amsterdam charges a per-night city tax on top of the room rate, usually already included in the quoted price — check at booking.

other.label: Opening-hour trap
other.text: Many independent shops in the Negen Straatjes open at 11:00 or later and close Sundays or Mondays; the Albert Cuyp and Dappermarkt run Monday–Saturday only.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 for police, fire and ambulance; canal water rescue is handled by the same number.

proTips: Buy Anne Frank House and Van Gogh Museum tickets the moment you fix your dates — both routinely sell out weeks ahead in the April–June and September windows.
Take the NDSM ferry (not the Buiksloterweg one) in the late afternoon on Day 5; it runs a longer, quieter crossing and times well with sunset at the Lookout.
Walk the Rijksmuseum's Gallery of Honour first, before the museum's own opening rush from tour buses arrives around 10:30.
The Noordermarkt's Saturday farmers' stalls thin out fast after 13:00 — go early for the good cheese.
Skip the fixed-route canal cruises: a GVB day ticket covering the IJ ferries plus a short Amstel stretch on tram 4 shows you more water for less money.
De Pijp empties of tourists after 21:00 even in July; it is the neighbourhood to walk for an unhurried evening.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: 55–70 km on foot, flat, plus several short IJ ferry crossings
raw.Who It Suits: First-time and repeat visitors who want depth over a checklist, families comfortable near bike lanes

typeSpecific.surface: 55–70 km on foot, flat, plus several short IJ ferry crossings
typeSpecific.audience: First-time and repeat visitors who want depth over a checklist, families comfortable near bike lanes

packingNotes: A proper rain shell — Amsterdam weather turns inside twenty minutes most of the year.
Flat, grippy shoes for cobbles and canal-house thresholds that are rarely level.
A cross-body bag rather than a backpack on trams and in markets.
A phone or card that supports contactless tap-in for OVpay; a physical OV-chipkaart is now mostly a backup.
A tote for the Albert Cuyp and Dappermarkt; stalls sell by weight and hand you paper, not bags.
Sunglasses and a hat for the Vondelpark and Sarphatipark stretches in late spring.
A light scarf or layer for the open ferry decks even in summer — the IJ has real wind.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Anne Frank House or Van Gogh Museum sells out your date.** Check the official sites for daily cancellation releases at 09:00, or shift the visit to a weekday morning slot if one remains.
**Rain wipes out a walking afternoon.** The Rijksmuseum, Van Gogh Museum, Tropenmuseum and EYE Filmmuseum all absorb two to three hours indoors without rebooking anything.
**A ferry line is suspended for maintenance or fog.** The Metro 52 Noord/Zuidlijn runs Centraal Station to Noorderpark on the same fare system as a backup route into Noord.
**You misjudge a bike lane.** Cross at marked points, look for the painted bike symbol, and never walk in the red asphalt strip even to take a photo.
**A market day falls on your planned rest day.** The Dappermarkt and Albert Cuyp run Monday–Saturday; only build market mornings into weekdays, not a Sunday.

trips.title: Kraków in Seven Days: Planty Ring, Kazimierz Nights, Nowa Huta Mornings
trips.subRegion: Lesser Poland (Małopolska) — Kraków and the Wieliczka–Oświęcim corridor

bestPeriod.window: late April to mid-June, then the second half of September
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (Rynek Główny gridlock, Wieliczka queues, Kazimierz stag noise) and the first fortnight of December

accommodation.note: €350–€620 (€50–€89/night, twin-share in Stare Miasto or Kazimierz)

food.note: €165–€270 (€24–€39/day, including one tasting menu)

transport.note: €45–€75 (MPK tickets, Wieliczka and Oświęcim trains, airport train)

activities.note: €120–€185 (Wawel, Rynek Underground, Wieliczka, Auschwitz guide, Schindler)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy

trips.gatewayAirport: Kraków–Balice (KRK), 11 km west. The Kraków Lotnisko–Kraków Główny train runs every 30 min, ~20 min, ~€4.65 (20 PLN, 2026 Koleje Małopolskie fare, luggage free). Rail from Warsaw Centralna 2h20 on EIP/IC; from Berlin via Warsaw or the direct night train.
trips.summary: Most people give Kraków a weekend and see the Cloth Hall, a dragon and a queue. Seven days is the length at which the city stops performing. You get the hejnał at 07:00 with nobody watching, a whole grey morning in…
trips.hook: Most people give Kraków a weekend and see the Cloth Hall, a dragon and a queue. Seven days is the length at which the city stops performing. You get the hejnał at 07:00 with nobody watching, a whole grey morning in Nowa Huta's Plac Centralny, an unhurried afternoon in the Podgórze quarry, and enough evenings in Kazimierz to have a regular table. It is flat, compact, cheap by Western European standards, and it rewards patience more than energy.

snapshot.Best period: Late April–mid June; second half of September
snapshot.Start / End: Kraków (Stare Miasto) → Kraków (single base, no relocation)
snapshot.Getting there: Kraków–Balice (KRK), 11 km west. The Kraków Lotnisko–Kraków Główny train runs every 30 min, ~20 min, ~€4.65 (20 PLN, 2026 Koleje Małopolskie fare, luggage free). Rail from Warsaw Centralna 2h20 on EIP/IC; from Berlin via Warsaw or the direct night train.

itinerary.title: The Planty Ring and the First Hejnał
itinerary.morning: Arrive, drop bags, and walk the Planty clockwise from Barbakan to Wawel — 4 km, about an hour, and the fastest way to internalise the city's shape. It replaced the walls after 1820; the surviving fragment at Brama Floriańska tells you how thick they were.
itinerary.afternoon: Rynek Główny, then the Sukiennice gallery of 19th-century Polish painting upstairs in the Cloth Hall. Stand under St Mary's on the hour for the **hejnał** — played to four windows, cut off mid-phrase.
itinerary.evening: **Miód Malina**, ul. Grodzka 40 — pierogi and duck; touristed and still good. Nightcap at **Café Camelot**, ul. św. Tomasza 17.
itinerary.dayStats: 5 km on foot

itinerary.title: Wawel and the Renaissance Courtyard
itinerary.morning: Be at the Wawel ticket office when it opens; take the State Rooms first, then the Crown Treasury & Armoury. Timed slots mean a 09:30 entry and a 12:00 entry can be two hours apart.
itinerary.afternoon: Wawel Cathedral on its separate ticket: the Sigismund Chapel from the nave, the Royal Tombs below, then the timber climb to the Sigismund Bell. Descend through ul. Kanonicza, the city's best-preserved street.
itinerary.evening: **Starka**, ul. Józefa 14 in Kazimierz — house-aged rye vodkas and Galician cooking. Reserve; the back room fills by 19:30 [VERIFY: current hours].
itinerary.dayStats: 4 km

itinerary.title: Under the Square, and Kazimierz After Dark
itinerary.morning: **Rynek Underground** — four metres below the square, the medieval market level with cloth stalls, cart ruts and a lead-smelting hearth. Ninety minutes is right.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross to Kazimierz. Szeroka's synagogue rectangle: the Old Synagogue (municipal museum), the Remuh with its 16th-century cemetery, then Izaak. Coffee and pistachio cake somewhere on ul. Józefa.
itinerary.evening: **Hamsa**, Szeroka 2, for hummus and mezze — the argument for Israeli food on this square is deliberate. Then a **zapiekanka** at the Okrąglak, the round former butchers' rotunda in the middle of Plac Nowy, roughly €4 (16–20 PLN) and open absurdly late [VERIFY: current prices and closing time].
itinerary.dayStats: 5 km

itinerary.title: Oświęcim
itinerary.morning: Train from Kraków Główny to Oświęcim, then the shuttle or a 2 km walk to the Auschwitz I gate. Your booked English-language guided tour covers Auschwitz I and the bus transfer to Birkenau; allow 3.5 hours minimum.
itinerary.afternoon: Birkenau's scale is the point — the ramp, the wooden barracks, the distance from the gate to the ruins of Crematoria II and III. Do not schedule anything after it.
itinerary.evening: Back in Kraków, eat quietly and early. **Café Camelot** or a bowl of żurek near your flat. No nightlife tonight; nobody wants it.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km each way, ~1h40 by train

itinerary.title: Podgórze, Zabłocie and the Ghetto Ground
itinerary.morning: Cross Kładka Bernatka to **Plac Bohaterów Getta** and its 70 empty bronze-and-steel chairs (Lewicki & Latak, 2005) — one per thousand deported. **Apteka pod Orłem**, the pharmacy on the square that stayed open through the ghetto, is a small, exact museum.
itinerary.afternoon: East into **Zabłocie**: Schindler's Factory on ul. Lipowa — a Kraków-under-occupation museum more than a Schindler shrine — then **MOCAK** next door.
itinerary.evening: **Bottiglieria 1881**, ul. Bocheńska 5 — tasting menu, Michelin-starred, book three to six weeks ahead; expect €90–€130 (380–550 PLN) per head with pairing [VERIFY: current menu price and hours].
itinerary.dayStats: 6 km

itinerary.title: Nowa Huta and the Socialist City
itinerary.morning: Tram 4 or 22 from Teatr Bagatela to **Plac Centralny im. Ronalda Reagana**, 25–35 minutes. Walk the arcades, then out along **Aleja Róż** — a parade axis turned quiet rose-bed, with a hole where Lenin stood until 1989.
itinerary.afternoon: The Nowa Huta Museum branch and the Nowa Huta Underground shelters, then the concrete ark of Arka Pana church in Bieńczyce, built 1967–77 after a decade of refused permits [VERIFY: current opening hours for the shelter tours].
itinerary.evening: Back to Kazimierz for a slower night — wine on ul. Józefa, then Plac Nowy's bars, which are at their best on a Friday around 22:00.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km east by tram

itinerary.title: Wieliczka, Hala Targowa and the Mound
itinerary.morning: If it is a Sunday, start at **Hala Targowa** on ul. Grzegórzecka — the flea market runs early and thins out by 11:00; enamel signs, Cepelia textiles, and the grilled-sausage van under the viaduct [VERIFY: current market hours].
itinerary.afternoon: Train from Kraków Główny to Wieliczka Rynek-Kopalnia (24 min) for the **Tourist Route**: about 800 steps down, 3 km of the mine's 245 km walked, two hours underground, ending at the Chapel of St Kinga carved entirely from salt. Guided groups only; the mine now prices the Tourist Route seasonally from 93 PLN (~€22) per person, with a normal Polish-language ticket running roughly 100–130 PLN (~€23–€30) depending on the month [VERIFY: current foreign-language Tourist Route ticket price, which carries a premium over the Polish tour].
itinerary.evening: Tram 1 to Salwator, up ul. Kościuszki past the Norbertine convent to **Kopiec Kościuszki** for the last light over the Vistula bend, then a final supper back in Stare Miasto.
itinerary.dayStats: 30 km round trip

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Copernicus
accommodationStrategy.description: on the quietest street inside the Planty, 200 m below Wawel, with a Renaissance-vaulted breakfast room and a rooftop looking straight at the cathedral. You walk everywhere and hear nothing at night.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–10 weeks ahead direct; rates jump for Corpus Christi and the Jewish Culture Festival.

accommodationStrategy.name: Karmel Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: one street off Szeroka but insulated from Plac Nowy's noise corridor, walking distance to Starka, Hamsa and the Kładka Bernatka footbridge to Podgórze. Best value for a seven-night stay.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead; ask for a courtyard-facing room.

accommodationStrategy.name: Apartments on ul. Józefa or ul. Meiselsa
accommodationStrategy.description: over a week a kitchen and a washing machine change the economics. Buy at Stary Kleparz and cook two nights.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–8 weeks ahead; check for a lift and street-side double glazing.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming; 5G across the centre and Nowa Huta, free wifi on most MPK trams.
logistics.emergency: 112. The 24-hour *apteka* on ul. Karmelicka is the reliable central pharmacy.
logistics.weather: continental. April and October swing 8–20 °C in a day; winter smog (*smog krakowski*) is a genuine problem from November to February — another reason for the shoulder seasons.
logistics.bookingWindows: Auschwitz ~90 days; Bottiglieria 1881 three to six weeks; Schindler's Factory 5–10 days; Wieliczka and Wawel 2–7 days in shoulder season, longer in July.
logistics.money: złoty, not euro. Cards everywhere, including trams and market stalls. Refuse dynamic currency conversion at the terminal — always pay in PLN. Avoid Euronet ATMs on Floriańska; use a bank-branded machine. Roughly €1 ≈ 4.25–4.35 PLN [VERIFY: current exchange rate].
logistics.transportRules: validate nothing if you bought a mobile ticket — activate it *before* boarding. Inspectors work the Nowa Huta trams hard. The Wieliczka and Oświęcim trains are Koleje Małopolskie/Polregio; buy at the machine, not on board.
logistics.permits: photography without flash is fine in most museums but forbidden inside the Sigismund Chapel and in parts of Auschwitz; large bags (over 30x20x10 cm) are refused at the Auschwitz gate and there is no left-luggage inside.

proTips: Hear the hejnał at 07:00 rather than at noon. Same trumpeter, same broken note, an empty square, and you can actually see him lean out of the window.
Book the Auschwitz slot for a **13:00–14:00 start**, not 09:00. The morning coaches from Kraków clear Auschwitz I by early afternoon and Birkenau is nearly empty by 16:00.
Skip the Wieliczka organised coach tour. The Kraków Główny train plus a ticket bought at the mine costs about a third and you choose your own group.
Do Kazimierz on a Tuesday or Wednesday. Plac Nowy on a Saturday belongs to stag parties; midweek it belongs to Kraków.
Eat lunch at a *bar mleczny* — the milk bars on ul. Grodzka and in Nowa Huta serve naleśniki and barszcz for €3–€5 (12–20 PLN). It is the cheapest good food in the city.
For the Wyspiański windows at the Franciscan church, go between 15:00 and 16:30 on a clear afternoon; the west light is what the glass was designed for, and entry is free.
Ask for *"poproszę rachunek"* (the bill) and *"na wynos"* (takeaway). Tipping is 10% in restaurants, nothing in milk bars.

raw.Walkable neighbourhood blocks: **Stare Miasto within the Planty** — the 4 km green ring on the line of the demolished walls, enclosing Rynek Główny, ul. Floriańska, ul. Grodzka and ul. Kanonicza; nothing inside is more than 12 minutes' walk from the Cloth Hall. **Kazimierz** — the Szeroka rectangle (Remuh and Old Synagogues), ul. Józefa for galleries and small plates, Plac Nowy for the Okrąglak. **Podgórze** across the Powstańców Śląskich bridge — Plac Bohaterów Getta, ul. Lwowska ghetto-wall fragment, and the **Zabłocie** post-industrial strip along ul. Lipowa. **Nowa Huta**, 9 km east — Plac Centralny im. Ronalda Reagana and the fan of Aleja Róż, Aleja Solidarności and Aleja Jana Pawła II. **Salwator/Zwierzyniec**, at the western terminus of tram 1, for the Norbertine convent, ul. Kościuszki and the climb to Kopiec Kościuszki.
raw.Transit passes and prices: MPK single tickets are time-based, and the March 2026 tariff replaced the old 20-minute ticket with a 15-minute one — 15 minutes ~€0.95 (4 PLN), 30 minutes or one journey ~€1.40 (6 PLN), 60 minutes ~€1.85 (8 PLN), 90 minutes ~€2.10 (9 PLN); a 24-hour Zone I ticket is ~€4.65 (20 PLN), while the 48-hour ~€9.30 (40 PLN) and 72-hour ~€12.80 (55 PLN) tickets are sold only as all-zone versions (2026 KMK tariff). Buy from the on-board machine (card accepted) or the Jakdojade app. The **Kraków Card** bundles unlimited MPK travel with roughly 40 museums at about €30 for 24h, €45 for 48h and €52 for 72h, with a transport-free 72-hour museum pass at €30 (2026 tariff); note that Wawel and Wieliczka are outside it. Do the maths honestly: on a seven-day stay where your two biggest tickets (Wieliczka, Auschwitz) are *not* covered, singles plus individual admissions almost always win. Buy the Card only if you compress five paid museums into one 48-hour block.
raw.Cultural booking timelines: **Auschwitz-Birkenau** is the hard constraint. The guided-entry band is far wider than most guides admit: from April to September entry between 07:30 and 17:00 is only possible on a booked guided tour with an educator (to 16:00 in March and October, 15:00 in February, 14:00 in January and November, 13:00 in December), and the free individual entry cards are only for the hours outside that. Slots are released on visit.auschwitz.org daily at 12:00 noon, 90 days ahead, and English tours in the shoulder season are gone within days of release; the individual 3.5-hour guided tour is 150 PLN (~€35) in a foreign language, 140 PLN in Polish, and the six-hour study tour 190/180 PLN (2026 tariff). Book this before you book flights. **Schindler's Factory** (Fabryka Emalia Oskara Schindlera, ul. Lipowa 4) sells out most days by mid-morning — buy online 5–10 days ahead. **Wawel** uses timed entry per exhibition, with separate tickets for the State Rooms, Crown Treasury & Armoury and the Dragon's Den, and a limited free allocation on one weekday [VERIFY: current free-entry day and timed-slot rules]. **Wawel Cathedral** is ticketed separately at the office opposite the entrance, covering the Royal Tombs and the Sigismund Bell tower. **Rynek Underground** (Podziemia Rynku, entrance in the Cloth Hall's northern end) caps numbers and closes on the second Monday of each month; admission is ~€10.50 (45 PLN), reduced 35 PLN, and Tuesday is the free day, on a short 10:00–15:00 shift with no advance booking (2026 Muzeum Krakowa tariff). **Wieliczka** admits the Tourist Route in guided groups only.
raw.Architectural focal points: Gothic — **Kościół Mariacki** (14th c., asymmetric towers) and Veit Stoss's limewood altarpiece, 1477–89. Renaissance — the arcaded **Wawel courtyard** (Francesco the Florentine, from 1507) and Bartolomeo Berrecci's **Sigismund Chapel**, 1519–33, the purest Italian Renaissance interior north of the Alps. Młoda Polska / Secession — **Stanisław Wyspiański's** stained glass and wall painting at the Franciscan Basilica, ul. Franciszkańska 2, above all the west window *Bóg Ojciec — Stań się*. Socialist realism — **Nowa Huta** (from 1949), the Renaissance-quoting arcades of Plac Centralny and the axial Aleja Róż.

trips.title: Lisbon on Foot: Seven Hills, Seven Days

bestPeriod.window: Mid-March–early June & mid-September–end October
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August — 35°C on the calçada, Alfama unwalkable by noon, peak prices.
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-March–early June & mid-September–end October

accommodation.note: Boutique guesthouse double, per-person share, Chiado or Príncipe Real

food.note: Tasca lunches €10–16, one €50–70 dinner, €6/day coffee and pastéis

transport.note: Navegante card, Sintra return, ferries, funiculars, airport metro

activities.note: Gulbenkian, MAAT, Azulejo, Jerónimos, two Sintra palaces

profile.difficultyNote: 2 — 8–12 km a day on steep basalt cobbles, 150–250 m cumulative ascent; hard on ankles, not on lungs.

trips.gatewayAirport: LIS — Humberto Delgado; Metro Red Line to Alameda 20 min, taxi to Baixa 20–25 min (€15–20)
trips.summary: Lisbon rewards people who accept that the city is a staircase. This week trades the tram-28 conveyor belt for a neighbourhood sequence: the Moorish tangle of Alfama and Mouraria, then the Pombaline grid and the literary hills of Chiado and Bairro Alto, then Príncipe Real, then the river — Belém's Manueline stonework west, Marvila's warehouse breweries east. Distances are short, gradients are not. A Sintra day breaks the week open with fog and Romantic follies. It suits travellers who want architecture and food weighted equally.

itinerary.title: Landing on the Grid: Baixa and Chiado
itinerary.morning: Metro to Baixa-Chiado, drop bags, walk the Pombaline grid from Praça do Comércio up Rua Augusta — note the standardised window bays, Manuel da Maia's prefab logic in stone. A *bica* standing at Confeitaria Nacional on Praça da Figueira, open since 1829.
itinerary.afternoon: The roofless **Convento do Carmo** (€7) is the truest surviving image of 1 November 1755. Then Museu Nacional de Arte Contemporânea–Chiado on Rua Serpa Pinto, and up via the **Elevador da Glória** to Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara.
itinerary.evening: **Taberna da Rua das Flores** (no. 103), no reservations — arrive 19:00, chalkboard menu, €25–35pp. Ginjinha at **A Ginjinha**, Largo de São Domingos, €1.60.
itinerary.dayStats: 5.5 km, 130 m ascent; Metro Red + Green; Navegante €0.50 + 24h pass €7.25; Carmo 10:00–19:00.

itinerary.title: Alfama and Mouraria end to end
itinerary.morning: Bus 737 from Praça da Figueira to **Castelo de São Jorge** (€15) for the 09:00 opening and empty ramparts, then walk down through Largo do Contador Mor.
itinerary.afternoon: Rua de São Pedro and Beco do Carneiro into lower Alfama; the **Sé** (Romanesque, 1147, twin fortress towers, cloister €5). Cross into **Mouraria** by Rua dos Cavaleiros for Largo da Severa and the grocers of Rua do Benformoso — the least gentrified inner quarter.
itinerary.evening: Fado at **Mesa de Frades**, Rua dos Remédios 139A, a tiled former chapel; 20:00 sitting, book 3–5 days ahead, ~€45 with food. Cheaper walk-in alternative: **Tasca do Chico**, Rua do Diário de Notícias 39.
itinerary.dayStats: 7.8 km, 210 m ascent; bus 737; castle €15, opens 09:00; fado 20:00–21:00 starts.

itinerary.title: Belém: Manueline stone, modern riverfront
itinerary.morning: Tram 15E from Praça da Figueira (25 min). **Mosteiro dos Jerónimos** on a 09:30 slot (€18 combined with Torre de Belém; church nave free). The two-storey cloister and Castilho's south portal are the reason to come.
itinerary.afternoon: **MAAT** (€11) — Levete's crouching pavilion plus the 1908 Central Tejo boiler hall, which is the better half. Torre de Belém from outside; the interior queue rarely repays 45 minutes.
itinerary.evening: **Cervejaria Ramiro**, Av. Almirante Reis 1 — garlic prawns, then a *prego* as dessert. No bookings; take a ticket, expect 30–50 min, €35–45pp.
itinerary.dayStats: 6.2 km flat; tram 15E ~€1.66; Jerónimos 09:30–18:00, closed Mon; MAAT closed Tue.

itinerary.title: Príncipe Real, Estrela, Gulbenkian
itinerary.morning: Up through **Praça das Flores** to **Praça do Príncipe Real** and its 1863 cedar canopy; Embaixada inside the neo-Moorish Ribeiro da Cunha palace. On to **Jardim da Estrela** and the 1790 **Basílica da Estrela** dome.
itinerary.afternoon: Metro Blue Line to São Sebastião for the **Calouste Gulbenkian** (€14, Founder's + Modern; free Sun after 14:00). Two hours minimum — the Lalique room, the Rembrandt wall, and Gonçalo Ribeiro Telles's garden.
itinerary.evening: **A Cevicheria**, Rua Dom Pedro V 129 (no reservations, leave your name, drink pisco next door), or **Cantinho do Avillez**, Rua dos Duques de Bragança 7, booked a week out, €40–55pp.
itinerary.dayStats: 7.1 km, 170 m ascent; Metro Blue; Gulbenkian €14, 10:00–18:00, closed Tue.

itinerary.title: Sintra day trip
itinerary.morning: Rossio 08:11 train, 40 min, ~€2.40. Bus 434 up to **Palácio da Pena** for a 09:30–10:00 slot (park + palace €20) — Ferdinand II's 1840s Romantic collage of Manueline quotation, Moorish tile and Bavarian battlement.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the **Castelo dos Mouros** ramparts (€12), then the **Palácio Nacional de Sintra** with its conical kitchen chimneys (€13). In heavy fog, swap for **Quinta da Regaleira** (€15) and its initiation well.
itinerary.evening: Back by 19:00. **Bistro 100 Maneiras**, Largo da Trindade 9 (book 2 weeks, €70–90pp) or petiscos at **Taberna Sal Grosso**, Calçada do Forte 22.
itinerary.dayStats: 9.4 km incl. Sintra hills, 320 m ascent; ~€4.80 train return; Pena last entry 18:00.

itinerary.title: Azulejos east: Xabregas, Marvila, Beato
itinerary.morning: Bus 794 to the **Museu Nacional do Azulejo** in the Madre de Deus convent (€8, closed Mon). The 23-metre panorama of pre-earthquake Lisbon upstairs explains what 1755 erased better than any text.
itinerary.afternoon: North into **Marvila/Beato**: Dois Corvos taproom on Rua Capitão Leitão, the Fábrica Braço de Prata warehouse, Underdogs Gallery's wall on Rua Fernando Palha. Industrial Lisbon converting itself in real time.
itinerary.evening: **Prado**, Travessa das Pedras Negras 2 — produce-led, book 2–3 weeks, €45–60pp. Late drink at Pensão Amor, Rua do Alecrim 19.
itinerary.dayStats: 8.6 km, flat; bus 794/210; Azulejo 10:00–13:00 & 14:00–18:00; taproom pints €4–5.

itinerary.title: Estuary morning and departure
itinerary.morning: Ferry Cais do Sodré → **Cacilhas** (10 min, ~€1.55) for the reverse skyline and lunch at **Ponto Final**, Rua do Ginjal 72, booked ahead. Or Elevador de Santa Justa at 08:30, before the queue.
itinerary.afternoon: Last pastéis at **Manteigaria**, Rua do Loreto 2 (€1.40, at the marble counter), then Metro Red Line to LIS from Alameda.
itinerary.evening: Flight out; a closing vermouth at Comida Independente, Rua Cais do Tojo 28, if the slot is late.
itinerary.dayStats: 4.5 km; ferry 10 min; airport 25 min from Baixa-Chiado with one change; allow 2 h before departure.

accommodationStrategy.name: Casa Balthazar
accommodationStrategy.description: Mid-slope between Baixa and Bairro Alto, so both are downhill and you never need a taxi. Private terraces, plunge pool, and a small lift up from Rossio that saves sixty steps a day. €160–210 double with breakfast; ask for a Tagus-facing room.

accommodationStrategy.name: Memmo Alfama
accommodationStrategy.description: The right base if Alfama is the priority: red-tiled pool terrace over the Tagus, in a lane no tour group reaches with wheeled bags. Steep approach — taxi to Largo de São Rafael on arrival. €190–260.

accommodationStrategy.name: Casa Amora
accommodationStrategy.description: Quieter and greener for a full week, with kitchenettes for the Mercado de Campo de Ourique haul and a flat ten minutes to Metro Rato. €130–180.

logistics.connectivity: Full EU roaming, no local SIM needed for EU residents. 4G/5G is complete; download offline maps only for the Pena woods, where signal drops.
logistics.emergency: 112 for everything. Tourist police post at Palácio Foz, Praça dos Restauradores. EU/EHIC applies; insurance still matters because timed monument tickets are strictly non-refundable.
logistics.weather: The *nortada*, a hard afternoon northerly, cools summer but leaves riverfront terraces cold after 19:00 even in June. Autumn downpours make calçada portuguesa genuinely slippery — rubber soles, never leather.
logistics.bookingWindows: Pena 5–7 days; Jerónimos/Belém 1–2 weeks; Prado and 100 Maneiras 2–3 weeks; fado houses 3–5 days. Gulbenkian, MAAT and Azulejo are same-day.
logistics.money: Euro, contactless everywhere, though small tascas prefer cash. Use Multibanco ATMs, not Euronet. Tip by rounding up, 5–10% at dinner. The *couvert* is chargeable — decline it.
logistics.transportRules: Validate on every boarding including trams and funiculars; inspectors work 28E and 15E hard. Some CP gates reject zapping for Sintra — buy at the Rossio counter if so. Santa Justa is €6.15 standalone but included in the 24h Carris pass.
logistics.permits: City tourist tax €4 per person per night, capped at seven nights, collected at check-out and usually absent from booking-site totals. Drones banned over the historic centre and all Parques de Sintra sites.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable and good. Real risks are pickpockets on tram 28 and at Santa Justa, and harmless drug-hawkers on Rua Augusta. Wet cobbles injure more visitors here than anything else.

proTips: Ride **tram 12E** on the same rails as the 28 for a shorter Alfama loop with a fraction of the crowd — or take the 28 eastbound from Martim Moniz at 07:15.
Load **zapping**, not the 24h pass, unless you'll make five-plus rides that day. Lisbon is a walking city; most days you use two.
For Pena, book the first slot, take bus 434 up and **walk down** through the Parque da Pena past the Chalet da Condessa d'Edla — the half everyone skips.
**Manteigaria over Pastéis de Belém** when time is tight: same custard tart, no 40-minute queue, and you watch the lamination through the window.
**Miradouro da Senhora do Monte** in Graça beats São Pedro de Alcântara at sunset and has a fraction of the buskers — 12 minutes uphill from Largo da Graça.
Most museums close **Monday** (Azulejo, Jerónimos, Ancient Art); the Gulbenkian closes **Tuesday**. Build Monday around the Castelo, Belém exteriors and Marvila.
If Sintra is fogged in before 11:00 — common in spring — reverse the day: Regaleira and the town palace first, Pena at 14:00 when cloud usually lifts.

raw.Day trip: Sintra on the **CP Linha de Sintra** from Rossio, 40 min, ~€2.40 each way, departures every 10–20 min from 06:00.

trips.title: Little Paris, Then the Bulldozers: Seven Days in Bucharest

bestPeriod.window: mid-May to mid-June and the whole of September — terrace weather without the 38 °C concrete oven
bestPeriod.avoid: mid-July to late August (heat, and half the good kitchens close for the month)

accommodation.note: €350–€630 (€50–€90/night for a good central room)

food.note: €175–€315 (€25–€45/day — Bucharest is still startlingly cheap for the quality)

transport.note: €25–€60 (metro and surface passes, one airport bus, two day-trip transfers)

activities.note: €90–€170 (Palace of Parliament, Primăverii, Village Museum, Therme)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy

trips.gatewayAirport: Henri Coandă (OTP), 17 km north. **Express bus 783** runs OTP → Piața Unirii via Piața Victoriei roughly every 20–30 min, ~40–60 min; buy the card at the STB kiosk in the arrivals hall before boarding. Rail links to Gara de Nord also run from the airport halt.
trips.summary: Bucharest does not tidy itself up for you. A Brâncovenesc monastery church sits in a hole below street level with an office block on top of it; a 1930s Modernist apartment slab by a Dada founder faces a boulevard…
trips.hook: Bucharest does not tidy itself up for you. A Brâncovenesc monastery church sits in a hole below street level with an office block on top of it; a 1930s Modernist apartment slab by a Dada founder faces a boulevard that ate a whole neighbourhood. Seven days here is not padding — it is the minimum needed to walk the belle-époque villas, the interwar concrete, the Ceaușescu Civic Centre and the parks, and to eat properly while doing it.

snapshot.Start / End: București → București
snapshot.Getting there: Henri Coandă (OTP), 17 km north. **Express bus 783** runs OTP → Piața Unirii via Piața Victoriei roughly every 20–30 min, ~40–60 min; buy the card at the STB kiosk in the arrivals hall before boarding. Rail links to Gara de Nord also run from the airport halt.

itinerary.title: Centrul Vechi, at ground level
itinerary.morning: Bus 783 in, drop bags, and walk straight into **Lipscani**. Start at **Stavropoleos monastery** (1724) — the finest Brâncovenesc stone carving in the city, a courtyard of salvaged tombstones, and total silence forty metres from the bar strip.
itinerary.afternoon: **Hanul lui Manuc**, the 1808 merchants' caravanserai, still built around its wooden-galleried courtyard. Then the ruins of the **Curtea Veche**, Vlad Țepeș's princely court, and the Old Princely Court church, the oldest in Bucharest.
itinerary.evening: **Caru' cu Bere** on Str. Stavropoleos — 1899, neo-Gothic vaults, stained glass, and yes it is touristed, and yes the *mici* and the house beer are still correct. Book, or queue.

itinerary.title: Calea Victoriei, end to end
itinerary.morning: From Piața Victoriei walk south. The **Romanian Athenaeum** (1888, Albert Galleron) — go inside; the circular fresco of Romanian history runs the full drum. Then the **Revolution Square** ensemble: the former **Central Committee** building and **the balcony** from which Ceaușescu addressed the crowd on 21 December 1989 and heard it turn on him.
itinerary.afternoon: South past the **CEC Palace** (1900, Paul Gottereau) with its glass dome, into **Cărturești Carusel** — a bookshop in a gutted 19th-century Chrissoveloni bank, six white floors of light.
itinerary.evening: **Lacrimi și Sfinți** on Str. Șepcari — Romanian ingredients, unfussy, a menu that changes on what came in. One of the few places doing serious regional cooking without folklore.

itinerary.title: The Civic Centre and what it replaced
itinerary.morning: **Palace of Parliament** tour — booked, ID in hand. The second-largest administrative building on earth by floor area after the Pentagon, 1,100 rooms, and a marble bill that beggared the country. The guide will give you the numbers; the roof terrace gives you the view down Bd. Unirii.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the boulevard east, then hunt the buried churches: **Schitul Maicilor** and **Mihai Vodă**, both moved on rails in the 1980s and now boxed behind apartment blocks. This half-day is the point of the trip.
itinerary.evening: Metro M2 south to **Bellu cemetery** if the light holds — Romania's Père-Lachaise, with Eminescu, Caragiale and Enescu, and funerary sculpture worth an hour. Then dinner at **Hanu' Berarilor**, in one of its restored 19th-century houses.

itinerary.title: Cotroceni, and the two great museums
itinerary.morning: **Cotroceni Palace** — the royal residence turned presidential complex; the museum wing is visited **by advance-booked guided tour with ID**, same rule as the Parliament [VERIFY: current Cotroceni booking procedure and price]. Then walk the surrounding streets: Dr. Lister, Dr. Clunet, the Neo-Romanian villa stock at its densest.
itinerary.afternoon: North to Piața Victoriei for the **Muzeul Țăranului Român** (Romanian Peasant Museum) — textiles, icons on glass, and a whole wooden church reassembled inside. It is a design object as much as an ethnographic one.
itinerary.evening: Next door, **Grigore Antipa** natural history museum stays open late enough on some days to combine [VERIFY: current Antipa closing time]. Dinner at **Zexe Zahana** — Bucharest's argument for its own historic recipes, cooked from archive menus.

itinerary.title: Armenească, Mântuleasa and the quiet streets
itinerary.morning: **Armenească**: the Armenian church of 1911, the low 19th-century houses, and the best-preserved fabric of pre-war residential Bucharest. Slow, flat, almost no traffic.
itinerary.afternoon: **Mântuleasa** — the street Mircea Eliade made into a novella — plus the **Foișorul de Foc** fire tower and Grădina Icoanei. Hunt Marcel Iancu's Modernist houses on Str. Negustori and around Dorobanți; several are marked.
itinerary.evening: **Kane** in the Dorobanți grid — tasting-menu cooking with Romanian produce, one of the city's best kitchens. Book a week out. Afterwards, **Nomad Skybar** in the old town for the rooftop, which is the only way to see the Civic Centre's scale at night.

itinerary.title: Out of town: Mogoșoaia and Snagov
itinerary.morning: **Mogoșoaia Palace**, 14 km north-west, built 1698–1702 by Constantin Brâncoveanu and the definitional example of the style named after him — loggia, carved stone, a lake behind. Forty minutes by car, or bus from Laromet [VERIFY: current Mogoșoaia entry price and opening days].
itinerary.afternoon: **Snagov** — the lake and the island monastery reached by boat, where tradition (not evidence) puts the grave of Vlad Țepeș. It is a genuinely peaceful afternoon and the woodland around the lake is the closest real forest to the city.
itinerary.evening: Back for something simple in the centre: *ciorbă*, *tochitură*, a glass of Fetească Neagră.

itinerary.title: Primăverii, the park, and the water
itinerary.morning: **Primăverii Palace** on Bd. Primăverii — the Ceaușescu family villa, opened to visitors in 2016 and left as it was: the peacock mosaics, the indoor pool, Elena's wardrobes. Timed tickets, book ahead.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk into **Herăstrău / Regele Mihai I park** and along the lake to the **Muzeul Satului (Village Museum)** — 300-odd relocated rural buildings from every Romanian region on 100 open-air hectares, one of the oldest such museums in Europe (founded 1936) [VERIFY: current Village Museum ticket price].
itinerary.evening: If your flight is late, **Therme București** at Balotești sits between the city and the airport — Europe's largest thermal water complex, palm houses, slides and quiet pools, with a shuttle from Piața Presei [VERIFY: 2026 Therme entry tiers and shuttle timetable]. Shower, change, and go straight to OTP.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Cișmigiu
accommodationStrategy.description: a 1912 building on the edge of Cișmigiu gardens, two minutes from the M1/M3 Izvor and Universitate axis, and walking distance to both the old town and the Civic Centre — the two poles of this itinerary.
accommodationStrategy.booking: online, 3–4 weeks ahead; ask for a room off the boulevard, which is loud.

accommodationStrategy.name: Rembrandt Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: inside the old town but on the quieter northern edge, so you get Lipscani on foot without the 03:00 bar noise. Small, long-established, and the staff genuinely know the restaurant scene.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct, 4–6 weeks ahead — it has few rooms and fills.

accommodationStrategy.name: Epoque Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: the quietest good hotel in the centre, with a pool and a parking option that matters if you hire a car for the Mogoșoaia and Snagov day. Ten minutes' walk to Calea Victoriei.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct or online, 4 weeks ahead.

logistics.connectivity: 5G across the whole city and free Wi-Fi on much of the metro and in cafés. Romanian mobile data is among the fastest and cheapest in the EU; a local eSIM is barely worth the trouble for a week if you have EU roaming.
logistics.emergency: **112**, English answered. Pharmacies marked *farmacie*; several near Piața Romană are 24-hour.
logistics.weather: Bucharest sits on a plain with no relief — July and August routinely exceed 35 °C and the concrete holds it overnight. May and September are the reason to come. Sudden violent thunderstorms in late spring flood underpasses; give the metro an extra fifteen minutes.
logistics.bookingWindows: Palace of Parliament 5–10 days (weekends longer). Primăverii Palace 3–7 days. Kane a week. Caru' cu Bere for dinner, 2–3 days. Everything else walk-in.
logistics.money: Romanian **leu (RON)**; €1 ≈ 5.10–5.25 RON. Cards are accepted almost everywhere including buses and markets; keep 100–150 RON cash for church donations, small markets and the Snagov boatman. Romania is in the EU but **not** the euro — do not assume euro acceptance.
logistics.transportRules: Validate or tap on entry to every STB vehicle; inspectors are active on the trams. Metro runs roughly 05:00–23:00. If you hire a car for the day trips, a **rovinietă** e-vignette is compulsory on national roads outside the city: category A costs **€3.50 (~18 RON)** for one day or **€6 (~31 RON)** for ten days — there is no seven-day product. Buy it at any fuel station or online before you drive.
logistics.permits: No permits. Photo ID is a hard requirement for Parliament and Cotroceni. Photography is restricted in parts of the Parliament and forbidden in Primăverii's private rooms; drone flying over the Civic Centre is prohibited.

proTips: Book the Palace of Parliament for **09:00 or 09:30**, the first slot. Groups arrive from 11:00, the rooms echo, and the early tour moves at half the pace.
Carry your passport every day, not a photocopy. Two of the best visits in this file — Parliament and Cotroceni — refuse entry on a photocopy or a phone photo.
Use the metro north–south (M2) and walk east–west. The M2 crosses the whole city in 20 minutes; the surface equivalent at rush hour is an hour.
Go to Bellu cemetery at 16:00 on a weekday. Low light, empty avenues, and the sculpture reads properly — it is the one place in Bucharest that rewards being slow.
Order *ciorbă de burtă* once and *ciorbă rădăuțeană* once, and decide. The first is tripe and garlic and sour cream; the second is chicken, gentler, and the one to start with.
Ask at any old-town bar for a *palincă* rather than a vodka. The Transylvanian double-distilled plum spirit runs 40–55% and is the house drink that locals actually order.
Do Therme on the way to the airport, not as a day trip. It is 20 minutes from OTP and 45 from the centre — the geography only works one way.

raw.Walkable neighbourhood blocks: **Centrul Vechi** (Lipscani, Str. Franceză, Hanul lui Manuc, Stavropoleos) — dense, flat, one hour end to end. **Calea Victoriei** — the spine, 2.7 km from Piața Victoriei to Splaiul Independenței, walkable in a morning with stops. **Cotroceni** — a grid of belle-époque and Neo-Romanian villas around the palace and the Botanical Garden, best on foot for two hours. **Dorobanți / Primăverii** — leafy, embassy-heavy, low-rise; the Ceaușescu family villa sits in it. **Armenească and Mântuleasa** — the two quietest historic quarters in the centre, half-restored, entirely residential. **Uranus / Casa Poporului** — not walkable in the ordinary sense; the Civic Centre was built at a scale that defeats pedestrians, and you cross it deliberately. **Herăstrău / Regele Mihai I** — the big northern park, 3 km of lakeside path.
raw.Transit passes and fares: The metro is run by **Metrorex** (lines **M1** circle-ish, **M2** north–south, **M3** west, **M4** north-west, **M5** Drumul Taberei); the buses, trams and trolleybuses are **STB**. They use different ticketing: STB sells the reloadable **Multiplu**/Activ card, metro sells its own card or contactless bank-card entry at the gates. Rough figures: STB single trip ~3 RON (€0.60), 24-hour ~10 RON, weekly ~20 RON; metro 2-trip ~6 RON, 10-trip ~25 RON, 24-hour ~10 RON, weekly ~30 RON; bus 783 to the airport carries a supplement over the standard fare [VERIFY: 2026 STB and Metrorex tariffs and the current 783 fare]. Contactless bank-card tap-in works on both networks and is the simplest option for a week.
raw.The honest transport note: Bucharest traffic is genuinely severe — among the worst-congested cities in Europe — and a 6 km taxi at 18:00 can take 45 minutes. **The metro plus walking beats taxis** for almost every itinerary in this file. Use Bolt or Uber for late nights and the two day trips only.
raw.Cultural booking timelines: The **Palace of Parliament** is the binding one: tours must be **booked in advance online** and you must carry a **passport or national ID card** matching the booking, checked at the entrance. Turn up without it and you are refused, no exceptions. Book 5–10 days ahead in season, longer for weekends; the standard tour runs ~45–75 minutes and costs around 60–70 RON [VERIFY: 2026 Palace of Parliament tour price and booking lead time]. The **Primăverii Palace** (Ceaușescu's residence) sells timed slots and sells out days ahead in summer [VERIFY: current ticket price]. Everything else — Antipa, the Peasant Museum, the Village Museum — is same-day.
raw.Architectural focal points, with periods: **Brâncovenesc** (late 17th–early 18th c.): Stavropoleos monastery church, Kretzulescu church, Antim monastery — carved stone, twisted colonnettes, deep porches. **Neo-Romanian** (from c. 1886): the national style invented by **Ion Mincu**, who fused Brâncovenesc detail with Beaux-Arts planning — Casa Vernescu and the Central School for Girls are his; the style saturates Cotroceni. **Interwar Bucharest Modernism** (1929–1940): **Horia Creangă**'s ARO Building on Bd. Magheru (now Cinema Patria), a landmark of European Modernism, and **Marcel Iancu** — who co-founded **Dada** at the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich in 1916 before returning to Bucharest to build some thirty houses, then emigrating to Palestine in 1941. **Socialist Civic Centre** (1980s): Bd. Unirii and the Palace of Parliament, designed under **Anca Petrescu**.
raw.Systematisation — what was destroyed: After the 1977 earthquake, Ceaușescu's *sistematizare* programme levelled roughly a fifth of the historic centre to build the Civic Centre: the Uranus and Antim quarters, some 40,000 people displaced, and around **two dozen churches** demolished or hidden. Several were physically **moved on rails** — Schitul Maicilor and the Mihai Vodă church were rolled hundreds of metres and walled in behind blocks, where they still stand, invisible from the street. Look for them; they are the best argument this city makes.

trips.title: Belgrade at the Confluence: Kafanas, Concrete and the Sava
trips.subRegion: Belgrade, with Vojvodina & Šumadija as gateways

bestPeriod.window: Late April–mid June & September–mid October
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (35°C in a valley basin, splavovi overrun); January–February brings the košava wind and grey days.
bestPeriod.raw: Late April–mid June & September–mid October

accommodation.note: Central boutique double, per-person share, Dorćol or Vračar

food.note: Kafana main 900–1,600 RSD (€8–14), coffee 200 RSD, rakija 250–400 RSD

transport.note: City transport is fare-free; cost is airport transfers and the Novi Sad rail day

activities.note: Tesla, Museum of Yugoslavia, Kalemegdan sites, Novi Sad entries

profile.difficultyNote: 2 — 7–10 km a day; the only real climbs are Kalemegdan's ramparts and the Karađorđeva escarpment up to Kosančićev Venac.

trips.gatewayAirport: BEG — Nikola Tesla Airport; A1 minibus to Slavija 30 min, bus 72 to Zeleni Venac 45 min, taxi with an official rank voucher ~2,200–2,500 RSD (€19–21)
trips.summary: Belgrade sits where the Sava meets the Danube and has been destroyed and rebuilt about forty times, which is why it reads as a collage rather than a set piece: Habsburg Zemun, Ottoman-then-Austrian Kalemegdan, 19th-century Stari Grad, socialist Novi Beograd across the river. This week walks all four, deliberately including the buildings most tourists ignore — the Genex Tower, the Museum of Yugoslavia's marble hush, the bomb-damaged General Staff ruins on Nemanjina. Eating is in kafanas, drinking is late and often on a river barge. Prices are the lowest of any capital in this collection. Serbia is outside the EU: budget for roaming and carry dinars.

itinerary.title: Arrival, Knez Mihailova, Kalemegdan
itinerary.morning: A1 minibus to Slavija, drop bags, walk down **Knez Mihailova**'s pedestrian spine. Coffee at **Kafeterija** on Kralja Petra.
itinerary.afternoon: **Kalemegdan Fortress** — the Sahat Kula clock tower, the Ružica church with its chandelier of spent shell casings, the **Military Museum** (300 RSD), and the Victor monument at the confluence viewpoint for the Sava-Danube junction.
itinerary.evening: **Skadarlija**, the 19th-century bohemian street: dinner at **Šešir Moj** (Skadarska 21) with *ćevapi* or *karađorđeva šnicla*, live tamburica after 20:00; 1,500–2,200 RSD (€13–19).
itinerary.dayStats: 6.1 km, 70 m ascent; A1 ~400 RSD; city buses fare-free; Kalemegdan open 24h, museums 10:00–17:00.
itinerary.sleep: Mama Shelter Belgrade, Kneza Miloša 60, Savski Venac.

itinerary.title: Tesla, Vračar and Saint Sava
itinerary.morning: **Nikola Tesla Museum**, Krunska 51 (600 RSD, tours in English hourly) — the urn with his ashes, the working Tesla coil demonstration, and original apparatus; book ahead.
itinerary.afternoon: **Temple of Saint Sava** (free) — the crypt's Byzantine-revival frescoes are darker and better than the main space, and the 2020 gold-ground dome mosaic is genuinely the largest of its kind. Then **Kalenić Market** and the Vračar streets around Njegoševa.
itinerary.evening: **Iva New Balkan Cuisine**, Ivan-begova 12 — Vojvodina produce reworked, tasting menu ~4,500–6,000 RSD (€38–51), book 5–7 days. Cheaper: **Zavičaj**, Gavrila Principa 77.
itinerary.dayStats: 7.3 km; trolleybus 19/22 fare-free; Tesla 10:00–18:00, closed Mondays; Saint Sava 07:00–19:00.

itinerary.title: Yugoslavia, Dedinje and the concrete
itinerary.morning: Bus 40/41 to the **Museum of Yugoslavia**, Botićeva 6 (500 RSD combined) — the **House of Flowers** holds Tito's tomb, the relay-baton collection is the sharpest object lesson in the country's history, and the Old Museum handles it critically rather than nostalgically.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk down to Dedinje's diplomatic villas, then to Nemanjina for **Dobrović's ruined General Staff** buildings — the 1999 damage left in place. Continue to the Beograđanka tower.
itinerary.evening: **Ambar** at Beton Hala, Karađorđeva 2–4 (Balkan small plates, riverside, book 3–4 days, €25–35pp), then a drink in **Savamala** at Ludost or KC Grad.
itinerary.dayStats: 8.5 km; buses 40/41 fare-free; Museum of Yugoslavia 10:00–18:00, closed Mondays.

itinerary.title: Novi Sad and Fruška Gora day trip
itinerary.morning: Soko train from **Beograd Centar (Prokop)**, ~35 min, 1,000–1,400 RSD. Walk Zmaj Jovina to **Trg Slobode** and the neo-Gothic **Name of Mary Church**, then over the bridge to **Petrovaradin Fortress** for the upside-down clock tower and the Danube panorama.
itinerary.afternoon: Taxi or arranged driver into **Fruška Gora** for two monasteries — **Krušedol** (1509, Branković endowment) and **Novo Hopovo** (16th-century frescoes). Budget 4,000–6,000 RSD for a half-day car.
itinerary.evening: Return train by 20:00. Late kafana at **Šumatovačka**, Šumatovačka 78, for grilled meat and a house rakija.
itinerary.dayStats: 7.4 km walked; train 35 min each way, ~2,400 RSD return; Petrovaradin grounds free, museum 400 RSD.

itinerary.title: Zemun and the Danube bank
itinerary.morning: Bus 15/84 to **Zemun** (fare-free). Walk **Gospodska** and the Baroque-fronted lanes, then climb to the **Gardoš Tower** (1896, Millennium tower, 200 RSD) for the confluence view.
itinerary.afternoon: Fish lunch on **Zemunski Kej** at **Šaran**, Kej Oslobođenja 53 (grilled *smuđ* or fish soup, 1,800–2,600 RSD), then walk the quay toward the Great War Island (Veliko Ratno Ostrvo) viewpoint.
itinerary.evening: Back into town for **splavovi** — river barges on the Sava and Danube banks. Freestyler and Barka are the mainstream end; Ludost and 20/44 the more interesting. No cover before 23:00 on most.
itinerary.dayStats: 8.8 km, 60 m ascent; buses 15/84 fare-free, 25–35 min; Gardoš 10:00–22:00 in summer.

itinerary.title: Art, markets and the old core
itinerary.morning: **National Museum of Serbia**, Trg Republike 1a (300 RSD, free Sundays) — the Miroslav Gospel facsimile, Vinča figurines, and a strong 19th–20th-century Serbian painting floor.
itinerary.afternoon: **Kosančićev Venac**, the cobbled bluff above the Sava with the burnt National Library site, then **Bajrakli Mosque** (1575, the city's only surviving Ottoman mosque) on Gospodar Jevremova, and the Dorćol streets around Strahinjića Bana.
itinerary.evening: **Salon 1905** in Zemun or **Dva Jelena** in Skadarlija for the traditional version. Rakija flight at **Rakia Bar**, Dobračina 5 — ask for *dunja* (quince) and *viljamovka*.
itinerary.dayStats: 6.7 km; National Museum 10:00–18:00, Thu to 20:00, closed Mondays; rakija 250–400 RSD a measure.

itinerary.title: Confluence morning and departure
itinerary.morning: Walk or cycle the **Sava Promenada** past Beton Hala to the Branko Bridge, or take the short boat to **Veliko Ratno Ostrvo** in summer. Coffee at Pastis, Strahinjića Bana.
itinerary.afternoon: Burek from **Trpković**, Nemanjina 32 (before 11:00 or it is gone), then A1 minibus or bus 72 to BEG.
itinerary.evening: Flight out.
itinerary.dayStats: 4.6 km; A1 30 min ~400 RSD; BEG needs 2 h for non-Schengen departures.

accommodationStrategy.name: Mama Shelter Belgrade
accommodationStrategy.description: Central without being in the Knez Mihailova crush, with a rooftop bar and a ten-minute flat walk to both Saint Sava and the Sava riverfront. Reliable air conditioning matters in a valley city that traps August heat. €80–120 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Moskva
accommodationStrategy.description: The 1908 Secessionist landmark, green Pécs ceramic on the façade, and the single most Belgrade address there is. Rooms are dated for the price but the location and the ground-floor café are the point. €110–150.

accommodationStrategy.name: Square Nine
accommodationStrategy.description: The best hotel in the country, a Leman-designed interior on a quiet square two minutes from Kalemegdan, with a pool and a serious breakfast. €200–280, and worth it if a week of kafanas needs one soft landing.

logistics.connectivity: **Non-EU roaming.** EU "roam like at home" does not apply, though most EU operators now apply a Western Balkans roaming cap — check your tariff before landing or you will pay per-megabyte. A local Yettel, A1 or MTS prepaid SIM costs about 500–1,000 RSD with several GB; passport required at purchase.
logistics.emergency: 112 works; direct lines are 192 police, 194 ambulance, 193 fire. Urgentni Centar on Pasterova is the main ER. **Serbia is outside the EU and outside EHIC** — take proper travel insurance with medical cover; treatment is not reciprocal.
logistics.weather: The **košava**, a strong south-easterly, blows in autumn and winter at 50–80 km/h, closing splavovi and making the Kalemegdan ramparts genuinely cold. Summer thunderstorms arrive over Novi Beograd fast in late afternoon.
logistics.bookingWindows: Tesla Museum 2–4 days; Iva New Balkan Cuisine 5–7 days; Ambar 3–4 days; Skadarlija kafanas 1–2 days at weekends; Soko trains to Novi Sad can be bought same-day but sell out on Friday and Sunday evenings.
logistics.money: **Serbian dinar (RSD)**, roughly 117 RSD to €1. Cards work in hotels, malls and modern restaurants; kafanas, markets, taxis and Skadarlija musicians are cash. Change money at licensed *menjačnica* booths, never at the airport, and never accept euro prices. Tip 10% in restaurants, round up in taxis.
logistics.transportRules: All regular city transport has been fare-free since January 2025 — no ticket, no card, no validation, and nobody will ask. Do not let a taxi driver refuse the meter; use the CarGo or Yandex app, or take a voucher taxi from the airport kiosk. Serbia is outside Schengen, so allow proper time for the passport queue at BEG.
logistics.permits: A small per-night residence tax (roughly 150–200 RSD) is added by hotels. Foreign visitors are technically required to be **registered with the police within 24 hours of arrival** — hotels do this automatically, private-apartment hosts sometimes do not, so ask for the *beli karton* registration slip. Photographing military and government buildings is prohibited.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable in Belgrade. Petty crime is low; the genuine risks are aggressive driving and unregulated taxis at the airport and Slavija. Smoking indoors is still common in kafanas.

proTips: Ask any hotel or private host for the **beli karton** police registration slip. It is rarely checked, but its absence at the border can cause a real problem on exit.
Take a taxi **only from the official airport kiosk**, which prints a fixed-price voucher by zone; the drivers who approach you in arrivals charge three to five times as much.

Belgrade's transport being fare-free makes the **bus 15 to Zemun and the 40/41 to Dedinje** the cheapest sightseeing in Europe — ride the trolleybus 19 the length of the ridge for the city section-view.
The **Museum of Yugoslavia is free on 25 May**, Tito's official birthday, when the relay batons come out and Yugonostalgics turn up in person; it is anthropology as much as history.
Order rakija by fruit, not brand — *dunja* (quince), *kajsija* (apricot), *viljamovka* (pear) — and never mix it with anything. A kafana will bring a house measure for 250–400 RSD.
**Beograd Centar (Prokop)**, not the old Glavna station, is where all intercity trains now leave; it is poorly signed and a 15-minute walk from Slavija, so allow extra time for the Novi Sad train.
Eat burek **before 11:00** — Serbian bakeries make it once, in the morning, and Trpković on Nemanjina sells out by mid-morning.

Splavovi move, close and rebrand every season, and the summer barges on the Danube bank at Zemunski Kej are different venues from the winter Sava ones — check current listings rather than a year-old guide.

raw.Walkable blocks: Stari Grad (Knez Mihailova → Kosančićev Venac → Kalemegdan, 1.4 km with the only real ascent); Dorćol (Cara Dušana → Strahinjića Bana → Skadarlija's cobbled 400 m); Savamala (Karađorđeva → Beton Hala → the Sava riverfront, 1.2 km flat); Vračar (Temple of Saint Sava → Njegoševa → Kalenić market, 1.5 km); Zemun (Gospodska → Zemunski Kej → Gardoš Tower, 1.6 km with a 60 m climb).
raw.Transit pass: none needed — **Belgrade abolished public transport fares on 1 January 2025**, so buses, trams, trolleybuses and BG Voz suburban trains carry no ticket and no validation. The exceptions are the **A1 airport minibus** and E-prefix express minibuses, where you pay the operator directly.
raw.Airport transfer: **A1 minibus**, BEG → Slavija Square, about 30 min, roughly 400 RSD (€3.40), paid on board. **Bus 72** to Zeleni Venac is fare-free but slower (45–55 min). Take a taxi only from the official kiosk in arrivals, which issues a fixed-price voucher by zone — central Belgrade is zone 2, about 2,200–2,500 RSD.
raw.Booking timeline: the **Nikola Tesla Museum** runs timed guided demonstrations and sells out same-day in season — book 2–4 days ahead on nikolateslamuseum.org. **Museum of Yugoslavia** is same-day. **Belgrade Philharmonic** and **National Theatre** release seats about a month out. Kafanas with live music (Šešir Moj, Tri Šešira in Skadarlija) want a 1–2 day call at weekends. Splav clubs are guest-list by Instagram DM on Fridays and Saturdays.
raw.Architectural focal points: the Austrian-rebuilt Baroque gates of Kalemegdan over Ottoman and Roman *Singidunum* foundations; Nikola Dobrović's 1965 General Staff complex on Nemanjina, still ruined from 1999 and now a live preservation argument; Mihajlo Mitrović's 1977 Genex Tower ("Western Gate"), the definitive Yugoslav brutalist object; Aleksandar Deroko and Bogdan Nestorović's Temple of Saint Sava, begun 1935, its 4,000-tonne dome lifted into place in 1989 and mosaics finished in 2020; Zemun's Central-European façades, an actual Habsburg town inside the city.
raw.Eating structure: kafana lunches and dinners (Šumatovačka, Zavičaj), a market morning at Kalenić, one modern kitchen (Iva New Balkan Cuisine or Salon 1905), and river-barge drinking. Reservations are needed only at weekends and for the modern places.
raw.Day trip: **Novi Sad** by Soko high-speed train from **Beograd Centar (Prokop)**, about 35 minutes, roughly 1,000–1,400 RSD (€8.50–12) each way; add Petrovaradin Fortress and, with a taxi or tour, the Fruška Gora monasteries.
