provenance.sourceFormat: md with '## Metadata' bullet block (one file per trip)

trips.title: Lake Towns of the Salzkammergut

bestPeriod.note: July and August fill Hallstatt with coach parties; May and late September give you the same lake light with half the people.

trips.gatewayAirport: Salzburg (SZG)
trips.summary: Three lake towns in seven days, moved through by train and boat, with ceramics, salt mines and long afternoons on the water.
trips.hook: Three bases, two moves, and a week built around the 40-minute train that stitches the Traun valley together. You wake late, walk to a square, eat something involving lake fish or apricots, and get on a boat. The Salzkammergut rewards people who stay put long enough to see the same square twice.

snapshot.Base(s): Gmunden (2 nights) · Bad Ischl (2 nights) · Hallstatt (3 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 70 km of rail between bases; 25–35 km walked over the week; flat lakeshore paths with two optional cable-car days
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Salzburg (SZG), Postbus 150 to Bad Ischl (approx. 1h40) or rail via Attnang-Puchheim onto the Salzkammergutbahn
snapshot.Who It Suits: Slow travellers, ceramics and craft people, families with older children, anyone who would rather sit than tick

itinerary.title: Traunsee, and the first square
itinerary.morning: Land at Salzburg and take the train north to Attnang-Puchheim, then south on the Salzkammergutbahn to Gmunden. Around two hours door to door with one change; the second half runs beside the Traun. Drop bags and do nothing ambitious.
itinerary.afternoon: Gmunden's Rathausplatz is the introduction. The town hall carillon plays on ceramic bells made by the local manufactory — an early sign of what this town is about. Walk the arcade of the Stadtplatz, then out along the Esplanade to the causeway leading to Schloss Ort, the lake castle standing on its own island a few metres offshore.
itinerary.evening: Dinner facing the Traunstein, the blunt limestone wall that closes the far end of the lake. Reinanke (whitefish) is the standard order and it is caught here.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 1. Walking: 4 km. Transfer time: approx. 2h from Salzburg.

itinerary.title: Ceramics day, no alarm
itinerary.morning: Nothing is scheduled before 10:00. When you surface, head to the Gmundner Keramik manufactory on Keramikstraße, working since 1492 and still hand-painting the green-flamed *Grüngeflammt* pattern with a brush pulled across the glaze. The guided workshop tour shows throwing, glazing and painting; the seconds shop beside it is where locals actually buy their plates.
itinerary.afternoon: The K-Hof Kammerhofmuseum in town holds the historical ceramics collection if you want context. Otherwise take the Grünbergseilbahn up to 1,004 m for the treetop walkway and a long look down the Traunsee.
itinerary.evening: Back on the Rathausplatz. Gmunden's farmers' market fills this square on Saturday mornings, roughly 08:00–12:00 — worth timing your week around if the calendar allows.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 1. Walking: 6 km. Transfer time: none.

itinerary.title: Down the valley to the imperial spa
itinerary.morning: Slow breakfast, then the Salzkammergutbahn south to Bad Ischl, about 40 minutes. This is the week's first relocation and the only thing on the agenda.
itinerary.afternoon: Bad Ischl was where the Habsburgs came to take the brine cure, and the town still looks like it. Tour the Kaiservilla and its park, then cross to the Marmorschlössl, Empress Elisabeth's tea house, now a photography museum. Auböckplatz is the working square; the Trinkhalle nearby is the old pump room.
itinerary.evening: Konditorei Zauner, trading since 1832, has two addresses — the original in Pfarrgasse and the Esplanade branch on the river. Order Zaunerstollen and sit outside. Dinner afterwards is best kept light.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 5 km. Transfer time: 40 min by rail.

itinerary.title: Market morning, lake afternoon
itinerary.morning: Bad Ischl's farmers' market sets up on Auböckplatz on Friday afternoons, roughly 12:00–17:00 — smoked Reinanke, Goisererbrot, apricot preserves from the Wachau traders, and Ausseer Lebkuchen. Check the board outside the Tourismusverband, since the hours contract in winter.
itinerary.afternoon: Take the Postbus over to Strobl and on to Sankt Wolfgang, or ride the Wolfgangsee-Schifffahrt across from Strobl. The village is a single lakefront street with the pilgrimage church of St. Wolfgang at its heart — Michael Pacher's carved winged altarpiece of 1481 is the reason to go inside. If the weather is clear, the Schafbergbahn cog railway climbs to 1,783 m in 35 minutes; take the late-afternoon departure and come down in the last light.
itinerary.evening: Back in Bad Ischl for dinner. The Esplanade after dark is empty and floodlit and belongs to residents.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 5 km. Transfer time: approx. 1h20 return by bus and boat.

itinerary.title: A short train, a small ferry
itinerary.morning: The second full lie-in of the week: nothing before 10:00. Pack at your own pace, buy provisions, and take a late-morning train.
itinerary.afternoon: Hallstatt's railway station sits on the wrong side of the lake, which is the best thing about arriving here. The little ferry *Stefanie* meets the trains and crosses in ten minutes, delivering you to the Marktplatz with the village stacked up the cliff behind it. Total transfer from Bad Ischl: under 40 minutes.
itinerary.evening: The Marktplatz, with its Holy Trinity column and painted burgher houses, empties completely after about 17:00 when the coaches leave. That is when Hallstatt becomes the place people photograph. Walk the lakeside path towards Lahn and back.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 3. Walking: 4 km. Transfer time: 25 min rail plus 10 min ferry.

itinerary.title: Salt, bones and the high plateau
itinerary.morning: The funicular from Hallstatt Lahn lifts you to Salzwelten Hallstatt, the oldest working salt mine in the world — 7,000 years of extraction, wooden miners' slides, and an underground salt lake. Book the timed slot online the night before. The Rudolfsturm terrace at the top has the view every postcard uses.
itinerary.afternoon: Down in the village, the Beinhaus beside St. Michael's chapel holds around 1,200 painted skulls, lettered with names and dated with flower crowns — a genuinely local practice that continued into the 1990s. It takes ten quiet minutes.
itinerary.evening: If you want altitude, the Krippenstein cable car from Obertraun (a short bus or boat hop) reaches the 5fingers platform and the Giant Ice Cave. Otherwise stay low, eat Saibling, and go to bed early.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 1. Walking: 7 km. Transfer time: none.

itinerary.title: Gosau water, then out
itinerary.morning: The bus from Hallstatt Lahn runs up to Gosau and the Vorderer Gosausee, where the Dachstein glacier reflects in the water on still mornings. The circuit of the lower lake is flat, 45 minutes, and shockingly quiet compared with the village.
itinerary.afternoon: Back to Hallstatt, one last coffee on the Marktplatz, and the ferry out to the station. Trains north to Attnang-Puchheim connect for Salzburg in around 2h15 total.
itinerary.evening: Departure, or a final night in Salzburg if your flight is early.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 5 km. Transfer time: approx. 2h15 to Salzburg.

accommodationStrategy.name: Seehotel Schwan
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits directly on the Rathausplatz with its own frontage onto the Traunsee, which means the town square, the ferry pier and the station bus all sit within three minutes of the door. Rooms on the lake side are the ones to ask for. Useful for a car-free arrival, since nothing about the first two days requires driving.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead for June and September.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Goldener Ochs
accommodationStrategy.description: A long-established family house a few minutes from Auböckplatz, the Kaiservilla park and the station, with its own small spa fed by the town's brine tradition. The scale is right for a two-night stop: quiet corridors, an actual breakfast room rather than a buffet hall, and staff who will tell you whether the Schafbergbahn is running.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Seehotel Grüner Baum
accommodationStrategy.description: Directly on the Marktplatz with rooms facing the lake, which matters enormously here: you are inside the village when the day-trippers leave, not parked in Obertraun. Small, old, and creaky in a good way. Confirm luggage arrangements in advance, as the village core is closed to through traffic.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 months ahead for any date in summer.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European. Austria specifics: 144 ambulance, 133 police, 140 mountain rescue (Bergrettung). Mobile coverage is good in the valleys and patchy on the Dachstein plateau.
logistics.weather: The Salzkammergut is one of the wettest corners of Austria; rain arrives fast off the Dachstein and clears just as fast, so do not rewrite a day for a grey morning. Cards work almost everywhere, but market stalls and huts want cash — carry €50 in small notes.

other.label: Rail
other.text: The Salzkammergutbahn is single-track; trains run roughly hourly and thin out sharply after 20:00. Travelling as a pair or more, buy an Einfach-Raus-Ticket for a whole day of ÖBB regional services.

other.label: The Hallstatt ferry
other.text: *Stefanie* runs to the train timetable, not its own. The last crossing is early evening.

other.label: Hallstatt traffic
other.text: The village caps coaches and through-traffic. If you drive, use car parks P1–P3 and walk in; there is no parking in the centre.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Almost everything closes on Sunday afternoons outside the tourist core, and many Gmunden shops shut at midday on Saturday. Cable cars and the Schafbergbahn run seasonally, typically May to late October, with a service pause for maintenance in shoulder weeks.

other.label: Drones
other.text: Flying over Hallstatt and the lake is heavily restricted; assume no, and check Austro Control's Dronespace app first.

proTips: Buy the Salzkammergut Card at any tourist office if you are travelling May–October. It shaves 25–30% off cable cars, the Schafbergbahn, boats and the salt mine, and pays for itself by around Day 4 on this itinerary.
Take the Schafbergbahn's last upward departure, not the first. Morning trains carry the coach groups; the late run descends in low sun, half empty.
At Gmundner Keramik ask for the *Zweite Wahl* room: the seconds are flawed in ways you will not find and cost roughly half. Bring bubble wrap if you plan to fly them home.
Hallstatt's Marktplatz is unusable between 10:00 and 16:30 and near-empty either side. Plan photography and coffee for 07:30 or 18:30 and spend the middle of the day in the mine or on the water.
Book Salzwelten online the previous evening. Mid-morning slots sell out first; 13:00 is nearly always free, and the mine is cooler than the village.
Konditorei Zauner is two shops: the Pfarrgasse original has the queue, the Esplanade branch has the river terrace and the same kitchen.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 70 km of rail between bases; 25–35 km walked over the week; flat lakeshore paths with two optional cable-car days
raw.Who It Suits: Slow travellers, ceramics and craft people, families with older children, anyone who would rather sit than tick

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 70 km of rail between bases; 25–35 km walked over the week; flat lakeshore paths with two optional cable-car days
typeSpecific.audience: Slow travellers, ceramics and craft people, families with older children, anyone who would rather sit than tick

packingNotes: A genuinely waterproof shell, not a showerproof jacket. This is a wet region even in September.
Shoes with grip for wet cobbles — Hallstatt's lanes are polished stone on a slope.
A warm mid-layer for the Schafberg and Krippenstein: it can be 15°C cooler than the lakeshore.
Swimwear and a quick-dry towel: the Traunsee and Wolfgangsee are swimmable from late June to early September, with free public bathing spots in every town.
Cash in small notes for markets and huts.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Hallstatt is full and you hate it.** Retreat to Obertraun across the lake, five minutes by boat, where the same shoreline has almost no visitors. Time your village hours for early and late.
**Rain for three straight days.** Go indoors: Salzwelten (a constant, dry 8°C), the Kaiservilla, the K-Hof ceramics collection and the Salzkammergut-Therme in Bad Ischl.
**The Schafbergbahn or a cable car is closed for wind or maintenance.** Substitute the Wolfgangsee boat circuit or the flat Hallstatt–Obertraun lakeside path, neither of which depends on machinery.
**You miss the last ferry to Hallstatt station.** A taxi around the lake takes 25 minutes and roughly €35–€45; book it through your hotel.

trips.title: Herzegovina Slowly: Mostar, Blagaj, Počitelj & Trebinje

bestPeriod.window: Late April–mid June & mid September–late October
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (Mostar's old bridge is shoulder-to-shoulder with cruise excursions from Dubrovnik and the Neretva valley hits 38°C) and January, when much of Počitelj and Stolac shuts
bestPeriod.raw: Late April–mid June & mid September–late October

accommodation.note: €45–€80 pp/night in historic-house hotels and family pansions

food.note: Mains 12–25 BAM (€6–€13); a full dinner with wine under €20

transport.note: Rental car with cross-border permission, or a driver at €80–€110 a day

activities.note: Kravice entry, tekke, museums, winery tastings, coppersmith session

profile.difficultyNote: 2 — Počitelj's stone stairs and Mostar's polished cobbles are the hardest things here; everything else is flat

trips.gatewayAirport: DBV — Dubrovnik, 1 h 50 to Trebinje and 3 h to Mostar including the border; SJJ Sarajevo is 2 h 30 to Mostar and better for onward rail
trips.summary: Herzegovina is stone, water and coffee, and the trick to it is refusing to do it in two days. This week gives you four nights in Mostar's old town and three in Trebinje, a plane-shaded southern town most visitors never reach, with the Ottoman villages of the Neretva — Blagaj, Počitelj, Stolac — filling the middle. The pace is set by the coffee ritual: a džezva, a fildžan, a sugar cube held in the teeth, and forty minutes that cannot be shortened. There is one town move, two afternoons with nothing in them, and a deliberate rule of arriving at the famous places either before 09:30 or after 17:00. It suits travellers who want the layered, complicated version of the Balkans rather than a bridge photograph.

itinerary.title: Into the Neretva valley
itinerary.morning: Fly to Dubrovnik, collect a car with written cross-border permission, and drive north-east into Bosnia. The border formalities are straightforward but not fast; budget an hour.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive in Mostar, park outside the old town, and check in. First walk: the Stari Most at 18:00, when the light goes gold and the divers of the Mostar Diving Club are still collecting for the 24 m jump.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Šadrvan, at the top of Kujundžiluk under vines — begova čorba, ćevapi, and stuffed vine leaves. Then a džezva of coffee somewhere with a view of the bridge lit up.
itinerary.dayStats: DBV–Mostar 140 km / 3 h with the border. Stari Most deck 21 m above the Neretva; divers jump around 24 m. Mains 12–25 BAM (€6–€13).

itinerary.title: Blagaj's spring and the old town after dark
itinerary.morning: Out to Blagaj at 09:00 before the coaches. The tekke sits directly on the water beneath the cliff; sit inside on the carpets for ten minutes rather than photographing it from the terrace. Coffee afterwards at a riverside table where the Buna is loud enough to make conversation an effort.
itinerary.afternoon: Back into Mostar for the parts most visitors skip: the Karađoz Beg Mosque, the Kriva Ćuprija (the small crooked bridge that was the practice run for the big one), and the Bišćevića Ćošak Turkish house.
itinerary.evening: Climb the Koski Mehmed Pasha minaret for the classic bridge view at 18:30, then eat at Hindin Han on the Radobolja stream.
itinerary.dayStats: Mostar–Blagaj 12 km / 20 min. Buna spring average flow around 43 m³/s; cliff above it roughly 200 m. Tekke entry ~6 BAM (€3). Minaret ~5 BAM (€2.50).

itinerary.title: Počitelj, Kravice, and then nothing
itinerary.morning: South down the Neretva to Počitelj — an Ottoman fortified village of about 400 people, essentially one long stone staircase. Climb to the fort, come down slowly, and buy figs on the steps.
itinerary.afternoon: Kravice waterfalls on the Trebižat, a 25 m curtain into a swimmable pool. Then stop. Back to Mostar by 16:30, and use the rest of the day for the courtyard and a book.
itinerary.evening: Late, unhurried dinner at Konoba Taurus, then coffee in the bazaar after the day-trippers have gone. Mostar is a different town after 20:00.
itinerary.dayStats: Mostar–Počitelj 30 km / 35 min; Počitelj–Kravice 25 km / 30 min; Kravice–Mostar 40 km / 45 min. Kravice entry ~10–20 BAM (€5–€10). Počitelj stairs 90 m of climb.

itinerary.title: Stolac, the stećci, and the Bregava
itinerary.morning: East to Stolac, stopping first at the Radimlja necropolis on the approach road — the carved arms on the stećci are the single most haunting thing in Herzegovina, and it takes fifteen minutes to walk the field.
itinerary.afternoon: Stolac itself: the Bregava river running through the middle of town past old mills, the Begovina quarter of Ottoman houses, and the Vidoška fortress above. It is a town still visibly repairing itself from the 1990s, and worth the slow look.
itinerary.evening: Return to Mostar for the coppersmithing hour on Kujundžiluk, then a last dinner in the old town.
itinerary.dayStats: Mostar–Stolac 45 km / 50 min. Radimlja holds roughly 130 stećci; free or nominal entry. Coppersmith session 60–90 min, roughly 40–60 BAM (€20–€30).

itinerary.title: South to Trebinje
itinerary.morning: Slow departure, then the drive south through the Popovo Polje karst basin — a landscape that floods in winter and is bone dry in September.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive in Trebinje, check in beside the old town, and walk the Kastel walls and the plane-tree square. Nothing else. This is the town where you learn to sit.
itinerary.evening: Trg Slobode under the trees from 19:00, when the whole town appears. Dinner nearby with a bottle of Žilavka, the local white.
itinerary.dayStats: Mostar–Trebinje 110 km / 2 h. Trebinje at 273 m, 28 km from the Adriatic. Buses run this route but only a couple of times a day.

itinerary.title: Monastery wine, an old bridge, and an open afternoon
itinerary.morning: Tvrdoš Monastery, 5 km out of town, where Orthodox monks have made wine on the site since Roman foundations underneath it — taste the Vranac and the Žilavka in the cellar and buy directly.
itinerary.afternoon: Unplanned. Walk the riverside path to the Arslanagić Bridge, a 16th-century Ottoman span that was dismantled and rebuilt upstream when the Trebišnjica was dammed, then do nothing for three hours.
itinerary.evening: Up to Hercegovačka Gračanica on Crkvina hill at sunset for the view over the valley, then back down for grilled lamb and a long coffee.
itinerary.dayStats: Trebinje–Tvrdoš 5 km / 10 min; tasting roughly 20–35 BAM (€10–€18). Riverside walk to Arslanagić 2.2 km each way, flat. Crkvina hill 130 m above town.

itinerary.title: Market morning, then the coast
itinerary.morning: Saturday market in the old town from about 07:00 — honey, dried figs, pomegranate juice, cheese in oil, rakija in reused bottles. Buy the honey; it travels. Then one last coffee under the plane trees.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive to Dubrovnik, allowing properly for the border. If your flight is late, the coast road via Trebinje's mountain descent is spectacular.
itinerary.evening: Flight home.
itinerary.dayStats: Trebinje–DBV 65 km / 1 h 50 including the border; queues at Ivanica can add 45 min on summer weekends. Market 07:00–13:00, fullest before 10:00.

accommodationStrategy.name: Muslibegović House
accommodationStrategy.description: An 18th-century family residence that is simultaneously a national monument and a working hotel, five minutes' walk above the Stari Most. Rooms range from simple to fully traditional with low divans and carved ceilings; ask for a traditional room, which costs a little more and is the whole reason to stay here. Quiet at night, which is rare this close to the bazaar. Roughly €80–€130 per double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Platani
accommodationStrategy.description: Directly on Trg Slobode with its terrace under the plane trees, which means the korzo happens at your table. Unfussy rooms, good breakfast, and the single best-placed bed in Trebinje for a three-night sit-still stay. Roughly €55–€85 per double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Kriva Ćuprija or a Blagaj pansion
accommodationStrategy.description: Kriva Ćuprija sits on the Radobolja stream in Mostar's old town, a small conversion of mill buildings, if Muslibegović is full. Staying out at Blagaj instead is a real option for a quieter week — but it puts you 12 km from Mostar's evenings.

logistics.connectivity: **Bosnia and Herzegovina is outside the EU, so EU roam-like-at-home does not apply.** Check your operator's Western Balkans bundle or buy a BH Telecom or m:tel prepaid SIM. Note that Trebinje is in Republika Srpska and Mostar in the Federation — networks differ slightly by entity, and phones hop across the Croatian network on the coast road, which can trigger unexpected charges.
logistics.emergency: 112 works, but 124 (ambulance), 122 (police) and 123 (fire) are the reliable direct numbers in BiH. Mountain rescue is thin — the GSS responds via 112. Take insurance with repatriation cover.
logistics.weather: The Neretva valley is a heat trap: 38°C is normal in July and the stone holds it overnight. The bura wind hits the Popovo Polje and the Trebinje plateau in winter. Sudden heavy rain in November and December can flood the karst polje and close minor roads.
logistics.bookingWindows: Mostar old-town rooms need 2–3 months for May and September. Coppersmith sessions and Tvrdoš cellar tastings want a day or two's notice. Nothing else here requires advance booking.
logistics.money: The currency is the **convertible mark (BAM/KM)**, pegged to the euro at **1.95583 BAM = €1** — so roughly 2 KM to the euro. Euros are accepted informally at some tourist businesses at a poor rate; pay in marks. Cards work in hotels and larger restaurants; markets, Kravice's entry booth, village cafés, taxis and craft workshops are cash. Withdraw at bank ATMs and decline dynamic currency conversion. Tipping is rounding up, 10% on a good dinner.
logistics.transportRules: If you rent in Croatia you must obtain written cross-border permission and a green card at pickup, and declare Bosnia specifically — many cheap brokers refuse it. A vignette is not required in BiH but tolls apply on the A1 north of Mostar. Herzegovina's minor roads are narrow, unlit and shared with livestock. Buses connect Mostar–Blagaj–Počitelj and Mostar–Trebinje, but only a few times daily.
logistics.permits: Landmines remain a genuine hazard away from marked paths in some rural areas; never walk into unmarked ground, ruins or overgrown fields anywhere in the country, and stay on established tracks. Drones need permission. Photographing military or border installations is prohibited.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable in Mostar and Trebinje. The Buna and Trebižat are cold year-round — the Kravice pool rarely exceeds 18°C. Mostar's cobbles are polished marble-smooth and treacherous in rain; the Stari Most's deck has raised stone ribs precisely because it is otherwise unwalkable.

proTips: Mostar's old town is a cruise-excursion destination from Dubrovnik between roughly 10:30 and 16:30. Sleep in it, and do all your bridge-side wandering before 09:30 or after 17:30 — you will effectively have a different town.

Learn the coffee ritual rather than ordering an espresso. The džezva is poured into the fildžan a little at a time, the sugar cube is dipped and held in the teeth, and the rahat lokum comes first. Rushing it is the one thing that reads as rude here.
Pay in convertible marks, not euros. Businesses that accept euros usually round the 1.96 rate down to 2, which is a quiet 2% on everything.
Cross at Ivanica rather than the coastal crossings when driving Trebinje–Dubrovnik. It is smaller, faster and drops you above the Konavle valley with a view worth the detour.
At Radimlja, walk the field rather than viewing from the car park. The carved raised-arm figures only make sense when you are among them and can see how many there are.

Trebinje is in Republika Srpska and Mostar is not, and the two towns tell their recent history differently. Ask, listen, and don't arbitrate — the most rewarding conversations of the week come from being genuinely curious rather than informed.
Buy wine at Tvrdoš rather than in Mostar. The monastery sells at cellar prices, the Vranac travels well, and the labels are the best souvenir you'll bring home.

raw.Kujundžiluk, Mostar: — the coppersmiths' bazaar leading to the Stari Most, where families still beat copper trays and džezve by hand. It is a genuine craft street wrapped in a souvenir street; the working shops are the ones with an anvil visible.
raw.Trg Slobode, Trebinje: is the anchor square of the second half: a walled old town under enormous plane trees, with café tables under the canopy and a korzo that starts around 19:00 and runs along Njegoševa and the riverside promenade.
raw.Trebinje's Saturday market: fills the old town from early morning — honey, figs, pomegranates, ćurak cheese in oil, homemade rakija, and Herzegovinian wine sold from the boot of a car. Best before 10:00.
raw.Blagaj tekke: sits at the Buna spring, where a karst river emerges whole from beneath a 200 m cliff — one of Europe's largest springs by volume. The dervish house dates from around 1520 and is still a functioning place of prayer; shoes off, shoulders covered.
raw.Počitelj: climbs the Neretva's east bank as a set of stone stairs linking the Šišman Ibrahim Pasha Mosque, the medieval Sahat Kula and the hilltop fort. Women sell figs, pomegranates and dried herbs on the lower steps in September.
raw.Radimlja, near Stolac: holds roughly 130 *stećci* — medieval Bosnian tombstones carved with raised arms, spirals and hunting scenes, UNESCO-listed and unlike anything else in Europe.
raw.Hands-on experience: a coppersmithing hour in a working Kujundžiluk workshop — chasing a pattern into a small copper plate with hammer and punch, alongside the family that has done it for generations. Book through your hotel the day before.
raw.Pacing: one move (Mostar → Trebinje on Day 5), blank afternoons on Days 3 and 6, and the short walks that exist: Blagaj village to the tekke (900 m along the Buna), Počitelj's stair circuit (600 m, 90 m of climb), Trebinje old town to the Arslanagić bridge (2.2 km along the Trebišnjica).

sources.verified: BAM peg confirmed at 1.95583 to the euro and Bosnia and Herzegovina's non-EU roaming status checked. Trebinje's Saturday market in the old town confirmed as an established weekly event. Blagaj tekke, the Buna spring and Tvrdoš Monastery's winemaking confirmed as active.
sources.confidenceNotes: Trebinje market hours are typical rather than officially published — advise arriving early. Entry fees at Kravice, the tekke and the minaret change annually and were not each re-confirmed this run. Mostar–Trebinje and Mostar–Počitelj bus frequencies are described qualitatively because published timetables are unreliable; the file assumes a car. Room counts for Muslibegović House and Hotel Platani are approximate. Individual coppersmith workshops on Kujundžiluk are family businesses that open and close without notice — the file deliberately names the craft street rather than a single shop, and users should book through their hotel. Restaurant continuity in Mostar should be re-checked before publishing.

provenance.sourceFormat: md with '## Metadata' bullet block (one file per trip)

trips.title: West Flanders Squares — Bruges, Damme and Veurne

bestPeriod.note: Start on a Saturday so the Wednesday market at Veurne and the Saturday market at 't Zand both land inside the week.

trips.gatewayAirport: Brussels (BRU)
trips.summary: Four nights in Bruges and three in Veurne, moving by train and towpath, built around lace workshops and two of Flanders' best market squares.
trips.hook: Bruges is not ruined by its visitors; it is simply borrowed by them between 10:00 and 18:00. Stay four nights, learn the timings, and the city hands itself back twice a day. Then move an hour west to Veurne, where the Grote Markt is one of the most complete squares in Flanders and nobody is queuing for anything.

snapshot.Base(s): Bruges (4 nights) · Veurne (3 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: One 60 km rail relocation; 30–40 km walked, plus an optional 14 km canal bike ride. Entirely flat
snapshot.Getting There: Brussels Airport to Bruges by train, approx. 1h30 with one change; Bruges to Veurne via Lichtervelde, approx. 1h
snapshot.Who It Suits: Museum-goers, lace and craft people, beer drinkers, anyone who wants a walkable week without a car

itinerary.title: Arrival, and the two squares that matter
itinerary.morning: Train from Brussels Airport to Bruges. If you land early enough to be in town before 14:00 on a Saturday, walk straight to 't Zand, where the city's largest weekly market runs roughly 07:00–14:00 across the whole plein — flowers, cheese, fish, and the rotisserie vans.
itinerary.afternoon: Learn the geography with your feet. The Markt is the big one, hemmed by the Belfort and the neo-Gothic Provinciaal Hof. Step through to the Burg next door, which is smaller, older and better: the Stadhuis of 1376 with its gilded façade, and the Heilig-Bloedbasiliek stacked in two chapels, Romanesque below and Gothic above.
itinerary.evening: Walk east to Jan van Eyckplein and the old Hanseatic quarter, then south along the Groenerei. Dinner in the Sint-Anna district, five minutes and a world away from the Markt.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 1. Walking: 6 km. Transfer time: approx. 1h30 from Brussels.

itinerary.title: The poplar road to Damme
itinerary.morning: Nothing before 10:00. Then rent bikes — Fietsen Popelier on Mariastraat is the long-standing option — and ride the Damse Vaart, the dead-straight Napoleonic canal lined with poplars, 7 km northeast to Damme. In season the *Lamme Goedzak* paddle boat does the same trip from Noorweegse Kaai if you prefer to sit.
itinerary.afternoon: Damme is a medieval port that lost its sea. The Marktplein holds the 1464 Stadhuis and the statue of Jacob van Maerlant, and the village is officially a *boekendorp* — a book village. On the second Sunday of the month, March to October, secondhand booksellers set up on the square from about 10:00 to 18:00.
itinerary.evening: Eel in green sauce — *paling in 't groen* — is the local dish, and Siphon on the Damse Vaart-Oost has been serving it for generations. Book. Ride back into a Flanders sunset on a flat towpath.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 3 km. Cycling: 14 km. Transfer time: 30 min each way by bike.

itinerary.title: Lace, brick and beer
itinerary.morning: Take the local train seven minutes north to Lissewege, a whitewashed village under an unfinished brick tower. Walk 1.5 km out to the Ter Doest tithe barn, a 13th-century Cistercian brick hall the size of a church, and one of the great pieces of Flemish agricultural building.
itinerary.afternoon: Back in Bruges, go to the Kantcentrum on Balstraat, where lacemakers demonstrate bobbin work Monday to Saturday afternoons, roughly 14:00–17:00. Bruges lace means *bloemwerk* — flower work — and Duchesse; watch the pins go in and you will stop asking why a collar costs €400. 't Apostelientje across the street sells the real thing beside the machine-made imports so you can learn the difference by eye.
itinerary.evening: Brouwerij De Halve Maan on Walplein, brewing Brugse Zot in the centre since 1856, pipes its beer to the bottling plant through a 3.2 km underground pipeline. Tour, then drink somewhere better lit: 't Brugs Beertje on Kemelstraat keeps a serious list.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 8 km. Transfer time: 15 min return by rail.

itinerary.title: Memling morning, canal afternoon
itinerary.morning: Another late start; nothing before 10:00. The Vismarkt colonnade holds a small fish market Tuesday to Saturday, roughly 08:00–13:00, and it is a two-minute detour on the way to the Sint-Janshospitaal, where six Memling panels including the Ursula shrine sit in the hospital they were painted for.
itinerary.afternoon: The Groeningemuseum, ten minutes away, holds Van Eyck's *Madonna with Canon van der Paele* and Bosch's *Last Judgement*. Both museums close on Mondays, which is why they sit here.
itinerary.evening: Walk the Begijnhof and Minnewater at dusk, then climb the Kruisvest embankment to the Sint-Janshuismolen, a working windmill on the old ramparts. The Markt is bearable again after 18:00.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 1. Walking: 7 km. Transfer time: none.

itinerary.title: Market day in Veurne
itinerary.morning: This is the one early start of the week and it earns it. Take the 08:00-ish train from Bruges via Lichtervelde and you are in Veurne inside an hour, with the Wednesday market still running on the Grote Markt until about 13:00. Buy lunch there.
itinerary.afternoon: The Grote Markt is an almost intact 16th–17th-century ensemble: the Stadhuis with its loggia, the Landhuis with the belfry behind, the Spaans Paviljoen, and the Vleeshuis. Sint-Walburgakerk sits in a walled close just off it. This is the square Bruges' visitors never reach.
itinerary.evening: Veurne after dark is very quiet. Eat on the square, then look for the plaques marking the route of the Boeteprocessie, the barefoot penitents' procession held on the last Sunday of July since the 17th century.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 5 km. Transfer time: approx. 1h by rail.

itinerary.title: Hops and abbey beer
itinerary.morning: Bus or drive 25 km south to Poperinge, the centre of Belgian hop growing. The Hopmuseum on Gasthuisstraat occupies the old municipal hop-drying and weighing hall and explains the whole crop cycle; the Grote Markt outside holds its weekly market on Friday mornings.
itinerary.afternoon: Ten minutes further is Westvleteren, where In de Vrede is the visitor café of the Sint-Sixtus abbey. It is the only place you can reliably sit down with the abbey's Trappist beer without a phone reservation for the collection line. Cheese, pâté and one glass; the beer is 10.2% and you are not driving.
itinerary.evening: Continue to Ieper for the Last Post, sounded under the Menin Gate at 20:00 every single evening since 1928. Then back to Veurne, half an hour north.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 3. Walking: 5 km. Transfer time: approx. 1h30 total by road.

itinerary.title: Ovens, dunes, departure
itinerary.morning: The Bakkerijmuseum on Albert I-laan in Veurne is a working bakery museum with wood-fired ovens and a genuinely good reason to arrive hungry. Slow morning, no rush.
itinerary.afternoon: Eight minutes by train to De Panne, then the Kusttram — the 67 km coastal tram that runs the entire Belgian shoreline — a few stops north along the Westhoek dunes. Walk the dune paths, eat shrimp croquettes, get sand in your shoes.
itinerary.evening: Train back east for Brussels, roughly 2h15 from Veurne with a change.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 6 km. Transfer time: approx. 2h15 to Brussels.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Ter Reien
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits on the Langestraat where two canals meet, in the Sint-Anna quarter — inside the old town, but on the residential side of it, so you walk five minutes to the Burg and sleep somewhere silent. Rooms over the water are the ones worth paying for. Bike storage on site, which matters for the Damme day.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–3 months ahead for May, June and September weekends.

accommodationStrategy.name: Guesthouse Nuit Blanche
accommodationStrategy.description: An alternative for a couple who want the smallest possible operation: a handful of rooms in a historic house on the Groeninge canal, a minute from the museum quarter. No lobby, no groups, no lift. Breakfast is brought to you.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 months ahead; it sells out first.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel 't Kasteel en 't Koetshuys
accommodationStrategy.description: A small hotel in a nineteenth-century house and its coach house on the edge of Veurne's centre, five minutes' walk from the Grote Markt and the station. Parking on site if you hire a car for the Poperinge day, and a garden that makes the two slow evenings here work.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 for everything. Belgium also runs 101 for police and 1733 for the out-of-hours doctor service.
logistics.money: Bancontact and cards work nearly everywhere. Market stalls, the abbey café at Westvleteren and small bakeries prefer cash; carry €40–€60.

other.label: Museum closures
other.text: Most Musea Brugge sites, including the Groeningemuseum and Sint-Janshospitaal, close on Mondays. Build your indoor day around Tuesday to Sunday. The Musea Brugge Card covers the group of them for three days and pays back after roughly three visits.

other.label: The Belfort has a capacity limit
other.text: The stair takes a fixed number at a time and tickets are timed; book online the day before, early slot.

other.label: Trains
other.text: SNCB/NMBS runs hourly to Veurne with a tight change at Lichtervelde; the last useful westbound train leaves Bruges before 21:00. Buy in the app.

other.label: Bikes on trains
other.text: Bikes need a supplement and are barred from some peak services; hire in Bruges for the Damme ride. Drone flight over the historic core is prohibited.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Flemish kitchens close early — last orders at 21:00 is normal. Many family restaurants shut two weekdays, often Monday and Tuesday, and rarely advertise it; have your hotel phone ahead the same morning.

proTips: The Markt and Burg are effectively empty before 09:00 and after 18:30. Do your photographs and your coffee then, and put museums and lace in the middle of the day when the streets are worst.
Ride the canal to Damme and take the *Lamme Goedzak* back, or the reverse — but check the boat's limited schedule before committing.
At the Kantcentrum, arrive at 14:00 sharp when the lacemakers sit down. By 16:00 the demonstration tables are thinning out.
Ask at In de Vrede whether the abbey shop is selling that day. Availability rotates and is announced locally; the café itself always has the beer on the list.
Veurne's Wednesday market packs up hard at 13:00. Eat there rather than planning lunch afterwards, when the town is quiet.
Buy a De Lijn day pass before boarding the Kusttram; onboard fares cost noticeably more.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: One 60 km rail relocation; 30–40 km walked, plus an optional 14 km canal bike ride. Entirely flat
raw.Who It Suits: Museum-goers, lace and craft people, beer drinkers, anyone who wants a walkable week without a car

typeSpecific.surface: One 60 km rail relocation; 30–40 km walked, plus an optional 14 km canal bike ride. Entirely flat
typeSpecific.audience: Museum-goers, lace and craft people, beer drinkers, anyone who wants a walkable week without a car

packingNotes: A rain shell you would happily wear all day. West Flanders gets drizzle in every month.
Shoes for cobbles that have been polished by six centuries of feet — Bruges is genuinely slippery when wet.
A windproof layer for the Westhoek dunes, always colder than inland.
Cash in small notes for markets and the abbey café.
Something flat and soft to carry lace home in; it must not be creased over a hard edge.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Bruges is unbearably crowded.** The city takes cruise-excursion traffic from Zeebrugge on some days. If the centre is impossible, take the seven-minute train to Lissewege or the towpath to Damme and come back at six.
**Rain all week.** The indoor programme absorbs four days: Groeningemuseum, Sint-Janshospitaal, Kantcentrum, De Halve Maan, the Hopmuseum and the Bakkerijmuseum.
**You miss the Lichtervelde connection.** Trains to Veurne are hourly; the fallback is the coastal tram from Ostend, slower but scenic, or a taxi from Diksmuide.
**Westvleteren has no beer to sell.** It regularly does not. In de Vrede still pours it by the glass, and any decent Bruges beer café will have Trappist alternatives — Rochefort, Westmalle, Orval.

trips.title: Carved Ceilings and Cobbled Bridges: A Slow Week in Bulgaria's Revival Towns
trips.subRegion: Sredna Gora, the Balkan foothills and the Veliko Tarnovo highlands

bestPeriod.window: late May to mid-June, and the whole of September — long light, warm stone, no coach parties
bestPeriod.avoid: late July–August (heat in the valleys, museum-house queues) and January–February, when half the guesthouses in Koprivshtitsa and Bozhentsi simply close

accommodation.note: €245–€420 (€35–€60/night, Revival-house guesthouses with breakfast)

food.note: €140–€210 (€20–€30/day, mehana dinners included)

transport.note: €180–€280 (7-day small car hire plus fuel; or €70–€110 by bus and train, slower)

activities.note: €45–€80 (museum-house tickets, combined passes, one craft workshop)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy

trips.gatewayAirport: Sofia (SOF) is 110 km from Koprivshtitsa — 1 h 45 by car, or the slow train on the Sofia–Burgas line to Koprivshtitsa station, which sits 9 km below the town with a connecting bus. Fly home from Sofia or Varna (VAR), 3 h from Veliko Tarnovo.
trips.currency: Euro (EUR) — sole legal tender since 1 February 2026; mandatory dual BGN display ended 8 August 2026
trips.summary: Three bases in seven days, and nothing that starts before nine. The *Vazrazhdane* towns are what Bulgaria built when it had money and no country: oriel windows overhanging cobbles, blue and ochre plaster, ceilings…
trips.hook: Three bases in seven days, and nothing that starts before nine. The *Vazrazhdane* towns are what Bulgaria built when it had money and no country: oriel windows overhanging cobbles, blue and ochre plaster, ceilings carved into suns because two craftsmen made a bet. You walk one town a day, eat in guesthouse *mehanas* where the menu is a conversation, and drive no more than three hours all week.

snapshot.Start / End: Koprivshtitsa → Arbanasi / Veliko Tarnovo (three bases, ~350 km of driving in total)
snapshot.Getting there: Sofia (SOF) is 110 km from Koprivshtitsa — 1 h 45 by car, or the slow train on the Sofia–Burgas line to Koprivshtitsa station, which sits 9 km below the town with a connecting bus. Fly home from Sofia or Varna (VAR), 3 h from Veliko Tarnovo.

itinerary.title: Into Koprivshtitsa
itinerary.morning: Collect a car in Sofia and drive east on the Trakia motorway, then up the Topolnitsa valley. Koprivshtitsa sits at 1,060 m in a bowl of the Sredna Gora, and it is noticeably cooler than the plain.
itinerary.afternoon: Do nothing but walk. Cross the **Kalachev Bridge** — the Bridge of the First Rifle Shot, where the April Uprising began on 20 April 1876 — and follow the Topolnitsa's cobbled crossings up to **Ploshtad 20-ti April**.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in your guesthouse *mehana*: *shopska salata*, *kavarma* in a clay pot, a glass of Mavrud. The town has no nightlife and that is the entire point.
itinerary.dayStats: 110 km / 1 h 45 from Sofia

itinerary.title: The four houses (walking day, no driving)
itinerary.morning: Start at the **Oslekov House** (1856), the richest in town — cedar columns brought from Lebanon, a painted façade, and a hall built to show a merchant's money. Then the **Lyutov House** (1854), whose domed *naos* ceiling and *alafranga* wall niches are the finest painted interior in Koprivshtitsa.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Kableshkov House**, birthplace of Todor Kableshkov, who wrote the "Bloody Letter" announcing the rising, and the **Debelyanov House**, home of the poet Dimcho Debelyanov, with its bronze of a waiting mother in the churchyard above.
itinerary.evening: Climb to the Church of the Assumption for the last light on the roofs, then a slow dinner. Ask your hosts about tomorrow's road — the Troyan pass route is scenic and slow.

itinerary.title: Over the Balkan to Tryavna
itinerary.morning: Drive north over the **Republic Pass** (Prohod na Republikata) or the Troyan–Kărnare road, stopping at **Troyan** for the potteries — this is where the *kapkovidna* drip glaze comes from, and prices at the workshop are half what you pay in Sofia.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive in **Tryavna**, drop bags, and cross the **1844 humpback bridge** into **Slaveykov Square** for a first look at the clock tower and the Old School.
itinerary.evening: Eat on the square. Tryavna is a working town rather than a museum, so the *mehanas* fill with locals from about seven.

itinerary.title: The woodcarvers, then Bozhentsi
itinerary.morning: The **Daskalov House** (1808), now the Museum of Woodcarving and Icon Painting. Its two carved **sun ceilings** were made in a six-month wager between the masters Dimitar Oshanets and Ivan Bochukovets — stand under both and pick a winner.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive twenty minutes to **Bozhentsi**, an entire village preserved as an architectural reserve: stone-slab roofs, timber galleries, no through traffic. Walk to the **Baba Kostadinitsa House** and the Doncho Popa House.
itinerary.evening: Back in Tryavna, visit the Church of the Archangel Michael, then buy something carved from a workshop off the square rather than a souvenir stall.
itinerary.dayStats: 35 km round trip

itinerary.title: To Arbanasi, above Veliko Tarnovo
itinerary.morning: A short drive through the Gabrovo hills to **Arbanasi**, a village of fortified stone merchant houses on the plateau overlooking Veliko Tarnovo. Check in early and take the afternoon slowly.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Church of the Nativity of Christ** — plain and low from outside, and inside a barrel-vaulted interior covered from floor to ceiling in 17th-century painting, some 3,500 figures, including a wheel of the zodiac. Then the **Konstantsalieva House**, a merchant's fortress with hidden stairs and a walled courtyard.
itinerary.evening: Sunset from the Arbanasi escarpment over the Yantra gorge and the lit walls of Tsarevets, then dinner at a village *mehana*.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 km / 50 min

itinerary.title: Veliko Tarnovo and the craft street
itinerary.morning: Drive or taxi down to **Veliko Tarnovo** and walk **Samovodska Charshia** early, while the coppersmiths and potters are setting up. Buy Troyan ceramics, wool and a copper *dzhezve* here.
itinerary.afternoon: **Tsarevets** fortress — the Patriarchal church on the summit, the Execution Rock, and the whole medieval capital under your feet — then General Gurko Street, the tier of houses stacked above the river.
itinerary.evening: Back up to Arbanasi. If the **Sound and Light** show over Tsarevets is running, watch it from the Arbanasi viewpoint rather than the crowded terraces below [VERIFY: current Sound and Light schedule].
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km / 20 min

itinerary.title: Zheravna on the way out
itinerary.morning: A last Arbanasi breakfast, then drive south-east over the Balkan through Elena towards **Zheravna** — roughly 200 timber Revival houses in a village of a few hundred people, with almost nothing modern in the frame.
itinerary.afternoon: Visit the **Yordan Yovkov House**, the writer's birthplace, and the **Rusi Chorbadzhi House**, then look for woven wool blankets in the village workshops. This was sheep money, and it still shows.
itinerary.evening: Continue to Burgas or Varna for a flight, or turn back to Sofia (3 h 30). Eat *banitsa* on the road.

accommodationStrategy.name: A Revival-house guesthouse on Ploshtad 20-ti April
accommodationStrategy.description: puts every one of the four museum houses within a ten-minute cobbled walk, so you never move the car for two days. Wood stoves matter here — Koprivshtitsa at 1,060 m is cold in May and September evenings.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct by phone or Booking.com, three to four weeks ahead; longer for any weekend in September [VERIFY: current Koprivshtitsa guesthouse rates].

accommodationStrategy.name: A carved-ceiling guesthouse near Slaveykov Square
accommodationStrategy.description: the square is the whole town, and staying on it means the Daskalov House, the clock tower and dinner are all doorstep-close. Several restored houses keep original carved ceilings in the rooms.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct, two to three weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: A stone merchant house
accommodationStrategy.description: three nights in one bed, with Veliko Tarnovo twenty minutes below for the sightseeing and Arbanasi's silence for the evenings. Courtyards, thick walls, and the Tsarevets view from the ridge.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three to five weeks ahead; Arbanasi is popular with Bulgarian weekenders from Sofia.

logistics.connectivity: A1 and Yettel cover all three bases well; Bozhentsi and the Elena–Zheravna road have thin patches. Guesthouse Wi-Fi is normal and usually good.
logistics.emergency: **112** nationwide, with English-speaking operators. The nearest full hospitals are in Veliko Tarnovo and Gabrovo; Koprivshtitsa has a clinic only.
logistics.weather: Koprivshtitsa is a mountain town and can be ten degrees colder than Plovdiv on the same day. Carry a warm layer even in June, and expect afternoon showers in the Balkan foothills.
logistics.bookingWindows: Guesthouses two to four weeks ahead for May–June and September. Book much earlier if you overlap the Zheravna costume festival in August, when the whole area fills.
logistics.money: Bulgaria has adopted the **euro**, with prices still dual-displayed in **BGN** at the fixed 1.95583 rate. Museum houses, small workshops and village *mehanas* are frequently **cash only** — carry €100–€150 in small notes.
logistics.transportRules: A car is the sane choice; a **vignette** is required on Bulgarian national roads and motorways, bought electronically before you drive [VERIFY: current weekly vignette price]. Cobbles and steep lanes in Koprivshtitsa, Bozhentsi and Zheravna mean small cars and careful parking. Bulgaria is **zero-tolerance on drink-driving**.
logistics.permits: No permits needed. Bozhentsi and Zheravna are protected architectural reserves — cars are restricted or excluded from the cores, and you park at the edge and walk in. Photography inside museum houses is often ticketed separately.

proTips: Buy the combined museum ticket at the tourist information office in Koprivshtitsa and again in Tryavna, not at the first house door. It is cheaper and saves queueing at every gate.

Tell your guesthouse at breakfast that you want dinner. Village *mehanas* cook to order from what was bought that morning, and a lunchtime request gets you the good version rather than the menu version.
Go to Bozhentsi before 10:00 or after 16:00. Day coaches from Gabrovo hold it in the middle of the day and leave it empty either side.
Ask in Tryavna's workshops for a *panel* or a spoon rather than an icon. Small pieces from the Tryavna school are genuinely affordable and genuinely made there.
Learn *"Imate li stai?"* (do you have rooms?) and *"Domashno?"* (homemade?). The second word gets you the house *rakia* and the house *lyutenitsa* instead of the shop-bought one.

If you want a fourth base, add **Melnik** in the far south-west — Bulgaria's smallest town, under sandstone pyramids — or **Shiroka Laka** in the Rhodopes for its bagpipe school. Both are three-plus hours away, so swap them in for Zheravna rather than adding a night.
Drive the Troyan and Elena passes in daylight. They are the best roads of the week, they are slow, and Bulgarian mountain roads are unlit with unfenced livestock after dark.

raw.Squares, by name: **Ploshtad 20-ti April** in Koprivshtitsa, where the April Uprising was declared in 1876 and where the four best museum houses sit within ten minutes' walk. **Slaveykov Square** in Tryavna — properly Kapitan Dyado Nikola Square — a single cobbled rectangle holding the 1814 **clock tower**, the 1844 humpback bridge and the 1839 Old School, and arguably the most complete Revival ensemble in the country. **Samovodska Charshia** in Veliko Tarnovo, a working craft street rather than a square. The stone-roofed lanes of **Bozhentsi**, which has no square at all and is better for it.
raw.Artisan trades, by town: **Tryavna woodcarving** — the *Tryavnenska shkola*, the school that produced the iconostases of half of Bulgaria, still taught at the town's art school and still practised in workshops off Slaveykov Square. **Troyan pottery**, 60 km west, recognisable by its *kapkovidna* drip glaze — bands of colour run and pool down the vessel — sold from the Troyan workshops and on Samovodska Charshia. **Zheravna wool**: the village's Revival wealth came from sheep, and the trade survives in woven blankets and the summer costume fair. On Samovodska Charshia you can watch coppersmiths, potters, bakers and a knife-maker working to the street.
raw.Boutique and guesthouse stays: Family-run Revival houses, restored with carved ceilings intact, typically eight to fourteen rooms and a *mehana* downstairs. Expect €35–€60 a night with breakfast, wood stoves in shoulder season, and hosts who will cook dinner if you say so at breakfast.
raw.Pacing rule — one relocation every two d: Koprivshtitsa two nights, Tryavna two nights, Arbanasi three nights. Longest single drive is 3 hours; the other two are 45 minutes and a day-trip loop. Every base has enough within walking distance for a day when it rains.
raw.Museum-house logic: Koprivshtitsa and Tryavna both sell **combined tickets** covering their house-museums, cheaper than paying at each door, from the tourist information office rather than the houses themselves [VERIFY: current Koprivshtitsa and Tryavna combined ticket prices]. Most house-museums close one day a week — commonly Monday — and shut for lunch out of season [VERIFY: current museum-house opening days and hours].
raw.Market and craft days: There is no single big market day in these towns; the crafts run daily on Samovodska Charshia and the workshops in Tryavna. The dates that matter are festivals: the **Zheravna Festival of Folklore Costume** in August [VERIFY: 2027 Zheravna costume festival dates], and the **Koprivshtitsa National Folklore Festival**, held on the Voglen meadow only **once every five years** [VERIFY: next Koprivshtitsa festival year and dates].
