trips.title: Painted Houses — An Appenzellerland Week

bestPeriod.note: The Landsgemeinde votes in the open air on the last Sunday of April; the decorated cattle come down off the alps in the first half of September.

trips.gatewayAirport: Zürich (ZRH)
trips.summary: Appenzell, Urnäsch, Stein and Gais in seven days — painted gables, working dairies, Biber bakers and narrow-gauge trains, with one hotel change.
trips.hook: Appenzellerland is small, stubborn and very good at making things: cheese, herbal bitters, honey cake pressed in carved wooden moulds, embroidery fine enough to sell to Paris. Two half-cantons, a landscape of green hummocks under the Alpstein wall, and towns where the house fronts are painted the colours of a Sunday waistcoat. This week takes four of them at walking pace, on a narrow-gauge railway, with a single change of hotel.

snapshot.Base(s): Appenzell (4 nights) · Gais (2 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: 40–50 km walked; rolling pasture paths, one cable-car day in the Alpstein, all village walking flat
snapshot.Getting There: Fly Zürich (ZRH); train to St. Gallen or Gossau, then Appenzeller Bahnen to Appenzell (approx. 2h in total)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Craft and folk-culture travellers, families, walkers who want a gondola rather than a rucksack

itinerary.title: Hauptgasse and the Landsgemeindeplatz
itinerary.morning: Zürich airport to St. Gallen by direct train, then the Appenzeller Bahnen narrow-gauge line up through Teufen and Bühler — about 45 minutes of climbing through pasture, with the Alpstein filling the windscreen. Total journey approx. 2 hours.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Hauptgasse. Appenzell's main street is a run of painted, deep-eaved gable fronts in ox-blood, ochre and green, each with the family's trade lettered across it; the Rathaus and the Pfarrkirche St. Mauritius anchor the top end. Then the Landsgemeindeplatz — the bare square where, on the last Sunday of April, citizens of Innerrhoden still vote on cantonal law in the open air by raising a hand.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in town: Appenzeller Chäshörnli, Siedwurst with Rösti, Chäsmagerone. Ask for the Appenzeller Bier from the Brauerei Locher, which has been brewing in the village since 1886, and finish with a small glass of Appenzeller Alpenbitter — a herbal digestif made here since 1902 from a recipe of some forty-two herbs.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 1 (Appenzell). Walking: 3 km. Transfer: approx. 2h from ZRH.

itinerary.title: Ebenalp, the cliff inn, and the Seealpsee
itinerary.morning: Take the little red train ten minutes up the valley to Wasserauen, then the cable car to Ebenalp at 1,640 m — approx. CHF 34 return (about €36). At the top, walk down through the Wildkirchli: three prehistoric caves in the cliff, a hermitage chapel, and then Berggasthaus Aescher, the inn pinned against the rock face under an overhang.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue down to the Seealpsee, a green lake in a bowl of limestone, roughly 1h15 from Aescher on a steep but made path. Alp dairies around the shore sell their own cheese and cold Most in summer. From the lake it is another hour of easy descent to Wasserauen and the train.
itinerary.evening: Back in Appenzell by 17:30. Sit outside on the Hauptgasse with a beer and watch the light go off the Säntis.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 1 (Appenzell) plus the Alpstein. Walking: 8 km, approx. 700 m descent. Transfer: 20 min by train, cable car.

itinerary.title: Urnäsch and the museum of customs
itinerary.morning: Twenty-five minutes by train west to Urnäsch, a long green village square lined with painted houses in Ausserrhoden. The Museum für Appenzeller Brauchtum on the square is the single best explanation of this culture anywhere: the Silvesterchläuse costumes — the "beautiful" ones with headdresses built as model farmhouses, the "ugly" ones in moss and pine cones — plus cow bells, harness, Streichmusik instruments and the yodelling tradition. Approx. CHF 10 (about €10.50).
itinerary.afternoon: Walk out of Urnäsch on the pasture paths toward Schwellbrunn, or simply sit on the square. This is the second of the week's slow afternoons and it is meant to be.
itinerary.evening: Return to Appenzell. If you are here between Christmas and mid-January, the Silvesterchlausen on 31 December and again on 13 January — the Old New Year of the Julian calendar — is the reason people come to Urnäsch at all.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Appenzell, Urnäsch). Walking: 6 km. Transfer: 50 min by train, return.

itinerary.title: Market morning, bitters and the Biber bakers
itinerary.morning: Appenzell's weekly market takes the Landsgemeindeplatz on Saturday mornings, usually from about 08:00 to 12:00 — alp cheese, dried meat, Öpfelbrot, honey, and stalls of cut flowers. Buy the day's food here. The Biber bakeries along the Hauptgasse make the region's honey-and-almond cake pressed in carved wooden moulds, so that a bear, a Senn or a cow comes out on the crust; they will show you the mould if the shop is not three deep.
itinerary.afternoon: Two working producers accept visitors in the village. The Alpenbitter distillery keeps a visitor room and shop explaining the herb recipe, and the Locher brewery runs a self-guided brewing experience with tasting, approx. CHF 20–30 (about €21–32). Between them, look into the Museum Appenzell on the Hauptgasse for the hand embroidery: Appenzell whitework, worked by outworking farmwomen through the 19th century and still practised by a handful of embroiderers.
itinerary.evening: Walk fifteen minutes out of the village on the Sitter riverside path for the view back at the painted fronts, then a last supper in Appenzell before the move.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 1 (Appenzell). Walking: 5 km. Transfer: none.

itinerary.title: Fifteen minutes to Gais
itinerary.morning: The only relocation of the week, and it takes a quarter of an hour: the Appenzeller Bahnen train north to Gais. Take the whole morning anyway — coffee, a last pass along the Hauptgasse, and a slow packing.
itinerary.afternoon: Gais's Dorfplatz is the reason to come: a complete ensemble of curved-gable houses, rebuilt after the village burned in 1780 and protected as a heritage site of national importance. There is nothing quite like the sweep of those rounded gables anywhere else in Switzerland. Gais also made its living from the whey cure in the 18th and 19th centuries, when visitors came to drink Molke from the alps.
itinerary.evening: Village kitchens here close early. Eat at 19:00, then walk out on the ridge toward the Stoss, where the Appenzellers defeated the Habsburg army in 1405 — the chapel and the view over the Rhine valley are ten minutes' walk from the last houses.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Appenzell, Gais). Walking: 5 km. Transfer: 15 min by train.

itinerary.title: Stein: the show dairy and the folk museum
itinerary.morning: Bus or train and bus west to Stein, roughly 30–40 minutes. The Appenzeller Schaukäserei is a working demonstration dairy: cheesemaking happens in the morning behind glass, from the copper vat through the cutting of the curd to the press, and the cellar with its brine-washed wheels is part of the visit. Come before midday or you will see clean equipment.
itinerary.afternoon: Next door, the Appenzeller Volkskunde-Museum is the craft half of the day: hand-weaving and hand-embroidery demonstrated on the original equipment, a reconstructed Sennenstube, and the naive Bauernmalerei — the painted milk pails, cow straps and Alpfahrt panels that are this region's true folk art. Approx. CHF 10 (about €10.50).
itinerary.evening: Back to Gais for the evening. In the first half of September, watch the roads: the Alpabfahrt brings the herds down from the alps, Sennen in yellow breeches and red waistcoats walking ahead of decorated cows, and it stops traffic in every village here.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Gais, Stein). Walking: 5 km. Transfer: approx. 1h20 return.

itinerary.title: The rack railway down to the Rhine, and out
itinerary.morning: From Gais, take the line to Altstätten Stadt — a narrow-gauge descent with a rack section that drops roughly 600 m off the Appenzell plateau into the Rhine valley in about twenty minutes, one of the most dramatic short rides in Swiss railways. Walk Altstätten's arcaded Marktgasse, then ride back up.
itinerary.afternoon: A last unhurried lunch on the Gais Dorfplatz, and time to buy what you decided against earlier in the week: Appenzeller cheese vacuum-packed for travel, a bottle of Alpenbitter, a Biber in its box.
itinerary.evening: Gais to St. Gallen is around 35 minutes by train, and St. Gallen to Zürich airport about 1h15. Allow three hours door to gate and do not attempt a flight before midday.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Gais, Altstätten). Walking: 4 km. Transfer: approx. 2h to ZRH.

accommodationStrategy.name: Romantik Hotel Säntis
accommodationStrategy.description: The painted facade on the Landsgemeindeplatz belongs to the hotel itself, which puts you on the square where the market sets up and thirty seconds from the Hauptgasse. It has a proper restaurant and a small spa, which matters after the Ebenalp descent, and the station is a four-minute walk with a bag.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead; Landsgemeinde weekend a year out.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Appenzell
accommodationStrategy.description: The quieter alternative on the same square, family-run, with a café-confiserie downstairs that makes its own Biber and pastries. Rooms are simple and calm; ask for one facing the square rather than the road behind. Good value by Swiss standards and easy about early breakfasts for the Wasserauen train.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Krone
accommodationStrategy.description: Directly on Gais's curved-gable square, a traditional Gasthof with a handful of rooms and a kitchen that feeds the village. Being on the Dorfplatz is the whole reason to sleep in Gais rather than commuting from Appenzell; the square is yours after 20:00. Station two minutes away for the Stein and Altstätten days.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 works everywhere; in Switzerland use 144 for ambulance, 117 police, 118 fire, and **1414 for Rega**, the air rescue service — relevant on the Ebenalp and Seealpsee paths. Save 1414 before you go up.
logistics.weather: The Alpstein manufactures its own afternoon cloud from June onward. The Ebenalp cable car stops in high wind or thunderstorms, and the descent to Seealpsee is dangerous in wet weather — the path is polished limestone.
logistics.money: Switzerland uses the Swiss franc; euros are sometimes accepted in tourist businesses at a poor rate and change comes in francs. Cards work everywhere including the market, but carry CHF 50–100 in coins and small notes for alp dairies and mountain inns, several of which are cash-only.
logistics.transportRules: A Half Fare Card (approx. CHF 120, about €126, valid one month) pays for itself in about three days at these fares, including the cable cars, which sell half-price tickets on it. A Swiss Travel Pass only makes sense if you are combining this with travel elsewhere in the country. Ask your hotel whether your stay comes with a regional guest card — several Appenzellerland hosts issue one covering local buses.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 works everywhere; in Switzerland use 144 for ambulance, 117 police, 118 fire, and **1414 for Rega**, the air rescue service — relevant on the Ebenalp and Seealpsee paths. Save 1414 before you go up.

other.label: Timetable discipline
other.text: Swiss trains and post buses leave to the second and connections are built on four-minute changes. Miss one and the next is typically 30 or 60 minutes. Check the last departure from Wasserauen and Stein before you set out.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Village shops close 12:00–13:30 for lunch, at 18:30 on weekdays, around 16:00 on Saturday, and all day Sunday. The Schaukäserei only makes cheese in the morning. Museums in Urnäsch and Stein often close Mondays outside high season.

other.label: Alpine paths
other.text: are waymarked yellow for hiking trails and white-red-white for mountain trails. The Ebenalp–Seealpsee–Wasserauen route is white-red-white: steep, exposed in places, and not a stroll in trainers.

other.label: Drones
other.text: are restricted near the cable cars and over the Alpstein wildlife zones; the Hoher Kasten and Ebenalp platforms give the shot legally.

other.label: Fires and foraging
other.text: Open fires are permitted only at marked fireplaces, and grazing land is private working pasture — close every gate, walk single file through herds, and never come between a cow and a calf.

proTips: Take the first Ebenalp cable car of the day, around 08:00. The Aescher path is a single-file cliff ledge and by 11:00 it is a queue; before 09:30 you will have the Wildkirchli caves to yourself.
Descend to Seealpsee rather than ascending to it. The climb from Wasserauen is 600 m of steady grind; the descent from Ebenalp puts the lake in front of you the whole way.
At the Schaukäserei, arrive by 10:00. Cheesemaking runs in the morning and what is on show at 15:00 is a clean vat and a shop.
Buy Appenzeller cheese at an alp dairy above Seealpsee or at the Saturday market, not at the airport. Ask for the *würzig* or the extra-mature — the mild export version is not what the region eats.
Ask a Biber baker on the Hauptgasse to show you the carved mould. The moulds are individual to each house and older than most of the shops.
The Gais–Altstätten rack descent is worth doing as a return trip in the morning, when the Rhine valley haze has not yet built up. Sit on the right going down.

If your dates touch the last Sunday in April, the Landsgemeinde is public and free to watch from the edge of the square. Arrive in Appenzell before 10:00; the trains are full and the village is closed to cars.
Book Berggasthaus Aescher for a drink, not a meal, unless you have reserved. It is small, famous, and the terrace turns over fast.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: 40–50 km walked; rolling pasture paths, one cable-car day in the Alpstein, all village walking flat
raw.Who It Suits: Craft and folk-culture travellers, families, walkers who want a gondola rather than a rucksack

typeSpecific.surface: 40–50 km walked; rolling pasture paths, one cable-car day in the Alpstein, all village walking flat
typeSpecific.audience: Craft and folk-culture travellers, families, walkers who want a gondola rather than a rucksack

packingNotes: Proper hiking boots with ankle support for the Ebenalp descent — the limestone is polished and slick, and trainers are the commonest cause of injury on that path.
A warm mid-layer and a windproof shell: the Ebenalp is 1,000 m above Appenzell and runs 6–8 °C colder, with wind.
Sunglasses and high-factor sunscreen — the pasture and limestone reflect hard even in September.
CHF 100 in small notes and coins for alp dairies, mountain inns and the market.
A soft cool bag or two for carrying cheese home; the Saturday market sells whole wedges that will not survive a warm car boot.
Trekking poles for the Seealpsee descent, especially with knees over fifty.
A light rain shell in any month; Appenzell's summer afternoon storms are brief and total.
Cash-friendly small wallet: several dairies have an honesty box rather than a till.
Modest, warm clothing if you attend the Landsgemeinde — it is a formal civic occasion held outdoors in April.
whatCouldGoWrong: **The Ebenalp cable car is closed for wind or maintenance.** Fallback: the Kronberg lift from Jakobsbad or the Hoher Kasten from Brülisau, both a short train or bus ride away, or the flat valley walk from Wasserauen toward Seealpsee, which is fine in poor visibility.

**Fog sits on the plateau all day.** It happens in October. Fallback: this is a museum-and-workshop itinerary at heart — the Urnäsch folk museum, the Stein dairy and craft museum, and the Appenzell distillery and brewery are all indoors and all better in bad weather.
**A Monday closes the museums.** Fallback: shift the Urnäsch and Stein days to Tuesday–Saturday and use Monday for Appenzell village, the producers and a valley walk.

**The costs bite.** Switzerland is expensive and this itinerary has two cable cars and several paid visits. Fallback: buy the Half Fare Card, eat your main meal at midday from the market, and use village Gasthof kitchens rather than hotel restaurants — the same food at two-thirds the price.

**You miss the last train from Stein or Wasserauen.** Services here stop early by city standards. Fallback: check the last departure at the stop when you arrive, and budget approx. CHF 60–90 for a taxi back to Gais or Appenzell if you overrun.

trips.title: Arcaded Squares of South Bohemia

bestPeriod.note: State chateaux shut from November to March and open weekends only in April and October; late October brings the Třeboň pond harvests.

trips.gatewayAirport: Prague (PRG)
trips.summary: Three arcaded Renaissance squares in seven days — Krumlov, Třeboň and Telč — with carp ponds, a Baroque theatre and two long lie-ins.
trips.hook: South Bohemia is a landscape of engineered water and unhurried squares. Three towns, two short drives, and a week spent walking arcades that have not changed shape since a fire in 1530 forced the rebuild. Nothing here needs to be rushed, and most of it closes on Mondays anyway.

snapshot.Base(s): Český Krumlov (3 nights) · Třeboň (2 nights) · Telč (2 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 260 km of driving across the whole week, all on flat to gently rolling secondary roads; 30–35 km walked
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Prague (PRG); direct coach to Český Krumlov in approx. 3h, or hire a car at the airport
snapshot.Who It Suits: Architecture readers, slow eaters, families, anyone who wants UNESCO towns without Prague's crowds

itinerary.title: Into the Vltava bend
itinerary.morning: Collect a car at Prague airport, or take the direct RegioJet coach south; either way you are in Český Krumlov in about three hours. The old town sits inside a tight double loop of the Vltava, and cars stay outside it.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk náměstí Svornosti, the small sloping main square with its 1716 plague column and Renaissance town hall arcade, then follow Horní to the church of St Vitus and back down Latrán, the trade street under the castle wall.
itinerary.evening: Eat early. The Eggenberg brewery has been working below the castle since the 16th century and its beer is the local pour. Then walk the riverbank after dark, when the town lights the castle tower and empties out.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 1. Walking: 5 km. Transfer time: approx. 3h from Prague.

itinerary.title: Monday rules, so walk
itinerary.morning: Nothing before 10:00. Czech state monuments close on Mondays, which makes this a day for streets rather than interiors. Cross the Plášťový most, the covered cloak bridge spanning the moat on three tiers of arches, and walk the castle gardens instead.
itinerary.afternoon: The Klášter complex — the former Minorite and Poor Clares monasteries on Klášterní — runs working craft workshops where you can watch, and often try, hand papermaking, blacksmithing and pottery. The marionette makers' shops on and around Radniční are the other Krumlov craft to look at properly: carved limewood heads, painted, strung by hand.
itinerary.evening: Dinner on Parkán, the lane along the river below the square. The Egon Schiele Art Centrum on Široká stays open some Mondays; check the board on your way past.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 1. Walking: 7 km. Transfer time: none.

itinerary.title: Castle, theatre, monastery
itinerary.morning: The Zámek Český Krumlov guided routes reopen today. Route I covers the Renaissance and Baroque state rooms; the Baroque Theatre of 1766 is a separate, tightly capped tour and it is the reason to be here. Original stage machinery, painted flats, thunder run and wind machine, all still worked by rope. Tours run roughly May to October and sell out days ahead — book online.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive 10 km north to the Cistercian monastery at Zlatá Koruna, founded 1263, whose chapterhouse is one of the finest early Gothic rooms in Bohemia. Twenty minutes of driving, an hour inside, and almost nobody there.
itinerary.evening: Back in Krumlov, climb the castle tower before it closes for the last long view down onto the roofs.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 6 km. Transfer time: 40 min return by car.

itinerary.title: Folk baroque and the pond town
itinerary.morning: Another slow start; nothing before 10:00. Then drive 20 km northeast to Holašovice, a UNESCO village whose green is ringed by 23 farmsteads with the curved, whitewashed, ornamented gables of *selské baroko* — south Bohemian rural baroque. It takes half an hour and it is unlike anything else in Europe.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue 55 km east to Třeboň, arriving mid-afternoon. Masarykovo náměstí is a long arcaded rectangle of gabled burgher houses; the Bílý koníček on the corner has carried its date of 1544 through everything since.
itinerary.evening: Carp is not a joke here — it is the local farmed fish and it is properly cooked. Order it grilled or *na černo* and follow it with Regent, brewed in the town since 1379.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 3. Walking: 4 km. Transfer time: approx. 1h30 driving.

itinerary.title: Engineered water
itinerary.morning: The Třeboň basin is a 16th-century fish-farming machine. Walk the dam of Rybník Svět straight out of town, then into the woods to the Schwarzenberg mausoleum, a neo-Gothic tomb standing alone above the water. Circuit of the lake: about 12 km, entirely flat; the short version to the mausoleum and back is 5 km.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive 15 km to the dam of Rybník Rožmberk, the largest pond in the country at 489 hectares, dug out between 1584 and 1590 by the estate engineer Jakub Krčín. The Zlatá stoka, the 45 km Golden Canal that feeds the whole system, was cut even earlier. If you are here in late October or early November, ask locally about the *výlov* — the pond harvest, when the water is drawn down and the carp are netted in front of a crowd.
itinerary.evening: Třeboň is a peat spa town; Bertiny lázně takes walk-ins for peat wraps. Otherwise, arcades and a beer.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 1. Walking: 9 km. Transfer time: 40 min return by car.

itinerary.title: Nativity figures and a narrow gauge
itinerary.morning: Drive 30 km northeast to Jindřichův Hradec. náměstí Míru is a broad arcaded square with a Trinity column; the castle behind it holds the Rondel, a free-standing Renaissance garden pavilion with a stucco ceiling that stops conversation.
itinerary.afternoon: The Muzeum Jindřichohradecka holds Krýzovy jesličky, a mechanical folk nativity built over sixty years by a local stocking-maker: nearly 1,400 figures, over 130 of them moving. If the 760 mm narrow-gauge line to Nová Bystřice is running a steam day, take that instead.
itinerary.evening: Continue 30 km to Telč and check in on the square. Arrive in time to see it empty at dusk.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 3. Walking: 5 km. Transfer time: approx. 1h20 driving.

itinerary.title: Telč, arcade by arcade
itinerary.morning: náměstí Zachariáše z Hradce is a long triangular space enclosed by continuous arcades and about forty gabled houses, each front different, rebuilt in Renaissance dress after the 1530 fire. Farmers' markets set up here on Saturday mornings, roughly 08:00–12:00, from spring to autumn — bread, honey, smoked fish, and Vysočina cheese.
itinerary.afternoon: The Státní zámek Telč tour takes in the Golden Hall with its coffered ceiling of thirty painted panels. Afterwards walk the causeway between the Štěpnický and Ulický ponds that make the town an island. If you have time before flying, Slavonice is 30 km south and its squares are covered in 16th-century sgraffito.
itinerary.evening: Telč to Prague airport is about 2h15 by road.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 5 km. Transfer time: approx. 2h15 to Prague.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Konvice
accommodationStrategy.description: On Horní, a minute from náměstí Svornosti and directly above the river bend, with rooms looking across to the castle. Small, old, wooden-floored, and inside the pedestrian zone — which matters, because the old town is closed to cars and this end of it has the shortest walk in from the parking areas.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead for May, June and September.

accommodationStrategy.name: Bílý koníček
accommodationStrategy.description: The oldest surviving house on Masarykovo náměstí, working as a modest hotel with a restaurant under the arcade. You are on the square, inside the walls, five minutes from the Svět dam walk and the Regent brewery gate — the two things you came to Třeboň for. Parking is outside the historic core.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead; longer if you come for the pond harvest.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Celerin
accommodationStrategy.description: Twelve or so rooms directly on náměstí Zachariáše z Hradce, several facing the arcades. Being on the square is the whole point in Telč: day visitors arrive at 10:00 and are gone by 17:00, and the hours either side belong to whoever sleeps here. Ask for a front room and accept the church bells.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead, more for summer weekends.

logistics.emergency: 112 works everywhere. Czech services direct: 155 ambulance, 158 police, 150 fire.
logistics.money: Czechia uses the koruna, not the euro. Decline dynamic currency conversion, and withdraw from bank ATMs rather than the independent machines in tourist streets.

other.label: Motorway vignette
other.text: A digital vignette (*dálniční známka*) is required on Czech motorways and is bought online at edalnice.cz against your plate; a ten-day one costs roughly CZK 270. Class II and III roads — most of this route — are free, and confirm with the rental desk whether a vignette is already registered.

other.label: Monday closures
other.text: State castles and chateaux, including Český Krumlov, Jindřichův Hradec and Telč, close on Mondays. They also close entirely from November to March and run weekends only in April and October.

other.label: Guided-tour language
other.text: Chateau tours run in Czech by default; English slots are fixed-time or need a minimum group. Book the English slot online.

other.label: Parking
other.text: All three old towns restrict traffic. Use the signed car parks outside the walls, roughly CZK 50–100 per day, and tip about 10% in restaurants as you pay.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Small-town Czech kitchens stop serving hot food around 21:00, and many close one weekday. Museums often shut for lunch between 12:00 and 13:00.

proTips: Book the Krumlov Baroque Theatre as soon as your dates are fixed. Capacity is tiny, the season short, and nothing else on this itinerary substitutes for it.
Krumlov's castle courtyards stay open long after the ticketed routes close. Walk them at 21:00, with no tour groups anywhere.
The Svět circuit is best walked anti-clockwise in the afternoon so the low sun is behind you over the water on the return leg.
Buy smoked carp fillets from the fish counter on Masarykovo náměstí and eat them on the dam. It is what Třeboň people do and it costs almost nothing.
Telč's square photographs badly at midday and beautifully at 07:30, when the arcades are in shadow and the gables catch the light.
If the weather collapses, Slavonice's houses hide rib-vaulted interiors and the town runs tours of its medieval underground passages.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 260 km of driving across the whole week, all on flat to gently rolling secondary roads; 30–35 km walked
raw.Who It Suits: Architecture readers, slow eaters, families, anyone who wants UNESCO towns without Prague's crowds

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 260 km of driving across the whole week, all on flat to gently rolling secondary roads; 30–35 km walked
typeSpecific.audience: Architecture readers, slow eaters, families, anyone who wants UNESCO towns without Prague's crowds

packingNotes: Comfortable shoes with a real sole: every square on this trip is cobbled and cambered.
A warm layer for evenings — the Vysočina plateau around Telč sits at 500 m and drops sharply after sunset even in June.
Insect repellent for the Třeboň wetlands from June to August. Mosquitoes there are serious.
Cash in koruna, around CZK 2,000, for markets, car parks and village pubs.
Offline maps and a light rain jacket: Vysočina signal is patchy and the pond basin makes its own weather.
whatCouldGoWrong: **You arrive on a Monday and everything is shut.** This itinerary assumes it. If your dates shift, move the walking day onto whichever day is Monday.
**The Baroque Theatre is sold out.** No substitute exists, but Krumlov's castle Route II and the Museum Fotoatelier Seidel, a preserved 1900s photographic studio on Linecká, fill the slot well.
**Rain for a full day.** Třeboň's spa, the Regent brewery tour, the Jindřichův Hradec museum and Krumlov's monastery workshops are all indoors.
**Your car is ticketed in an old town.** The zones are enforced; if your hotel sits inside one, have them register your plate for loading access before you drive in.

trips.title: Slate and Riesling — The Mosel Village Week

bestPeriod.note: September and early October give harvest activity and warm slate; many small hotels close from January to mid-March.

trips.gatewayAirport: Frankfurt (FRA)
trips.summary: Seven slow days between Bernkastel and Cochem — timber squares, slate vineyards, Fuder cellars and river boats, with only two moves all week.
trips.hook: The Mosel bends so hard that villages three kilometres apart by water are twenty by road, which is why nobody here has ever been in a hurry. This week strings four of them together — Bernkastel-Kues, Traben-Trarbach, Beilstein, Cochem — using boats, a branch-line train and a great deal of walking between vine rows. Two changes of hotel in seven nights, and both of them downstream.

snapshot.Base(s): Bernkastel-Kues (3 nights) · Beilstein (2) · Cochem (2)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: 60 km of river covered by boat and bus; 40–50 km walked; riverside towpath flat, vineyard paths steep and slate-loose
snapshot.Getting There: Fly Frankfurt (FRA); ICE to Koblenz, Mosel line to Bullay or Wittlich, then regional bus or boat
snapshot.Who It Suits: Wine-curious slow travellers, couples, anyone who wants a river week without a cruise ship

itinerary.title: Into Bernkastel, and the Marktplatz at dusk
itinerary.morning: Frankfurt to Koblenz by ICE (about 1h20), then the Moselstrecke regional train along the river to Wittlich Hauptbahnhof and a regional bus down into Bernkastel-Kues — roughly 25 minutes, and the bus drops you at the bridge between the two halves of the town.
itinerary.afternoon: Bernkastel's Marktplatz is a closed timber box of a square: the Rathaus of 1608, the Michaelsbrunnen fountain in the middle, and on the corner of Karlstraße the Spitzhäuschen of 1416, so narrow at the base and so wide at the top that it looks like a mistake. Sit for an hour. Then walk the Graacher Straße and Burgstraße lanes behind it, which are where people actually live.
itinerary.evening: Cross to Kues for the St.-Nikolaus-Hospital, the almshouse Nikolaus von Kues endowed in 1458 for thirty-three poor men and which still houses residents. The vaulted cellar holds the Mosel-Vinothek — around 150 wines from the whole middle Mosel open by the glass or by flat-rate tasting, approx. €20–28. This is the fastest legitimate education in Mosel Riesling available anywhere.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 1 (Bernkastel-Kues). Walking: 4 km. Transfer: approx. 3h45 from FRA.

itinerary.title: The Doctor, the sundials, and a walk to Wehlen
itinerary.morning: Climb into the Bernkasteler Doctor, the small, absurdly steep parcel directly above the town — twenty minutes of switchbacks and you are standing in the most expensive vineyard soil in Germany, looking down on your own hotel roof. Continue up to Burg Landshut, the ruined bishop's castle on the spur, for the classic bend-of-the-river view.
itinerary.afternoon: Take the riverside path downstream to Graach (3 km) and on to Wehlen (5 km total), flat the whole way. Above Wehlen stands the Sonnenuhr — the vineyard sundial built in 1842 so pickers on the slope could tell the time — and the Graacher Domprobst and Himmelreich slopes run in between. Growers here are small and serious: Weingut Willi Schaefer in Graach and Weingut Markus Molitor at Bernkastel-Wehlen both receive visitors, strictly by appointment, usually arranged by email a week or more ahead.
itinerary.evening: Return by the Kolb or Mosel line passenger boat if the timetable suits, otherwise walk back. Eat in Bernkastel's old town; Riesling with Mosel trout or Schwenkbraten is the standard pairing and it works.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 3 (Bernkastel, Graach, Wehlen). Walking: 11 km, approx. 180 m ascent. Transfer: none.

itinerary.title: Market morning, cellars and casks
itinerary.morning: Bernkastel-Kues holds its weekly market on Thursday mornings, usually about 08:00 to 13:00 — bread, Eifel cheese, smoked ham, and in autumn plums and Federweisser, the cloudy half-fermented must that is only drinkable within days of pressing. Buy lunch and take it to the riverbank.
itinerary.afternoon: A cellar visit. Ask your host to book you into a working Weingut rather than a tasting bar: Weingut Dr. Loosen occupies a house on the Bernkastel bank with an old vaulted cellar, and Weingut Fritz Haag at Brauneberg, ten minutes upstream, is another benchmark estate that takes appointments. What you are looking for down there is the Fuder — the traditional 1,000-litre oval Mosel cask. The cooper's trade that builds and maintains them is nearly gone from the valley; ask which cooperage still hoops their casks and you will get a proper answer and probably a second glass.
itinerary.evening: A last slow evening on the Marktplatz. If you are here in the first days of September, the Weinfest der Mittelmosel takes over both banks — glorious, and completely incompatible with an early night.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 1–2 (Bernkastel-Kues, optionally Brauneberg). Walking: 5 km. Transfer: none.

itinerary.title: Downstream via Traben-Trarbach to Beilstein
itinerary.morning: Move day, taken gently. The bus or boat to Traben-Trarbach takes under an hour. The town is the odd one out on this river: it got rich on the wine trade around 1900 and hired the Berlin architect Bruno Möhring, who left it a Jugendstil bridge gate of 1899 and a scatter of villas that look imported from Charlottenburg.
itinerary.afternoon: The Traben-Trarbacher Unterwelt — kilometres of interlinked wine cellars under the streets, entered on a guided tour, approx. €8, cool enough to need a jacket in August. Above the town, the earthworks of Mont Royal, Louis XIV's abandoned fortress of 1687, make a 45-minute walk with the best view of the double bend.
itinerary.evening: Continue downstream to Beilstein — train to Bullay, then bus or the Kolb passenger boat, depending on the day. Beilstein has around 140 residents, one square the size of a large room, and once the day visitors leave it goes completely silent. Dinner at your guesthouse; there are only a handful of kitchens and they all close early.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 3 (Bernkastel, Traben-Trarbach, Beilstein). Walking: 6 km. Transfer: approx. 2h30 including stops.

itinerary.title: Beilstein, Burg Metternich and the tithe cellar
itinerary.morning: The whole of Beilstein takes twenty minutes to walk and a morning to appreciate: the stepped Marktplatz, the Zehnthaus — the tithe house where the lord's share of the harvest was collected, now a wine bar in its vaulted cellar — and the Karmeliterkirche up the steps, which holds a Black Madonna brought from Cologne.
itinerary.afternoon: Burg Metternich, the ruined castle on the crag above, is a ten-minute climb and approx. €3.50; the terrace looks straight down the river. Afterwards take the car-and-passenger ferry across to Ellenz-Poltersdorf — a two-minute crossing, a couple of euros — and walk the far bank for the view back at Beilstein, which is the one worth having.
itinerary.evening: The Zehnthaus cellar, candle-lit and vaulted, pours the local Ellenzer and Beilsteiner Rieslings. Ask for something dry — the valley's off-dry style dominates the shelves but the growers keep trocken bottles back.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Beilstein, Ellenz-Poltersdorf). Walking: 6 km, approx. 150 m ascent. Transfer: ferry only.

itinerary.title: Cochem, the mustard mill and the chairlift
itinerary.morning: A slow start, then the short hop downstream to Cochem — 12 km by boat or bus, about 30 minutes. Cochem is the biggest town of the week at around 5,000 people and it feels metropolitan after Beilstein. Check in, then walk the Marktplatz with its Rathaus of 1739 and the St.-Martin-Brunnen.
itinerary.afternoon: The Historische Senfmühle on Endertstraße is a working mustard mill using a stone grinder from the 1810s; the tour is short, the tasting generous, and the coarse Riesling mustard is the single best thing to carry home from this valley. Approx. €4. Then the Sesselbahn — a single-seat chairlift from the Endertstraße up to the Pinnerkreuz, approx. €8 return — and walk back down through the vines in 35 minutes.
itinerary.evening: Reichsburg Cochem sits above everything: a medieval castle destroyed by the French in 1689 and rebuilt in 1868–77 by the Berlin businessman Louis Ravené, which makes it more 19th-century fantasy than fortress. Guided tours run through the day, approx. €8. Go for the last slot, when the light is low over the river.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Beilstein, Cochem). Walking: 7 km. Transfer: 30 min.

itinerary.title: Market morning and the way out
itinerary.morning: Cochem's weekly market takes the Marktplatz on Thursday mornings, roughly 08:00–12:00, small and entirely local. If your day falls otherwise, the bakers on Bernstraße open at 06:30 and the riverside promenade before 09:00 belongs to dog walkers and swans.
itinerary.afternoon: One last option before the train: the former Bundesbank bunker beneath Cochem's Bundesbankstraße, built in secret in 1962 to hold emergency currency for the Federal Republic and declassified only recently — a genuinely strange 90-minute tour, approx. €12, booked online.
itinerary.evening: Cochem has its own station on the Koblenz–Trier line. Koblenz is 40 minutes away, Frankfurt Airport around 2h30 in total with one change. Buy your Riesling before you leave the valley; the growers ship, but the mustard does not travel by post well.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 1 (Cochem). Walking: 4 km. Transfer: approx. 2h30 to FRA.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Zur Post
accommodationStrategy.description: On the Gestade quay, one minute from the Marktplatz and two from the bridge to Kues and the Cusanusstift cellar. Long-running and family-managed, with parking behind — useful if you drive in, irrelevant if you arrive as this itinerary suggests. Rooms on the river side hear the promenade until about 22:00, then nothing.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months for September; the Weinfest weekend goes a year out.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Haus Lipmann
accommodationStrategy.description: A 1795 house on the Mosel bank, run by the same family for generations, with a terrace over the water and a vaulted cellar of its own. In a village this small there is no chain alternative and no reason to want one; you eat where you sleep, and the last diners leave by 22:00.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four months ahead for May–October; closed in deep winter.

accommodationStrategy.name: Weinhaus Lohspeicher
accommodationStrategy.description: A narrow converted warehouse on the stepped Obergasse, above the tourist crush of the riverfront and a two-minute walk from the Marktplatz. Nine rooms, a serious kitchen, and stairs instead of a lift — pack light. It is the one address in Cochem that feels like the villages upstream.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two to three months ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 everywhere; 110 for police. Mobile coverage is good in the towns and patchy in the deeper bends — expect dead spots on vineyard paths above Graach and on the Mont Royal plateau.
logistics.weather: Mosel passenger services run roughly Easter to late October, thin out sharply in April and November, and stop entirely for high water. Never build a same-day connection on the last boat; check the posted board at the landing stage each morning.
logistics.money: Village guesthouses, the ferry at Beilstein and market stalls often take cash only. ATMs exist in Bernkastel-Kues, Traben-Trarbach and Cochem; Beilstein has none.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 everywhere; 110 for police. Mobile coverage is good in the towns and patchy in the deeper bends — expect dead spots on vineyard paths above Graach and on the Mont Royal plateau.

other.label: High water (Hochwasser)
other.text: is the valley's real hazard, mostly December–March but possible after heavy summer rain. Riverside promenades and some ground-floor hotels close at short notice. Check the Mosel gauge readings before a winter or early-spring trip.

other.label: Cellar visits are appointment-only
other.text: at the good estates — email a week or more ahead, name a time, and expect a charge of approx. €15–35 per person, usually credited against bottles bought.

other.label: Drink-driving is not worth risking
other.text: Germany's limit is 0.5‰ and 0.0 for drivers within their first two years of licence. This itinerary is built on trains, buses and boats precisely so you never face the question.

other.label: Opening hours
other.text: Small-village kitchens serve lunch 12:00–14:00 and dinner 18:00–20:30, and many close one weekday entirely (Ruhetag). Sunday shopping does not exist outside bakeries.

other.label: Trains
other.text: The Bullay–Traben-Trarbach branch (the Moselweinbahn) is a ten-minute shuttle timed to the main line; the Koblenz–Trier trains take bikes without reservation outside peak hours.

proTips: Walk the vineyards in the morning and the riverbank in the afternoon. The slopes face south and become genuinely punishing after 13:00 in September; the towpath is shaded by then.

Buy the day's wine at the estate, not the restaurant. Mosel guesthouses almost universally allow you to bring a bottle bought from a local grower for a small corkage — ask first, it is a normal request here.
At any tasting, ask for the *Kabinett* before the Spätlese. The Mosel's genius is low alcohol and high acid, and Kabinett shows it best; it is also the cheapest tier on the list.
Take the boat downstream and the bus back, not the reverse. Downstream sailings are faster, and the bends unfold in the right order for the light.
The Beilstein ferry runs on demand rather than a strict timetable. If it is on the far bank, stand at the slipway where the skipper can see you — that is the signal.
Cochem's Reichsburg tours sell out mid-afternoon in summer. The 09:00 and the last slot of the day are the ones with room and without a coach group.
Ask at any Weingut who still coopers their Fuder casks. It is the question that separates a tourist tasting from a real cellar conversation, and it usually earns you a walk into the barrel room.
Carry a small bottle to fill with Traubensaft — unfermented Riesling grape juice — sold at market stalls in September. It is the best non-alcoholic thing in the valley.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: 60 km of river covered by boat and bus; 40–50 km walked; riverside towpath flat, vineyard paths steep and slate-loose
raw.Who It Suits: Wine-curious slow travellers, couples, anyone who wants a river week without a cruise ship

typeSpecific.surface: 60 km of river covered by boat and bus; 40–50 km walked; riverside towpath flat, vineyard paths steep and slate-loose
typeSpecific.audience: Wine-curious slow travellers, couples, anyone who wants a river week without a cruise ship

packingNotes: Shoes with a stiff sole and grip: the vineyard paths are loose Devonian slate on gradients up to 60%, and it rolls underfoot like broken tile.
A light windproof layer — the river channels wind hard even on warm days, especially on the boats.
One warm mid-layer for cellar visits; working Mosel cellars sit at 10–12 °C year-round.
Sun hat and high-factor sunscreen for the slopes; the south-facing slate reflects heat brutally in September.
A padded wine sleeve or two if you plan to fly bottles home — very few estates here package for air travel.
Cash in small notes for the ferry, market and village kitchens.
A refillable bottle: the vineyard walks above Graach and Wehlen have no water points at all.
Insect repellent for riverside evenings in June and July.
whatCouldGoWrong: **High water cancels the boats.** Fallback: the Koblenz–Trier railway and the regional buses run regardless, and every leg in this itinerary has a road equivalent within 30 minutes' extra travel.

**You arrive and every good cellar is closed to walk-ins.** Fallback: the Mosel-Vinothek in the Cusanusstift cellar at Kues is open daily in season and pours across the whole region — book nothing, walk in, taste 150 wines.

**A village kitchen is shut for its Ruhetag and there is no alternative.** In Beilstein this is real. Ask your guesthouse the day before which places are open, and keep bread, cheese and ham from the Bernkastel market as insurance.

**Harvest week makes estates unavailable.** From mid-September to late October growers are picking and genuinely cannot host. Book cellar visits before you travel or shift them to the Vinothek and the Traben-Trarbach Unterwelt.

**Winter closures.** Many of the small hotels named here shut from January to mid-March, and the boats stop entirely. This is not a winter itinerary; if you must come then, base in Cochem, which stays open year-round.

trips.title: Franconian Squares — Rothenburg, Dinkelsbühl and the Ries

bestPeriod.note: Late September gives warm stone, thin crowds and the first Federweisser; December is beautiful but the Reiterlesmarkt fills Rothenburg.

trips.gatewayAirport: Nürnberg (NUE)
trips.summary: Three walled Franconian towns in seven days — Rothenburg, Dinkelsbühl and Nördlingen — with market mornings, Riemenschneider altars and only two moves.
trips.hook: Three towns that never grew. Rothenburg kept its walls because it went broke after 1631, Dinkelsbühl because nobody bothered to knock them down, and Nördlingen because it sits in a meteorite crater with nowhere to sprawl. This week walks all three at the speed of a market morning, with two relocations in seven days and a great deal of sitting on squares.

snapshot.Base(s): Rothenburg ob der Tauber (3 nights) · Dinkelsbühl (2) · Nördlingen (2)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 95 km of driving in total; 45–55 km walked over the week; flat cobbles, wall parapets, one gentle river valley
snapshot.Getting There: Fly Nürnberg (NUE); train to Steinach (b Rothenburg) and the branch line in, or rent a car at the airport
snapshot.Who It Suits: Slow travellers, families with children over six, anyone who wants medieval Germany without a coach-park itinerary

itinerary.title: Arrival and the first circuit of the wall
itinerary.morning: Land at Nürnberg, collect the car, and drive the 90 km southwest to Rothenburg — about 1h10 on the A6 and B25. Leave the car outside the walls; the Altstadt is closed to through traffic and hotel guests get a permit for loading only. Park P1 (Schwäbsche Hall Straße) or P5 by the Bahnhof, approx. €5–7 per day.
itinerary.afternoon: Do nothing ambitious. Walk the covered parapet of the Stadtmauer, joined at the Rödertor and followed anticlockwise — roughly 2.5 km of the 4 km circuit is walkable, free, and mostly empty after 17:00. Come down at the Klingentor, cut through to the Marktplatz, and look at the Rathaus: Gothic tower behind a Renaissance front by Leonhard Weidmann, 1572.
itinerary.evening: The Plönlein — the fork where Untere Schmiedgasse splits, with the yellow house wedged between the Kobolzeller Tor and the Siebersturm — is unbearable at noon and beautiful at 19:30. Then dinner in the Herrngasse end of town, and the Nachtwächter round: the night watchman leaves the Rathaus arcade on the Marktplatz at 20:00 in English, April to December, approx. €10, no booking, just turn up.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 1 (Rothenburg). Walking: 5 km. Transfer: 1h10 by car from NUE.

itinerary.title: Creglingen, a Riemenschneider altar and a museum of thimbles
itinerary.morning: A late breakfast, then 20 km north up the Tauber to Creglingen — 25 minutes on the L1020 through Detwang and Bettwar. The Herrgottskirche stands alone in a field 2 km south of the village. Inside is Tilman Riemenschneider's Marienaltar, carved around 1505–10 in limewood and never painted; in the second half of the morning the south windows put light straight onto it. Approx. €4.
itinerary.afternoon: Fifty metres away, the Fingerhutmuseum — a genuine one-room obsession, thimbles from Roman bronze to 19th-century Creglingen porcelain, built on the town's own thimble-making industry. Approx. €3. Afterwards, the Jüdisches Museum Creglingen in the old village of Archshofen, or simply the walk along the Tauber meadows.
itinerary.evening: Back to Rothenburg by 18:00. Eat early, then drop through the Kobolzeller Tor into the Burggarten for the last light over the Taubertal — this is the one view in town that turns gold rather than orange.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Rothenburg, Creglingen). Walking: 6 km. Transfer: 45 min driving, return.

itinerary.title: Market morning, craftsmen's house, and the Tauber loop
itinerary.morning: Market day. Rothenburg's Wochenmarkt sets up on the Marktplatz on Wednesday and Saturday mornings, usually from about 07:00 until 12:30 — Franconian asparagus in May, Zwetschgen and Bamberger Hörnla potatoes in September, plus a cheese van and a smoked-fish stall. Buy lunch here, not in a restaurant.
itinerary.afternoon: The Alt-Rothenburger Handwerkerhaus at Alter Stadtgraben 26 is a 700-year-old artisans' house left as its coopers, weavers, dyers, potters and shoemakers used it — eleven rooms, original workbenches, approx. €3.50. Then walk down through the Kobolzeller gate to the Doppelbrücke, the double-decked stone bridge over the Tauber, past the Topplerschlösschen of 1388 to Detwang, whose village church holds a second Riemenschneider — the Kreuzaltar, older and rougher than the Creglingen one. It is 1.5 km down and 1.5 km back up, all on a made path.
itinerary.evening: Schneeballen — the fist-sized fried pastry knot — is Rothenburg's edible cliché, and the honest way to eat one is at a working bakery on Untere Schmiedgasse rather than a souvenir shop. One is enough for two people.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 1 (Rothenburg + Detwang). Walking: 8 km. Transfer: none.

itinerary.title: South to Dinkelsbühl
itinerary.morning: An unhurried morning: coffee on the Marktplatz, the Rathausturm if the weather is clear (220 steep steps and a ladder at the top, approx. €2.50, best before 11:00), then load the car.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive 47 km south on the B25 — the old Romantic Road alignment through Schillingsfürst and Feuchtwangen, about 50 minutes. Check in inside Dinkelsbühl's walls and walk the Weinmarkt, the town's long spine of a square: the Deutsches Haus of 1440 with its carved timber front, the Schranne, and the Münster St. Georg at the end, one of the purest late-Gothic hall churches in southern Germany, its nave startlingly white.
itinerary.evening: Dinkelsbühl's night watchman walks nightly at 21:00 from the Münster, April to October, in German, singing rather than lecturing — free, tip the horn. Before that, the Rothenburger Weiher on the town's east side gives the whole wall reflected in water at dusk.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Rothenburg, Dinkelsbühl). Walking: 4 km. Transfer: 50 min / 47 km.

itinerary.title: Dinkelsbühl slowly, and Feuchtwangen's cloister
itinerary.morning: Market morning again — Dinkelsbühl's weekly market usually runs Wednesday and Saturday mornings from about 07:30 to 12:30 on the Altrathausplatz. Then the Haus der Geschichte in the old town hall, which does an honest job on the Thirty Years' War and the Kinderzeche, the children's festival held every third weekend of July since 1897.
itinerary.afternoon: Optional 25 km north to Feuchtwangen for the Romanesque Kreuzgang — a cloister used as an open-air theatre every summer by the Kreuzgangspiele — and the Fränkisches Museum's peasant furniture and painted cupboards. Or skip the car entirely and walk the full ring of Dinkelsbühl's wall from the outside: 2.5 km, sixteen towers, no crowds, wholly flat.
itinerary.evening: Wine on the Weinmarkt. Franconia's dry Silvaner in the squat Bocksbeutel is the local pour and it goes with Schäufele — roast pork shoulder — better than beer does.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Dinkelsbühl, Feuchtwangen). Walking: 7 km. Transfer: 45 min driving, return.

itinerary.title: Into the crater: Nördlingen
itinerary.morning: A long breakfast, then 32 km south on the B25 to Nördlingen, about 35 minutes. You cross the crater rim near Maihingen without noticing it — a 15-million-year-old impact basin 25 km wide, which is why the fields go suddenly flat.
itinerary.afternoon: Nördlingen is the only town in Germany with a completely walkable circular wall: 2.6 km, covered for most of its length, five gates, eleven towers, free and open all day. Do the whole ring, then the Rieskrater-Museum in the Klösterle barn of 1503, which explains the impact and displays a lunar sample lent by NASA — approx. €4.50.
itinerary.evening: Climb the Daniel, the 90 m tower of St.-Georgs-Kirche, 350 steps, approx. €5. The tower keeper still lives up there and calls "So, G'sell, so" across the roofs on the half hour between 22:00 and midnight. From the top the crater rim is a visible ring on the horizon.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Dinkelsbühl, Nördlingen). Walking: 6 km. Transfer: 35 min / 32 km.

itinerary.title: Market on the Marktplatz, then Harburg
itinerary.morning: Nördlingen's weekly market fills the Marktplatz on Wednesday and Saturday mornings, usually 07:00–12:30, in front of the Rathaus with its outdoor stone staircase of 1618. Ries onion, Swabian Spätzle flour, farm eggs. Eat breakfast off the stalls sitting on the Rathaus steps.
itinerary.afternoon: Twelve kilometres south, Schloss Harburg sits over the Wörnitz gorge — one of the oldest and least restored castles in southern Germany, with a real dungeon tower and a courtyard you can loiter in. Approx. €8 with a tour.
itinerary.evening: Return the car at Nürnberg (1h15 via the B25/A6) or take the train from Nördlingen via Donauwörth. If you have the evening, spend it back on the Nördlingen Marktplatz — it empties by 19:00 and the town belongs to its 20,000 residents again.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Nördlingen, Harburg). Walking: 4 km. Transfer: 25 min to Harburg; 1h15 to NUE.

accommodationStrategy.name: Burg-Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: Fifteen rooms built into the town wall at Klostergasse, with a terrace that hangs directly over the Tauber valley. It is inside the pedestrian zone, so you unload with a permit and then forget the car for three days — which is the whole point of basing here. Ask for a valley-side room; the town-side ones face a quiet lane but see nothing.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead for September; six for December.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Deutsches Haus
accommodationStrategy.description: The 1440 timber facade on the Weinmarkt is the most photographed building in town and the rooms behind it are plain, comfortable and quiet after the square empties at 22:00. You are thirty seconds from the night watchman's start point and the Saturday market, and the kitchen serves Franconian standards late by small-town standards.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead; avoid the Kinderzeche weekend in July unless that is the point.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel-Restaurant Klosterhof
accommodationStrategy.description: A calm, family-run house a few minutes' walk inside the wall, with parking on site — important, because Nördlingen's centre is tight and market mornings take the Marktplatz spaces. Good base for a two-night finish: you can walk the whole wall from the door and be at the Daniel in five minutes.
accommodationStrategy.booking: one month ahead outside festival dates.

logistics.emergency: 112 for everything across Germany; 110 for police. Pharmacies rotate a night service — the roster is posted in every Apotheke window as the *Notdienst*.
logistics.bookingWindows: The night watchman tours take no reservations. Restaurant tables inside Rothenburg's walls need a call by mid-afternoon in season. December accommodation in Rothenburg goes six to nine months out.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 for everything across Germany; 110 for police. Pharmacies rotate a night service — the roster is posted in every Apotheke window as the *Notdienst*.

other.label: Cash still matters
other.text: Franconian market stalls, small bakeries, church donation boxes and most tower climbs are cash-only. Carry €80–100 in small notes; there is an ATM on the Rothenburg Marktplatz and one on Dinkelsbühl's Segringer Straße.

other.label: The opening-hour trap
other.text: Small-town Germany closes at 18:00 on weekdays and around 14:00 on Saturdays, and shuts entirely on Sundays — bakeries excepted, which usually open Sunday morning for two or three hours. Buy anything you need on Saturday morning.

other.label: Monday closures
other.text: Museums in all three towns commonly close on Mondays outside high summer. The wall walks, churches and squares never do, which is why Day 1 and Day 4 are built around walls rather than exhibits.

other.label: Driving and parking
other.text: No environmental zone (Umweltplakette) applies in these towns, unlike Nürnberg city centre — if you detour into Nürnberg you need the green sticker. All three old towns restrict access; use the marked P lots outside the gates and pay at the machine.

other.label: Car-free version
other.text: Rothenburg is reachable by train via Steinach; Nördlingen sits on the Aalen–Donauwörth line. Dinkelsbühl has no railway at all — regional buses connect it to Rothenburg and Nördlingen but run a handful of times a day and thin out badly on Sundays. If you refuse to drive, spend four nights in Rothenburg and three in Nördlingen and treat Dinkelsbühl as a weekday bus excursion.

other.label: Drones
other.text: are effectively unusable over these old towns: the walls, towers and dense residential roofs put you inside flight restrictions and within earshot of everybody.

proTips: Rothenburg empties between 17:30 and 09:30. Coach groups arrive around 10:00 and are gone by 16:30 — stay inside the walls and you get the Plönlein, the Marktplatz and the wall walk to yourself twice a day.
Walk the Rothenburg wall clockwise from the Rödertor in the evening; the low sun is then behind you and the Taubertal side is lit rather than backlit.
The Herrgottskirche altar in Creglingen is unlit by design. Go between 11:00 and 13:00, when daylight from the south windows falls across the carving — much better than any spotlight.
In Nördlingen, do the wall circuit before the Daniel climb. From the parapet you learn the town's shape; from the tower you then read the crater rim, which otherwise looks like ordinary hills.
Buy Franconian wine at the market stalls, not in the souvenir shops on Herrngasse — the same growers from the Tauber valley sell direct, roughly a third cheaper.
Order Schneeballen fresh from a bakery counter rather than pre-bagged. They stale within a day and the vacuum-packed ones on the tourist streets are often weeks old.
If you are here on a Wednesday or Saturday, plan the day around the market and eat your main meal at midday. Kitchens in all three towns do their best work at lunch.
Schloss Harburg is 12 km from Nördlingen and almost nobody on the Romantic Road stops there. Go in the last hour before closing.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 95 km of driving in total; 45–55 km walked over the week; flat cobbles, wall parapets, one gentle river valley
raw.Who It Suits: Slow travellers, families with children over six, anyone who wants medieval Germany without a coach-park itinerary

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 95 km of driving in total; 45–55 km walked over the week; flat cobbles, wall parapets, one gentle river valley
typeSpecific.audience: Slow travellers, families with children over six, anyone who wants medieval Germany without a coach-park itinerary

packingNotes: Shoes with real grip: Franconian cobbles are rounded river stone, slick after rain, and the wall parapets have worn stone steps.
A compact rain shell — May and September both deliver 20-minute downpours with no warning.
A torch or phone light for the Daniel stair and the Rothenburg wall towers, which are unlit.
€100 in coins and small notes for markets, church boxes and tower turnstiles.
Binoculars: the Riemenschneider altars are roped off at three metres and the detail is the whole point.
A folding tote for market shopping — no stall in Germany gives you a bag.
One layer warmer than you expect for evenings; the Ries and the Tauber valley both drop sharply after sunset in autumn.
A refillable bottle: public fountains on the Marktplatz in Rothenburg and Nördlingen run drinking water unless posted *kein Trinkwasser*.
whatCouldGoWrong: **You arrive on a Monday and everything is shut.** Fallback: the wall circuits, all three parish churches and the market squares are open daily and free. Shift museum days to Tuesday and Wednesday.
**Rothenburg is overwhelming at midday.** If the crowd ruins it, walk out through the Kobolzeller gate to Detwang — twenty minutes down the valley and you will meet six people instead of six hundred.

**The Dinkelsbühl bus doesn't run on Sunday.** If you are car-free and get stranded, taxis operate between Dinkelsbühl and Ansbach or Nördlingen at roughly €70–90; book a day ahead through your hotel.
**December crowds and prices.** Rothenburg's Reiterlesmarkt triples room rates and fills the lanes. If you want Advent, base in Dinkelsbühl or Nördlingen and day-trip in on a weekday morning.

**Bad weather kills the tower climbs.** The Daniel and the Rathausturm close in high wind or ice. Substitute the Rieskrater-Museum, the Handwerkerhaus and a long lunch — both towns are built for weather.

trips.title: South Funen Archipelago: Ærø, Faaborg & Svendborg

bestPeriod.window: May to September. June for long light and open island ferries; late August for warm sea and fewer Danish holidaymakers; December for the Ærøskøbing Christmas streets
bestPeriod.raw: May to September. June for long light and open island ferries; late August for warm sea and fewer Danish holidaymakers; December for the Ærøskøbing Christmas streets

accommodation.note: €100–180 per night, double, in a kro or town hotel; €220+ for a manor stay

food.note: €50–80 per day; a kro dinner €40–65

transport.note: €120–200: train to Svendborg, inter-island ferries, bike hire €70–100 per week

activities.note: €60–110: Egeskov Castle, Faaborg Museum, Marstal Maritime Museum, distillery visit

trips.summary: A seven-day cozy towns trip itinerary in Det Sydfynske Øhav (South Funen Archipelago), Denmark.

itinerary.title: Svendborg and Christmas Cove
itinerary.morning: Train from Odense to Svendborg (about 45 minutes; Odense is 75 minutes from Copenhagen on the InterCity). Svendborg is the maritime capital of the archipelago, with wooden schooners still in the harbour.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the old town's hilly streets, the harbour, and the Danish Maritime Museum branch. Rent bikes for the week.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in the harbour quarter. Svendborg is where Bertolt Brecht lived in exile from 1933 to 1939 — the house is in Skovsbostrand, just outside town.

itinerary.title: Tåsinge: Troense and Valdemars Slot
itinerary.morning: Cycle over the bridge to Tåsinge and along to Troense, a single street of half-timbered captains' houses with hollyhocks against the walls — the most photographed village street in Funen.
itinerary.afternoon: Valdemars Slot, a 17th-century Baroque manor built by Christian IV for his son, with a beach and a restaurant in the old tea pavilion below it. Then the Bregninge church tower for the archipelago panorama.
itinerary.evening: Back to Svendborg, or stay in Troense for the quietest night of the week.

itinerary.title: Ferry to Ærø: Ærøskøbing
itinerary.morning: The Ærøfærgen from Svendborg to Ærøskøbing, about 75 minutes across the archipelago. The approach into the harbour is half the pleasure.
itinerary.afternoon: Ærøskøbing is the best-preserved 18th-century small town in Denmark: cobbled lanes, 1700s doorways, no building out of period, and gaslight-style street lamps. It takes ninety minutes to walk and a day to absorb. The Bottle Peter Museum holds 1,700 ships-in-bottles made by one obsessive man.
itinerary.evening: Eat at one of the town's handful of restaurants, then walk out to the Vesterstrand beach huts — a row of small painted bathing houses on the shore, protected as heritage.

itinerary.title: Ærø by bicycle: Marstal and Søby
itinerary.morning: Cycle east to Marstal, once one of the largest sailing-ship ports in Northern Europe and the setting for Carsten Jensen's novel *We, the Drowned*. The Marstal Maritime Museum is exceptional and run partly by retired sailors.
itinerary.afternoon: Return west along the south coast lanes past Store Rise's prehistoric long barrow and church. If you have the legs, continue to Søby at the northern tip with its shipyard and harbour.
itinerary.evening: Ærø's distillery and brewery both run tastings; the island has a small but serious drinks scene for its 6,000 inhabitants.
itinerary.dayStats: 35 km, gentle hills

itinerary.title: Ærø slow day: Voderup Klint and the artisan circuit
itinerary.morning: Voderup Klint, a stepped cliff of grass terraces sliding gently into the sea, with cattle grazing on the ledges — a genuinely strange and beautiful landscape, 15 minutes by bike from Ærøskøbing.
itinerary.afternoon: The island's makers: ceramicists, a weaver or two, the ship-in-bottle tradition, and the small galleries that open when their owners feel like it. Ærø has been a wedding destination for a century, which supports more craft than the population would suggest.
itinerary.evening: Sunset swim at Vesterstrand, then a long dinner.

itinerary.title: Faaborg and the small islands
itinerary.morning: Ferry Søby–Faaborg (about an hour). Faaborg is a merchant town with a leaning bell tower, cobbled streets and the Faaborg Museum — purpose-built in 1915 for the Funen Painters, and one of the loveliest small museums in Denmark, including its Kaare Klint furniture.
itinerary.afternoon: The Ø-færgen from Faaborg calls at Lyø, Avernakø and Bjørnø — islands with populations in the dozens, one shop, and a rhythm that has not changed. A half-day round trip to Lyø, with its village pond and stone maze, is the archipelago in miniature.
itinerary.evening: Faaborg's Torvet square and a harbour dinner.

itinerary.title: Egeskov and out
itinerary.morning: Cycle or bus to Egeskov Castle near Kværndrup — a moated Renaissance castle from 1554 standing on oak piles in its own lake, with gardens, a maze and a vintage vehicle collection.
itinerary.afternoon: Train from Kværndrup or Svendborg to Odense and on to Copenhagen.

accommodationStrategy.name: Pension Vestergade 44
accommodationStrategy.description: A 1784 merchant's house run as a guesthouse, with a walled garden and breakfast served on mismatched china. Six or so rooms. It is the reason people come back to Ærø, and it books out a season ahead for July.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Ærøhus / Det Lille Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: Two long-established town hotels within the historic centre, both with restaurants. Practical, warm, and 200 m from the ferry berth, which matters when you are arriving with bikes.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Ærø / Svendborg harbour hotels
accommodationStrategy.description: Base for the first and last nights, on the water, close to the station and the ferry. Good bike storage and a kitchen that stays open later than anything on the islands.

logistics.emergency: 112. Ærø has a health centre but the nearest hospital is on Funen — a ferry away. Factor this if you travel with anyone with a chronic condition.
logistics.weather: Mild, but this is an archipelago: wind is the variable. A hard southwesterly makes the exposed Ærø south coast slow and the ferries occasionally cancel.
logistics.bookingWindows: July on Ærø: 4–6 months for the good guesthouses. Danish schools' summer holiday (roughly late June to early August) is when the archipelago fills with Danish families. September is wide open.
logistics.money: DKK. Cards everywhere, including the island honesty stalls that sell eggs, flowers and potatoes by the roadside with an app payment code taped to the box.

other.label: Ferries are the timetable of this trip
other.text: Ærøfærgerne runs Svendborg–Ærøskøbing and Faaborg–Søby; the small-island Ø-færgen from Faaborg serves Lyø, Avernakø and Bjørnø on a fixed daily pattern. Foot passengers and cyclists rarely need to book; cars in July absolutely do. Sailings thin dramatically outside the summer season. `verify: true`

other.label: Cycling
other.text: Funen and Ærø are gently rolling, well signposted, and comprehensively bike-friendly; the national route 8 crosses this area. Lights are mandatory after dark. Ærø's lanes are narrow and hedged — ride single file.

other.label: Shop hours
other.text: Small-town Denmark closes early and Sunday hours are limited outside the summer season. Buy provisions on Saturday.

proTips: Take the ferry to Ærø **on foot or by bike, never by car**. Car spaces are the scarce commodity, the island is 30 km end to end, and Ærøskøbing's centre is barely drivable anyway.
Ærøskøbing at **07:00** — before the day-ferry arrives — is a town of eighteenth-century silence. That single hour is what the whole itinerary is built around.
The **Ø-færgen small-island run** is a public service, not a tour: it costs a few euros, the timetable allows 3–5 hours ashore, and you will be the only visitor on Lyø.
Danish *kro* (inn) dinners are a fixed institution and typically better value than anything calling itself a restaurant. Ask for the daily *dagens ret*.

Ærø is one of Europe's most self-sufficient renewable-energy communities, with community-owned wind and solar and an electric ferry on the Ærø routes. Ask about it; islanders are proud of it and will tell you the whole story.
Book Egeskov for a weekday. Weekend afternoons in summer are full-family territory and the gardens lose their calm.

raw.artisan_focus: Ship-in-bottle making, boat building, ceramics, small-batch whisky and brewing, hand-knitting
