trips.title: Pueblos Blancos: Grazalema, Setenil & the Road Down to Vejer
trips.subRegion: Sierra de Grazalema & the Cádiz–Málaga white villages

bestPeriod.window: Late March–early June & mid September–early November
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (inland highs of 38–42°C, sierra trails closed for fire risk 1 June–15 October) and late November–January, when Grazalema takes Spain's heaviest rainfall
bestPeriod.raw: Late March–early June & mid September–early November

accommodation.note: Two bases; €70–€120 pp/night in small village hotels

food.note: €10–€16 venta mains, one €45 tasting dinner in Vejer

transport.note: Rental car essential — rural buses run 1–2 times a day

activities.note: Cooking class, cheese dairy, Vía Verde bike hire, park permits

profile.difficultyNote: 2 — steep whitewashed lanes, one optional 12 km greenway ride and short sierra walks; nothing technical

trips.gatewayAirport: XRY — Jerez de la Frontera, 1 h 15 to Grazalema; AGP Málaga is the bigger-choice alternative at 2 h to Grazalema, 1 h 20 to Ronda
trips.summary: Two bases, one long descent. You spend four nights high in Grazalema at 823 m, where the sierra rains hardest and the wool is still woven, then drop three nights to Vejer de la Frontera within sight of the Atlantic. In between are the villages that make the route famous — Zahara on its castle rock, Setenil built under an overhanging cliff, Olvera at the head of a disused railway now turned greenway. The pacing is unhurried by design: one move, two open afternoons, and no day that asks for more than 70 km of driving. It suits people who like a village square at 21:00, cheese bought from the person who made it, and a week where the best hours are the ones with nothing scheduled.

itinerary.title: Up into the sierra
itinerary.morning: Land at Jerez, pick up the car, and take the A-382 then A-372 east through El Bosque. Stop at the Centro de Visitantes El Bosque to pick up park information and, if you plan restricted-zone walking, to sort permits.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive in Grazalema, park below the centre and check in. Walk the village end to end — it takes twenty minutes — and end on Plaza de España with a beer and a plate of chicharrones.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Cádiz El Chico on the square: sierra stews, local lamb, and a wine list that leans Cádiz rather than Rioja.
itinerary.dayStats: XRY–Grazalema 95 km / 1 h 15. Grazalema at 823 m. Village walk 1.4 km. Shops shut 14:00–17:30.

itinerary.title: Wool, cheese and the highest village
itinerary.morning: Artesanía Textil de Grazalema when the looms are running — the mill weaves merino blankets and ponchos the village has made since the 18th century. Buy the plain undyed manta, not the souvenir throw.
itinerary.afternoon: The 12 km run south to Villaluenga del Rosario for Queso Payoyo: taste the semicurado, the sheep's cheese rolled in rosemary, and the manteca-cured wheels. Walk the village's stone bullring, oval and set into the rock, then look into the sinkhole of the Sima de Villaluenga at the edge of town.
itinerary.evening: Back in Grazalema, Mesón El Simancón for tagarninas and payoyo-stuffed pork.
itinerary.dayStats: Grazalema–Villaluenga 12 km / 20 min. Villaluenga at 858 m — highest in Cádiz province. Cheese €12–€22/kg. Mill mornings roughly 09:00–14:00.

itinerary.title: Zahara, a mountain pass, and an empty afternoon
itinerary.morning: Drive the CA-9104 over Puerto de las Palomas to Zahara de la Sierra — the best road in Andalucía, with the reservoir opening below you at the top. Climb to the Nazrid keep for the view down the Zahara–El Gastor lake.
itinerary.afternoon: Nothing. Back over the pass by 14:30, then a book and a terrace. The sierra light between 17:00 and 20:00 does the work for you.
itinerary.evening: Tapas rather than dinner — work along Plaza de España and Calle Agua, ordering one plate per bar.
itinerary.dayStats: Grazalema–Zahara 17 km / 30 min via Puerto de las Palomas, 1,357 m. Castle path 1.2 km / 180 m ascent. Zahara village at 511 m.

itinerary.title: Setenil under the rock, Olvera above the greenway
itinerary.morning: Setenil de las Bodegas, where Calle Cuevas del Sol and Cuevas de la Sombra run under a genuine overhanging cliff — houses with a mountain for a roof. Coffee at a terrace table with 30 metres of rock above it.
itinerary.afternoon: North to Olvera: the church of Nuestra Señora de la Encarnación and the Moorish castle share one small ridge, and La Cilla below explains the Vía Verde. Hire bikes at the old station and ride out towards the Peñón de Zaframagón to watch griffon vultures.
itinerary.evening: Return to Grazalema for the last night; eat at a venta on the way rather than arriving late and hungry.
itinerary.dayStats: Grazalema–Setenil 33 km / 45 min; Setenil–Olvera 16 km / 25 min; Olvera–Grazalema 38 km / 50 min. Vía Verde 36 km total, 30 tunnels; Olvera–Zaframagón 12 km each way, near-flat. Bike hire €12–€18/day.

itinerary.title: Down through Arcos to the Atlantic light
itinerary.morning: Leave the sierra westward via Ubrique, the leather town, where workshops still cut and stitch for luxury houses. Then Arcos de la Frontera: Plaza del Cabildo on its cliff edge, the Basílica de Santa María, and the balcony over the Guadalete.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue south-west to Vejer de la Frontera. Park outside the walls — the old town's lanes are barely car-width — and check in. First walk: the Arco de la Segur, the Judería, and the walls at sunset.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at El Jardín del Califa, in the Moorish garden of the Califa hotel: Moroccan-leaning cooking, tagines, and a courtyard that stays cool.
itinerary.dayStats: Grazalema–Arcos 60 km / 1 h; Arcos–Vejer 65 km / 1 h. Vejer at 190 m, 10 km from the Atlantic. Walls circuit 1.8 km.
itinerary.sleep: La Casa del Califa, Vejer de la Frontera

itinerary.title: Market, cooking class, and an open afternoon
itinerary.morning: Shop the Mercado de Abastos with Annie B's Spanish Kitchen, then cook the haul — retinto beef, Barbate tuna, sherry from El Puerto — through a long, unhurried session with a roof terrace to eat it on.
itinerary.afternoon: Blank on purpose. Sleep it off, or drive 12 km to El Palmar for a flat empty beach and a chiringuito.
itinerary.evening: Late tapas inside the Mercado de Abastos itself, where the old market stalls now serve small plates from about 20:00.
itinerary.dayStats: Cooking class roughly 5–6 h, around €130–€160. Vejer–El Palmar 12 km / 18 min. Market tapas from 20:00, closed Sunday evening.
itinerary.sleep: La Casa del Califa, Vejer de la Frontera

itinerary.title: Last plaza, then out
itinerary.morning: Coffee on Plaza de España with the tiled fountain, then a slow last loop of the walls before the town wakes properly.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive north to Jerez — an hour — with time for a sherry bodega if your flight is late.
itinerary.evening: Flight home.
itinerary.dayStats: Vejer–XRY 65 km / 1 h; Vejer–AGP 195 km / 2 h 15. Add 45 min for the Jerez return in August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Casa de las Piedras
accommodationStrategy.description: A plain, long-running family hotel a minute off Plaza de España, with a mix of simple older rooms and renovated ones in the annexe. It is not luxurious, and that is why it works: parking nearby, breakfast from 08:00 for early sierra walks, and staff who know exactly which trails are open. Roughly €65–€95 per double.

accommodationStrategy.name: La Casa del Califa
accommodationStrategy.description: A warren of interconnected buildings on Plaza de España with Moorish and 16th-century fabric, a garden restaurant, and rooms reached by staircases you will get lost in for two days. Directly on the plaza, so you can go out for one drink and come back. Roughly €120–€180 per double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Fuerte Grazalema or Casa Rural La Mimbrera
accommodationStrategy.description: If Casa de las Piedras is full, take a rural house on the Grazalema–Benamahoma road instead of dropping to a chain in Ronda; the point of this week is waking inside the park boundary, not near it.

logistics.connectivity: Spain is in the EU roaming zone. 4G is fine in every village named here; the Vía Verde tunnels, Garganta Verde and the Puerto de las Palomas road have dead patches. Download the Cádiz–Málaga area offline.
logistics.emergency: 112 covers everything including mountain rescue and Guardia Civil. Sierra de Grazalema trails have no phone coverage in the gorges — leave a route note at your hotel.
logistics.weather: Grazalema records the highest annual rainfall in Spain, roughly 2,000 mm, concentrated November–March; a wet day here is genuinely wet. Summer inland highs hit 38–42°C while Vejer stays 6–8°C cooler thanks to the Atlantic levante and poniente winds, which blow hard enough on the coast to close beach umbrellas.
logistics.bookingWindows: Restricted-zone park permits (Garganta Verde, El Pinsapar, Llanos del Rabel) must be requested in advance through the Junta de Andalucía's Sierra de Grazalema reservation system — do it 2–4 weeks out for spring weekends. Annie B's classes book weeks ahead in spring and autumn. El Jardín del Califa needs 2–3 days.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards are standard in hotels and town restaurants, but ventas, cheese dairies and market stalls often want cash — carry €80–€100. Tipping is light: round up, or 5% on a full dinner.
logistics.transportRules: A car is effectively mandatory. Rural bus links exist — Transportes Generales Comes between Cádiz, Ubrique and Grazalema, and Los Amarillos between Ronda and Zahara/Grazalema — but typically run once or twice a day and not at all on Sundays. Village centres in Vejer, Arcos and Setenil are too narrow to drive; use the outer car parks. Fuel up in Ronda, Olvera or El Bosque, not in the small villages.
logistics.permits: The high-risk fire season (1 June–15 October) closes several sierra routes entirely. Wild camping is prohibited in the natural park. Drones need authorisation over the park and are banned over the villages.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable throughout. The sierra is limestone with sudden drops and no railings on the castle paths; take proper shoes. Sun exposure inland is severe from May — the villages are white for a reason.

proTips: Drive the CA-9104 from Grazalema to Zahara in the late afternoon rather than the morning: the Puerto de las Palomas viewpoint faces so that the reservoir lights up around 18:00, and the coach traffic has gone.
Buy your payoyo at the Villaluenga dairy, not in Grazalema's souvenir shops. Ask for vacuum-packing if you're flying — it doubles the safe carry time.
Setenil is a two-hour town swamped by day-trippers between 11:00 and 16:00. Arrive at 09:30, and eat in Olvera instead.
The Vía Verde is best ridden Olvera-to-Zaframagón and back rather than end-to-end: you get the vulture colony, the tunnels and the viaducts without needing a shuttle from Puerto Serrano.

Learn the sierra eating clock. Ventas serve lunch 13:30–16:00 and often shut afterwards; village restaurants don't take dinner orders before 20:30. Plan a late lunch and a very late dinner, not the reverse.
In Grazalema, ask at your hotel each morning which park zones are open. Permit availability, fire risk and rain all shift the answer daily, and the posted signs lag reality.
Vejer's Mercado de Abastos is a functioning food market by day and a tapas hall at night. Do both — morning for the tuna and the retinto, evening for the small plates.

raw.Plaza de España, Grazalema: is the hinge of the week: the church of Nuestra Señora de la Aurora on one side, three bar terraces on the others, and a fountain that the whole village passes twice a day. Shops shut 14:00–17:30; the square refills from 20:00 and is fullest at 21:30, an hour later than northern Spain.
raw.Plaza de España, Vejer: works to a different clock — Andalusian-tiled, palm-shaded, and busy from 19:30, with the paseo running out through the Arco de la Segur and along the walls.
raw.Artesanía Textil de Grazalema: on the A-372 at the village edge still weaves pure merino blankets on the town's centuries-old looms (the Merino Royale line). Weekday mornings are when you'll see the machines running; call before a Friday afternoon visit.
raw.Queso Payoyo, Villaluenga del Rosario: — the dairy and shop for the goat and sheep cheese named after the payoya goat breed. Villaluenga is the smallest municipality in Cádiz province and sits at 858 m, the highest village in the sierra.
raw.Vía Verde de la Sierra: 36 km of former railbed between Olvera and Puerto Serrano, through 30 tunnels and over four viaducts, passing the Peñón de Zaframagón griffon vulture colony. Bike hire at both end stations; an out-and-back from Olvera to Zaframagón is 12 km each way and almost flat.
raw.Venta culture: roadside ventas are where sierra cooking actually lives — sopa de tomate, chicharrones, venison in season, plates at €8–€14. They open early, close mid-afternoon, and rarely take cards.
raw.Hands-on experience: a day cooking class at **Annie B's Spanish Kitchen** in Vejer — market shopping first, then sherry, tapas and Andalusian technique in a house with a roof terrace over the plain.
raw.Pacing: one town move all week (Grazalema → Vejer on Day 5), full unstructured afternoons on Days 3 and 6, and short village-to-village walks where they exist — Grazalema to Benamahoma on the old Camino (7 km downhill), Zahara's castle path (1.2 km, 180 m).

sources.verified: Artesanía Textil de Grazalema (the Merino Royale blanket mill) confirmed as still operating. Queso Payoyo confirmed as operating at Villaluenga del Rosario with a second outlet in Grazalema. Vía Verde de la Sierra route length, tunnel count and Zaframagón vulture colony spot-checked.
sources.confidenceNotes: Mill and dairy opening hours are seasonal and were not confirmed day-by-day — advise users to phone ahead. Sierra de Grazalema restricted-zone permit rules and the fire-season closure window change annually; re-verify against the Junta de Andalucía before publishing. Room counts for Casa de las Piedras and La Casa del Califa are approximate. Annie B's Spanish Kitchen class pricing and calendar should be re-checked directly. Comes and Los Amarillos rural bus frequencies are volatile and were not timetable-verified this run — the file deliberately treats a car as mandatory. Villaluenga's cheese fair is annual but its date moves; no date is asserted here.

trips.title: Four Walled Villages of the Alsace Wine Road

bestPeriod.note: Start on a Thursday so Ribeauvillé's Saturday market and Colmar's covered market both fall inside the week; September brings the harvest and October the colour.

trips.gatewayAirport: Basel-Mulhouse EuroAirport (BSL/MLH)
trips.summary: Three fortified wine villages in seven days, nine kilometres apart, with grand cru footpaths, a 1715 cask and two mornings that start at ten.
trips.hook: The villages on the Route des Vins sit so close together that a week here needs almost no driving. You move three times, never more than twelve kilometres, and spend the rest of the days walking between vine rows and cellar doors. The trick is being inside the walls at seven in the morning and seven at night, when the coaches are somewhere else.

snapshot.Base(s): Riquewihr (3 nights) · Kaysersberg (2 nights) · Eguisheim (2 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 120 km driven all week; 35–45 km walked, including one 500 m ascent to the Ribeauvillé castles
snapshot.Getting There: EuroAirport Basel-Mulhouse to Colmar by rail via Saint-Louis, approx. 1h; or TGV Paris–Colmar in 2h40
snapshot.Who It Suits: Wine drinkers, slow walkers, food-market people, couples and families who want short days

itinerary.title: Inside the Riquewihr walls
itinerary.morning: Land at Basel-Mulhouse, pick up a car and drive north to Colmar and on to Riquewihr — about an hour in total. Park outside the ramparts; the village core is pedestrian.
itinerary.afternoon: Riquewihr survived the wars with its 16th-century fabric intact. Walk rue du Général-de-Gaulle from the lower gate to the Dolder, the 1291 belfry-gate that closes the top of the street, and look up: dated lintels, oriel windows, and courtyards with wooden galleries behind every arch.
itinerary.evening: Eat in a winstub — the Alsatian tavern format, long tables, tarte flambée and a pitcher of Riesling. Then walk the empty street; by 19:30 the day visitors have gone and Riquewihr belongs to about 1,200 residents.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 1. Walking: 4 km. Transfer time: approx. 1h from Basel.

itinerary.title: Cooperage, then the vine path
itinerary.morning: Nothing before 10:00. Then the Tour des Voleurs and the Maison de Vigneron beside it: a winemaker's house set out as it worked, with the cooper's bench, the hooping tools, the shaving horse and a great beam wine press. This is what village cooperage actually looked like, and it explains the shape of every cask you will see this week.
itinerary.afternoon: Pick up the marked sentier viticole behind the village and walk up through the Grand Cru Schoenenbourg — steep marl and gypsum, the reason Riquewihr Riesling ages — then across to Hunawihr with its fortified church, and back via Zellenberg. About 7 km, two hours, no navigation required.
itinerary.evening: Tastings in the village. Hugel & Fils has been in Riquewihr since 1639; ask to see the Sainte-Catherine foudre, in continuous use since 1715. Dopff au Moulin, a few doors down, makes the Crémant.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 3. Walking: 9 km. Transfer time: none.

itinerary.title: Market morning in Ribeauvillé
itinerary.morning: Five kilometres north, Ribeauvillé holds its weekly market on Saturday mornings, roughly 08:00–12:30, spreading along the Grand'Rue around the Place de la Sinne and its fountain. Munster from the valley farms, bretzels, charcuterie, fruit. Buy lunch.
itinerary.afternoon: Two workshops in one town. Beauvillé, on the edge of Ribeauvillé, still prints table linen by hand on flat screens in a former mill, and sells seconds and ends at the factory shop. The Cave de Ribeauvillé, founded in 1895 and the oldest wine cooperative in France, pours across the Grand Cru Kirchberg de Ribeauvillé and Geisberg.
itinerary.evening: If you have legs left, climb to the Trois Châteaux — Saint-Ulrich, Girsberg and Haut-Ribeaupierre — on the marked path above town. Roughly 500 m of ascent, two hours up, and the ruins look straight down the plain to the Black Forest.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 10 km. Transfer time: 20 min return by car.

itinerary.title: Nine kilometres, one grand cru
itinerary.morning: The second lie-in: nothing before 10:00. Pack slowly and drive the nine kilometres to Kaysersberg, which sits in the mouth of the Weiss valley under a ruined keep.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the fortified bridge of 1514, then the church of Sainte-Croix for its carved and painted altarpiece of 1518. Neighbouring Kientzheim, ten minutes on foot, holds the Grand Cru Schlossberg — the first Alsace vineyard classified, in 1975 — and Domaine Paul Blanck's tasting room at its foot.
itinerary.evening: Kaysersberg's main street empties completely after dinner. Domaine Weinbach, at the Clos des Capucins on the edge of the village, receives by appointment only; arrange it before you travel.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 6 km. Transfer time: 20 min driving.

itinerary.title: Up the valley for cheese and eau-de-vie
itinerary.morning: Drive 12 km up the Weiss to Lapoutroie. The Fromagerie Haxaire has been making and ageing Munster AOP here for generations — washed-rind, straw-mat matured, and eaten with cumin seeds rather than in spite of the smell. The cellars can be visited.
itinerary.afternoon: In the same village, the G. Miclo distillery works the Alsatian eaux-de-vie: kirsch, mirabelle, framboise, poire williams. Tastings are small and strictly for the passenger seat.
itinerary.evening: Back in Kaysersberg, the Albert Schweitzer museum occupies the house where he was born in 1875, three minutes from the bridge. Dinner in the village.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 2. Walking: 4 km. Transfer time: 45 min return by car.

itinerary.title: Jam, a watchman, and the ring village
itinerary.morning: Drive south, stopping at Niedermorschwihr, where Christine Ferber makes her copper-pan preserves at Maison Ferber on rue des Trois Épis. Opening hours are short and idiosyncratic — check before you set out — and the queue is worth it.
itinerary.afternoon: Twelve kilometres on to Eguisheim, whose lanes run in concentric rings around the Place du Château Saint-Léon and its fountain and chapel. Walk the outer ring twice: once for the flowers and once for the dated doorways. Domaine Léon Beyer and Domaine Bruno Sorg both pour in the village, on Grand Cru Eichberg and Pfersigberg.
itinerary.evening: In summer, Turckheim's night watchman still makes his round from the Place Turenne at 22:00, lantern, halberd and horn, from May to October. It is five kilometres away and it is not a re-enactment invented for visitors.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 3. Walking: 6 km. Transfer time: 40 min driving.

itinerary.title: Colmar, and out
itinerary.morning: Colmar is fifteen minutes away. Start at the Marché Couvert on rue des Écoles, the 1865 brick-and-iron hall trading Tuesday to Saturday, roughly 08:00–18:00 — oysters, Munster, horseradish, bretzels.
itinerary.afternoon: The Musée Unterlinden, in a Dominican convent with a 2015 Herzog & de Meuron extension, holds Grünewald's Isenheim altarpiece; it closes on Tuesdays, which is why it sits on this day. Walk out past the Koïfhus of 1480, the Maison Pfister of 1537 and the canals of the Petite Venise.
itinerary.evening: Colmar to Basel-Mulhouse is about an hour by road, less by train and shuttle.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns visited: 1. Walking: 6 km. Transfer time: approx. 1h to Basel.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel de la Couronne
accommodationStrategy.description: A handful of rooms in a stone house on rue de la Couronne, within the ramparts and a minute from the Dolder. Sleeping inside the walls is the entire argument: you get Riquewihr at 07:00 and 21:00, which is the only time it resembles the village in the photographs. Ask about the loading permit for driving in with bags.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3 months ahead for September and October.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Constantin
accommodationStrategy.description: A former winegrower's house on rue du Père Kohlman, quiet, small, with a courtyard and its own parking — which is not a given in a village where the street is closed to traffic. Two minutes from the fortified bridge and the church, and ten minutes on foot to the Schlossberg vines at Kientzheim.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2 months ahead; the Advent weekends sell out by summer.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hostellerie du Château
accommodationStrategy.description: Directly on the Place du Château Saint-Léon, facing the fountain and the chapel, in a half-timbered house with about a dozen rooms. Being on the square means the ring lanes are a doorstep walk at dawn, and you can leave the car parked for two full days.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–3 months ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 across Europe; in France, 15 for the SAMU medical service and 17 for police. Pharmacies display the on-duty rota for nights and Sundays.
logistics.money: Cards everywhere; market stalls and small producers still prefer cash. Carry €60.

other.label: Drink-driving
other.text: The French limit is 0.5 g/L of blood, and 0.2 g/L for licence-holders of under three years. Every serious tasting room has a spittoon and expects you to use it. Colmar taxis will do village runs, and a designated driver is the norm here.

other.label: Tasting appointments
other.text: Village co-operatives and the larger houses have walk-in tasting rooms. Named domaines — Weinbach, Zind-Humbrecht, Trimbach — are appointment-only, by email, usually a few weeks out. Expect a €10–€20 tasting fee, often waived on purchase.

other.label: Village traffic
other.text: Riquewihr, Eguisheim and Kaysersberg close their cores to cars. Use the paid car parks outside the walls, around €5–€8 per day, and ask your hotel to authorise a short loading window.

other.label: Crit'Air
other.text: France's air-quality sticker is required in Strasbourg's low-emission zone. Order one online before travelling if your route touches Strasbourg; Colmar and the villages do not currently require it.

other.label: Closing days
other.text: Many Alsatian restaurants close Sunday evening and all day Monday and Tuesday. Museums generally close Tuesday, and the covered market in Colmar closes Monday.

other.label: Harvest
other.text: The *vendanges* run roughly mid-September to mid-October. Cellars are working, tasting rooms may shut without notice, and tractors own the vineyard lanes.

proTips: Walk the sentier viticole between Riquewihr and Hunawihr in the late afternoon: the path faces east, so the light comes over your shoulder onto the Schoenenbourg slope rather than into the lens.
Ask at Hugel to see the 1715 Sainte-Catherine cask. It is not on the standard tasting and they will usually show it if the cellar is quiet.
Buy from the Cave de Ribeauvillé rather than the village boutiques: co-operative pricing on grand cru bottlings runs meaningfully below the shop shelves ten metres away.
Order Munster with cumin and eat it at the end, not with dessert. Ask for the Haxaire *fermier* by name on any cheese board in the valley.
Riquewihr and Eguisheim take their coach traffic between 10:30 and 17:00. Do interiors and tastings then; walk the streets at 07:30 and after 19:00.
Book the Turckheim watchman round for a clear evening. He does not go out in heavy rain, and there is no schedule to appeal to.
A wine box from any co-operative ships or travels far better than bottles in a suitcase; most cellars sell purpose-made six-bottle flight cases for a few euros.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 120 km driven all week; 35–45 km walked, including one 500 m ascent to the Ribeauvillé castles
raw.Who It Suits: Wine drinkers, slow walkers, food-market people, couples and families who want short days

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 120 km driven all week; 35–45 km walked, including one 500 m ascent to the Ribeauvillé castles
typeSpecific.audience: Wine drinkers, slow walkers, food-market people, couples and families who want short days

packingNotes: Shoes that handle both cobbles and a chalky vineyard path; the sentier viticole is dusty in summer and slick after rain.
A layer for the Weiss valley, which sits higher and colder than the plain.
Sun protection for the vine paths, which have no shade at all between May and September.
A folding six-bottle carrier or padded wine sleeves if you plan to fly home with anything.
Cash for markets, car parks and the Lapoutroie cellars.
A light waterproof — Vosges foothill weather turns fast in the afternoon.
Something smarter than walking clothes for one dinner; Alsatian restaurants are informal but not scruffy.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Every village is full of coaches.** Restructure rather than relocate. Hunawihr, Zellenberg, Niedermorschwihr and Kientzheim take almost no group traffic and are all within five kilometres.
**A domaine cancels because it is harvest.** Cellar doors in the co-operatives stay open through the vendanges; switch to the Cave de Ribeauvillé or Wolfberger at Eguisheim.
**Rain for two days.** Unterlinden, the Beauvillé works, the Haxaire cellars, the Miclo distillery and the Riquewihr museums make a full wet-weather week between them.
**You cannot park at your hotel.** Alsace village cores are genuinely closed. Confirm the loading arrangement at booking, and travel with bags you can wheel or carry 300 m over cobbles.
**Someone has to drive after tastings.** Build the week around one non-drinking driver per day, or use Colmar-based taxis for the Ribeauvillé and Lapoutroie legs.

trips.title: The Périgord Noir, Slowly

bestPeriod.note: Truffle and foie gras season runs November to March, outside this window; these dates instead catch the walnut harvest and the start of autumn markets without July's crowds.

trips.gatewayAirport: Bergerac Dordogne Périgord (EGC)
trips.summary: A slow week between Sarlat's market streets and the Vézère's river villages, with one relocation, walnut mills and honey-stone bastides.
trips.hook: This is a week for a single valley, walked twice rather than four valleys walked once. Sarlat's golden stone streets, the cliff villages on the Dordogne, and the quiet Romanesque churches of the Vézère all sit within a short drive of each other — close enough that the right pace is no pace at all.

snapshot.Base(s): Sarlat-la-Canéda (4 nights), then Saint-Léon-sur-Vézère (3 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Under 200 km of driving all week, flat river walks, occasional hilltop climbs
snapshot.Getting There: 20 min from Bergerac Airport to Sarlat; TGV to Bordeaux then a rental car (2h15)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Slow travellers, food-focused couples, families who like rivers more than motorways

itinerary.title: Settling into Sarlat-la-Canéda
itinerary.morning: Arrive and walk into the old town through Rue de la République. The daily produce market fills the Sainte-Marie hall — a deconsecrated church redesigned as a covered market by Jean Nouvel in 2001 — every morning except Monday.
itinerary.afternoon: Wander Rue de la Salamandre and Rue des Consuls, lined with 14th- to 17th-century hôtels particuliers in honey-coloured limestone, then the Lanterne des Morts beside the cathedral.
itinerary.evening: Dinner near Place du Marché aux Oies, the old goose market square, on Périgourdine staples: confit, walnut salad, Cabécou.
itinerary.dayStats: 3 km walking · relocations: 0 · market: Sarlat daily produce market (except Monday), 08:00–13:00.

itinerary.title: Sarlat's Saturday market and a walnut mill
itinerary.morning: Time this day for a Saturday: the market spreads through every street of the old town, 08:00–13:00, alongside a smaller Wednesday version. Walnuts, cèpes in season, foie gras, duck confit and Cabécou cheese fill the stalls.
itinerary.afternoon: A 15-minute drive to Sainte-Nathalène for the Moulin de la Tour, a 19th-century stone mill still pressing walnut and hazelnut oil on its original millstones, with tastings at the end of the visit.
itinerary.evening: Return to Sarlat for a quiet dinner; the town empties out fast once the market stalls are gone.
itinerary.dayStats: 20 km round trip, 30 min driving · relocations: 0.

itinerary.title: La Roque-Gageac and Domme
itinerary.morning: La Roque-Gageac, built into a cliff face above the Dordogne, has a small riverside market on Friday mornings in season. Walk the single street and the troglodyte fort cut into the rock above it, then take a gabare river boat — flat-bottomed barges once used to carry goods downriver, now running short scenic loops.
itinerary.afternoon: Domme, a bastide founded in 1281 on a limestone spur, has its own Thursday morning market on Place de la Halle. Walk through the Porte des Tours gate, stand at the Belvédère de la Barre for the whole valley in one view, and cool off in the show cave below the town, the Grotte de Domme.
itinerary.evening: Back to Sarlat, 12 km.
itinerary.dayStats: 26 km round trip, 45 min driving · relocations: 0 · markets: La Roque-Gageac (Friday, seasonal), Domme (Thursday, 08:00–13:00).

itinerary.title: Beynac-et-Cazenac
itinerary.morning: Château de Beynac, an 11th- to 13th-century fortress on a sheer cliff above the river, is one of the best-preserved in the valley and was used as a filming location for its unbroken medieval silhouette. Climb the narrow lanes below it slowly — there is no reason to rush a village this small.
itinerary.afternoon: A short riverside walk toward La Balme or a second gabare run from Beynac's own landing, looking back up at the château from the water.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Beynac, then back to Sarlat to pack for tomorrow's move.
itinerary.dayStats: 24 km round trip, 40 min driving · relocations: 0.

itinerary.title: Relocating to the Vézère: Saint-Léon-sur-Vézère
itinerary.morning: The one relocation of the week: Sarlat to Saint-Léon-sur-Vézère, 35 km, about 40 minutes on quiet D-roads. The village is listed among France's most beautiful, built around a Romanesque church, Saint-Léonce, from the 11th and 12th centuries, and a bend in the river with a shallow beach.
itinerary.afternoon: Check into the new base and walk the riverside path past the private Château de la Salle and Château de Clérans, visible only from outside.
itinerary.evening: A slow dinner in the village; there is little else to do here after dark, which is the point.
itinerary.dayStats: 35 km, 40 min driving · relocations: 1.

itinerary.title: Montignac market and Vézère prehistory
itinerary.morning: Montignac-Lascaux holds a market on Wednesday and Saturday mornings along the riverbank, smaller and less touristy than Sarlat's.
itinerary.afternoon: Lascaux IV, the Centre International de l'Art Pariétal designed by Snøhetta in 2016, needs a timed ticket — book at least a few weeks ahead in summer. Alternatively, or as a second stop, the Renaissance Château de Losse near Thonac sits directly on the Vézère with formal gardens running down to the water.
itinerary.evening: Dinner back in Saint-Léon-sur-Vézère or Montignac.
itinerary.dayStats: 18 km round trip, 25 min driving · relocations: 0 · market: Montignac, Wednesday and Saturday, 08:00–13:00.

itinerary.title: Les Eyzies and departure
itinerary.morning: Les Eyzies-de-Tayac, self-styled capital of prehistory, holds the Musée National de Préhistoire, built into the cliff itself by architect Jean-Pierre Buffi in 2004, and the Abri Pataud rock shelter beside it.
itinerary.afternoon: Last stop for foie gras, walnut oil and duck products at a producer shop in Les Eyzies or back through Sarlat, depending on your route to Bergerac.
itinerary.evening: If the flight is late, a final dinner in Bergerac's own old town near the Cyrano statue before the airport.
itinerary.dayStats: 25 km to Les Eyzies, then 55 km to Bergerac, about 1h15 total driving · relocations: 0 (departure).

accommodationStrategy.name: La Hoirie
accommodationStrategy.location: Route de la Chapelle-Péchaud, just outside Sarlat
accommodationStrategy.description: A 17th-century manor with its own park and pool a five-minute drive from Sarlat's old town, useful for Days 1–4 when you want quiet evenings after a day of walking cobbles and market crowds. Ask for a room facing the garden, not the car park.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–10 weeks ahead for Saturday-market weeks.

accommodationStrategy.name: La Villa des Consuls
accommodationStrategy.description: A 16th-century town house on a quiet street inside the old town walls, close enough to the Sainte-Marie market hall to walk over for coffee before the Saturday crowds build. Good for travellers who want to be inside Sarlat rather than driving in each morning.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Moulin de la Beune
accommodationStrategy.description: An old mill building on the Beune, a short walk from the Vézère confluence and the prehistory museum, and a 15-minute drive from Saint-Léon-sur-Vézère — a good last-night option if your flight leaves early from Bergerac.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 for all services; French mountain and river rescue also routes through 112.
logistics.money: Cards work in restaurants and larger shops; carry cash for market stalls and small producers.
logistics.health: The Vézère's beach at Saint-Léon-sur-Vézère is unsupervised — check current speed after rain before letting children swim.

other.label: A car is essential
other.text: Public transport between these villages is sparse to nonexistent; rent from Bergerac or Bordeaux and plan on under 200 km for the whole week.

other.label: Parking in Sarlat
other.text: The old town is largely pedestrian on market mornings; use the Sainte-Marie or Plaine de la Rode car parks and walk in — do not attempt to drive into the centre on a Saturday before 13:00.

other.label: Market rhythm
other.text: Sarlat: daily except Monday, biggest Saturday. Domme: Thursday mornings. La Roque-Gageac: Friday mornings, seasonal. Montignac: Wednesday and Saturday mornings. Build the week around whichever falls where you are.

other.label: Truffle and foie gras seasonality
other.text: Fresh Périgord black truffle (Tuber melanosporum) is a December-to-March product, sold at winter truffle markets in Sarlat and at Sainte-Alvère's Monday afternoon truffle market; outside those months, shops sell preserved or frozen truffle and jarred foie gras rather than fresh.

other.label: Opening-hour trap
other.text: Small village shops and even some château ticket desks close for lunch, typically 12:30–14:00, and many are shut on Mondays outside peak summer.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 for all services; French mountain and river rescue also routes through 112.

proTips: Arrive so that Day 2 lands on a Saturday; Sarlat's market is markedly bigger than the Wednesday version and worth building the whole week around.
Reach Beynac and La Roque-Gageac by 09:30 — both fill with coach groups from Sarlat and Périgueux by midday.
The Moulin de la Tour tasting is free with a visit; buy the walnut oil there rather than in a Sarlat shop, it is noticeably fresher.
Book Lascaux IV tickets for a late-morning slot; the light in the reconstructed caves reads better before the afternoon groups thicken the queue.
The Grotte de Domme stays a cool 13°C year-round — a good midday escape from a hot Périgord afternoon.
Château de Losse draws far fewer visitors than Beynac despite being just as photogenic from the river.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Under 200 km of driving all week, flat river walks, occasional hilltop climbs
raw.Who It Suits: Slow travellers, food-focused couples, families who like rivers more than motorways

typeSpecific.surface: Under 200 km of driving all week, flat river walks, occasional hilltop climbs
typeSpecific.audience: Slow travellers, food-focused couples, families who like rivers more than motorways

packingNotes: Flat, grippy shoes — Sarlat's cobbles and Domme's ramparts are uneven underfoot.
A light layer for the show caves and mill interiors, which stay around 12–14°C even in July.
Swimwear for the Vézère beach at Saint-Léon-sur-Vézère.
A reusable tote for market shopping; stallholders weigh and wrap, they do not bag.
Cash in small notes and coins for market stalls and church donation boxes.
A hat and sun protection for the exposed viewpoints at Domme and the Belvédère de la Barre.
A cool bag if you plan to buy foie gras or fresh duck products to take home.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Lascaux IV is sold out for your date.** Font-de-Gaume near Les Eyzies runs limited daily tickets to see original polychrome paintings, a genuine and often quieter alternative.
**Sarlat's car parks are full on Saturday morning.** Park at Plaine de la Rode and walk the ten minutes in rather than circling for a closer spot.
**A château or mill closes for a private event.** Most post updates on their own websites the week before; check the morning you plan to go rather than assuming a summer schedule holds.
**Midsummer heat makes midday walking unpleasant.** Shift to a Domme-cave or museum interior between 13:00 and 16:00, and save exposed viewpoints for morning or early evening.
**Narrow D-roads and blind bends catch first-time drivers.** Speeds are naturally low; treat every hilltop bend as blind and give way at unmarked village junctions.

trips.title: Pelion Kalderimia: Mansions, Plane Trees and the Little Train
trips.subRegion: Thessaly — Mount Pelion & the Pagasetic Gulf

bestPeriod.window: Mid-May–late June & mid-September–early November
bestPeriod.avoid: August — Greek domestic holidays fill every archontiko and the east-coast beach road jams; January–February closes many village kitchens and can snow the Chania pass shut.
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-May–late June & mid-September–early November

accommodation.note: Restored archontiko double €90–€160 per room; per-person share

food.note: Village taverna mains €8–€14; a Volos tsipouradiko round €6–€9 with meze

transport.note: Small hire car for the week plus fuel; or KTEL buses at a fraction of it

activities.note: Moutzouris train, Milies library, co-op visit, museum entries

profile.difficultyNote: 2/5 — optional cobbled walks of 40 minutes to 2 hours with real descent; everything else is sitting down

trips.gatewayAirport: SKG Thessaloniki — 2 h 30 min drive to Makrinitsa; VOL Nea Anchialos (seasonal) 45 min; ATH Athens 3 h 30 min, or 3 h by train to Volos with a change at Larissa
trips.summary: Pelion is the mountain the centaurs were given, a 1,600 m ridge that drops on one side into the flat Pagasetic Gulf and on the other straight into the Aegean, and it is stitched together by *kalderimia* — cobbled mule paths, laid by hand, that were the only roads until the 1960s. The villages on it are unlike anywhere else in Greece: slate-roofed stone mansions with painted ceilings, built by a merchant class that got rich on silk and never quite left. This week uses three bases and no more, walks between villages rather than driving where possible, rides the metre-gauge Moutzouris train down to Milies, and spends deliberate hours doing nothing under thousand-year-old plane trees. It is a slow week by design: two moves, two long walks, several blocks of afternoon with nothing in them at all.

itinerary.title: Up to Makrinitsa, and the balcony at dusk
itinerary.morning: Drive up from Volos or SKG to **Makrinitsa** and park at the village entrance — the core is cobbled and closed to cars. Walk in with a bag; someone will help.
itinerary.afternoon: Nothing scheduled. Sit on the square, look at the **Theophilos mural** in the old kafeneio, and let the coach tours leave.
itinerary.evening: Dinner on a terrace above the gulf; the lights of Volos come on 600 m below you, and the mountain goes quiet at about nine.
itinerary.dayStats: Drive Volos→Makrinitsa 17 km / 30 min; village altitude ≈600 m; walking 1.5 km

itinerary.title: The kalderimi to Portaria and back
itinerary.morning: Walk the **Makrinitsa → Portaria kalderimi**, 40–50 minutes down through the Karavos gorge past the Mana springs. Coffee in Portaria's square under the planes.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk back up, slowly, or take the road. Then the Museum of Folk Art and History of Pelion in Makrinitsa's Topali mansion — one hour, no more.
itinerary.evening: Grilled meats and *spetsofai* — the Pelion sausage-and-pepper stew that is the mountain's actual signature dish — with a carafe of local tsipouro.
itinerary.dayStats: 5 km walking / 150 m descent and ascent / kalderimi 2.5 km, 40–50 min each way

itinerary.title: Move to Vizitsa; Milies and the painted ceiling
itinerary.morning: Drive over to **Vizitsa**, 30 km of hairpins and 50 minutes. Park at the edge and walk your bags into the car-free core.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the **Vizitsa → Milies kalderimi**, 35–45 minutes under chestnuts, to **Milies**. See the **Church of Agioi Taxiarches** and its zodiac-painted vault, and the **Public Historical Library of Milies**, founded 1814 — a genuine Enlightenment collection in a mountain village of a few hundred people.
itinerary.evening: Eat in Milies' square and walk the kalderimi back in the dark with a torch, or take the five-minute road transfer.
itinerary.dayStats: Drive 30 km / 50 min; kalderimi 2.2 km each way, 35–45 min; Milies ≈400 m

itinerary.title: The Moutzouris, and a deliberately empty afternoon
itinerary.morning: If it is a Saturday or Sunday and the line is running, drive down to **Ano Lechonia** for the **10:00 Moutzouris departure** — 15 km of 60 cm gauge built by Evaristo de Chirico, over stone viaducts and through hand-cut cuttings, with a halt at **Ano Gatzea**, arriving Milies about 90 minutes later. Otherwise walk the old alignment from Milies down toward Ano Gatzea.
itinerary.afternoon: **Do nothing.** The archontiko *sala*, a book, the shade. This is the point of the week, not a gap in it.
itinerary.evening: Vizitsa has one or two kitchens and they close early. Eat at eight, sleep at ten.
itinerary.dayStats: Train €10 single / €18 return, 15 km in ≈90 min, Sat–Sun, dep. Ano Lechonia 10:00 / Milies 15:00; drive Vizitsa→Ano Lechonia 12 km / 25 min

itinerary.title: Cross the mountain to Tsagarada
itinerary.morning: Drive east over the ridge to **Tsagarada** — 35 km, a full hour, endless hairpins through beech and chestnut, with the Aegean appearing suddenly on the far side.
itinerary.afternoon: Find the **plane tree in the square of Agia Paraskevi**: a thousand years old, roughly 14 m around, with a stone bench built into the roots. Sit under it. Walk the lanes between the four hamlets, which are further apart than any map suggests.
itinerary.evening: Dinner and the bar at the **Lost Unicorn**, or a taverna in Agios Stefanos.
itinerary.dayStats: Drive 35 km / 1 h; Tsagarada ≈500 m; four hamlets spread over ≈3 km

itinerary.title: Zagora apples, and the co-op
itinerary.morning: **Nothing before eleven.** Breakfast slowly.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive to **Zagora**, 18 km and 35 minutes north, for the **Agricultural Cooperative of Zagora** — the shop, the packing line if it is October, and the terraced orchards of **Mila Zagoras Piliou PDO** and **Firiki Piliou**. Walk the four quarters and look into the 1762 library.
itinerary.evening: Down to **Chorefto** for fish on the beach, or back to Tsagarada.
itinerary.dayStats: Drive 18 km / 35 min each way; harvest season late Sept–end Oct; walking 3 km

itinerary.title: Down to Damouchari, and Volos tsipouradika
itinerary.morning: Walk the **kalderimi from Agia Paraskevi down to Damouchari**, 4 km and 450 m of descent in 1 h 10–1 h 30, ending at the only natural harbour on Pelion's east coast — a pebble cove of stone houses and a ruined Venetian tower, used as a location for *Mamma Mia!*. Swim. Arrange a lift back up rather than walking it.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive down to **Volos**, 55 km and 1 h 20.
itinerary.evening: The **tsipouradika** ritual, which is Volos's real institution: you order tsipouro by the small bottle and a plate of meze arrives with each round, different every time, chosen by the kitchen. Go to **Kavouras**, Hatziargiri 3 near the port, one of the oldest; or into **Nea Ionia** for **Demiris**, Efremidou 23, for shellfish and *kolitsiani*, or **Bokos**, Meandrou 143, where the tables are entirely local. A round is €6–€9. Three rounds is dinner.
itinerary.dayStats: Kalderimi 4 km / 450 m descent / 1 h 10–1 h 30; drive to Volos 55 km / 1 h 20; tsipouro round €6–€9
itinerary.sleep: Volos waterfront hotel, or out on an evening flight from SKG

accommodationStrategy.name: Archontiko Repana
accommodationStrategy.description: A genuine merchant's archontiko of roughly eight to ten rooms on the upper lanes, with carved wooden ceilings, a stone-flagged breakfast room and the whole Pagasetic Gulf below the windows. There is no vehicle access — you park at the village entrance and walk in on cobbles, which is the trade for sleeping inside a car-free village. Roughly €90–€140 per room with breakfast. **Archontiko Xiradaki** and **Archontiko Karamarli** are equivalents on the same lanes.

accommodationStrategy.name: Archontiko Karagiannopoulou
accommodationStrategy.description: Vizitsa's core is entirely pedestrian and its archontika are the reason the village is protected. Six to nine rooms around a shared *sala*, wood-burning stoves that matter in May and October, and a hostess who will cook if you ask by lunchtime. **Archontiko Blana** is the near-neighbour alternative. Around €80–€130 per room.

accommodationStrategy.name: Lost Unicorn Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: Ten or so rooms, a proper library, a bar that stays open, and a garden — the right base for the east side because Tsagarada's four hamlets have almost no evening life of their own. Two minutes from the Agia Paraskevi plane tree and the head of the Damouchari kalderimi. Roughly €100–€160 per room.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming applies, no surcharge. 4G is good in Volos, Makrinitsa, Portaria and Zagora, patchy in the Tsagarada hamlets and on the cross-mountain road, and effectively absent on the kalderimi in the gorges. Download offline maps: the cobbled paths are unnumbered and the junctions are ambiguous.
logistics.emergency: 112 nationwide; ambulance 166. The referral hospital is **Achillopouleio General Hospital in Volos** — 1 h 20 from Tsagarada on hairpins, which is the real argument for driving carefully. Greece is in the EU, so EHIC/GHIC covers state care; carry travel insurance for repatriation.
logistics.weather: Pelion is far wetter and cooler than the Greek stereotype — the ridge catches Aegean moisture and Tsagarada is one of the rainiest inhabited places in Greece. Expect fog on the ridge road, sudden autumn downpours, and 10 °C between the gulf shore and the villages. Snow closes the Chania pass several times each winter. Cobbles become genuinely dangerous when wet.
logistics.bookingWindows: Archontika for late September and October need **6–10 weeks**; for August, months. The Moutzouris train should be booked ahead at weekends through Hellenic Train — capacity is small and it sells out. The Zagora co-op visit needs a phone call a week ahead. Village tavernas rarely need booking except at weekends.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards are widely taken in Volos and at hotels, but **village kafeneia, kalderimi-side tavernas and the co-op shop often prefer cash** — carry €100–€150. The train sells tickets onboard **cash only**. Tipping is rounding up or 5–10%.
logistics.transportRules: A small car is strongly preferable to a large one — the Pelion roads are narrow, cambered and hairpinned, and several village approaches end in a wall. **Do not attempt to drive into Makrinitsa or Vizitsa's cores.** KTEL Magnisias buses serve the west side well and the east side barely; a Volos→Tsagarada return by bus commits you to two departures a day. Greek motorway tolls to Volos are cash or card at barriers. Cross-border rental to North Macedonia or Albania needs written permission.
logistics.permits: No park fees. The villages of Makrinitsa, Vizitsa, Milies and parts of Tsagarada are **protected traditional settlements** — hence the cobbles, the slate roofs and the parking restrictions. Drones need Greek CAA registration and are restricted over settlements. Foraging chestnuts and herbs on private terraces is not yours to do; ask.
logistics.health: Tap water in the Pelion villages is spring-fed and excellent — the fountains on the squares are drinkable. Ticks are present in the chestnut and beech woods spring to autumn. Adders exist but are rarely seen. The genuine hazards are the **wet kalderimi** and the **descent to Damouchari**, where a 450 m drop on uneven cobbles turns knees to mush — take poles.

proTips: **Confirm the Moutzouris is actually running before you build a day on it.** The line has been suspended for extended periods in recent years and reinstated at short notice. Check Hellenic Train's Pelion page in the week of travel and have Day 4 work without it — the old railway alignment on foot from Milies is a good substitute.
**Stay in Makrinitsa overnight rather than visiting it.** Between 11:00 and 15:00 it is a coach stop; from 17:00 to 10:00 it is one of the loveliest villages in Greece, and only guests are there.
**Walk the kalderimia downhill and arrange a lift back.** Makrinitsa→Portaria and Tsagarada→Damouchari are both far better descended, and every guesthouse can organise the return leg for €15–€25.

**Order tsipouro the Volos way.** Do not order food. Order a round of tsipouro — *me anise* or *choris* — and the meze comes with it, different each round. Ordering a menu marks you out immediately and costs more.

**Come in October if you can.** Apple harvest at Zagora, chestnuts at Xourichti, the *kazania* firing for tsipouro, empty guesthouses at shoulder rates, and the beech woods turning. It is the single best month on the mountain.

**Book one archontiko room with a *sala* and a stove.** The shared sitting room is the architecture — carved ceilings, low divans, stained glass — and the point of paying for a mansion rather than a hotel.

**Cross the mountain in daylight.** The Portaria–Chania–Tsagarada road is beautiful and completely unlit, with a hairpin every two hundred metres and free-ranging goats. An hour becomes ninety minutes after dark, in fog it becomes two.
**Ask your host about a *kazani* in late October.** Tsipouro distillation is licensed, communal and entirely social; there is no ticket and no schedule, only an invitation.
**Eat spetsofai at least twice.** It is Pelion's own dish — country sausage, peppers, tomato — and every village kitchen makes it differently.

raw.Makrinitsa (≈600 m), the \"balcony of Pe: the square is a shelf hanging over Volos with a marble fountain, four enormous plane trees, the Church of Agios Ioannis Prodromos, and the old kafeneio holding a **mural by Theophilos Hatzimihail**. Rhythm: dead until 09:00, coffee and *loukoumades* until noon, a coach-tour surge 11:00–15:00, then genuinely empty and beautiful from 17:00.
raw.Portaria (≈600 m): a working village rather than a museum, plane-shaded square by Panagia Portarea, busiest at the 18:00–20:00 *volta*.
raw.Vizitsa (≈500 m): no vehicles reach the core — you park at the edge and walk cobbles in. A single small square, one or two kitchens, silent by 22:00.
raw.Milies (≈400 m): the square holds the **Church of Agioi Taxiarches (1741)**, whose vaulted ceiling is painted with a cosmological scheme including the zodiac, and the **Public Historical Library of Milies**, founded in 1814 by Anthimos Gazis. Life peaks around the train's arrival late morning at weekends.
raw.Tsagarada (≈500 m): four separate hamlets — Agios Stefanos, Agia Paraskevi, Agioi Taxiarches, Agia Kyriaki — each with its own square. **Agia Paraskevi's plane tree is around a thousand years old with a trunk roughly 14 m in circumference.** The square is a place people sit for hours; join them.
raw.Zagora (≈500 m): the largest and least prettified village, four quarters around Agios Georgios, with the historic Zagora Public Library (1762) and the apple co-op at its economic centre.
raw.Agricultural Cooperative of Zagora: , Zagora — the growers' co-operative behind **Zagorin** apples and the PDO **Mila Zagoras Piliou**. Its shop sells apples, juice and preserves on weekday working hours; the **harvest runs roughly late September to the end of October** and is when the whole village is in the orchards.
raw.Firiki Piliou PDO: — the small, elongated heritage apple, picked **October**, sold at village shops and as spoon sweet.
raw.Volos Municipal Market (Dimotiki Agora): — Monday to Saturday mornings, the place to buy Pelion olive oil, herbs and *tsipouro*.
raw.Tsipouro distillation (*kazania*): fires in Pelion villages **from mid-October through November**, by permit; ask your host, because these are family events, not attractions.
raw.Chestnuts: around Xourichti and Tsagarada, **October**; **olive pressing** on the Pagasetic side, **November–December**.
raw.Small named archontika and boutique stay: **Archontiko Repana**, Makrinitsa — a restored 19th-century mansion of roughly 8–10 rooms on the upper lanes. **Archontiko Xiradaki**, Makrinitsa — similar scale, painted ceilings, gulf views. **Archontiko Karamarli**, Makrinitsa. **Archontiko Karagiannopoulou** and **Archontiko Blana**, Vizitsa — both inside the car-free cobbled core, typically 6–9 rooms each, with a shared *sala* and wood-burning stoves. **Lost Unicorn Hotel**, Tsagarada — an English-run country house of around 10 rooms with a library and a proper bar. **Aegli Hotel**, Portaria — larger and more conventional, useful if you want a lift and a pool.
raw.Pacing: **Two base moves in the whole week** (Makrinitsa → Vizitsa on Day 3, Vizitsa → Tsagarada on Day 5). Three explicit do-nothing blocks: the whole of Day 4 afternoon, Day 6 morning, and Day 7 afternoon. No day contains more than one "sight".
raw.Makrinitsa → Portaria: , ≈2.5 km, **40–50 minutes**, 150 m of descent on well-kept cobbles through the Karavos gorge and the Mana springs.
raw.Vizitsa → Milies: , ≈2.2 km, **35–45 minutes**, one of the best-preserved kalderimia on the mountain, chestnut shade the whole way.
raw.Milies → Ano Gatzea: along the old railway alignment, ≈5 km, **1 h 15**, nearly flat.
raw.Tsagarada (Agia Paraskevi) → Damouchari: , ≈4 km, **1 h 10–1 h 30 descending**, roughly 450 m down through plane and oak to a stone-built cove. Walk down, get a lift back — the ascent is a different proposition.
notes: Cobbles are slick when wet and uneven throughout: proper shoes, not sandals.
raw.Named transport lines and drive legs: **KTEL Magnisias** runs Volos → **Portaria/Makrinitsa** frequently through the day, about 30 minutes; Volos → **Milies/Vizitsa** a few times daily, about 1 hour; Volos → **Tsagarada/Agios Ioannis** typically only **two or three services a day**, around 2 hours — check the timetable before relying on it, and never on a Sunday. **Hellenic Train's Moutzouris line** runs **Ano Lechonia → Milies**, 15 km in about 90 minutes with a 15-minute halt at **Ano Gatzea**; the standard pattern is **Saturdays and Sundays, departing Ano Lechonia at 10:00 and Milies at 15:00**, at roughly **€10 single / €18 return** (children 4–12 €6/€10). Drive legs: Volos→Makrinitsa 17 km / 30 min; Makrinitsa→Vizitsa 30 km / 50 min; Vizitsa→Tsagarada 35 km / 1 h on continuous hairpins; Tsagarada→Zagora 18 km / 35 min; Tsagarada→Volos 55 km / 1 h 20.
raw.One named hands-on experience: The **Agricultural Cooperative of Zagora** — arrange in advance to join the October apple harvest and see the grading and packing line that turns Zagorin fruit into the crate stamped with the PDO. Out of season, the co-op shop and a walk through the terraces still explain the village better than any museum.

sources.verified: Hellenic Train's official Pelion page — the **Ano Lechonia–Milies route, 15 km in roughly 90 minutes with a 15-minute halt at Ano Gatzea, the Saturday/Sunday pattern with 10:00 and 15:00 departures, and fares of €10 single / €18 return (€6/€10 children 4–12), with onboard purchase cash only**. Critically, the same page has carried a standing notice that services were **cancelled from 19 September 2024 until further notice**, and Greek press reported the line returning to service from **14 December 2024** following hotelier protest. Named Volos tsipouradika and addresses — **Kavouras (Hatziargiri 3), Demiris (Efremidou 23, Nea Ionia), Bokos (Meandrou 143, Nea Ionia)** — from a Greek travel-press round-up.
sources.confidenceNotes: Re-verify before publishing — (1) the **Moutzouris operating status, days and fares** are the single most volatile fact in this file; the line has been suspended and reinstated repeatedly and the schedule differs between summer and shoulder season. Do not publish a fixed departure time without checking hellenictrain.gr in the fortnight before travel. (2) **KTEL Magnisias frequencies** to Tsagarada and Vizitsa, which are seasonal and thin out sharply outside July–August. (3) **Room counts and rates for Archontiko Repana, Xiradaki, Karamarli, Karagiannopoulou, Blana and the Lost Unicorn** — all indicative, none checked against a 2026 rate sheet, and several Pelion archontika change ownership or close for winter. (4) **Agricultural Cooperative of Zagora** visitor access and whether harvest participation can actually be arranged — this needs a direct call; the shop is confirmed, the hands-on element is not. (5) The **Theophilos mural** in Makrinitsa's kafeneio and the **Milies library** opening hours. (6) The **Tsagarada plane tree's** age and girth are traditional claims widely repeated locally rather than measured facts. (7) Kalderimi distances and walking times, estimated from route descriptions rather than surveyed, and condition after winter storms — several Pelion paths have been damaged by flooding in recent years and repairs are ongoing.

trips.title: The Bend and the Hills: Szentendre, Esztergom and the Palóc Villages
trips.subRegion: Danube Bend (Dunakanyar) & the Cserhát Hills, Nógrád County

bestPeriod.window: late April to early June, and the whole of September into mid-October
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (Szentendre's Fő tér is shoulder-to-shoulder, Danube boats sold out) and January–February (Hollókő shuts down)

accommodation.note: €300–€500 (€43–€72/night, panzió and village house, 2 bases)

transport.note: €90–€150 (small hire car for days 4–7, or rail + ferry throughout)

activities.note: €60–€105 (Skanzen, citadel, basilica cupola, Hollókő castle, museums)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy

trips.gatewayAirport: Budapest Liszt Ferenc (BUD). The **HÉV H5** suburban railway from Batthyány tér reaches Szentendre in about 40 min: a 500 HUF Budapest single plus a suburban supplementary ticket of about 450 HUF for the Békásmegyer–Szentendre section, roughly 950 HUF (~€2.40) each way. A party is better off with MÁV's HÉV *kirándulójegy*, 6,200 HUF for unlimited Békásmegyer–Szentendre travel for up to ten people in a day (2026 tariff). From Day 4, a small hire car picked up in Vác or Budapest makes the Cserhát practical.
trips.summary: Budapest is forty minutes behind you and it may as well be a different country. This week runs along the Danube where it turns hard south — Serbian church towers in Szentendre, a citadel above Visegrád, Hungary's…
trips.hook: Budapest is forty minutes behind you and it may as well be a different country. This week runs along the Danube where it turns hard south — Serbian church towers in Szentendre, a citadel above Visegrád, Hungary's largest basilica staring across a bridge into Slovakia — then turns inland into the Cserhát, where Hollókő's whitewashed Ófalu has fifty-eight protected houses, an embroidery tradition still worked by hand, and no traffic. Two beds all week. Ferries, slow trains, long lunches.

snapshot.Best period: Late April–early June; September to mid-October
snapshot.Start / End: Szentendre → Hollókő → Budapest (one-way, ~180 km total)
snapshot.Getting there: Budapest Liszt Ferenc (BUD). The **HÉV H5** suburban railway from Batthyány tér reaches Szentendre in about 40 min: a 500 HUF Budapest single plus a suburban supplementary ticket of about 450 HUF for the Békásmegyer–Szentendre section, roughly 950 HUF (~€2.40) each way. A party is better off with MÁV's HÉV *kirándulójegy*, 6,200 HUF for unlimited Békásmegyer–Szentendre travel for up to ten people in a day (2026 tariff). From Day 4, a small hire car picked up in Vác or Budapest makes the Cserhát practical.

itinerary.title: Serbian Szentendre
itinerary.morning: HÉV H5 from Batthyány tér. Drop bags, walk into **Fő tér** and stand at the Merchants' Cross while the day-trippers are still on the train.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Blagovestenska church** on Fő tér itself (1752, an iconostasis behind a plain baroque street front), then up to the Belgrade Cathedral and the Serbian Ecclesiastical Art Collection in the episcopal quarter — the surviving trace of the Serbs who fled north in 1690.
itinerary.evening: Climb Templom tér for the roofs and the river, then dinner in the old town.
itinerary.dayStats: 4 km on foot

itinerary.title: Skanzen and Marzipan
itinerary.morning: Bus or a 4 km ride out to **Skanzen**, the Hungarian Open Air Museum on Sztaravodai út — 300-plus relocated buildings across regional villages, including a full Nógrád street. Allow three hours; the internal narrow-gauge railway is running and saves legs, on its own ticket of 1,400 HUF (1,200 HUF reduced). Admission is 4,000 HUF (~€10) full and 2,000 HUF reduced, rising to 5,000/2,500 HUF on festival days such as Easter, Pentecost and St Martin's; under-6s and over-70s free, and free for under-26s on the second Sunday of the month (2026 tariff).
itinerary.afternoon: Back into town for the **Szabó Marzipan** museum and shop on Dumtsa Jenő utca, then the Margit Kovács ceramic collection — Szentendre's best single art holding.
itinerary.evening: A slow supper on Bogdányi utca; Szentendre empties dramatically after the last HÉV crowd goes home.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km round trip

itinerary.title: Visegrád by Water
itinerary.morning: Take the **MAHART** boat upriver to Visegrád if the timetable serves, otherwise the H5 to Szentendre station and the bus. The **Royal Palace** of Matthias Corvinus — the Renaissance loggia and the Hercules fountain — sits at river level.
itinerary.afternoon: Up to the **Fellegvár citadel**, 300 m above the river. The bend is the whole point: the Danube swings 90 degrees below you with the Börzsöny on the far bank. Walk or take the shuttle from the Nagyvillám road.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **Malomkert Panzió** in Visegrád, then the last boat or bus back to Szentendre.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 km round trip

itinerary.title: Esztergom, and a Bridge into Slovakia
itinerary.morning: Train or car to **Esztergom**. The **Basilica** is the largest church in Hungary — climb the cupola for the Danube and the Slovak hills, and go into the **Bakócz Chapel**, red marble, 1506, dismantled and reassembled stone by stone inside the newer building.
itinerary.afternoon: The Christian Museum in the Primate's Palace, then walk the **Mária Valéria bridge** across to **Štúrovo** in Slovakia — ten minutes, no formalities inside Schengen, and a coffee on the far bank looking back at the dome.
itinerary.evening: Return via **Vác** if the schedule allows: **Március 15. tér**, the 1764 **Triumphal Arch** built by Isidore Canevale for a visit by Maria Theresa, and dinner at **Vén Hajó** on the embankment. Then back to Szentendre and pack.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 km each way

itinerary.title: Over the Cserhát to Hollókő
itinerary.morning: Collect the car and drive east and north via the M3 and Pásztó. Stop at the **Nógrád** castle ruins on their basalt knoll for twenty minutes and the view over the Cserhát.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive in **Hollókő** and walk **Ófalu** end to end — two rows of whitewashed houses with carved timber galleries, the wooden-towered church of 1889 at the fork, and the craft houses: weaving, pottery, embroidery, the doll collection.
itinerary.evening: Settle into **Hollókői Vendégház**. Village dinner, a glass of Nógrád wine, and a street with no cars on it after dark.

itinerary.title: The Castle, and the Palóc Museum
itinerary.morning: Climb to **Hollókő castle** above the village — 13th century, restored, 25 minutes up through oak wood, with the Cserhát ridges laid out in every direction.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive to **Szécsény** for the Forgách castle and the **Kubinyi Ferenc Museum**, then on to **Balassagyarmat** for the **Palóc Museum** — costume, embroidery, the reconstructed Palóc house in the garden [VERIFY: current opening hours for the Palóc Museum and Kubinyi Ferenc Museum].
itinerary.evening: Back to Hollókő the slow way through the villages. Eat where you are staying.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km round trip

itinerary.title: Last Morning in Ófalu, then Budapest
itinerary.morning: Buy embroidery directly from the workshop rather than the gift counter, and one piece of black burnished pottery. If it is Easter weekend, stay for the **Húsvéti Fesztivál** — the Palóc costumes come out and the water-throwing *locsolkodás* is real, not staged; the autumn **wine and harvest weekend** is quieter and better for eating [VERIFY: 2027 Hollókő Easter and wine festival dates].
itinerary.afternoon: Drive back to Budapest, dropping the car at the airport or in the city.
itinerary.evening: Fly out, or one last dinner in Budapest with the week's embroidery in your bag.

accommodationStrategy.name: A Fő tér-area panzió
accommodationStrategy.description: four nights without repacking, with the HÉV, the MAHART pier and the bus station all within 10 minutes on foot. That combination is what makes the whole Danube leg car-free.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead; longer for the September wine weekend.

accommodationStrategy.name: Malomkert Panzió
accommodationStrategy.description: the alternative Danube base if you prefer the citadel side of the bend to Szentendre's crowds — quieter, greener, its own kitchen, and the Nagymaros ferry five minutes away for the rail connection.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–5 weeks ahead direct [VERIFY: current rates].

accommodationStrategy.name: Hollókői Vendégház
accommodationStrategy.description: sleeping inside the UNESCO village, not in a hotel below it. Thick whitewashed walls, a timber gallery, and the street to yourself once the coaches leave at five.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–10 weeks ahead, and much further for Easter weekend, when the village is fully booked months out.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming; 4G/5G along the Danube, thinner in the Cserhát but fine in Hollókő.
logistics.emergency: 112. Hospitals at Vác, Esztergom and Salgótarján; Hollókő has no pharmacy, so stock up in Szécsény.
logistics.weather: the Danube Bend funnels wind and the citadel is 300 m above the river, routinely 5 °C colder and much windier than the bank. Cserhát mornings in October drop close to freezing. Spring Danube high water occasionally closes the Szentendre and Vác embankments and suspends ferry services.
logistics.bookingWindows: Hollókő 6–10 weeks (Easter: months); Szentendre 4–6 weeks; MAHART boats a few days ahead in season, same-day midweek; nothing else requires reservation.
logistics.money: forint, roughly **€1 ≈ 390–405 HUF** [VERIFY: current exchange rate]. Cards are near-universal, including on MÁV trains and at Skanzen; carry HUF cash for the Hollókő craft houses, the Nagymaros ferry and village markets. Always decline dynamic currency conversion and pay in HUF.
logistics.transportRules: Hungarian motorways require an **e-matrica** vignette — a county sticker is enough if you stay off the M3, but the M3 leg needs a national one; hire cars usually include it, so confirm. Trains on the Szob line are MÁV; buy at the machine or the Vonatinfó app. Bikes travel on the HÉV and on Danube boats for a supplement. Drink-driving limit is zero.
logistics.permits: Ófalu is a living village with residents — photography of house exteriors is fine, of interiors and people only with permission. Drones are prohibited over the Hollókő World Heritage core and over Esztergom Basilica.

proTips: Do Szentendre's Fő tér **before 10:00 or after 18:00**. The HÉV delivers Budapest day-trippers in a wave mid-morning and reclaims them by early evening; the square is a genuinely quiet baroque space on either side of that.

Take the **Nagymaros–Visegrád ferry** rather than driving round via Vác. Five minutes across, costs a couple of euros, and the approach to the citadel from the water is the view the palace was designed for.
At Esztergom, buy the **cupola climb** ticket, not just basilica entry. The nave is free to enter; the dome and the Bakócz Chapel are what you are paying for.
Eat lunch at **Vén Hajó** in Vác on a weekday. Weekend Danube-side tables are booked out by Budapest families by Friday evening.
In Hollókő, the craft houses close around 17:00 with the coaches. Arrange your **embroidery purchase in the afternoon of Day 5** so you are not scrambling on the last morning.
Skanzen's Nógrád section is the same architecture you sleep in three days later. Walk it first, in that order — it turns Hollókő from a pretty street into something you can read.
Useful Hungarian: *"Egy kávét kérek"* and *"a számlát, legyen szíves"*. Tipping is 10%, often already added as *szervizdíj* — check the bill.

raw.Village and town squares by name: **Fő tér**, Szentendre — the triangular baroque square with the 1763 Merchants' Cross, ringed by former Serbian merchant houses. **Március 15. tér**, Vác — the Danube-facing main square with its Dominican church, above which lies the crypt where the 18th-century mummies were found. **Széchenyi tér**, Esztergom, in the Vízivárosi lower town beneath the basilica hill. **Ófalu**, Hollókő — not a square but a single forked street of 58 protected houses on the slope below the castle, UNESCO-listed in 1987 as the surviving example of a pre-agricultural-revolution Palóc village. **Szécsény's** Kubinyi Ferenc square below the Forgách castle and the leaning fire tower.
raw.Market days and artisan specialities: the **Palóc embroidery** of the Nógrád villages — dense red-and-blue floral work on white linen, distinct from Kalocsa's brighter style and still stitched to order in Hollókő and Balassagyarmat. **Palóc pottery**, black-fired and burnished, sold in the Ófalu craft houses. **Szabó Marzipan** in Szentendre, Dumtsa Jenő utca, with its museum room and Hungarian Parliament sculpted in almond paste. Szentendre's produce market off Bükkös part runs strongest on Friday and Saturday mornings; Vác's covered market and Balassagyarmat's weekly market follow the standard Hungarian rhythm of early mornings and Wednesday/Saturday peaks [VERIFY: current market days for Szentendre, Vác and Balassagyarmat]. The **Palóc Museum** in Balassagyarmat, founded 1891, is the reference collection for both traditions.
raw.Boutique and characterful stays: **Malomkert Panzió** in Visegrád, a mill-garden guesthouse with its own restaurant a short walk from the Royal Palace [VERIFY: current rates and restaurant hours]. **Hollókői Vendégház** — village houses inside the protected Ófalu, whitewashed, timber-galleried, some with a *kemence* stove [VERIFY: current rates and which houses are let]. **Vén Hajó** in Vác, the moored-boat restaurant on the Danube embankment, for a long lunch [VERIFY: current hours and seasonal operation]. **Prima Pékség** for morning pastry and coffee — the reliable small-town bakery counter for a *kakaós csiga* before a train [VERIFY: exact branch locations in Szentendre and Vác].
raw.Deliberate slow-travel pacing (max one r: **two bases only.** **Szentendre nights 1–4** covers Szentendre itself, Visegrád, Esztergom and Vác by boat, ferry and train, with no packing. **Hollókő nights 5–7** covers Nógrád, Szécsény and Balassagyarmat within a 35 km radius. The single relocation is Szentendre → Hollókő, about 95 km and 1h40 by car via the M3 and the road through Pásztó. Everything on the Danube leg can be done without a car: the **MAHART PassNave** hydrofoil and boat services run Budapest–Szentendre–Visegrád–Esztergom on a seasonal timetable. In 2026 the Budapest–Szentendre–Leányfalu–Visegrád excursion boat ran 22 June to 30 August, Thursday to Sunday, at 7,500 HUF one-way and 9,000 HUF return; the *Bíbic* hydrofoil ran May to September on selected weekends, 11,000 HUF to Visegrád and 13,000 HUF to Esztergom one-way, advance booking only because there is no on-board sale. Treat the timetable as conditional: low water on the Danube suspended or rerouted the Budapest–Szentendre, Budapest–Visegrád and hydrofoil services from 13 July to 13 September 2026, so check mahartpassnave.hu before you build a day around a boat; the Budapest Nyugati–**Szob** line stops at **Nagymaros-Visegrád** and at **Szob**, and the small **Nagymaros–Visegrád ferry** crosses in five minutes, on demand, all year.
