trips.title: Passes and Valleys — Bernina to the Gotthard

bestPeriod.note: The San Bernardino and Gotthard Tremola pass roads are normally open only from late May or June to October; confirm current status before booking.

trips.gatewayAirport: Zürich (ZRH)
trips.summary: A week of high passes and warm valleys, from the Bernina and San Bernardino to the Gotthard's cobbled Tremola and the Verzasca and Maggia.
trips.hook: This is Switzerland's grand traverse in miniature: three high passes, a UNESCO railway line running alongside your car, and a landing in Ticino's palm-lined valleys at the end. Drive it in summer, when every pass road named here is actually open, and budget real time for the hairpins rather than trusting the map's straight-line distance.

snapshot.Base(s): St. Moritz/Pontresina (3 nights), then Locarno/Ascona (3 nights), one night in transit
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 780 km driving, three passes over 2,000 m, valley roads with hairpins
snapshot.Getting There: Rental car from Zürich Airport; return the car in Zürich at trip's end
snapshot.Who It Suits: Confident drivers, couples and families who want mountains and lake towns in one loop

itinerary.title: Zürich to St. Moritz over the Julier Pass
itinerary.morning: Collect the rental car at Zürich Airport and drive south on the A3/A13 to Chur (120 km, 1h15), the gateway to Graubünden's valleys.
itinerary.afternoon: From Chur, climb the Julier Pass (Pass dal Güglia, 2,284 m), one of the rare Alpine passes that stays open year-round; expect grades up to 8% and switchbacks above the treeline. Stop at the Julier's Roman-era cairns near the summit before descending to Silvaplana and St. Moritz (85 km from Chur, roughly 1h30 with stops).
itinerary.evening: Settle into Pontresina and walk the lakeside promenade at St. Moritz for the evening light on the Piz Corvatsch face.
itinerary.dayStats: 205 km, approx. 3h driving · Julier Pass summit 2,284 m.

itinerary.title: Bernina Pass and a dip into Tirano
itinerary.morning: Drive the Bernina Pass road (2,328 m), open year-round though occasionally closed briefly after heavy snowfall even in season. The road runs alongside the UNESCO World Heritage Rhaetian Railway line — watch for the red Bernina Express crossing the Lago Bianco causeway. Stop at the Ospizio Bernina and the lake itself.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue down into Val Poschiavo to Poschiavo village, then cross into Italy at Tirano — a Schengen border with no checkpoint, but carry passports and confirm your rental agreement covers Italy before you go. Walk to the Santuario della Madonna di Tirano and have lunch in the piazza.
itinerary.evening: Return over the Bernina to St. Moritz or overnight in Poschiavo itself.
itinerary.dayStats: 90 km round trip, approx. 2h30 driving · Bernina Pass summit 2,328 m.

itinerary.title: Over the Julier again to San Bernardino
itinerary.morning: Retrace the Julier to Tiefencastel and on to Thusis (95 km from St. Moritz, about 1h45), stopping at the Viamala gorge, a 300 m-deep limestone cut the old Chur–Chiavenna trade route had to cross.
itinerary.afternoon: From Thusis, take the historic San Bernardino Pass road (2,065 m) rather than the road tunnel — it closes roughly November to May, so this only works in the window this trip is built for. Grades reach 9–10% through tight hairpins to San Bernardino village.
itinerary.evening: Overnight in San Bernardino or nearby Mesocco, below the ruined Castello di Mesocco.
itinerary.dayStats: 135 km, approx. 2h45 driving · San Bernardino Pass summit 2,065 m.

itinerary.title: Into Ticino: Bellinzona's three castles
itinerary.morning: Descend the Mesolcina valley to Bellinzona (45 km, 50 min) and walk the UNESCO World Heritage trio of 15th-century castles — Castelgrande, Montebello and Sasso Corbaro — connected by a signed footpath through the old town.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Locarno (25 km, 30 min), Switzerland's warmest corner, and walk the Piazza Grande and the lakeside promenade toward Ascona.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Locarno's old town, arcaded streets a world away from the passes behind you.
itinerary.dayStats: 70 km, approx. 1h20 driving.

itinerary.title: Verzasca Valley
itinerary.morning: Drive up the Val Verzasca to Lavertezzo and the Ponte dei Salti, a Roman-arched stone bridge over turquoise pools that are genuinely swimmable in summer.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Corippo, Switzerland's smallest municipality, a single street of stone-roofed houses declared a heritage site, then to the Verzasca Dam at Vogorno — a 220 m wall known internationally as the GoldenEye bungee-jump site, worth the stop even just to watch.
itinerary.evening: Back to Locarno.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 km round trip, approx. 1h15 driving.

itinerary.title: Maggia Valley
itinerary.morning: Drive the Val Maggia to Cevio, then into the Val Bavona, one of the Alps' most dramatically vertical side valleys, its stone ronchi hamlets clinging to the cliff base.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk to the Foroglio waterfall, which drops straight into the valley floor beside the hamlet of the same name, then stop for a swim in the Maggia's clear pools near Ponte Brolla on the way back.
itinerary.evening: Return to Locarno or Ascona for a last Ticino dinner.
itinerary.dayStats: 65 km round trip, approx. 1h30 driving.

itinerary.title: The Gotthard Tremola and home to Zürich
itinerary.morning: Drive Locarno to Airolo on the A2 (60 km, 45 min), then climb the Tremola San Gottardo, the cobbled historic road with 24 hairpins built between the 1830s and 1940s, grades to 9%, up to the Passo del San Gottardo (2,106 m). Stop at the Museo Nazionale del San Gottardo and the old hospice.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend the north side into Andermatt and the Urseren valley.
itinerary.evening: Drive on to Zürich via the A2 (150 km, approx. 2h) for the flight home, or take one last night in Andermatt if your schedule allows.
itinerary.dayStats: 215 km, approx. 3h30 driving · Gotthard Pass summit 2,106 m, Tremola grades to 9%.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Walther
accommodationStrategy.description: A 1907 hotel in the Engadin's grand-hotel style, a short walk from the Bernina Express station and well placed for both the Julier and Bernina legs. Ask for a valley-facing room over the Roseg side rather than the road.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–10 weeks ahead for July and August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel San Bernardino
accommodationStrategy.description: A mid-century hotel built for the pass road itself, right at the base of the old San Bernardino climb — useful for breaking the long Julier-to-Ticino day into two manageable legs rather than one exhausting one.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Belvedere
accommodationStrategy.description: An Art Nouveau-era hotel on the hill above Locarno's old town, with lake views and easy walking down to Piazza Grande, and a good base for both the Verzasca and Maggia valley days.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead.

logistics.connectivity: Coverage drops in the Bavona and on the Tremola's upper hairpins; download offline maps for Graubünden and Ticino before setting out each morning.
logistics.emergency: 112 for general emergencies; Rega, the Swiss air rescue service, on 1414 for anything in the mountains.
logistics.money: Cards are widely accepted, but small village kiosks, parking meters and mountain huts often want Swiss franc coins.

other.label: The motorway vignette is mandatory
other.text: An annual sticker or e-vignette, CHF 40 (approx. €42) for the calendar year, is required on all Autobahn/Autostrasse sections (green signs) including the A2 and A13 used on this route. Buy it at the border, at fuel stations, or online before crossing in — driving without one risks a CHF 200 fine.

other.label: Fuel up before the side valleys
other.text: Val Bavona and much of the upper Verzasca have no petrol stations; fill the tank in Locarno or Bellinzona before each valley day.

other.label: Pass closures
other.text: The San Bernardino and Gotthard Tremola pass roads close roughly November to May depending on snow; both have year-round tunnel alternatives (San Bernardino road tunnel, Gotthard road and rail tunnels) if weather forces a detour even in season.

other.label: Cross-border rental
other.text: Confirm before pickup that your rental agreement and insurance cover Italy for the Tirano dip — most Swiss agencies allow it, but not all, and one-way returns to a different depot carry a separate fee.

other.label: Parking realities
other.text: Bellinzona's Castelgrande has a small paid car park at the base; the Ponte dei Salti car park in Lavertezzo fills by mid-morning in July and August — a shuttle bus runs from Tenero on the busiest days.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 for general emergencies; Rega, the Swiss air rescue service, on 1414 for anything in the mountains.

proTips: Drive the Tremola westbound in the early morning — the light comes from behind you on the hairpins and the coach traffic hasn't arrived yet.
Reach the Ponte dei Salti before 09:00; by 11:00 in August the car park is full and the pools are three-deep with people.
Watch the Bernina Express cross the Lago Bianco causeway from the roadside layby just past the Ospizio — the classic angle everyone photographs, for free, from the car.
The San Bernardino old pass road carries a fraction of the Gotthard's traffic for nearly the same drama — treat it as the quiet warm-up before the Tremola.
Buy the vignette online before you land rather than at the border kiosk, where queues build fast on summer weekends.
If you want to watch (or make) a bungee jump at the Verzasca Dam, check the operator's board at the dam car park for the day's jump window rather than assuming it runs continuously.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 780 km driving, three passes over 2,000 m, valley roads with hairpins
raw.Who It Suits: Confident drivers, couples and families who want mountains and lake towns in one loop

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 780 km driving, three passes over 2,000 m, valley roads with hairpins
typeSpecific.audience: Confident drivers, couples and families who want mountains and lake towns in one loop

packingNotes: Layers for pass summits that sit 15–20°C colder than the Ticino valleys below, even in August.
Swimwear and a quick-dry towel for the Verzasca and Maggia pools.
Sunglasses — the glare off high-altitude snow patches and white limestone is sharp even in summer.
A phone mount and offline map download for stretches with no signal.
Comfortable walking shoes for the short climbs at Bellinzona's castles and the Val Bavona hamlets.
Cash in Swiss francs, small denominations, for parking meters and mountain kiosks.
A cool bag or small cooler for picnic stops at passes with no services.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A pass closes for snow, rockfall or maintenance even in summer.** The Gotthard and San Bernardino road tunnels run year-round as fallbacks, and the Bernina Express covers the Bernina corridor by rail if the road shuts.
**The Ponte dei Salti car park is full.** Use the Tenero park-and-ride shuttle rather than circling Lavertezzo's narrow lanes.
**A sudden mountain thunderstorm hits on an exposed pass.** Pull into a marked layby and wait it out — Alpine storms are usually short and visibility on hairpins in heavy rain is genuinely dangerous.
**Your rental car isn't cleared for Italy.** Confirm this at booking, not at the Tirano border — if it isn't covered, skip the dip and spend the extra time at Poschiavo's Baroque old town instead.
**You run low on fuel mid-valley.** Val Bavona and the upper Verzasca have none; treat Locarno and Bellinzona as your last-chance fill-ups before each side trip.

trips.title: The Pass Quadrilateral — Furka, Grimsel, Susten, Nufenen
trips.subRegion: Bernese Oberland, Uri and Goms (Upper Valais)

bestPeriod.note: The Nufenen is usually the last of the four to open, often not until mid-June.

trips.gatewayAirport: Zürich (ZRH)
trips.summary: Four high passes inside one small triangle of Switzerland — 2,478 m at the top, granite everywhere, and a season that lasts about four months.
trips.hook: Four passes, three valleys, and barely 900 km all week. The Furka, Grimsel, Susten and Nufenen enclose a compact block of granite around the head of the Rhône, and the point of the trip is to drive each of them in the right direction at the right hour. They are also shut for more than half the year, which concentrates the mind.

snapshot.Base(s): Meiringen (2 nights), Andermatt (2), Oberwald / Goms (2), Grimsel (1)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 865 km; four high passes, sustained 8–13% gradients, hundreds of hairpins
snapshot.Getting There: Zürich (ZRH); vignette on arrival, then A4/A2 to Luzern and the Brünig
snapshot.Who It Suits: Confident mountain drivers; anyone who likes hydro-engineering as much as scenery

itinerary.title: Vignette, Brünig, Haslital
itinerary.morning: Collect the car at Zürich. If it is a Swiss rental the motorway vignette is already on the screen; if not, buy one before the first motorway metre. Then A4 and A2 to Luzern.
itinerary.afternoon: The Brünigpass (1,008 m) drops you into the Haslital. It is open year-round and is the gentle overture. Stop at Meiringen and walk the Aareschlucht, a 1.4 km gorge on galleries bolted to the rock.
itinerary.evening: The Reichenbachfall funicular runs to the falls where Conan Doyle disposed of Holmes. Meiringen is small, has fuel, and is the last cheap supermarket before the passes.
itinerary.dayStats: 138 km · 2 h drive · Brünigpass (1,008 m) · max altitude 1,008 m

itinerary.title: The Susten, the engineered one
itinerary.morning: From Innertkirchen the **Sustenpass (2,224 m)** climbs east through Gadmen. Built between 1938 and 1945 as a strategic route, it is the widest and most forgiving of the four: gradients rarely exceed 9%, the radii are generous, and long gallery tunnels take the worst of the avalanche terrain. Normally open from early June to late October.
itinerary.afternoon: Stop at the Steingletscher, where a moraine lake sits below the retreating ice and there is a large free layby. Cross the summit tunnel and descend to Wassen in the Reuss valley — the eastern side is tighter than the western.
itinerary.evening: Return the same way to Meiringen; the light on the Gadmertal in the late afternoon is the reason to drive it twice.
itinerary.dayStats: 96 km · 2 h 30 drive · 1 pass (Susten, twice) · max altitude 2,224 m

itinerary.title: Grimsel and Furka in one afternoon
itinerary.morning: South from Innertkirchen up the **Grimselpass (2,164 m)**: long ramps over bare granite slabs, dammed lakes stacked one above another, gradients to 11%. Break at Handegg for the Gelmerbahn, a former works funicular with a maximum gradient of 106%; seats must be reserved.
itinerary.afternoon: At the summit, park by the Totensee and walk five minutes for the view down into the Rhône valley. Descend the hairpins to Gletsch, then turn up the **Furkapass (2,429 m)** — the narrowest and most exposed of the four, with a switchback stack past the derelict Belvédère hotel and the Rhône Glacier ice grotto (approx. CHF 10, open roughly June to October).
itinerary.evening: Down the eastern side to Realp and Andermatt for two nights.
itinerary.dayStats: 112 km · 3 h 15 drive · Grimsel and Furka · max altitude 2,429 m

itinerary.title: Oberalp and the Schöllenen
itinerary.morning: East from Andermatt over the **Oberalppass (2,044 m)** to Sedrun: broad, open, less dramatic than its neighbours and a good rest for tyres. A 45-minute walk from the summit lake reaches the Tomasee, the source of the Rhine.
itinerary.afternoon: Back to Andermatt and north into the Schöllenenschlucht, where the Teufelsbrücke crosses a granite slot that blocked north–south traffic for a thousand years. Park at the Devil's Bridge layby, not on the road.
itinerary.evening: Andermatt has fuel, a supermarket and the last proper garage before the Goms. Use it.
itinerary.dayStats: 84 km · 2 h drive · Oberalppass (2,044 m) · max altitude 2,044 m

itinerary.title: Nufenen, the high one
itinerary.morning: West over the Furka again — the Valais descent is better driven downhill — through Gletsch to Oberwald and Ulrichen in the Goms.
itinerary.afternoon: From Ulrichen the **Nufenenpass / Passo della Novena (2,478 m)** climbs to the highest point of any road lying entirely within Switzerland. Opened only in 1969, it is the last of the four to clear each spring, and the Ticino side pitches to 13%. A wind turbine turns on the summit ridge; the layby there is the coldest place on the trip.
itinerary.evening: Drop to Airolo for a coffee in Italian, then climb straight back over. Base in Oberwald or Obergesteln.
itinerary.dayStats: 152 km · 3 h 30 drive · Furka and Nufenen (twice) · max altitude 2,478 m

itinerary.title: Goms, glacier and the steam railway
itinerary.morning: In July and August the Dampfbahn Furka-Bergstrecke runs restored steam trains over the old Furka mountain line between Realp and Oberwald. Book weeks ahead; it is the only way to see the abandoned upper trackbed.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive down-valley to Fiesch and take the cable car to the Eggishorn for the Aletsch Glacier — 20 km of ice, the largest in the Alps, and unreachable by road.
itinerary.evening: A short detour into the Binntal, a dead-end side valley on a single-lane road with passing places, for the quietest hour of the week.
itinerary.dayStats: 114 km · 2 h 20 drive · no passes · max altitude 1,400 m at Fiesch (2,869 m by cable car)

itinerary.title: Grimsel northbound, then out
itinerary.morning: Back up the Rhône to Gletsch and over the **Grimselpass** northbound — the direction that gives the reservoir staircase in sequence. Coffee at the Grimsel Hospiz on its rock spur above the lake.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend to Innertkirchen and Meiringen, then the Brünig to Luzern.
itinerary.evening: A2 and A4 to Zürich, 110 km from Luzern, roughly 1 h 15 outside rush hour.
itinerary.dayStats: 204 km · 3 h drive · Grimsel and Brünig · max altitude 2,164 m

accommodationStrategy.name: Parkhotel du Sauvage
accommodationStrategy.description: A 19th-century grand hotel in its own park, with proper parking and a five-minute walk to the Aareschlucht bus. It sits at the junction of the Susten and Grimsel approaches, so two nights here covers both without moving.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2 months for July–August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel 3 Könige & Post
accommodationStrategy.description: On the old village street, family-run for generations, with a garage and a kitchen that serves after mountain hours. Andermatt is the hinge of the whole route — Furka, Oberalp, Susten and the Schöllenen all start within ten minutes.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks.

accommodationStrategy.name: Historisches Alpinhotel Grimsel Hospiz
accommodationStrategy.description: Perched on a rock spur above the Grimselsee at 1,980 m, hydro-powered and reachable only while the pass is open. One night here puts you above the day-trippers for sunset and sunrise on the granite, and it is the single most atmospheric bed on the trip.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 months; it sells out first.

logistics.emergency: 112 works; 144 for ambulance, 117 police, and 1414 for Rega air rescue. Mobile coverage is good on the roads and patchy in the Binntal.
logistics.weather: Snow above 2,000 m is possible in any month. A summit can go from 20°C to sleet in an hour, and passes close at short notice in September.
logistics.money: Swiss francs; euros are often accepted at a poor rate and change comes in francs. Cards are universal, including at summit kiosks.

other.label: The vignette is CHF 40 and there is no shorter option
other.text: No day pass, no week pass. It is valid from 1 December of the previous year to 31 January of the following — fourteen months for everyone, whether you stay two days or two months. Buy the sticker at the border, a post office or a petrol station, or an e-vignette online tied to the plate. Driving without one costs CHF 200 plus the price of the vignette.

other.label: The passes are closed all winter
other.text: Susten, Grimsel, Furka, Nufenen and Oberalp all shut, typically from late October to late May or June, with the Nufenen last to open. The **Furka Base Tunnel car shuttle** between Realp and Oberwald runs year-round, roughly CHF 30–35 per car, several times an hour — the only way through when the Furka is white.

other.label: Headlights on, day and night
other.text: , everywhere in Switzerland. It is a legal requirement and it is enforced.

other.label: Uphill has priority
other.text: where a pass road narrows, and PostAuto coaches have absolute right of way, announced by the three-tone horn. On blind hairpins, expect one.

other.label: Gradients and brakes
other.text: Nufenen (13%), Furka and Grimsel (11%) all reward engine braking. Descending an automatic in D with the brakes on for 12 km is how rentals end up smoking at Gletsch.

other.label: Fuel
other.text: Fill in Meiringen, Andermatt, Ulrichen or Airolo. There is nothing at Realp, Gletsch or any summit, and nothing at all after 20:00 in the Goms.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Village shops close 12:00–14:00 and all day Sunday. Mountain restaurants stop serving hot food around 20:00.

other.label: Cross-border rental
other.text: Swiss hires can enter Italy, France, Austria and Germany freely. One-way drops into another country add CHF 200–500, and picking up in Italy or Germany means buying your own vignette.

proTips: Drive every pass **before 09:30 or after 16:30** on summer weekends. Between those hours the motorcycle traffic makes overtaking on the hairpins unpleasant.
Reserve the **Gelmerbahn** online the moment dates are fixed. Walk-up slots vanish by mid-morning, and the funicular stops running at the first real cold snap.
Take the **Furka westbound in the morning and eastbound in the evening**: the Valais side faces west and is backlit until midday.
Check the **cantonal pass-status pages** at breakfast, not the night before. Uri, Bern and Valais each publish live opening data and a September closure can be decided at 06:00.
The **Grimsel Hospiz stays open past the last car** most years; if the pass shuts while you are up there, staff know the timing before anyone else does.
Buy a **half-price rail card only if you plan the Eggishorn and the steam railway** — otherwise pay per ride; three cable-car trips will not recover the fee.
Park at the **Steingletscher layby rather than the summit** for lunch. Same altitude, a glacier lake instead of a car park, and no coach traffic.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 865 km; four high passes, sustained 8–13% gradients, hundreds of hairpins
raw.Who It Suits: Confident mountain drivers; anyone who likes hydro-engineering as much as scenery

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 865 km; four high passes, sustained 8–13% gradients, hundreds of hairpins
typeSpecific.audience: Confident mountain drivers; anyone who likes hydro-engineering as much as scenery

packingNotes: A warm jacket and hat that live in the car, not in the boot — the Nufenen summit runs 15°C below the valley.
Sunglasses and high-factor cream; UV at 2,400 m is brutal even under cloud.
Motion-sickness remedies for passengers. The Furka's Valais side is 30 hairpins in 10 km.
Offline maps and downloaded pass-status bookmarks; signal drops in the Schöllenen and Binntal.
Walking boots for the Tomasee and the Aareschlucht galleries.
A CHF coin float for summit toilets and small laybys.
Swimwear for the Goms thermal pools at Brigerbad if a pass shuts.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A pass closes mid-trip.** Fresh snow shuts the Nufenen or Furka at any time from September. Fallback: the Furka Base Tunnel car shuttle keeps Realp–Oberwald open year-round, and the Grimsel usually stays open longest.
**Brake fade on a long descent.** Fallback: pull into a layby, let the brakes cool for fifteen minutes, and use low gears afterwards. Do not coast in neutral.
**The Gelmerbahn or Eggishorn is shut for wind.** Both stop above roughly 60 km/h gusts. Fallback: the Aareschlucht and the Binntal are wind-immune.

**Rental without a vignette.** Cars hired in Germany, Italy or France often arrive without one, and the first Swiss motorway camera does not care. Fallback: buy at the border crossing before joining the motorway.
**Weekend gridlock at the Grimsel.** On fine August Sundays the summit car parks overflow onto the road. Fallback: reverse the day and drive it in the opposite direction after 16:00.

trips.title: Bohemia by Car — Spa Colonnades, Ore Mountains and Sandstone
trips.subRegion: West Bohemia, Krušné hory and the Elbe sandstone

bestPeriod.note: The Krušné hory ridge road is snow-cleared but slow from November to March; the sandstone gorge boats run April to October only.

basecamps: Karlovy Vary, Mezní Louka and Kutná Hora
trips.gatewayAirport: Prague (PRG)
trips.summary: A 950 km Bohemian loop from Prague through the spa triangle, along the Ore Mountains ridge and into the sandstone gorges of Bohemian Switzerland.
trips.hook: Czechia does not do alpine passes, so this drive earns its scenery a different way: forest ridges at a thousand metres, spa towns built to be walked in, and a sandstone canyon where the road simply stops at the German border. The legs are short, the second-class roads are free, and the car is the point only about half the time.

snapshot.Base(s): Karlovy Vary (3 nights), Mezní Louka / Hřensko (2), Kutná Hora (1)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 950 km; motorway D6/D8 plus long ridge and forest roads, max altitude approx. 1,100 m
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Prague (PRG); collect the car at the airport, never in the centre
snapshot.Who It Suits: Slow drivers who want castles, colonnades and one serious gorge walk

itinerary.title: Out of Prague, west to the Ohře
itinerary.morning: Collect the car at Václav Havel Airport. Confirm the e-vignette is registered to the plate — Czechia has had no windscreen sticker since 2021 — and that dipped headlights come on automatically, because they are compulsory day and night, year round.
itinerary.afternoon: Take the D6 west, then drop south to **Křivoklát**, a royal hunting castle in the Berounka woods. The village car park is below the walls; the last 300 m is on foot. Rejoin the D6 for Karlovy Vary.
itinerary.evening: Detour to **Loket**, a granite spur town wrapped in a river meander, with a 12th-century castle above the square. Then 15 km on to Karlovy Vary. Park in a garage below the spa zone — the Lázeňská zóna is permit-only for cars and the enforcement is camera-based.
itinerary.dayStats: 175 km · 2h40 driving · no passes · max altitude 430 m.

itinerary.title: Karlovy Vary on foot, Bečov by car
itinerary.morning: Leave the car. Walk the Mlýnská, Tržní and Sadová colonnades, buy a porcelain **lázeňský pohárek** cup from a kiosk, and taste the springs in ascending temperature — Vřídlo, the geyser spring, runs at 73°C and is drunk cooled.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive 25 km south to **Bečov nad Teplou** for the Reliquary of St. Maur, the Romanesque shrine found under the castle chapel floor in 1985. Entry is by timed guided tour only and small groups sell out; book online the day before.
itinerary.evening: Back in Karlovy Vary, walk up to the Diana lookout tower by funicular and down through the forest path.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km · 1h10 driving · no passes · max altitude 620 m.

itinerary.title: The spa triangle
itinerary.morning: West on the R6/D6 to **Cheb**, whose Špalíček merchant houses lean into the square, then 6 km to **Františkovy Lázně** — the smallest and flattest of the three UNESCO-listed Great Spas of Europe here, laid out in yellow neoclassical terraces.
itinerary.afternoon: South on the 21 and 230 to **Mariánské Lázně**: the cast-iron colonnade, the singing fountain on the hour, and forest roads through the Slavkovský les on the way back.
itinerary.evening: Return to Karlovy Vary on the 20/6. Third night in the same bed, which is the whole reason to base here.
itinerary.dayStats: 165 km · 2h50 driving · no passes · max altitude 780 m.

itinerary.title: The Ore Mountains ridge
itinerary.morning: Climb the hairpins of the 25 to **Jáchymov**, the silver and uranium town that gave the word "dollar" its root, then on to **Boží Dar** at 1,028 m — the highest town in Central Europe. The spur road to the **Klínovec** car park (1,244 m summit) tops out around 1,100 m; the last stretch is on foot or by chairlift.
itinerary.afternoon: Take the ridge road east — the 219 and 254 through Loučná pod Klínovcem, Hora Svaté Kateřiny and Nová Ves v Horách. This is the finest driving of the week: long open moorland curves at 800–900 m with the Bohemian basin dropping away to the south. Descend the switchbacks to Litvínov, then the D8 to Ústí nad Labem and Děčín.
itinerary.evening: Follow the Labe (Elbe) gorge road to **Hřensko**, the lowest point in Czechia at 115 m, and sleep at Mezní Louka. Parking in Hřensko itself is cramped, paid and slow; the Mezní Louka lot is bigger.
itinerary.dayStats: 210 km · 4h00 driving · 3 ridge saddles (Boží Dar, Hora Svaté Kateřiny, Nová Ves) · max altitude approx. 1,100 m.

itinerary.title: Bohemian Switzerland
itinerary.morning: Walk from Mezní Louka to **Pravčická brána**, Europe's largest sandstone arch, on the red-marked trail — about 3 km each way, entry approx. CZK 200 (€8). The Czech waymarking is a coloured stripe between two white ones and the network is dense; follow colours, not compass.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive down to Hřensko and take the punts through the **Edmundova soutěska** and **Divoká soutěska** gorges of the Kamenice. Ferrymen pole the boats between walls 50 m high; tickets are sold at the landing stage and the last departure is mid-afternoon.
itinerary.evening: Optional cross-border run to Bad Schandau and the **Bastei** bridge in Saxon Switzerland — 25 km, no border formalities, no German car toll.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 km · 1h10 driving · no passes · max altitude 415 m.

itinerary.title: Down the Labe to the silver town
itinerary.morning: Retrace the gorge to Děčín, then follow the river to **Litoměřice** for its arcaded square and the Chalice house, and stop at **Terezín**, the fortress town used as a ghetto and transit camp. Allow two unhurried hours; parking is free outside the Small Fortress.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue via **Mělník**, where the Vltava meets the Labe below a castle terrace planted with Ludmila vines, then cross-country on the 16 and 38 to Kutná Hora.
itinerary.evening: Walk the Barborská terrace above the Jesuit college at dusk, after the coaches leave.
itinerary.dayStats: 205 km · 3h20 driving · no passes · max altitude 380 m.

itinerary.title: Kutná Hora and back to Prague
itinerary.morning: The **Sedlec Ossuary** opens early and issues timed tickets; take the first slot and combine it with the cathedral of the Assumption next door. Then the cathedral of **St. Barbara**, a late-Gothic hall church funded by silver miners.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive the 111 and 125 through the Sázava woods to **Český Šternberk**, a castle on a rock spine still held by the family that built it in 1241. Guided tours in Czech with printed English text.
itinerary.evening: D1 into Prague and drop the car at the airport or a peripheral depot. Do not drive into Prague 1 with luggage; the tram is faster.
itinerary.dayStats: 100 km · 1h50 driving · no passes · max altitude 460 m.

accommodationStrategy.name: Grandhotel Pupp
accommodationStrategy.description: The anchor of the town since the 18th century, at the top of the pedestrian spa street with its own garage — which solves Karlovy Vary's real problem, that the centre is closed to unpermitted cars. Three nights here means three days without repacking.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead; longer for film-festival week in early July.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Mezní Louka
accommodationStrategy.description: A 19th-century hunting lodge at the trailhead for Pravčická brána, with a large open car park and a kitchen that serves late enough for walkers coming off the gorge trails. Staying here rather than in Hřensko avoids the morning parking scrum in the gorge village.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks for weekends in high summer.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Mědínek Old Town
accommodationStrategy.description: On Palackého náměstí, three minutes from St. Barbara's and with parking behind the building — useful because Kutná Hora's old-town streets are narrow, one-way and heavily signed. Good position for the early ossuary slot.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three weeks.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; 155 ambulance, 158 police, 150 fire. Mountain rescue (Horská služba) is **1210** and covers the Krušné hory and the sandstone parks.
logistics.money: Koruna, not euro. Cards work almost everywhere, but gorge boats, small car parks and village pubs are cash-first. Refuse dynamic currency conversion at ATMs.

other.label: E-vignette
other.text: Motorway and expressway use (D-class roads: D6, D8, D1, D11) requires a plate-linked electronic vignette bought at edalnicnizname.cz or the app — approx. CZK 300 (€12) for 10 days, CZK 480 (€19) for 30 days, CZK 2,570 (€105) annual. There is no sticker and no physical proof. First-class roads numbered 6, 13, 20 and so on are free, and several exempt sections are signposted.

other.label: Rental cars
other.text: Czech rentals normally include the vignette; check the plate on your confirmation. Cross-border into Germany, Austria, Poland and Slovakia is standard; the Balkans are usually excluded or surcharged €30–€60. One-way drops to Dresden or Vienna start around €150.

other.label: Germany's Umweltplakette
other.text: The Bastei detour needs nothing — neither Dresden nor Saxon Switzerland has a low-emission zone. If you extend to Leipzig, Halle or Berlin you need a green Umweltplakette on the windscreen, sold for €6–€20 at TÜV/DEKRA stations; rentals registered in Germany usually already carry one, Czech-plated cars usually do not.

other.label: Driving rules that are actually enforced
other.text: Dipped headlights 24/7 all year. Blood alcohol limit is zero — no glass of wine at lunch. Winter tyres are compulsory from 1 November to 31 March whenever there is snow, ice or slush. Speed cameras and section control are common on the D8 and around Ústí.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 pan-European; 155 ambulance, 158 police, 150 fire. Mountain rescue (Horská služba) is **1210** and covers the Krušné hory and the sandstone parks.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Czech castles close entirely from November to March and run weekends-only in April and October; most shut on Mondays even in season. Guided tours are the only way in and the last tour is often 90 minutes before closing.

proTips: Book the Bečov reliquary tour and the St. Barbara / Sedlec combined ticket online the previous evening. Both cap group sizes and both sell out by mid-morning in summer.
Drive the Krušné hory ridge west to east. Eastbound, the Bohemian basin is on your right all afternoon and the light stays behind you.
At Hřensko, park at Mezní Louka and walk down to the gorge boats rather than driving in. The village road is a single lane between rock and river, and it gridlocks by 10:00.
Buy the spa cup, not bottled water: the Karlovy Vary springs are free, and the porcelain spout is designed to cool 73°C water on the way to your mouth.
Fill up in Czechia before crossing to Saxony. Czech fuel is consistently cheaper, and the border stations at Hřensko know it.
If rain kills the sandstone day, swap in Děčín castle's rose garden and the Ústí funicular to Větruše — both are ten minutes away and mostly indoors.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 950 km; motorway D6/D8 plus long ridge and forest roads, max altitude approx. 1,100 m
raw.Who It Suits: Slow drivers who want castles, colonnades and one serious gorge walk

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 950 km; motorway D6/D8 plus long ridge and forest roads, max altitude approx. 1,100 m
typeSpecific.audience: Slow drivers who want castles, colonnades and one serious gorge walk

packingNotes: Grippy shoes with an edge: the sandstone steps at Pravčická brána stay damp and greasy even in August.
A light waterproof — the Elbe gorge makes its own weather.
Cash in koruna, roughly CZK 3,000, for boats, car parks and rural pubs.
Swimwear for a spa afternoon in Karlovy Vary or Mariánské Lázně.
A phone holder and offline maps; the ridge road loses signal in the border forests.
Something warm: Boží Dar sits at 1,028 m and runs 8–10°C below Prague.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Forest-fire or storm closure in Bohemian Switzerland.** Sections of the park have been closed for restoration since the 2022 fire and trails change year to year. Fallback: the Tisá rock town and the Děčínský Sněžník plateau, both 30 minutes away and unaffected.

**You drove a D-road without a vignette.** Fines are issued to the plate and follow the rental company back to you with an admin fee. Fallback: buy the vignette on your phone before you touch a D-road — activation is immediate.
**Castle shut on a Monday.** It will be. Fallback: build Mondays around towns, not castles — Kutná Hora, Litoměřice and Loket all work as walking days.
**Prague airport drop at rush hour.** The D1 and the Prague ring seize up 07:00–09:00 and 15:00–18:00. Fallback: leave Kutná Hora before 07:00 or after 10:00; the difference is 45 minutes.

trips.title: The B500 — Schwarzwaldhochstrasse, Panoramastrasse and Baden Wine
trips.subRegion: Schwarzwald and the Baden wine terraces, Baden-Württemberg

bestPeriod.note: The B500 ridge is open all year but drifts and freezing fog close sections in midwinter; late September brings the wine harvest and the clearest air.

basecamps: Baden-Baden, Triberg and Freiburg im Breisgau
trips.gatewayAirport: Karlsruhe/Baden-Baden (FKB) or Basel–Mulhouse–Freiburg (BSL/MLH/EAP)
trips.summary: The Schwarzwaldhochstrasse and Panoramastrasse driven end to end, with Baden vineyards, the Kandel hairpins and a Kaiserstuhl finish.
trips.hook: Germany's oldest scenic road runs along a fir ridge above the Rhine plain, and on a clear evening you can see the Vosges from it. Below the ridge the same trip becomes something else entirely: hairpins into vine terraces, a wine village every eight kilometres, and cake taken seriously.

snapshot.Base(s): Baden-Baden (2 nights), Freudenstadt (1), Triberg (1), Freiburg im Breisgau (3)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 780 km; ridge roads and hairpin descents, gradients to 10%, max altitude 1,241 m
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Karlsruhe/Baden-Baden (FKB), Stuttgart (STR) or Basel (EAP); rail to Offenburg also works
snapshot.Who It Suits: Unhurried drivers, cake enthusiasts, anyone who wants scenery without altitude sickness

itinerary.title: Baden-Baden and the Ortenau terraces
itinerary.morning: Collect the car and check for a green **Umweltplakette** on the windscreen. Baden-Baden and Freiburg itself no longer run low-emission zones, but Karlsruhe still does, and the sticker is what gets you in there.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive the Badische Weinstrasse north-south through **Neuweier** and **Varnhalt**, terraced Riesling slopes where the local bottle shape is the flat-sided Bocksbeutel, then **Sasbachwalden**, half-timbered and steep. Small Winzergenossenschaft tasting rooms sit directly on the road with free parking.
itinerary.evening: Baden-Baden. Leave the car in the Kongresshaus garage and walk the Lichtentaler Allee to the Trinkhalle; the historic Friedrichsbad and the Caracalla Therme are five minutes apart.
itinerary.dayStats: 70 km · 1h40 driving · no passes · max altitude 420 m.

itinerary.title: Schwarzwaldhochstrasse
itinerary.morning: The **B500 Schwarzwaldhochstrasse** proper: 60 km from Baden-Baden to Freudenstadt, opened in 1930 and never tolled. It climbs quickly to the ridge at Sand and stays between 800 and 1,000 m the whole way, with the Rhine plain on the right and spruce on the left.
itinerary.afternoon: Stop at the **Mummelsee** (1,036 m) — a glacial tarn with a large paid car park that fills by 11:00 on summer Sundays — and walk 25 minutes up to the **Hornisgrinde**, 1,164 m, the northern Black Forest's highest point, with a boardwalk across the moor and a viewing tower. Continue to the **Nationalparkzentrum Ruhestein**, a striking stack of cantilevered timber boxes above the pass at 915 m, then **Schliffkopf** (1,055 m) and the **Kniebis** saddle (935 m).
itinerary.evening: Freudenstadt, whose market square is the largest in Germany and is essentially a car park with arcades. Free parking, which is unusual and welcome.
itinerary.dayStats: 80 km · 2h00 driving · 3 saddles (Ruhestein, Schliffkopf, Kniebis) · max altitude 1,036 m.

itinerary.title: Kinzig valley and the clock country
itinerary.morning: South on the B294 to **Alpirsbach** and its Romanesque monastery church, then **Schiltach**, a raft-builders' town of white-and-black timber houses stacked up a hillside. Park below the Marktplatz; the square itself is on a slope and cobbled.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Vogtsbauernhof** open-air museum at Gutach preserves real Black Forest farmhouses moved from across the region, including the low-slung roofs that run down to the ground. Then **Triberg**: the waterfall drops 163 m in seven cascades and charges entry; the upper Wasserfall car park saves the climb.
itinerary.evening: Stay in Triberg or Schonach. Ask your hotel for the **KONUS Gästekarte** — it makes all regional buses and trains free for overnight guests, which is worth knowing on a driving trip too.
itinerary.dayStats: 115 km · 2h30 driving · no passes · max altitude 1,000 m.

itinerary.title: Schwarzwald-Panoramastrasse and the Kandel
itinerary.morning: Join the signposted **Schwarzwald-Panoramastrasse**, a 275 km route that links the high plateaux. Take it via Furtwangen — the Deutsches Uhrenmuseum has the original cuckoo mechanisms and the world's largest clock collection — over the **Thurner** at 1,036 m to **St. Märgen** and **St. Peter**, whose Baroque abbey library is one of the finest interiors in Baden.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Kandelstrasse**: 11 km of tight, cambered hairpins from the Kandel pass at 1,241 m down to Waldkirch, with gradients to 10% and a well-earned reputation among motorcyclists. Drive it downhill in the afternoon with the Rhine plain opening ahead.
itinerary.evening: Into Freiburg im Breisgau for three nights. The city centre is largely pedestrianised (its Umweltzone was lifted in May 2025); use the Schlossberg or Rotteckring garages and walk.
itinerary.dayStats: 140 km · 3h20 driving · 2 passes (Thurner, Kandel) · max altitude 1,241 m.

itinerary.title: Schauinsland, Belchen and the Münstertal
itinerary.morning: The **Schauinslandstrasse** climbs from Horben in about 170 curves — a former hill-climb course, now speed-limited and camera-watched — to a summit car park near 1,220 m. Parking is paid; the tower is a ten-minute walk.
itinerary.afternoon: Over the **Notschrei** pass (1,121 m) and down to Todtnau, then up to Multen for the **Belchen**, 1,414 m. Private cars are banned from the last stretch to the summit: you park at Multen and take the Belchen-Seilbahn cable car or the shuttle bus. This is the region's best 360-degree view — Vosges, Jura, and the Alps on a clear autumn day.
itinerary.evening: Over the **Wiedener Eck** (1,037 m) and down through the **Münstertal** to Staufen, where the Fausthaus faces the market square, then back to Freiburg.
itinerary.dayStats: 130 km · 3h10 driving · 3 passes (Schauinsland, Notschrei, Wiedener Eck) · max altitude 1,220 m.

itinerary.title: Höllental, Feldberg and the Wutach
itinerary.morning: East on the **B31 through the Höllental**, a narrow rock gorge with the Hirschsprung statue on a ledge above the road, to **Titisee**. Then the **Feldbergpass** at 1,231 m, the highest through-road in the Black Forest, under the 1,493 m Feldberg summit.
itinerary.afternoon: Round the **Schluchsee**, then **St. Blasien**, whose enormous domed cathedral is a shock in a village of that size. Loop east to the **Wutachschlucht** gorge — the Schattenmühle car park is the standard access point for the two-hour walk in.
itinerary.evening: Return via Titisee and the Höllental. Watch for evening deer on the B500 stretches south of Hinterzarten.
itinerary.dayStats: 165 km · 3h20 driving · 1 pass (Feldbergpass) · max altitude 1,231 m.

itinerary.title: Kaiserstuhl and out
itinerary.morning: West to the **Kaiserstuhl**, a volcanic hill island in the Rhine plain planted almost entirely with vines. Drive the loess terraces via Ihringen, Achkarren and Oberbergen; the Vulkanfelsen and Badberg viewpoints look across to Alsace.
itinerary.afternoon: **Breisach** on the Rhine, with the Stephansmünster on its rock and the French bank in walking distance. Lunch, a last Spätburgunder tasting at a village cooperative, then the A5 north or south.
itinerary.evening: Drop the car. If flying from Basel's EuroAirport, note the terminal has separate French and Swiss sectors — return to the sector your contract names, since the Swiss side implies the Swiss motorway vignette.
itinerary.dayStats: 80 km · 1h50 driving · no passes · max altitude 560 m.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel am Markt
accommodationStrategy.description: A modest, long-run house on the market square by the Stiftskirche, uphill from the spa quarter and inside the old town — so the Friedrichsbad, the Trinkhalle and the Lichtentaler Allee are all walkable. Parking is arranged nearby rather than on site, which is normal in Baden-Baden's old streets.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks; longer for the Iffezheim race meetings.

accommodationStrategy.name: Parkhotel Wehrle
accommodationStrategy.description: A 17th-century inn with its own park in the middle of Triberg, five minutes from the waterfall entrance and with proper on-site parking — which matters, because Triberg's centre is a narrow valley floor with very little of it. It also fixes the trip's weak spot: the middle Black Forest is short on characterful beds.
accommodationStrategy.booking: a month.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Zum Roten Bären
accommodationStrategy.description: Documented from 1120 and arguably the oldest inn in Germany, on the Oberlinden by the Schwabentor. Its garage is the practical point: Freiburg's centre is pedestrianised and crossed by tram lines and Bächle water channels, and having a parked car inside the ring for three nights is worth paying for.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months in September.

logistics.emergency: 112 for everything; 110 for police. Bergwacht Schwarzwald handles gorge and forest rescues through 112.
logistics.weather: Winter tyres are legally required in winter conditions (the *situative Winterreifenpflicht*), and the B500 above 900 m gets freezing fog and drifting snow from November. Sections around Ruhestein and Schliffkopf close for hours at a time.
logistics.money: Cards are widely taken but small Winzergenossenschaften, mountain Gasthäuser and cake counters still prefer cash or Girocard. Shops shut at 20:00 and everything closes on Sunday except bakeries and petrol stations.

other.label: No car toll, but a sticker
other.text: Germany charges cars nothing for Autobahn use. What you do need is the green **Umweltplakette** for Umweltzonen — in this region Karlsruhe, Stuttgart, Mannheim and Heidelberg (Freiburg's zone was lifted in May 2025). It costs €6–€20 at TÜV, DEKRA or a workshop; German rentals normally carry one, foreign-plated cars usually do not, and the fine is charged per entry.

other.label: Cross-border
other.text: Alsace is 20 minutes from Freiburg and Basel is 60. In France you need a **Crit'Air** sticker for the Strasbourg zone; in Switzerland the motorway **Autobahnvignette** costs CHF 40 and is sold only as an annual, valid from 1 December to 31 January of the following year, now also as an e-vignette linked to the plate.

other.label: Rental restrictions
other.text: German rentals allow France, Switzerland, Austria and the Benelux as standard; eastward travel is often restricted and one-way drops abroad — Freiburg to Basel or Strasbourg — attract fees from €100. Confirm the Swiss vignette question before crossing.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 for everything; 110 for police. Bergwacht Schwarzwald handles gorge and forest rescues through 112.

other.label: Speed and cameras
other.text: The Schauinslandstrasse, the Kandel and the B500 all carry permanent speed and noise cameras, aimed mainly at motorcycles. Limits drop to 50 or 60 km/h without much warning.

proTips: Take the **KONUS Gästekarte** from any participating hotel: free regional trains and buses for overnight guests. Use it to ride up to Feldberg or Schauinsland and walk down, leaving the car behind.
Drive the Kandel and the Schauinsland downhill in late afternoon. Both face west, and both are jammed with motorcycles on Sunday mornings.
Do the Mummelsee before 10:00 or after 17:00. The car park is the bottleneck for the whole northern B500 on summer weekends.
You cannot drive up the Belchen — build in the cable car at Multen or the road is a dead end with a barrier.
Café Schäfer in Triberg still makes Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte to the documented original recipe. It is a small shop, and it sells out.
In the Kaiserstuhl, aim for a village cooperative rather than a roadside shop: Achkarren, Oberrotweil and Ihringen all pour Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder for a couple of euros a glass.
The Wutachschlucht is best walked one way with the bus back, which the KONUS card makes free.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 780 km; ridge roads and hairpin descents, gradients to 10%, max altitude 1,241 m
raw.Who It Suits: Unhurried drivers, cake enthusiasts, anyone who wants scenery without altitude sickness

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 780 km; ridge roads and hairpin descents, gradients to 10%, max altitude 1,241 m
typeSpecific.audience: Unhurried drivers, cake enthusiasts, anyone who wants scenery without altitude sickness

packingNotes: Walking shoes with tread: the Wutach gorge path is rooty, wet and unimproved.
A warm layer for the ridge — Hornisgrinde in May is often 10°C colder than Baden-Baden.
Swimwear and flip-flops for the Baden-Baden thermal baths; the Friedrichsbad is textile-free, the Caracalla is not.
A cool bag for wine bought at cooperatives; car boots in the Rhine plain reach 50°C in summer.
Cash, roughly €150, for parking meters, small tastings and cake.
Insect repellent for the Wutach and the moorland boardwalks in June.
Sunglasses — the ridge road runs west-facing all afternoon.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Snow or fog shuts the B500 ridge.** Fallback: the parallel B462 and B33 through the Kinzig and Murg valleys stay open and reach the same towns; you lose the view, not the day.
**You enter Karlsruhe without an Umweltplakette.** Fallback: buy one at a TÜV or DEKRA station on the edge of the city before driving in, or park at a Park-and-Ride tram stop outside the zone.
**Sunday closures strand you without food.** Fallback: Autobahn service areas and bakery cafés open Sunday mornings; buy provisions on Saturday before 20:00.
**Motorcycle weekend traffic on the passes.** Fallback: move the Kandel, Schauinsland and Mummelsee legs to weekdays and use Saturday and Sunday for the Kaiserstuhl and the wine villages.

trips.title: Andalucía: Ronda, the Alpujarras & Cabo de Gata
trips.subRegion: Andalucía — Serranía de Ronda, Sierra Nevada's southern slope and Almería

bestPeriod.window: April–early June & mid-September–early November
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (Sevilla-side inland temperatures over 42°C, coastal traffic); December–February for Puerto de la Ragua snow closures
bestPeriod.raw: April–early June & mid-September–early November

accommodation.note: Ronda parador-adjacent, an Alpujarra cortijo, Cabo de Gata

food.note: Menú del día €14–€18; Granada tapas come free with drinks

transport.note: Rental, fuel (~€1.60/l), minimal tolls, city parking

activities.note: Alhambra €19, Torcal, Rodalquilar mine, Tabernas

profile.difficultyNote: 2 — driving-led, with a 2 h Torcal karst loop and a stepped 1 h in Ronda's gorge

trips.gatewayAirport: AGP — Málaga Costa del Sol; 100 km / 1 h 40 to Ronda via the A-357 and A-367, or 1 h 25 on the A-397
trips.summary: Andalucía has more good driving roads than any other region in Spain, and this loop links three completely different ones: the cliff-edge A-397 up from the coast to Ronda, the ledge road through the Alpujarras that Gerald Brenan wrote about, and the empty desert straights of Almería. In between you climb Puerto de la Ragua at 2,000 m over the eastern shoulder of the Sierra Nevada — a crossing that goes from Moorish terraces to alpine pine to lunar badlands in ninety minutes. The week ends in the volcanic coves of Cabo de Gata, the driest place in Europe, where the roads are wide, empty and the light in October is extraordinary. It suits drivers who want variety of terrain and can navigate Spain's expanding low-emission zones without collecting fines.

itinerary.title: Málaga to Ronda by the cliff road
itinerary.morning: Collect the car at AGP. Head west on the A-7 to San Pedro de Alcántara — 55 km of coastal sprawl, but it is the price of admission to the A-397.
itinerary.afternoon: The A-397 climbs 1,000 m in 49 km with the Mediterranean falling away behind. Stop at the Puerto del Madroño layby for the view back to Gibraltar and, on a clear day, the Rif. Arrive Ronda mid-afternoon and park in the Martínez Astein or Socorro underground lots.
itinerary.evening: Walk the Puente Nuevo at sunset — the 98 m bridge over the El Tajo gorge is best from the Mirador de Aldehuela on the north side, or from the Jardines de Cuenca below. Dinner at Tragatá, Benito Gómez's tapas bar.
itinerary.dayStats: 105 km / 2 h; A-397 climbs to 950 m; AP-7 avoided; Ronda garage €14–€18/day.
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Montelirio, Ronda — a clifftop 18th-century mansion with valet parking.

itinerary.title: Grazalema, the white villages and El Torcal
itinerary.morning: West on the A-372 into the Sierra de Grazalema, over the Puerto del Boyar at 1,103 m, and down to Grazalema village. Continue to Zahara de la Sierra for the reservoir view, then the CA-9104 over the Puerto de las Palomas — 1,357 m, and one of the great white-village panoramas.
itinerary.afternoon: Return east and cross to **El Torcal de Antequera**. The upper car park is accessed by a narrow 4 km road with a barrier system in high season — arrive before 11:00 or park at the lower lot and take the shuttle. Walk the Ruta Amarilla (2.9 km) through the karst pinnacles.
itinerary.evening: Drive to Antequera and eat at Arte de Cozina for porra antequerana. Or return to Ronda if you prefer one base.
itinerary.dayStats: 210 km / 4 h with stops; Puerto del Boyar 1,103 m; Puerto de las Palomas 1,357 m; El Torcal free entry, parking €2.
itinerary.sleep: Parador de Antequera, or return to Hotel Montelirio, Ronda.

itinerary.title: Across to Granada and the Alhambra
itinerary.morning: The A-92 east from Antequera is fast, free dual carriageway through olive country. Two hours to Granada.
itinerary.afternoon: **Do not drive into central Granada.** The ZBE covers the historic core. Park at the Alhambra's own visitor car park (€6/day) or the Parking San Agustín, and use taxis or the C30/C32 microbuses thereafter. Your Alhambra ticket carries a strict half-hour entry slot for the **Nasrid Palaces** — miss it and it is void.
itinerary.evening: Sunset from the Mirador de San Nicolás in the Albaicín — go 40 minutes before sunset for a spot on the wall. Then free tapas crawl on Calle Navas: Los Diamantes for fried fish, Bodegas Castañeda for the classics.
itinerary.dayStats: 100 km / 1 h 40; A-92 toll-free; Alhambra €19 general, Nasrid Palaces timed entry; Granada ZBE camera-enforced.
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Casa 1800 Granada (Albaicín, arranges permitted access and a garage) or Alhambra Palace.

itinerary.title: The Alpujarra ledge road
itinerary.morning: Leave Granada south on the A-44, exit at Lanjarón and pick up the A-348 / A-4132. Órgiva is the last big fuel stop. Then the Poqueira gorge: Pampaneira, Bubión and Capileira stacked on the mountainside, all with lower car parks and lanes too tight to drive.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue east to **Trevélez** at 1,476 m — Spain's ham-curing village, where the jamón is air-dried at altitude. The road beyond, through Juviles and Bérchules to Cádiar, is the quietest and best-surfaced section of the whole Alpujarra.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Mesón La Fragua in Trevélez, or at your cortijo. The night sky here is exceptional — the Sierra Nevada blocks the coastal light dome.
itinerary.dayStats: 120 km / 3 h 15 with village stops; road runs 700–1,600 m; Trevélez 1,476 m; last supermarket fuel at Órgiva.
itinerary.sleep: Hotel La Fragua II, Trevélez, or Alquería de Morayma near Cádiar — both have their own parking.

itinerary.title: Puerto de la Ragua, Tabernas and the desert coast
itinerary.morning: Climb the A-337 from Laroles to **Puerto de la Ragua at 2,000 m** — 15 km of steady, narrow, well-graded ascent through pine into open moorland at the col. There is a small refuge, a picnic area and a nordic ski trailhead. Descend the north side to La Calahorra, whose Renaissance castle sits on a bare hill above the Marquesado plain.
itinerary.afternoon: East on the A-92 through Guadix's cave-house quarter, then into the **Tabernas desert** — Europe's only true desert, and the backdrop to A Fistful of Dollars. Fort Bravo / Texas Hollywood is the surviving film set worth stopping at.
itinerary.evening: Drop south to Cabo de Gata. Dinner at La Ola in San José for grilled red prawns.
itinerary.dayStats: 230 km / 5 h; Puerto de la Ragua 2,000 m, snow-closed in spells December–March; A-92 free; Tabernas gets to 42°C in summer.
itinerary.sleep: MC San José or Cortijo El Sotillo, San José — both with secure lots, which matters here.

itinerary.title: Rodalquilar, Las Negras and the cove roads
itinerary.morning: Drive north to **Rodalquilar**, an abandoned gold-mining village in a volcanic amphitheatre with the mill ruins standing open to walk through. Then over to **Las Negras**, a whitewashed fishing hamlet at the end of a long straight road.
itinerary.afternoon: The Playa de los Muertos car park is on the AL-5106 above the beach; the descent is a 20-minute rough path. Alternatively, the **Playa de Mónsul and Playa de los Genoveses** track south of San José is **closed to private cars in summer** — a shuttle bus runs from San José and the barrier is enforced. Out of season you can drive the piste, which is graded gravel and fine for a normal car.
itinerary.evening: Sunset from the **Mirador de la Amatista** on the AL-3115 between Rodalquilar and La Isleta — the best coastal viewpoint in the park, and it faces the right way for the last hour of light.
itinerary.dayStats: 85 km / 2 h; Mónsul/Genoveses track 7 km gravel, seasonal vehicle ban; shuttle €5 return; park entry free.
itinerary.sleep: MC San José or Cortijo El Sotillo (second night).

itinerary.title: The coast road back to Málaga
itinerary.morning: Head west on the A-7 along the Almería and Granada coast. The stretch through the Sierra de Gádor and the Salobreña plain is a series of viaducts and tunnels with genuine sea views. Stop at Salobreña's castle above the sugar-cane fields.
itinerary.afternoon: Optional detour to Nerja for the caves, or straight through to Málaga. Return the car at AGP — refuel at the Cepsa on the A-7 approach, not at the airport.
itinerary.evening: If you have hours to spare, park at the Muelle Uno garage and walk Málaga's centre — Picasso Museum, the Alcazaba, and the roof terrace at AC Málaga Palacio.
itinerary.dayStats: 220 km / 2 h 45; A-7 toll-free (AP-7 optional, €3–€9 per section); Málaga ZBE — use Muelle Uno or Alcazaba garages.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Montelirio
accommodationStrategy.description: Built into the cliff edge beside the Puente Nuevo, with a valet service that removes the problem of Ronda's near-impossible old-town parking. Terrace rooms look straight down the El Tajo gorge, and it is 60 seconds' walk from the bridge, so you can shoot the blue hour without moving the car. €150–€230.

accommodationStrategy.name: Alquería de Morayma
accommodationStrategy.description: A working farm estate on the eastern Alpujarra with its own wine, olive oil and generous open parking — useful, because every other Alpujarra village has none. It sits at the base of the A-337, meaning the Puerto de la Ragua climb starts 15 minutes after breakfast rather than an hour. €90–€130.

accommodationStrategy.name: Cortijo El Sotillo
accommodationStrategy.description: Just outside San José with a large gated car park, which is the practical point: San José's street parking is metered, contested and the Genoveses shuttle leaves from the village. Stables, a pool for the flat afternoon hours, and a five-minute walk to the harbour restaurants. €120–€190.

logistics.connectivity: Spain is in the EU roaming zone. Coverage is good almost everywhere including the Alpujarra villages; the exceptions are the Puerto de la Ragua col and the interior of Cabo de Gata's tracks. Download offline maps for the park.
logistics.emergency: 112 across Spain. Guardia Civil 062; mountain rescue in the Sierra Nevada is run by the Guardia Civil's GREIM via 112. Road assistance is through your rental's own number — RACE is 900 100 992.
logistics.weather: The **terral**, a hot dry offshore wind, can push Málaga past 40°C for days in summer. Grazalema records Spain's highest rainfall and produces dense fog on the A-372 with little warning. Cabo de Gata is genuinely arid — under 200 mm of rain a year — but a **levante** easterly makes the eastern coves unswimmable and blows fine grit.
logistics.bookingWindows: **The Alhambra is the hard constraint** — tickets go on sale up to three months ahead on alhambra-patronato.es and the Nasrid Palaces slots sell out weeks in advance for April–October. Buy from the official site only; resellers charge triple. Cabo de Gata accommodation books out for August and Semana Santa.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards work everywhere including village bars and fuel pumps. Keep €20 in coins for blue-zone street meters. Tipping is minimal: rounding up, or 5% for a full dinner. Granada is one of the last cities where a drink comes with a free tapa.
logistics.transportRules: No vignette. Motorway tolls are limited to the AP-7 Costa del Sol on this route. Speed limits are 120 on autovías, 90 on conventional roads, 30 in most urban single-lane streets. Speed cameras are frequent and signed; radar detectors are illegal. Two warning triangles were replaced by the mandatory **V-16 connected beacon from 1 January 2026** — confirm your rental has one. Alcohol limit 0.05% (0.03% for drivers under two years).
logistics.permits: Cabo de Gata-Níjar is a natural park: the Genoveses and Mónsul access track is closed to private vehicles in high season with a paid shuttle instead, and wild camping and campervan overnighting are prohibited and actively fined. Drones require registration and are banned over the park and over the Alhambra. Sierra Nevada National Park restricts vehicle access above certain points on the Hoya de la Mora road.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable throughout, though Almería's is very hard and most people buy bottled. Heatstroke is the real risk in Tabernas and at El Torcal — go early, carry water. Sea urchins and occasional Portuguese man o' war after easterly winds on the Almería coast. Puerto de la Ragua at 2,000 m needs no acclimatisation but can be 15°C colder than the coast.

proTips: Buy the Alhambra ticket the day it opens for your month, and choose a **Nasrid Palaces slot before 09:00 or after 18:00**. The half-hour entry window is enforced to the minute, and midday slots put you in the Court of the Lions with 400 other people.
Drive the A-397 **upward from the coast**, not down. The sea views open behind you on the ascent and you are on the inside of the drops; descending it puts you on the cliff edge for 49 km.

Park outside every ZBE. In Granada use the Alhambra visitor lot or Parking San Agustín; in Málaga use Muelle Uno. Camera-enforced ZBE fines are €200 and arrive via the rental company months later with an admin fee on top.

Check the Puerto de la Ragua before committing on Day 5. There is no barrier and no live feed — the Junta de Andalucía's traffic information and the Laroles village bar are both better sources than any app.
Reach El Torcal's upper car park before 11:00. In peak season a barrier system diverts arrivals to the lower lot and a shuttle, adding an hour to a two-hour walk.

The Genoveses and Mónsul beach track is closed to cars in summer. If you visit in October or April you can drive the gravel piste yourself — a normal hatchback handles it at 20 km/h, and you get Spain's best beach with a dozen people on it.

Shoot the Alpujarra villages from the road **below** Pampaneira in the late afternoon; the classic stacked-white-village shot only works when the western sun is on the terraces. Mornings there are entirely in shadow.
Trevélez's ham cellars offer free tastings and will vacuum-pack for travel. A whole leg is not hand-luggage; a sliced 100 g pack is, and it is a fifth of the price of the same ham in Málaga.

Confirm your rental carries the V-16 emergency beacon rather than triangles. Since January 2026 the beacon is the legal requirement, and standing on a hard shoulder placing triangles is now both illegal and dangerous.

raw.Total distance: ~1,000 km over 7 days. Longest leg is Day 5, Granada–Cabo de Gata via the full Alpujarra road and Puerto de la Ragua, 230 km in a genuine 5 h.
raw.A-397 (San Pedro de Alcántara–Ronda), 49: the famous one. Climbs from sea level to 1,000 m over the Serranía de Ronda with sweeping engineered curves, a 950 m summit near Puerto del Madroño, and long unguarded drops. Excellent surface, no toll, but it is a favourite of motorcyclists and Guardia Civil speed patrols in equal measure. Allow 1 h 10, not 50 minutes.
raw.A-372 (Ronda–Grazalema–El Bosque), 52 km: narrower and more technical than the A-397, threading the Sierra de Grazalema — the wettest place in Spain, which means fog and wet limestone even in May. Puerto del Boyar at 1,103 m has a proper viewpoint layby.
raw.A-4132 Alpujarra road (Lanjarón–Órgiva–P: roughly 90 km of continuous contour-hugging two-lane road at 700–1,600 m, with the Poqueira gorge villages (Pampaneira, Bubión, Capileira) stacked above it. Trevélez at 1,476 m is among the highest villages in Spain. Village streets are one-car-wide with 90° turns — park at the lower lots.
raw.Puerto de la Ragua (A-337), 2,000 m: the only paved crossing of the Sierra Nevada's eastern end, linking the Alpujarra to the Marquesado plain and Guadix. Narrow, well-surfaced, ~15 km of climb from La Calahorra, with a cross-country ski centre at the col. **Closes on snow, typically for spells between December and March**, and there is no live barrier — check before committing.
raw.Tolls: Andalucía is almost entirely toll-free. The **AP-7 Málaga–Estepona (AP-7 Costa del Sol)** is the exception, costing roughly €3–€9 per section and up to ~€12 in high season for the full Málaga–Guadiaro run; the parallel free A-7 is slower and busier. The AP-4 Sevilla–Cádiz became toll-free in 2019. No vignette exists in Spain.
raw.Low-emission zones (ZBE): the item most likely to cost you money. **Málaga's ZBE** covers the centre and is camera-enforced; **Granada's ZBE** covers the historic core including the Realejo and much of the Albaicín approach. Rental cars registered in Spain carry a DGT environmental sticker (etiqueta ambiental) — a modern petrol car gets a "C" label which is currently admitted in both, but non-resident and unregistered vehicles are not automatically exempt. The safe practice is to park in a designated underground car park outside the zone and walk.
raw.Car rental & cross-border: Málaga is one of Europe's cheapest rental markets, which is also why the counter upsell is aggressive — decline the fuel-purchase option and take a card with a large enough limit for the excess hold. Gibraltar is permitted by most companies but frequently requires declaration; Morocco is refused by nearly all. Cross into Portugal is generally free of charge on Spanish rentals. One-way AGP-to-Almería drops are €60–€120.
raw.Fuel & hazards: fuel is plentiful except on the Alpujarra road above Órgiva (fill at Órgiva) and across Puerto de la Ragua (fill at Cádiar or Guadix). Hazards: goats and Iberian ibex on the A-4132 at dawn and dusk, fog banks in Grazalema, and the fact that Andalucian villages have unmarked speed bumps that will destroy a low rental's sump.

sources.verified: Málaga and Granada both operate camera-enforced ZBE low-emission zones covering their historic centres, with the DGT environmental sticker system determining access; Spain has no vignette and Andalucía is largely toll-free apart from the AP-7 Costa del Sol; Puerto de la Ragua's altitude (~2,000 m) and its status as the paved crossing of the eastern Sierra Nevada, subject to snow closure.
sources.confidenceNotes: ZBE rules are the most volatile element — Spanish municipalities have been phasing in enforcement on different timetables and the treatment of foreign-plated and non-resident vehicles differs between Málaga and Granada; re-verify against each ayuntamiento's own page before publishing. Puerto de la Ragua has no fixed closure dates and no live status feed; the December–March window is typical, not guaranteed. AP-7 Costa del Sol section prices vary seasonally and should be re-quoted. Alhambra ticket pricing and the three-month sales window are revised periodically. The Genoveses/Mónsul vehicle restriction dates are set annually by the park authority. The V-16 beacon requirement took effect 1 January 2026 — confirm rental fleet compliance.

food.note: €55–90 per day; heimablídni home dinners €70–110 pp

trips.summary: A seven-day road trips & scenic drive itinerary in Streymoy, Eysturoy, Norðoyar, Sandoy, Vágar, Faroe Islands.

itinerary.title: Vágar: Gásadalur and the western edge
itinerary.morning: Land at Vágar, collect the car. Drive first to Bøur, a village of turf roofs facing the sea stacks of Tindhólmur.
itinerary.afternoon: Through the old single-lane tunnel — or the new one — to Gásadalur, a village of sixteen people that had no road access until 2004; the postman used to walk over the mountain three times a week. The Múlafossur waterfall drops straight off the cliff beside it into the Atlantic.
itinerary.evening: Sørvágur or Miðvágur for the night. Buy food; shops close early and are shut on Sundays.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 km

itinerary.title: Streymoy: Saksun, Tjørnuvík and the old high road
itinerary.morning: Take the Oyggjarvegur, the old mountain road over Streymoy, rather than the tunnel — it climbs into cloud with the whole island beneath it.
itinerary.afternoon: Saksun: a turf-roofed church, a tidal lagoon that empties completely at low water, and a handful of farms in an amphitheatre of cliffs. Then across to Tjørnuvík on the north coast, facing the Risin og Kellingin sea stacks — the giant and the witch, petrified while trying to drag the Faroes to Iceland.
itinerary.evening: Drive to Tórshavn. Walk Tinganes, the peninsula of red turf-roofed government buildings where the Løgting has met since Viking times — arguably the oldest continuous parliamentary site in the world.
itinerary.dayStats: 90 km

itinerary.title: Eysturoy: Gjógv, Funningur and the pass
itinerary.morning: Through the Eysturoy subsea tunnel, past the illuminated undersea roundabout with its light installation and jellyfish sculpture. North to Funningur, said to be the first Norse settlement in the islands.
itinerary.afternoon: The Eiðisskarð pass beneath Slættaratindur (882 m, the highest point), then Gjógv, built around a 200 m natural sea gorge that served as its harbour.
itinerary.evening: Stay in Gjógv. There is one guesthouse, no restaurant, and complete silence.
itinerary.dayStats: 110 km

itinerary.title: Norðoyar: Klaksvík, Viðareiði and Kalsoy
itinerary.morning: The Norðoya tunnel to Klaksvík, the second town and the fishing capital, with the extraordinary Christianskirkjan — a modern church with a Viking longhouse form and a rowing boat hung from the ceiling.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive to Viðareiði, the northernmost settlement, under Enniberg — one of the highest sea cliffs in Europe at 754 m. Alternatively take the small ferry from Klaksvík to Kalsoy and drive its chain of single-lane tunnels to Trøllanes for the Kallur lighthouse walk, the most photographed ridge in the Faroes. Ferry capacity is tiny; queue early. `verify: true`
itinerary.evening: Klaksvík. The town brewery is a national institution.
itinerary.dayStats: 120 km + ferry

itinerary.title: Vestmanna bird cliffs and Sandoy
itinerary.morning: The Vestmanna sea-cliff boat trip: two hours through sea caves and under 600 m cliffs stacked with guillemots, fulmars and puffins. It cancels in swell, so treat it as first-choice-if-calm.
itinerary.afternoon: Through the new Sandoy tunnel to Sandoy — sand dunes, the village of Skopun, and Húsavík with its medieval ruins. Sandoy is where Faroese people go when they want to be somewhere quiet, which tells you something.
itinerary.evening: Back to Tórshavn.
itinerary.dayStats: 100 km + boat

itinerary.title: Tórshavn, Kirkjubøur and a home dinner
itinerary.morning: Kirkjubøur, the medieval episcopal seat: the roofless Gothic Magnus Cathedral begun around 1300, the small St Olav's church still in use, and Kirkjubøargarður, a farmhouse continuously inhabited for centuries.
itinerary.afternoon: Tórshavn properly — the National Museum, the Nordic House, the old town's black tarred houses with grass roofs, and the harbour.
itinerary.evening: Book a **heimablídni**: dinner in a Faroese family's home, several courses of lamb, fish and rhubarb, with the family eating alongside you. It is the single best thing you can do in the islands.
itinerary.dayStats: 40 km

itinerary.title: Trøllkonufingur, Sørvágsvatn or Mykines, then out
itinerary.morning: Depending on wind: the Mykines boat for puffins, or the short walk to the Trælanípa cliff over Sørvágsvatn.
itinerary.afternoon: Fly out from Vágar. Allow generous slack for weather.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Føroyar or Hotel Brandan
accommodationStrategy.description: Two contrasting bases in the capital: Føroyar is turf-roofed on the hill with the harbour view; Brandan is newer, in town, with a spa. Both have secure parking, which matters more than it sounds in a place where the wind removes car doors.

accommodationStrategy.name: Gjáargarður
accommodationStrategy.description: The guesthouse at the gorge village, with home-cooked dinners booked at check-in. Essential for Day 3 because the alternative is an hour's drive back to Tórshavn on a mountain road in the dark.

accommodationStrategy.name: Klaksvík guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: Simple, cheap, and positioned so that the Kalsoy ferry and the Viðareiði drive both start from your door rather than 90 minutes away. Book the ferry morning and stay the night before — this is the sequencing that makes Day 4 work.

logistics.emergency: 112. The national hospital is in Tórshavn with smaller facilities in Klaksvík and Suðuroy. Helicopter evacuation is available and used.
logistics.weather: Wind, not rain, drives the itinerary. Above 15 m/s, mountain roads and ferries stop. Build two flexible days into seven and reorder daily around the forecast rather than fighting it.
logistics.bookingWindows: Cars: 2–3 months for summer. Heimablídni dinners: 3–6 weeks. Vestmanna boats: a few days, but expect cancellation. Guesthouses in Gjógv and Viðareiði: 2–3 months.

other.label: Tunnel tolls
other.text: The Vágar, Eysturoy and Sandoy subsea tunnels are tolled by automatic plate recognition and billed to the rental company, typically with an administration fee. Expect a bill after you get home. `verify: true`

other.label: Single-lane tunnels
other.text: Several older mountain tunnels — notably on Kalsoy and in the outer islands — are one lane with passing bays (marked **M**). The rule: the vehicle with the bay on its side pulls in. They are unlit, wet, and rock-walled. Drive slowly with headlights on.

other.label: Sheep
other.text: There are more sheep than people and they own the roads. Hitting one makes you liable to the owner. Assume a sheep behind every blind crest.

other.label: Ferries
other.text: Strandfaraskip Landsins runs the inter-island ferries; the Kalsoy and Mykines routes have small capacity and fill in summer. The Suðuroy ferry (2 h) is large and reliable. `verify: true`

other.label: Sundays
other.text: Shops, most restaurants and many attractions close. Fuel stations are largely automated. Plan food on Saturday.

proTips: Always take the **old mountain road** where one exists beside a tunnel. The Oyggjarvegur, the Norðradalsskarð and the Eiðisskarð are the three best drives in the North Atlantic and everyone else is underground.
Check **wind, not rain**. A Faroese 4 mm rain day with 6 m/s wind is a great day out; a dry day at 18 m/s is not.

The **Faroese helicopter** service links remote villages at subsidised fares and is one of Europe's great transport oddities. Seat release is scheduled and tourists may be limited to one-way sectors — check the current rules well ahead. `verify: true`
Fill the tank whenever you are below half. Fuel stations outside Tórshavn, Klaksvík and Vágar are sparse and several are card-only automats.

Photograph Saksun and Gásadalur **before 09:00 or after 20:00**. Both are tiny private settlements where residents have had real problems with visitor volume — arrive early, stay on marked paths, park only in the designated areas.
If a storm eats a day, the Nordic House, the National Museum and the Tórshavn swimming baths absorb it well — and a storm-day heimablídni is better than a calm-day one.

raw.driving_character: Short legs on excellent tarmac, punctuated by subsea tunnels, single-lane mountain tunnels with passing bays, and hairpin descents into fjord villages
raw.mountain_passes: The old Oyggjarvegur high road over Streymoy, the Eiðisskarð pass on Eysturoy, and the Norðradalsskarð — all worth taking instead of the tunnel
raw.tunnels: Vágatunnilin (2002), Norðoyatunnilin (2006), Eysturoyartunnilin (2020, with the world's only undersea roundabout), Sandoyartunnilin (2023)
raw.cross_border_rules: The Faroes are outside the EU and the Schengen customs union though within the Nordic passport area; hire cars cannot leave the archipelago
