raw.Who It Suits: Experienced hut hikers comfortable with fixed cable and glacier-adjacent exposure; not a beginner's first hut trip

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 55–65 km, 5,200 m ascent / 5,200 m descent; glacier-moraine paths, cable-secured rock steps, T3–T4
typeSpecific.audience: Experienced hut hikers comfortable with fixed cable and glacier-adjacent exposure; not a beginner's first hut trip

packingNotes: A proper via-ferrata set (harness, lanyard with shock absorber, karabiners) for the Mörchenscharte — this is the mandatory item, not the over-pack.
Hüttenschlafsack for every hut night.
Trekking poles for the long descents on Days 2, 5 and 7.
A headtorch for dorm rooms and early starts.
Cash in small notes, more than you think you need.
A lightweight hard-shell for the exposed scharten.
Sun protection — the glacier-adjacent cols reflect UV even under cloud.
What people over-pack: hiking food for the whole week. Every hut sells meals and packed lunches; carry snacks for between huts, not seven days of rations.
What people under-pack: gloves for the cabled sections — bare hands on cold morning steel wear through fast.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Berliner Hütte fully booked.** Fallback: stay at Furtschaglhaus one extra night and do a longer single push to Greizer Hütte the next day, or check for late cancellations by phone the morning of.

**Old snow on the Mörchenscharte.** Fallback: ask the Berliner Hütte warden the evening before; in a heavy-snow year the crossing is sometimes deferred until conditions are confirmed safe by hut staff who cross it daily.
**Afternoon storm building near a scharte.** Fallback: retreat to the hut just left — both Berliner and Greizer are within 2–3 hours of the Mörchenscharte for most of its approach.
**Fatigue after the Day 3 crux.** Fallback: Kasseler Hütte is a genuinely restful hut; treat Day 4 as the easier day it is rather than pushing straight through to the valley.
**Bus timing from Ginzling to Finkenberg on Day 6.** Fallback: confirm the regional timetable the night before at the gasthof, or use a local taxi — the gap between buses can be over an hour.

trips.title: The Stubai Höhenweg Hut Circuit

bestPeriod.note: The Peiljoch and Niederl saddles hold hard snow into early July; late September brings the first hut closures.

trips.gatewayAirport: Innsbruck (INN)
trips.summary: A six-hut circuit around the Stubai Alps from Neustift, crossing five glacier-rimmed saddles between 2,700 m and 3,000 m.
trips.hook: The Stubai Höhenweg is a ring of Alpenverein huts strung around a horseshoe of 3,000 m peaks, and you spend the week walking the inside of that horseshoe with the glaciers never far from view. Every day ends at a staffed hut with a hot meal and a bed, and every day in between crosses a saddle that makes you work for the next valley. Neustift, at the mouth of the Stubaital, is the only base you need.

snapshot.Base(s): Neustift im Stubaital (start/finish), six huts en route
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 60–68 km, 5,600 m ascent / 5,600 m descent; high alpine path on scree, slab and moraine, T3 with T4 sections
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Innsbruck (INN), then IVB regional bus 4166 up the Stubaital to Neustift (about 40 minutes)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Fit hikers with hut experience and no fear of exposed, cable-secured ground; not a first alpine trek

itinerary.title: Neustift to Starkenburger Hütte
itinerary.morning: Bus or taxi from Neustift to the Kampl trailhead above Fulpmes, or walk straight out of Neustift village if you want the full vertical. Either way the path climbs through spruce forest onto the open Schlick valley flank.
itinerary.afternoon: Steady switchbacks above the treeline to Starkenburger Hütte (2,237 m), an Alpenverein hut with a wide terrace looking straight down the Stubaital. Book it in advance through the Alpenverein's online hut-booking portal; July and August weekends fill two to three weeks out.
itinerary.evening: Dinner is Tiroler Gröstl or a hut goulash; pay the overnight fee in cash, as most Stubai huts still prefer it for lodging even when the bar takes cards.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 1,300 m ascent, negligible descent, 4.5–5.5 hours. Grade T2–T3, forest track then open alpine path, no exposure.

itinerary.title: Starkenburger Hütte to Franz-Senn-Hütte
itinerary.morning: The path contours north below the Kalkwand and drops briefly into the Oberbergtal before climbing again — an undulating traverse rather than one clean pass, past the Bremer Hütte junction (worth the 20-minute detour for coffee if the timing works).
itinerary.afternoon: A final pull over rough moraine brings you to Franz-Senn-Hütte (2,147 m), one of the largest and oldest huts in the range, with its own small alpine museum and a view straight up the Alpeiner Ferner glacier.
itinerary.evening: The Franz-Senn-Hütte's kitchen runs late for a hut; a Kaiserschmarrn here is a fair reward. Book through the DAV/ÖAV portal — this hut sells out fastest of the six.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 850 m ascent, 650 m descent, 5–6 hours. Grade T3, exposed traverse sections with fixed cable on the steepest rock steps.

itinerary.title: Franz-Senn-Hütte to Dresdner Hütte
itinerary.morning: The big day. Climb past the Alpeiner Ferner's lower moraine to the Schwarzenbergscharte (2,919 m), a narrow notch with fixed steel cable on both approaches — the first genuinely alpine crossing of the week.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend scree and old snow patches (common into mid-July) into the Gletschertal, then climb again to Dresdner Hütte (2,308 m), the circuit's biggest hut, sitting directly below the Stubai glacier ski area's lift infrastructure.
itinerary.evening: Dresdner Hütte has real showers and a bigger dining room than most; it is also the easiest hut to reach by cable car from Mutterberg, so it fills with day visitors as well as trekkers. Book ahead regardless.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km, 950 m ascent, 800 m descent, 6–7 hours. Grade T4 at the Schwarzenbergscharte (fixed cable, exposed), T3 elsewhere. Snow risk: the scharte's north side can hold névé into early July — carry poles at minimum, microspikes are sensible before mid-July.

itinerary.title: Dresdner Hütte to Nürnberger Hütte
itinerary.morning: Climb past the glacier ski lifts (surreal in July, with skiers overhead on the Eisgrat) to the Peiljoch (2,997 m), the highest point on the whole circuit and a genuine mountaineer's saddle with cable protection on the final metres.
itinerary.afternoon: A long, knee-testing descent past the Sulzenauferner's outwash into the Neder valley, then a short reclimb to Nürnberger Hütte (2,297 m), tucked under the Wilder Freiger.
itinerary.evening: Quieter than Dresdner or Franz-Senn; a good hut for an early night before the next crossing.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 750 m ascent, 950 m descent, 6 hours. Grade T4 at Peiljoch (short fixed-cable scramble, real exposure), T3 on the descent. Old snow on the Peiljoch's shaded side into July.

itinerary.title: Nürnberger Hütte to Sulzenauhütte
itinerary.morning: Drop into the valley floor near the Grünausee, a small glacial lake worth the five-minute detour, then begin the climb to the Niederl (2,700 m).
itinerary.afternoon: The Niederl is broad and less exposed than the previous two saddles, but the approach crosses a stretch of permanent scree that shifts underfoot — go slowly. Beyond it, Sulzenauhütte (2,191 m) sits below the Sulzenauferner glacier with the best glacier panorama of the week from its terrace.
itinerary.evening: This hut is popular with day-trippers from the Stubai valley floor via the Grawa waterfall path, so the terrace is lively; the dorms quiet down fast after 21:00.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km, 650 m ascent, 850 m descent, 5 hours. Grade T3, one loose scree traverse, no fixed protection required.

itinerary.title: Sulzenauhütte to Neue Regensburger Hütte
itinerary.morning: Climb to the Grawagrubennieder (2,900 m), the last of the big saddles, with views back over the whole horseshoe you have just walked.
itinerary.afternoon: The descent into the Oberissalm side is long and rocky; the Neue Regensburger Hütte (2,286 m) appears late, perched above the Oberiss reservoir.
itinerary.evening: This is the most remote of the six huts and the one most likely to have space without weeks of notice — still book ahead, but it is the fallback if others are full.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 800 m ascent, 750 m descent, 6 hours. Grade T3–T4, short fixed-cable step below the saddle, exposure moderate.

itinerary.title: Neue Regensburger Hütte to Neustift
itinerary.morning: A long, mostly downhill walk past the Oberiss reservoir and into the Milders valley on a good path used by farm traffic in the lower half.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive in Milders or Neustift by early-to-mid afternoon; the regional bus runs frequently back into Neustift centre if you finish in Milders.
itinerary.evening: A last Tiroler dinner in Neustift — Bacher Wirt or any of the Gasthöfe on the main street serve knödel and Kaspressknödelsuppe without pretension.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km, 100 m ascent, 1,650 m descent, 4.5–5.5 hours. Grade T1–T2, farm track and forest road, no exposure.

accommodationStrategy.name: Alpenverein huts en route
accommodationStrategy.description: All six huts (Starkenburger, Franz-Senn, Dresdner, Nürnberger, Sulzenau, Neue Regensburger) are ÖAV/DAV huts bookable through the Alpenvereinshütten online reservation system; a handful still take direct phone bookings when the online calendar shows a hut as full but a warden holds back emergency beds. Book the full week as one block the day online reservations open for the season — Franz-Senn and Dresdner sell out first.
accommodationStrategy.booking: as early as the season's booking window allows, minimum 6–8 weeks ahead for August.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €25–€40 half-board per night for Alpenverein members, €45–€60 for non-members (join the Alpenverein or a reciprocal club before the trip — it pays for itself in three nights)

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Jagdhof or a Gasthof in Neustift
accommodationStrategy.description: Neustift has a deep bench of family-run hotels used to trekkers dropping bags before and after the circuit; ask any of them about secure luggage storage for the six days you are on the huts, which most offer informally.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead for peak August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Self-catering apartment in Neustift or Fulpmes
accommodationStrategy.description: A cheaper way to cover the arrival and departure nights, with a kitchen for restocking hut snacks before you start.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Austrian alpine rescue (Bergrettung) is reached fastest on **140**. Every hut has a landline and usually a radio even where mobile signal fails.
logistics.weather: Afternoon thunderstorms build from around 13:00 in July and August; start each stage by 07:00–07:30 to be off the saddles before the build-up.
logistics.bookingWindows: The Alpenvereinshütten portal opens hut calendars roughly 6–12 months ahead depending on the hut; Franz-Senn and Dresdner (glacier-adjacent, cable-car accessible) fill first because they also serve day visitors and via-ferrata parties.

other.label: Hüttenschlafsack is mandatory
other.text: , not optional — huts will rent one if you forget, but at a markup, and it is one more thing to queue for at check-in.

other.label: Cash for huts
other.text: Bar tabs and lodging at most huts still run on cash; carry €300–€400 in €20s and €50s for the week, since the nearest ATM after Neustift is nonexistent until you return.

other.label: Snow on the saddles
other.text: Schwarzenbergscharte, Peiljoch and Grawagrubennieder can all hold hard old snow into the first half of July; ask the hut warden the evening before, since they update conditions daily.

other.label: Camping is prohibited
other.text: in the Tyrolean alpine zone outside designated sites — the huts are the accommodation, not a fallback for a tent.

proTips: Reserve the whole six-hut chain the same day the booking calendar opens; a broken chain is the single most common thing that unravels this trip.
Carry a printed confirmation for each hut — a warden checking a paper list moves faster than one hunting for a booking app with patchy signal.
Eat the Kaiserschmarrn at Franz-Senn-Hütte before 15:00, before the afternoon rush from the Alpeiner Ferner trail arrives.
Fill water bottles at every hut tap without exception — above 2,200 m there is almost no reliable surface water between saddles.
Cross the Peiljoch and Schwarzenbergscharte before 10:00; loose scree that is frozen firm at dawn turns to ball-bearings by early afternoon.
Ask each warden about the next day's saddle conditions at dinner — huts compare notes by radio and know about fresh snow before any app does.
If a saddle is genuinely bad, the valley-floor alternative from most huts is a straightforward descent to a Stubaital bus stop.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 60–68 km, 5,600 m ascent / 5,600 m descent; high alpine path on scree, slab and moraine, T3 with T4 sections
raw.Who It Suits: Fit hikers with hut experience and no fear of exposed, cable-secured ground; not a first alpine trek

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 60–68 km, 5,600 m ascent / 5,600 m descent; high alpine path on scree, slab and moraine, T3 with T4 sections
typeSpecific.audience: Fit hikers with hut experience and no fear of exposed, cable-secured ground; not a first alpine trek

packingNotes: Hüttenschlafsack (hut sleeping liner) — genuinely mandatory, not a suggestion, at every ÖAV/DAV hut.
A headtorch with spare batteries for dorm rooms and pre-dawn starts.
Trekking poles, non-negotiable for the long descents on Days 3, 4 and 7.
Microspikes or light crampons if walking before mid-July, for old snow on the three high saddles.
A 30–40 L pack that carries well loaded — you are on your feet 5–7 hours most days.
Cash in small notes, more than feels necessary.
A lightweight hard-shell — the exposed saddles get genuine wind even on a clear day.
Earplugs for shared dorms.
What people over-pack: a full change of clothes for each day. Two hiking sets and one dry hut set is enough.
What people under-pack: sun protection. The glacier-adjacent saddles reflect UV hard even in cloud.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A hut in the chain is full.** Fallback: Neue Regensburger and Sulzenauhütte usually have more late availability than Franz-Senn or Dresdner; a broken chain can sometimes be patched by descending to the valley for one night and rejoining by bus and a shorter re-ascent the next day.
**Old snow on a saddle you're not equipped for.** Fallback: ask the warden the evening before; most huts can suggest a lower, longer alternative path that avoids the steepest snow-holding gully.

**Afternoon storm building on a saddle.** Fallback: turn back to the hut you left rather than push over an exposed crossing — every saddle on this circuit has a hut within 1–2 hours behind you for most of the ascent.
**Knees give out on the long descents.** Days 3, 4 and 7 drop 750–1,650 m each. Fallback: poles from day one, and a rest morning built around a late start rather than skipping a hut night.

**Bus timing back from Milders or Neustift.** Fallback: the Stubaital regional bus runs regularly in season, but confirm the last departure the night before at the hut, since Day 7 timing depends on how the descent goes.

trips.title: Sutjeska and Zelengora: Maglić, Perućica and the Via Dinarica White Trail
trips.subRegion: Sutjeska National Park, Zelengora & the upper Drina — Republika Srpska

bestPeriod.window: Mid-June–early October, with late June for the Zelengora wildflowers and September for stable rock on Maglić
bestPeriod.avoid: November–May — the Prijevor road is unploughed, katuns close and the Maglić chains ice
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-June–early October, with late June for the Zelengora wildflowers and September for stable rock on Maglić

accommodation.note: Hotel Mladost approx. 70–110 BAM pppn; katun and mountain-hut beds 30–50 BAM

food.note: Mains 12–22 BAM, a beer 3–4 BAM; katun half board 45–70 BAM

transport.note: Sarajevo transfer, hire car or driver, the rough Prijevor and Zelengora tracks

activities.note: Park entry 10 BAM pp, mandatory Perućica ranger, Trnovačko ranger fee, guide days

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5 — one 900 m ascent with chain-protected rock to the national high point, plus three plateau days at 1,500–2,000 m

trips.gatewayAirport: SJJ Sarajevo, 2 h 45 min to Tjentište via Foča; TGD Podgorica 2 h 30 min; TIV Tivat 3 h
trips.summary: Sutjeska is Bosnia's oldest national park and the only place in Europe where you can walk from a Yugoslav-modernist war memorial into an untouched primeval forest and up the country's highest mountain in three days. **Maglić, 2,386 m**, is a proper limestone peak with chains on its upper gully; **Perućica** is 1,400 hectares of virgin beech and fir that you may only enter with a ranger; **Zelengora** behind it is a rolling green plateau strung with a dozen glacial lakes the locals call *gorske oči*, mountain eyes. It is empty, cheap, logistically rough and among the finest walking in south-east Europe. It suits self-sufficient hikers who are comfortable with cash economies, bad roads and unmarked ground.

itinerary.title: Foča, Tjentište and the Valley of Heroes
itinerary.morning: Drive Sarajevo → Foča → **Tjentište**, roughly 2 h 45 min on the M18/M20 along the Drina and Sutjeska rivers. Pay the **10 BAM park entry in cash** at the checkpoint and register your week's plans at the National Park office.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk to the **Battle of Sutjeska memorial** — Miodrag Živković's two 19 m concrete wings from 1971, one of the great Yugoslav *spomeniks* — and the adjoining Memorial House with its Krsto Hegedušić frescoes. Then an easy 6 km along the Sutjeska river gorge.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Hotel Mladost: *pastrmka* (Drina trout), *sač*-baked lamb, *ajvar*, and a Nektar beer. Book tomorrow's Perućica ranger at reception before the office closes.
itinerary.dayStats: 130 km drive / 2 h 45 min / Tjentište 500 m / park entry 10 BAM cash per person / 6 km riverside walk

itinerary.title: Perućica with a ranger
itinerary.morning: Meet the **National Park ranger** at 08:00 — **independent entry into Perućica is prohibited**. Drive the forest road to the **Dragoš sedlo viewpoint at about 1,500 m**, looking down the full length of one of Europe's last primeval forests, roughly 1,400 hectares of untouched beech, fir and spruce with individual trees over 300 years old and 50 m tall.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend with the ranger on the permitted line toward the **Skakavac waterfall**, a single 75 m fall at the head of the forest, then back out. Nothing here is cut, cleared or tidied: fallen trunks lie where they fell, which is the whole point of a reserve.
itinerary.evening: Back at Tjentište. Dinner at the hotel, and repack for two nights up at Prijevor with everything you need in one bag.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km walking / 400 m ascent / Dragoš sedlo approx. 1,500 m / Skakavac approx. 75 m / ranger fee 50–100 BAM per group / 5–6 h

itinerary.title: Up to Prijevor and the Maglić summit
itinerary.morning: 4x4 or high-clearance vehicle up the rough 20 km track to **Prijevor, 1,657 m**, the saddle between Maglić and Volujak, with the katun and mountain hut and a view straight into Montenegro.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb **Maglić, 2,386 m** — Bosnia and Herzegovina's highest mountain. Grass and scree to the base of the summit wall, then the **chained gully**: roughly 80–100 m of Grade I/II rock with fixed steel chains and pegs, straightforward in the dry, genuinely serious in the wet. The summit ridge looks down on Trnovačko jezero on one side and the whole Zelengora plateau on the other.
itinerary.evening: Katun supper at Prijevor — soup, cheese pie, *pršut*, and *rakija* pressed by whoever poured it. No electricity beyond a solar lamp; the night sky here is exceptional.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km / 730 m ascent / summit 2,386 m / chains 80–100 m at Grade I/II / 4–4 h 30 min up, 3 h down / dry from Prijevor to the top

itinerary.title: Trnovačko jezero and the Montenegrin border
itinerary.morning: From Prijevor, cross into Montenegro on foot to **Trnovačko jezero, 1,517 m** — a heart-shaped glacial lake in a cirque of grey limestone under **Trnovački Durmitor, 2,594 m**. The Montenegrin ranger collects **€1–€2 per person** in season. Be clear-eyed about this: it is an **unofficial border crossing**, tolerated in practice for day walkers but not an authorised entry point, so carry your passport, do not continue further into Montenegro, and return the same way.
itinerary.afternoon: Return over the saddle to Prijevor, then a long descent on the Via Dinarica line toward the Sutjeska valley and a transfer round to **Orlovačko jezero, 1,470 m**, on the Zelengora side.
itinerary.evening: The planinarski dom at Orlovačko has bungalows, a stove and grilled trout. Swim if you can stand 14 °C.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km / 450 m ascent / 600 m descent / Trnovačko jezero 1,517 m / ranger €1–€2 / 5–6 h plus a 90 min transfer
itinerary.sleep: Planinarski dom / bungalows, Orlovačko jezero, 1,470 m

itinerary.title: Zelengora's mountain eyes: Donje and Gornje Bare
itinerary.morning: Walk the **Via Dinarica White Trail** west across the plateau — beech, then open pasture, then bare rolling ridges — to **Donje Bare, 1,490 m**, the most photographed of the Zelengora lakes, ringed by spruce.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to **Gornje Bare** and over the ridge below **Bregoč (approx. 2,014 m)**, the plateau's high point, with the Maglić–Volujak–Bioč wall filling the whole southern horizon. Waymarking thins out here; keep the GPX running.
itinerary.evening: Back to Orlovačko, or on to the katun at **Kotlaničko jezero** for a night with the herds. Dinner is whatever the family cooked, in quantity.
itinerary.dayStats: 18 km / 800 m ascent / 700 m descent / Donje Bare 1,490 m / Bregoč approx. 2,014 m / 7 h realistic / marking sparse between lakes
itinerary.sleep: Katun at Kotlaničko jezero, or Orlovačko jezero

itinerary.title: Kotlaničko, Štirinsko and down to Tjentište
itinerary.morning: A loop of the eastern lakes — **Kotlaničko jezero** and **Štirinsko jezero** — on cattle traces and Via Dinarica marks, with the plateau's characteristic mix of sinkholes, springs and horse pasture.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend the old forest road and marked path off Zelengora's eastern rim to **Tjentište, 500 m**, roughly 1,000 m of loss through beech. Stay strictly on the marked line: unmarked ground in Bosnia is where the mine-risk conversation starts, and there is no reason to be off-path here.
itinerary.evening: Last dinner at Hotel Mladost or at a *vodenica* fish restaurant on the Drina near Foča — trout, *kajmak*, and Herzegovinian Blatina.
itinerary.dayStats: 19 km / 400 m ascent / 1,000 m descent / Tjentište 500 m / 7 h realistic / stay on marked trail

itinerary.title: The Drina, Foča and out
itinerary.morning: Drive north down the Drina. If you have half a day, the **Tara river canyon** and the rafting put-in above Foča are 40 minutes away, and the Drina's confluence with the Ćehotina at Foča is a good stop for the Aladža mosque, rebuilt in 2019.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Sarajevo (2 h 45 min) for Baščaršija, the Latin Bridge and the Tunnel of Hope, or south-west to Mostar (3 h) if you are flying from Dubrovnik.
itinerary.evening: *Ćevapi* at Željo or Petica in Sarajevo, Bosnian coffee in a copper *džezva*, and the flight out the following morning.
itinerary.dayStats: Tjentište–Sarajevo 130 km / 2 h 45 min / Tjentište–Mostar approx. 3 h / spend leftover BAM before the border, it is not convertible abroad

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Mladost
accommodationStrategy.description: The only real hotel inside the park, a socialist-era block that has been progressively renovated, with the memorial 300 m away, the park office at reception, secure parking and a restaurant. Roughly 70–110 BAM per person. It is where you arrange the Perućica ranger and the Prijevor 4x4, which is worth more than the room.

accommodationStrategy.name: Prijevor katun
accommodationStrategy.description: A working shepherd station and simple hut on the saddle beneath Maglić, reachable only by rough track. Blankets, a wood stove, an outside tap and no electricity — and the only bed that makes a Maglić ascent a half-day rather than an epic. 30–50 BAM, cash, booked by phone the day before.

accommodationStrategy.name: Planinarski dom Orlovačko jezero
accommodationStrategy.description: Wooden bungalows and a hikers' house beside a lake on the Zelengora side, with a kitchen, trout, and vehicle access for luggage. It is the natural base for two plateau days and much warmer at night than a katun. 40–70 BAM per person.

logistics.connectivity: **Bosnia and Herzegovina is outside the EU roaming zone.** The Western Balkans regional roaming agreement covers movement between the six regional economies, not EU visitors; EU SIMs are charged at reduced but non-zero non-EU rates. Buy an m:tel or BH Telecom prepaid SIM in Sarajevo or Foča. There is **no signal at Prijevor, on most of Zelengora, or in Perućica**. Download offline maps and the Via Dinarica GPX before you leave Foča.
logistics.emergency: 112 general, 122 police, 124 ambulance. Mountain rescue is the volunteer GSS; **there is no routine helicopter service** and a ground evacuation from Zelengora will take most of a day. Nearest hospitals: Foča (which has a university clinical centre) and Sarajevo. **EHIC/GHIC is not valid in Bosnia** — insure for mountain walking to 2,500 m plus repatriation, and note that a rescue at Trnovačko jezero involves Montenegro.
logistics.weather: Afternoon thunderstorms build over Maglić and Volujak from around 14:00 in July and August, and the summit chains are a poor place for one — start by 08:00. Zelengora holds fog well into the morning after a cold night. Snow is possible above 1,800 m in any month.
logistics.bookingWindows: Perućica rangers 1–2 days ahead through the Tjentište office, more on August weekends. Prijevor katun and the 4x4 transfer 2–3 days. Hotel Mladost 2–4 weeks in summer. Nothing here uses an online booking portal; phone and Viber are the channels.
logistics.money: The currency is the **convertible mark (BAM/KM), pegged at 1 EUR = 1.95583 BAM**. Euros are sometimes accepted at poor rates; **use marks**. **There is no ATM inside the national park** — draw 400–600 BAM in Foča or Sarajevo before you go up, in small notes. Cards work at Hotel Mladost and nowhere above it. Tipping is rounding up, or 10% for a full meal.
logistics.transportRules: No vignette in Bosnia; roads are tolled only on the A1. **Cross-border rental permissions matter here** — confirm your hire contract allows Montenegro and Croatia, and that the green card lists them, before driving anywhere near Trnovačko. The Prijevor track needs genuine ground clearance; hiring a local driver is cheaper than the damage waiver. The Tjentište–Sarajevo M20 is scenic and slow.
logistics.permits: Park entry 10 BAM per person, cash. **Perućica may only be entered with a National Park ranger — independent access is prohibited and enforced.** Camping is restricted to designated areas at Tjentište; wild camping in Perućica and the strict reserve is forbidden. Fires outside katun hearths are prohibited. Drones need park permission. Do not remove deadwood or plants from Perućica.
logistics.health: **Landmine awareness is a real and non-negotiable part of walking in Bosnia.** The national park's core routes are cleared and in regular use, but BiH still has suspected hazardous areas and the rule is absolute: **stay on marked, worn trails, never shortcut through untrodden ground, never enter ruins, trenches or fenced areas, and heed any red-and-white skull-and-crossbones or "MINE" sign.** Check BHMAC guidance before travelling. Elsewhere: treat all water, expect livestock guardian dogs at katuns (stop, do not run), and note that ticks and TBE are present in the beech forest up to about 1,500 m.

proTips: Arrange the **Perućica ranger and the Prijevor 4x4 on your first evening**, in person at the Tjentište office or hotel reception. Phone and email in advance frequently go unanswered; showing up and booking face to face works.
Draw **BAM cash in Foča**, not Tjentište. There is no ATM in the park, katuns cannot change a €50, and euros above the valley get you a bad rate at best.

Climb Maglić on your **second day at Prijevor** if the forecast allows a choice — the chains dry within a couple of hours of sun, and wet limestone in that gully is what turns a Grade I scramble into an accident.
Ask the Prijevor katun to point out the Trnovačko path before you set off. The border saddle is obvious in clear weather and not obvious at all in cloud.

Treat **Trnovačko jezero as an out-and-back day walk**, not a route into Montenegro. Continuing to Gusinje or Plav from there without an official crossing is an immigration problem you do not want in the Balkans.

Carry a GPX for Zelengora specifically. The Via Dinarica marks are good in principle and intermittent in practice between Donje Bare and Kotlaničko, where the ground is open pasture with cattle traces in every direction.
Buy cheese and *kajmak* at the katuns. It is the entire local economy up there, it costs a few marks, and it is better than anything in Sarajevo.

Go in the **last week of June** for the Zelengora meadows or the **first fortnight of September** for Maglić. July and August bring heat on the Sutjeska valley floor and the only crowds the park ever sees.
Spend your leftover marks before you cross out. BAM is a closed currency and is effectively worthless once you leave.

raw.Hut-to-hut booking path: There is no formal hut chain here. The sequence is **Hotel Mladost at Tjentište (500 m, park-owned)** → **the katun and mountain hut at Prijevor (1,657 m)** → **the planinarski dom and bungalows at Orlovačko jezero (1,470 m)** → **the katun at Kotlaničko jezero / Zelengora** → back to Tjentište. All bookings go **direct by phone or Viber/WhatsApp to the operator, or through the National Park Sutjeska office at Tjentište**; nothing is on a booking portal, and email replies are slow. **Everything is cash in convertible marks (BAM)** — expect **30–50 BAM (€15–€26) for a bed** and **45–70 BAM (€23–€36) for half board** at a katun, and **70–110 BAM per person** at Hotel Mladost. **There are no card terminals above Tjentište and no ATM inside the park.** Bring a **sleeping-bag liner and a light sleeping bag** — katun bedding is blankets, and the huts sit at 1,500–1,700 m where August nights fall to 4–6 °C. **If a katun is full**, the shepherd family will make space on the floor or in a second building; there is no alternative within walking distance, so ring ahead the day before rather than turning up.
raw.Ranger permits and park fees: Park entry is **10 BAM / €5 per person**, collected at the checkpoint on the M20 at Tjentište, **cash only**. **Entry to Perućica is strictly guided and independent access is prohibited** — you must be accompanied by a National Park ranger, arranged the day before at the Tjentište office, with a guide fee typically **50–100 BAM per group** depending on size and route. The standard visit is the **Dragoš sedlo viewpoint** over the forest and the **Skakavac waterfall (about 75 m)**; walking into the forest floor itself is permitted only on the ranger's chosen line. **A separate ranger sits seasonally at Trnovačko jezero on the Montenegrin side and collects €1–€2 per person.**
raw.Safety markers and waymarking: Bosnia uses the standard ex-Yugoslav **planinarska markacija — a red circle with a white centre** (the same family as Slovenia's Knafelc blaze), painted on rock and tree, plus wooden signposts giving hours. The **Via Dinarica White Trail**, the alpine line of the three-corridor Via Dinarica network, is additionally marked with its own **blue-and-white logo** and crosses Zelengora and Sutjeska. Marking quality is good on the Maglić and Perućica routes and around Orlovačko, and **poor to absent on the Zelengora plateau between lakes**, where the "path" is often a cattle trace. Carry a GPX. **There are no via ferratas**, but Maglić's upper gully has **fixed chains and steel pegs over roughly 80–100 m of Grade I/II rock**.
raw.Elevation and gear essentials: High points: **Maglić 2,386 m** (the highest mountain in Bosnia and Herzegovina), Trnovački Durmitor 2,594 m on the Montenegrin side, Bregoč on Zelengora at about 2,014 m, Prijevor 1,657 m, Trnovačko jezero 1,517 m. Cumulative ascent across the walking days is roughly **3,200 m**. **Snow lies in the Maglić north gully and the Zelengora shaded corries into late June**; before 25 June carry microspikes. Gloves for the chains, a helmet if there is any party above you in the gully, and B-rated boots. No ferrata set needed, though a short sling and carabiner is reassuring on the chains in the wet.
raw.Water, food resupply and rubbish: Zelengora is unusually well watered for karst — springs, streams and lakes throughout — but the plateau is grazed by cattle and horses all summer, so **filter or treat everything**. The Maglić route from Prijevor is **dry from the katun to the summit**: carry 2 litres. Katuns sell milk, *kajmak*, cheese, *pita* and coffee for a few marks. **Resupply only in Foča or Tjentište**; there is no shop in the park interior. **All rubbish comes out with you** — the park has minimal collection and burning is the local default.
raw.Bail-out options, rescue and insurance: Prijevor is reachable by 4x4 on a rough 20 km track from Tjentište, so a Maglić evacuation is a drive, not a carry. Orlovačko has vehicle access. The remote stretch is the Zelengora plateau between Kotlaničko and Donje Bare, which is 3–4 hours from a road. **112 is the general emergency number; 122 police and 124 ambulance also work.** Mountain rescue is the volunteer **GSS (Gorska služba spašavanja)** and there is **no routine helicopter rescue** — plan on a ground evacuation taking most of a day. **Bosnia is outside the EU and EHIC/GHIC does not apply**; buy insurance naming Bosnia and Herzegovina, mountain walking to 2,500 m, and repatriation. Note that a rescue at Trnovačko jezero may involve **Montenegrin** services, which is a separate jurisdiction and a separate insurance question.
raw.Realistic walking times: Bosnian signposts and shepherd estimates are quick. Add **30–35%**. Prijevor to Maglić is quoted at 3 h; plan 4–4 h 30 min with the chains and any queue. Prijevor to Trnovačko jezero is quoted 1 h 30 min–2 h; plan 2 h–2 h 30 min.

typeSpecific.technicalRating: Bosnia uses the standard ex-Yugoslav **planinarska markacija — a red circle with a white centre** (the same family as Slovenia's Knafelc blaze), painted on rock and tree, plus wooden signposts giving hours. The **Via Dinarica White Trail**, the alpine line of the three-corridor Via Dinarica network, is additionally marked with its own **blue-and-white logo** and crosses Zelengora and Sutjeska. Marking quality is good on the Maglić and Perućica routes and around Orlovačko, and **poor to absent on the Zelengora plateau between lakes**, where the "path" is often a cattle trace. Carry a GPX. **There are no via ferratas**, but Maglić's upper gully has **fixed chains and steel pegs over roughly 80–100 m of Grade I/II rock**.
typeSpecific.hutBooking: There is no formal hut chain here. The sequence is **Hotel Mladost at Tjentište (500 m, park-owned)** → **the katun and mountain hut at Prijevor (1,657 m)** → **the planinarski dom and bungalows at Orlovačko jezero (1,470 m)** → **the katun at Kotlaničko jezero / Zelengora** → back to Tjentište. All bookings go **direct by phone or Viber/WhatsApp to the operator, or through the National Park Sutjeska office at Tjentište**; nothing is on a booking portal, and email replies are slow. **Everything is cash in convertible marks (BAM)** — expect **30–50 BAM (€15–€26) for a bed** and **45–70 BAM (€23–€36) for half board** at a katun, and **70–110 BAM per person** at Hotel Mladost. **There are no card terminals above Tjentište and no ATM inside the park.** Bring a **sleeping-bag liner and a light sleeping bag** — katun bedding is blankets, and the huts sit at 1,500–1,700 m where August nights fall to 4–6 °C. **If a katun is full**, the shepherd family will make space on the floor or in a second building; there is no alternative within walking distance, so ring ahead the day before rather than turning up.

sources.verified: Sutjeska National Park entry at **10 BAM / €5 per person, cash only** at the checkpoint; that **entry into Perućica is strictly guided and independent access is prohibited by park regulation**; **Trnovačko jezero at 1,517 m** on the Bosnia–Montenegro border, reached in **1.5–2 hours from the Prijevor saddle**, with a **seasonal Montenegrin ranger collecting €1–€2 per person**; Maglić at 2,386 m as the country's highest mountain; the BAM peg to the euro.
sources.confidenceNotes: The Perućica ranger fee is quoted as a range and is negotiated per group — confirm with the Tjentište office. Katun and mountain-hut rates at Prijevor, Orlovačko and Kotlaničko are 2025 estimates set in cash and vary by family; none is bookable online. The precise length and grade of the fixed chains on Maglić, and Bregoč's elevation on Zelengora, should be spot-checked against a current Bosnian hiking club description. Hotel Mladost's operating status and renovation state have changed repeatedly — re-verify before publishing. The legal status of the on-foot crossing to Trnovačko jezero is grey and locally tolerated rather than formally authorised; this should be checked with the park and worded carefully. Landmine guidance must be re-verified against the current BHMAC map before publication. Perućica's protected area is variously cited between about 1,400 and 1,500 hectares, and the Skakavac waterfall between 70 and 80 m.

trips.title: The GR57 Ourthe Valley Walking Week

bestPeriod.note: Summer school holidays (July–August) bring the kayak and campsite crowds to the river villages; late spring and September keep the valley quiet.

trips.gatewayAirport: Brussels (BRU)
trips.summary: A week of GR57 river-valley walking along the Ourthe from La Roche-en-Ardenne, through gorges, dams and the Ardennes' oldest bourgs.
trips.hook: This is not alpine walking and it does not pretend to be. The Ourthe cuts a deep, wooded valley through the Ardennes plateau, and the GR57 follows it — up one bank, down the other, through beech forest, past castle ruins and into small stone towns that have been market centres since the Middle Ages. A week here is quiet, well-marked and genuinely hilly, without a single lift or hut.

snapshot.Base(s): La Roche-en-Ardenne, with day loops and two out-nights toward Hotton and Durbuy
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 95–115 km, 2,600–3,200 m cumulative ascent; forested valley slopes, riverside path, farm track, waymarked red-and-white GR
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Brussels (BRU), train to Marloie or Melreux-Hotton, then TEC bus to La Roche-en-Ardenne
snapshot.Who It Suits: Steady walkers who want real daily distance and hills without alpine exposure; a good first multi-day hiking trip

itinerary.title: La Roche-en-Ardenne orientation loop
itinerary.morning: Arrive and climb straight to the Château de La Roche-en-Ardenne, a ruined feudal fortress on its rock spur above the Ourthe, to get the shape of the valley before walking it for real.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop out to Le Deister, the wooded viewpoint above town, and back down through the old streets near the market square.
itinerary.evening: A first Ardennes dinner — jambon d'Ardenne and a local Orval or Rochefort — at one of the riverside restaurants along the Quai de l'Ourthe.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km, 250 m ascent, 250 m descent. Waymarking: local yellow-rectangle circuit around town, not yet the GR57.

itinerary.title: La Roche to Nisramont
itinerary.morning: Join the GR57 heading upstream along the Ourthe Occidentale, following the riverbank through mixed forest with the water never far below the path.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb to the Nisramont dam and its reservoir, a working hydroelectric barrage that also created a quiet lake popular with local anglers; loop back on the opposite bank.
itinerary.evening: Return to La Roche by the same waymarked route or by a short taxi transfer if legs are tired — this is a there-and-back day, deliberately, to keep the same base.
itinerary.dayStats: 20 km, 550 m ascent, 550 m descent. Waymarking: GR57 red-and-white horizontal bars throughout, well maintained.

itinerary.title: Ourthe Occidentale toward Ortho
itinerary.morning: Continue upstream past Maboge, where the valley narrows and the path climbs onto the wooded slope above the river before dropping back to water level.
itinerary.afternoon: Reach Ortho, a small hamlet with a working watermill history, then return via a higher forest track that gives long views back down the valley toward La Roche.
itinerary.evening: A rest evening — this stretch is the longest out-and-back of the week and legs earn an early night.
itinerary.dayStats: 22 km, 600 m ascent, 600 m descent. Waymarking: GR57, with a short shared stretch on a local yellow-marked variant near Ortho.

itinerary.title: La Roche to Marcourt and the château ruins loop
itinerary.morning: Shorter day, deliberately. Walk downstream and cross to Marcourt, where the ruins of another Ardennes château sit above the confluence of the Ourthe's two branches.
itinerary.afternoon: A forest loop above Beausaint gives a genuinely quiet stretch of the valley, with beech and oak canopy and almost no other walkers outside peak summer weekends.
itinerary.evening: Back in La Roche by mid-afternoon; use the extra time to visit the small Musée de la Bataille des Ardennes, a reminder of how contested this valley was in December 1944.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 400 m ascent, 400 m descent. Waymarking: GR57 to Marcourt, local blue-marked circuit for the Beausaint loop.

itinerary.title: Transfer to Hotton, walk to Barvaux
itinerary.morning: Bus or taxi transfer downstream to Hotton, known locally for its show caves (Grottes de Hotton) carved into the valley's limestone band — a genuine geological break from the schist and sandstone upstream.
itinerary.afternoon: Pick up the GR57 heading downstream along the Ourthe toward Barvaux-sur-Ourthe, a flatter, more open stretch of valley than the upper river, with willow and alder lining the banks.
itinerary.evening: Overnight in Barvaux, a small riverside town with a long tradition of Ourthe kayak tourism, quiet outside July and August.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km, 300 m ascent, 300 m descent. Waymarking: GR57 red-and-white, flat and well-signed.

itinerary.title: Barvaux to Durbuy and back
itinerary.morning: Follow the riverside path from Barvaux to Durbuy, popularly (if imprecisely) marketed as the smallest town in the world — a genuinely well-preserved stone bourg with a topiary garden and a medieval street plan.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop back via the wooded ridge above the river rather than retracing the flat bank path, for a different angle on the valley before returning to Barvaux.
itinerary.evening: Transfer back to La Roche-en-Ardenne by bus in the early evening to close the loop on the same base for the final night.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km, 350 m ascent, 350 m descent. Waymarking: GR57 to Durbuy, local yellow-marked ridge path for the return.

itinerary.title: Nadrin and the Belvédère des Six Ourthes
itinerary.morning: A short bus or taxi ride to Nadrin, where the GR57 passes the Belvédère des Six Ourthes, a viewing tower over the river's tightest meanders — six loops of the Ourthe visible at once from the top.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the loop trail beneath the belvedere and back into La Roche-en-Ardenne along the final stretch of river valley, closing the week where it started.
itinerary.evening: A last dinner in La Roche, unhurried.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 300 m ascent, 300 m descent. Waymarking: GR57 throughout, the week's final and most scenic river-meander stretch.

accommodationStrategy.name: Gîte or chambre d'hôtes in La Roche-en-Ardenne
accommodationStrategy.description: La Roche has a long tradition of hosting Ardennes walkers and kayakers, and small guesthouses near the Quai de l'Ourthe are used to muddy boots and early breakfasts. Staying here for five of the seven nights keeps logistics simple.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead for summer weekends, less pressure outside July–August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Small hotel or gîte in Barvaux-sur-Ourthe
accommodationStrategy.description: The one night away from La Roche, chosen to make the Hotton–Barvaux–Durbuy stretch a two-day out rather than a long there-and-back; riverside guesthouses here are used to walkers arriving on foot with packs.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–3 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Self-catering cottage near La Roche
accommodationStrategy.description: A number of Ardennes gîtes rent by the week with a kitchen, useful for keeping food costs down across seven days.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead in season.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European, the standard number across Belgium for police, fire and ambulance.
logistics.money: Small-town shops and boulangeries often close on Mondays and for a long lunch; stock up on picnic supplies the afternoon before a long walking day.
logistics.transportRules: TEC regional buses link La Roche-en-Ardenne, Hotton, Barvaux and Nadrin, but frequency drops sharply outside weekday commuting hours — check the return timetable before setting out each transfer day.

other.label: Waymarking system
other.text: Belgium uses the same GR convention as France: a horizontal red bar over a horizontal white bar means continue straight; the same two bars crossed into an X means wrong way; an angled double bar means turn. Local circuit walks (PR, Promenades) use single-colour rectangles — yellow, blue or green — maintained by local tourism offices rather than the GR federation, and often overlap the GR57 for short stretches.

other.label: River levels
other.text: After heavy rain the lowest riverside stretches near Hotton and Barvaux can flood the path; a higher parallel forest track exists at most points and is signed as an alternative.

other.label: Hunting season
other.text: Parts of the Ardennes forest are open to organised hunts (chasse) from autumn through winter, signed at access points; this trip's May–June/September window largely avoids it, but check local signage in September.

other.label: Wild camping is not permitted
other.text: on the marked GR network in Wallonia; overnight stops are gîtes, chambres d'hôtes or hotels in the valley towns.

proTips: Walk the Nisramont and Ortho out-and-backs (Days 2–3) in the morning light heading upstream — the river runs roughly east–west here and the low sun sits behind you on the return leg.

Buy Ardennes ham and a wedge of Orval-washed cheese at a Hotton or Barvaux boulangerie for a riverside picnic rather than eating in a restaurant every midday — it is cheaper and lets you time the walk around the food, not the other way round.
Visit the Grottes de Hotton first thing on Day 5, before the transfer walk — the caves get warm foot traffic from midday coach groups in season.
Climb the Belvédère des Six Ourthes on a clear morning rather than late afternoon; low-angle morning light shows the river meanders far better than a flat midday sun.
Ask your La Roche gîte host about the Musée de la Bataille des Ardennes' opening hours before Day 4 — it is a small, volunteer-run museum with limited hours outside peak season.
Time the Durbuy loop for a weekday. The town is genuinely small and a summer Saturday brings coach parties that overwhelm its narrow streets.
Carry a paper IGN or NGI 1:25,000 map alongside the waymarking — GPS signal is reliable in the valley but the marking itself is the more dependable navigation tool here, as it should be.

raw.Who It Suits: Steady walkers who want real daily distance and hills without alpine exposure; a good first multi-day hiking trip

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 95–115 km, 2,600–3,200 m cumulative ascent; forested valley slopes, riverside path, farm track, waymarked red-and-white GR
typeSpecific.audience: Steady walkers who want real daily distance and hills without alpine exposure; a good first multi-day hiking trip

packingNotes: Sturdy trail shoes rather than heavy boots — the terrain is wooded valley slope, not alpine rock, and drains well.
A light rain shell; Ardennes weather turns from sun to drizzle with little warning even in a good week.
A 20–25 L daypack is enough; nights are spent in guesthouses, not huts, so no sleeping gear is needed.
A refillable water bottle — village fountains and café taps cover most days, but carry 1–1.5 L for the longer out-and-back stages.
Insect repellent for the river-adjacent forest stretches in early summer.
A paper NGI/IGN Ardennes walking map as backup to the GR waymarking.
Cash in small denominations — several village boulangeries and small gîtes are cash-preferred.
What people over-pack: technical hiking gear. This is a serious walking week, but it is hills and forest, not mountains — trail shoes and a rain shell cover nearly everything.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Heavy rain floods the lowest riverside path.** Fallback: take the signed higher forest alternative that parallels most of the GR57's low sections near Hotton and Barvaux.
**A TEC bus transfer is missed or delayed.** Fallback: La Roche and the river towns are close enough (12–20 km) that a taxi transfer is a realistic, inexpensive backup.
**A gîte in Barvaux has no room on short notice.** Fallback: book that one mid-week night well ahead, since it is the trip's only fixed away-night and the town's guesthouse stock is small.
**Tired legs after the long Day 3 out-and-back.** Fallback: Day 4 is deliberately shorter and closer to base — treat it as the built-in recovery day it is.
**Hunting activity signed near a forest section in early autumn.** Fallback: respect the posted diversion and use the parallel valley-floor GR57 route, which hunts rarely close.

trips.title: Marble and Granite: A Pirin Hut-to-Hut Week from Bansko
trips.subRegion: Pirin National Park (Северен и Централен Пирин)

bestPeriod.window: the second half of September — snow gone from Koncheto, huts half-empty, storm frequency dropping
bestPeriod.avoid: before mid-June (old snow on the Vihren north side and in the Kazana couloirs) and the 6 September and 22 September national holidays, when every hut fills with Bulgarian parties

accommodation.note: €70–€120 (€10–€18/night in BTS huts, dormitory)

food.note: €140–€210 (€20–€30/day — hut menus are short and you carry the gap)

transport.note: €45–€90 (Sofia–Bansko bus, Bunderitsa jeep taxi, Bezbog chairlift, Dobrinishte–Sofia)

activities.note: €0–€180 (park entry is free; a guide day for Koncheto is the variable)

profile.difficultyNote: Hard

trips.gatewayAirport: Sofia (SOF) airport, then a direct bus to Bansko from Sofia Central Bus Station (2 h 45–3 h 15) or the narrow-gauge Septemvri–Dobrinishte railway, the slowest and best-looking train in the Balkans. Plovdiv (PDV) is a 3 h 30 alternative.
trips.currency: Euro (EUR) — sole legal tender since 1 February 2026; mandatory dual BGN display ended 8 August 2026
trips.summary: Pirin changes underfoot halfway through the week. The north is white Triassic marble — bright, sharp, waterless, murder on boot rands — and the centre is grey granite that holds a hundred lakes in its hollows. In…
trips.hook: Pirin changes underfoot halfway through the week. The north is white Triassic marble — bright, sharp, waterless, murder on boot rands — and the centre is grey granite that holds a hundred lakes in its hollows. In between sits Koncheto, a knife-edge with a fixed cable and a genuine death toll. You sleep in unheated BTS huts, pay cash, eat bean soup, and stand on the second-highest summit in Bulgaria before most of Bansko is awake.

snapshot.Best period: July–September, best in the second half of September
snapshot.Start / End: Bansko → Dobrinishte (point-to-point, ~62 km, ~5,200 m ascent)
snapshot.Getting there: Sofia (SOF) airport, then a direct bus to Bansko from Sofia Central Bus Station (2 h 45–3 h 15) or the narrow-gauge Septemvri–Dobrinishte railway, the slowest and best-looking train in the Balkans. Plovdiv (PDV) is a 3 h 30 alternative.

itinerary.title: Bansko to the Bunderitsa
itinerary.morning: Arrive in Bansko (925 m), a town of stone-and-timber Revival houses with a ski resort bolted on. Draw hut cash at an ATM on Pirin Street — your last machine for six days — and eat at a *mehana* on the old square.
itinerary.afternoon: Take the **Bansko gondola** to Banderishka polyana, or share a **jeep taxi up the Bunderitsa road** from the gondola base — the road is rough, unsurfaced above Hizha Banderitsa, and driven by locals in vehicles you would not rent [VERIFY: current summer gondola fare and jeep-taxi rate]. Stop at **Baikushev's Pine**, a Bosnian pine (*Pinus heldreichii*) estimated at **over 1,300 years old**, standing in the forest just below Hizha Banderitsa.
itinerary.evening: Walk the last stretch to **Hizha Vihren (1,950 m)**, the busiest hut in the range and the base for everything that follows. Confirm your onward beds by phone from the warden's desk while there is still signal.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km / +330 m with mechanical assist

itinerary.title: Vihren, 2,914 m, by the Kazana cirque
itinerary.morning: Leave by 06:30. The red trail climbs to the **Kazana** ("the cauldron") cirque, a marble amphitheatre that holds snow into July, then zigzags to the summit ridge. Four to four and a half hours up.
itinerary.afternoon: **Vihren, 2,914 m** — Bulgaria's second-highest summit after Musala, with the Banski Suhodol wall one side and the granite south the other. Descend the same way; polished wet marble is treacherous.
itinerary.evening: Back at Hizha Vihren, walk twenty minutes to the **Banderishki lakes**, a granite-rimmed chain below Todorka, then bean soup and an early night [VERIFY: current Hizha Vihren bed and half-board rates].

itinerary.title: Kutelo, Koncheto and the long drop to Yavorov
itinerary.morning: The decision day. Up the red line to **Premkata** saddle and **Kutelo (2,908 m)**, Bulgaria's third summit, in about three hours. Check the wind on the col; if it pushes you around, turn back.
itinerary.afternoon: **Koncheto** — the cabled knife-edge — then **Banski Suhodol (2,884 m)** and a long, loose, waterless descent to **Hizha Yavorov (1,740 m)**. Allow eight to ten hours door to door and carry three litres.
itinerary.evening: Yavorov is small, wood-heated and cash-only, the Kutelo wall filling the window. No shop, no card machine [VERIFY: current Hizha Yavorov rates and warden's phone].

itinerary.title: Down to Razlog, round to the Bunderitsa
itinerary.morning: The green trail down the Suhodol ridge to the **Predel** road, then a bus or shared transfer into **Razlog** [VERIFY: current Predel–Razlog bus times] — the honest way to reposition, because there is no low traverse under the marble wall.
itinerary.afternoon: Bus Razlog to **Bansko** (20 minutes), resupply at the Kaufland on the edge of town, then a jeep taxi back up the Bunderitsa road to **Hizha Vihren**.
itinerary.evening: A short day is not a wasted one. Wash socks, eat two dinners, and study the Vasilashki plateau on the hut's wall map — tomorrow is the longest stretch above 2,300 m.

itinerary.title: The classic high crossing to Tevno Ezero
itinerary.morning: Climb to the **Banderishka porta** under **Todorka (2,746 m)**, then traverse south past the upper **Banderishki lakes** on granite slab. After yesterday's marble the change of rock is unmistakable underfoot.
itinerary.afternoon: Over the **Todorina porta** and down into the **Vasilashki lakes** — a basin of a dozen tarns — then the long rise to **Hizha Tevno Ezero (2,510 m)**, sitting on the shore of its own black lake. Seven to eight hours.
itinerary.evening: Pirin's highest hut and its most spartan: bunks, blankets, a gas ring, no shower, sometimes no warden late in the season. Sunset over Dzhengal is the compensation.

itinerary.title: Popovo Lake and the granite south
itinerary.morning: Contour east under **Dzhengal (2,730 m)** on the red E4 line. If the weather has broken, escape south over the **Mozgovishka porta** to **Hizha Pirin (Kamenitsa, 1,640 m)** and the Sandanski road — know this before you need it.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop to **Popovo Lake (2,234 m)**, the largest and deepest glacial lake in Pirin, then round the Dzhano shoulder and descend to **Hizha Bezbog (2,236 m)** in three to four hours.
itinerary.evening: Bezbog has electricity, a proper kitchen and a card machine — the first hot shower since Bansko [VERIFY: current Hizha Bezbog rates].

itinerary.title: Bezbog Lake, then the chairlift out
itinerary.morning: A pre-breakfast lap to **Bezbogsko Lake**, then the 45-minute pull to **Bezbog peak (2,645 m)** for a last look north along the ridge you walked.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Bezbog chairlift** down to Hizha Gotse Delchev, then the shuttle road to **Dobrinishte** [VERIFY: current Bezbog chairlift fare and operating hours]. If the lift is down, the forest path adds two hours.
itinerary.evening: Soak in Dobrinishte's mineral pools, eat *kavarma* with a grape *rakia*, then take the narrow-gauge train or a bus back to Sofia.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km / +180 / −1,050 m with lift

accommodationStrategy.name: Hizha Vihren
accommodationStrategy.description: the only sensible base for both Vihren and Koncheto, and the one hut with dependable signal for confirming the rest of the chain. Dormitories, hot food, cash only.
accommodationStrategy.booking: phone direct, two to four weeks ahead midweek; longer for the September holiday weekends.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hizha Tevno Ezero
accommodationStrategy.description: the only bed on the central plateau, which is what makes the classic high crossing two manageable days instead of one brutal one. Expect nothing beyond a bunk.
accommodationStrategy.booking: phone direct the week before, and confirm it is staffed at all — the season is short.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hizha Bezbog
accommodationStrategy.description: the chairlift on the doorstep makes it both the natural finish and the easiest mid-week bail-in. Showers, power, cards accepted.
accommodationStrategy.booking: phone or the hut's own online form, one to two weeks ahead.

logistics.connectivity: A1 and Yettel cover Bansko, Dobrinishte and most of the northern ridge; Tevno Ezero and the Vasilashki basin have none. Download offline maps at Hizha Vihren.
logistics.emergency: **PSS 1470** or **112**. Give your position as a named hut, lake or saddle plus the waymark colour — Bulgarian rescuers navigate by hut names, not coordinates. Response is on foot and slow.
logistics.weather: Storms build from about 13:00 in July and August. Koncheto in lightning is unsurvivable, and the marble stays greasy for hours after rain. Be off the ridge by early afternoon.
logistics.bookingWindows: Two to four weeks by phone covers most of the season; the exceptions are the weekends around 6 and 22 September, when Bulgarian clubs book the range out.
logistics.money: Bulgaria has adopted the **euro**, with prices still dual-displayed in **BGN** at the fixed 1.95583 rate. Every hut except Bezbog is **cash only** — carry €150–€200 in small notes; a warden with no float will not break a €50.
logistics.transportRules: The Bunderitsa road above Hizha Banderitsa is unsurfaced and no place for a rental car; use the gondola or a jeep taxi. The Bezbog chairlift runs a short summer season with weather stops.
logistics.permits: Pirin is a **national park and a UNESCO World Heritage site**. There is no entry fee, but: **no wild camping** outside the marked bivouac zones beside huts, **no open fires anywhere**, **no dogs**, no drones, no picking or collecting, and marked trails only.

proTips: Phone the huts in the evening, between 19:00 and 21:00, when the warden is behind the bar rather than out on the hill. Open with *"Dobar vecher, imate li svobodni mesta?"* — good evening, do you have free beds?
Reverse the week if the forecast is bad early. Bezbog and Tevno Ezero first, Koncheto last, gives the ridge four extra days to dry out; the transport works in either direction.
Fill at the **Hizha Vihren spring** and again at the Banderishki lakes. Between Kutelo and Hizha Yavorov the marble swallows every drop in the mountain — nothing to drink for six hours.
Carry cash in €5, €10 and €20 notes. There is no ATM above Bansko, and wardens genuinely cannot change large denominations.
Take the second half of September. The huts empty after 22 September, the ridge is dry, and beds appear at a week's notice.
If Koncheto is out, the **Vlahini lakes** circuit from Hizha Vihren is the best consolation day in northern Pirin — granite, water and views of the wall you are not walking.
Book the jeep taxi down the Bunderitsa road through your warden the night before. That road with a full pack is a joyless 15 km.

raw.Hut chain and booking channel: Bulgarian huts belong to the **BTS (Български туристически съюз** — Bulgarian Tourist Union**)** and its member clubs. There is **no central booking system**: you phone the hut, or the hut warden's mobile, usually in Bulgarian, and you pay **cash on arrival**. Written confirmations barely exist. The counterweight is the old BTS **no-turn-away tradition** — a hut finds you floor space rather than send you down in the dark. Do not treat that as a booking strategy. Chain: **Hizha Vihren** (1,950 m, phone) → **Hizha Yavorov** (1,740 m, phone) → back to Vihren → **Hizha Tevno Ezero** (2,510 m, phone, seasonal, very basic) → **Hizha Bezbog** (2,236 m, phone/online) [VERIFY: current bed rates at each hut] [VERIFY: Hizha Tevno Ezero 2026 opening and closing dates].
raw.Waymarks: The **KKS/BTS** system, run by the Commission for Maps and Signalisation: a horizontal three-band blaze, **white–colour–white**, painted on rock and on the marble itself. **Red** carries the main Pirin ridge line and the European **E4**; **blue**, **green** and **yellow** are approaches and connectors. Above the treeline, tall marker poles supplement the paint — essential in cloud on the Vasilashki plateau. Junction signs give hours, not kilometres.
raw.Daily ascent/descent: Day 1 +330 m. Day 2 +985/−985 m (Vihren and back). Day 3 +1,020/−1,230 m over Kutelo and Koncheto. Day 4 −950 m plus road transfer, then +330 m. Day 5 +900/−340 m to Tevno Ezero. Day 6 +420/−700 m to Bezbog. Day 7 +180/−1,050 m with a chairlift assist. Roughly 5,200 m of ascent across the week.
raw.The geology split: Northern Pirin (Vihren, Kutelo, Koncheto, Banski Suhodol) is **marble**: white, blinding, fissured and **dry** — rain vanishes into the karst, so between Hizha Vihren and Hizha Yavorov there is **no reliable water at all**. Central Pirin (Todorka south to Bezbog) is **granite**: grey slab and blocky boulder fields, impermeable, which is why the Banderishki, Vasilashki and Popovo lake groups sit where they do. Marble edges shred soft soles; bring stiff boots.
raw.Koncheto — say it plainly: *Konchéto* ("the little horse") is a **marble knife-edge ridge at around 2,810 m**, roughly 400 m long, with drops of several hundred metres on both sides and a **fixed steel cable** along the crest. It is a marked red route, not a climb, but it has **killed people** — falls in wind, in verglas, and in cloud. It is unsuitable in wet, snow, strong wind, or for anyone troubled by exposure. If in doubt, take the Kazana route to Vihren and skip the ridge; there is no lost objective.
raw.Gear tied to altitude: Hizha Tevno Ezero at 2,510 m is above every tree in Bulgaria and gets frost in September. Non-negotiable: stiff boots, hardshell, warm mid-layer, gloves, headtorch, **3 L water capacity** for the marble days, a **sleeping bag or liner** (huts give blankets of uncertain history), and a power bank.
raw.Rescue and insurance: **Planinska Spasitelna Sluzhba (PSS)**, the mountain rescue service of the Bulgarian Red Cross: **1470** from a Bulgarian mobile, or 112. Response is by ground team from Bansko or Dobrinishte and can take hours; helicopter availability is not something to plan around. Insure explicitly for **unroped mountain walking above 3,000 m** and search-and-rescue costs.
raw.Food reality: Pirin huts are **basic**: *bob chorba* (bean soup), *shopska salata*, sausage, bread, instant coffee, beer and little else; Tevno Ezero may run to soup and tea only. Carry every lunch, plus two days of emergency food for the ridge.

There is **no central booking system**: you phone the hut, or the hut warden's mobile, usually in Bulgarian, and you pay **cash on arrival**. Written confirmations barely exist. The counterweight is the old BTS **no-turn-away tradition** — a hut finds you floor space rather than send you down in the dark. Do not treat that as a booking strategy. Chain: **Hizha Vihren** (1,950 m, phone) → **Hizha Yavorov** (1,740 m, phone) → back to Vihren → **Hizha Tevno Ezero** (2,510 m, phone, seasonal, very basic) → **Hizha Bezbog** (2,236 m, phone/online) [VERIFY: current bed rates at each hut] [VERIFY: Hizha Tevno Ezero 2026 opening and closing dates].

trips.title: Berner Oberland Hut Chain — Kandersteg to Grindelwald

bestPeriod.note: The Hohtürli approach and Sefinenfurgge can hold hard snow into July; the cable-secured Chindbetti step near Hohtürli is safest dry.

trips.gatewayAirport: Zürich (ZRH)
trips.summary: A hut-to-hut week on the Via Alpina from Kandersteg over Hohtürli to Blüemlisalphütte, then on through Griesalp and Mürren to Grindelwald.
trips.hook: This is the Berner Oberland at its most classic: a steep, cable-assisted climb from Kandersteg's Oeschinensee to the Hohtürli pass and Blüemlisalphütte, a glacier-fringed SAC hut with the Blüemlisalp icefall at the door, then a Via Alpina traverse through Griesalp and over the Sefinenfurgge to Mürren, finishing along the Eiger's north face to Grindelwald. Four valleys, one waymarked national route, and a genuinely alpine week.

snapshot.Base(s): Kandersteg to start, Grindelwald to finish, huts and villages between
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 75–85 km, 5,800–6,400 m combined ascent; white-red-white T3 throughout, one cable-secured step near Hohtürli
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Zürich (ZRH), train to Spiez, change for Kandersteg (about 2h total)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Fit hut-to-hut hikers comfortable with a steep cable-assisted pass and consecutive long days

itinerary.title: Kandersteg and the Oeschinensee
itinerary.morning: Arrive Kandersteg by train from Spiez. Walk or take the gondola up to Oeschinensee, one of the most photographed alpine lakes in Switzerland, sitting at 1,578 m below the Blüemlisalp wall.
itinerary.afternoon: Circle the lake on the lower path, checking the Hohtürli route's condition board at the Berghotel before returning to Kandersteg.
itinerary.evening: Early dinner; the Hohtürli climb starts before sunrise tomorrow to beat the afternoon cloud buildup.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km, 350 m ascent, 350 m descent. Grade T1–T2, well-graded lakeside path.

itinerary.title: Hohtürli and Blüemlisalphütte
itinerary.morning: From Oeschinensee, climb the long switchbacked path toward Hohtürli (2,778 m), steepening through the final section known locally as the Chindbetti, where fixed cable assists a short exposed rock step.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross Hohtürli and drop the short distance to Blüemlisalphütte (2,834 m), a Swiss Alpine Club hut sitting directly beside the Blüemlisalp glacier, with the Blüemlisalphorn and Morgenhorn filling the skyline.
itinerary.evening: The hut terrace looks straight onto the icefall — arrive with enough daylight to sit and watch it before dinner.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 1,250 m ascent, negligible descent. Grade T3, cable-secured rock step near the pass, otherwise steady switchback trail.

itinerary.title: Descent to Griesalp via the Gamchi side
itinerary.morning: From Blüemlisalphütte, descend the glacier-carved Gamchi valley on the hut's western approach, a quieter and less-trodden line than the Kandersteg side.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue down through alp pasture to Griesalp, a small road-end hamlet in the Kiental, reachable only by postbus or on foot — no through road.
itinerary.evening: Griesalp is tiny; the single guesthouse is the only option, so confirm the booking before setting out.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 100 m ascent, 1,350 m descent. Grade T3, steep scree and switchback upper section, easing to forest track lower down.

itinerary.title: Sefinenfurgge to Mürren
itinerary.morning: Climb from Griesalp on the Via Alpina Route 1 waymarking toward the Sefinenfurgge (2,612 m), a demanding pass with loose rock on both approaches and, in a heavy year, old snow into July.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend into the Sefinental, passing below the Rottal glacier's outwash, and climb the final stretch to Mürren, the car-free village terraced above the Lauterbrunnen valley.
itinerary.evening: Mürren's Eiger–Mönch–Jungfrau panorama from the village promenade is one of the best in the region — worth the walk before dinner.
itinerary.dayStats: 18 km, 950 m ascent, 850 m descent. Grade T3–T4, loose rock near the Furgge, genuinely demanding in poor visibility.

itinerary.title: Gimmelwald and down to Lauterbrunnen
itinerary.morning: An easier day after Sefinenfurgge: walk or ride the cable car down to Gimmelwald, one of the smallest and least-changed villages in the valley, then continue on foot along the valley-side path.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend to Lauterbrunnen itself, in the valley of 72 waterfalls, with time to see the Staubbach Fall directly above the village.
itinerary.evening: A valley-floor rest night; gear dries out properly for the first time since Kandersteg.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km, 150 m ascent, 950 m descent. Grade T1–T2, well-graded path and some cable-car assistance.

itinerary.title: Wengen and the Kleine Scheidegg balcony
itinerary.morning: Train from Lauterbrunnen up to Wengen, a car-free terrace village, then continue on foot along the balcony trail toward Kleine Scheidegg, with the Eiger's north face rising directly overhead.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue on the classic Männlichen or Eigergletscher path, contouring below the face before dropping toward Grindelwald.
itinerary.evening: Grindelwald marks the end of the high walking; a proper final dinner is in order.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km, 550 m ascent, 750 m descent. Grade T2, wide balcony trail, no exposure despite the dramatic setting.

itinerary.title: Bachalpsee and departure
itinerary.morning: A last short walk: gondola to First, then the easy path out to Bachalpsee, a glacier-fed tarn that mirrors the Wetterhorn and Schreckhorn on a calm morning.
itinerary.afternoon: Return to Grindelwald, train to Interlaken and onward toward Zürich for the flight home.
itinerary.evening: Depart.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km, 200 m ascent, 200 m descent (excluding lift-assisted sections). Grade T1, easy path throughout.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel or B&B in Kandersteg
accommodationStrategy.description: Close to the Oeschinensee gondola and the train station, useful for the pre-dawn Hohtürli start on Day 2.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead for August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Blüemlisalphütte
accommodationStrategy.description: Book directly through the SAC/CAS online hut reservation portal well ahead — this is one of the most popular huts in the Berner Oberland and regularly sells out on August weekends.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–12 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Gasthaus in Griesalp or Mürren
accommodationStrategy.description: Griesalp has a single small guesthouse that is the only overnight in the hamlet; Mürren has more choice but fills fast in high season, given its car-free status and Eiger-north-face views.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–10 weeks ahead, especially for Griesalp.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Switzerland's alpine and helicopter rescue is Rega, on **1414**.
logistics.weather: Afternoon storms build over the glaciated peaks from around 13:00 in summer; both Hohtürli and Sefinenfurgge should be crossed in the morning.
logistics.bookingWindows: Blüemlisalphütte runs on the SAC's online reservation system; book it as soon as dates are set, since demand consistently outstrips beds through August.

other.label: Waymarks
other.text: White-red-white blazes mark the mountain trail standard used throughout this route (Bergweg, T2–T3); the short cable-secured step below Hohtürli is the only section approaching Alpine-trail character.

other.label: Griesalp access
other.text: No through road serves Griesalp; the postbus from Kiental is the only vehicle link, useful to know if weather forces an early exit from Day 3.

other.label: Via Alpina waymarking
other.text: Route 1 signage overlays the standard Swiss trail network with its own logo; follow the white-red-white blazes as the primary reference where the two diverge.

other.label: Cash
other.text: Griesalp's guesthouse and the hut bar both prefer cash; carry Swiss francs in small notes.

proTips: Book Blüemlisalphütte before anything else on this trip — it is the hardest bed on the route to secure.
Start the Hohtürli climb by 07:00; the Chindbetti cable step is far more pleasant with cool rock and no queue.
Take the Gamchi-side descent to Griesalp rather than retracing to Kandersteg — it is the quieter, more rewarding line and avoids doubling back.
Confirm the Griesalp postbus timetable before Day 3, since it is the only backup if legs or weather demand an early exit from the valley.
Walk the Kleine Scheidegg balcony in the morning; afternoon cloud regularly hides the Eiger face by early afternoon in July and August.
Reserve the First gondola for an early Day 7 slot — Bachalpsee gets crowded by mid-morning in high season.
Eat Alpkäse at the Griesalp or Mürren guesthouse rather than waiting for Grindelwald; both sit close to working alp dairies.
