packingNotes: Trekking poles, essential for the long Day 6 descent (1,650 m).
A lightweight hard-shell — Écrins afternoon storms are a real, recurring feature of the range.
Cash in small notes for refuge lodging and bar tabs.
A headtorch for refuge dorms and any storm-avoidance early start.
Sun protection — the glacier-adjacent cols reflect strong UV even under high cloud.
A refuge sleeping liner if not using CAF-provided bedding; policy varies between the four refuges.
A 30–35 L pack; refuges provide meals, so there's no need to carry food beyond the between-hut stretches.
What people over-pack: crampons and ice axe. The Col d'Arsine crossing here is a walking col, not a glacier traverse — check conditions with the warden first.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Refuge du Chatelleret fully booked.** Fallback: Refuge du Carrelet, lower in the same valley, has more capacity and a shorter approach; treat Day 2 as a day walk from Carrelet rather than a relocation.

**Bus connection over the Col du Lautaret missed on Day 3.** Fallback: the Lautaret road carries frequent seasonal bus and shuttle services in summer; confirm the day's timetable the morning of rather than the night before, since schedules shift with school-holiday dates.

**Snow lingering on the Col d'Arsine in early July.** Fallback: ask the Alpe du Villar-d'Arêne warden the evening before — if the col is genuinely bad, the plateau above the refuge itself makes a satisfying shorter alternate day.
**Afternoon storm building near the Col d'Arsine.** Fallback: turn back to whichever refuge is closer rather than pushing over an exposed moraine crest in a lightning risk.
**Refuge du Pigeonnier unreachable by phone.** Fallback: the Alpe du Villar-d'Arêne warden usually has a radio line to neighbouring huts and can confirm space before you commit to the col crossing.

trips.title: Mount Olympus Refuges: Petrostrouga, the Muses Plateau and Mytikas
trips.subRegion: Central Macedonia & Thessaly — Olympus National Park, Pieria

bestPeriod.window: Mid-June–early October, with mid-September the best mix of stable rock and empty refuges
bestPeriod.avoid: November–May — Mytikas becomes a winter mountaineering route, refuges close and the Kaki Skala ices
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-June–early October, with mid-September the best mix of stable rock and empty refuges

accommodation.note: Refuge dorms €18–€25 pppn; Litochoro rooms €55–€90

food.note: Refuge dinner €14–€18, breakfast €7–€9; Litochoro taverna mains €9–€15

transport.note: Thessaloniki transfer, Gortsia and Prionia taxis €25–€40 each, hire car for two days

activities.note: Dion archaeological park €8, Platamonas castle €3–€4, optional guide for Mytikas

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5, spiking to 5/5 on the Mytikas day — an exposed Grade II/III scramble on loose rock at 2,900 m

trips.gatewayAirport: SKG Thessaloniki Makedonia, 1 h 10 min to Litochoro; ATH Athens 4 h 30 min by car or 4 h by train to Litochoro station
trips.summary: Olympus is far more mountain than its mythology suggests: a limestone massif rising from a beach to 2,918 m in 18 kilometres, with a summit that is a genuine scramble rather than a walk. This week climbs it the sensible way — up the forested Gortsia ridge to Petrostrouga, onto the Plateau of the Muses, over Mytikas and Skolio, and then a long descent through the Enipeas gorge to Litochoro and the sea. The refuges are cheap, sociable and Greek in character, meaning enormous dinners and no nonsense about check-in times. It suits fit hikers with scrambling experience; the summit ridge is the crux and not everyone should attempt it.

itinerary.title: Litochoro, the lower Enipeas and the sea
itinerary.morning: Arrive from Thessaloniki to **Litochoro, 300 m**, a stone town wedged at the gorge mouth with the massif filling the whole western sky. Register your route at the Olympus National Park information office and confirm the refuge bookings by phone.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the **lower Enipeas gorge** from the town's Mylos to the **Agios Dionysios monastery ruins** and back — wooden footbridges, river crossings, plane trees, and a cold pool at the Enipeas springs.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **Gastrodromio En Olympo** on the main square, the best kitchen in Pieria — wild greens, Olympus mushrooms, goat, and a Rapsani red from the mountain's own vineyards.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km round trip / 350 m ascent / Litochoro 300 m / 3 h 30 min realistic / national park registration completed
itinerary.sleep: Villa Drosos or Hotel Enipeas, Litochoro

itinerary.title: Gortsia to the Petrostrouga refuge
itinerary.morning: Taxi 40 minutes to the **Gortsia trailhead at 1,100 m** (€25–€40). Start the E4 through beech and black pine, past the **Barba** clearing, on a broad ridge that gains height steadily rather than steeply.
itinerary.afternoon: Reach **Petrostrouga refuge, 1,920 m**, sitting on a shoulder with the tree line just above and the whole Thermaic Gulf below. Afternoon here is deliberate acclimatisation — you have gained 800 m and will gain 800 more tomorrow.
itinerary.evening: Refuge dinner — bean soup, pasta, plenty of it — and an early night. The refuge is the friendliest on the mountain and often has climbers coming down off Stefani.
itinerary.dayStats: 6 km / 820 m ascent / Gortsia 1,100 m / Petrostrouga 1,920 m / 3 h 30 min–4 h realistic / bed €18–€22 cash

itinerary.title: Skourta and the Plateau of the Muses
itinerary.morning: Above Petrostrouga the forest ends within an hour. Climb the **Skourta ridge to 2,475 m**, then traverse the exposed **Lemos** ridge with the **Stefani** north face — the Throne of Zeus, the most dramatic thing on the mountain — appearing across the Kazania cirque.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross onto the **Plateau of the Muses at about 2,650 m** and check into **Giosos Apostolidis, 2,697 m**, the highest refuge in Greece, with **Christos Kakalos** a few hundred metres away.
itinerary.evening: Sunset from the plateau over the Kazania. Nights up here drop to 3–6 °C in August; the refuge has blankets but the dorm is not heated. Buy water now — there is none on the plateau.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km / 900 m ascent / 150 m descent / Skourta 2,475 m / refuge 2,697 m / 4–5 h realistic / no water source above the tree line

itinerary.title: Mytikas, 2,918 m, and down to Refuge A
itinerary.morning: Leave at 06:00 with helmets on. Traverse the **Zonaria** below Stefani to **Skala, 2,866 m**, then the **Kaki Skala** — 30–45 minutes of exposed Grade II/III scrambling on loose limestone to the **summit of Mytikas, 2,918 m** and its metal box of a summit register. The direct **Louki couloir** from the plateau is shorter and considerably more dangerous.
itinerary.afternoon: Reverse to Skala, add the easy 20-minute ridge to **Skolio, 2,911 m** for the view down the 500 m Kazania wall, then take the long zigzagging descent to **Spilios Agapitos (Refuge A), 2,060 m**, in its stand of Bosnian pine.
itinerary.evening: Refuge A is the busiest and best-run hut on the mountain: dinner at 18:00, lights out at 22:00, and a warden's briefing on tomorrow's weather. Ouzo on the terrace as the Thermaic Gulf turns pink.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km / 450 m ascent / 1,100 m descent / summit 2,918 m / Kaki Skala 30–45 min each way at Grade II/III / 7–8 h realistic

itinerary.title: Prionia and the full Enipeas gorge
itinerary.morning: Descend the classic mule path through beech and Bosnian pine to **Prionia, 1,100 m**, where a taverna sells bean soup, grilled sausage and the coldest spring water on the mountain.
itinerary.afternoon: Instead of taking the road, walk the **full Enipeas gorge** — 12 km and roughly 800 m of descent past the **monastery of Agios Dionysios**, the cave chapel, and a dozen plank bridges and cable-assisted river crossings — all the way back down to Litochoro at 300 m. It is the finest gorge walk in northern Greece and almost nobody does it in this direction.
itinerary.evening: Swim at Plaka Litochorou, five minutes from town, then dinner at To Pazari for grilled octopus and tsipouro.
itinerary.dayStats: 18 km / 150 m ascent / 1,760 m descent / Prionia 1,100 m / gorge 12 km / 7–8 h realistic — the longest day of the week
itinerary.sleep: Villa Drosos or Hotel Enipeas, Litochoro

itinerary.title: Dion, Platamonas and Palaios Panteleimonas
itinerary.morning: Drive 15 minutes to the **archaeological park of Dion**, the Macedonian sanctuary city at the mountain's foot where Alexander sacrificed before crossing into Asia — mosaics, a submerged sanctuary of Isis and an excellent museum (€8).
itinerary.afternoon: South to the **Platamonas castle**, a 13th-century Crusader fortress on a bluff above the sea, and up to the restored stone village of **Palaios Panteleimonas** at 500 m for the best view back at the whole Olympus escarpment.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Palaios Panteleimonas's plane-shaded square — grilled lamb, local wine, and the massif you walked over silhouetted opposite.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km driving / Dion €8 / Platamonas €3–€4 / Palaios Panteleimonas 500 m / 3 km of village walking
itinerary.sleep: Villa Drosos or Hotel Enipeas, Litochoro

itinerary.title: Rapsani, the Tembi gorge and out
itinerary.morning: Drive the mountain's south flank to **Rapsani**, the PDO wine village at 700 m, for a tasting of xinomavro-krassato-stavroto blends at Dougos or the Rapsani co-operative.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue through the **Vale of Tembi**, the gorge between Olympus and Ossa where the Pineios cuts to the sea, then north to Thessaloniki (1 h 10 min from Litochoro) or south to catch the Athens train from Litochoro station.
itinerary.evening: Thessaloniki's Ladadika or Modiano market for bougatsa, mezedes and the flight out.
itinerary.dayStats: Rapsani 700 m / Tembi gorge 10 km / Litochoro–SKG 1 h 10 min / Litochoro–Athens 4 h by train

accommodationStrategy.name: Spilios Agapitos (Refuge A)
accommodationStrategy.description: The best-organised bed on Olympus, with 110 places, a real kitchen, hot food all day, and a warden family who have run it for generations and give an honest weather briefing. It is also the standard base for a Mytikas attempt from the Prionia side. Roughly €20–€25 for a bed, cash. Book on mountolympus.gr or by phone well ahead for July and August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Giosos Apostolidis
accommodationStrategy.description: The highest refuge in Greece, on the Plateau of the Muses, and the only bed that puts you within 90 minutes of Mytikas at dawn. Spartan, cold at night, no water source on the plateau, but the position is unmatched and the sunrise over the Aegean is the reason you came. Open roughly early June to end of October.

accommodationStrategy.name: Villa Drosos
accommodationStrategy.description: Quiet, ten minutes' walk from the gorge trailhead and the town square, with parking, secure storage for the bag you do not take up the mountain, and breakfast early enough for a Gortsia start. Roughly €60–€90 double, and a pool that matters after the Enipeas descent.

logistics.connectivity: Greece is in the EU roaming zone. Signal is surprisingly good on the Muses Plateau (line of sight to the coast) and at Refuge A, and poor in the Enipeas gorge and on the Gortsia forest ridge. Download offline maps — the Anavasi 1:25,000 Olympus sheet is the standard reference.
logistics.emergency: 112 for all emergencies, 166 for EKAB ambulance. Mountain rescue is the volunteer Hellenic Rescue Team with Air Force helicopter support; expect hours, not minutes, above 2,600 m. Nearest hospital: Katerini. Insurance must cover scrambling and mountaineering — many travel policies exclude ground above Grade II.
logistics.weather: Olympus makes its own weather; cloud caps the summit ridge by mid-morning on many summer days and the Kaki Skala in cloud is a genuinely serious place. Afternoon thunderstorms are frequent in June and September. Summit attempts start at 06:00 for this reason. Check the EMY (Hellenic National Meteorological Service) mountain forecast and the refuge boards.
logistics.bookingWindows: Refuges 2–4 weeks for July and August, less otherwise; reconfirm 48 hours ahead by phone. Litochoro hotels 3–6 weeks in August. Gortsia and Prionia taxis a day ahead. Guides for Mytikas 2–3 weeks in high season.
logistics.money: Euro. **The refuges are cash-only in practice** — carry €250–€300 in small notes. Litochoro has ATMs; Prionia and above have none. Tipping is rounding up, or 5–10% in a taverna.
logistics.transportRules: No vignette in Greece; the A1 Athens–Thessaloniki motorway is tolled at roughly €14–€18 for the Litochoro–Thessaloniki stretch of the network. The Prionia road is narrow, unsurfaced in its last kilometres and hard on a small hire car — use a taxi. Litochoro railway station is 5 km from the town and is served by the Athens–Thessaloniki intercity line.
logistics.permits: No permit or entry fee for Olympus National Park. **Register your route** at the refuge or the Litochoro office. Wild camping and open fires are prohibited in the park core; drones need authorisation. Do not remove rocks or plants — the massif has 1,700 plant species, 23 of them endemic.
logistics.health: Water above 2,000 m is bought, not found. The dominant hazard is **rockfall on the Kaki Skala and in the Louki couloir** — wear a helmet and never climb directly beneath another party. Heat is a genuine issue on the lower Enipeas in July and August, where the gorge floor exceeds 35 °C. Vipers occur on the lower slopes; ticks in the beech forest.

proTips: Climb **upward** across the week — Petrostrouga at 1,920 m, then Apostolidis at 2,697 m, then the summit — rather than the usual one-night dash from Refuge A. Two nights of acclimatisation transforms the Kaki Skala from an ordeal into a scramble.
Be on the Kaki Skala by **07:30**. After 09:30 there are parties above you on loose rock, and the summit block gets a queue that turns 45 minutes into two hours.
If the ridge is wet, in cloud, or busy, take **Skolio (2,911 m)** instead. It is a walk, it is 7 m lower than Mytikas, and it has the better view — of Mytikas.
Walk the **Enipeas gorge downhill from Prionia**, not up from Litochoro. Everyone does it the other way; downhill you get the monastery, the bridges and the pools with nobody on them.
Carry a helmet even if you plan only to walk. The Zonaria traverse below Stefani takes rockfall from the faces above regardless of what you personally are climbing.
Buy water at Apostolidis the evening before, not the morning of. The Muses Plateau has no source and the refuge's stock is helicoptered in and finite.
Book the Gortsia taxi through your Litochoro hotel the night before and ask for 07:00. The trailhead is unserved by public transport and the drivers know the forest road.
Rapsani on the last day is the mountain's own appellation and almost nobody links it to the hike. The co-operative pours the xinomavro blends for a few euros.

raw.Hut-to-hut booking path: **Petrostrouga (1,920 m, 72 places, effectively open year-round)** → **Giosos Apostolidis (2,697 m, 80 places, early June to end of October, run by the SEO mountaineering association of Thessaloniki)** → **Spilios Agapitos, universally called Refuge A (2,060 m, 110 places, early May to end of October, run by the Zolotas family for the Greek mountaineering club)**. The fourth hut, **Christos Kakalos (2,648 m, 17 places, late May to early November)**, sits on the Muses Plateau beside Apostolidis and is the overflow. **There is no central booking portal.** Refuge A books through mountolympus.gr and by phone on **+30 23520 81800**; Apostolidis and Petrostrouga take phone and email bookings, and Apostolidis will confirm by SMS. Expect **€18–€25 for a dormitory bed, dinner €14–€18 and breakfast €7–€9**, so a de facto half board of €40–€50. **All three are cash-only in practice** — the card machines are satellite-linked and rarely work — so carry €250–€300 for the week. **Bring a sleeping-bag liner**; blankets are provided and full sleeping bags are discouraged in the dorms for hygiene. **If a refuge is full:** Kakalos absorbs the Apostolidis overflow, and Greek refuge custom means a mattress on the dining-room floor rather than a refusal, but it is not a plan — phone two weeks out and reconfirm 48 hours before.
raw.Safety markers and waymarking: Olympus is threaded by the **E4 European long-distance path**, marked with the standard **black-on-yellow E4 square** and supported by **red paint blazes and red-white diamond markers** on the national-park network, with numbered wooden signposts at every junction (E4, the Gortsia route, the Prionia route, Louki, Zonaria). Above the tree line the marking becomes cairns and painted dots on rock, which vanish in cloud — the Zonaria traverse and the Skala–Mytikas section are where people get lost. **There are no via ferratas and no fixed cables anywhere on Olympus.**
raw.The Kaki Skala grade and helmet reality: The **Kaki Skala ("Bad Staircase")** runs from **Skala, 2,866 m**, along the west side of the summit ridge to **Mytikas, 2,918 m** — roughly **30–45 minutes each way of exposed Grade II/III scrambling (YDS Class 3)** on limestone that is loose, polished in the popular lines, and sits above 300–500 m drops. The alternative from the Muses Plateau, the **Louki couloir**, is shorter and steeper and is a **rockfall funnel**. **A helmet is the single most important item on this mountain** — the hazard is not your own fall so much as the stones dislodged by the party above you, and on an August morning there will be one. Guides run fixed-rope handrails for clients; independent scramblers should carry a short rope and know how to use it, or turn around at Skala and take **Skolio, 2,911 m**, which is a walk and only 7 m lower.
raw.Registration and park rules: Olympus has been a national park since 1938, Greece's first. Walkers are asked to **register at the refuge or at the Litochoro information office** before going high, giving route and expected return — this is what search and rescue works from. **Wild camping and fires are prohibited inside the park core**; bivouacking above the tree line is tolerated only in emergency. Drones need authorisation.
raw.Elevation and gear essentials: Cumulative ascent for the four mountain days is roughly **2,700 m**, with a single **1,800 m descent** on the Enipeas day that punishes knees more than anything on the way up. High points: **Mytikas 2,918 m, Skolio 2,911 m, Stefani (the Throne of Zeus) 2,909 m, Skala 2,866 m, Apostolidis 2,697 m, Skourta 2,475 m**. **Snow lingers in the Kazania cirque and the Louki couloir into late June**, and microspikes plus an axe are appropriate before roughly 20 June; after that it is a dry-rock mountain. Bring a **helmet**, sticky-soled B-rated boots, gloves and 3 litres of water capacity.
raw.Water, food resupply and rubbish: **Olympus is dry above 2,000 m.** There is a good spring at **Prionia (1,100 m)** and one at Petrostrouga; the **Muses Plateau has no water at all** and Apostolidis sells it. Refuge A has water. Carry **2.5–3 litres** for the summit day. Resupply only in Litochoro — there is no shop above 300 m. **All rubbish comes down with you**; refuges are supplied by mule and helicopter and will not take your packaging.
raw.Bail-out options, rescue and insurance: From the Muses Plateau the escape is the Zonaria traverse down to Refuge A and Prionia (3–4 h), or the long Gortsia descent. From Refuge A, Prionia is 2 h and has a road. **112 is the emergency number; EKAB ambulance is 166**, and mountain rescue on Olympus is run by the volunteer **Hellenic Rescue Team** with helicopter support from the Hellenic Air Force. Response above 2,600 m is measured in hours, not minutes. Rescue is not billed as a rule, but **medical evacuation and repatriation are not covered by EHIC/GHIC** — insure for mountaineering and scrambling, and check the policy does not exclude "climbing above Grade II".
raw.Realistic walking times: Greek signposts are optimistic and were largely written for local club members. Add **30%**. Gortsia to Petrostrouga is signed 3 h; plan 3.5–4 h. Refuge A to Mytikas and back is signed 5–6 h; plan 7–8 h, more if you queue on the Kaki Skala.

typeSpecific.technicalRating: Olympus is threaded by the **E4 European long-distance path**, marked with the standard **black-on-yellow E4 square** and supported by **red paint blazes and red-white diamond markers** on the national-park network, with numbered wooden signposts at every junction (E4, the Gortsia route, the Prionia route, Louki, Zonaria). Above the tree line the marking becomes cairns and painted dots on rock, which vanish in cloud — the Zonaria traverse and the Skala–Mytikas section are where people get lost. **There are no via ferratas and no fixed cables anywhere on Olympus.**
typeSpecific.hutBooking: **Petrostrouga (1,920 m, 72 places, effectively open year-round)** → **Giosos Apostolidis (2,697 m, 80 places, early June to end of October, run by the SEO mountaineering association of Thessaloniki)** → **Spilios Agapitos, universally called Refuge A (2,060 m, 110 places, early May to end of October, run by the Zolotas family for the Greek mountaineering club)**. The fourth hut, **Christos Kakalos (2,648 m, 17 places, late May to early November)**, sits on the Muses Plateau beside Apostolidis and is the overflow. **There is no central booking portal.** Refuge A books through mountolympus.gr and by phone on **+30 23520 81800**; Apostolidis and Petrostrouga take phone and email bookings, and Apostolidis will confirm by SMS. Expect **€18–€25 for a dormitory bed, dinner €14–€18 and breakfast €7–€9**, so a de facto half board of €40–€50. **All three are cash-only in practice** — the card machines are satellite-linked and rarely work — so carry €250–€300 for the week. **Bring a sleeping-bag liner**; blankets are provided and full sleeping bags are discouraged in the dorms for hygiene. **If a refuge is full:** Kakalos absorbs the Apostolidis overflow, and Greek refuge custom means a mattress on the dining-room floor rather than a refusal, but it is not a plan — phone two weeks out and reconfirm 48 hours before.

All three main refuges require booking before arrival and none is served by a central portal.
sources.confidenceNotes: Refuge bed and meal prices are indicative 2025 figures and are not published consistently — re-verify with each refuge for 2026. The Refuge A phone number and the mountolympus.gr booking flow should be spot-checked. Gortsia and Prionia taxi fares, Dion and Platamonas entry fees, and A1 toll totals are seasonal estimates.

trips.title: Alta Via 1 in Seven Days: Braies to the Civetta Wall
trips.subRegion: Dolomiti Bellunesi & Ampezzane — Fanes-Sennes-Braies, Lagazuoi, Civetta

bestPeriod.window: Late June–mid-September, with 10 July–10 September the fully staffed window
bestPeriod.avoid: October–mid-June — rifugi shut, Forcella del Lago and Forcella Coldai hold hard snow, and the Lagazuoi cable car stops mid-October
bestPeriod.raw: Late June–mid-September, with 10 July–10 September the fully staffed window

accommodation.note: Six rifugio half-board nights €70–€95 plus one valley hotel

food.note: Lunches, a beer at €5–€7, packed lunch (pranzo al sacco) €10–€13

transport.note: Venice transfers, Dolomiti Bus, Lagazuoi cable car, Passo Duran taxi

activities.note: Ferrata set hire €12–€18/day, tourist tax, Lagazuoi tunnel head torch, CAI membership

profile.difficultyNote: 4/5 — seven consecutive days of 550–950 m ascent and up to 1,350 m descent at 1,500–2,750 m, with exposed but non-technical ground

trips.gatewayAirport: VCE Venice Marco Polo, 2 h 40 min to Lago di Braies via Dobbiaco; INN Innsbruck 2 h; TSF Treviso 2 h 45 min
trips.summary: The Alta Via 1 is the Dolomites' introductory grand traverse and the one that actually delivers on the postcard: turquoise Braies, the high karst desert of Fanes and Sennes, the Great War tunnels bored through Lagazuoi, then a full day walking beneath the 1,200 m Civetta wall. Compressed into seven days it becomes serious walking — 5 to 8 hours daily, twelve passes, and no rest day — but it stays a hiking route, not a climbing one. You sleep in rifugi with duvets, three-course dinners and a wine list, which is why the beds vanish in February. It suits confident hill walkers who want altitude and scenery without needing rope work.

itinerary.title: Lago di Braies to Rifugio Biella
itinerary.morning: Transfer to **Lago di Braies (Pragser Wildsee), 1,494 m**. Note that private cars need a pre-booked slot in summer; arrive by the Dobbiaco bus instead. Walk the lake's east shore, then start path 1 up the Valle di Braies Vecchia.
itinerary.afternoon: A steady 850 m climb on scree and rock steps to **Forcella Sora Forno, 2,388 m**, then a short traverse to **Rifugio Biella** at 2,327 m under the Croda del Becco. Fit walkers add the 1 h 15 min ascent of **Croda del Becco (Seekofel), 2,810 m**, the finest first-day view on the route.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Biella — barley soup, *canederli*, apple strudel. The hut is small and social; sit at the long table and swap the next four days' bookings with everyone else.
itinerary.dayStats: 6.5 km / 850 m ascent / 50 m descent / high point 2,388 m / 3 h 30 min–4 h realistic
itinerary.sleep: Rifugio Biella, 2,327 m (dorm half board approx. €70–€80)

itinerary.title: The Sennes plateau, Pederü and the climb to Fanes
itinerary.morning: A long, gentle karst crossing on path 6/26 past **Rifugio Sennes (2,116 m)** and Rifugio Fodara Vedla — treeless limestone pavement, marmots, and no water at all.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop 570 m on the jeep road to **Pederü, 1,548 m** (the only shop and the day's bail-out), then climb 500 m up the Val dai Tamersc to the twin huts **Rifugio Lavarella and Rifugio Fanes** at 2,050–2,060 m.
itinerary.evening: Lavarella runs the highest brewery in Europe — drink its unfiltered Sisyphus. Fanes next door does the better *casunziei*. Book whichever you sleep in; they are separate businesses.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km / 700 m ascent / 900 m descent / Pederü low point 1,548 m / 6–7 h realistic / zero water between huts
itinerary.sleep: Rifugio Lavarella or Rifugio Fanes, Alta Badia

itinerary.title: Forcella del Lago and the ascent to Lagazuoi
itinerary.morning: South on path 11 past Lago Limo and the Passo Tadega, then the day's crux: a steep, sometimes snow-filled couloir to **Forcella del Lago, 2,486 m**, with a fixed cable on the final rock step.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend to Lago di Lagazuoi, then climb again over **Forcella Lagazuoi, 2,573 m** and up the ridge to **Rifugio Lagazuoi, 2,752 m**, the highest bed of the week and directly above the WW1 galleries.
itinerary.evening: Lagazuoi's terrace at sunset is the picture everyone comes for; the sauna is genuinely good after 900 m of ascent. Book this hut the day reservations open.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km / 950 m ascent / 400 m descent / two passes above 2,480 m / 6–6 h 30 min realistic / hut at 2,752 m

itinerary.title: The Lagazuoi tunnels, Cinque Torri and Nuvolau
itinerary.morning: Descend through the **Galleria del Lagazuoi**, the Italian mine tunnel driven into the mountain in 1916–17 — 1 km of stepped, wet, unlit gallery losing 600 m. **Helmet and head torch essential**, ferrata set recommended. The Kaiserjäger path is the exposed alternative. Cable car for anyone who would rather not.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross **Passo Falzarego, 2,105 m** (coffee, bus stop, gear shop) and climb path 440/439 past the **Cinque Torri** climbing towers and the restored Italian trench museum to **Rifugio Averau**, then the final 25-minute pull to **Rifugio Nuvolau, 2,575 m**.
itinerary.evening: Nuvolau is a stone box on a summit with a 360° horizon and eighteen beds. Eat at Averau below if you want the best kitchen on the route (its *casunziei all'ampezzana* is the local benchmark) and walk up after.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km / 700 m ascent / 950 m descent / tunnel 1 km, −600 m / Falzarego 2,105 m / 5 h 30 min–6 h 30 min
itinerary.sleep: Rifugio Nuvolau, 2,575 m (or Rifugio Averau, 2,413 m)

itinerary.title: Passo Giau, Forcella Ambrizzola and Monte Pelmo
itinerary.morning: Descend to **Forcella Nuvolau** and traverse under Ra Gusela to **Passo Giau, 2,236 m**, then climb the grassy shoulder on path 436 to **Forcella Ambrizzola, 2,277 m** — the day's pivot, with Monte Pelmo suddenly filling the south.
itinerary.afternoon: Contour on path 467 over Forcella Col Duro and Forcella Roan, then down through larch to **Rifugio Città di Fiume, 1,918 m**, sitting on a meadow directly beneath Pelmo's north wall.
itinerary.evening: Città di Fiume is the friendliest kitchen on the AV1 — polenta with *schiz* cheese, venison ragù. The dinosaur footprint slab on Pelmo is a 40-minute walk if you still have legs.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km / 600 m ascent / 1,250 m descent / three forcelle / 6–7 h realistic / Dolomiti Bus at Passo Giau

itinerary.title: Passo Staulanza to the Civetta: Coldai and Tissi
itinerary.morning: Path 472 to **Passo Staulanza, 1,766 m** (bar, bus stop, last resupply), then the sustained 400 m climb on path 556 through pine to **Rifugio Coldai, 2,132 m**.
itinerary.afternoon: Over **Forcella Coldai, 2,191 m** to the emerald **Lago Coldai**, then a rising traverse on path 560 beneath the **Civetta north-west wall** — 1,200 m of vertical limestone, one of the great faces of the Alps — to **Rifugio Tissi, 2,250 m** on its rock knoll.
itinerary.evening: Tissi at sunset turns the Civetta orange and the queue for the terrace bench is real. Small hut, big view; book it in February or accept Coldai.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km / 900 m ascent / 600 m descent / Forcella Coldai 2,191 m / 6–7 h realistic / Civetta wall 1,200 m

itinerary.title: Vazzoler, Carestiato and out at Passo Duran
itinerary.morning: Descend path 560/555 past the Col Reàn to **Rifugio Vazzoler, 1,714 m**, whose alpine botanical garden sits under the Torre Venezia. This is the quietest, greenest hour of the week.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb path 554 over **Forcella del Camp, 1,933 m** to **Rifugio Carestiato, 1,834 m** under the Moiazza, then down to **Passo Duran, 1,601 m**, where the pre-booked taxi runs you to Agordo and the Belluno bus. Purists continue three more days to La Pissa and Belluno.
itinerary.evening: Belluno's Piazza dei Martiri: dinner at Al Borgo in Anzù for *pastin* and Prosecco Superiore, or a simpler *osteria* plate in the old town before the train to Venice.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km / 700 m ascent / 1,350 m descent / Passo Duran 1,601 m / 7–8 h realistic / taxi Duran–Agordo €40–€60
itinerary.sleep: Hotel in Belluno, or Rifugio Carestiato if you extend the route

accommodationStrategy.name: Rifugio Lagazuoi
accommodationStrategy.description: The highest and most comfortable bed on the AV1, with hot showers, a sauna, private rooms as well as dorms and a terrace over the entire Ampezzo basin. Booked through its own website months ahead; roughly €85–€100 dorm half board. Cable-car access means you can send a bag up or bail out cleanly.

accommodationStrategy.name: Rifugio Città di Fiume
accommodationStrategy.description: Low enough for warm nights, positioned directly under Monte Pelmo, and the best value on the route at around €70–€78 half board with the CAI discount. Bookable via prenotarifugi.cai.it, with parking and bus access at nearby Passo Staulanza for a partial-week itinerary.

accommodationStrategy.name: Rifugio Tissi
accommodationStrategy.description: Twenty-odd beds on a knoll facing the Civetta wall, and the single most contested night on the trail. Small, spartan and cash-friendly. If it will not book, take Rifugio Coldai an hour back and walk the traverse in the early morning light instead.

logistics.connectivity: Italy is in the EU roaming zone, so an EU SIM works at no extra cost. Coverage is good at Lagazuoi, Nuvolau and Falzarego, weak on the Sennes plateau and in the Val dai Tamersc, and absent in the tunnels. Download the Tabacco 03, 031 and 025 sheets offline.
logistics.emergency: 112 or 118 for Soccorso Alpino. Give the CAI path number and the nearest forcella name, not GPS alone. Italian helicopter rescue is charged — insure specifically for it or join CAI, whose subscription includes cover. Nearest hospitals: Cortina (Codivilla-Putti) and Belluno.
logistics.weather: Convective thunderstorms build from 13:00–15:00 on most July and August afternoons and the exposed forcelle are lightning traps. Aim to be inside by 15:00. Late-August cold fronts can drop snow above 2,500 m overnight. Check meteo.provincia.bz.it and arpa.veneto.it.
logistics.bookingWindows: Rifugi open the following summer's diary between February and April; Lagazuoi, Nuvolau and Tissi go within days. Lago di Braies car access needs a summer slot booked online. Ferrata hire in Cortina is walk-in but thin on August weekends.
logistics.money: Euro. Several huts take cards but the satellite terminals fail regularly; carry €300–€400 cash for the week. Tipping is not customary; round up the bar bill.
logistics.transportRules: Dolomiti Bus and SAD serve Falzarego, Passo Giau and Passo Staulanza; buy tickets on the app or at bars, not from the driver. Lago di Braies has a summer traffic ban for private cars in the middle of the day. The Lagazuoi cable car runs roughly 6 June–18 October.
logistics.permits: No permit is needed to walk the AV1. Fanes-Sennes-Braies and the Dolomiti Bellunesi are protected areas: **wild camping and bivouacking are prohibited**, as are fires and drones without authorisation. Do not remove WW1 artefacts from the Lagazuoi galleries — unexploded ordnance still surfaces.
logistics.health: Hut tap water is usually potable but signed where it is not; assume rainwater cisterns at Nuvolau and Tissi are non-potable unless told otherwise. Altitude is modest but 2,750 m sleeping affects poor sleepers. The main injury risk is a twisted ankle on wet limestone on the long descents.

proTips: Join CAI (or use a reciprocal UIAA club card) before booking. It cuts €12–€15 a night off four of the seven huts, includes rescue cover, and moves you up the waiting list.
Book Lagazuoi, Nuvolau and Tissi on the first morning their diaries open, then build the rest of the week around whatever they give you. Trying the reverse wastes February.
Walk the Lagazuoi tunnel **downhill** as the route does. Uphill through 600 m of wet stepped gallery in a queue is a different and much worse experience.
Order the *pranzo al sacco* at dinner, not at breakfast. By 07:00 the kitchen is on breakfast service and will hand you whatever is left.
Stop at Rifugio Averau for lunch even if you sleep at Nuvolau. It is 25 minutes below, has the best food on the trail, and Nuvolau's kitchen is tiny.
Fill two litres at every hut and treat the day between huts as waterless. The Sennes plateau in August has caught out more walkers than any pass on the route.
Take the Croda del Becco summit on Day 1 while you are fresh and the pack is at its lightest — it is the only 2,800 m viewpoint on the itinerary.
Carry a €50 note reserve in a separate pocket. When the card terminal at a CAI hut fails at 21:00, that is the difference between paying and an awkward morning.

raw.Hut-to-hut booking path: Rifugio Biella (2,327 m, CAI) → Rifugio Lavarella or Rifugio Fanes (2,050–2,060 m, both private, Alta Badia families) → Rifugio Lagazuoi (2,752 m, private, Pompanin family) → Rifugio Nuvolau (2,575 m, CAI Cortina — the oldest refuge in the Dolomites, 1883) → Rifugio Città di Fiume (1,918 m, CAI Fiume) → Rifugio Tissi (2,250 m, CAI) with Rifugio Coldai (2,132 m, CAI Venezia) as the fallback → Rifugio Carestiato (1,834 m, CAI Agordo). **There is no central portal.** CAI-managed huts take bookings through prenotarifugi.cai.it; private huts (Lagazuoi, Fanes, Lavarella) use their own website or email plus a phone confirmation. Most open the following summer's diary between **early February and April**, and the Lagazuoi and Nuvolau nights sell out within days of opening. Half board runs **€70–€95 in a dorm and €110–€140 in a small room**, plus a **tourist tax of €1.50–€2.50 per person per night**. Several huts still prefer cash and card readers fail when the satellite link drops — **carry €300–€400**. A **sleeping-bag liner (*sacco lenzuolo*) is mandatory**; full sleeping bags are refused. If a hut is full: ring the *gestore* directly rather than trusting the online form, ask to be put on the *lista d'attesa*, and take the standard fallback for each stage — Sennes or Pederü for Biella, Averau for Nuvolau, Coldai for Tissi, Vazzoler for Carestiato. Under Italian mountain custom a *rifugio* may not turn away a walker in danger, but that means a mattress on the dining-room floor, not a bed.
raw.CAI membership discount: A CAI or reciprocal UIAA/Alpine Club membership cuts roughly **€12–€15 per night** off a CAI hut and gives priority on waiting lists. Over four CAI nights it broadly pays for itself.
raw.Safety markers and waymarking: The Dolomites use **red-white-red CAI paint blazes with the path number stencilled in black**, plus wooden signposts giving hours to the next rifugio. The Alta Via 1 is additionally marked with a **blue triangle containing the numeral 1**. The route follows CAI paths 1, 6, 7, 10, 11, 20, 26, 436, 467, 472, 554, 556, 558, 560 and 563 in sequence — the AV1 triangle is the reliable identifier where numbers conflict. **Via ferrata:** the AV1 itself has no obligatory ferrata, but two optional Lagazuoi variants are graded — the **Galleria del Lagazuoi** WW1 tunnel descent (easy, but requires helmet, head torch and ideally a set) and the **Kaiserjäger path** (ferrata grade A/B). The Piz Dles Cunturines and Averau ferratas nearby are grade B/C.
raw.Elevation and gear essentials: Cumulative ascent for the seven days is roughly **4,900 m and 5,700 m of descent**. High points: Rifugio Lagazuoi 2,752 m, Forcella Lagazuoi 2,573 m, Nuvolau 2,575 m, Forcella del Lago 2,486 m, Forcella Coldai 2,191 m. **Snow patches** persist on the north side of Forcella del Lago and above Lago di Coldai until **early July**; before 10 July carry microspikes, and a walking axe only for a June crossing. A **ferrata set (harness, lanyard, helmet) plus head torch** is needed only for the Lagazuoi tunnel and Kaiserjäger — hire in Cortina at Cooperativa di Cortina or K2 Sport, €12–€18/day.
raw.Water, food resupply and rubbish: The Dolomites are karst and **the route is dry between huts** — there are no reliable springs on the Sennes plateau or the Civetta traverse. Every rifugio sells drinking water, some at €1–€3 a litre; fill 2 litres each morning and carry 3 on the Fanes-to-Lagazuoi day. Order a *pranzo al sacco* the evening before (€10–€13). Resupply villages: Pederü, Passo Falzarego, Passo Staulanza, Passo Duran. **Pack out all rubbish** — rifugi are supplied and cleared by helicopter and cargo cableway, and they will ask you to carry your own waste down.
raw.Bail-out options and cable-car shortcuts: Day 2 bails at **Pederü** (1,548 m, shuttle jeep to San Vigilio). Day 3–4 bails at **Passo Falzarego** via the **Lagazuoi cable car** — summer 2026 season runs roughly **6 June to 18 October**, first cabin 09:00, last up 16:40, last down 17:00, cabins every 15 minutes, with a small online-booking discount. Day 5 bails at Passo Giau or Passo Staulanza on Dolomiti Bus. Day 7 ends at **Passo Duran**, where a pre-booked taxi to Agordo (€40–€60) connects to Belluno buses. Cortina's Dolomiti Bus lines 30/31 serve Falzarego.
raw.Rescue and insurance: **118 or 112** reaches the Soccorso Alpino e Speleologico Veneto/Alto Adige. Helicopter rescue in Italy is **billed** — commonly €80–€120 per minute of flight in the Veneto — and EHIC/GHIC does not cover it. Either buy alpine-trekking insurance naming helicopter recovery, or take CAI membership, which includes a rescue and repatriation package.
raw.Realistic walking times: Dolomite signposts quote fit local times. For an averagely fit walker with a 9–11 kg pack, add **25–35%** and a further 20 minutes per hour in wet limestone. The signed "5.30 h" from Nuvolau to Città di Fiume is honestly 6.5–7 h with photo stops.

trips.title: Liechtenstein Panorama — Malbun, Fürstensteig and the Rätikon Rim

bestPeriod.note: The Naafkopf ridge and Pfälzerhütte approach can hold snow into June; the Fürstensteig is best walked dry, after a settled spell.

trips.gatewayAirport: Zürich (ZRH)
trips.summary: A full week built from Liechtenstein's compact high country — Fürstensteig, the Fürstin-Gina-Weg and Pfälzerhütte — with two honest cross-border days into Vorarlberg.
trips.hook: Liechtenstein is 25 km long, and no honest week pretends otherwise — this trip owns it, basing entirely in Malbun and Steg and using the country's real assets: the cable-secured Fürstensteig, the high traverse to Pfälzerhütte under the Naafkopf, and two sections of the new Liechtenstein Trail. Two days cross into neighbouring Vorarlberg, because that is where the Rätikon actually continues, and pretending otherwise would waste good trail.

snapshot.Base(s): Malbun (1,600 m), with day trips from Steg
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 65–75 km, 4,200–4,800 m combined ascent; alpine ridge (white-red-white T2–T3), one secured via-ferrata-style traverse
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Zürich (ZRH), train to Sargans or Buchs SG, then LIEmobil bus 11 to Malbun (about 2h15 door to door)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Confident hikers who want a genuinely small-country week without padding, comfortable with cables and drops

itinerary.title: Arrival and the Sareis warm-up
itinerary.morning: Arrive via Buchs SG, LIEmobil bus to Malbun. LIEmobil covers the whole principality for a flat low fare — buy the day pass at the Malbun terminus.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the Sareisbahn chairlift to Sareis (2,000 m) and walk the short ridge loop back down through Alp Sücka, an easy leg-stretch with the whole Malbun bowl below.
itinerary.evening: Settle in Malbun; check tomorrow's forecast at the tourist information kiosk.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km, 250 m ascent (lift-assisted), 650 m descent. Grade T1–T2, no exposure.

itinerary.title: Fürstin-Gina-Weg to the Bettlerjoch
itinerary.morning: From Steg, walk the Fürstin-Gina-Weg, Liechtenstein's high panoramic path named for the former princess, climbing through larch to the Valünapass area.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to the Bettlerjoch (2,109 m) on the Austrian border, with views into the Samina valley and across to the Drei Schwestern ridge, then descend to Malbun.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Malbun; this was the acclimatization day for tomorrow's longer push.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 850 m ascent, 850 m descent. Grade T2–T3, well-graded alpine path, brief exposed sections near the Joch.

itinerary.title: Up to Pfälzerhütte under the Naafkopf
itinerary.morning: From Malbun, climb via the Bettlerjoch route or the direct Naafkopf path toward Pfälzerhütte (2,108 m), run by DAV Sektion Pfalz — Liechtenstein's only staffed mountain hut, sitting almost exactly on the tripoint of Liechtenstein, Austria and Switzerland.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop packs and climb the Naafkopf (2,570 m) itself, a straightforward scramble from the hut with views over three countries at once.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at the hut; book ahead, since it is the only overnight option on this side of the ridge and fills on summer weekends.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km, 950 m ascent, negligible descent (day pack for the summit). Grade T3, rocky trail with short scrambling to the Naafkopf summit.

itinerary.title: The high traverse and down to Valüna
itinerary.morning: From Pfälzerhütte, traverse south-west along the ridge on marked alpine trail into Swiss territory above the Valünatal, a quiet stretch that sees far fewer boots than the Malbun side.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend into the Valünatal and follow the valley path back down to Steg, closing the loop.
itinerary.evening: Bus back to Malbun; an easier evening after two demanding days.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 300 m ascent, 1,350 m descent. Grade T2–T3, loose scree on the upper traverse.

itinerary.title: Cross-border to Nenzinger Himmel
itinerary.morning: Bus and connecting Postbus over the Bielerhöhe road corridor is not direct — instead take the LIEmobil/ÖBB connection via Feldkirch to Nenzen, then the seasonal shuttle bus up the closed valley road to Nenzinger Himmel, a high alpine meadow basin in Vorarlberg.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk up through Nenzinger Himmel toward the Vorarlberg high country, a broad, gentle basin that is one of the range's classic soft-landing days after the Naafkopf traverse.
itinerary.evening: Return by the same shuttle; overnight back in Malbun or, for a shorter transfer next morning, in Nenzen village.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 500 m ascent, 500 m descent. Grade T1–T2, wide valley path, no exposure.

itinerary.title: The Fürstensteig
itinerary.morning: Transfer to Gaflei above Triesenberg. The Fürstensteig begins here: a narrow, cable-secured ledge path blasted into the Drei Schwestern's flank in 1898, with iron stemples and handrails across the exposed sections.
itinerary.afternoon: The path continues to Bergstation Sareis, where the chairlift offers a fast return to Malbun for tired legs, or continue on foot back down through Alp Sücka.
itinerary.evening: This is the trip's other headline day — a quieter dinner and an early night afterwards is the usual pattern.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km, 550 m ascent, 350 m descent (to Sareis) or 950 m descent (all the way down). Grade T4 with continuous fixed cable, genuinely exposed; not a route for vertigo or wet rock.

itinerary.title: Gafadura Hütte and departure
itinerary.morning: Second cross-border day: Postbus toward Vorarlberg's Gamperdonatal via Frastanz, up to the Gafadura Hütte, run by the Alpenverein Vorarlberg on the ridge above the Ill valley.
itinerary.afternoon: Short loop from the hut for the view back across Liechtenstein and the Rhine valley, then descend and connect back to Buchs SG for the onward train.
itinerary.evening: Depart via Zürich.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km, 650 m ascent, 650 m descent. Grade T2, forest and alp path, no exposure.

accommodationStrategy.name: Gasthof Restaurant Turna or Hotel Alpina
accommodationStrategy.description: Small family-run hotels a few minutes from both the Sareisbahn and the Bettlerjoch trailhead, and the only realistic single base for a week that returns to Malbun most nights. Ask for a room with drying space for wet boots after the Fürstensteig.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead for July–August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Pfälzerhütte
accommodationStrategy.description: The only staffed hut on the route and the logical overnight for the Day 3–4 high traverse; book directly through the hut's own reservation channel (linked from the Alpenverein Sektion Pfalz website) or by phone, especially for weekend dates.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Pension in Steg
accommodationStrategy.description: A quieter, cheaper alternative to Malbun for the first two nights, with the Fürstin-Gina-Weg trailhead at the door.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Liechtenstein has no separate alpine rescue number, and 112 routes to the same Rega-coordinated Swiss/Austrian mountain rescue network used across the border.
logistics.weather: The Rätikon builds afternoon cloud quickly off the Rhine valley; plan the Fürstensteig and Naafkopf days for clear mornings and be off exposed ground by early afternoon.
logistics.transportRules: Both Vorarlberg legs (Nenzinger Himmel, Gafadura) need Austrian Postbus or ÖBB connections that do not run on a Liechtenstein timetable — check the seasonal shuttle schedule to Nenzinger Himmel before committing to Day 5, as it operates a reduced summer service only.

other.label: LIEmobil
other.text: Liechtenstein's bus network is inexpensive and covers Malbun, Steg and Vaduz thoroughly; a multi-day pass is the simplest option for a week that starts and ends by bus.

other.label: Currency
other.text: Liechtenstein uses the Swiss franc; Vorarlberg uses the euro. Carry both in small amounts for hut bars and bus fares.

other.label: Hüttenschlafsack
other.text: Required at Pfälzerhütte and at Gafadura Hütte, as at any DAV or Alpenverein hut.

other.label: Cash
other.text: Card acceptance is patchy at both mountain huts; carry cash in both currencies.

proTips: Book Pfälzerhütte before anything else — it is the only bed on that side of the ridge and the pinch point of the week.
Walk the Fürstensteig on a weekday morning; it is narrow enough that a busy Saturday means real queuing at the ladder sections.
Confirm the Nenzinger Himmel shuttle bus schedule the day before — it is genuinely seasonal and thinner than it looks online.
Buy the LIEmobil multi-day pass on arrival rather than single tickets; it pays for itself by Day 3.
Ask at the Malbun tourist office about current Naafkopf and Fürstensteig conditions — both close temporarily after heavy rain.
Eat at least one dinner of Käsknöpfle, the Liechtenstein-Vorarlberg staple, at a Malbun gasthof rather than saving it for a city trip elsewhere.
Time the Sareisbahn descent on Day 6 for late afternoon light across the Rhine valley toward the Swiss side.

raw.Who It Suits: Confident hikers who want a genuinely small-country week without padding, comfortable with cables and drops

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 65–75 km, 4,200–4,800 m combined ascent; alpine ridge (white-red-white T2–T3), one secured via-ferrata-style traverse
typeSpecific.audience: Confident hikers who want a genuinely small-country week without padding, comfortable with cables and drops

packingNotes: Via-ferrata gloves for the Fürstensteig's steel cable sections — bare hands get raw fast.
A climbing-style helmet for both the Fürstensteig and the Naafkopf summit scramble.
Hüttenschlafsack for the two hut nights.
CHF and EUR cash in small denominations.
Sturdy boots with ankle support; this is not a sneaker week.
A light rain shell — Rätikon weather turns quickly even on a forecast-clear day.
A printed or offline map of the Vorarlberg legs; mobile signal is unreliable in the Gamperdonatal and Nenzinger Himmel basins.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Fürstensteig closed after rain.** The path management closes it when the rock is wet or icy. Fallback: swap Day 6 with Day 2's Fürstin-Gina-Weg leg and reattempt later in the week.
**Nenzinger Himmel shuttle not running.** Fallback: walk the lower Gamperdonatal instead from Frastanz, a gentler valley day that needs no seasonal shuttle.
**Pfälzerhütte fully booked.** Fallback: day-trip to the Naafkopf ridge from Malbun without the overnight, returning to Malbun the same evening — longer, but keeps the itinerary intact.
**Cross-border bus connections missed.** Fallback: a taxi from Malbun to Nenzen or Frastanz is not cheap but is far cheaper than losing a whole day of a short week.
**Bad weather strands the whole week in Malbun.** Fallback: the lower Vaduz old-town and Rhine valley cycle path are genuine half-day options that need no ridge conditions at all.

trips.title: The Escapardenne Eisleck Trail — Kautenbach to La Roche
trips.subRegion: Éislek plateau, northern Luxembourg and Belgian Ardennes

bestPeriod.note: The Éislek's schist plateau holds water after rain; late spring and early autumn give firmer paths and cooler walking than midsummer.

trips.gatewayAirport: Luxembourg (LUX)
trips.summary: A seven-day thru-walk on the Escapardenne Eisleck Trail from Kautenbach to La Roche-en-Ardenne, plus a Lee Trail sampler from Vianden.
trips.hook: Luxembourg's north is quiet, folded, and thoroughly walkable: the Escapardenne Eisleck Trail crosses the Éislek plateau from the rail junction at Kautenbach to the Belgian Ardennes town of La Roche-en-Ardenne in five waymarked stages, dropping into river valleys and climbing back onto open farmland between them. This week walks the whole thing, then adds a taste of its northern sister route, the Escapardenne Lee Trail, out of Vianden before heading home — a genuine week's plateau-and-valley trek, not a single long day stretched thin.

snapshot.Country: Luxembourg (with the trail's final stages in Belgium)
snapshot.Base(s): Kautenbach to start, La Roche-en-Ardenne to finish, Vianden for the closing add-on
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 120–135 km, 2,800–3,300 m combined ascent; rolling plateau, river valley, forest track, no exposure
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Luxembourg (LUX), bus 16 into the city, then train to Kautenbach (about 45 minutes)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Steady multi-day walkers who want a low-exposure, forest-and-farmland thru-hike with real villages every night

itinerary.title: Kautenbach and the trailhead
itinerary.morning: Train from Luxembourg City to Kautenbach, a small station on the main Luxembourg–Liège line that doubles as the Eisleck Trail's start point. Drop bags at the guesthouse.
itinerary.afternoon: Short orientation walk along the Wiltz river below the village, checking the trail's stylised waymark (a white-and-orange "É" on green background) before the real distance begins tomorrow.
itinerary.evening: Early dinner; the week's longest stage is next.
itinerary.dayStats: 6 km, 150 m ascent, 150 m descent. Grade easy forest and riverside path, no exposure.

itinerary.title: Stage 1: Kautenbach to Wiltz
itinerary.morning: Climb out of the Wiltz valley onto open plateau farmland, the trail alternating between hedgerowed fields and beech forest.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend into Wiltz, the Éislek's largest town, known for its open-air festival amphitheatre and its château.
itinerary.evening: Wiltz has the week's best choice of restaurants; a good night to eat properly.
itinerary.dayStats: 22 km, 480 m ascent, 460 m descent. Waymark: white-and-orange Escapardenne blaze on green post, standard forest and field track.

itinerary.title: Stage 2: Wiltz to Boulaide
itinerary.morning: The trail leaves Wiltz through the Wiltz forest, one of the larger continuous woodland blocks on the route, before opening onto the plateau again.
itinerary.afternoon: Rolling farmland to Boulaide, a small village near the Luxembourg–Belgium border, with the plateau's characteristic long sightlines over hedgerowed pasture.
itinerary.evening: Boulaide's single guesthouse is the only overnight option — confirmed ahead is essential.
itinerary.dayStats: 24 km, 420 m ascent, 400 m descent. Grade easy, gravel and forest track throughout.

itinerary.title: Stage 3: Boulaide to Insenborn
itinerary.morning: The trail turns toward the Lac de la Haute-Sûre, Luxembourg's largest reservoir, through forest that thickens as the ground drops toward the water.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive at Insenborn on the lake's southern shore, with an afternoon free to walk the lakeside path or simply sit by the water — the only substantial lake on the whole route.
itinerary.evening: Fish features on every local menu here; the lake is stocked and actively fished.
itinerary.dayStats: 19 km, 380 m ascent, 420 m descent. Grade easy, lakeside and forest track.

itinerary.title: Stage 4: Insenborn to Nadrin, crossing into Belgium
itinerary.morning: The trail follows the lake shore before climbing away from the water and crossing the unmarked Luxembourg–Belgium border into the southern Ardennes.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue through Belgian forest to Nadrin, a small village on a bend of the Ourthe, with a viewpoint over the river's horseshoe loop at nearby Le Hérou.
itinerary.evening: First night in Belgium; note the transport pattern changes here — Belgian regional buses are not part of Luxembourg's free network.
itinerary.dayStats: 23 km, 500 m ascent, 480 m descent. Grade easy to moderate, more forest track, occasional root and stone underfoot.

itinerary.title: Stage 5: Nadrin to La Roche-en-Ardenne
itinerary.morning: The final stage follows the Ourthe valley's forested flank, with repeated views down to the river's meanders.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend into La Roche-en-Ardenne, the trail's terminus, a small town below a ruined medieval castle at the river's most dramatic bend.
itinerary.evening: A proper finish-line dinner; La Roche has more restaurant choice than anywhere since Wiltz.
itinerary.dayStats: 18 km, 380 m ascent, 460 m descent. Grade easy, forest track, one steady climb out of Nadrin.

itinerary.title: Transfer to Vianden and the Lee Trail
itinerary.morning: Bus from La Roche to Bastogne, then train back into Luxembourg and up to Vianden, gateway to the Escapardenne Lee Trail, the Eisleck Trail's northern sister route.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Lee Trail's opening stretch from Vianden along the Our valley toward Stolzembourg, a shorter sampler day that shows the second trail's character — tighter valley, more river, less open plateau — before looping back to Vianden.
itinerary.evening: Depart from Vianden or return to Luxembourg City for the flight home.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 320 m ascent, 320 m descent. Grade easy to moderate, valley path with one climb above Stolzembourg.

accommodationStrategy.name: Gîte or Gasthaus in Kautenbach
accommodationStrategy.description: Right at the rail station and trailhead, so no transfer is needed before or after the walking days. Book the night before Day 2's long stage.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead for summer.

accommodationStrategy.name: Village B&Bs along the route
accommodationStrategy.description: Each village has one or two small B&Bs or gîtes rurales serving the trail directly; Boulaide in particular has a single realistic option, so book the whole chain together before departure rather than village by village.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead, especially for Boulaide.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel in La Roche-en-Ardenne
accommodationStrategy.description: A comfortable finish-line base with a full choice of restaurants, useful for a rest evening before the transfer to Vianden.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European throughout both Luxembourg and Belgium.
logistics.weather: The plateau is exposed to wind and rain with little tree cover on the open farmland stretches; forest sections offer real shelter, valley sections can be humid and midge-prone in early summer.
logistics.bookingWindows: Boulaide and Nadrin have very few beds; book the whole week's accommodation chain before setting out, not village by village en route.
logistics.transportRules: Luxembourg abolished fares on all domestic trains and buses in 2020 — the Kautenbach train and any connecting local bus within the country cost nothing. This ends at the Belgian border; budget normally for Bastogne–Vianden legs.

other.label: Waymarking
other.text: The Escapardenne Eisleck Trail and Lee Trail both use a white-and-orange stylised "É" blaze on a green background, distinct from Luxembourg's national and local GR markings — confirm you are following the right one where routes cross.

other.label: Luggage transfer
other.text: Several Éislek gîtes offer informal bag-forwarding between villages on request; arrange it a day ahead rather than assuming it is automatic.

other.label: Cash and cards
other.text: Village guesthouses in the Éislek increasingly take cards, but Boulaide and Nadrin are safer with cash in hand.

proTips: Confirm Boulaide's single guesthouse before booking anything else — it is the genuine pinch point of the itinerary.
Ride the Kautenbach–Wiltz branch line at least once if you have spare time; it is one of the more scenic short rail hops in the country.
Eat the Ardennes ham and Éislek-style smoked charcuterie in Wiltz or La Roche rather than waiting for a city — this is the region it comes from.
Use Luxembourg's free transit to scout Day 7's Vianden approach the evening before, rather than discovering the bus timetable cold.
Walk the Le Hérou viewpoint detour near Nadrin even off-schedule; it is a five-minute add for one of the best river views on the route.
Carry a printed stage map for the Belgian sections — trail apps sometimes lose the Escapardenne overlay once across the border.
Time Day 4's lakeside stretch at Insenborn for a swim if the weather allows; it is the only real water-break of the week.

raw.Who It Suits: Steady multi-day walkers who want a low-exposure, forest-and-farmland thru-hike with real villages every night

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 120–135 km, 2,800–3,300 m combined ascent; rolling plateau, river valley, forest track, no exposure
typeSpecific.audience: Steady multi-day walkers who want a low-exposure, forest-and-farmland thru-hike with real villages every night

packingNotes: Trail shoes rather than stiff boots — nothing on this route demands rigid soles, and the terrain rewards lighter footwear.
A proper rain shell; the Éislek plateau gets more rain than its low elevation suggests.
Insect repellent for the river valley evenings, especially Insenborn and the Our valley near Vianden.
A lightweight daypack if using luggage transfer, full pack if not — confirm which before setting out.
A printed Escapardenne stage map as backup to any phone app.
A refillable bottle; village fountains and cafés are reliable, but the open plateau stretches have no taps.
Cash in small denominations for Boulaide and Nadrin.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Boulaide's guesthouse is full.** Fallback: base in Wiltz for two nights and taxi to and from the Boulaide stage start, adding cost but keeping the trail intact.
**Persistent rain turns plateau paths to mud.** Fallback: the route stays walkable in wet weather, but expect stages to run 20–30% slower — build in a buffer rather than rushing to a booked dinner.
**Belgian bus connection from La Roche to Bastogne is missed.** Fallback: a taxi covers the same distance in 30 minutes and is affordable for one leg of an otherwise low-cost week.

**A stage day proves longer than fitness allows.** Fallback: several stages have a mid-point village with a bus link back to the nearest rail line, letting you shorten a day without abandoning the trail.

**Bag-forwarding arrangement falls through.** Fallback: every village on the route is small enough to walk end-to-end with a full pack if forwarding fails; build 30 extra minutes per stage into the plan as insurance.

trips.title: Jotunheimen Hut-to-Hut: Besseggen to Fannaråken

bestPeriod.window: The staffed hut season runs roughly late June to mid-September, and that is the window. Early July still has snow on the high traverses; late August and the first week of September give the most stable conditions
bestPeriod.raw: The staffed hut season runs roughly late June to mid-September, and that is the window. Early July still has snow on the high traverses; late August and the first week of September give the most stable conditions

accommodation.note: DNT staffed huts €45–80 per night for members in dormitory or room, plus €25–40 for dinner and €15–20 for breakfast; DNT membership pays for itself in three nights

food.note: €55–85 per day if eating hut meals; €25–35 self-catering from hut provision stores

transport.note: €180–280: Oslo–Otta train and Valdresekspressen/local buses, the Gjende boat, one taxi transfer

activities.note: Included; optional guided glacier day €120–180

profile.difficultyNote: Hard. 5–8 hours of walking daily, 800–1,300 m of ascent, high exposed terrain and Norway's two highest summits as options

trips.summary: A seven-day hiking & alpine trekking itinerary in Jotunheimen National Park, Innlandet & Vestland, Norway.

itinerary.title: Oslo to Gjendesheim
itinerary.morning: Train Oslo–Otta (about 3 h 30), then the connecting bus over Valdresflye to Gjendesheim at the eastern end of Lake Gjende. The road itself is one of Norway's national tourist routes.
itinerary.afternoon: Check in at Gjendesheim, the DNT lodge at the trailhead. Walk up toward Besshøe for an hour to see tomorrow's ridge in profile and to test your legs at altitude.
itinerary.evening: Hut dinner at a set time — DNT lodges serve one seating, and it is a communal, three-course, genuinely good affair. Fill water bottles; check the morning boat time.
itinerary.dayStats: travel day, 4 km acclimatisation walk

itinerary.title: Besseggen: Memurubu to Gjendesheim
itinerary.morning: The M/S Gjende boat from Gjendesheim to Memurubu, 20 minutes up the lake. Walk the route in this direction — it is the standard, the ascent is on the good side, and the ridge unfolds in front of you.
itinerary.afternoon: The climb to Veslfjellet and then the Besseggen ridge itself: a rock arête with green Lake Gjende on one side, 400 m below, and deep blue Lake Bessvatnet on the other, 100 m higher. There is one steep scrambling step near Bandet where hands are needed. Norway's most walked mountain route and worth every one of its visitors.
itinerary.evening: Descend to Gjendesheim. **Water:** the Bessvatnet shore and the streams below Veslfjellet; the ridge is dry for 5 km.

itinerary.title: Gjendesheim to Memurubu by the north shore, or Gjendebu
itinerary.morning: Take the marked north-shore route toward Memurubu — the quieter, lower alternative that traverses beneath yesterday's ridge.
itinerary.afternoon: Alternatively take the boat the full length of Gjende to Gjendebu, the oldest DNT hut in Jotunheimen (1871), tucked at the western head of the lake with the Svartdalen valley behind it.
itinerary.evening: Memurubu is privately run and the only building on the lake's north shore. Book ahead — it is not a DNT hut and it fills. `verify: true`

itinerary.title: Memurubu to Spiterstulen over Memurubreen
itinerary.morning: The long crossing north-west through the Memurudalen valley into the heart of the range. This is proper high wilderness: no road, no signal, red T-marks on rock.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive Spiterstulen (1,106 m), a family-run mountain lodge at the foot of Galdhøpiggen with a hundred years of climbing history and its own bridge over the Visa river.
itinerary.evening: Early dinner and an early night. **Water:** abundant glacial streams all day — take them from fast-flowing clear tributaries rather than milky glacial melt.

itinerary.title: Galdhøpiggen, 2,469 m
itinerary.morning: From Spiterstulen, the standard route up Northern Europe's highest mountain: a long, steady, non-glaciated ascent over Svellnosbrean's flank on boulder and snowfield. Start at 07:00.
itinerary.afternoon: The summit has a small stone hut and, on a clear day, a view over the entire Jotunheimen massif and west to the Hurrungane. Descend the same way — the descent is where tired legs turn ankles.
itinerary.evening: Spiterstulen again. If you want a glacier experience, book the guided Juvasshytta route with rope and crampons instead — it crosses a live glacier and is guided only. **Water:** streams to about 1,900 m, then nothing.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km return, 1,470 m, 7–9 h

itinerary.title: Spiterstulen to Leirvassbu and on toward Fannaråken
itinerary.morning: Over the Kyrkjeoyme pass to Leirvassbu (1,400 m), a big DNT lodge on a lake beneath the Kyrkja pyramid.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue west toward the Fannaråken approach, or take the bus link toward Krossbu on the Sognefjellet road — at 1,434 m, the highest mountain pass road in Northern Europe.
itinerary.evening: Krossbu or Leirvassbu. Both are working mountain stations with drying rooms and enormous breakfasts.

itinerary.title: Fannaråkhytta and out
itinerary.morning: The climb to Fannaråkhytta at 2,068 m — the highest staffed lodge in Norway, standing on a summit plateau above the Hurrungane peaks and the Sognefjord system. On a clear day you see to Jostedalsbreen, and there is a sauna at the top.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend to Turtagrø on the Sognefjellet road. Bus to Sogndal or back over the pass to Lom, then onward to Oslo or Bergen.

accommodationStrategy.name: DNT staffed lodges
accommodationStrategy.description: The Norwegian Trekking Association's network: bunk or private rooms, three-course dinners, packed-lunch tables where you build your own *matpakke*, drying rooms and boot halls. **Join DNT before you travel** — membership is inexpensive and cuts each night's cost substantially. The huts operate a principle that nobody is turned away, so mattresses on the floor are the overflow, not a locked door.

accommodationStrategy.name: Spiterstulen
accommodationStrategy.description: Privately run since the 19th century, at 1,106 m in the Visdalen valley, with rooms, a campsite and a restaurant. The right base for two nights because the mountain deserves an unhurried start and a real recovery.

accommodationStrategy.name: Memurubu
accommodationStrategy.description: The only accommodation on Gjende's north shore, served by boat. It converts Besseggen from a day hike into a two-way itinerary and gives you the lake at dawn. Book separately from DNT and book early.

logistics.emergency: 113 medical, 112 rescue. Install the **Hjelp 113** app. Norwegian Red Cross and Norsk Folkehjelp staff summer patrols on Besseggen. Signal exists at the huts and on high ridges, not in the valleys.
logistics.weather: Snow can fall on the high passes in any summer month. Yr.no's point forecasts at 1,500 m and 2,000 m are the ones that matter. If a front is coming, huts will advise you plainly — take the advice; DNT staff are not being cautious for insurance reasons.
logistics.bookingWindows: DNT huts are booked through the association's online system; staffed huts take reservations for the summer season and the popular ones — Fannaråkhytta and Gjendesheim in particular — fill for August weekends. Unstaffed self-service huts are unlocked with the standard DNT key, which must be obtained in advance. `verify: true`

other.label: What you must bring
other.text: A **sleeping bag liner (lakenpose) is mandatory** in every DNT hut. Also: cash is not needed — huts are card-based — but signal is not guaranteed, so bring a physical card. Boots with ankle support, gaiters, four-season shell, hat and gloves in any month, sunglasses and high-factor sun cream for snowfield glare.

other.label: Route marking
other.text: Red **T** marks painted on rock and cairns. In fog the T-route is your lifeline; never leave it to shortcut. Snow cover in early season hides marks entirely.

other.label: Glacier rule
other.text: Never step onto a glacier unroped and unguided. Galdhøpiggen from Spiterstulen avoids glacier travel; from Juvasshytta it does not, and the guided crossing there is a scheduled daily service.

other.label: Gear essentials list
other.text: Map (Turkart Jotunheimen 1:50,000) and compass, headtorch, 1.5 l water capacity, blister kit, spare socks, poles, a warm layer you have not used yet, and a foil blanket.

other.label: Booking windows
other.text: DNT huts: as soon as summer bookings open, typically several months ahead for the marquee nights. Memurubu: 3+ months for July and August. The Gjende boat: same-day is usually fine, but the 08:30 sailing is the busy one.

proTips: Walk Besseggen **Memurubu → Gjendesheim**, and take the earliest boat. Two thousand people can be on that ridge on an August Saturday; leaving at 08:00 puts you an hour ahead of the mass.

**Join DNT.** Membership costs less than one night's non-member surcharge across a week, and it also gets you the hut key for the self-service network — which opens up a far quieter version of this route.
Hut breakfasts include a **make-your-own packed lunch table**. Build it properly: this is your entire day's food, and there is nowhere to buy anything.
Fannaråkhytta's **sauna at 2,068 m** is a defensible reason to reorganise your entire week.

Take the **Sognefjellet road** at least one way, by bus. It is the highest pass road in Northern Europe and the transition from the Jotunheimen plateau down toward the fjords is one of Europe's great descents.
Ask hut staff about the next day's snow conditions at breakfast, not the night before. They will have spoken to the walkers who came the other way that morning.
