typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 45 km on the Chemin du Vignoble and bisses paths, gently graded with some steeper vineyard sections
typeSpecific.audience: Native-grape hunters, raclette purists, anyone happy to walk an irrigation channel for an hour to earn a tasting

packingNotes: Comfortable walking shoes for the bisses paths, some of which run along narrow ledges with a rail rather than open ground.
A warm layer for the Val d'Anniviers evening, which cools quickly once the sun drops behind the ridge.
Sun protection; the Valais gets more annual sunshine than almost anywhere else in Switzerland.
A small amount of Swiss franc cash for cooperative cellars and mountain villages.
A light daypack for the Bisse de Clavau and Sentier Viticole walks.
A reusable water bottle; several bisses have safe refill points along the path.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Domaine Chappaz can't fit you in.** Cave La Romaine in Chamoson and Provins in Sion both pour comparable native-grape flights without a booking.
**A thunderstorm closes a bisse path.** Retreat to Château de Villa's cellar-restaurant or the Sion old town museums for the afternoon.
**The last CarPostal down from Grimentz is missed.** A taxi from the village runs the same route in about 35 minutes; arrange it through the raclette cave before dinner rather than after.
**A cooperative cellar is closed for its midday break.** Time cellar visits for mid-afternoon rather than around noon.

**You want Vin des Glaciers and none is available that day.** It is poured irregularly from a communal barrel; ask the Grimentz tourist office which cellar is serving it that week rather than any single address.

trips.title: Moravian Cellars and Bohemian Lager
trips.subRegion: South Moravia, Plzeň Region and Prague

bestPeriod.note: September through mid-October is harvest (vinobraní) season in Moravia; cellars are busiest and most alive but book further ahead.

trips.gatewayAirport: Prague (PRG)
trips.summary: A week from Prague's beer halls to Pilsner Urquell's cellars and on to Moravia's VOC wine villages and cliffside sklepy lanes.
trips.hook: Czechia runs two drinking cultures on two very different clocks: Bohemian lager, brewed to a method fixed at Plzeň in 1842, and Moravian wine, made in villages that still write their own quality rules through a local appellation system. This week does both — three nights in Prague and Plzeň for beer, four in the Mikulov–Znojmo wine country, with a rental car for the cellar lanes where no train goes.

snapshot.Base(s): Prague (2 nights) · Plzeň (1 night) · Mikulov (4 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 480 km by train and car across the week; flat to gently rolling vineyard walking in Moravia, 5–10 km per cellar day
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Prague (PRG); Airport Express bus into the centre, 35–45 min
snapshot.Who It Suits: Drinkers happy to switch registers mid-week, from pub to appellation wine, with a car for the last four days

itinerary.title: Prague, on tap
itinerary.morning: Land in Prague, settle into the centre, and walk down to the Vltava for orientation — Charles Bridge, then up into the Old Town.
itinerary.afternoon: Klášterní pivovar Strahov, the monastery brewhouse inside Strahov Monastery, brews on-site and takes walk-in visitors; the terrace looks out over the whole city. No reservation needed outside peak lunch hours.
itinerary.evening: U Fleku, trading continuously since 1499, serves only its own dark 13° lager, brewed downstairs. It's a tourist fixture, but a genuine one — go for the beer and the fact of the place rather than the food.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 6. Approx. tasting spend: €12–€18.

itinerary.title: Vinohrady, then west
itinerary.morning: Walk Vinohrady, Prague's turn-of-the-century residential district, and stop at a neighbourhood pub for lunch: vepřo-knedlo-zelo, roast pork with bread dumpling and braised cabbage, the baseline Czech plate against which everything else is measured.
itinerary.afternoon: Train to Plzeň, about an hour on a fast regional service from Praha hlavní nádraží. Check in near the historic centre.
itinerary.evening: Walk Plzeň's main square (náměstí Republiky) and the Gothic Cathedral of St. Bartholomew, then dinner at a pub pouring unfiltered, unpasteurised Pilsner Urquell straight from tank — noticeably different from the bottled export version.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 95. Approx. tasting spend: €15–€20.

itinerary.title: Where lager was invented
itinerary.morning: Pilsner Urquell Brewery tour: book online in advance for an English-language slot, since groups fill fast even on weekdays. The tour covers the original 1842 brewhouse and the historic underground cellars, cut 9 kilometres into the sandstone beneath the town, where the beer was matured in oak before refrigeration existed.
itinerary.afternoon: Train back toward Prague, changing there for a fast train south to Brno (total journey around 4h with the connection); alternatively, take an earlier Plzeň departure to make the connection comfortably. Collect a rental car in Brno for the Moravia leg.
itinerary.evening: Drive to Mikulov, about 55 minutes south of Brno. Settle into your base for the next four nights; an easy dinner in the main square.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1 (Pilsner Urquell). Km travelled: 340 (rail plus drive). Approx. tasting spend: €10–€15.

itinerary.title: Mikulov, and the VOC system
itinerary.morning: Walk Mikulov's main square and climb to Mikulov Castle for the view over the Pálava hills and, on a clear day, into Austria. The Dietrichstein family crypt beneath the Church of St. Wenceslas is a quiet ten-minute stop.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive out to Sedlec, one of the villages inside the VOC system — "Vinařská obec," or wine municipality, a set of quality rules that individual village associations write and police themselves, on top of the standard EU designation. VOC Mikulov requires single-variety, single-vintage wines that pass a blind tasting panel before they can carry the local seal; it's stricter, and more locally meaningful, than the regional PDO alone. Look for the VOC seal on the bottle neck at any cellar you visit.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Mikulov: svíčková, marinated beef sirloin in a cream vegetable sauce with bread dumpling and cranberries, alongside a Sedlec Riesling or Pálava (a Moravian cross-variety grown almost nowhere else).
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 30. Approx. tasting spend: €15–€22.

itinerary.title: Velké Pavlovice and the sklepy lanes
itinerary.morning: Drive about 35 minutes to Velké Pavlovice, the unofficial capital of Moravian red wine — Frankovka and André both do well on these south-facing slopes. Walk the village's cellar lane and stop at a family-run sklep with posted tasting hours; several take walk-ins on weekend mornings, but a phone call the day before secures a proper sit-down flight rather than a bottle at the counter.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive on to Nechory near Velké Bílovice for the sklepní uličky — rows of small, low, whitewashed cellar buildings built directly into the hillside, none grander than a garage, each belonging to one family. This is the working, unpolished version of Moravian wine culture, distinct from the château-style tasting rooms further west.
itinerary.evening: Back in Mikulov. Order Moravský vrabec, "Moravian sparrow," a roast pork dish with caraway and garlic, nothing to do with the bird.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 2–3 (village cellars). Km travelled: 60. Approx. tasting spend: €20–€30.

itinerary.title: Znojmo and Šobes
itinerary.morning: Drive about 40 minutes to Znojmo. Znovín Znojmo runs a walk-in visitor centre with a tasting room in town — no reservation needed for a standard flight, though the vineyard tour up to Šobes itself, a dramatically steep site on a bend of the Dyje river inside Podyjí National Park, should be booked a few days ahead through the winery.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk Znojmo's old town and, if time allows, the Znojmo underground — a network of medieval cellar tunnels beneath the streets, unrelated to wine storage but a good wet-weather hour. Znojmo is also known for pickled cucumbers (Znojemské okurky), a protected regional product; buy a jar at the town market if it's running.
itinerary.evening: Last dinner in the Mikulov area. If your week lines up with September, ask about vinobraní — the harvest festival atmosphere spills into ordinary weeknights across the wine villages at this time of year.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 80. Approx. tasting spend: €15–€22.

itinerary.title: Brno market, then home
itinerary.morning: Drive to Brno, about an hour, and drop the rental car. Walk to Zelný trh, the Cabbage Market — a working produce and flower market that has operated on this square since the Middle Ages, open daily (best Tuesday to Saturday mornings).
itinerary.afternoon: Lunch in Brno: a last svíčková or a plate of Moravian cheeses, with a glass of whatever VOC wine the kitchen is pouring by the glass.
itinerary.evening: Train to Prague (about 2h30) to connect with your flight, or fly out of Brno–Tuřany if your itinerary allows it.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 220. Approx. tasting spend: €10–€15.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel near Old Town Square
accommodationStrategy.description: Central enough to walk to Strahov and Vinohrady, with easy access to the airport bus and the train station for the onward leg to Plzeň. Two nights is enough for the beer-culture half of the trip without over-committing to the capital.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Rohatý Krokodýl or similar central Mikulov guesthouse
accommodationStrategy.description: A short walk from the main square and castle, with easy driving access to Sedlec, Velké Pavlovice and Znojmo — the natural hub for a car-based four-night wine stay, since none of the villages themselves have much lodging.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead for September harvest season.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European. Czechia specifics: 155 ambulance, 158 police, 150 fire.
logistics.bookingWindows: Pilsner Urquell tours fill on weekends — book at least a week ahead. Šobes vineyard tours at Znovín should be arranged a few days out. Village sklep visits in Velké Pavlovice and Nechory are best confirmed by phone the day before.
logistics.money: Czechia uses the koruna (CZK), not the euro; cards are widely accepted in cities, but small village cellars often prefer cash.

other.label: Drink-drive alternative
other.text: A designated non-drinking driver is the realistic solution in the wine villages, since cellars are spread across hillsides with no public transport between them; several Mikulov hotels can also arrange a local driver for a half-day cellar circuit. In Prague and Plzeň, walk or use trams and buses — do not drive at all.

other.label: Rental car
other.text: Pick up in Brno on Day 3, not before — there is no need for a car in Prague or Plzeň, and city parking there is a genuine hassle.

other.label: Vignette
other.text: Czech motorways require an electronic vignette; buy it online or at a border kiosk before driving out of Brno.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Rural sklepy keep informal hours, often weekend-only outside harvest season — don't assume a weekday walk-in will find anyone home.

proTips: Order lager "tankové pivo" (tank beer) wherever it's offered in Plzeň — unpasteurised and unfiltered, served straight from insulated tanks rather than kegs, and noticeably softer than the bottled version most people know abroad.
Ask specifically for the VOC seal on a bottle in Moravia; it signals the producer submitted to blind tasting, which is a genuinely useful shortcut when a cellar's whole list is unfamiliar.
Nechory's cellar lane is at its best in late afternoon light — plan the Velké Bílovice stop for 16:00–18:00 rather than midday.
Zelný trh in Brno is a working market, not a tourist stall row — go early for the best produce and to see it as locals use it.
If you can only fit one Moravian appellation village beyond Mikulov, choose Velké Pavlovice for reds or Znojmo for whites and the Šobes vineyard — they represent the two ends of the region's range.
Buy Znojmo pickles at the source; the protected-name product tastes markedly different from supermarket versions elsewhere in the country.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 480 km by train and car across the week; flat to gently rolling vineyard walking in Moravia, 5–10 km per cellar day
raw.Who It Suits: Drinkers happy to switch registers mid-week, from pub to appellation wine, with a car for the last four days

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 480 km by train and car across the week; flat to gently rolling vineyard walking in Moravia, 5–10 km per cellar day
typeSpecific.audience: Drinkers happy to switch registers mid-week, from pub to appellation wine, with a car for the last four days

packingNotes: Comfortable shoes for cobbled town squares and gently sloped vineyard paths.
A light jacket for cellar visits — sklepy and underground tunnels run cool even in summer.
Cash in koruna for rural cellars and market stalls.
International driving permit if your home licence isn't EU-format, plus your rental car documents for the Brno pickup.
A phrasebook or app for Czech; English coverage thins out fast once you leave Prague, Plzeň and the main wine-tourism addresses.
A soft bag or box for wine bottles bought at cellar doors.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A village sklep is shut when you arrive.** Treat any unconfirmed cellar as a bonus; Sedlec and Velké Pavlovice both have enough density that another will usually be open nearby.
**The Plzeň–Brno rail connection runs late.** Build in a buffer day if possible, or collect the rental car a day later and start the Moravia leg from Day 4 instead.
**Harvest season overbooks the Mikulov area.** Book accommodation 8+ weeks ahead for September, and have Znojmo as a lodging backup if Mikulov itself is full.
**Rain washes out a vineyard walk.** Znojmo's underground tunnels and Zelný trh's covered stalls are solid wet-weather alternatives.

trips.title: Baden Wine and the Black Forest Table

bestPeriod.note: Early April brings almond blossom to the Kaiserstuhl; late September and October bring harvest and the first Straußwirtschaften of the year.

trips.gatewayAirport: EuroAirport Basel-Mulhouse-Freiburg (EAP)
trips.summary: A week on Germany's warmest wine hills, from Kaiserstuhl cooperatives and Ortenau growers to the Black Forest kitchen and Freiburg's daily market.
trips.hook: The Kaiserstuhl is an extinct volcano wearing a skirt of loess, and it runs hotter than anywhere else in Germany — which is why Spätburgunder ripens here the way it does nowhere else north of Burgundy. This week works two ends of Baden at once: the cooperative-driven villages of the Kaiserstuhl and Ortenau, and the smoked-ham, cherry-cake kitchen of the Black Forest above them, with Freiburg's cathedral-square market as the daily anchor.

snapshot.Base(s): Freiburg im Breisgau (7 nights, with day trips)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 250 km of day-trip driving; volcanic hill roads with grades up to 15% in the Kaiserstuhl
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to EuroAirport Basel-Mulhouse-Freiburg (EAP), approx. 45 minutes by airport bus to Freiburg
snapshot.Who It Suits: Spätburgunder drinkers, cooperative-cellar tasters, anyone who wants ham, cake and wine in the same afternoon

itinerary.title: Freiburg orientation
itinerary.morning: Land at EuroAirport and take the airport bus to Freiburg, about 45 minutes. Drop bags near the Altstadt.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Münsterplatz, where Freiburg's daily market runs Monday to Saturday, roughly 07:30–13:30, thickest on Wednesday and Saturday — the cathedral's red sandstone tower rises directly over the stalls. Note the Bächle, the shallow water channels threading the old town.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in the Altstadt: Bibeleskäs mit Bubespitzle, fresh herbed quark with hand-rolled potato noodles, a genuine Baden farmhouse dish, with a Freiburg Spätburgunder.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 4 km on foot. Approx. tasting spend: €0.

itinerary.title: Into the Kaiserstuhl
itinerary.morning: Drive west into the Kaiserstuhl, about 25 minutes to Ihringen, the warmest point in Germany and the source of most of the region's Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder. Walk the terraced Winklerberg vineyard, cut into volcanic loess with dry-stone retaining walls.
itinerary.afternoon: Weingut Dr. Heger in Ihringen shows appointment-led tastings; email ahead. For a walk-in alternative, the Winzergenossenschaft Achkarren, one of Germany's oldest wine cooperatives, opened in 1929, pours a full flight with no booking needed.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at a Straußwirtschaft if the calendar allows — these seasonal taverns, licensed by Baden-Württemberg law for a few weeks a year, are the classic setting for Zwiebelkuchen mit Federweißer, onion tart with the cloudy, half-fermented new wine. Outside that window, order Flammkuchen (locally "Dünnele"), the thin-crust tart of cream, onion and bacon, instead.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1–2. Km travelled: 45 km round trip. Approx. tasting spend: €20–30.

itinerary.title: Volcanic villages and the Franz Keller table
itinerary.morning: Drive on to Oberrotweil and Oberbergen, the Kaiserstuhl's highest villages, for a walk along the Vulkanpfad, the marked path explaining the extinct volcano's geology among the vines.
itinerary.afternoon: Weingut Salwey in Oberrotweil pours by appointment; the Winzergenossenschaft Oberbergen/Bickensohl area cooperatives are walk-in.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Schwarzer Adler in Oberbergen, the Keller family's long-established restaurant-with-rooms, built directly into its own vineyard and known for Baden classics done precisely — Schäufele, roasted pork shoulder blade with a dark gravy and Kartoffelsalat, is the dish to order.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 2. Km travelled: 55 km round trip. Approx. tasting spend: €25–35.

itinerary.title: Freiburg market day and the Umweltzone
itinerary.morning: A full morning at the Münsterplatz market: farm cheese, Schwarzwälder Schinken (Black Forest ham, smoked over fir and spruce), stone fruit in season, and bread from the surrounding villages.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Altstadt properly — the university quarter, the Augustinerplatz, the Schwabentor gate. If driving into the city, remember Freiburg's Umweltzone: only cars with a green environmental sticker (Feinstaubplakette) may enter the centre, checked at the ring boundary.
itinerary.evening: Slice of Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte, Black Forest cherry cake, made properly with Schwarzwälder Kirschwasser, the region's protected cherry brandy, at a Konditorei in the old town.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 5 km. Approx. tasting spend: €15–20.

itinerary.title: Ortenau and Durbach
itinerary.morning: Drive north to Durbach, about an hour, where Riesling is grown under its old local name, Klingelberger, on granite rather than the Kaiserstuhl's loess.
itinerary.afternoon: The Durbacher Winzergenossenschaft is walk-in and pours the full Klingelberger range. For a private grower, the historic Schloss Staufenberg estate above the village keeps a public Vinothek with terrace views over the Rhine plain.
itinerary.evening: Return to Freiburg. A lighter dinner: Flädlesuppe, pancake-strip broth, ahead of a Winzergenossenschaft Spätburgunder.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 2. Km travelled: 110 km round trip. Approx. tasting spend: €20–25.

itinerary.title: Up into the Black Forest kitchen
itinerary.morning: Drive up into the hills above Freiburg — the Schauinsland or the villages around Kandel — for the Black Forest side of the trip: working smokehouses and farm kitchens that supply the ham and Kirschwasser tasted on Day 4.
itinerary.afternoon: A farmhouse Vesper plate (cured meats, farm bread, mountain cheese) at a Schwarzwaldhof; several of the working farms sell direct and will explain the smoking process, which takes weeks over cold fir smoke.
itinerary.evening: Back down to Freiburg. A last Kaiserstuhl bottle with dinner in the Altstadt.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 60 km round trip. Approx. tasting spend: €15–20.

itinerary.title: Königschaffhausen and departure
itinerary.morning: A final Kaiserstuhl stop at Königschaffhausen, whose cooperative cellar is known for a particularly structured Spätburgunder from the Steingrüble vineyard. Walk-in tasting, no appointment.
itinerary.afternoon: Last errands at the Münsterplatz market if it is a market day, then the airport bus back to EuroAirport.
itinerary.evening: Departure.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 50 km round trip plus airport transfer. Approx. tasting spend: €10–15.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Oberkirch
accommodationStrategy.description: Faces the cathedral and the market stalls directly, putting the daily food anchor and the old town's restaurants within a two-minute walk; useful for a car-free base between Kaiserstuhl and Ortenau day trips.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Colombi Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: A long-standing Freiburg address a short walk from the Altstadt with private parking, which matters given the number of driving day trips this itinerary needs; ask for a car with the green Umweltzone sticker if renting locally.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead for April and September.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Germany specifics: 110 police, 112 fire/ambulance.
logistics.bookingWindows: Dr. Heger, Salwey, and other private Kaiserstuhl growers pour by appointment; email a week or more ahead, or ask the Kaiserstuhl Tourismus office to arrange it. Cooperative (Winzergenossenschaft) cellars are walk-in with posted hours.
logistics.money: Cards work in Freiburg; village cooperatives and farm stalls often prefer cash.

other.label: The Umweltzone
other.text: Freiburg's low-emission zone requires a green Feinstaubplakette sticker on any car entering the ring road; rental cars from German agencies carry one by default, but check.

other.label: Rail alternative
other.text: The Breisgau-S-Bahn reaches Endingen and the Kaiserstuhlbahn branch serves several villages, though the highest hill villages (Oberrotweil, Achkarren) are car- or taxi-only.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Cooperative tasting rooms usually close Sundays; the Münsterplatz market does not run on Sunday at all.

other.label: Drink-drive alternatives
other.text: With driving days built in, designate a non-tasting driver each day, use a wine-tour minibus service booked through Freiburg or Kaiserstuhl Tourismus, or ride the flat Kaiserstuhl-Radweg between villages by rental or e-bike instead of driving.

proTips: Time a visit for early April if you can: the Kaiserstuhl's almond trees blossom around Ihringen before anywhere else in Germany, and the Mandelblütenweg path is at its best for about two weeks.
Ask any Winzergenossenschaft which single vineyard (Einzellage) a pour comes from — Kaiserstuhl cooperatives blend widely but usually keep a few site-specific bottlings back for tasting only.
Buy Schwarzwälder Schinken direct from a farm smokehouse rather than a supermarket; ask how many weeks it hung, and expect to pay more for it.
The Münsterplatz market is calmest before 09:00; by 11:00 it is standing room only.
Straußwirtschaften post a wreath of fir branches (Besen or Kranz) over the door when open — there is no fixed calendar, so check the current list at the village tourist office.
Ask Schwarzer Adler and similar restaurants for the Kirschwasser used in their Kirschtorte by name; several buy from named local Brennereien worth seeking out separately.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 250 km of day-trip driving; volcanic hill roads with grades up to 15% in the Kaiserstuhl
raw.Who It Suits: Spätburgunder drinkers, cooperative-cellar tasters, anyone who wants ham, cake and wine in the same afternoon

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 250 km of day-trip driving; volcanic hill roads with grades up to 15% in the Kaiserstuhl
typeSpecific.audience: Spätburgunder drinkers, cooperative-cellar tasters, anyone who wants ham, cake and wine in the same afternoon

packingNotes: A car adaptor or app for German fuel-price comparison; Kaiserstuhl villages have few stations.
Comfortable shoes for vineyard-hill walking; loess paths turn to mud after rain.
A cooler bag for ham and cheese bought at farm stalls.
Light layers: the Kaiserstuhl runs several degrees warmer than the Black Forest hills above it.
Cash in small notes for cooperatives and farm sales.
A printed list of Straußwirtschaft opening dates from the tourist office; online listings lag.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A private grower doesn't reply to your email.** Fall back on the local Winzergenossenschaft, which is always walk-in and pours a comparable range.
**You can't find an open Straußwirtschaft.** Order Zwiebelkuchen and Federweißer at any Weinstube during the autumn weeks instead; most kitchens keep it on the menu regardless.
**Rain washes out a hill walk.** Retreat to a cooperative cellar tasting or the K3 ceramics-and-glass museum in Freiburg.
**You've had too much to drive back from the Kaiserstuhl.** Book a taxi in advance — village mobile coverage can be thin — or overnight at a Kaiserstuhl inn rather than returning to Freiburg.
**The Umweltzone catches you without a sticker.** Rental agencies at EuroAirport stock compliant vehicles by default; confirm at pickup rather than after a fine arrives.

trips.title: Riesling on the Mosel Slate

bestPeriod.note: Late September and October bring the Weinfeste and full cellars; May and June give quiet tasting rooms and the same growers pouring last year's vintage.

trips.gatewayAirport: Frankfurt-Hahn (HHN)
trips.summary: A week on the Mosel's blue-slate slopes, tasting Riesling by Prädikat and Grosse Lage from cooperative doors to appointment-only cellars.
trips.hook: The river doubles back on itself six times between Bernkastel and Traben-Trarbach, and the vines follow it up slopes steeper than a staircase. This week is built around slate: the blue-grey Devonian rock that heats the vineyards from below and gives Mosel Riesling its wet-stone bite. You taste at cooperative counters that never close for lunch, and at cellar doors that answer one email a week.

snapshot.Base(s): Bernkastel-Kues (4 nights) · Traben-Trarbach (3 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 60 km between villages by train, bus and river boat; vineyard slopes up to 65% gradient, walked on graded paths only
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Frankfurt-Hahn (HHN), approx. 45 minutes by taxi or the Bernkastel-Kues–Hahn Flughafenshuttle to the Markt
snapshot.Who It Suits: Riesling drinkers, terroir obsessives, anyone who wants to understand why the same grape tastes different fifty metres up a hill

itinerary.title: Arrival on the river bend
itinerary.morning: Land at Frankfurt-Hahn and transfer by taxi or shuttle to Bernkastel-Kues, about 45 minutes through the Hunsrück hills. Drop bags at the Markt.
itinerary.afternoon: Bernkastel's half-timbered market square, the Spitzhäuschen and the St. Michael fountain are the orientation walk. Cross the Balduinbrücke to Kues and back for the view of the town stacked against the vineyard.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at a Straußwirtschaft if one is open — these seasonal wine taverns, licensed for a few weeks a year, serve Zwiebelkuchen mit Federweißer, onion tart with the cloudy, half-fermented new wine, a pairing that only exists in autumn. Outside that window, order the tart with a young Kabinett instead.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 3 km on foot. Approx. tasting spend: €0.

itinerary.title: The Doctor and the Prädikat ladder
itinerary.morning: Walk up into the Bernkasteler Doctor, the vineyard immediately behind the town whose name has been a byword for quality since the 1900s. The path to the Doctor-und-Graben viewpoint gives the full angle of the slope.
itinerary.afternoon: Dr. Loosen's Vinothek on St. Johannishof is walk-in, no appointment needed, and pours a flight across the Prädikat system: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese and, in the right vintage, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, each named for the sugar ripeness (Oechsle) of the grapes at picking, from lightest to most concentrated. Ask them to explain Eiswein alongside it — grapes picked frozen, usually in December. The Mittelmosel-Museum in the same building holds the region's viticultural history, including the wooden monorail carts still used on the steepest rows.
itinerary.evening: Riesling-poached Saibling (char) at a Markt-facing Weinstube, with a Kabinett from the afternoon's tasting.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 5 km. Approx. tasting spend: €20–30.

itinerary.title: Graach, Wehlen and the appointment-only door
itinerary.morning: Regional bus to Graach, then on foot along the Mosel-Weinwanderweg to Wehlen. The path runs through the Wehlener Sonnenuhr, the sundial-marked vineyard that gives the wine its name, and the neighbouring Graacher Himmelreich.
itinerary.afternoon: Joh. Jos. Prüm, in Wehlen, keeps no public tasting room and no signage worth photographing. Visits are by written appointment only, arranged weeks ahead by email through the estate, and the same discretion applies at Willi Schaefer in Graach, a tiny production seen only by prior arrangement. Book both well before the trip if you want in; otherwise taste the same sites' wines, by the glass, at the Weinstube am Markt in Bernkastel that evening.
itinerary.evening: Cross back by the passenger ferry from Zeltingen if it is running, or the regional bus, for dinner in Bernkastel-Kues.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0–1 (reservation-dependent). Km travelled: 9 km. Approx. tasting spend: €15–25.

itinerary.title: Ürzig's red slate and the VDP pyramid
itinerary.morning: Bus or train to Ürzig. The Ürziger Würzgarten sits on reddish, iron-rich slate rather than the usual blue-grey, and the wines carry a spice note locals will tell you comes straight from the soil.
itinerary.afternoon: Markus Molitor's Vinothek in Bernkastel (Trabener Straße) sells across the range and pours a walk-in flight; the cellars themselves, spread over more than twenty parcels in Bernkastel, Wehlen, Zeltingen and Erden, are shown only by arrangement. Ask for a Grosses Gewächs if they are pouring one: the VDP (Verband Deutscher Prädikatsweingüter) classifies its members' best single vineyards as VDP.Grosse Lage, roughly the Mosel's equivalent of a grand cru, and a dry wine from a Grosse Lage site labelled Grosses Gewächs (GG) is hand-harvested and released later than everyday bottlings.
itinerary.evening: Erden, next door, holds the Erdener Prälat and Erdener Treppchen sites. Dinner in Ürzig, river trout with new potatoes.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 12 km. Approx. tasting spend: €20–30.

itinerary.title: Downriver to Traben-Trarbach
itinerary.morning: Take the Kolb-Linie passenger boat (seasonal) or the regional bus from Bernkastel-Kues, past Kröv, to Traben-Trarbach — about 40 minutes either way.
itinerary.afternoon: Traben-Trarbach's fortune came from the wine trade, and the Jugendstil villas along the Moselufer, built by wine merchants around 1900, are the result. Walk up to the ruined Grevenburg or across to Mont Royal, the earthworks of a 17th-century French fortress on the hillside above town, for the long view down the valley.
itinerary.evening: Selbach-Oster's Vinothek in neighbouring Zeltingen is walk-in and worth the short detour if timed with the boat; otherwise taste the Traben-Trarbach range at a riverside Weinstube.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 8 km. Approx. tasting spend: €20–25.

itinerary.title: Calmont, the steepest vineyard in Europe
itinerary.morning: Drive or take a taxi from Traben-Trarbach to Bremm, about 40 minutes downriver, for the Calmont — Europe's steepest vineyard, worked on slopes over 65% gradient with monorail carts (Schrägaufzüge) because no tractor can climb it. The Calmont-Klettersteig via ferrata runs along its top edge for those with a head for exposure; the lower Calmont-Panoramaweg gives the same view without the cable.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Zell, home of the "Schwarze Katz" (black cat) vineyard, an old marketing name now attached to a real Ortslage. Lunch on the river.
itinerary.evening: Back to Traben-Trarbach. A quiet dinner; this is the longest driving day of the week.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0–1. Km travelled: 80 km round trip. Approx. tasting spend: €10–20.

itinerary.title: Piesport, the Roman ship, and departure
itinerary.morning: Regional bus or train to Neumagen-Dhron, the oldest documented wine town on the Mosel, where a Roman relief of a wine ship — the Neumagener Weinschiff — was excavated; a replica stands by the church. Walk on to Piesport.
itinerary.afternoon: The Piesporter Goldtröpfchen forms a natural amphitheatre above the village, one of the Mosel's best-known south-facing sites. A last tasting at a village cooperative counter, then transfer back toward Frankfurt-Hahn.
itinerary.evening: Departure from Hahn, or an overnight near the airport if the flight is early.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 15 km plus approx. 60 km transfer. Approx. tasting spend: €15–20.

accommodationStrategy.name: Romantik Hotel zur Post
accommodationStrategy.description: On the Markt, a few steps from the bridge and the bus stop, this long-established house has hosted the wine trade for generations; the restaurant pours deep into the local list, and staff will call ahead to arrange the reservation-only cellar visits.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–10 weeks ahead for September and October.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Bellevue
accommodationStrategy.description: The Art Nouveau hotel that anchors the Moselufer, built by the wine trade at its 1900s peak and still trading. Rooms on the river side put you steps from the boat pier and the bridge to Trarbach.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Germany specifics: 110 police, 112 fire/ambulance. Mobile coverage is reliable along the valley, patchy on the high vineyard tracks above Calmont.
logistics.bookingWindows: J.J. Prüm, Willi Schaefer and similarly small growers do not run tasting rooms; email the estate directly, weeks ahead, stating your dates and group size, or ask the Bernkastel-Kues tourist office (part of Moselwein e.V.'s network) to make the introduction.
logistics.money: Cards are accepted at hotels and larger Weinstuben; small growers and market stalls prefer cash — carry €50–€80 in small notes.

other.label: Rail and bus
other.text: Bernkastel-Kues has no passenger rail station; the nearest is Wittlich, connected by bus. Piesport and Neumagen-Dhron sit on the Trier–Koblenz line. A VRT (Verkehrsverbund Region Trier) day ticket covers buses and trains across the valley.

other.label: The Kolb-Linie boats
other.text: run seasonally, roughly Easter to October, and stop for weather; check the day's schedule at the pier before planning a one-way trip.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Village Vinotheken often close Sunday and Monday outside the main season; cooperative tasting rooms keep the most reliable hours.

other.label: Drink-drive alternatives
other.text: Do not drive between tastings. Use the VRT buses, the Kolb-Linie boat, a pre-booked taxi (ask your hotel), or spread tastings across a walking or e-bike day on the flat Mosel-Radweg between villages.

proTips: Email reservation-only estates at least six weeks out; the smallest growers answer correspondence once a week and September fills first.
Ask any Vinothek to pour a "vertical by Prädikat" — the same vineyard's Kabinett through Auslese side by side — it explains the whole system in fifteen minutes.
The Bernkasteler Doctor viewpoint is best walked in late afternoon light, when the slate visibly darkens the closer rows.
Buy futures (Subskription) if a grower offers it; VDP estates release Grosses Gewächs the following September at a lower price than the finished bottle.
Skip the Calmont via ferrata cable if you are short on time — the Panoramaweg gives the same view from the same ridge without the harness.
Ask cooperative staff which Ortsteil (village subsection) a pour comes from; Mosel labels can be confusing and locals read them instantly.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 60 km between villages by train, bus and river boat; vineyard slopes up to 65% gradient, walked on graded paths only
raw.Who It Suits: Riesling drinkers, terroir obsessives, anyone who wants to understand why the same grape tastes different fifty metres up a hill

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 60 km between villages by train, bus and river boat; vineyard slopes up to 65% gradient, walked on graded paths only
typeSpecific.audience: Riesling drinkers, terroir obsessives, anyone who wants to understand why the same grape tastes different fifty metres up a hill

packingNotes: Comfortable shoes with grip; vineyard tracks are steep gravel, not pavement.
A light rain shell; the valley catches river-borne showers even on sunny forecasts.
A soft cooler bag or bottle sleeves for anything you buy at cellar doors.
A phrasebook or app for German wine terms (trocken, feinherb, süß) — not every small grower's English extends to nuance.
Cash in small notes.
A daypack for the Neumagen-to-Piesport and Calmont walks.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A reservation-only estate doesn't answer.** Have a walk-in backup ready (Dr. Loosen, Markus Molitor's Vinothek, Selbach-Oster) for the same afternoon.
**The Kolb-Linie boat is cancelled for high water or wind.** Fall back to the regional bus; the ride is less scenic but the same journey time.
**Rain closes out a vineyard walk.** Retreat to the Mittelmosel-Museum or a cellar tasting; slate paths get genuinely slippery wet.
**Calmont's via ferrata is closed for maintenance.** The lower Panoramaweg stays open and gives comparable views.
**You've tasted too much to drive back from Bremm.** Book a taxi for the return leg in advance; mobile signal on that stretch can be weak.

trips.title: The Sherry Triangle: Solera, Tabanco & the Bajo de Guía
trips.subRegion: Marco de Jerez — Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María, Sanlúcar de Barrameda & Cádiz

bestPeriod.window: Late February–early June & late September–early November
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (38–42°C inland, bodegas hot and half-staffed) and Feria del Caballo week in May, when Jerez prices double
bestPeriod.raw: Late February–early June & late September–early November

accommodation.note: Jerez palacete €90–€140 pppn; Sanlúcar and Cádiz €70–€120

food.note: Tabanco tapas €2.50–€5; Bajo de Guía langostinos €28–€45; one tasting menu €80–€120

transport.note: Regional trains, taxis between the three towns, one hired driver day

activities.note: 8–10 bodega visits €18–€50, sherry-vinegar visit, cookery class €75–€110

profile.difficultyNote: 1/5 — flat towns, one beach walk, sand at Bajo de Guía

trips.gatewayAirport: XRY Jerez, 15 min taxi to Jerez centre; SVQ Seville 1 h 15 min by car, 1 h 10 m by train
trips.summary: Three towns, twenty kilometres apart, producing wines that cannot legally be made in each other's cellars. You spend the week learning why: albariza chalk, the flor yeast veil, the fractional blending of the solera, and the sea humidity that makes Sanlúcar's manzanilla thinner and saltier than Jerez's fino from identical grapes. Between visits it is a tapas trip — tabancos where a copa costs €1.60, Cádiz's Mercado Central, langostinos at the Guadalquivir mouth, retinto beef from the Vejer marshes. Cheap for what it is, and the most technically interesting wine week in Spain.

itinerary.title: Jerez: albariza, flor, first copa
itinerary.morning: Arrive at XRY, drop bags, and walk Jerez's old town to the Alcázar and the Cathedral of San Salvador, which stands above the historic bodega quarter.
itinerary.afternoon: The orientation visit at **González Byass (Tío Pepe)** — the Gustave Eiffel-attributed La Concha bodega, the venencia demonstration, and the Colors of Sherry flight covering fino through PX.
itinerary.evening: Tabanco crawl on Calle Santa María: **El Pasaje** for sherry from the butt and a 22:00 flamenco set, then **Tabanco Plateros** for chicharrones.
itinerary.dayStats: 1 bodega / González Byass tours €25.50–€50 / tabanco copa €1.60–€2.60, tapa €2.50–€4 / 15 min airport transfer
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Bodega Tío Pepe or Casa Palacio María Luisa, Jerez

itinerary.title: Old wines and the almacenista idea
itinerary.morning: **Bodegas Tradición** for VOS and VORS only — amontillado and palo cortado with 30-plus years of average age, plus the Zurbarán and Goya canvases upstairs.
itinerary.afternoon: **Bodegas Lustau** for the almacenista range, which bottles other people's soleras under their names — the clearest lesson in how the trade actually works.
itinerary.evening: **Mantúa** (Michelin-starred, Jerez) if you want the modern kitchen, or **Albalá** for a shorter, cheaper version of the same idea.
itinerary.dayStats: 2 bodegas / Tradición €40–€60, Lustau €18–€30 / VORS bottle band €55–€120 / all walking, no car
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Bodega Tío Pepe or Casa Palacio María Luisa, Jerez

itinerary.title: El Puerto de Santa María and the river bodegas
itinerary.morning: Train from Jerez to El Puerto (12 min). Visit **Gutiérrez Colosía**, whose butts sit metres from the Guadalete mouth — the humidity gives a visibly thicker flor than Jerez.
itinerary.afternoon: **Bodegas Osborne** and the Toro bull, then fried fish from a *freiduría* on Calle Misericordia, eaten in a paper cone with a copa from the bar next door, which is legal and expected.
itinerary.evening: **Aponiente**, Ángel León's three-star in a tidal mill on the salt marsh, if you booked months ago; otherwise **Romerijo** for a kilo of prawns.
itinerary.dayStats: Train €4 return / 2 bodegas / Colosía €18–€25 / freiduría cone €8–€14 / Aponiente tasting menu €250+
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Bodega Tío Pepe or Casa Palacio María Luisa, Jerez

itinerary.title: Sanlúcar: manzanilla and the Bajo de Guía
itinerary.morning: Transfer to Sanlúcar (35 min). **Barbadillo** in the Barrio Alto for Solear and the manzanilla pasada, then a walk down to the Barrio Bajo.
itinerary.afternoon: **La Guita** or **Hidalgo-La Gitana** for the second angle, then the Doñana view across the Guadalquivir from the Fábrica de Hielo.
itinerary.evening: **Casa Bigote** at Bajo de Guía: langostinos de Sanlúcar, acedías, and a cold half-bottle of manzanilla en rama that costs less than the starter.
itinerary.dayStats: 35 min transfer / 2 bodegas / fees €15–€30 / langostinos €28–€45 per ración / manzanilla bottle €7–€14
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Posada de Palacio, Sanlúcar de Barrameda

itinerary.title: Cádiz market day
itinerary.morning: Drive or bus to Cádiz (45 min) and go straight to the **Mercado Central de Abastos** — the Rincón Gastronómico stalls sell erizos, tuna mojama and a plate of gambas you eat standing up.
itinerary.afternoon: The sea wall from La Caleta to the Castillo de San Sebastián, then the **Torre Tavira** camera obscura for the peninsula's rooftop geography.
itinerary.evening: **Taberna Casa Manteca** in La Viña for chicharrón especial de Cádiz on waxed paper, then **El Faro de Cádiz** for a proper sit-down.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 min each way / market plates €3–€9 / Torre Tavira €8 / no bodega today, palate rest
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Posada de Palacio, Sanlúcar de Barrameda

itinerary.title: Vejer: retinto, vinegar and a kitchen
itinerary.morning: Drive inland to **Vejer de la Frontera**, a white hill town above the Barbate marshes, and take the cookery class at **Annie B's Spanish Kitchen** — tortillitas de camarones and a sherry reduction.
itinerary.afternoon: Retinto beef tasting at **Venta El Toro** or a visit to a sherry-vinegar solera at **Bodegas Páez Morilla** in Jerez on the way back, where the acetification bodega smells nothing like the wine one.
itinerary.evening: **Restaurante Trafalgar** on Vejer's Plaza de España, or back in Jerez at **Tabanco San Pablo**.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 min Sanlúcar–Vejer / class €75–€110, 4 h / vinegar visit €12–€20 / retinto steak €22–€32

itinerary.title: Pagos, horses and out
itinerary.morning: A vineyard morning, not a cellar one: ask a bodega to run you into the **Macharnudo** or **Balbaína** pago to see albariza chalk, white and spongy, holding winter rain through a rainless summer.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Real Escuela Andaluza del Arte Ecuestre** in Jerez for the Thursday or Friday "Cómo bailan los caballos andaluces" show, then last bottles at **La Casa del Jerez**.
itinerary.evening: Early flight from XRY, 15 minutes away, or the 1 h 10 m train to Seville.
itinerary.dayStats: Vineyard visit €25–€45 / equestrian show €22–€30 / XRY 15 min / duty-free sherry travels badly in the hold — pack upright
itinerary.sleep: Airport hotel or overnight in Seville

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Bodega Tío Pepe
accommodationStrategy.description: Inside the González Byass complex, so the Day 1 tour starts downstairs and you can walk to every tabanco on Calle Santa María. Rooms overlook the cellar courtyards; €120–€200 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Casa Palacio María Luisa
accommodationStrategy.description: An eighteenth-century palace on Calle Tornería with a courtyard and a serious sherry list, two minutes from the cathedral. Better rooms, no bodega noise; €160–€260.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Posada de Palacio
accommodationStrategy.description: A converted eighteenth-century house minutes from Barbadillo and ten minutes' walk down to the Bajo de Guía seafood strip, which matters because you will not be driving after dinner. €80–€140 double.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming, no surcharge. 4G/5G throughout; the only dead spots are inside thick-walled bodega naves.
logistics.emergency: 112, including Salvamento Marítimo for the Guadalquivir mouth. Hospital Universitario de Jerez is the main hospital; EHIC/GHIC accepted.
logistics.weather: Two winds define the trip. **Levante**, hot and easterly, dries the air and shrinks the flor; **poniente**, humid and westerly off the Atlantic, feeds it. Bodegas open windows for the poniente. Summer inland highs hit 42°C; Cádiz stays 8–10°C cooler.
logistics.bookingWindows: Aponiente 3–6 months. Bodegas Tradición 3–4 weeks by email. González Byass and Barbadillo 3–7 days online. Almacenista visits are arranged through Lustau or a specialist guide, not directly. Feria del Caballo hotels sell out six months out.
logistics.money: Eurozone. Cards work almost everywhere; tabancos and market stalls are quicker with coins. Tipping is minimal — round up, or 5–10% for a full restaurant meal.
logistics.transportRules: The Renfe C-1 line links Jerez, El Puerto and Cádiz cheaply and frequently; Sanlúcar has no rail service, only buses and taxis. Blood-alcohol limit is 0.5 g/l, 0.3 for drivers licensed under two years, and roadside checks around Jerez are routine. Parking inside Cádiz's old town is close to impossible — use the Canalejas underground car park.
logistics.permits: Bodega visits are timed and ticketed; walk-ins are refused at González Byass and Tradición. Shipping a case costs €25–€60 within Europe.
logistics.health: Tap water is drinkable across all three towns. Fino and manzanilla are 15% abv and drink deceptively like white wine — a tabanco round is stronger than it tastes. Sun on the Bajo de Guía sand is unshaded from noon.

proTips: Buy fino and manzanilla by bottling date, not vintage. Anything over a year old has lost the flor character you came for; the *saca* date is usually on the back label or the neck.
Do González Byass first and Bodegas Tradición second, never the reverse. The big tour teaches the solera mechanics you need to appreciate a 30-year VORS.

Order the same style in all three towns on consecutive days — fino in Jerez, fino-manzanilla in El Puerto, manzanilla in Sanlúcar — from the same producer where possible. That comparison is the whole trip in three glasses.
Ask to see the venencia used properly. In a real bodega the venenciador draws through the flor without breaking the veil, and the pour from arm's length is aeration, not theatre.
Tabancos are not tourist bars: they were wine shops that grew a counter. Order by the copa from the butt behind the bar rather than from the bottle list, and expect chalk marks instead of a receipt.
In Sanlúcar, eat at Bajo de Guía at 21:00, not 20:00. The langostinos land in the afternoon and the good places serve the day's catch late.
Sherry vinegar deserves a purchase alongside the wine. A Reserva vinegar from a solera costs €10–€18 and is the single most useful souvenir of the week.
If your dates fall near an *en rama* saca — March–April or September–October — ask the bodega to open one. It is the release that changes materially year to year.

raw.The DOs: **DO Jerez-Xérès-Sherry** and **DO Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda** share a production zone but manzanilla may only be aged in Sanlúcar. **DO Vinagre de Jerez** covers the vinegars. Grapes: **Palomino Fino** for almost everything, **Pedro Ximénez** and **Moscatel** for the sweet wines. The best vineyards are **albariza** chalk in the pagos of Macharnudo, Balbaína, Carrascal and Añina — Macharnudo Alto is the grand cru.
raw.Styles: **Fino** and **manzanilla** age biologically under flor, 15–15.5% abv, and are living wines — buy the most recent bottling. **Amontillado** starts under flor and finishes oxidatively; **oloroso** never has flor, fortified to 17%+; **palo cortado** is the anomaly, the aromatics of amontillado with the body of oloroso. **PX** is raisined and sweet to 400+ g/l. **VOS** (aged over 20 years) and **VORS** (over 30) are certified by cask analysis. **En rama** means minimally filtered, released in seasonal *sacas*, usually spring and autumn.
raw.Solera and criadera: Butts stack in scales: the *solera* is the floor row wine is drawn from, the *criaderas* the rows above that replenish it. Fractional blending means no vintage exists and average age is a property of the extraction rate — ask each guide what percentage they draw a year.
raw.Bodegas, large and small: **González Byass (Tío Pepe)**, Calle Manuel María González 12, Jerez, books online at tiopepe.com: the Tío Pepe Experience around €25.50, Colors of Sherry €28.50, tapas versions €30.50–€33.50, and a Premium VORS tour at €50; Tuesday–Sunday, advance reservation required, English guides standard, phone +34 956 357 016. **Bodegas Tradición** (Jerez) is the counterpoint — VOS/VORS only plus a private Spanish painting collection, small groups, email weeks ahead, roughly €40–€60. **Bodegas Lustau** runs an almacenista programme. In Sanlúcar, **Barbadillo** sells tours online; **La Guita** and **Hidalgo-La Gitana** run smaller visits. In El Puerto, **Osborne** and riverfront **Gutiérrez Colosía**. *Almacenistas* — stockholders who age but never bottle — are the connoisseur's visit, arranged through Lustau or a specialist guide.
raw.Producers beyond wine: **Tabanco El Pasaje**, Calle Santa María 8, Jerez — the oldest surviving tabanco, sherry from the butt, daily flamenco. **Tabanco Plateros** and **Tabanco San Pablo** complete the crawl. **Casa Balbino** on Plaza del Cabildo, Sanlúcar, for tortillitas de camarones. **Casa Bigote** and **Joselito Huerta** at Bajo de Guía for langostinos de Sanlúcar. In Cádiz, the **Mercado Central de Abastos** and its Rincón Gastronómico stalls. **Venta El Toro** and **Trafalgar** in Vejer for retinto. Sherry vinegar at **Bodegas Páez Morilla** and Lustau's vinegar soleras.
raw.Season and timing: *Vendimia* runs mid-August to mid-September, brutally hot, with Jerez's **Fiesta de la Vendimia** in early September. *En rama* sacas land around March–April and September–October, the best weeks for flor wine. Avoid **Feria del Caballo** in May unless you want horses more than wine.
raw.Hands-on element and driving: A half-day class at **Annie B's Spanish Kitchen** in Vejer de la Frontera — tortillitas de camarones, a sherry reduction, retinto — €75–€110, English-taught, two weeks' notice. Spain's limit is 0.5 g/l (0.3 under two years' licence) and checks are routine. Use **Renfe** C-1: Jerez–El Puerto 12 min, Jerez–Cádiz 40 min, €4–€7. Sanlúcar has no station — taxi or the M-050 bus. **Sherry Explorers** and **Turismo Sabor** run English-speaking driver days at €280–€450 per car.

sources.verified: González Byass / Tío Pepe's own experiences page listing the Tío Pepe Experience at €25.50, Colors of Sherry at €28.50, Between Tapas at €30.50, Between Wines and Tapas at €33.50 and Premium VORS at €50, Tuesday–Sunday with advance reservation and telephone booking on +34 956 357 016; Barbadillo's public visits page for Sanlúcar; the existence and separate legal status of DO Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda.
sources.confidenceNotes: Tradición, Lustau, La Guita, Hidalgo and Gutiérrez Colosía fees are estimated bands — re-check, as several bodegas moved to timed online-only ticketing. Aponiente's season, price and closures change annually; confirm before building Day 3 around it. Casa Bigote and Casa Balbino close on varying weekdays. Annie B's runs a seasonal calendar. En rama saca timing varies by producer and is not fixed. Hotel rates are prior-season estimates.

trips.title: The Côte d'Or, Climat by Climat
trips.subRegion: Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune, Burgundy

bestPeriod.note: Late September to mid-October overlaps harvest (vendange); domaines are busiest and some close tasting rooms for a week at a time.

trips.gatewayAirport: Lyon-Saint-Exupéry (LYS)
trips.summary: A week walking the Côte d'Or's Grand Cru and Premier Cru climats, from Beaune's covered market to domaines that answer email in weeks, not days.
trips.hook: A single ridge, barely 60 km end to end, carries more named, legally defined vineyard parcels than anywhere else on earth — the climats, mapped by monks and refined for eight centuries, now a UNESCO World Heritage landscape. This week is built on foot and by train along that ridge, from the Côte de Nuits' reds down through Beaune to the Côte de Beaune's whites, with the market, the Hospices and the protocol for actually getting a domaine to say yes.

snapshot.Base(s): Beaune (7 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 70 km by train and bike across the week; flat vineyard paths, 8–15 km per walking/cycling day
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Lyon-Saint-Exupéry (LYS) or Paris; TGV to Le Creusot TGV or Dijon, then TER to Beaune (approx. 20 min)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Serious wine drinkers willing to email ahead and walk between villages rather than be driven

itinerary.title: Beaune, inside the ramparts
itinerary.morning: Arrive via TGV to Dijon or Le Creusot TGV, then the short TER connection into Beaune. Walk the old town's ramparts, the fortified circuit that still rings the centre, and get your bearings from the Place Carnot.
itinerary.afternoon: Approach the Hôtel-Dieu from outside first — the polychrome tile roof is the image everyone has of Beaune, and the courtyard is free to view. Save the interior museum for tomorrow.
itinerary.evening: Dinner near the ramparts: oeufs en meurette, poached eggs in a reduced red wine sauce with lardons and pearl onions, is the dish to start the week on. A village-level Beaune red or a Hautes-Côtes de Beaune sits well with it.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 4. Approx. tasting spend: €15–€20.

itinerary.title: The market, and two walk-in cellars
itinerary.morning: Beaune's Saturday market fills Place Carnot and nearby streets from about 08:00 to 13:00 — cheese, produce, a proper crowd of locals. Structure the week so this day lands on a Saturday if you can; a smaller Wednesday market is the fallback.
itinerary.afternoon: Two walk-in tastings, no reservation needed: the Marché aux Vins, a cellar tasting cut into the town's old church crypts, and Patriarche Père et Fils, holder of the largest cellars in Burgundy — around 5 km of tunnels under the former Couvent des Visitandines — with a self-guided route through them.
itinerary.evening: Dinner: jambon persillé, a cold terrine of ham set in parsleyed white wine aspic, a Burgundian Easter dish served year-round in Beaune's better bistros.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 2 (walk-in). Km travelled: 5. Approx. tasting spend: €20–€30.

itinerary.title: Pommard and Volnay, on foot
itinerary.morning: Walk south from Beaune on the vineyard paths toward Pommard, about 4 km — the first village of the Côte de Beaune, known for structured, mineral reds. The path runs directly between the rows; note the small stone signs (bornes) marking where one climat ends and the next begins.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Volnay, another 3 km, through Premier Cru sites like Clos des Chênes and Caillerets. This is the practical way to learn the hierarchy: Bourgogne regional at the base, village appellation (Volnay, Pommard) above that, Premier Cru naming a specific parcel, and Grand Cru — the rarest tier, about 1% of production — reserved for a short list of the most prized sites.
itinerary.evening: Reservation tasting at a small Pommard or Volnay domaine, booked by email 4–6 weeks ahead, or via the Beaune tourist office's list of domaines open to visitors. Expect a modest fee and a real expectation you'll buy a bottle or two.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 14 (round trip). Approx. tasting spend: €25–€40.

itinerary.title: Clos de Vougeot and the Côte de Nuits
itinerary.morning: TER train north from Beaune to Vougeot (about 12 minutes), then walk to the Château du Clos de Vougeot — seat of the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin and the walled Grand Cru vineyard itself, one of the Côte de Nuits' oldest sites, planted by Cistercian monks. The château interior is open without reservation, small entrance fee.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue on foot or by local bus to Vosne-Romanée. You will not get inside Domaine de la Romanée-Conti — it receives no public visitors, and that scarcity is itself the lesson: some of Burgundy's most quoted names are not for sale as an experience, only as a very expensive bottle. Walk the lane past the Romanée-Conti and La Tâche parcels from the public road instead.
itinerary.evening: Reservation tasting at Domaine Faiveley in Nuits-Saint-Georges, booked several weeks ahead by email — a long-established, serious Côte de Nuits house that does receive visitors in a proper cellar setting.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1 (plus Clos de Vougeot château). Km travelled: 10. Approx. tasting spend: €30–€45.

itinerary.title: Gevrey-Chambertin, and Dijon's mustard
itinerary.morning: Train to Gevrey-Chambertin, home to nine Grand Cru climats including Chambertin itself, the vineyard Napoleon reportedly never travelled without. Walk the short loop through the village and up into the lower rows.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue by train to Dijon, 20 minutes further north, for a change of register: the Maille boutique on Rue de la Liberté sells mustard drawn straight from the tap, an old Dijon tradition, and the half-timbered old town is worth an unhurried two hours.
itinerary.evening: Back to Beaune. Dinner built around Époisses, the pungent washed-rind cheese from a village 30 minutes northwest, paired with a structured Gevrey-Chambertin.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0 (village walking + Dijon). Km travelled: 45 (rail). Approx. tasting spend: €10–€15.

itinerary.title: Cycling the Côte de Beaune
itinerary.morning: Rent a bike in Beaune and ride the Voie des Vignes, the region's dedicated vineyard cycle route, south toward Santenay — about 16 km one-way, quiet lanes and greenway, flat and well-signed.
itinerary.afternoon: Stop in Chassagne-Montrachet and Puligny-Montrachet, straddling the Grand Cru Montrachet vineyard — split between the two communes, considered by many the finest dry white vineyard anywhere. A reservation tasting at a village-level producer (arranged by email in advance) is more realistic than any Grand Cru bottle, but standing at the parcel's edge is worth the ride alone.
itinerary.evening: Return to Beaune by bike or by folding the bike onto a TER service. Dinner: coq au vin, the other Burgundian standard, paired with a Chassagne-Montrachet white if the day's tasting has put you in the mood for more.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 32 (round trip cycling). Approx. tasting spend: €25–€35.

itinerary.title: Last cellar, and out
itinerary.morning: A final reservation tasting somewhere you didn't reach earlier in the week — Bouchard Père & Fils or Louis Jadot in Beaune both run structured cellar visits by appointment, and take bookings a day or two ahead outside peak season.
itinerary.afternoon: Buy at the source: most domaines ship, but a hand-carried case is part of the week for most visitors.
itinerary.evening: TER to Dijon or Le Creusot TGV, connecting onward to Lyon or Paris for the flight home.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 40 (rail). Approx. tasting spend: €30–€50.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Le Cep
accommodationStrategy.description: A cluster of 16th- and 17th-century buildings inside the ramparts, a short walk from the Hôtel-Dieu, the market square and the station — the best-located base for a week run almost entirely on foot and rail.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–10 weeks ahead for autumn.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel des Remparts
accommodationStrategy.description: A quieter courtyard hotel a few streets from Place Carnot, useful if Le Cep's rates push the budget too far while keeping the same walkable position.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: A chambre d'hôtes in Pommard or Volnay
accommodationStrategy.description: Trades city convenience for waking inside the vineyard rows; a fair alternative for the middle nights if you'd rather walk to a domaine than take a train. Confirm the owner can store bikes and bottles securely.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; also 15 (SAMU medical), 17 (police), 18 (fire) work directly in France.
logistics.weather: Summer afternoons on the open vineyard paths offer no shade at all; carry water on the Pommard–Volnay and Voie des Vignes days.
logistics.bookingWindows: Email 4–6 weeks ahead in French or English; state party size and whether you plan to buy. The Beaune Office de Tourisme and the BIVB (Bureau Interprofessionnel des Vins de Bourgogne) both maintain lists of domaines currently open to visitors and can relay requests to smaller producers.
logistics.money: Cards are accepted everywhere in Beaune; smaller cellar-door sales sometimes prefer cash for round numbers.

other.label: Minimum spend
other.text: Small domaines rarely charge a hard tasting fee but expect a purchase; treat €40–€80 in bottles as the unwritten cost of a good visit.

other.label: Drink-drive alternative
other.text: Do not rent a car. The TER Dijon–Beaune–Chalon-sur-Saône line stops at or near most villages named here (Vougeot, Nuits-Saint-Georges, Gevrey-Chambertin), and the Voie des Vignes cycle route covers the Côte de Beaune villages Beaune does not reach by rail.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Harvest (usually mid-September to early October) can close small domaines' tasting rooms without much notice — confirm the week of your visit, not just when you first book.

proTips: Learn the hierarchy before Day 3: regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru. Every list and domaine explains itself in these terms — the fastest way to read a Burgundy label correctly.
Walk past Romanée-Conti's vines deliberately — how small and unremarkable the parcel looks against its reputation is itself the point of Day 4.
Visit the Hôtel-Dieu interior late morning; tour groups cluster earlier and the museum is far quieter after 11:30.
At Patriarche, walk the route slowly — the tasting cup (tastevin) given at the start is yours to keep, and refills are unlimited within it.
Rent bikes the evening before the Voie des Vignes day; ramparts shops run low on good bikes by 09:30 in peak season.
Ask any domaine whether they're a récoltant (grower-producer) or buy in grapes — it changes what you're tasting, and most are glad to explain it.

raw.Who It Suits: Serious wine drinkers willing to email ahead and walk between villages rather than be driven

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 70 km by train and bike across the week; flat vineyard paths, 8–15 km per walking/cycling day
typeSpecific.audience: Serious wine drinkers willing to email ahead and walk between villages rather than be driven

packingNotes: Comfortable walking shoes for vineyard paths that turn to packed dirt or light gravel.
A sunhat; the Côte's open rows offer almost no shade between villages.
A soft-sided wine bag or two, or ship bottles home via a domaine's export service rather than carrying a full case.
Smart-casual layers for evening — Beaune's better restaurants expect more than trail wear.
A phrasebook or app; smaller domaines outside Beaune are less consistently English-speaking than the town itself.
A printed copy of tasting confirmations; rural cellar signal can be unreliable.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A reservation-only domaine doesn't reply.** Fall back to Beaune's walk-in cellars (Patriarche, Marché aux Vins, Bouchard) — genuinely serious tastings without an appointment.
**Harvest closes a domaine mid-visit-window.** This is normal in late September; the Beaune tourist office can usually redirect you same-day to an open alternative.

**Rain washes out the Pommard–Volnay walk or the Voie des Vignes ride.** Both routes are entirely rideable/walkable in light rain with a shell jacket; heavier rain, retreat to Beaune's covered cellars for the day.
**You've bought more wine than you can carry.** Most domaines and the Beaune tourist office can point you to a shipping service; do not attempt to drive it out yourself if you didn't rent a car.

trips.title: Champagne, Chalk to Cork
trips.subRegion: Reims, Épernay, Côte des Blancs and Côte des Bar

bestPeriod.note: Late September into October is harvest (vendange) — the region is at its most alive, but book grande marque cellar tours further ahead.

trips.gatewayAirport: Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG)
trips.summary: A week from Reims' Roman chalk cellars to Épernay's Avenue de Champagne and the grower villages of the Côte des Blancs and Côte des Bar.
trips.hook: Under Reims and Épernay run more than a hundred kilometres of chalk galleries, some dug by the Romans, all cool and dark enough to age a wine for decades undisturbed — the UNESCO-listed "Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars." This week works from the grande marque crayères of Reims through the Avenue de Champagne to the grower villages of the Côte des Blancs, then south to the quieter, Pinot Noir-driven Côte des Bar, with the RM-versus-NM distinction as the thread that ties it together.

snapshot.Base(s): Reims (3 nights) · Épernay (4 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 140 km by train and car across the week; flat town walking, gently rolling vineyard paths in the Côte des Blancs
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG); TGV from CDG-2 direct to Reims, approx. 45 min
snapshot.Who It Suits: Wine drinkers ready to book grande marque tours weeks ahead and take a full day for the quieter Aube

itinerary.title: Reims, cathedral first
itinerary.morning: Fly into CDG and take the direct TGV to Reims, about 45 minutes from the airport station. Walk straight to Notre-Dame de Reims, the coronation cathedral of French kings, and look for the Chagall windows in the axial chapel.
itinerary.afternoon: Settle into central Reims and walk the streets around Place Drouet d'Erlon, the city's main dining artery.
itinerary.evening: Dinner built around jambon de Reims (a cooked, herbed ham specific to the city) and a glass of grande marque Champagne by the glass — an easy, low-commitment introduction before the cellar visits start.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 5. Approx. tasting spend: €18–€25.

itinerary.title: Into the crayères
itinerary.morning: Reservation tour at Veuve Clicquot or Pommery — both age Champagne in Roman-era chalk pits (crayères) beneath Reims, and neither takes walk-ins; book online several weeks ahead, especially for weekend slots. Pommery's cellars are the more theatrical of the two, with contemporary art installed among the galleries.
itinerary.afternoon: If your week lands on a Wednesday, Friday or Saturday, the covered Halles du Boulingrin market runs its morning session — a restored Art Deco hall worth the detour.
itinerary.evening: Fossier, the biscuiterie that has made the biscuit rose de Reims since 1756, keeps a shop in town; buy a box and eat one dipped in a glass of Champagne after dinner, the traditional way it's served locally.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 6. Approx. tasting spend: €35–€55.

itinerary.title: Taittinger, and south to Épernay
itinerary.morning: A second Reims crayère tour, at Taittinger — partly built into the cellars of the old Saint-Nicaise abbey, some sections 13th-century. Book online in advance; same-day availability is rare in season.
itinerary.afternoon: Train to Épernay, about 25 minutes on the regional line. Check into your base for the next four nights and walk the Avenue de Champagne, the single street where Moët & Chandon, Mercier, Perrier-Jouët and de Castellane all keep their headquarters above more than 100 km of combined cellars.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Épernay: andouillette if you want the local specialty in full, or a gentler potée champenoise (a slow-cooked pork and vegetable stew) if not.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 2 (Reims). Km travelled: 30. Approx. tasting spend: €45–€65.

itinerary.title: The Avenue, properly
itinerary.morning: Reservation tour at Moët & Chandon, the largest house on the avenue and the most tour-ready — book online well ahead for a specific time slot, since capacity per day is genuinely limited despite the scale of the operation.
itinerary.afternoon: De Castellane, further down the avenue, keeps a walk-in-friendly visitor centre built around its own tower — climb it for a rooftop view over Épernay before the cellar visit. Mercier, next door, still runs a version of its historic laser-guided electric train through the cellars; check current booking requirements online, as reservation policy shifts by season.
itinerary.evening: Dinner with chaource, the soft, bloomy-rind cheese from the Aube, as a preview of Day 6.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 2. Km travelled: 4. Approx. tasting spend: €50–€70.

itinerary.title: Hautvillers and the Côte des Blancs
itinerary.morning: Bus or taxi to Hautvillers, the hilltop village where Dom Pérignon is buried in the abbey church — the myth of Champagne's invention is overstated, but the abbey and the village's painted wrought-iron shop signs (each depicting a different Champagne-related trade) are genuinely worth the half-day.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive or taxi south into the Côte des Blancs — Cramant, Avize, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger — Chardonnay country and the source of blanc de blancs. Look at any bottle's small print for the producer code: RM (récoltant-manipulant) means a grower who grows the grapes and makes the wine themselves; NM (négociant-manipulant) means a house that buys in grapes, which covers most of the grande marque names visited earlier this week.
itinerary.evening: Reservation tasting at Pierre Péters in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger or Agrapart & Fils in Avize, both long-established grower estates — email a few weeks ahead, since these are small operations without a dedicated visitor programme, and expect to buy a bottle or two rather than just taste and leave.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 35. Approx. tasting spend: €25–€40.

itinerary.title: South to the Côte des Bar
itinerary.morning: This is the long day. Drive or take the train (Épernay–Troyes, changing if needed, roughly 1h30–2h) into the Aube département — the Côte des Bar, a Pinot Noir-heavy sub-region far enough from Reims and Épernay that it sees a fraction of the visitors.
itinerary.afternoon: Reservation visit at Drappier in Urville, a long-established grower house that has farmed the same site since the 18th century — email ahead, and expect a warmer, less scripted welcome than the grande marque tours earlier in the week. If time allows, drive on to Les Riceys, the only commune in France permitted to produce three separate appellations (Champagne, Coteaux Champenois and Rosé des Riceys still wine).
itinerary.evening: Dinner nearby built around chaource at its actual source, alongside a Côte des Bar Champagne — almost entirely Pinot Noir, rounder and less mineral than Côte des Blancs bottlings.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 200 (round trip). Approx. tasting spend: €25–€35.

itinerary.title: Last glass, and out
itinerary.morning: Back in Épernay, a final walk down the Avenue de Champagne for any house you didn't reach, or a return visit to buy bottles directly from a producer you liked earlier in the week.
itinerary.afternoon: Train to Paris (TGV via Reims or direct regional connections, roughly 1h30–2h total) or back to CDG for the flight home.
itinerary.evening: Departure, or a final night in Paris if your flight is early the next morning.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 140. Approx. tasting spend: €20–€40 (bottle purchases).

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel near Place Drouet d'Erlon
accommodationStrategy.description: Walking distance to the cathedral, the crayère visitor entrances, and the station for the short hop to Épernay — the right base for the Reims-focused first nights.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel on or near the Avenue de Champagne
accommodationStrategy.description: Puts you inside walking distance of Moët, Mercier and de Castellane, with taxis and rental pickup easy to arrange for the Côte des Blancs and Côte des Bar days.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–10 weeks ahead for autumn.

accommodationStrategy.name: A chambre d'hôtes in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger or Cramant
accommodationStrategy.description: An alternative for the middle of the week if you'd rather be inside grower-Champagne country than commuting to it; several growers rent rooms above or beside their own cellars.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; also 15 (SAMU medical), 17 (police), 18 (fire) work directly in France.
logistics.bookingWindows: Moët & Chandon, Veuve Clicquot, Pommery and Taittinger require online reservation weeks ahead, especially for weekends; walk-up availability is rare in season. De Castellane and Mercier are the most walk-in-friendly of the well-known houses, though booking is still recommended.
logistics.money: Cards are accepted everywhere in Reims and Épernay; smaller growers in the Aube may prefer cash for round-number purchases.

other.label: Booking grower estates
other.text: Email 3–4 weeks ahead for Pierre Péters, Agrapart or Drappier; these are small teams without a dedicated booking office, and a purchase after tasting is the expected norm rather than an option.

other.label: Drink-drive alternative
other.text: Do not rent a car for the Reims–Épernay core of the trip; TER trains connect them in about 25 minutes. For the Côte des Blancs and Côte des Bar, hire a local driver through the Épernay tourist office, or rent a car and appoint a strict non-drinking driver for those two days only.

other.label: Cycling option
other.text: Signed vineyard cycling loops run out of Épernay and Hautvillers for a lower-key alternative to a car on the Côte des Blancs day.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Halles du Boulingrin in Reims runs Wednesday, Friday and Saturday mornings only — plan around it rather than assuming a daily market.

proTips: Learn RM versus NM before Day 5; once you can read the two letters on a label, every Champagne shelf in France reads differently.
Book Moët & Chandon and one crayère tour (Pommery or Veuve Clicquot) on different days, not back to back — both run 60–90 minutes and stacking them dulls the second visit.
Climb the de Castellane tower before, not after, its cellar tour — the light is better in late morning and the queue is shorter.
On the Côte des Blancs day, taste Cramant, Avize and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger back to back if you can arrange more than one grower stop; the chalk-driven minerality shifts noticeably village to village.
The Côte des Bar day rewards an early start — Drappier's morning slots are quieter, and it leaves time for Les Riceys without rushing the drive back.
Buy biscuit rose de Reims at the Fossier shop itself rather than a supermarket version; the texture difference is real, and it's the one local product built specifically to eat with Champagne.
