packingNotes: A light jacket for the crayères and cellars — chalk galleries run a constant 10–12°C year-round.
Comfortable shoes for cobbled town streets and the Avenue de Champagne's long blocks.
A soft wine bag or case box for bottles bought at Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Avize or Drappier.
Smart-casual layers for grande marque tastings, which run more formal than a village cellar.
A phrasebook or app; Reims and Épernay are tourist-fluent in English, but the Aube less so.
A printed copy of tour confirmations for houses that check names against a booking list at the door.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A grande marque tour is sold out.** Book the moment your dates are fixed; if you're shut out, De Castellane and Mercier usually have shorter lead times than Moët, Veuve Clicquot or Taittinger.
**The Côte des Bar day runs long and you miss dinner reservations.** Build a two-hour buffer into the return drive or train; the Aube connections are less frequent than the Reims–Épernay core.

**A grower estate doesn't reply to your email.** The Épernay tourist office (Maison du Champagne / Office de Tourisme) keeps an updated list of growers currently welcoming visitors and can suggest an alternative in the same village.
**Rain washes out the Hautvillers or Côte des Blancs walking.** Cellars absorb a wet day easily; shift the vineyard walking to Day 7 morning if the forecast clears.

trips.title: Crete End to End: Horta, Graviera & the Raki Fires

bestPeriod.window: Late April–early June & late September–early November
bestPeriod.avoid: Mid-July–late August — 36–40°C, coastal villages overwhelmed, and mountain producers shut through the afternoon
bestPeriod.raw: Late April–early June & late September–early November

accommodation.note: Chania Venetian-house rooms €80–€140 pppn; Archanes agroturismo €55–€90

food.note: Taverna mains €9–€16; a full mezedopoleio spread €22–€30 pp; raki almost always free

transport.note: Rental car 6 days €180–€300, fuel, one driver day for the wine circuit

activities.note: Winery tastings €12–€30, cheese dairy, oil mill, cookery class €65–€95, foraging walk €45–€70

profile.difficultyNote: 2/5 — a gorge-edge herb walk, olive-terrace slopes, otherwise flat markets and tavernas

trips.gatewayAirport: CHQ Chania, 20 min to Chania old town; HER Heraklion, 25 min to Archanes; 2 h 30 min CHQ–HER by road
trips.summary: Crete's food identity is older than the mainland's: a Minoan-rooted diet of wild greens, barley rusk, sheep's cheese and raw olive oil that epidemiologists spent the 1960s writing down. The week runs west to east — Chania's covered market, Rethymno's mountain villages, Heraklion's PDO wine zones, then the Lasithi olive country around Sitia. You eat dakos most days, learn six wild greens by leaf, and drink Vidiano and Liatiko from grapes grown nowhere else. In late autumn the island smells of pomace: raki distilling is a licensed communal event you can be invited to.

itinerary.title: Chania: the covered market and the harbour
itinerary.morning: Land at CHQ, drive 20 minutes into Chania and walk the Venetian harbour to the Egyptian lighthouse before the heat.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Chania Municipal Market**, the 1913 cross-shaped hall: graviera cut from the wheel, barrels of olives, herbs by the sack, and butchers who will explain apaki.
itinerary.evening: **To Stachi** or **Tamam** in the old town for chochlioi boubouristi and boiled horta, closed with a carafe of raki the kitchen will not charge you for.
itinerary.dayStats: 20 min from CHQ / market stalls, graviera €12–€18/kg / taverna dinner €18–€26 pp / no driving after 19:00
itinerary.sleep: Casa Delfino or Serenissima, Chania old town

itinerary.title: Akrotiri, Kolymvari oil and the Kissamos dairies
itinerary.morning: Drive west to **Terra Creta** at **Kolymvari** for a mill visit and a structured PDO oil tasting — bitterness and pungency as quality markers, not faults.
itinerary.afternoon: On to the **Kissamos** hinterland for a sheep dairy making graviera and pichtogalo, then the beach at Falassarna if the day allows.
itinerary.evening: **Ntounias** on the Akrotiri road above Chania — wood-fired, no electricity in the kitchen, everything from the farm below; order whatever the greens are that week.
itinerary.dayStats: 78 km round trip / 1 mill + 1 dairy / oil tasting €10–€20 / PDO Kolymvari 500 ml €9–€16 / Ntounias mains €10–€15
itinerary.sleep: Casa Delfino or Serenissima, Chania old town

itinerary.title: Into the mountains: Vamos, herbs and a kitchen
itinerary.morning: A guided **wild-herb walk** in the Apokoronas hills out of Vamos — stamnagathi, vlita, radikia, fennel and the difference between the ones you boil and the ones you fry.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive east to the Amari valley and **Enagron** at Axos for the cookery session: kalitsounia, a horta pie, and the staka you will meet again in gamopilafo.
itinerary.evening: Eat at Enagron; the farm's own lamb and a bottle of Vidiano.
itinerary.dayStats: Herb walk €45–€70, 3 h / class €65–€95, 4 h / 95 km Chania–Axos, 1 h 40 m / Vidiano bottle €12–€22

itinerary.title: Rethymno, Margarites and the dakos standard
itinerary.morning: Down to **Rethymno** old town — the Fortezza, the Venetian loggia, and a coffee in the Rimondi fountain square.
itinerary.afternoon: The pottery village of **Margarites** and Arkadi monastery, with a village-taverna dakos: rusk barely softened, tomato grated not chopped, mizithra crumbled, oil poured until it pools.
itinerary.evening: **Avli** in Rethymno, a Venetian courtyard restaurant with the island's deepest Cretan wine list, for gamopilafo and a Liatiko.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 km / dakos €5–€8 / Avli mains €18–€28 / Liatiko by the glass €6–€10
itinerary.sleep: Avli Lounge Apartments or Casa Vitae, Rethymno

itinerary.title: Peza and Dafnes: the indigenous grapes
itinerary.morning: Driver day east to **Lyrarakis** at Alagni for Dafni, Plyto and Vidiano — varieties this estate personally brought back from single-figure hectares.
itinerary.afternoon: **Douloufakis** at Dafnes for the Vidiano benchmark and a Liatiko in both dry and sweet form, then a stop at **Domaine Paterianakis** if the schedule holds.
itinerary.evening: **Peskesi** in Heraklion, which farms its own supply and reconstructs pre-war Cretan recipes; order apaki and the ancient-grain bread.
itinerary.dayStats: 2–3 wineries / fees €12–€35 each / driver day €250–€400 per car / 62 km circuit / PDO Peza bottle €10–€20
itinerary.sleep: Lato Boutique Hotel, Heraklion, or an Archanes guesthouse

itinerary.title: Archanes, Knossos and the raki fires
itinerary.morning: **Knossos** at opening time, then up to **Archanes**, a restored wine village at 400 m below Mount Juktas with the Fourni Minoan cemetery on its edge.
itinerary.afternoon: In October and November, attend a **kazanema** — a licensed raki distillation. The still runs a fixed permitted period; first and last runs are discarded, the middle is the tsikoudia, and it lasts as long as the fire does.
itinerary.evening: Village taverna in Archanes for gamopilafo and grilled lamb straight off the kazani fire.
itinerary.dayStats: Knossos entry €20 / 25 min Heraklion–Archanes / raki 40–45% abv / kazanema is an invitation, not a ticket
itinerary.sleep: Lato Boutique Hotel, Heraklion, or an Archanes guesthouse

itinerary.title: East to Lasithi, Sitia oil, and out
itinerary.morning: Drive east on the E75 toward **Agios Nikolaos** and inland to the Lasithi olive country. Visit the **Sitia Union of Agricultural Cooperatives** for PDO Sitia oil, the most-awarded on the island.
itinerary.afternoon: **Xygalo Siteias** and apaki from a Sitia deli, then the drive back west along the Mirabello gulf.
itinerary.evening: Last dinner at **Chrisofyllis** in Agios Nikolaos or back at Heraklion's waterfront before an evening flight from HER.
itinerary.dayStats: 145 km Heraklion–Sitia, 2 h 15 m / PDO Sitia 500 ml €10–€18 / allow 45 min HER return / oil in hold baggage only
itinerary.sleep: Airport hotel near HER, or fly out

accommodationStrategy.name: Casa Delfino
accommodationStrategy.description: A seventeenth-century house with a pebble-mosaic courtyard, three minutes from the market and inside the pedestrian zone, so the car goes in a garage and stays there for two nights of eating and raki. €180–€300 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Enagron Ecotourism Village
accommodationStrategy.description: The reason to spend a night in the mountains: stone cottages at 600 m, the farm supplies the kitchen, and both the cookery class and the herb walks are on site rather than an hour away. €90–€150 double, half board available.

accommodationStrategy.name: Lato Boutique Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: Faces the Venetian fortress and the port, walkable to Peskesi and the archaeological museum, with parking — the practical base for the Peza and Dafnes days and the eastern drive. €110–€180.

logistics.connectivity: Greece is in EU roaming. 4G is strong along the north coast, weak in the Amari valley and on the Lasithi plateau roads. Download offline maps: village signage is often only in Greek script.
logistics.emergency: 112, plus 166 for ambulance. Hospitals in Chania, Rethymno, Heraklion and Agios Nikolaos. EHIC/GHIC accepted. Mountain roads have no barriers — carry insurance covering rental excess.
logistics.weather: The **meltemi** blows hard from the north July–September and grounds ferries; the south coast stays sheltered. Autumn brings brief violent rain that floods gorge roads.
logistics.bookingWindows: Cookery classes and herb walks 1–2 weeks; Lyrarakis and Boutari a few days online; Douloufakis and small estates 3–7 days by phone. Domaine Economou months, if at all. Chania old-town hotels 2–3 months for May and September.
logistics.money: Eurozone. Cards work in cities and wineries; mountain tavernas, dairies and honey stands are cash — carry €150. Tipping is 5–10%. Raki arrives free at the end of a meal and refusing it politely takes practice.
logistics.transportRules: Blood-alcohol limit 0.5 g/l, 0.2 g/l for licences under two years, and Greece enforces it hard. KTEL coaches cover Chania–Rethymno–Heraklion frequently at €8–€16. Village roads are single-track with unfenced drops and goats; do not drive them at night. Fuel stations close early in the interior.
logistics.permits: Raki distilling is licensed and time-limited per household; you attend by invitation, and buying home-distilled raki commercially is not legal. Foraging greens for personal use is customary but not inside Samaria and the other park zones. Knossos is busiest 10:00–13:00.
logistics.health: Tap water is drinkable in Chania, Rethymno and Heraklion; in villages and on the Lasithi plateau, drink bottled. Raki runs 40–45% abv and is poured generously and repeatedly. Sun exposure from May onwards is severe on unshaded terraces.

proTips: Ask for *horta* by asking what was picked, not from a menu. The word covers a dozen plants and the good tavernas boil whatever came in that morning — stamnagathi in spring is the one to hold out for.
Judge olive oil by bitterness and a peppery catch at the back of the throat. Both are polyphenol markers and both are what the PDO Sitia and Kolymvari mills will teach you to look for.
Go in late October and you get raki season, the olive harvest starting, warm sea and half the summer prices. It is comfortably the best week of the Cretan year.
Order Vidiano everywhere and Assyrtiko nowhere. Assyrtiko is Santorini's grape; Crete's own white was nearly extinct twenty-five years ago and is now the island's most interesting bottle.
A kazanema is not a paid experience. Mention to a village taverna owner or your guesthouse in October that you would like to see one and you will usually be taken along; bring something to the fire.
Buy graviera cut from the wheel at the Chania market, not pre-packed. Ask for a piece aged over a year — the crystalline older cheese never leaves the island.
Dakos is assembled at the last moment. If the rusk arrives fully soft, the kitchen made it early; a good one still has a bite at the edge.

raw.Appellations: **PDO Peza** (Heraklion, Kotsifali–Mandilari reds and Vilana whites) and **PDO Dafnes** (100% Liatiko, dry and sweet) are the historic zones; **PDO Archanes** and **PDO Sitia** complete the four. **PGI Crete**, **PGI Heraklion** and **PGI Chania** cover most modern bottlings and allow the indigenous varieties more freely. Grapes: **Vidiano**, the best white — stone fruit with weight, rescued from near-extinction since 2000; **Vilana**, lighter and citric, the Peza workhorse; **Thrapsathiri** and **Dafni** as aromatic minorities; **Liatiko**, pale, early-ripening, hugely perfumed; **Kotsifali** for aroma and **Mandilari** for structure, nearly always blended.
raw.PDO foods: **Graviera Kritis PDO** — hard sheep's milk (up to 20% goat), aged minimum five months, nutty and crystalline. **Sitia PDO** olive oil from the Koroneiki groves of eastern Lasithi is the most decorated; **Kolymvari Chania PDO** is the western equivalent. Also **Xygalo Siteias PDO**, a soured spreadable cheese, **Pichtogalo Chanion PDO**, and **staka**, the sheep's-milk clotted butter spooned onto gamopilafo.
raw.Dishes by name and where: **Dakos** — barley rusk, grated tomato, mizithra, oil — is best in the Rethymno hinterland; the canonical version is served at village tavernas around **Margarites** and **Archanes**. **Gamopilafo**, the wedding rice cooked in goat and lamb broth and finished with staka butter, is a Chania-region dish. **Apaki**, vinegar-marinated pork smoked over aromatic herbs, is eastern. **Chochlioi boubouristi** — snails fried face-down and deglazed with vinegar — is the test dish; **Ntounias** on Akrotiri and **To Stachi** in Chania do them properly. **Horta**, boiled wild greens with lemon and oil, is the actual centre of the diet. **Peskesi** in Heraklion is the benchmark modern kitchen, sourcing from its own farm.
raw.Named producers and visit logistics: **Lyrarakis** at Alagni (Peza) rescued Dafni and Plyto from extinction and runs scheduled tastings and vineyard tours, roughly €15–€35, booked online, English standard. **Douloufakis** at Dafnes is the Vidiano reference, bookable by email or phone with days' notice. **Boutari Fantaxometocho** at Skalani has a large visitor centre near Knossos; **Domaine Paterianakis** (organic, Melesses) and **Idaia** near Venerato want a phone call. In the east, **Domaine Economou** at Ziros is a cult Liatiko producer with almost no visitor infrastructure. For cheese and oil: the **Kissamos** dairies, **Terra Creta** at Kolymvari (mill visit and tasting, about €10–€20), and the **Sitia Union of Agricultural Cooperatives**.
raw.Season and timing: Grape harvest is early — Liatiko and Vilana come in from **early August to early September**, weeks before the mainland. **Raki/tsikoudia distilling runs mid-October to late November**, once the pomace has fermented; each still needs a licence and a fixed number of days, and the *kazanemata* are social occasions with grilled meat and singing. Olive harvest and pressing runs **November to January**. Wild-greens foraging is a **winter and spring** activity, best February–April. Sheep's cheese is at its best in spring.
raw.Hands-on element: A half-day cookery class at **Agreco Farm** near Rethymno or **Enagron Ecotourism Village** at Axos — picking greens, hand-rolling kalitsounia, baking in a wood oven; €65–€95 with lunch, English-taught, a week's notice. For foraging, book a **wild-herb walk**: guided walks run out of Vamos and the Apokoronas villages, and Enagron's own herb walks are led by resident farmers.
raw.Transport and the sober-driving plan: Greece's limit is 0.5 g/l, 0.2 g/l under two years' licence, and checks around Heraklion are common. There is no useful rail. The **KTEL Chania–Rethymno–Heraklion** coach is frequent and €8–€16 a leg, covering the three city bases; villages need a car. For the Peza and Dafnes circuit book a driver — **Cretan Wine Tours** and **Wine Roads of Crete** run English-speaking days at €250–€400 per car.

sources.verified: Lyrarakis Winery operating public tastings and tours near Heraklion with online booking; the Cretan tsikoudia/raki distilling season falling in the October–November post-harvest window as a licensed communal event; the four historic Cretan PDO wine zones and the indigenous status of Vidiano, Vilana, Liatiko and Kotsifali.
sources.confidenceNotes: All winery tasting fees are estimated bands — re-check Lyrarakis, Douloufakis, Boutari and Paterianakis directly, and confirm whether Paterianakis and Idaia currently take walk-in bookings. Domaine Economou's visitor access is uncertain and may be closed entirely; do not promise it. Terra Creta's mill-tour format and price should be re-verified, as should the Sitia cooperative's visitor opening. Cookery-class and herb-walk operators run seasonal calendars and named guides change year to year — confirm Enagron and the Vamos walks before publishing. Knossos entry price and opening hours change by season. Kazanema attendance cannot be booked and should never be sold as a scheduled activity. Hotel rates are prior-season estimates.

trips.title: Istria in Truffle Season: Motovun Forest, Malvazija & the World's Best Oil
trips.subRegion: Central Istria, the Mirna valley & the west coast

bestPeriod.window: Mid-September–late November for white truffle; late April–June for a quieter, cheaper version
bestPeriod.avoid: Mid-July–late August — coastal towns are gridlocked, inland hill villages hit 35°C, and there is no white truffle
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-September–late November for white truffle; late April–June for a quieter, cheaper version

accommodation.note: Hill-village guesthouse €90–€150 pppn; Rovinj boutique €120–€190

food.note: Konoba mains €14–€24; a fresh white-truffle dish €35–€70; Rovinj fish €25–€40

transport.note: Rental car 6 days, Učka tunnel toll, fuel, one driver day

activities.note: Truffle hunt €80–€150, oil tastings €12–€25, winery visits €15–€35

profile.difficultyNote: 2/5 — a two-hour truffle hunt on wet forest floor, steep hill-village lanes, olive-grove walking

trips.gatewayAirport: PUY Pula, 50 min to Motovun; TRS Trieste 1 h 30 min; ZAG Zagreb 3 h; VCE Venice 2 h 45 min
trips.summary: Istria in autumn is the only place in Europe where the white truffle, world-class olive oil and a serious indigenous white grape occupy the same forty kilometres. You base inland among the hill villages — Motovun on its 277 m cone, Grožnjan, Buzet — hunt Tuber magnatum in the oak and poplar woods of the Mirna floodplain, and eat it grated over fuži by the gram. Between truffle days you work through Malvazija Istarska and Teran, taste down a Flos Olei shortlist, meet boškarin ox, and finish at Rovinj with Kvarner scampi. No drive exceeds an hour.

itinerary.title: Pula, then up into the hills
itinerary.morning: Land at PUY, see the Roman amphitheatre and the Temple of Augustus, then drive inland before lunch.
itinerary.afternoon: Up to **Motovun**, walled and 277 m above the Mirna floodplain, and walk the ramparts for the view over the truffle forest you will be standing in tomorrow.
itinerary.evening: **Konoba Mondo** just below the town gate — fuži with truffle, and a Malvazija from Benvenuti up the road.
itinerary.dayStats: 50 min PUY–Motovun / 1,052 steps up from the car park, or the shuttle / truffle fuži €28–€45 / Malvazija bottle €10–€20
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Kaštel or Roxanich Wine & Heritage Hotel, Motovun

itinerary.title: The hunt in the Motovun forest
itinerary.morning: A two-hour hunt with **Karlić Tartufi** at Paladini or **Prodan Tartufi** — lagotto romagnolo dogs working the poplar and oak floodplain, then a tasting of truffle products in the farmhouse.
itinerary.afternoon: **Livade** and the **Zigante** shop to see the market itself: fresh magnatum weighed on a jeweller's scale, and which preserved products are worth buying.
itinerary.evening: **Zigante Restaurant** at Livade for the full truffle menu, or **Konoba Dolina** at Gradinje for the same ingredient at half the price.
itinerary.dayStats: Hunt €80–€150 pp, 2 h / fresh white truffle €2,500–€5,000/kg / 12 km Motovun–Livade / boots essential

itinerary.title: Momjan: Malvazija, Muškat and amphorae
itinerary.morning: North to **Momjan** for **Kozlović** — a cantilevered concrete winery cut into the hillside, with a structured Malvazija flight from fresh to acacia-aged.
itinerary.afternoon: **Kabola** next door for organic and amphora-aged Malvazija buried in the courtyard, then the sweet **Muškat Momjanski**.
itinerary.evening: **Konoba Rino** in Momjan or down to **Buje** for dinner; order the boškarin carpaccio if it is on.
itinerary.dayStats: 2 wineries / fees €15–€30 each / 35 km / Muškat Momjanski 0.5 l €18–€30 / driver day recommended

itinerary.title: Vodnjan olive oil and the Flos Olei shortlist
itinerary.morning: South to **Vodnjan** and **Chiavalon** for a structured tasting: single-variety Buža, Istarska bjelica and Karbonaca poured blind against a supermarket oil.
itinerary.afternoon: **Ipša** at Ipši, a hilltop mill with a terrace over the Mirna valley — and, from mid-October, a live pressing you can watch. Buy here rather than at the coast.
itinerary.evening: **Konoba Boškarin** or a Vodnjan konoba for ox stew and pljukanci.
itinerary.dayStats: 2 mills / tastings €12–€25 each / 68 Istrian producers in Flos Olei 2026 / 500 ml single-variety €18–€30 / 95 km round trip

itinerary.title: Grožnjan, Roč to Hum and the Glagolitic Alley
itinerary.morning: **Grožnjan**, the artists' village, near-abandoned in the 1960s and now full of galleries and one very good gelato counter.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Glagolitic Alley** from **Roč to Hum** — 7 km punctuated by eleven sculptural monuments to the Glagolitic script, ending at Hum, which bills itself the world's smallest town at around twenty inhabitants. Biska at **Aura** in Buzet on the way.
itinerary.evening: **Humska Konoba** at Hum for maneštra and a shot of the mistletoe brandy.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km Roč–Hum, 11 monuments / Hum population ~20 / Aura tasting €8–€15 / biska bottle €14–€22

itinerary.title: Buzet, Subotina and a hands-on kitchen
itinerary.morning: If your dates hit the second Saturday of September, be in **Buzet** for **Subotina** and the giant truffle omelette. Otherwise, book a **truffle and fuži cookery class** at Karlić or a Motovun agroturizam — rolling fuži by hand, then shaving truffle over them.
itinerary.afternoon: Buzet's old town on its ridge, then the Mirna valley road back.
itinerary.evening: **Toklarija** at Sovinjsko Polje, a slow-food restaurant in a 500-year-old olive mill with a single long tasting menu and no choices.
itinerary.dayStats: Class €70–€110, 3 h / Subotina omelette uses 1,000+ eggs in a 2 m pan / Toklarija menu €90–€140, book 2–3 weeks

itinerary.title: Rovinj, scampi and out
itinerary.morning: Down to **Rovinj**, the Venetian fishing town on its peninsula, and up to St Euphemia's campanile.
itinerary.afternoon: **Kvarner scampi** and grilled fish at **Konoba Batelina** in Banjole near Pula — David Skoko's restaurant, still the region's best seafood — or **Monte** in Rovinj for the Michelin-starred version.
itinerary.evening: PUY is 40 minutes from Rovinj and 15 from Banjole. Truffle products travel; fresh truffle does not.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 min Motovun–Rovinj / Batelina mains €18–€32, book 2–4 weeks / Monte menu €150–€220 / PUY 40 min
itinerary.sleep: Airport hotel near Pula, or fly out

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Kaštel
accommodationStrategy.description: The only real hotel inside Motovun's walls, on the main square with parking below and its own spa. Central to every inland drive, and you can walk to Konoba Mondo after a bottle. €110–€180 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Roxanich Wine & Heritage Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: A converted cooperative building on the hill below town, with a working cellar of long-macerated Malvazija and Teran underneath. Tasting and bed in the same place, which resolves the 0.0-limit problem for younger drivers. €160–€260.

accommodationStrategy.name: San Canzian Village & Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: An abandoned stone village rebuilt as a hotel between Momjan and Grožnjan, well placed for the wine and oil days and quieter than Motovun in October. €180–€300.

logistics.connectivity: Croatia is in EU roaming — no surcharge. 4G is good in hill towns, weak in the Mirna floodplain and the Učka foothills. Download offline maps; agroturizam addresses are hamlet names, not streets.
logistics.emergency: 112. The main hospital is in Pula. Croatia is in the EU, so EHIC/GHIC applies; add rental-excess cover for the narrow inland roads.
logistics.weather: The **bura** hits the eastern side and the Učka pass with gusts over 100 km/h, closing bridges and exposed motorway sections; the Mirna valley is sheltered but fogs heavily on autumn mornings. Rain makes the truffle season — a wet October is good news you must dress for.
logistics.bookingWindows: Truffle hunts 1–2 weeks in October–November, longer for weekends. Toklarija 2–3 weeks. Batelina 2–4 weeks. Kozlović and Chiavalon a few days online. Motovun hotels 2–3 months for the truffle peak.
logistics.money: Croatia adopted the **euro in 2023** — no kuna. Cards are widely accepted; hunt operators, small mills and konobas in hamlets often want cash, so carry €150.
logistics.transportRules: Blood-alcohol limit 0.5 g/l, and **0.0 for drivers under 25 or with under two years' licence** — stricter than most of the EU and enforced. The Učka tunnel costs about €5 each way; the A8/A9 Istrian Y is ticket-tolled. Headlights are mandatory in daylight in the winter half of the year. Croatia is in Schengen, so the Slovenian and Italian borders are open.
logistics.permits: Truffle hunting requires a licence and registered dogs — you attend, you do not dig. Fresh truffle moves freely within the EU but is declarable beyond it. Oil and truffle products are hold-baggage items.
logistics.health: Tap water is drinkable. The forest floor in truffle season is deep mud and standing water — the operator supplies boots but rarely in every size. Ticks are present in Istrian woodland into November.

proTips: Book the hunt directly with Karlić or Prodan rather than through a coastal agency. You get the family's own forest, a smaller group and a real tasting instead of a bus stop.
Buy truffle by the gram in a restaurant before you buy any at a shop. A 7–10 g shaving over fuži tells you what fresh magnatum actually smells like, and most jarred products bear no relation.
Read the label on truffle oil. Almost all of it, including brands sold in Istria, is flavoured with synthetic bis(methylthio)methane — the mills and honest shops will tell you so.

Taste olive oil at the mill in the second half of October and you can drink the *novello* straight from the press, cloudy and stinging. It is a different substance from the filtered version sold in spring.
Ask for single-variety Istarska bjelica. It is the bitterest and most pungent of the four local varieties, the one that wins the Flos Olei entries, and the one supermarkets blend away.
Malvazija comes in two entirely different styles from the same estates — fresh stainless and acacia-aged or macerated. Always ask for both; the price difference is smaller than the flavour gap.
The first two weeks of November stack white-truffle peak, olive pressing and empty hill villages. September Subotina is more fun but the truffles are smaller and wetter.

raw.Truffle species and seasons: **Tuber magnatum**, the Istrian white, runs roughly **1 September–31 January** with the peak in **October and November**; the Motovun forest floodplain around Livade produces the largest specimens in Europe, including a record-setting 1.31 kg find. Black truffles split into summer **Tuber aestivum** (May–September, cheap, mild) and winter **Tuber melanosporum/brumale** (November–March). The price gap is the point: white runs €2,500–€5,000/kg at source in a normal year and climbs in a dry autumn; summer black is €200–€400.
raw.Hunting and the named names: **Zigante Tartufi**, based at **Livade** in the Mirna valley, is the region's dominant house — a shop, a truffle-focused restaurant and organised hunts. **Karlić Tartufi** at Paladini near Buzet is the long-established family operation whose hunts include a tasting in the farmhouse; **Prodan Tartufi** and **Miro Tartufi** are the other reliable family hunters. A hunt runs about two hours with lagotto dogs, costs roughly **€80–€150 per person** with a tasting, needs a week's notice in October and November, and is wet underfoot. Book direct, not through a coastal desk.
raw.Appellations and wine: Croatia's system uses PDO/ZOI at regional level: **Hrvatska Istra** is the designation. **Malvazija Istarska** is the flagship white — fresh and acacia-scented young, or macerated and aged in acacia wood for the amber style; **Teran** is the high-acid local red, distinct from Slovenian Kras Teran and the subject of a long-running EU naming dispute; **Muškat Momjanski** from the Momjan hills near Buje is the sweet speciality. Estates to book: **Kozlović** at Momjan (architecturally the best visit, €15–€30, online booking, English fluent), **Kabola** at Momjan (organic, amphora Malvazija), **Benvenuti** at Kaldir, **Matošević** at Krunčići, **Coronica** at Koreniki, and **Roxanich** at Motovun, which pairs long-macerated wines with a hotel. Two weeks' notice is comfortable; Saturdays fill first.
raw.Olive oil: Istria has topped the **Flos Olei** guide as the world's best olive-growing region for nine editions, with **68 Istrian producers in the 2026 guide** — 13.6% of the 500 worldwide. **Uljara Mate** of Savudrija scored a perfect 100/100 in the Hall of Fame for the third time, and **OPG Rheos** of Novigrad took Best Blended Medium Fruity. Others around **Vodnjan** and **Buje**: **Chiavalon** (purpose-built tasting room, €12–€25, book online), **Ipša** (hilltop mill with a terrace near Livade), **Meloto** and **Belci**. Varieties to ask for: **Buža**, **Istarska bjelica**, **Karbonaca**, **Rosinjola** — Bjelica is the bitter, pungent one.
raw.Dishes and other producers: **Fuži** (rolled quills) and **pljukanci** (hand-rolled spindles) are the two Istrian pastas; both are the correct vehicle for truffle. **Boškarin**, the near-extinct Istrian ox, appears as carpaccio, stew and salami — **Konoba Boškarin** and the butchers around Kanfanar handle it. **Kvarner scampi** (*Nephrops norvegicus*) are the region's protected shellfish, best simply boiled. **Aura** distillery at Buzet makes biska, the mistletoe brandy, and medica.
raw.Festivals and timing: **Subotina** in **Buzet**, on the second Saturday of September, opens the season with a giant truffle omelette cooked in a two-metre pan using upwards of a thousand eggs. **Tuberfest / Truffle Days** run at Livade and across central Istria through **October and November**. The olive harvest and pressing runs **mid-October to late November**, overlapping the truffle peak perfectly — the single best fortnight of the Istrian year is the first half of November.
raw.Transport and the sober-driving plan: Croatia's limit is **0.5 g/l, and 0.0 for drivers under 25 or with under two years' licence**. Inland roads are narrow, wet and unlit in autumn, and the Pula–Buzet rail line is minimal — plan two driver days with **Istria Wine Tours** or a Rovinj-based transfer operator, roughly €280–€450 per car. The **Učka tunnel** costs about €5 each way; the A8/A9 Istrian Y is ticket-tolled. Croatia is in the EU, Schengen and the eurozone, so the borders are open.

sources.verified: Istria named the world's best olive-oil region by Flos Olei for a ninth time, with 68 Istrian producers in the 2026 guide representing 13.6% of the global top 500, Uljara Mate of Savudrija scoring 100/100 in the Hall of Fame for a third time, and OPG Rheos of Novigrad taking Best Blended Medium Fruity; the Istrian white-truffle season running through autumn with an October–November peak and Livade/Motovun forest as its centre; Zigante's Livade base.
sources.confidenceNotes: Truffle hunt prices (€80–€150) and winery/mill tasting fees are estimated bands and must be re-checked with Karlić, Prodan, Kozlović, Kabola, Chiavalon and Ipša directly. Fresh white-truffle per-kilo prices swing enormously with rainfall and should never be quoted as fixed. Subotina's exact date moves within early September and should be confirmed against Buzet's tourist board each year. Toklarija, Konoba Batelina and Monte have seasonal closures and Batelina in particular closes for extended periods — confirm before building Day 7 around it. The Zigante restaurant's format and the Livade shop's opening have changed in recent years. Croatia's 0.0 limit for under-25 drivers should be re-confirmed against current traffic law before publishing. Hotel rates are prior-season estimates.

trips.title: Bull's Blood and Noble Rot: Seven Days Between Eger and Tokaj
trips.subRegion: Eger and the Bükk foothills, then Tokaj-Hegyalja on the Bodrog

bestPeriod.window: the last week of September through the third week of October — Eger's reds are in, Tokaj's aszú pickers are out
bestPeriod.avoid: December–March (many Hegyalja cellars open by appointment only, and the Szépasszony-völgy row half-shuts)

accommodation.note: €380–€640 (€55–€92/night; Eger guesthouse plus a Mád or Tarcal manor)

food.note: €200–€320 (€29–€46/day, including two tasting menus)

transport.note: €230–€360 (hire car 7 days €140–€230, fuel, motorway e-vignette, or rail plus a driver on tasting days)

activities.note: €190–€330 (cellar visits €15–€60; an aszú vertical runs higher)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy

trips.gatewayAirport: Budapest Liszt Ferenc (BUD) then hire car; Eger is 130 km northeast, about 1 h 50 on the M3. Rail: Budapest Keleti–Eger, roughly 2 h with a change at Füzesabony. Leaving from Tokaj, Debrecen (DEB) is ~100 km and often cheaper than driving back to Budapest.
trips.summary: Two Hungarian wine regions, three hours apart, that share almost nothing. Eger is rhyolite tuff, Kékfrankos, and a horseshoe of cellar doors cut into a valley wall where you drink standing up. Tokaj is loess over…
trips.hook: Two Hungarian wine regions, three hours apart, that share almost nothing. Eger is rhyolite tuff, Kékfrankos, and a horseshoe of cellar doors cut into a valley wall where you drink standing up. Tokaj is loess over volcanic rock, grey mould furring the cellar ceilings, and sweet wine measured in *puttony* baskets. Come in October: the Bükk turns copper, aszú pickers work berry by berry, and the cellars smell of fermenting must and damp stone.

snapshot.Best period: Late September to mid-November; aszú picking runs into November
snapshot.Start / End: Budapest → Eger (3 nights) → Tokaj-Hegyalja (4 nights) → Debrecen or Budapest
snapshot.Getting there: Budapest Liszt Ferenc (BUD) then hire car; Eger is 130 km northeast, about 1 h 50 on the M3. Rail: Budapest Keleti–Eger, roughly 2 h with a change at Füzesabony. Leaving from Tokaj, Debrecen (DEB) is ~100 km and often cheaper than driving back to Budapest.

itinerary.title: Eger: Castle, Minaret, Cellar Row
itinerary.morning: Collect the car at BUD and drive the M3 to Eger. Buy the motorway e-vignette (*e-matrica*) online or at the first petrol station before you join the motorway.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk Dobó István tér, climb to **Eger Castle** for the 1552 siege story and the casemates, then out to the 40 m Ottoman **minaret** — the northernmost surviving in Europe.
itinerary.evening: First pass through the **Szépasszony-völgy**, the horseshoe of cellar doors below the town. Do not try to do all of it. Pick three doors, drink small, and eat afterwards at **Macok Bistro & Wine Bar** under the castle wall [VERIFY: current Macok hours].
itinerary.dayStats: 4 km on foot

itinerary.title: Egerszalók, Noszvaj and Bikavér Properly
itinerary.morning: **St. Andrea** at Egerszalók, 8 km southwest. Taste *Áldás* against *Lőrinc*, then go up the range; this is the cleanest introduction to what modern Eger is trying to be.
itinerary.afternoon: North to **Thummerer** at Noszvaj for the classical counterweight — deep tuff cellars, long-aged Bikavér Superior, and a family archive worth asking about.
itinerary.evening: Back to Egerszalók for the **Saliris** thermal complex and its travertine "salt hill", then a quiet dinner in Eger.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 km

itinerary.title: Quarry, Fúzió and the Nagy-Eged Climb
itinerary.morning: **Bolyki** — a winery built into a disused rhyolite quarry on the town's edge, with tanks under the rock face. Taste the Kékfrankos and the Egri Csillag.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk or drive up **Nagy-Eged**, Eger's steep limestone hill and the region's most ambitious vineyard site, then down into town for **Gál Tibor Fúzió** on Széchenyi utca.
itinerary.evening: **Kovács Nimród** for the single-vineyard bottlings, then dinner at **Imola Udvarház** above the castle. Pack tonight; tomorrow is a relocation.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, +300 m on foot

itinerary.title: East to Hegyalja: Mezőzombor and Mád
itinerary.morning: Drive Eger → Tokaj-Hegyalja on the M3 and route 37. Stop at **Disznókő** near Mezőzombor — the estate at the region's western gate, with the modern Makovecz-school winery building and a tasting that lays out aszú against dry Furmint.
itinerary.afternoon: Into **Mád**. Walk up to the **Szent Tamás** and **Betsek** slopes for the lie of the land: south-facing, volcanic, terraced.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **Percz** in Mád — Hungarian cooking with a serious Hegyalja list [VERIFY: current Percz opening days].

itinerary.title: Mád: Szepsy, Royal Tokaji, Barta
itinerary.morning: **Szepsy István**, by appointment. The dry Furmints from Szent Tamás and Úrágya are the reference point for the whole region's shift toward dry wine.
itinerary.afternoon: **Royal Tokaji**'s Mád cellar for the first-growth aszú range, then **Barta** in the Rákóczi cellar beneath Kővágó, whose terraced Öreg Király vineyard was rebuilt from scrub.
itinerary.evening: **First Estate** in Mád for dinner, or back to Percz. If it is late October, ask anyone whether the aszú pickers are still out — a second and third pass through the same rows can run into November.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km

itinerary.title: Tarcal and Tokaj Town
itinerary.morning: **Gróf Degenfeld** at Tarcal — manor, park and a broad range including szamorodni. Then the short climb to the Tarcal hillside for the view over the Bodrog plain.
itinerary.afternoon: Lunch at **Sárga Borház** on the Tarcal slope, then into **Tokaj** town itself for **Demeter Zoltán**, a one-man cellar in the old town, and a walk to the Bodrog–Tisza confluence.
itinerary.evening: Stay in Tarcal or Tokaj. Order **halászlé** and drink dry Furmint with it; the sweet wines come after the fish, not with it.
itinerary.dayStats: 35 km

itinerary.title: Tolcsva, Sárospatak and Out
itinerary.morning: **Oremus** at **Tolcsva** — Vega Sicilia's Tokaj estate, with a long cellar system and a rigorous tasting; ask for Mandolás alongside the aszú.
itinerary.afternoon: Lunch at **Gusteau** in Tolcsva, the region's most consistent kitchen. Then 20 km to **Sárospatak** for the Rákóczi castle if you have the hours.
itinerary.evening: Out via **Debrecen** (100 km) or back to Budapest (240 km, ~2 h 40). Buy at the cellars, not at the airport: EU-bound flights allow a case in hold luggage and estates ship [VERIFY: current estate shipping options].
itinerary.dayStats: 80 km

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Senator-Ház
accommodationStrategy.description: on the main square, 300 m from the castle ramp, and walkable to Macok and the taxi rank you need for a Szépasszony-völgy evening. No car use after tasting.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–5 weeks ahead; Eger fills for the September Bikavér events.

accommodationStrategy.name: Botrytis Hotel or a Mád guesthouse
accommodationStrategy.description: Mád puts Szepsy, Royal Tokaji, Barta, Holdvölgy, Percz and the Szent Tamás slope inside a 2 km radius, so the densest tasting day of the week needs no driving at all.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead; harvest weekends go first [VERIFY: current Mád accommodation availability and rates].

accommodationStrategy.name: Gróf Degenfeld Castle Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: sleeping on a working Tokaj estate, with a park, a restaurant and the vineyard behind the house; a good last two nights and an easy run to Debrecen.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead direct, bundled with a tasting.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming applies. Coverage is solid in Eger and along route 37; thinner in the Zemplén side valleys above Tolcsva.
logistics.emergency: 112. Pharmacies are *gyógyszertár*; Eger and Sátoraljaújhely have the nearest hospitals to Hegyalja.
logistics.weather: October swings 6–20 °C in a day, and Hegyalja mornings are foggy — that river fog off the Bodrog is precisely what makes botrytis possible. Cellars sit at 10–12 °C year-round; take a jacket.
logistics.bookingWindows: Szepsy and Demeter Zoltán 3–6 weeks; Barta, Holdvölgy, Oremus, Disznókő and Royal Tokaji 5–10 days; St. Andrea and Thummerer 2–3 days; Gusteau and Percz a week in harvest season.
logistics.money: forint, not euro, at roughly 390–410 HUF to €1 [VERIFY: current exchange rate]. Cards work at estates and restaurants; carry cash for Szépasszony-völgy cellar doors, some of which still take notes only. Refuse dynamic currency conversion on card terminals.
logistics.transportRules: **Hungary enforces a 0.00 blood-alcohol limit** — no glass of wine, no beer, no exceptions, and roadside checks are routine in wine regions during harvest. Either nominate a non-drinking driver each day or hire a local driver for the two heavy tasting days (roughly €90–€140 per day) [VERIFY: current driver rates]. Motorways require an **e-matrica** vignette bought in advance by number plate; on the 2026 D1 tariff a 10-day national pass is 6,900 HUF (~€17.50), a monthly 11,170 HUF (~€28) and an annual 61,760 HUF, with a single day at 5,550 HUF. County-only vignettes are 7,190 HUF each for the year and cover Heves and Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén far more cheaply if you avoid the M3 — though two of them together cost more than a 10-day national pass, so for one week take the national one.
logistics.permits: none for cellar visits. Vineyard walking is generally tolerated on tracks but never between rows during harvest — ask at the cellar first.

proTips: Do the Szépasszony-völgy on your first evening, not your last. It is a cellar row, not a fine-wine destination — treating it as orientation rather than climax saves the week's palate.
In Tokaj, taste **dry Furmint first, aszú last**, and ask for a **szamorodni** in between. Going straight to the sweet wine wastes the region's best current argument.
Ask every Hegyalja cellar for the *dűlő*. Szent Tamás, Betsek, Úrágya and Király are the names that separate a good bottle from a great one, and the answer is usually on the back label.
Base in **Mád**, not Tokaj town. Tokaj has the name and the confluence; Mád has the producers, and you can walk to five of them.
Book Szepsy before you book flights. It is the single hardest appointment in the region and the rest of the week can be arranged around it.
Time Day 7 for late October and you may catch **aszú picking** — two or three passes through the same rows, berry by berry. Ask a cellar whether you can walk out with the pickers for an hour.
Learn *"Egészségedre"* (cheers) and *"Egy pohár száraz furmintot kérek"* (a glass of dry Furmint, please). Tipping is 10–12%, and increasingly added to the bill — check before doubling it.

raw.Appellations and classifications: **Eger PDO** (*Egri* DHC): **Egri Bikavér** is a red blend led by Kékfrankos, with Bikavér **Superior** and **Grand Superior** as tightened tiers — lower yields, longer ageing, and at Grand Superior level a single named *dűlő* (vineyard) on the label [VERIFY: current Egri DHC yield and ageing thresholds]. **Egri Csillag** is the white counterpart, a multi-variety blend built on Carpathian Basin grapes. **Tokaj-Hegyalja PDO** covers 27 settlements on the volcanic foothills of the Zemplén. **Aszú** is made from individually picked botrytised berries (*Botrytis cinerea*) kneaded into a base wine; since the 2013 vintage the legal minimum sits at the old 5-puttonyos level, so *puttonyos* on a label is now optional shorthand rather than the grading it once was. **Szamorodni** ("as it came") is pressed from whole bunches, dry or sweet; **fordítás** is a second wine drawn from already-pressed aszú paste. The black fur on Hegyalja cellar walls is **Cladosporium cellaris**, and it is a sign of correct humidity, not neglect.
raw.Reservation-only cellars: **Szepsy István** (Mád) and **Demeter Zoltán** (Tokaj) are appointment-only and can be booked out weeks ahead; **Barta** (Mád, in the Rákóczi cellar under Kővágó hill) and **Holdvölgy** (Mád) run booked tasting programmes, not drop-in bars. **Royal Tokaji**, **Disznókő** (Mezőzombor) and **Oremus** (Tolcsva) take scheduled visits, still best booked 5–10 days out. In Eger, **St. Andrea** (Egerszalók), **Thummerer** (Noszvaj) and **Kovács Nimród** want a day or two's notice; **Bolyki** and **Gál Tibor Fúzió** in town are walk-in-friendly [VERIFY: current visitor hours at Bolyki and Fúzió].
raw.Producers and wines to ask for: Eger: **St. Andrea** — *Áldás* (Egri Csillag) and *Lőrinc* (an approachable Bikavér), then the Nagy-Eged bottlings if the cellar will pour them. **Thummerer** for the classic Superior style, **Gál Tibor** for Fúzió and Kékfrankos, **Kovács Nimród** for single-vineyard Battonage Chardonnay and Syrah, **Bolyki** for the quarry site as much as the wine. Tokaj: **Szepsy** for dry Furmint that redefines the region, **Royal Tokaji** for its first-growth range, **Disznókő** for aszú with clarity, **Oremus** for Mandolás dry Furmint, **Gróf Degenfeld** at Tarcal, **Barta** for terraced Öreg Király, **Holdvölgy** and **Demeter Zoltán** for small-scale precision.
raw.First-growth vineyards: The 1737 royal classification named the crus you will hear about all week: **Szent Tamás** and **Betsek** above Mád, **Úrágya** on the Mád–Tarcal ridge, **Király** at Mád/Tarcal, with Nyulászó, Percze and Mézes Mály close behind. Ask which *dűlő* a bottle came from; in Hegyalja the answer is the wine.
raw.Signature dishes: **Halászlé** (river-fish soup, paprika-red, Tisza style with carp), **töltött káposzta** (stuffed cabbage), **Mangalica** (the curly-haired pig, best as a slow-cooked shoulder or cured *szalonna*), **körözött** (sheep's-cheese and paprika spread, the standard cellar snack), and **somlói galuska** for pudding.

trips.title: West Cork Larder: Ballymaloe to Skibbereen
trips.subRegion: County Cork — East Cork, Kinsale and West Cork

accommodation.note: €130–240 per night, double; country-house rooms €250–400

trips.summary: A seven-day culinary & wine tour itinerary in County Cork — East Cork, Kinsale and West Cork, Ireland.

itinerary.title: Cork city and the English Market
itinerary.morning: Land at Cork. Straight to the **English Market**, a covered Victorian food market trading since 1788, with tripe and drisheen butchers, spiced beef, buttered eggs and On the Pig's Back's charcuterie counter.
itinerary.afternoon: Lunch upstairs at the Farmgate Café overlooking the market floor — the single best introduction to Cork food culture. Then the Butter Museum in Shandon, which sounds like a joke and is actually the history of Ireland's export economy.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Cork city. The city has developed real depth in recent years, including internationally recognised kitchens. `verify: true`

itinerary.title: East Cork: Ballymaloe and Midleton
itinerary.morning: Drive east to Shanagarry. **Ballymaloe House** is where modern Irish food began — Myrtle Allen opened the dining room in 1964 on the family farm and turned local, seasonal cooking into a national argument. Lunch here, or better, book a **one-day course at the Ballymaloe Cookery School** at Kinoith, with its organic farm and gardens.
itinerary.afternoon: Midleton and the Jameson distillery for the whiskey story, or the smaller producers around Ballycotton for fish landed that morning.
itinerary.evening: Ballymaloe's dinner is a set five-course menu built from the farm and the garden. Book far ahead.

itinerary.title: Kinsale
itinerary.morning: Kinsale, Ireland's self-declared gourmet capital since the 1970s, in a harbour of painted houses. Charles Fort on the headland gives you the walk before lunch.
itinerary.afternoon: The town's restaurant density is real — everything from a Michelin-recognised small room to fish shacks on the pier. Blacks of Kinsale brews and distils in the town.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Kinsale, then the harbour walk. This is the last "town" night before the west gets rural.

itinerary.title: Clonakilty, Timoleague and the pudding belt
itinerary.morning: **Clonakilty** black pudding has been made by the same family butchers since the 1880s and is the Irish benchmark. The town also has a Friday market and Deasy's out at Ring for lunch on the water.
itinerary.afternoon: **Ummera Smokehouse** at Timoleague — cold-smoked salmon, chicken and bacon over oak, in tiny batches, by arrangement. Then Inchydoney beach.
itinerary.evening: Stay in Clonakilty or move on to Skibbereen. Traditional music in Clonakilty's pubs is unforced and excellent.

itinerary.title: Skibbereen, Drimoleague and the cheese run
itinerary.morning: **Skibbereen's Saturday market** is one of the best food markets in Ireland — cheese, vegetables, bread, oysters, and the producers themselves behind the tables. Time your week to land here on a Saturday.
itinerary.afternoon: The farmhouse cheese circuit: **Durrus** on the Sheep's Head road, **Gubbeen** at Schull with Fingal Ferguson's smokehouse and salami operation next to Giana's cheese room, and **Glenilen Farm** at Drimoleague for butter and cream. Visits are by arrangement and worth every email.
itinerary.evening: **West Cork Distillers** in Skibbereen, then dinner in town.

itinerary.title: Schull, Baltimore and the sea
itinerary.morning: Schull's Sunday market and the harbour. **Sally Barnes's Woodcock Smokery** near Castletownshend smokes only wild fish, over beech, with salt — one of the most uncompromising food producers in Europe.
itinerary.afternoon: Baltimore, and the ferry to Sherkin Island or Cape Clear — Cape Clear has a goat farm making ice cream and a bird observatory, and the crossing is 45 minutes of Atlantic.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Baltimore, where the standard is startlingly high for a village of a few hundred people. `verify: true`

itinerary.title: Bantry, the Beara edge and out
itinerary.morning: **Bantry's Friday market** if the day fits; otherwise the drive around Bantry Bay with Whiddy Island offshore, and Milleens cheese country on the Beara peninsula — where Veronica Steele made the cheese in 1976 that started Irish farmhouse cheesemaking.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive back to Cork Airport (about 2 h from Bantry). Buy vacuum-packed cheese and smoked fish at the last market you pass; almost all of it travels well.

accommodationStrategy.name: Ballymaloe House
accommodationStrategy.description: A working farm, a country house, and the origin point of the whole story. Rooms are comfortable rather than luxurious; the point is the dining room, the gardens and the atmosphere of a place that has been doing this for sixty years. Book months ahead, especially for a course week.

accommodationStrategy.name: Kinsale townhouses
accommodationStrategy.description: Walkable to every restaurant in town, which matters when the whole day's plan ends in a tasting menu. Good breakfasts and secure parking.

accommodationStrategy.name: Skibbereen and Baltimore small hotels and guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: The West Cork base for Days 5 and 6, close to the markets, the cheese farms and the harbour. Baltimore in particular lets you walk to dinner and take the island ferry in the morning without moving the car.

logistics.emergency: 112 or 999. Cork University Hospital is the regional centre; West Cork's local facilities are limited and distances are long — Bantry to Cork is nearly two hours.
logistics.weather: Mild, wet, and Atlantic. This does not disrupt a food itinerary but it will disrupt the island ferries from Baltimore and the outdoor legs. Have a wet-day plan: the English Market, the Butter Museum and a distillery tour all work in rain.
logistics.bookingWindows: Ballymaloe House and its cookery-school courses: 3–6 months. Starred restaurants in Cork and West Cork: 4–8 weeks and longer for weekends. Summer accommodation in Kinsale and Baltimore: 3 months.

other.label: Market days are the skeleton of this trip
other.text: Skibbereen on Saturday, Bantry on Friday, Schull on Sunday, Midleton on Saturday, Clonakilty on Friday. Build the week around them rather than fitting them in. `verify: true`

other.label: Producer visits are a favour, not a service
other.text: Farmhouse cheesemakers and smokehouses are small businesses with animals and schedules. Email two weeks ahead, confirm, arrive on time, and buy something.

other.label: Driving and drinking
other.text: Ireland's limit is 50 mg/100 ml and enforcement is active. West Cork's distances are short but the roads are dark and narrow; plan a driver or stay within walking distance of dinner.

other.label: Bringing food home
other.text: Vacuum-packed cheese, smoked fish and cured meat travel fine within the EU. Check current rules if you are flying to the UK or beyond, which has changed post-Brexit.

proTips: Book a **single-day course at Ballymaloe Cookery School** rather than trying to get a table at everything. It is the highest-value day in this itinerary and it recalibrates how you cook afterwards.
Ask a cheesemaker who else you should visit. West Cork's producers are a network with forty years of history between them and the introductions they make will open doors no booking system will.
The **English Market at 09:00 on a weekday** is a working market with butchers who will talk. At 13:00 on a Saturday it is a scrum.
Irish farmhouse cheese has a **season**. Summer-milk cheeses eaten in autumn are a different product from winter ones; ask which wheel is drinking best right now, exactly as you would with wine.
Kinsale is where most food tourists stop. Skibbereen, Schull and Ballydehob are where the producers actually are, and the price and quality difference is stark.

If a market day is rained out, the **Bantry and Skibbereen indoor food halls and delis** carry the same producers' goods, and Toonsbridge Dairy's buffalo mozzarella at Macroom is a reliable indoor stop.

raw.appellations_and_terroir: No wine appellations — this is a dairy, shellfish and smokehouse terroir. The relevant protected names are Irish farmhouse cheeses and Irish whiskey; the defining conditions are mild wet Atlantic pasture, a long grass-growing season, and cold clean inshore water
raw.reservation_only: Farm and smokehouse visits are by arrangement — these are working producers, not visitor attractions. Email a week or two ahead

trips.title: Sangiovese Spine: Chianti Classico, Montalcino & the Pecorino Hills
trips.subRegion: Chianti Classico, Montalcino, Val d'Orcia & Cortona

bestPeriod.window: Mid-May–late June & mid-September–late October
bestPeriod.avoid: Late July–mid-August — 35–38°C and Ferragosto closures; also 20 Sept–5 Oct, when owners are on the crushpad and answer nothing
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-May–late June & mid-September–late October

accommodation.note: Chianti agriturismo €120–€180 pppn; Montalcino relais €160–€240

food.note: Trattoria mains €14–€22; Cecchini set menus €35–€60; one blowout €120–€180

transport.note: Car 6 days €260–€400, fuel, parking, one shared driver day

activities.note: 9–11 tastings at €25–€60, cheese dairy €12, cookery class €120–€160

profile.difficultyNote: 2/5 — cellar stairs, sloping vineyard rows, two hours standing at a butcher's counter

trips.gatewayAirport: FLR Florence Peretola, 55 min drive to Greve in Chianti; PSA Pisa 1 h 40 min; BLQ Bologna 1 h 55 min
trips.summary: One grape, three denominations, and a 90 km transect explaining why they taste nothing alike. You start on the galestro ridges between Greve and Radda, where Chianti Classico has just redrawn itself into eleven named sub-zones; drop south to Montalcino, where Sangiovese Grosso ripens earlier and spends five years in wood; and finish among Pienza's pecorino dairies and Cortona's Etruscan terraces. Three estates a day is a hangover, two is an education. It suits people who want to leave able to taste Panzano against Lamole blind.

itinerary.title: Florence to Greve, the Gallo Nero briefing
itinerary.morning: Land at Peretola, collect the car and leave on the SR222 Chiantigiana rather than fighting Florence's ZTL, passing San Casciano where the UGA map begins.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk Greve's funnel-shaped Piazza Matteotti, then use **Le Cantine di Greve in Chianti**, a self-serve enoteca of roughly 140 wines — the cheapest way to calibrate Annata against Riserva against Gran Selezione before spending money at estates.
itinerary.evening: **Ristoro di Lamole**, up the hairpins at 550 m, for peposo and a terrace over the Lamole terraces.
itinerary.dayStats: 42 km / 55 min from FLR / 1 enoteca, 8–10 pours at €2–€6 / Annata bottle band €14–€22

itinerary.title: Panzano: the Conca d'Oro and the butcher
itinerary.morning: 8 km south to **Fontodi**, organic since the 1980s, on the floor of the Conca d'Oro amphitheatre; ask to walk out and see galestro shale in section.
itinerary.afternoon: Second estate at **Il Molino di Grace** or **Vecchie Terre di Montefili**, then the ridge path for the view that explains the UGA boundary.
itinerary.evening: **Officina della Bistecca** at Cecchini — fixed communal menu built on the bistecca, oil, salt and Dario's own Chianti. The sitting starts as one; be on time.
itinerary.dayStats: 22 km driving / 2 estates / fees €35–€50 each / Cecchini fixed menu about €60 with wine / Gran Selezione €38–€75

itinerary.title: Radda, Gaiole and the art of ageing
itinerary.morning: **Radda in Chianti** at 530 m: **Montevertine** if your email landed, otherwise **Val delle Corti** or **Poggerino**. Altitude reads as acidity and red fruit, not weight.
itinerary.afternoon: The strada bianca to **Castello di Ama**, Gaiole — San Lorenzo Gran Selezione, Vigneto Bellavista, and site-specific work by Kapoor, Kounellis and Chen Zhen through the cellars.
itinerary.evening: **Badia a Coltibuono**'s restaurant in the eleventh-century abbey for ribollita and pappardelle sul cinghiale; **Osteria Le Panzanelle** at Lucarelli is the cheaper call.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 km / 2 estates / Ama €40–€70 including the art park / 8 km white gravel, drive at 30 km/h

itinerary.title: Pici by hand, then south to Montalcino
itinerary.morning: The cookery class at **Badia a Coltibuono**: hand-rolled eggless pici, a sauce, a dessert, eaten with the abbey's wines.
itinerary.afternoon: Through **Castellina in Chianti** for the Via delle Volte tunnel-street, then the SR2 Cassia past Siena into the Val d'Orcia.
itinerary.evening: **Osticcio** in Montalcino, a wine bar over the Ombrone — a first Brunello flight and cinta senese salumi.
itinerary.dayStats: Class 4 h, €120–€160 / 78 km, 1 h 25 min Gaiole–Montalcino / Brunello by the glass €9–€16

itinerary.title: Brunello: north slope, south slope
itinerary.morning: North first — **Il Marroneto** below the walls or **Canalicchio di Sopra** at Montosoli, tasting Rosso beside Brunello to see what four extra years does.
itinerary.afternoon: South to **Sant'Angelo in Colle** for **Il Poggione** or **Argiano**, then the Romanesque **Abbazia di Sant'Antimo** below Castelnuovo dell'Abate — twelfth-century travertine that glows at 17:00.
itinerary.evening: **Il Leccio** at Sant'Angelo in Colle for pinci all'aglione. Driver day: book Sunny Tuscany Transfers or use the hotel's car.
itinerary.dayStats: 46 km / 2 estates / fees €25–€45, usually waived on two bottles / Brunello €40–€90, Riserva €70–€180, Rosso €18–€28

itinerary.title: Pienza pecorino and Montepulciano's Nobile
itinerary.morning: Across the Val d'Orcia to **Pienza**, Pius II's Renaissance grid town, and **Podere Il Casale** or **Caseificio Cugusi** for the pecorino sequence: fresco, semi-stagionato, stagionato, then the leaf- and ash-aged wheels.
itinerary.afternoon: **Montepulciano** at 605 m: Vino Nobile at biodynamic **Avignonesi** at Valiano, or the medieval cellars of **Contucci** and **De' Ricci** under Piazza Grande, among the few here that tolerate short notice.
itinerary.evening: **La Grotta**, opposite San Biagio, or **Osteria Acquacheta** for bistecca priced by the etto.
itinerary.dayStats: 62 km / 1 dairy + 2 cellars / cheese tasting €10–€15 / Vino Nobile €18–€35, Pieve €35–€60

itinerary.title: Cortona, the oil mill, and out
itinerary.morning: East to **Cortona**, Etruscan walls above the Valdichiana, for the MAEC museum's bronze lamp. Cortona DOC is Syrah country — a useful palate reset.
itinerary.afternoon: **Frantoio Pruneti** at San Polo in Chianti for a guided oil tasting — or, in November, a live pressing — then hand the car back at Peretola.
itinerary.evening: **Trattoria Cammillo** or **Il Santo Bevitore** in Florence if you fly the next morning.
itinerary.dayStats: 115 km Montalcino–Cortona–Florence / oil tasting €12–€20 / DOP Chianti Classico oil 500 ml €18–€26 / allow 2 h to the airport

accommodationStrategy.name: Villa Bordoni
accommodationStrategy.description: On a dirt lane 4 km from Greve, putting Panzano, Lamole and Radda inside 25 minutes. Free parking, a real cellar list, and a kitchen that still feeds you after a late Gaiole finish. €220–€340 double B&B.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Vecchia Oliviera
accommodationStrategy.description: Just outside Porta Cerbaia with its own car park, two minutes from Osticcio and the Fortezza enoteca, west-facing over the Val d'Orcia. Best value for the Brunello days at €150–€220 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Castello di Velona
accommodationStrategy.description: The splurge: an eleventh-century castle above Sant'Antimo with thermal pools, isolated enough to force the driver arrangement the week needs anyway. €350–€600 double.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming, no surcharge. 4G is reliable in towns, patchy on the strade bianche between Radda and Gaiole. Download offline maps — several estate entrances are unsigned gates with a number.
logistics.emergency: 112. Nearest hospitals are Campostaggia (Poggibonsi) for Chianti and Nottola (Montepulciano) for the Val d'Orcia. EHIC/GHIC accepted; add rental-excess cover.
logistics.weather: Hail between mid-May and July is the real hazard and closes roads fast. September afternoons still reach 30°C.
logistics.bookingWindows: Cecchini's Officina 4–8 weeks; Biondi-Santi and Montevertine 6–12 weeks; Ama and Antinori 2–4 weeks; Coltibuono classes 3–4 weeks. Small Montalcino estates answer Italian email faster than English.
logistics.money: Eurozone. Cards near-universal, but frantoi, dairies and farm stands prefer cash; carry €150. Service is normally included — round up. The €2–€4 coperto is not a tip.
logistics.transportRules: Florence, Siena, Montalcino and Montepulciano enforce **ZTL** camera zones; fines arrive months later via the rental company, so park outside the walls always. Rural fuel stations close 13:00–15:30 and Sundays, though most have unattended card pumps. Autostrada tolls pay at the barrier.
logistics.permits: Tasting fees of €25–€60 are standard and often credited against two to six bottles — ask when booking, not at the till. Intra-EU shipping is simple; UK and US runs €30–€90 a case plus duty.
logistics.health: Tap water is drinkable, fountains included. The blood-alcohol limit of 0.50 g/l is less than one tasting flight — use the spittoons and treat the driver rota as fixed. Ticks in woodland edges April–October.

proTips: Ask every Gran Selezione producer which UGA is on the label and why. That tier is the only one permitted to name a sub-zone, so it is the only bottle that tells you where in Chianti Classico you actually are.
Taste Rosso di Montalcino beside Brunello at the same estate. Identical fruit, four years apart — more education in ten minutes than a vertical costing five times as much.
Book Cecchini's lunch counter instead of dinner if you are driving. Dario DOC plus a glass costs a fraction of the Officina and leaves you sober by 15:00.
Estates on the Radda–Gaiole gravel open on the hour and do not wait. Arrive five minutes early or lose the slot to tomorrow.
Late October is the sweet spot: harvest done so owners will talk, mills running, vineyard colour at peak. Late September fails all three tests.
Buy oil at the frantoio, not the estate. November olio nuovo under a DOP Chianti Classico seal is a different product from supermarket Toscano IGP, and the price gap is narrower than you think.
Enoteca La Fortezza inside Montalcino's fortress pours four producers' Brunello side by side for the cost of one estate visit — use it on arrival to decide which two estates to book.
Ship, don't carry. Two cases of Brunello break most baggage allowances, and estate shippers handle the paperwork better than a courier found later.

raw.Chianti Classico DOCG: — minimum 80% Sangiovese; Gran Selezione since the 2023 revision requires 90% and bans international varieties. Tiers: Annata (12 months), Riserva (24 months), Gran Selezione (30 months, estate fruit only). The eleven **UGA** sub-zones — San Casciano, Montefioralle, Panzano, Lamole, Greve, Radda, Gaiole, Castellina, Vagliagli, Castelnuovo Berardenga, San Donato in Poggio — may be printed **only on Gran Selezione labels**. Lamole at 500–650 m on sandstone gives floral, high-toned wine; Panzano's Conca d'Oro gives grip; Castelnuovo Berardenga is warmest and roundest.
raw.Brunello di Montalcino DOCG: — 100% Sangiovese Grosso, 4 years' ageing (2 in oak), released 1 January of the fifth year; Riserva 5 years. **Rosso di Montalcino DOC** is the same fruit at one year and is the sane weekday drinking; **Sant'Antimo DOC** covers the rest. North slope (Montosoli, Torrenieri) is perfumed; Sant'Angelo in Colle in the south ripens hardest. **Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG** — 70% minimum Sangiovese, locally Prugnolo Gentile, 24 months; the new **Pieve** tier needs 85% from twelve named parish districts. **Bolgheri DOC** is the coastal outlier: Cabernet and Merlot on beach gravel.
raw.Reservation-only estates: Nobody takes weekday walk-ins. **Castello di Ama** (Gaiole; San Lorenzo Gran Selezione plus a contemporary art park) books via castellodiama.com, roughly €40–€70, English standard, 3–4 weeks ahead. **Antinori nel Chianti Classico** at Bargino sells timed online tours, €45–€75. **Fontodi** (Panzano) answers email, two weeks' notice, €35–€50 usually credited against a case. **Montevertine** (Radda) takes very few visitors, email only, 6–8 weeks. In Montalcino, **Biondi-Santi Tenuta Greppo** books months ahead at €80–€150 for verticals; **Il Marroneto**, **Poggio di Sotto** and **Salvioni** are email-only; **Argiano** and **Il Poggione** reply within days.
raw.Producers beyond wine: **Antica Macelleria Cecchini**, Via XX Luglio 11, Panzano — Dario Cecchini's butcher shop and three eating rooms: Officina della Bistecca (fixed, about €60, communal, one sitting), Solociccia (€35–€40), and the Dario DOC burger counter at lunch; book on dariocecchini.com. **Caseificio Cugusi**, Via della Boccia 8, Montepulciano, and **Podere Il Casale** above Pienza for Pecorino di Pienza aged in ash, walnut leaves or hay, €10–€15. **Frantoio Pruneti** at San Polo presses Moraiolo, Frantoio and Leccino. **Forno Lombardi** (Greve) for unsalted pane sciocco.
raw.Harvest timing: Chianti Classico picks roughly 15 September–10 October; Montalcino starts a week earlier. The last week of September is the worst week for an owner's attention and the best for seeing a crushpad — choose. **Olive pressing runs 25 October–late November** and is the most rewarding hands-on window.
raw.Hands-on element: A half-day pici and sauce class in the abbey kitchen at **Badia a Coltibuono**, Gaiole — €120–€160 with lunch and estate wine, English-taught, 3–4 weeks' notice. In November swap it for a dawn pressing at Frantoio Pruneti, following your own crate through the mill.
raw.Designated-driver strategy: Italy's limit is 0.50 g/l, and zero for licences under three years old. Chianti has no useful public transport. Budget two driver days: **Tuscany Wine Tours by Massimo** and **Grape Tours Florence** run English-speaking drivers at roughly €450–€600 per car per day for 2–4 people; **Sunny Tuscany Transfers** covers the Montalcino leg. Trains only help at the edges — Florence SMN–Siena 1 h 30 m, Chiusi-Chianciano for Montepulciano plus a 20-minute taxi.

trips.summary: A seven-day culinary & wine tour itinerary in Vilnius, Aukštaitija (northeast Lithuania), Biržai, Dzūkija, Lithuania.

itinerary.title: Vilnius: the old town table
itinerary.morning: Arrive Vilnius. The old town is the largest surviving baroque old town in Eastern Europe, on the UNESCO list, and walkable end to end in forty minutes.
itinerary.afternoon: **Halės Turgus**, the covered market since 1906: rye bread, smoked meats, curd cheese, forest mushrooms and honey. Lunch here. Then Užupis, the self-declared artists' republic across the Vilnia river with its own constitution on a wall in thirty languages.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at one of the restaurants reinterpreting Lithuanian historical cuisine — the Grand Duchy's kitchen, with its game, rye and preserved fruit, is being seriously researched and cooked in Vilnius right now. `verify: true`

itinerary.title: Vilnius: beer bars and the modern kitchen
itinerary.morning: The Gediminas Tower and the Palace of the Grand Dukes for the context that explains the food: this was the capital of a state that stretched to the Black Sea.
itinerary.afternoon: Vilnius's **farmhouse-beer bars** are the point of this day. A handful of small bars in the old town and in Naujamiestis serve rotating *kaimiškas alus* from named village brewers — often unfiltered, low-carbonation, and unlike anything in the German or Belgian traditions.
itinerary.evening: Snack culture: smoked pig ears, *kepta duona* (fried garlic rye), curd cheese and salted peas, which exist specifically to be eaten with farmhouse ale.

itinerary.title: Trakai and the Karaim kitchen
itinerary.morning: Trakai, 30 minutes west: the island castle on Lake Galvė, red brick on water, rebuilt in the 20th century and unmistakable.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Karaim** community — a Turkic people brought here in the 14th century by Grand Duke Vytautas — still lives on the town's main street in three-windowed wooden houses. Their **kibinai**, a baked pastry of lamb and onion, is one of the region's great dishes and is made properly only here.
itinerary.evening: Return to Vilnius, or drive north to start the Aukštaitija leg.

itinerary.title: Aukštaitija: the farmhouse brewing heartland
itinerary.morning: Drive north toward Panevėžys and Pasvalys (about 2 h). This is flat, fertile, barley country and the last place in Europe where farmhouse brewing survived without a revival — it simply never stopped.
itinerary.afternoon: Visit an actual farm brewery. **Jovarų Alus** is the most famous, brewed by hand in a village with equipment that looks agricultural because it is. Arrangements must be made ahead and a Lithuanian-speaking guide helps enormously.
itinerary.evening: Biržai, the beer capital: a castle, a lake, and two large regional breweries in town alongside the farm producers. Dinner with local ale and *skilandis*.

itinerary.title: Biržai karst, Anykščiai and the fruit wines
itinerary.morning: The **Kirkilai karst lakes** outside Biržai — a landscape of sinkholes where the gypsum bedrock collapses, with a viewing tower over dozens of small water-filled craters.
itinerary.afternoon: South to Anykščiai for the fruit-wine tradition — Lithuania's berry and apple wines are a serious regional industry — plus the treetop walkway in the Anykščiai pine forest and the narrow-gauge railway.
itinerary.evening: Anykščiai or back toward Vilnius.

itinerary.title: Stakliškės mead and the Dzūkija forest
itinerary.morning: **Stakliškės**, south of Vilnius, is where Lithuanian mead is made to a documented traditional method — honey, water, hops and herbs, fermented and matured for months rather than fortified. The tasting explains why *midus* is closer to a wine than to the sweet mead most people expect.
itinerary.afternoon: Into **Dzūkija National Park**: pine forest, sand, and villages like Zervynos and Musteika, where the UNESCO-listed **tree-beekeeping** tradition is still practised — hives hollowed into living pines, worked with a rope and a climbing seat.
itinerary.evening: Mushrooms. Dzūkija is Lithuania's foraging heartland and in September the entire region is in the forest at dawn. A guesthouse dinner here will be built around what was picked that morning.

itinerary.title: Vilnius return and departure
itinerary.morning: Last market run at Halės or the Tymo market for honey, black bread, smoked cheese and a bottle of mead.
itinerary.afternoon: Vilnius airport is fifteen minutes from the old town.

accommodationStrategy.name: Vilnius old town boutique hotels
accommodationStrategy.description: Small hotels in restored baroque and 19th-century buildings, €80–150. Everything on Days 1–3 is walkable, which matters on a beer itinerary. Look for a property between the cathedral and Užupis.

accommodationStrategy.name: Biržai / Aukštaitija country guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: Simple, warm, and often with a sauna and a host who brews or knows who does. This is the region where the accommodation is the introduction — a guesthouse owner will get you into a farm brewery that no website lists.

accommodationStrategy.name: Dzūkija forest homesteads
accommodationStrategy.description: Wooden houses in pine forest near Merkinė or Marcinkonys, €50–90, with home cooking and mushroom knowledge. The right ending for the week and a completely different Lithuania from Vilnius.

logistics.emergency: 112. Vilnius has excellent hospitals; rural Aukštaitija and Dzūkija are 40–90 minutes from one.
logistics.bookingWindows: Vilnius restaurants: 1–3 weeks. Brewery visits: 2–4 weeks via a guide. Guesthouses in mushroom season: 3–4 weeks, and note that September weekends in Dzūkija are busy with Lithuanian foragers.

other.label: Farmhouse breweries are farms
other.text: They are not visitor centres, several do not have websites, and the brewer may speak only Lithuanian. Either go with a specialist beer guide from Vilnius or have your guesthouse arrange it. Turning up unannounced is not the custom. `verify: true`

other.label: What farmhouse ale is
other.text: Often unboiled or briefly boiled wort, family yeast cultures, farm-grown hops, low carbonation, served fresh and sometimes cloudy. Shelf life is short and it does not travel — which is precisely why you go to it.

other.label: Alcohol law
other.text: Lithuania has some of the EU's strictest alcohol regulation: a **0.0‰ drink-drive limit for drivers with under two years' experience and 0.4‰ otherwise**, retail sale restricted by hour, and a minimum purchase age of 20. Plan drivers accordingly. `verify: true`

other.label: Foraging
other.text: Mushroom and berry picking on public forest land is legal and is a national obsession. Do not pick in strict nature reserves, and never eat anything a local has not confirmed — Lithuania has genuinely dangerous lookalikes.

other.label: Driving
other.text: Good roads, headlights on at all times, winter tyres compulsory 10 November–1 April. Rural drink-driving enforcement is strict and checkpoints are common.

proTips: Hire a **specialist beer guide** for the Aukštaitija day. It costs less than a good dinner and it is the difference between drinking farmhouse ale in a Vilnius bar and drinking it out of the fermenter with the man who made it.

Ask for the **beer snack menu** (*užkandžiai*) rather than a main course. Smoked pig ears, fried rye with garlic, salted peas, curd cheese and dried meat is the correct meal with farmhouse ale and it costs €10.

**Šaltibarščiai** — the neon-pink cold beetroot and kefir soup with hot potatoes on the side — is a summer-only dish and Lithuanians are passionate about it. Order it any time between May and September.
Mead from **Stakliškės** is the single best thing to bring home from this trip: it is unlike commercial mead, it ages, and it is difficult to find outside the country.
Go in **late September**. Mushroom season, honey harvest, apple wine, warm days and beer festivals in the Aukštaitija towns all coincide.

Vilnius's food scene has changed dramatically in the last decade and the historical-cuisine research movement is the most interesting thing happening in Baltic food. Book one such dinner deliberately, early in the week — it frames everything you eat afterwards.

raw.appellations_and_terroir: Not a wine country — this is Europe's last living **farmhouse ale** tradition, plus honey. Lithuanian *kaimiškas alus* uses raw or lightly boiled wort, local landrace yeasts kept in families for generations, and hops grown on the farm. Stakliškės mead is made to a documented traditional recipe; Lithuanian and Polish **tree beekeeping** was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2020
