trips.title: Crémant and the Luxembourg Moselle

bestPeriod.note: Whit Monday brings Grevenmacher's wine market and June the vines in full leaf; September is harvest, when the smallest domaines are hardest to reach.

trips.gatewayAirport: Luxembourg (LUX)
trips.summary: A week along the Route du Vin tasting Crémant de Luxembourg, Riesling and Elbling from cooperative caves to appointment-only biodynamic growers.
trips.hook: Luxembourg's Moselle is a 42-kilometre ribbon of river between Schengen and Wasserbillig, and it is worked by two very different hands: the Vinsmoselle cooperative, whose cellars anchor half the villages, and a handful of small, independent domaines who answer their own email. All of it moves on the country's free public transport, which means this is a week of tasting without ever calculating a taxi fare.

snapshot.Base(s): Remich (4 nights) · Grevenmacher (3 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 40 km along the Route du Vin, flat riverside paths with gentle vineyard slopes above each village
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Luxembourg (LUX), free RGTR bus or a short taxi to Remich, approx. 30 minutes
snapshot.Who It Suits: Crémant drinkers, appellation-system nerds, anyone who wants a wine week with zero transport cost

itinerary.title: Arrival on the river
itinerary.morning: Land at Luxembourg Airport and take the free RGTR bus to Remich, about 30 minutes.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Remich Esplanade, the riverside promenade that is the town's social spine, and get oriented: the Route du Vin runs both directions from here, Schengen downstream, Grevenmacher and Wormeldange upstream.
itinerary.evening: Friture de la Moselle, small fried river fish, at a promenade restaurant, with a glass of Elbling — the oldest grape variety still grown here, planted since Roman times.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 4 km on foot. Approx. tasting spend: €0.

itinerary.title: Crémant and the Marque Nationale
itinerary.morning: Domaine Mathis Bastian in Remich pours a walk-in tasting and is a good place to start with the appellation system: any bottle carrying Luxembourg's Marque Nationale seal has passed an official state tasting panel and chemical analysis, the country's own quality guarantee, distinct from and layered on top of the EU's Moselle Luxembourgeoise appellation.
itinerary.afternoon: A short bus ride to Stadtbredimus for Domaine Cep d'Or, another walk-in cellar, focused on Crémant de Luxembourg, the traditional-method sparkling wine that has carried its own AOP since 1991 — made the same way as Champagne, second fermentation in the bottle, but from Mosel-grown Pinot Blanc, Auxerrois, Chardonnay and Riesling.
itinerary.evening: Bouneschlupp, green bean soup with potatoes, bacon and smoked sausage — one of Luxembourg's two unofficial national dishes — back in Remich.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 2. Km travelled: 8 km plus bus. Approx. tasting spend: €25–35.

itinerary.title: The email-only grower
itinerary.morning: Domaine Sunnen-Hoffmann, a small biodynamic producer near Remich, is well regarded but does not run a public tasting room; visits are by appointment, arranged by email at least two to three weeks ahead, or through the Entente Touristique de la Région Moselle. Book this before the trip if you want the slot.
itinerary.afternoon: Without a confirmed appointment, spend the afternoon on the Sentier Viticole path above Remich instead, through the vineyards toward Bech-Kleinmacher, where the A Possen open-air museum shows the region's older farming and wine-growing life.
itinerary.evening: Judd mat Gaardebounen, smoked pork collar with broad beans, Luxembourg's other national dish, at a Remich restaurant, paired with a Pinot Gris.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0–1 (reservation-dependent). Km travelled: 10 km. Approx. tasting spend: €15–30.

itinerary.title: Up the Route du Vin to Grevenmacher
itinerary.morning: Free RGTR bus along the Route du Vin through Wintrange, Ahn and Wormeldange, about 30 minutes to Grevenmacher. Wormeldange is worth a stop for the Vinsmoselle cooperative's Caves de Wormeldange, a walk-in cellar known for Riesling and Auxerrois from the steep Koeppchen vineyard.
itinerary.afternoon: Grevenmacher itself is Bernard-Massard territory: Caves Bernard-Massard, family-owned since 1921 and the country's largest private Crémant producer, runs a public tour and tasting through its rock-cut cellars, walk-in but worth booking the tour slot a day ahead in high season.
itinerary.evening: Settle into Grevenmacher; a quiet dinner facing the river.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 2. Km travelled: 6 km plus bus. Approx. tasting spend: €25–30.

itinerary.title: Ahn, Ehnen and the small domaines
itinerary.morning: Walk or take the free bus back down to Ahn and Ehnen, two of the prettiest villages on the river, for Domaine Krier Bisenius, a family estate with a walk-in Vinothek, pouring Auxerrois and Pinot Gris from vineyards immediately behind the village.
itinerary.afternoon: Ehnen's small wine museum, the Musée du Vin, occupies a former winegrower's house and covers the valley's shift from Elbling-heavy production to today's varietal range.
itinerary.evening: Back to Grevenmacher. Kachkéis, a soft, spreadable cooked cheese, with bread and a glass of Rivaner, as a simple evening plate.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 9 km. Approx. tasting spend: €15–20.

itinerary.title: Wäimaart and Wormeldange's Koeppchen
itinerary.morning: If the trip falls near Whit Monday (Pentecost), Grevenmacher's Wäimaart — a wine market with stalls from growers up and down the valley — fills the town centre; otherwise spend the morning walking the marked vineyard path above Wormeldange to the Koeppchen site.
itinerary.afternoon: A second look at Vinsmoselle's cooperative range, this time comparing a Crémant Brut against a Crémant Rosé, both walk-in pours, to understand the house style against the smaller independents tasted earlier in the week.
itinerary.evening: Quetschentaart, plum tart, for dessert — the valley's harvest-season standard.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 6 km. Approx. tasting spend: €15–20.

itinerary.title: Luxembourg City market and departure
itinerary.morning: Free train or bus into Luxembourg City, about 25 minutes, for the Place Guillaume II market, running Wednesday and Saturday mornings, roughly 07:30–13:30 — a last chance at farm cheese, charcuterie and produce from across the country.
itinerary.afternoon: A walk through the Grund and along the casemates before heading to the airport.
itinerary.evening: Departure from Luxembourg (LUX).
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 5 km plus transfers. Approx. tasting spend: €10–15.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel St. Nicolas
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits directly on the Esplanade with river-facing rooms, putting the promenade restaurants, the Route du Vin cycle path and the free bus stop all within a few minutes' walk — a good base for the week's first, gentler days.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel-Restaurant Simmer
accommodationStrategy.description: A long-established address on the Route du Vin between Grevenmacher and Remich, with a kitchen built around the local wine list; useful as a base for the Wormeldange and Ahn cellars without depending on bus timetables for dinner.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European, covers police, fire and ambulance in Luxembourg.
logistics.weather: The river moderates temperatures; sudden showers are more common than long rain in May and June.
logistics.bookingWindows: Independent growers such as Sunnen-Hoffmann do not run drop-in tasting rooms; email at least two to three weeks ahead, or route the request through the Entente Touristique de la Région Moselle. Vinsmoselle's cooperative caves and Bernard-Massard are walk-in.
logistics.money: Cards are accepted almost everywhere in Luxembourg, including small cellar shops.
logistics.transportRules: All RGTR buses and trains within Luxembourg have been free of charge since 2020; the Route du Vin bus and the Luxembourg City line both cost nothing.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Village Vinothèques often close Monday; check ahead if your plan depends on one specific stop.

other.label: Drink-drive alternatives
other.text: With buses and trains free, there is no financial reason to drive between tastings — use the Route du Vin bus line, or walk the flat riverside path between neighbouring villages.

proTips: Ask any Marque Nationale bottle's back label for its control number — it is a genuine state-issued mark, not a marketing sticker, and growers are proud to explain it.
Book the Bernard-Massard cellar tour a day ahead in summer; the walk-in tasting room stays open even when the guided tour is full.
Compare an Elbling against a Crémant base wine if a cellar offers it; Elbling's high acidity is exactly what makes the valley's sparkling wine work.
Time a Whit Monday visit around Grevenmacher's Wäimaart for the widest single-day tasting of small growers in one place.
Ask for Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc back to back — the valley's two most-planted white grapes taste more different from each other here than in most other regions.
Use the free train to Luxembourg City for the Saturday Place Guillaume II market rather than the smaller village markets, which run irregularly.

packingNotes: Comfortable shoes for the Sentier Viticole vineyard paths, which are dirt and grass rather than pavement.
A light rain layer; river-valley showers arrive with little warning.
A small cooler bag for Crémant or Kachkéis bought at a cellar door.
A phrase or two of French or German; Luxembourgish is the everyday language but both are widely spoken.
Cash in small denominations for market stalls, though cards work almost everywhere else.
A daypack for the vineyard walk above Wormeldange.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Sunnen-Hoffmann or another small domaine doesn't reply in time.** Fall back on Vinsmoselle's cooperative caves or Bernard-Massard, both reliably walk-in.
**You visit outside Whit Monday and miss the Wäimaart.** Grevenmacher's cellars and the Ehnen wine museum give the same context any week of the season.
**Rain washes out the vineyard walk.** The Musée du Vin in Ehnen and the A Possen museum near Bech-Kleinmacher are solid indoor alternatives.
**A bus runs late or is cancelled.** Services are frequent along the Route du Vin, but build a 20-minute buffer before any timed cellar appointment.
**You've tasted more than planned.** With transport free and frequent, simply wait for the next bus rather than walking a vineyard road at dusk.

trips.hook: Moldova is the only wine country where you tour two of the cellars by car, windows down, headlights on, past street signs that read *Cabernet* and *Feteasca*. Above ground it is quieter than that sounds: low Codru hills of walnut and vine, villages of blue-painted gates, and a capital that eats plăcinte at 08:00. Come in the last week of September and you will smell fermentation from the road. It suits drinkers who want producers, not pageantry.

Overland: Iași (Romania) is 3 h by road, Odesa 4 h. There is a slow overnight train from Bucharest to Chișinău.

itinerary.title: Chișinău, Landing and the First Glass
itinerary.morning: Land at KIV, drop bags, and orient on Bulevardul Ștefan cel Mare — the Arcul de Triumf, the Catedrala Nașterea Domnului with its free-standing belfry, the Ștefan cel Mare monument at the park gate. Twenty minutes fixes the city's grid in your head.
itinerary.afternoon: **Piața Centrală** for the food groundwork: barrels of *must* in season, sheep's brânză, walnuts, dried plums, and the divin counter. Then late plăcinte at **La Plăcinte** on Ștefan cel Mare.
itinerary.evening: A structured by-the-glass flight at **Carpe Diem**, the city's serious wine bar — ask for Viorica, then a Rara Neagră, then a Fetească Neagră, in that order [VERIFY: current hours and address]. Dinner at **Vatra Neamului** for zeamă and mămăligă.
itinerary.dayStats: city walking, 4 km

itinerary.title: The Two Underground Cities
itinerary.morning: North to **Cricova**. The tour runs by electric train through galleries quarried for limestone and converted to wine storage in the 1950s; it holds 12–14 °C, so bring a jacket even in September. Finish in the tasting rooms on the traditional-method sparkling.
itinerary.afternoon: South through Chișinău to **Mileștii Mici**, driven along the underground avenues past the *Golden Collection* to a tasting hall; the scale, not the wine list, is the point. Allow an hour of city traffic between the two.
itinerary.evening: Eat lightly — **Propaganda Cafe**, or a bowl of zeamă near Parcul Catedralei. Two big lunches are coming.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km driving

itinerary.title: East to the Dniester: Bulboaca and Purcari
itinerary.morning: Out on the R30 to **Castel Mimi** at Bulboaca, 35 km east. Tour the restored 1893 cellar, then taste the Codru whites; with its garden, spa and restaurant this is the one stop here that works for a non-drinker.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue southeast to **Château Purcari**, 60 km on, for the **Negru de Purcari** vertical: Cabernet Sauvignon with Saperavi and Rara Neagră in French oak, and the 1878 Paris story told properly.
itinerary.evening: Stay at the **Purcari Wine Resort** — villas on the estate lake. Dinner is estate cooking with estate wine, which is exactly the point of driving this far [VERIFY: current villa rates and restaurant hours].
itinerary.dayStats: 120 km

itinerary.title: Ștefan Vodă Proper: Crocmaz and the Way Home
itinerary.morning: Walk the Purcari vineyard blocks before breakfast — the Dniester valley light at 07:30 is the photograph of the week. Then 20 km to **Et Cetera** at Crocmaz, the Luchianov brothers' domain: small, precise, and the best place in the country to understand Rara Neagră on its own.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop back northwest to **Asconi** at Puhăceni for a courtyard lunch — grilled meats, mămăligă, house Fetească Neagră — in the reconstructed village-street setting the estate built around its cellar.
itinerary.evening: Into Chișinău by early evening: sarmale and a glass of Fetească Regală somewhere unambitious. The week's second half is the harder driving.
itinerary.dayStats: 150 km

itinerary.title: Orheiul Vechi, the Non-Wine Day
itinerary.morning: North on the R14 to **Orheiul Vechi**, 55 km. Park at Butuceni and walk up the limestone promontory above the meander of the Răut to the **cave monastery** — a 13th-century hermitage cut into the cliff, with a bell tower on the ridge above and the church of the Ascension beside it. Cover shoulders; it is an active place of prayer.
itinerary.afternoon: Lunch in **Butuceni** — plăcinte, chicken zeamă, house wine from a plastic bottle, the honest other half of Moldovan wine culture. Then 18 km to **Chateau Vartely** above **Orhei**, tasting on the terrace.
itinerary.evening: Stay in a Butuceni guesthouse. No light pollution, and the promontory at dusk is worth walking twice.
itinerary.dayStats: 100 km

itinerary.title: South to Valul lui Traian: Tigheci and Cimișlia
itinerary.morning: The long day. Drive south from Chișinău through Hîncești and Leova toward the **Tigheci** hills for **Fautor** — the most convincing modern estate in the south, and the reference point for Moldovan Viorica and for late-harvest whites.
itinerary.afternoon: East across the Valul lui Traian earthwork toward Cimișlia for **Gitana**, whose reds are the broad, sun-driven counterweight to everything you drank in Codru. Ask to taste Rara Neagră from both zones back to back if the cellar will pour it.
itinerary.evening: Back in Chișinău around 19:00: a Bardar XO or Călărași divin, then an early night [VERIFY: current Fautor and Gitana visitor days].
itinerary.dayStats: 280 km round trip

itinerary.title: Codru Garagistes and Wine Day
itinerary.morning: Small Codru producers within 40 km of the capital: **Equinox**, **Novak**, **Atu Winery**. Two of the three in a morning is realistic; all three is not. Here you meet the winemaker, not a guide.
itinerary.afternoon: If the trip is timed to the **first weekend of October**, this is **Ziua Națională a Vinului** — a hundred-odd producers pouring in Piața Marii Adunări Naționale. Buy the glass, walk the rows, find the four-hectare estates you will never see abroad.
itinerary.evening: Last supper at **Gustar** or back at **Carpe Diem**, then Piața Centrală in the morning for divin and walnuts to carry home. Duty-free allowances into the EU are two litres of wine and one of spirits per adult [VERIFY: current EU allowance for Moldova].
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km

accommodationStrategy.name: Nobil Luxury Boutique Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: central but off the Ștefan cel Mare noise line, walkable to Carpe Diem and Piața Centrală, breakfast early enough for a 07:30 departure.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks direct; four months for the Wine Day weekend, when the city sells out.

accommodationStrategy.name: Purcari Wine Resort
accommodationStrategy.description: it removes the worst decision on this itinerary — driving 120 km back to Chișinău after a Negru de Purcari vertical. Lakeside villas, estate restaurant, vines at the door.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–8 weeks through the château, bundled with the tasting.

accommodationStrategy.name: Butuceni Eco-Resort
accommodationStrategy.description: restored *casa mare* rooms with clay stoves, a kitchen doing zeamă and plăcinte, five minutes from the cave monastery path.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–3 weeks ahead; ask whether dinner is included [VERIFY: current rates and dinner arrangement].

logistics.connectivity: Moldova is not in EU roaming. Buy a local SIM or eSIM (Orange, Moldcell) at the airport; 4G is good on main roads, patchy in the Tigheci hills.
logistics.emergency: 112 nationwide, English is not guaranteed. Carry your driver-guide's number and your accommodation's; rural pharmacies close by 18:00.
logistics.weather: sharply continental. Late September runs 20–27 °C by day, dropping to 8 °C at night in the Codru; October rain turns unsurfaced vineyard tracks to mud within an hour.
logistics.bookingWindows: Mileștii Mici, Cricova, Purcari 1–3 weeks (longer in autumn); Fautor and Et Cetera 1–2 weeks; Castel Mimi, Asconi, Vartely 3–7 days; Chișinău hotels four months for Wine Day.
logistics.money: the leu (MDL), roughly 19–20 to the euro [VERIFY: current rate]. Cards work in Chișinău and at the big estates; carry cash for guesthouses, monastery donations and market stalls. Change at a bank or a *casa de schimb valutar* in town, never at the airport rate.
logistics.transportRules: **Moldova enforces a 0.00 blood-alcohol limit.** No "one glass" tolerance, penalties include vehicle seizure — which is why a hired driver-guide is the structural requirement this itinerary is built around, at €65–€95 a day with car and fuel [VERIFY: current driver-guide day rate]. Self-driving on a non-tasting day: headlights on outside built-up areas year-round, signs Romanian-only.
logistics.permits: no permits for any winery here. Transnistria (the left bank of the Dniester, Tiraspol and Bender) is outside Chișinău's control and hire cars are often contractually barred from entering; this itinerary never crosses. Purcari sits on the right bank, well clear of it.

proTips: Book Cricova at 10:00 and Mileștii Mici at 15:00 on the same day. They sit either side of Chișinău and the afternoon slot dodges the 17:00 traffic.
Take a fleece underground. Both cellars hold 12–14 °C all year and tours run 90 minutes; September T-shirts are misery by the third gallery.
If you can taste only one native, ask for **Rara Neagră** over Fetească Neagră — rarer, lighter, and almost never exported.
Buy *must* roadside between about 20 September and 5 October — unfiltered fermenting juice in reused bottles, drinkable for two days, and the taste of Moldovan autumn.

Time Day 7 to the first Saturday of October. Ziua Națională a Vinului puts a hundred producers on one square for the price of a glass — the fastest way to find domains you would otherwise never locate.
Learn *"Un pahar de vin roșu, vă rog"* and *"Cât costă?"*. Russian works everywhere, but Romanian is noticeably better received in the villages.
Ship rather than carry — Purcari, Castel Mimi and Vartely arrange EU shipping. Six bottles in hold luggage is a false economy once you pay the excess-baggage fee.

raw.Appellations (IGP): **Codru** — the forested central hills around Chișinău, 150–350 m, the coolest zone; whites and mid-weight reds, home of Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală and the aromatic modern crossing **Viorica**. **Ștefan Vodă** — the southeast toward the Dniester and the Black Sea influence; warmer, longer autumns, the classic terroir for **Rara Neagră** and **Fetească Neagră**, the natives that give Negru de Purcari its spine. **Valul lui Traian** — the south, named for the Roman earthwork; the biggest, warmest zone, broad ripe reds around Cimișlia and the Tigheci hills. All three are IGP (*Indicație Geografică Protejată*) [VERIFY: current PDO/IGP labelling practice].
raw.Reservation-only domains — treat as abso: **Mileștii Mici**, **Cricova** and **Château Purcari** must be booked ahead; at the two underground cities walk-ins are effectively impossible, because a tour means a vehicle and a guide allocated to you. Book them 1–3 weeks out by email or web form, longer in harvest month; all three still refuse walk-ins and take reservations by phone or web form only. Budget per person (2026): **Cricova** from 250 MDL (about €13) for the weekday-morning tour alone, 400 MDL with a souvenir bottle, 700 MDL for the tour with a three-wine tasting and 950 MDL for six wines with cheese; **Mileștii Mici** 350 MDL (450 MDL evenings and weekends) for the 50-minute drive-through including the Golden Collection, 800 MDL for the tour with three wines and charcuterie; **Château Purcari** 300 MDL for the château tour alone and 450 MDL for the Classic tasting of four wines, rising to 600–1,000 MDL for the Reserve, Parcela and Academia flights, most of which carry a two- to five-person minimum. **Fautor** (Tigheci) and **Et Cetera** (Crocmaz) are small and also appointment-only. **Castel Mimi**, **Asconi** and **Chateau Vartely** run scheduled tours and a restaurant, so they tolerate short notice — but not on a September Saturday.
raw.Named producers: **Cricova**, 15 km north — 120 km of limestone galleries at 60–80 m depth, streets named after the wines stored along them, traditional-method sparkling. **Mileștii Mici**, 20 km south — the Guinness-record collection, roughly 1.5 million bottles in some 200 km of galleries, around 55 km in use; you are driven through it. **Château Purcari** (1827, Ștefan Vodă) — Negru de Purcari, the Cabernet–Saperavi–Rara Neagră blend whose ancestor took gold at the 1878 Paris Exposition. **Castel Mimi** at Bulboaca — Constantin Mimi's 1893 château, restored, with a serious restaurant. Then **Asconi** (Puhăceni), **Et Cetera** (Crocmaz, the Luchianov brothers), **Fautor** (Tigheci), **Gitana** in the south, **Chateau Vartely** above Orhei, and the small Codru names **Equinox**, **Novak** and **Atu Winery** [VERIFY: current tasting-room days at Equinox, Novak and Atu].
raw.Signature dishes: **plăcinte** (coiled pastry with brânză, cartofi, varză or cherries), **zeamă** (sour chicken-and-noodle broth lifted with borș de tărâțe), **mămăligă cu brânză și smântână** (polenta, sheep's cheese, sour cream — cut with a wooden knife, never metal), **sarmale** in cabbage or vine leaves, **must** (cloudy fermenting juice, roadside for about ten days a year), and **divin**, the aged brandy — Bardar and Călărași Divin are the names.

trips.title: Vranec & Stanušina: The Tikveš Basin and the Vardar Road
trips.subRegion: Tikveš & Povardarie — Kavadarci, Negotino, Demir Kapija, Štip & Skopje

bestPeriod.window: Late April–mid-June & September–late October
bestPeriod.avoid: July–mid-August — the Tikveš basin is the hottest place in the country at 38–42°C with almost no shade
bestPeriod.raw: Late April–mid-June & September–late October

food.note: Restaurant mains MKD 350–700 (€6–€11); a full winery dinner MKD 1,500–2,500 (€24–€41)

transport.note: Rental car 6 days, fuel, one driver day, Skopje taxis

activities.note: Tastings MKD 600–1,800 (€10–€29), Stobi entry, ajvar session, rakija visit

profile.difficultyNote: 2/5 — vineyard walking, the Stobi site on gravel, a short climb at Marko's Towers

trips.gatewayAirport: SKP Skopje, 1 h 20 min drive to Negotino, 1 h 35 min to Kavadarci; OHD Ohrid 2 h 30 min
trips.summary: Tikveš is the largest continuous vineyard region in the Balkans and almost nobody visits it. The basin sits between the Vardar and the Kožuf mountains, gets around 270 sunny days a year, and grows Vranec — the black, tannic national grape — alongside Stanušina, a pale indigenous red found nowhere else. The week runs south from Skopje through Negotino, Kavadarci and Demir Kapija, staying in wineries that built their own rooms because there were no hotels, then east to Štip for pastrmajlija. Come in September and the whole country is outdoors making ajvar over open fires.

itinerary.title: Skopje: Bit Pazar and the Old Bazaar
itinerary.morning: Land at SKP, 20 minutes from the centre. Walk the Stone Bridge into the **Old Bazaar**, the largest surviving Ottoman bazaar in the Balkans outside Istanbul.
itinerary.afternoon: **Bit Pazar** — pepper mountains in September, ajvar pots, dried beans for tavče gravče, sheep cheese, rakija sold by the funnel.
itinerary.evening: **Pivnica An** in a restored caravanserai for kebapi and tavče gravče, or **Stara Kuća** for the fuller spread.
itinerary.dayStats: SKP 20 min / bazaar meal MKD 400–800 (€7–€13) / market ajvar 1 kg jar MKD 300–500 (€5–€8) / no driving today

itinerary.title: South to Stobi and Negotino
itinerary.morning: The A1 down the Vardar to **Stobi**, the Roman and early Byzantine city at the Crna–Vardar confluence — mosaics, a theatre, the Episcopal basilica, and effectively empty midweek.
itinerary.afternoon: **Stobi Winery** next door for a first Vranec and a Temjanika, then on to **Bovin** at Negotino, the country's first private winery.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Popova Kula on arrival at Demir Kapija; the kitchen pairs the winery's own range.
itinerary.dayStats: 95 km Skopje–Stobi, 1 h 10 m / Stobi entry MKD 120–300 (€2–€5) / 2 wineries / tastings MKD 600–1,500 (€10–€24) each

itinerary.title: Demir Kapija and the Stanušina question
itinerary.morning: **Popova Kula**'s own tasting, working through Vranec, Kratošija, Temjanika and — the reason to be here — **Stanušina** as both a light red and a rosé.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Demir Kapija** gorge, the "iron gate" where the Vardar cuts through the mountains, then the winery's collection of dozens of local varieties grown side by side.
itinerary.evening: Stay in; Demir Kapija has little else, which is exactly why the winery built rooms.
itinerary.dayStats: 1 winery / Keif-style tasting MKD 900–1,800 (€15–€29) / Stanušina bottle MKD 500–900 (€8–€15) / no driving

itinerary.title: Kavadarci, Tikveš Winery and Lake Tikveš
itinerary.morning: Driver day. **Tikveš Winery** at Kavadarci — founded 1885, the largest in south-east Europe — and its Barovo and Lepovo single-vineyard programme.
itinerary.afternoon: Out to **Lake Tikveš**, the reservoir on the Crna, for a boat hour and the vineyard slopes above it.
itinerary.evening: A Kavadarci kafana for tavče gravče baked to order in its earthenware dish, and a carafe of house Vranec.
itinerary.dayStats: 32 km / 1 winery / tasting MKD 700–1,600 (€11–€26) / driver day €150–€280 per car / Vranec Reserve MKD 700–1,400 (€11–€23)

itinerary.title: Ajvar over the fire, and rakija
itinerary.morning: In September, the hands-on morning: an **ajvar session** — crates of red peppers roasted over an open grill, peeled hot, minced and slow-cooked in oil for hours. Arranged through your host, not sold as a tour.
itinerary.afternoon: A **rakija distillation** visit in a Tikveš village if you are here in October or November; otherwise a cellar visit at **Lazar Winery** or **Château Sopot**.
itinerary.evening: Eat what you made. Ajvar with sheep cheese, bread and grilled meat is the correct end to the day.
itinerary.dayStats: Ajvar session 4–6 h / ~10 kg peppers yields ~3 kg ajvar / rakija 40–50% abv / visit fees MKD 500–1,200 (€8–€20)

itinerary.title: East to Štip for pastrmajlija
itinerary.morning: Drive north-east to **Štip**, the textile city on the Bregalnica, and climb to the **Isar** fortress above it.
itinerary.afternoon: Pastrmajlija from a dedicated *pastrmajlijarnica* — the oval bread with cubed pork and a cracked egg, ordered by size and eaten with a hot pepper and a beer.
itinerary.evening: Back west toward Skopje, or a night in Štip. Stop at **Chateau Kamnik** on the Skopje approach for a last serious tasting.
itinerary.dayStats: 105 km Demir Kapija–Štip, 1 h 30 m / pastrmajlija MKD 200–400 (€3–€7) / Kamnik tasting MKD 900–1,800 (€15–€29)

itinerary.title: Matka, last market, and out
itinerary.morning: **Matka Canyon**, 30 minutes from Skopje — a gorge, a reservoir and Vrelo cave, and the country's easiest morning off.
itinerary.afternoon: Last buys at Bit Pazar: ajvar, dried peppers, sheep cheese and a bottle of Stanušina that will be almost impossible to find at home.
itinerary.evening: SKP is 25 minutes from the centre. Wine over one litre goes in the hold; there are duty limits leaving for the EU.
itinerary.dayStats: Matka 30 min each way / boat to Vrelo MKD 300–600 (€5–€10) / SKP 25 min / EU duty allowance 4 l still wine per adult

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Popova Kula
accommodationStrategy.description: A hilltop winery with around 25 rooms, a restaurant and terrace over the Vardar gorge, and a variety collection of indigenous grapes in the grounds. Tasting, dinner and bed in one building solves the driving problem for three nights. MKD 3,700–6,200 (€60–€100) double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Solun
accommodationStrategy.description: Central, walkable to the Old Bazaar and Bit Pazar, with parking — the practical bookend for the first and last nights. MKD 3,000–5,000 (€49–€81).

accommodationStrategy.name: Tikveš Winery guest accommodation / Kavadarci town hotels
accommodationStrategy.description: If you want to be inside the vineyard basin rather than at its southern edge, Kavadarci has plain, cheap town hotels and Tikveš's own estates offer limited guest capacity — book by email, as online listings are patchy. MKD 2,500–4,500 (€40–€73).

logistics.connectivity: **Non-EU, so EU roaming does not apply** — check your operator's Western Balkans tariff or buy a local A1 or Telekom prepaid SIM at the airport for a few euros. 4G coverage is good along the Vardar corridor and in the towns, weaker in the Kožuf foothills.
logistics.emergency: 112, plus 192 police, 193 fire, 194 ambulance. Main hospitals are in Skopje; Kavadarci and Negotino have clinics only. **EHIC/GHIC does not apply** — full travel insurance with medical repatriation is essential.
logistics.weather: The basin is the hottest, driest part of the country, 38–42°C in July and August with no shade in the vineyards. The **Vardarec**, a cold northerly funnelled down the valley, drops temperatures sharply in winter and spring.
logistics.bookingWindows: Popova Kula rooms 2–4 weeks, longer in September. Tikveš, Stobi and Kamnik visits a week by email. Ajvar and rakija sessions are arranged informally through your host, not booked online. Skopje hotels a few days.
logistics.money: The currency is the **Macedonian denar (MKD)**, pegged at roughly **61.5 MKD to €1**. Cards work in Skopje, wineries and larger restaurants; markets, village kafanas and rural fuel stations are cash. Withdraw denars from ATMs rather than changing euros at the airport, and do not accumulate denars — they are hard to change back. Tipping is 10%.
logistics.transportRules: Blood-alcohol 0.5 g/l, **0.0 for drivers with under two years' licence and professionals**; on-the-spot fines are normal. A **green card** is required for a car brought from abroad, and most EU rental agreements prohibit or surcharge entry into North Macedonia — hire locally in Skopje instead. The A1 is tolled in short sections, cash or card, and Skopje–Gevgelija tolls total a few euros. Headlights on at all times.
logistics.permits: North Macedonia is outside the EU and the Schengen area, so there is a **customs border** — the EU duty allowance on return is 4 litres of still wine and 1 litre of spirits per adult, and larger wine purchases must be declared. **Wild Ohrid trout is protected**; buying or ordering it is not something to encourage.
logistics.health: Tap water is drinkable in Skopje and the main towns; use bottled in villages. Rakija is 40–50% abv and is poured as hospitality rather than as a drink you ordered. Summer sun in the basin is severe and vineyards offer no shade.

proTips: Ask for Stanušina at every winery, even when it is not on the tasting list. It grows nowhere else, several producers make only a few thousand bottles, and it is the single thing you cannot buy at home.
Taste Vranec and Kratošija side by side. Kratošija is Zinfandel under another name, and the comparison instantly explains why Vranec tastes as black and structured as it does.
Book the winery that has rooms. Tikveš has almost no hotel infrastructure and Popova Kula's model — cellar, kitchen and bed in one building — is the only way to drink properly without a driver.
Go in September for ajvar. Every household in the basin is roasting peppers outdoors, and being invited to help is genuinely easy if you ask your host rather than an agency.
Buy a local SIM at Skopje airport. EU roaming does not reach North Macedonia and a week of data costs a couple of euros against potentially punitive roaming charges.

Do not hire the car in Greece or Bulgaria and drive in. Most EU rental contracts exclude North Macedonia or charge a heavy cross-border fee; renting in Skopje is cheaper and avoids the green-card problem entirely.
Eat pastrmajlija in Štip rather than Skopje. It is a Štip dish, the ovens there are set up for it, and the version sold in the capital is a pale copy.

raw.Appellation structure: The wine law divides the country into three regions and sixteen districts; **Povardarie** (the Vardar River Valley) is the largest and contains the **Tikveš** district, which alone makes roughly two-thirds of national production. The PDO/PGI framework is being aligned to EU practice under accession, so labels carry *kontrolirano poteklo* rather than a DOC-style term — expect "Tikveš" as the geographical claim.
raw.Grapes: **Vranec** ("black stallion") is the flagship: deep, tannic, 14%+, ageing well in oak. **Kratošija** is the same variety as Zinfandel and Primitivo and gives a rounder, redder-fruited wine. **Stanušina** is endemic to Tikveš — pale, low-tannin, high-acid, made as a light red and a rosé, and effectively unavailable outside the country. Whites: **Temjanika** (Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains) is the aromatic star, **Smederevka** the high-acid workhorse.
raw.Wineries with rooms and how to book: **Popova Kula** at **Demir Kapija** is the model — a hilltop winery with a hotel, restaurant and a variety collection including Stanušina, with structured tastings and email booking, English fluent; the "Keif" style tastings and dinner-plus-room packages are its published formats. **Tikveš Winery** at **Kavadarci**, founded 1885 and the largest in south-east Europe, runs a visitor programme at its Barovo and Lepovo estates. **Stobi Winery** near **Gradsko** has a modern visitor centre beside the archaeological site; **Chateau Kamnik** near Skopje, **Bovin** at Negotino (the first private winery) and **Lazar Winery** complete the list. Most want a **week's email notice**; small producers prefer a phone call, and English is reliable at Popova Kula, Stobi, Kamnik and Tikveš but not at every family cellar.
raw.Producers beyond wine: **Rakija** — grape *lozova rakija* and plum — is distilled at household level across the basin from **late September through November**, and several wineries and village households run visits. **Ajvar**, the roasted red-pepper relish, is made communally in **September**, when the whole country buys peppers by the crate: the Kavadarci and Negotino markets are stacked with them and any guesthouse will let you join. **Ohrid trout** (*Salmo letnica*) is protected and wild catch is banned or tightly restricted — what you are served is farmed or another species. **Bit Pazar** in Skopje is the biggest open market, with the **Old Bazaar** above it for burek, kebapi and Turkish coffee.
raw.Dishes by name: **Tavče gravče** — baked beans with red pepper in an earthenware *tava*, the national dish, best in a village *kafana* rather than a city restaurant. **Pastrmajlija**, the boat-shaped bread with cubed pork and egg, belongs to **Štip**, which holds the **Pastrmajlijada** festival there each autumn. **Selsko meso**, **shopska salad** and **turli tava** fill the rest. For benchmarks: **Restaurant Popova Kula** at Demir Kapija for the winery pairing, **Stara Kuća** or **Pivnica An** in Skopje's Old Bazaar for the traditional register.
raw.Season and timing: Harvest is **late August to early October**, Vranec last; the **Tikveš harvest festivals** in Kavadarci fall in September. **Ajvar season is September**, the pepper harvest peak. **Rakija distilling runs October–November.** The last week of September combines all three but is also when winemakers are least available — pick your priority.
raw.Transport and the sober-driving plan: The limit is **0.5 g/l, 0.0 for professionals and licences under two years**; A1 checks are frequent and fines payable on the spot. The Vardar rail line (Skopje–Veles–Gradsko–Demir Kapija–Gevgelija) is slow and infrequent — one leg, not a week. Hire a driver: Skopje operators including **Macedonia Travel** and **Wine Tour Macedonia** run English-speaking Tikveš days at roughly €150–€280 per car. Skopje taxis are metered and cheap; agree a price for intercity runs.

sources.verified: Popova Kula operating as a winery with hotel rooms, restaurant and structured tastings at Demir Kapija, with bookable tasting and dinner-plus-accommodation formats; Tikveš Winery at Kavadarci as a visitable estate founded 1885 and the largest in south-east Europe; Tikveš's position within the Povardarie/Vardar Valley wine region; the endemic status of Stanušina to the Tikveš basin.
sources.confidenceNotes: All prices are estimated bands converted at roughly 61.5 MKD to €1 — the peg is stable but the tasting and room prices themselves are unconfirmed against 2026 lists and must be re-checked with Popova Kula, Tikveš, Stobi and Kamnik directly. English-language availability at smaller cellars is variable. The named Skopje driver operators and their day rates are indicative and should be verified. Ajvar and rakija sessions are informal, host-arranged activities and cannot be sold as scheduled products. The exact date of the Štip Pastrmajlijada and the Kavadarci harvest festivals moves each year. Ohrid trout regulations have changed repeatedly — confirm the current position before publishing anything about ordering it. Rental-car cross-border rules into North Macedonia vary by company and should be checked per supplier. Stobi entry prices and opening hours should be spot-checked.

trips.title: Cheese, Genever and the North Holland Table
trips.subRegion: North Holland and the Schiedam distilleries

bestPeriod.note: The Alkmaar and Edam demonstration markets run April to September, and Hollandse Nieuwe herring reaches the stalls from late May or early June.

trips.gatewayAirport: Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS)
trips.summary: A week from Amsterdam's brown cafés to Alkmaar's cheese-carrier guild and Schiedam's tall malt-mill distilleries, timed to the new herring season.
trips.hook: This week runs on three engines: cheese, grain spirit and the North Sea. Alkmaar's cheese carriers still work the Waagplein in white uniforms and coloured guild hats; Schiedam's windmills were built absurdly tall for one reason, to catch wind over the malt-house roofs for jenever distilling; and Amsterdam ties it together with a herring cart on every other corner once the new season starts.

snapshot.Base(s): Amsterdam (5 nights) · Alkmaar (2 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 120 km of train travel across the week; flat city and polder walking throughout
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS), direct train to Amsterdam Centraal, approx. 20 minutes
snapshot.Who It Suits: Cheese and spirits obsessives, herring-season completists, anyone happy eating standing up

itinerary.title: Amsterdam, brown cafés and herring
itinerary.morning: Land at Schiphol and train to Amsterdam Centraal, about 20 minutes. Drop bags near the Jordaan.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Jordaan's canals and find a bruine kroeg, a "brown café" named for decades of tobacco-stained walls, for an orientation Genever borrel — poured to the brim in a tulip glass, traditionally sipped without lifting it first.
itinerary.evening: Broodje haring at a herring cart if the new season (Hollandse Nieuwe) has started; if not, order the cured, onion-topped version instead, and bitterballen with mustard as a bar snack.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 4 km on foot. Approx. tasting spend: €0.

itinerary.title: Albert Cuypmarkt and craft jenever
itinerary.morning: The Albert Cuypmarkt in De Pijp runs Monday to Saturday, roughly 09:00–17:00, the country's largest daily street market — cheese stalls, stroopwafel griddles, and produce from the polders sit side by side.
itinerary.afternoon: A. van Wees "De Ooievaar," a small working jenever distillery in the Jordaan, still distils on-site and runs walk-in tastings through its tiny proeflokaal (tasting room), though a guided tour is best booked a day ahead by email.
itinerary.evening: Kaassoufflé, a deep-fried cheese-filled pastry, and a jenever tasting flight comparing jonge (young, neutral) against oude (old, malty) styles.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 6 km. Approx. tasting spend: €20–30.

itinerary.title: North to Alkmaar
itinerary.morning: Train from Amsterdam Centraal to Alkmaar, about 35 minutes. Check into Alkmaar and walk the Waagplein.
itinerary.afternoon: If it is a Friday between April and early September, the Alkmaar cheese market runs 10:00–13:00 — worth stressing plainly: this is a seasonal demonstration for visitors, staged by the historic cheese-carriers' guild on the Waagplein, not a working wholesale trade (that moved to closed auction decades ago). The ceremony is still genuine: guild members in white with coloured straw hats carry wheels on wooden barrows, weigh them at the 14th-century Waaggebouw, and settle the price with a ritual hand-clap.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Alkmaar; smoked eel if a stall or restaurant has it, with a young Dutch Gouda to compare against the market wheels.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 4 km. Approx. tasting spend: €15–20.

itinerary.title: Edam and the smaller market
itinerary.morning: Train and bus (or a direct regional bus) to Edam, about 45 minutes from Alkmaar. Edam runs its own, smaller cheese demonstration market on Wednesdays in July and August, roughly 10:30–12:30, on Jan van Nieuwenhuizenplein — again a folkloric event rather than a trading market, on a shorter season than Alkmaar's.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk Edam's canals and the Grote Kerk; a working cheese farm near Volendam, such as the well-known Catharina Hoeve, gives a hands-on demonstration of traditional Edam-making outside market hours.
itinerary.evening: Back to Alkmaar. A plate of Dutch cheeses by age — jong, belegen, oud — tasted side by side.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 8 km plus transfers. Approx. tasting spend: €15–20.

itinerary.title: Volendam, Marken and North Sea fish
itinerary.morning: A short bus or boat hop from Edam to Volendam, the old fishing harbour on the IJsselmeer, still selling smoked eel (paling) straight off the boats.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross to Marken, a former island village of green-black wooden houses, on foot along the causeway or by the seasonal ferry from Volendam. The contrast between the two — Volendam loud and commercial, Marken quiet — is the point.
itinerary.evening: Return to Amsterdam by train via Amsterdam Centraal. Settle into the second Amsterdam base with a North Sea seafood dinner — mussels or plaice, depending on the season.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 12 km plus transfers. Approx. tasting spend: €20–25.

itinerary.title: Schiedam, city of tall mills
itinerary.morning: Train from Amsterdam to Schiedam Centrum, about an hour. Schiedam's skyline is genuinely unusual: its windmills, including De Noord and De Vrijheid, are among the tallest traditional mills in the world, built that height specifically to catch clean wind over the malt-house roofs that once ringed the town.
itinerary.afternoon: The Nationaal Jenevermuseum, housed in a former distillery on the Lange Haven, covers the malt-wine spirit's full history. Nolet's Distillery, family-run since 1691 and still producing genever alongside its better-known vodka, offers the House of Nolet visitor experience by advance booking only — reserve online at least a week ahead, more in summer.
itinerary.evening: Dinner back in Amsterdam; a last jenever, this time an oude style, with Kachkéis-style farm cheese and rye bread.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1–2 (Nolet reservation-dependent). Km travelled: 6 km plus transfers. Approx. tasting spend: €20–30.

itinerary.title: Amsterdam market close and departure
itinerary.morning: A last pass through the Albert Cuypmarkt or the Noordermarkt farmers' market (Saturdays, roughly 09:00–16:00) for cheese and preserves to take home.
itinerary.afternoon: A canal walk through the Nine Streets, then the train to Schiphol.
itinerary.evening: Departure from Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS).
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 5 km plus airport transfer. Approx. tasting spend: €10–15.

accommodationStrategy.name: The Hoxton, Amsterdam
accommodationStrategy.description: A well-known, centrally placed hotel in a row of converted canal houses, close to the Nine Streets, De Pijp trams and the train to both Alkmaar and Schiedam — a practical hub for a week built on day trips.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8 weeks ahead for May and September.

accommodationStrategy.name: NH Alkmaar
accommodationStrategy.description: A short walk from the Waagplein and the station, useful for being inside the old town before the market crowds arrive on a Friday morning and for the short hop to Edam and Volendam.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead, earlier for a market Friday.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; the Netherlands uses 112 for all services.
logistics.bookingWindows: The House of Nolet tour in Schiedam is by advance reservation only, made online; walk-ins are not accommodated.
logistics.money: Cards, including contactless, are near-universal in the Netherlands; some very small stalls are card-only, the reverse of much of Europe.

other.label: The Alkmaar and Edam markets are demonstrations, not trade
other.text: Alkmaar's runs Fridays only, April to early September, 10:00–13:00; Edam's runs Wednesdays only, July and August, 10:30–12:30. Both are seasonal and weather can shorten a session; check the tourist board's calendar before travelling for one specifically.

other.label: Trains
other.text: NS regional trains connect Amsterdam, Alkmaar and Schiedam directly and frequently; buy an OV-chipkaart or use contactless bank card tap-in/tap-out on all trains, trams and buses.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Many Amsterdam shops open late on Sunday and Monday mornings; cheese farms outside the main towns often close for a midday break.

other.label: Drink-drive alternatives
other.text: This trip runs entirely on foot, tram and train; there is no driving leg, so the only rule is timing trains around tastings rather than rushing between them.

proTips: Arrive in Alkmaar the night before a Friday market and walk the empty Waagplein at 08:00 — the guild sets up in the hour before the ceremony starts.

Ask a herring cart to serve it "Hollandse Nieuwe" only once the season is confirmed open, usually late May or early June; earlier in the year it is last year's catch, still good but a different thing.
Book A. van Wees's guided distillery tour a day ahead by email; the walk-in proeflokaal is available without booking but the tour explains the copper stills.
Reserve Nolet's House of Nolet the moment dates are fixed — slots in June and September fill weeks out.

Compare Edam and Alkmaar cheese: Edam is traditionally the smaller, ball-shaped export cheese with a red wax coat; Alkmaar's market historically traded the flatter, larger Gouda-style wheels, which is why Alkmaar's ceremony is the bigger of the two.
Catch the Noordermarkt farmers' market on Saturday morning for organic and small-producer cheese away from the tourist stalls.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 120 km of train travel across the week; flat city and polder walking throughout
raw.Who It Suits: Cheese and spirits obsessives, herring-season completists, anyone happy eating standing up

typeSpecific.surface: Approx. 120 km of train travel across the week; flat city and polder walking throughout
typeSpecific.audience: Cheese and spirits obsessives, herring-season completists, anyone happy eating standing up

packingNotes: Comfortable, flat shoes; Amsterdam and market-town cobbles punish anything else.
A rain shell that packs small — North Sea weather turns quickly even in June.
A small cooler bag or vacuum-seal option for cheese or smoked eel to take home.
Cash in small notes for herring carts and market stalls, even though cards work almost everywhere else.
A tote or basket bag; Dutch markets expect you to bring your own.
Sunglasses; the flat polder light off the IJsselmeer is sharper than it looks on a grey forecast.
whatCouldGoWrong: **You arrive expecting Alkmaar's market to be a real trading floor.** It closed as a wholesale market long ago; go for the guild ceremony and the atmosphere, not for wholesale prices.
**Nolet's Distillery is fully booked.** The Nationaal Jenevermuseum in the same town gives comparable historical depth without a reservation.
**The herring season hasn't started yet.** Cured herring and smoked eel are available year-round at the same stalls.
**Rain washes out Marken or Volendam.** Both have enough covered cafés and the Marken church and Volendam's fishing museum to fill an hour.

**A market Friday or Wednesday falls outside the April–September window.** Alkmaar and Edam's cheese farms, including Catharina Hoeve near Volendam, run demonstrations independent of the town market calendar.

trips.title: Solaris and Smoked Plums: A Małopolska Eating and Drinking Week from Kraków

bestPeriod.window: the second half of September into the first ten days of October — *winobranie* harvest, plum-smoking in Szydłów, apples in Łącko and *oscypek* still coming off the Podhale pastures
bestPeriod.avoid: November–March (most vineyards shut to visitors, the *bacówki* are empty, and the mountain roads are a lottery)

accommodation.note: €350–€600 (€50–€85/night, Kraków dearer than Podhale)

food.note: €260–€420 (€37–€60/day — one tasting-menu night skews this hard)

transport.note: €290–€430 (driver-guide days, or car hire plus a hired driver for tasting days)

activities.note: €120–€220 (vineyard tastings €10–€25 each, salt mine, cheese dairy visits)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy

trips.gatewayAirport: Kraków–Balice (KRK). The **SKA1** train runs airport → Kraków Główny in 20 minutes, **20 PLN** (~€4.70) one-way, luggage free.
trips.summary: Poland has 500-plus registered vineyards and almost nobody outside the country has drunk one. This week runs from a Kraków bread ring you eat standing up, through a hillside vineyard below a monastery where the monks…
trips.hook: Poland has 500-plus registered vineyards and almost nobody outside the country has drunk one. This week runs from a Kraków bread ring you eat standing up, through a hillside vineyard below a monastery where the monks still refuse women entry, up to shepherd huts on Podhale where smoked sheep cheese is made over an open fire, and down into the Carpathian foothills where the plums are dried in wood smoke. Easy walking, serious drinking, and a driver every single day.

snapshot.Start / End: Kraków → Kraków (loop, ~620 km driven)
snapshot.Getting there: Kraków–Balice (KRK). The **SKA1** train runs airport → Kraków Główny in 20 minutes, **20 PLN** (~€4.70) one-way, luggage free.

itinerary.title: Kraków, standing up (city walking, no driving)
itinerary.morning: Land, SKA1 into Kraków Główny, drop bags, then walk to **Stary Kleparz**, the market that has traded on the same ground since the 14th century. Buy an **obwarzanek krakowski** from a blue cart — poppy, salt or sesame — and eat it in the first ten minutes, because after that it turns to cardboard, which is the point of the PGI.
itinerary.afternoon: Lunch at **Bar Mleczny Pod Temidą** on Grodzka, a working *bar mleczny*: a state-subsidised milk bar, the surviving institution of the People's Republic, where you queue, order at a hatch and eat *żurek*, *pierogi ruskie* and *naleśniki* for the price of a coffee elsewhere. Cash helps.
itinerary.evening: **Karakter** on Brzozowa for the modern counterweight — offal, fire, short menu, no ceremony. Book ahead; it is small [VERIFY: current opening days].

itinerary.title: Salt, sausage and the Wieliczka hillside
itinerary.morning: Driver collects you for **Wieliczka**. The Tourist Route through the medieval salt mine explains more about Małopolska's food than any restaurant will: salt was the region's wealth from the 13th century, it preserved the meat and fish that fed Kraków, and the royal salt monopoly built the Wawel you will walk past. Tickets from **93 PLN** (~€22); expect 100–130 PLN in season, and foreign-language tours cost more [VERIFY: 2026 foreign-language adult ticket price].
itinerary.afternoon: Up the hill to **Winnica Wieliczka** for the first tasting: Solaris, Johanniter, a Rondo. Then west to **Liszki** for **kiełbasa lisiecka** (PGI) straight from a village butcher — coarse-ground, subtly smoked, a completely different animal from supermarket *kiełbasa*.
itinerary.evening: Back in Kraków, dinner at **Pod Nosem** below Wawel — Polish cooking taken seriously, with a cellar that actually lists Polish bottles. Ask for the Srebrna Góra pour before you visit the vineyard tomorrow.
itinerary.dayStats: ~60 km driven

itinerary.title: The monastery hillside and the food hall
itinerary.morning: **Winnica Srebrna Góra**, on the Kraków slope below the **Camaldolese hermitage at Bielany** — one of the largest vineyards in the country, planted on limestone, inside the city limits, and a fifteen-minute drive from the Rynek. Tour the parcels, then taste through the Solaris, Johanniter and the Riesling that only exists in good years [VERIFY: current tasting fee and booking channel].
itinerary.afternoon: **Hala Forum**, the food hall in the brutalist carcass of the old Hotel Forum across the Vistula — the best cross-section of what young Polish cooks are doing, eaten on a concrete terrace with the Wawel skyline opposite.
itinerary.evening: The set-piece: **Bottiglieria 1881** on Bocheńska, Kraków's Michelin-starred tasting room, in a former wine warehouse. It pours Polish wine alongside the classics without apology. Book six to eight weeks ahead [VERIFY: current tasting-menu price].
itinerary.dayStats: ~25 km driven

itinerary.title: Over the Beskids to Podhale
itinerary.morning: Leave south on the Zakopianka. Break at **Bochnia**, the older of the two royal salt mines — mined since 1248, quieter than Wieliczka, and the underground chamber where local schoolchildren still sleep for their asthma.
itinerary.afternoon: Into Podhale and up to a working **bacówka** — a shepherd's hut on the high pasture, where **oscypek** and **bryndza podhalańska** are made by hand: sheep's milk curdled, pressed into carved spindle moulds, brined, then hung in the smoke above the fire. The season closes in early autumn, so this is a late-September ask [VERIFY: 2026 bacówka season end dates].
itinerary.evening: **Morskie Oko** on Krupówki in Zakopane — the old-guard *góralska* dining room: *kwaśnica* (sour cabbage and pork rib soup), grilled oscypek with cranberry, and a highlander band that plays whether you want it or not.

itinerary.title: Nowy Targ market and the Dunajec apples
itinerary.morning: **Nowy Targ**'s Thursday market is the largest in the Polish Carpathians — sheepskin, wooden butter moulds, sacks of dried mushrooms, and cheese sold by women who made it. Go before 09:00.
itinerary.afternoon: East down the Dunajec to **Łącko**, home of **jabłka łąckie** (PGI) and of *śliwowica łącka*, the plum spirit the valley has distilled, legally and otherwise, for a century. Orchard visits in early October coincide with pressing.
itinerary.evening: Cross to **Nowy Sącz** for the night. Eat simply — *placki ziemniaczane*, trout from the Poprad — and save the appetite.
itinerary.dayStats: ~90 km

itinerary.title: Podkarpacie: Jasiel and the smoked plums
itinerary.morning: East into the **Beskid Niski** to **Winnica Jasiel**, near the Slovak border in one of the emptiest corners of Poland — depopulated after 1947, now vines. Rondo, Regent, Solaris, and a producer who will explain frankly why Riesling is a gamble at this latitude [VERIFY: current visit arrangements and tasting fee].
itinerary.afternoon: The plum detour: **śliwka szydłowska** (PGI), dried for days over a slow beech-and-alder fire in the *suszarnia*, comes out dense, dark and faintly savoury. It is the single most distinctive preserved food in southern Poland and it goes into *pierogi*, into pork, and into *nalewka*.
itinerary.evening: Nalewka session — the domestic fruit-infusion tradition that survived vodka's industrial century. *Wiśniówka* (sour cherry), *pigwówka* (quince), *dereniówka* (cornelian cherry). Poured at cellar temperature, never over ice.

itinerary.title: Back to Kraków, and the last table
itinerary.morning: Drive back north-west via Tarnów. If it is a Sunday, take the detour to **Hala Targowa** on Grzegórzecka in Kraków for the flea market and the *maczanka po krakowsku* stall — slow-braised pork neck with the cooking juices soaked into a *kajzerka* roll, the city's true street sandwich and older than the kebab by a century.
itinerary.afternoon: Last shopping: Polish bottles from a specialist merchant rather than the airport, and a vacuum-packed **oscypek** — which is legal to fly within the EU. Fresh *bryndza* is not worth the risk of a warm hold.
itinerary.evening: **Fiorentina** on św. Marka, the long-running Italian-Polish room that Kraków's own cooks eat in on their nights off. Order the ossobuco, drink a Solaris, and put the €80 tasting menus behind you.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Copernicus
accommodationStrategy.description: on the quietest medieval street in the city, four minutes' walk from Wawel and Pod Nosem, with a rooftop terrace and — the point for this trip — a concierge who can actually get a Bottiglieria table and arrange a licensed driver at short notice.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct or by email, 8–10 weeks ahead for late September.

accommodationStrategy.name: Aries Hotel & Spa
accommodationStrategy.description: a base for the Podhale cheese days that is not on Krupówki, so you sleep. Secure parking for the hire car, a proper drying room, and the Nowy Targ road is fifteen minutes away for the market start.
accommodationStrategy.booking: online, 4–6 weeks ahead; avoid Polish long weekends.

accommodationStrategy.name: Dwór Kombornia
accommodationStrategy.description: a restored Podkarpacie manor within 40 minutes of Winnica Jasiel and the Beskid Niski vineyards, with its own kitchen — which matters, because rural Podkarpacie has almost no dinner options after 20:00.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct, 3–4 weeks ahead.

logistics.connectivity: 4G/5G is excellent across Małopolska and patchy only in the Beskid Niski valleys near the Slovak border. Download offline maps for the Jasiel day; several vineyard access lanes are unnamed forest tracks.
logistics.emergency: **112** everywhere. Pharmacies (*apteka*) are widespread; a 24-hour one operates near Kraków Główny.
logistics.weather: September in the Carpathian foothills swings 25 °C to 6 °C within a week. Harvest dates move accordingly — a vineyard that promised you a picking day may bring it forward five days at 48 hours' notice.
logistics.bookingWindows: Bottiglieria 1881 six to eight weeks. Every vineyard one to two weeks minimum, more in harvest. Wieliczka same-week online is usually fine outside July–August. Bacówka visits are arranged through the hotel or a guide, never cold.
logistics.money: Poland uses the **złoty**; €1 ≈ 4.25 PLN. Cards are near-universal — but milk bars, village butchers, market stalls and most *bacówki* are cash. Carry 300–400 PLN.
logistics.transportRules: Limit **0.02% BAC**, enforced with roadside checks that are routine, not exceptional, in wine districts during harvest. Hire a driver. Motorway A4 (Kraków–Tarnów) and the S7 are tolled in sections; the *e-TOLL* app handles it for cars [VERIFY: current A4 Kraków–Katowice car toll].
logistics.permits: No permits needed. Note that **oscypek** sold on Krupówki in Zakopane is frequently cow's-milk imitation sold to tourists; genuine PDO oscypek is sheep's milk, seasonal, and carries the producer's registration. If it is on sale in February, it is not oscypek.

proTips: Book the vineyards **before** the flights. Polish estates open for a booked party and not otherwise; three of the seven producers here have no fixed opening hours at all.

Ask any vineyard for the *"wino z winnicy"* — the wine actually made from that estate's own fruit, as opposed to bought-in juice. It is a legally meaningful distinction in Poland and the answer tells you everything.
Eat the *obwarzanek* within ten minutes of purchase. Locals buy them at 07:00 for a reason; the cart rings sold at 16:00 on the Rynek have been out since dawn.
Use the milk bars for lunch every day you are in Kraków. Twelve euros buys two people a full lunch, and the *Pod Temidą* queue moves faster than any café.
Go to Nowy Targ market on a Thursday, not a Saturday. Thursday is the trading day locals use; Saturday is the version arranged for visitors.
Buy your Polish wine at the estate. Retail distribution is thin, mark-ups at Kraków wine shops are steep, and several of these producers sell out their entire vintage at the cellar door.
Learn *"Poproszę"* (I'd like) and *"Na zdrowie"*. In a milk bar the first is the entire transaction, and in a cellar the second gets you a second pour.

raw.The wine regions: Poland's commercial viticulture is barely thirty years old: the communist state grew no wine, and the modern industry restarted only in the **1990s**, with the first legal commercial bottlings arriving after Poland's 2004 EU accession forced a proper register. There are now **500+ registered vineyards**. Two named PGI-scale zones matter: **Małopolski Przełom Wisły** — the Vistula gorge terraces between Kazimierz Dolny, Puławy and Janowiec — and **Podkarpacie**, the Carpathian foothill belt running from the Dunajec east to the Slovak border. Neither behaves like a French appellation; think of them as geographical indications wrapped around a scatter of small estates.
raw.Producers you can actually visit: **Winnica Srebrna Góra** — planted on the south-facing Kraków hillside directly below the **Camaldolese monastery at Bielany**, inside the city boundary, and one of the largest vineyards in Poland. **Winnica Wieliczka**, above the salt town, on the Małopolska Wine Trail. **Winnica Nad Dworskim Potokiem**, a small family estate on the same trail east of Kraków [VERIFY: current tasting-room address and hours]. **Winnica Jasiel** in the Beskid Niski near the Slovak frontier, one of Podkarpacie's serious names. **Winnica Płochockich** in the Małopolski Przełom Wisły. For national context: **Winnica Turnau** in Pomerania, near Szczecin — the country's most commercially visible producer, and 600 km away, so it is a bottle to buy rather than a stop to make — and **Winnica Silesian** in Lower Silesia.
raw.Grapes: Poland is a cold-climate country and the varieties that work are the disease-resistant hybrids: **Solaris** (the workhorse white — early, ripe, capable of real weight), **Johanniter**, **Seyval Blanc**, and for red **Rondo** and **Regent**. **Zweigelt** succeeds in warm sites; **Riesling** ripens only at the margin, in the best years, on the best slopes, and the producers who bottle it will tell you so.
raw.PDO and PGI foods: **Obwarzanek krakowski** (PGI) — a boiled-then-baked plaited ring, chewier and drier than a bagel and legally makeable only in Kraków and two neighbouring districts. **Oscypek** (PDO) — smoked, brine-cured spindle cheese from Podhale sheep's milk, made only between roughly May and September. **Bryndza podhalańska** (PDO) — the soft, salty, spreadable sheep cheese from the same season. **Kiełbasa lisiecka** (PGI) from **Liszki**, coarse-cut, lightly smoked pork. **Śliwka szydłowska** (PGI) — plums dried over beech and alder smoke. **Jabłka łąckie** (PGI) — apples from the Dunajec valley around Łącko.
raw.Reservation-only, without exception: Every vineyard on this itinerary is **appointment-only**. There are no drop-in cellar doors in Poland; most estates are family-run and open a tasting room only when someone has booked. Email or phone at least a week ahead, two in harvest.
raw.Driving rule — non-negotiable: Poland's legal limit is **0.02% BAC (0.2‰)**, effectively zero tolerance, and the offence band above 0.05% is criminal, not administrative. Every tasting day on this trip needs a hired driver or a driver-guide. Budget €120–€180 (520–780 PLN) per driver day [VERIFY: current driver-guide day rates].
