trips.title: Douro Field Blends: Quintas, Tawnies & the Pocinho Line
trips.subRegion: Alto Douro Vinhateiro — Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo & Douro Superior

bestPeriod.window: Late April–mid-June & mid-September–end October
bestPeriod.avoid: July–early August — Douro Superior regularly exceeds 40°C in schist canyons with no shade; also January–February, when many quintas close entirely
bestPeriod.raw: Late April–mid-June & mid-September–end October

accommodation.note: Quinta guesthouse €100–€170 pppn; two nights in Gaia/Porto €90–€140

food.note: Quinta lunch €25–€40; Régua tasca mains €10–€16; one starred dinner €90–€150

transport.note: Car 5 days, Linha do Douro tickets, one rabelo leg, driver day

activities.note: 9–11 tastings €12–€45, port lodge tours €20–€35, olive mill, treading session

profile.difficultyNote: 2/5 — steep terrace walking on loose schist, long cellar stairs, one optional treading session

trips.gatewayAirport: OPO Porto Francisco Sá Carneiro, 1 h 45 min drive to Peso da Régua, 2 h 10 min to Pinhão
trips.summary: The Douro is a landscape argument: pre-phylloxera field blends of forty varieties planted together on schist terraces so steep the region needed UNESCO protection to justify farming them at all. The week runs upriver from the softer, wetter Baixo Corgo through the Cima Corgo heartland at Pinhão to the near-desert Douro Superior, learning the port hierarchy — ruby, LBV, tawny, colheita, vintage — before circling back to Vila Nova de Gaia to see where those casks actually age. Dry Douro DOC reds are now half the story and get equal time. Trains, a rabelo leg and a driver day mean nobody has to stay sober on the switchbacks.

itinerary.title: Porto, Gaia lodges, and the shape of port
itinerary.morning: Land at OPO, drop bags in Porto and walk the Ribeira down to the Dom Luís I bridge.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross to **Vila Nova de Gaia** for **Taylor's** (scale, the 20-year tawny) and **Graham's 1890 Lodge** (museum, a vintage flight). The point is the cool damp lodge air that makes tawny possible and the Douro heat impossible.
itinerary.evening: **Taberna dos Mercadores** in the Ribeira, or **The Yeatman**'s cellar list if you want the full vertical.
itinerary.dayStats: 2 lodges / tours €20–€35 each / 20-year tawny bottle €40–€60, 40-year €120–€180 / no driving today
itinerary.sleep: Hotel in Porto Ribeira or Gaia

itinerary.title: The Linha do Douro to Régua and the Baixo Corgo
itinerary.morning: Train from Porto Campanhã to **Peso da Régua**, roughly 2 h, sitting on the right after Mosteirô for the first river views.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Museu do Douro** for demarcation history, then **Quinta do Vallado** outside town — Baixo Corgo fruit, a schist-clad modern winery, and a side-by-side of Douro DOC red against port.
itinerary.evening: **Castas e Pratos** in the converted railway warehouse; order posta and the house Douro red.
itinerary.dayStats: Train €13–€18, 2 h / 1 quinta / Vallado tasting €15–€30 / museum €7.50 / Douro DOC red €12–€30
itinerary.sleep: Quinta do Vallado or Hotel Régua Douro, Peso da Régua

itinerary.title: Pinhão, Bomfim and the Cima Corgo
itinerary.morning: Régua–Pinhão by train (25 min) for the station's azulejo panels, then **Quinta do Bomfim** — terrace tasting above the line, Dow's and Warre's, and the walk through the vineyard blocks.
itinerary.afternoon: A rabelo hour on the river from Pinhão quay, then **Quinta de la Rosa** for a second, smaller-scale visit and its riverside terrace.
itinerary.evening: **Restaurante DOC** at Folgosa, on a deck built over the water, for Rui Paula's tasting menu — or the far cheaper **Veladouro** in Pinhão.
itinerary.dayStats: Train 25 min, €3–€5 / 2 quintas / Bomfim €20–€45 / rabelo €15–€25, 1 h / DOC menu €90–€150
itinerary.sleep: Quinta de la Rosa or Vintage House Hotel, Pinhão

itinerary.title: Field blends, Crasto and treading if the season allows
itinerary.morning: Driver day. **Quinta do Crasto** above Gouvinhas for the Vinha Maria Teresa old-vine field blend and the infinity pool that appears in every photograph of the region.
itinerary.afternoon: **Quinta Nova de Nossa Senhora do Carmo** at Covas do Douro — vineyard trail, wine museum, and the best quinta lunch on the river.
itinerary.evening: In late September, a **lagar treading session** where one is offered — barefoot in granite tanks, two hours of cutting and liberdade, and a real understanding of why port is fortified mid-ferment.
itinerary.dayStats: 48 km driving, all switchbacks / 2 quintas / fees €25–€45 / driver day €300–€450 per car / treading session €30–€60 where offered
itinerary.sleep: Quinta de la Rosa or Vintage House Hotel, Pinhão

itinerary.title: Favaios moscatel, bread and olive oil
itinerary.morning: Climb 400 m out of the valley to **Favaios** on the plateau. The **Adega Cooperativa de Favaios** pours Moscatel do Douro, a style unrelated to port and made from Moscatel Galego Branco.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Museu do Pão e do Vinho** and the bakery for *pão de Favaios*, then down to **Quinta do Salgueiral** for a Douro DOP olive-oil tasting and a mill walk.
itinerary.evening: **O Lagar** in Régua for posta mirandesa cooked rare on a hot stone, and bola de carne from the morning's bakery for tomorrow's train.
itinerary.dayStats: 62 km / 1 co-op + 1 mill / Moscatel tasting €8–€15 / oil tasting €10–€18 / posta €18–€26 / Moscatel bottle €7–€14
itinerary.sleep: Quinta de la Rosa or Vintage House Hotel, Pinhão

itinerary.title: Douro Superior: Vale Meão and the Côa
itinerary.morning: Train east from Pinhão toward **Pocinho**, the end of the line, roughly 1 h 10 m through the tightest gorges of the route.
itinerary.afternoon: **Quinta do Vale Meão** at Foz Côa — the estate that once made Barca Velha, now the benchmark for Douro Superior concentration. Pair it with the **Côa Valley** Palaeolithic rock-art park if you hold a slot.
itinerary.evening: Back west, or overnight locally at **Quinta do Vallado Douro Superior**. Eat simply: grilled cabrito and a bottle of the estate's own red.
itinerary.dayStats: Train 1 h 10 m each way, €6–€10 / 1 quinta / Vale Meão tasting €25–€45 / Côa park visit €18 / Douro Superior red €25–€60
itinerary.sleep: Quinta do Vallado Douro Superior or back at Pinhão

itinerary.title: Tawny logic, and out via Gaia
itinerary.morning: Drive or train back west along the N222 Régua–Pinhão stretch, routinely called one of the world's best drives, stopping at the **Miradouro de São Leonardo de Galafura** at 640 m.
itinerary.afternoon: A last Gaia lodge — **Kopke** for colheitas, since it holds the deepest run of single-vintage tawnies and pours them by the glass by decade.
itinerary.evening: **Cantinho do Avillez** or **Casa Guedes** for a pernil sandwich before OPO.
itinerary.dayStats: 120 km Pinhão–Gaia, 2 h / 1 lodge / Kopke colheita flight €20–€45 / colheita bottle €35–€90 / OPO 25 min from Gaia
itinerary.sleep: Airport hotel, or fly out same evening

accommodationStrategy.name: Quinta de la Rosa
accommodationStrategy.description: On the river below Pinhão with its own winery, restaurant and pool, so the Day 3 tasting is a walk downstairs and you never drive after dinner. €140–€230 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Quinta do Vallado
accommodationStrategy.description: Schist-and-slate modern building attached to a historic Baixo Corgo estate, five minutes from Régua station, which makes the train days frictionless. Its Douro Superior sister property at Vila Nova de Foz Côa lets you split the week without backtracking. €160–€260.

accommodationStrategy.name: Vintage House Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: The reliable non-quinta option, a converted eighteenth-century estate building on the quay next to the rabelo moorings and 400 m from the station. Large rooms, river-facing terrace, €150–€240.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming applies. 4G is good in Régua and Pinhão, unreliable in the gorges east of Tua and on the Favaios plateau road. Download offline maps; quinta driveways are unnumbered.
logistics.emergency: 112. The main hospital is Centro Hospitalar de Vila Real, 40 min from Régua. Terrace falls on loose schist are the commonest injury — wear grip, not deck shoes.
logistics.weather: The valley is a heat trap — Pinhão runs up to 12°C warmer than Porto on the same afternoon, and the Douro Superior tops 40°C in July. Autumn river fog blanks the N222 viewpoints before 10:00.
logistics.bookingWindows: Quintas 2–4 weeks, longer for September; Crasto and Vale Meão 4–8 weeks. DOC Folgosa 3–6 weeks. Treading sessions sell out by August. Côa Valley rock-art slots are capped and released online ahead.
logistics.money: Eurozone. Cards accepted at quintas and restaurants; village bakeries and the Favaios co-op shop are easier with cash. Tipping is 5–10% or rounding up.
logistics.transportRules: Blood-alcohol limit 0.5 g/l, and 0.2 g/l for licences under three years. The N222 and N323 are narrow, blind and unforgiving — do not drive them after tasting. Motorway tolls on the A4 use electronic gantries; take the rental company's transponder. CP changed Linha do Douro timetables and some Porto services now require a change at Caíde or Régua — verify on cp.pt before relying on a connection.
logistics.permits: Tasting fees of €12–€45 are standard and often credited against a purchase. The Alto Douro Vinhateiro is a UNESCO cultural landscape: no drones over quintas without permission, and terraces are private property.
logistics.health: Tap water is drinkable. Port is 19–20% abv — a five-glass flight is close to a bottle of table wine. Sun exposure on unshaded schist terraces is severe from May; carry water on any vineyard walk.

proTips: Sit on the right-hand side leaving Porto and the left returning. East of Mosteirô the Linha do Douro runs at water level and the wrong seat costs you the best forty minutes of the trip.
Taste an LBV and a 10-year tawny side by side at the same house. Same base wine, two ageing philosophies — it explains the whole port hierarchy faster than any tour.
Ask any quinta to show you a *vinha velha* block. The interplanted forty-variety field blends are being replanted to single varieties, and the old parcels are finite.
Buy port at the quinta, not in Gaia. The same bottle is routinely 20–30% cheaper upriver, and colheitas from small houses never reach the lodges' shops.
Book the Côa Valley rock-art park at the same time as your Douro Superior quinta. Both are near Vila Nova de Foz Côa, both are capped, and doing them separately wastes a two-hour drive.
Treading in a lagar is real work, not a photo op — two hours of chest-deep marching in cold must. Wear nothing you value and eat first.
The last ten days of October give harvest-free owners, full autumn colour and no 40°C afternoons. It is the single best week of the year here.

raw.The two DOCs: **DOC Porto** (fortified) and **DOC Douro** (unfortified) share one demarcated zone, the world's oldest at 1756. Three sub-regions: **Baixo Corgo** in the west, wettest and coolest, historically ruby and volume; **Cima Corgo** around Pinhão and Tua, the vintage-port heartland; **Douro Superior**, east to the Spanish border, hottest and least planted, now the source of the most concentrated dry reds.
raw.Grapes and field blends: The modern five are **Touriga Nacional**, **Touriga Franca**, **Tinta Roriz** (Tempranillo), **Tinta Barroca** and **Tinto Cão**. Old vineyards are **vinha velha** field blends — up to forty varieties interplanted and co-fermented, never separately identified.
raw.Port styles: **Ruby** and **LBV** (Late Bottled Vintage, from one year, bottled 4–6 years after harvest; unfiltered versions need decanting) age in bulk. **Tawny** with an indication of age — 10, 20, 30, 40 years — is a blend whose stated age is an average, aged oxidatively in small casks in Gaia's cool lodges. **Colheita** is a single-vintage tawny, minimum seven years in wood, with the year on the label. **Vintage** is declared only in outstanding years, roughly three times a decade, bottled after two years and aged in glass; each house declares independently, subject to IVDP approval. **Moscatel do Douro** from Favaios is a separate sweet speciality.
raw.Quintas open to visitors: **Quinta do Bomfim** (Symington, Pinhão) is the best-organised visit on the river — terrace tasting above the railway line, tours bookable online at roughly €20–€45 by flight, English standard, several daily. **Quinta Nova de Nossa Senhora do Carmo** (Covas do Douro) has a wine hotel, restaurant and vineyard trail. **Quinta do Crasto** (Gouvinhas) is known for the infinity pool and the Vinha Maria Teresa old-vine field blend; email well ahead. **Quinta do Vallado** (Régua) and **Quinta do Vale Meão** (Foz Côa) best show the west–east contrast; **Quinta de la Rosa** at Pinhão has rooms and a riverside restaurant. All need reservations, most answer email within days and prefer 2–4 weeks' notice, longer in September.
raw.Producers beyond wine: In **Favaios**, the **Adega Cooperativa de Favaios** for Moscatel and the **Museu do Pão e do Vinho**, where the four-cornered *pão de Favaios* is still baked. **Quinta do Salgueiral** near Régua for Douro DOP olive oil and mill visits. The essential dishes are **posta mirandesa** — a thick PDO Mirandesa steak served rare, canonically at **Restaurante O Lagar** in Régua — and **bola de carne**, the layered meat bread in every Régua bakery. **Restaurante DOC** at Folgosa (Rui Paula) is the river's benchmark kitchen; **Castas e Pratos** in Régua fills an old railway warehouse.
raw.Season and timing: Harvest runs roughly 25 August–end September, earliest in the Douro Superior. Foot treading in *lagares* runs through September and a few quintas let visitors join, usually in the evening — but that fortnight is also when owners have no time for you. Olive pressing follows in November; vine colour peaks in the last ten days of October.
raw.Transport and the sober-driving plan: Portugal's limit is 0.5 g/l, and 0.2 g/l for licences under three years. The **Linha do Douro** is the answer: Porto Campanhã–Régua roughly 2 h, Régua–Pinhão 25 min, Pinhão–Pocinho about 1 h 10 m, €5–€15, running at water level east of Régua. CP has restructured Douro schedules and some services now require a connection — check cp.pt the week before. Add a **rabelo** leg from Pinhão quay (€15–€25 an hour) and one driver day with **Douro Exclusive** or **Living Tours** at €300–€450 per car.

sources.verified: Symington's own visitor page for Quinta do Bomfim confirming it as a bookable visit-and-tasting site at Pinhão; CP's published alert that Linha do Douro schedules changed and services were restructured; the three-sub-region structure of the demarcated Douro and the separate legal existence of DOC Porto and DOC Douro; vintage-declaration practice, in which each house declares individually subject to IVDP approval.
sources.confidenceNotes: Tasting fees are estimated bands; Bomfim, Crasto, Vale Meão and Quinta Nova each price several tiers and change them seasonally. Linha do Douro journey times and through-service availability are the most volatile item here — confirm on cp.pt close to travel. Visitor treading sessions are offered by only some quintas in some vintages; do not promise one. Restaurante DOC and Castas e Pratos have seasonal closures. Rabelo quay prices are informal. Hotel rates are prior-season estimates.

trips.title: Fetească and Fire Water: A Week Through Dealu Mare and Drăgășani
trips.subRegion: Dealu Mare (Prahova & Buzău), the Buzău Land Geopark, and Drăgășani on the Olt

bestPeriod.window: mid-September to mid-October — the *culesul viilor* harvest, warm days, cellars open and working
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (35 °C on the terrace, cellars shut for holidays) and February–March (nothing is happening)

accommodation.note: €350–€560 (€50–€80/night, mostly winery guesthouses)

food.note: €175–€280 (€25–€40/day — Romanian restaurant prices are low, winery lunches are not)

transport.note: €260–€400 (driver-guide or private transfers; a car you cannot legally drink and drive)

activities.note: €140–€260 (tastings €12–€35 per person per estate)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy

trips.gatewayAirport: Bucharest Otopeni (OTP). Dealu Mare is 70–90 min north-east by road; Drăgășani 3 h west. Trains reach Ploiești and Drăgășani but not the cellars — this is a road trip with a hired driver.
trips.currency: Romanian leu (RON) — roughly 5.0–5.3 RON to the euro during 2026
trips.summary: Romania makes more wine than New Zealand and Austria combined and almost nobody outside it drinks any. This week fixes that: a sun-facing terrace of Carpathian foothill vineyard where Fetească Neagră ripens like a…
trips.hook: Romania makes more wine than New Zealand and Austria combined and almost nobody outside it drinks any. This week fixes that: a sun-facing terrace of Carpathian foothill vineyard where Fetească Neagră ripens like a Rhône grape, a fortnight-old plum spirit poured before breakfast, mud volcanoes bubbling in a bare grey badland, and a second, cooler valley on the Olt growing a grape that exists nowhere else. Easy driving, hard-to-find bottles, and a driver you must hire.

snapshot.Start / End: Bucharest → Bucharest (loop, ~620 km driven)
snapshot.Getting there: Bucharest Otopeni (OTP). Dealu Mare is 70–90 min north-east by road; Drăgășani 3 h west. Trains reach Ploiești and Drăgășani but not the cellars — this is a road trip with a hired driver.

itinerary.title: Bucharest to the terrace
itinerary.morning: Land at Otopeni, meet the driver, and go straight north-east on the DN1 and DJ102 towards Urlați. The vineyard appears as soon as the plain tilts: a continuous south-facing bench under wooded Subcarpathian hills.
itinerary.afternoon: **Crama Basilescu** at Urlați for the first flight — a house rebuilt on a 19th-century estate, strong on Fetească Neagră and Tămâioasă. Ask for the dry Tămâioasă alongside the sweet to understand the grape's range [VERIFY: current visiting hours].
itinerary.evening: Check into a guesthouse around Ceptura or Urlați. Dinner of *ciorbă rădăuțeană* then *tochitură* with *brânză de burduf*; a small *țuică* first, poured by the host, refused at your peril.
itinerary.dayStats: 95 km

itinerary.title: Davino, and the benchmark
itinerary.morning: **Davino** at Ceptura, booked well ahead. The estate is the reference point for modern Romanian wine: Domaine Ceptura Blanc from Fetească Albă and Sauvignon, the Rouge from Fetească Neagră with Cabernet and Merlot, and Flamboyant at the top.
itinerary.afternoon: Lunch at the winery restaurant if the booking allows, then **SERVE** — founded by the Corsican Count Guy de Poix in 1994, the first foreign-owned Romanian estate after 1989, and still the maker of Cuvée Charlotte and Terra Romana.
itinerary.evening: Back to Ceptura. Walk the vineyard tracks at dusk; if it is late September the pickers are still out and the crush pads are running past dark.
itinerary.dayStats: 30 km

itinerary.title: Fintești, Șarînga and the eastern end
itinerary.morning: **Lacerta** at Fintești, a purpose-built modern winery with a gravity-flow cellar and a wide range — the Cuvée X and the Fetească Neagră reserve are the ones to taste side by side.
itinerary.afternoon: **Aurelia Vișinescu** at Șarînga, one of Romania's most respected winemakers working under her own name; the Anima and Nomad ranges. Then **Rotenberg** further east, where Mihai Rotenberg makes some of the country's most serious Merlot on iron-red clay [VERIFY: whether Rotenberg accepts same-day visits].
itinerary.evening: Move base to Pietroasele or Sărata-Monteoru in Buzău county. Dinner: *pastramă de oaie* grilled over vine cuttings, and *mămăligă*.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 km

itinerary.title: Mud volcanoes and the Geopark
itinerary.morning: The **Buzău Land UNESCO Global Geopark** — a designated territory of salt karst, fossil beds, ophiolites and living mud vents across the Buzău Subcarpathians. Start at the *vulcanii noroioși* at **Berca** (Pâclele Mari and Pâclele Mici), where cold methane pushes grey clay slurry up through cones into a landscape with almost nothing growing on it [VERIFY: current entry fee and opening hours at Pâclele Mari].
itinerary.afternoon: North to the **Focul Viu** natural gas flames at Lopătari and the rock-cut chambers around **Aluniș** and **Nucu-Bozioru**, hollowed into sandstone and used as hermitages. The **Sarea lui Buzău** salt outcrops are the geological story in one place.
itinerary.evening: Back down to Pietroasele — the site of the 1837 Pietroasele gold hoard and a working vineyard since Roman times. Eat *sarmale* and drink a Tămâioasă Românească off-dry.
itinerary.dayStats: 70 km, no wine

itinerary.title: West to the Olt
itinerary.morning: A long transfer day, west on the A1 and DN65. Break it at **Domeniile Sâmburești** in Olt county, historically the source of Romania's best Cabernet Sauvignon, a genuinely different terroir from Dealu Mare.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive **Drăgășani**, a small Vâlcea town on the right bank of the Olt with vineyards on the slope behind it. The valley is cooler and windier than Dealu Mare and the wines show it — higher acid, more aromatics.
itinerary.evening: Guesthouse dinner in or near Drăgășani. *Ciorbă de burtă* if you have the stomach for it, then grilled trout from the Olt tributaries.
itinerary.dayStats: 250 km

itinerary.title: Crâmpoșie, Novac, Negru
itinerary.morning: **Prince Știrbey**, the estate revived by Baroness Ileana Kripp-Costinescu and Jakob Kripp on restituted family land, and the reason Crâmpoșie Selecționată exists commercially at all. Taste the Crâmpoșie, then the Novac and the Negru de Drăgășani back to back — both bred at the local research station in the 20th century, both dark and black-peppered.
itinerary.afternoon: **Avincis**, the architecturally striking neighbour, built around the restored Vila Dobrușa. Their Cuvée Petit and the Crâmpoșie are the markers. Book both estates as one day, ideally with lunch at whichever offers it [VERIFY: current lunch availability and price at Avincis].
itinerary.evening: If time and the driver allow, a bottle of **Crama Oprișor** from Mehedinji further south-west — the Smerenie and La Cetate labels — bought locally rather than visited; it is a two-hour detour you do not need.
itinerary.dayStats: 35 km

itinerary.title: Back to Bucharest, and what to carry home
itinerary.morning: Drive east on the DN65 and A1. Stop in Pitești only for fuel; there is nothing you need.
itinerary.afternoon: Bucharest. A closing tasting flight at a city wine bar covers what the week missed — a **Petro Vaselo** from the Banat, a **Liliac** from Transylvania, a **Grasă de Cotnari** from Moldavia — the three regions this itinerary deliberately skipped.
itinerary.evening: *Mici* with mustard and a beer at a *berărie*, then *papanași*. Fly out, or stay a night. EU passengers can carry wine home without limit for personal use; the 100 ml liquid rule still applies to hand luggage, so it all goes in the hold.
itinerary.dayStats: 200 km

accommodationStrategy.name: Casa Timiș
accommodationStrategy.description: a full estate hotel with its own vineyard and restaurant, up in the Prahova hills within an hour of the Ceptura and Urlați cellars, which means one relocation instead of three. Real kitchen, real wine list, secure parking for the driver.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct or by booking platform, 4–6 weeks ahead, longer for harvest weekends [VERIFY: current nightly rate].

accommodationStrategy.name: Conacul Bellu / guesthouses at Urlați
accommodationStrategy.description: puts you inside the Dealu Mare vineyard rather than at its edge, walking distance from at least one cellar, and *pensiune* hosts cook the regional dishes better than any restaurant will.
accommodationStrategy.booking: by phone or email, 2–3 weeks ahead; many take cash only.

accommodationStrategy.name: Pensiuni at Drăgășani / Vila Dobrușa area
accommodationStrategy.description: Drăgășani has thin hotel stock, so a guesthouse on the vineyard slope is both the best and the only sensible option; you are ten minutes from Știrbey and Avincis and can walk between vineyard blocks before breakfast.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead, direct; confirm whether breakfast is included, as many quote room-only.

logistics.connectivity: 4G/5G is good and cheap across Prahova, Buzău and Vâlcea — Romania has some of the fastest fixed and mobile internet in the EU. Signal drops in the Geopark's deeper valleys around Nucu-Bozioru.
logistics.emergency: **112**, English-speaking operators. Pharmacies (*farmacie*) are widespread; many in towns run *non-stop*.
logistics.weather: September days reach 25–28 °C on the terrace and drop to 8 °C at night. October brings the first real rain and the clay tracks between vineyard blocks turn to grease — do not take a low car onto them.
logistics.bookingWindows: Estates 1–2 weeks ahead, longer in harvest; Davino, SERVE and Prince Știrbey closer to 2–3 weeks in late September. Accommodation 3–6 weeks. Confirm by phone the day before — email replies can be slow.
logistics.money: Cards work in towns and at the larger estates. Small *pensiuni*, village shops and roadside honey and *zacuscă* stalls are cash. Carry 400–600 RON (€75–€115) in small notes. ATMs are in every town; avoid the standalone Euronet machines and their conversion offer — always choose to be charged in RON.
logistics.transportRules: Blood alcohol limit **0.00%**. If you self-drive at all, you need a **rovinietă** e-vignette for national roads — category A, **1 day €3.50 (~18 RON), 10 days €6 (~31 RON), 30 days €9.50 (~50 RON)**; there is no 7-day product. Rental cars usually include it — verify at pickup, because the fine falls on the driver.
logistics.permits: No permits for the vineyards. The Buzău Land Geopark charges site by site rather than as a whole; the mud volcano reserves have small entry fees and marked paths — the crust is thin and people do go through it.

proTips: Book Davino and Prince Știrbey first and build the week around the two dates they give you. Everything else in this itinerary is flexible; those two are not.
Go at *culesul viilor* — the second half of September into early October. You get crush-pad access, must straight off the press, and winemakers who are exhausted but talking.
Ask specifically for **DOC-CT** and **DOC-CIB** bottlings of Tămâioasă Românească. The late-harvest and noble-rot tiers rarely leave the country and are the best value on any Romanian list.
Say *"Un pahar de Fetească Neagră, vă rog"* and *"Nu conduc"* (I'm not driving). The second sentence changes the pour.

Buy your *țuică* from the estate or a *pensiune* host, not a supermarket. Ask whether it is *de prună*, single-distilled, and expect 28–40% — if they say *pălincă* and hand you 50%+, treat it accordingly.
Skip the Prahova Valley castle circuit on this trip. Peleș is 90 minutes away and swallows a full day; Dealu Mare and Buzău are the reason you came.
Have the driver collect a case at each estate rather than carrying bottles between hotels. Most cellars will hold and consolidate a purchase for a same-week pickup.

raw.Appellations (DOC): **Dealu Mare** is the headline: a 60-km south-facing terrace at 150–550 m along the Subcarpathian foothills of Prahova and Buzău counties, where the Carpathians shelter the slope and the aspect gives it more heat than the latitude should allow — Romania's serious red country. **Drăgășani DOC** sits on the right bank of the Olt in Vâlcea, cooler, sandier, more aromatic, and the historic home of two native varieties. For context: **Recaș** and **Miniș** in the Banat (west, Hungarian-influenced, Cadarcă country), **Cotnari** in Moldavia (sweet whites from Grasă), and **Murfatlar** behind the Black Sea coast. Romanian labels carry the DOC plus a ripeness sub-tier — **DOC-CMD** (harvest at full maturity), **DOC-CT** (late harvest), **DOC-CIB** (noble-rot harvest).
raw.Native grapes to hunt: **Fetească Neagră** — the flagship red, black-cherry and dried plum, tannin that needs three years. **Fetească Albă** and **Fetească Regală** — the whites; Regală is the crisper, later crossing. **Tămâioasă Românească** — the "frankincense grape", a Muscat relative, made dry, off-dry and botrytised. **Grasă de Cotnari** — thin-skinned, rot-prone in the best way, the base of Cotnari's sweet whites. **Crâmpoșie Selecționată** — Drăgășani's own, a 1970s clonal selection of an ancient local white, sharp and saline. **Novac** and **Negru de Drăgășani** — modern Romanian crossings bred at the Drăgășani research station, both dark and peppery. **Băbească Neagră** — pale, high-acid, the Gamay of the east.
raw.Named producers: Dealu Mare: **Davino** at Ceptura (the benchmark — Domaine Ceptura Rouge, Flamboyant, Revelatio), **SERVE** (Guy de Poix's estate, Cuvée Charlotte), **Lacerta** at Fintești, **Budureasca**, **Rotenberg** (a Merlot specialist at Dealu Mare's eastern end), **Aurelia Vișinescu** at Șarînga (Anima, Nomad), **Crama Basilescu** at Urlați. Elsewhere: **Domeniile Sâmburești** in Olt, **Avincis** and **Prince Știrbey** at Drăgășani, **Crama Oprișor** in Mehedinți, **Petro Vaselo** in the Banat, **Liliac** in Transylvania.
raw.Appointment-only, without exception: Romanian estates are not drop-in cellar doors. **Davino, SERVE, Rotenberg, Aurelia Vișinescu, Prince Știrbey and Avincis all require a booking**, usually 5–10 days ahead, by email or their web form, with a stated party size. Lacerta and Budureasca have more restaurant-like set-ups but still ask you to call. Turning up unannounced at harvest gets you a polite no. Tastings run roughly €12–€35 a head depending on the flight [VERIFY: current 2026 tasting fees at each estate].
raw.Signature dishes, correct names: *Sarmale* (cabbage-rolled minced pork, with *mămăligă* and sour cream), *mici* or *mititei* (skinless grilled minced-meat rolls, ordered by the piece), *ciorbă de burtă* (tripe soup, garlic and cream), *ciorbă rădăuțeană* (its chicken cousin from Rădăuți), *zacuscă* (autumn roast-vegetable relish, every household makes it in October), *tochitură* (pork stew with polenta, cheese and a fried egg), *papanași* (fried cheese doughnuts, sour cream and sour-cherry jam), *cozonac* (the enriched walnut loaf), *pastramă de oaie* (cured, smoked mutton — the autumn dish), and *brânză de burduf*, sheep's cheese matured in a fir-bark or sheepskin casing.
raw.Țuică vs palincă: Both are fruit spirits and they are not the same. ***Țuică*** is plum, generally single-distilled, and sits around **28–40% ABV** in its common commercial and household forms. ***Palincă*** is double-distilled, legally protected, made from plum, apple, pear or apricot mostly in Transylvania and Maramureș, and lands at **40–55% ABV** — homemade *pălincă de casă* is often stronger still. Both are served before, not after, the meal.
raw.Zero tolerance: Romania's drink-drive limit is **0.00%** in blood alcohol, criminally enforced above 0.08% with prison exposure. There is no "one glass" allowance. **A hired driver is mandatory** on this itinerary, not a nicety — budget €80–€120 a day for a car and driver-guide [VERIFY: current driver-guide day rate].

trips.subRegion: Skåne — Österlen, Kullahalvön and the Malmö–Lund axis

trips.summary: A seven-day culinary & wine tour itinerary in Skåne — Österlen, Kullahalvön and the Malmö–Lund axis, Sweden.

itinerary.title: Malmö: the modern Swedish table
itinerary.morning: Arrive via Copenhagen and the Öresund bridge train — 35 minutes from Kastrup to Malmö Central. Collect a car later; today is on foot.
itinerary.afternoon: Malmö Saluhall in the old freight depot for charcuterie, cheese and coffee, then the Västra Hamnen waterfront and the Turning Torso.
itinerary.evening: Malmö is Sweden's most interesting food city for its size, with a strong Middle Eastern layer alongside the New Nordic one. Book a tasting menu at one of the city's fine-dining rooms, or eat falafel on Möllevångstorget, which is equally correct.

itinerary.title: Kullabygden: the northwest vineyards
itinerary.morning: Drive north to the Kulla peninsula (about an hour). This is Sweden's most concentrated wine district: **Kullabergs Vingård** near Nyhamnsläge and **Arilds Vingård** above the fishing village of Arild, which pairs its own Solaris and Souvignier Gris with a restaurant in the vines.
itinerary.afternoon: Book both tastings in advance — Swedish vineyards are small, family-run, and almost never open for walk-ins. Then Kullaberg nature reserve: cliffs, a lighthouse, and Nimis, the driftwood sculpture that has been quietly at war with the county administration since 1980.
itinerary.evening: Mölle or Arild. Dinner at the vineyard restaurant if you can get the slot.

itinerary.title: Hallandsåsen and the road east
itinerary.morning: **Thora Vingård** on the southern slope of the Hallandsåsen ridge — a larger estate with a good visitor operation and sparkling wine made by traditional method.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive southeast across Skåne toward Österlen, stopping at **Hällåkra Vingård** near Anderslöv, one of Sweden's earliest serious commercial plantings, with a shop and a lunch service.
itinerary.evening: Arrive Österlen. Simrishamn or Kivik for the night.

itinerary.title: Österlen: apples, cider and the coast
itinerary.morning: **Kiviks Musteri**, the apple works at Kivik, has pressed must and cider here since 1888 and is the anchor of Sweden's apple industry. Tasting, orchard walk, and the museum.
itinerary.afternoon: The Österlen coast road: Baskemölla, Vitemölla, Skillinge and Brantevik, fishing hamlets turned artists' villages with smokehouses on the harbour. Buy smoked herring and eat it on a wall.
itinerary.evening: Ale stenar at Kåseberga — a 67 m stone ship of 59 boulders on a headland over the Baltic — at sunset, then smoked fish from the harbour hut below.

itinerary.title: The Österlen producers day
itinerary.morning: Österlen's small-producer density is remarkable: cheese-makers, a saffron pancake tradition, rapeseed oil pressers, a mustard maker, several bakeries doing serious sourdough and *spettekaka*, the tall spun-sugar cake that is Skåne's protected regional speciality.
itinerary.afternoon: Glimmingehus, the best-preserved medieval fortified manor in the Nordic countries, with a herb garden and a good kitchen.
itinerary.evening: Stenshuvud National Park for the walk up to the sea view, then dinner in Kivik.

itinerary.title: Åhus, Absolut and the eel coast
itinerary.morning: North to Åhus, where the wheat for **Absolut Vodka** is grown within a defined local radius and the whole product is distilled — the visitor experience explains the single-source claim well.
itinerary.afternoon: The Skåne eel coast: *ålagille* — the autumn eel feast in traditional huts along the shore — is one of Sweden's most particular food traditions, though eel is now heavily restricted for conservation reasons and the tradition is changing. `verify: true`
itinerary.evening: Return west toward Lund or Malmö. Dinner at a *gästgiveri* — the old Swedish coaching-inn format that still serves the best value food in the province.

itinerary.title: Lund and departure
itinerary.morning: Lund: the Romanesque cathedral with its astronomical clock, the university town's cafés, and Sweden's oldest still-operating market hall.
itinerary.afternoon: Öresund train to Copenhagen Airport, 40 minutes.

accommodationStrategy.name: Arild / Mölle coastal hotels
accommodationStrategy.description: Grand Hôtel Mölle and the smaller Arild guesthouses sit on the cliff above the Öresund. Being on the peninsula means the two most important vineyard visits are ten minutes away and you can taste properly without a drive afterwards.

accommodationStrategy.name: Vineyard and orchard stays
accommodationStrategy.description: Several Skåne producers have rooms or cottages on the estate, from simple to designed. Sleeping where you taste is the single best structural decision on a wine itinerary in a country with a 0.2‰ blood alcohol limit for driving.

accommodationStrategy.name: Malmö or Lund city hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: Bookend the week in the city: better restaurant access, no car needed, and a 35-minute train to Copenhagen Airport on the last morning.

logistics.emergency: 112. Skåne University Hospital in Lund and Malmö. Ticks are present in Skåne's woodland — check after walks in Stenshuvud.
logistics.bookingWindows: Swedish wineries are small, seasonal, and staffed by the owners. Tastings are scheduled, often on fixed days, and a booked slot 2–6 weeks ahead is the norm. Turning up unannounced generally means a locked gate.

other.label: The alcohol rules shape everything
other.text: Sweden's drink-drive limit is 0.2‰ — effectively one drink is too many. Systembolaget, the state monopoly, is the only retailer of wine and spirits above 3.5%, closes early on Saturdays and is shut on Sundays. Vineyards may now sell their own wine at the farm gate under recent reforms — confirm before planning to buy on site. `verify: true`

other.label: What Swedish wine actually is
other.text: Cool-climate, aromatic, high-acid whites — Solaris above all — plus increasingly credible traditional-method sparkling and light reds from Rondo and Regent. Judge it as northern-frontier wine, not as a Burgundy substitute; the best bottles are genuinely good and the price reflects tiny production.

other.label: Harvest
other.text: Late September to mid-October. Visiting then means seeing the work; it also means the owners are busy, so book earlier and accept shorter visits.

other.label: Driving
other.text: Roads are excellent. Rural speed limits 70–90 km/h. Wildlife collisions (deer, wild boar) at dawn and dusk are the main hazard; boar are increasingly common in Skåne.

other.label: Booking windows
other.text: Destination restaurants: 2–4 months and some run ticketed release dates. Coastal hotels in July: 3 months. Vineyard tastings: 2–6 weeks. Midsummer weekend (late June): everything is closed or full.

proTips: Structure the week so one person is a **designated driver** each day, or stay at the estate. Skåne's vineyard geography and Sweden's alcohol law are in direct conflict and this is the only clean resolution.

Visit in **harvest**. Swedish producers are unusually open about their process because the industry is young and they are proud of it; you will get a two-hour conversation instead of a fifteen-minute pour.
Kiviks Musteri's **must and cider range** is far more interesting than its supermarket presence suggests — ask for the single-orchard and the ice-cider tastings specifically.
Skåne's *gästgiveri* inns serve a fixed *husmanskost* lunch, usually until 14:00, for a third of the evening price. It is the best-value meal in the province and the most traditional.
**Systembolaget's Saturday closing time** ends any hope of a Sunday bottle. Buy on Friday.
If you want the one unmissable non-wine food stop: the harbour smokehouses on the Österlen coast at Brantevik and Skillinge, mid-morning, when the racks come out.

raw.appellations_and_terroir: Sweden is a cool-climate frontier region. Skåne is the country's warmest county, on chalk and clay-over-limestone soils, with the Öresund moderating spring frost. Production sits under EU rules with Swedish protected geographical indication frameworks — labels you will see include county and estate names rather than a long-established appellation hierarchy

trips.subRegion: Vipava Valley, the Karst & eastern Goriška Brda

trips.gatewayAirport: TRS Trieste–Ronchi, 45 min to Štanjel and 55 min to Vipava; LJU Ljubljana 1 h 15 min; VCE Venice 1 h 50 min
trips.summary: Two adjoining regions divided by a wind and a rock. The Vipava Valley is flysch and green terraces growing two white grapes that exist almost nowhere else, Zelen and Pinela, under the burja funnelling off the Trnovo plateau. Twenty minutes south the Karst is red terra rossa over limestone, where the same wind cures pršut in unheated lofts and Teran is defined by acidity. Between them sits the osmica — a farm licensed to sell its own wine and meat for eight days at a time, announced by an ivy branch on a pole. The week is built to catch two.

itinerary.title: Into the Vipava, and the shape of the wind
itinerary.morning: Land at Trieste, pick up the car, buy the e-vinjeta online, and drive up the H4 into the Vipava Valley.
itinerary.afternoon: **Vipavski Križ**, a walled hill village of about 100 people, then a first tasting at **Sutor** or **Slavček** to meet Zelen and Pinela.
itinerary.evening: **Gostilna Pri Lojzetu** at Dvorec Zemono, a Palladian-style manor on a mound above the valley — the region's benchmark kitchen, and one of the few places serving a full Vipava flight by the glass.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 min from TRS / 1 winery / tasting €12–€25 / Zelen bottle €12–€20 / vignette €16 weekly
itinerary.sleep: Majerija, Slap pri Vipavi, or Hiša Torkla, Vipava

itinerary.title: Guerila, Burja and the flysch terraces
itinerary.morning: Up to **Planina** for **Guerila** — biodynamic, high terraces, and the clearest expression of Zelen's saline herbal edge. Ask to see the burja damage on the exposed rows.
itinerary.afternoon: **Burja Estate** at Podnanos for old-vine parcels and Schioppettino, then up to the Trnovo plateau rim to see the wind gap the valley sits under.
itinerary.evening: **Majerija** at Slap, whose dining room is a converted farmhouse and whose bedrooms are underground; the tasting menu leans on valley produce.
itinerary.dayStats: 2 wineries / fees €15–€30 each / 42 km / burja gusts recorded above 180 km/h at the valley mouth / menu €55–€85

itinerary.title: Amber wine, Batič, and an osmica if the calendar allows
itinerary.morning: **Mlečnik** or **Batič** at Šempas for the maceration tradition: whites fermented on skins for weeks, aged in large wood, tannic and orange in the glass.
itinerary.afternoon: Check osmize.com the night before; if a Vipava or lower-Karst farm is inside its eight days, go — a plate of pršut, cheese, boiled egg and a jug of the farm's own wine for €12–€18.
itinerary.evening: Back to Vipava town for the informal **Gostilna Podfarovž** on the river.
itinerary.dayStats: 1–2 wineries + 1 osmica / amber tasting €15–€25 / osmica cash only, €12–€18 pp / ivy sprig = open, no sprig = closed

itinerary.title: Over to the Karst: Štanjel, terra rossa, Teran
itinerary.morning: Drive south to **Štanjel**, a fortified hill village whose **Ferrari Garden**, designed by Maks Fabiani, is the architectural set piece of the Karst.
itinerary.afternoon: First Teran at **Renčel** in Dutovlje or **Štoka** at Krajna Vas — high acid, low alcohol, iron-red, and a wine that only makes sense with pršut in front of it.
itinerary.evening: **Gostilna Ražman** at Dutovlje or **Grande** at Tomaj for jota, boiled beef and Teran by the litre.
itinerary.dayStats: 38 km Vipava–Štanjel, 45 min / 1–2 wineries / Teran bottle €9–€16 / Štanjel garden entry €4–€6
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Tabor Lokev or a Dutovlje farm guesthouse

itinerary.title: Pršut day: Lokev, Dutovlje, Lipica
itinerary.morning: A curing-loft visit at **Lokev**, where the racks hang in open-shuttered rooms and the whole method is wind rather than smoke or heat. Taste twelve-, eighteen- and twenty-four-month legs side by side.
itinerary.afternoon: **Lipica Stud Farm**, founded 1580 and the origin of the Lipizzaner, ten minutes away — a working break from eating.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at a Dutovlje or Tomaj gostilna; order the pršut cut by hand rather than machine and a glass of Vitovska for contrast.
itinerary.dayStats: Pršut visit €10–€20 / Lipica tour €18–€28 / 22 km circuit / Kraški pršut min. 12 months' cure / whole leg €180–€280
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Tabor Lokev or a Dutovlje farm guesthouse

itinerary.title: The blending session and the Brda edge
itinerary.morning: The hands-on morning: a **cellar blending session** back at **Guerila** or **Batič**, building and bottling your own Zelen–Rebula cuvée from cask samples.
itinerary.afternoon: North to eastern **Goriška Brda** — **Šmartno**'s walled core and a Rebula tasting at **Ščurek** at Plešivo, where the maceration style goes furthest.
itinerary.evening: **Klinec** in Medana, one sitting only, for slow-cooked lamb and the estate's amber wines. Book days ahead.
itinerary.dayStats: Blending session €35–€60, 2 h / 1 winery / 48 km Karst–Brda, 55 min / Rebula bottle €14–€28
itinerary.sleep: Hiša Marica, Šmartno, or back on the Karst

itinerary.title: Cross-border Carso, and out
itinerary.morning: Drop into the Italian **Carso** above Trieste for **Zidarich** or **Vodopivec** — the same limestone, the same Vitovska, a different country and a noticeably different price list.
itinerary.afternoon: Trieste itself: a coffee at **Caffè San Marco**, and last buys at the covered market before the airport.
itinerary.evening: Fly from TRS, 25 minutes from the Carso villages.
itinerary.dayStats: 2 Schengen crossings, no checks / 1 winery / Carso tasting €20–€35 / 35 km / TRS 25 min
itinerary.sleep: Airport hotel at Ronchi, or fly out

accommodationStrategy.name: Majerija
accommodationStrategy.description: Bedrooms built into the hillside below the dining room, so the tasting menu and the bed are the same building — the correct arrangement in a valley with a 0.0 limit for new drivers. €90–€140 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Tabor Lokev
accommodationStrategy.description: Beside the Karst curing lofts and ten minutes from Lipica and Dutovlje, with parking and a kitchen that serves its neighbours' pršut. Plain rooms, excellent position, €70–€110.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hiša Marica
accommodationStrategy.description: Inside Šmartno's medieval walls with a terrace kitchen, useful if you extend the Brda day into a second night rather than driving back over the Karst. €110–€145 double.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming applies. 4G is good in both valleys, patchy on the Trnovo rim and in Karst dolines. Download offline maps — osmica signage is a hand-painted board and a branch, not a pin.
logistics.emergency: 112 for all services. Nearest hospitals are Šempeter pri Gorici and Izola. EHIC/GHIC accepted; add rental-excess cover.
logistics.weather: The **burja** is the defining hazard: dry north-easterly gusts routinely exceed 120 km/h through the Vipava gap, closing the H4 to caravans and high-sided vehicles and making side roads dangerous. Check promet.si and meteo.si daily in winter and spring.
logistics.bookingWindows: Guerila, Burja and Batič 2–3 weeks; Klinec and Pri Lojzetu 1–2 weeks; blending sessions 3–4 weeks by request. Osmice cannot be booked — check the published calendar and turn up.
logistics.money: Slovenia is in the eurozone. Cards work at wineries and restaurants, but **osmice, pršut cellars and farm stands are cash-only** — carry €150. Tipping means rounding up or 10% for a full meal.
logistics.transportRules: A weekly **e-vinjeta** of about €16 is required for Slovenian motorways including the H4 — buy online before crossing, as there are no toll booths. Blood-alcohol limit 0.5 g/l, **0.0 for licences under two years and drivers under 21**. Cross-border rental into Italy is normally free but must be declared. Carry ID for Schengen crossings.
logistics.permits: Osmice may sell only the farm's **own** production, which is why the menu is fixed and short — do not expect a wine list. Kraški pršut PGI and Kras PDO Teran are protected names with specific minimums.
logistics.health: Tap water is drinkable, fountains included. Ticks are a real risk in Karst scrub and Vipava woodland April–October, and Slovenia has one of Europe's highest tick-borne encephalitis rates — consider vaccination. Karst dolines and abandoned shafts are unfenced; stay on paths.

proTips: Check osmize.com the week before you travel and build the itinerary around whichever farms are inside their eight days. There is no way to reserve, and the calendar shifts every year.
Look for the ivy. A fresh green sprig on the signpost means the licence is running; a browning one means the eight days are nearly up and the wine may already be finished.
Taste Zelen and Pinela side by side at the same estate before you taste anything international. They are the reason to come, and both disappear from your palate after a Merlot.
Order Teran only with Kraški pršut or jota. The acidity that makes it awkward alone is exactly what the fat needs, and every Karst gostilna will tell you the same thing.
Ask a pršut curer to open the shutters. The whole method is visible in one gesture: burja in, moisture out, no smoke and no heat anywhere in the building.
Book the blending session as a specific request, not from a website. Neither Guerila nor Batič advertises it, and both will run one for two or three people with enough notice.
Cross into the Italian Carso for one morning. Zidarich and Vodopivec make Vitovska from the identical limestone at roughly double the Slovenian price — the comparison is worth the border hop.

raw.Appellations: **Vipavska dolina PDO** covers the valley: **Zelen** (herbal, saline, low-yielding, indigenous), **Pinela** (softer, apple and almond), plus Rebula, Malvazija and Laški Rizling. **Kras PDO** is the Karst: **Teran**, made from Refošk on terra rossa, defined by high minimum acidity and modest alcohol; also Vitovska and Malvazija. **Goriška Brda PDO** to the north-west is Rebula country. The **orange/amber** tradition — extended skin maceration of white grapes in wood or amphora — is native here, with Rebula the classic vehicle.
raw.Wineries and how to reach them: Nobody has a tasting room open on spec. **Guerila** at Planina above Vipava is biodynamic and the reference for Zelen and Pinela; it takes bookings through its website and by phone, tastings roughly €15–€30, English fluent. **Burja Estate** at Podnanos (Primož Lavrenčič) works old parcels of Zelen and Schioppettino and needs email a week ahead. **Batič** at Šempas is the natural-wine name, with a restaurant attached. **Sutor**, **Slavček (Tilia)** and **Mlečnik** are the others worth a morning; Mlečnik is amber-only and answers slowly. In the Karst, **Renčel** at Dutovlje, **Štoka** at Krajna Vas and **Vinakras** at Sežana; over the border in Italian Carso, **Zidarich** and **Vodopivec** for Vitovska. Two to three weeks' notice is normal, most owners prefer a phone call, and Saturdays book out first.
raw.The osmica system: Historically a Habsburg-era right to sell your own wine tax-free for **eight days** (*osem*), the osmica survives as a licensed home tavern: a farm registers dates with the municipality, hangs a wooden signpost topped with an **ivy sprig** that stays green for exactly the eight days, and serves its own wine, pršut, cheese and boiled eggs at farmhouse prices. Some farms run two per year, usually spring and autumn. The calendar is published by the Karst tourist board and on osmize.com — check it before fixing dates, because which farms are open is genuinely random. Names that recur: **Pri Krčarju**, **Leban–Lipa**, **Kosmina**, **Ostrouška–Pelicon**.
raw.Pršut and other producers: **Kraški pršut PGI** is dry-cured in the burja without smoke, minimum twelve months, and tastes drier and more mineral than Italian prosciutto because the wind does the work a heated chamber otherwise would. Visit the curing lofts at **Lokev** and the family curers around **Dutovlje** and **Tomaj**; guided visits with tasting run €10–€20 and want a day or two of notice. Add a Karst sheep dairy for cheese, and the dried-fruit and olive producers near Vipavski Križ.
raw.Season and timing: Harvest runs roughly **10 September–10 October**, valley first, Karst later. Pršut curing is a winter craft — the burja does its best work December–March — but the cellars are visitable year-round. Osmice cluster in **March–May and October–December**. Avoid the last fortnight of September if you want owners' attention; take it if you want to see fermenting amber wine in open vats.
raw.Hands-on element: A **cellar blending session** at **Guerila** or **Batič**: build a Zelen–Pinela–Rebula blend from cask samples, bottle and label it — €35–€60 per person, two hours, arranged by request rather than advertised. In winter, a pršut salting and pressing demonstration at Lokev instead.
raw.Transport and the sober-driving plan: Slovenia's limit is 0.5 g/l and **0.0 for drivers with under two years' licence or under 21**; enforcement is strict. Public transport between Vipava villages is close to useless. Book at least two driver days — **Vipava Valley Wine Tours** and **Trieste-based Karst transfer operators** run English-speaking days at roughly €250–€400 per car. Trains help only at the edges: Ljubljana–Sežana and the Trieste–Villa Opicina line reach the Karst rim. A Slovenian **e-vinjeta** (weekly around €16) is required for the H4 motorway through the Vipava valley — buy online before crossing.

sources.verified: The osmica tradition as an eight-day licensed direct-sale period marked by a wooden signpost and an ivy sprig that stays fresh for exactly those eight days, with farms sometimes running two per year and a published seasonal calendar naming farms including Pri Krčarju, Leban–Lipa, Kosmina and Ostrouška–Pelicon; Guerila's biodynamic status and its public wine-tourism listing for Vipava Valley visits; Kraški pršut's burja-cured, unsmoked method.
sources.confidenceNotes: All tasting fees are estimated bands and unconfirmed against 2026 price lists — re-check Guerila, Burja, Batič, Renčel and Štoka directly. The named osmice above appeared on a prior-year calendar and will not necessarily be open on your dates; the calendar must be re-checked at the time of travel and no osmica should be presented as bookable. Pršut cellar visit formats and prices at Lokev and Dutovlje vary by producer and were not confirmed. The blending session is described as arrangeable by request and is not a published product — verify before selling it. Lipica tour prices and Štanjel garden entry should be spot-checked. The Slovenian weekly e-vinjeta price changes annually. Hotel rates are prior-season estimates.

activities.note: €120–€220 (tastings €8–€25, open-cellar ticket, museum entries)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy

trips.gatewayAirport: Bratislava (BTS) or Vienna (VIE, 60 km, direct bus). Return from Košice (KSC). ZSSK regional trains Bratislava hl. st. → Pezinok in ~25 min, twice hourly.
trips.summary: Twenty minutes by train from Bratislava the vines start and do not stop for forty kilometres. This is the Malokarpatská route: Grüner Veltliner from limestone slopes, a Slovak-bred white nobody outside the country…
trips.hook: Twenty minutes by train from Bratislava the vines start and do not stop for forty kilometres. This is the Malokarpatská route: Grüner Veltliner from limestone slopes, a Slovak-bred white nobody outside the country has heard of, cellars you enter through a house door, and *burčiak* drunk cloudy and still fermenting in September. Then a long eastward jump to the seven Slovak villages that are legally, genuinely Tokaj. Easy, cheap, and almost entirely undiscovered.

snapshot.Start / End: Bratislava → Košice (point-to-point, with a 380 km transfer east on Day 5)
snapshot.Getting there: Bratislava (BTS) or Vienna (VIE, 60 km, direct bus). Return from Košice (KSC). ZSSK regional trains Bratislava hl. st. → Pezinok in ~25 min, twice hourly.

itinerary.title: Rača and Svätý Jur (Bratislava base, by train)
itinerary.morning: Arrive and take the S-line train to **Bratislava-Rača**, the city's own vineyard suburb. **Villa Vino Rača** occupies the old cooperative cellar and takes visitors without an appointment.
itinerary.afternoon: Train on to **Svätý Jur**, ten minutes further — a tiny walled wine town of gated cellar courtyards below the ruin of Biely Kameň. Walk the Šúr nature reserve boardwalk east of town.
itinerary.evening: Back into Bratislava. Eat *bryndzové halušky* and drink Frankovka in the Old Town, and note that with a **0.0‰** limit, the train was not optional.

itinerary.title: Pezinok and the press museum (Pezinok base)
itinerary.morning: Relocate to Pezinok, 25 minutes by rail. The **Malokarpatské múzeum** on Štefánikova holds the largest collection of historic wine presses in central Europe — vast oak beam presses from the 17th century onward — plus a cellar tasting under the building [VERIFY: current museum entry and tasting price].
itinerary.afternoon: **Pavelka** on the edge of town for a structured tasting through Veltlínske zelené, Rizling vlašský and Devín. Book ahead.
itinerary.evening: *Kapustnica* and roast duck with *lokše* at a Pezinok cellar restaurant. In September, order *burčiak* — partly fermented must, cloudy, sweet, mildly alcoholic and available for about three weeks only.

itinerary.title: Modra, majolica and Štúr (Pezinok base)
itinerary.morning: Bus or ride to **Modra**, the route's heart. The **Slovenská ľudová majolika** workshop still hand-throws and hand-paints the blue-and-white Modra ware; you can watch the painters at the bench [VERIFY: current workshop visiting hours].
itinerary.afternoon: The **Ľudovít Štúr Museum** — Štúr, who codified written Slovak in the 1840s, died in Modra in 1856 and is buried here. Then **Elesko** on the town's edge: a glass cube of a winery with the **Zoya Museum** collection inside, and a proper restaurant.
itinerary.evening: Drive or taxi ten minutes to **Limbach** for a hillside cellar with a view down to the Danube plain, then back. Nominate a driver or use a local taxi — there is no evening bus worth the wait.

itinerary.title: Doľany, Častá and Trnava
itinerary.morning: North along the route through **Doľany** — small, stone-cellared, unfashionable — to **Častá** and **Červený Kameň**, the Fugger-built Renaissance fortress whose cellars are among the largest vaulted spaces in Europe [VERIFY: current Červený Kameň tour times].
itinerary.afternoon: East to **Trnava**, "little Rome" for the ring of church towers inside its intact brick town walls — St Nicholas, the vast Jesuit University Church, the Trinity. **Mrva & Stanko** are based here; book a tasting before you travel.
itinerary.evening: Trnava's square at dusk with a glass of Dunaj. Sleep here, or return to Pezinok.
itinerary.dayStats: Pezinok → Trnava, 55 km

itinerary.title: East to Tokaj
itinerary.morning: Long transfer day. D1 motorway the whole way to Košice, then 70 km south-east to the Tokaj villages. By rail it is IC to Košice and a regional connection to Slovenské Nové Mesto [VERIFY: current ZSSK IC fares].
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive in **Malá Tŕňa**. The landscape changes completely: volcanic tuff hills, loess, and cellars cut horizontally into the rock, furred with *Cladosporium cellare* mould.
itinerary.evening: **Tokaj Macik Winery** for the first tasting: dry Furmint, then Lipovina, then a *Tokajský výber* sweet wine. Dinner at the winery; it also has rooms.
itinerary.dayStats: Trnava → Malá Tŕňa, 380 km / 4 h

itinerary.title: Viničky and the puttony ladder (Malá Tŕňa base)
itinerary.morning: **J&J Ostrožovič** at Veľká Tŕňa — a tour of the deep cellar galleries and a vertical through the *výber* levels, three to six puttony, plus *Tokajská esencia* if they have it open [VERIFY: current Ostrožovič tour and tasting rates].
itinerary.afternoon: Drive to **Viničky** for the cellar street and the view across the Bodrog to Hungary. The Slovak and Hungarian Tokaj are one geological region divided by the 1920 Trianon border.
itinerary.evening: Local cooking — bean soup, *pirohy*, and the sweet wine after rather than with dessert, which is how it is drunk here.

itinerary.title: Košice and out
itinerary.morning: Drive back to Košice via the vine terraces at Čerhov. If you are here on the right weekend, the Tokaj open-cellar day runs in May [VERIFY: 2027 Tokaj open-cellar dates].
itinerary.afternoon: Košice's Hlavná ulica and St Elisabeth Cathedral, the largest church in Slovakia and the easternmost Gothic cathedral in Europe. Buy bottles here rather than at the airport.
itinerary.evening: Fly out of Košice, or take the evening IC back to Bratislava (about 5 h 30).
itinerary.dayStats: Malá Tŕňa → Košice, 90 km

accommodationStrategy.name: Penzión Grand Matysová
accommodationStrategy.description: five minutes from the Pezinok station, so the whole Small Carpathian half of the week runs on trains and short taxis with nobody driving. Parking if you do rent, and cellar restaurants within walking distance.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct or Booking.com, 4 weeks ahead; much earlier for an open-cellar weekend [VERIFY: current nightly rate].

accommodationStrategy.name: Elesko Wine Park
accommodationStrategy.description: sleeping at the winery removes the driving problem entirely for one night, and the on-site restaurant and gallery mean an evening with no logistics. Good for a mid-week upgrade.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct, 3–4 weeks ahead; weekends fill with weddings.

accommodationStrategy.name: Tokaj Macik Winery
accommodationStrategy.description: there is essentially no other accommodation in the Slovak Tokaj villages, and staying with a producer gets you into the cellar in the evening and a breakfast that includes the estate's own bread and *lekvár*. Walking distance to nothing, which is the point.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct by email, 3–6 weeks ahead; the winery is small.

logistics.connectivity: Full 4G/5G along the Small Carpathian route. Signal drops inside the Tokaj rock cellars, obviously, and thins on the back roads between Čerhov and Viničky.
logistics.emergency: 112. Bratislava and Košice have major hospitals; Pezinok and Trebišov have district ones. If you walk the Malé Karpaty ridge (the red-marked Štefánikova magistrála), mountain rescue is **HZS 18 300** and is chargeable without insurance.
logistics.weather: Harvest weather is fine and warm, but the first fortnight of October can turn cold and wet fast. Cellars sit at 10–12 °C year-round; take a jacket into every tasting.
logistics.bookingWindows: Cellars 3–7 days by phone. **Deň otvorených pivníc** — the Small Carpathian open-cellar day, run twice yearly in May and November — is ticketed, capped, and the ticket includes a glass and a passport stamped at each cellar; buy online the moment sales open and book your bed the same day [VERIFY: 2027 Deň otvorených pivníc dates and ticket price].
logistics.money: Euro. Big producers take cards; village cellars often do not. Carry €150–€200 cash for the week, more if you intend to buy Tokaj sweet wines, which run €25–€60 a half-bottle.
logistics.transportRules: **Slovakia enforces 0.0‰ blood alcohol — zero tolerance, no allowance whatsoever.** Either nominate a non-drinking driver or run the western half on the Bratislava–Pezinok–Modra rail and bus corridor, which is frequent and cheap. Motorway driving requires the plate-registered **e-vignette** from eznamka.sk.
logistics.permits: None for tasting. There is no duty limit moving wine within the EU for personal use, but airline hold-baggage rules and 100 ml cabin limits still apply — ship or check a wine box.

proTips: Anchor the trip on **Deň otvorených pivníc**. One ticket, one glass, dozens of cellars in Pezinok, Modra, Vinosady and Limbach open on the same day, and shuttle buses between them — it solves the appointment problem and the driving problem at once.

Come in the second half of September for **burčiak**. It is sold by the litre from barrels on the squares, it must be transported with the cap loose because it is still fermenting, and it disappears by mid-October.
Email cellars in advance in Slovak or German rather than English. Many growers over 50 have better German, and a booking request that opens *"Dobrý deň, radi by sme ochutnali…"* gets answered faster.

Taste **Devín** at three producers before deciding what you think of it. It is Slovakia's own crossing, made nowhere else in quantity, and it swings from lychee-aromatic to almost Riesling-taut depending on the maker.
Buy Modra majolica at the workshop, not the town-square stalls. Seconds with tiny glaze flaws sell at a third of the price and are indistinguishable on a table.
In Tokaj, ask for the **dry Furmint** first. The Slovak side has quietly gone very good at dry wine, it is a fraction of the price of the sweet bottles, and no producer will offer it unprompted.

Take the train from Bratislava to Svätý Jur, walk the two kilometres of vine track to Pezinok, and train home. It is the cheapest good day in Slovak wine and costs under €4 in fares [VERIFY: current ZSSK regional fare].

raw.Appellations: The **Malokarpatská vinohradnícka oblasť** (Small Carpathian wine region) is the largest and best-known of Slovakia's six regions, running along the south-east foot of the Malé Karpaty from Bratislava-Rača to Trnava. The **Malokarpatská vínna cesta** is the signed wine route through it. In the far east, the **Vinohradnícka oblasť Tokaj** covers just seven cadastral villages — Malá Tŕňa, Veľká Tŕňa, Viničky, Čerhov, Černochov, Slovenské Nové Mesto and Bara — a small, legally protected Tokaj on the Hungarian border. Slovak Tokaj is made under the same rules of *výber* puttony counts as its Hungarian neighbour.
raw.Grapes: Whites: **Veltlínske zelené** (Grüner Veltliner, the regional workhorse — white pepper, green apple, high volume), **Rizling vlašský** (Welschriesling), **Devín** — a Slovak-bred crossing of Tramín červený and Veltlínske červenobiele, aromatic and unmistakably local — and **Muškát moravský**. Reds: **Frankovka modrá** (Blaufränkisch), **Svätovavrinecké** (St Laurent), **Dunaj** (another Slovak crossing, dark and dense) and **Alibernet**, a teinturier with black juice. Tokaj: **Furmint**, **Lipovina** (Hárslevelű) and **Muškát žltý** (Sárgamuskotály).
raw.Named producers: **Elesko** (Modra — big glass winery with the Zoya art gallery attached), **Karpatská Perla** (Šenkvice), **Mrva & Stanko** (Trnava/Skalica, one of the country's benchmark makers), **Château Belá** (Belá, near Štúrovo — **Egon Müller**'s Slovak Riesling project, and the reason serious wine people know Slovakia exists), **Villa Vino Rača**, **Pavelka** (Pezinok), **Repa Winery** (Vinosady). In Tokaj: **J&J Ostrožovič** (Veľká Tŕňa) and **Tokaj Macik Winery** (Malá Tŕňa).
raw.Reservation-only, flagged clearly: Most Small Carpathian cellars are family operations with no tasting-room staff: **you must book, by phone or email, usually 3–7 days ahead**, and many will not open for fewer than four people. Elesko and Villa Vino Rača have proper visitor centres and take walk-ins; Château Belá, Mrva & Stanko and both Tokaj producers are appointment-only [VERIFY: current tasting fees and minimum group sizes at each producer].
raw.Signature dishes: *Bryndzové halušky* (potato dumplings with sheep bryndza and bacon — the national dish), *kapustnica* (sauerkraut soup with sausage and dried mushrooms, richest at Christmas), *lokše* (thin potato flatbreads, served with goose in the November season), *šúľance s makom* (poppy-seed rolled dumplings), *trdelník* — which is a Hungarian-Slovak *kürtőskalács* originating in Skalica in western Slovakia, not a Czech invention, whatever the Prague stalls claim.
