trips.title: Grandvalira & Pal-Arinsal: Andorra's Six-Sector Week

bestPeriod.window: Mid-January–mid-March, with the second half of January the sweet spot for snow depth against crowds
bestPeriod.avoid: 26 December–6 January (Spanish and French holidays collide, Pas de la Casa queues double) and after 10 April, when south-facing Encamp and El Tarter go to slush by 11:00
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-January–mid-March, with the second half of January the sweet spot for snow depth against crowds

accommodation.note: Soldeu/El Tarter 3–4 half board €90–€150 pppn; Andorra la Vella cuts this by a third

food.note: Mountain restaurant mains €14–€22; valley menú del dia €16–€20; Andorran alcohol duty is low

transport.note: Toulouse or Barcelona shared transfer €55–€90 each way; local L4/L2 bus €2–€5 per hop

activities.note: 6-day area pass roughly €300–€360, Caldea 3 h ~€45, one day of ski school or hire extras

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5 — six lift-served days with 4,000–7,000 vertical metres of descent, no touring required, but two long circuits demand a full day on your feet at 2,000–2,600 m

trips.gatewayAirport: TLS Toulouse–Blagnac, 3 h–3 h 30 by road to Soldeu; BCN Barcelona El Prat, 3 h–3 h 45; LEU Andorra–La Seu d'Urgell, 45 min but almost no scheduled traffic
trips.summary: Andorra sells itself on volume, and for once the claim survives contact: Grandvalira alone strings six sectors across two valleys and a border ridge, and the joint Grandvalira Resorts ticket bolts on Pal-Arinsal and Ordino-Arcalís on the far side of the country. The week is built as a west-to-east sweep — start soft on Encamp and Canillo, spend the middle days working the Soldeu–Grau Roig spine and the Avet World Cup pitch, cross to Pas de la Casa for the French-facing snow, then break out to Arcalís for the one genuinely serious freeride mountain in the principality. It suits confident intermediates and better, families who want a lot of blue mileage without repetition, and anyone who likes the idea of finishing a ski day in a duty-free thermal spa. What it does not suit is the skier chasing Alpine altitude: the top here is 2,640 m and the bottom stations sit at 1,550–1,710 m, so snowmaking, not elevation, is what holds the week together.

itinerary.title: Land, transfer, and open the legs on Canillo
itinerary.morning: Fly into Toulouse or Barcelona and take a pre-booked shared transfer up the CG2. From Barcelona the road climbs through La Seu d'Urgell and the Andorran customs post at Sant Julià de Lòria; from Toulouse you come over the Pas de la Casa side and drop past Grau Roig, which is the better first view.
itinerary.afternoon: Collect hire gear at Viladomat in El Tarter, then ride the Canillo gondola from 1,550 m and ski the wide, quiet blues off Tossal de la Llosada. Canillo is the least-skied sector and the right place to find your feet.
itinerary.evening: Sol i Neu in Soldeu — the village's long-running restaurant-bar on the main road — for grilled meats and a first look at the après crowd next door.
itinerary.dayStats: Transfer 3 h–3 h 45 / Canillo gondola 1,550 m base / 2–3 h skiing, roughly 1,200 m vertical / hire €90–€140 for the week

itinerary.title: Soldeu, Espiolets and a first look at the Avet
itinerary.morning: Up the Soldeu gondola to Espiolets at 2,250 m, the biggest beginner plateau in the country and also the hub for everything above it. Warm up on Esparver and Àliga, then take the Solanelles chair for the long reds toward Riba Escorjada.
itinerary.afternoon: Inspect the **Avet**, Soldeu's FIS-homologated World Cup black that drops back into the village. The top pitch is steeper and narrower than its reputation; ski it once early, then again after 15:00 when the surface has been scraped clean and honest.
itinerary.evening: L'Abarset at the Soldeu base for the ski-boot après hour, then dinner at Ibaya in the Sport Hotel Hermitage if you want the fine-dining end of the valley.
itinerary.dayStats: 25–30 piste km / roughly 4,500 m descent / Espiolets 2,250 m / Avet vertical about 500 m to the village

itinerary.title: The Funicamp run: Encamp to Grau Roig and the Pessons cirque
itinerary.morning: Take the L4 bus down to Encamp at 1,300 m and ride the **Funicamp** — roughly 6 km of gondola to Cortals d'Encamp. It is a 20-plus-minute ride; do it before 10:00 or queue behind the day-trippers from Andorra la Vella.
itinerary.afternoon: Work west into **Grau Roig** and lap the **Pessons cirque**, a natural amphitheatre of chairs at 2,300–2,600 m with the best-preserved snow in Grandvalira. Lunch at the Refugi dels Llacs de Pessons. Then decide: return over the ridge to Soldeu, or drop back down the Funicamp.
itinerary.evening: Bus into Andorra la Vella and eat at Borda Estevet, a converted stone farm building on the Carretera de la Comella — escudella, grilled lamb and a Costers del Segre red.
itinerary.dayStats: Funicamp roughly 6,000 m of cable, 1,300 m to over 2,500 m / Pessons cirque 2,300–2,600 m / 30+ piste km / last ridge crossing to Soldeu by 15:30

itinerary.title: Pas de la Casa, the French frontier and duty-free
itinerary.morning: Ski the full eastern traverse from Soldeu through Grau Roig and over the Coll Blanc ridge into **Pas de la Casa**. This is the north- and east-facing corner of the resort at 2,050–2,640 m and it holds cold snow when everything else is turning.
itinerary.afternoon: Lap Pic Blanc and the Font Negre bowl, then ski down into Pas de la Casa town itself, which is less a village than a duty-free retail park at 2,050 m. Buy alcohol, tobacco, perfume or electronics here at Andorran rates, but know the allowances before you cross a border with them.
itinerary.evening: Return over the ridge no later than 15:00, or accept the L4 bus home. Dinner at El Rusc or Borda Xixerella over in the Erts/La Massana side if you have a car; otherwise Slalom in Soldeu.
itinerary.dayStats: Pas de la Casa 2,050–2,640 m / traverse Soldeu–Pas roughly 15 km each way / hard turnaround 15:00 / L4 bus fallback €2–€5

itinerary.title: Weather-contingency and rest day: Caldea, Canillo and the valley
itinerary.morning: This is the designed flex day. If the forecast is a whiteout or a foehn wind has shut the high chairs, take it now; if the week has been kind, take it anyway on day five when legs are worst. Start at the **Palau de Gel** in Canillo — Olympic rink, pool, and a warm building.
itinerary.afternoon: Bus to Escaldes-Engordany for **Caldea**, the glass tower fed by 70°C sulphur springs, or its adults-only sibling **Inúu**. Three hours is the standard ticket, roughly €45; the outdoor lagoon in falling snow is the reason people come.
itinerary.evening: Can Manel on Carrer Mestre Xavier Plana in Andorra la Vella for Catalan-Andorran cooking, then walk the Meritxell shopping strip. Andorra has no VAT in the EU sense — a 4.5% IGI instead — which is why the strip exists.
itinerary.dayStats: Caldea 3 h ~€45, Inúu supplement / Palau de Gel entry €10–€18 / zero vertical metres, which is the point / snowshoe alternative at Grau Roig, 2–3 h circuits

itinerary.title: Cross the country: Ordino-Arcalís and the freeride day
itinerary.morning: Drive or bus west across Andorra to **Ordino-Arcalís** — the far northern valley, 1,940–2,625 m, high, north-facing and the only sector here that feels like a proper mountain rather than a lift network. Your multi-day Grandvalira pass already covers it.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the Creussans chair and work the terrain toward **Port de Rat** and under **Pic de Casamanya**. If there is fresh snow, book a guide through Andorra Guies rather than pointing at a line yourself; carry transceiver, shovel and probe and check meteo.ad before you leave the hotel.
itinerary.evening: Eat in Ordino village at Restaurant Armengol or the Quo Vadis, then drive back over the Coll d'Ordino. Allow 45–60 minutes.
itinerary.dayStats: Ordino-Arcalís 1,940–2,625 m, roughly 30 km pisted / drive from El Tarter 50–70 min / avalanche bulletin meteo.ad, EAWS 1–5 / guide €280–€400 per day for a group

itinerary.title: Pal-Arinsal, then out
itinerary.morning: Last ski day at **Pal-Arinsal**, the third resort on your pass — 1,550–2,560 m, about 63 km, tree-lined at Pal and open above Arinsal, and the friendliest sector for a relaxed final morning. The Vallnord-era gondolas from La Massana and Arinsal put you on snow fast with luggage left at the hotel.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski until 13:00, return hire gear, then transfer. From La Massana the run to Barcelona is 3 h–3 h 45; to Toulouse 3 h–3 h 30 including the customs stop, which is a real stop with real queues on Sunday afternoons.
itinerary.evening: If your flight is early, sleep at the border in La Seu d'Urgell or at an airport hotel rather than chancing the CG1 in snow.
itinerary.dayStats: Pal-Arinsal 1,550–2,560 m, roughly 63 km / half-day 2,500–3,000 m descent / customs queue allowance 30–60 min on Sundays / airport transfer 3 h+

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Nordic
accommodationStrategy.description: On the road at El Tarter within a short walk or shuttle hop of the gondola, with ski room, pool and half board that matters when the nearest supermarket is a bus ride away. Central on the valley axis: Canillo, Soldeu and the Funicamp at Encamp are all inside 20 minutes on the L4. Roughly €90–€140 pppn half board in high season.

accommodationStrategy.name: Sport Hotel Hermitage & Spa
accommodationStrategy.description: The luxury anchor at the foot of the Soldeu gondola, with the Sport Wellness Mountain Spa and two serious restaurants, Ibaya and the Japanese Koy Hermitage. Ski to the door and pay for it: €300–€500 per room. Book it if comfort, not mileage, is the point.

accommodationStrategy.name: Andorra Park Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: The counter-strategy: sleep in the capital, save 30–40% on the bed, walk to Caldea and the shops, and commute to snow via the Funicamp at Encamp ten minutes away, which lands you high. The cost is 25–40 minutes each way and no ski-in/ski-out. Roughly €130–€220 per room.

logistics.connectivity: Andorra Telecom (Mobiland) is the sole operator and Andorra sits **outside EU roaming** — EU and UK bundles do not apply and charges are steep. Kill data roaming at the border, use lift-station wifi, and download offline maps and the Grandvalira app first.
logistics.emergency: 112 reaches the Bombers d'Andorra, who run mountain rescue. Andorra is **not in the EU**, so EHIC/GHIC does not apply — carry insurance naming winter sports, off-piste and helicopter recovery. The hospital is Nostra Senyora de Meritxell, Escaldes-Engordany.
logistics.weather: The **foehn** can lift freezing levels 1,000 m in hours and shut top chairs on wind; Mediterranean lows dump heavy wet snow on the eastern sectors and close the **Port d'Envalira** at 2,408 m, Europe's highest paved pass and the road to France. Check the CG2 before any Pas de la Casa plan.
logistics.bookingWindows: Season passes cheapest in the Early Booking window closing 30 June; day and multi-day passes are dynamic and cheapest 7–14 days ahead online. February half-term beds in Soldeu and El Tarter go 3–4 months out. Caldea weekend slots 2–3 days ahead. Freeride guides are unbookable on a powder morning — reserve on spec.
logistics.money: Andorra uses the **euro** by monetary agreement but is outside the EU and has no VAT — a 4.5% IGI instead. Cards are universal; small refuges prefer cash. Tipping is rounding up.
logistics.transportRules: Winter tyres or chains are legally required in winter conditions and enforced. **Customs checks apply entering and leaving at both the Spanish and French borders** — carry passports and know your duty-free allowance. Multi-day passes upgrade automatically to the three-resort ticket; the Mobile Pass runs on Bluetooth, so keep the phone charged and out of a metal-lined pocket.
logistics.permits: No park fees. Drones require Andorran authorisation and are banned over the ski areas. Off-piste is legal, but ducking closure ropes voids resort liability and, in practice, your insurance.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable. Altitude is modest at 2,640 m top, but Pas de la Casa at 2,050 m plus alcohol plus dehydration produces the classic day-two headache. The avalanche bulletin is **meteo.ad** — read it yourself, not the hotel's summary.

proTips: Never buy two consecutive single-day passes. Any Grandvalira pass of two or more days automatically becomes the Grandvalira Resorts area pass and hands you Pal-Arinsal and Ordino-Arcalís for nothing.
Sleep at El Tarter or Canillo rather than Soldeu — same lift network, 15–25% cheaper beds, and a fraction of the 09:00 gondola queue.
Ride the Funicamp from Encamp on the busiest day of the week. Everyone else drives to Soldeu; Encamp's 1,300 m base puts you at 2,500 m in one ride and bypasses the crush entirely.
Ski the Avet twice in a day — 10:00 on the overnight groom, and after 15:00 once it has been scraped to the boilerplate the racers actually deal with. It is a different run.
Book Caldea for a weekday afternoon, and book Inúu instead if you are over 16: identical thermal source, a fraction of the population.
Turn off data roaming at the customs post. Andorra sits outside the EU roaming zone and this is the single most common bill shock of the trip.
Treat 15:00 as the latest you leave Pas de la Casa for Grau Roig. Missing it costs a €45–€60 taxi or a slow L4 bus in ski boots.
If fresh snow lands, abandon the plan and go to Ordino-Arcalís that morning, not two days later. It is the only place in Andorra where powder survives a full day of traffic.

raw.Pass tiers by name: The **Grandvalira pass** covers the six eastern sectors — indicatively **€60–€72 adult/day**, **€330–€390 for 6 days adult**, **€215–€260 child (6–11)**, all dynamic. Critically, any pass of **two or more consecutive days upgrades automatically to the Grandvalira Resorts area pass**, adding Pal-Arinsal and Ordino-Arcalís free. The regional super-pass is the **Andorra Pass** season ticket across all three, published for 2026/27 at **€885 non-resident in Early Booking to 30 June, €1,019 from 1 July**; the northern-valleys **Nord Pass** at €668 rising to €788. Buy online for up to ~15% off gate price and use the **Mobile Pass** — 244 Bluetooth gates went in for 2025/26, replacing the keycard and its deposit. Night skiing is not a Grandvalira product; budget no floodlit supplement.
raw.Lift network and circuits: The spine runs Encamp → Grau Roig → Pas de la Casa one way, Encamp → Canillo → El Tarter → Soldeu → Grau Roig the other. The **Funicamp gondola** from Encamp at 1,300 m is the key piece — roughly 6 km of cable to Cortals d'Encamp above 2,500 m, one of Europe's longest, letting you sleep in the valley and reach Grau Roig in 25 minutes. Coll Blanc and the Pessons bowls carry you over the 2,500 m ridge to Pas de la Casa; the **Canillo–El Forn gondola** lifts 1,550 m into Canillo, which links east over Tossal de la Llosada and Espiolets. The **Encamp-to-Pas-and-back-to-Canillo circuit is a full day**: 40–45 piste km, eight to ten lifts.
raw.Last lift home: Lifts run roughly 09:00–16:30. The two links that strand people are Pas de la Casa back to Grau Roig, and the Espiolets/Tossal chain from Soldeu to Canillo — treat **15:00 as the hard turnaround at Pas de la Casa, 15:30 at Soldeu**. The patch is the road: the **L4 bus** works the CG2 between Encamp, Canillo, El Tarter, Soldeu and Pas de la Casa for €2–€5; a taxi Pas–Soldeu is €45–€60.
raw.Snow reliability: Grandvalira spans **1,710–2,640 m**, Pal-Arinsal 1,550–2,560 m, Ordino-Arcalís 1,940–2,625 m. Pas de la Casa and Grau Roig face north and east onto the French frontier and hold natural snow; Encamp, Canillo and El Tarter are lower, sunnier, snowmaking-dependent. Roughly **€11 m went into snow production for 2025/26** — 53 new guns plus 118 replacements at about 90% less energy, a 100,000 m³ reservoir at Lake Vaquer, 36,000 m³ at Ordino-Arcalís, 3 km of new Soldeu–El Tarter pipe. Coverage is high, plausibly ~70% of pisted km, but unpublished — treat as unverified. **Season: late November to mid-April.** In a bad year the resort retreats to the Grau Roig–Pas de la Casa bowls and the Espiolets plateau, closes the valley returns and sends you down by gondola.
raw.Off-piste and touring: The freeride mountain is **Ordino-Arcalís** — terrain skier's left of the Creussans chair and the bowls under **Pic de Casamanya** and **Port de Rat**, with a lift-accessed freeride zone and transceiver checkpoint. In Grandvalira the **Pessons cirque** gives long mellow off-piste, and the old **TK Bosc** drag at Soldeu was removed for 2025/26 to open a tree-freeride sector. Bulletin: **Servei Meteorològic Nacional d'Andorra** (meteo.ad), EAWS 1–5. No legal guide requirement, but this is a persistent-weak-layer snowpack with slow rescue: use **Andorra Guies** or a Grandvalira freeride guide, €280–€400 per day per group.
raw.Piste breakdown: Grandvalira publishes about **210 km over 130 runs**; Pal-Arinsal adds ~63 km, Ordino-Arcalís ~30 km — around **300 km** on the joint ticket, roughly 20% green, 30% blue, 35% red, 15% black. **Beginners** belong at Encamp's Cortals plateau, El Tarter's Riba Escorjada and lower Pal. **Intermediates** own the Soldeu–Grau Roig axis, lapping Solanelles and Coll Blanc. **Experts** get three things: the **Avet** black at Soldeu (the FIS World Cup piste of the 2019 Finals, steeper and narrower up top than its reputation), the Pic Blanc blacks at Pas de la Casa, and Arcalís.
raw.Non-ski days: **Caldea and Inúu** at Escaldes-Engordany, southern Europe's largest thermal complex on 70°C sulphur springs — three hours around €45, Inúu the adults-only annexe. **Palau de Gel** in Canillo has an Olympic rink and pool. Marked **snowshoe circuits at Grau Roig and the Juclà lakes**, dog-sledding at Grau Roig, and the 5 km-plus **Tobotronc** alpine coaster at Naturlandia.
raw.Hire, lockers and schools: Every base has a Grandvalira rental; **Viladomat** (Soldeu, El Tarter, Canillo) is the reliable independent — **€90–€140 a week** standard, €160–€220 performance. Lockers at Espiolets and Grau Roig €5–€8 a day. The **Escola d'Esquí i Snowboard de Grandvalira** runs roughly **€150–€220 for five half-day group mornings**, **€60–€90 an hour** private.

The regional super-pass is the **Andorra Pass** season ticket across all three, published for 2026/27 at **€885 non-resident in Early Booking to 30 June, €1,019 from 1 July**; the northern-valleys **Nord Pass** at €668 rising to €788. Buy online for up to ~15% off gate price and use the **Mobile Pass** — 244 Bluetooth gates went in for 2025/26, replacing the keycard and its deposit. Night skiing is not a Grandvalira product; budget no floodlit supplement.

Roughly **€11 m went into snow production for 2025/26** — 53 new guns plus 118 replacements at about 90% less energy, a 100,000 m³ reservoir at Lake Vaquer, 36,000 m³ at Ordino-Arcalís, 3 km of new Soldeu–El Tarter pipe. sources.verified: Grandvalira Resorts' published €39 m investment for 2025/26 (€32.1 m Grandvalira, €2.9 m Pal Arinsal, €4 m Ordino Arcalís), including ~€11 m on snowmaking, 53 new plus 118 replacement guns, the 100,000 m³ Lake Vaquer and 36,000 m³ Ordino reservoirs, 3 km of new Soldeu–El Tarter pipe, the TK Eslàlom extension to 556 m / 229 m vertical, the new 70 m TK Refugi, the removal of TK Bosc at Soldeu for a freeride area, and 244 Bluetooth Mobile Pass gates. sources.confidenceNotes: **The 6-day adult and child prices quoted (€330–€390 and €215–€260) are an estimated band, not a confirmed tariff.** Grandvalira publishes no fixed multi-day price; the only firm reference found was a November 2024 sample of €378 adult / €240 child for six days. Re-verify against the live booking assistant for actual travel dates. Senior rates (~€43.50 for 65–69, ~€25 for 70–74, free at 75+) are also sample-date dependent. Keycard deposit amount unconfirmed and possibly obsolete under the Mobile Pass. **Snowmaking coverage as a percentage of pisted km is not published by Grandvalira** — the ~70% figure is inference and must be sourced or cut. Piste kilometres and the difficulty split are indicative. Funicamp length is widely quoted near 6 km but unconfirmed to the metre. Season dates, lift hours and last-crossing times shift year to year. Ski school, hire, Caldea and Palau de Gel prices are prior-season bands.

trips.title: Ski Arlberg — St. Anton, the Flexenbahn and the Valluga

bestPeriod.note: January and February hold the most reliable snow; March gives longer days but softer afternoon off-piste.

trips.gatewayAirport: Innsbruck (INN)
trips.summary: A week based in St. Anton am Arlberg, using the Flexenbahn interconnect to ski Lech, Zürs and Warth, with a guided off-piste day and the Weisse Ring circuit.
trips.hook: Ski Arlberg is Austria's biggest interconnected area, and St. Anton is its loud, steep, powder-hungry end of it. This week uses St. Anton as a base, rides the Flexenbahn across to the quieter, pricier villages of Lech and Zürs, and spends one full day with a guide off the marked runs — because on the Arlberg the best terrain is exactly where the piste map stops being useful.

snapshot.Base(s): St. Anton am Arlberg (7 nights)
snapshot.Best Period: December–March; January and February most snow-secure
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Ski Arlberg: approx. 305 km piste, 200 km marked ski routes, base 1,304 m to top 2,811 m
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Innsbruck (INN), 1h10 transfer; or Zürich (ZRH), 2h30 transfer
snapshot.Who It Suits: Strong intermediates and advanced skiers comfortable with steep, often ungroomed terrain

itinerary.title: Arrival and the Galzig shakedown
itinerary.morning: Land in Innsbruck, transfer by rail to St. Anton (1,304 m). The direct train from Innsbruck Hauptbahnhof takes about an hour and drops you a five-minute walk from most central hotels.
itinerary.afternoon: Rent skis on the Dorfstrasse and buy the Ski Arlberg pass online in advance — a pre-loaded card saves the first-morning Galzigbahn queue. Ride the Galzigbahn gondola to 2,185 m for an easy recon lap back to the valley.
itinerary.evening: Early dinner and an early night. St. Anton's après-ski culture, centred on the Krazy Kanguruh at the base of the Galzig slope, runs loud from mid-afternoon; skip it on arrival day and save it for later in the week.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 600 m vertical · Galzig sector only · 2 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Rendl, the sunny side
itinerary.morning: Rendl is St. Anton's own separate sector, reached by a gondola from the southern edge of the village rather than through the main Galzig–Gampen lift chain. It faces south-east, so ski it on a cold, clear morning and avoid it by early afternoon in a hot spell, when the lower snow softens fast.
itinerary.afternoon: Rendl has the area's best lift-served, patrolled freeride-adjacent terrain: wide ridge bowls plus a dedicated freeride zone the ski patrol opens and closes by avalanche bulletin. Check the noticeboard at the Rendlbahn base before heading off-piste even within the marked zone — "open" here means avalanche-controlled, not risk-free.
itinerary.evening: Walk the short Dorfstrasse loop; St. Anton's old core is compact and everything is within ten minutes of the lifts.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 5,200 m vertical · Rendl sector · 5.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: The Weisse Ring
itinerary.morning: The Weisse Ring is a 22 km circular ski safari linking St. Anton, St. Christoph, Stuben and back, strung together on the Vallugabahn, Albonabahn and the Rendl/Gampen lift chains rather than one dedicated lift. Start at Galzig and ski clockwise via St. Christoph (1,800 m) to Stuben; a confident intermediate manages it in three to four hours.
itinerary.afternoon: From Stuben, the Albonabahn and Alberjoch chair carry you back to the St. Anton side, closing the loop past Rendl. The circuit's weak link is timing: the last connecting lift at Stuben closes earlier than the main Galzig lifts, and missing it means a bus back rather than a ski-back.
itinerary.evening: St. Christoph's small hamlet, one of the birthplaces of Austrian ski instruction, is worth a coffee stop if you have time before the last lift — otherwise save it for a future lap.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 22 km circuit, 4,300 m vertical · St. Anton–St. Christoph–Stuben sectors · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Flexenbahn to Zürs and the Valluga
itinerary.morning: The Flexenbahn cable car, opened in 2016, is what actually makes "Ski Arlberg" one area rather than four resorts strung along a road. It runs from Alpe Rauz, above St. Anton, to Zürs in about six minutes, replacing an old bus transfer. Ride it early — wind holds are common above 2,000 m and the Flexenbahn is the first lift to suspend in a storm, splitting the interconnect in two.
itinerary.afternoon: From Zürs, ski across to Lech via the pistes and lifts around Zürsersee and the Rüfikopf. Lech is the quieter, more manicured half of the area — old wooden farmhouses, a slower pace than St. Anton. The Valluga cable car, the area's highest point at 2,811 m, is visible from most of Zürs; Valluga II, the upper stage, only carries skiers with a certified guide, because the descent is a narrow, exposed, glaciated ridge with real avalanche and fall exposure and no marked piste down.
itinerary.evening: Ride the Flexenbahn back to Alpe Rauz before the last car — check the posted last-departure time each morning, since it shifts with daylight and weather through the season — and bus or ski back into St. Anton.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 4,800 m vertical · Zürs–Lech sectors via Flexenbahn · 5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Guided off-piste day
itinerary.morning: Book a full day with a certified mountain guide through Piste to Powder, the town's established freeride and touring outfit, or the Skischule St. Anton's guided freeride programme. A guide is non-negotiable for the classic Arlberg lines off the back of Valluga and Kapall. Groups run four to six skiers; transceiver, probe and shovel are provided or checked on the spot.
itinerary.afternoon: A typical day runs a couloir or bowl off the Valluga or Schindlergrat, checking slope angle and aspect against the morning's avalanche bulletin, and finishes with a longer valley run toward St. Anton or St. Christoph. The guide reads the five-level European avalanche danger scale (1 Low to 5 Very High) posted daily and will change or cancel terrain choices on the spot — that flexibility is the point of paying for local knowledge.
itinerary.evening: A debrief drink is standard practice with these groups — worth staying for, since guides here often flag which slopes are worth another look later in the week.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,200–1,600 m vertical off-piste · Valluga/Schindlergrat/St. Christoph sectors · full guided day.

itinerary.title: Warth-Schröcken and the far end of the interconnect
itinerary.morning: Take the Flexenbahn again, continuing past Zürs and Lech to Warth-Schröcken, the interconnect's western end, joined to Lech only since a 2013 lift upgrade. Warth sits slightly higher and more sheltered than St. Anton's lower slopes, and in a thin-snow year is often the better sector by February.
itinerary.afternoon: Warth's terrain is broader and less crowded than St. Anton's — a good contrast day for tired legs. If the snowpack low down has been marginal — St. Anton's village-level runs sit at 1,304 m and suffer first in a warm spell — this is the bad-snow plan B for the week: stay high, on Warth-Schröcken and upper Zürs above 1,700 m, and treat any day below that as optional.
itinerary.evening: The return trip from Warth to St. Anton by lift needs a firm early-afternoon turnaround; missing the last Flexenbahn car means a long road transfer by bus around the valley, well over an hour.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 3,800 m vertical · Warth-Schröcken sector · 4.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Last laps and departure
itinerary.morning: A short final session on Gampen-Kapall, St. Anton's steep home sector above the village, suits those who want one more real run before packing.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop skis at the rental shop, shower, and train to Innsbruck. Build in a two-hour buffer — Sunday afternoon trains from the Arlberg run full with changeover traffic.
itinerary.evening: Flight home from Innsbruck.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,800 m vertical · Gampen-Kapall sector · 2 lift hours.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Post St. Anton
accommodationStrategy.description: A long-established Dorfstrasse hotel two minutes from the Galzigbahn base, with ski storage and boot dryers — the shortest walk from bed to lift matters on a week built around early Flexenbahn starts.
accommodationStrategy.booking: August for the following winter.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €220–€320 per night for two, half board

accommodationStrategy.name: Aparthotel Rosanna
accommodationStrategy.description: Modern apartments near the station and the Nassereinbahn lift, useful for controlling the food budget and drying gear after a guided off-piste day.
accommodationStrategy.booking: October.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Alte Post
accommodationStrategy.description: A 700-year-old former coaching inn on the main street, with an early breakfast service that suits the 07:00 starts a guided day or Flexenbahn wind-window requires.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €190–€280 per night for two, half board

logistics.connectivity: Good in the villages and most mid-mountain lift stations; it drops out in the couloirs and bowls a guide will take you into, one more reason to ski off-piste with one.
logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Austrian alpine and mountain rescue is **140**. Ski patrol responds fast within resort boundary; off-piste rescue is a helicopter call — confirm your insurance covers it.
logistics.weather: The Flexenbahn and Valluga cable car are high, exposed lifts and the first to suspend in strong wind; build a spare half-day into the itinerary.
logistics.bookingWindows: Christmas and February half-term weeks sell out St. Anton's better hotels by September; book the guided off-piste day two to three weeks ahead in high season.
logistics.money: Cards work everywhere on the mountain and in town; carry cash for smaller Alm huts on the Rendl and Warth sides.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 pan-European; Austrian alpine and mountain rescue is **140**. Ski patrol responds fast within resort boundary; off-piste rescue is a helicopter call — confirm your insurance covers it.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Lift last-departure times shift through the season and are posted each morning at the base stations — check the Zürs-side last Flexenbahn time before heading that way.

other.label: Avalanche equipment
other.text: Anyone skiing off-piste, guided or not, must carry a transceiver, probe and shovel and know how to use them; guide offices check kit but this does not substitute for self-rescue competence.

proTips: Load the Ski Arlberg pass online before arrival — the Galzigbahn queue on a Saturday changeover morning is the worst of the week.
Ski Rendl in the morning and the Gampen-Kapall side in the afternoon; the aspect works with the light both times.
Do the Weisse Ring on a weekday, not a Saturday, when the connecting Stuben lifts are busiest with changeover traffic from both directions.
The Valluga II summit stage sells out its guided slots first on bluebird days — ask your guide to book it at the start of the week, not the morning of.
St. Christoph's small hamlet on the Weisse Ring route is quieter for lunch than the Galzig mid-station self-service.
Warth-Schröcken's slopes hold better snow later in the season than St. Anton's lower runs — save Warth for the back half of a March trip.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Ski Arlberg: approx. 305 km piste, 200 km marked ski routes, base 1,304 m to top 2,811 m
raw.Who It Suits: Strong intermediates and advanced skiers comfortable with steep, often ungroomed terrain

typeSpecific.surface: Ski Arlberg: approx. 305 km piste, 200 km marked ski routes, base 1,304 m to top 2,811 m
typeSpecific.audience: Strong intermediates and advanced skiers comfortable with steep, often ungroomed terrain

packingNotes: Transceiver, probe and shovel if you own them; otherwise confirm your guide outfit supplies and checks a set.
A helmet — mandatory in practice on Ski Arlberg's steeper pitches and required by most guide operators.
Goggles with a low-light lens for flat-light days; the upper Valluga terrain loses definition fast in cloud.
A base layer system for temperature swings between the sheltered Lech side and the wind-exposed Flexenbahn crossing.
Cash in small notes for mountain huts that do not take cards.
A daypack for the guided day, sized for extra layers, water and emergency kit.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Wind closes the Flexenbahn.** Fallback: ski the St. Anton–St. Christoph–Stuben side on the Weisse Ring lifts, lower and more wind-sheltered, and try the Lech/Zürs crossing again the next clear morning.
**Low snow at village level.** Fallback: stay on lift-served terrain above 1,700 m — Rendl's upper bowls, Galzig, Warth-Schröcken — and treat any low-altitude run as optional.
**Guided day fully booked in high season.** Fallback: book Skischule St. Anton's group freeride clinic instead, or move the guided day earlier in the week.
**Missed last lift back from Zürs or Warth.** Fallback: the regional Arlberg bus network covers the same villages by road, slower but running into the evening.

trips.title: KitzSki — the Streif, the Tree Runs and Pass Thurn

bestPeriod.note: Kitzbühel's low base altitude makes January and February the safer bet for reliable snow at valley level.

trips.gatewayAirport: Innsbruck (INN)
trips.summary: A week skiing KitzSki from Kitzbühel — the Streif, Bichlalm tree runs, and the Jochberg–Pass Thurn side — honest about the resort's low-altitude snow risk.
trips.hook: Kitzbühel is a ski town that happens to sit at 762 m, which is low for the Alps and means its snow record is a story of snowmaking, not glaciers. What it has instead is one of the great race pistes in the world, genuinely good tree skiing at Bichlalm, and a town worth the detour even on a thin-snow afternoon. This week treats the low base altitude honestly and builds the week around the terrain that holds up regardless.

snapshot.Base(s): Kitzbühel (7 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: KitzSki: approx. 179 km piste, base 762 m (Kitzbühel) to 2,000 m (Pengelstein/Steinbergkogel)
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Innsbruck (INN), 1h drive/rail transfer; Salzburg (SZG) is a similar distance
snapshot.Who It Suits: Intermediate to advanced skiers, families wanting a proper town alongside the slopes

itinerary.title: Arrival and the Hahnenkammbahn
itinerary.morning: Transfer from Innsbruck by train (change at Wörgl, roughly 1h20 total) or direct road transfer, arriving into Kitzbühel Hauptbahnhof, a short walk from the old town and the Hahnenkammbahn gondola base.
itinerary.afternoon: Buy the KitzSki pass and ride the Hahnenkammbahn up to Ehrenbachhöhe, 1,700 m, for an orientation lap on the groomed runs above town. This gondola replaced the old cable car in 2020 and is the fastest way onto the Hahnenkamm massif from the town centre.
itinerary.evening: Walk the old town — Vorderstadt and Hinterstadt — where the medieval street plan and painted facades are worth seeing even in ski boots.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 800 m vertical · Hahnenkamm sector · 2 lift hours.

itinerary.title: The Streif
itinerary.morning: The Streif is the Hahnenkamm downhill World Cup race course, and outside race week (it hosts the Hahnenkamm races in mid-to-late January and is closed to the public for several days around the event) it is open to any skier as a marked black run. Ride the Hahnenkammbahn to Ehrenbachhöhe and take it in stages — the Mausefalle start section is genuinely steep and best approached after a warm-up lap elsewhere on the mountain, not as the first run of the day.
itinerary.afternoon: Below the Steilhang and Alte Schneise sections the gradient eases; finish at the Zielschuss into the valley near Kitzbühel town. The full course is roughly 3.3 km with 860 m of descent — treat it as a serious black run, not a novelty.
itinerary.evening: The Streif-side huts along the lower run, including the Hahnenkamm-stube area, are a good stop for the traditional Kitzbüheler Brettljause, a cold cured-meat and cheese board.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,600 m vertical · Hahnenkamm/Streif sector · 3.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Kirchberg and the Fleckalmbahn link
itinerary.morning: KitzSki's interconnect runs from the Hahnenkamm side over the Pengelstein and Steinbergkogel ridge to Kirchberg's Fleckalmbahn, joining the two towns into one lift-served area. This link is the area's weak point in poor visibility: the ridge run between Steinbergkogel and Pengelstein is exposed to wind and closes first in a storm, which strands skiers on whichever side they started from.
itinerary.afternoon: Kirchberg's slopes are broader and less crowded than the Kitzbühel side on a weekday; the Gaisberg sector above Kirchberg has good intermediate cruising with reliable snowmaking cover down to the valley.
itinerary.evening: Kirchberg's centre is quieter and cheaper than Kitzbühel's; worth a dinner detour if staying central Kitzbühel starts to feel pricey by mid-week.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 3,400 m vertical · Kirchberg/Kirchberg-Kitzbühel link · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Bichlalm tree skiing
itinerary.morning: Bichlalm is a small, separate lift-served sector above Kitzbühel, reached by its own gondola from the Bichlalm base near town, and it is the area's real tree-skiing terrain — wide-spaced forest glades below the tree line rather than groomed piste. It runs on limited hours and closes earlier than the main KitzSki lifts, so plan it as a half-day rather than a full one.
itinerary.afternoon: Book a guided glade session with Skischule Rote Teufel, Kitzbühel's long-established ski school (the "Red Devils," founded in the 1930s and closely tied to the town's racing history), which runs small-group off-piste and tree-skiing sessions here. A guide matters at Bichlalm because the glades are unpatrolled in the same way the main pistes are, and tree wells and variable snow depth under the canopy are real hazards after a fresh fall.
itinerary.evening: Return to Kitzbühel for an early dinner; Bichlalm's last lift down is notably earlier than the Hahnenkamm side's.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,800 m vertical off-piste/glade · Bichlalm sector · 3 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Jochberg and Pass Thurn
itinerary.morning: Ski the connecting runs south from the Hahnenkamm side down toward Jochberg, joined into KitzSki via the Resterhöhe lifts. This is the area's higher, more sheltered flank, and the sector to favour if the Kitzbühel town-side slopes are looking thin.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to the Pass Thurn sector, KitzSki's southernmost and highest-altitude piste area, topping out near 1,975 m. Pass Thurn faces north and holds snow noticeably later into spring than the Kitzbühel-facing slopes — the honest bad-snow plan B for this whole week is to spend more time here and less on the low, sun-exposed Streif-facing runs whenever the forecast turns mild.
itinerary.evening: The bus/lift combination back from Pass Thurn to Kitzbühel takes longer than a same-sector return; check the last-lift board at Resterhöhe before heading up in the afternoon.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 4,200 m vertical · Jochberg/Pass Thurn sector · 4.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Guided off-piste day
itinerary.morning: Book a guided freeride day through Skischule Rote Teufel or Element3 Kitzbühel, both established local ski schools running certified-guide off-piste programmes. KitzSki's off-piste is more modest than the high-alpine terrain further west in Austria, but the Kitzbüheler Horn's north side and pockets off the Hahnenkamm ridge hold worthwhile lines after a fresh snowfall, and local knowledge of where the snowmaking-groomed base gives way to natural cover is exactly what a guide provides here.
itinerary.afternoon: Guides check the daily Tyrolean avalanche bulletin, rated on the standard five-level European avalanche danger scale (1 Low to 5 Very High), before committing to any specific slope; on a lower-altitude area like KitzSki the bigger real hazard is often thin or rocky early-season cover rather than deep-snow avalanche risk, but guides carry and check transceiver, probe and shovel regardless.
itinerary.evening: A free evening in town — Kitzbühel's restaurant scene is a genuine reason to base here over a purely functional ski village.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,000–1,400 m vertical off-piste · Kitzbüheler Horn/Hahnenkamm sectors · half-day guided.

itinerary.title: Kitzbüheler Horn and departure
itinerary.morning: The Kitzbüheler Horn, on the opposite side of town from the Hahnenkamm, is KitzSki's other main sector and worth a final morning — less crowded than the Hahnenkamm side and with good views back over the Kitzbühel basin.
itinerary.afternoon: Return skis, and take the train back to Innsbruck via Wörgl with a comfortable buffer before an evening flight.
itinerary.evening: Flight home from Innsbruck.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,600 m vertical · Kitzbüheler Horn sector · 2.5 lift hours.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Tennerhof
accommodationStrategy.description: A traditional Tyrolean farmhouse-style hotel a short walk from the Hahnenkammbahn base, with ski storage and a genuinely early breakfast for race-piste starts.
accommodationStrategy.booking: August for the January race-week period, otherwise 2–3 months ahead.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €260–€380 per night for two, half board

accommodationStrategy.name: Aparthotel Andreas Hofer
accommodationStrategy.description: Central apartments between the old town and the Kitzbüheler Horn base station, useful for controlling food costs in one of Austria's pricier resort towns.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Rasmushof
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits directly beside the Streif's finish area on the Hahnenkamm, genuinely ski-in ski-out for the Hahnenkamm sector and a short taxi from the old town for evenings out.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead; sells out fastest around race week.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €220–€320 per night for two, half board

logistics.connectivity: Reliable in town and at all major lift stations; patchy in the Bichlalm glades, which is one more reason to ski them with a guide who carries a working radio.
logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Austrian alpine rescue **140**. KitzSki patrol response on-piste is fast given the area's proximity to town and road access.
logistics.bookingWindows: Hahnenkamm race week (mid-to-late January) sells out Kitzbühel's hotels up to a year ahead and closes the Streif to public skiing for several days; avoid that week entirely unless the race itself is the point of the trip.
logistics.money: Cards standard everywhere; Kitzbühel is one of the pricier Austrian resort towns for food and drink.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 pan-European; Austrian alpine rescue **140**. KitzSki patrol response on-piste is fast given the area's proximity to town and road access.

other.label: Snowmaking reality
other.text: KitzSki has one of the densest snowmaking networks in Austria and can guarantee a skiable base down to the valley through most of a normal winter, but a genuinely warm or dry spell still closes lower runs — check the daily piste report rather than assuming coverage.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Bichlalm's lift closes earlier than the main KitzSki network — check the posted time each morning rather than assuming a uniform closing hour across sectors.

other.label: Avalanche equipment
other.text: Mandatory for any off-piste terrain, including the Kitzbüheler Horn's north side glades — transceiver, probe, shovel, and the training to use them.

proTips: Ski the Streif in the first two hours after lift opening, before the lower sections get skied off and icy in the afternoon sun.
Favour the Pass Thurn and Jochberg side of the area in a mild spell; it holds snow longest.
Book Bichlalm's guided tree-skiing session for the morning slot — the lift's limited hours make afternoon availability tight in high season.
The Fleckalmbahn ridge link between Kirchberg and Kitzbühel is the first lift to close in wind; check both sides' status before committing to a full loop.
Kirchberg's restaurants run noticeably cheaper than central Kitzbühel's for an equivalent meal — worth the short bus or ski-bus hop.
Race week aside, the town's old streets are genuinely worth an afternoon off skis if a low-snow day makes the lower slopes unappealing.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: KitzSki: approx. 179 km piste, base 762 m (Kitzbühel) to 2,000 m (Pengelstein/Steinbergkogel)
raw.Who It Suits: Intermediate to advanced skiers, families wanting a proper town alongside the slopes

typeSpecific.surface: KitzSki: approx. 179 km piste, base 762 m (Kitzbühel) to 2,000 m (Pengelstein/Steinbergkogel)
typeSpecific.audience: Intermediate to advanced skiers, families wanting a proper town alongside the slopes

packingNotes: Transceiver, probe and shovel for any glade or off-piste terrain, including Bichlalm.
A helmet, particularly for the Streif's steeper pitches.
Layers that handle a wide temperature range — Kitzbühel's low base altitude means milder days than higher Austrian resorts.
Edge-sharp skis or a rental with fresh tuning; snowmaking-groomed pistes ice up harder than natural snow.
Cash for smaller mountain huts on the Jochberg and Pass Thurn side.
A daypack for the guided freeride day, sized for spare layers and water.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A warm spell strips the lower slopes.** Fallback: shift to the higher, north-facing Pass Thurn and Jochberg sector, which holds cover longest, and treat any day on the low Streif-facing runs as conditional.
**Wind closes the Kirchberg–Kitzbühel ridge link.** Fallback: ski each side of KitzSki independently that day and reconnect once the Fleckalmbahn or Steinbergkogel lift reopens.

**Bichlalm's guided session sells out.** Fallback: book with the alternate school — if Rote Teufel is full, Element3 Kitzbühel runs comparable small-group programmes, or shift the guided day to the Kitzbüheler Horn's off-piste pockets instead.

**Trip coincides accidentally with Hahnenkamm race week.** Fallback: the Streif itself is closed to the public, but the rest of KitzSki remains fully open — treat it as a spectating bonus rather than a lost ski day.

trips.title: Jahorina & Bjelašnica: Sarajevo's Olympic Mountains in Winter
trips.subRegion: Jahorina, Bjelašnica & Igman — the 1984 Olympic mountains above Sarajevo

bestPeriod.window: Late January–early March, with the first three weeks of February the most reliable window for depth on both mountains
bestPeriod.avoid: Late December–7 January, when Serbian and regional Orthodox holidays fill every Jahorina bed and the Poljice access road gridlocks; and after 20 March, when 1,300 m bases turn to mud
bestPeriod.raw: Late January–early March, with the first three weeks of February the most reliable window for depth on both mountains

accommodation.note: Jahorina 3–4 half board 90–160 BAM (€46–€82) pppn; Sarajevo city hotels €45–€90 per room

food.note: Mountain restaurant mains 14–25 BAM (€7–€13); Sarajevo ćevapi 8–12 BAM; coffee 2–3 BAM

transport.note: Airport transfer 60–90 BAM each way; hire car €30–€45/day; ski bus 10 BAM

activities.note: 6-day Jahorina pass 316–373 BAM, plus Bjelašnica days, Lukomir guided snowshoe, Trebević cable car

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5 — five lift-served days on modest vertical, plus one full-day snowshoe traverse to Lukomir at 1,450–1,600 m that demands six hours on your feet

trips.gatewayAirport: SJJ Sarajevo International, 30 km / 45–60 min to Jahorina, 27 km / 40–50 min to Bjelašnica's Babin Do
trips.summary: Sarajevo is the only European capital with two Olympic ski mountains inside forty minutes of its trams, and the week works because you can move between them. Jahorina, which held the 1984 women's alpine events, is the bigger and better-lifted of the pair — a broad forested dome of long blue and red motorway with a good gondola and the largest floodlit night-ski operation in the region. Bjelašnica, which held the men's, is the harder, colder, wind-scoured mountain, its summit plateau rolling out into the shepherd villages of Umoljani and Lukomir above the Rakitnica canyon. The arc is Jahorina first for volume, Bjelašnica second for character, Sarajevo as the constant bolt-hole, and one non-ski day given over to the city's Olympic ruins. It suits confident intermediates who care more about atmosphere and value than vertical, and anyone who wants a European ski week for half the Alpine price.

itinerary.title: Land at Sarajevo, Baščaršija, and up to the mountain
itinerary.morning: Fly into SJJ, which sits in the Butmir plain ten minutes from the city. Collect a hire car if you have booked one — it is worth it here, because the two mountains are on opposite sides of Sarajevo and the bus schedule is thin. Change a little money: Bosnia uses the **konvertibilna marka (BAM/KM)**, pegged at 1.95583 to the euro.
itinerary.afternoon: Do not go straight to the snow. Spend three hours in **Baščaršija**, the Ottoman quarter — the **Sebilj** fountain, the **Gazi Husrev-beg mosque**, the coppersmiths of Kazandžiluk — and eat ćevapi standing up at **Ćevabdžinica Željo**. Then drive the 30 km up to Jahorina, a climb of some 900 m on a road that is properly winter-maintained but needs winter tyres.
itinerary.evening: Check in, collect hire gear from one of the shops on the Jahorina hotel road, and eat at **Koliba** at Hotel Termag — the best-executed traditional cooking on the mountain, in a stone-and-timber room.
itinerary.dayStats: SJJ to Jahorina 30 km / 45–60 min / climb from 500 m to 1,300 m / hire gear 120–200 BAM for six days / keycard deposit 10 BAM

itinerary.title: Poljice gondola, Skočine, and the width of Jahorina
itinerary.morning: Buy the **6-day Jahorina pass** at the Poljice window and ride the **Poljice 10-person gondola** up onto the ridge before 09:30. Warm up on the wide blues off Ogorjelica — Jahorina's pistes are unusually broad, which makes it a forgiving place to find your rhythm after a travel day.
itinerary.afternoon: Move west onto the **Skočine six-seater** and lap the long north-facing reds beneath it. These are the resort's best-preserved snow and its longest continuous descents; three or four laps here is a real day's skiing.
itinerary.evening: **Ski Bar Cassiopeia** at the Termag for the après hour, then dinner at **Restoran Vučko** in the hotel of the same name.
itinerary.dayStats: Jahorina 1,300–1,916 m / roughly 52 km of piste, 18 lifts / 6-day pass 316–373 BAM adult, 230–287 BAM child / lifts 09:00–16:00

itinerary.title: The Olympic run, Rajska Dolina, and skiing under lights
itinerary.morning: Ski the **Olimpijska staza** — the 1984 women's Olympic course — early, on the overnight groom, when the pitch is honest and the traffic is not. Then drop into **Rajska Dolina**, the sheltered eastern gully, and lap it; on a windy day this is where the whole mountain ends up, so take it first.
itinerary.afternoon: Lunch at **Rajska Vrata**, the timber hut restaurant at the foot of the Rajska Dolina lift and the most-photographed building on the mountain — order the beans with smoked meat and the somun bread. Ski until 16:00, then rest deliberately, because the evening is the point.
itinerary.evening: **Night skiing.** Jahorina runs the largest floodlit operation in the region — a session ticket is 58–69 BAM, a two-night pass 99–117 BAM, and the surface at −8°C under lights is usually the best of the whole day. Eat late at **Restoran Poljice** or back at the hotel.
itinerary.dayStats: Olympic run vertical roughly 400 m / night ski session 58–69 BAM (€30–€35) / floodlit hours typically 19:00–22:00 / two-night pass 99–117 BAM

itinerary.title: Cross to Bjelašnica: Babin Do and the men's downhill
itinerary.morning: Drive down through Sarajevo and up the other side — around 60 km and 75–90 minutes door to door, or take the ski bus for a 10 BAM supplement. Buy a **Bjelašnica day ticket, 59 BAM adult / 47 BAM teen / 42 BAM child**, at **Babin Do**, and ride to the 2,067 m summit ridge.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the **1984 men's downhill and slalom lines**. Bjelašnica is a colder, more exposed, more serious mountain than Jahorina, with less width and more consequence; if the wind is up, the top lifts will be on hold and you will spend the day in the lower half. Look across the plateau toward **Trnovo** and **Šator**, the newer lift development on this side.
itinerary.evening: Eat on the mountain at **Restoran Benetton** at Babin Do before driving back, or drop into Sarajevo and go to **Dveri** on Prote Bakovića for Bosnian home cooking in a room the size of a wine cellar.
itinerary.dayStats: Bjelašnica 1,266–2,067 m / day ticket 59 BAM (€30) adult / Jahorina–Bjelašnica by road 60 km, 75–90 min / no ski link between the two mountains

itinerary.title: Weather-contingency and rest day: Trebević, the bobsleigh track and the city
itinerary.morning: This is the designed flex day — take it early if a Dinaric low is dumping wet snow and closing the Jahorina road, otherwise take it here. Drive or bus into Sarajevo, leave the car, and ride the **Trebević cable car** from Bistrik: nine minutes and roughly 600 m of ascent to 1,164 m.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk fifteen minutes from the top station to the **abandoned 1984 bobsleigh and luge track** — a graffiti-covered concrete run through the pines that was used as an artillery position during the siege. Then descend and do the **Tunel spasa (Tunnel of Hope) Museum** at Butmir, which explains how the city survived. Finish with a steam at the restored **Isa-Begov Hamam**.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **Inat Kuća** ("the House of Spite") across the river from the City Hall, then rakija at **Barhana** in the old town.
itinerary.dayStats: Trebević cable car roughly 9 min, base 583 m to 1,164 m / bobsleigh track free and unfenced / zero vertical metres skied / Tunnel Museum entry ~10 BAM

itinerary.title: Snowshoe to Lukomir, the highest village in Bosnia
itinerary.morning: Meet a guide — **Green Visions** is the established operator for this — and drive round to the Bjelašnica plateau, parking at or above **Umoljani**. Fit snowshoes and set off across the plateau. This is open, wind-blasted, treeless karst at 1,400–1,600 m and it does not forgive poor navigation.
itinerary.afternoon: Reach **Lukomir**, at roughly 1,495 m the highest permanently inhabited village in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a cluster of stone houses with stećci tombstones on the rim of the **Rakitnica canyon**, 800 m deep. In deep winter the village is largely empty and reached only on foot; the point is the walk and the emptiness, not a café.
itinerary.evening: Back down to Sarajevo. Eat at **4 Sobe Gospođe Safije** for something more ambitious, or **Kod Bibana** on the hillside above Vratnik for the view over the whole basin at dusk.
itinerary.dayStats: 12–16 km round trip on snowshoes / 5–7 hours moving / plateau 1,400–1,600 m / guided day roughly 120–200 BAM per person in a group / no EAWS avalanche bulletin — guide strongly advised

itinerary.title: A last morning on Jahorina, then out
itinerary.morning: Ski the Skočine side until midday on the last day of your six-day pass — the mountain is emptiest on a Sunday morning before the Sarajevo day-trippers arrive around 10:30. Return hire gear and reclaim the 10 BAM keycard deposit.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop into Sarajevo, eat a final burek standing up at **Buregdžinica Sač** on Bravadžiluk, and spend the last hour in the Baščaršija buying coffee and a džezva. Allow 60 minutes to SJJ with luggage.
itinerary.evening: Fly out. If your flight is early, sleep in the city rather than on the mountain — the Jahorina road at 05:00 in fresh snow is not a race you want to run.
itinerary.dayStats: Half-day skiing, roughly 1,500–2,000 m descent / keycard refund 10 BAM / Jahorina to SJJ 45–60 min / airport check-in 2 h for regional flights
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Colors Inn, Sarajevo (if overnighting before an early flight)

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Termag
accommodationStrategy.description: Stone, timber and sheepskin, a proper ski room, a spa, and **Koliba**, the mountain's benchmark kitchen. On the hotel road with quick shuttle access to Poljice and Rajska Dolina; half board matters because Jahorina has no real village and no supermarket. Roughly 130–200 BAM (€66–€102) pppn half board.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Bistrica
accommodationStrategy.description: The 1984 Games hotel, refurbished, still the biggest bed-block on the mountain and sitting at the Rajska Dolina base. Choose it for ski-in/ski-out and Olympic-legacy atmosphere rather than finesse — the practical family and group option. Roughly 90–150 BAM (€46–€77) pppn.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Colors Inn
accommodationStrategy.description: The counter-strategy: sleep in the city, ten minutes from Baščaršija, and drive to whichever mountain has the better snow. Halves the bed cost, doubles the food quality, makes the Trebević and Tunnel days trivial — at 45–90 minutes each way and no ski-in/ski-out. Roughly €55–€90 per room.

logistics.connectivity: Good on the pistes, patchy on the Bjelašnica plateau. Bosnia sits **outside EU roaming**, so EU and UK bundles do not apply — though the **Western Balkans "Roam like at home" agreement** and the 2023 EU–WB6 roaming reduction have cut charges sharply. Check your operator's zone before you land or buy a BH Telecom or m:tel prepaid SIM. Download offline maps: the plateau has dead ground.
logistics.emergency: **112** works; **124** is the ambulance. Mountain rescue is the volunteer **Gorska služba spašavanja (GSS)**, organised separately in the Federation and Republika Srpska, and helicopter recovery is not routine — assume a long ground evacuation. Bosnia is **not in the EU**, so EHIC/GHIC does not apply: carry insurance naming winter sports, off-piste and repatriation, and check that night skiing is not excluded.
logistics.weather: The Dinarics turn Adriatic lows into very heavy, wet snowfalls — 40–60 cm overnight is unremarkable, and the **jugo** that brings it can lift the freezing level above 1,500 m and ruin Jahorina's lower half in twelve hours. Behind it comes the **bura**, which puts Bjelašnica's summit lifts on wind hold. Sarajevo sits in a basin that traps a **severe winter inversion** — the city at −5°C under smog while Jahorina is at +2°C in sun.
logistics.bookingWindows: Jahorina beds for Orthodox Christmas and New Year (roughly 1–10 January) go three to four months out at double price; February half-term is the second crunch. Lift tickets need no advance purchase. The **Lukomir snowshoe day must be booked a week ahead** — it runs on demand. Trebević takes no reservations but queues on sunny weekends.
logistics.money: The **konvertibilna marka (BAM/KM)**, pegged at **1 EUR = 1.95583 BAM**. Cards work in hotels and larger restaurants; huts, the ski bus, taxis and Lukomir are cash. Jahorina ATMs run dry at weekends — draw in Sarajevo. Tip by rounding up to 10%.
logistics.transportRules: **Winter tyres are legally required from 1 November to 15 April**, with chains carried on mountain routes; verify the hire car is equipped. There is no vignette — A1 tolls are per section. Crossing into Croatia, Montenegro or Serbia needs the **green card** and written cross-border permission. Lift access is RFID keycard: 10 BAM deposit at Jahorina, 5 BAM token at Bjelašnica.
logistics.permits: No park entry fee. Bjelašnica parking is 2 BAM per started hour, 10 BAM daily. Drones need civil-aviation permission and are banned over the ski areas. **Landmine contamination remains a real hazard in parts of the Bjelašnica and Igman uplands** — BHMAC maps the residual risk; stay on marked pistes, marked routes and roads.
logistics.health: Sarajevo tap water is potable and good. There is **no daily five-point EAWS avalanche bulletin for Bosnia and Herzegovina** — FHMZBiH and RHMZ RS publish snow and weather data only, so treat all off-piste as unbulletined and carry transceiver, shovel and probe. Altitude is a non-issue at 2,067 m.

proTips: Buy the flexible **10-day combined Ski Card** rather than a six-day Jahorina pass if you intend to ski both mountains. It is valid non-consecutively across Jahorina, Bjelašnica, Ravna planina and Vlašić, which means you can chase snow between mountains instead of committing to one on day one.

Ski Jahorina on a weekday and Bjelašnica at the weekend, not the other way round. Jahorina takes the Sarajevo and Belgrade weekend crowd; Bjelašnica's weekend traffic is smaller and its lift queues barely exist.

Take the night-ski session seriously. At 19:00 in February the piste has refrozen into a fast, grippy surface that is better than anything you skied at midday, and the ticket is a third of a day pass.
Sleep in Sarajevo for the first two nights and on the mountain for the last four. You get the city's food and museums when your legs are fresh, and ski-in access when they are not.
Draw cash in Sarajevo before you drive up. Jahorina's ATMs are few and are routinely empty from Friday evening; the mountain huts, the ski bus and Lukomir are cash-only.
Walk to the bobsleigh track from the top of the Trebević cable car rather than driving the Trebević road. The road is often unploughed above the tree line and the walk is fifteen easy minutes.

Book English-language ski instruction in writing, ahead of time. Lessons here are extraordinarily cheap — 40–70 BAM an hour private — but the default working language is Bosnian/Serbian and turning up at the desk on the day rarely produces an English-speaking instructor in February.
Never leave marked ground on the Bjelašnica and Igman plateau without a local guide. This is landmine country as well as unbulletined avalanche terrain, and the two hazards compound.
Eat the mountain lunch at **Rajska Vrata** at 11:30 or 14:00, never at 12:30. It has perhaps sixty covers and everyone on Jahorina wants one of them.

raw.Pass tiers by name: Three products, not one system. **Jahorina (Olympic Centre Jahorina)** sells a resort ticket: **73–86 BAM adult/day (€37–€44)**, **53–73 BAM child (€27–€37)**, sliding across Pre/Post, Mid and Peak bands (peak roughly 22 Dec–15 Jan and 9–27 Feb). **6-day adult 316–373 BAM (€162–€191)**, **6-day child 230–287 BAM (€118–€147)**. **Bjelašnica–Igman (OC Bjelašnica)** is separate: **59 BAM adult (€30)**, **47 BAM teen 13–18 (€24)**, **42 BAM child under 12 (€21)**; Igman alone **30 BAM (€15)**. The regional super-pass is the **combined Ski Card**, a flexible **10-day ticket, most recently 350 BAM (~€179)**, usable non-consecutively across **Jahorina, Bjelašnica, Ravna planina and Vlašić** — over 100 km on one card. **Night skiing** is separate: Jahorina **58–69 BAM** a session, **99–117 BAM** for two nights; Bjelašnica **42 BAM**. **Keycard deposit 10 BAM at Jahorina, a 5 BAM token at Bjelašnica.** Buy at the Poljice and Rajska Dolina windows, at Babin Do, or online — no dynamic pricing and no early-bird on multi-day tickets, only autumn season-pass presale.
raw.Lift network and interconnects: Jahorina's spine runs from **Poljice** at roughly 1,300 m, where the **Poljice 10-person gondola** does the heavy lifting, up to the Ogorjelica ridge. The **Skočine six-seater** serves the long, wide, north-facing runs on the western flank; the **Rajska Dolina** ("Paradise Valley") chair works the sheltered eastern gully, the tree-protected option on a windy day; and the **Olimpijska** lift feeds the **Olympic run**, the 1984 women's course. Poljice, Rajska Dolina and Skočine are the three ticket-and-parking bases and interconnect on snow — roughly 52 km over 20-odd runs without touching a road. **Bjelašnica is a separate mountain with no ski link to Jahorina**: lifts climb from **Babin Do at 1,266 m** to the 2,067 m ridge, the men's 1984 downhill and slalom still in use, connecting across the plateau toward the **Igman** nordic area at Veliko and Malo Polje. **Trnovo** and **Šator** are the newer lift development on that side. **Last lifts 16:00**; the gap between mountains is patched by road only — **ski bus supplement 10 BAM**, with daily Sarajevo services to both.
raw.Snow reliability: Jahorina spans **1,300–1,916 m**, Bjelašnica **1,266–2,067 m**. Both sit in a continental Dinaric snow climate that produces genuinely heavy falls — this is one of the snowiest parts of Europe by annual total — but at low altitude and on a mountain whose upper dome is largely treeless. Jahorina's Rajska Dolina and Skočine sides face broadly north and east and hold; the Poljice base is the first thing to go. Both resorts run substantial snowmaking on the main descents, with Jahorina claiming near-full coverage of its principal pistes, but **no resort publishes snowmaking as a percentage of pisted kilometres — treat any figure you are quoted as marketing**. **Season: roughly 5 December to mid-April**, with the honest window mid-January to mid-March. In a bad snow year Jahorina retreats to Rajska Dolina and the upper Skočine runs and closes the ski-home to Poljice, sending you down in the gondola; Bjelašnica, higher and colder, usually keeps its summit runs when Jahorina's lower half has gone.
raw.Off-piste and touring: The serious ground is on Bjelašnica. The classic is the **plateau tour from Babin Do toward Šehitluci and the Studeni Potok drainage**, and the longer traverse to **Umoljani** and the rim of the **Rakitnica canyon**. Jahorina's off-piste is short tree skiing between the Skočine and Rajska Dolina pistes. **Critically, Bosnia and Herzegovina publishes no EAWS-standard daily avalanche bulletin.** The **Federalni hidrometeorološki zavod BiH (FHMZBiH)** and the **Republički hidrometeorološki zavod RS** give weather and snow-depth data, not a five-point hazard rating — read the snowpack yourself or hire someone who can. There is also **residual landmine risk around both massifs**: stay on marked ground and treat BHMAC hazard mapping as non-negotiable. **Guides: Green Visions**, the Sarajevo ecotourism operator, is the established outfit for Bjelašnica plateau snowshoe and touring days and for Lukomir; **Gorska služba spašavanja (GSS)** is mountain rescue.
raw.Piste breakdown: **Jahorina: roughly 52 km over 20 runs — about 25 km easy (48%), 24 km intermediate (46%), 3 km difficult (6%)**, plus 18 lifts. **Bjelašnica and Igman together add roughly 20 km** of steeper, more exposed terrain including the Olympic men's downhill. **Beginners** belong on the Poljice plateau and the wide lower half of the Skočine runs, where the pitch is gentle and the pistes are absurdly wide by Alpine standards. **Intermediates** own Jahorina outright: the Skočine reds and the full-width cruising off the Ogorjelica ridge are what this mountain does best. **Experts** get two things and should not expect a third — the **1984 Olympic run at Jahorina**, still a proper pitch, and the men's downhill line on Bjelašnica, which on a firm morning is the most serious piste in the country.
raw.Non-ski days: The **Trebević cable car** climbs from Bistrik in about nine minutes to 1,164 m; fifteen minutes' walk from the top station is the **abandoned 1984 bobsleigh and luge track**, a graffitied concrete serpent used as a wartime firing position — free, unfenced, affecting. In the city: the **Tunel spasa (Tunnel of Hope) Museum** at Butmir, the **Gazi Husrev-beg mosque and bezistan**, the **Historical Museum of BiH** siege exhibition, the **Svrzo House**. On the mountain: the **guided snowshoe traverse to Lukomir** (~1,495 m, the country's highest inhabited village) from Umoljani, and Jahorina's **tubing and Alpine Coaster** at Poljice. For warm water, **Terme Ilidža** west of the city and the restored **Isa-Begov Hamam** in the old town.
raw.Hire, lockers and schools: This is the cheapest instruction in ski Europe. Rental at the Poljice and Rajska Dolina bases and from the shops along the Jahorina hotel road runs roughly **25–40 BAM/day (€13–€20)** for a standard ski-boot-pole package, **120–200 BAM (€61–€102) for six days**; performance skis add 40–60%. Lockers at the base stations are 5–10 BAM/day. The **OC Jahorina ski school** and the independent schools attached to the larger hotels charge in the region of **40–70 BAM (€20–€36) per hour for a private lesson** and **150–260 BAM (€77–€133) for a five-morning group course** — roughly a third of Austrian rates. Book English-language instruction ahead; it exists but is not the default.

typeSpecific.liftNetwork: Three products, not one system. **Jahorina (Olympic Centre Jahorina)** sells a resort ticket: **73–86 BAM adult/day (€37–€44)**, **53–73 BAM child (€27–€37)**, sliding across Pre/Post, Mid and Peak bands (peak roughly 22 Dec–15 Jan and 9–27 Feb). **6-day adult 316–373 BAM (€162–€191)**, **6-day child 230–287 BAM (€118–€147)**. **Bjelašnica–Igman (OC Bjelašnica)** is separate: **59 BAM adult (€30)**, **47 BAM teen 13–18 (€24)**, **42 BAM child under 12 (€21)**; Igman alone **30 BAM (€15)**. The regional super-pass is the **combined Ski Card**, a flexible **10-day ticket, most recently 350 BAM (~€179)**, usable non-consecutively across **Jahorina, Bjelašnica, Ravna planina and Vlašić** — over 100 km on one card. **Night skiing** is separate: Jahorina **58–69 BAM** a session, **99–117 BAM** for two nights; Bjelašnica **42 BAM**. **Keycard deposit 10 BAM at Jahorina, a 5 BAM token at Bjelašnica.** Buy at the Poljice and Rajska Dolina windows, at Babin Do, or online — no dynamic pricing and no early-bird on multi-day tickets, only autumn season-pass presale.
typeSpecific.snowReliability: Jahorina spans **1,300–1,916 m**, Bjelašnica **1,266–2,067 m**. Both sit in a continental Dinaric snow climate that produces genuinely heavy falls — this is one of the snowiest parts of Europe by annual total — but at low altitude and on a mountain whose upper dome is largely treeless. Jahorina's Rajska Dolina and Skočine sides face broadly north and east and hold; the Poljice base is the first thing to go. Both resorts run substantial snowmaking on the main descents, with Jahorina claiming near-full coverage of its principal pistes, but **no resort publishes snowmaking as a percentage of pisted kilometres — treat any figure you are quoted as marketing**. **Season: roughly 5 December to mid-April**, with the honest window mid-January to mid-March. In a bad snow year Jahorina retreats to Rajska Dolina and the upper Skočine runs and closes the ski-home to Poljice, sending you down in the gondola; Bjelašnica, higher and colder, usually keeps its summit runs when Jahorina's lower half has gone.

sources.verified: OC Jahorina's published Winter 2025/26 pricelist in BAM (1-day adult 73–86, child 53–73; 6-day adult 316–373, child 230–287; night 58–69, two-night 99–117; keycard deposit 10, replacement 10; Pre/Mid/Peak bands with peak 22 Dec–15 Jan and 9–27 Feb). OC Bjelašnica's announced 2025/26 daily rates (59 adult, 47 teen 13–18, 42 child under 12, 42 night; season pass 960 with 580/535 autumn presale; Igman 30). Bjelašnica parking 2 BAM/hour and 10 BAM daily, 10 BAM bus supplement, 5 BAM token, 20 BAM season-pass replacement. The joint Jahorina–Bjelašnica–Ravna planina–Vlašić flexible 10-day Ski Card at 350 BAM over 100+ km. Jahorina's profile: 1,300–1,890/1,916 m, roughly 52 km at 48% easy / 46% intermediate / 6% difficult, 18 lifts, floodlit night skiing, 1984 women's alpine venue, Pale II 10-person gondola listed as a future addition. The BAM peg at 1.95583.

Bjelašnica's altitude range (1,266–2,067 m) and the km attributed to Bjelašnica plus Igman are indicative.
