trips.title: Hautes Fagnes Cross-Country — and the Honest Plan B

bestPeriod.note: Snow cover reliable enough for cross-country grooming is not guaranteed most winters: build this trip expecting a good chance of little or no skiable snow.

trips.gatewayAirport: Liège (LGG)
trips.summary: A week based at Malmedy for Hautes Fagnes cross-country skiing when snow allows, with a genuine bad-snow plan built around winter hiking, Spa and Liège.
trips.hook: This is a snow-sports trip written for the winter you will probably get, not the one on the brochure. The Hautes Fagnes plateau is Belgium's coldest, highest ground, and in a properly cold winter it holds a genuine cross-country base at Ovifat and Elsenborn. Most winters, it does not — or it holds one for a matter of days. This itinerary skis when there is snow, walks the same landscape on boardwalks when there is not, and spends two full days on Spa and Liège so the week works either way.

snapshot.Base(s): Malmedy (7 nights)
snapshot.Best Period: January–February; snow depth is never guaranteed
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Plateau at 550–694 m; groomed loipe (when present) 5–15 km at Ovifat/Elsenborn
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Liège (LGG) or Brussels (BRU); rail to Liège then a rental car for the plateau
snapshot.Who It Suits: Skiers who accept the odds honestly, and anyone who wants a slower, fog-and-heather winter week regardless of snow

itinerary.title: Arrival and the snow report
itinerary.morning: Fly into Liège or Brussels and pick up a rental car; the Hautes Fagnes plateau has no rail access and only a limited seasonal weekend bus, so a car is the honest requirement for this trip. Drive to Malmedy, a compact Ardennes town with a good base for both the plateau and the day trips ahead.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive up to the Centre Nature de Botrange, the reserve's visitor centre near the Signal de Botrange (694 m, the highest point in Belgium), and check the actual snow depth and grooming status at the desk — this single stop determines how the rest of the week gets weighted between skis and boots.
itinerary.evening: Settle into Malmedy; the old town's arcaded streets and its cathedral are worth a first-evening wander regardless of what the snow report said.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 8 km on foot, plateau orientation only · 0 m elevation gain of consequence · no lift or trail infrastructure involved.

itinerary.title: Ovifat and Ferme Libert, snow permitting
itinerary.morning: If the Centre Nature reported a workable base — in practice at least 15–20 cm of settled snow, which the plateau's exposed, wind-scoured terrain does not hold reliably even when it falls — head to Ferme Libert at Ovifat, the long-established cross-country centre that grooms loipe on the plateau's western flank and rents classic and skate skis on-site. If there is no base, skip to the boardwalk alternative and treat this as a hiking day instead.
itinerary.afternoon: On a good-snow day, Ferme Libert's groomed loops run through open heath and spruce plantation, 2–5 km circuits linking into a longer network in a strong year; there is no lift infrastructure at all — flat, gently rolling classic and skate terrain, and the "interconnect" that matters is simply how far the grooming machine has reached that week, which shrinks fast after a thaw. On a no-snow day, walk the boardwalked Sentier des Fagnes from the Baraque Michel car park instead, a raised timber walkway built because hikers used to get lost and, in a few historic cases, die of exposure crossing the open bog in fog. The walk passes close to the Croix des Fiancés, a memorial cross marking one such 19th-century death, a sober but real waypoint.
itinerary.evening: Either way, dinner in Malmedy; the town's brasseries lean toward hearty Ardennes cooking — game, boudin, and local beer — which suits a cold day outdoors.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 8–12 km skied or walked · Ovifat sector or Sentier des Fagnes boardwalk · half-day.

itinerary.title: Signal de Botrange and a guided fen crossing
itinerary.morning: Some zones of the Hautes Fagnes Nature Reserve — including parts of the Fagne de la Poleur and Fagne des Deux Séries — are closed to unaccompanied visitors and open only with an authorised reserve guide, a genuine legal protection for the peat bog habitat rather than a marketing device. Book a guided walk through the Centre Nature de Botrange, which runs regular ranger-led crossings into these normally closed sections.
itinerary.afternoon: The guided route, on skis if there is a base or on foot with gaiters if not, covers ground most visitors never see: open sphagnum bog, dwarf pine, and — in a real winter — rime-iced heather that looks genuinely arctic for a country at 50°N and under 700 m.
itinerary.evening: Return to Malmedy; an early night, since day trips start tomorrow.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 10 km guided route · restricted-access reserve zones · half-day, guide-led.

itinerary.title: Spa
itinerary.morning: Drive the 45 minutes to Spa, the town that gave the word "spa" to the world. The Thermes de Spa, a modern thermal bathing complex fed by the same mineral springs Peter the Great and generations of European aristocracy came for, is the day's anchor — book a half-day pass in advance for the busier weekend slots.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the town's historic Pouhon Pierre-le-Grand pavilion, where you can still taste the sparkling ferruginous spring water for free, and browse the belle-époque Casino quarter.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Spa or back in Malmedy; either works, since the drive is short.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 3 km walked in town · thermal bathing, no elevation of note · full day.

itinerary.title: Liège
itinerary.morning: Drive or take the connecting train from a nearby station to Liège, the region's real city, for a full day away from the plateau. Start in the old town around the Place Saint-Lambert and the Curtius museum quarter.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb (or ride the lift on) the Montagne de Bueren, the 374-step stair up to the citadel, then cross to La Boverie on its river island for contemporary art, or spend the afternoon in the Outremeuse district's market streets instead.
itinerary.evening: Liège's food scene — boulets à la liégeoise, the Sunday-market energy even on a weekday, and a proper Belgian beer bar — makes this the week's best dinner night.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 8–10 km walked, city terrain · no plateau activity · full day.

itinerary.title: Elsenborn and the second snow window
itinerary.morning: Return to the plateau and try the Elsenborn side, near the military training area of the same name, which has its own groomed loipe network on the years when conditions allow — a genuine second chance if the Ovifat side melted out mid-week or was never skiable to begin with.
itinerary.afternoon: On a good-snow day, ski the Elsenborn loops, generally quieter than Ovifat since they sit slightly further from the main visitor routes. On a no-snow day, drive the 25 minutes to Robertville and walk the shoreline of the Lac de Robertville, a reservoir lake with a forested loop path — a gentler, lower-altitude contrast to the open plateau, and a fair substitute activity that still uses the same base.
itinerary.evening: A last dinner in Malmedy.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 10 km skied or walked · Elsenborn sector or Lac de Robertville · half-day.

itinerary.title: Baraque Michel and departure
itinerary.morning: A final short walk or ski from Baraque Michel — the plateau's historic crossroads inn and the trailhead for most of the marked routes — before returning the car.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive back to Liège or Brussels for the flight home, allowing extra time in winter for potential fog on the plateau roads themselves.
itinerary.evening: Flight home.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 5 km, plateau finale · Baraque Michel sector · half-day.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Le Grand Bau
accommodationStrategy.description: A central Malmedy hotel within easy driving distance of both the plateau (20 minutes) and the day-trip roads to Spa and Liège, with secure parking that matters for a car-dependent week.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Baraque Michel
accommodationStrategy.description: A working inn at the plateau's main crossroads since the 19th century, useful for one night if you want to be on-site for an early guided crossing rather than driving up each morning.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two to three weeks ahead; rooms are limited.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €80–€120 per night for two, often half board

accommodationStrategy.name: Chalet or gîte near Ovifat
accommodationStrategy.description: A short walk from the Ferme Libert cross-country base, useful if the snow report looks promising and you want to be first on the grooming each morning.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two weeks ahead in a confirmed-snow week; further ahead is a gamble given the forecast uncertainty.

logistics.connectivity: Reasonable in Malmedy and Spa; patchy on the open plateau, which matters for fog navigation — carry a paper map of the marked routes, not just a phone.
logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European, the correct number for both police and rescue on the plateau; there is no dedicated alpine rescue service, but local fire and civil protection teams know the fen terrain well.
logistics.weather: The plateau's fog can close in within minutes and is the area's real hazard, historically more dangerous than any snow or cold on its own — stay on marked boardwalks, and treat reserve-guide advice on closures as final.
logistics.bookingWindows: Guided restricted-zone walks should be booked at least a week ahead; Thermes de Spa slots a few days ahead for weekends.
logistics.money: Cards standard everywhere; small huts and the Baraque Michel inn take cards too.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 pan-European, the correct number for both police and rescue on the plateau; there is no dedicated alpine rescue service, but local fire and civil protection teams know the fen terrain well.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Ferme Libert's rental desk and the Centre Nature de Botrange keep shorter winter weekday hours — check before driving up.

other.label: Reserve access rule
other.text: Some sections of the reserve are legally closed to unaccompanied entry to protect the peat bog; this is enforced, and the guided-walk booking is the only legitimate way in.

proTips: Check the Centre Nature de Botrange's snow report the evening before deciding each day's plan, not once at the start of the week — plateau conditions change fast.
If snow does arrive, ski Ovifat in the morning before any afternoon thaw softens the base, which happens quickly at this altitude and latitude.
Book the Thermes de Spa for a weekday afternoon; weekends draw crowds from both Liège and the Ardennes.
Treat the Liège day as fixed regardless of snow — it is the week's strongest single day either way, and planning it independent of the forecast removes one variable.
The Sentier des Fagnes boardwalk is worth doing even in a good snow year: it reaches ground the ski loops do not.
Pack for both scenarios from day one rather than deciding gear at the airport; hedging halfway through the week wastes a day.

raw.Who It Suits: Skiers who accept the odds honestly, and anyone who wants a slower, fog-and-heather winter week regardless of snow

typeSpecific.surface: Plateau at 550–694 m; groomed loipe (when present) 5–15 km at Ovifat/Elsenborn
typeSpecific.audience: Skiers who accept the odds honestly, and anyone who wants a slower, fog-and-heather winter week regardless of snow

packingNotes: Waterproof hiking boots and gaiters — the bog terrain is wet underfoot even without snow.
Cross-country ski layers (breathable base and mid-layer) in case a base materialises; rental skis are available at Ferme Libert.
A compass or offline GPS track for the marked routes, given the fog risk.
A proper windproof shell — the open plateau has little shelter and Belgium's strongest winter winds.
Swimwear for the Thermes de Spa.
Comfortable city shoes for the Liège day, separate from the plateau boots.
whatCouldGoWrong: **No snow arrives all week.** Fallback: this itinerary already assumes it — the boardwalk hikes, guided fen crossing, Spa and Liège days carry the week on their own.
**Fog closes the plateau on a planned walk day.** Fallback: swap in the Spa or Liège day early, and wait for a clearer window later in the week.
**A brief snowfall melts within 48 hours.** Fallback: ski the first available morning rather than waiting — at this altitude, the first clear morning after a fall is often the only skiable window.
**Rental stock runs low on a rare good-snow weekend.** Fallback: Elsenborn's smaller rental point, or book Ovifat a day ahead by phone once the snow report turns positive.

trips.title: Bansko: Seven Days Under Todorka, Gondola Queue Included
trips.subRegion: The Pirin, Blagoevgrad province — Bansko, Bunderishka Polyana and Dobrinishte

bestPeriod.window: mid-January to mid-March — cold, settled snow on the north-facing upper mountain
bestPeriod.avoid: 27 December–6 January (peak tariff, two-hour gondola queues) and after mid-April (lifts closed)

accommodation.note: €280–€520 (€40–€75/night; apartment or 4-star with shuttle)

food.note: €145–€230 (€21–€33/day; mehana dinners run €12–€20 a head)

transport.note: €110–€180 (Sofia airport transfer ~€25–€35 each way, plus road shuttles and one day trip)

activities.note: €400–€520 (6-day lift pass €341, plus a guided touring day and equipment hire)

profile.difficultyNote: Moderate

trips.gatewayAirport: Sofia (SOF), 160 km north; road transfer 2 h 30–3 h via the E79 and Simitli. Bansko Express, the established airport shuttle, has published its **26 December 2026 – 22 March 2027** shared winter fares at **£25–£39 per person each way (roughly €29–€45)** depending on party size — cheapest at four or more, plus a £1 per person booking fee — and runs the shared service only for flights landing or leaving Sofia between 10:00 and 23:55. The public Sofia–Bansko coach is about **€17** and takes 2 h 45–3 h. Plovdiv (PDV) is 190 km east. The narrow-gauge Septemvri–Dobrinishte railway reaches Bansko slowly and beautifully, but not usefully with ski bags.
trips.currency: Euro (EUR) — sole legal tender since 1 February 2026; mandatory dual BGN display ended 8 August 2026
trips.summary: Bansko is the cheapest serious ski week in Europe and it makes you earn it. The whole mountain hangs off one gondola out of a town at 990 m, and at 08:30 in February that gondola has a queue you can see from three…
trips.hook: Bansko is the cheapest serious ski week in Europe and it makes you earn it. The whole mountain hangs off one gondola out of a town at 990 m, and at 08:30 in February that gondola has a queue you can see from three streets away. Beat it and you get north-facing snow, a 16 km run home, and a stone-built old town where dinner with wine costs less than a lift ticket in the Alps. Skiers who plan mornings win here.

snapshot.Start / End: Sofia → Bansko → Sofia (single base, no relocation)
snapshot.Getting there: Sofia (SOF), 160 km north; road transfer 2 h 30–3 h via the E79 and Simitli. Bansko Express, the established airport shuttle, has published its **26 December 2026 – 22 March 2027** shared winter fares at **£25–£39 per person each way (roughly €29–€45)** depending on party size — cheapest at four or more, plus a £1 per person booking fee — and runs the shared service only for flights landing or leaving Sofia between 10:00 and 23:55. The public Sofia–Bansko coach is about **€17** and takes 2 h 45–3 h. Plovdiv (PDV) is 190 km east. The narrow-gauge Septemvri–Dobrinishte railway reaches Bansko slowly and beautifully, but not usefully with ski bags.

itinerary.title: Arrival, Fitting, and the Old Town (walking only)
itinerary.morning: Sofia transfer down the E79 through Blagoevgrad and Simitli, then the climb east into the Pirin. Two and a half to three hours.
itinerary.afternoon: Hire skis in town rather than at the gondola — the shops on Pirin Street and around Nikola Vaptsarov Square fit faster and store gear overnight for a few euro.
itinerary.evening: Walk the old town: the 1835 **Sveta Troitsa** church and its heavy stone tower, **Velyanova Kashta** with its painted interiors, the Vaptsarov house-museum. Dinner at **Dedo Pene Inn** — bean soup, kavarma, sipped rakia.

itinerary.title: First Turns and the Queue Lesson (gondola, 990 → 2,560 m)
itinerary.morning: Be in the gondola line by **08:00**, not 08:30. In peak season the difference between those two times is 40 minutes to an hour.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the **Plato** area to find your legs, then take the Bunderitsa chairs to the top station under Todorka for the first big view over the Pirin ridge.
itinerary.evening: Ski the **Alberto Tomba** road back to town at around 15:45 when it empties, then eat at **Baryakova Mehana** — the courtyard grill in a 19th-century house off Pirin Street [VERIFY: current mehana opening hours].

itinerary.title: The Road Alternative and Balkaniada (2,560 → 1,635 m)
itinerary.morning: Skip the gondola entirely: take a **jeep-taxi or minibus up the 12 km mountain road** to Shiligarnika or Bunderishka Polyana, roughly €10–€15 per person, 25–35 minutes, and be on snow before the gondola's first cabins arrive [VERIFY: current road shuttle fares]. In heavy snowfall the road needs chains and can close.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the **Balkaniada** race piste repeatedly while the crowds are still queuing below, then the Todorka side for the steeper pitches.
itinerary.evening: **Come Prima** on Pirin Street for pizza and pasta when you have had enough grilled meat; it is the town's most consistently busy non-Bulgarian table.

itinerary.title: Ski Touring into the Pirin (900–1,100 m ascent on skins)
itinerary.morning: Meet your guide at Bunderishka Polyana and skin south into the **Bunderitsa valley** toward the Vihren massif — dwarf pine, then open bowls, then a summit or col depending on the avalanche bulletin.
itinerary.afternoon: Transceiver check, then descend. National park terrain: no infrastructure, no patrol, long carries if it goes wrong.
itinerary.evening: A quiet night. **Victoria** for a sit-down dinner, then the sauna at your hotel; tomorrow is a long day.

itinerary.title: Day Trip: Borovets or Dobrinishte
itinerary.morning: Two options, opposite characters. **Borovets** in the Rila, 130 km and about 2 h 15 by road, gives tree-lined pistes off the Yastrebets gondola and different snow entirely; the last published Borovets tariff is 2025/26, at **100 BGN (about €51)** for an adult day pass and 520 BGN (about €266) for six non-consecutive days, with 2026/27 prices not yet out. **Dobrinishte**, 6 km down the valley, is the cheap local alternative with almost no queue.
itinerary.afternoon: Whichever you chose, get back for the last hour of light. Dobrinishte makes this easy; Borovets does not.
itinerary.evening: Thermal soak at the Dobrinishte mineral baths if you went short, then dinner back in Bansko.
itinerary.dayStats: 130 km or 6 km

itinerary.title: The Full Vertical Day (1,570 m of lift-served descent)
itinerary.morning: Gondola at 08:00, straight to the top station, and lap the upper mountain while the mid-station crowds churn. Coffee at the Bunderishka Polyana huts, not at the base.
itinerary.afternoon: Work the **Plato → Shiligarnika → Balkaniada** circuit, then take the long way home: top station to town on the **Alberto Tomba** in one run, 16 km, ideally around 15:30.
itinerary.evening: Après on **Pirin Street** — this is the night for it. The mehanas run live folk music from about 20:00 and the tables fill from 19:30.

itinerary.title: Half Day and Out (gondola return €27)
itinerary.morning: A last three hours on the mountain, or the **gondola return ticket at €27 (52.81 BGN)** if you are done skiing but want the ridge view one more time.
itinerary.afternoon: Lunch, gear return, then the market street for lyutenitsa, banitsa for the road and a bottle of Melnik red from the Struma valley an hour west.
itinerary.evening: Transfer to Sofia. Allow three hours plus a buffer; the E79 through the Kresna gorge slows badly in bad weather.

accommodationStrategy.name: Kempinski Hotel Grand Arena
accommodationStrategy.description: effectively at the gondola station, which on this mountain is the most valuable thing money buys. Ski storage, boot dryers, spa, and you can watch the queue from the window before joining it.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–12 weeks ahead for February; longer for the New Year fortnight.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Perun Lodge
accommodationStrategy.description: 10 minutes' walk from the gondola, a reliable morning ski-bus, and a boot room that actually dries boots. Better value than the gondola-side hotels for a week.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead; check whether the shuttle runs to the road drop-off as well as the gondola [VERIFY: current hotel shuttle arrangements].

accommodationStrategy.name: Self-catering apartment in the Grand Manastira or Terra Complex quarter
accommodationStrategy.description: a kitchen, a washing machine and a supermarket 200 m away change the economics of a family week. Take one with ground-floor ski storage.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–8 weeks ahead; confirm heating is included in the rate, not metered.

logistics.connectivity: EU roaming applies. 4G/5G is good in town and along the gondola line, patchy in the Bunderitsa valley beyond the ski area — do not rely on a phone for touring navigation.
logistics.emergency: 112, which routes to mountain rescue (PSS). Carry transceiver, shovel and probe for anything off-piste, and note that the town clinic handles fractures but serious cases go to Blagoevgrad or Sofia. Check that your travel insurance covers off-piste skiing *with a guide* — many policies do not.
logistics.weather: Mediterranean-fed storms arrive from the southwest; 40–60 cm in 24 hours happens, and closes the mountain road before it closes the gondola. Wind holds on the upper chairs are common, and Plato keeps running when the top station does not.
logistics.bookingWindows: hotels 6–12 weeks for February half-term; ski hire on arrival is fine; guided touring 2–3 weeks; lift passes are bought on the spot, with no meaningful online discount [VERIFY: current online pass purchase options].
logistics.money: Bulgaria has adopted the euro, and lift prices are published in EUR alongside BGN at the fixed rate of 1.95583 BGN to €1. Cards are accepted at the lift office, hotels and most mehanas; carry some cash for jeep-taxis and small shops. Refuse dynamic currency conversion at terminals.
logistics.transportRules: winter tyres are compulsory on Bulgarian roads from **15 November to 1 March**, and the mountain road demands them plus chains after snowfall. A vignette is required on national roads — hire cars normally include it, transfers always do. Drink-driving limits are strictly enforced.
logistics.permits: no permit for skiing, but the zone abuts **Pirin National Park**, where camping, fires and off-trail vehicle access are restricted. Uphill skinning is tolerated at the piste edges — ask patrol, and never skin a groomed race slope in opening hours.

proTips: Use the **mountain road** at least twice. A €10–€15 jeep seat up to Shiligarnika buys back an hour of queue every time, and on a powder morning it is the difference between first tracks and third.
Ski down to the gondola mid-station at the end of the day rather than riding down. The 16 km **Alberto Tomba** run is nearly empty after 15:30 and it is the resort's best single piece of skiing.
Buy the **6-day pass, not six 1-day passes**: €341 against €354 at peak, and you skip the ticket window every morning.
Eat where the queue is Bulgarian. **Dedo Pene** and **Baryakova** are the old-town benchmarks; a full dinner with wine lands around €15–€20 a head, less than a mountain-restaurant lunch in the Alps.
If a storm shuts the top station, do not write the day off — head to **Dobrinishte**, 6 km away, which often keeps running when Bansko's upper lifts are wind-held.
Learn *"Едно кафе, моля"* (one coffee, please) and note the head-shake reversal: a nod can mean no, a shake can mean yes. It matters when you are asking whether a lift is open.
Take an afternoon off for the old town. Bansko is a working Bulgarian town of 18th- and 19th-century stone houses, not a purpose-built resort, and the museums are open when the queue is worst.

raw.Lift pass pricing (2025/26 tariff, publi: Season ran **1 December 2025 – 12 April 2026**. **Peak, 27 December – 31 March:** 1-day adult **€59 (115.39 BGN)**, child 7–11.99 **€30 (58.67 BGN)**; 6-day adult **€341 (666.94 BGN)**, child **€164 (320.76 BGN)**. **Spring, 1–12 April:** 1-day adult **€45 (88.01 BGN)**, child €20; 6-day adult **€259**, child €110. A **gondola return ticket is €27 (52.81 BGN)**, unchanged across the season — the pedestrian/non-skier option. Treat all of the above as 2025/26 rates: **as of early September 2026 Ulen has not published a 2026/27 tariff** — banskoski.com still shows only the 2025/26 table and the last early-bird season-pass promotion it ran was the December 2025 one — so budget on the figures above plus a single-digit percentage and re-check from about mid-November.
raw.Lift network and interconnects: Everything starts with the **Bansko gondola** from the edge of town (990 m) to **Bunderishka Polyana** (1,635 m), roughly 25 minutes. Above it the mountain splits into two linked bowls: the **Shiligarnika** side (chairlifts to the Plato area, around 1,700–2,000 m) and the **Bunderitsa** side climbing to the top station at **2,560 m** beneath **Todorka** peak (2,746 m). The **Balkaniada** race piste under Shiligarnika is the FIS slope; **Plato** is the wide intermediate playground; the **Alberto Tomba** run is the ski road home, about 16 km from the upper mountain to the gondola base — the longest continuous descent in the country and a genuine reason to ski until the light goes. The old **Chalin Valog** sector on the lower slopes is worth knowing only as a bad-weather fallback [VERIFY: current Chalin Valog lift operation].
raw.Snow reliability: The 990 m base is too low to hold snow — hence the gondola, and hence the heavy snowmaking on the lower ski road. Above 1,600 m the bowls are predominantly **north- and northeast-facing**, shaded through short days, with mid-winter temperatures at 2,000–2,500 m below freezing for weeks. Mid-January to mid-March is when the upper mountain skis like a proper alpine resort; April is corn on top, slush below.
raw.Off-piste, touring and guiding: Lift-served terrain is modest; the reason to bring skins is the **Pirin National Park**, a UNESCO site whose boundary sits immediately beyond the pistes. Objectives from Bunderishka Polyana run toward **Vihren** (2,914 m), the Bunderitsa valley huts and the Todorka ridgelines. Take a guide: convex, wind-loaded, lightly trafficked terrain with long rescue times. Bulgarian operators running Pirin ski touring and freeride include **Traventuria** and **Odysseia-In** out of Sofia, plus Bansko-based guides working through the ski schools [VERIFY: current Bansko-based guiding operators and day rates]. Mountain rescue is the Bulgarian Red Cross **Planinska Spasitelna Sluzhba (PSS)**; call 112 and ask for mountain rescue [VERIFY: current PSS direct number].
raw.The constraint nobody advertises: Bansko's ski zone is a concession bounded by the national park, so it cannot build its way out of the queue. Lift capacity has grown far more slowly than bed capacity, and that mismatch — not snow, not terrain — defines a week here.

trips.title: Engelberg-Titlis: The Laub, Steinberg and Galtiberg Descents

bestPeriod.note: The Titlis glacier holds snow all season; the Laub and Galtiberg exits lower down need a settled, well-bonded snowpack, best from late January.

trips.gatewayAirport: Zürich (ZRH)
trips.summary: A week of guided big-mountain freeride at Engelberg-Titlis, built around the Laub, Steinberg and Galtiberg descents and the single Rotair bottleneck that controls access to all of them.
trips.hook: Engelberg's off-piste reputation is built on a handful of genuinely serious descents off a genuinely serious glacier, and every one of them is reached through the same narrow gate: the Rotair, the world's first revolving cable car, running from Stand to the Titlis summit. This week is built around that bottleneck, the glacier hazard above it, and the guiding that makes the terrain safe to use.

snapshot.Base(s): Engelberg
snapshot.Best Period: January–March; late January onward for the lower off-piste exits to be properly filled in
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Engelberg-Titlis network plus the Brunni sector; base 1,050 m at Engelberg, top 3,020 m at Titlis
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Zürich (ZRH); direct train via Lucerne to Engelberg, roughly 1h30–1h45
snapshot.Who It Suits: Expert skiers and riders wanting guided glacier and big-mountain off-piste, comfortable with long, committing descents and variable exit terrain

itinerary.title: Arrival and gear check
itinerary.morning: Train from Zürich via Lucerne to Engelberg. Check into the base hotel and walk to a rental shop for skis or a splitboard, boots and a full avalanche kit — transceiver, probe, shovel.
itinerary.afternoon: Register with Outventure or a certified Bergführer for the week's guided glacier and off-piste days, and check the Titlis Xpress gondola and Rotair status for the coming days.
itinerary.evening: Read the Swiss avalanche bulletin (SLF) and plan the week's day order around the forecast.
itinerary.dayStats: 0 vertical metres skied · 0 sectors · 0 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Orientation: Trübsee and Jochpass
itinerary.morning: Ride the Titlis Xpress gondola from Engelberg to Trübsee (1,796 m), a scenic lake basin and the hub for the whole area. Ski the Trübsee and Jochpass sectors to read the group's form on genuinely varied terrain before the bigger days.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Stand and take a first, lighter look at the Rotair queue — this cable car to the Titlis summit is the area's single bottleneck, and getting a feel for its rhythm on a quieter day pays off later in the week.
itinerary.evening: Early dinner; tomorrow starts at opening.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,800 m vertical · 2 sectors (Trübsee, Jochpass) · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Titlis summit and the Laub
itinerary.morning: Be at the Titlis Xpress base by 08:00 to beat the Rotair queue, which builds fast once the day-tripper sightseeing crowd arrives — the Rotair serves both skiers and non-skiing visitors to the summit, and it is the one lift in the network with genuinely limited throughput.
itinerary.afternoon: With Outventure or a Bergführer, ski the Laub: a steep, north-facing off-piste descent from the upper mountain back down toward Trübsee, one of Engelberg's classic big-mountain lines and exposed enough — in avalanche terms and in consequence of a fall — to require a guide regardless of how confident the group feels.
itinerary.evening: Recovery dinner in the village.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,200 m vertical · 1 itinerary (the Laub) · 2.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Steinberg glacier descent
itinerary.morning: Back up through Trübsee and Stand to the Titlis summit via the Rotair. The upper Steinberg glacier basin below the summit station is crevassed and requires roped travel on the approach in most snow years — this is guide-mandatory terrain, not an optional extra.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the open Steinberg descent, a wide glacier bowl with sustained pitch, before the route funnels back toward the lift infrastructure at Stand or Trübsee.
itinerary.evening: Gear check; tomorrow is a lower-key sector day.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,000 m vertical · 1 itinerary (Steinberg) · 2.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Brunni: the sunny bad-snow plan B
itinerary.morning: Take the Brunni cable car from the south side of Engelberg village up to Brunni-Ristis and Klostermatte — a smaller, lower, south-facing sector, genuinely different terrain and microclimate from the glacier side, and the honest fallback when Titlis is wind-closed or the glacier snowpack has been declared unstable.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski Brunni's groomed and lightly off-piste terrain at a relaxed pace; it also serves as a legitimate rest day for legs worked hard by two consecutive big descents.
itinerary.evening: Village evening; Brunni's shorter lift hours mean an earlier finish than the Titlis side.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,800 m vertical · 1 sector (Brunni) · 3.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Galtiberg: the long exit
itinerary.morning: With the guide, ride back to the Titlis summit for the week's longest and most serious objective: the Galtiberg, a sustained, roughly 2,000 m descent down a remote side valley, ending well below the lift network in forest terrain that typically requires a walk-out to a road pickup point or the Engelberg-Stäfeli bus. This is a full-day commitment and is only run when the guide confirms conditions and group fitness support it.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue the descent through changing snow conditions — glacier, open bowl, then forest — with the guide managing route-finding and timing against the light.
itinerary.evening: Transport pickup and return to Engelberg; allow a late, unhurried dinner.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,000 m vertical · 1 itinerary (Galtiberg) · 2 lift hours plus a walk-out.

itinerary.title: Final morning and departure
itinerary.morning: A short, easy session on Trübsee or Brunni, whichever is skiing better, followed by gear return.
itinerary.afternoon: Train back to Zürich via Lucerne for the flight home.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,200 m vertical · 1 sector · 2 lift hours.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Terrace
accommodationStrategy.description: Close to both the Titlis Xpress base and the village centre, with ski storage and a drying room — practical given how early the Titlis-side days need to start to beat the Rotair queue.
accommodationStrategy.booking: eight weeks ahead for February.

accommodationStrategy.name: Ski Lodge Engelberg
accommodationStrategy.description: A smaller, more informal base popular with freeriders and guides, a short walk from the Titlis Xpress and well placed for an early Galtiberg-day departure.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Bänklialp
accommodationStrategy.description: Set slightly above the village with valley views and a slower pace, a good fit for the Brunni rest day and for anyone wanting distance from the Titlis-side crowds in the evening.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Switzerland's air rescue service Rega is 1414 — save it before any glacier or backcountry day.
logistics.weather: The Titlis summit and Rotair are wind-sensitive; check the resort's lift-status page each morning before committing to a glacier-side plan.
logistics.bookingWindows: Outventure and independent Bergführer availability tightens in February half-term and around Easter; book the Laub, Steinberg and Galtiberg days as soon as travel dates are fixed.
logistics.money: Switzerland uses the Swiss franc; cards are accepted almost everywhere, cash useful for smaller mountain huts.
logistics.health: The SLF's European 1–5 danger scale applies; transceiver, probe and shovel are mandatory for every off-piste day, and a rope is added by the guide for any crevassed glacier approach.

other.label: Pass tiers, approx. 2026
other.text: The whole-destination Engelberg-Titlis day pass, covering Trübsee, Stand and the Titlis summit via the Rotair, runs approx. CHF 85–100 (approx. €90–€105) for an adult under the resort's dynamic pricing model; the smaller Brunni/Klostermatte sector alone is considerably cheaper, roughly CHF 48–69 (approx. €50–€73) for a full day — worth knowing on the Day 5 fallback, when you may not need the full-price pass at all.

other.label: Engelberg-Titlis is not on the Magic Pass
other.text: Like most large, glacier-served resorts, it sells its own ticket independent of Switzerland's forty-plus-resort Magic Pass network.

other.label: Where the bottleneck actually is
other.text: Every route to the summit, the Laub, the Steinberg and the Galtiberg funnels through the Rotair, a single revolving cable car shared with non-skiing sightseers visiting the glacier attraction — arrive at opening on any Titlis-side day, since the queue compounds through the morning and does not meaningfully shorten until mid-afternoon.

proTips: Ride the first Titlis Xpress cabin of the day, every glacier-side day — the Rotair queue is driven as much by sightseers as by skiers, and it only gets longer after mid-morning.
Schedule the Laub and Steinberg earlier in the week and Brunni as the recovery day — both big descents are physically taxing and benefit from fresh legs.
Confirm the Galtiberg's exit transport (road pickup or the Stäfeli bus) with the guide the night before, not on the mountain — this route does not return to the lift network.
Use the Brunni pass, not the full destination pass, on the fallback day — no reason to pay for Rotair access you will not use.
Check the SLF bulletin before booking the Steinberg or Galtiberg — both cross genuinely crevassed or remote terrain and the guide will reorder the week around the forecast, not the itinerary.
Keep a spare unscheduled day loose if possible; Engelberg's best guided days are weather windows, not calendar dates.

typeSpecific.surface: Engelberg-Titlis network plus the Brunni sector; base 1,050 m at Engelberg, top 3,020 m at Titlis
typeSpecific.audience: Expert skiers and riders wanting guided glacier and big-mountain off-piste, comfortable with long, committing descents and variable exit terrain

packingNotes: Full avalanche kit: transceiver, probe, shovel, mandatory for every guided descent this week.
Wide freeride skis or a freeride splitboard; there is little reason to bring narrow piste skis for this trip.
A climbing harness may be requested by the guide for the Steinberg glacier approach — ask when booking.
A hardshell and warm midlayers; the Titlis summit at 3,020 m is routinely 15–20°C colder and windier than the village.
A day pack with room for skins (if the guide requests a short boot-pack or skin section) plus food and water for the long Galtiberg day.
Sturdy off-mountain boots for the Galtiberg's forest walk-out, which can be on unbroken snow.
whatCouldGoWrong: **The Rotair queue eats the morning.** Fallback: use the earlier orientation day to learn its rhythm, and always take the first cabin on a big-descent day rather than a mid-morning one.

**Titlis is wind-closed.** Fallback: Brunni's lower, more sheltered sector keeps the week skiable — this is a genuine plan B, not a consolation prize, and is scheduled into the week for exactly this reason.

**The Galtiberg is called off for crevasse or avalanche risk.** Fallback: the guide substitutes a shorter, better-secured glacier line off Titlis, or moves the day to Brunni and reschedules Galtiberg for later in the week if a weather window opens.

**Guided days are fully booked.** Fallback: book Outventure or a Bergführer before arrival; walking in to Engelberg without a pre-booked guide is the most common reason visiting freeriders miss the area's signature descents.
**A member of the group is not fit for the Galtiberg's full length.** Fallback: split the group — Outventure can run a shorter Steinberg repeat for anyone not up for the long exit.

trips.title: Verbier and the 4 Vallées: Mont-Fort, Tortin and the Stairway to Heaven

bestPeriod.note: The Mont-Fort glacier holds snow all season; the Tortin face and lower Verbier slopes need a genuine cold spell to ski well, best from mid-January.

trips.gatewayAirport: Geneva (GVA)
trips.summary: A week in Verbier and the 4 Vallées built around Mont-Fort, the Stairway to Heaven and Tortin, with an honest read of where the lift interconnect actually breaks down.
trips.hook: Verbier's reputation rests on one glacier cable car and the terrain it unlocks. The 4 Vallées network is genuinely vast — four linked valleys, over a hundred lifts between them — but almost everything this trip is built for depends on a single chain running from Verbier village to Mont-Fort at 3,330 m, and that chain has a well-known weak link at the top. This week is planned around it, not surprised by it.

snapshot.Base(s): Verbier
snapshot.Best Period: January–March; mid-January onward for the Tortin face to be properly filled in
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: 4 Vallées network (Verbier, La Tzoumaz, Nendaz, Veysonnaz, Thyon, Siviez); base 820 m at Le Châble, top 3,330 m at Mont-Fort
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Geneva (GVA); shuttle or train via Martigny/Le Châble, roughly 2h to 2h30 total
snapshot.Who It Suits: Advanced and expert skiers and riders wanting guided glacier freeride and steep off-piste, comfortable in variable, ungroomed snow

itinerary.title: Arrival and gear check
itinerary.morning: Fly to Geneva; shuttle or train (Geneva-Martigny, then the Le Châble gondola) up to Verbier at 1,500 m.
itinerary.afternoon: Check into the base hotel and visit a rental shop for skis or a splitboard, boots and full avalanche kit — transceiver, probe, shovel. Register with La Fantastique or the Bureau des Guides de Verbier for the week's guided days.
itinerary.evening: Buy the 4 Vallées pass and check the Valais avalanche bulletin for the coming days.
itinerary.dayStats: 0 vertical metres skied · 0 sectors · 0 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Local orientation: Savoleyres and Lac des Vaux
itinerary.morning: Ride the Savoleyres gondola on Verbier's quieter, south-facing side — a good first day to read the group's ability on varied but non-glacial terrain.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross to Lac des Vaux and the lower Attelas sector, working toward the base of the Mont-Fort lift chain to see current conditions and queue length before committing a full day to it.
itinerary.evening: Early dinner; tomorrow starts early to beat the Mont-Fort queue.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 3,000 m vertical · 2 sectors (Savoleyres, Lac des Vaux) · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Mont-Fort and the Stairway to Heaven
itinerary.morning: Be at the Médran lift base in Verbier by 08:00. Ride up through Les Ruinettes to Attelas (2,727 m), then the Mont-Fort cable car to 3,330 m — the single access point to the glacier terrain and the most wind-sensitive lift in the network; it is the first thing to close in a storm and the reason this day is scheduled early in the week, not the last possible morning.
itinerary.afternoon: With a guide, ski the Stairway to Heaven: from the Mont-Fort glacier or Col des Gentianes, a long, roughly 2,000 m off-piste descent down the Combe de Tortin to the Tortin lift base. Crevasses on the upper glacier and variable snow on the lower combe make this a guided itinerary, run by La Fantastique or the Bureau des Guides de Verbier, not a solo line regardless of visible tracks.
itinerary.evening: Recovery dinner; this is the physically hardest day of the week.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,700 m vertical · 1 itinerary (Stairway to Heaven) · 3 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Tortin face and Siviez
itinerary.morning: Ride the Jumbo gondola from Le Châble/Verbier toward Attelas, then down into the Tortin sector via the Chassoure-Tortin cable car. The Tortin piste itself is one of the network's steepest marked runs, north-facing and mogul-prone by midday; ski it early while it is still firm rather than broken up.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue into Siviez and across toward Nendaz, sampling the interconnect's mid-mountain pistes, which are considerably gentler than the Verbier side.
itinerary.evening: Return via the same chain to Verbier.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,900 m vertical · 2 sectors (Tortin, Siviez/Nendaz) · 4.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: The full 4 Vallées traverse
itinerary.morning: A long point-to-point day linking Verbier through Siviez to Veysonnaz and on to Thyon, using the full chain of gondolas and chairlifts that gives the area its name. This is a logistics exercise as much as a ski day — plan lift closing times at each valley in advance, since missing the last connection strands you a taxi ride from Verbier.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the Thyon/Veysonnaz pistes, generally sunnier and lower-altitude than Mont-Fort, then begin the return traverse in good time.
itinerary.evening: Confirm the last uphill connection back over Attelas before it closes; if in doubt, descend to Le Châble by road transport rather than risk it.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 3,400 m vertical · 4 sectors (Verbier, Siviez, Veysonnaz, Thyon) · 5.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Second glacier day or La Tzoumaz bad-snow plan B
itinerary.morning: Check Mont-Fort's status before deciding: if it is running and the snowpack has stabilised, a second guided glacier itinerary off Col des Gentianes extends the week's off-piste tally. If the top chain is on wind hold or the lower slopes are worn thin by traffic and sun, switch to La Tzoumaz on the sunnier, more sheltered side of the valley — lower altitude but more forgiving and typically less crowded.
itinerary.afternoon: Either continuation of the glacier plan, or a relaxed tree-lined afternoon on La Tzoumaz's runs, a genuine fallback rather than a consolation prize.
itinerary.evening: Gear rinse and pack check ahead of the last day.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,200-2,700 m vertical · 1 sector (Mont-Fort or La Tzoumaz) · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Final morning and departure
itinerary.morning: A short session on the Savoleyres side, the most reliable sector for a low-key last morning regardless of what the top of the mountain is doing.
itinerary.afternoon: Return gear, shuttle to Geneva.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,300 m vertical · 1 sector (Savoleyres) · 2 lift hours.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Nevaï
accommodationStrategy.description: Close to the Médran lift base, the start point for the Mont-Fort chain — useful given how early Day 3 and any repeat glacier day need to start. Spa and sauna help with recovery after the Stairway to Heaven.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead for February.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Verbier
accommodationStrategy.description: A straightforward central base within walking distance of Médran, Savoleyres and the village restaurants, without the design-hotel price premium.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Chalet-style guesthouse, Le Châble
accommodationStrategy.description: A lower-cost option in the valley-floor town at the base of the Verbier gondola, useful for a longer stay or a group happy to add ten minutes to each lift-base commute.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Switzerland's air rescue service Rega is 1414, the number to know for any serious off-piste incident.
logistics.weather: Check MeteoSwiss and the resort's own lift-status page each morning; Mont-Fort's status is the one figure that reshapes the whole day's plan.
logistics.bookingWindows: La Fantastique and the Bureau des Guides de Verbier fill February and Easter dates weeks ahead; book the Stairway to Heaven day as soon as your dates are fixed.
logistics.money: Switzerland uses the Swiss franc; cards are near-universal but small mountain restaurants sometimes prefer cash.
logistics.health: The Swiss avalanche bulletin (SLF) uses the same European 1–5 danger scale; carry transceiver, probe and shovel on every off-piste or glacier day, without exception.

other.label: Pass tiers, approx. 2026
other.text: A 4 Vallées adult one-day pass runs approx. CHF 94 (approx. €99); a six-day pass approx. CHF 409 (approx. €430). Buying online at least ten days ahead typically carries a discount over walk-up prices — book the week in advance rather than at the lift base.

other.label: Verbier is not on the Magic Pass
other.text: Switzerland's popular multi-resort Magic Pass covers roughly forty smaller and mid-sized areas, but Verbier/4 Vallées, like most premium big-name resorts, sells its own standalone pass — do not assume cross-honour with a Magic Pass bought elsewhere in Switzerland.

other.label: Where the interconnect breaks down
other.text: The entire glacier side of the network funnels through the Attelas-Mont-Fort cable car chain; this is the most wind-exposed lift in the system and the first to close in poor weather, at which point Tortin, Siviez and the glacier terrain all become unreachable from Verbier until it reopens.

proTips: Ski Mont-Fort and the Stairway to Heaven early in the week, not the last possible day — it is the lift most likely to be closed by wind, and a mid-week backup day only works if you have not saved everything for Day 7.
Ride the first cabin up Médran; the queue for Attelas and Mont-Fort builds fast after 09:00 in high season.
Ski Tortin before midday — its steep, mogulled face is far more manageable firm than it is broken up by an afternoon of traffic.
Buy the 4 Vallées pass online at least ten days ahead for the standard advance discount rather than at the lift-base ticket office.
On the full-traverse day, write down each connecting lift's last-departure time before setting out — the return chain over Attelas closes earlier than the village lifts.
If Mont-Fort is closed, do not wait it out at the base — La Tzoumaz's sheltered side is often skiing perfectly well while the glacier chain sits idle.
