A small pack for skins, water and a spare layer on the full-traverse day.
Comfortable off-mountain shoes for Verbier's steep village streets, which see plenty of foot traffic between hotel and lift.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Mont-Fort is closed by wind.** Fallback: switch immediately to La Tzoumaz or the Tortin/Siviez sector if already accessible, and hold a spare mid-week day to retry the glacier chain.
**Tortin is icy or bare after a dry, cold spell.** Fallback: this face needs real snow depth; default to Savoleyres or the Nendaz side, which hold artificial and natural cover better.

**The full-traverse day runs long and a connection is missed.** Fallback: descend to the nearest valley-floor town (Nendaz, Veysonnaz or Thyon all have road transport) and return to Verbier by taxi or bus rather than pushing a closing lift.

**Guided departures are fully booked.** Fallback: book La Fantastique or the Bureau des Guides de Verbier before arrival, not on Day 1 — this is the single most common reason groups miss the Stairway to Heaven.

**A storm cycle closes the upper mountain for several days.** Fallback: Savoleyres and the lower Verbier pistes, more sheltered and tree-lined, keep the week skiable while waiting the glacier terrain out.

trips.title: Krkonoše — Špindlerův Mlýn, Pec and the Ridge Tour

bestPeriod.note: The ridge above 1,300 m holds a reliable base longest; valley snow at Špindlerův Mlýn is now heavily snowmaking-dependent by comparison.

trips.gatewayAirport: Prague (PRG)
trips.summary: A week skiing Špindlerův Mlýn and Pec pod Sněžkou, with a guided ski-touring day on the Krkonoše ridge and the national park's real winter access closures explained.
trips.hook: Krkonoše is not the Alps, and it does not try to be — the whole range tops out at 1,603 m, at Sněžka. What it has instead is a genuinely wild, wind-scoured summit ridge, two well-built but not-quite-connected valley resorts, and a national park administration that closes large parts of the high ground every winter to protect it. This week skis both valley resorts, respects the closures, and spends one day on the ridge itself with a certified guide.

snapshot.Base(s): Špindlerův Mlýn (5 nights), Pec pod Sněžkou (2 nights)
snapshot.Best Period: January–March; the ridge holds snow longest, valley slopes are snowmaking-supported
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Base approx. 715 m (Špindlerův Mlýn), top approx. 1,603 m (Sněžka, ridge tour only); resort lift-served terrain tops around 1,235–1,299 m
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Prague (PRG); bus or shared shuttle to Špindlerův Mlýn, roughly 2h30
snapshot.Who It Suits: Intermediate skiers who want a lower-key, lower-cost Central European week, plus anyone keen to try ski touring on gentle, well-marked terrain

itinerary.title: Arrival and Medvědín
itinerary.morning: Bus from Prague's Florenc station to Špindlerův Mlýn, arriving into the town at 715 m, wedged along the young Elbe (Labe) river at the foot of two separate ski mountains.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the Medvědín gondola on the north side of the valley for an orientation lap — Medvědín's runs are broad, mostly red-graded, and reliably snowmaking-covered from top to bottom.
itinerary.evening: Walk the short riverside street; Špindlerův Mlýn is small enough to see in twenty minutes, and most restaurants sit within that stretch.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 700 m vertical · Medvědín sector · 2 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Svatý Petr and the interconnect that isn't
itinerary.morning: Cross the valley — literally, since Medvědín and the Svatý Petr/Hromovka sector on the opposite mountain are not lift-connected. This is the week's first honest interconnect lesson: Špindlerův Mlýn markets itself as one resort, but skiing between its two halves means riding down to the valley floor and taking the free ski bus (or a ten-minute walk in good conditions) rather than a direct lift.
itinerary.afternoon: Svatý Petr's slopes, served by a modern gondola from town, include the FIS-graded Svatý Petr race piste, one of the steeper pitches in the Czech resort scene, plus gentler blues off to the side for a mixed-ability group.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in town; the bus link between the two sectors stops running by early evening, so plan any sector-hopping for daylight hours.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 3,600 m vertical · Svatý Petr/Hromovka sector · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: National park boundaries and a low-key touring intro
itinerary.morning: The Krkonoše National Park (KRNAP) enforces a genuinely strict winter access regime: large sections of the highest ground, including most of the main ridge above the tree line, sit in Zone I, the strict nature reserve, where travel off marked and specifically winter-permitted routes is prohibited, and several connecting ridge paths are closed outright from 1 November to 31 May to protect overwintering chamois and capercaillie. This is enforced by park rangers, not a suggestion — check the current KRNAP winter route map at the Špindlerova bouda information point before planning any ridge walking or touring.
itinerary.afternoon: Take an introductory ski-touring lesson on the permitted, gentle terrain near Labská bouda, reached by a marked winter route from the top of the Medvědín lift system. This is the low-commitment version of tomorrow's bigger day: skins, touring bindings, and a guide explaining how the park's permitted-route system works before anyone commits to the full ridge.
itinerary.evening: Early dinner; tomorrow's ridge day starts early.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 400 m vertical touring · Labská bouda approach, permitted route · half-day.

itinerary.title: Guided day on the Krkonoše ridge
itinerary.morning: Book a full guided ski-touring day through a certified guide from the Asociace horských vůdců ČR (the Czech Mountain Guides Association), which trains and certifies guides who legally operate within the park's permitted winter corridors. A guide here is the practical way to use the ridge's permitted routes correctly and read conditions on genuinely exposed, wind-loaded terrain that looks deceptively gentle from below.
itinerary.afternoon: A typical route runs from Labská bouda along the permitted ridge section toward Luční bouda, with wide views into Poland on the border ridge; the guide checks the daily avalanche bulletin from Horská služba ČR (the Czech Mountain Rescue Service), rated on the standard five-level European avalanche danger scale (1 Low to 5 Very High), before committing — wind slab on the exposed ridge is the real hazard here, not steep-slope avalanche terrain in the alpine sense.
itinerary.evening: Return to Špindlerův Mlýn; a guided ridge day in genuinely raw weather is tiring even on gentle gradients, and an early night is standard.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 12 km, 500 m vertical touring · Krkonoše main ridge, permitted corridor · full guided day.

itinerary.title: Transfer to Pec pod Sněžkou
itinerary.morning: Bus or taxi transfer over to Pec pod Sněžkou, on the eastern side of the range and the base for the Sněžka cable car. Check into Pec and ski the afternoon on the Hnědý vrch sector directly above town.
itinerary.afternoon: Pec's slopes, part of the larger SkiResort Černá hora–Pec network that also links Zahrádky and, via ski bus rather than direct lift, the separate Černá hora mountain above Janské Lázně, are gentler on average than Špindlerův Mlýn's, which makes this a good rest-legs day after the touring effort.
itinerary.evening: Pec's small centre sits directly below Sněžka, Czechia's highest peak (1,603 m) and the border ridge with Poland — worth a look up at the summit weather station even from the valley floor.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,400 m vertical · Hnědý vrch sector · 3 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Černá hora and the honest snow check
itinerary.morning: Take the ski bus over to Janské Lázně and ride the Černá hora cable car, a modern gondola that replaced the Czech Republic's historic first chairlift, up to the summit area near 1,299 m. Černá hora sits slightly higher and more sheltered than either Špindlerův Mlýn sector, and in a marginal-snow year this is genuinely the more reliable of the three main areas.
itinerary.afternoon: This is the trip's honest bad-snow plan B in practice: if the valley base at Špindlerův Mlýn or Pec has looked thin earlier in the week, weight the second half of the trip toward Černá hora's higher runs rather than the lower-altitude sectors, and treat any run below about 900 m as conditional on the week's actual snow report rather than assumed.
itinerary.evening: Return to Pec for a final evening; the walk around the small town centre, with views up to Sněžka, is a good way to close the trip.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 3,000 m vertical · Černá hora sector · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Last morning and departure
itinerary.morning: A final short session on Pec's Zahrádky sector, quieter than Hnědý vrch and a gentle way to end the week.
itinerary.afternoon: Return skis, and take the bus back toward Prague, allowing a comfortable buffer — the Pec–Prague road route runs through smaller towns and can be slow in winter weather.
itinerary.evening: Flight home from Prague.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,400 m vertical · Zahrádky sector · 2 lift hours.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Start
accommodationStrategy.description: A straightforward hotel a short walk from both the Medvědín gondola and the Svatý Petr shuttle bus stop, useful given the two sectors' lack of direct lift connection.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks ahead for peak February weeks.

accommodationStrategy.name: Horský hotel Krakonoš
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits directly at the base of the Hnědý vrch lifts in Pec, with ski storage and an easy walk to the Sněžka cable-car connection point in Janské Lázně's direction.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four weeks ahead.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €65–€100 per night for two, often half board

accommodationStrategy.name: Labská bouda
accommodationStrategy.description: A working mountain hut directly on the plateau near the touring route used on Day 3 and Day 4; staying a night here (rather than commuting up each day) suits anyone wanting an early start on the guided ridge tour.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three weeks ahead; beds are limited and often taken by touring groups.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €45–€75 per night for two, half board typical

logistics.connectivity: Reliable in both resort towns; drops out fast on the open ridge, which the guide accounts for with radio and offline maps — do not rely on phone signal above the tree line.
logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; mountain rescue in the Krkonoše is handled by Horská služba ČR, reachable via 112 or the regional line posted at every lift base.
logistics.bookingWindows: Czech school holiday weeks (staggered by region through February) sell out both resorts; check the specific week against the holiday calendar before booking.
logistics.money: Czechia uses the koruna (CZK); cards are widely accepted, but smaller mountain huts, including Labská bouda, often prefer cash.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 pan-European; mountain rescue in the Krkonoše is handled by Horská služba ČR, reachable via 112 or the regional line posted at every lift base.

other.label: National park rules
other.text: Off-route travel in KRNAP's Zone I is illegal, and rangers do check; the permitted winter corridor system exists so guided and independent skiers can still use the ridge responsibly. Confirm the current permitted-route map before any touring day.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: The inter-sector ski bus in Špindlerův Mlýn runs a reduced-frequency winter timetable — check current times rather than assuming an Alpine-style continuous shuttle.

other.label: Avalanche equipment
other.text: Mandatory for the ridge tour: transceiver, probe and shovel, generally supplied and checked by the guide association's outfitters — confirm when booking.

proTips: Ski Medvědín in the morning and Svatý Petr in the afternoon on a clear day, rather than trying to bounce between them more than once — the bus transfer eats real time.
Book the guided ridge day for the clearest forecast window in the week, even if it means shuffling the itinerary; the ridge in poor visibility is a washout regardless of snow quality.
Černá hora is consistently the least crowded of the three main areas on a weekday — worth weighting toward it if Špindlerův Mlýn or Pec feel busy.
The Sněžka summit weather station and the short walk up from the top of the Pec-side lifts (in good visibility only) gives a view into Poland that most week-long visitors skip entirely.
Czech ski school and guide pricing runs well below equivalent Austrian or Swiss rates — a genuinely good-value place to try touring for the first time.
Buy multi-day lift tickets covering both Špindlerův Mlýn's sectors together; the combined ticket is cheaper than paying per sector per day.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Base approx. 715 m (Špindlerův Mlýn), top approx. 1,603 m (Sněžka, ridge tour only); resort lift-served terrain tops around 1,235–1,299 m
raw.Who It Suits: Intermediate skiers who want a lower-key, lower-cost Central European week, plus anyone keen to try ski touring on gentle, well-marked terrain

typeSpecific.surface: Base approx. 715 m (Špindlerův Mlýn), top approx. 1,603 m (Sněžka, ridge tour only); resort lift-served terrain tops around 1,235–1,299 m
typeSpecific.audience: Intermediate skiers who want a lower-key, lower-cost Central European week, plus anyone keen to try ski touring on gentle, well-marked terrain

packingNotes: Transceiver, probe and shovel for the ridge touring day.
Touring bindings or a rental set booked in advance at Labská bouda or in Špindlerův Mlýn — stock is limited outside the main resort towns.
A windproof shell rated for genuinely raw exposed-ridge conditions; the Krkonoše ridge is famous locally for wind, not cold in isolation.
Layers that adapt between snowmaking-groomed valley runs and the more variable natural snow on the ridge.
Cash in koruna for mountain huts and the ski bus if it is not card-enabled.
A map or offline GPS track of the current KRNAP permitted winter routes.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Valley snow is thin at Špindlerův Mlýn.** Fallback: weight the week toward Černá hora's higher, more sheltered runs, already scheduled for the second half.
**Poor visibility cancels the ridge tour.** Fallback: reschedule it for the last clear day, and use the freed day for an extra session at Pec.
**The inter-sector ski bus runs late or crowded.** Fallback: ski one sector fully in the morning and commit to it for the afternoon rather than chasing a tight connection.
**A booked hut bed on the ridge falls through.** Fallback: base the touring day from the valley instead — an early start, but no overnight needed.

trips.title: Garmisch-Partenkirchen: The Classic Area and the Zugspitze Glacier

bestPeriod.note: The Classic area sits low (750-2050 m) and is snow-dependent; the Zugspitze glacier above 2000 m holds snow reliably from December into April.

trips.gatewayAirport: Munich (MUC)
trips.summary: A week on Garmisch-Partenkirchen's Classic area and the Zugspitze glacier, with an honest plan for the low-altitude snow years Bavaria actually has.
trips.hook: Garmisch-Partenkirchen skis two different mountains with two different personalities: a low, historic race-piste area that needs real winter to work, and a genuine glacier that does not. This week uses both, treats the Zugspitzplatt as the honest fallback it is, and builds in the queue-avoidance logic the Eibsee cable car demands.

snapshot.Base(s): Garmisch-Partenkirchen
snapshot.Best Period: January–March; the Classic area's lower slopes are marginal outside a cold, snowy winter
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Garmisch-Classic (Kandahar, Hausberg, Kreuzeck, Alpspitze), base 720 m to 2,050 m; Zugspitze glacier, 2,000 m to 2,962 m
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Munich (MUC); direct train from Munich Hauptbahnhof to Garmisch-Partenkirchen, roughly 1h20
snapshot.Who It Suits: Intermediate to advanced skiers who want race-pedigree pistes plus a high-altitude glacier day; families on the gentler Hausberg slopes

itinerary.title: Arrival and the town area
itinerary.morning: Train from Munich to Garmisch-Partenkirchen. Check into the base hotel and walk to a rental shop on Marienplatz or Zugspitzstraße for skis, boots and, if the week includes any touring, skins.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the Hausbergbahn, the gentlest of the four Classic sectors, to get a first read on snow depth low in the valley — this tells you within an hour whether the week needs to lean on the glacier earlier than planned.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in the old Partenkirchen quarter around Ludwigstraße, with its painted Lüftlmalerei house façades.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,400 m vertical · 1 sector (Hausberg) · 3 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Kandahar and Kreuzeck
itinerary.morning: Bus or walk to the Kreuzeckbahn. The Kreuzeck sector links across to the Kandahar piste, home of the annual FIS World Cup downhill and slalom — steep, race-groomed, and the benchmark run of the Classic area.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the Kandahar itself if conditions allow (it demands real snow cover to be worthwhile — a thin year turns it icy and unpleasant) or stay on the connecting Kreuzeck blues and reds, which hold snow better on their partly shaded aspect.
itinerary.evening: Free evening in town; the Partnachklamm gorge trailhead is a short taxi ride for anyone wanting a non-ski outing.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,200 m vertical · 2 sectors (Kreuzeck, Kandahar) · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Alpspitze and the Gatterl freeride zone
itinerary.morning: Ride the Alpspitzbahn cable car to Osterfelderkopf (2,050 m), the highest and most reliably snow-holding point in the Classic area, with views onto the Zugspitze massif and the Höllental below.
itinerary.afternoon: For confident skiers, the marked-but-ungroomed Gatterl zone near the top station offers short, steep off-piste pitches inside the ski area boundary — check the local avalanche and closure signage before dropping in, since it is patrolled but not pisted.
itinerary.evening: Early return; this sector's cable car has limited late-afternoon capacity in high season.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,900 m vertical · 1 sector (Alpspitze) · 3.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Rest and valley day, or bad-snow Plan B
itinerary.morning: This is the week's flex day. If the Classic area's lower slopes are thin — a real possibility in a mild Bavarian winter — skip them entirely and go straight to the Zugspitze glacier instead (see Day 5); otherwise use the morning for a valley activity: the Olympic Ski Stadium (1936 Winter Games venue) or the Partnachklamm.
itinerary.afternoon: Sauna and recovery, or a short cross-country loop on the valley-floor Loipe network if snow is present at town level.
itinerary.evening: Early dinner and an early night before the glacier day.
itinerary.dayStats: 0-1,900 m vertical (conditional) · 0-1 sector · flexible lift hours.

itinerary.title: Zugspitze glacier day
itinerary.morning: Take the Eibsee-Seilbahn cable car from the Eibsee lake shore — one of the world's steepest cable cars — direct to the Zugspitze summit at 2,962 m, or the Bayerische Zugspitzbahn cogwheel train via Grainau if the cable car queue is long, which connects into the glacier system at the Sonn Alpin/Zugspitzplatt station.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the Zugspitzplatt glacier ski area, a compact but genuinely snow-sure zone between roughly 2,000 m and 2,600 m, well above the rain line that troubles the valley slopes. The terrain is short and lift-served rather than expansive — plan on repeated laps rather than long point-to-point runs.
itinerary.evening: Ride back down; both the cable car and the cogwheel train stop running by late afternoon in winter, so do not linger past the posted last-descent time.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,600 m vertical · 1 sector (Zugspitzplatt) · 3.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Second Classic day or the Höllental approach
itinerary.morning: With good snow cover and a guide, the Höllental — the dramatic valley between the Alpspitze and the Zugspitze — is the area's serious off-piste and ski-mountaineering objective, descending from near the Zugspitze summit through glaciated and then forested terrain to Hammersbach station. This is a committing, guided-only day: crevasses on the upper Höllentalferner and a roped downclimb section make it unsuitable without a certified mountain guide, arranged through the German Alpine Club's Summit Club alpine school or a local Bergführer.
itinerary.afternoon: For everyone not doing the Höllental, a second lap of Kreuzeck-Kandahar-Alpspitze, mixing sectors based on which aspect is skiing best that day.
itinerary.evening: Relaxed dinner; this is the last full ski day.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,000-2,700 m vertical · 1-3 sectors · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Final morning and departure
itinerary.morning: A short session on Hausberg's forgiving slopes, gear return, and a last coffee on Marienplatz.
itinerary.afternoon: Train back to Munich for the flight home.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,000 m vertical · 1 sector (Hausberg) · 2 lift hours.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Zugspitze
accommodationStrategy.description: Central location within walking distance of the Hausbergbahn and Kreuzeckbahn base stations, with ski storage and a drying room — useful on the days the plan pivots at short notice between Classic-area sectors.
accommodationStrategy.booking: eight weeks ahead for February.

accommodationStrategy.name: Reindl's Partenkirchner Hof
accommodationStrategy.description: A long-established family-run hotel in the old Partenkirchen quarter, close to the Alpspitzbahn base and an easy walk to the Ludwigstraße restaurants for the evening after a glacier day.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two to three months ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel am Kurpark
accommodationStrategy.location: near the Kurpark and spa quarter
accommodationStrategy.description: A quieter, lower-cost base within a short bus ride of both the Classic-area lift stations and the Eibsee-Seilbahn departure point, good for a family group balancing skiing with spa time.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four to six weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Bavarian mountain rescue (Bergwacht Bayern) is reached via 112.
logistics.weather: The Föhn wind can strip the valley of cloud in hours but also brings rapid warming that softens or ruins lower-mountain snow; check the Deutscher Wetterdienst mountain forecast each morning.
logistics.bookingWindows: Reindl's and other Partenkirchen hotels fill for the Kandahar World Cup weekend (check the FIS calendar) — avoid or book many months ahead if that weekend falls inside your dates.
logistics.money: Cards are near-universal; the regional GVB day ticket covers Garmisch's local buses between hotel and lift base stations.

other.label: The ZugspitzCard
other.text: Combines Garmisch-Classic and the Zugspitze glacier under one ticket; useful precisely because the two areas need such different snow conditions to work — check current pricing at the ticket office or zugspitze.de before buying single-area passes.

other.label: Snow reality
other.text: Garmisch town sits at 720 m and the lower Classic-area slopes can be thin, wet or closed in a mild winter; the Zugspitze glacier above 2,000 m is the honest Plan B and should be treated as a scheduled day, not an emergency backup.

other.label: Eibsee-Seilbahn queues
other.text: This cable car is extremely popular with sightseers as well as skiers; arrive at opening or use the Bayerische Zugspitzbahn cogwheel train from Garmisch station as the less crowded alternative on peak days.

other.label: Avalanche awareness
other.text: The Gatterl zone and any Höllental approach are avalanche terrain rated on the same European 1–5 scale as the Alps generally — carry a transceiver, probe and shovel for both, and check the Bavarian avalanche report (Lawinenwarndienst Bayern).

proTips: Check the Lawinenwarndienst Bayern snow depth chart before booking which day is the glacier day — moving Day 5 earlier in a thin week salvages the trip.
Ride the Bayerische Zugspitzbahn cogwheel train up and the Eibsee-Seilbahn cable car down (or vice versa) rather than doing both legs on the same lift — it halves your time in each queue.
Ski the Kandahar piste in the first two hours after opening; by midday it is heavily skied off and considerably rougher.
The Gatterl freeride zone skis best the morning after fresh snow — by afternoon the short pitches are tracked out.
Use the ZugspitzCard rather than buying Classic-area and glacier tickets separately if your week genuinely mixes both areas; work out the break-even against your planned day split before committing.
Book Höllental with a guide at least a week ahead in high season — the Summit Club and local Bergführer run limited group sizes on this route.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Garmisch-Classic (Kandahar, Hausberg, Kreuzeck, Alpspitze), base 720 m to 2,050 m; Zugspitze glacier, 2,000 m to 2,962 m
raw.Who It Suits: Intermediate to advanced skiers who want race-pedigree pistes plus a high-altitude glacier day; families on the gentler Hausberg slopes

typeSpecific.surface: Garmisch-Classic (Kandahar, Hausberg, Kreuzeck, Alpspitze), base 720 m to 2,050 m; Zugspitze glacier, 2,000 m to 2,962 m
typeSpecific.audience: Intermediate to advanced skiers who want race-pedigree pistes plus a high-altitude glacier day; families on the gentler Hausberg slopes

packingNotes: Layers for a genuine altitude and temperature range: 720 m in town to 2,962 m at the Zugspitze summit.
A hardshell rather than just a softshell — the glacier can be windy and wet valley snow at low altitude needs waterproofing too.
Goggles for two very different light conditions: flat valley light in the Classic area, intense glare on the glacier.
Transceiver, probe and shovel if any off-piste or Höllental day is planned.
Comfortable warm boots for the Eibsee cable car queue, which is often an outdoor wait.
A base-layer change for the transition between the low, potentially wet Classic-area slopes and the cold, dry glacier.
whatCouldGoWrong: **The Classic area is thin or closed at low altitude.** Fallback: shift days to the Zugspitze glacier, which holds snow independent of valley conditions; this is why Day 4 is built as a flex day.
**The Eibsee-Seilbahn is fully booked or queued for hours.** Fallback: the Bayerische Zugspitzbahn cogwheel train from Garmisch station reaches the same glacier system with a shorter wait most days.
**Föhn wind brings rapid warming mid-week.** Fallback: move remaining Classic-area days to the shadier Kreuzeck aspect and prioritise glacier time while it lasts.
**The Kandahar piste is icy after a thin, cold spell.** Fallback: Hausberg's gentler, more sheltered slopes ski better in exactly these conditions.

**A planned Höllental day is cancelled for crevasse or weather risk.** Fallback: the guide will substitute a lower-risk glacier tour on the Zugspitzplatt at short notice — never attempt the descent independently if the guided day falls through.

trips.title: Baqueira Beret: Val d'Aran on the Atlantic Side

bestPeriod.window: Mid-January–mid-March; the second half of February combines the deepest base with lengthening days
bestPeriod.avoid: 26 December–7 January and Spanish Semana Santa, when Barcelona and Madrid arrive together and the C-28 queues at Baqueira 1500 start at 08:15
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-January–mid-March; the second half of February combines the deepest base with lengthening days

accommodation.note: Salardú/Arties guesthouses €80–€130 pppn; Baqueira 1500 slopeside €180–€300

food.note: Menú del dia €18–€25; mountain restaurant mains €18–€28; one Casa Irene dinner €70–€100

transport.note: Toulouse transfer or hire car €55–€90/day; free ski bus within Val d'Aran

activities.note: 6-day forfait roughly €300–€360, Banhs de Tredòs €18–€25, one guided freeride day

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5 — lift-served days of 4,000–6,000 vertical metres, with one optional ski-touring or freeride day that pushes to 4/5

trips.gatewayAirport: TLS Toulouse–Blagnac, 2 h 30–3 h to Vielha via Bossòst; ILD Lleida–Alguaire 2 h 30; BCN Barcelona El Prat 4 h–4 h 30
trips.summary: Val d'Aran is the only Spanish valley that drains north into the Atlantic, and that single geographic accident is the whole trip: the weather arrives wet off the Bay of Biscay, dumps on the Aran side of the watershed, and leaves Baqueira with the most reliable snow in Spain. The week works as three concentric rings — the groomed Baqueira and Beret bowls for the first days, the Bonaigua and Cara Nord flanks for the harder pistes and long descents, and then the off-piste terrain around Baciver and the Escornacrabes couloir for anyone who brought a transceiver. Between ski days you drop into a valley of Romanesque churches, Aranese-speaking villages and thermal water at Tredòs. It suits strong intermediates and experts, especially those who care more about snow quality and freeride potential than about vertical drop or lift-network glamour.

itinerary.title: Toulouse to Vielha, and a first afternoon on Baqueira
itinerary.morning: Fly to Toulouse and drive south through Saint-Gaudens and over into Spain at Bossòst — the Aran side of the border, which is why this is the fast route. Roughly 2 h 30 without snow.
itinerary.afternoon: Collect the forfait and hire kit at Baqueira 1500, ride the **Blanhiblar** gondola up to the 1,800 m plateau, and ski the wide blues off the Bosque and Argulls chairs for two hours to find your feet.
itinerary.evening: Tauèrna Urtau in Arties for pintxos and a Somontano red, or Era Lucana in Vielha if you are staying in the capital.
itinerary.dayStats: Drive Toulouse–Vielha 2 h 30–3 h / Baqueira 1500 base / 8–12 piste km, roughly 1,500 m descent / hire €120–€190 for the week

itinerary.title: Beret plateau and the Baciver traverse
itinerary.morning: Drive or take the free ski bus to the **Beret** access at Pla de Beret, about 1,850 m — a broad sunlit shelf that skis nothing like the rest of the resort. Warm up on the plateau blues, then push out to the **Baciver** chairs.
itinerary.afternoon: Traverse back over the ridge into the Baqueira bowl and ski laps of the long reds down to 1,800 m. Lunch at the Pla de Beret restaurant rather than descending.
itinerary.evening: Salardú, and the Romanesque church of Sant Andreu with its 12th-century Crist de Salardú, then dinner at the hotel.
itinerary.dayStats: Pla de Beret ~1,850 m / Cap de Baqueira ~2,510 m / 25–30 piste km, roughly 4,500 m descent / free Val d'Aran ski bus Vielha–Baqueira

itinerary.title: Bonaigua and the long fall lines
itinerary.morning: Cross to the **Bonaigua** sector on the far side of the **Port de la Bonaigua (2,072 m)** — check the C-28 road status before you leave, because this is the pass that closes. The Bonaigua flank has the resort's longest sustained pitches and its best blacks.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the Bonaigua reds and blacks until the linking chair closes around 16:15, then return over the ridge to the Baqueira bowl. Do not leave this to 16:30.
itinerary.evening: Casa Irene in Arties — the valley's long-established restaurant, where the Aranese-French cooking and the game dishes justify the bill. Book ahead.
itinerary.dayStats: Port de la Bonaigua 2,072 m / Bonaigua linking chair last run ~16:15 / 28–33 piste km, roughly 5,500 m descent / C-28 closes in heavy snow, no alternative from that side

itinerary.title: Cara Nord and the freeride day
itinerary.morning: Read the **Lauegi d'Aran** bulletin over breakfast — if it is 3 or above, this becomes a piste day. If it is 1 or 2 and there is fresh, meet a guide from Camins or the Escola d'Esquí freeride programme at Baqueira 1500 with transceiver, shovel and probe.
itinerary.afternoon: Work the shaded **Cara Nord** above Argulls and Ta Dossau, and if conditions allow, the **Escornacrabes** couloir off the Baqueira ridge. Otherwise take the guide onto the Baciver backcountry, which is safer-angled and skis just as well.
itinerary.evening: Après at Moët in Baqueira 1500 while the road empties, then back to Salardú.
itinerary.dayStats: Bulletin: lauegi.conselharan.org, EAWS 1–5 plus Aran's own ATES terrain classification / guide €300–€400 per day per group / Escornacrabes is an itinerary, not a piste / transceiver, shovel, probe mandatory

itinerary.title: Weather-contingency and rest day: Tredòs, Vielha and the Romanesque valley
itinerary.morning: The designed flex day, and the one to move if the Bonaigua closes or a foehn shuts the top chairs. Drive up the Aiguamòg valley to the **Banhs de Tredòs** at about 1,750 m and sit in sulphurous water at 34–37°C with snow on the rim.
itinerary.afternoon: Down to **Vielha** for the **Musèu dera Val d'Aran** and the church of **Sant Miquèu** with its Crist de Mijaran, then walk the old town. Aranese — a variety of Gascon Occitan — is co-official here alongside Catalan and Spanish, and the street signs are the clearest evidence of it.
itinerary.evening: Era Lucana in Vielha for **olla aranesa**, the valley's cabbage, bean and pork winter stew, and a **civet** of wild boar or chamois. This is the meal the trip is really about.
itinerary.dayStats: Banhs de Tredòs ~€18–€25, water 34–37°C, altitude ~1,750 m / Vielha 974 m / zero vertical metres / snowshoe alternative up the Valarties, 2–3 h

itinerary.title: The full traverse day
itinerary.morning: The big one. Start at Baqueira 1500 on first lifts, up the **Blanhiblar** gondola, over the top to Beret, out to the far edge of **Baciver**, and back across the plateau.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross the Bonaigua flank, take the longest reds you can find, and finish the day by skiing the whole vertical from around 2,500 m back to the 1,500 m road base. Lunch is a sandwich in a lift queue; that is the deal.
itinerary.evening: Baqueira 1500 après at Moët, then a taxi or the ski bus back down. Do not drive the C-28 after a session there.
itinerary.dayStats: 30–35 piste km / roughly 6,000 m descent / 1,500–2,510 m, the full 1,000 m in one run at the end / 173 km total resort terrain across ~169 runs

itinerary.title: Half day on Beret, then out
itinerary.morning: Final morning on the **Pla de Beret** plateau — high, sunny, and the easiest place to ski with luggage already in the car. Two hours is enough.
itinerary.afternoon: Return hire kit by 13:00, then drive north over Bossòst to Toulouse. Allow extra: the Bossòst road and the Vielha tunnel both stack up on Sunday afternoons and the border is a real bottleneck in bad weather.
itinerary.evening: Overnight near Toulouse rather than chancing an early flight after a mountain drive.
itinerary.dayStats: Half day ~2,000 m descent / drive Salardú–Toulouse 2 h 45–3 h 30 with Sunday traffic / Vielha tunnel keeps the southern route open year-round / winter tyres or chains required by signage

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Rafael Leret
accommodationStrategy.description: Salardú at 1,268 m is the strategic base: five minutes from Baqueira 1500 by free ski bus, ten from the Beret road, and with a real village around it rather than a car park. Ski storage, early breakfast, and a bill roughly 40% below the slopeside equivalents. Around €80–€130 pppn.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Val de Neu
accommodationStrategy.description: The ski-in/ski-out option at the foot of the lifts, with a spa and the shortest possible morning. You are buying twenty minutes a day and paying heavily for it: roughly €250–€450 per room, and there is no village outside the door. Worth it with small children or a short trip.

accommodationStrategy.name: Parador de Arties
accommodationStrategy.description: Built around the Casa de Don Gaspar de Portolà in Arties at 1,143 m, midway between Vielha and Salardú, with the valley's best restaurant cluster on the doorstep. A 15-minute ski-bus run to the lifts. Roughly €120–€200 per room, and the most characterful bed in Aran.

logistics.connectivity: 4G is good in the villages, on the Baqueira bowl and across Beret, and unreliable on the Bonaigua back side and in the Aiguamòg valley. EU roaming applies. Download the Baqueira app and offline maps; the resort's own **Ski Track App**, new for 2025/26, logs descents and shares live location, which is genuinely useful on a big traverse day.
logistics.emergency: 112 reaches the **Bombers de la Generalitat** and the **GRAE** mountain rescue unit. Spain is EU, so EHIC/GHIC covers state care, but not off-piste rescue or repatriation — carry winter-sports insurance that names off-piste and helicopter recovery. The valley hospital is Espitau Val d'Aran in Vielha.
logistics.weather: Atlantic fronts arrive wet and heavy and can drop a metre in 36 hours, which is the resort's strength and its main disruptor. The **Port de la Bonaigua closes** in those events, cutting the C-28 to Esterri d'Àneu — the **Vielha tunnel** on the N-230 is the year-round southern lifeline. Foehn on the Spanish side can also spike freezing levels and shut top chairs on wind.
logistics.bookingWindows: Baqueira 1500 and Salardú beds for February and Semana Santa go 4–6 months out. Casa Irene needs a week. Guides for a powder day should be reserved in advance, not on the morning. Forfaits are cheapest bought online at least seven days ahead.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards work everywhere including the Banhs de Tredòs; small village bars still like cash. Tipping is rounding up, or 5–10% for a full restaurant meal.
logistics.transportRules: Winter tyres or chains are required by signage on the C-28 and enforced by the Mossos when it snows — a hire car from Toulouse may not come chained, so ask. The **BaqueiraPASS** keycard is reloadable and gets a better per-day rate than a gate ticket. The Val d'Aran ski bus is free; parking at Baqueira 1500 is the daily bottleneck, so use it.
logistics.permits: No park fees within the resort, but the **Aigüestortes i Estany de Sant Maurici National Park** boundary lies immediately south of the Bonaigua and has its own rules for ski touring — check before crossing. Drones require AESA compliance and are banned over the ski area. Off-piste is legal and unpatrolled; the resort does not rescue you for free outside the marked terrain.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable throughout the valley. Altitude is not an issue below 2,510 m. The real hazards are avalanche and the Bonaigua road. Read the **Lauegi d'Aran** bulletin daily and use Aran's published **ATES** terrain map when planning any touring — it is one of very few places in southern Europe where that resource exists.

proTips: Sleep in Salardú or Arties, not at Baqueira 1500. The free ski bus makes the slopeside premium pointless, the villages have restaurants, and you avoid the 08:15 car queue on the C-28 entirely.
Use the Blanhiblar gondola from Baqueira 1500 in the morning and drive to the Beret access in the afternoon. Splitting your entry points halves your time in lift queues on a Saturday.
Check the C-28 status over the Port de la Bonaigua before committing to that sector. If it closes while you are on the far side, the only way home is around the mountain.

Read the Lauegi bulletin yourself rather than asking the hotel. Aran publishes in five languages to EAWS standards and, uniquely for the Pyrenees, an ATES terrain classification — it is better information than most Alpine valleys give you.
Book the Banhs de Tredòs for a snowy afternoon rather than a clear one. Outdoor sulphur pools at 1,750 m in falling snow is the single best photograph of the week.

Order olla aranesa on a day you have skied hard. It is a slow winter stew of cabbage, beans, pork and pasta, it appears on menus only in the cold months, and it is the local dish that is actually local.
Buy the forfait online at least a week ahead and load it to a BaqueiraPASS card. The gate price is the worst price available and the card carries over to next season.
If the resort is wind-held above 2,200 m, go to Beret rather than home. The plateau sits low and open enough that its lifts often keep turning when the Baqueira and Bonaigua top chairs stop.

raw.Pass tiers by name: Baqueira sells a single resort **forfait** — there is no local-versus-area distinction here because there is only one area, and no regional super-pass equivalent to Dolomiti Superski. For 2025/26 the **one-day adult forfait reached €71.50**, up 3.6% on the previous season's €69 and the smallest rise in five years; the **weekend day rate ran about €66.50** and a **five-day package worked out around €60 per day**. A **6-day adult pass falls in the region of €300–€360**, with **children (roughly 7–12) around €200–€245** — banded, because Baqueira prices dynamically by date and the published multi-day tariff moves. A **season pass runs roughly €1,200–€1,300 adult.** There is a dedicated **beginner ticket at about €25 adult and €15 child**, covering the learning lifts only, plus a free conveyor at Beret. Passes load onto the reloadable **BaqueiraPASS** keycard, which reduces the per-day rate against gate prices; expect a small refundable card charge on first issue. Buy at least a week ahead online for the best rate. **There is no night skiing at Baqueira** — the resort has never run a floodlit product, so budget nothing for it.
raw.Lift network and the circuits you can sk: Three sectors on one continuous lift network. **Baqueira** rises from the roadside base at **Baqueira 1500** — the **Blanhiblar** and **Vaquèira** gondolas are the main access, lifting the morning crowd off the C-28 and up to the 1,800 m plateau — and tops out around Cap de Baqueira. **Beret** sits over the ridge to the north on the broad Pla de Beret plateau at about 1,850 m, sunnier, gentler and the family sector, with its own road access from Salardú. **Bonaigua** hangs on the far side of the **Port de la Bonaigua**, the 2,072 m pass on the C-28, and gives the longest fall-line pitches in the resort. The signature day is the **full traverse: Baqueira 1500 up to Cap de Baqueira, over into Beret, out to Baciver, back over the Bonaigua flank and home** — around 30–35 piste kilometres. **Cara Nord**, the north face above Argulls and Ta Dossau, is the shaded, cold-snow annexe that holds powder longest.
raw.Last lift and the bus that patches the g: Lifts run roughly **09:00–17:00** and the sector-linking chairs above Beret and Bonaigua close first, typically 16:15–16:30. The gap-patcher is the **free Val d'Aran ski bus**, which runs Vielha–Arties–Salardú–Tredòs–Baqueira 1500 through the day. If you are caught on the Bonaigua side after the last chair, the only way home is the **C-28 over the Port de la Bonaigua** — which is exactly the road that closes in snow.
raw.Snow reliability: The resort spans roughly **1,500 m at Baqueira 1500 to about 2,510 m at Cap de Baqueira / Tuc de Baciver**. The critical fact is aspect and airmass, not altitude: Val d'Aran is on the **Atlantic watershed**, so it takes the full moisture load of Biscay fronts that never reach the Catalan Pyrenees to the south. **173 km of skiable terrain** across roughly 169 marked runs plus four itineraries were published for 2025/26, with the season announced as **29 November 2025 to 6 April 2026** (other listings quote 12 December to 21 April — the gap is real and must be re-checked). Snowmaking is extensive and was extended for 2025/26 with 14 new guns at Ta Dossau, 12 old units replaced by six efficient ones, two new winch groomers and 2 km of additional wind fencing; **coverage is commonly given as around 50–60% of pisted kilometres, but Baqueira does not publish a firm percentage.** In a bad snow year the resort concentrates on the high Beret plateau and the shaded Cara Nord, and the return to Baqueira 1500 shuts, sending everyone down the gondolas.
raw.Off-piste and touring: This is the reason strong skiers come. **Escornacrabes** — literally "goat-scarer" in Aranese — is the resort's famous couloir, a narrow steep line off the Baqueira ridge that is skied as an itinerary rather than a piste. **Tuc de Salana**, **Tuc de Baciver** and the bowls beyond Baciver toward the Marimanya massif give the touring terrain, and the Aiguamòg valley toward Colomèrs is the classic ski-tour approach. The avalanche bulletin is the **Butlletí de Perill d'Allaus issued by the Centre de Lauegi d'Aran, the avalanche service of the Conselh Generau d'Aran** (lauegi.conselharan.org), published to EAWS standards in five languages — and uniquely for the Pyrenees, Aran also publishes an **ATES avalanche-terrain classification** for the valley, which is genuinely useful for planning. A guide is not legally mandated but is the practical default: local outfits include **Camins** and the freeride programme run through the **Escola d'Esquí Baqueira Beret**. Transceiver, shovel and probe are non-negotiable beyond the ropes.
raw.Piste breakdown: Of the roughly **173 km**, the split runs approximately 10% green, 35% blue, 40% red and 15% black. **Beginners** belong on the **Pla de Beret** plateau, which is wide, sunny and almost flat by Pyrenean standards, and on the free conveyor learning zone. **Intermediates** should live on the Baqueira bowl reds and the Beret–Baciver link, where the mileage is. **Experts** get the **Bonaigua** fall-line blacks, the **Cara Nord** shaded pitches, and — with a guide and a bulletin reading below 3 — Escornacrabes and the Baciver backcountry.
raw.Non-ski days: The **Banhs de Tredòs**, thermal pools at about 1,750 m up the Aiguamòg valley above Tredòs, fed by sulphurous springs and open outdoors in the snow, is the single best rest-day in the valley — roughly €18–€25 for a session. Beyond that: the Romanesque church of **Sant Miquèu** in Vielha with its Crist de Mijaran, **Santa Maria d'Arties**, the **Musèu dera Val d'Aran** in Vielha, marked snowshoe routes up the Aiguamòg and Valarties valleys, and the Nordic circuit at Beret.
raw.Hire, lockers and schools: Rental clusters at Baqueira 1500 and 1700 and in Salardú and Vielha; expect **€120–€190 a week** standard and **€220–€300** for performance or freeride skis with touring bindings. Slopeside lockers at Baqueira 1500 and Beret run **€6–€10 a day** and are worth it because the road base is where the parking chaos is. The **Escola d'Esquí Baqueira Beret** is the resort school: roughly **€250–€330 for five half-day group mornings**, **€65–€90 an hour** private with a lower hourly rate for full days, plus dedicated freeride and touring programmes.

trips.title: Levi & Ylläs: Lapland Twin-Resort Ski Week

bestPeriod.window: Late November to early May. **February–April is the sweet spot** — returning daylight, deep cold-dry snow and long cross-country conditions. December is dark (the sun barely clears the horizon at this latitude); late April gives spring skiing with 18 hours of light
bestPeriod.raw: Late November to early May. **February–April is the sweet spot** — returning daylight, deep cold-dry snow and long cross-country conditions. December is dark (the sun barely clears the horizon at this latitude); late April gives spring skiing with 18 hours of light

accommodation.note: €120–260 per night for a 2–4 person ski cabin; hotel doubles €150–280; peak Christmas–New Year and Easter can double this

food.note: €55–95 per day; cabins have full kitchens and the supermarket is far cheaper than the slope restaurants

transport.note: €250–420: flights to Kittilä (Levi is 15 minutes away) or Kolari rail, plus airport transfer and a ski bus pass

activities.note: Lift passes €55–70 per day, roughly €250–320 for six days; add €150–350 for a husky or reindeer day, snowmobile safari or a guided off-piste day

trips.summary: A seven-day winter sports & skiing itinerary in Kittilä & Kolari, Finnish Lapland, Finland.

itinerary.title: Arrival at Levi and the first laps
itinerary.morning: Fly to Kittilä — the airport is 15 minutes from Levi, one of the shortest ski transfers in Europe. Collect your lift pass and hire skis at the base.
itinerary.afternoon: Warm up on the front-face pistes served by the gondola. Levi's fell is broad and rounded rather than steep; the pleasure here is width, grooming and empty snow, not vertical.
itinerary.evening: Levi village has an actual après scene by Nordic standards. Eat early; Finnish kitchens close earlier than Alpine ones.

itinerary.title: Levi's full network and the floodlit evening
itinerary.morning: Ski the whole mountain: the World Cup slalom face on the front side, the longer blues on the back, and the tree runs on the lower flanks where the *tykky* — crown snow-load — turns the pines into white sculptures.
itinerary.afternoon: The freestyle parks and the family areas, or a lesson if you are new to Nordic conditions, which are colder and faster than Alpine snow.
itinerary.evening: **Floodlit skiing** is the answer to the short winter day: several Levi slopes are lit into the evening, and skiing under lights with the temperature at −15 °C is genuinely wonderful.

itinerary.title: Cross-country: the Levi track network
itinerary.morning: Finland's real ski culture is Nordic. Levi has around 230 km of machine-groomed track, including illuminated loops, running through forest and out onto the open fell.
itinerary.afternoon: Hire classic gear and take an instructor for two hours; the technique differs enough from alpine that a lesson transforms the week. Stop at a *laavu* — an open wooden shelter with a fire pit — and grill sausages, which is the correct Finnish lunch.
itinerary.evening: Smoke sauna, then a cold plunge or a roll in the snow. Non-negotiable.

itinerary.title: Transfer to Ylläs and the long runs
itinerary.morning: Drive or transfer 40 minutes to Ylläs. The fell rises to 718 m with 63 slopes across two sides, and it feels twice as empty as Levi.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the long blue from the top of the Ylläsjärvi side — around 3 km, the longest run in Finland — then cross the fell to the Äkäslompolo side. The views from the top run all the way to the Pallas fells.
itinerary.evening: Äkäslompolo is a village, not a resort strip: wooden houses in pine forest around a lake. Self-cater or eat at one of the handful of restaurants.

itinerary.title: Ylläs off-piste, tree skiing and the ski bus
itinerary.morning: Ylläs's tree skiing between the marked runs is the best lift-served off-piste in Finland, and after a snowfall the low-density powder in the *tykky* forest is extraordinary. Take a **local guide** — the fells are rounded and disorienting in flat light, and the tree zones are easy to get lost in.
itinerary.afternoon: The two base areas are linked by piste and by a frequent ski bus; use the bus to ski both sides without repeating.
itinerary.evening: Northern lights. Ylläs's low light pollution and the fell tops make it one of the better aurora bases in Lapland; the season runs roughly September to April on clear, dark nights.

itinerary.title: A day off the skis: huskies, reindeer or the Pallas fells
itinerary.morning: A husky safari, a reindeer farm visit with a Sámi host, or a snowmobile route — all standard, all bookable in advance, all better booked with the smaller local operators.
itinerary.afternoon: Alternatively, ski-tour or snowshoe into **Pallas–Yllästunturi National Park**, which surrounds both resorts — the same fells as the summer traverse in Trip 18, under two metres of snow.
itinerary.evening: Ice fishing on a frozen lake, or a last sauna.

itinerary.title: Last laps and departure
itinerary.morning: Morning skiing on the pass you have already paid for — most passes run to the day's end regardless of your flight.
itinerary.afternoon: Transfer to Kittilä (from Ylläs, about 1 h 15) and fly out.

accommodationStrategy.name: Levi ski-in/ski-out hotels and apartments
accommodationStrategy.description: Levi Hotel Spa and the Panorama-style properties on the fell put you on the snow with a pool and a spa. The village is compact, the ski bus is frequent and free with the pass, and the supermarket is walkable — which matters, because self-catering halves the food budget.

accommodationStrategy.name: Äkäslompolo log cabins
accommodationStrategy.description: Traditional Finnish *mökki* in pine forest: two to four bedrooms, a full kitchen, a drying room, a fireplace and a private sauna. €140–260 for the cabin, not per person, which makes Ylläs the best value in Lapland for a group of four. Ski-track access from the door is standard.

accommodationStrategy.name: Ylläsjärvi slope-side apartments
accommodationStrategy.description: The quieter southern base, closest to the longest run and the gondola-side lifts. Fewer restaurants, more snow, and a shorter transfer to the national park trailheads.

logistics.emergency: 112 and the **112 Suomi** app for GPS location. Pisteside first aid at both resorts; the hospital is in Kittilä with the main facility in Rovaniemi.
logistics.bookingWindows: Christmas–New Year and the Finnish and Central European school holiday weeks in February–March are the peaks — cabins go 6–12 months ahead. Late March to April is quieter, sunnier and cheaper.

other.label: Lift pass tiers
other.text: Passes are sold per resort by day, with meaningful discounts from three days upward and further reductions for children and seniors. Regional multi-resort options and combined Levi/Ylläs products have existed in some seasons — check the current arrangement before buying two separate passes. Prices and structures change every season. `verify: true`

other.label: Darkness is the real planning variable
other.text: At 67.8° N the sun does not rise for a period around the winter solstice, and even in January the skiable daylight is short. This is why floodlit slopes and headtorch Nordic loops exist. From late February onward the light is generous and by April it is endless.

other.label: Cold
other.text: −20 °C is a normal January morning and −30 °C happens. Goggles not sunglasses, a face covering, mittens over gloves, and battery-warmed insoles if you feel the cold. Phones die fast — keep them inside a layer.

other.label: Off-piste guides
other.text: Finnish fells are avalanche-poor by Alpine standards because of the low angles, but the risks here are different: whiteout on featureless rounded terrain, tree wells, extreme cold, and getting lost. Use local guides; several operate from both resorts.

other.label: Sámi culture
other.text: Reindeer herding is a living livelihood, not a show. Choose operators run by Sámi families, do not photograph people or corrals without asking, and be aware that "Lapland Sámi experiences" vary enormously in authenticity.

proTips: Come in **March**. You get full winter snow, ten hours of daylight, aurora still active at night, and prices well below the Christmas peak.
Rent a **cabin, not a hotel room**. Finnish self-catering cabins with a private sauna are the local standard, are cheaper for groups, and are the actual cultural experience.
Give **cross-country a proper half day** even if you came to ski downhill. The Levi and Ylläs track networks are among the best in the world and this is what Finns are really doing out there.
The *laavu* shelters on the track networks have firewood and a grill. Carry sausages and a thermos and lunch costs €3 instead of €25.
**Book Levi first, Ylläs second.** Arriving at the bigger, busier resort while you are fresh and finishing in the quiet forest at Äkäslompolo gives the week the right shape.

Aurora tip: you do not need a tour. Walk 15 minutes from the village edge, away from lights, on a clear night, and check an aurora forecast app. At this latitude a modest geomagnetic reading is enough.

raw.resort_profile: Two large fell resorts 40 minutes apart. Levi is Finland's biggest and busiest, with the country's most complete lift network, a World Cup slalom slope and a real village; Ylläs has more pistes and the longest run in Finland, spread across two quiet villages
raw.lift_network: Levi: roughly 43 slopes and 26 lifts including a gondola, with floodlit skiing. Ylläs: about 63 slopes and 29 lifts across two base areas (Äkäslompolo and Ylläsjärvi) linked by piste and ski bus
raw.snow_reliability: Very high — this is Arctic Finland. Cold, dry, low-density snow from late November to early May, with extensive snowmaking to guarantee an early-season opening. The limitation is darkness and cold, not snow cover
