trips.title: Chamonix Freeride: Grands Montets, Vallée Blanche and the Off-Piste Circuit

bestPeriod.note: February and March give the most stable glacier crossings; January can be colder but the Vallée Blanche moraine exit is icier.

trips.gatewayAirport: Geneva (GVA)
trips.summary: A week of guided and self-directed freeride in Chamonix, built around the Vallée Blanche, Grands Montets and Le Tour, with avalanche and crevasse discipline throughout.
trips.hook: Chamonix does not have one ski area — it has five separate mountains stitched together by a valley bus and a shared lift pass, and the best skiing on most of them is off the marked piste. This week uses all five, ends with the Vallée Blanche glacier descent from the Aiguille du Midi, and treats avalanche and crevasse risk as the daily planning question it actually is.

snapshot.Base(s): Chamonix-Mont-Blanc, with two nights positioned toward Argentière
snapshot.Best Period: January–March; February and March for the most reliable Vallée Blanche exit
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Five linked sectors (Brévent-Flégère, Grands Montets, Le Tour-Balme, Aiguille du Midi/Vallée Blanche); base 1,035 m at Chamonix, top 3,842 m at the Aiguille du Midi
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Geneva (GVA); shuttle or train (via Saint-Gervais and the Mont-Blanc Express) to Chamonix, roughly 1h15–1h45
snapshot.Who It Suits: Confident off-piste skiers and riders comfortable on variable snow, roped glacier travel and long unmarked descents

itinerary.title: Arrival and orientation
itinerary.morning: Fly into Geneva and take the shuttle or the Léman Express/Mont-Blanc Express rail combination to Chamonix. Check into the base hotel and rent skis or a splitboard, boots and an avalanche kit (transceiver, probe, shovel) from a rental shop on Rue Joseph Vallot or Rue du Docteur Paccard.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk to the Maison de la Montagne on Place de l'Église, home of the Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix and the Office de Haute Montagne (OHM), the free walk-in service where guides brief on snowpack, glacier conditions and the daily avalanche bulletin (Météo-France BRA). Buy the Chamonix Le Pass covering Brévent-Flégère, Grands Montets, Le Tour-Balme and Les Houches.
itinerary.evening: Group briefing with the guide if pre-booked, or a solo transceiver practice session in the search field most rental shops keep near their counters.
itinerary.dayStats: 0 vertical metres skied · 0 sectors · 0 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Brévent-Flégère, orientation day
itinerary.morning: Take the Téléphérique du Brévent from Chamonix centre up to 2,525 m. This south-facing sector catches the sun earliest and holds up best after fresh snow blows through the Grands Montets side, so it is the sensible opener while you read how the group skis together.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride across to La Flégère (1,877 m base, Index at 2,385 m) via the valley traverse, and ski the open bowls below the Refuge de Bellachat side of the ridge, staying inside the pisted boundary until the guide has assessed the day's danger rating on the European five-level scale.
itinerary.evening: Aprés-ski on Rue du Docteur Paccard; check tomorrow's Grands Montets lift status before dinner — the sector is wind-exposed and the Argentière side often closes above Lognan when the valley itself is calm.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 3,200 m vertical · 1 sector (Brévent-Flégère) · 4.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Grands Montets and the Argentière glacier
itinerary.morning: Bus to Argentière and ride the Télécabine de Plan-Joran. Note before you go: the historic cable car from Lognan to the Aiguille des Grands Montets summit (3,295 m) has been shut since a 2018 fire destroyed the mid-station, and the upper mountain has run on a reduced, rebuilt lift configuration since — check the current top station with the lift company before committing a day to this sector, the interconnect most likely to have changed since last season.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the accessible pistes and marked off-piste variants above Lognan, with views onto the Argentière glacier and the Aiguille Verte. With a guide, the Pas de Chèvre passage links this basin toward the Mer de Glace system for skiers planning ahead to the Vallée Blanche exit later in the week.
itinerary.evening: Early return to Chamonix; the Argentière-side buses thin out after 17:00.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,600 m vertical · 1 sector (Grands Montets) · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Le Tour-Balme and the Vallée du Trient
itinerary.morning: Bus to Le Tour and ride the Télécabine de Charamillon to Col de Balme (2,270 m), the highest and most north-facing sector in the valley and the most snow-reliable when the lower mountain is thin.
itinerary.afternoon: With the Compagnie des Guides, this is the launch point for the Vallée du Trient ski tour: a short skin over the col into Switzerland, then a long glacier and forest descent past the Trient glacier toward Vallorcine, finishing at the train station. Crevasses on the upper glacier make this a roped, guided day only.
itinerary.evening: Train back from Vallorcine on the Mont-Blanc Express, a scenic 25-minute ride down the valley.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,900 m vertical (plus one uphill skin) · 1 sector (Le Tour-Balme) · 3 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Vallée Blanche, guided
itinerary.morning: Early start at the Aiguille du Midi téléphérique — arrive before 07:30 to beat the queue, since the ride to 3,842 m runs in two stages. Meet the Compagnie des Guides party at the top; the guide fits harnesses and rope for the exposed ridge walk off the summit station, the single most consequence-heavy few minutes of the week.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski or ride the Vallée Blanche itself: roughly 20 km and 2,700 m of descent down the Géant and Mer de Glace glaciers to Chamonix or, in low-snow years, to a shuttle pickup partway down. Crevasses are real and hidden by snow bridges; the route is skied roped and guided, never solo, regardless of how many tracks are already visible.
itinerary.evening: A long, satisfied dinner — this is the trip's centrepiece and most parties are tired by 18:00.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,700 m vertical · 1 itinerary (Vallée Blanche) · 1 lift ride (Aiguille du Midi).

itinerary.title: Second freeride day, weather-dependent
itinerary.morning: Check the Aiguille du Midi status before making plans — it is the valley's most wind-sensitive lift, with holds common above 60–70 km/h at altitude, so keep this day flexible. If it is running and conditions are stable, a second glacier tour (the Envers du Plan variant off the Vallée Blanche, or a return to Grands Montets) extends the week's off-piste mileage.
itinerary.afternoon: If the Midi is on hold, default to Grands Montets or Le Tour, both of which sit lower and are less exposed to wind than the Aiguille du Midi's summit ridge.
itinerary.evening: Gear rinse and dry — wet skins and rope need to dry overnight before packing.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 2,400 m vertical · 1 sector (weather-dependent) · 3.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Final morning and departure
itinerary.morning: A short session at Brévent-Flégère, the most forgiving last-morning sector, then return skis and boots by the shop's midday deadline.
itinerary.afternoon: Shuttle or train to Geneva for the flight home.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,200 m vertical · 1 sector (Brévent-Flégère) · 2 lift hours.

accommodationStrategy.name: Heliopic Hôtel & Spa
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits at the base of the Aiguille du Midi téléphérique, which matters directly on the Vallée Blanche day: no valley transfer, no early bus, just a walk to the lift queue before 07:30. Ski/boot storage and a drying room are standard.
accommodationStrategy.booking: October for a February–March week.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Les Grands Montets
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits in Argentière itself, a two-minute walk from the Plan-Joran gondola base, so the Grands Montets and Le Tour days start without a bus. Quieter and slightly cheaper than central Chamonix.
accommodationStrategy.booking: eight weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Faucigny
accommodationStrategy.description: A straightforward central option on Rue Joseph Vallot, close to the Maison de la Montagne, rental shops and the Brévent lift base — useful for the orientation and departure days.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; French mountain rescue (PGHM) is reached via 112.
logistics.weather: The Aiguille du Midi cable car suspends in high wind several times most winters; build a spare day into the itinerary rather than scheduling the Vallée Blanche on the last possible morning.
logistics.bookingWindows: Compagnie des Guides Vallée Blanche departures fill weeks ahead in February half-term and around Easter; book on arrival or before.
logistics.money: Cards are accepted everywhere in town; carry cash for the smaller Argentière bakeries and the OHM donation box.

other.label: Avalanche bulletin
other.text: Météo-France issues the BRA daily for the Mont-Blanc massif on the European 1–5 danger scale; read it every morning at the OHM or online before choosing a sector.

other.label: Mandatory kit for anything off-piste
other.text: Transceiver, probe and shovel, carried and switched on, for every skier — rental shops and guides check this and will refuse an unequipped client.

other.label: Lift pass logistics
other.text: The Chamonix Le Pass does not automatically include the Aiguille du Midi téléphérique or Vallée Blanche access — these are ticketed separately, often bundled into a guided day.

other.label: Insurance
other.text: Standard travel insurance rarely covers off-piste or glacier skiing — check for an off-piste/ski-touring extension before you go.

proTips: Ride the Aiguille du Midi before 07:30; the queue triples by 09:00 and any wind hold usually shows by mid-morning.
Ski Brévent-Flégère on the first storm-cycle morning — its south aspect sheds new snow into rideable corn faster than the shadier Grands Montets side.
Confirm the Grands Montets top-lift configuration with the lift company on the day, not from a website the night before — this sector has changed more than any other since the 2018 fire.
The Vallée du Trient tour finishes at Vallorcine station; buy the return train ticket that morning rather than searching for a machine with skis on.
Use the OHM's free morning briefing even on days you ski without a guide — it is the most current route-condition source in the valley.
Eat mountain lunch before 12:00 or after 13:30; Flégère and Lognan are packed in the standard slot.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Five linked sectors (Brévent-Flégère, Grands Montets, Le Tour-Balme, Aiguille du Midi/Vallée Blanche); base 1,035 m at Chamonix, top 3,842 m at the Aiguille du Midi
raw.Who It Suits: Confident off-piste skiers and riders comfortable on variable snow, roped glacier travel and long unmarked descents

typeSpecific.surface: Five linked sectors (Brévent-Flégère, Grands Montets, Le Tour-Balme, Aiguille du Midi/Vallée Blanche); base 1,035 m at Chamonix, top 3,842 m at the Aiguille du Midi
typeSpecific.audience: Confident off-piste skiers and riders comfortable on variable snow, roped glacier travel and long unmarked descents

packingNotes: Full avalanche kit: transceiver, probe, shovel — rent locally if you are not bringing your own.
A climbing harness is provided by the guide for the Vallée Blanche but bring your own gloves thin enough to clip a carabiner.
Glacier glasses or goggles with a category 4 lens; the Vallée Blanche at midday is blindingly bright.
A buff or balaclava for the Aiguille du Midi summit ridge, which is routinely 15–20°C colder than valley Chamonix.
Wide-platform freeride or all-mountain skis; piste skis are the wrong tool for every sector on this trip bar the final morning.
A small day pack with space for skins, a spare layer and water — most days involve at least one short walk or skin.
whatCouldGoWrong: **The Aiguille du Midi is on wind hold.** Fallback: swap the Vallée Blanche day for Grands Montets or Le Tour and keep a spare day at the end of the week for a rescheduled attempt.
**The Grands Montets top section is closed or reconfigured.** Fallback: the lower Plan-Joran sector still skis well after a fresh dump; Le Tour-Balme is the better full-mountain alternative.
**A storm cycle strips the valley of visibility for two days.** Fallback: Brévent-Flégère's tree-lined lower slopes remain skiable in flat light when the higher glacier terrain does not.
**Vallée Blanche departures are fully booked.** Fallback: book on Day 1 at the Maison de la Montagne rather than waiting, and hold a mid-week weather window as backup.
**Someone in the group is not fit for a full glacier day.** Fallback: split the party — the guide can choose a shorter, gentler Vallée Blanche variant depending on conditions and ability.

trips.title: Les 3 Vallées from Méribel — Courchevel to Val Thorens

bestPeriod.note: February and March give the most reliable snow across all altitudes; late-season March offers longer light for the Val Thorens and Orelle sectors.

trips.gatewayAirport: Chambéry (CMF)
trips.summary: A week based in Méribel using the full 3 Vallées interconnect to reach Courchevel, Val Thorens and Orelle, with pass tiers explained and a guided off-piste day.
trips.hook: Les 3 Vallées is the largest lift-connected ski area on earth, and Méribel sits at its geographic middle, which is exactly why it works as a base: Courchevel is one valley over, Val Thorens the other, and neither requires a car. This week uses the interconnect properly — including the two points where it actually breaks down — and spends a full day off the marked pistes with a certified guide.

snapshot.Base(s): Méribel (7 nights)
snapshot.Best Period: December–March; February/March most snow-secure across all altitudes
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Les 3 Vallées: approx. 600 km piste; base 1,450 m (Méribel) to 3,230 m (Cime de Caron, Val Thorens)
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Chambéry (CMF), 1h30 transfer; Geneva (GVA) or Lyon (LYS) also viable, 2h30
snapshot.Who It Suits: Confident intermediates and advanced skiers who want to actually use the scale of the area, not just one valley

itinerary.title: Arrival and Méribel orientation
itinerary.morning: Transfer from Chambéry to Méribel (1,450 m), roughly 90 minutes by road up the Tarentaise valley and the Méribel access road.
itinerary.afternoon: Buy the appropriate pass tier for the week (see Smart Logistics below) and take the Saulire Express or Roc de Fer chairs above Méribel centre for an easy orientation lap, finishing down toward Méribel-Mottaret at 1,700 m, the resort's higher and snow-surer satellite village.
itinerary.evening: Méribel's centre, deliberately built in traditional chalet style since the resort's 1938 founding by a British skier fleeing the newly annexed Austrian Alps, is compact enough to explore on foot.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 900 m vertical · Méribel/Mottaret sectors · 2 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Méribel valley in full
itinerary.morning: Ski the Méribel valley's own terrain properly before crossing anywhere else: the Mont Vallon cable car above Mottaret reaches 2,952 m, the valley's highest point, with a long, varied descent back down.
itinerary.afternoon: The Plattières and Tougnète sectors on the valley's eastern flank connect toward Les Menuires and St Martin de Belleville — worth a look even on a Méribel-focused day, since the lift network here is genuinely open rather than needing a specific "linking" chair.
itinerary.evening: A Méribel Valley pass (the resort's own local ticket, cheaper than the full 3 Vallées pass) genuinely covers everything skied so far — worth knowing before paying for the full interconnect ticket on day one.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 4,200 m vertical · Méribel/Mottaret/Tougnète sectors · 4.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Courchevel, and the Saulire bottleneck
itinerary.morning: Cross into the Courchevel valley via the Saulire cable car, the historic link between the two valleys and, on a busy day, the single biggest queue in the 3 Vallées — arrive by 08:45 to beat the mid-morning crush, since this cabin is the actual chokepoint of the whole interconnect. In strong wind it is also the first lift on this side to suspend, stranding skiers on whichever side of the ridge they started from.
itinerary.afternoon: Courchevel's four linked villages — Courchevel 1850 (the luxury end), 1650, Moriond and Le Praz — offer a different character: wider, more manicured pistes and noticeably higher prices in 1850's restaurants. Ski down through the Bel Air and Ariondaz sectors for a varied return.
itinerary.evening: Return over the Saulire before its last-departure time, checked each morning at the base — missing it means a long piste-and-lift detour back via Méribel-Mottaret rather than a direct crossing.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 4,500 m vertical · Courchevel valley (1850/1650/Moriond/Le Praz) · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Val Thorens and the Col de Chanrossa
itinerary.morning: Cross into the Val Thorens/Belleville valley via the Col de Chanrossa or Mont de la Chambre lift chain from Méribel-Mottaret — a smoother link than the Saulire, though it too closes first in genuinely severe wind since it runs along an exposed ridge.
itinerary.afternoon: Val Thorens itself sits at 2,300 m, the highest resort centre in Europe, and its lift-served terrain reaches the Cime de Caron at 3,230 m by cable car — the area's highest point and, on a clear day, a view stretching to Mont Blanc. This altitude is also the honest reason Val Thorens holds snow later into spring than either Méribel or Courchevel; if the week has been marginal for snow lower down, weight more time here.
itinerary.evening: Return to Méribel via the same link chain; Val Thorens' own centre, purpose-built and functional rather than picturesque, is not worth an overnight detour on this itinerary.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 4,800 m vertical · Val Thorens/Belleville valley · 4.5 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Orelle, the Maurienne-side extension
itinerary.morning: Orelle is the 3 Vallées' fourth access point, added in 2011 specifically to give the area a direct link from the Maurienne valley and the A43 motorway, avoiding the longer Tarentaise approach — useful context for why it exists, and also why it is the area's most exposed single link. The Bouquetin tri-cable gondola climbs from the Orelle valley floor up to the Cime de Caron ridge in one long span; it is the lift most likely to suspend in high wind of anything in the network, and when it closes, Orelle is effectively cut off from the rest of the 3 Vallées.
itinerary.afternoon: Approach Orelle from the Val Thorens side instead — ski down to the Bouquetin's upper station and ride it down, then back up, for a genuinely different, quieter pocket of the area with good tree-line skiing lower down that the higher valleys lack.
itinerary.evening: Return to Méribel via Val Thorens and the Col de Chanrossa link, timed against the posted last-lift schedule.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 3,600 m vertical · Orelle/Val Thorens link · 4 lift hours.

itinerary.title: Guided off-piste day
itinerary.morning: Book a full day with the Bureau des Guides de Méribel or the off-piste programme run by ESF Méribel (École du Ski Français), both established local operations offering certified-guide freeride days. The Vallée des Encombres, accessed from the ridge above St Martin de Belleville, is the area's best-known off-piste itinerary: a long, unpatrolled descent through wild, partially wooded terrain that is genuinely not a place to go without a guide who knows the current line and snowpack.
itinerary.afternoon: Depending on conditions, the guide may instead choose lines off the Mont Vallon or Col de Chanrossa ridges, checking the daily Météo-France avalanche bulletin, rated on the standard five-level European avalanche danger scale (1 Low to 5 Very High), before committing. Transceiver, probe and shovel are standard kit for the day, either brought or supplied and checked by the guide office.
itinerary.evening: A debrief with the group is normal practice; guide offices here often flag which lines are worth another look before the snow changes character later in the season.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,200–1,800 m vertical off-piste · Vallée des Encombres/Mont Vallon sectors · full guided day.

itinerary.title: St Martin de Belleville and departure
itinerary.morning: A gentler final morning in the quieter St Martin de Belleville sector, a genuine working Savoyard village rather than a purpose-built resort, with good tree-lined runs back toward the valley.
itinerary.afternoon: Return to Méribel, hand back rental gear, and transfer to Chambéry with a comfortable buffer before an evening flight.
itinerary.evening: Flight home from Chambéry.
itinerary.dayStats: approx. 1,800 m vertical · St Martin de Belleville/Méribel sectors · 2.5 lift hours.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Le Coucou
accommodationStrategy.description: A short walk from the Saulire lift base, positioned for the early starts the Courchevel crossing rewards, with ski storage and boot warmers standard.
accommodationStrategy.booking: August for the February peak.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €280–€400 per night for two, half board

accommodationStrategy.name: Résidence Le Village Montana
accommodationStrategy.description: Apartments at 1,700 m, closer to the Mont Vallon cable car and the Val Thorens-direction lifts, and generally cheaper than central Méribel for an equivalent standard.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two to three months ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Le Grand Coeur
accommodationStrategy.description: A well-established Méribel hotel a short walk from the centre, with an early breakfast service that suits the 08:45 start needed to beat the Saulire queue.
accommodationStrategy.booking: August for Christmas and February school-holiday weeks.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €320–€460 per night for two, half board

logistics.connectivity: Reliable in all four resort centres; drops out on the high ridge lifts and in the Vallée des Encombres, one more reason the guided day carries a radio.
logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; French mountain rescue (PGHM) also reachable via 112. Piste patrol response within resort boundaries is fast given the density of lift infrastructure.
logistics.weather: The Saulire cable car and the Orelle-side Bouquetin gondola are the two most wind-sensitive links; build a spare half-day into the week rather than assuming every crossing will run.
logistics.bookingWindows: French Christmas/New Year and February school-holiday weeks (staggered by zone) sell out Méribel's better properties up to a year ahead; book the guided off-piste day two to three weeks ahead in high season.
logistics.money: Cards standard everywhere; RFID pass cards are used at every lift gate — keep it accessible rather than buried in a pack.

other.label: Ski pass tiers
other.text: A Méribel Valley pass (local only, covering Méribel and Mottaret) runs approx. €65–€72 per day or €330–€370 for six days in 2026 and is genuinely enough for a Méribel-only week. The full 3 Vallées pass, needed for Courchevel, Val Thorens and Orelle, runs approx. €78–€86 per day or €400–€450 for six days. There is no meaningful middle tier — local valley or the whole interconnect.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 pan-European; French mountain rescue (PGHM) also reachable via 112. Piste patrol response within resort boundaries is fast given the density of lift infrastructure.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Last-lift times on the inter-valley links shift through the season and are posted each morning — check the return-crossing time before heading to Courchevel or Val Thorens.

other.label: Avalanche equipment
other.text: Mandatory for the Vallée des Encombres and any off-piste terrain — transceiver, probe and shovel; guide offices check kit but this does not substitute for self-rescue competence.

proTips: Cross to Courchevel before 09:00; the Saulire queue by 10:30 on a Saturday changeover morning can run 30–40 minutes.
Weight the back half of the week toward Val Thorens and Orelle if the season has run mild — the altitude difference from Méribel's 1,450 m base is real.

A Méribel Valley pass genuinely pays for itself over a full 3 Vallées pass if you are not planning to cross into Courchevel or Val Thorens more than once or twice — do the arithmetic before buying the full tier by default.
Book the Vallée des Encombres guided day for the clearest forecast window in the week; visibility on the exposed St Martin ridge approach matters as much as snow quality.
St Martin de Belleville's village restaurants run noticeably cheaper than Courchevel 1850's for an equivalent meal.
Check the Bouquetin gondola's live status before committing to an Orelle-side day in anything but calm weather.

raw.Who It Suits: Confident intermediates and advanced skiers who want to actually use the scale of the area, not just one valley

typeSpecific.surface: Les 3 Vallées: approx. 600 km piste; base 1,450 m (Méribel) to 3,230 m (Cime de Caron, Val Thorens)
typeSpecific.audience: Confident intermediates and advanced skiers who want to actually use the scale of the area, not just one valley

packingNotes: Transceiver, probe and shovel for the guided off-piste day.
A helmet, standard practice on the steeper Courchevel and Mont Vallon terrain.
Goggles with a low-light lens for the exposed ridge crossings in flat light.
Layers for a wide range: Val Thorens at 2,300–3,230 m runs noticeably colder than Méribel's 1,450 m base village.
Cash in small notes for mountain restaurants that prefer it.
A daypack for the guided day, sized for spare layers, water and emergency kit.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Wind closes the Saulire cable car.** Fallback: ski Méribel's own extensive terrain that day, or cross to Val Thorens via the more sheltered Chanrossa link instead.
**The Bouquetin gondola suspends, stranding an Orelle-side plan.** Fallback: retreat to the Val Thorens sector, fully accessible from Méribel regardless of Orelle's status.
**Low snow at Méribel's 1,450 m base.** Fallback: spend more time at Val Thorens and Mottaret's higher terrain, both holding cover longer.

**The Vallée des Encombres guided day is fully booked.** Fallback: book the alternate operator — ESF Méribel if the Bureau des Guides is full — or shift to Mont Vallon's more accessible off-piste pockets.

trips.title: Parnassos & Arachova: Skiing Above the Oracle
trips.subRegion: Mount Parnassos, Arachova & Delphi, Central Greece

bestPeriod.window: Late January–late February, the only weeks in which Parnassos can be relied on to have both sectors open
bestPeriod.avoid: 24 December–6 January, when Arachova doubles in price and the access road gridlocks; and after mid-March, when the mountain is usually finished regardless of what the calendar says
bestPeriod.raw: Late January–late February, the only weeks in which Parnassos can be relied on to have both sectors open

accommodation.note: Arachova guesthouses €70–€140 per room; Delphi and Polydrosos 30–40% less

food.note: Taverna mains €10–€18; tsipouro €4–€6; mountain canteen food is poor and overpriced — eat in the villages

transport.note: Hire car €35–€55/day plus fuel and tolls; snow chains are a legal requirement, budget for hire

activities.note: Lift tickets €20 weekday / €35 weekend, Delphi site and museum, one guided snowshoe day

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5 — four short lift-served days on modest vertical, plus a snowshoe day on the Livadi plateau and a lot of walking at Delphi; the demand is weather patience, not fitness

trips.gatewayAirport: ATH Athens Eleftherios Venizelos, 200 km / 2 h 30–3 h to Arachova; the ski centre is a further 27 km / 35–45 min above the town
trips.summary: Parnassos is the strangest ski week in Europe, and the reason to do it is not the skiing. It is the fact that you can spend a morning on a lift-served bowl at 2,200 m looking south over the Gulf of Corinth, and an afternoon walking the Sacred Way at **Delphi**, ten kilometres down the mountain, where the Greeks located the centre of the world. **Arachova**, a vertical stone village at 950 m clinging to the mountainside between the two, has spent thirty years turning itself into Greece's winter social capital — the ratio of fur coats to ski boots in its bars on a Saturday night is genuinely remarkable. The ski centre itself is state-run, with two linked sectors, **Kelaria** and **Fterolakka**, a third at **Gerontovrachos**, and Greece's first and only gondola lifts. The honest framing is this: the mountain is small, the season is short, the snow is unreliable, and you must build the week so that a bad snow report does not ruin it. This itinerary therefore alternates ski days with Delphi, the Corycian Cave, the north-side villages of **Agoriani/Eptalofos** and **Polydrosos**, and the tsipouro-and-formaela circuit — so that skiing is the bonus, not the premise.

itinerary.title: Athens to Arachova, and the first look at the mountain
itinerary.morning: Land at **ATH** and pick up a hire car. **Confirm the car has snow chains and that you know how to fit them before you leave the airport** — on the Parnassos access road they are a legal requirement in snow conditions and the police turn cars back without them.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive northwest, roughly 200 km and 2 h 30–3 h via Thiva and Livadeia, climbing the last stretch to **Arachova** at 950 m. Check in, then walk up the **264 steps to Agios Georgios** at the top of the village for the view down the Pleistos gorge toward the Gulf of Corinth.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **Taverna Dasargyris**, the village's long-standing kitchen — order the **formaela** fried at the table, kokoretsi if it is on, and a carafe of **tsipouro**. Then check tomorrow's snow report at snowreport.gr before you sleep.
itinerary.dayStats: ATH–Arachova ≈ 200 km / 2 h 30–3 h / Arachova 950 m / snow chains legally required on the access road / Delphi 10 km west

itinerary.title: Kelaria: the gondola, and learning the mountain
itinerary.morning: Drive the 27 km up to **Kelaria** — 35–45 minutes and around 800 m of climb, on a road that is properly maintained but genuinely alpine. Arrive before 09:00 on a weekday and the car park is empty. Buy the **weekday ticket at €20**, or **€35 if it is a weekend or holiday**, with **5% off if you buy online**.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the **Ermis gondola**, the first gondola built in a Greek ski resort, and spend the day working the Kelaria blues and reds. The terrain is wide, sunny and forgiving; the views south over the Gulf of Corinth from the top are the reason people photograph this place.
itinerary.evening: Back down to Arachova. The village's bars fill from about 20:00 and do not empty; **Taverna Panagiota** for dinner first, then whichever bar on the main street has the crowd.
itinerary.dayStats: Arachova–Kelaria 27 km / 35–45 min / Kelaria base ≈ 1,750 m / weekday ticket €20, weekend €35 / lifts 08:30–16:00 high season, 09:00–15:00 low

itinerary.title: Delphi, the Charioteer, and a deliberate non-ski day
itinerary.morning: Do not ski. Drive 10 km west to **Delphi** and be at the gate when it opens. Walk the Sacred Way up past the treasuries to the **Temple of Apollo**, then on to the theatre and the stadium at the top — in February you will have most of it to yourself, and snow on the Phaedriades cliffs above is worth the trip alone.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Delphi Archaeological Museum** and the bronze **Charioteer**, then walk 15 minutes east to the **Tholos at the Sanctuary of Athena Pronaia**, which is the building on every postcard. Lunch in Delphi village looking down the olive valley toward Itea.
itinerary.evening: Eat in Delphi rather than driving back hungry — **Taverna Vakhos** on the upper street has the view. Then back to Arachova for a quiet night.
itinerary.dayStats: Arachova–Delphi 10 km / 15 min / site plus museum 3–4 h minimum / combined ticket typically €12–€20 winter rate / zero vertical metres skied

itinerary.title: Fterolakka, Gerontovrachos and the full width of the centre
itinerary.morning: Start from the lower base at **Fterolakka**, roughly 1,640 m and more sheltered than Kelaria, and ski the linking terrain across the ridge. This is the whole of the ski centre in one traverse and it takes a morning.
itinerary.afternoon: If the wind allows, take the chair up into **Gerontovrachos**, the highest and most exposed sector at around 2,250 m, which holds the coldest snow and is the first thing to close. **Be back on your own base's side of the ridge by 15:00** — a wind hold on the connecting lift means the car-park shuttle.
itinerary.evening: Drive down the north side instead of back to Arachova and eat in **Agoriani (Eptalofos)** or **Polydrosos** — fir-forested villages with wood stoves, half Arachova's prices, and no fur coats at all.
itinerary.dayStats: Fterolakka ≈ 1,640 m, Gerontovrachos to ≈ 2,250–2,260 m / ≈ 23 km of piste, 17 lifts / vertical band ≈ 650 m / ridge turnaround 15:00

itinerary.title: Weather-contingency and rest day: Livadi, the Corycian Cave and warm food
itinerary.morning: This is the designed flex day, and on Parnassos it is more likely than anywhere else in this collection to become a forced one — if the mountain has not opened, or a southerly has stripped it, take it now. Drive up to the **Livadi plateau** above Arachova, around 1,100–1,200 m, and either sledge with the Greek families or fit snowshoes.
itinerary.afternoon: Snowshoe from Livadi to the **Corycian Cave (Korykion Antron)**, the enormous stalactite cavern that Pausanias described and that was sacred to Pan and the nymphs — a 3–4 hour round trip in snow, best done with a guide from **Trekking Hellas** or the local mountaineering club, because the plateau navigation is not obvious in cloud.
itinerary.evening: Back to Arachova and eat properly: **Taverna Kaplanis** for slow-cooked meat, more formaela, and the local hilopites. Buy a rug or a length of woven cloth in one of the village workshops on the way.
itinerary.dayStats: Livadi plateau ≈ 1,100–1,200 m / Corycian Cave round trip 3–4 h on snowshoes / guided day ≈ €50–€90 pp / no EAWS avalanche bulletin in Greece — guide advised

itinerary.title: Best-conditions ski day, or the tour to Liakoura
itinerary.morning: Keep this day flexible and spend it wherever the mountain is best. If the snow has come good, this is the day to ski Kelaria and Gerontovrachos properly and to take the **4-day combined ticket at €95** if you have not already — it pays for itself on the third day.
itinerary.afternoon: If conditions are settled and you have booked a guide, the alternative is the **ski tour or winter ascent to Liakoura, the 2,457 m summit of Parnassos**, from the top of the lifts: a modest skin in good weather, a serious mountain day in bad. The view takes in the Gulf of Corinth, Giona, Vardousia and, on the clearest days, the Peloponnese.
itinerary.evening: Last night in Arachova. Start with tsipouro and mezedes somewhere on the main street, then dinner wherever the locals are, which will not be the place with the English menu outside.
itinerary.dayStats: Liakoura 2,457 m / summit day 4–6 h round trip from the lifts / 4-day combined ticket €95 / guide €150–€300 per group per day

itinerary.title: Down the mountain, and back to Athens
itinerary.morning: If the lifts are turning and your flight is late, take a **€15 low-season afternoon ticket** for a final couple of hours — Parnassos's short hours mean a morning-only ski is a genuinely good-value option here.
itinerary.afternoon: Return hire gear and chains in Arachova, then drive back to **ATH**: 200 km, 2 h 30–3 h, and add an hour if it is a Sunday evening in February, when the whole of Athens is coming down this road at once.
itinerary.evening: Fly out, or spend the last night in Athens — the drive is manageable but the Sunday return traffic on the Athens–Lamia motorway is the single most reliably unpleasant part of this trip.
itinerary.dayStats: Half-day afternoon ticket €15 low season / €20 high / Arachova–ATH 200 km / 2 h 30–3 h, +1 h Sunday evening / allow 2 h 30 at ATH

accommodationStrategy.name: Xenonas Generali
accommodationStrategy.description: A stone *xenonas* in the old part of the village, with fireplaces, thick walls and the sort of breakfast that assumes you are going up a mountain. It puts you inside walking distance of the tavernas and bars — which matters, because Arachova's streets are narrow, vertical and impossible to park on. Roughly €80–€140 per room.

accommodationStrategy.name: Domotel Anemolia Mountain Resort
accommodationStrategy.description: The comfortable option, set on the ridge with pool, spa and a long view down the Pleistos valley toward the sea. Choose it for the parking, the family space and the ability to reach both Delphi and the ski road quickly without navigating Arachova's lanes. Roughly €110–€200 per room.

accommodationStrategy.name: Polydrosos or Eptalofos guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: The counter-strategy: sleep on the quiet, forested northern flank of Parnassos, pay 30–40% less, eat better and more cheaply, and approach the ski centre from the north road. The cost is distance from Delphi and total absence of nightlife — which for many travellers is the point. Roughly €50–€90 per room.

logistics.connectivity: Coverage is good in Arachova, Delphi and at the ski bases, patchy on the Livadi plateau and absent in the Corycian Cave approach. Greece is **inside EU roaming**, so EU and most UK bundles apply at home rates. Download offline maps for the plateau.
logistics.emergency: **112** works nationally; **166** is the ambulance (EKAB) and **199** the fire service. Mountain rescue is provided by **EMAK**, the fire service's special disaster response unit, and the volunteer **Hellenic Rescue Team**; helicopter availability is weather- and asset-dependent and cannot be assumed. Greece is **in the EU**, so **EHIC/GHIC applies** to state healthcare — but not to rescue costs or repatriation. The nearest hospitals are at Amfissa and Livadeia.
logistics.weather: Parnassos lives and dies by Mediterranean cyclogenesis. A single depression tracking up the Ionian can deliver a metre in 48 hours; a warm **southerly (the *notias*)** behind it can take most of it away in a day. Wind is the other constant — **Gerontovrachos is exposed and closes on wind more often than on snow**, and the linking traverse between Kelaria and Fterolakka goes with it. Fog on the plateau is common and total. Check **snowreport.gr** and the ski centre's own bulletin every evening; do not plan more than a day ahead.
logistics.bookingWindows: Arachova beds for **Christmas–6 January and for weekends in February** need booking two to three months out and prices roughly double; midweek is available almost on the day. Lift tickets need no advance purchase, though the **5% online discount** is worth two minutes. Guided snowshoe or summit days should be arranged a week ahead. Delphi needs no booking in winter.
logistics.money: The **euro**. Cards are accepted in Arachova hotels and the larger tavernas; village kafeneia, the smaller north-side tavernas and some ski-centre kiosks prefer cash. ATMs exist in Arachova and Delphi. Tipping is rounding up, 5–10%.
logistics.transportRules: **Snow chains are a legal requirement on the Parnassos access road when conditions and signage demand, and this is actively enforced** — the police stop cars at the junction above Arachova and turn back those without them. Confirm your hire car carries a set, know how to fit them, and practise once in daylight. The Athens–Lamia motorway is tolled in several sections. Winter tyres are not legally mandated in Greece as they are in the Balkans, which makes chains all the more important. There is no vignette.
logistics.permits: The ski centre is on **state land managed by ETAD**; there is no separate park fee, but **parts of Parnassos are within a National Park and a Natura 2000 site**, which restricts off-road driving and camping. Drones need Greek civil aviation authorisation and are banned over the archaeological sites — Delphi in particular, where staff will intervene. Photography rules at Delphi permit personal stills but not tripods without permission.
logistics.health: Tap water in Arachova and Delphi is potable. **Greece publishes no daily EAWS avalanche bulletin** — the **EMY (Hellenic National Meteorological Service)** issues mountain weather forecasts and the ski centre issues a snow bulletin, but there is no five-point hazard rating for Parnassos. Treat all off-piste and touring as unbulletined, carry transceiver, shovel and probe, and go with someone who knows the mountain. Thin cover over rock is the most common cause of injury here in a poor year — ski conservatively on the marked routes when the base is shallow.

proTips: **Ski Monday to Friday and sightsee at weekends** — the inverse of every other resort in this collection. A weekday lift ticket is €20 against €35 at weekends, and Arachova on a Saturday belongs to Athens.
Take the **4-day combined ticket at €95** if you intend to ski three or more days. Against €35 weekend days it pays for itself immediately, and against €20 weekdays it still wins on the fourth.
**Buy your ticket online for the 5% electronic discount** and to avoid the window queue, which on a snowy Saturday is the longest line on the mountain.

Structure the week so that **the skiing is optional**. Parnassos may not open, may open only at weekends, or may open with two lifts. Delphi, the Corycian Cave and the north-side villages do not depend on snow, and a week built around them with skiing on top never fails.
**Hire skis in Arachova, not at the base.** They are cheaper, better fitted, and available — the Kelaria and Fterolakka shops are picked clean by 09:30 on a busy day.
**Fit the chains once in daylight in the hotel car park** before you need them on a dark, sleeting road. The police check at the junction above Arachova is routine and unsympathetic.

Cross the ridge back to your own base by **15:00**. Parnassos's lift hours are short — 16:00 in high season, 15:00 in low — and a wind hold on the linking chair means a shuttle between car parks in ski boots.

Eat on the **north side of the mountain** at least twice. Agoriani (Eptalofos) and Polydrosos have wood-fired tavernas at half Arachova's prices, and the fir forest up there is a completely different mountain from the bare southern slopes.

Go to **Delphi at opening time on a weekday in February**. The site takes snow beautifully, the tour buses do not run, and you will have the Temple of Apollo essentially alone — which is not a sentence that can be written about it in any other season.

raw.Pass tiers by name: There is one product and one operator: the **Parnassos Ski Centre**, run by the state property company **ETAD**, sells a single-resort ticket with no area or regional super-pass — there is nothing else within range to link to. The pricing is by **day of the week, not by season band**: **high season (weekends and public holidays) €35 adult**, **low season (weekdays) €20 adult** — the sharpest weekday/weekend spread in European skiing. **Afternoon tickets** (after 13:00 in high season, 12:00 in low) are **€20 and €15**. A **family ticket is €70** in high season. **School students pay €20 / €10** and **university students €35 / €20**. The nearest thing to a multi-day product is a **combined 4-day ticket at €95**, which is the value buy for anyone skiing more than two days. The **season pass is €450 individual, €1,000 for a "family plus"**. There is no dynamic pricing and no early-bird, but there is a **5% discount for buying electronically online** rather than at the window. **Lockers run €30–€250** depending on duration, and **instructor season passes €600–€1,000**. Operating hours are **08:30–16:00 in high season, 09:00–15:00 in low season**, which is short by Alpine standards and worth planning around. **There is no night skiing at Parnassos** — budget no floodlit supplement.
raw.Lift network and interconnects: Two sectors work as one. **Fterolakka**, the lower and more sheltered base at roughly **1,640 m**, and **Kelaria**, the main base at around **1,750 m**, are linked on snow across the ridge between them and are the whole of the everyday skiing. Above and east sits **Gerontovrachos**, the highest and most exposed sector, reached by chair from the Kelaria side and the first thing to shut in wind. The signature lift is the **Ermis (Hermes) gondola at Kelaria — the first and still one of the only gondola lifts in a Greek ski resort** — with the **Iraklis** chair and a further dozen or so chairs and conveyors making up a fleet of roughly **17 lifts**. **The two base areas are connected by road as well as by piste**, and the ski centre runs a shuttle between the Kelaria and Fterolakka car parks; that shuttle is what saves you when the linking traverse is closed by wind, which is often. **Last lifts are 16:00 in high season and 15:00 in low season** — and the practical rule is that **you must be back on your own base's side of the ridge by about 15:00**, because a wind hold on the connecting chair leaves you facing a car-park shuttle in ski boots.
raw.Snow reliability: This is the central problem and the file should not pretend otherwise. Parnassos spans roughly **1,600 m at the Fterolakka base to about 2,250–2,260 m at the top of Gerontovrachos** — a vertical band of only 650–670 m, on a mountain 25 km from the Gulf of Corinth at latitude 38°N. Aspects are mostly north and northeast, which is what makes the resort viable at all. Snowfall arrives in large, infrequent dumps from Mediterranean depressions and can vanish in a single warm southerly. **Snowmaking exists but covers only a fraction of the terrain, and the ski centre does not publish coverage as a percentage of pisted kilometres — do not quote one.** **Season: mid-December to early April**, but the reliable window is roughly 20 January to 28 February. **In a bad snow year Parnassos may open only at weekends, may run only the upper Kelaria and Gerontovrachos lifts, and in the worst years opens very late or barely at all** — which is exactly why this itinerary front-loads Delphi and the villages and treats every ski day as conditional. Check **snowreport.gr** and the ski centre's own daily bulletin the night before, every night.
raw.Off-piste and touring: The lift-served off-piste is the open ground on the **Gerontovrachos** flanks and the gullies between the Kelaria and Fterolakka pistes — short, and rocky when thin. The real objective is the **ski tour to Liakoura, the summit of Parnassos at 2,457 m**, from the top of the lifts: a straightforward but exposed skin in good conditions and a serious undertaking in bad ones, with weather that turns faster than anywhere in the Alps. Across the valley, **Giona** and **Vardousia** offer bigger and wilder touring for those with a guide and a week to spare. **Greece publishes no national daily avalanche bulletin on the EAWS scale.** The available sources are the **Hellenic National Meteorological Service (EMY, emy.gr)** for mountain weather, the ski centre's own snow bulletin, and **snowreport.gr**. Rescue is the **Hellenic Rescue Team (Ελληνική Ομάδα Διάσωσης)** and **EMAK**, the fire service's special disaster unit. **Take a guide.** The mountaineering clubs — **EOS Amfissas** and the Athens EOS — and commercial operators such as **Trekking Hellas** run guided winter ascents and snowshoe days; freelance-touring on Parnassos without local knowledge is how people get killed on a mountain that looks benign.
raw.Piste breakdown: The published figure is around **23 km in total: roughly 17 km easy (about 72%), 6.5 km intermediate (28%), and no officially graded black runs**, plus around 10 km of ungroomed marked ski routes, over some 19–20 named pistes and 17 lifts. **Beginners** are extremely well served — this is a resort of wide, gentle, sunny blue terrain and it is a genuinely good place to learn, with cheap weekday lift tickets to match. **Intermediates** get the Kelaria reds and the Gerontovrachos sector and will have seen everything in a day and a half. **Experts** should come for the ski tour to Liakoura and the view, not for the pistes; there is no lift-served steep skiing here in the Alpine sense, and anyone told otherwise has been sold something.
raw.Non-ski days: This is where the week earns its keep. **Delphi**, 10 km west of Arachova, is one of the great archaeological sites of the world — the Temple of Apollo, the theatre, the stadium and the **Delphi Archaeological Museum** with the bronze Charioteer, all of it near-empty in February and spectacular under snow. The **Livadi plateau** above Arachova at around 1,100–1,200 m is the local sledging and snow-play ground and the trailhead for the snowshoe walk to the **Corycian Cave (Korykion Antron)**, the huge stalactite cavern sacred to Pan and the nymphs. On the north side, **Agoriani (officially Eptalofos)** and **Polydrosos** are fir-forested villages with tavernas and a fraction of Arachova's prices. And Arachova itself has the **Church of Agios Georgios** at the top of its 264 steps, the weaving and rug workshops, and a food culture built on **formaela**, the PDO sheep's cheese fried at the table, and **tsipouro**.
raw.Hire, lockers and schools: Rental is available at both **Kelaria** and **Fterolakka** base areas and, better and cheaper, from the ski shops along Arachova's main street — expect roughly **€15–€25/day** for a standard ski-boot-pole package and **€70–€120 for six days**. Lockers at the ski centre run **€30–€250** depending on the rental period. Ski schools operate out of both bases; expect roughly **€40–€60 an hour for a private lesson** and **€150–€250 for a five-morning group course**, with English widely spoken. Two practical notes: **hire your snow chains at the same time as your skis** if the car did not come with them, and **rent in Arachova rather than at the base** — the base shops run out on a busy Saturday by 09:30.

sources.confidenceNotes: **The altitude range is not settled.** One authoritative aggregator gives 1,581–2,250 m with a 669 m vertical; the resort and local sources are commonly quoted at 1,640–2,260 m. The text uses banded figures (≈1,640 m Fterolakka base, ≈1,750 m Kelaria base, ≈2,250–2,260 m top of Gerontovrachos) and these must be confirmed against ETAD's own technical data before publishing. **Individual lift names beyond the Ermis (Hermes) gondola are not fully verified** — the Iraklis chair is named on good authority but the full fleet naming and the exact lift serving Gerontovrachos should be checked against the current trail map. **No snowmaking coverage figure is published and none is asserted here.** **Season dates are indicative and unusually volatile at this resort** — in poor years opening slips by weeks and sectors run only at weekends; the daily source of truth is the ski centre bulletin and snowreport.gr. Delphi's winter combined-ticket price (€12–€20) is a band, not a quoted figure, and the reduced winter rate should be checked with the Ephorate. Rental, ski-school, guide and snowshoe prices are indicative bands. Arachova and Delphi hotel and taverna names are real and long-established but seasonal opening should be confirmed. The snow-chain enforcement described is a real and current practice on the access road but the legal citation should be re-checked against the Greek Highway Code before publishing as law.

trips.title: Sellaronda Week: Alta Badia & Val Gardena on One Pass
trips.subRegion: Alta Badia & Val Gardena, Dolomites, South Tyrol

bestPeriod.window: Mid-January–mid-March; late February and early March give the longest lift days with the Sellaronda still comfortably completable
bestPeriod.avoid: 27 December–6 January (Italian holiday peak, Sellaronda bottlenecks at Passo Pordoi) and after mid-April, when the low Corvara and Ortisei returns close
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-January–mid-March; late February and early March give the longest lift days with the Sellaronda still comfortably completable

accommodation.note: Corvara/Selva 4 half board €130–€250 pppn; La Villa and Colfosco run 15–20% cheaper

food.note: Rifugio pasta €14–€20, secondi €22–€30; one gourmet dinner adds €120–€250

transport.note: Airport transfer €70–€120 each way; SkiBus free with the guest card; two ski-taxi legs

activities.note: 6-day Dolomiti Superski pass roughly €420–€480, MyDolomiti card, Lagazuoi horse tow €5

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5 — the Sellaronda is a six-hour day of continuous but not steep skiing; the Gran Risa and Saslong are technical rather than aerobic

trips.gatewayAirport: VCE Venice Marco Polo, 2 h 45–3 h 15 to Corvara; VRN Verona 3 h–3 h 30; INN Innsbruck 2 h–2 h 30 over the Brenner
trips.summary: This is the week the Dolomites were built for: one keycard, twelve ski areas, and a ring road on snow around a 3,152 m limestone block. The structure is simple — bed down in Alta Badia, spend the first days learning the local network at Corvara, La Villa and San Cassiano, run the **Sellaronda** once in each direction mid-week, take a day off the circuit for the **Hidden Valley** behind Lagazuoi, and cross into **Val Gardena** for the Saslong and Seceda. The skiing is overwhelmingly blue and red, immaculately groomed and rarely steep; what makes it remarkable is the scale, the light on the Sella and Sassolungo, and a rifugio culture in which lunch is a two-hour Ladin meal rather than a tray of chips. It suits confident intermediates above all, families who want distance without difficulty, and experts who accept that their hard skiing here is two World Cup pistes and a handful of couloirs rather than a whole mountain.

itinerary.title: Arrive Corvara, orient on Col Alt and Piz La Ila
itinerary.morning: Transfer from Venice or Verona up the Val Badia. The road from Brunico climbs through San Lorenzo and San Martino; from the south you come over the Passo Falzarego, which is the more dramatic and the more likely to be chained.
itinerary.afternoon: Collect skis at Sport Kostner in Corvara and buy the 6-day Dolomiti Superski pass online the night before to take the 5% discount. Ride Col Alt for the easy reds above the village, then cross to **Piz La Ila** for a first look at the Gran Risa from the side.
itinerary.evening: La Stüa de Michil at Hotel La Perla in Corvara if you want the Michelin start to the week; otherwise Ristorante Stüa dla Lâ, or a plate of casunziei in the hotel.
itinerary.dayStats: Transfer 2 h 45–3 h 30 / Corvara 1,568 m / 12–15 piste km, roughly 2,000 m descent / pass 5% cheaper bought online

itinerary.title: Alta Badia network and the Gran Risa
itinerary.morning: Work the local 130 km: Corvara to Colfosco, back over to La Villa via Piz La Ila, then down into San Cassiano and up Piz Sorega. This is intermediate cruising at its most efficient — long, wide, empty reds.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the **Gran Risa** at La Villa, the World Cup giant-slalom hill: short at about 1.25 km but with pitches past 50%, and best attempted at 14:00 once you have found your edges. Then a long lunch at Ütia de Bioch or Rifugio Piz Arlara.
itinerary.evening: Après at the Piz Arlara terrace or the Corvara base bars, then dinner at La Siriola in Ciasa Salares, San Cassiano, if you booked it.
itinerary.dayStats: 30–35 piste km / roughly 5,500 m descent / Gran Risa 1.25 km, ~450 m vertical, max gradient past 50% / free Alta Badia SkiBus with the guest card

itinerary.title: Sellaronda clockwise (orange)
itinerary.morning: Leave Corvara by **08:45**. Up over **Passo Campolongo (1,875 m)** to Arabba, then the Porta Vescovo cable car and across to **Passo Pordoi (2,239 m)**. Arabba is the steepest section of the whole circuit and the only place the orange route bites.
itinerary.afternoon: Over **Passo Sella (2,244 m)** into Val Gardena, up Plan de Gralba and **Dantercepies**, then over **Passo Gardena (2,121 m)** to Colfosco and home. Lunch fast and standing if you left late — the circuit does not forgive a two-hour rifugio.
itinerary.evening: Corvara, feet up. You have done roughly 26 km on skis and a dozen lifts.
itinerary.dayStats: Sellaronda orange ~40 km total, ~26 km skied / four passes 1,875–2,244 m / 6 h including lifts / start by 10:00, last pass by 15:30

itinerary.title: The Hidden Valley and Lagazuoi
itinerary.morning: Ski via San Cassiano and Capanna Alpina, or take the ski taxi, to **Passo Falzarego**, then the **Lagazuoi cable car** to 2,732 m. Have a coffee on the Rifugio Lagazuoi terrace first — it is the best single view in the Dolomites.
itinerary.afternoon: Ski the **Armentarola** red, 8.5 km down the Val Travenanzes between frozen waterfalls, stopping at **Rifugio Scotoni** for the grill. At the bottom, join the **horse-drawn rope tow** — €5, cash — which drags a line of skiers back toward the Armentarola lift.
itinerary.evening: San Cassiano for dinner; take the free SkiBus home to Corvara rather than the last lift chain.
itinerary.dayStats: Lagazuoi cable car every ~15 min, 09:00–16:40, 3 min ride, top 2,732 m / Armentarola run 8.5 km red / horse tow €5 pp / Capanna Alpina→Piz Sorega taxi ~€5 pp; Armentarola→Falzarego ~€8 pp cash

itinerary.title: Weather-contingency and rest day: Ortisei, Ladin culture, tobogganing
itinerary.morning: This is the flex day — take it here, or move it to whichever day the Sella passes close on wind, which they do several times a season. Ride the **Ortisei–Alpe di Siusi** cable car onto the plateau and ski two or three gentle blues in the sun, or skip skis entirely.
itinerary.afternoon: Ortisei's woodcarving workshops and the Museum Gherdëina, or the **Museum Ladin Ćiastel de Tor** at San Martino in Badia — the Ladin language survives in about 30,000 speakers across these five valleys and this is where it is explained properly. Then the **Rasciesa toboggan run**, roughly 6 km from the funicular back to Ortisei.
itinerary.evening: Anna Stuben or Concordia in Ortisei; take the free Val Gardena SkiBus and the Alta Badia connection home, or stay over.
itinerary.dayStats: Alpe di Siusi plateau ~1,800–2,000 m / Rasciesa toboggan ~6 km / zero World Cup pistes, deliberately / SkiBus free with guest card

itinerary.title: Val Gardena, Seceda and the Saslong
itinerary.morning: Ride into Val Gardena over Passo Gardena, then take the **Seceda** gondola from Ortisei to **2,518 m** for the Odle ridge view and the long descent back toward Santa Cristina.
itinerary.afternoon: Up **Ciampinoi** from Selva and ski the **Saslong**, the FIS World Cup downhill piste, including the Gobbe di Cammello camel humps that eat racers every December. Lunch at **Rifugio Emilio Comici**, which serves seafood and champagne at 2,150 m and is exactly as absurd as it sounds.
itinerary.evening: Selva for après at the Ciampinoi base, then the last lifts over Passo Gardena — **do not be later than 16:00** on this crossing.
itinerary.dayStats: Seceda 2,518 m / Saslong FIS downhill, roughly 3.4 km, start ~2,250 m to ~1,420 m / Val Gardena–Alpe di Siusi 175 km on 79 lifts / Passo Gardena return hard cutoff ~16:00

itinerary.title: Sellaronda counter-clockwise (green), then out
itinerary.morning: Run the circuit the other way if you have a late flight: **green, counter-clockwise**, out over Passo Gardena to Selva and Plan de Gralba first, then Sella, Pordoi, Arabba and Campolongo home. It skis completely differently — flatter early, steeper late.
itinerary.afternoon: If your flight is early, do half the loop to Arabba and take the SkiBus back. Return hire kit by 17:00; most shops shut at 18:30.
itinerary.evening: Overnight near Venice or Verona rather than driving the Falzarego in the dark after snowfall.
itinerary.dayStats: Sellaronda green ~40 km / half-loop escape via Arabba + SkiBus ~45 min / transfer to VCE 2 h 45–3 h 15 / winter tyres or chains mandatory 15 Nov–15 Apr

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Col Alto
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits at the foot of the Col Alt lift in the centre of Corvara, which is the single best Sellaronda start point because you can leave clockwise or counter-clockwise from the same door. Ski depot, spa, and half board that gets you fed before an 08:45 departure. Roughly €150–€250 pppn half board.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Portillo Dolomites 1966
accommodationStrategy.description: On the pass itself between Corvara and Arabba, so you start the circuit already 300 m higher and ahead of the village queues, and the Arabba side is a ski-out. The trade is isolation: no village to walk to in the evening. Roughly €130–€200 pppn.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Gran Baita
accommodationStrategy.description: The Val Gardena alternative if the Saslong and Seceda matter more to you than Alta Badia. Walking distance to the Ciampinoi and Dantercepies stations, so both Sellaronda directions and the World Cup piste are on the doorstep. Roughly €140–€230 pppn half board.

logistics.connectivity: 4G and 5G are good in both valleys and on most of the Sellaronda, weak in the Val Travenanzes on the Hidden Valley. EU roaming applies. Download the Dolomiti Superski and Alta Badia apps for live lift status — the Sella passes close on wind without much warning.
logistics.emergency: 112. Piste rescue is charged in Italy and the bill for a sled-and-ambulance can run into hundreds of euros; helicopter recovery is far more. Italy is EU, so EHIC/GHIC covers state healthcare, but not rescue costs — insurance naming winter sports is essential and many Italian resorts now require third-party liability cover by law.
logistics.weather: The dominant pattern is high pressure and cold, dry air, with occasional Adriatic lows delivering heavy snow to the south side. The real disruptor is **wind on the four passes**, which shuts the exposed Pordoi and Sella lifts and breaks the circuit mid-day. A **temperature inversion** is common: Corvara at −12°C and Piz La Ila at −2°C.
logistics.bookingWindows: Half-board hotels for February half-term and Christmas go 6–9 months out. Michelin tables at La Siriola and La Stüa de Michil need 3–6 weeks. Rifugio Scotoni and Club Moritzino take lunch bookings and fill by 11:00 on a bluebird day. Ski school for a peak week: 2–3 months.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards are accepted essentially everywhere including rifugi, but the **Lagazuoi horse tow and the Armentarola ski taxis are cash** — carry €30–€40 in small notes. Tipping is rounding up; a coperto of €2–€4 per head is normal and is not a tip.
logistics.transportRules: **Winter tyres or onboard chains are legally required in South Tyrol and Veneto from 15 November to 15 April**, and the Falzarego and Pordoi roads are enforced. Passes load onto the reloadable MyDolomiti Card, €5 to replace. Free SkiBus travel comes with the local guest card issued by your hotel — ask for it at check-in, it is not automatic.
logistics.permits: The Dolomites are a UNESCO World Heritage site; drones are effectively banned over the ski areas and need ENAC compliance elsewhere. Italian law requires **helmets for under-18s** and mandates **third-party liability insurance for all skiers** — most lift passes now bundle it, but confirm.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable. Altitude tops out around 2,700 m and is not a medical issue. The Sella couloirs (**Val Mezdì, Val Setus, Val Lasties**) are unpatrolled ski routes with terrain traps and no phone signal — take a guide, transceiver, shovel and probe, and read **lawinen.report** every morning.

proTips: Do the Sellaronda on a Tuesday or Wednesday. Weekends bring Italian day-trippers up from Bolzano and Belluno and the Pordoi bottleneck can add 40 minutes to the loop.
Leave Corvara by 08:45, not 09:30. The circuit is timed by the last pass crossing at 15:30, and every ten minutes you lose in the morning is ten minutes off your lunch.
Buy the pass online the night before for the 5% discount, and put it on a MyDolomiti Card you keep between trips — it reloads and saves the queue entirely.
Book Rifugio Scotoni by phone before you ride the Lagazuoi cable car. It is the best lunch on the mountain and by the time you ski down to it the terrace is gone.
Ride Lagazuoi at 09:00 sharp. The Hidden Valley is a one-way run served by a single cable car; by 11:30 you are skiing in a queue and by 15:00 the horse tow has a twenty-minute line.
Ski the Gran Risa in the afternoon and the Saslong in the morning. The Gran Risa is south-facing and needs sun on it; the Saslong is best on hard overnight groom before it gets chopped.
Ask for the local guest card at hotel check-in. It makes the Alta Badia and Val Gardena SkiBus free, which is what rescues you when a pass closes on wind.
Carry €40 in cash purely for the horse tow and the two Armentarola ski taxis. Card readers do not exist on any of them.
If the Sella passes shut, do not sit in the hotel — take the SkiBus to Ortisei and ski the sheltered Alpe di Siusi plateau, which stays open in almost anything.

raw.Pass tiers by name: Three products. The **local Val Gardena–Alpe di Siusi pass** covers 79 lifts and 175 km — **€72–€80 adult per day**, **€50–€56 junior under 16**, **€65–€72 senior over 65**. The **Alta Badia local pass** covers roughly 130 km on 53 lifts at similar money. The area/regional super-pass is **Dolomiti Superski**: 12 areas, about **1,200 km** and 450 lifts on one card, at **€77–€86 adult per day**, **€54–€60 junior**, **€69–€77 senior**. A **6-day Dolomiti Superski adult pass falls in the region of €420–€480** in high season with juniors around 30% less — banded, not confirmed, because Dolomiti Superski now prices through a calculator rather than a fixed tariff. There is a **5% discount for buying online**, and the **Superdays** bundle gives 10 non-consecutive days at **€660 adult / €460 junior**. Passes load onto the **MyDolomiti Card**, a reloadable keycard: rather than a deposit you pay a **€5 replacement charge** if you lose it. Season 2025/26 ran **29 November 2025 to 3 May 2026**. There is no meaningful night skiing here — the after-dark product is floodlit tobogganing, not floodlit pistes.
raw.The Sellaronda, both directions: The circuit rings the Sella massif over four passes: **Campolongo (1,875 m), Pordoi (2,239 m), Sella (2,244 m) and Gardena (2,121 m)**, through Selva, Canazei, Arabba, Corvara and Colfosco. Total **roughly 40 km, of which about 26 km is on skis** and the rest on lifts, across a dozen installations. **Orange is clockwise** — from Val Gardena via the **Dantercepies** gondola out of Selva; **green is counter-clockwise**, entering through Plan de Gralba. Allow **six hours including lifts and lunch**. The governing rule is timing: **start by 10:00 at the latest, and cross your last pass by 15:30.** Miss that and you are in a taxi.
raw.Named lifts that structure the week: **Ciampinoi** and **Dantercepies** out of Selva; **Piz Sella** and Plan de Gralba on the Sella side; **Seceda** gondola from Ortisei to 2,518 m; the Ortisei–Alpe di Siusi cable car; **Piz La Ila** and Piz Sorega from La Villa and San Cassiano; **Boè** from Corvara up toward the Vallon and the highest lift-served point in Alta Badia; Col Alt above Corvara. The bus links that patch gaps are the free **SkiBus** networks in both valleys — the Alta Badia line between Corvara, Colfosco, La Villa, San Cassiano and Badia, and the Val Gardena line between Ortisei, Santa Cristina and Selva.
raw.Snow reliability: Bases sit at **1,236 m (Ortisei), 1,433 m (La Villa), 1,563 m (Selva) and 1,568 m (Corvara)**, tops at **2,518 m (Seceda)** and around 2,550 m at Vallon. That is not a high resort by Alpine standards, and the Dolomites' answer is engineering: Dolomiti Superski publishes snowmaking coverage of **roughly 97% of pisted kilometres**, one of the highest figures in the Alps, drawing on reservoirs across all twelve areas. It is also a dry, cold, high-pressure climate — natural snowfall is modest but what falls stays. **In a bad snow year the Dolomites out-perform almost everywhere else**, because the machine-made base is laid in late November and holds; what suffers is the off-piste, which is often simply absent, and the low returns into Ortisei and Corvara, which close first.
raw.Off-piste and touring: This is not a freeride destination, and the honest lines are few. The **Vallon bowl** above Corvara holds the best lift-accessed powder in Alta Badia. **Val Mezdì**, the great couloir splitting the Sella massif from the Pordoi cable car, and its neighbours **Val Setus** and **Val Lasties**, are the classic Dolomite descents — steep, committing, terrain-trapped and **effectively guide-only**: they are ski routes, not pistes, unpatrolled, and people die in them most seasons. The avalanche bulletin is the **Euregio bulletin at lawinen.report** covering Tyrol, South Tyrol and Trentino, with **AINEVA** the national umbrella. Guides: the **Guide Alpine Alta Badia** and **Catores** in Val Gardena.
raw.Piste breakdown: Dolomiti Superski's 1,200 km runs approximately 30% easy, 60% intermediate and 10% difficult — an unusually intermediate-heavy mountain. **Beginners** belong on the Alpe di Siusi plateau above Ortisei, which is a vast, gentle, sunny shelf, and on the Piz Sorega side of San Cassiano. **Intermediates** own everything, and should simply ski the Sellaronda twice and the Alta Badia network in between. **Experts** get the **Saslong** in Val Gardena, the FIS downhill dropping from Ciampinoi to Santa Cristina with its Gobbe di Cammello camel humps; the **Gran Risa** at La Villa, a short, brutal giant-slalom pitch of roughly 1.25 km and 450 m vertical with gradients past 50%; and the Sella couloirs with a guide.
raw.The Hidden Valley: The single best non-circuit day. Ride the **Lagazuoi cable car** from Passo Falzarego to **2,732 m**, which runs about every 15 minutes from 09:00 to 16:40 on a three-minute lift, then ski the **8.5 km Armentarola red** down the Val Travenanzes past frozen waterfalls. At the bottom you are pulled back toward the Alta Badia lifts by a **horse-drawn rope tow — €5 per person**, two horses and a long rope, genuinely the last of its kind. A shuttle taxi from Capanna Alpina to the Piz Sorega base is about **€5 per person**; Armentarola back to Passo Falzarego runs about **€8 per person, cash only**.
raw.Non-ski days and rifugio culture: Lunch is the point: **Rifugio Scotoni** on the Hidden Valley for grilled meat, **Club Moritzino** on Piz La Ila, **Ütia de Bioch** and **Rifugio Piz Arlara** in Alta Badia, **Rifugio Emilio Comici** above Selva for its improbable seafood and champagne list, **Baita Sofie** on Seceda. Off snow: the **Rasciesa toboggan run** above Ortisei, roughly 6 km; night tobogganing from Piz Sorega; the **Museum Ladin Ćiastel de Tor** at San Martino in Badia for the Ladin language and culture; woodcarving workshops and the Museum Gherdëina in Ortisei; the Pranives ice rink in Selva.
raw.Hire, lockers and schools: **Sport Kostner** in Corvara and the **Rent and Go** and Skiservice outlets across Selva, La Villa and Ortisei cover hire at roughly **€110–€180 a week** standard and **€200–€280** performance; boot-and-ski depots at most lift bases run **€6–€10 a day** and save you carrying kit through villages. Schools: **Scuola Sci & Snowboard Alta Badia** (Corvara), **Ski School Dolomites La Villa**, **Scuola Sci Selva Val Gardena** and **Scuola Sci Ortisei**. Expect roughly **€250–€350 for five half-day group mornings** and **€65–€90 an hour** for a private, with the hourly rate dropping on full-day and multi-day bookings.
