trips.title: Pelicans, Beech and Bujtina: Eastern Albania Off the Grid

bestPeriod.window: Mid-May–late June & September–mid-October
bestPeriod.avoid: December–March — the Shebenik glacial-lake tracks are snowbound, most Prespa homestays close, and the Rrajcë road ices badly
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-May–late June & September–mid-October

accommodation.note: Bujtina homestays 2,500–4,000 ALL (€25–€40) per person with dinner; Korçë and Pogradec hotels €35–€60 a double

food.note: Village dinners are usually included; town mains 600–1,200 ALL (€6–€12)

transport.note: High-clearance rental €40–€60/day, fuel around 200 ALL/litre (€2.00), no motorway tolls except the Kalimash tunnel (not on this route)

activities.note: Guides, Maligrad boat, Voskopojë church keyholders, a pelican morning; both national parks are free to enter

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5 — walks of 8–15 km with 400–800 m ascent on shepherd paths and forest track; nothing technical, but way-marking in Shebenik is thin and a guide changes the day

trips.gatewayAirport: TIA Tirana, 2 h 30 to Korçë via Elbasan and 1 h 40 to Librazhd; OHD Ohrid (North Macedonia), 50 min to Pogradec via the Qafë Thanë border
trips.summary: Eastern Albania is the country's quiet half: a high plateau of lakes at 700–900 m, walled in by 2,200 m ridges, with the Greek and Macedonian borders on three sides and almost no coach tourism. This week starts in Korçë among Ottoman bazaar streets and the painted churches of Voskopojë, drops to the Prespa lakes where a Macedonian-speaking minority farms beans on the shore of a lake full of Dalmatian pelicans, then works north through Lin and Pogradec on Lake Ohrid before finishing in the beech forest of Shebenik-Jabllanicë — a UNESCO primeval-beech site and the best-documented Albanian habitat of the Balkan lynx. You sleep almost entirely in *bujtina*, family homestays where dinner is not optional and the rakia is homemade. It suits people who want genuinely empty landscape, are relaxed about rough road, and accept that most of the week is cash, no signal, and a wood stove.

itinerary.title: Into Korçë
itinerary.morning: Drive from Tirana over the Krrabë and through Elbasan and Librazhd, then up the Devoll to Korçë at 850 m — a city of low nineteenth-century houses, a serious Ottoman-era bazaar restored in the 2010s, and the country's first Albanian-language school, now a museum.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Old Bazaar, the Mirahori mosque (founded in the 1490s), and the National Museum of Medieval Art, which holds the best collection of Albanian icons in the country, including work by the Onufri school. Buy a week's supplies here — it is the last full supermarket before the mountains.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in the bazaar on Korçë staples: lakror pie, kernacka sausages, and a Birra Korça, brewed in the city since 1928.
itinerary.dayStats: 180 km drive / 2 h 30 / Korçë 850 m / last full supermarket for 3 days / museum entry roughly 700 ALL (€7)
itinerary.sleep: Hani i Pazarit or a bazaar guesthouse, Korçë

itinerary.title: Voskopojë churches and Dardhë
itinerary.morning: Drive 21 km west to Voskopojë, which in the eighteenth century was one of the largest cities in the Balkans with a printing press and an academy, and is now a village of a few hundred among the ruins. Five post-Byzantine churches survive with extensive frescoes — St Nicholas, St Athanasius and the Prodromos among them. Several are locked; the keyholder lives nearby and is found by asking in the café.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue over to Dardhë, a stone village at 1,344 m in beech forest, then walk one of the loops above it. Slow afternoon by design; this is acclimatisation and the pleasantest air in eastern Albania.
itinerary.evening: Eat where you sleep — grilled meat, mountain trout, and the local honey and walnut everything.
itinerary.dayStats: 21 km to Voskopojë / Dardhë 1,344 m / 8 km walk, 350 m ascent / keyholder tip 300–500 ALL per church (€3–€5) / five surviving frescoed churches
itinerary.sleep: Guesthouse in Dardhë, or back in Korçë

itinerary.title: Over the ridge to Prespa
itinerary.morning: Drive north-east from Korçë through Zvezdë and over the ridge into the Prespa basin, dropping to Greater Prespa at 850 m. The moment the lake appears, the character changes: the villages here — Pustec, Gollomboç, Gorica e Madhe, Zaroshkë, Cerje — are Macedonian-speaking, and the municipality is bilingual.
itinerary.afternoon: Take a boat from Gorica or Pustec to Maligrad, the small rock island in Albanian water, where the fourteenth-century cave church of Shën Maria is built into an overhang with surviving frescoes. Back on shore, walk up to the rock-cut hermitages above Zaroshkë, cut into the cliff face and reached by a steep scramble.
itinerary.evening: Homestay dinner: Prespa beans, which are the local pride, lake fish, and rakia poured by the host until you stop him.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 km drive / 1 h 15 / Prespa 850 m, Ohrid 695 m, 155 m apart and connected through karst / Maligrad boat roughly 3,000–5,000 ALL (€30–€50) per boat / homestay 2,500–4,000 ALL per person with dinner

itinerary.title: A slow day on the lake
itinerary.morning: Be on the shore at first light with binoculars. Dalmatian pelicans move between Lesser and Greater Prespa and are most reliably seen on the water early; from the northern shore near Gorica you also look straight across at Golem Grad, the Macedonian island in the middle of the lake, notorious for its tortoises and water snakes and closed to Albanian-side boats.
itinerary.afternoon: Deliberately nothing. Swim — Prespa is warm and clean by August. Walk the shore path between two villages. Watch the bean harvest if it is September. There is no attraction to tick here and that is the point.
itinerary.evening: Sunset from the Zaroshkë cliffs, then back for dinner. Ask your host about the winter, when the lake sometimes freezes at the edges and the village halves.
itinerary.dayStats: 0–8 km walking / Prespa NP Albania roughly 27,750 ha, declared 1999 / Lesser Prespa holds the world's largest Dalmatian pelican colony / no entry fee / power cuts common, charge everything when you can

itinerary.title: Lin, Pogradec and the Ohrid shore
itinerary.morning: Drive north around the lakes and over to Lake Ohrid's Albanian shore. Stop at Lin, a peninsula village of steep lanes where a hilltop early-Christian basilica keeps sixth-century floor mosaics, and where excavation from 2023 revealed a Neolithic pile-dwelling settlement in the shallows dated to around 6000 BC — among the oldest lakeside villages known in Europe.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Pogradec and Tushemisht, where the Drilon springs feed a channel of clear water under plane trees. This is a resort strip by Albanian standards; treat it as the week's shower-and-laundry day.
itinerary.evening: Grilled koran — the Ohrid trout, subject to catch restrictions, so ask what is actually on the plate — on the lakefront.
itinerary.dayStats: 75 km drive / 1 h 40 / Lin basilica mosaics 6th c., pile dwellings dated to roughly 6000 BC / Ohrid 695 m / Qafë Thanë border 20 min from Pogradec
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Enkelana or a Pogradec lakefront hotel

itinerary.title: Rrajcë, the primeval beech, and up into Shebenik
itinerary.morning: Drive north on the SH3 to Rrajcë in Librazhd municipality. The beech forest above the village is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list as part of the transnational Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe — old, structurally complex, full of deadwood, and completely unlike the grazed hillsides around it. Walk it slowly with a park guide.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrange the 4x4 up from Fushë-Studë towards the glacial lakes. Shebenik-Jabllanicë covers about 34,500 hectares and holds fourteen glacial lakes between roughly 1,500 and 1,900 m, most of them shallow, cold and completely silent. Walk in from wherever the track gives up.
itinerary.evening: Back down to a Rrajcë or Fushë-Studë bujtina. Wood stove, spring water, no signal, dinner from the garden and the flock.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km drive / 4x4 track 9–12 km from Fushë-Studë / lakes at 1,500–1,900 m / park roughly 34,500 ha, free entry / 14 glacial lakes / Shebenik peak 2,262 m

itinerary.title: Jabllanica ridge, çaj mali, and out
itinerary.morning: A last walk on the Jabllanica side towards Stëblevë, the border village, on slopes where çaj mali grows in dry limestone grassland. In July and August you will meet people cutting it; watch how they do it — knife, above the wood, never the root — before you touch any yourself.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend and choose an exit. Qafë Thanë into North Macedonia puts you at Ohrid airport in under an hour; the SH3 west takes you to Tirana in two and a half. Clear the rental agency's cross-border paperwork in advance if you are leaving through Macedonia.
itinerary.evening: Last dinner in Librazhd or Elbasan, or on the Ohrid lakefront if you have crossed.
itinerary.dayStats: 8–12 km walk, 400–600 m ascent / çaj mali harvest July–August / Qafë Thanë border 55 min to OHD / Tirana 2 h 30 from Librazhd / green card and written permission needed for a border crossing in a rental
itinerary.sleep: Ohrid, Tirana or an airport hotel

accommodationStrategy.name: A Prespa bujtina
accommodationStrategy.location: Pustec, Gollomboç or Gorica e Madhe
accommodationStrategy.description: The village homestay network on the Albanian Prespa shore is the reason to come here rather than to the Greek side: a room in a family house, dinner and breakfast included, roughly 2,500–4,000 ALL (€25–€40) per person. Book by phone or through the municipality rather than online — many are not on booking platforms. Expect no card machine, no English beyond basics, and Macedonian as the household language.

accommodationStrategy.name: A Shebenik bujtina at Rrajcë or Fushë-Studë
accommodationStrategy.description: These are the only beds within reach of the glacial lakes, and they double as the way you arrange the 4x4 and the guide. Wood stove, spring water, solar or intermittent mains, no shop worth the name. The trade-off for the isolation is that you eat what the household eats, at their hour, which is the best deal on this trip.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hani i Pazarit
accommodationStrategy.description: A comfortable, central base inside the Old Bazaar with parking and a proper breakfast, useful as bookends at either end of the week when you want a shower, a laundry and a restaurant with a menu. Around €40–€70 a double. It is also the last place to draw serious cash before the mountains.

logistics.connectivity: Albania is not in the EU, so EU roam-like-home does not apply; Western Balkans operators run a regional scheme among themselves, and EU–Western Balkans rates were reduced in late 2023 but you can still be billed. A Vodafone AL or One Albania prepaid SIM costs a few hundred lek with generous data. The real trap is border spillover — near Prespa, Qafë Thanë and Stëblevë your phone may register on a Greek or Macedonian network. Lock the network manually.
logistics.emergency: 112 is the single European number and works; 127 for ambulance, 129 police, 128 fire, are still in circulation. Organised mountain rescue in Albania is thin and largely volunteer — assume self-rescue and long evacuation times from Shebenik. Albania is outside the EU health system: travel insurance naming hiking, remote evacuation and repatriation is not optional. The nearest serious hospitals are in Elbasan and Korçë; Tirana for anything major.
logistics.weather: The eastern plateau is continental, not Mediterranean — Korçë and Prespa are genuinely cold, with hard frost from November and snow that closes upland tracks. Summer afternoon thunderstorms build over Shebenik and Jabllanica from mid-afternoon; on the open ridge there is no shelter. Prespa gets sudden lake winds that make small-boat crossings to Maligrad unwise; the boatmen will tell you and they are right.
logistics.bookingWindows: Nothing here needs months of notice except beds in Korçë during the mid-August diaspora return and the Carnival week, when the city fills. Prespa and Shebenik homestays want two or three days' warning, mainly so someone shops. The 4x4 to the Shebenik lakes should be arranged the day before, not on the morning.
logistics.money: The lek (ALL) trades at roughly 97–100 to the euro, so treat 100 ALL as €1. Cards work in Korçë, Pogradec and Elbasan and essentially nowhere else on this route. Draw 40,000–60,000 ALL in Korçë for the week and carry small notes; homestays, boatmen, guides, church keyholders and village shops are all cash. Tipping is rounding up; guides expect 10%.
logistics.transportRules: No vignette, and no tolls on this route. Albanian roads are much improved on the main SH corridors and still poor everywhere else — assume half the map speed on anything unnumbered. Rental cars need explicit written permission plus a green card to cross into North Macedonia or Greece, and many desks refuse; arrange it at booking if you plan to fly out of Ohrid. Drink-driving enforcement is strict and the limit is low.
logistics.permits: Both Prespa and Shebenik-Jabllanicë national parks are free to enter and open year-round; there is no gate and no ticket. Camping in the strict-protection zones is not permitted, and the Rrajcë UNESCO core zone should be walked with a park guide. Commercial collection of medicinal and aromatic plants including çaj mali requires authorisation; household picking does not. Drone flight over the Prespa lakes, the pelican areas and within the border strip is a bad idea legally and ethically — do not.
logistics.health: Tap water in Korçë and Pogradec is chlorinated and generally fine; village spring water is usually excellent but filter above grazing. Ticks are present April–October in the beech belt. Nose-horned viper lives on sunny limestone across the region and antivenom is in hospitals, not villages. Livestock guard dogs at the Shebenik stani are serious animals — stop, do not run, wait for the shepherd. Prespa's shallow shore is safe swimming but the lake drops off fast off the rock spurs.

proTips: Arrange the Shebenik 4x4 through the bujtina you are sleeping in, not through an agency in Tirana. It is half the price, and the driver knows which section of the track failed this spring.
Go to Voskopojë on a weekday morning and ask at the café for the keyholder before you walk to the churches — turning up at a locked door and waiting is the standard tourist experience there.
Lock your phone to a specific Albanian network by hand while you are within 10 km of Prespa or Qafë Thanë. Automatic selection will find a Greek or Macedonian mast and bill you for it.

Buy Prespa beans and çaj mali directly from the household you stay with. It is the cleanest way to leave money in a village that has almost no other income, and the tea is a fraction of Tirana airport prices.
Time Prespa for early morning: the pelicans are on the water, the light is on the Macedonian shore, and by 11:00 the wind is usually up.
Treat Pogradec as the mid-week reset. It is the only town on the route with reliable laundry, a pharmacy, an ATM that works and a hotel shower with pressure.

If you want the Balkan lynx story rather than the animal, contact PPNEA in Tirana before travelling — their camera-trap and monitoring work in Shebenik is the reason the park exists, and they occasionally take visitors.
September is the strongest single month: the pelicans are back on Greater Prespa, the beans are being harvested, the Shebenik track has dried out, and the heat has gone off Korçë.
Carry a small first-aid kit and any prescription you need for the whole week. There is no pharmacy in Pustec, Rrajcë or Fushë-Studë, and Librazhd's closes in the evening.

raw.Remote access — the tracks that matter: The Prespa shore road from Zvezdë to Pustec, Gollomboç and Zaroshkë is asphalt but narrow, unlit and rockfall-prone; a normal car is fine. Everything worth doing in Shebenik-Jabllanicë is not. The track from Fushë-Studë up to the glacial lakes at 1,500–1,900 m is roughly 9–12 km of stone and washed-out clay and genuinely needs a 4x4 or a high-clearance pickup; after rain the last section is winch territory, and snow patches block it until early June. The Rrajcë–Prevall forest road and the Stëblevë spur towards the border are the same story on a smaller scale. The main SH3 through Librazhd and Prrenjas is good asphalt throughout.
raw.Last-mile walk-ins and transfers: From the highest driveable point above Fushë-Studë it is 45–90 minutes on foot to the lake basins depending on where the track has failed that year. Zaroshkë's rock-cut hermitages are a 20–30 minute scramble above the shore. Maligrad island is boat-only, 20 minutes from Gorica or Pustec. Transfers are arranged through the homestay you are staying in — every valley has a cousin with a Mitsubishi L200 — and cost roughly 5,000–8,000 ALL (€50–€80) for a half-day, cash, agreed the night before.
raw.Wilderness isolation — Level 4 of 5 in t: Roughly 50–60 minutes to paved road at Fushë-Studë, no neighbours within 5 km once the summer stani are empty, nearest shop in Fushë-Studë or Rrajcë (small, erratic hours), nearest fuel and pharmacy in Librazhd (about 35 km / 1 h 10 from the trailhead), nearest hospital the regional hospital in Elbasan, roughly 1 h 50 from the lakes. Prespa is Level 3: Pustec has a shop and a health post, but the nearest full pharmacy and hospital are in Korçë, about 1 h 15 away over the Zvezdë ridge.
raw.Off-grid reality: Prespa villages are on mains power but suffer cuts; the Shebenik uplands are solar, generator or nothing. Bujtina water comes from mountain spring boxes and is usually excellent — filter or boil anyway above grazing. Heating and cooking are wood stove, and firewood is the household's own; in Shebenik it is cut and stacked in autumn, so do not burn through it casually. Wastewater is soakaway; there is no drainage system in the upland villages, so nothing goes down a sink that would not go on a garden. Bring what you cannot buy: head torch, power bank, a water filter, cash in small notes, and any medication — there is no pharmacy in Pustec, Rrajcë or Fushë-Studë.
raw.Phone signal: Vodafone AL and One Albania cover Korçë, Pogradec, Librazhd and most of the Prespa shore. There is no usable signal in the Shebenik lake basins, in the Rrajcë forest, or on the Zaroshkë cliffs, and phones near the borders latch onto Greek and Macedonian networks — a real bill risk. Download offline maps for the whole region before Korçë; Shebenik's way-marking is patchy and some marked routes on hiking apps are shepherd tracks that no longer exist.
raw.Foraging and çaj mali: Albania is one of Europe's largest exporters of wild-collected medicinal and aromatic plants, and mountain tea — *çaj mali*, the ironwort *Sideritis raeseri* — is the flagship. It is harvested in July and August on the dry limestone slopes of Shebenik, Jabllanica and the Prespa ridges, cut with a knife above the woody base so the plant regrows, never uprooted. Wild collection for household use is normal and unremarked; collection for sale falls under the forest and biodiversity legislation and needs authorisation from the municipality or forest service, and heavy wild harvesting has pushed the species enough that much commercial supply is now cultivated. Wild mushrooms and berries are gathered freely for the pot, with no functioning public mycological inspection service anywhere in eastern Albania — the only sensible rule is to eat nothing you did not have identified by the household you are staying with. Collection of anything inside a national park's strict-protection zone is prohibited, and protected species — including several Prespa and Shebenik endemics and all orchids — are photograph-only.
raw.Named places to sleep and their characte: The Prespa homestays are a village-scale network in Pustec, Gollomboç, Gorica e Madhe and Zaroshkë, developed with conservation-NGO support, where you sleep in a family's spare room and eat beans, lake fish and pickles at their table. In Shebenik, the bases are Rrajcë and Fushë-Studë, with the park's visitor infrastructure at Rrajcë. Korçë has proper hotels — Hani i Pazarit sits inside the restored Old Bazaar — and Pogradec has the long-established lakeside Hotel Enkelana. Dardhë, at 1,344 m above Korçë, is a stone-built summer and ski village with several guesthouses and the coldest air in the region.
raw.Wildlife: Lesser Prespa holds the world's largest breeding colony of Dalmatian pelicans, mostly on the Greek side but ranging across the whole basin; birds are on the water from February, breeding through spring, and the colony is still rebuilding after the avian-influenza outbreak that killed a large share of the adults in early 2022. Greater Prespa carries pygmy cormorant, great white pelican and wintering wildfowl. Shebenik-Jabllanicë is a core Albanian site for the Balkan lynx, alongside brown bear, grey wolf, chamois and wildcat — the lynx is monitored by camera trap by PPNEA and effectively unseeable in person. Ethical rules: watch pelicans from the shore or a boat kept well off, never approach a raft of birds, no drones over the lakes or colonies at any time of year, and no playback.
raw.Fire and open flame: Albania's high fire-risk season runs roughly 1 June to 30 September, when open fires, stubble burning and barbecues outside built fireplaces in and near forest are banned, and enforcement has hardened after several severe seasons. Cook on the stove. In Prespa the shore reedbeds burn easily and are legally protected habitat; a discarded cigarette there is a serious matter.

sources.verified: Shebenik-Jabllanicë National Park area of roughly 34,500 ha, free entry, 14 glacial lakes at 1,500–1,900 m, Balkan lynx / brown bear / grey wolf presence, and the Rrajca beech forest's inscription as part of the UNESCO Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe; Lesser Prespa as the world's largest Dalmatian pelican breeding colony and the catastrophic avian-influenza outbreak that struck it in early 2022; Balkan Lynx Recovery Programme monitoring in Albania run by PPNEA.
sources.confidenceNotes: No named Prespa or Shebenik homestay is given because none could be confirmed against a live source this run — the file describes the village homestay network instead, and specific *bujtina* names, phone numbers and prices must be inserted and verified before publishing. Hani i Pazarit (Korçë) and Hotel Enkelana (Pogradec) should be re-checked as trading. The legal position on commercial *çaj mali* / medicinal-plant collection is described in general terms because no current statutory text or permit threshold was confirmed this run; have it checked against the Albanian forest and biodiversity legislation before publication. The Prespa NP area figure (roughly 27,750 ha, declared 1999) and the Fushë-Studë track distance and driveability were not confirmed against an official source and vary year to year. Maligrad boat prices, museum entries and keyholder tips are indicative only. The current Dalmatian pelican population figure after the 2022 outbreak was not established this run and should be sourced from the Society for the Protection of Prespa or PONT before publishing. Lek-to-euro conversions and fuel prices need refreshing at publication.

provenance.sourceFormat: md with '## Metadata' bullet block (one file per trip)

trips.title: A Self-Catering Week in the Gesäuse Gorge
trips.subRegion: Gesäuse National Park, Ennstal Alps, Styria

bestPeriod.note: The Alm access track is unploughed and closed by snow from roughly late October to April; June evenings are still cold enough for the wood stove.

trips.gatewayAirport: Graz (GRZ)
trips.summary: Seven off-grid nights in a self-catering Almhütte above the Enns gorge, splitting wood, hauling water and watching chamois on the Xeis crags.
trips.hook: Gesäuse is Austria's most vertical national park: the Enns River saws a green-white gorge straight through the limestone Xeis massif, and the side valleys above it hide a scatter of rentable Almhütten with no electricity, no neighbours and a wood stove that is the only heat you get. This week is not a hike with a hut attached — it is a hut with hikes attached. You haul your own water, split your own kindling, and the payoff is a night sky over the Johnsbachtal that most of Austria lost fifty years ago.

snapshot.Base(s): A self-catering Almhütte in the Johnsbachtal, above Johnsbach (7 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 45–60 km walking, 2,200–2,800 m cumulative ascent; forestry track, alpine meadow, gorge path
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Graz (GRZ), train to Admont via Selzthal, then a pre-arranged pickup or taxi up the Johnsbachtal (no bus serves the upper valley)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Self-sufficient couples or small groups happy to fetch water, feed a fire and go two days without a shower

itinerary.title: Gstatterboden to the Alm
itinerary.morning: Train from Graz to Admont via Selzthal, then a taxi or the pre-arranged hut owner's pickup along the B146 to Gstatterboden, where the road turns up the Johnsbachtal. Buy final groceries in Admont before you leave — this is your last real shop for a week.
itinerary.afternoon: The last stretch to the hut is a narrow, partly gravel forestry road that a normal car manages in dry summer conditions; after rain the final switchbacks are better done in a vehicle with good clearance, and the last 15–20 minutes is a walk-in with your packs from the parking pull-out, since no vehicle is left running at the hut itself. Light the wood stove, find the spring, learn the composting toilet.
itinerary.evening: No signal up here beyond one bar near the ridge. Cook on the wood stove, read by gas lamp, watch the gorge walls go black.
itinerary.dayStats: 4 km walk-in with packs, 220 m ascent. No phone signal at the hut; nearest reliable signal is on the ridge path above, 25 minutes up.

itinerary.title: Settling in: the Johnsbachtal loop
itinerary.morning: Short orientation walk down to Johnsbach village — its plain 15th-century church, the mountain guides' cemetery, and the small Alpine Club information point. Confirm your firewood allowance with the hut owner if it isn't already stacked.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop back via the Kölblwirt inn, useful as a fallback meal if you don't want to cook, then up through larch pasture to the hut. Split and stack a day's wood — you'll need it.
itinerary.evening: Dinner from your carried supplies. First proper dark-sky test: step outside once your eyes adjust.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km, 350 m ascent/descent. Grade easy, gravel lane and meadow path.

itinerary.title: Haindlkarhütte and the Xeis balcony
itinerary.morning: Climb the marked path from Johnsbach toward the Haindlkarhütte (Alpine Club hut, seasonal refreshments), a steady pull through spruce forest into dwarf pine.
itinerary.afternoon: From the hut terrace the Xeis crest — Hochtor, Planspitze — fills the skyline; chamois are routinely visible on the scree bands above. Descend the same path, refilling water bottles at the hut's spring tap.
itinerary.evening: Wood-stove stew. Watch for bats working the meadow at dusk.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 950 m ascent/descent. Grade moderate, well-marked alpine path, no technical exposure.

itinerary.title: Rest day and resupply run
itinerary.morning: Deliberately slow. Drive or get a lift down to Admont for the one resupply run of the week — go before 12:00 on a weekday. Austrian shops shut for good by 18:30 on weekdays and by early afternoon on Saturday, and everything, without exception, is closed on Sunday.
itinerary.afternoon: Wander Admont itself: the Benedictine Admont Abbey and its library are worth the detour if you've never seen it. Back at the hut by mid-afternoon.
itinerary.evening: Restock the woodpile, hang washing, do nothing.
itinerary.dayStats: Effectively a rest day; under 3 km on foot at the hut end.

itinerary.title: The Enns gorge trail
itinerary.morning: Drive to Gstatterboden and pick up the Gesäuse gorge path, which runs along the true right bank of the Enns beneath the Hochtor and Planspitze cliffs — the park's signature walk, with the river running turquoise-white over limestone slabs below.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue toward the Kummerbrücke area and back, watching the cliffs for peregrine falcons, which nest on these walls. Return to the hut by late afternoon; the forestry track access closes to vehicle traffic after dark in places, so time your return.
itinerary.evening: A simpler dinner — you'll be tired from the heat down in the gorge, which sits noticeably warmer than the hut.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km, 250 m ascent/descent. Grade easy-moderate, riverside path, some exposed sections with fixed cable near the narrows.

itinerary.title: Kölbleck ridge and the deer rut listening walk
itinerary.morning: Climb from the hut onto the Kölbleck ridge for open views across the Ennstal to the Gesäuse's northern peaks, including the Admonter Reichenstein.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend through the Kalktal side valley, watching the treeline for red deer — in late September, stags roar across the valley at dusk.
itinerary.evening: Last full evening — finish the firewood, pack out every scrap of rubbish you've generated all week; nothing is collected up here.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km, 900 m ascent/descent. Grade moderate-demanding, some steep forest sections.

itinerary.title: Departure
itinerary.morning: Clean the hut properly — ash out, floor swept, toilet serviced per the owner's instructions — and carry down every bag of rubbish and recycling with you; there is no bin.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive or taxi to Admont, train back to Graz via Selzthal.
itinerary.evening: Flight home from Graz.
itinerary.dayStats: 4 km walk-out with packs, then transfer day.

accommodationStrategy.name: The Almhütte, Johnsbachtal
accommodationStrategy.description: The whole point of this trip: a single, isolated, wood-heated hut booked through Erlebnisregion Gesäuse's short list of self-catering Alm properties in the Johnsbachtal and around Weng im Gesäuse. Confirm before booking exactly what's included — bedding is often not provided, only a mattress, so bring or hire a sleeping bag and liner. Ask specifically about the water source (piped spring vs. cistern) and whether firewood is stacked or you split your own.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 10–12 weeks ahead for July–August.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €55–€90 per night for the whole hut

accommodationStrategy.name: Kölblwirt, Johnsbach
accommodationStrategy.description: Not where you sleep, but worth knowing as your one nearby fallback for a cooked meal, a hot shower arrangement if the hut's is basic, or a place to wait out a bad-weather afternoon. Useful psychologically as much as practically: a 20-minute walk from most Johnsbachtal Alm huts.
accommodationStrategy.booking: no booking needed, but check it's open — smaller Gasthöfe close one weekday.

accommodationStrategy.name: A guesthouse in Admont
accommodationStrategy.description: Book one night here either side of the Alm stay if your flight times are tight or you want a proper shower and a supermarket at hand before or after a week without either. Admont also has the region's best selection of shops and a pharmacy, useful for topping up first-aid supplies.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–3 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; Austrian mountain rescue (Bergrettung) **140**; the hut owner's number should be saved before you lose signal.
logistics.weather: The gorge traps heat and the ridges trap wind; afternoon thunderstorms build fast over the Xeis massif in summer — start exposed ridge walks early.
logistics.money: Cards work in Admont; carry cash for the hut deposit, firewood top-ups and the Gasthof.

other.label: Isolation, specifically
other.text: No phone signal at the hut itself; the nearest doctor is in Admont (approx. 25–30 minutes by car); the nearest shop is Admont's Nah&Frisch or Spar.

other.label: Foraging
other.text: Outside the national park boundary, Styrian law allows personal mushroom picking up to roughly 2 kg per person per day. Inside the Gesäuse National Park itself — which includes most of the Johnsbachtal slopes — picking anything, mushrooms included, is prohibited; this is enforced by park rangers, not a courtesy rule.

other.label: Fire
other.text: Open fires outside the hut's own stove and any designated ring are prohibited under Austrian forest law without landowner permission, and are banned outright within the national park. The wood stove indoors is the only fire you get.

other.label: Water and waste
other.text: Treat the spring supply as untreated — boil or filter if you have any doubt after heavy rain. There is no rubbish collection: everything you bring in, you carry out, including food waste that could draw wildlife to the hut.

other.label: Opening hours
other.text: Austrian shops close by 18:30 on weekdays, early on Saturday, and are shut all day Sunday — plan the one resupply trip around this, not around it being convenient.

proTips: Ask the hut owner for the water source before booking. A piped spring is reliable in a dry August; a rain-fed cistern is not.
Do the single resupply run on Day 4, not Day 1 — you arrive with enough for two days, and shopping mid-week means fresher bread and no rush before the long drive up.
Time the Enns gorge path for morning; by early afternoon the valley floor is noticeably hotter than the hut, and the light on the limestone walls is better before noon.
Bring a head torch stronger than you think you need — Alm huts use gas or battery lamps, and the walk to the composting toilet at 2 a.m. is genuinely dark.
If you're here in the second half of September, sit outside near dusk on the Kölbleck side and listen for the stags; you don't need to hike far to hear the rut.
Ask about buying pre-split firewood at the hut rather than relying only on what's stacked — a week's stove use burns more than first-timers expect.
Check trail-condition notices at the Gesäuse National Park visitor centre in Admont before the Kölbleck ridge day; a wet week makes it slick.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 45–60 km walking, 2,200–2,800 m cumulative ascent; forestry track, alpine meadow, gorge path
raw.Who It Suits: Self-sufficient couples or small groups happy to fetch water, feed a fire and go two days without a shower

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 45–60 km walking, 2,200–2,800 m cumulative ascent; forestry track, alpine meadow, gorge path
typeSpecific.audience: Self-sufficient couples or small groups happy to fetch water, feed a fire and go two days without a shower

packingNotes: A warm sleeping bag or liner — bedding is frequently not supplied in self-catering Alm huts, even in July.
A head torch, spare batteries, and a lighter or matches for the stove.
A day pack for hut resupply, plus a proper hiking pack for the walk-in itself.
Water purification tablets or a filter as backup for the spring.
Sturdy boots for the gorge path's cable sections and the Kölbleck's rougher ground.
Bin bags for carrying out all rubbish — you will generate more than you expect.
Tick repellent and a tick-removal tool; Styria is a TBE-endemic region and vaccination is worth discussing with a travel doctor before you go.
Binoculars for chamois on the Xeis crags and peregrines on the gorge walls.
Cash in small denominations for the hut deposit and any village Gasthof meals.
A basic first-aid kit — the nearest doctor is a 25–30 minute drive away.
whatCouldGoWrong: **The access track is washed out after heavy rain.** Fallback: park at the lower pull-out and treat the last stretch as a longer walk-in; tell the hut owner in advance.
**You misjudge firewood and run low mid-week.** Fallback: most Alm owners keep a small reserve stack for this — ask in advance whether extra wood is available on request.

**A thunderstorm traps you on the Kölbleck ridge.** Fallback: descend immediately via the nearest marked path into the Kalktal rather than continuing along the exposed crest; there is no shelter on the ridge itself.

**Someone gets sick or hurt with no signal at the hut.** Fallback: know the short walk up to the ridge point where signal returns, and carry the Bergrettung number written down, not just saved on a phone that may be dead.

**The Sunday closing catches you out and you're low on food.** Fallback: Kölblwirt in Johnsbach serves meals most days even when shops are shut; treat it as your emergency kitchen, not your default one.

trips.title: The Una's Green Water: Cabins, Travertine and Krajina Forest

bestPeriod.window: Late May–early July & September–mid-October
bestPeriod.avoid: December–March — riverside cabins close or run cold, forest tracks to Klekovača are snowbound, and the Una runs high and brown
bestPeriod.raw: Late May–early July & September–mid-October

accommodation.note: Riverside wooden cabins €50–€90 per unit; NP camping 20 KM (€10) pp/night

food.note: Mains 12–22 KM (€6–€11); a whole grilled trout with sides under €15

transport.note: Rental car from Zagreb €40–€60/day, fuel, green card, cross-border fee

activities.note: NP zone tickets 4–12 KM, rafting €45–€60, NP guide 100 KM/day, fishing permit 50–60 KM

profile.difficultyNote: 2/5 — riverside walking, one 900 m forest ascent, and a rafting day; nothing technical

trips.gatewayAirport: ZAG Zagreb, 2 h 30 to Bihać via the Maljevac crossing; ZAD Zadar 2 h 45; SJJ Sarajevo 4 h 30
trips.summary: The Una is a limestone river that builds its own bed: dissolved calcium precipitates out as travertine, forming stepped barriers, terraces and curtains that shift over decades, so the waterfalls here are alive rather than eroded. Una National Park, declared in 2008, protects 198 km² of that river plus the Unac tributary and the forest above. This week is deliberately low-mileage — a rafting day from Štrbački buk, a slow day of village bread and travertine at Martin Brod, a forest day toward Klekovača's old-growth beech and spruce, and evenings on a wooden deck with the water going past at walking pace. It suits people who want genuine quiet, low prices and a country that still surprises Western visitors, and who will take the landmine briefing seriously enough to stay on marked ground.

itinerary.title: Cross the border, land on the river at Bihać
itinerary.morning: Drive from Zagreb to the Maljevac or Ličko Petrovo Selo crossing — passports out, green card in the glovebox — and into Una-Sana canton. Change money and buy a local SIM in Bihać.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk Bihać's riverside: the Captain's Tower, the Fethija mosque (a Gothic church converted in the 16th century, unmistakable from its buttresses), and the Japodski otoci, a chain of wooded river islands linked by footbridges that the town uses as its swimming and picnic ground.
itinerary.evening: Grilled Una trout and a Bosnian coffee at a riverside restaurant on the Kostela cascade below town, with the falls audible over dinner.
itinerary.dayStats: 240 km / 2 h 30 plus border / BAM pegged at 1.95583 to €1 / local SIM roughly 10–20 KM / hospital in Bihać, the only one for 100 km

itinerary.title: Štrbački buk and the upper river
itinerary.morning: Drive to Orašac and take the forest spur to Štrbački buk, the Una's signature fall — a 24 m travertine drop into a green pool, viewed from wooden platforms that put you close enough to be soaked in spray. Buy the zone ticket at the entrance gate.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the riverside path downstream and swim in one of the flat reaches; the water sits around 12–14°C even in August, so this is a plunge, not a lounge. Cross into the Lohovo zone on the way back for the quieter Troslap and Dvoslap cascades.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Kulen Vakuf below the Ostrovica fortress, a 14th-century hilltop ruin above a village of 300 people.
itinerary.dayStats: NP zone ticket 12 KM adult (≈€6.10), 8 KM child, 4 KM senior / Lohovo entrance 4 KM / Štrbački buk 24 m / 12 km gravel spur from Orašac / water 12–14°C
itinerary.sleep: Riverside cabin or pension, Kulen Vakuf

itinerary.title: Rafting the Štrbački buk section
itinerary.morning: Raft the classic run from below Štrbački buk down to Lohovo — grade II–III at normal levels, with a few genuine drops over travertine steps and long green flat stretches between. Operators supply wetsuit, helmet and shuttle; the park charges a separate small water-use fee of 15 KM for this section.
itinerary.afternoon: Dry out at the take-out, eat the standard rafting lunch of grilled meat and bread, then do nothing for three hours. This is not a filler — the river week only works if you let some days empty out.
itinerary.evening: Back in Kulen Vakuf, walk up to the Ostrovica ruins for sunset over the Una's confluence with the Krušnica.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km river / grade II–III / operator price typically €45–€60 pp incl. equipment and shuttle / NP rafting fee 15 KM Štrbački buk–Lohovo / minimum age usually 12

itinerary.title: Martin Brod, Milančev buk and a slow village day
itinerary.morning: Drive south to Martin Brod, where the Unac joins the Una and the river disintegrates into a fan of travertine steps — Milančev buk and the Veliki and Mali buk, a hundred small falls rather than one big one. Buy the separate zone ticket.
itinerary.afternoon: Visit the 15th-century Rmanj Monastery at the confluence, then walk the village lanes past the old mills. Eat lunch where the sign is handwritten. In late September the road here smells of plum rakija being distilled in every second yard.
itinerary.evening: Nothing planned. Read on a deck. If you are here in late July, the Una Regatta — a mass descent of the river that has run since the 1990s and draws thousands of boats — turns this stretch into a festival and you should either join it or avoid the week entirely.
itinerary.dayStats: Martin Brod / Milančev buk zone ticket 5 KM adult, 3.50 KM child / 45 km from Kulen Vakuf / family package 20 KM in April–May and October–November
itinerary.sleep: Village house or cabin, Martin Brod

itinerary.title: Forest day toward Osječenica and Klekovača
itinerary.morning: With a park guide or a local driver, take the forest roads east toward Osječenica and the flanks of Klekovača (1,962 m), where some of the last old-growth beech and spruce in Bosnia stands in the Lom reserve. This is the one day that genuinely needs a 4x4 and genuinely needs someone who knows which side tracks are cleared ground.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk 8–10 km through the forest, looking for bear sign on the beech and listening for black woodpecker. Stay on the track. Mushroom season here is late September–early November and the ceps are extraordinary, within personal-use quantities and outside the park's strict zones.
itinerary.evening: Return to the valley for lamb slow-cooked under a sač (an iron bell buried in embers) — order it in the morning, it takes four hours.
itinerary.dayStats: 40–50 km of forest road / Klekovača 1,962 m / guide 100 KM (≈€51) up to 8 h / zero mobile signal for 5 h / mine-marking signs mean stop, no exceptions
itinerary.sleep: Cabin, Martin Brod or Kulen Vakuf

itinerary.title: Krušnica source, Ostrožac castle and the lower valley
itinerary.morning: Drive north to Bosanska Krupa and paddle or walk the Krušnica, a 5 km spring-fed tributary so clear it looks like the boats are floating on air. Canoe hire is cheap and the current is gentle.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Ostrožac, a fortress above the Una begun by the Habsburgs on a medieval base, half-ruined, half-restored, and virtually unvisited on a weekday.
itinerary.evening: Back to Bihać. Eat ćevapi in the old town, then coffee by the water while the swifts work the river.
itinerary.dayStats: 5 km Krušnica / canoe hire roughly 30–50 KM / Ostrožac 25 km from Bihać / river temperature 9–11°C at the Krušnica source

itinerary.title: Last morning on the water and out
itinerary.morning: Walk the Japodski otoci once more at 07:00, when the mist is still on the river and the town is empty, or fish a morning beat with a park permit — the Una's grayling and brown trout are the reason people fly here with rod tubes.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive north to the border and Zagreb, allowing an hour of contingency for the crossing on a summer weekend.
itinerary.evening: Zagreb, or straight to the airport.
itinerary.dayStats: Fishing permit 50–60 KM/day, 120–140 KM for three days / 240 km to ZAG / border queues of 1–2 h on July and August weekends

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Kostelski Buk
accommodationStrategy.style: riverside hotel on a travertine cascade
accommodationStrategy.description: Ten kilometres from Bihać and built directly over a working waterfall, so the sound is constant and the terrace is the point. Secure parking, a proper restaurant, reliable hot water and Wi-Fi that works — the right first and last night when everything else on this trip is deliberately basic. Roughly €70–€110 a double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Camp Lučica
accommodationStrategy.style: national park campsite and simple cabins
accommodationStrategy.description: Park-run riverside pitches and huts at 20 KM (about €10) per person per day, with the river a few metres away and the park's own staff on site. Basic sanitation, no restaurant, wood available. The cheapest legitimate way to sleep inside the park boundary and the best for early-morning otter watching.

accommodationStrategy.name: Rafting-operator wooden bungalows
accommodationStrategy.description: The rafting clubs on the Una's Bihać stretch run clusters of timber cabins with shared fire pits, outdoor kitchens and a boat trailer permanently parked outside. Rough, friendly, €50–€90 a cabin, and they will bundle the rafting day and the shuttle with the room. Book by phone or Facebook message, not through booking platforms.

logistics.connectivity: Bosnia is outside the EU and outside EU roaming. Reduced Western Balkans roaming caps exist under a 2023 EU declaration, but rates are still not domestic — buy a BH Telecom or m:tel prepaid SIM in Bihać. No signal at all on the forest roads or in the Unac canyon; download offline maps.
logistics.emergency: 112 works; 122 police, 124 ambulance. Mountain rescue in Una-Sana canton is volunteer-based (GSS) and slow to reach the Klekovača forest roads — coordinates and a working local SIM matter more than anything in your first-aid kit. Nearest full hospital: Kantonalna bolnica "Dr. Irfan Ljubijankić", Bihać. EHIC/GHIC does **not** cover Bosnia; carry travel insurance that explicitly names rafting and hiking, and be ready to pay cash and reclaim.
logistics.weather: The Una valley is humid and thunderstorm-prone from late May, with storms building over Osječenica in mid-afternoon. River level is the volatile variable: after two days of rain the rafting grade jumps and operators cancel. Autumn brings dense valley fog that does not lift until 10:00 and makes the gravel spur to Štrbački buk genuinely dangerous.
logistics.bookingWindows: Rafting on Una Regatta weekend in late July is booked out months ahead and the whole valley is full; either commit early or move your dates. Cabins otherwise need two to four weeks in July–August, and almost nothing in September. Park guides should be requested at least three days out through the NP office in Bihać.
logistics.money: The convertible mark (BAM/KM) is pegged to the euro at 1.95583, so 10 KM ≈ €5.11. Euros are accepted informally at some tourist businesses at a poor rate — change money properly. Cards work in Bihać hotels and supermarkets and nowhere else that matters: village shops, park gates, mills, fishing permits and most cabins are cash. Draw 300–400 KM on arrival. Tipping is rounding up.
logistics.transportRules: Bosnia has no motorway vignette; the short A1 sections are tolled at barriers. You need a green card for the rental — confirm with the hire desk in Zagreb before you leave and expect a cross-border fee of €30–€60. Headlights on during the day are compulsory. Winter equipment rules run 1 November–15 April. Fuel is cheaper than in Croatia; fill up before returning.
logistics.permits: Una NP charges by zone — 12 KM for the Štrbački buk–Lohovo zone, 4 KM for the Lohovo entrance, 5 KM for Martin Brod/Milančev buk, free under 7, with April–May and October–November family packages at 20 KM. Rafting sections carry small additional fees (15 KM Štrbački buk–Lohovo, 8 KM Martin Brod–Kulen Vakuf). Fishing permits are 50–60 KM per day. Camping outside designated sites is prohibited in the park. Drones need permission from the park and are restricted near the border zone with Croatia, which the river partly forms.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable in Bihać and Kulen Vakuf; treat spring and well water at cabins. Ticks are abundant in the Krajina forest April–October and TBE is present in the region — check nightly. Nose-horned viper occurs on sunny limestone. And above all: the landmine issue is real, historic front-line ground runs through this landscape, and the rule is absolute — stay on paths, roads and grazed land.

proTips: Go to Štrbački buk before 09:00 or after 17:00. Between 11:00 and 15:00 in July it fills with day-trippers bussed from the Croatian coast, and the platforms are only so wide.
Buy the April–May or October–November family package at 20 KM if there are three or more of you — it undercuts individual zone tickets across two entrances.
Ask your cabin host to order sač lamb or veal in the morning for that evening. It is the single best meal in this valley and it cannot be done on demand.

The park's own guide at 100 KM for a full day is the cheapest serious wildlife guiding in Europe and the only way to read the Klekovača forest roads correctly. Book it for the day you would otherwise waste.
Carry small notes. A 100 KM note at a village mill or a park gate will produce a genuinely awkward five minutes.
Time your visit around the Una Regatta in late July deliberately — either in it, for one of the great river parties of the Balkans, or a fortnight either side, for an empty river.
The Krušnica is more beautiful than the Una at its own confluence and almost nobody outside Bosanska Krupa paddles it. Two hours, gentle, and the clearest water of the week.
Photograph the travertine at Martin Brod in the hour after sunrise, when mist sits in the steps and the whole fan glows. By 10:00 the light is flat and the picture is gone.
Fill the tank in Bihać or Kulen Vakuf before any forest day. There is no fuel between Martin Brod and Drvar, and the tracks drink more than you expect.

raw.Remote access — which tracks need what: The asphalt from Bihać to Kulen Vakuf (M14.1, roughly 40 km) is fine in any car, if slow and narrow. The 12 km spur from Orašac to the Štrbački buk viewing platforms is a graded gravel forest road: passable in a standard car dry, but rutted and slick after rain, and locals will tell you a high-clearance vehicle is the honest answer in October. The forest roads climbing toward Osječenica and Klekovača from Drvar and Martin Brod are genuine 4x4 ground — 18–25 km of loose limestone, logging traffic, no barriers and no phone signal. After snow they are impassable until May.
raw.Last-mile walk-ins and transfers: Štrbački buk is a 400 m walk and 150 wooden steps down from the upper car park. Martin Brod's Milančev buk is reached on foot through the village in under 15 minutes. The park office in Bihać (JP NP Una) arranges guides at 100 KM (about €51) for up to eight hours, and rafting operators shuttle you and your car between put-in and take-out as part of the price — the only practical way to do the upper river.
raw.Wilderness isolation — Level 3 of 5 at M: 5 min to paved road but 45 min to a supermarket in Bihać, nearest fuel at Kulen Vakuf or Bosanski Petrovac, nearest pharmacy Bihać, nearest hospital Kantonalna bolnica "Dr. Irfan Ljubijankić" in Bihać (55–70 min from Martin Brod). Klekovača forest days push this to Level 4: two hours to a hospital, no neighbours within 8 km, no signal.
raw.Off-grid reality: Riverside cabins are mostly grid-connected but with thin supply — expect a wood-burning stove as the real heat source, firewood stacked outside and included, an electric shower that dislikes being run twice at once, and septic wastewater that will not take anything but paper. Water is generally municipal and drinkable in Bihać and Kulen Vakuf, but cabin supply drawn from springs or wells should be treated. Carry a head torch, a power bank, a filter bottle, insect repellent and any specific food you need: village shops sell bread, ajvar, cheese, coffee and beer, and nothing else.
raw.Phone signal: BH Telecom and m:tel cover the valley floor and both towns; nothing in the Klekovača forest or the Unac canyon. Bosnia is **not** in the EU roaming zone — EU SIMs roam at non-domestic rates even with the reduced Western Balkans caps agreed in 2023, so buy a BH Telecom or m:tel prepaid SIM in Bihać for a few euros and stop worrying.
raw.Named cabins and character: Hotel Kostelski Buk at Kostela sits directly on a travertine cascade 10 km from Bihać, with the noise of the falls in every room. Camp Lučica, run by the national park, offers riverside pitches and simple cabins at 20 KM per person per day. Rafting operators around Golubić and Ćelije run clusters of wooden bungalows with shared fire pits — rustic, cheap, and loud on regatta weekends.
raw.Foraging rules: Bosnia's mushroom culture is strong and largely informal — vrganj (cep), lisičarka (chanterelle) and smrčak (morel) are the prizes, and the season peaks late September to early November. Federation forestry rules require permission from the cantonal forestry authority for commercial collection; personal-use picking is tolerated without paperwork, but collecting inside Una NP's protected zones needs park permission and is prohibited in the strict-protection core. There is no reliable public mycological inspection point in Una-Sana canton — assume you are on your own and do not eat anything you cannot identify with total confidence. Wild garlic, rosehips, elderflower, cornel cherries and blackberries are freely picked by everyone.
raw.Landmine awareness — non-negotiable: BHMAC reports more than 820 km² of Bosnia still suspected of contamination, roughly 1.6% of the country, from an original 4,180 km²; clearance is running at about 75 km² per year and the country is not expected to be mine-free before the early 2030s. The former front line ran through this region. Stay on marked paths, roads, and land that is obviously farmed or grazed. Do not walk into unused meadow, ruined villages, or forest edge to photograph a building. Yellow-and-red skull signs and red-painted stones mean stop. Report anything suspicious rather than moving it.
raw.Wildlife: Brown bear and grey wolf both use the Osječenica–Klekovača massif; otter is genuinely common on the Una and the Unac and is the realistic sighting — look at dawn from the Martin Brod bridges and the quiet reaches above Lohovo. Kingfisher, dipper and grey heron work the travertine steps all day. Ethical viewing: no baiting, no drones over roosts or otter holts, keep to hides and bridges, and give any bear a wide, upwind exit.
raw.Fire risk and open flame: Federation forest law bans open fire in and within 150 m of forest during the declared high-risk summer period, typically 1 June–31 October, with cantonal variations. Use only the built fire pits at cabins and campsites, never leave one unattended, and expect campfires to be flatly refused inside national park zones.

sources.verified: Una National Park official price list — Štrbački buk/Lohovo zone 12 KM adult, 8 KM child 7–14, 4 KM senior 65+, free under 7; Lohovo entrance 4 KM; Martin Brod/Milančev buk 5 KM adult, 3.50 KM child; family packages 20 KM in April–May and October–November; rafting-section fees 15 KM (Štrbački buk–Lohovo) and 8 KM (Martin Brod–Kulen Vakuf); camping at Lučica 20 KM per person per day; tourist guide 100 KM up to 8 hours; fishing 50–60 KM daily and 120–140 KM for three days. BHMAC landmine contamination figures: over 820 km² still suspected, roughly 1.6% of territory, about 3,360 km² cleared of an original 4,180 km², clearance targeted at 75 km² a year.
sources.confidenceNotes: The park price list checked was the most recent published version and may not reflect a 2026 revision — re-verify before publishing. Named accommodation other than the park's own Camp Lučica needs confirmation of current operation, rates and season; the rafting-operator bungalow cluster is described generically for that reason and should have a specific verified operator inserted. Rafting per-person prices are operator-set and were not confirmed this run. The Klekovača/Osječenica forest-road condition, logging activity and which tracks are cleared ground must be confirmed locally on the day — treat every figure about them as indicative. EU–Western Balkans roaming rates changed in 2023 and are being revised again; check current caps. Una Regatta dates shift annually. Cross-border rental fees from Croatia vary by company.

trips.title: Heathland Week — Cabin Days in the Hoge Kempen
trips.subRegion: Hoge Kempen National Park, Belgian Limburg

bestPeriod.note: Late May–June brings breeding nightjars and orchids on the heath; August turns the Mechelse Heide purple with flowering heather.

trips.gatewayAirport: Brussels (BRU)
trips.summary: A gentle week of forest-cabin nights around Belgium's only national park, from heather-clad dunes to a former coal mine turned nature gate.
trips.hook: The Hoge Kempen is a small, flat, deeply un-alpine kind of wild — 6,000 hectares of drift-sand heath, juniper scrub and Scots pine stitched together from old military and mining land into Belgium's only national park. It rewards patience more than fitness: sit still at dusk on the Mechelse Heide and nightjars churr past your head. This week bases you in a forest cabin at the park's southern edge and works outward through its five gates on foot and by bike, with one former colliery site as a reminder of what this landscape used to be.

snapshot.Base(s): Maasmechelen, forest cabin at the Terhills site (7 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 60–80 km on foot and by bike; flat sand paths, boardwalk, forest track — no significant elevation change
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Brussels (BRU), train to Maastricht or Genk then local bus/taxi to Maasmechelen, or hire a car for the whole week
snapshot.Who It Suits: Families and slow walkers who want genuine nature immersion without altitude or exposure

itinerary.title: Arrival and the Terhills lakes
itinerary.morning: Train to Genk or Maastricht, then transfer to Maasmechelen. Check into the forest cabin at Terhills, built on the grounds of the former Eisden colliery.
itinerary.afternoon: Easy orientation walk around the Terhills lakes — flooded former quarry water, now clear enough for the swimming area — and along the first stretch of marked heath path toward the park boundary.
itinerary.evening: Cook in; the cabin kitchens are fully equipped, unlike a wilderness hut. Settle in properly for the week.
itinerary.dayStats: 6 km, flat. No ascent worth naming.

itinerary.title: Mechelse Heide
itinerary.morning: Drive or cycle the short distance to the Mechelse Heide gate, the largest contiguous heather expanse in the Benelux. Walk the marked loop past grazing Galloway cattle, kept here specifically to browse back birch and pine seedlings and keep the heath open.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to the viewpoint dune and look for sand lizards basking on bare sand patches — a species this heath is specifically managed for. Cycle back via the quieter forest edge paths rather than retracing the outbound route.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Maasmechelen; the town centre has a reasonable spread of everyday restaurants.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km combined walking and cycling, flat sand and gravel paths.

itinerary.title: Lieteberg and Kattevennen
itinerary.morning: Drive to As and the Kattevennen gate, home to Connecterra, the park's flagship nature-discovery centre — worth an hour before you walk, especially with kids, for its hands-on exhibits on the park's sand, water and forest systems.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb the short path to the Lieteberg lookout tower, the park's best single viewpoint, giving a full sweep across the dune ridges and pine blocks toward Genk. Picnic at the base rather than on the exposed platform if the wind is up.
itinerary.evening: Back to the cabin. Early night — Day 4 starts before dawn.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km, one short climb to the Lieteberg summit (a dune, not a mountain — under 30 m of ascent).

itinerary.title: Dawn wildlife walk and Cicindria pines
itinerary.morning: Out before sunrise for the best wildlife window: roe deer feeding at the forest edge, and — if you're lucky and quiet — a fox or the tail end of a wild boar family moving between cover. Boar numbers have grown across the park in recent years; keep dogs leashed and give any sounder a wide, calm berth.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive to the Cicindria gate near Zutendaal and walk the pine forest paths, quieter and more shaded than the open heath, good for a hot afternoon.
itinerary.evening: Rest at the cabin. Sauna or lake swim if the Terhills facilities are booked for you.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km across the two sessions, flat.

itinerary.title: Pietersheim and the Lanaken loop
itinerary.morning: Drive to the Pietersheim gate at Lanaken, entered through the grounds of Kasteel Pietersheim, and pick up the marked trail into the park's northwestern block.
itinerary.afternoon: A longer loop through mixed heath and forest, with a stop at one of the park's bird hides — bring binoculars for tree pipit and, at dusk, nightjar in the right season. Return via the castle grounds.
itinerary.evening: Dinner out in Lanaken or back at the cabin.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km, flat, mostly sand and gravel track.

itinerary.title: Bike day: the knooppunten network
itinerary.morning: Rent bikes in Maasmechelen and ride the numbered junction (knooppunten) cycle network looping through the park's southern gates — a genuinely different way to cover ground here compared to on foot.
itinerary.afternoon: Stop at a café along the route, then finish with a slow ride back through the Terhills site itself, past the old mine infrastructure now repurposed as adventure and leisure ground.
itinerary.evening: Last cabin dinner. Pack for departure.
itinerary.dayStats: 35–45 km cycling, flat, mixed asphalt and gravel.

itinerary.title: Departure
itinerary.morning: A final short walk from the cabin door before checkout — no need to drive anywhere for one more taste of the heath.
itinerary.afternoon: Transfer to Maastricht or Genk station, train onward to Brussels.
itinerary.evening: Flight home from Brussels.
itinerary.dayStats: 3 km, then transfer day.

accommodationStrategy.name: Forest cabin, Terhills, Maasmechelen
accommodationStrategy.description: The best-located base for this trip: a wood-and-glass cabin set directly in forest on the former Eisden colliery grounds, a short drive or ride from three of the park's five gates, with the Terhills lakes on the doorstep for an evening swim. Cabins here have real kitchens and proper beds — comfort, not survival — which suits a week built around long days outdoors.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead for summer weekends.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €140–€220 per night for a two-to-four-person cabin

accommodationStrategy.name: A guesthouse in As
accommodationStrategy.description: A quieter alternative if you'd rather be close to the Lieteberg and Connecterra side of the park than the Maasmechelen side. As is a small, workaday Kempen village with limited eating options, so plan to drive out most evenings.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: A hotel in Genk
accommodationStrategy.description: Useful as a one-night bookend if your train times don't line up with the cabin check-in or checkout, and it puts you near C-mine, Genk's own former-colliery cultural site, if you want an extra half-day of industrial-heritage context before or after the park.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–3 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; this covers police, fire and ambulance throughout Belgium.
logistics.money: Cards are near-universal in Belgium, including at the cabin resort and most cafés; carry some cash for small village shops.

other.label: Isolation, specifically
other.text: This is a gentle trip by Nature Escapes standards: mobile signal is reliable across nearly the whole park, the nearest supermarket (Maasmechelen town centre) is a 5–15 minute drive from any gate, and Maasmechelen and Lanaken both have general practitioners and a pharmacy.

other.label: Foraging
other.text: The park is a strict nature reserve. Picking anything — mushrooms, berries, flowers, deadwood — is prohibited across almost all of it; this is actively enforced, unlike the more relaxed rules in ordinary Belgian forest.

other.label: Fire
other.text: Open fires and barbecues are banned throughout the park at all times, and the heath itself is genuinely fire-prone in a dry summer — Flanders issues public fire-risk codes, and access to parts of the reserve can be temporarily closed on high-risk days. Check the day's status before an August visit.

other.label: Wild boar
other.text: Numbers have risen across the Kempen; keep dogs on a lead, never approach a sounder with young, and store food properly at the cabin.

other.label: Ticks
other.text: Present on the heath in warmer months; check after every walk, particularly around ankles and knees.

other.label: Opening hours
other.text: Belgian supermarkets generally run normal weekday and Saturday hours with reduced Sunday opening — plan your one bigger shop for a weekday.

other.label: Cycling
other.text: The knooppunten junction-number network covers the whole region; download the map or grab a paper one from Connecterra before setting out.

proTips: Do the dawn wildlife walk on your second or third morning, not your first — you'll have learned the trail junctions by then and won't waste the best light finding your way.

Visit Connecterra before your first heath walk, not after; its exhibits explain why the cattle, the sand patches and the controlled burns are there, and the rest of the week reads differently once you know.
August heather bloom draws weekend crowds to Mechelse Heide specifically — walk it on a weekday morning, or shift that visit to a Tuesday if your itinerary allows.
Ask at the Terhills reception about lake swimming hours and whether a sauna slot is included; it is the single best way to end a hot walking day here.
Nightjars are most active in the first 45 minutes after sunset in June–July — pick a heath edge near cover, stay still, and switch phone torches off entirely.
Rent bikes for Day 6 rather than driving it; the knooppunten network is built for exactly this kind of loop and covers ground a walking day can't.
Check the park's fire-risk status before an August trip — on the highest-risk days, some heath sections close to visitors entirely.
