raw.Who It Suits: Families and slow walkers who want genuine nature immersion without altitude or exposure

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 60–80 km on foot and by bike; flat sand paths, boardwalk, forest track — no significant elevation change
typeSpecific.audience: Families and slow walkers who want genuine nature immersion without altitude or exposure

packingNotes: Comfortable walking shoes rather than boots — the terrain is flat sand and gravel, not mountain ground.
A light rain layer; Belgian weather turns quickly even in a "good" week.
Binoculars for nightjar, tree pipit and sand lizard spotting.
A tick-removal tool and insect repellent for heath walking in warmer months.
Swimwear for the Terhills lakes.
A bike lock if you bring your own bikes rather than renting.
Sun protection — the open heath has zero shade at midday.
A printed or downloaded knooppunten cycle map as backup to your phone.
Cash for small village purchases and any hide-side honesty-box refreshments.
A cool bag for cabin groceries if you're doing one big weekday shop.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A high fire-risk day closes part of the heath.** Fallback: shift to the forested Cicindria or Pietersheim gates, which stay open under most fire-risk levels, and save the open Mechelse Heide sections for a cooler day.
**Weekend crowds at Mechelse Heide during heather bloom.** Fallback: walk it before 09:00 or move that visit to a weekday; use the quieter Cicindria pine trails on the Saturday instead.
**Rain washes out a full cycling day.** Fallback: the Terhills site and Connecterra both have solid indoor content, and the forest trails under tree cover stay walkable in lighter rain.
**You encounter a wild boar sounder on a narrow path.** Fallback: back away slowly the way you came, keep any dog close and leashed, and do not attempt to move around them off-path.
**A missed local train connection at Genk or Maastricht.** Fallback: both stations run frequent onward services throughout the day; budget a buffer rather than a tight connection on departure day.

trips.title: Reserve Country: Central Balkan Huts, Karst Caves and the Rhodope Vulture Gorges
trips.subRegion: Central Balkan National Park (Stara Planina), the Lovech karst, and the Eastern Rhodopes

bestPeriod.window: late May to mid-June (waterfalls at full flow, vultures on eggs, meadows in flower)
bestPeriod.avoid: November–April on the ridge (Botev is a full winter mountain), and August in the Rhodopes (40 °C, rivers down to a trickle)

food.note: €110–€170 (€16–€24/day; hut half-board where offered)

transport.note: €180–€300 (a hire car is effectively compulsory: €30–€45/day plus fuel)

activities.note: €40–€80 (Devetashka, Krushuna, Ökocentrum-style visitor centres, a guided vulture hide)

profile.difficultyNote: Moderate

trips.gatewayAirport: Sofia (SOF) or Plovdiv (PDV). Kalofer is 2 h from Sofia on the A1/I-6 via Karlovo. Finish near the Greek border: Madzharovo is 3 h 30 from Sofia, 2 h 15 from Plovdiv. Hire the car at the airport.
trips.currency: Euro (EUR) — sole legal tender since 1 February 2026; mandatory dual BGN display ended 8 August 2026
trips.summary: A week in the two wildest blocks of Bulgaria: a beech-and-granite national park where nine strict reserves are sealed off from everything but a marked footpath, and a semi-desert river gorge where griffon vultures…
trips.hook: A week in the two wildest blocks of Bulgaria: a beech-and-granite national park where nine strict reserves are sealed off from everything but a marked footpath, and a semi-desert river gorge where griffon vultures ride the thermals over a rewilded valley. You sleep in unheated *hizha* bunkrooms at 1,800 m, drive forest roads that will take a hire car's sump off, and go two days without a signal. Not comfortable. Genuinely remote.

snapshot.Best period: Late May to mid-June, or September
snapshot.Start / End: Kalofer → Madzharovo (point-to-point, ~600 km driving)
snapshot.Getting there: Sofia (SOF) or Plovdiv (PDV). Kalofer is 2 h from Sofia on the A1/I-6 via Karlovo. Finish near the Greek border: Madzharovo is 3 h 30 from Sofia, 2 h 15 from Plovdiv. Hire the car at the airport.

itinerary.title: Kalofer and the highest waterfall in Bulgaria
itinerary.morning: Drive Sofia–Karlovo–**Kalofer**, the birthplace of Hristo Botev, and register your route intention at the **Central Balkan National Park** Kalofer information point [VERIFY: current Kalofer visitor point opening hours].
itinerary.afternoon: The Byala reka valley trail to **Raysko Praskalo** — "Paradise Spray" — which drops **124.5 m** in a single fall off the Botev cirque, the highest waterfall in Bulgaria and the Balkans. Full volume in late May, a thin thread by August.
itinerary.evening: Continue to **Hizha Rai** at roughly 1,950 m beneath the fall. Bean soup, a wood stove, a generator that dies at 22:00 [VERIFY: current Hizha Rai bed and half-board rates].

itinerary.title: Botev peak, 2,376 m
itinerary.morning: Leave at 06:30 for **Botev**, the Stara Planina's highest summit at **2,376 m**, crowned by an incongruous television mast and meteorological station. Two to three hours from Rai on marked trail, exposed to the ridge wind throughout.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the rim above **Dzhendema** reserve, the great south-facing wall of the range and the most strictly protected ground in Bulgaria. Look; do not enter.
itinerary.evening: Descend to Kalofer and drive the **Beklemeto (Troyan) pass** at about 1,525 m to a *vila* in **Cherni Osam** or **Apriltsi** — hot water, a real bed, and signal for the first time in 36 hours.

itinerary.title: Steneto and the beech forests
itinerary.morning: Up the Cherni Osam forest road to **Hizha Pleven** at about 1,300 m, gateway to the **Steneto** reserve — a Bulgarian component of UNESCO's *Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests* inscription of 2017.
itinerary.afternoon: The marked through-route into the Steneto gorge: limestone walls, the Cherni Osam river, caves in the flank, beech never cut. Marked trail only; the reserve permits nothing else.
itinerary.evening: Back down for the **Natural History Museum in Cherni Osam**, a serious taxidermy and habitat collection built by one family over decades [VERIFY: current Cherni Osam museum hours].

itinerary.title: Kozya Stena and the ridge huts
itinerary.morning: Park at the **Troyan Pass** monument on Beklemeto and walk the ridge west on **Kom–Emine** (E3) waymarks to **Kozya Stena** reserve, a narrow limestone crest holding Balkan endemics including edelweiss.
itinerary.afternoon: Down to **Hizha Kozya Stena** for soup, then across to **Hizha Dobrila** at roughly 1,800 m, the stone staging post on the ridge [VERIFY: current Hizha Dobrila rates and midweek staffing].
itinerary.evening: Stay at Dobrila. No signal, spring water, and the stars over the Steneto forest. Carry cash — there is no card machine on the ridge.

itinerary.title: Down to the karst: Devetashka and Krushuna
itinerary.morning: North to **Lovech** (about 1 h 15), then 20 km to **Devetaki** village and the **Devetashka Cave** — a colossal karst hall with seven ceiling openings and a floor the size of a stadium, holding a large bat colony. **Access is restricted in the bat breeding season, roughly June–July** [VERIFY: current Devetashka Cave seasonal closure dates and hours].
itinerary.afternoon: East to the **Krushuna waterfalls**, a travertine staircase of terraces and moss below the village — boardwalks, low gradient, and the busiest thing on this itinerary. Before 10:00 or after 16:00.
itinerary.evening: The long transfer south: Lovech to **Madzharovo** is roughly 290 km and 4 hours via Stara Zagora and Haskovo. Do it in daylight — the last hour is narrow gorge road.

itinerary.title: Vultures above the Arda
itinerary.morning: At first light, up to the viewpoint above the **Madzharovo** gorge on the Arda — the core breeding area of Bulgaria's **griffon vulture** colony and a last stronghold of the **Egyptian vulture**, the small migratory one that winters in Africa and is critically endangered in Europe.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Bulgarian Society for the Protection of Birds (BSPB/BDZP) Eastern Rhodopes Nature Conservation Centre** runs the field station, exhibition and guided hides. Book a hide in advance — it starts before dawn and there are few seats [VERIFY: current BSPB Madzharovo hide booking process and fee].
itinerary.evening: Stay at the centre. The old mining valley below is among the emptiest inhabited landscapes in the EU: black stork, sombre tit, and a river with nobody on it.

itinerary.title: Studen Kladenets and the Byala Reka wilderness
itinerary.morning: West along the Arda to the **Studen Kladenets** reservoir, focus of the Rhodope rewilding work — reintroduced **fallow and red deer** built up as a prey base for the vultures, and a feeding site above the water.
itinerary.afternoon: With high clearance and dry weather, run south into the **Byala Reka** basin towards Kroumovgrad: oak savanna, dry gorges, tortoises on the track, one of the least visited protected areas in the country. In a 2WD car on a wet day, do not.
itinerary.evening: Out via Kardzhali. Eat *patatnik*, drink Rhodope wine, and note that the week cost less than three nights in the Alps.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hizha Rai
accommodationStrategy.description: the only bed that puts you on Botev's rim at dawn instead of climbing 1,400 m from the valley. Wood stove, generator hours, spring water, bunkrooms.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct by phone a few days ahead midweek, 2–3 weeks for a summer weekend. Cash only; bring a liner.

accommodationStrategy.name: Village *vila* rentals
accommodationStrategy.description: the midweek reset — hot water, drying space and a kitchen, 20 minutes from the Steneto trailhead and inside the Kom–Emine corridor. Wood-stove heating; ask whether wood is included.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–4 weeks ahead via Booking.com or direct with the owner. September is the tight month, because of the mushrooms.

accommodationStrategy.name: BSPB Eastern Rhodopes Nature Conservation Centre
accommodationStrategy.description: you sleep at the research station above the gorge, with the people who ring the birds. Simple rooms, shared facilities, exhibition on site, hides arranged at the desk.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct with BSPB well ahead for spring migration and the breeding season — the building is small [VERIFY: current BSPB Madzharovo room rates].

logistics.connectivity: A1 and Yettel cover Kalofer, Troyan, Apriltsi, Lovech and the Rhodope villages. There is **no signal at Hizha Rai, Hizha Dobrila or in the Steneto gorge** and patchy coverage on the Botev ridge. Download offline maps — Kom–Emine waymarks are good but sparse in cloud.
logistics.emergency: **112**, routing to the **Planinska spasitelna sluzhba** (Bulgarian Red Cross mountain rescue). Response to the Botev ridge is measured in hours. Leave your route with the hut warden and stick to it.
logistics.weather: The ridge makes its own weather. Botev is among the windiest points in Bulgaria and can go sun-to-whiteout in twenty minutes in any month; snow patches persist into June. The Rhodopes are the opposite problem — 40 °C and no shade in August.
logistics.bookingWindows: Huts, a few days to three weeks. The BSPB centre and any vulture hide, weeks to months in spring. The hire car as early as possible for September — Bulgarian fleets run out.
logistics.money: Bulgaria uses the **euro**, lev fixed at 1 EUR = 1.95583 BGN. **Every hut here is cash-only** and there is no ATM above the valley towns; carry €200–€250 in small notes. Cards work in Lovech, Troyan and Kardzhali.
logistics.transportRules: An electronic **vignette** is required on Bulgarian republican roads and motorways — buy it online or at a fuel station before driving. Check the rental agreement's unsurfaced-road exclusion. Fuel in Troyan and again in Haskovo; Rhodope stations are far apart and close early.
logistics.permits: No entry fee or permit for the national park. **Marked trails only in all nine reserves**; no camping or bivouac in reserves; camping only in designated park zones; **no open fires anywhere in the park**; no drones; dogs leashed and banned in reserves. Collecting plants, fungi or wood is prohibited in the core and reserves and permit-regulated elsewhere.

proTips: **Take Raysko Praskalo in the last week of May.** Snowmelt is what makes a 124 m waterfall look like one; by August it is a stain on a cliff.
**Phone the hut the day before, in Bulgarian if you can.** Wardens do not reliably answer email, and a hut listed as open may be shut for a week for supplies.

**Ask a Cherni Osam or Apriltsi host about mushrooms instead of searching alone.** Village knowledge of which slope is producing is decades deep, freely given, and keeps you legally outside the park core.
**Book the Madzharovo hide before anything else.** It is the one genuinely scarce thing here, and only the dawn session is worth doing.
**Use the Beklemeto pass as your bad-weather switch.** If the ridge is in cloud, drop north to Devetashka and Krushuna a day early and take Botev on the better morning.
**Carry 3 litres and a filter.** Kom–Emine ridge springs are reliable in June and unreliable in September; Rhodope tributaries in August are stagnant.
**Learn *"Има ли мечки тук?"*** — "are there bears here?" The answer is always yes, and the advice that follows beats anything written down.

raw.Access requirements: Three grades. **Asphalt throughout**: the Beklemeto (Troyan) pass road at ~1,525 m and the Kalofer approach. **Rough but 2WD-passable when dry**: the Cherni Osam forest road to **Hizha Pleven**, broken concrete then gravel, fine in a hatchback if you crawl. **High clearance genuinely required**: the upper forest road above Kalofer, the tracks around **Studen Kladenets**, and everything off tarmac in the **Byala Reka** basin, where the road is a dry riverbed with a name. Rain downgrades all three within an hour, and Bulgarian hire cars are almost always barred from unsurfaced roads — read the agreement.
raw.Isolation level: 4 of 5: Two nights in huts with no road access and no mains power; the Rhodope nights in a village of a few hundred with one shop. Not 5 — there is always a warden or a village within three hours' walk — but nowhere here is help fast.
raw.Wild camping vs bivouac — the distinctio: Bulgarian law prohibits camping outside designated sites, and inside **Central Balkan National Park** camping is allowed only at the directorate's **designated camping and bivouac zones**, mostly at or beside the huts. In practice a **bivouac** — one night, late in, early out, no established camp, no fire, pitched beside a hut or at a marked bivouac place — is accepted by wardens. A **camp** — several nights, a fire ring, gear spread out, off-zone — is not, and is fined. Inside the nine **strict reserves** (Boatin, Tsarichina, Kozya Stena, Steneto, Sokolna, Peeshtite Skali, Severen Dzhendem, Dzhendema, Stara Reka) there is **no camping and no bivouac at all**: the marked through-trail and nothing else — no leaving the path, no fire, no picking, no dogs, no drone [VERIFY: current Central Balkan NP bivouac zone list and seasonal reserve closures].
raw.Foraging: Medicinal plants fall under the **Medicinal Plants Act (Zakon za lechebnite rastenia)**: personal-quantity picking on state forest land is free, **commercial collection needs a municipal permit**, and several species are under annual quota or banned from wild collection outright — **Sideritis scardica** (*mursalski chay*) and **Rhodiola rosea** are the two you will be tempted by and must not take [VERIFY: current banned/quota species list]. Mushrooms — *manatarka* (cep), chanterelle — are free for personal use on state forest land in the Troyan and Apriltsi valleys, the classic September activity. **Inside the reserves and the park core, all collecting of plants, fungi and firewood is prohibited.**
raw.Bear and wolf protocol: The Central Balkan holds a resident **brown bear** population and the beech reserves are prime habitat. Make noise on blind bends and in dense beech, avoid dusk in berry season, never approach a cub, keep food out of the tent, and if you meet one do not run — back away facing it, talking level. Wolves are present in both ranges and are not a practical concern. The likelier problem is a livestock guardian dog at a *kolibi* sheepfold: stop, do not turn your back, let the shepherd call it off.
raw.Off-grid utilities: The high huts (Rai, Dobrila, Kozya Stena) run **generator or solar on fixed evening hours**, with wood stoves, spring water, dry toilets, cold showers, and are **cash-only**; blankets are provided, bedding often is not. Village *vila* rentals in Cherni Osam, Apriltsi and Ribaritsa have mains power and hot water but frequently no central heating, only a wood *pech* — ask before booking a May night.

trips.title: Stay on the Path: A Week in the Swiss National Park

bestPeriod.note: Chamanna Cluozza opens roughly mid-June to mid-October only; the Val Trupchun red deer rut in September draws the heaviest foot traffic of the year.

trips.gatewayAirport: Zurich (ZRH)
trips.summary: A week inside the strictest nature reserve in the Alps: marked paths only, nothing picked, no camping and no dogs, from Zernez to a hut with no road and Val Trupchun's ibex and red deer.
trips.hook: Founded in 1914, the Swiss National Park is the oldest in the Alps and by far the strictest: leaving the marked path is forbidden everywhere, picking anything — a flower, a mushroom, a pinecone — is forbidden everywhere, and dogs, camping, cycling off the pass road and fires are all simply not allowed. What that discipline buys you is an ecosystem left almost entirely alone for over a century: bearded vultures reintroduced from nothing, ibex on the scree in plain sight, and Val Trupchun's red deer herds that draw wildlife watchers from across Switzerland every September.

snapshot.Base(s): Zernez (5 nights), Chamanna Cluozza (1 night), Zernez again (1 night)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 60–70 km walking, 3,000–3,400 m cumulative ascent; marked mountain path throughout, no off-path travel permitted anywhere
snapshot.Getting There: Zurich (ZRH) → Rhaetian Railway via Chur and the Vereina line to Zernez (approx. 3h30)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Disciplined, patient walkers who want serious wildlife and can accept strict rules without exception

itinerary.title: Zurich to Zernez
itinerary.morning: Train from Zurich via Chur, through the Vereina tunnel, to Zernez — no car is needed anywhere on this trip, and the park itself has no internal road network beyond the Ofenpass (Pass dal Fuorn) that skirts its southern edge.
itinerary.afternoon: Visit the Nationalparkzentrum in Zernez, the park's excellent visitor centre, before entering — it explains the rule set clearly and is worth the hour, since rangers assume you have read it.
itinerary.evening: Settle into Zernez; the village is small but has several restaurants and a supermarket, the last full resupply point before several days of hut and trail food.
itinerary.dayStats: 4 km, negligible vert. Village paths. Water: Zernez shops. Bail-out: village is the base itself.

itinerary.title: Val Trupchun: ibex, deer and the park's best wildlife valley
itinerary.morning: Bus to S-chanf and the Val Trupchun trailhead, then walk in along the marked valley path — no vehicle goes further than the car park.
itinerary.afternoon: Val Trupchun is the park's best wildlife valley: ibex work the scree above the path in full view, red deer graze the floor, and in September the rut is loud and constant. Stay strictly on the marked path — rangers patrol here specifically because of the crowds it draws.
itinerary.evening: Bus back to Zernez.
itinerary.dayStats: 18 km, 550 m vert. Marked valley path, well-graded, no exposure. Water: none inside the park — carry 2 L, since no picking, foraging or off-trail refill is permitted and streams are not treated water sources. Bail-out: the valley path is a straightforward there-and-back to the trailhead at any point.

itinerary.title: Il Fuorn and the Ofenpass forests
itinerary.morning: Bus along the Ofenpass road to Il Fuorn, where the Parc Naziunal's own historic hotel sits directly inside the park boundary — one of the very few permitted buildings within it.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk one of the marked loop trails from Il Fuorn through old-growth stone-pine and larch forest, some of the least disturbed subalpine forest in the Alps, precisely because a century of strict protection has kept it that way.
itinerary.evening: Bus back to Zernez, or dine at Il Fuorn's hotel restaurant before returning.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 400 m vert. Marked forest path. Water: Il Fuorn hotel. Bail-out: the Ofenpass road bus runs regularly in both directions.

itinerary.title: Walk in to Chamanna Cluozza
itinerary.morning: Full pack on. Walk from Zernez (or a short bus hop to Punt la Drossa) along the marked path into the Cluozza valley, climbing steadily through forest and open slope.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive at Chamanna Cluozza (1,882 m), the only overnight accommodation inside the park and reachable solely on foot — no road comes near it. It runs off-grid: solar power for lighting, water piped from a mountain source, a dry or low-flush toilet system, and a strict carry-out policy for anything you bring in that isn't food waste handled by the hut itself.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at the hut (advance booking essential; the hut sells out on clear-forecast weekends in its short season). No fires, no dogs, and quiet hours are taken seriously here.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 750 m ascent from Zernez. Marked mountain path, some steeper switchbacks, no technical exposure. Water: none en route, arrive with a full bottle — refill at the hut. Bail-out: the path back down to Zernez is the same trail, roughly 2.5–3 hours.

itinerary.title: A quiet day around Cluozza, then back to Zernez
itinerary.morning: A short marked loop above the hut for views over the Cluozza gorge and, with luck, bearded vultures riding the thermals — the species was reintroduced to the Alps starting in 1991, with the Engadin among the first release sites, and sightings here are genuinely common, not a rarity to hope for.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend the marked path back to Zernez, retracing the previous day's route.
itinerary.evening: A full dinner and a proper bed in Zernez after the hut's simpler facilities.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 750 m descent. Marked mountain path. Water: hut supply at the start, Zernez at the end. Bail-out: the descent path has no alternative exits — commit to the full return once started.

itinerary.title: S-charl valley and Zernez museum
itinerary.morning: Bus to S-charl, a quiet side valley with a small hamlet and a history of silver mining, sitting just outside the park's strictest core zone with a gentler network of marked paths.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk one of the S-charl loops, then return to Zernez for a lighter final full day before departure.
itinerary.evening: Return to the Nationalparkzentrum's exhibition for anything missed on arrival, or a last dinner in Zernez.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 400 m vert. Marked path, gentle grades. Water: S-charl hamlet. Bail-out: the S-charl postbus runs on a fixed schedule back to Scuol or Zernez.

itinerary.title: Zernez to Zurich
itinerary.morning: A short valley walk near Zernez if time allows, otherwise pack and confirm the return train.
itinerary.afternoon: Rhaetian Railway back to Zurich via Chur.
itinerary.evening: Onward flight from Zurich.
itinerary.dayStats: Transfer day, short optional walk only.

accommodationStrategy.name: Guesthouse in Zernez
accommodationStrategy.description: The obvious base: on the railway line, at the Nationalparkzentrum's doorstep, and the last point with a full supermarket and pharmacy before the park's interior. Book ahead for September, when rut-season wildlife watchers fill the village.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead for September; 3–4 weeks otherwise.

accommodationStrategy.name: Chamanna Cluozza
accommodationStrategy.description: The only overnight accommodation permitted inside the park, reached on foot only, with a short season (roughly mid-June to mid-October) dictated by snow and staffing. Off-grid facilities: solar lighting, piped mountain-source water, and a low-impact toilet system; bring a sleeping-bag liner, since bedding at Swiss huts is typically a shared dormitory mattress and blanket only.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–10 weeks ahead — this is the single hardest reservation of the trip and the hut fills months out for peak-season weekends.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Il Fuorn
accommodationStrategy.description: One of the only buildings permitted inside the park boundary, useful as an alternative or additional night if Chamanna Cluozza is unavailable, with easier road access via the Ofenpass bus and a proper restaurant.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead in summer.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European, or Switzerland's Rega mountain rescue on 1414. Note the signal gaps in the Cluozza valley to hut staff on arrival — they have radio contact.
logistics.money: Swiss franc (CHF); cards work widely, including at Cluozza and Il Fuorn, but carry cash as backup where connectivity is unreliable.

other.label: Access
other.text: Zernez is reached entirely by rail, no 4x4 needed; within the park, movement is on foot only, since private vehicles are restricted to the Ofenpass through-road and its trailhead car parks. Chamanna Cluozza has no vehicle access in any season.

other.label: Isolation level
other.text: The nearest full shop, pharmacy and doctor are in Zernez; once inside the park, there is no resupply beyond the Il Fuorn hotel and the Cluozza hut kitchen. Signal is reliable in Zernez and along the Ofenpass but patchy to absent in Val Trupchun and around Cluozza — treat the park interior as out of contact.

other.label: Resupply
other.text: Zernez has a Coop or Volg-style general store; buy everything needed for hut days there.

other.label: Foraging and fire law — the strictest in this itinerary
other.text: Nothing may be picked anywhere: no flowers, berries, mushrooms, wood or rocks. Marked paths only, enforced by wardens with real fines. Dogs are not permitted anywhere, including on a lead. Camping, bivouacking, off-road cycling, drones and open fires are all prohibited, as is swimming in the park's streams and lakes.

other.label: Wildlife
other.text: Ibex and bearded vulture are the signature sightings, best looked for on the open scree and thermals above Val Trupchun and the Cluozza gorge; the red deer rut runs through September and draws the year's biggest crowds to Val Trupchun. Marmots are common at lower elevations.

other.label: Ticks
other.text: Graubünden carries TBE risk at lower elevations; vaccination or careful checks are sensible for S-charl and the lower Cluozza valley.

proTips: Book Chamanna Cluozza first — its short season and single-hut status inside the whole park make it the binding constraint on the week.
Walk Val Trupchun on a weekday if possible; September weekends draw dedicated wildlife-watching groups and the trailhead car park fills early.
Bring your own binoculars rather than relying on shared hut equipment — sightings reward patience, not proximity, which the rules prohibit anyway.
Read the park's rule leaflet, free at the Nationalparkzentrum and every trailhead board, before Day 2 — rangers do check.
S-charl on Day 6 sits just outside the strictest core and feels noticeably gentler — a good rest day after the core-zone discipline.
Ask the Nationalparkzentrum for that week's ranger-guided walk schedule — the only way to get expert spotting without leaving the marked path.
Aim for a weekday arrival at Cluozza; the small dining room gets genuinely crowded on a clear Friday or Saturday in high season.
