trips.title: Suðuroy & Mykines: Faroese Isolation Week

bestPeriod.window: **Mid-May to late August** — the Mykines ferry and the puffin colony operate only in this window. September gives the clearest air and the emptiest villages but Mykines access closes
bestPeriod.raw: **Mid-May to late August** — the Mykines ferry and the puffin colony operate only in this window. September gives the clearest air and the emptiest villages but Mykines access closes

accommodation.note: €100–180 per night for a guesthouse or a self-catering house; village houses rented whole from €130

food.note: €45–75 per day; self-catering is near-obligatory outside Tvøroyri and Vágur

transport.note: €350–500: flights, the Suðuroy ferry (2 h), the Mykines ferry, and a hire car

activities.note: €80–180: hiking fees where charged, a guided cliff walk, boat trips

trips.summary: A seven-day nature escapes & cabin stay itinerary in Suðuroy (southernmost island) and Mykines (westernmost island), Faroe Islands.

itinerary.title: Tórshavn and the Smyril ferry to Suðuroy
itinerary.morning: Arrive Vágar, drive to Tórshavn, buy a week of food — the supermarkets in the capital are far better stocked than anything in the south.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Smyril ferry** from Tórshavn to Tvøroyri takes about two hours across open water. Take the car; Suðuroy has no other way to move.
itinerary.evening: Tvøroyri, a town strung along a fjord with a black wooden church moved here from Norway in the 18th century. Settle in.

itinerary.title: The west coast cliffs: Beinisvørð and Sumba
itinerary.morning: Drive south to **Beinisvørð**, a 470 m sheer cliff face dropping into the Atlantic — the most imposing sea cliff on the island and reachable by a short walk from the road.
itinerary.afternoon: Sumba, the southernmost village, and Akraberg lighthouse beyond it at the island's tip, where the next land south is Scotland. Wind here is a physical force.
itinerary.evening: Village house or Vágur guesthouse. There is no restaurant in most of these settlements: cook.

itinerary.title: Fámjin and Hvannhagi
itinerary.morning: **Fámjin**, reached over a mountain road, is a village of perhaps thirty houses on the west coast. Its church holds the original **Merkið**, the Faroese flag, sewn by students in 1919.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Hvannhagi** hike from Tvøroyri — a hanging valley of boulders and small lakes with a view to the island of Lítla Dímun, the smallest of the eighteen islands and the only uninhabited one. About three hours return, steep, and stunning.
itinerary.evening: Long light, no traffic, nothing scheduled.

itinerary.title: Vágur, Ásmundarstakkur and the bird cliffs
itinerary.morning: Vágur, the island's second town, and the walk out to **Ásmundarstakkur**, a sea stack with a natural arch, on a headland covered in nesting seabirds.
itinerary.afternoon: The eastern coast road and the abandoned village sites; Suðuroy has lost population steadily for a century, and the empty houses are part of the landscape.
itinerary.evening: If you have arranged one, a **heimablídni** dinner in a Suðuroy home — the island's version is warmer and less commercial than the capital's.

itinerary.title: Ferry back and reposition to Vágar
itinerary.morning: The Smyril back to Tórshavn, then west to Sørvágur on Vágar.
itinerary.afternoon: Prepare for Mykines: check the ferry status, pack for a night with everything you need, including all food.
itinerary.evening: Sørvágur. Early night — the Mykines boat goes early and decisions get made at first light.

itinerary.title: Mykines
itinerary.morning: The **Mykines ferry** from Sørvágur takes about 45 minutes and runs only in the summer season. It cancels frequently in swell. Landing at the village jetty involves a steep climb up steps from the boat.
itinerary.afternoon: The walk out along the ridge to **Mykineshólmur**, over a footbridge above a chasm, to the lighthouse and the **gannet colony** — the only one in the Faroes. The path passes through dense puffin burrows; a hiking fee applies and a guide may be required on parts of the route. `verify: true`
itinerary.evening: Stay overnight in the village guesthouse if you can get it. When the day boat leaves, Mykines has perhaps a dozen people on it and the silence is total.

itinerary.title: Return and departure
itinerary.morning: The morning boat back — or the helicopter, if the sea is up and you have a seat.
itinerary.afternoon: Vágar airport is twenty minutes from Sørvágur. Build slack: a Mykines cancellation can strand you a day, and this is the known risk of the itinerary.

accommodationStrategy.name: Whole-house rentals in Suðuroy villages
accommodationStrategy.description: Faroese families rent out village houses — turf roof, thick walls, a kitchen, sometimes a hot tub facing the Atlantic. €110–180 for the house. This is level-2 isolation: no shop, no restaurant, no traffic, and the best value on the islands.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Bakkin / Tvøroyri and Vágur guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: The practical bases with a restaurant, a shop and fuel. Choose one of these for the first and last Suðuroy nights and a village house in between.

accommodationStrategy.name: Mykines guesthouse
accommodationStrategy.description: A handful of beds on an island of ten residents, with meals cooked by your host because there is no alternative. It books out for the entire summer within weeks of opening. If you want one night of genuine North Atlantic isolation, this is it — and it requires planning months ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112. Suðuroy has a hospital in Tvøroyri; Mykines has nothing, and evacuation is by boat or helicopter and weather-dependent. This is a genuine consideration for anyone with a medical condition.
logistics.weather: Wind is the operating variable. Above roughly 15 m/s, boats stop, cliff walks become dangerous and mountain roads close. Cliff edges here are unfenced, wet, and grassed — the classic accident is a slip on a 35° grass slope above a 400 m drop.
logistics.bookingWindows: Mykines guesthouse: as soon as the season opens, 6+ months. Suðuroy village houses: 2–3 months. Cars: 2–3 months for summer.

other.label: There is no right to roam
other.text: Faroese land is owned and hiking access is regulated. Several routes charge a landowner fee, some require a guide, and a few close during the sheep gathering and the bird-nesting season. Never assume a path is public. `verify: true`

other.label: Wild camping is not permitted
other.text: outside designated campsites. This is different from Norway, Sweden and Finland and catches out Nordic-experienced travellers regularly.

other.label: Ferries and cancellation
other.text: The Suðuroy ferry is large and reliable. The **Mykines ferry is small and cancels often** — plan a two-night buffer, and never book a next-morning flight after a Mykines day.

other.label: Supplies
other.text: Buy food in Tórshavn. Suðuroy's shops are adequate; Mykines has none at all. Shops close early and on Sundays.

other.label: Bird ethics
other.text: Do not walk on puffin burrows — the ground is undermined and collapses. Keep to paths, do not use drones over colonies, and give gannets and their nests wide berth.

proTips: **Stay a night on Mykines.** The day-trip crowd leaves on the afternoon boat and the island becomes what it actually is. It is the single best decision available on this itinerary and the hardest to book.

Take the **helicopter** one way if you can. The subsidised inter-island service serves Mykines and Suðuroy at a remarkably low fare for a scheduled sector, and it flies when the boats do not. Rules on tourist bookings and one-way sectors change — check the current position. `verify: true`

Suðuroy is the one island where the Faroese ferry is worth taking **with a car**. Everything else is walkable; here, distances and mountain roads make a car the difference between two villages and eight.

Ask your host about the **grindadráp** debate if you are curious about it, and listen rather than argue. It is a real and complex part of Faroese life and the visitor's confident opinion is rarely welcome.
Faroese village houses often have an outdoor **hot tub facing the sea**. Booking one in Fámjin or Sumba turns a wet, wind-blasted day into the reason you came.
Build a **spare day** into the end. Not as a luxury — as the mechanism that stops a cancelled Mykines boat from becoming a missed flight.

raw.remote_access: No 4x4 needed — roads are surfaced. The remoteness is structural: Suðuroy is a two-hour ferry from the capital with no air link, and Mykines is a small boat or a helicopter, both weather-dependent, with about ten year-round residents

isolation_levels.level_1: Tvøroyri or Vágur — small towns on Suðuroy with a shop, a bank and a restaurant
isolation_levels.level_2: A rented village house in Fámjin, Sumba or Hvalba — a handful of houses, no shop, roads that end
isolation_levels.level_3: Mykines — one settlement, no shop, no road link, ferry cancelled roughly one day in three, and total silence after the last boat leaves

raw.foraging_rules: All land in the Faroes is owned, either privately or as *útmark* commons. There is no Nordic-style right to roam: hiking off marked routes and any picking, camping or fire needs the landowner's permission. Wild camping is restricted to designated campsites
raw.wildlife: Atlantic puffin, northern gannet on Mykineshólmur, fulmar, guillemot, storm petrel; no native land mammals apart from introduced hares and mice

trips.title: Hautes-Chaumes — A Marcairie Week on the Vosges Crest
trips.subRegion: Parc naturel régional des Ballons des Vosges, Haut-Rhin

bestPeriod.note: Marcairies and fermes-auberges on the hautes-chaumes generally open only from late May to October, when cattle are up on summer pasture.

trips.gatewayAirport: Bâle-Mulhouse-Freiburg (EAP/BSL/MLH)
trips.summary: A week of nights in working marcairies and fermes-auberges on the Vosges high pastures, walking the Route des Crêtes from the Grand Ballon to Lac Blanc.
trips.hook: The Vosges' high pastures — the hautes-chaumes — are one of France's odder landscapes: treeless, wind-combed grassland sitting directly above dense beech and fir forest, grazed all summer by cattle whose milk still goes into real Munster cheese at working farmhouses called marcairies. Several of these farms take overnight guests as fermes-auberges, and this week strings a run of them together along and below the Route des Crêtes, from the Grand Ballon's summit dome to the cliffs above Lac Blanc, with the smell of woodsmoke and warm cheese as the constant.

snapshot.Base(s): Munster valley, with two nights at a hautes-chaumes marcairie (7 nights total)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 65–85 km walking, 2,600–3,200 m cumulative ascent; forest track, open pasture, granite ridge path
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Bâle-Mulhouse-Freiburg (EuroAirport), train to Colmar, then bus or taxi to Munster; a car is genuinely useful for the crest days
snapshot.Who It Suits: Families and moderate walkers who want real farm hospitality alongside their hiking, not a wilderness survival week

itinerary.title: Arrival in Munster
itinerary.morning: Train from Colmar to Munster, the small town that gives its name to the cheese and the valley. Settle into your base and buy provisions for the coming marcairie nights, where meals are often simple and self-catering supplements are welcome.
itinerary.afternoon: Easy orientation walk along the Fecht river through town and out to the edge of the valley's pasture, getting a first look at the hautes-chaumes rising above.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Munster — the town has a proper choice of restaurants, your last for a couple of nights.
itinerary.dayStats: 7 km, gentle.

itinerary.title: Petit Ballon and first marcairie night
itinerary.morning: Drive to the trailhead near Sondernach and climb through beech forest onto the open chaume of the Petit Ballon (1,267 m), a gentler warm-up before the bigger crest days.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue along the ridge to a working marcairie for the night. The last stretch to most hautes-chaumes farms is an unpaved farm track, generally fine for an ordinary car in dry weather but rutted enough after rain that a higher-clearance vehicle is safer; expect a 10–20 minute walk-in with your overnight bag from the nearest parking turn-out.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at the farm: tourte, munster with cumin, a simple tarte aux myrtilles if the season's right. Lights are early here — everyone's up with the cattle.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 700 m ascent. Grade moderate, forest track then open pasture.

itinerary.title: Along the chaume to Le Markstein
itinerary.morning: Walk the ridge path south along the hautes-chaumes toward Le Markstein, through classic high-pasture terrain grazed by Vosgienne cattle, with views opening east toward the Rhine plain and the distant line of the Black Forest.
itinerary.afternoon: Détour to a second ferme-auberge for lunch, a good way to compare the region's cheese-and-charcuterie plates.
itinerary.evening: Return to Munster by car or taxi for a proper shower and a night in a real bed.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 400 m ascent/descent. Grade easy-moderate, open chaume path.

itinerary.title: Grand Ballon and the Route des Crêtes
itinerary.morning: Drive the Route des Crêtes, the WWI-era military road that runs the Vosges skyline, to the base of the Grand Ballon (1,424 m), the range's highest point, topped by a radar dome and a First World War memorial to army engineers.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the short summit loop, then follow the crest road's parallel footpath toward Col Amic, watching the exposed rock for chamois — reintroduced to the Vosges in the 1950s and now established near Hohneck and the Grand Ballon.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Munster.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km, 350 m ascent/descent. Grade easy, exposed to wind on the summit plateau.

itinerary.title: Hohneck and second marcairie night
itinerary.morning: Drive to the Col de la Schlucht and climb to the Hohneck (1,362 m), one of the most panoramic summits in the range, with the Lac Blanc cirque visible to the north and the Alsace plain spread out east.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend along the ridge to a second marcairie for the night, a different farm from Day 2 to see the variation in the tradition — some run larger dairy herds, others focus more on the auberge side.
itinerary.evening: Farm dinner again; ask about the cheese-making schedule, since some marcairies let guests watch or even help with the morning milking.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km, 750 m ascent/descent. Grade moderate, ridge path and pasture track.

itinerary.title: Lac Blanc and the Rocher du Hang
itinerary.morning: Walk down from the marcairie toward Lac Blanc, a glacial lake beneath dramatic granite cliffs near Orbey, formed by the same Quaternary glaciation that shaped the whole crest.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop around the lake and up to the Rocher du Hang viewpoint above it — a well-known local paragliding launch, worth watching from below even if you're not flying. Continue to Col du Calvaire and pick up return transport to Munster.
itinerary.evening: Last full evening — dinner in Munster, pack for departure.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km, 550 m ascent/descent. Grade moderate, forest and lakeside path, some rocky steps near the Rocher du Hang.

itinerary.title: Departure
itinerary.morning: A short farewell walk from Munster into the nearest pasture edge before checkout.
itinerary.afternoon: Bus or taxi to Colmar, train onward to Bâle-Mulhouse-Freiburg.
itinerary.evening: Flight home.
itinerary.dayStats: 4 km, then transfer day.

accommodationStrategy.name: A marcairie/ferme-auberge on the hautes-chaumes
accommodationStrategy.description: The heart of this trip: two separate nights at different working dairy farms that also take overnight guests, chosen for their setting directly on the crest rather than for any particular comfort standard. Rooms are simple, sometimes dormitory-style, and the appeal is entirely the setting and the food — fresh munster, farm charcuterie, and a fire going by evening even in August.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead for July–August, since many marcairies take only a handful of overnight guests at a time.

accommodationStrategy.name: A guesthouse in Munster
accommodationStrategy.description: Your comfortable middle-of-week base, with a proper shower, a full choice of restaurants, and easy access to the Route des Crêtes trailheads by car. Munster's cheese market and dairy heritage make it a genuinely relevant base rather than just a convenient one.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead for summer.

accommodationStrategy.name: A hotel near Col de la Schlucht
accommodationStrategy.description: Useful if you'd rather stay right on the Route des Crêtes for the Hohneck and Lac Blanc days rather than driving up from the valley each morning; several small hotels sit directly on or near the col.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; French mountain rescue is reached via 112, which routes to the relevant gendarmerie or PGHM unit.
logistics.money: Cards are near-universal in Munster and at most fermes-auberges; carry cash for the smaller, more remote marcairies.

other.label: Isolation, specifically
other.text: Munster has full supermarkets and a pharmacy; the marcairies themselves have no shop at all, phone signal on the open chaume is generally workable but drops in the forested approach sections, and the nearest hospital is in Colmar, roughly 30–40 minutes from Munster.

other.label: Foraging
other.text: Mushroom picking is broadly tolerated in French state and communal forest for personal consumption within informal reasonable limits, but is prohibited or restricted within the park's designated nature reserves, including the Tanet-Gazon du Faing reserve near Hohneck — check signage before picking anywhere near a reserve boundary.

other.label: Fire
other.text: Open fires are prohibited in and near Vosges forest under standing prefectural rules, tightened further during dry summer spells when burn bans are common; the marcairies' own hearths are the fire you get.

other.label: Grand tétras (capercaillie)
other.text: A small, protected population survives in the old-growth stands near Hohneck and the Tanet massif; some paths in this zone carry seasonal or permanent off-trail restrictions to protect breeding birds — stay on marked routes through these sections regardless of season.

other.label: Wildlife
other.text: Chamois are the headline sighting on the rockier crest faces; red deer are present lower in the forest, with the rut running through October; wild boar are common and best given space, especially with dogs.

other.label: Ticks
other.text: Present through the Vosges forest and pasture edges in warmer months; check after every walk.

other.label: Opening hours
other.text: French village shops often close on Monday rather than Sunday, the reverse of the Austrian and German pattern — check the specific day before relying on a small-town boulangerie.

proTips: Book the two marcairie nights first and build driving legs around them — the good ones fill early in July and August precisely because they take so few overnight guests.
Ask each marcairie directly whether you can watch or join the evening milking; it's often offered informally rather than advertised, and it's the most memorable hour of the trip.
Walk the Route des Crêtes on foot for the Grand Ballon–Col Amic stretch rather than only driving it; the parallel footpath gets you off the road and onto genuine pasture within ten minutes.
Time Lac Blanc for a weekday morning — it's one of the most visited spots in the southern Vosges on a fine summer weekend, largely for its paragliding launch and lake views.
Order the munster fermier with cumin seeds specifically, and ask which marcairie made it — much of what's served on the crest comes from the very farm you're eating in.
If chamois-spotting matters to you, glass the rockier north faces near Hohneck in the first two hours after sunrise, before day-hikers are on the ridge.
Carry small cash even at farms that technically take cards — connectivity on the open chaume is patchy enough that terminals sometimes fail.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 65–85 km walking, 2,600–3,200 m cumulative ascent; forest track, open pasture, granite ridge path
raw.Who It Suits: Families and moderate walkers who want real farm hospitality alongside their hiking, not a wilderness survival week

typeSpecific.surface: approx. 65–85 km walking, 2,600–3,200 m cumulative ascent; forest track, open pasture, granite ridge path
typeSpecific.audience: Families and moderate walkers who want real farm hospitality alongside their hiking, not a wilderness survival week

packingNotes: Sturdy walking shoes for the mix of forest track, pasture and the rockier Rocher du Hang steps.
A proper windproof layer — the open hautes-chaumes are exposed with no tree cover at all.
A change of clothes light enough to carry for the two marcairie nights, since these are walk-in stays.
Cash in small denominations for the more remote farms.
Binoculars for chamois and, in October, listening for the deer rut.
Tick repellent and a tick-removal tool.
A basic first-aid kit — the nearest hospital is 30–40 minutes from Munster.
Sun protection; the chaume has essentially no shade at midday.
A refillable water bottle; farms along the route are generally happy to refill it, but carry enough for the exposed stretches between them.
A camera or phone with a full battery for the Route des Crêtes viewpoints — signal, and therefore charging temptation to check it constantly, is unreliable up there anyway.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A marcairie is fully booked for your preferred date.** Fallback: the park has a genuine network of these farms along the crest; ask the Munster tourist office for current availability.
**Rain turns the farm access track to mud.** Fallback: park at the lower turn-out and walk the last stretch in; call ahead so the farm knows.
**Wind or storm makes the exposed Grand Ballon–Hohneck stretch unpleasant.** Fallback: drop into the forest paths just below the crest line, which run roughly parallel and stay sheltered.

**A summer burn ban is in effect and you're relying on an open fire for warmth.** Fallback: the marcairies' indoor hearths are unaffected; just don't expect or ask for anything outdoors during a dry-spell restriction.

**Lac Blanc is unpleasantly crowded on a summer Saturday.** Fallback: shift that leg to Sunday morning instead, or walk the quieter approach from Col du Calvaire rather than the main Orbey-side car park route.

trips.title: Velebit Stone and Lika Forest: A Karst Cabin Week

bestPeriod.window: Mid-June–mid-July & early September–mid-October
bestPeriod.avoid: November–April — the Oltari–Zavižan road is snow-blocked, the NP shepherd huts close, and bura closes the coastal roads
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-June–mid-July & early September–mid-October

accommodation.note: NP shepherd huts €100–€200 per hut; Zavižan bunk ~€20; coastal hotels €80–€120

food.note: Lika konoba mains €10–€16; two nights are self-catered because there is no restaurant

transport.note: Rental car with genuine ground clearance €45–€70/day, fuel, A1 tolls

activities.note: Two NP tickets, Velebit House, Cerovac caves, Manita peć, a guided bear/wolf morning

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5 — daily walks of 8–16 km with 400–900 m ascent on sharp karst; no technical ground, but the rock punishes soft footwear

trips.gatewayAirport: ZAD Zadar, 55 min to Starigrad-Paklenica and 2 h 05 to Krasno; RJK Rijeka 2 h 10 to Krasno; ZAG Zagreb 2 h 40
trips.summary: Velebit is 145 km of waterless limestone standing between the Adriatic and the forested plateau of Lika, and this week works both sides of it. You start soft in the Gacka valley among watermills and trout springs, climb to Zavižan where Croatia's highest year-round weather station sits beside an alpine botanical garden, then walk the Premužić Trail — a 1930s dry-stone path engineered so beautifully that it crosses cliffs without a single exposed step. The middle of the week is deliberately slow: a day in the old-growth spruce of Štirovača, an afternoon at Kuterevo's bear refuge, a cave day underground. It ends on the seaward face at Paklenica, where the mountain drops 1,700 m to the sea in eight kilometres. It suits people who want silence, a wood stove, and no phone signal, and who accept that on this mountain you carry your own water.

itinerary.title: Gacka springs and the slow entry to Lika
itinerary.morning: Pick the car up at Zadar and drive north on the A1 to Otočac, stopping at Majerovo vrilo, one of the Gacka's three karst source springs, where the water rises at a constant 8–10°C and the restored watermill sits over the outflow. Walk the short circuit and look for grayling holding in the weed.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Tonkovića vrilo and the Gacka fly-fishing beats — day permits are sold through the Otočac angling association and the river's brown trout are famously hard. Buy a week's food in Otočac; this is the last full supermarket before Krasno.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Otočac on Lika staples — sour cabbage, lamb, and the local basa cheese spread.
itinerary.dayStats: 118 km drive / 1 h 40 / Gacka springs at 452 m / river temperature 8–10°C year-round / last full supermarket for 4 days

itinerary.title: Kuterevo bears and the climb to Zavižan
itinerary.morning: Drive 20 km to Kuterevo for the Velebit Refuge for Young Bears, a volunteer-run sanctuary founded in 2002 that keeps orphaned bears that could never be returned to the wild. It opens roughly 09:00–17:00 in spring, summer and autumn, closes in winter so the animals are not disturbed, and asks for a donation rather than a ticket. Rules are strict and non-negotiable: no feeding, no noise, no reaching over barriers.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive via Krasno — stop at Velebit House (Kuća Velebita), the park's interpretation centre — then up through Oltari onto the macadam to Zavižan. Walk the Velebit Botanical Garden loop below the hut, established 1967 in a dolina at 1,480 m, and the 15-minute path to Vučjak (1,644 m) for the whole Kvarner archipelago at once.
itinerary.evening: Dinner is whatever the hut is cooking — usually soup and something stewed — eaten at long tables with mountaineers. Cash only.
itinerary.dayStats: 62 km drive / last 8.5 km unsealed / Zavižan 1,594 m / NP 1-day ticket €7, Velebit House €6, combined €10 / hut has generator power only

itinerary.title: Premužić Trail to Alan
itinerary.morning: Start at 07:00 on the Premužić Trail, the dry-stone path built 1930–33 by forest engineer Ante Premužić across the most broken limestone in the range. The Zavižan–Alan section runs roughly 16 km with modest cumulative ascent but constant undulation, threading the Rožanski kukovi strict reserve — a chaos of towers and shafts including Lukina jama, one of the deepest caves in the world at over 1,400 m.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop into the Lubenovac basin, a grassy karst polje ringed by rock where shepherds summered until the 1960s. This is the day's best chance of wolf or bear sign — scat, hair on fence posts, torn stumps.
itinerary.evening: At Alan, the park's restored shepherd huts have wood stoves and solar lighting. Cook what you carried, then sit outside; on a clear night the Adriatic light pollution stops at the ridge and the sky is genuinely dark.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km walk / 450 m cumulative ascent, 600 m descent / 5–6 h / no water source en route, carry 3 L / Alan hut €140–€200 for 7–10 people
itinerary.sleep: Alan shepherd huts, Northern Velebit NP

itinerary.title: A slow day in Štirovača old-growth forest
itinerary.morning: Deliberately unhurried. Drive or arrange a park lift down the Alan spur and across to Štirovača, a valley of old-growth Norway spruce at 1,050–1,200 m that feels nothing like the bare ridge — moss, deadwood, cold air pooling even in August. Walk 6–8 km on the forest track and the marked loop, slowly, looking up.
itinerary.afternoon: Nap, read, do nothing. If it is September or October and you are outside the national park boundary, this is legal mushroom country: ceps, chanterelles, saffron milkcaps, within the 3 kg personal limit. Take nothing you cannot name twice.
itinerary.evening: Grill on the hut's built fireplace if the fire ban permits, otherwise the stove. Wolves in this valley call most often in the two hours after dark in late autumn.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km forest road, high-clearance advised / 6–8 km walk / valley floor 1,050 m / mushroom limit 3 kg pp/day, zero inside NP boundaries / no signal all day
itinerary.sleep: Alan shepherd huts or Lubenovac hut (€100, sleeps 4)

itinerary.title: Cerovac caves and the crossing to the sea
itinerary.morning: Descend the eastern flank via Baške Oštarije (928 m), the historic pass village where the road crosses the range, then drive south to the Cerovac caves near Gračac — three linked systems in the Crnopac massif, with the Upper and Lower caves developed for visitors, Pleistocene cave-bear bones in the sediment and a constant 8°C inside. Take a fleece.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Starigrad-Paklenica and walk the first, easy hour of the Velika Paklenica canyon, past the anchor-studded Anića kuk wall where climbers have been working 350 m of limestone since the 1930s.
itinerary.evening: Fish and grilled squid on the coast road, with the whole Velebit wall behind you turning orange.
itinerary.dayStats: 165 km drive / Baške Oštarije pass 928 m / cave interior 8°C / Paklenica 1-day adult €9.50 May–Sep, €7.60 Mar–Apr & Oct, €4.75 winter

itinerary.title: Paklenica canyon, Manita peć and the mountain hut
itinerary.morning: Walk Velika Paklenica to the Manita peć cave (an add-on ticket, opening days limited outside summer — usually a few fixed days a week in spring and autumn), 90 minutes up with a 500 m climb off the canyon floor and a guided 30-minute tour inside.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Lugarnica, the forester's house that serves soup and beer in season, then to Planinarski dom Paklenica at 480 m. Those with legs left can push toward Vaganski vrh (1,757 m), the range high point, but it is a full day in itself.
itinerary.evening: Eat at the hut. Below you the canyon funnels cold air down after sunset — even in July it drops sharply.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km round trip / 850 m ascent / Manita peć at 570 m, interior 400 m of passage / hut at 480 m / 600+ equipped climbing routes in the canyon
itinerary.sleep: Planinarski dom Paklenica, or back down in Starigrad

itinerary.title: Bura, the coast road and out
itinerary.morning: Check the wind before anything else. If the bura is running, the Adriatic Highway under Velebit is where it hits hardest — gusts over 200 km/h have been recorded near Maslenica, and Croatian police impose vehicle-category bans rather than closing the road outright. If it is calm, walk the short Mala Paklenica canyon, far quieter than its big sister.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive the old coast road south through Seline and Rovanjska, then over the Maslenica bridge with the whole karst wall on your left.
itinerary.evening: Last dinner in Zadar's old town before the airport, 20 minutes away.
itinerary.dayStats: 85 km to ZAD / bura gusts recorded above 200 km/h at Maslenica / A1 Sveti Rok–Maslenica is the alternative when the coast road is restricted / vehicle bans posted by HAK

accommodationStrategy.name: Planinarski dom Zavižan
accommodationStrategy.description: Staffed year-round beside the meteorological station and the botanical garden, with bunkrooms, a wood stove and a kitchen serving whatever is on. It is the only way to be on the ridge at dawn without a tent, and the price is a fraction of anything on the coast. Bring cash, a sleeping bag liner and earplugs.

accommodationStrategy.name: Alan and Lubenovac shepherd huts
accommodationStrategy.description: The park rents restored shepherds' huts as whole units: Alan sleeps 7–10 for roughly €140–€200 a night, Lubenovac sleeps 4 for around €100, tourist tax extra. Solar lighting, wood stove with firewood supplied, cistern water, no shop for 25 km. Book direct with the park office — this is the trip's defining night.

accommodationStrategy.name: A family hotel in Starigrad-Paklenica
accommodationStrategy.location: coastal base for the canyon days
accommodationStrategy.description: Starigrad's small family-run hotels sit within 10 minutes of the Paklenica gate, have parking, and give you a shower and a washing machine after three off-grid nights. Around €80–€120 a double in shoulder season, more in August. The trade-off is traffic noise from the coast road: ask for a rear room.

logistics.connectivity: Croatia is in the EU, so EU roaming applies with no surcharge. Coverage is good on the coast and in Lika villages, absent in Štirovača, Lubenovac and most of the Premužić Trail. Download offline tiles for the whole massif before Krasno.
logistics.emergency: 112 for everything; it dispatches HGSS, the Croatian Mountain Rescue Service, which has stations in Gospić and Zadar. Carry the HGSS app, which transmits coordinates. Rescue on Velebit is slow because access roads are bad — expect hours, not minutes. Insurance should name off-trail hiking and caving if you enter Cerovac beyond the tourist route.
logistics.weather: The bura is the defining phenomenon — a katabatic north-easterly that accelerates over the ridge and slams the Velebit Channel, strongest between Senj and Maslenica, most frequent October–April but possible any month. It arrives fast and can make ridge walking impossible. Summer thunderstorms build over the plateau from mid-afternoon; on bare karst there is no shelter, so be off the ridge by 15:00.
logistics.bookingWindows: NP shepherd huts at Alan and Lubenovac go early for July–August weekends — book two to three months ahead by email. Zavižan cannot be reliably reserved for individuals in peak weeks; phone ahead. Manita peć runs on a limited weekly schedule outside summer, so check the Paklenica site before committing a day to it.
logistics.money: Croatia uses the euro (since January 2023) and is in Schengen. Cards work in towns; the mountain huts, Kuterevo's donation box and the Štirovača area are cash. Carry €150 in small notes. Tipping is rounding up, or 10% for a sit-down meal.
logistics.transportRules: The A1 is tolled — Zagreb to Zadar is roughly €20 by car — and paid at barriers by card or cash; there is no vignette. Rental agreements often prohibit unsealed roads: read the contract, because Oltari–Zavižan and Štirovača are exactly the sort of track that voids a CDW. Cross-border into Bosnia or Slovenia needs a green card and prior permission from the rental desk.
logistics.permits: Northern Velebit NP charges €7 for a basic one-day ticket, €6 for Velebit House, €10 combined; guided ranger days run around €60 per adult. Paklenica charges €4.75–€9.50 per day depending on season, with 3- and 5-day passes. Camping and open fires are banned in both parks. The Rožanski and Hajdučki kukovi are strict reserves: stay on the Premužić Trail. Drones need Croatian CAA registration and are banned over national parks without written permission.
logistics.health: Tap water in Lika towns is potable; cistern water at the huts should be treated. Ticks are abundant April–October in Lika's forest and grassland, and tick-borne encephalitis is present in continental Croatia — consider vaccination and check nightly. Nose-horned viper (*Vipera ammodytes*) lives on sunny Velebit scree; watch where you put your hands, and the antivenom is in Zadar and Gospić hospitals, not in the mountains. There is no water on the ridge — dehydration is the single most common problem HGSS deals with here.

proTips: Do the Premužić Trail south to north from Alan if you can arrange a car swap — the light is better on your back, and you finish at Zavižan with a hut instead of a hut-less saddle.
Ask the Northern Velebit park office to leave the Alan hut key at the Babić Siča entrance station rather than Krasno; it saves a 40-minute detour on a bad road.
Kuterevo's refuge runs on volunteers and donations, not ticket revenue. Turn up mid-morning on a weekday, buy something from the wood-carving stall, and skip the weekend coach hours.
Fill every water container in Krasno. There is no potable tap between Oltari and Baške Oštarije, a distance of 40 km along the ridge.
If the bura forecast is above force 8, move the Paklenica days earlier and the Zavižan days later — the ridge is unpleasant but the coast road is the part that actually gets restricted.
Štirovača is state forest with active logging. Phone Hrvatske šume in Gospić the day before, or simply reverse out of the valley if you meet a loaded lorry — they cannot.
Buy the Paklenica 3- or 5-day ticket if you plan two canyon days plus Manita peć; the arithmetic beats two singles.
September is the best week of the year here: beech mast brings bears low, mushrooms are up, the bura has not started, and the huts are half empty after the Croatian holiday exodus ends.
Carry a 20-litre dry bag as your Zavižan-to-Alan luggage. Nothing on this trip is wheelable, and the park's vehicle transfer is not guaranteed.

raw.Remote access — the Oltari–Zavižan road: From Krasno the asphalt runs 12 km to Oltari (1,050 m), after which 8.5 km of narrow, potholed macadam climbs to Zavižan at 1,594 m. A normal hatchback manages it dry and slowly (allow 35–40 minutes); after heavy rain the gravel scours into ruts and a high-clearance vehicle earns its money. It is snow-blocked roughly late November to mid-May, and the park closes the barrier at Babić Siča. The Štirovača forest road from Baške Oštarije is 14 km of active logging track — genuinely 4x4 or high-clearance after rain, and closed without notice when timber lorries are working.
raw.Last-mile walk-ins: Alan shepherd huts sit at the end of a rough 6 km spur from the Alan saddle; Lubenovac is a 25-minute walk from the nearest turning circle. Zavižan hut is a 400 m walk from the car park. Budget a rucksack, not a wheeled case.
raw.Transfers: Northern Velebit NP (npsv@np-sjeverni-velebit.hr, +385 53 665 380) will arrange a ranger vehicle to the huts for luggage on request; local taxi and shuttle work out of Otočac and Senj rather than Krasno. There is no bus to Zavižan at any time of year.
raw.Wilderness isolation — Level 4 of 5 at Z: 45 min to paved road at Krasno, no permanent neighbours within 6 km, nearest shop and fuel in Krasno (roughly 25 km, closes 19:00 and Sunday afternoons), nearest pharmacy in Otočac (48 km), nearest hospital Opća bolnica Gospić (about 1 h 20). Paklenica drops this to Level 2: Starigrad has shops, a pharmacy and Zadar hospital 50 minutes away.
raw.Off-grid reality: Velebit is pure karst — no springs, no streams, no surface water anywhere on the ridge. The huts run on rainwater cisterns and delivered tanks, and cistern water should be boiled or filtered even where locals drink it. Zavižan has a generator and limited hours of power; the shepherd huts at Alan and Lubenovac are solar with a wood-burning stove, firewood provided by the park, dry composting or chemical toilets, and no shower in some units. Bring 3 litres per person per day, a head torch, a power bank, matches, and all food: the last shop is Krasno.
raw.Phone signal: Patchy A1/HT coverage on the Zavižan summit ridge, nothing in Štirovača or the Lubenovac basin, good on the Paklenica coast. Download offline maps; the Premužić Trail is well marked but the side branches to Alan are not.
raw.Foraging rules: Croatia's protected-species ordinance caps wild mushrooms at 3 kg per person per day for personal use, with commercial collection requiring a permit and a certified sorter; picking is banned outright inside national park zones (Northern Velebit and Paklenica), and permitted with the personal-use limit in the surrounding Velebit Nature Park and Lika state forests. Berries and herbs are capped separately (typically 2 kg of berries, 1 kg of dried herb material). Edelweiss, Velebit degenia (*Degenia velebitica*, the massif's endemic yellow crucifer) and all orchids are strictly protected — photograph only. Have any mushroom haul checked at a mycological inspection point; the nearest reliable ones are in Gospić and Rijeka, run through the county public-health institutes.
raw.Wildlife: Brown bear (roughly 1,000 in Croatia, concentrated in Gorski kotar and Lika) is active at dawn and dusk from April to November, feeding on beech mast in September–October. Grey wolf packs use the Štirovača–Lubenovac corridor; Eurasian lynx, reintroduced to the Dinarides in 1973 and still numbering only a few dozen in Croatia, is present but effectively unseeable. Ethical rules: no baiting, no playback calls, no approaching a sow with cubs, keep dogs leashed, and never leave food outside a hut. Kuterevo's refuge is a sanctuary, not a zoo — bears there are orphans that cannot be released.
raw.Fire and open flame: Croatia's high fire-risk season on the coastal slope runs 1 June–31 October, when open fires, barbecues outside built fireplaces and stubble burning are banned in and near forest; fines run into four figures. Cooking is on hut stoves only. Inland Lika is less restricted but the same common sense applies in an August drought.

sources.verified: Northern Velebit NP price list (basic 1-day €7, Velebit House €6, combined €10, ranger day €60, Alan shepherd huts €140–€200 for 7–10 people, Lubenovac €100 for 4, tourist tax from €1.90, office +385 53 665 380 / npsv@np-sjeverni-velebit.hr); Paklenica online ticket pricing tiers (€9.50 peak, €7.60 shoulder, €4.75 low season, 5-day €28.50, Manita peć and visitor centre ticketed separately, 600+ equipped climbing routes); Kuterevo bear refuge open spring–autumn, closed in winter for hibernation, roughly 09:00–17:00, volunteer-staffed.
sources.confidenceNotes: The 3 kg per person per day mushroom limit is the widely cited Croatian personal-use figure but the ordinance is amended periodically — re-verify against the current *Pravilnik* before publishing, and confirm the Gospić mycological inspection point still operates. Cerovac caves ticket prices and tour times were not confirmed this run. Manita peć opening days vary week to week outside July–August. The Oltari–Zavižan road surface and the Štirovača logging-track condition change every season; both should be checked with the park office within a week of travel. Alan spur road condition and whether park vehicle transfers are currently offered need direct confirmation. Bura gust figures near Maslenica are historical records, not typical conditions. Specific Otočac and Starigrad hotels were deliberately left generic — insert verified named properties before publishing.

trips.title: Puszta, Karst and Szer: A Week in Hungary's Three Quietest National Parks

bestPeriod.window: mid-October to early November for the crane migration — the single best wildlife spectacle in Hungary
bestPeriod.avoid: July–August on the puszta (35 °C, heat shimmer kills the birding, and the grassland is bleached)

accommodation.note: €230–€400 (€33–€57/night — village guesthouses, forest cabins, park lodges)

food.note: €130–€200 (€19–€29/day; self-catering brings this down further)

transport.note: €230–€330 (car hire €160–€250, fuel ~€110 for ~1,150 km, e-matrica 6,900 HUF)

activities.note: €90–€150 (cave tours, guided puszta drives, narrow-gauge railway, park entries)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy

trips.gatewayAirport: Budapest Ferenc Liszt (BUD). A car is effectively required — the Őrség hamlets and the Aggtelek villages have one or two buses a day, and the puszta has none.
trips.summary: Three landscapes that share nothing except emptiness: the scattered ridge-hamlets of the Őrség, where a farmstead is its own village; the Hortobágy, Europe's largest continuous natural grassland, where in late…
trips.hook: Three landscapes that share nothing except emptiness: the scattered ridge-hamlets of the Őrség, where a farmstead is its own village; the Hortobágy, Europe's largest continuous natural grassland, where in late October tens of thousands of cranes come down onto the fishponds in a noise you feel in your chest; and the Aggtelek karst, where a 25-kilometre cave system runs under the border into Slovakia. Low budget, low light pollution, very few people.

snapshot.Best period: May, September, and mid-October to early November for cranes
snapshot.Start / End: Budapest → Budapest (loop, ~1,150 km)
snapshot.Getting there: Budapest Ferenc Liszt (BUD). A car is effectively required — the Őrség hamlets and the Aggtelek villages have one or two buses a day, and the puszta has none.

itinerary.title: West to the scattered hamlets
itinerary.morning: Collect the car at BUD, buy the 10-day e-matrica (**6,900 HUF**, ~€17.50), and take the M1/M86 west to Vas county. Stop in Körmend for supplies — the Őrség has village shops with limited hours and no supermarket.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive **Szalafő**, the Őrség's western edge, seven hamlets on separate ridges. Walk to **Szalafő-Pityerszer**, the open-air museum of *kerített ház* farmsteads — timber-framed houses built around an enclosed yard, the local answer to a landscape with no defensible village centre.
itinerary.evening: Settle into the cabin. Dinner is *dödölle*, potato dumpling under sour cream, and everything under **pumpkin-seed oil (*tökmagolaj*)** — the Őrség's cold-pressed oil is the region's one export-grade product. Stars from about 20:30.

itinerary.title: Őrség on foot
itinerary.morning: The **Őrségi Nemzeti Park** trails from Szalafő through the Csörgő-szer and Felsőszer hamlets: beech and oak, wet meadows, and the *szer* pattern visible from every rise. Marked in the Hungarian national system — coloured bands on trees.
itinerary.afternoon: **Vadása-tó** near Hegyhátszentjakab: a small forest lake with a circular path, swimmable in summer, and the park's best short family walk. Then **Pankasz** for the 1755 shingled wooden bell tower.
itinerary.evening: **Velemér**, whose Romanesque church holds Johannes Aquila's frescoes of 1378. Then back to the cabin for a wood-stove night [VERIFY: current Velemér church opening hours and key-holder arrangement].
itinerary.dayStats: 12–15 km walking

itinerary.title: Across the country to the grassland
itinerary.morning: The long transfer: M86 to the M1, round Budapest on the M0, then the M3 east across the Great Plain. It is a genuinely dull four hours; leave early and treat it as the price of admission.
itinerary.afternoon: Arrive **Hortobágy** village. The **Kilenclyukú híd**, the Nine-Arch Bridge of 1833, carries the old salt road over the Hortobágy river — 167 m of stone, the longest stone road bridge in historical Hungary. Beside it, the **Hortobágyi Csárda** of 1781.
itinerary.evening: First reconnaissance drive on road 33 at dusk. In late October the sky begins to fill from about 16:30 as **common cranes (*Grus grus*)** move from the stubble fields to the fishponds to roost.

itinerary.title: The crane day
itinerary.morning: Out before sunrise for the **morning flight** — cranes leave the roost at first light in ragged skeins and spread onto the maize stubble. The best line is the field roads east of the **Hortobágyi-halastó** and along the Kunkápolnási marsh edge; stay in or beside the car, which birds tolerate far better than a standing human.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Hortobágyi-halastó** fishponds, a Ramsar site, with a **narrow-gauge railway** running visitors out along the dykes to a lookout tower — the only way to reach the pond interior. Spoonbill, great white egret, marsh harrier, and in autumn a wall of noise from the roost [VERIFY: 2026 narrow-gauge railway timetable and fare].
itinerary.evening: The main event: build the whole day around the **evening roost flight**. From about an hour before sunset, tens of thousands of cranes come in over the water in waves, calling continuously. Bring a scope or good binoculars, a hat, and patience; it runs 45–60 minutes and ends in near-darkness.
itinerary.dayStats: all day, ~40 km driving

itinerary.title: Grey cattle, racka, and dark sky
itinerary.morning: The **Pusztai Állatpark** at Hortobágy and the **Mátai Ménes** stud: grey cattle, racka sheep, buffalo, and **Nonius horses** — the breed the puszta herdsmen created. The horse-show is touristy; the breeding stock and the guided cart ride onto the range are not [VERIFY: current Pusztai Állatpark and Mátai Ménes ticket prices].
itinerary.afternoon: A **guided puszta drive** into the core zone with a park guide — the only legal way into the interior grassland — for the great bustard flocks and the pumping stations. Arrange it the previous day at the park visitor centre [VERIFY: current guided puszta programme prices].
itinerary.evening: Stay out for the **Hortobágy Starry Sky Park**. From a field road 3 km from any village the Milky Way is unmistakable; late October gives you full dark by 18:30 and Andromeda naked-eye.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km / 1 h

itinerary.title: North to the karst
itinerary.morning: North-west through Tiszafüred and Miskolc into the Aggtelek hills. The plain ends abruptly; within twenty minutes you are in limestone, dolines and beech forest.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Baradla cave**, the Hungarian half of the **Baradla–Domica** system: about **25 km of surveyed passage**, of which roughly 5.6 km lies across the border in **Slovakia as Domica**. Tours run from three entrances — **Aggtelek** (the short tour, about 1 km / 1 hour), **Vörös-tó** (the middle tour, about 2.3 km / 1.5 hours) and **Jósvafő** (about 1.5 km / 1 hour). The long tour, Aggtelek to Jósvafő end-to-end, runs about 7 km and takes 5–7 hours, by arrangement and with a minimum group [VERIFY: current Baradla tour prices and departure times].
itinerary.evening: **Jósvafő** — 300 residents, one shop, one church, karst springs. The cave air is 10 °C year-round; bring a fleece regardless of the surface temperature.

itinerary.title: Karst surface, then home
itinerary.morning: The surface trails above **Jósvafő** and **Aggtelek**: the Tohonya-Kuriszlán educational trail, the Szádvár ruin above Szögliget, and the sinkhole meadows. This is the UNESCO-listed "Caves of Aggtelek Karst and Slovak Karst" landscape seen from above.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Vörös-tó** entrance middle tour if you skipped it, or the Rákóczi cave at Bódvarákó. Lunch in Aggtelek village.
itinerary.evening: M30/M3 back to Budapest, 230 km, 2 h 30 with the vignette already valid.

accommodationStrategy.name: Őrségi vendégház, Szalafő-Pityerszer
accommodationStrategy.description: you sleep inside the settlement pattern the park exists to protect, on a ridge with three neighbours, wood stove, no street light, and the Pityerszer museum and trailheads on foot from the door. Isolation 4.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead; October fills first. Confirm whether firewood and bed linen are included.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hortobágy Club Hotel / village guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: five minutes from the Nine-Arch Bridge and the visitor centre where the guided puszta programmes are booked, with parking for a pre-dawn start and somewhere to leave a scope. The village is your only realistic base for the crane days.
accommodationStrategy.booking: **crane season (mid-Oct to early Nov) needs 2–3 months** — Hungarian and Austrian birders book it out.

accommodationStrategy.name: Tengerszem / Jósvafő park lodges
accommodationStrategy.description: five minutes' walk from the Jósvafő cave entrance and the Tohonya trailhead, in a hamlet that goes silent at nine, with the Vörös-tó entrance a ten-minute drive for the middle tour.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead; school groups take the lodges in May and September midweek.

logistics.connectivity: 4G is reliable in all three park villages and patchy on the puszta field roads. **No signal underground** in Baradla, obviously. Download offline maps — the Hortobágy field-road network is barely mapped by satnav.
logistics.emergency: **112**. On the puszta, give your position by the nearest *csárda*, pumping station or road-33 kilometre post; there are no addresses. In the caves, you go nowhere without a guide, which is precisely why the rule exists.
logistics.weather: The Great Plain has the widest temperature range in Hungary — frost in late October mornings, 20 °C by afternoon. There is **no shade and no shelter** on the puszta; a storm crossing it is fully exposed. The karst gets fog that sits in the valleys until midday.
logistics.bookingWindows: Crane-season beds in Hortobágy 2–3 months. Baradla long tour and guided puszta drives, a few days to a week. Őrség cabins 4–6 weeks.
logistics.money: Forint. Cards are accepted at park ticket offices and larger *csárda*, but village shops, cave car parks and small guesthouses may be cash-only — carry 30,000–40,000 HUF (~€75–€100). ATMs in Debrecen, Körmend, Szentgotthárd and Putnok, not in the villages.
logistics.transportRules: 10-day e-matrica **6,900 HUF** covers the M1, M0, M3 and M30 legs. **0.0‰ alcohol limit** — total, not nominal. **Dipped headlights are compulsory outside built-up areas.** Watch for horse carts, herds crossing and unlit tractors at dusk on the plain.
logistics.permits: **The Hortobágy core grassland requires a park guide or a written permit from the park directorate in Debrecen** — do not simply walk in off a field road. Aggtelek caves: guided tour only. All three parks: no wild camping, no drones without permission, no off-path walking in strict reserves. Mushrooms must go past a **gombaszakellenőr** before they go in a pan.

proTips: **Book the crane week before you book anything else.** The roost flight peaks late October into the first days of November, and Hortobágy village has a few hundred beds against several thousand European birders.

**Watch the roost from inside the car.** Cranes accept a stationary vehicle at 200 m and will not accept a person on foot at 500 m. The field roads east of the Halastó are the position; arrive an hour early and switch the engine off.

**Take your mushrooms to the market inspector.** Any county-town market with a *gombavizsgáló* booth checks a private basket, usually free, usually before 11:00. It is the difference between a good dinner and a liver transplant, and locals do it as routine.
**Choose the Vörös-tó middle tour** over the short Aggtelek tour. It is the best formation-density-per-forint in the system, and it starts from a car park most coach groups skip.

**Buy pumpkin-seed oil from a named Őrség press**, not a supermarket. Ask the guesthouse whose oil they use — the cold-pressed product is dark green, smells of toasted seed, and does not survive heating.
**Do the long Baradla traverse only if you are four or more.** It needs a minimum group and 5–7 hours; splitting the cost across a party makes it the standout day of the week.

**Bring a red torch and stay out after 21:00 on the puszta.** The Starry Sky Park designation is real, the horizon is flat in every direction, and there is no other night sky like it this close to Budapest.

raw.Access requirements: **Őrség NP**: everything reachable on sealed lanes; no 4x4 needed, but the forest tracks between *szer* hamlets are clay and rut badly after rain. **Hortobágy NP**: the visitor sites (Nine-Arch Bridge, Pusztai Állatpark, Mátai Ménes, the fishpond boardwalk) are freely accessible on foot or by ticket, **but the grassland interior is not open access** — the core zones require either a **National Park guide** or a written **entry permit from the Hortobágyi Nemzeti Park Igazgatóság** in Debrecen, and the guided *puszta* drives are the ordinary way in. **Aggtelek NP**: the caves may be entered **only on a guided tour**, no exceptions; the surface trails around Jósvafő and Aggtelek are free and marked.
raw.Isolation rating (1 = suburban, 5 = genu: Őrség: **4** — hamlets of five to fifteen houses, no street lighting, nearest supermarket 20 minutes away. Hortobágy village: **2**; the puszta itself once you are 3 km from the road: **5**, with no shade, no water and no landmarks. Aggtelek and Jósvafő: **3** — small villages, one shop each, the karst plateau above them empty.
raw.Off-grid utilities: Most Őrség guesthouses are on mains power and well or mains water but have **wood stoves as primary heating** — ask whether firewood is included. Puszta *csárda* lodges and shepherd huts on the plain run on limited hot water and sometimes solar; the Aggtelek park lodges are conventional. Everywhere on this route: **no fuel after about 20:00** in villages, and no ATMs outside the towns.
raw.Foraging and the mushroom rule: Hungary has a distinctive and strictly applied system: **wild mushrooms may only be sold or, in practice, safely eaten after inspection by a licensed *gombaszakellenőr*** — a state-certified mushroom inspector. **Public mushroom inspectors sit at municipal markets** (Debrecen's Nagypiac and most county-town markets keep one during the season, usually mornings), and the service to a private picker is free or nominal. Picking for personal use is generally tolerated in state forests up to about 2 kg per person per day; picking is **banned outright in national-park core zones and strict reserves**. Take your basket to the inspector before you cook anything. Berries, wild pear, rosehip and elderflower are unrestricted outside core zones [VERIFY: current statutory personal-use mushroom quota].
raw.Wildlife protocol: There are **no resident brown bears in Hungary**, though individuals occasionally wander into the northern Borsod and Aggtelek hills from Slovakia — if you meet one, back away, do not run, make yourself heard. Wolves are re-establishing in the same northern karst in very small numbers and are not a practical hazard. The real animals you will meet are **Hungarian grey cattle (*magyar szürke szarvasmarha*)**, **racka sheep** with their corkscrew horns, **Nonius horses** and water buffalo on the Hortobágy — all semi-wild, all on open range, all to be given distance. Grey cattle bulls with calves in the herd are the one genuine risk: stay outside the fence line.
raw.Dark skies: The **Hortobágy Starry Sky Park** is an International Dark Sky Park covering much of the national park; the Milky Way is naked-eye across the whole southern sky on a moonless night. The Őrség is similarly dark. Bring a red-filter torch.
