trips.title: A Surf Week in Hossegor, Seignosse and Capbreton

bestPeriod.note: September and October bring the biggest, most consistent groundswell with warm water and thinner crowds than the August peak; June offers smaller, friendlier surf for building confidence.

trips.gatewayAirport: Biarritz (BIA)
trips.summary: A week of Atlantic beach-break surfing across Hossegor, Seignosse and Capbreton, shaped by the deep Gouf de Capbreton canyon offshore.
trips.hook: Most of the French Atlantic coast is a long, gently sloping sandbar. Hossegor is not, because a few hundred metres off its beach the seabed drops into the Gouf de Capbreton, a submarine canyon plunging to over 3,000 m within a few kilometres of the sand. That canyon focuses and steepens incoming Atlantic swell before it reaches the beach break, which is why this stretch of the Landes coast — Hossegor, Seignosse, Capbreton — produces some of the heaviest beach-break waves in Europe, and why it has trained a large share of France's competitive surfers. This week surfs all three towns, respects the canyon's power, and eats well in the Landes pine forest behind the dunes.

snapshot.Base(s): Hossegor (4 nights), Seignosse (2 nights), Capbreton (1 night)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Beach breaks across roughly 12 km of coast between Capbreton and Seignosse; the Gouf de Capbreton canyon offshore
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Biarritz, hire a car for the 30–40 minute drive north; a car is genuinely useful for moving between beach breaks by conditions each morning
snapshot.Who It Suits: Intermediate to advanced surfers ready for powerful, sometimes heavy beach-break waves, and beginners committed to lesson time in the gentler spots

itinerary.title: Arrival and the Gouf explained
itinerary.morning: Fly into Biarritz, collect the hire car, drive 30–40 minutes north to Hossegor. Check into base and walk to the Plage Centrale to see the beach break at work.
itinerary.afternoon: Register with a Hossegor surf school affiliated to the Fédération Française de Surf (FFS) for a conditions briefing. The instructor explains the Gouf de Capbreton's effect directly: the canyon channels swell energy toward shore with less of the usual dissipation over a shallow shelf, so waves break bigger, steeper and closer together than the swell height alone suggests — a real hazard for anyone used to gentler beaches.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Hossegor's Bourg, the town's old quarter around the Lac d'Hossegor rather than the beachfront.
itinerary.dayStats: 1 h in water · orientation and lesson at a gentler spot · softboard, 3/2 mm wetsuit.

itinerary.title: Hossegor beach breaks
itinerary.morning: The Atlantic here runs a fairly consistent west to north-west groundswell most of the year, met by a light morning offshore wind, typically from the east, that holds the wave faces clean before the sea breeze fills in. Check the surf report and tide table together — several Hossegor peaks, including La Gravière and La Nord, work best mid-tide and turn to dangerous, fast close-outs at others.
itinerary.afternoon: Surf La Sud or a mellower peak if the swell is running large, since La Gravière is known as one of the most powerful, heaviest beach breaks in Europe and is not a spot to underestimate on a big day.
itinerary.evening: Walk the boardwalk along the Lac d'Hossegor at sunset, or watch from the dune above La Gravière — this beach hosts World Surf League Championship Tour events and the standard in the water is genuinely high.
itinerary.dayStats: 2.5 h in water · W/NW groundswell, light morning offshore · shortboard, 3/2 mm wetsuit, leash and fins check.

itinerary.title: Seignosse and the rip picture
itinerary.morning: Drive 15 minutes to Seignosse, whose beaches — Les Bourdaines, Les Culs Verts, Penon — sit along the same canyon-shaped swell but spread the crowd out from Hossegor's peaks. Breaks here shift with every storm, so the bank and rip location changes week to week; ask the lifeguard post which channel is running before paddling out.
itinerary.afternoon: A second session, or a lesson upgrade for less experienced members at one of Seignosse's more forgiving banks, still supervised by CRS lifeguards in season.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Seignosse-Bourg, a genuine Landes village inland from the beach hamlets, with a market square and slower pace than the coast.
itinerary.dayStats: 2.5 h in water · W/NW swell, variable rip position · shortboard, 3/2 mm wetsuit.

itinerary.title: Rest tide and the Landes pine forest
itinerary.morning: A lighter day. Cycle or walk into the Landes pine forest behind the dunes, the largest man-made forest in Western Europe, planted from the 19th century to stabilise the dunes and drain the marshy Landes plain — resin-tapping scars still visible on older pines recall the region's turpentine industry.
itinerary.afternoon: Return to the beach for a lighter session at a mellow spot if the swell has dropped, or bodysurfing and skimboarding on the shorebreak if it hasn't — the shorebreak alone here is punchy enough to be worth respecting.
itinerary.evening: Capbreton's harbour for dinner — the town retains a working fishing fleet, one of the last on this stretch of coast, right beside the canyon that gives it its name.
itinerary.dayStats: 1.5 h in water or forest cycling · variable · shortboard or bike.

itinerary.title: Capbreton and the canyon's edge
itinerary.morning: Surf directly off Capbreton, where the Gouf's canyon head comes closest to shore — a short walk from the harbour mole. The bathymetry produces a distinctly punchy, hollow wave when swell direction and tide line up, a spot locals and visitors treat with real respect.
itinerary.afternoon: A second session or, for stronger surfers, the more exposed reef and jetty peaks near the canal — experienced surfers only, given the proximity to harbour structures and the canyon-focused power.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at the Capbreton harbourside, watching the fishing boats return.
itinerary.dayStats: 3 h in water · canyon-focused swell, tide-dependent · performance shortboard, 3/2 mm wetsuit.

itinerary.title: Best-conditions day, wherever that is
itinerary.morning: With five days of local knowledge built up, choose whichever of the three towns has the best combination of swell size, wind and tide that morning — standard practice here, and the short 10–20 minute drives between spots make it easy.
itinerary.afternoon: A longer freesurf session, plus a stop at a surf shop along the Avenue du Touring Club in Hossegor for wax, fin checks or a board repair — the town has one of France's densest concentrations of surf retail, a legacy of decades as a competition hub.
itinerary.evening: A farewell dinner back in Hossegor, with Landes specialties — duck, in various forms, is the region's defining ingredient well before seafood.
itinerary.dayStats: 3 h in water · best available conditions · own board and wetsuit.

itinerary.title: Final session and departure
itinerary.morning: A last dawn-patrol session, timed to the best tide of the day and the typically cleanest, least crowded window.
itinerary.afternoon: Return gear, shower, and drive back to Biarritz (30–40 minutes, add margin for August or a busy Saturday).
itinerary.evening: Flight home from Biarritz.
itinerary.dayStats: 1.5 h in water · variable, whatever the tide and swell allow · own or final rental kit.

accommodationStrategy.name: Surf lodge or guesthouse near the Hossegor Bourg / Lac d'Hossegor
accommodationStrategy.description: A base a short bike ride from the beach breaks and close to the town's surf shops, avoiding peak-season parking pressure at the Plage Centrale.
accommodationStrategy.booking: eight to ten weeks ahead for September–October.

accommodationStrategy.name: Chalet or B&B near Seignosse-Bourg or Les Bourdaines
accommodationStrategy.description: Convenient for Days 3 and 4, and generally quieter and better value than beachfront Hossegor.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel near the Capbreton harbour
accommodationStrategy.description: A short walk to the canal-mouth surf and the working fishing port, a genuinely different atmosphere from the resort feel further north.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four to six weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: Emergency number is 112. At sea, the maritime distress channel is VHF 16; search-and-rescue coordination for this coast runs through CROSS Étel.

other.text: Emergency number is 112. At sea, the maritime distress channel is VHF 16; search-and-rescue coordination for this coast runs through CROSS Étel.

Lifeguard (poste de secours, staffed by CRS lifeguards) season on the main beaches typically runs mid-June to mid-September. Outside those dates, beaches are unsupervised and the rips genuinely dangerous for anyone not confident reading them.

The flag system is standard French coastal practice: green (safe), orange (caution — the usual flag on a solid swell day here), red (surfing outside designated zones prohibited). Always surf within the marked zone when lifeguards are on duty.

The Gouf de Capbreton's effect on wave power is the key local fact: swell that would be moderate elsewhere can produce genuinely heavy, fast-breaking waves here, and shorebreak alone has caused serious injuries. Respect any "attention, vagues dangereuses" signage.
A car is genuinely useful: Hossegor, Seignosse and Capbreton are 10–20 minutes apart by road, and checking conditions across all three each morning is standard local practice.
Weather and swell can shift materially within a day; check a Landes-specific surf forecast (swell height, period, direction, wind) each morning.
Cash and card both work at surf shops and restaurants; smaller beach-hut rental kiosks can be cash-preferred in peak season.

Book surf lessons and board rental at least a few days ahead in the September–October and August windows — this coast's surf schools are numerous but the well-established ones fill quickly around a good forecast.

proTips: Ask a local surf shop or school which peak is working best that morning before committing — banks shift with every winter storm and shop staff surf here daily.
Surf the mid-tide window at La Gravière or La Nord rather than dead low or dead high, when both spots tend to close out fast and hard.
Choose September or October over August if flexible: swell is typically bigger and more consistent, the water still warm, and lineups noticeably thinner.
Check the tide and swell forecast the evening before, not the morning of — the best dawn sessions require an early start timed to a specific tide state.
Rent or buy a slightly higher-volume board than elsewhere; the extra paddle power helps against the canyon-steepened waves' quicker take-off.
Visit a surf shop on the Avenue du Touring Club for a repair or fin swap — Hossegor's shaping culture is deep and same-day turnaround is common in season.
Walk or cycle the Landes forest trails on a flat or overpowering-swell day; a proper change of pace from the open beach.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Beach breaks across roughly 12 km of coast between Capbreton and Seignosse; the Gouf de Capbreton canyon offshore
raw.Who It Suits: Intermediate to advanced surfers ready for powerful, sometimes heavy beach-break waves, and beginners committed to lesson time in the gentler spots

typeSpecific.surface: Beach breaks across roughly 12 km of coast between Capbreton and Seignosse; the Gouf de Capbreton canyon offshore
typeSpecific.audience: Intermediate to advanced surfers ready for powerful, sometimes heavy beach-break waves, and beginners committed to lesson time in the gentler spots

packingNotes: A 3/2 mm wetsuit for June and September–October; a thinner spring suit is fine at height of summer.
A leash rated for your board, plus a spare — Hossegor's power breaks leashes more than most beaches.
Reef-safe sunscreen and a rash vest for paddling-heavy sessions.
A dry bag for phone, keys and the surf forecast printout.
A rental bike for moving around Hossegor's Bourg and lake path without the car.
A warm layer for early dawn-patrol starts, even in September.
Comfortable walking or cycling shoes for the Landes forest.
Euro cash for beach kiosks, board-hire deposits and village restaurants.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Overestimating the beach break.** Waves here are genuinely heavier than they look. Start at a gentler spot like Les Bourdaines or a supervised lesson beach before progressing to La Gravière on a big day.
**A flat spell.** Groundswell is generally reliable in the shoulder season but can drop for a day or two. Fall back to the Landes forest, a Capbreton harbour walk, or a day trip toward Biarritz.
**A strong, shifting rip.** Rips move with every swell and can be hard to spot. Always ask the lifeguard post which channel is running, and surf within the flagged zone.
**Overcrowded peak-season lineups.** August brings heavy crowds. Shifting toward September–October, or surfing dawn patrol, avoids the worst of it.
**A big swell arriving faster than expected.** The Gouf can turn a moderate forecast into serious, closed-out conditions quickly. Check the morning report and be willing to sit a session out.

trips.title: Quiberon and the Golfe du Morbihan by Board and Kayak

bestPeriod.note: July and August bring the most reliable thermal afternoon breeze on the Côte Sauvage; June and September keep the Golfe's currents just as strong with far fewer boats.

trips.gatewayAirport: Nantes Atlantique (NTE)
trips.summary: A week of surf on the Côte Sauvage, sea kayaking the Golfe du Morbihan's tidal currents, and a Belle-Île crossing, based at Quiberon.
trips.hook: Two very different bodies of water sit either side of the Quiberon peninsula, ten kilometres apart. On the west, the Côte Sauvage takes the full Atlantic swell onto rock and beach break. On the east, the Golfe du Morbihan is nearly closed, and the tide has to force the same volume of water through a narrow mouth twice a day — currents that reach several knots and have humbled plenty of confident paddlers. This week surfs one and reads the other, with a day on Belle-Île and an evening at Carnac's alignments between.

snapshot.Base(s): Quiberon (5 nights), Vannes or Locmariaquer for the Golfe day (2 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Côte Sauvage beach and reef breaks along roughly 8 km; Golfe du Morbihan tidal basin approx. 20 km across with currents to 4–5 knots at the Barre du Grand Vezid
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Nantes, hire a car for the 1 h 30 drive to Quiberon; a car is genuinely useful for reaching Golfe put-in points and the Belle-Île ferry terminal
snapshot.Who It Suits: Surfers and sea kayakers comfortable reading a swell forecast and a tide table, who want two contrasting Breton waters in one week

itinerary.title: Arrival and first look at the Côte Sauvage
itinerary.morning: Fly into Nantes, collect the hire car, drive 1 h 30 to Quiberon. Check into base and walk the Côte Sauvage, the peninsula's exposed western shore, a run of small coves and reef points fully open to the Atlantic.
itinerary.afternoon: Register with a Quiberon surf school affiliated to the Fédération Française de Surf (FFS) for a conditions briefing and, for less experienced surfers, a first lesson at a sheltered sandy cove such as Port Blanc, gentler than the exposed points further south.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Quiberon town; an early one given tomorrow's tide-timed session.
itinerary.dayStats: 1 h in water · orientation and lesson · softboard, spring wetsuit.

itinerary.title: Côte Sauvage surf
itinerary.morning: The Atlantic swell here is usually a clean groundswell from the west to north-west, met most mornings by a light offshore or cross-shore breeze before the local thermal builds; check the surf forecast and tide table together, since several breaks work only within specific tide windows and turn to close-out mush or exposed rock at the wrong state. Surf a mid-tide session at Port Bara or Port Blanc depending on swell direction.
itinerary.afternoon: A second session or a rest, watching the more advanced reef break at Beg er Vil work at the right swell size — experienced surfers only, with rock hazards close to the surface.
itinerary.evening: Walk the Côte Sauvage coastal path (part of the GR34) at sunset, one of the finest stretches of the entire Breton coastal trail.
itinerary.dayStats: 2.5 h in water · SW groundswell, light offshore morning wind · shortboard or funboard, 3/2 mm wetsuit.

itinerary.title: Belle-Île crossing
itinerary.morning: Ferry from Quiberon's Port Maria to Le Palais on Belle-Île, roughly 45 minutes, the largest of Brittany's islands and a genuine day trip rather than a stretch.
itinerary.afternoon: Explore the Aiguilles de Port-Coton, the needle rocks Monet painted in 1886, and the Grand Phare lighthouse. If swell and wind align, a surf or bodyboard session is possible on the island's exposed western coves; otherwise this is a walking day.
itinerary.evening: Ferry back to Quiberon, dinner at the port.
itinerary.dayStats: 0–1.5 h in water depending on conditions · variable · own gear if surfing.

itinerary.title: Transfer to the Golfe and first paddle
itinerary.morning: Drive to Locmariaquer or Vannes on the Golfe du Morbihan's shore, about 45 minutes from Quiberon. This gulf is nearly landlocked, connected to the Atlantic by a mouth only about 1 km wide near Port-Navalo, and the tide pushes its full volume through that gap — currents at spots like the Barre du Grand Vezid can run 4–5 knots at springs, among the strongest on the French coast.
itinerary.afternoon: Register with a Golfe-based sea kayak club (several operate from Vannes, Larmor-Baden and Arradon, generally FFCK-affiliated) for a guided introductory paddle timed to slack water — the only sensible time for a first outing, since ebb and flood both run hard enough to overpower an unprepared paddler.
itinerary.evening: Vannes old town, with its half-timbered houses and ramparts around the port; dinner near the Place des Lices.
itinerary.dayStats: 2 h paddling · slack-water window · sea kayak, spray deck, buoyancy aid.

itinerary.title: The Golfe's islands
itinerary.morning: A longer guided kayak circuit among the Golfe's islands — popularly said to number 365, though the true count is closer to forty. Île aux Moines and Île d'Arz are the two largest, reachable by paddle or the small local ferries.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue the circuit or land on Île aux Moines for a walk and lunch; timing the return leg to ride the tide rather than fight it is the entire skill of paddling here, and the guide plans the route around that day's specific tide times.
itinerary.evening: Locmariaquer, where the Grand Menhir Brisé and the Table des Marchands passage tomb sit close to the water — among the oldest standing stone monuments in Europe, predating Carnac's alignments.
itinerary.dayStats: 3.5 h paddling · tide-timed circuit · sea kayak, wetsuit top.

itinerary.title: Carnac and a return surf session
itinerary.morning: Drive back toward Quiberon via Carnac, and spend the morning among the alignments — over 3,000 standing stones dating to the Neolithic, the largest such concentration in the world, with the Ménec and Kermario alignments walkable from marked paths.
itinerary.afternoon: Back on the Côte Sauvage for a final surf session, timed again to the tide and the day's swell forecast.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Carnac-Plage or Quiberon, with fresh oysters from the Golfe's beds, a genuine local specialty of Locmariaquer.
itinerary.dayStats: 2 h in water · variable swell and wind · surfboard, 3/2 mm wetsuit.

itinerary.title: Final session and departure
itinerary.morning: A last surf check on the Côte Sauvage or a short flat-water paddle from Quiberon's own sheltered eastern shore if the swell has dropped.
itinerary.afternoon: Return gear, shower, and drive back to Nantes (1 h 30, add margin on summer Saturdays).
itinerary.evening: Flight home from Nantes.
itinerary.dayStats: 1.5 h in water · variable · own or final rental kit.

accommodationStrategy.name: Guesthouse or hotel near Port Maria, Quiberon
accommodationStrategy.description: Within walking or short-drive distance of both the Côte Sauvage breaks and the Belle-Île ferry terminal — this single base covers Days 1, 2, 3, 6 and 7 without moving.
accommodationStrategy.booking: eight weeks ahead for July–August; four weeks for June or September.

accommodationStrategy.name: B&B near the Vannes or Locmariaquer waterfront
accommodationStrategy.description: A short drive from the Golfe's kayak clubs and put-in points, walking distance to Vannes old town.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four to six weeks ahead.

accommodationStrategy.name: Chambre d'hôtes near Carnac-Plage
accommodationStrategy.description: An option for splitting the last two nights closer to the alignments and final surf sessions, without the full drive back to Quiberon each evening.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four weeks ahead.

logistics.emergency: Emergency number is 112. At sea, the maritime distress channel is VHF 16, and search-and-rescue coordination on this coast runs through the CROSS (Centre Régional Opérationnel de Surveillance et de Sauvetage) Étel station, the CROSS covering the whole Breton Atlantic coast.

other.text: Emergency number is 112. At sea, the maritime distress channel is VHF 16, and search-and-rescue coordination on this coast runs through the CROSS (Centre Régional Opérationnel de Surveillance et de Sauvetage) Étel station, the CROSS covering the whole Breton Atlantic coast.

The Golfe du Morbihan's tidal currents are a genuine hazard, not a scenic detail: at spring tides the flow near Port-Navalo and around the Barre du Grand Vezid can exceed 4–5 knots, faster than most paddlers can make headway against. Guided or slack-water-timed paddling is the only sensible approach without strong local experience.

The Côte Sauvage lives up to its name: several coves have serious rip and rock hazards and are unsupervised outside the main patrolled beaches. Check the day's flag colour (green, yellow, orange, red, ascending restriction) and never surf an unsupervised break alone in unfamiliar conditions.
Lifeguard (poste de secours) season on the main Quiberon and Carnac beaches generally runs mid-June to early September; outside those dates, beaches are unsupervised.

Learn to read the SHOM tide table (coefficient and times of high/low water) before the first Golfe paddle — the coefficient, roughly 20 to 120, indicates that day's current strength, and a guide will not run a serious circuit on a high-coefficient day with inexperienced paddlers.

A car is genuinely useful: the Golfe's put-in points, Carnac's alignments and the Quiberon ferry terminal are spread wider than a single walkable base can cover, though local buses connect Quiberon, Carnac and Vannes.
Cash and card both work at rental counters and restaurants; smaller Golfe-side kiosks near the islands can be cash-only.
Book the Belle-Île ferry (Compagnie Océane) ahead in July–August, when sailings fill, and reserve Golfe guided kayak trips at least a few days out in peak season.

proTips: Check the tide coefficient before any Golfe paddle day — above about 90, even a guided group sticks to a short, sheltered route near slack water only.
Surf Port Blanc or sheltered coves on a small swell day and save the exposed points for a clean, moderate groundswell with light offshore wind.
Take the earliest reasonable Belle-Île ferry crossing for the fullest island day, since return sailings can be tight on the last boat in peak season.
Buy Golfe oysters directly from a producer's stall near Locmariaquer rather than a restaurant plate — noticeably fresher and cheaper.
Walk a stretch of the GR34 along the Côte Sauvage even on a non-water day; it gives the clearest sense of where each spot sits relative to the rocks.
Visit Carnac's alignments early morning or the last two hours before closing to avoid midday coach-tour crowds.
Ask the kayak guide to explain the Golfe's slack-water timing on the water, not just in the briefing — seeing the current slow and reverse near the islands is the best lesson in reading it.

raw.Total Distance / Terrain: Côte Sauvage beach and reef breaks along roughly 8 km; Golfe du Morbihan tidal basin approx. 20 km across with currents to 4–5 knots at the Barre du Grand Vezid
raw.Who It Suits: Surfers and sea kayakers comfortable reading a swell forecast and a tide table, who want two contrasting Breton waters in one week

typeSpecific.surface: Côte Sauvage beach and reef breaks along roughly 8 km; Golfe du Morbihan tidal basin approx. 20 km across with currents to 4–5 knots at the Barre du Grand Vezid
typeSpecific.audience: Surfers and sea kayakers comfortable reading a swell forecast and a tide table, who want two contrasting Breton waters in one week

packingNotes: A 3/2 mm wetsuit for July–August; step up to 4/3 mm for June or September mornings.
Reef booties for the rockier breaks.
A spray deck and proper buoyancy aid for the Golfe days — non-negotiable given the current strength.
A dry bag for phone, keys and the tide-table printout or app.
Sunglasses with a strap and high-factor sunscreen; the Golfe's flat water reflects glare all day.
Comfortable walking shoes for Carnac and the GR34.
A warm layer for Golfe mornings, often cooler and stiller than the open coast.
Euro cash for ferry kiosks, oyster stalls and smaller guesthouses.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Underestimating the Golfe's currents.** Paddling against a flooding or ebbing tide near the mouth can pin even a strong kayaker in place. Always paddle with a guide or strictly at slack water, treating the tide table as the actual schedule.

**A flat or blown-out swell on the Côte Sauvage.** Groundswell is generally reliable but not guaranteed; a flat week converts naturally into more Golfe paddling, Belle-Île time and the Carnac alignments.
**Missed Belle-Île ferry return.** Peak-season sailings can sell out. Book the return leg in advance and build slack rather than catching the last boat.
**Rock and rip hazards on unsupervised coves.** Several breaks have no lifeguard cover outside the main season. Stick to flagged, supervised beaches unless surfing with a school or experienced local.
**A sudden Atlantic frontal system.** Weather can turn quickly here. Check the CROSS Étel marine forecast each morning and treat any strong-wind warning as a reason to shift to the sheltered Golfe.

trips.title: Meltemi Weeks: Paros & Naxos on Board and Kite

bestPeriod.window: Mid-June–mid-September for wind; late May and late September for wind plus swimmable calm
bestPeriod.avoid: November–March — most centres shut, ferries cancel on southerlies, and water drops to 15–16°C
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-June–mid-September for wind; late May and late September for wind plus swimmable calm

accommodation.note: Mikri Vigla and Golden Beach studios €80–€140 per night double in August; €55–€90 in June

food.note: Taverna mains €10–€18, beach-club club sandwich €9, half-litre of local white €6

transport.note: Paros–Naxos ferry €13–€35, ATV or small car hire €35–€55/day, airport transfers

activities.note: Six days of kite or windsurf rental €270–€380, one refresher lesson €90–€120, one dive or freedive session €60–€90

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5 — no long-distance effort, but six days of 3–5 hours on the water in 20–30 knots is genuinely tiring on shoulders, forearms and neck

trips.gatewayAirport: JTR is wrong for this trip — use PAS Paros National (seasonal Athens and limited European) 20 min to Golden Beach, JNX Naxos Island National 10 min to Naxos Town, or ATH Athens + Blue Star ferry to Paros 3 h 45 min / Naxos 4 h 30 min
trips.summary: This is a week built around a wind that arrives on a timetable. From roughly mid-June the meltemi settles into the Cyclades as a northerly, filling in through the early afternoon and blowing itself out around sunset, and Paros and Naxos sit in the channel where it accelerates hardest. You base first on Paros — Chrisi Akti and New Golden Beach for windsurfing, Pounda for kite in the Antiparos channel — then take the 30-to-45-minute ferry to Naxos, where Mikri Vigla splits into a flat lagoon at Limanaki and a wave side at Orkos in the same ten-minute walk. The rhythm is the same every day: slow mornings, snorkelling and coffee, then a hard three-hour session from about 13:00. It suits an independent intermediate more than a first-timer, because in the second half of July the wind is often too strong for a beginner lesson to even run.

itinerary.title: Land on Paros, rig at New Golden Beach
itinerary.morning: Arrive at Paros (PAS) or off the Blue Star from Piraeus into Parikia. Collect a small car or ATV and drive 20–25 minutes across the island to the Chrisi Akti / New Golden Beach strip on the east coast. Register at Force7 at New Golden Beach: sign the waiver, get sized, and agree the week's rate rather than paying by day.
itinerary.afternoon: Deliberately soft first session. The meltemi is cross-onshore here so a mistake washes you back onto sand, which makes it the right place to shake off a winter. Sail or ride between 13:30 and 16:30, then stop before your forearms decide for you.
itinerary.evening: Taverna Tsachpinis at Drios, five minutes south, for grilled gopa, fava and a carafe of white. Older, cheaper and quieter than the beach-club strip.
itinerary.dayStats: Airport to Golden Beach 20 min / typical afternoon 18–24 knots NNE in June, 22–30 knots in August / water 24–26°C / sail 5.0–5.8 m, kite 8–9 m for 75 kg

itinerary.title: Pounda, the channel and the ferry lane
itinerary.morning: Cross to the west coast to Pounda while the wind is still building. Check in at Paros Kite Pro Center and walk the beach first: the Antiparos ferry lane is the single most important thing on this trip and you need to see where it runs before you are powered up. Rig, then use the light morning breeze for a downwinder-free warm-up.
itinerary.afternoon: Full session at Pounda from about 13:00. Flat sandy shallows close in, chop further out, side-shore meltemi. Set a personal turnaround marker well inside the ferry track and hold it.
itinerary.evening: Drive 25 minutes north to Naoussa. Eat at Siparos on Santa Maria bay if you want the good meal of the week, or at one of the fishing-harbour tavernas in Naoussa itself for grilled octopus and ouzo at half the price.
itinerary.dayStats: Golden Beach to Pounda 25 min / Antiparos ferry crosses every 20–30 min, 07:00–00:30 in summer / Pounda kite day rental €60–€80 / channel Venturi adds roughly 3–6 knots over open-sea forecast

itinerary.title: Kolimbithres, freediving and a windless-morning boat
itinerary.morning: Off the water. Drive to Kolimbithres on the far side of Naoussa Bay, where wind and salt have sculpted the granite into smooth hollows, and snorkel or freedive the rock shelves — 6–12 m of visibility on a calm morning, octopus in the crevices, urchins everywhere, so wear shoes. Aegean Diving College in Naoussa runs guided dives and can put a competent snorkeller onto better ground.
itinerary.afternoon: Either an afternoon session back at New Golden Beach if the meltemi has filled, or the Antiparos option: the ferry from Pounda takes about 10 minutes and lands you in a village that is genuinely quieter than anywhere on Paros.
itinerary.evening: Volcano or Glafkos in Naoussa's old harbour. Order whatever came in that morning, by the kilo.
itinerary.dayStats: Pounda–Antiparos ferry ~10 min, roughly €1.50–€2 foot passenger, €6–€8 with a car / Kolimbithres visibility typically 6–12 m / guided dive €55–€90 / snorkel set hire €10–€15

itinerary.title: Ferry to Naxos, first look at Mikri Vigla
itinerary.morning: Drop the Paros car, take the ferry from Parikia to Naxos Town — Blue Star runs it in about 45 minutes, the fast cats in 25–35. Book the day before in August; the Cycladic ferry network is the trip's one genuine single point of failure. Pick up a car at Naxos port.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive 20 minutes south to Mikri Vigla and walk the headland before you rig. Limanaki on the north side, Orkos on the south, and the granite spine between them — see the difference in water state with your own eyes. Register at Flisvos Kite Centre or Naxos Kitelife. If you want to ride, ride Limanaki.
itinerary.evening: Axiotissa Taverna between Kastraki and Mikri Vigla — vegetable-forward Naxian cooking, its own garden produce, a wine list better than the setting suggests. Book, it fills.
itinerary.dayStats: Parikia–Naxos ferry 25–45 min, roughly €13–€18 conventional, €25–€35 fast / Naxos port to Mikri Vigla 20 min / Limanaki flat-to-chop, Orkos wave and reef

itinerary.title: Limanaki flat water and the Orkos question
itinerary.morning: Coffee at the Flisvos Kite Centre and a slow rig. If you hold an IKO Level 3 card, bring it; without it you will be assessed before you get independent gear. Use the morning for a technique hour — a private lesson here is worth more than three unstructured afternoons.
itinerary.afternoon: Long session on Limanaki. If the meltemi is over 28 knots and clean and you are genuinely a wave rider, cross to Orkos with a partner and a briefed plan; if you are hesitating, that is your answer, and Limanaki will not disappoint you.
itinerary.evening: Kontos Fish Tavern on the Mikri Vigla road, or drive 15 minutes to Plaka for sundown at Kavuras. **Plan B if the wind fails:** swap the afternoon for the Temple of Demeter at Sangri and the Melanes kouros lying unfinished in his orchard.
itinerary.dayStats: Naxos private kite tuition €90–€140/hour / kite day rental €60–€80, six-day €270–€380 / Orkos advanced only, reef and rock section / afternoon peak 14:00–17:00

itinerary.title: Plaka, Laguna and a downwind run
itinerary.morning: Drive the coast road north and look at Plaka's 4 km of open sand and at the Laguna flats behind Agios Prokopios. Laguna is the shallowest, flattest water on the island and the best place on the trip to try a new trick without paying for it.
itinerary.afternoon: Run a supported downwinder — Mikri Vigla to Plaka is the classic, cross-onshore the whole way with sand under you and a road behind the dunes for the pick-up. Arrange the shuttle with your centre in the morning, not at 15:00.
itinerary.evening: Agios Prokopios or Agia Anna for the beach tavernas. Order the Naxian potatoes and the graviera saganaki; this island grows and makes both.
itinerary.dayStats: Mikri Vigla–Plaka downwinder roughly 4–5 km / shuttle €15–€25 pp / Laguna knee-to-waist depth over sand / typical August afternoon 25–32 knots N/NNE

itinerary.title: Agios Georgios, Koufonisia option, Portara at sunset
itinerary.morning: Move to Naxos Town. Agios Georgios is the town beach and a waist-deep lagoon — an easy last wing or windsurf session with Flisvos Sportclub, or the place to put a nervous partner on a board for the first time without any consequence at all.
itinerary.afternoon: If you have a spare day and calm sea, the Small Cyclades day boat to Koufonisia — an hour or so from Naxos — gives you the clearest snorkelling water of the whole trip at Pori and the sea caves along the north shore. Otherwise, wash and return kit and swim off Agios Georgios.
itinerary.evening: Walk the causeway to the Portara — the unfinished 6th-century BC marble doorway of the Temple of Apollo — for sunset, then eat at To Elliniko in the old town.
itinerary.dayStats: Naxos–Koufonisia ferry roughly 55–90 min depending on operator, €18–€30 each way / Agios Georgios sandy and waist-deep 100 m out / Portara free, no fence, no ticket
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Grotta or Nissaki Beach, Naxos Town

accommodationStrategy.name: Golden Beach Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: Directly on the windsurf beach, which removes the single biggest daily friction on a trip like this: you can look at the water from the balcony and decide whether to rig. Rooms are simple, there is outdoor rinse space for kit, and the centres are a two-minute walk. Roughly €90–€150 double in August, €60–€95 in June.

accommodationStrategy.name: Mikri Vigla Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits on the neck of land between Limanaki and Orkos, so both spots are on foot and you can re-check conditions hourly without driving. Kitchenettes matter here because Mikri Vigla has few dinner options and the good tavernas are a drive. Roughly €95–€160 double in season.

accommodationStrategy.name: Nissaki Beach Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: The last-night option: on the Agios Georgios lagoon, walking distance to Flisvos Sportclub, the ferry port and the Portara, which is exactly what you want when you are packing kit and catching a morning boat. Roughly €160–€260 double, and worth it for one night rather than seven.

logistics.connectivity: 4G and increasingly 5G across both islands, weak in the Naxos interior valleys and at Orkos behind the headland. Greece is in the EU so roaming is at domestic rates for EU/EEA SIMs; UK SIMs vary by operator. Download the Windy and Ferryhopper apps and set an offline map before you rely on them at a beach car park.
logistics.emergency: 112 for everything; **Hellenic Coast Guard 108** for anything on the water. Naxos has a general hospital in Naxos Town; Paros has a health centre at Parikia. Serious cases are transferred to Athens by air, which is a real reason to carry insurance that names kitesurfing and windsurfing explicitly — many policies exclude both by default, and freediving below 10 m almost always needs a rider.
logistics.weather: The meltemi is the whole story. It arrives with little visible warning beyond a hard blue sky and a white-capped horizon, it can jump 10 knots in an hour, and it does not respect the "dies at sunset" folklore once it is properly established. Watch the Poseidon System (poseidon.hcmr.gr) alongside Windy, and treat any forecast over 35 knots as a ferry-disruption day as much as a sailing day.
logistics.bookingWindows: August accommodation at Mikri Vigla and Golden Beach goes three to five months out and is the hardest thing to fix late. Ferries: book the Paros–Naxos leg at least 24–48 hours ahead in August, and the Piraeus legs two to four weeks ahead if you are bringing a car. Kite and windsurf week-passes rarely sell out but the good boards do — reserve gear by email a fortnight ahead. Axiotissa needs a day's notice.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards are accepted almost everywhere including beach bars, but Greek island card terminals fail with unhelpful regularity, so carry €100–€150 in cash. Tipping is 5–10% or rounding up; it is not obligatory and nobody chases it.
logistics.transportRules: An ATV or quad is the local default but is genuinely dangerous on gravel and, importantly, most travel insurance voids for quad accidents without a category A licence — a small car costs €35–€55 a day and carries a board bag. Taking a hire car between Paros and Naxos on the ferry needs the rental company's written permission and usually costs extra; it is almost always cheaper to hire separately on each island. Ferry tickets must be exchanged for boarding passes at the port for some operators — allow 30 minutes.
logistics.permits: No permit is needed to kite or windsurf, but Greek beach regulation increasingly separates swimmer zones from watersports zones with buoys in high season — respect them, port police do enforce. Anchoring on *Posidonia* seagrass is illegal. Drones need EASA/HCAA registration and are banned over archaeological sites including the Portara and the Temple of Demeter. Spearfishing with scuba is illegal in Greece; removing antiquities from the seabed is a serious criminal matter, and both islands' waters have plenty.
logistics.health: Tap water on Paros is generally not drinkable and on Naxos varies by village — buy or filter. Sea urchins are the number-one injury; carry reef shoes and a needle. Mauve stinger jellyfish come in patches, not blooms, and vinegar is not the recommended treatment for them — hot water immersion is. The meltemi's dry heat masks dehydration badly; two litres per session is a floor, not a target.

proTips: Do your independent-riding paperwork before you leave home. An IKO Level 3 card in your wallet is the difference between renting gear at Mikri Vigla on day one and spending two hours being assessed on day two.

Buy the six-day rental pass at your first centre, not day-by-day. Every centre on both islands discounts hard past four days, and the pass usually includes board storage, which saves you loading a hire car twice a day.
Ride the mornings in July and August. Everyone shows up at 14:00 for the peak; 10:00–12:00 gives you 15–20 knots, an empty beach and a session you can actually repeat the next day.
At Pounda, pick a physical landmark on Antiparos and never go beyond it. The ferry lane is not marked on the water, the ferries are not slow, and the meltemi pushes you toward it.

Take the conventional Blue Star ferry rather than the fast catamaran on any day forecast over 30 knots. The big ships keep sailing when the cats cancel, and a cancelled fast ferry in August rebooks two days later.
Kolimbithres before 09:00. The rock pools are shadeless, the tour boats from Naoussa start at 10:30, and the water is glassiest before the thermal starts.

On Naxos, check both sides of the Mikri Vigla headland every single day. A 3-knot shift or a 20-degree veer turns Limanaki from perfect to unrideable and Orkos from terrifying to sublime, and the walk between them is four minutes.

Eat inland at least twice. Halki, Apeiranthos and Sangri feed you Naxian graviera, kitron and slow-cooked goat for what a beach club charges for a salad, and it is the only way to see that Naxos is a farming island that happens to have beaches.
Book your last night in Naxos Town rather than at the beach. Rinsing salt out of a kite at 22:00 and then driving 20 km to a 06:30 ferry is a bad end to a good week.

raw.Prevailing wind — the meltemi (μελτέμι),: a dry north to north-northeast flow between a Balkan high and an Anatolian low. Season runs May to late September with roughly 70% of episodes falling June–September; July and August are the peak. Typical strength is 4–5 Beaufort (11–21 knots); established episodes commonly run 5–7 Beaufort (17–33 knots) and the strongest August days push 35 knots-plus in the channels. The daily cycle is the thing to plan around: it usually builds from late morning to early afternoon, peaks 14:00–17:00, and softens at sunset — but a properly set-in meltemi does not follow that curve and simply blows for three to ten days without stopping, day and night. In the Paros–Naxos strait, a Venturi between the two islands adds a reliable 3–6 knots over open-sea forecast.
raw.Kit sizing reality: a 75 kg rider in July at Pounda or Mikri Vigla is typically on a 7 m or 8 m kite in the afternoon and a 9 m only in the morning or in September; June and late September more often give 9–12 m. Windsurfers should expect 4.2–5.2 m sails on August afternoons and 5.5–6.5 m in June. Every centre's rental fleet is sized for this, so hiring beats flying kit for a single week.
raw.Launch spots, Paros: *Chrisi Akti (Golden Beach)* — east-facing, coarse sand, cross-onshore in the meltemi, chop building to short 1–1.5 m wind swell by mid-afternoon, intermediate; the historic World Cup windsurf venue on the island. *New Golden Beach (Néa Chrisi Akti)*, immediately north over the headland — the same wind with a longer sandy runway and slightly cleaner water state. *Santa Maria*, north coast — sheltered turquoise bays, sand and seagrass patches, best for SUP, wing and beginner windsurf in lighter morning wind, plus decent snorkelling on the rocky spurs. *Pounda*, west coast facing Antiparos — the island's kite spot, a shallow sandy shelf with side-shore meltemi, flat to light chop, and one serious hazard: the Antiparos car ferry crosses the channel every 20–30 minutes and you must stay out of its lane.
raw.Launch spots, Naxos: *Mikri Vigla* is really two spots either side of a granite headland. *Limanaki*, the north side, is flat-to-choppy, sandy, side-onshore, and the beginner and freestyle side; *Orkos*, the south side, is the wave side with a reef and rock section, more swell, and a stronger, more side-offshore feel — advanced only. *Plaka*, 4 km of west-facing sand between Mikri Vigla and Agios Prokopios — cross-onshore, sandy bottom, big empty runway, the sensible fallback when Mikri Vigla is crowded. *Agios Georgios*, the town beach, is a waist-deep sandy lagoon that stays walkable 100 m out — the safest teaching water in the Cyclades. *Laguna*, behind Agios Prokopios, is a genuinely shallow flat-water lagoon, best in the top half of the tide-free day when the sea breeze is filling.
raw.Equipment hubs and certification: on Naxos, *Flisvos Sportclub* at Agios Georgios (windsurf, wing, SUP, VDWS-affiliated) and its sister *Flisvos Kite Centre* at Mikri Vigla, which teaches to IKO standard and requires an IKO Level 3 card or an on-site competence assessment before it will rent you kite gear independently. *Naxos Kitelife* and *Thalasea Sports* also operate at Mikri Vigla. On Paros, *Paros Kite Pro Center* and *Paros Kite Center* at Pounda, and *Force7 Surf & Kite Center* at New Golden Beach. Indicative 2026 rates: kite equipment day rental €60–€80, six-day pass €270–€380; windsurf funboard rental €25–€50 per hour or €280–€330 per week; a beginner IKO/VDWS kite course of 6–9 hours runs €300–€450 depending on group size, private tuition €90–€140 per hour. Board and rig storage is €5–€10 per day where offered.
raw.Tides and currents — be honest: the Aegean is effectively tideless. Astronomical range at Paros and Naxos is on the order of 0.1–0.3 m, and a strong meltemi's wind set-up moves the waterline more than the moon does. There are no tide windows to plan around. What does matter is wind-driven current: in the Paros–Naxos and Paros–Antiparos channels a sustained northerly pushes a persistent southbound surface drift, so an upwind-limited rider ends up progressively downwind and offshore. Headland acceleration at the Mikri Vigla rock and at Cape Ai Giannis is real and abrupt. Offshore-component danger is concentrated at Orkos and on the north-facing pockets of Santa Maria: if the meltemi backs to NNW, a spot that felt cross-shore becomes cross-offshore and the next land is a long way south.
raw.Sea conditions and safety: water temperature runs roughly 18–19°C in May, 21–22°C in June, 24°C in July, 25–26°C in August, 23–24°C in September and 21–22°C in October. In July and August a shorty or even boardshorts and a lycra is enough for a two-hour session; June and late September justify a 2 mm shorty or 3/2 because 25 knots of dry northerly strips heat fast even off warm water. *Pelagia noctiluca* mauve stingers appear in patchy blooms, worst in late summer and after several calm days — annoying rather than dangerous. Sea urchins are the actual injury statistic here: the rocky ledges at Mikri Vigla's headland, Kolimbithres and Santa Maria's spurs are covered in them, and reef shoes are not optional. Lifeguard coverage on Cycladic beaches is thin and inconsistent even in August; assume there is none. **Hellenic Coast Guard: 108. General emergency: 112.**
raw.Boat and kayak logistics: Greece requires a boat licence for rentals above 30 hp; the standard tourist rental is a 4.7–5.5 m open boat with a 15–30 hp outboard, hireable without a licence for roughly €80–€140 per day plus fuel from Naoussa, Pounda, Aliki and Naxos Town. You sign a declaration and are given a fixed permitted area — typically "no crossing to Naxos" from Paros. Anchoring on *Posidonia oceanica* seagrass is prohibited under Greek law and enforced with fines; anchor on the visible pale sand patches. Small-boat hire is a bad idea on a 30-knot afternoon regardless of licence; do it on a windless morning.
raw.Weather-contingency plan: *No wind* — freedive and snorkel Kolimbithres in Naoussa Bay, dive with an operator out of Naoussa, take the 10-minute Pounda–Antiparos ferry and do the cave, or run the Naxos interior to Apeiranthos and the Melanes kouros. *Too much wind (35 kt+)* — Mikri Vigla's Limanaki side and Naxos's Laguna hold up when Orkos and Golden Beach are unrideable; failing that, this is the day for the Portara at sunset, the Naxos citadel museums, or a Naxian cheese-and-kitron tasting at Halki, and for the fact that Blue Star's big ferries keep running when the fast cats cancel.

sources.confidenceNotes: All rental, lesson and storage prices are indicative and were not confirmed against 2026 published price lists — re-verify with each centre directly. The brief refers to "Pounda's PWA history"; the documented Professional Windsurfers Association World Cup venue on Paros is Chrisi Akti / New Golden Beach on the east coast, with Pounda established later as the kite spot — this file reflects that and the attribution should be double-checked before publishing. Force7 Surf & Kite Center's current operating status at New Golden Beach should be confirmed for 2026. trips.subRegion: Central Dalmatia — Split, Brač, Hvar & the Pakleni Islands, Vis, Šolta

bestPeriod.window: Late May–late June and early September–early October — reliable maestral, warm sea, no August berth war
bestPeriod.avoid: November–March — bura season, most island restaurants and the Blue Cave transfer service shut, and charter fleets are hauled out
bestPeriod.raw: Late May–late June and early September–early October — reliable maestral, warm sea, no August berth war

accommodation.note: Bareboat share (4 pax on a 45 ft) €550–€950, or land-based hotels €90–€180/night double

food.note: Konoba mains €14–€26, Hvar town markup 30–50%, provisioning at Tommy Split cuts this hard

transport.note: Ferries, taxi boats, Split airport transfer, car hire for the Brač days

activities.note: Marina berths, Blue Cave entry, Kornati park ticket, guided kayak days, windsurf rental

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5 — sailing is low-effort, but two kayak days of 14–18 km on open water with afternoon chop is a real day out

trips.gatewayAirport: SPU Split, 25 min to ACI Marina Split and 30 min to ACI Marina Trogir; ferry Split–Supetar (Brač) 50 min
trips.summary: Central Dalmatia's afternoon is a machine. From roughly 11:00 the maestral fills from the northwest, builds through the early afternoon, holds 12–20 knots until about 17:00 and then switches off with the sun — which means every sailing leg, every kayak crossing and every windsurf session in this week has the same window and the same deadline. The trip is built around that: mornings on flat glass for kayaking, snorkelling and the Blue Cave, afternoons under sail or on a board. You move Split–Šolta–Vis–Hvar–Pakleni–Brač–Trogir, either on a bareboat if someone in the party holds a skipper's ticket and an SRC, or as a land-based version stitched together with car ferries and taxi boats. It suits competent, organised people who like a plan with a clock in it.

itinerary.title: Split, provisioning, and the shakedown to Šolta
itinerary.morning: Land at SPU and go straight to ACI Marina Split or ACI Trogir for the charter check-in. Present originals — skipper's ticket and SRC — and walk the boat with the base engineer properly: through-hulls, bilge pump, anchor windlass counter, tender outboard, and the location of the second reef. Land-based travellers instead check into Split and book the Šolta ferry.
itinerary.afternoon: Provision at the big Tommy or Konzum near the marina rather than on the islands, where the same basket costs 40% more. Sail out on the first of the maestral through the Split gate and cross to Šolta, anchoring in Šešula bay — deep, sheltered, thick mud holding.
itinerary.evening: Konoba Šišmiš at Šešula, on the water at the head of the bay, with a dinghy dock. Order the peka if you call ahead — it takes three hours and cannot be ordered on arrival.
itinerary.dayStats: Split–Šešula roughly 11 nm / maestral fills 11:00–13:00, 12–18 knots by mid-afternoon / Šešula anchor in 8–12 m over mud / peka must be ordered 3 h ahead
itinerary.sleep: At anchor, Šešula bay, Šolta — or Hotel Martinis Marchi, Maslinica

itinerary.title: The crossing to Vis and Komiža
itinerary.morning: Early departure while the sea is glass. The Šolta–Vis crossing is open water and best done before the maestral has any chop in it. Round the north coast of Vis to Vis town or continue west to Komiža under the flank of Hum.
itinerary.afternoon: Komiža is the working fishing town and the Blue Cave departure point. Walk the harbour, look at the *falkuša* fishing boats in the Fishermen's Museum in the Venetian tower, then swim off Kamenica beach. Divers: the Komiža centres run the *Teti* wreck and the B-17 bomber.
itinerary.evening: Konoba Jastožera in Komiža, built over the old lobster pens with the sea running under the floor. Order lobster with pasta if the budget allows, or the fish stew if it does not.
itinerary.dayStats: Šolta–Vis roughly 22–25 nm / Komiža town quay or Vis ACI marina, roughly €9.50–€11.50/m/day for a monohull / crossing best before 11:00
itinerary.sleep: At anchor or on the quay, Komiža — or Hotel San Giorgio, Vis town

itinerary.title: Biševo, the Blue Cave, and Stiniva
itinerary.morning: Biševo early. The Blue Cave's light peaks between about 11:00 and 12:00, and the queue at Mezuporat is worst from 11:30, so aim to be there by 10:00. No private boat enters the cave — the entrance is roughly 1.5 m by 2.5 m — so you buy a ticket at the Mezuporat jetty and transfer into a small licensed dinghy for a five-to-ten-minute circuit inside. Bring cash.
itinerary.afternoon: Sail back around the south coast of Vis to Stiniva, the pebble cove behind its rock gate. Boats hold off outside; swim or dinghy in. Then the Green Cave at Ravnik, which you can actually swim into, and where the light comes through a hole in the roof.
itinerary.evening: Return to Vis town and eat at Pojoda, in a courtyard of orange trees behind the waterfront — old-school Dalmatian, and the best cooking on the island.
itinerary.dayStats: Blue Cave entry ~€24 high season / ~€18 shoulder, cash only, no ATM on Biševo / cave open roughly 1 April–1 November, closed on southerly swell / peak light 11:00–12:00 / taxi boat from Komiža ~€35 pp, 15–20 min
itinerary.sleep: Vis town, at anchor or on the ACI quay

itinerary.title: Vis to Hvar and the Pakleni islands
itinerary.morning: Depart Vis on the first breeze for the run northeast to the Pakleni archipelago. This is the week's best sailing leg: 18–20 nm with a building maestral on the beam.
itinerary.afternoon: Berth at ACI Marina Palmižana on Sv. Klement or anchor off Vinogradišće on the island's sheltered south side. Palmižana bay is north-facing and exposed to any bura, so check the forecast before committing to an anchor there overnight.
itinerary.evening: Taxi boat into Hvar town — they run until late and cost a few euros. Eat at Konoba Menego in the stepped lanes above the square, then walk up to the Fortica for the view back over the Pakleni. **Plan B if jugo is forecast:** skip Hvar town, stay on the protected south side, and eat at Toto's or Laganini on Vinogradišće.
itinerary.dayStats: Vis–Palmižana roughly 18–20 nm / ACI Palmižana premium berth, budget €130–€200/night for a 13 m monohull in August / Hvar taxi boat runs to ~01:00 in season / Fortica climb 20 min, roughly €10

itinerary.title: Sea-kayaking the Pakleni archipelago
itinerary.morning: The kayak day, and it must be a morning. Launch from Palmižana or from Hvar town and thread the channels of the archipelago — Sv. Klement, Marinkovac, Jerolim, Stipanska — on flat water with 15–20 m visibility over white sand and seagrass. Guided groups typically cover 12–16 km with two swim stops.
itinerary.afternoon: Off the water before the maestral has the channels white-capping. Snorkel the shallow ledges off Jerolim, then a long lunch at Palmižana. The gardens above the bay were planted by the Meneghello family in the 1900s and are worth the walk.
itinerary.evening: Back into Hvar town for the Franciscan monastery and Zoraić or Gariful on the harbour. **Plan B if wind is up:** stay island-side; the guided kayak operators cancel above about 15 knots and will move you to the following morning.
itinerary.dayStats: Pakleni kayak day 12–16 km / guided day €70–€110 pp with boat, spray deck, dry bag and lunch / visibility typically 15–20 m / operators cancel above ~15 knots

itinerary.title: Bol, Zlatni Rat and the channel's afternoon
itinerary.morning: Cross the Hvar channel north to Bol on Brač. This is the compression zone: expect 4–8 knots more than the open-water forecast once you are in the channel, and expect it earlier in the day than elsewhere. Berth in Bol's small marina or take a mooring off Borak.
itinerary.afternoon: The reason you came. Rig at Big Blue Sport on Beach Borak, immediately west of the Zlatni Rat spit — side-shore maestral, pebble bottom, flat inshore water and short chop outside. If the wind is under 12 knots, take their sea kayak or SUP option and paddle west along the cliffs instead.
itinerary.evening: Konoba Mlin in Bol, in an old olive mill in the back lanes. Order the lamb and ask for a Brač Plavac Mali. **Plan B for a windless afternoon:** drive or taxi up to the Blaca hermitage — a 15th-century monastery in a gorge, reachable only on foot for the last kilometre.
itinerary.dayStats: Hvar channel crossing 8–10 nm / Big Blue Sport funboard ~€50/hour or ~€310/week; beginner course ~€200 for 6 hours; private advanced ~€140/hour / board storage €5–€7/day / Bol channel adds 4–8 knots
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Kaštil, Bol — or at anchor off Borak

itinerary.title: Milna, Trogir and the hand-back
itinerary.morning: Sail west along the south coast of Brač and round to Milna, or run straight for the base. If you are still hungry for one more open-water leg and the maestral is early, the Kornati day-sail option leaves from further north and needs a full day plus a park ticket — treat it as an add-on rather than a day-seven squeeze.
itinerary.afternoon: Return the boat at ACI Trogir or ACI Split. Trogir is the better hand-back because the UNESCO old town is a five-minute walk over the bridge and you can spend the dead hours in the Cathedral of St Lawrence looking at Radovan's 1240 portal instead of in a marina car park.
itinerary.evening: Konoba Trs in Trogir, in a stone courtyard off the main lane. Then a last walk on the Riva.
itinerary.dayStats: Bol–Trogir roughly 26–30 nm / hand-back typically 09:00 with a fuel and damage inspection / Kornati one-day boat ticket for 11–17.99 m roughly €95 in season bought in advance, about double on-site
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Bellevue or Palace Derossi, Trogir — or an airport hotel

accommodationStrategy.name: The bareboat itself
accommodationStrategy.location: 42–47 ft monohull from ACI Split or ACI Trogir
accommodationStrategy.description: Sleeping aboard is what makes the itinerary work: you are already at the anchorage when the light is right at Stiniva and the Blue Cave, and you skip the ferry timetable entirely. A 45 ft four-cabin monohull in June runs roughly €3,200–€4,800 a week plus a transit log of €100–€200 and berthing, which lands at €550–€950 per person for a full boat. Requires a skipper's ticket and an SRC in the crew.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Kaštil
accommodationStrategy.location: 15th-century stone building on the Bol waterfront
accommodationStrategy.description: The land-based anchor for the Brač days. Directly on the harbour and a ten-minute walk along the seafront promenade to Beach Borak and Big Blue Sport, so you can carry a rig if you have to and check the channel from the terrace. Roughly €140–€230 double B&B in season.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Martinis Marchi
accommodationStrategy.style: restored 18th-century castle with its own small marina
accommodationStrategy.description: The one splurge, and the only place on Šolta with a proper berth attached to a hotel room. Useful as a first or last night if you are land-based, because Šolta is 50 minutes from Split by ferry and feels an order of magnitude quieter than Hvar. Roughly €260–€420 double.

logistics.connectivity: 4G is good along the whole coast and in every town on this route; it drops in the lee of Vis's Hum and inside the Pakleni channels. Croatia is in the EU and Schengen, so EU roaming applies at domestic rates. Download Navionics or a chart app with offline vector charts before you leave the marina — the Pakleni are full of unmarked rock heads.
logistics.emergency: **195 for maritime search and rescue**, 112 for everything else, VHF Channel 16 monitored by MRCC Rijeka and the coastal radio stations. Split has the regional hospital (KBC Split); Hvar and Vis have health centres only, and a serious case is a helicopter or fast-boat transfer to Split. Travel insurance must name sailing and, separately, sea kayaking — many policies treat "watersports" as a bolt-on. Decompression chamber: Split.
logistics.weather: Check DHMZ (meteo.hr) and its dedicated coastal-waters forecast alongside Windy; Croatian marinas post the daily forecast at the capitanerie office. The bura arrives faster than any other Adriatic wind and its gusts are two to three times the mean, so a "35 knot bura" means 60-knot hits. The jugo announces itself a day ahead with a greasy swell from the southeast and falling pressure. Neither is a summer certainty, but both happen in June and September.
logistics.bookingWindows: Bareboats for July and August go six to nine months ahead; June and September, three to four months. Charter paperwork — skipper's ticket, SRC, crew list, sojourn tax — should be with the base four to six weeks before departure. ACI berths in Hvar, Palmižana and Trogir cannot be pre-booked cheaply and in August you should be in the marina by 15:00. Kornati tickets: buy online at the parks system in advance to halve the price. Restaurants on Hvar and Vis in August need two to three days.
logistics.money: Croatia adopted the euro on 1 January 2023, so prices are in EUR and older kuna price lists you find online are historic. Cards work in towns and marinas. Carry cash for the Blue Cave (cash only), taxi boats, island konobas and Biševo generally. Tipping is 10% at a sit-down meal.
logistics.transportRules: Bringing a rental car onto a car ferry needs the rental company's permission, which is usually granted for domestic island routes and refused for Bosnia and Montenegro. Jadrolinija's Split–Supetar car ferry runs roughly hourly in summer and takes 50 minutes; catamarans to Hvar and Vis are foot-passenger only. Croatian motorway tolls apply on the A1 from Zagreb; there is no vignette.
logistics.permits: National-park entry is charged per boat per day and enforced by park rangers who board. Anchoring on *Posidonia oceanica* seagrass is prohibited; anchor on sand. Inside Kornati and Telašćica, anchoring is confined to designated bays and overnight stays often require a mooring buoy. Spearfishing requires a permit and is banned in national parks and near-total for non-residents in some zones. Drones need HCAA-compliant operation and are banned over Diocletian's Palace and Trogir's old town. A vessel over 15 m or carrying more than 12 people has additional reporting duties.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable throughout Croatia including on the islands, though tanked marina water is best filtered. Sea urchins are the dominant injury — the entire coast is rock and pebble. The weever fish (*Trachinus*) buries in sand in shallow water and its spine hurts badly; hot-water immersion is the treatment. Sunburn on a boat is systematically underestimated because the maestral cools you. No sharks worth thinking about and no dangerous jellyfish.

proTips: Get your SRC before you get excited about the boat. Croatia enforces the VHF radio operator's certificate as hard as the skipper's ticket, it is the requirement most crews discover four weeks out, and no charter base will hand over keys without the original.
Every long crossing goes in the morning. The maestral means the sea is glass at 08:00 and choppy at 15:00, so a Vis crossing planned for after lunch is a crossing planned badly.
Buy the Kornati boat ticket online before you sail. Bought at a ranger's boat inside the park it is roughly double, and rangers do board.

Arrive at Mezuporat on Biševo by 10:00 with cash. The light in the Blue Cave peaks 11:00–12:00 and the queue peaks 11:30 — those two facts are why the trip so often disappoints, and why arriving an hour early fixes it.
Take a berth by 15:00 in July and August, or plan to anchor. Palmižana, Hvar and Trogir fill in the late afternoon and there is no reservation system that reliably saves you.
Provision in Split, not on the islands. A trolley at the big Tommy near ACI Split is 30–40% cheaper than the same trolley in Hvar town, and island shops close for a long lunch.
Order peka three hours ahead. Every konoba on this route will make it and none will make it on demand — a phone call from the anchorage at midday is the difference.

At Bol, ride the channel edge rather than the beach edge. The compression between Brač and Hvar means the wind five hundred metres out is meaningfully stronger and cleaner than the wind at the launch, and the pebble spit's tip genuinely moves with the season.
Keep one flexible day in the middle of the week. Jugo and bura both cost a day when they come, and a week with no slack turns a weather event into a cancelled Blue Cave you have paid for.

raw.Prevailing wind — the maestral (also *ma: a thermal northwesterly generated by the temperature difference between the heated Dalmatian hinterland and the cooler sea. It is the summer wind and the reason this coast works. Typical cycle: nothing at 08:00, first ripples 10:30–11:30, 8–12 knots by 13:00, peak 12–20 knots from 14:00 to 17:00, easing from 18:00 and gone by sunset. Occasional 22–25 knot days in June and September. It is strongest and most reliable in the channels — the Bol channel between Brač and Hvar and the Split gate — where compression adds 4–8 knots over open water. This is exactly why Bol is the Adriatic's windsurf capital.
raw.The two winds that end the plan — bura a: the *bura* (bora) is a dry, cold, brutally gusty northeasterly that falls off the Dinaric wall. Its season is October to April but summer episodes happen, usually 12–36 hours, arriving fast, gusting to 40–60 knots in the accelerating gaps (Velebit channel, the Vrulja gap on the Makarska riviera, the Split channel) and leaving a hard blue sky behind it. Bura gusts are the reason charter contracts forbid certain anchorages. The *jugo* (sirocco) is the opposite personality: a warm, humid southeasterly that builds slowly over a day or more, brings low cloud and rain, and — crucially — builds real swell, 1.5–3 m in the open channels. Jugo is what closes the Blue Cave and cancels catamaran ferries. A third, the *levanat* easterly, is short-lived and mostly a nuisance.
raw.Launch spots and sailing water: *Zlatni Rat / Beach Borak, Bol (Brač)* — the famous shifting shingle spit; the windsurf launch is off Borak beach immediately west, side-shore maestral, smooth pebble bottom, flat inshore water building to short chop, superb for intermediates, with the hazard being the Bol channel current and the fact that the spit's tip and the water depth around it move. *Šešula bay, Šolta* — deep, protected, thick holding mud, the archetypal first-night anchorage. *Stiniva, Vis* — a pebble cove behind a 10 m rock gate, no anchoring inside, boats hold off; the swim in is the point. *Palmižana bay, Sv. Klement (Pakleni)* — north-facing, sand and seagrass, exposed to bura, home to ACI Marina Palmižana. *Vinogradišće* on the same island's south side — the kayak lunch stop. *Jerolim and Stipanska*, the inner Pakleni — flat, sheltered, 10 minutes by taxi boat from Hvar town.
raw.Equipment hubs and certification: *Big Blue Sport* on Beach Borak at Bol is the anchor operation — VDWS-affiliated, running roughly 40 Flikka boards and 60 Severne rigs plus sea-kayak, SUP and mountain-bike programmes, with a café and shop on the beach. Indicative rates: beginner windsurf course €200 for 6 hours, advanced private tuition around €140/hour, school-board rental from about €25/hour, funboard about €50/hour or €310 for the week, board storage €5–€7 per day and rig storage €5–€8. For kayaking, Split-based operators run the Pakleni archipelago and the Split–Čiovo coast as guided day trips at roughly €70–€110 per person including boat, spray deck, dry bag and lunch. Diving is PADI and SSI both — centres cluster at Komiža (Vis), Hvar town and Bol.
raw.Tides — the honest number: Central Dalmatia is near-tideless. Spring range at Split is roughly 0.3–0.5 m and neaps under 0.2 m; the northern Adriatic around Venice reaches a metre or so, but you are not there. There are no tidal gates, no tide-dependent breaks and no reason to consult a tide table for a launch. What *does* move the water is meteorological: a strong jugo can pile 0.3–0.5 m of water into the bays on top of the astronomical tide, and a hard bura pushes it back out. Currents are weak — generally under 1 knot, running broadly northwest along the coast — but they accelerate around headlands and through the narrow channels, and the Bol channel and the Split gate both reward a look at the water before a kayak crossing.
raw.Sea conditions and safety: water temperature runs roughly 17–19°C in May, 22–23°C in June, 24–25°C in July, 25–26°C in August, 23–24°C in September and 20–21°C in October. June to September needs nothing more than a lycra for a session; May and October justify a 3/2 shorty for windsurfing and a light top for kayaking, because the maestral is cooling even when the sea is warm. Jellyfish are a minor issue — occasional *Pelagia noctiluca* and the harmless fried-egg *Cotylorhiza*. Sea urchins are the real hazard and Dalmatian pebble-and-rock entries are full of them; reef shoes on every rocky entry, without exception. Lifeguards exist on the main managed beaches (Zlatni Rat, Bačvice) in July and August and nowhere else. **Croatian search and rescue at sea: 195. General emergency: 112.** MRCC Rijeka coordinates; VHF Channel 16 is monitored.
raw.Bareboat charter, the licence and the pa: Croatia requires at least one person aboard with a recognised skipper's qualification **and** a VHF radio operator's certificate — SRC, LRC or GMDSS. The VHF certificate is the requirement people forget and it is strictly enforced by the harbourmaster and coastguard; photocopies are not accepted, originals only. RYA Day Skipper and an ICC for coastal waters are both recognised, alongside qualifications from the many countries with which the Croatian ministry has bilateral recognition. Expect to submit documents four to six weeks before the charter, to pay a transit log of roughly €100–€200, and to file a crew list — the Croatian system requires the crew list and sojourn tax to be lodged electronically before departure, and the charter base normally does this for you. Charter companies typically also want a logbook showing five to fifteen documented sailing days depending on yacht size.
raw.Marina and park fees: ACI marina daily berthing for a 10–20 m monohull averages roughly €9.50–€11.50 per metre per day, with ACI Split, ACI Trogir and ACI Palmižana at the expensive end of the network; catamarans run 50–100% more, around €16.50–€20.50 per metre. Budget €130–€200 a night for a 13 m monohull at a premium Central Dalmatian ACI berth in August, less in June. National-park entry is charged per boat per day: for an 11.00–17.99 m vessel, Kornati is roughly €95 in peak season (June–September) and €50 outside it when bought in advance — bought inside the park at a mobile reception desk it is around double, so buy online. Kornati tickets run 00:00–24:00 and stay valid until 12:00 the next day. The Blue Cave at Biševo charges roughly €24 per adult in high season (about 20 June–10 September) and €18 in shoulder season, cash only at the island, with no ATM.
raw.Weather-contingency plan: *No maestral* — this is the good problem. Use it: kayak the Pakleni channels on glass, dive or freedive the Green Cave at Ravnik, motor to Stiniva, do the Blue Cave in the 10:30–13:00 light window. *Jugo* — get to a protected marina early, because everyone else will want the same berth by 16:00; the Blue Cave closes on southerly swell even under a clear sky, and ferry catamarans cancel before the big car ferries do. *Bura* — do not cross channels; stay put, and if you are on a bareboat, expect the charter base to phone you with instructions rather than the other way round. Land alternatives: Diocletian's Palace and the Split cellars, Trogir's Radovan portal, the Blaca hermitage on Brač, and Vis's Tito's Cave and the abandoned military tunnels.

sources.confidenceNotes: Marina rates vary by month and by exact length band — confirm the specific ACI tariff for your boat and dates. Charter prices for a 45 ft monohull are indicative market figures, not quotes. Blue Cave season dates and the exact high-season window shift year to year and the cave closes at short notice on swell; re-verify before publishing. Kayak day-trip prices and the ~15-knot cancellation threshold are operator-dependent. Restaurant status on Vis, Šolta and the Pakleni changes between seasons — Jastožera, Pojoda, Šišmiš, Menego, Mlin and Trs should each be re-checked for 2026 opening. Distances in nautical miles are planning approximations from chart, not measured routes. Croatia's national SAR number 195 and MRCC Rijeka coordination should be confirmed against the current official listing. The maestral figures are climatological norms; June and September deliver it less reliably than July and August even though they are better months to travel.
