trips.hook: Hungary has no coastline and never has. What it has instead is a 77 km inland sea that behaves like open water in a squall, and a flooded forest on a dammed river that behaves like a maze. This week is four days of wind on Balaton — keelboat sailing out of Balatonfüred, wingfoiling off the Kenese bluffs — and three of quiet paddling through the willow labyrinth of Lake Tisza. No tides, no swell, and one genuinely serious hazard you must learn to read.

snapshot.Start / End: Balatonfüred → Tiszafüred (point-to-point, ~250 km between the two lakes)
snapshot.Getting there: Budapest Ferenc Liszt (BUD). MÁV line 29 from Déli/Kelenföld to Balatonfüred, ~2 h; line 30 to Siófok on the south shore. Lake Tisza is 2 h by car from Budapest on the M3; rail to Tiszafüred via Füzesabony.

itinerary.title: Balatonfüred, the sailing capital
itinerary.morning: Train from Budapest to **Balatonfüred**. Walk the Tagore sétány promenade and the Vitorlás tér harbour, and check in with your school or charter — paperwork and licence checks happen before anything gets untied.
itinerary.afternoon: A first sail on the eastern basin as the thermal fills after 13:00. Reaching towards Tihany, tacking back, learning what 3.3 m of water does to wave shape.
itinerary.evening: Fish soup on the promenade and the **Kékszalag** history: the Blue Ribbon, run since 1934, is Europe's longest round-the-lake race, roughly 155 km from Balatonfüred to Balatonkenese, Keszthely, Tihany and back, held in **mid-July** [VERIFY: 2026 Kékszalag dates].

itinerary.title: The Tihany narrows
itinerary.morning: Ashore on the **Tihany peninsula**: the Benedictine abbey, the Inner Lake, and the view down onto the narrows where the lake constricts to about 1.5 km.
itinerary.afternoon: Sail the narrows on the afternoon breeze — the strongest, gustiest water on Balaton, with the 12 m well underneath and noticeably colder water on your hands.
itinerary.evening: Ride the **Szántód–Tihany car ferry** across and back for the crossing itself, then eat at Zamárdi on the shallow south shore [VERIFY: current Szántódrév ferry season and timetable].

itinerary.title: Kenese and the wing day
itinerary.morning: Drive or take the train 25 km east to **Balatonkenese** under the Akarattya loess bluffs. Rig on the Vak Bottyán strand and wait; nothing happens before midday.
itinerary.afternoon: The northwesterly comes in side-on across a long fetch — the best windsurf and wingfoil water on the lake. Beginners should be at **Balatonalmádi** or the southern shore instead, where you can stand up.
itinerary.evening: Watch the **viharjelző** lamp on the shore mast as the light goes. Learn to count the flash rate now, in calm weather, so you are not doing it for the first time in a squall.

itinerary.title: The shallow south shore
itinerary.morning: Cross to **Siófok** or **Zamárdi**. The southern shore shelves so gently you can walk 300 m out in waist-deep water at 25 °C — this is where every Hungarian learns, and where a first windsurf or SUP lesson belongs.
itinerary.afternoon: A long SUP paddle along the Zamárdi shoreline, or a beginner windsurf session. Nothing here is deeper than you are tall, which is the whole point.
itinerary.evening: Drive east to **Tiszafüred**, about 3 h via the M7 and M3. Alternatively, spend the evening on **Lake Velence** at Agárd, halfway, and finish the transfer in the morning.

itinerary.title: Into the flooded forest
itinerary.morning: At **Poroszló**, start at the **Tisza-tavi Ökocentrum** — the freshwater aquarium and the marsh walkway give you the map of the labyrinth before you enter it.
itinerary.afternoon: Kayak from the Poroszló port into the **Tiszavalki basin**: dead-straight cut channels opening into willow and poplar standing in the water, storks, terns and herons overhead. Carry a compass or GPS track; the channels look identical.
itinerary.evening: Tiszafüred for *halászlé* — Tisza fish soup, river carp, far hotter with paprika than the Balaton version.

itinerary.title: Tiszafüred, birds and open water
itinerary.morning: The **Tiszafüredi madárrezervátum** bird reserve is part of Hortobágy National Park, and its core zone can only be entered **with a guide or a permit** — book a guided paddle rather than blundering into it [VERIFY: current Hortobágy NP guided-paddle booking and permit rules].
itinerary.afternoon: SUP on the open water of the **Sarud basin**, where the lake widens and behaves like a lake rather than a forest. Wind here is lighter and more variable than on Balaton.
itinerary.evening: Sunset from the Tiszafüred embankment. Lake Tisza is a reservoir on a dammed river, so unlike Balaton it has a **slow but real current** near the main channel and at the Kisköre dam — stay clear of both.

itinerary.title: Szigetköz or the drive home
itinerary.morning: Either a last Tisza paddle, or the long option: drive northwest to the **Szigetköz**, the Danube's braided side-branch system above Győr, and put a canoe in at **Lipót** or **Ásványráró**.
itinerary.afternoon: The Szigetköz branches are gravel-bedded, cold, clear and genuinely flowing — the only moving water on this trip. Go with a local outfitter; the branches are shallow and shift annually.
itinerary.evening: Győr or Budapest for the flight home, three water bodies and three different rulebooks behind you.

accommodationStrategy.name: Harbour-side hotels and pensions
accommodationStrategy.description: walking distance to the yacht harbour, so you are on the boat when the thermal fills rather than driving to it. Board and rig storage is normal; ask when booking.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–10 weeks ahead for June, and avoid Kékszalag week unless you are racing [VERIFY: current Balatonfüred June rates].

accommodationStrategy.name: Beach-side apartments
accommodationStrategy.description: the eastern-basin wind ground, strand 200 m away, space for a board bag and a wing. Much cheaper than Füred and better water for foiling.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 4–6 weeks ahead; weekly lets are standard and cheaper than nightly.

accommodationStrategy.name: Port guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: paddle-in access, drying space, and a 06:00 launch onto flat water before the day-trippers. Both towns are quiet, cheap and built around the water.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead in July–August; a few days outside that.

logistics.connectivity: Full coverage on both lakes. Install the OMSZ weather app and bookmark the **viharjelző** status page; the warning is also broadcast on lakeside loudspeakers and shown at every harbour.
logistics.emergency: **112**, reaching the **Balatoni vízirendészet** and the Hungarian water-rescue service. Give the nearest named strand or harbour. Life jackets are compulsory on small craft; wear one on a SUP regardless of what the locals do.
logistics.weather: The defining risk. Cold fronts cross the Bakony fast, the lake builds steep chop within minutes, and the shallow depth means no swell warns you first. **Check the storm warning before every launch and again at 12:00.** Second degree means everyone off the water, swimmers included.
logistics.bookingWindows: Charters and courses 6–10 weeks for June, longer around the Kékszalag; guided Hortobágy paddles 2–3 weeks. Everything else is short-notice.
logistics.money: Hungary uses the **forint**, roughly 395–400 HUF to €1 [VERIFY: current HUF/EUR rate]. Cards work at harbours, schools and restaurants; beach kiosks and small rentals are often cash. Decline dynamic currency conversion at ATMs.
logistics.transportRules: MÁV serves both Balaton shores (lines 29 and 30) and Tiszafüred via Füzesabony; the **Szántód–Tihany ferry** links the shores in season. **Petrol and diesel motorboats are banned on Balaton.** Skipper alcohol limits follow the road **KRESZ** rules, and the water police test.
logistics.permits: No licence for boards, wings, kayaks or SUPs. **A Hungarian licence or recognised equivalent (typically an ICC) is required to skipper a keelboat** — confirm in writing with the charter company before paying. The Tiszafüred reserve core zone needs a guide or permit, and parts of Lake Tisza close in the breeding season.

proTips: **Learn the flash rate on a calm day.** Forty-five per minute means come in; ninety means get out now. Counting for ten seconds and doubling is the whole skill, and it is the one that matters.
**Sail Balaton mornings for practice, afternoons for fun.** The thermal is a clock. Schools run drills before noon because there is nothing else to do with the water.
**Send your ICC to the charter company before you pay the deposit.** Licence recognition is the most common reason a Balaton bareboat booking collapses at the desk.
**Beginners go south, foilers go east.** Zamárdi and Siófok for waist-deep warm water; Kenese and Almádi for the side-on northwesterly. Do not learn at Tihany.
**Take a GPS track into the Tiszavalki channels.** The flooded forest is genuinely a maze, the willow stands look identical, and phone batteries die.
**Go the first week of September.** The water is still 22–23 °C, the wind is back to its May reliability, and the strands that were impassable in August are empty.

**Eat the two fish soups in the right order.** Balaton *halászlé* is milder and pike-perch-based; the Tisza version is carp, darker and far hotter. Doing Balaton first makes the Tisza one land properly.

raw.Prevailing wind: The dominant direction is **northwesterly**, funnelled and accelerated by the Bakony hills. The reliable pattern is a **thermal building from about 13:00** and holding to early evening, usually 10–18 knots, strongest through the **Tihany narrows** where the lake pinches to about 1.5 km. Mornings are light — schools use them for drills. Most consistent wind in **May, June and September**; July and August are hotter, busier and often glassy until mid-afternoon.
raw.There are no tides: Balaton is a closed inland lake: **no tide, no swell, no current worth the name**. The hazards are different and entirely real. First, **squall lines** — a cold front crossing the Bakony arrives with almost no warning. Second, the **chop**: with a mean depth of about **3.3 m** (maximum roughly 12 m in the Tihany well), the lake cannot absorb energy, so wind that would raise a long swell at sea instead raises a **short, steep, vicious chop within minutes** that stops a dinghy dead and swamps a SUP. Third, **cold** — the deep basin off Tihany stays markedly colder than the shallows, and going from 26 °C at Zamárdi into the channel is a genuine shock. A slow wind-driven **seiche** shifts water end to end; that matters for moorings, not for you.
raw.The viharjelző — storm warning system: The most important thing on the lake, and not advisory. Orange-yellow lamps on masts around the whole shoreline flash at a rate that encodes the alert. **First degree: 45 flashes per minute** — storm possible; leave deep water and stay within roughly 500 m of shore. **Second degree: 90 flashes per minute** — storm imminent or in progress; **leave the water immediately**, no exceptions. Read the rate, not the colour: count for ten seconds and double it. Warnings come from the national meteorological service and are enforced by the water police [VERIFY: current viharjelző flash rates, lamp colours and issuing authority]. Never gamble on outrunning a second degree — the chop builds faster than you can reach a harbour.
raw.Launch spots by name: **Balatonfüred** — the Balatonfüredi Yacht Club harbour and the town marina, the keelboat centre of the lake. **Balatonkenese** and **Balatonalmádi** — the eastern basin under the Akarattya bluffs, side-on northwesterly, the windsurf and wingfoil ground. **Tihany** — the narrows, strongest and gustiest, experienced only. **Siófok** and **Zamárdi** — the shallow warm southern shore where you can wade 300 m out; beginner ground, and where every school teaches. **Lake Tisza** — the harbours at **Poroszló** and **Tiszafüred**. **Szigetköz** — canoe put-ins at **Dunakiliti**, **Lipót** and **Ásványráró**. **Lake Velence** — Agárd and Gárdony, shallow and reed-fringed.
raw.Rental and school hubs: Sailing schools and charter fleets cluster at Balatonfüred and Balatonlelle; windsurf and wing bases sit on the Balatonkenese (Vak Bottyán strand), Balatonalmádi (Wesselényi strand) and Zamárdi beaches. Kayak, canoe and SUP hire on Lake Tisza runs from the **Tisza-tavi Ökocentrum** port at Poroszló and the Tiszafüred harbours [VERIFY: current school and rental operator names and season dates at each site]. Reckon €50–€90 a day for windsurf or wing gear with a lesson, €12–€25 for a kayak or SUP, €200–€400 for a skippered keelboat [VERIFY: current 2026 charter and gear rates].
raw.Licences and boating rules: To **skipper a keelboat** on Hungarian waters you need a Hungarian small-craft licence (*kedvtelési célú kishajóvezetői*, with the sailing endorsement) **or a recognised equivalent — an ICC is the usual accepted foreign qualification**. This catches people out: charter firms will not release a yacht on a foreign club membership, and a bareboat booking made without checking is a booking you lose [VERIFY: current licence thresholds and which foreign certificates are recognised]. **Petrol and diesel motorboats are banned on Balaton** for recreational use — sail, paddle and electric only, with exemptions for authorities and rescue. Boards, wings, kayaks and SUPs need no licence. The **Balatoni vízirendészet** enforces the code, with life jackets required on small craft and alcohol limits matching the road **KRESZ** rules.

trips.title: The Bonifacio Funnel: Porto Pollo, La Maddalena and Gallura on the Wind
trips.subRegion: Northern Sardinia — Gallura, Porto Pollo & the La Maddalena Archipelago

bestPeriod.window: Mid-May–June and September — the maestrale is at its most reliable, the water is swimmable, and the archipelago is not yet rationed by August boat traffic
bestPeriod.avoid: August (Gallura's roads, beaches and permit quotas are all at their worst and prices roughly double) and November–March (most centres closed, water 14–15°C)
bestPeriod.raw: Mid-May–June and September — the maestrale is at its most reliable, the water is swimmable, and the archipelago is not yet rationed by August boat traffic

accommodation.note: Camping Isuledda pitch or bungalow €35–€90; Palau three-star double €90–€160; Santa Teresa €110–€190 in September

food.note: Trattoria main €14–€22, seafood by weight €55–€80/kg, Vermentino di Gallura by the glass €4–€6, coffee €1.20

transport.note: Hire car €40–€70/day plus fuel; Palau–La Maddalena ferry €14–€20 return with car; airport transfer

activities.note: Six days of kit hire €330–€450, one coached session €80–€90, park permit for a rental boat €15–€55/day, Cala Coticcio guided access €25–€40, one dive at Tavolara €50–€75

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5 — five to six days of afternoon sessions in 20–30 knots, plus a guided scramble into Cala Coticcio and a freedive day at Tavolara

trips.gatewayAirport: OLB Olbia Costa Smeralda — 45 min to Palau and Porto Pollo, 1 h to Santa Teresa Gallura, 25 min to Porto San Paolo for Tavolara. AHO Alghero is 2 h 15.
trips.summary: Porto Pollo exists because of a geographical accident: eleven kilometres of open water between Sardinia and Corsica, and a northwest wind that has to squeeze through it. The Bocche di Bonifacio behaves like a venturi, and the maestrale that arrives at the sandy isthmus of the Isola dei Gabbiani has been accelerated on the way in. What makes the spot rather than merely windy is the isthmus itself, which splits the water into two entirely different sports within two hundred metres — a shallow, glassy lagoon on one side for learning and freestyle, an open bay with chop and a swell line on the other for wave riding and blasting. You spend the week on that isthmus, with three days out: one into the La Maddalena Archipelago National Park with its permit system and its no-go zones, one west to Capo Testa and the granite of Santa Teresa Gallura, one south to freedive the wall at Tavolara. The rhythm is fixed and generous — the maestrale is a genuine afternoon wind, so mornings are for coffee, boats and snorkelling, and from about one o'clock you sail.

itinerary.title: Olbia to Porto Pollo, register, first lagoon session
itinerary.morning: Land at OLB, collect a car and drive 45 minutes north through Arzachena to **Palau** and on to the Porto Pollo isthmus. Check in, then walk the isthmus end to end — five minutes — and look at both bays. This is the single most useful orientation on the trip: flat glass one side, chop and a swell line the other.
itinerary.afternoon: Register at your centre (Sporting Club Sardinia or Wind Porto Pollo if you want FIV/IKO structure and rescue-boat cover, MB Pro Center for the biggest fleet) and take an easy first session in the **sheltered lagoon**. Sand bottom, waist-deep, and the correct place to recalibrate.
itinerary.evening: Drive into Palau for dinner at La Gritta, on the water at Porto Faro looking across at La Maddalena, or Da Robertino in town for Gallurese cooking and a bottle of Vermentino di Gallura.
itinerary.dayStats: OLB–Porto Pollo 45 km, 45 min / lagoon knee-to-chest deep over sand / maestrale fills 11:00–13:00, peaks 14:00–18:00 at 15–30 knots / kit hire €60–€90/day, six-day €330–€450

itinerary.title: The open bay, the venturi and a coached hour
itinerary.morning: Coffee and a slow rig. Book a **private hour** with your centre for the morning — €80–€90 buys a technique correction that will pay for itself across five remaining afternoons, and morning wind is the right strength for coaching.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross to the **open western bay** for the real session. Side-onshore maestrale, building chop, and by mid-afternoon a short wind swell you can actually ride. Respect the marked kite and windsurf corridors, and note the centres' rescue boat positions before you launch.
itinerary.evening: Aperitivo at the Isuledda beach bar while the wind drops off the isthmus, then dinner at Da Thomas in Palau — the pasta with bottarga is the local thing to order.
itinerary.dayStats: Bocche di Bonifacio ~11 km wide, accelerates the maestrale by several knots over regional forecast / private lesson €80–€90/h, 6 h package €420–€540 solo, ~€120 pp for three / 75 kg rider on a typical afternoon: 7–9 m kite, 4.7–5.5 m sail

itinerary.title: La Maddalena Archipelago by boat: permits, Budelli, Spargi
itinerary.morning: A morning boat day, because the maestrale makes the archipelago unpleasant after 14:00. Hire a **40 hp gommone** in Palau (no licence needed — Italy's threshold is 40.8 hp / 30 kW) or take a licensed day boat, and **buy the park navigation authorisation online before you leave the dock**. Run north to **Spargi** and **Cala Corsara**, then **Santa Maria** and the **Cala Napoletana** anchorage, anchoring only on visible clean sand.
itinerary.afternoon: Approach **Budelli**. The **Spiaggia Rosa is inside a Zone A integral reserve — no landing, no anchoring, no close approach**, and the pink sand is viewed from the boardwalk on the island's authorised route or from the water at the prescribed distance. Then back through the Passo dei Monaci to Palau ahead of the wind, or leave the boat and take the 15-minute **Palau–La Maddalena ferry** for an evening in La Maddalena town.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in La Maddalena town on Piazza Umberto I, or back at Porto Pollo.
itinerary.dayStats: Park navigation permit roughly €15–€55/day, ~40% reduction for sail / 40 hp gommone €180–€350/day plus fuel / Palau–La Maddalena ferry 15 min, €14–€20 return with car / Spiaggia Rosa: Zone A, no landing, no anchoring / anchor on sand only, Posidonia protected

itinerary.title: Cala Coticcio with a guide, then the afternoon wind
itinerary.morning: Drive or ferry across to **Caprera** and walk in to **Cala Coticcio**, the granite twin cove known as "Tahiti" — **access is only with an authorised guide in capped daily groups and must be booked in advance**; unaccompanied entry is fined. The walk is a rough 40-minute scramble over granite, so wear shoes. The water inside is as clear as anywhere in the Mediterranean; snorkel the eastern lobe.
itinerary.afternoon: Back to Porto Pollo for the session. If the maestrale is over 28 knots, ride the lagoon side; if it has backed west, do not ride the lagoon side at all — that shift makes it offshore with open strait downwind.
itinerary.evening: Also on Caprera is the **Compendio Garibaldino**, Garibaldi's house and tomb, which is a better hour than it sounds. Dinner in Palau or self-catered at the campsite.
itinerary.dayStats: Cala Coticcio guided access only, capped daily numbers, roughly €25–€40 pp / approach walk ~40 min over granite / water 23–25°C in September / offshore risk when maestrale backs W/WSW

itinerary.title: Capo Testa, the Valle della Luna and Santa Teresa Gallura
itinerary.morning: Drive an hour west to **Capo Testa** — a granite headland eroded into rounded, hollowed shapes, with the **Valle della Luna** behind it and small deep coves like **Cala Spinosa** cut into the rock. Snorkel from the rocks: 15–25 m visibility, granite boulders, and shoals in the gullies. Reef shoes for the urchins.
itinerary.afternoon: Into **Santa Teresa Gallura** for lunch and a swim at **Rena Bianca**, then look across 11 km of the Bocche to Bonifacio's white cliffs on Corsica. If you want a session, Porto Liscia on the way back takes the same maestrale with far more room than Porto Pollo.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Papè Satan in Santa Teresa Gallura — a long-standing kitchen with proper Sardinian cooking — before the drive back.
itinerary.dayStats: Porto Pollo–Capo Testa 40 km, 55 min / Bocche di Bonifacio 11 km across, Corsica visible / Rena Bianca sheltered, sandy, family water / Gallura tidal range 0.2–0.4 m — no tide planning required
itinerary.sleep: Camping Isuledda, Isola dei Gabbiani, or Hotel Corallaro, Santa Teresa

itinerary.title: Tavolara: the wall, and a day of depth instead of wind
itinerary.morning: Drive an hour south to **Porto San Paolo** and cross to **Tavolara**, the limestone slab that rises 560 m straight out of the sea inside the **Area Marina Protetta Tavolara–Punta Coda Cavallo**. Dive or freedive with a local centre: the walls drop past 40 m, the granite and limestone architecture is dramatic, and **Secca del Papa** is one of the best-known dive sites in the western Mediterranean.
itinerary.afternoon: Lunch on Tavolara's Spalmatore di Terra beach at one of the two seasonal restaurants, then snorkel the shallows before the boat back. This is a deliberate no-wind day; if the maestrale is exceptional, keep it in reserve and ride instead.
itinerary.evening: Back north. Dinner in Palau, or a last plate of seafood in Cannigione on the Golfo di Arzachena.
itinerary.dayStats: Porto Pollo–Porto San Paolo 65 km, 1 h / Tavolara summit 565 m / marine protected area, zoned, dive with a licensed centre only / guided dive €50–€75, freedive session €45–€70 / visibility commonly 20–30 m

itinerary.title: Last session on the isthmus, then out
itinerary.morning: Final morning at Porto Pollo. Use the light wind window for a **wingfoil session in the lagoon** if you have not tried it — this is one of the best places in Europe to learn it, and every centre now has kit and a shallow, forgiving flat area to fall in.
itinerary.afternoon: Wash and return gear, then take the coast road east via **Capo d'Orso** — the wind-eroded bear-shaped granite above Palau, a fifteen-minute walk from the car park with the whole archipelago below it — before the drive to Olbia.
itinerary.evening: If time allows, eat in Olbia's Corso Umberto before the flight; otherwise the airport.
itinerary.dayStats: Wingfoil kit €70–€100/day / Capo d'Orso 15 min walk, small entry fee / Porto Pollo–OLB 45 min / return kit before 17:00, most centres close at 18:00

accommodationStrategy.name: Camping Isuledda
accommodationStrategy.description: The obvious base: it occupies the isthmus itself, so both bays, all four water-sports centres and the launching areas are on foot, and you can re-check conditions hourly without moving a car. Pitches, mobile homes and bungalows, a shop, a bar and rinse facilities. Roughly €35–€60 a pitch, €70–€130 for a bungalow in season.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel La Vecchia Fonte
accommodationStrategy.description: Ten minutes from Porto Pollo and in walking distance of the La Maddalena ferry, Palau's restaurants and the boat-rental quays, which makes it the right choice for the archipelago and Capo d'Orso days. Parking, air conditioning and a proper breakfast, which the campsite does not offer. Roughly €100–€180 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Corallaro
accommodationStrategy.description: Worth one night at the western end of the week: directly above Rena Bianca beach, walking distance into Santa Teresa's old centre and twenty minutes from Capo Testa, with the Bocche and Corsica in front of you. Roughly €140–€230 double in September.

logistics.connectivity: Good 4G/5G in Palau, Santa Teresa and along the SP90; patchy on the Isola dei Gabbiani's seaward side and genuinely poor in the archipelago's channels. Italy is in the EU, so EU/EEA SIMs roam at domestic rates. Download Windguru and the park's authorisation portal before you need them at a boat quay.
logistics.emergency: **112** for everything and **1530** for the Guardia Costiera, plus **VHF Channel 16** on the water. Hospitals at Olbia (the main one for the north-east) and La Maddalena; serious cases go to Sassari or Cagliari. Check that your policy names kitesurfing and windsurfing — many European policies exclude both, and freediving below 10 m almost always needs a rider.
logistics.weather: The maestrale is the whole timetable. It can jump ten knots in an hour and it does not respect the "dies at sunset" rule once properly established. **It also cancels ferries:** a hard maestrale stops the Palau–La Maddalena service and the archipelago day boats, and it is the single most common cause of a lost boat day. The scirocco brings haze, gust and a heavy sea in the Bocche.
logistics.bookingWindows: July and August accommodation in Gallura goes four to six months out and roughly doubles in price. **Cala Coticcio's guided access has a daily cap and must be booked days in advance in high season.** La Maddalena park navigation authorisations are bought online per day and are best purchased the evening before. Six-day kit passes rarely sell out but the good boards do — email your centre a fortnight ahead. Boat rentals in Palau book out in August.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards are accepted almost everywhere including beach kiosks, but carry €80–€120 in cash for parking, small beach bars and the occasional rural trattoria. Tipping is not obligatory in Italy — round up, or leave 5% for genuinely good service; note the *coperto* (cover charge) of €2–€4 per person on many restaurant bills is not a tip.
logistics.transportRules: A car is essential. Gallura's beach parking is almost universally paid in summer (€1.50–€3/hour, often via app) and the Porto Pollo and Capo Testa car parks fill by 11:00 in August. Taking a hire car on the Palau–La Maddalena ferry is straightforward and cheap but requires the rental company's permission in some contracts — check. **The 40.8 hp / 30 kW licence threshold and the six-mile limit are the two numbers that govern boat hire**; both are enforced by the Guardia Costiera and the archipelago is patrolled.
logistics.permits: **Every boat needs a paid daily La Maddalena park authorisation.** Zone A areas are closed to entry, anchoring and stopping. **Anchoring on *Posidonia oceanica* is illegal and fined**, and Sardinia enforces this hard. Landing on Spiaggia Rosa is prohibited; Cala Coticcio needs a guide. Sardinia also bans removing sand, pebbles and shells from its beaches — this carries fines running to hundreds of euros and airport checks are real. Drones need ENAC registration and are restricted over the national park.
logistics.health: Tap water is drinkable in Palau and Santa Teresa but many locals drink bottled; ask at your accommodation. **Sea urchins on every granite ledge are the leading injury** — reef shoes and a needle. Mauve stinger jellyfish come in patches; hot-water immersion, not vinegar. The maestrale's dry heat conceals dehydration badly. Sardinian sun in June and July is stronger than the air temperature suggests — sail in a rash vest.

proTips: Buy the six-day pass at your centre on day one. Every Porto Pollo centre discounts hard past four days and the pass normally includes beach storage, which removes two car loadings a day from your life.

Walk both sides of the isthmus every morning before you rig. A twenty-degree veer turns the lagoon from perfect to offshore and the open bay from choppy to sublime, and the walk between them is three minutes.

Buy your La Maddalena park authorisation online the night before, not at the quay. The desks queue in August and the permit is per-day and non-transferable — arriving without one means either a wasted morning or a fine.

Book Cala Coticcio's guide slot before you leave home for a July or August trip. The daily cap is small, it sells out, and being turned back at the trailhead is a genuinely miserable way to lose a morning.
Do the archipelago in the morning, always. The maestrale peaks at 14:00–18:00 and a 5 m gommone crossing the Passo dei Monaci at four in the afternoon in 28 knots is not a pleasant boat.
Take a coached hour in the first two days rather than the last. In this lagoon a single instructor correction, applied over five remaining afternoons, is worth more than the whole rest of the rental.

Learn wingfoil here rather than anywhere else. The Porto Pollo lagoon is shallow, flat, sandy and forgiving, all four centres have current kit, and it is the one spot in the Mediterranean where the learning curve is genuinely pleasant.
Do not take sand, pebbles or shells home. Sardinia prosecutes this, airport baggage checks look for it, and the fines start in the hundreds of euros.

Eat inland once. Arzachena, Luogosanto and the Gallura stazzi feed you suckling pig, *zuppa gallurese* and Vermentino at half the coastal price, and it is the only way to see that Gallura is a granite farming country that happens to have the Costa Smeralda attached to it.

raw.Prevailing wind — the maestrale and the: The **maestrale** is a northwest wind, the Mediterranean's dominant summer flow in this corner, generated by pressure gradients across the Gulf of Lion and the Tyrrhenian. The **Bocche di Bonifacio**, the roughly 11 km strait between Sardinia and Corsica, compresses that flow between two granite coasts and accelerates it measurably — Porto Pollo sits directly in the outfall, which is why a 15-knot regional forecast routinely delivers 20–25 knots at the isthmus. Season runs roughly **April to early November**, with the strongest and most consistent months **May, June and September**; July and August are windy but with more light days and far more people. Typical working strength is **15–30 knots in the afternoon**. The daily cycle overlays a thermal on the synoptic wind: light or nothing in the morning, filling from **11:00–13:00**, peaking **14:00–18:00**, easing at sunset. A properly established maestrale ignores that cycle and blows through the night for three or four days. The counter-wind is the **scirocco** from the southeast, which brings humid haze, a longer swell and gustier, less pleasant conditions; the **ponente** westerly is the mid-season alternative.
raw.Launch spots — the twin bays of Porto Po: The sandy isthmus connecting the mainland to the **Isola dei Gabbiani (Isuledda)** divides the water. The **western/open bay** takes the maestrale side-onshore across open water with building chop and a genuine wind swell by mid-afternoon — this is the wave, freeride and advanced side. The **eastern/sheltered lagoon** behind the isthmus is knee-to-chest deep over sand, glassy flat in the same wind, and is where every beginner course, freestyle session and wingfoil first flight happens; it is one of the best learning lagoons in the Mediterranean. **The two areas are formally separated into kite and windsurf zones with marked corridors** — the centres enforce this and you will be told where to launch. Bottom is sand across the isthmus with granite outcrops at the edges. Elsewhere in Gallura: **Rena Bianca** at Santa Teresa Gallura (sheltered, sandy, family water, good for SUP), **Cala Spinosa** and the coves at **Capo Testa** (granite, deep, superb snorkelling, no launching), and **Porto Liscia**, the long beach west of Porto Pollo, which takes the same wind with more space and fewer people.
raw.Equipment hubs and certification: Porto Pollo has four established centres clustered at the isthmus and on the Isola dei Gabbiani. **MB Pro Center** (Windsurf Village, operating since 2009, a very large RRD fleet plus wingfoil boards and kites, with a kids' academy). **Sporting Club Sardinia** (on the Isola dei Gabbiani, running since 1988, affiliated to **FIV, VDWS and IKO**, multilingual, kite from age nine). **Wind Porto Pollo Centre** (Isola dei Gabbiani, **FIV and IKO** certified, Duotone equipment, with its own rescue boat). **PKS / FH Academy** (Isola dei Gabbiani, **IKO**, kite, wingfoil, windsurf and eFoil). Indicative 2026 pricing: **private lesson €80–€90/hour; a six-hour package €420–€540 one-to-one, around €190 per person for two, around €120 per person for three; kite or windsurf day hire €60–€90; a six-day rental pass €330–€450; wingfoil kit €70–€100/day.** Board and rig storage on the beach is included in most week passes and €5–€10/day otherwise. Rescue-boat cover is standard at the two FIV/IKO centres and is a real reason to hire from them rather than the cheapest option.
raw.Tides and currents — the honest Mediterr: Northern Sardinia is effectively tideless: **astronomical range in Gallura is on the order of 0.2–0.4 m**, and a hard maestrale's wind set-up shifts the waterline more than the moon. There are no tide windows in this file and there should be none in your planning. What is real is current. The **Bocche di Bonifacio carries a significant wind-driven surface current**, generally eastward under a maestrale, and it strengthens in the narrows and between the archipelago's islands; a channel that looks like a two-minute crossing on a chart can hold two knots of drift. Headland acceleration is pronounced at **Capo d'Orso, Punta Sardegna and Capo Testa**. Offshore-wind danger at Porto Pollo is a specific, named risk: **if the wind backs west or west-southwest, the sheltered lagoon side becomes offshore, and downwind of you is the open strait toward Corsica.** Every centre briefs this; take the briefing seriously.
raw.Sea conditions and safety: Water temperature: roughly 15–16°C in April, 18–19°C in May, 21–23°C in June, 24–25°C in July, 25–26°C in August, 23–24°C in September, 21–22°C in October. **A 2 mm shorty or long john is right for May and October; boardshorts and a lycra do July and August, but take a 2 mm top for a three-hour session, because 28 knots of dry maestrale strips heat fast even off warm water.** *Pelagia noctiluca* mauve stingers appear in patches, particularly after several calm days. **Sea urchins live on every granite ledge in Gallura** — at Capo Testa, Cala Coticcio and the rocky edges of the Porto Pollo bays — and reef shoes are essential. Lifeguard coverage exists on the main managed beaches in July and August only; at Porto Pollo the practical rescue cover is the centres' own boats during opening hours. **Emergency 112; Guardia Costiera 1530; VHF Channel 16.**
raw.La Maddalena Archipelago National Park —: The park covers 62 islands and islets and **every boat navigating in its waters needs a daily online authorisation purchased in advance**; cost scales with hull length and propulsion, running roughly **€15–€55 per day for the small-to-mid craft most visitors hire, with sailing vessels receiving a reduction of around 40% on the motor rate.** The park is divided into graded protection zones: **Zone A areas are integral reserves where entry, anchoring and stopping are prohibited outright**, and the waters around **Budelli's Spiaggia Rosa** are exactly that — the pink beach has been closed to landing and to close approach since the 1990s, and there is no version of the trip in which you walk on it; authorised operators view it from the Budelli boardwalk instead. **Anchoring is permitted only on clean sand, never on *Posidonia oceanica* seagrass**, which is both an offence and the main cause of dragged anchors in the archipelago; overnight anchoring is allowed only in permitted zones with sand or mud bottoms and with per-cove boat caps. **Cala Coticcio ("Tahiti") on Caprera is accessible only with an authorised guide**, in capped daily groups, booked in advance — unaccompanied entry is fined.
raw.Boat logistics and the Italian 40 hp rul: Italy's threshold is clear and generous: **a boating licence (*patente nautica*) is required only for engines over 40.8 hp / 30 kW, or for vessels over 24 m, or for navigation more than six nautical miles from shore.** That makes the standard 5–6 m gommone with a 40 hp outboard rentable by anyone over 18 without a licence — the workhorse of a Gallura week. Expect **€180–€350 per day in season plus fuel**, from Palau, Cannigione or Santa Teresa Gallura, with the park permit either included or bought separately at the desk. The six-mile limit matters here: it keeps you comfortably inside the archipelago but rules out a Corsica crossing. Harbour fees at Palau and Cannigione for a day berth run €25–€60 for a small craft in high season; Porto Cervo is another matter entirely.
raw.Weather-contingency plan: *No wind:* the archipelago boat day, Capo Testa and the Valle della Luna, or a freedive at Tavolara. *Too much wind (30 knots+):* the lagoon side at Porto Pollo holds when the open bay does not, and Porto Liscia gives more room; if that fails, La Maddalena town, the Garibaldi museum at Compendio Garibaldino on Caprera, or the Nuraghe Albucciu and the Gallura interior around Arzachena. *Scirocco:* Rena Bianca at Santa Teresa is sheltered from the southeast, and the Bocche crossing gets uncomfortable — do not book the boat day. **Note that a hard maestrale also cancels the Palau–La Maddalena ferry and the archipelago day boats**, so hold one flexible day.

sources.verified: Porto Pollo's four established centres and their affiliations — MB Pro Center (founded 2009, Windsurf Village, large RRD fleet plus wingfoil and kite), Sporting Club Sardinia (founded 1988, Isola dei Gabbiani, FIV/VDWS/IKO, kite from age nine), Wind Porto Pollo Centre (founded 2000, Isola dei Gabbiani, FIV and IKO, Duotone, rescue service), and PKS / FH Academy (Isola dei Gabbiani, IKO); indicative 2026 lesson pricing of €80–€90 for a private hour and six-hour packages at €420–€540 solo, ~€190 pp for two and ~€120 pp for three; the flat shallow lagoon versus open-sea wave split at the Isola dei Gabbiani and the existence of separated kite and windsurf zones; maestrale afternoon strengths of 15–30 knots from April to November; Italy's boat-licence threshold of 40 hp engine power (with the statutory figure being 40.8 hp / 30 kW) and 24 m length; the La Maddalena Archipelago National Park's daily online navigation authorisation with cost scaling by size and a roughly 40% reduction for sailing vessels, its graded protection zones with Zone A closed to entry and anchoring, its anchor-on-clean-sand-only rule protecting *Posidonia oceanica*, per-cove caps on overnight anchoring, and the total prohibition on landing at or closely approaching Budelli's Spiaggia Rosa.

Windfinder's Porto Pollo station is no longer reporting, so the wind figures here rest on centre-published and regional climatology rather than a live station record — treat the "venturi adds several knots" claim as well-attested locally but not quantified from data in this run. Named hotels (Camping Isuledda, Hotel La Vecchia Fonte, Hotel Corallaro) and restaurants (La Gritta, Da Robertino, Da Thomas, Papè Satan) should be confirmed as still trading. trips.title: Curonian Lagoon: Svencelė & Nida Kite Week
trips.subRegion: Curonian Lagoon and the Baltic coast, Klaipėda region

bestPeriod.window: **May to early October.** May–June and September have the strongest and most consistent wind; July–August is warmest with reliable afternoon thermals and the busiest water
bestPeriod.raw: **May to early October.** May–June and September have the strongest and most consistent wind; July–August is warmest with reliable afternoon thermals and the busiest water

accommodation.note: €60–140 per night, double, in Svencelė, Kintai or Nida; camp beds €30–50

food.note: €30–55 per day

transport.note: €120–200: flights to Palanga or Vilnius plus transfer, car hire €40–55 per day, Curonian Spit ferry and eco-fee

activities.note: Kite or wing gear rental €50–80 per day; lessons €60–90 per hour, a full beginner course €300–450

trips.summary: A seven-day water sports & coastal trip itinerary in Curonian Lagoon and the Baltic coast, Klaipėda region, Lithuania.

itinerary.title: Arrive Klaipėda, transfer to Svencelė
itinerary.morning: Fly to Palanga (30 minutes from Klaipėda) or Vilnius and drive four hours. Klaipėda for supplies and a look at the old Memel warehouse quarter.
itinerary.afternoon: Transfer to **Svencelė**, a peninsula on the eastern shore of the Curonian Lagoon and the best flatwater kite spot in the Baltics: a huge shallow bay where you can stand across most of the riding area.
itinerary.evening: Rig check, kit hire, and a briefing on the local wind pattern.

itinerary.title: Svencelė: the flatwater week begins
itinerary.morning: Morning wind is often light; use it for a lesson, a foil session or SUP.
itinerary.afternoon: The thermal fills. Svencelė's combination of waist-deep water, a long fetch and a side-shore southwesterly is close to ideal for learning and for freestyle progression — flat water and a standing depth means falls have no consequences.
itinerary.evening: The camps here are social and international; evening barbecues are the norm.

itinerary.title: Kintai and the eastern shore
itinerary.morning: Kintai, further south, is a quieter bay with the same shallow-water character and fewer riders. Good for a long downwinder with a shuttle back.
itinerary.afternoon: Nearby is **Ventės Ragas**, one of Europe's oldest bird-ringing stations — a genuinely worthwhile hour off the water, especially in migration season.
itinerary.evening: Return to Svencelė.

itinerary.title: Cross to the spit: Nida and Preila
itinerary.morning: Ferry from Klaipėda to Smiltynė and drive down the **Curonian Spit** to Nida (about an hour, with the Neringa eco-fee for vehicles).
itinerary.afternoon: The lagoon side at Nida and Preila offers launches with the Parnidis dune as a backdrop. Note that the spit is a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape and **launching is restricted to designated areas** — check locally before rigging anywhere new. `verify: true`
itinerary.evening: Nida's harbour: smoked fish, weather vanes, and the best evening light on the trip.

itinerary.title: Baltic side: waves and the open sea
itinerary.morning: Cross the spit to the open Baltic beach. In autumn, a northwesterly builds rideable wind swell here; in summer it is a 50 km beach for swimming, running and kayaking.
itinerary.afternoon: **Melnragė** and **Giruliai** north of Klaipėda are the accessible open-sea spots, with the Melnragė pier as the marker. Waves are short-period and messy compared to the North Sea — the Baltic is a small, shallow, non-tidal sea and it behaves like one.
itinerary.evening: Klaipėda for dinner.

itinerary.title: Big session day or downwinder
itinerary.morning: Whichever spot the forecast favours. With a car and both shores available, this coast rarely blanks between May and October.
itinerary.afternoon: A guided **lagoon downwinder** from Kintai toward Svencelė, or Preila to Nida on the spit side, with a support boat.
itinerary.evening: Last night. If it is late summer, watch for the **cyanobacteria advisories** — the shallow lagoon warms and blooms in hot still spells, and swimming is discouraged when a bloom is posted. `verify: true`

itinerary.title: Dawn session and departure
itinerary.morning: Early wind, pack the kit.
itinerary.afternoon: Palanga airport is an hour from Svencelė; Vilnius is four.

accommodationStrategy.name: Svencelė kite camps and cabins
accommodationStrategy.description: On-site accommodation at the spot: cabins, glamping tents and camp rooms, with gear storage, rinse facilities, a rescue boat and instructors on the water. €50–110. Being able to walk from bed to launch is the entire logic of a kite week and this is the only place on the lagoon that offers it properly.

accommodationStrategy.name: Kintai and Dreverna guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: Small village guesthouses on the eastern shore, quieter and cheaper, with easy access to the southern bays. Better if you want the lagoon's fishing-village character alongside the sport.

accommodationStrategy.name: Nida wooden guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: For the two nights on the Curonian Spit. More expensive and more beautiful, with the dune, the Baltic beach and the lagoon all within walking distance. See Trip 10 for the fuller version of Nida.

logistics.emergency: 112. Klaipėda has the regional hospital, 30–45 minutes from most spots. Camps run rescue boats during operating hours; outside them, there is no cover.
logistics.bookingWindows: Kite camps in July–August: 2–3 months. Nida accommodation in high summer: 3–4 months. May and September: 2–3 weeks.
logistics.health: Standing depth is what makes Svencelė forgiving, and it is also what makes a bad crash different: injuries here come from hitting a hard sand bottom, not from drowning. Helmet and impact vest are sensible, not optional, for anyone jumping.
logistics.gettingThere: A car makes the week: the two shores are separated by a ferry and an hour of driving, and the ability to chase wind between them is what turns four good days into six.

other.label: The Baltic has no meaningful tide
other.text: Water level here is a **wind-driven** variable: sustained westerlies raise the lagoon, easterlies drain it, and the difference over a week can be substantial in a bay this shallow. Ask the camp what the level is doing before assuming yesterday's depth.

other.label: Protected landscape
other.text: The Curonian Spit is a UNESCO site with strict dune and habitat protection: designated launches only, no walking on the dunes off boardwalks, no fires, and seasonal restrictions in bird areas. Fines are real.

other.label: The border
other.text: The southern half of the spit is in Russia's Kaliningrad exclave. Do not ride, sail or drift south of the marked boundary — this is a hard international border on the water as well as the land.

other.label: Water quality
other.text: Late-summer cyanobacteria blooms occur in the warm shallow lagoon. Advisories are posted; take them seriously, particularly for children and dogs.

proTips: **Learn here.** Svencelė is one of the best beginner kite spots in Europe: standing depth over a large area, consistent side-shore thermal, warm water in summer, and prices roughly half of Tarifa or the Netherlands.
Ride the **afternoon thermal**, and use the mornings for a foil session, a lesson or the spit. The wind pattern in midsummer is predictable enough to plan the day around.
Base at Svencelė and take **two nights in Nida** rather than commuting daily. The ferry, the eco-fee and the spit's speed limits make a daily round trip a waste of wind.
Bring or hire a **wing** as well as a kite. On light thermal days, wing foiling gets you on the water when kites are sitting on the beach — and this lagoon is close to perfect for it.
The lagoon's shallow warm water means a **shorty in July** is enough. Do not overpack neoprene for the Baltic's reputation; this is not the North Sea.
Combine with **Trip 10** if you want a partner or family who does not ride to enjoy the same week — Nida, the dunes and the cycle path are twenty minutes from the launch.

raw.prevailing_wind: Southwest to west dominant, with reliable summer sea-breeze thermals building through the afternoon. Northeasterlies are offshore on the mainland shore and side-shore at Svencelė's spit
raw.wind_statistics: Spring and autumn deliver the strongest gradient wind; midsummer relies on the thermal, which typically fills in early afternoon and holds until evening
launch_spots: Preila and Nida on the lagoon side
Melnragė and Giruliai on the Baltic side near Klaipėda
raw.equipment_hubs: Svencelė is the centre — schools, storage, rescue boats and rental on site; Nida has smaller operations
raw.tidal_awareness: The Baltic is effectively **non-tidal** — the range is a few centimetres. Water level is driven by wind instead: a sustained westerly pushes water into the lagoon and raises it, a strong easterly drains it and can leave the shallows unrideable. Plan by wind history, not by a tide table
raw.water_temp_c: 14–17 in May, 20–24 in July–August in the shallow lagoon, 15–18 in late September
raw.wetsuit_guidance: Shorty or 3/2 in midsummer; 4/3 in May and late September; the lagoon is far warmer than the open Baltic
