packingNotes: A 4/3 mm wetsuit as the default, with a thicker 5/3 mm or 5/4 mm for shoulder-season open-coast sessions.
Wetsuit boots; both the lake and open-coast entries have shell and stone sections.
A wing and a kite if bringing personal gear for both disciplines — rental covers either but not always both at short notice.
A tide table or app for the Oosterschelde days specifically; the Grevelingenmeer and dam sides do not need one.
A dry bag for the sea-kayak day on the Oosterschelde.
Layers for the car park between sessions; Zeeland's open coast is windier and several degrees cooler than the sheltered lake side even a few hundred metres away.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Wrong-side wind direction.** A day that is unrideable on the open coast is often fine on the lake. Check both spots' live conditions before writing off the day.

**Missed slack water on the Oosterschelde.** Turning up even thirty minutes late can mean a genuinely strong current running against a paddler or a swimmer. Build the whole day's plan around the tide table, not the other way round.
**A September–November storm system.** Force 7 or above on the open coast is not a session, it is a hazard. Retreat to the lake for lighter riding or take a full rest day.
**Gear left rigged unattended.** Zeeland's wind can pick up fast; an unweighted kite or wing on the beach is a known cause of minor injuries and lost gear here.

**No rental availability for a specific discipline.** Wing foil demand has outpaced kite rental stock at some Brouwersdam operators in peak season; book gear two to three days ahead if a specific session is essential.

trips.title: Flat Water and Side-Shore: Masurian Sailing and a Kite Week on the Hel Peninsula
trips.subRegion: Great Masurian Lakes and the Hel Peninsula / Zatoka Pucka

bestPeriod.window: the second half of June — long days, warm bay water, and wind before the August lull
bestPeriod.avoid: the first three weeks of August (Masurian marinas full, Hel road jammed, lightest wind of the year)

accommodation.note: €300–€520 (€43–€74/night, including two nights aboard)

transport.note: €180–€280 (Warsaw or Gdańsk transfer, one-way car hire Masuria→Hel, SKM trains)

activities.note: €280–€450 (yacht charter share, kayak hire, two kite lessons or gear rental)

profile.difficultyNote: Easy–Moderate

trips.gatewayAirport: Warsaw (WAW/WMI) → Giżycko by train via Olsztyn/Korsze, 4–5 h. Gdańsk (GDN) is the exit airport: SKM/PKM to Gdynia, then the Hel line train down the peninsula, ~1 h 45.
trips.summary: Poland gives you two entirely separate water worlds in one week. Inland, a chain of connected lakes big enough to lose sight of the shore, linked by nineteenth-century canals and hand-cranked locks, where the whole…
trips.hook: Poland gives you two entirely separate water worlds in one week. Inland, a chain of connected lakes big enough to lose sight of the shore, linked by nineteenth-century canals and hand-cranked locks, where the whole country goes sailing in July. On the coast, a 35 km sandbar with a warm, shallow, flat bay on one side and open Baltic swell on the other — which is exactly why it became Poland's kite and windsurf capital. Two boats, two disciplines, one long drive between them.

snapshot.Start / End: Giżycko → Hel (point-to-point, ~330 km between the two halves)
snapshot.Getting there: Warsaw (WAW/WMI) → Giżycko by train via Olsztyn/Korsze, 4–5 h. Gdańsk (GDN) is the exit airport: SKM/PKM to Gdynia, then the Hel line train down the peninsula, ~1 h 45.

itinerary.title: Giżycko, the swing bridge, and taking the boat
itinerary.morning: Train to **Giżycko**, the capital of the lakes, sitting on the isthmus between **Niegocin** and **Kisajno**. Collect a charter from **Ekomarina Giżycko** on the Niegocin waterfront [VERIFY: current 2026 charter rates for a 30–34 ft lake yacht].
itinerary.afternoon: Watch the **most obrotowy**, the 1889 hand-cranked rotating bridge over the Łuczański Canal — one person turns a hundred tonnes of iron, on the hour, and boat traffic queues on both sides. Then a shakedown sail on Niegocin.
itinerary.evening: Provision at the marina, walk the Boyen Fortress ramparts, and eat fried *sielawa* (vendace) on the promenade.

itinerary.title: North into Mamry and Sztynort
itinerary.morning: Sail north through Kisajno into **Mamry**, the second-largest lake in Poland and the most open water on the chain. The whole northern basin is exposed — reef early.
itinerary.afternoon: Into **Marina Sztynort**, the biggest charter base in Masuria, under the ruined Lehndorff palace. Lunch, then on to **Węgorzewo** at the top of the system, 12 km further, where **Ekomarina Węgorzewo** is the northern charter hub.
itinerary.evening: Overnight in Węgorzewo. The town is quieter and cheaper than Giżycko and the pizza at the port is better than it has any right to be.
itinerary.dayStats: 25 km sailing

itinerary.title: Śniardwy, the big one
itinerary.morning: Back south through the Giżycko bridge — check the opening times posted at the marina — and down Niegocin and the Kula canal.
itinerary.afternoon: Out onto **Śniardwy**, at about 114 km² **the largest lake in Poland**: shallow, wide, and famous for turning nasty faster than its size suggests. Keep the shoreline in sight, watch for the marked shoals, and get off it if a squall line builds.
itinerary.evening: Into **Mikołajki**, the noisiest and most enjoyable port on the lakes — Port Mikołajki, the Kurki, the wooden promenade. Book a berth ahead in July [VERIFY: current Mikołajki marina berth fee].
itinerary.dayStats: 35 km sailing

itinerary.title: Bełdany, the Guzianka locks, and the Krutynia
itinerary.morning: Sail south down **Bełdany**, the long, forested, wind-sheltered lake, to the **Śluza Guzianka** — the 1879 lock connecting Bełdany with Jezioro Guzianka Małe and the Nidzkie system, now doubled by the newer Guzianka II chamber. Locking through is the single most Masurian hour of the week.
itinerary.afternoon: Leave the yacht at Ruciane-Nida and hire kayaks for the last stage of the **Krutynia** — the classic Polish flatwater descent, roughly **91–100 km from Sorkwity to Ruciane-Nida**, normally paddled in **eight to ten day-stages** (Sorkwity → Bieńki → Babięta → Spychowo → Krutyń → Ukta → Nowy Most → Ruciane-Nida). The Krutyń–Ukta stage is the beautiful one: clear water over sand, alder tunnels, kingfishers.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at the Krutyń waterfront, then back to the boat. The **Mazurska Pętla Żeglarska**, the EU-funded Masurian Sailing Loop, is why every port on this route now has fuel, water and pump-out.
itinerary.dayStats: 18 km sailing + 12 km paddling

itinerary.title: Handover, and the long move to the coast
itinerary.morning: Return the yacht at Giżycko or Mikołajki. Charter handovers are usually Saturday morning — check yours before booking flights.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive or ride to the coast: roughly **330 km, 4 h 15**, Giżycko → Elbląg → Gdańsk → Władysławowo → **Chałupy**. The last 10 km down the peninsula can take an hour in August.
itinerary.evening: Check the wind for tomorrow, walk the sandbar from bay to open sea in four minutes, and eat smoked flounder at a Chałupy fish shack.

itinerary.title: Chałupy and Kuźnica, flat-water day
itinerary.morning: **Chałupy 3** and **Chałupy 6** at first thermal. On a W/NW wind this is textbook side-shore, waist-deep for 200 m, with a sandy bottom and no rock. A first kite lesson lives here.
itinerary.afternoon: Move 4 km to **Kuźnica** as the breeze fills — the narrowest, shallowest, flattest part of the whole bay and the reason beginners come to Hel at all. Rig small; the thermal peaks around 15:00.
itinerary.evening: Swap the bay for the open Baltic beach on the north side for the sunset and a swim. Water is honestly **17–20 °C in July–August**, 14–16 °C in June, and can drop to 11–12 °C overnight after an upwelling — the bay side runs 2–4 °C warmer than the open sea.

itinerary.title: Jastarnia, Rewa, and the end of the sandbar
itinerary.morning: **Jastarnia** for stronger-wind day: deeper water, more space, a proper harbour. If the forecast is light, take the train to **Hel** at the tip for the Fokarium seal centre and the wartime coastal battery.
itinerary.afternoon: If you have a car, cross to **Rewa** on the mainland shore and walk out along **Cypel Rewski**, the Ryf Mew spit — a sand tongue running a kilometre into the bay, knee-deep either side, and the best flat-water launch on the whole Gulf.
itinerary.evening: Train from Hel or Władysławowo to Gdynia and Gdańsk, about 1 h 45. Last dinner on Gdańsk's Długie Pobrzeże.

accommodationStrategy.name: Chartered yacht
accommodationStrategy.description: on the Masurian lakes the boat is the accommodation, and every port on the Mazurska Pętla has showers, power and water. A 30–34 ft lake cruiser with an inboard sleeps 6–8.
accommodationStrategy.booking: **December to February** for a July charter — the good boats go at the boat shows. Direct with the base, not through an aggregator.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Ekomarina
accommodationStrategy.description: the first and last nights on land, thirty seconds from the charter pontoon, with secure luggage storage while you are on the water and a laundry.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6–8 weeks ahead in season [VERIFY: current rates].

accommodationStrategy.name: Camping Chałupy 6 / Ośrodek Chałupy
accommodationStrategy.description: you sleep on the sandbar, 60 seconds from the launch on the bay side, with gear storage, rinse tanks and an on-site school — the single biggest quality-of-life factor on a wind trip.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 2–3 months ahead for July–August; the peninsula genuinely runs out of beds [VERIFY: current 2026 pitch and cabin rates].

logistics.connectivity: Good 4G/5G across the lakes and the whole peninsula. Use **Windguru** or **Windy** for both halves — the Hel spot pages are the standard reference, and the Masurian forecast that matters is the squall risk on Śniardwy.
logistics.emergency: **112**; water rescue is **WOPR on 601 100 100**. On the lakes, Mazurskie WOPR runs patrol boats out of Giżycko and Mikołajki; on the coast, lifeguarded beaches fly the standard red/yellow flags — a **red flag means swimming is prohibited**, not "be careful".
logistics.weather: Masurian squalls arrive fast and from the west; the standard warning is a siren and a flashing light at the ports, and the rule is to be off Śniardwy and Mamry before a front. On Hel, the thermal collapses at dusk — do not launch at 18:00 expecting the afternoon breeze.
logistics.bookingWindows: Yacht charters **6–9 months** for July. Kite courses 3–4 weeks. Hel accommodation 2–3 months. Marina berths in Mikołajki and Giżycko can be reserved by phone the same morning outside August.
logistics.money: The złoty, roughly 4.3 PLN to the euro. Cards everywhere, including marinas and most fish shacks; carry 200 PLN for lock fees, berth fees at small ports and beach car parks.
logistics.transportRules: The Hel Peninsula has **one road and one railway**, and the road is the bottleneck — in August, park at Władysławowo and use the **Hel line train**, which runs the full length of the sandbar and takes bikes and boards. Polish rail carries a bicycle for a flat **11.90 PLN** on PKP Intercity services with bike spaces.
logistics.permits: The **patent żeglarski** matters. Polish law lets you sail **without any licence** on inland waters in a sailing yacht of up to **7.5 m hull length**, and drive a motorboat with an engine up to **10 kW**; anything larger requires at minimum the **żeglarz jachtowy** certificate, and charter bases will ask to see it or supply a skipper for around 350–500 PLN a day [VERIFY: current 2026 skipper day rate and the exact hull-length threshold under the current regulation]. On the sea, **kitesurfing is restricted to designated zones** on the Hel bay shore in high season and banned from the main lifeguarded swimming areas — the zones are marked and enforced by municipal patrols [VERIFY: 2026 Hel municipal kite-zone boundaries and hours].

proTips: **Check the wind direction, not just the strength, on the bay side.** W and NW are side-shore and safe; **S and SW are offshore and dangerous**. This one distinction separates a good Hel day from a rescue call.

**Jellyfish are a non-issue and worth knowing about anyway.** What you will meet is *chełbia modra*, the moon jelly — translucent, four purple rings, completely harmless. The occasional lion's mane (*bełtwa festonowa*) drifts in on easterlies and stings mildly. Nothing in the Baltic is dangerous.
**Go in the second half of June.** You get 17 hours of daylight, water already at 17 °C in the bay, statistically better wind than August, and the Polish school holidays have not started.
**Book the Krutynia as a one-way with transfer.** Every Masurian kayak operator will shuttle you and the boats; paddling upstream back to Sorkwity is a genuinely miserable idea.
**Time the Giżycko swing bridge.** It opens on a published schedule, not on demand, and a missed opening costs an hour. Read the board at Ekomarina before you plan the day's leg.
**Learn *"Jaki jest wiatr?"*** — what is the wind? — and *"Czy jest wolne miejsce?"* for a berth. Masurian harbourmasters answer both instantly.

**Do not swim outside the flags on the open Baltic side.** The rip currents run out through the gaps in the offshore bar, they are invisible from the beach, and the peninsula's unguarded stretches are where the drownings happen.

raw.Prevailing wind: direction, force, month: Both halves of this trip run on **westerlies**. On the Hel Peninsula the dominant flow is **W to NW**, typically **4–6 Bft in May–June and September**, softening in July–August to a **thermal sea breeze** that builds from around 12:00–13:00 and dies at dusk. May, June and September are the reliable statistical months; August is the warmest water and the weakest wind. On the bay side a **W/NW wind is beautifully side-shore** — flat water, steady pressure, safe drift back toward the sandbar.
raw.The offshore danger, stated plainly: A **southerly or south-westerly on the Zatoka Pucka shore blows straight offshore**, away from the peninsula and out into a bay 10–15 km wide. It looks perfect — flat, warm, sunny — and it will take a downed kite or a broken mast foot far beyond swimming range. Do not launch on the bay side in S/SW without a rescue boat. The reverse applies on the open-sea beaches with a northerly.
raw.Launch spots by name: **Chałupy 3** and **Chałupy 6** — the historic centre of Polish windsurfing, waist-deep water hundreds of metres out. **Kuźnica** — the narrowest point of the peninsula, the shallowest, flattest water, and the classic beginner spot. **Jastarnia** — deeper, more room, better in strong wind. **Jurata** — quieter, the same bay water. **Cypel Rewski** at Rewa, on the mainland side of the bay: the Ryf Mew sandspit, where you can walk out a kilometre in knee-deep water. Open-sea launches exist at Władysławowo and Hel but are for wave riders, not learners.
raw.Rental and school hubs: Chałupy and Kuźnica are wall-to-wall stations in season, with kite and wing gear, IKO-certified instruction, and storage. Jastarnia has the windsurf-focused operators. Book courses ahead in July — the good instructors sell out [VERIFY: current 2026 kite course prices and specific school names in Chałupy and Jastarnia].
raw.Tide, current and the real hazards: **The Baltic is effectively non-tidal** — the astronomical range in the Gulf of Gdańsk is a few centimetres and no one plans around it. What actually moves the water is **wind-driven set-up (*spiętrzenie wiatrowe*)**, which can raise or drop the level by half a metre or more over a day and floods the low Hel beaches in autumn gales; **seiches**, the slow sloshing oscillation of the Gulf of Gdańsk after a wind event; **upwelling**, which can drop open-sea water temperature by 8–10 °C overnight when the wind turns; and **rip currents** on the open Baltic side, which run out through the sandbar gaps and are the commonest cause of Polish drownings. On the lakes the equivalent risk is not current but fetch: **Śniardwy** builds a short, vicious 1 m chop in twenty minutes.

typeSpecific.windConditions: Both halves of this trip run on **westerlies**. On the Hel Peninsula the dominant flow is **W to NW**, typically **4–6 Bft in May–June and September**, softening in July–August to a **thermal sea breeze** that builds from around 12:00–13:00 and dies at dusk. May, June and September are the reliable statistical months; August is the warmest water and the weakest wind. On the bay side a **W/NW wind is beautifully side-shore** — flat water, steady pressure, safe drift back toward the sandbar.

activities.note: Board and wetsuit hire €20–€30/day or €100–€150/week, 3–4 coached sessions €35–€60 each, Berlengas boat €23–€30, Nazaré fort €2

trips.gatewayAirport: LIS Lisbon Humberto Delgado — 45 min to Ericeira, 1 h 20 to Peniche, 1 h 45 to Nazaré. OPO Porto is 2 h 15 to Nazaré if you run the trip in reverse.
trips.summary: This is Portugal's densest stretch of good waves and it fits inside a 70 km drive. You start in Ericeira, the only World Surfing Reserve in Europe, where seven or eight genuinely world-class reefs sit inside four kilometres of coast and a beginner can still find a sand-bottomed beach break at Foz do Lizandro. Then you move to Peniche, which is not a town so much as a peninsula — and because it sticks out into the Atlantic with waves on both sides, it works in almost any wind, which is the single most useful geographical fact in Portuguese surfing. You finish north at Nazaré, where a 230 km submarine canyon focuses swell into Praia do Norte and where, in the right season, you stand on the fort headland and watch waves that do not look real. Two hard truths shape the week: the nortada, a thermal north wind that ruins the afternoon most days from spring to early autumn, and a 3.5 m spring tidal range that turns each break on and off. Learn both and this is one of the best surf weeks in Europe.

itinerary.title: Land in Lisbon, Foz do Lizandro to shake off the flight
itinerary.morning: Land at LIS, collect the car — take the electronic toll transponder, the A8 and A21 both use it — and drive 45 minutes northwest to Ericeira. Check in, then walk the clifftop path from Praia dos Pescadores north past Praia do Norte and Matadouro so you can see the reserve's geography from above before you paddle into it.
itinerary.afternoon: First session at **Foz do Lizandro**, the sand-bottomed river-mouth beach at the southern end of town. Multiple peaks, forgiving, and the correct place to recalibrate after a winter. Note where the river rip runs on the dropping tide.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Tik Tapas in the old town, or grilled fish at Marisqueira César. Ericeira is a fishing town before it is a surf town and the fish shows it.
itinerary.dayStats: LIS–Ericeira 50 km, 45 min / Foz do Lizandro sand bottom, all levels / board + wetsuit hire €30–€45/day / water 17–19°C in September, 3/2 full suit
itinerary.sleep: Ericeira Chill House or Rapture Surfcamp Ericeira

itinerary.title: Ribeira d'Ilhas at dawn, then the reserve on foot
itinerary.morning: Be in the water at Ribeira d'Ilhas at first light — the amphitheatre bay 2 km north of town, a long right-hand reef point and the most accessible of the reserve's serious waves. On a smaller day the inside section is genuinely intermediate-friendly. Check the tide: it wants mid-to-high.
itinerary.afternoon: Nortada will be up. Walk the reserve — Ribeira d'Ilhas, Reef, Cave, Pedra Branca and Coxos are all within a few kilometres, and watching Coxos from the cliff on a solid day is an education in what a point break can do. Do not paddle out at Coxos on your first visit.
itinerary.evening: Beer and petiscos at the Ribeira d'Ilhas beach bar while the wind drops, then dinner at Prim or Mar d'Areia in town.
itinerary.dayStats: Ericeira–Ribeira d'Ilhas 2 km / spring tidal range 3.2–3.6 m, neaps 1.2–1.6 m / nortada fills 11:00–13:00, peaks 15:00–19:00, 15–25 knots / Coxos advanced only, urchin-covered reef
itinerary.sleep: Ericeira Chill House or Rapture Surfcamp Ericeira

itinerary.title: São Julião, coaching, and a tide-planned second session
itinerary.morning: Drive 15 minutes south to **São Julião**, an exposed beach break with multiple peaks that holds swell when the rest of the coast is flat and takes a bigger day than Lizandro. Book a coached session here or at Lizandro — one video-analysis hour with an FPS-certified coach is worth three unstructured surfs.
itinerary.afternoon: Second short session timed to the tide rather than the clock — if the morning was high water at Ribeira d'Ilhas, the afternoon low opens Matadouro and the Lizandro banks. Then Ericeira's Sunday-market streets and the Ericeira Surf Clube's clubhouse.
itinerary.evening: Canastra or Tasca do Joel for percebes, ameijoas à Bulhão Pato and a bottle of Colares white — the tiny sand-grown wine region is 20 minutes down the coast.
itinerary.dayStats: Ericeira–São Julião 12 km, 15 min / coached session €35–€60, private €60–€90/h / two tides in 12 h 25 min — plan sessions around them, not lunch
itinerary.sleep: Ericeira Chill House or Rapture Surfcamp Ericeira

itinerary.title: North to Peniche: Baleal, Cantinho da Baía and Lagide
itinerary.morning: Drive 70 minutes north to Peniche, dropping bags at Baleal. Warm up at **Cantinho da Baía** on the sheltered south side of the Baleal isthmus — soft, sandy and the least consequential water in the region, which is exactly what you want on a travel day.
itinerary.afternoon: If there is northwest swell and the tide is mid-to-high, paddle out at **Lagide**, the left-hand reef on Baleal's north side. If the nortada is already up, this is when the peninsula pays: cross to the south side and check Supertubos and Molho Leste.
itinerary.evening: Bar do Bruno on the Baleal isthmus for sunset, then dinner at Tasca do Joel in Peniche — one of the best fish kitchens on this coast, and you should book.
itinerary.dayStats: Ericeira–Peniche 70 km, 1 h 10 / Baleal isthmus splits north- and south-facing beaches within 400 m / Lagide left reef, NW swell, mid-to-high tide / Cantinho da Baía all levels
itinerary.sleep: Baleal Surf Camp or Surfers Lodge Peniche

itinerary.title: Supertubos, Cabo Carvoeiro and the fort
itinerary.morning: Dawn at **Supertubos**, on the south side. Whether you surf it or watch it depends entirely on the swell and honestly on you — on a 1.5 m day with a light north wind and a dropping tide it is one of the best waves in Europe, and on a 3 m day it is a sand-bottomed guillotine. **Molho Leste** next door is the sensible compromise.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive out to **Cabo Carvoeiro** at the tip of the peninsula — the lighthouse, the Nau dos Corvos sea stack, and the cliff path round to the Papôa. Then the **Fortaleza de Peniche** and its Museu Nacional Resistência e Liberdade, the former political prison of the Estado Novo, which is a serious and worthwhile hour.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Nau dos Corvos on the cape with the light going down over the Berlengas, or Marisqueira Mirandum in town for shellfish by weight.
itinerary.dayStats: Supertubos best on W/NW swell, N/NE wind, dropping tide / Peniche fort museum entry roughly €3–€5 / Cabo Carvoeiro to Berlengas 10 km, visible on a clear day
itinerary.sleep: Baleal Surf Camp or Surfers Lodge Peniche

itinerary.title: Berlengas: the 350-person island
itinerary.morning: Take the first boat from Peniche's fishing harbour to **Berlenga Grande** — 30 minutes, and the crossing is genuinely rough on any residual swell, so take something for it. The island is a Nature Reserve and UNESCO Biosphere Reserve with a daily cap of roughly 350 visitors, so your ticket is your permit. Walk up to the lighthouse, then down the causeway to the **Forte de São João Baptista**, the seventeenth-century fort on its own islet.
itinerary.afternoon: Snorkel the clear water off Carreiro do Mosteiro — visibility here is far better than the mainland beaches — or take the operator's cave tour round to the Furado Grande tunnel. Last boat back is usually mid-to-late afternoon; miss it and you are staying.
itinerary.evening: Back in Baleal, an easy evening session at Prainha if the wind has dropped, then dinner at Casa Vieira or a plate of caldeirada at the harbour.
itinerary.dayStats: Peniche–Berlenga Grande 10 km, ~30 min / daily visitor cap ~350 / return boat €23–€30 / cave tour €15–€25 extra / service roughly May–September, cancels on swell
itinerary.sleep: Baleal Surf Camp or Surfers Lodge Peniche

itinerary.title: Nazaré's Praia do Norte, then Lisbon
itinerary.morning: Drive 45 minutes north to **Nazaré** and go straight to the **Forte de São Miguel Arcanjo** on the Sítio headland — the red lighthouse fort, now a small big-wave museum, standing directly above Praia do Norte. The **Nazaré Canyon**, roughly 230 km long and 5 km deep at its head, funnels and focuses Atlantic swell into this one beach, which is why the world's largest surfed waves happen here. From October to March you may see tow-in sessions; in September you will at least see why. Take the funicular down to Praia and walk the seafront.
itinerary.afternoon: A final surf at **Praia do Norte's** southern end or at Salgado, or if the swell is big, at sheltered **Praia da Nazaré** in front of town. Then the drive to Lisbon.
itinerary.evening: If you have time before the flight, dinner in Lisbon's Cais do Sodré or a last plate of grilled sardines at a Nazaré seafront restaurant. Return the car with a full tank; the toll transponder settles automatically.
itinerary.dayStats: Peniche–Nazaré 55 km, 45 min / fort and museum entry roughly €2 / Nazaré Canyon ~230 km long, up to 5 km deep / big-wave season October–March / Nazaré–LIS 1 h 45
itinerary.sleep: Departure, or an airport hotel in Lisbon

accommodationStrategy.name: Rapture Surfcamp Ericeira
accommodationStrategy.description: A full-package camp on the beginner-to-intermediate beach with boards, wetsuits, coaching, transport to whichever break is working, and secure gear storage — which matters because Ericeira's reefs are spread over several kilometres and the camp van solves the tide-timing problem for you. Dorms from roughly €40/night, private doubles €90–€140, week packages €450–€750 with half board.

accommodationStrategy.name: Baleal Surf Camp
accommodationStrategy.description: On the isthmus itself, which means both the north- and south-facing beaches are within a few hundred metres and you can re-check both sides of the peninsula on foot rather than by car. Board and wetsuit hire on site, drying racks, a good social kitchen. Roughly €35–€55 dorm, €80–€130 double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Surfers Lodge Peniche
accommodationStrategy.description: The step up: a proper hotel with a pool, rooftop, decent food and a surf programme attached, for anyone travelling as a couple where only one person surfs. Walking distance to Cantinho da Baía, and it stays open and comfortable in November when the camps get bleak. Roughly €130–€230 double.

logistics.connectivity: Very good 4G/5G along the whole coast; thin in the Berlengas and in the cliff coves. Portugal is in the EU so EU/EEA SIMs roam at domestic rates. Download Windguru or Surfline and the Instituto Hidrográfico tide tables offline — the beach car parks at Coxos and São Julião have poor signal.
logistics.emergency: **112** for everything. **MRCC Lisboa +351 214 401 919** and **VHF Channel 16** for maritime incidents; the Polícia Marítima handle beach enforcement. Hospitals in Torres Vedras and Caldas da Rainha; major trauma to Lisbon. Standard travel insurance usually covers surfing but check whether it covers *tow-in* or reef breaks if you are going anywhere near Nazaré.
logistics.weather: The nortada is the daily constant from April to September; treat any afternoon plan as provisional. Autumn and winter bring genuine Atlantic storm systems, and a 4 m swell here does not just make surfing hard, it closes coastal roads and the Nazaré promenade. Sea fog (*nevoeiro*) rolls in with startling speed on the Ericeira cliffs.
logistics.bookingWindows: Surf camps in Ericeira and Peniche sell out three to four months ahead for July–September. The Berlengas boat should be booked online several days ahead in July–August because of the 350-person cap, and same-day is often possible in May, June and September. Nazaré accommodation is impossible during the big-wave events — check the WSL and Nazaré Tow Surfing Challenge calendars before fixing dates. Restaurants like Tasca do Joel need a day's notice.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards are near-universal including Multibanco everywhere, but small tascas and beach kiosks still prefer cash — carry €50–€80. Tipping is 5–10% at a sit-down meal, rounding up elsewhere. Motorway tolls are electronic: take the transponder from the rental desk or you will get a bill with fees attached.
logistics.transportRules: A car is close to essential — the good breaks in both areas are strung along 15 km of coast and the buses do not follow surf. Board-carrying: most rental cars will not take a longboard inside; camps provide transport. Parking at Ribeira d'Ilhas, Coxos and Supertubos fills by 09:00 in summer, and break-ins from beach car parks are a genuine and well-documented problem — leave nothing visible.
logistics.permits: No permit is needed to surf. The Ericeira World Surfing Reserve is a protection designation, not a permit system, but respect for local priority at Coxos and Pedra Branca is enforced socially and firmly. The Berlengas Nature Reserve caps visitors and restricts anchoring, camping (advance ICNF permit only) and any collection of flora or fauna. Beach flags are legally binding during the June–September bathing season. Drones require ANAC registration and are restricted over the reserve and over Berlengas.
logistics.health: Tap water is drinkable throughout. Cold-water shock is the underrated risk — 15°C in July after an upwelling week is a genuine hazard for someone who packed a shorty. Rips at Foz do Lizandro's river mouth and the Baleal channels are the most common rescue cause; if caught, paddle parallel to the beach, not against the flow. Urchins on the Ericeira reefs — bring booties. Portuguese man o' war triggers occasional red flags; treat with hot water, not vinegar.

proTips: Surf at dawn, every day, without negotiation. Between April and September the nortada makes the afternoon a lottery and the morning a certainty; the whole trip's quality is decided by what time you set the alarm.
Learn the peninsula rule at Peniche before you need it: north wind means south-side spots, south wind means north-side spots. It is why Peniche is surfable roughly 340 days a year.

Pull the tide table each morning and pick the break to fit it, not the other way round. Lagide on mid-to-high, Coxos and Pedra Branca on mid-to-low, Supertubos on the drop — with a 3.5 m spring range, getting this wrong wastes the session.

Book the first Berlengas boat of the day, not the second. The island's cap means the later arrivals share the one path and the one beach with everyone, and the sea is almost always calmer before the wind builds.

Watch Coxos from the cliff before you ever consider paddling out. It has a strict local hierarchy, an urchin-covered reef and a shallow take-off, and turning up unannounced on a good day is the fastest way to have a bad week.

Take a video-analysis session in your first two days, not your last. Ericeira and Peniche coaches all offer it, and applying corrections over five remaining days is worth ten times as much as being told them on day six.
Nazaré is best visited in the morning even outside big-wave season, because the Sítio headland catches the same nortada and by afternoon the viewing platform is a wind tunnel full of coaches.

Eat inland once. Óbidos, Atouguia da Baleia and the Colares wine villages between Ericeira and Sintra all feed you better and cheaper than the seafront, and Colares' sand-grown Ramisco is one of the strangest and best wines in Portugal.

If you only have one wetsuit, make it a 3/2 with a chest zip, and bring a thermal top. Portuguese upwelling means summer water here is colder than the Irish Sea in August, and half the visiting surfers underdress for it.

raw.Prevailing wind — the nortada: A north to north-northwest thermal wind driven by the contrast between the cold Atlantic and the heating Iberian interior. It is the defining daily rhythm of the Portuguese coast from roughly April to September. Typical cycle: glassy or light-offshore at dawn, first ripples around 10:00–11:00, filling hard through midday, peaking 15:00–19:00 at 15–25 knots and occasionally 30, then easing after sunset. October–March is synoptic rather than thermal, with cleaner all-day windows but bigger, stormier swell. **The practical consequence is absolute: surf at dawn.** By 13:00 in July most of the exposed coast is a wind-blown mess.
raw.The peninsula trick at Peniche: Peniche's headland points west, with beaches facing north and beaches facing south within a few minutes' drive. In a nortada, the north-side spots (Baleal, Lagide, Praia do Norte, Almagreira) go onshore while the south side (**Supertubos**, **Molho Leste**, Consolação) turns offshore and clean. In a southerly, it reverses exactly. Ericeira has less of this flexibility — most of the reserve faces west to northwest — which is why you base the second half of the week in Peniche.
raw.Ericeira World Surfing Reserve — the bre: Designated in 2011, the first World Surfing Reserve in Europe, protecting roughly 4 km of coast and a cluster of world-class waves. *Coxos* — a powerful right point/reef over urchin-covered rock, best at mid-to-low tide, the best wave in the reserve and firmly advanced-only with a serious local pecking order. *Pedra Branca* — a fast, hollow left over a flat, shallow slab; the region's best lefthander and dangerous at low tide. *Ribeira d'Ilhas* — a long, forgiving right-hand reef point that has hosted WSL Challenger Series events, workable by intermediates and, on the inside on a small day, by beginners with an instructor. *Reef* and *Cave* — short, heavy and technical. *Matadouro* and *Praia do Norte* — reef peaks with a more manageable reform inside. *Foz do Lizandro* — a sand-bottomed river-mouth beach break with multiple peaks, the reserve's beginner and intermediate anchor, and the fallback whenever the reefs are too big. *São Julião*, a few kilometres south, is an exposed beach break with multiple peaks that is remarkably consistent even in flat summer weeks and takes a bigger swell than Lizandro.
raw.Peniche and Baleal — the breaks: *Supertubos* — a shallow, ferociously fast sand-bottomed barrel on the south side, the WSL tour venue, working best on a solid W/NW swell with north or northeast wind and dropping tide; it breaks close to dry sand and it is not a spot to learn heavy-water surfing on. *Molho Leste* — the jetty-protected spot next door, technical and fast, good on southwest swells at mid tide. *Cantinho da Baía* and *Prainha* on the Baleal isthmus — soft, sheltered, sandy and the reason Peniche has two dozen surf schools. *Lagide* — a left-breaking reef on the north side of the Baleal peninsula, best on northwest swell and mid-to-high tide, and the goofy-footer's favourite. *Almagreira* and *Praia do Norte/Belgas* — wilder, less crowded beach breaks north of town. *Consolação* — a two-in-one beach with a soft sandy north end and a sharp reef to the south.
raw.Equipment hubs and certification: Ericeira: **Ericeira Surf Clube** (the local club, founded in the late 1980s, the institutional heart of the reserve), **Rapture Surfcamp Ericeira** at Foz do Lizandro, and the **Ultimar** and **Ericeira Surf & Skate** shops for board hire and repairs. Peniche and Baleal: **Baleal Surf Camp** (one of Portugal's oldest, on the isthmus), **Peniche Surf Camp**, **Surfers Lodge Peniche**, and **Surf Stash** for board and wetsuit rental without a package. Indicative 2026 prices: soft-top or shortboard hire €20–€30/day, €100–€150/week; wetsuit hire €10–€15/day; a two-hour group lesson €30–€45; private coaching €60–€90/hour; a seven-night surf-camp package with board, wetsuit, two daily sessions and half board €450–€750. Instructors work to ISA and Federação Portuguesa de Surf standards; ask to see the FPS instructor card. Board storage is included in camps and costs €3–€5/day at shops.
raw.Tides and currents — this is the real At: Spring range on this coast runs roughly **3.2–3.6 m**, neaps roughly **1.2–1.6 m**, with two highs and two lows a day. That is not a detail: Ribeira d'Ilhas works differently across a 3 m swing, Lagide needs mid-to-high, Coxos and Pedra Branca prefer mid-to-low, and Supertubos changes character entirely over a tide. **Do not plan from a memorised table — pull the Instituto Hidrográfico tide times for Peniche or Cascais each morning.** Rips are the primary hazard: at Foz do Lizandro the river-mouth rip runs hard on a dropping tide, and at Baleal and Almagreira the channel rips are strong enough to carry a competent surfer 200 m out in minutes. Use them to paddle out, never to swim. Headland acceleration around Cabo Carvoeiro and the Papôa is severe, and the offshore-wind danger on this coast is real for anyone on a SUP or inflatable — an offshore land breeze at Baleal puts open Atlantic downwind of you.
raw.Sea conditions, wetsuits and safety: This coast is cold for its latitude because the nortada drives upwelling. Water temperature: roughly 14–15°C January–March, 15–16°C April–May, 16–17°C June, 17–19°C July–August (but capable of dropping to 15°C after a hard nortada week), 18–19°C September, 17–18°C October, 16°C November. **A 3/2 full suit is the summer minimum; a 4/3 with boots from November to April; add a hood in January–February.** Swell height: roughly 0.8–1.5 m in June–August, 1.2–2.5 m in September–October, 2–4 m November–February with 5 m-plus events. Jellyfish are a minor issue compared with the Mediterranean, though Portuguese man o' war occasionally arrives on westerly weather; the real injury risks are the urchin-covered basalt at the Ericeira reefs (booties for Coxos and Pedra Branca) and the sand-bottom impact at Supertubos. Lifeguards (*nadadores-salvadores*) operate on the designated bathing beaches from roughly 15 June to 15 September only, and the flag system is legally binding. **Emergency 112; MRCC Lisboa +351 214 401 919; VHF Channel 16. Maritime Police enforce beach rules.**
raw.Boat, kayak and Berlengas logistics: Portugal has no meaningful licence-free horsepower allowance of the Italian or Greek kind — recreational motorboats require a *carta de navegador de recreio*, so the practical water options here are guided boats, kayaks and SUPs. The **Berlengas** archipelago, 10 km off Peniche, is a Nature Reserve and UNESCO Biosphere Reserve with a **daily visitor cap of around 350 people on Berlenga Grande**, enforced through the boat operators' allocation, so you book a numbered return ticket rather than turning up. Licensed operators from Peniche's fishing harbour include **Viamar**, **Berlengatur**, **Berlenga Turpesca** and **Julius Boat**; the crossing takes about 30 minutes and costs roughly €23–€30 return, with cave tours around the island priced separately. The service runs roughly May to September and cancels routinely on swell — it is a calm-day activity, not a scheduled ferry. Camping on the island requires a separate advance permit from the ICNF. Anchoring inside the reserve is restricted.
raw.Weather-contingency plan: *Flat and windy:* São Julião takes swell when everything else is flat, and Cantinho da Baía is surfable in almost anything. *Blown out by nortada:* switch to the south side of the Peniche peninsula and surf Supertubos or Molho Leste, which the same wind cleans up. *Too big for you:* this is the Nazaré day — drive north and watch, which is a legitimate and unforgettable use of a bad-surf morning. *Sea state cancels Berlengas:* Cabo Carvoeiro, the Gruta da Furninha and the Peniche fort's Museu da Resistência e Liberdade fill the day properly. *Nothing works at all:* Óbidos, 25 minutes from Peniche, is a walled medieval town and a decent rainy afternoon.

sources.verified: Ericeira as a World Surfing Reserve and the character of its named breaks — Ribeira d'Ilhas as a long right reef point and WSL Challenger Series venue, Coxos as a powerful advanced right point best at mid-to-low tide, Pedra Branca as a fast left over flat reef that should be avoided at low tide, Foz do Lizandro and São Julião as all-level beach breaks; Peniche's spot roster and characters — Supertubos as the powerful tubing WSL venue, Molho Leste as a jetty-protected technical wave on southeast swell at mid tide, Lagide as a left reef on the north side working on NW swell at mid-to-high, Prainha and Cantinho da Baía as the beginner beaches, Consolação's split sandy/reef character, Almagreira as a wilder beach break; the Berlengas daily visitor cap of approximately 350 people, the roughly 30-minute crossing from Peniche, operators including Viamar, Berlengatur, Berlenga Turpesca and Julius Boat, and return fares in the region of €23–€30 with a June–September high season of multiple daily departures; Portugal's lack of a licence-free horsepower allowance comparable to Italy or Greece.

trips.hook: Half of this week is spent below the reeds, in a kayak on channels where the horizon is two metres of *stuf* and the only sound is a coot. The other half is on a coast that runs from a lagoon full of kites to a scruffy, beloved village on the Bulgarian border. It is a trip of ferries you cannot rush, boatmen who know where the pelicans are, and a sea that has no tide but plenty of current.

itinerary.title: Tulcea, paperwork and the waterfront (transfer day)
itinerary.morning: Travel from Bucharest to Tulcea, the delta's only real gateway town, and buy or collect the ARBDD access permit before doing anything else. Carry it on the water.
itinerary.afternoon: Check the Navrom Delta timetable in person at the passenger terminal. Classic slow ferries and faster boats run on fixed weekdays to Sulina, Sfântu Gheorghe and the Chilia line, and the pattern changes by season [VERIFY: current Navrom sailing days and departure times].
itinerary.evening: Walk the Tulcea quay and visit the Danube Delta Eco-Tourism Museum Centre for the aquarium of Danube fish. Eat by the water and buy repellent, sun cream and cash before you leave town.

itinerary.title: Down the Sulina arm to Crișan
itinerary.morning: Take the Navrom boat down the Sulina arm past Partizani and Maliuc. This is the working delta: dredgers, cargo, reed-cutters' barges and the occasional white-tailed eagle over the willows.
itinerary.afternoon: Land at Crișan and take a kayak straight onto the Dunărea Veche, the Old Danube, the abandoned meander that loops behind the village. Pure flatwater, high reed walls, and terns working the channel.
itinerary.evening: Stay at Ivan Pescar in Crișan, a fisherman's pensiune on the bank [VERIFY: current rates and board arrangement]. Dinner is *borș de pește* or fried carp; the delta eats what it caught that day.
itinerary.dayStats: ferry + 10 km paddle

itinerary.title: The Crișan–Mila 23 canal
itinerary.morning: Paddle the Crișan–Mila 23 canal, the classic delta kayak line: a straight cut that opens into the Old Danube's meanders, with pelican rafts on the wider stretches in the early hours.
itinerary.afternoon: Reach Mila 23, a Lipovan fishing village of one street, painted boats and Russian spoken at the fence line. The village produced Romania's canoeing dynasty; the boats on the bank are still working craft.
itinerary.evening: Return by paddle or arrange a lift back with a local boat. Sunset over Lake Roșu, reached from the Mila 23 side, is the delta's stock photograph for a reason.
itinerary.dayStats: 18–20 km paddle

itinerary.title: Caraorman, Letea and why you need a boatman (guided boat day)
itinerary.morning: Hire a local boatman rather than navigating alone. The channels toward Caraorman are unmarked, silt seasonally and dead-end into private fishing grounds; a Crișan or Mila 23 driver knows which cut is open this month [VERIFY: current guided-boat day rate].
itinerary.afternoon: Caraorman's sand dunes and old oak stand sit behind the village, an inland dune field in the middle of a wetland. Letea, the older and stranger forest with its feral horses, is the northern equivalent and is entered only with a licensed guide on marked routes.
itinerary.evening: Take the ferry or a boat transfer down to Sulina. The town is Romania's easternmost, an old free port that shrank; nothing is quick to reach and that is part of it.

itinerary.title: Sulina, Mile 0 and the sea
itinerary.morning: Walk to Mile 0, where the Sulina arm is measured out into the sea between two long jetties. The old lighthouse in town, once at the waterline, now stands several hundred metres inland — the river built the land beneath it.
itinerary.afternoon: The Maritime Cemetery holds British, Greek, Turkish and Russian graves from the Danube Commission era. Then cycle or walk east to Sulina beach, a wide unguarded strand where the freshwater plume meets the sea.
itinerary.evening: Eat at a Sulina fish table — La Cherhana is the name to ask for, cherhana being the old fish-landing station [VERIFY: current location and hours]. Watch the pilot boats work the mouth.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km walking or cycling

itinerary.title: Sfântu Gheorghe and out to the coast
itinerary.morning: Boat south to Sfântu Gheorghe, the delta's third arm and its most isolated village, where the Danube ends in a shifting sandbar. Green Village is the established stay if you break the journey here [VERIFY: current rates and open season].
itinerary.afternoon: Walk or take the village tractor-trailer 2 km to the wild beach: unguarded, enormous, with strong outflow current where the arm meets the sea. Swim inshore of the bar, not across it.
itinerary.evening: Ferry back to Tulcea, collect a car and drive south past Corbu's wild beach and the Năvodari lagoon to Mamaia. Pensiunea Delta Marina is a practical Tulcea-side fallback if the ferry runs late [VERIFY: current operation and location].
itinerary.dayStats: ferry + 130 km driving

itinerary.title: Siutghiol, then the southern villages
itinerary.morning: Rig on Lake Siutghiol behind Mamaia. Flat water, steady onshore breeze from mid-morning, and a lagoon big enough to ride out without crossing shipping. Beginners take the lagoon; the sea side is for swell days.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive south through Costinești, the old student resort, to 2 Mai and Vama Veche — two villages a kilometre from the Bulgarian border that have been Romania's alternative summer for fifty years. Casa Coral and Stuf Vama Veche are the recognised beds [VERIFY: current operation and rates].
itinerary.evening: Grilled fish, a guitar, and a beach that is unguarded at both ends. Constanța is 50 km back north for the airport, or Bucharest 300 km on the A2 — about three hours.
itinerary.dayStats: 75 km driving

accommodationStrategy.name: Ivan Pescar
accommodationStrategy.description: on the bank of the Sulina arm at the exact point where the Old Danube and the Mila 23 canal both begin, so both kayak days start from the jetty. Boat, kayak and local knowledge come with the house.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct by phone 4–6 weeks ahead for May–June; confirm whether the rate is half or full board, because there is no alternative kitchen.

accommodationStrategy.name: Green Village
accommodationStrategy.description: the only substantial accommodation in the most isolated of the three arms, with its own boat transfers and reliable food. It makes the wild beach and the Sacalin sandbar area viable without camping.
accommodationStrategy.booking: well ahead for the August film-festival week; the operating season is shorter than the calendar suggests [VERIFY: current season dates].

accommodationStrategy.name: Stuf Vama Veche
accommodationStrategy.description: walkable to the beach and to every table in the village, which matters because Vama Veche is a walking-and-drinking place, not a driving one. Simple, cheap, loud in August, calm in September.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–5 weeks for September; August is a domestic scramble and worth avoiding entirely.

logistics.connectivity: 4G covers Tulcea, Crișan, Sulina and Sfântu Gheorghe but drops out on the channels between them. Download offline charts; the delta's canals are poorly rendered on standard map apps.
logistics.emergency: 112. In the delta, response comes by boat and is slow — tell your pensiune your paddling plan and expected return, and carry a whistle and a dry-bagged phone.
logistics.weather: the delta is flat and exposed. A sudden squall raises short, steep chop on Lake Roșu and the wide channels within minutes. Get into a reed-sheltered cut rather than trying to cross open water.
logistics.bookingWindows: May–June and September pensiuni need 4–6 weeks. Boatmen are arranged the day before, in person, through your host — not online.
logistics.money: Romanian lei. Tulcea, Constanța and Mamaia take cards everywhere; the delta villages largely do not. Draw 1,500–2,000 RON in Tulcea for boatmen, permits, tips and village purchases.
logistics.transportRules: a *rovinietă* road vignette is required in Romania — hire cars usually include it; confirm. Navrom ferries carry bicycles and kayaks for a supplement and cannot be booked far in advance; arrive at the terminal early.
logistics.permits: the ARBDD permit is compulsory and checked. Strictly protected zones are closed outright, no fires or wild camping outside designated spots, no approaching bird colonies, and fishing requires its own separate licence. Rangers do patrol.

proTips: Paddle between 06:00 and 09:00. Wind is nil, the channels are glass, pelicans and herons are feeding, and by 11:00 the tour boats have pushed everything into cover.
Buy the ARBDD permit before you reach the water, not after a ranger asks. Enforcement is real and the fine costs far more than the permit.
Take a boatman for one full day even if you paddle the rest. The difference between seeing the delta and finding the delta is entirely local knowledge of which cut is open.
Bring a head net, long sleeves and DEET even in June. Evening on a Crișan terrace in still air is not survivable in shorts.
Ride the classic slow Navrom ferry in at least one direction. It is cheaper than the fast boat, it stops at villages the fast boat skips, and it is the way the delta actually travels.
On the coast, go to Vama Veche in September rather than August. Same village, a tenth of the crowd, and the sea is warmer than it was in June.

raw.Prevailing wind: Summer on the Dobrogea coast runs a north-easterly to easterly sea breeze that fills through the afternoon — light in the morning, 12–20 knots from mid-afternoon, fading at dusk. September adds the first synoptic northerlies, stronger and more consistent, which is when Mamaia's lagoon works best. Winter's *crivăț* from the north-east is out of season but explains the local rigging habits.
raw.Launch spots: On the sea side, Lake Siutghiol behind the Mamaia strip is the region's flat-water kite and wing venue — shallow, no swell, onshore breeze across a 5 km lagoon, and far more forgiving than the open beach two hundred metres away on the other side of the road. The Năvodari end of the lagoon and Corbu's wild beach take the overflow. In the delta, kayaks launch from Crișan's waterfront, Mila 23 and Sfântu Gheorghe.
raw.Equipment and hubs: Mamaia's watersports strip runs kite, wing and SUP schools through the summer season with English instruction [VERIFY: current Mamaia school rates and season dates]. In the delta, most pensiuni either keep kayaks or will call the neighbour who does; Crișan and Mila 23 are the reliable hire points, and a hired local boat with a driver is the standard way to reach anything beyond paddling range.
raw.Tidal and current awareness: The Black Sea is effectively non-tidal: the astronomical range is a few centimetres, so tide tables are irrelevant to launching, landing or beach camping here. The real hazards are wind-driven longshore currents that sweep parallel to shore on any sustained cross-shore breeze, rip currents off the long sandy bays at Corbu, Năvodari, Mamaia and Sfântu Gheorghe, and seiches — basin-scale oscillations that shift water level and flow inside enclosed bays. In the delta the current is riverine and constant: the Sulina arm runs hard and carries commercial traffic, so paddle the side channels and cross the main arm square, quickly and only with a clear sightline.
raw.Permits, mosquitoes and wildlife: Every visitor to the Danube Delta Biosphere Reserve needs an ARBDD access permit, and it is cheap rather than bureaucratic: **5 RON (about €1) per person per day, 15 RON (about €3) per person per week, 30 RON (about €6) per person per year** under Order 610/2009, with children, students and pensioners exempt along with residents of the reserve and its adjacent communes. A car needs its own permit — **10 RON per day or 100 RON per year** — and a private boat **20 RON per stay or 100 RON per year** (HG 538/2015). Buy online at permise.ddbra.ro, by SMS to **7494**, from the ARBDD permit machines in Tulcea and the delta villages and at SelfPay terminals nationwide, or over the counter at ARBDD headquarters in Tulcea (Mon–Thu 08:00–16:30, Fri 08:00–14:00) and the information centres at Chilia Veche, Sulina, Crișan and Murighiol. Rangers check it on the water — carry the SMS or the printout. A tour operator's boat fare does not include your personal permit unless they say so in writing. Strictly protected zones — Roșca-Buhaiova, the Letea and Caraorman cores, Sacalin-Zătoane, Periteașca-Leahova among them — are closed to visitors entirely, with no permit that opens them. Great white and Dalmatian pelicans nest here; both are strictly protected and you must not approach, circle or flush a raft of birds — keep several hundred metres and let them drift to you. Mosquitoes in July and August are genuinely brutal after 18:00; May, June and September are the reason to come then.
